en: Salutations to the illustrious Goddess Durgā.
[This is] the *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavata-māhātmya*:
she who is Sṛṣṭī in the form of creation, and she who is Pālinī in the act of protecting the world, and she who is Raudrī.
May she whose entire universe is her play even during its dissolution, who is known as the supreme (Parā),

and who subsequently manifests as the goddess Vaikharī in the form of articulate speech— consisting of the Paśyantī and Madhyamā stages— being propitiated by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, may she graciously adorn our speech. || 1 ||
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men,
as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Jaya."
The sages said:
O Sūta, may you live long! You who cause us to hear here many captivating and meritorious stories, O high-minded disciple of Vyāsa.
We have listened with devotion to this wonderful and meritorious account of Viṣṇu’s deeds, which removes all sins and is endowed with narratives of his incarnations. ||4||
The divine life-story of Śiva, as well as that of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, along with their greatness and the associated histories, has been heard from your lotus-like mouth. (5)
Now we wish to hear about that which is supremely purifying even among the purifying,
which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men with ease in every respect.
"O illustrious one, tell us the truth by which men may attain perfection;
for even in this Kali age, we know of no other than you who can sever our doubts.
Sūta said:
Well asked, O fortunate ones, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
I shall explain to you in its entirety that which is the essence of all the scriptures.
Ancient sacred fords and religious observances roar only so long as the Devībhāgavata is not properly heard by men.
The forest of sin remains dense with thorns, inflicting suffering upon men,
only so long as the axe named Devībhāgavata has not been obtained.
The great darkness of calamities that brings affliction to human beings persists only so long as the sun of the Devībhāgavata has not yet risen.
The sages said:
O Sūta, O Sūta, O highly fortunate one, best among speakers, tell us:
what is that Purāṇa like, and what is the procedure for hearing it?
In how many days should this be heard, and what is its mode of worship? By which men was it heard previously, and what various desires do they attain? (13)
Sūta said:
A portion of Viṣṇu was born as a sage from Parāśara upon Satyavatī;
having divided the Vedas into four, he taught them to his disciples in ancient times.
How can those who are outcasts (vrātyas), mere kinsmen of the twice-born, those lacking authority regarding the Vedas, women, and men of dull intellect, come to possess knowledge of dharma? (15)
Having reflected upon this with his mind, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa meditated upon a Purāṇa-saṃhitā, desiring to establish the dharma for them.
Having composed the eighteen Purāṇas, that venerable sage taught them to me alone, as well as the narrative known as the Bhārata.
There, he himself recited the Devībhāgavata Purāṇa, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, to King Janamejaya. (18)
Formerly, his father King Parīkṣit was bitten by the serpent Takṣaka;
for the sake of his purification, the king heard the Bhāgavata.
Having worshipped the Goddess, the Mother of the Three Worlds, according to the prescribed rites for nine days from the lotus-like mouth of the illustrious Vedavyāsa,
King Parīkṣit, once the nine-day sacrifice was completed—
Assuming a divine form, he attained the same world as the Goddess at that very moment. ||21||
Having beheld his father’s divine departure, King Janamejaya honored the sage Vyāsa and attained supreme joy.
Among the eighteen Purāṇas, the supreme and most excellent is the one named Devībhāgavata, which bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa. 23.
For those who always listen with devotion to the Bhāgavata narrative of the Goddess, spiritual perfection is not far off; therefore, it should always be cultivated by men.
Whether for half a day, or half of that, or for a single muhūrta, or even for a mere moment,
those men who listen with devotion shall never face an evil rebirth.
Whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices, all sacred fords, and all acts of charity, a person obtains that same fruit by listening to a Purāṇa even once. || 26 ||

Many duties have been performed [in other ages], but in the Kali age, there is only one duty for men; there exists no other than listening to the Purāṇas. For men in the Kali age who are devoid of righteous conduct and possess short lifespans, [this alone remains].
Vyāsa, for the benefit [of the world], composed the nectar-like essence known as the Purāṇas. ||28||
Just as a single man drinking nectar would become free from old age and death, so too the nectar of the Goddess’s story makes the entire family free from old age and death. 29.
There is no restriction here regarding months, nor is there any restriction regarding days;
the Devībhāgavata should always be served, always served by men. (30)
In the month of Āśvina, or the month of Madhu, or likewise in the month of Tapas or Śuci,
it yields especially great fruit during the four Navarātras.
Therefore, this nine-day sacrifice is declared to be the bestower of merit for men, as it yields a greater fruit than all other meritorious deeds.
Those who are ill-intentioned, devoted to evil, deluded, betrayers of friends, revilers of the Vedas,
addicted to violence, and attached to the path of atheism— they purify themselves in the Kali age by means of the nine-day sacrifice.

Those men who are greedy for the wives of others, who bear the burden of sin, and who lack devotion to cows, deities, and Brahmins—how can they become pure without knowledge of the nine-fold path? (34)

Whatever fruit is obtained by men through fierce austerities, the service of vows and sacred fords, various gifts, observances, sacrifices, burnt offerings, and recitations— that is attained by the nine-day sacrifice.
O Brahmins, neither the Gaṅgā, nor Gayā, nor Kāśī, nor Naimiṣa, nor Mathurā, nor Puṣkara purifies as instantly as this sacrifice to the Goddess at Badarīvana does. (36)
Therefore, the Bhāgavata Purāṇa of the Goddess is considered the highest of all, the supreme means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (37)
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, when the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Virgo,
one should worship [the deity] seated upon the great lion-throne on the Mahā-aṣṭamī day.
One who, out of devotion, gives a manuscript of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata—the source of the Goddess's delight—to a worthy brāhmaṇa, shall attain the station of the Goddess. (39)
Whoever daily recites even a single verse or half-verse of the Devībhāgavata with devotion shall become a recipient of the Goddess’s affection.
Merely by hearing it, one destroys the terrible state of calamities arising from great pestilence, as well as all portents whatsoever. (41)
Whatever fear is caused by child-seizing spirits (bālagraha), or by ghosts and goblins (bhūta-preta),
departs far away upon hearing this Devībhāgavata.
But that man who reads or listens with devotion to the Bhāgavata of the Goddess attains dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Upon hearing this, Vasudeva rejoiced greatly when he recovered his beloved son Kṛṣṇa, who had been delayed while searching for Prasenajit.
Whoever hears this narrative of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata with devotion,
or whoever reads it with devotion, attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One without a son obtains a son, and the poor man becomes wealthy;
the sick person shall be liberated from disease upon hearing this nectar of the Bhāgavata. (46)
Whether she be barren, or one who bears only female offspring, or a woman whose children have died,
by hearing the Devībhāgavata, she shall obtain a long-lived son.
That house in which the book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata is always worshipped indeed becomes a sacred pilgrimage site, destroying the sins of those who dwell there. 48.
He who, endowed with devotion, reads or even listens to this on the eighth, the fourteenth, or the ninth lunar day, attains supreme perfection. (49)
A twice-born man who recites it shall become a preeminent knower of the Vedas; one born of the arms [a Kṣatriya] shall become a lord of the earth;
a Vaiśya who recites it attains abundance of wealth; and even a Śūdra, by hearing it, shall become excellent in his own station.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Mānasa-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa, within the Māhātmya of the Devībhāgavata. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter.
The sages said:
"O highly fortunate one, how did Vasudeva obtain a son?"
Where was Prasena sought by Kṛṣṇa as he wandered about, and how? ||1||
O Sūta of noble intellect, tell this story: by what rite and for what reason was the Devībhāgavata heard by Vasudeva? 2.
Sūta said:
Satrājit, a scion of the Bhoja dynasty, lived happily in Dvāravatī;
he was devoted to the propitiation of the Sun, his supreme friend. (3)
Then, after some time, the Sun became pleased;
out of devotion and affection for him, he revealed his own world.
To him who had thus gained confidence, the Blessed One gave the Syamantaka jewel;
wearing that jewel around his neck, he returned to Dvārakā.
Seeing him, the citizens were bewildered by his splendor, thinking him to be the sun;
they approached Kṛṣṇa as he sat in the Sudharmā hall and spoke to him.
"O Lord of the World, here comes Savitṛ, desiring to see you.
Having heard those words, Kṛṣṇa laughed and spoke in the assembly: (7)
"O children, this is not the sun; it is Satrājit coming along, blazing with the Syamantaka jewel, the radiant gem bestowed by the Sun."
Then, having summoned the Brahmins and performed the rite of invoking blessings (*svastivācana*),
Satrājit caused them to enter his house after honoring them, and [offered] the jewel.
There is no plague there, nor famine, nor fear of calamities anywhere,
wherever that jewel— which constantly yields eight measures of gold— remains.
Then once, Satrājit’s brother, named Prasena, having fastened the jewel around his neck, immediately mounted a horse from the Sindhu region. ||11||
Having gone to the forest for the sake of hunting, the lion saw him;
having killed Prasena along with his horse, the lion seized that jewel.
Then Jāmbavān, the king of the bears, seeing the monkey Maṇidhara,
killed him at the entrance of the cave and, being full of valor, seized the jewel.
The lord gave that jewel to his son for the purpose of play;
then, having obtained the radiant jewel, the boy too began to play with it.
When Prasena had not returned, Satrājit was filled with distress:
"I do not know by whom Prasena has been slain, seeking the jewel. (15)
Then a rumor issued from the mouths of the people spread through the city:
"Surely Prasena has been killed by Kṛṣṇa, who was desirous of the jewel.
Kṛṣṇa also heard that ill-repute being smeared upon himself.
To wipe away that [stain], he went forth to his destination together with the citizens. || 17 ||
Having gone into the forest, he saw Prasena killed by a lion;
following the path marked by drops of blood, he went in pursuit of the king of beasts.
Then, seeing the slain lion at the entrance of the cave, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa spoke these words out of compassion to the inhabitants of the city: (19)
"Stay right here until my return;
I shall enter this cave to obtain the necklace of jewels. (20)
Having said, "So be it," those inhabitants of Dvārakā remained right there;
Kṛṣṇa went into the inner cave where the abode of Jāmbavān was located.
Upon seeing the son of the bear-king wearing that jewel, Kṛṣṇa then desired to seize the gem; at that moment, the nurse cried out in fear.
Hearing the cry of the nurse, the King of Artha immediately arrived and then fought with his master incessantly, day and night.
Thus, for twenty-seven nights, a great battle took place between the two;
meanwhile, the citizens remained at the gate, awaiting the arrival of Kṛṣṇa.
Then, out of fear, they returned to their own homes for twelve days;
there, overwhelmed with grief, they all recounted the entire account from the beginning while cursing Satrājit. (25)
Having heard that account of his son, the highly fortunate Vāsudeva fainted along with his retinue out of supreme grief;
he then reflected in many ways on how his own welfare might be secured.
Then the blessed celestial sage arrived from the world of Brahmā;
Vasudeva rose, bowed to him, and honored him.
Having inquired after the welfare of the high-minded Vāsudeva, Nārada [proceeded].
And he asked the best of the Yadus, "Tell me, what are you reflecting upon? (29)
Vasudeva said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, my son, who is very dear to me, went to the forest with the citizens to search for Prasena; he then beheld him slain."
Seeing Hari dead at the entrance of the cave, having killed Prasenajit,
he stationed the citizens at the gate and entered the cave himself.
Many days have passed, yet my son still does not emerge.
Therefore, O Sage, I grieve; tell me that by which I may obtain a son.
Nārada said:
O best of the Yadus, worship the goddess Ambikā for the sake of obtaining a son;
by her very propitiation, you shall indeed attain immediate welfare. (33)
Vasudeva said:
"O Blessed One, who indeed is that goddess, and what is the power of that Great Sovereign?
O divine sage, please tell me how she is to be propitiated. (34)
Nārada said:
O illustrious Vasudeva, listen to my account in brief;
who is capable of describing in detail the incomparable majesty of the Goddess? (35)
She who is the Blessed Lady, eternal, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, the Goddess higher than the highest, by whom this entire world is pervaded. (36)
By worshipping whom Brahmā creates this world of the moving and the unmoving, and by praising whom he was liberated from the fear arising from Madhu and Kaiṭabha. (37)
By whose grace the Lord Viṣṇu sustains this universe, and by the glance from the corner of whose eye Rudra withdraws it. (38)
That which is the cause of bondage for those to be saved is itself the bestower of liberation;
she is the supreme Goddess Vidyā, she alone is the Sovereign of all sovereigns. (39)
Having worshipped the Mother of the Universe according to the rites of Navarātra,
listen for nine days to the Devī-bhāgavata Purāṇa;
by the mere hearing of which you shall immediately obtain a son.
For men who read and listen, enjoyment and liberation are not far away. ||41||
Thus addressed by Nārada, Vasudeva bowed to him and spoke with supreme affection to Nārada, the best of sages.
Vasudeva said:
"O Blessed One, by your word my own past life has been remembered;
listen as I shall relate that which arose from the majesty of the Goddess."
Long ago, the wicked Kaṃsa, having learned from the voice in the sky that his own death would come from Devakī’s eighth pregnancy, imprisoned me along with my wife out of fear.
I lived in prison together with my wife Devakī;
moreover, the evil-doing Kaṃsa killed every son as soon as he was born.
His six sons having been slain by him, the blameless Queen Devakī was then deeply overwhelmed with grief and suffered day and night. 46.
Then, having summoned the sage Garga, bowed to him, and honored him, I informed him of Devakī’s sorrow and spoke out of a desire for a son:
"O Blessed One, ocean of compassion, you are the preceptor of the Yādavas."
O Sage, tell me the means for obtaining long-lived sons.
Then Garga, whose soul was serene and who was a treasure-house of compassion, said to me:
"O illustrious Vasudeva, listen to that supreme means of accomplishment."
Worship that auspicious Goddess Durgā, who removes the distress of her devotees; indeed, you shall immediately attain the highest good. 50.
By propitiating her, all may attain all their desires;
for men who worship Durgā, nothing in this world is difficult to obtain. (51)
Thus addressed, filled with joy, I bowed to that bull among sages together with my wife,
and with palms joined in reverence, I spoke with supreme devotion.
Vasudeva said:
"O Blessed One, O ocean of compassion, if you have affection for me, then in the past you should have propitiated Caṇḍikā for my sake. (53)
"Having been confined in Kaṃsa's house, I am unable to do anything;
therefore, O high-minded one, you alone must rescue me from this ocean of misery. (54)
Thus addressed by me, that bull among sages, being pleased, said:
"O Vasudeva, out of affection for you, I shall do what is beneficial for you. (55)
Then, having been entreated by me with affection,
the sage Garga departed for the Vindhya mountain along with other brahmins, desiring to propitiate Durgā.
Having gone there, the sage, devoted to the recitation of prayers, worshipped the Mother of the World, who grants the desires of her devotees.
For when the observance was completed, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"O sage, I am pleased; the accomplishment of your purpose shall come to pass. (58)
For the purpose of removing the burden of the earth, Hari has been sent forth by me;
he shall descend through his own portion into Devakī, the wife of Vasudeva.
Out of fear of Kaṃsa, Ānakadundubhi will immediately take that child and deliver him to the house of Nanda in Gokula;
meanwhile, he will bring Yaśodā’s daughter to his own home for King Kaṃsa.
Then Kaṃsa will give her away, and he will also hurl her to the ground to kill her.
Emerging from his hand, she will immediately assume a divine form;
as a portion of my own self, she shall bring about the welfare of the world on the Vindhya mountain.
Having heard those words and having bowed to the Mother of the World,
the sage Garga, with a tranquil soul, went to the city of Mathurā.
Having heard the granting of the boon by Mahādevī, which brought happiness to Garga Ācārya,
he, together with his wife, was well-pleased and attained supreme joy.
Since that time, O divine sage, I have known the supreme and most excellent majesty of the Goddess;
indeed, even now it has been heard by me from the lotus of your mouth.
Therefore, O Lord, you yourself must cause the *Bhāgavata* to be heard by the Goddess;
it is solely through my good fortune, O divine sage, O ocean of mercy, that you have arrived here. (66)
Having heard the words of Vasudeva, Nārada, with a delighted mind,
then began the narration on an auspicious day under a favorable constellation.
To dispel obstacles to the discourse, the twice-born recited the nine-syllable mantra;
likewise, they chanted the hymn to the Goddess as declared in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Beginning from the first book, Vasudeva listened with devotion to the nectar of the Bhāgavata as it issued from the mouth of the venerable Nārada.
On the ninth day, when the narration was completed, the high-minded Vasudeva, being well-pleased, honored both the book and the reciter.
Then, in that battle within the cave between Kṛṣṇa and Jāmbavat,
Jāmbavat’s limbs became limp from the impact of Kṛṣṇa’s fist.
Then, his mindfulness restored, he bowed to the Blessed One and spoke with supreme devotion, seeking forgiveness for his transgression:
"O best of the Raghus, you have been recognized by me, through whose wrath the lord of rivers [the ocean] was agitated."
Lanka was thrown into agitation, and Rāvaṇa, along with his followers, was slain.
"You are indeed that very same Kṛṣṇa; O Lord, forgive my wickedness!
Speak what must be done by me; I am your servant in every respect. (74)
Having heard the words of Jāmbavān, the Lord of the World replied:
"O Lord of the Bears, we have come here to this cave for the sake of the jewel. (75)

Then the twice-born, along with his wife, and the celestial sage Nārada, as well as the king of the bears, having honored Kṛṣṇa together with his wife, affectionately gave their own daughter Jāmbavatī to Kṛṣṇa, as well as the Syamantaka jewel.
Taking his wife with him and placing the jewel upon her neck,
he consecrated the king of bears with mantras and set out toward Dvārakā.
On the day the story concluded, the noble-minded Vasudeva fed the brahmins and gratified them with sacrificial fees.
While the twice-born were offering their benedictions at that moment, Hari arrived with his wife, wearing a jewel.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa together with his wife, those led by Vasudeva, their eyes filled with tears of joy, attained supreme delight. (80)
Then the celestial sage Nārada, delighted by Kṛṣṇa’s arrival,
took leave of Vasudeva, and Kṛṣṇa went to the assembly hall of Brahmā.

Whoever, with a pure heart and stainless devotion, reads or hears this account of Hari’s deeds which destroys ill-repute, shall always be filled with happiness and attain all his desires; and at the end of his body, he shall obtain the path to liberation in this world.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Mānasakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Purāṇa, within the Devībhāgavata-māhātmya. || 2 ||
Sūta said:
Now, O best of sages, listen to another ancient narrative (itihāsa) in which the majesty of this Devībhāgavata is sung.
Once, the sage born from a jar, the husband of Lopāmudrā,
went to Kumāra, worshipped him, and inquired about various matters.
To him, the blessed Skanda related at great length various discourses enriched by the majesty of gifts, sacred fords, vows, and other such practices.
The greatness of Vārāṇasī, as well as that of Maṇikarṇikā, and also of the Gaṅgā and its various holy sites (tīrthas), has been described in great detail. ||4||
Having heard this, the sage born from a jar, being delighted, questioned the youth of great splendor once more for the benefit of the worlds.
Agastya said:
O Blessed One, O Enemy of Tāraka, please tell me, O Lord, the procedure for hearing the greatness of the Devībhāgavata.
The Purāṇa named Devībhāgavata is the most supreme; therein the eternal Mother of the three worlds is directly glorified. (7)
Skanda said:
Who is capable of describing the greatness of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata in detail?
Listen, O Brahmā; I shall now relate it to you in brief. (8)
She who is eternal, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, the Mother of the Universe,
who directly resides therein as the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Therefore, O Sage, in the Devībhāgavata, that form consisting of speech [is described];
for one who reads or hears it, nothing whatsoever in this world is difficult to attain.
Vivasvat had a son known as Śrāddhadeva;
being childless, that king, with the permission of Vasiṣṭha, performed a sacrifice.
Then Śraddhā, the beloved wife of Manu, requested Hotṛ:
"O Brahmin, let her become my daughter; likewise, let a means be devised. (12)
Mentally reflecting, the Hotṛ priest offered the maiden herself as the oblation;
consequently, through that transgression, she became known by the name Ilā. || 13 ||
Then the king, seeing his daughter, spoke dejectedly to the preceptor:
"O Lord, how has this discrepancy in your resolve come about here?"
Having heard that, the sage reflected; and perceiving the transgression of the Hotṛ priest, he sought refuge in the Lord out of a desire for Ilā to attain manhood.
And through the power of the Sage’s asceticism, as well as by the grace of the Supreme Lord,
while all the worlds were looking on, the earth attained the state of a man.
Then Sudyumna, the son of Manu, having been consecrated with the purificatory rites by his preceptor,
became a treasury of sciences, just as the ocean is the repository of rivers.
Then, in the course of time, Sudyumna, having attained youth,
went to the forest for the sake of hunting, having mounted a horse from the Sindhu region.
Wandering from forest to forest with his followers, he roamed extensively;
by chance, that prince entered a forest at the foot of the Golden Mountain (Hemādri).
At a certain time, the blessed Śaṅkara, the God of gods, was sporting with joy together with his wife Aparṇā. At that moment,
the sages there were longing for a vision of Śiva.
Then, having seen them arrive, Girijā became ashamed.
Seeing those two, Giriśa and his consort, engaged in dalliance, the sages of rigid vows then withdrew and departed for their abode in Vaikuṇṭha.
Seeking to do what was pleasing to his beloved, Śiva cursed the forest, saying:
"From this day forward, whatever man enters here shall become a woman. (23)
From that time on, men indeed avoided that region;
yet Sudyumna, having entered there, became a most excellent woman.
Seeing his horse followed by female beings and a mare, he was struck with wonder;
then that beautiful woman wandered from forest to forest.
Once, she went to the vicinity of Budha’s hermitage;
having seen her, whose every limb was beautiful and whose breasts were full and elevated, [he was struck with desire]. (26)

The venerable Budha, his limbs pierced by the arrows of the bodiless god of love, desired her who had lips like the bimba fruit, teeth like kunda flowers, a beautiful face, and eyes like blue lotuses.
That fair-browed woman also desired the prince, the delighter of Soma;
thereafter, she dwelt in his hermitage, sporting with Budha.
Then, after some time, he who was born from Mitra and Varuṇa begot a son named Purūravas upon her.
Then, after some years had passed, she once remembered her own former history at Budha’s hermitage and, filled with sorrow, departed.
Then, having gone to the hermitage of the preceptor Vasiṣṭha and bowed down to him, she reported what had occurred and sought refuge, desiring manhood. (31)
Vasiṣṭha, having learned the news, went to Mount Kailāsa;
having worshipped Śambhu, he praised him, endowed with supreme devotion.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Salutations again and again to Śiva, to Śaṃkara, to the one with matted hair;
salutations to you whose body has half its limbs as the daughter of the mountain, and to the moon-crested one. (33)

Salutations to you, Mṛḍa, the bestower of happiness; salutations to the dweller of Kailāsa; salutations to the blue-throated one, who grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation to his devotees. ||34||
Salutations to Śiva, whose form is auspicious, who removes the fear of those who have sought refuge, who has the bull as his vehicle, who is the worthy protector, and the Supreme Self. (35)
Salutations to the one who assumes the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa during creation, preservation, and dissolution; salutations to the God of gods, the giver of boons, the enemy of Tripura.
Salutations again and again to you who take the form of sacrifice and bestow the fruits of those who perform it;
salutations to you, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, whose eyes are the sun, the moon, and fire.
Thus praised, the Blessed Lord, the Master of the World, appeared,
mounted upon his bull and accompanied by Ambikā, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Resembling the silver mountain, three-eyed, and moon-crested,
he, with a highly gratified soul, spoke to the best of sages who stood before him in prostration.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Choose a boon, O brahmin-sage, whatever dwells in your mind.
Thus addressed, the sage bowed to him and requested manhood.
Then the Blessed One, being pleased, said to that best of sages:
"For one month he shall be a man, and for one month he shall be a woman."
Having thus obtained the boon from Śambhu,
the great sage prostrated before the Great Goddess, the Mother of the World, who was intent on granting the boon.
And having worshipped her who possesses the luster of ten million crescent moons and who smiles beautifully, he constantly praised her with devotion, desiring for Ilā the attainment of manhood. 43.
Victory to you, O Goddess, Great Goddess, who bestows grace upon your devotees!
Victory to you, who are worshipped by all the gods; victory to you, the abode of infinite virtues! 44.
Salutations, salutations to you, O Goddess of gods, who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge!
Victory to you, O Durgā, destroyer of suffering, slayer of the wicked Daityas! 45.
Obeisance to you, O Great Illusion, who are accessible through devotion, Mother of the World, whose lotus feet have become a boat for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra. 46.
Even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, attain the sovereignty over the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe through service to Your lotus feet. (47)
Be gracious, O Goddess of gods, bestower of the four aims of life!
Who is capable of praising you, O Goddess? I am merely prostrate before you. 48.
Thus praised with devotion by the sage Vasiṣṭha, the supreme Goddess Durgā, the consort of Nārāyaṇa, became gracious at that very moment.
Then the Great Goddess, who removes the suffering of those who bow before her, said to the sage:
"Go to the palace of Sudyumna and perform my worship with devotion. (50)
O best of the twice-born, out of affection, cause Sudyumna to hear the ancient Purāṇa known as the Devībhāgavata, which brings me joy, in nine days.
"Merely by hearing this constantly, his manhood shall be restored.
Having spoken thus, Śiva and Īśvarī vanished from sight.
Vasiṣṭha, having bowed in that direction and returned to his own hermitage,
summoned Sudyumna and instructed him in the worship of the Goddess.
Having worshipped the Mother of the World according to the rites of Navarātra during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, he caused the king to hear [the sacred texts]. (54)
Having heard the nectar of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata with devotion, Sudyumna bowed down and honored his guru, and thereby attained manhood permanently. 55.
Having been consecrated upon the royal throne by the great seer Vasiṣṭha,
he ruled the earth with righteousness, delighting his subjects.
He worshipped with various sacrifices accompanied by complete and excellent sacrificial fees;
having entrusted the kingdom to his sons, he attained the same world as the Goddess.

Thus has everything been told, along with its history, O brahmins; if a human being reads this with true devotion or hears it, he shall attain all desires in this world through the grace of the Goddess, and at the end, he goes to the supreme nectar—the realm of the Goddess. (58)
Thus ends the third chapter in the Mānasakhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa, within the Devībhāgavata-māhātmya. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Sūta said:
Having thus heard this divine and wonderful narrative, the Pot-born Sage (Agastya) [was filled with wonder].
Desirous of hearing, he, full of humility, spoke this again to Viśākha. || 1 ||
Agastya said:
"O Lord, General of the Divine Armies, this wonderful story has been heard;
tell me again another account of the greatness of the Bhagavata."
Skanda said:
O sage born of Mitra and Varuṇa, listen to this narrative,
wherein the greatness of even a single portion of the Bhāgavata is proclaimed.
The expansion of Dharma is described with reference to the Gāyatrī;
that wherein the greatness of the Gāyatrī is found is intended as the Bhāgavata. (4)
Because this [work] belongs to the Blessed Lady (Bhagavatī), they know it as Bhāgavata;
for she, the Supreme Bhagavatī, is indeed worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. (5)
There was a highly intelligent sage renowned as Ṛtavāk;
in due time, a son was born to him under the final degree of the constellation Puṣya at the end of Gaṇḍānta.
He performed for him the birth rites and other ceremonies according to the prescribed rules;
he also performed the sacraments such as the tonsure and the initiation ceremony.
From the moment that son was born to that great-souled one, [he performed these rites].
Then, for that very reason, the sage became overwhelmed by grief and affliction.
His mother likewise had her soul overwhelmed by anger and greed;
she was constantly tormented by intense passion and was deeply afflicted by grief and suffering.
The sage Ṛtavāk, being deeply distressed, fell into reflection:
"What is the cause of this that has occurred? My son has become exceedingly wicked-minded."
He forcibly abducted the wife of a certain son of a sage;
that man of deluded intellect paid no heed to the instruction of his father nor to that of his mother. (11)
Then, with a dejected heart, Ṛtavāk spoke these words:
"For men, childlessness is better than ever having a wicked son. (12)
A wicked son causes even his deceased ancestors to fall into hell;
as long as he lives, he is a constant source of suffering to his parents. (13)
Fie on the birth of a wicked son who brings sorrow to his parents;
he is of no benefit to his friends, nor does he cause harm to his enemies.
Blessed are those men in this world in whose home dwells a good son—one who is inclined toward helping others and brings happiness to his father and mother. (15)
By a bad son the family is ruined; by a bad son one's reputation is destroyed;
through a bad son there is suffering both in this world and the next—the agonies of hell.
A lineage is ruined by a bad son; birth is ruined by a bad wife;
a day is ruined by bad food; and where is there happiness with a bad friend? (17)
Skanda said: Thus, constantly tormented by the wicked conduct of his wicked son, the sage went to Garga at the proper time and questioned him.
Ṛtavāk said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to question you; tell me that, O Lord, teacher of the science of astrology, what was the cause of my son's wicked character? (19)
The Vedas were studied by me according to the rules through service to my guru;
having fulfilled the vow of celibacy, marriage was performed according to the prescribed rites. ||20||
Together with my wife, I constantly practiced the duties of a householder,
and I performed the ritual of the five great sacrifices according to the prescribed rules.
O Brahmin, fearing hell and not out of a desire for sensual pleasure, I performed the rite of conception according to the rules for the sake of obtaining a son. (22)

"O Sage, this son of mine has been born ill-behaved, bringing sorrow to his parents and causing grief to his kinsmen, due to the fault of either my mother or myself. Having heard these words of the sage, Garga Ācārya then—
Having deliberated upon all that and its cause, he spoke these words to the astrologer: ||24||
Garga said:
"O sage, this is not your fault, nor that of your mother, nor of your lineage.
Rather, the Gaṇḍānta ending with Revatī is the cause of your son's ill character. (25)
O Sage, because the birth of your son occurred at an inauspicious time, that alone is the cause of your sorrow; there is not even the slightest other cause.
O Brahmin, for the sake of pacifying that suffering, diligently propitiate the auspicious Durgā, the mother of the worlds and the destroyer of misfortune.
Having heard Garga’s words, Ṛtavāk, overcome with anger, cursed Revatī: "Let Revatī fall from the sky! (28)
When he had thus pronounced the curse upon Pūṣan,
the sun’s orb fell from the sky onto Mount Kumuda, while all the world looked on.
Due to his falling there, that mountain became known as Raivataka;
from that time forward, it also became exceedingly beautiful.
Having pronounced a curse upon Revatī according to the procedure prescribed by Garga,
the sage propitiated the goddess Ambikā and became a partaker of happiness and good fortune.
Skanda said:
From the splendor of the constellation Revatī, a maiden was born;
she was peerless in beauty in the world, like a second Śrī. ||32||
Then, having seen that maiden born of Revatī’s splendor,
the sage Pramuca joyfully gave her the name Revatī.
Then he led her to his own hermitage and nourished her according to dharma,
just as the Brahmarṣi named Pramuca did for his daughter on Mount Kumuda.
Then, seeing that she had reached maturity and was endowed with beauty, the sage reflected: "Who might be a suitable husband for her? (35)
Though he searched for her in many ways, he did not find a suitable husband;
thereupon, entering the fire-sanctuary, the sage praised the Fire-god.
Then the Fire-god, being pleased, also prophesied for that maiden a husband who would be most righteous,
powerful, heroic, sweet-spoken, unconquered,
difficult to subdue, and a lord of the earth, O Sage.
Having heard these words of Agni, the sage then became serene.
By chance, under the pretext of hunting, the wise king named Durdama arrived at that moment at the hermitage of that sage.
The son of Vikramaśīla, born from the womb of Kālindī, was powerful and exceedingly heroic, originating from the lineage of Priyavrata.
Having entered the hermitage of the sage and not seeing that great ascetic, the king addressed Revatī, saying "O beloved," and questioned her. (41)
The king said:
"O beloved, that venerable great seer has departed from this hermitage. O auspicious one, tell me truly: I wish to see his feet."
The maiden said:
"O Great King, having heard those words, the great sage arrived at the fire-sanctuary and quickly emerged from the hermitage; the king also [acted] upon hearing that speech. (43)
Likewise, the sage saw King Durdama, endowed with the marks of royalty, standing at the door of the fire-sanctuary and bowing with humility.
The king bowed down to him, and the sage said to his disciple:
"O Gautama, let the guest-offering be brought; this king is worthy of the arghya."
"Since my son-in-law has returned after such a long time," he said, and specifically offered him the guest-offering (arghya); he too accepted it while reflecting.
Then, having greeted the king— who was seated upon his sage-like throne and had accepted the water of honor—
with blessings, he inquired after his welfare.
"O King, O lord of men, is all well with your army, your treasury, your friends,
your servants, your ministers, your city, your country, and likewise with yourself?"
Your wife is well, since she remains right here;
therefore, I do not ask about her welfare, but tell me of the welfare of these others.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace I am free from ailment in every respect.
But this is my curiosity, O Brahmin: who is this woman who exists as my wife? (50)
The sage said:
"O lord of the earth, you have a wife named Revatī, peerless in beauty on this earth; how is it that she exists as your wife and yet you do not know her?"
The king said:
"O Lord, those wives of mine such as Subhadrā and others who are in my house, I know them, O Blessed One; but I do not know Revatī. (52)
The sage said:
O King of great intelligence, that woman whom you have just now called "dear"— she who is your most praiseworthy beloved— has been forgotten by you in an instant.
The king said:
"O sage, that which was spoken by you is not false; we were invited by me in exactly that manner. My intention was not wicked; you should not be angry. (54)
The sage said:
"O King, you have spoken the truth; your intention has not been corrupted. These words were uttered by you in this manner because you were impelled by Agni. (55)
Today I asked the Fire-god, "Who shall become her husband?
He replied, "King Durdama will certainly be her husband. (56)
Therefore, O lord of the earth, accept this maiden given by me;
she was previously addressed as "Priyā" (the Beloved), so do not hesitate, my friend.
Having heard this, he remained silent, reflecting upon the words of the sage;
the sage then prepared to perform the marriage rite for him.
Then, seeing him prepared for the marriage, the maiden said to the sage:
"O father, you ought to perform my marriage when the constellation Revatī is in the sky. (59)
The sage said:
"O child, there are indeed many constellations suitable for marriage;
why then the wedding at Revatī? The asterism of Pūṣan (Revatī) is not situated in the heavens [for this purpose]."
The maiden said:
"There is no time suitable for my marriage except during the asterism of Revatī;
therefore, I entreat you, perform this wedding under the constellation of Puṣya. (61)
The sage said: "In former times, the constellation Revatī was cast down by the sage Ṛtavāk;
if you have no affection for it, how can your marriage take place?"
The maiden said:
"What penance has this one performed? He is merely a speaker of truth.
Have you not likewise performed such penance through speech, body, and mind?"
"You are capable of creating the world; I know the power of your asceticism.
O Father, having fixed the constellation Revatī in the sky, perform my marriage.
The sage said:
"So be it; may prosperity be yours, just as you tell me.
For your sake, I shall today establish the asterism of Puṣya on the path of the moon."
Skanda said:

Having spoken thus, O Pot-born one, the sage immediately restored the constellation of Puṣya to its former state by the power of his asceticism, so that it returned to its course in the path of the Moon. 66.
Under the constellation named Revatī, the sage gave Revatī to the high-souled King Durdama according to the rites of marriage.
Having performed the marriage with the maiden, the sage said to the king:
"O hero, tell me what you desire; I shall fulfill it. (68)
The king said:
"O sage, I am born in the lineage of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu;
by your grace, I desire a son who shall be the lord of a Manvantara. (69)
The sage said:
"If you have this desire, perform the propitiation of the Goddess;
you shall indeed have a son who will be a Manu, the sovereign of a Manvantara."
Having heard that Purāṇa named Devībhāgavata, which is the fifth, five times, you shall obtain the desired son.
The fifth Manu will be named Raivata, the son of Revatī;
he will be a knower of the Vedas, one who understands the true principles of the scriptures, a follower of dharma, and unconquered.
Thus addressed by the sage, the wise king, having bowed down joyfully to the sage, went with his wife to his own city. (73)
That high-minded one ruled the kingdom inherited from his father and grandfather;
that righteous soul protected his subjects like his own biological sons.
Once, a high-souled sage named Lomaśa arrived;
having prostrated before him and honored him, the king spoke with palms joined in reverence.
The King said:
"O Blessed One, O Sage, by your grace I desire to hear the Purāṇa named Devībhāgavata for the sake of obtaining a son. (76)
Having heard the words of the Lord of Creatures, Lomaśa, being pleased, said:
"O King, you are blessed; devotion has arisen in you toward the Mother of the Three Worlds."
If devotion has arisen toward her—the Supreme Mother of the World, who is worshipped by gods, demons, and men—then the accomplishment of your purpose will come to pass. (78)
Therefore, O King, I shall cause you to hear the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, by the mere hearing of which nothing whatsoever remains difficult to attain. (79)
Having spoken thus, O Brahmin, he began the narration on an auspicious day;
he listened to it five times according to the prescribed rite together with his wife.
On the day of completion, the righteous king, filled with supreme joy, honored both the Purāṇa and the sage.
Having offered oblations with the nine-syllable mantra and fed the young maidens,
he gratified the Brahmins along with their wives with sacrificial fees.
Then, after some time, by the grace of the Blessed One, that queen conceived a child who was to bring about the welfare of the world. (83)
Then, when an auspicious time had arrived and the planets were situated in favorable positions, Revatī gave birth to a son amidst all manner of auspiciousness. (84)
Upon hearing of his son's birth, the king, filled with joy, bathed and performed the postnatal rites,
such as the *jātakarman*, using water mixed with gold.
Having bestowed gifts according to the prescribed rules and gratified the Brahmins,
the king had the boy undergo the initiation ceremony and taught him the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches.
Born as a treasury of all sciences, most righteous, and the best among those skilled in weapons,
he was the powerful one named Raivata, both a speaker and a practitioner of dharma.
Then Brahmā appointed Raivata to the station of Manu;
that illustrious lord of the Manvantara ruled the earth according to righteousness.
Thus has this power of the Goddess been described in brief;
who is capable of describing the greatness of the Purāṇa in detail? (89)
Sūta said:
Having heard the greatness and the ritual procedure of the Bhāgavata, the pot-born sage (Agastya) worshipped Kumāra and returned once more to his own hermitage.
O Brahmins, this majesty of the Blessed Lord has been recounted by me in your presence.
He who hears it with devotion or recites it here, having enjoyed all worldly pleasures, attains liberation in the end.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Śrī Devībhāgavata-māhātmya within the Mānasa-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 4 ||
Now begins the fifth chapter.
The sages said:
"O Sūta, O Sūta, O highly fortunate one, we have heard this most excellent majesty."
Now we wish to hear the procedure for listening to the Purāṇas.
Sūta said:
O all you sages, listen to the rule for hearing the Purāṇas, by which those men who hear it shall attain success in all their desires. (2)
At the outset, the wise man, having summoned an astrologer, should determine an auspicious moment;
beginning from the month of Śuci, a period of six months brings good fortune.

Listening to the Purāṇas is auspicious when performed under the asterisms of Hasta, Aśvinī, Mūla, and Puṣya; during the constellations of Brahmā (Rohiṇī), Maitra (Anurādhā), Indu (Mṛgaśiras), and Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇa); on an auspicious lunar day and on a favorable weekday. ||4||
Through the sequence of the numbers eight, four, four, one, five, six, four, and three,
there is respectively the attainment of dharma, the acquisition of wealth, success in one's purpose, and supreme happiness.
Suffering, fear of the king, and the attainment of knowledge are the results in successive order.
One should purify the wheel spoken by Śiva during the listening of the Purāṇas.
Alternatively, for the pleasure of the Goddess during the four Navarātras,
one may listen [to this] even in another month, provided the lunar day, weekday, and asterism have been purified.
The wise should diligently prepare such provisions for this new sacrifice as are required for a marriage and other such ceremonies. (8)
One should employ many assistants who are free from deceit and greed,
men who are clever, generous, and devoted to the Goddess.
"Let this news be diligently dispatched to every land and among every person:
'One must certainly come here; there will be a discourse with the Goddess. (10)
Whether they be Sauras, Gāṇapatyas, Śaivas, Śāktas, or Vaiṣṇavas—for all of them she is to be served, since the gods are always accompanied by their Śaktis. (11)
Those who are intensely devoted to love and who long for the nectar-like essence of the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata should especially come for the sake of this discourse.
The castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, as well as women and those in the stages of life (āśramas)—whether possessing desire or free from desire—should drink this nectar of the narrative. 13.
There shall never be an occasion for them even to hear the word "no";
they must come at the proper time, for the auspicious moment of the sacrifice is fleeting.
The summoning of men must be carried out with propriety; likewise, for those who have arrived, a suitable place of residence must be provided. 15.
A place for discourse should be prepared on the ground, preceded by sweeping; then, in a spacious area, it should be made beautiful by smearing with cow dung. (16)
A beautiful pavilion should be constructed, adorned with pillars of plantain trees, with a canopy above and resplendent with flags and banners. (17)
And a divine seat for the speaker, provided with a comfortable covering, should be prepared with great care, facing either the east or the north. (18)
He should provide appropriate seats for the listeners—for both men and women—in order for them to hear the discourse. (19)

One who is eloquent, self-controlled, learned in the scriptures, devoted to the worship of the Goddess, compassionate, free from desire, skillful, steadfast, and an excellent speaker is considered [fit]. (20)

Devoted to Brahman, devoted to the deity, intent on the essence of the sacred narrative, magnanimous, free from greed, humble, and indeed abstaining from violence and other such acts—such a person is a true listener. || 21 ||
One who is devoted to heresy, greedy, addicted to women, a hypocrite, cruel, wrathful, or a harsh speaker is not praised at a sacrifice to the Goddess. (22)
To sever doubts, there should be one assistant who is learned, possesses such qualities, awakens the understanding of the listeners, remains composed, and acts as an aid to the speaker. (23)

Within a *muhūrta* before the day [ends], the acts of shaving and so forth should be performed by the people, such as the speaker and the listener; thereafter, the formulation of the observances (*niyama*) follows.
At the time of dawn, having performed purification, one should bathe;
one should daily perform the twilight prayers and the libation rite in brief.
To achieve fitness for hearing sacred narratives, one should cause cows to be given as gifts.
First, one should worship Gaṇapati, the remover of all obstacles.
Having also established the water-pots (kalaśas), one should worship there the deities belonging to the directions:
Vaṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, the Yoginīs, and likewise the Mātṛkās.
Having also worshipped Tulasī, the planets, Viṣṇu, and Śaṅkara,
one should worship the Mother of the Universe with the nine-syllabled mantra.
Having worshipped the book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata with all ritual offerings—as the very embodiment of the speech of the Goddess Śrī, composed in beautiful script—according to the rules. 29.
For the sake of pacifying obstacles to the discourse, he should also invite Brahmins;
by them, the nine-syllable mantra is to be recited as a prayer, and the Saptashati hymn is to be chanted.
Having performed circumambulations and prostrations, one should offer praise at the conclusion:
"O Kātyāyanī, O Mahāmāyā, O Bhavānī, O Bhuvaneśvarī! (31)
O Compassionate One, lift me up who am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra;
O Mother of the Universe, worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, be gracious! 32.
"O Goddess, grant the boon desired by my mind; salutations be unto you.
Having thus prayed, one should listen to the story with a restrained mind. (33)
Then, that self-possessed person, having honored the speaker with the thought that he is Vyāsa himself,
and having adorned him with garlands, ornaments, garments, and other gifts, should pray to him.
O knower of all scriptures and histories, O you who are Vyāsa in form, salutations be unto you!
Dispel the mass of inner darkness with the rising moon of this narrative.
Prior to that, the observances (niyamas) must be performed for nine days.
Having first seated the Brahmins and others, and having honored them, he himself should sit down.
One should listen attentively for the sake of attaining the fruits of the four aims of life, having cast aside all anxiety regarding home, sons, wife, and wealth. (37)
Starting from sunrise until a small portion of the sun remains,
the wise person should rest for just one muhūrta and then recite [the text] at midday.
For the sake of conquering excrement and urine, a light meal is prescribed for them;
however, one who desires the sacred narrative should eat only once a day, preferably sacrificial food (haviṣyānna).
Alternatively, one may subsist on fruits, consume only milk, or eat only ghee;
the wise should act in such a way that there is no obstacle to the recitation of the story. 40.
O twice-born ones, I shall declare the rule for those devoted to hearing this narrative:
those who perceive a distinction between Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa; (41)
Those who are devoid of devotion to the Goddess, heretics, violent, wicked, hostile toward Brahmins, and atheists—they are not fit to hear this narrative. (42)

Those who are greedy for seizing the property of Brahmins, for the wives and wealth of others, and for seizing the property of the gods—there is no qualification for them even to hear the sacred stories. 43.
Practicing celibacy, sleeping on the ground, speaking the truth, and having conquered his senses, he, being self-controlled, should eat from a leaf-plate at the conclusion of the recitation. 44.
One observing a vow should avoid eggplant, the *kalinda* gourd, oil, split pulses, honey, burnt food, stale food, and anything that is mentally impure. (45)
Food mixed with meat, lentil soup, and that which has been seen by a woman in her courses;
as well as garlic, radish, asafoetida, onion, and leek. (46)
One who observes the vow of silence (kathāvratī) should not eat the vegetables kūṣmāṇḍa and nalikā;
he should also avoid lust, anger, intoxication, greed, hypocrisy, and pride. ||47||

One who observes the vow of silence should not converse with those who harm Brahmins, the fallen, Vratyas, dog-cookers, Yavanas, outcastes, a woman in her courses, or those outside the Vedic fold. 48.
One should not even hear the censure of the Vedas, gurus, Brahmins, women, kings, great souls, the gods, or those devoted to the gods. (49)
He who observes the vow of sacred narrative (kathāvratī) should practice discipline, straightforwardness, purity, compassion, moderation in speech, and a noble state of mind. (50)
Whether she be barren, or one whose children are like crows, or unfortunate, or whose offspring have died;
or whether he be poor and childless—if such a person listens to this narrative with devotion, [he shall attain success]. (51)

This story should likewise be told to those who are barren, or those who give birth only to female children, or those who are unfortunate, or those whose children have died, or to women whose fetuses are lost. 52.
He who desires dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa without exertion must listen with diligence to the Bhāgavata of the Blessed One.
Indeed, these days beginning with Kathā are equal to the sacrifices of the masters of logic;
what is given, offered in sacrifice, or chanted during them yields infinite fruit. (54)
Having thus observed the vow for nine days, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana);
those desiring the fruit should act exactly as prescribed for the Mahāṣṭamī vow. || 55 ||
For those who are free from desire, merely by hearing [this], they become purified and indeed attain liberation;
since the Supreme Goddess bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men. (56)
One should always perform worship of both the book and the speaker;
one should receive the grace bestowed by the speaker with devotion. (57)
He who constantly worships young maidens, feeds them, and makes requests to them, as well as to married women and Brahmins, will attain success; of this there is no doubt. (58)
At the conclusion, one should recite the thousand names of Gāyatrī or the thousand names of Viṣṇu for the pacification of all defects. (59)
Since by remembering him and uttering his name during acts of austerity, sacrifice, and ritual performance,
whatever is deficient attains completeness, one should therefore glorify Viṣṇu.
At the conclusion [of the recitation] with the mantras of the *Devī-saptaśatī*,
one should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) using either the root mantra of the *Devīmāhātmya* or the nine-syllable mantra.
Alternatively, the oblation may be performed with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra;
for this Bhāgavata is said to be composed of the essence of the Gāyatrī.
One should properly satisfy the reciter with garments, ornaments, wealth, and other gifts;
when the reciter is pleased, all the deities are pleased with him.
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion and satisfy them with sacrificial fees;
for they are like gods upon this earth, and when they are pleased, the desired fruit is attained.
One should feed married women and young maidens with devotion to the Goddess;
having given them sacrificial fees as well, one should pray for one's own spiritual success.
One should also give other gifts—gold, milch cows, horses, elephants, and land; for him, the fruit thereof shall be inexhaustible.
And this Devībhāgavata, written in beautiful characters,
should be placed upon a golden throne and wrapped in a silken cloth.

On the eighth or the ninth [lunar day], he should give gifts to the reciter and to the one who has been honored; having enjoyed worldly pleasures here, he shall attain liberation, which is difficult to obtain. 68.
Whether he be poor, weak, a child, a youth, or even an old man, a physician who knows the ancient [medical] sciences is always worthy of honor and respect. (69)
There are many teachers in the world by virtue of their birth in excellence;
yet among all of them, the knower of the Purāṇas is the supreme teacher.
A Paurāṇika Brāhmaṇa, however, while seated upon the seat of Vyāsa,
should not offer salutations to anyone until his discourse is concluded.
Even those who listen to this divine ancient narrative without devotion possess no fruit of merit; they shall be partakers of suffering and poverty. (72)
Those who listen to the story of the Goddess without first honoring the Purāṇa with betel, flowers, and other offerings will indeed become impoverished. 73.
Those men who, abandoning a story being narrated, go elsewhere, will find their wives and wealth destroyed in the midst of their enjoyments. (74)
Those hypocrites who, seated upon high thrones, listen to the discourse,
shall become crows here after suffering the torments of hell.
Those who sit upon opulent seats and those who sit in the *vīrāsana* posture [shall likewise suffer].
And those who hear this divine narrative shall become branches of Arjuna. 76.
Those who utter difficult or improper replies while this narrative is being recited become donkeys in this world, and thereafter become lizards.
Those wicked ones who revile those who know the Purāṇas or the sin-removing narrative shall undoubtedly become dogs for a hundred births. || 78 ||
Those who listen to the discourse while seated on the same seat as the speaker go to the abode of hell and incur a sin equal to that of violating the preceptor’s bed. ||79||
Those who listen without bowing down become poisonous trees;
even those who listen while lying down become pythons.
Those men who never listen to the ancient stories,
having experienced a terrible hell, become village pigs.
Those deceitful ones who do not approve of the discourse and who create obstacles, having suffered in hell for ten million years, become village pigs. 82.
Those who give a seat, a vessel, a substance, fruit, garments,
or a woolen blanket to one who knows the Purāṇas go to the abode of Hari.
Those men who provide a new, auspicious silk cloth and fine thread for an ancient manuscript are partakers of happiness. (84)
Whatever fruit one may obtain from hearing all the Purāṇas, one shall obtain a hundred times that merit from the Devībhāgavata. (85)
Just as the Gaṅgā is preeminent among rivers, Śaṅkara among the gods, the Rāmāyaṇa among poems, and the sun among luminous bodies; ||86||
He was like the moon among things that give delight, like fame among riches, like the earth among those who possess forbearance, and like the ocean in depth. (87)
Among mantras, the Sāvitrī is supreme for the destruction of sin, as is the remembrance of Hari;
likewise, among the eighteen Purāṇas, the Devībhāgavata is supreme.
If one hears [this] nine times by any means whatsoever, it is impossible to describe its fruit; he indeed becomes liberated while living. (89)

When fear of kings or enemies has arisen, likewise when there is fear of a great pestilence, during famine, or when the kingdom is in ruin—one should listen to this for the sake of pacifying those calamities. (10)
O twice-born ones, one should listen to the Devībhāgavata for the destruction of ghosts and spirits, for the attainment of a kingdom from enemies, and for the acquisition of a son.
Whoever reads or even hears the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam—
be it half a verse or even a quarter of a verse— attains the supreme goal.
That very [teaching] was revealed by the Blessed Goddess herself in half a verse; it has been expanded through the lineage of disciples and grand-disciples. (93)
There is no dharma higher than the Gāyatrī; there is no austerity higher than the Gāyatrī;
there is no god equal to the Gāyatrī; there is no mantra higher than the Gāyatrī. 94.
Because it protects the singer (gātṛ), it is called Gāyatrī;
that Goddess, along with her secret doctrine, is established here in this Bhāgavata. (95)
Therefore, even the great Purāṇas are not worth a sixteenth part of this Bhāgavata, which brings delight to the Goddess. 96.
The Śrīmad Bhāgavata Purāṇa is the stainless wealth of the brāhmaṇas,
wherein the pure dharma was proclaimed by Nārāyaṇa, the son of Dharma;
herein also the secret of the Gāyatrī and Maṇidvīpa are described.
And the Blessed Gītā was sung by the Goddess herself to the Lord of the Snowy Mountains. ||97||
Therefore, O twice-born ones, there is nothing else in this world equal to this Purāṇa; for this reason, the Devībhāgavata should always be reverently served. 98.

Salutations evermore to that Mother of the World, whose entire power neither the Creator, nor Hari, nor Giriśa, nor even Ananta knows; how much less, then, can the partial incarnations of these, or other gods, know it? 99.

Salutations forever to that Mother of the Universe, having obtained the dust of whose lotus feet Brahmā creates the universe daily, Viṣṇu sustains it, and Rudra destroys it; otherwise, they would not be capable of such tasks. 100.

Having meditated upon the Mother, who shines within the heart of Supreme Śiva—smiling-faced, residing in a house made of wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi) on the Jewel Island (maṇidvīpa), which is adorned with groves of celestial trees at the edge of the ocean of nectar, and is wonderfully beautiful—a man indeed enjoys worldly enjoyment and attains liberation. || 101 ||
May she, the presiding deity of Maṇidvīpa, who is worshipped by Brahmā, Īśa, Acyuta, Śakra, and other great sages, exist for the welfare of the world. 102.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Piercing [the Ears]," in the *Devībhāgavata-māhātmya* within the *Mānasa-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Skanda Purāṇa*.
This *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavata-Māhātmya* belonging to the Skanda-purāṇa is completed.
The question of Śaunaka:
Oṃ, let us meditate upon that primordial knowledge, whose form is universal consciousness.
May she who shall impel our intellect. || 1 ||
Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, O Sūta, you are highly fortunate, O bull among men;
for you have properly studied these auspicious Purāṇa compendiums.
O sinless one, the eighteen divine Purāṇas were narrated by the sage Kṛṣṇa; they have been studied by you, O sinless one.
O giver of honor, you have learned from Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, all these [teachings] endowed with five characteristics, together with their secret mysteries.
By the power of our merit, you have arrived at this supreme field—
divine, all-inspiring, holy, and free from the defects of the Kali age.
"O Sūta, this assembly of sages indeed desires to hear the meritorious Purāṇa-saṃhitā; therefore, with a concentrated mind, please speak it to us."
"May you be long-lived, O Omniscient One, and free from the threefold afflictions;
O highly fortunate one, please narrate today the Purāṇa which is equal to the Veda."
O Sūta, those men who possess the faculty of hearing but are unskilled in discerning the true taste [of dharma] do not listen to the Purāṇas; indeed, they have been deceived by fate.
Just as the gratification of the sense of taste is experienced through the six flavors,
so too is the gratification of the sense of hearing held to be achieved by the words of the wise.
Indeed, hooded serpents, being without ears, may at will be deluded by the qualities of the sky;
but how is it that those who possess ears yet do not listen are no different from those without ears? (10)
Therefore, O gentle one, all these twice-born ones in the sacred field of Naimiṣa Forest remain composed and desirous of hearing [this], being afflicted by the fear of the Kali age. (11)
It is taught that the passing of time by whatever means possible is for fools in this world through vices, but for the wise through reflections on the scriptures. (12)
The scriptures are also diverse, consisting of disputations and debates;
the Purāṇas are of three kinds, and the various Śāstras are filled with cavil,
quibbling, and the provocation of pride and resentment.
They are endowed with various meaningful expressions, are logical, and are extensive. || 13 ||
Among those, the Vedānta is considered sāttvika, Mīmāṃsā is regarded as rājasa,
and the Nyāya-śāstra, which is constrained by the logic of causal arguments, is tāmasa.
In that very same way, O gentle one, you have narrated the Purāṇas, which consist of three qualities and possess five characteristics, through various stories.
Among those, the meritorious Bhāgavata, which is equal to the Vedas and endowed with all characteristics, was previously described by you. (16)
At that time, this most wonderful [account] was proclaimed merely by way of summary;
it bestows liberation upon those seeking liberation, and likewise grants all desires and dharma.
"Relate that supreme Purāṇa in detail with reverence;
all these twice-born ones desire to hear the divine and auspicious Bhāgavata. (18)
But you, O knower of dharma, being a refuge of the quality of goodness, surely know the ancient compendium spoken by Kṛṣṇa due to your devotion to your guru. (19)
O Omniscient One, we have heard many other things issuing from your mouth, yet even now we do not reach satiety, just as the immortals never tire of drinking nectar. (20)
Fie upon milk, O Sūta! For those who drink it, there is never liberation at any time;
whereas by drinking the Bhāgavata, a person is immediately released from distress.
O Sūta, although thousands of sacrifices have been performed by us for the sake of drinking the nectar of immortality,
we do not attain peace in our whole being.
For the fruit of sacrifices is heaven, and from heaven there is a falling back;
thus, in this wheel of saṃsāra, there is incessant wandering. (23)
O Omniscient One, without knowledge there is never liberation for men wandering here in this wheel of time composed of the three qualities. (24)
Therefore, recite the Bhāgavata, which is endowed with all aesthetic flavors, meritorious,
purifying, bestowing liberation, secret, and always dear to those seeking release.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Inquiry of Śaunaka," in the First Book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 1 ||
Description of the Number of Verses and the Subject Matter.
Sūta said:
"I am blessed, I am exceedingly fortunate, and I have been purified by these great-souled ones."
That which was asked is a very great merit, an ancient narrative renowned in the Vedas.
Therefore, I shall fully proclaim that which is in accord with the meaning of all the Vedas, the secret of all scriptures, and the unsurpassed essence of all the Āgamas. || 2 ||
Having bowed to that beautiful lotus-foot which bestows liberation upon yogis.
Served even by Brahmā and others who are intent on praise, and always meditated upon by the lords of sages—
I shall today describe in detail this glorious and supreme Purāṇa, which possesses manifold aesthetic flavors.
O twice-born ones, with devotion [he visited] that which is the abode of all aesthetic flavors and is renowned by the name Bhagavatī. || 3 ||
That power which is called "Vidyā" in the path of the Vedas is the supreme Śakti, beginning with Sat and the rest.
Omniscient, skilled in severing the bonds of existence, and abiding within the hearts of all,
she is difficult to know for those of evil nature, yet has been brought by sages to the state of being the object of meditation.
In this world, that Blessed Lady becomes manifest; she shall always be the bestower of spiritual accomplishments.
Having created this entire universe, which consists of the nature of both the existent and the non-existent,
she protects the world by means of her own power composed of the three qualities; and at the time of the kalpa's end, having withdrawn it all, she rejoices alone.
I remember her with my mind, the mother of the entire universe. || 5 ||
It is well known that Brahmā creates this entire universe, as indeed declared by those conversant with the Purāṇas who are learned in the Vedas;
yet it is said that his birth occurred within the lotus from Viṣṇu’s navel.
They said: "He creates only that which has already been spoken; for he is not independent."
While Viṣṇu was sleeping upon the couch of Śeṣa, at that time his birth indeed occurred within the bud of his navel;
it is said that the thousand-headed one (Śeṣa) became the support for this [birth].
How indeed can that Blessed One, the Enemy of Mura, be awakened?
The water of the single ocean exists only in the form of taste; indeed, without a vessel, there can be no persistence of taste whatsoever—
that which is truly the very nature of power (*śakti*) within the sphere of all beings.
I have gone for refuge to her, the mother of all beings. || 8 ||
Having seen Viṣṇu seated upon the lotus with his eyes closed in yogic sleep, the unborn Brahmā praised that Goddess; I have gone for refuge to her.
Having meditated upon that Māyā, which possesses attributes and likewise bestows liberation when devoid of attributes, I shall proclaim the entire Purāṇa; let the sages here listen.
The Purāṇa known as the Śrīmad Bhāgavata is the most excellent and meritorious;
it contains eighteen thousand refined verses. (11)
In this work, Kṛṣṇa has composed twelve auspicious sections;
it is recorded as containing three hundred chapters in full, augmented by eighteen.
There are twenty in the first, twelve indeed in the second, thirty in the third, and twenty-five in the fourth. || 13 ||
Likewise, thirty-five chapters are proclaimed in the fifth [book];
thirty-one in the sixth; and forty in the seventh. (14)
In the eighth [chapter], the enumeration of the principles (tattvas) is fifty; likewise in the ninth;
and thirteen, it is said by the Sage, are proclaimed in the tenth.
And likewise, O best of sages, twenty-four chapters are declared in the eleventh book, while there are exactly fourteen chapters in the twelfth.
Thus has the number been declared by the Great-Souled One in this Purāṇa;
this number is proclaimed to be eighteen thousand.
Primary creation, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manvantaras, and the history of the dynasties—thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics. (18)
She who is always devoid of qualities, eternal, all-pervading, unchanging, and auspicious;
she who is attainable through yoga, the support of all, and who abides as the fourth state (turīyā). || 19 ||
Her powers are indeed of the nature of sattva, rajas, and tamas;
those women are Mahālakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Mahākālī.
The assumption of bodies by these three powers for the purpose of creation has been described as "sarga" (emanation) by those learned in the scriptures. (21)
From that, the origin of Hari, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Rudra is recorded;
indeed, that is remembered as the secondary creation (pratisarga) for the purpose of protection, origination, and destruction.
Therein is the proclamation of the lineages of kings born from the Moon and the Sun;
those dynasties, beginning with Hiraṇyakaśipu and others, have been fully described.
And there is a detailed description of the Manus beginning with Svāyambhuva,
as well as the calculation of their time and their respective Manvantaras.
The recounting of their lineages is known as the *vaṃśānucarita*;
O best of sages, these [episodes] possess five characteristics. (25)
And likewise, the Bhārata consisting of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses was composed by the Sage;
it is proclaimed as the fifth Itihāsa, which is equal to the Vedas. (26)
Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, tell us in detail what those Purāṇas are;
O omniscient one, how many in number are they? For we here are desirous of hearing them.
"We, the inhabitants of the Naimiṣa forest, are terrified by the Kali age;
we have been commanded here by Brahmā after he gave us a mind-made discus. (28)
He said to us all: "Go behind him;
wherever his rim shatters, that place is remembered as sacred. (29)
At that time, Kali will never be able to enter there;
let them remain right there until the Satya Yuga returns once more.
Having heard those words of his and taken up that narrative,
he set out quickly, shaking [the earth] with the desire to see all lands.
Because he set the wheel in motion here both after death and in this world, and because the rim was shattered here as he watched,
this most purifying sacred field is called Naimiṣa by him.
"There is no entry for the Kali age here; therefore, this place was established by me, as well as by the high-souled sages and hosts of Siddhas who were afraid of the Kali age. (33)
"Indeed, sacrifices were rendered devoid of animals by means of sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and the like;
one must simply pass the time until the arrival of the Satya Yuga. (34)
O Sūta, you have arrived here entirely through the power of destiny;
therefore, please narrate today this purifying Purāṇa, which is esteemed by Brahmā.
O Sūta, we are all desirous of hearing, and you are a wise speaker;
we are indeed free from other occupations and likewise one-pointed in mind. (36)
O Sūta, may you be long-lived and free from the threefold afflictions;
today, indeed, narrate the auspicious and meritorious Bhāgavata Purāṇa.
In this work, there is a description of dharma, artha, and kāma according to the prescribed rules;
and having obtained knowledge through it, liberation (mokṣa) is indeed said to be attained by the Sage. 38.
O Sūta, we are not satiated by hearing this delightful narrative, which was told by the sage Dvaipāyana and which is purifying. (39)

Reveal that ancient [name] of the Blessed One, which is the singular vessel for all multitudes of virtues, the pure [name] of the Mother of the entire world, as wondrous as a dramatic performance, the destroyer of the entire mass of impurities, and the root of desire. (40)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Description of the Number of Verses and the Subject Matter," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The description of the Vyāsas belonging to their respective ages, preceded by a description of the Purāṇas.
Sūta said:
"O lords of sages, listen; I shall fully proclaim the Purāṇas."
Just as they were heard in their true essence from Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī.
Two *mats*, two *bhas*, three *vrats*, and four *vacas*—
these are the ancient *anāpaliṅgakūs* (unfit for marriage), each distinct from the others.
And the first Matsya Purāṇa is proclaimed to consist of fourteen thousand verses.
Likewise, a thousand planets [honored] the most wonderful Mārkaṇḍeya. || 3 ||
Fourteen thousand and five hundred.
The future has been fully enumerated by the sages who perceive the truth.
The Bhāgavata is indeed said to consist of eighteen thousand verses,
and likewise, there is the Purāṇa named Brahma, which consists of ten thousand verses.
The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa consists of exactly twelve thousand verses and one hundred more;
likewise, the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa consists of eighteen thousand verses.
O Śaunaka, there are ten thousand [verses] known as the Vāmana, six hundred for the Vāyavya,
and twenty-four thousand [verses].
The Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa is most wonderful, consisting of twenty-three thousand verses; the Vārāha Purāṇa is most wonderful, consisting of twenty-four thousand verses.
The Purāṇa known as Agni consists of exactly sixteen thousand verses;
the supreme Nārada Purāṇa is considered to consist of twenty-five thousand verses.
The extensive [Purāṇa] known as Padma is considered to consist of fifty-five thousand verses;
and that known as Liṅga consists of eleven thousand verses and is exceedingly well-remembered.
The Gāruḍa Purāṇa, spoken by Hari, consists of nineteen thousand verses; and the Kūrma Purāṇa, spoken by Kūrma, consists of seventeen thousand verses.
O sinless ones, I have related in detail the number known as the Purāṇas, which consists of eighty-one thousand verses and is called the Skanda, most wonderful to behold.
In the same manner, O best of sages, listen to the Upapurāṇas:
first Sanatkumāra, and after that Nārasiṃha.
The Nāradīya, the Śiva, the unsurpassed Daurvāsasa, the Kāpila, the Mānava, and likewise the Smṛti of Uśanas. || 14 ||
The Vāruṇa, the one called Kālika, the auspicious Sāmba composed by Nandin, the Saura spoken by Pārāśara, and the very extensive Āditya. || 15 ||
The Māheśvara, the Bhāgavata, and the Vāsiṣṭha in detail—these are the Upapurāṇas declared by the high-souled ones. || 16 ||
Having composed the eighteen Purāṇas, the son of Satyavatī created the incomparable narrative known as the Bhārata, which was augmented by them.
In all the Manvantaras, in every Dvāpara age,
he who seeks righteousness manifests the Purāṇas according to the prescribed rule.
In every Dvāpara age, Viṣṇu always assumes the form of Vyāsa and,
desiring the welfare of the world, divides the single Veda into many parts.
Then, perceiving that the Brahmins in the Kali age would be short-lived and of small intellect,
he composed this meritorious Purāṇa-saṃhitā in every age.
The hearing of the Vedas is not prescribed for women, Śūdras, and the kin of the twice-born;
it was for their benefit alone that the Purāṇas were composed. (21)
O best of sages, in this auspicious seventh Manvantara named Vaivasvata,
when the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age had arrived.
Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, my preceptor and the foremost knower of dharma, shall become the son of Droṇa when the twenty-ninth year has arrived. (23)
Likewise, there were twenty-seven past Vyāsas,
and by them the Purāṇa-saṃhitās were narrated in age after age.
The sages said:
O highly fortunate Sūta, tell us of the Vyāsas born in former ages,
who were the speakers of the Purāṇas in every Dvāpara Yuga.
Sūta said: In the first Dvāpara age, the Vedas were divided by Svayambhū himself;
in the second Dvāpara age, however, Prajāpati performed the work of Vyāsa.
In the third [age] Uśanas was the Vyāsa; in the fourth, Bṛhaspati;
in the fifth, Savitṛ was the Vyāsa; and in the sixth, Mṛtyu, and others likewise.
Maghavā is recorded as occurring in the seventh [Manvantara], Vasiṣṭha in the eighth;
Sārasvata in the ninth, and likewise Tridhāman in the tenth.
Then in the eleventh [Manvantara] was Trivṛṣa Bharadvāja;
after that, in the thirteenth, Antarikṣa; and Dharma in the fourteenth.
Trayyāruṇi was in the fifteenth, while Dhanañjaya was in the sixteenth;
Medhātithi was in the seventeenth, and Vratī likewise in the eighteenth.
Then Atri was the nineteenth, and after him Gautama;
Uttama was the twenty-first, and then Haryātmā is celebrated.
Vena, Vājaśravas, Soma Āmuṣyāyaṇa, Tṛṇabindu, Vyāsa, and after that Bhārgava. (32)
Then Śakti Jātūkarṇya, and then Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana;
this number twenty-eight which has been recounted by me is what I have heard.
I have heard from Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana this Purāṇa, the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, which is meritorious and the destroyer of the flood of all miseries. (34)

It bestows both worldly desires and liberation, is enriched with the meaning of the Vedas, is a pleasure-garden for the essence of all scriptures, and is always dear to those seeking release. || 35 ||
Vyāsa, having composed this most auspicious Purāṇa, indeed taught it to his high-souled son Śuka,
who was endowed with detachment.
And having understood it for the sake of its production from the fire-drill (araṇi). || 36 ||
O lords of sages, I have heard from the mouth of Vyāsa and grasped exactly as it was taught that entire secret of the Purāṇas in its true sense.
