And by the grace of the Guru, who is an ocean of compassion. || 37 ||
Questioned by Sūta, Dvaipāyana then related the entirety of that ancient mystery to him,
who was of wondrous intellect and not born from a womb.
I have heard of its great power there. || 38 ||
O best of beings, Śuka, desiring to cross the waters of the ocean of worldly existence so difficult to traverse, took great delight in tasting the fruit of the divine tree of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata*;
with his ears as vessels, he listened with love to this wonderful work, which is the abode of the essence of various narratives.
Having heard that, who on earth of such a kind would not be liberated from the fear of the Kali age? (39)
Even a wicked person, devoid of the Vedic dharma and lacking proper conduct and intention, [is not to be despised].
Whoever hears this supreme and glorious Purāṇa, even by way of a pretext,
shall enjoy an abundant array of pleasures here in this world, and at the end of the body, shall attain that beautiful, immovable state reached by yogis, marked with the name of the Blessed Goddess.
That knowledge which is devoid of attributes, unattainable even by Hari, Hara, and others, most beloved by the virtuous, and accessible through meditative absorption—
that very knowledge produces its state of being within the hollow of his heart.
Whoever constantly listens to this Satī Purāṇa, || 41 ||
Having obtained a human birth complete in all its limbs— a vessel for crossing the waters of the ocean of existence at will—
the fool, alas, does not listen even when he has found a teacher.
He has been deceived here by fate regarding that which is ancient and bestows happiness. || 42 ||
He who, having obtained a pair of keen ears in human form, being full of passion, constantly listens to the slanders of others—
[he misses] this ancient, stainless treasure-house of nectar that bestows all goals.
Why does that dull-witted man, though ruined, not hear this on earth? || 43 ||

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Vyāsas of Their Respective Ages Following the Description of the Purāṇas," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Regarding the statement that the Goddess is the most excellent,
the sages said:
"O gentle one, in which wife of Vyāsa was the son Śuka born?"
Or how, and of what kind was he, by whom this well-compounded [text] was recited? || 1 ||
You have stated that Śuka was not born from a womb and likewise not born from an egg;
there is a great doubt regarding this, so please explain it today, O high-minded one.
It was previously heard that there was a practitioner of yoga named Śuka, a man of great austerity;
how did he formerly study the Purāṇa of such great extent?
Sūta said: Formerly, on the bank of the Sarasvatī, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī,
was filled with wonder upon seeing two sparrows in his hermitage.
A charming infant, just born in the nest, released from its eggs, with a copper-colored beak and beautiful limbs, yet devoid of the sprouts of plumage. || 5 ||
But those two, being exceedingly intent on pleasure and devoted to their exertion,
repeatedly placed food into the beak of their young one.
Filled with joy, they rubbed their own limbs against those of the child,
and out of love, they kissed the auspicious face of the infant like two young sparrows.
Beholding that wonderful love there between the two young sparrows,
Vyāsa became anxious with thought and reflected deeply in his mind.
What wonder is there that even animals display such love for their offspring? It is no surprise that humans, who desire the fruits of service, should do so as well.
"Will these two sparrows, having arranged his marriage—the means to happiness—become happy upon seeing the auspicious face of the bride? (10)
Or else, when old age has arrived, a most righteous son will perform service for the two sparrows for the sake of merit.
Or, having acquired wealth, he will satisfy his parents;
or else, he will perform the funeral rites according to the prescribed rules.
Or rather, what will the boy achieve by going to Gayā and performing the śrāddha rite, or by duly performing the release of a dark-colored bull? (13)
In this saṃsāra, it is declared that the highest happiness among all pleasures is the embrace of a son's body and, in particular, his caressing.
For one who has no son, there is no destination, neither heaven nor anything else;
there is no means for achieving the world beyond other than a son. (15)
And it has been declared by the sages such as Manu and others in the Dharmaśāstras:
"One who has a son attains heaven, but one who is sonless does so in no way whatsoever. (16)
This is seen here before one's very eyes; it is not established by means of inference.
One who has a son is released from sin, and the word of a trustworthy person is eternal. (17)
Even at the time of death when he is afflicted, a man who lacks a son, lying upon the ground as his bed, becomes distressed and directs his thoughts toward his son. (18)
"I have abundant wealth in my house and various kinds of vessels;
this palace is beautiful as well—who will become its master? (19)
Since his mind wanders in distress at the time of death, one whose consciousness is thus deluded will certainly fall into an evil rebirth in every way. (20)
Having thus engaged in many kinds of reflection, the son of Satyavatī sighed repeatedly with hot breath and became despondent.
Having reflected deeply with his mind and having reached a firm resolution within his heart,
he went to the vicinity of Mount Meru to perform ascetic penance.
He reflected in his mind: "Which god shall we worship—one who is skilled in granting boons and likewise bestows the objects of our desire?"
Viṣṇu, Rudra, or the Lord of the Gods (Indra), or Brahmā, or the Sun;
Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya, as well as Pāvaka and Varuṇa. || 24 ||
While he was reflecting thus, Nārada, the best of sages,
arrived there by chance, his hand holding a lute, composed in mind.
Seeing him, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, was exceedingly pleased;
having offered the guest-offering (arghya) and provided a seat, he inquired after the welfare of the sage.
Having heard the inquiry regarding his welfare, the best of sages asked: "O Dvaipāyana, why are you troubled by anxiety? Tell me. (27)
Vyāsa said:
Since there is no destination for one without a son, nor any happiness in the mind, I am therefore distressed and reflect upon this again and again. (28)
"Whom among the gods shall I propitiate today with austerity, who will grant my desired object?
Thus distressed by such thoughts, I have now come to you for refuge. (29)
"O Great Sage, you are omniscient; speak quickly, O treasury of compassion!
To which deity shall I go for refuge, who will grant me a son? (30)
Sūta said:
Thus questioned by Vyāsa, the high-minded sage Nārada, a knower of the Vedas,
spoke with supreme affection regarding Kṛṣṇa.
Nārada said:
O illustrious son of Parāśara, regarding that very matter which you ask me here, Madhusūdana was previously questioned by my father.
Seeing Hari established in meditation, my father was filled with wonder;
he questioned the Lord of Gods, Śrīnātha, the Master of the World.
He was divine, resplendent with the Kaustubha gem, bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
he wore yellow garments, had four arms, and his chest was marked with the Śrīvatsa.
The cause of all worlds, the god of gods, the teacher of the universe,
Vāsudeva, the lord of the world, was performing great austerities.
Brahmā said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Master of the past, the future, and the present, why do you perform penance? What do you meditate upon, O Janārdana? (36)
This is a source of great wonder to me: you are the Lord of all the worlds;
yet you are absorbed in meditation, O Lord of Gods—what could be more marvelous than this? (37)
"O Lord of Māyā, born from the lotus of your navel, I am indeed the creator of everything;
tell me, O God, if there is anyone here who is superior to you."
I know you, O Lord of the World, to be the primordial source and the cause of all;
the creator, the protector, and the destroyer, the capable performer of every deed. (39)
O Great King, by your will I create this world;
and Hara, too, always acts according to your word when it is time for dissolution.
The sun revolves in the sky, the wind blows auspiciously and inauspiciously, fire burns, and the rain-cloud pours down, O Lord, by Your command. (41)
"But whom do you meditate upon, O God? This is a great doubt of mine;
for I see no god superior to you in the three worlds. (42)
Having shown compassion, speak to me today, for I am your devotee, O you of noble vows;
indeed, it is a traditional teaching that there is generally nothing that should be hidden from the great. (43)
Having heard those words of his, Hari said to Prajāpati:
"Listen with a one-pointed mind, O Brahmā; I shall tell you what is in my heart."
Although all people—including gods, asuras, and humans—know you, Śiva, and me to be the causes of maintenance, creation, and destruction; || 45 ||
"You are the creator and I am the protector, while Hara is the agent of destruction; all these have been brought about by Śakti"—such is the reflection made by those who have mastered the Vedas.

The power pertaining to the quality of passion (rājasī) resides in you for the creation of the world; that pertaining to goodness (sāttvikī) resides in me, and that pertaining to darkness (tāmasī) is proclaimed to reside in Rudra.
Separated from her, you are not capable of performing that task;
nor am I able to protect it, nor even Śaṅkara is able to destroy it.
O All-pervading Lord, we all exist perpetually dependent upon you, both in your presence and in your absence; hear an illustrative example, O observer of noble vows. (49)
"I sleep on my couch only when there is a remainder; I am dependent, without a doubt.
Subject to that [remainder], I always rise at the appointed time, having fallen under the power of time. (50)
I constantly perform penance, and I am always dependent upon that;
yet at times, I sport with Lakṣmī according to my pleasure.
"Sometimes I engage in a fierce battle with the Dānavas, one that subdues the body and strikes terror into all the worlds. (52)
O knower of dharma, it was witnessed by you directly in the past how, in that single ocean,
I engaged in a hand-to-hand combat with him for five thousand years.
Those two wicked Dānavas, born from the ear-wax and arrogant with pride,
Madhu and Kaiṭabha, were slain by the grace of the Goddess.
At that time, O illustrious one, did you not know the cause that is supreme beyond the supreme, whose form is Śakti? Why do you ask again and again? 55.
Becoming whatever I desire, I wander through the great ocean— appearing as a tortoise, a boar, a lion, and a dwarf in age after age.
Birth among the animal species is not dear to anyone in this world;
nor did I come into being by my own will in wombs such as those of boars and other such creatures.
Who, having abandoned sporting with his beloved, would go among inferior wombs such as those of fish;
or who, having left his bed, would sit upon the seat of Garuḍa?
I shall wage a great war as one who is independent. || 58 ||
Formerly, O Unborn One, my head went somewhere before you due to the snapping of a bowstring;
at that time, you took up the horse-head.
It was joined together once more by the most excellent craftsman. || 59 ||
"I am proclaimed as Hayānana (the horse-faced one),
and this is manifest before you, O Creator of the World; indeed, this is but a mockery in the midst of the world."
How could there be self and other if I were to exist? (60)
Therefore, I am not independent; I am entirely dependent upon Śakti.
I meditate upon that very Śakti constantly and without interruption. (61)
"O Lotus-born One, I know nothing superior to this.
Nārada said:
Thus was it spoken by Viṣṇu in the presence of the Lotus-born One.
And by him also, O bull among sages, I have been told exactly the same thing;
therefore, you too, O auspicious one, [should act] for the sake of attaining the goals of human existence. (63)
Without doubt, worship the lotus feet of the Goddess within the lotus of your heart;
that Goddess will grant you whatever is desired by you. 64.
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by Nārada, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī and one who was proficient in the lotus-feet of the Goddess, departed for the mountain to perform austerities.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Declaration that the Goddess is Supreme over All," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Narration of the Incarnation of Hayagrīva.
The sages said:
O Sūta, our minds are submerged in an ocean of doubt.
As it has been said: "It is a great marvel, causing wonder to the world. (1)
The head of Mādhava, having departed from his body, went once again to the Supreme;
from that, Hayagrīva was born, the Janārdana who is the creator of all. || 2 ||
Even the Veda praises that God, upon whom all the gods depend;
he is the primordial god, the Lord of the universe, and the cause of all causes.
O high-minded one, tell me all that in detail and quickly: how was his face also severed by the turn of fate at that time?
Sūta said: Let all you sages listen attentively on every side to the life-story of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, who possesses supreme splendor.
Once, after engaging in a fierce battle for ten thousand years, the eternal Lord Janārdana became utterly exhausted.
In a pleasant place within the same region, the Lord assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) and took hold of his strung bow, which rested against his neck.
Having placed his burden upon the tip of his bow, the Lord of Ramā fell asleep;
due to exhaustion and the turn of fate, he became deeply slumbering there.
Then, after some time, all the gods, including Indra, together with Brahmā and Śiva, prepared to perform a sacrifice.
Then they all went to Vaikuṇṭha to see the god Janārdana,
the Lord and sovereign of sacrifices, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
Not seeing him there at that time, those gods searched with their vision of knowledge and then went to where the Blessed Viṣṇu was staying.
They beheld the Lord Īśāna, who had fallen under the power of yogic sleep; seeing the all-pervading Viṣṇu unconscious, the gods sat down there.
While all the gods remained present and the Lord of the World was fast asleep,
all the deities, led by Brahmā and Rudra, fell into anxiety.
Then Śakra said to them, "O best of gods, what must be done? O best of gods, consider how their sleep may be interrupted. (14)
Then Śambhu said to him: "O best of gods, there is a fault in interrupting my sleep; furthermore, the work of the sacrifice must indeed be performed."
Then the ant was created by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin in order for it to devour the tip of the bow that was resting upon the earth.
When it has been consumed first, then the bow will sink down;
at that time, the God of gods will awaken from his sleep. || 17 ||
"Then all the work of the gods will be accomplished; of this there is no doubt.
Then the eternal God of gods commanded the ant.
Then the female ant said to him: "How can the sleep of the God of gods, the Lord of Māyā, the Teacher of the worlds, be interrupted? (19)
Breaking someone's sleep, interrupting a conversation, causing a rift between a husband and wife,
and creating discord between a child and its mother are recorded as equal to the sin of killing a Brahmin.
So how can I bring about the destruction of the happiness of the God of gods?
O Lord, what fruit is there from eating [this] that I should commit such a sin? (21)
"Indeed, the entire world acts out of sin under the influence of self-interest;
therefore, I shall accomplish my own interest by devouring [him]. (22)
Brahmā said: "We shall provide for your share within the midst of the sacrifice; listen as to how.
By that means, you must accomplish our purpose; awaken Viṣṇu without delay. (23)
"In the rite of fire-offering, by the side, it will fall from the presentation of the oblation;
know that to be your portion, and perform your task with haste. (24)
Sūta said:
Thus addressed by Brahmā, the ant, acting with haste, bit the tip of the bow that was resting on the ground; at that moment, the bowstring was released.
When Pratyajñā was liberated, ten million others were likewise freed;
a terrible sound then arose, and by it the gods were terrified.
The entire cosmic egg was agitated and the earth trembled at that time;
the oceans were tossed in distress, and the aquatic creatures quaked with fear. || 27 ||
Fierce winds blew and the mountains trembled; portents such as the falling of meteors occurred, foreboding misery. (28)
The quarters became most terrible and even the sun set; all the gods fell into anxiety, wondering, "What will happen on this ill-omened day? (29)
O ascetics, as they were thinking thus, the head of Viṣṇu, the God of gods— complete with its earrings and crown— vanished somewhere.
Then, while that terrible darkness was subsiding and Brahmā and Hara were at peace,
they both beheld a headless body of extraordinary appearance.
Having seen the headless trunk of Viṣṇu, the best of the gods were struck with wonder;
submerged in an ocean of anxiety, they wept, emaciated by grief.
"Alas, O Lord! O Master! What is this most wonderful and superhuman calamity that has occurred for all the gods, O eternal God of Gods? (33)
Whose illusion is this, by which your head has been taken away today?
You are forever uncuttable, impenetrable, and incapable of being burned.
When you have thus departed, O Lord, the deities will perish;
what kind of affection do we have for you? We weep only for our own sake. (35)
"This obstacle was not created by the Daityas, nor by the Yakṣas, nor by the Rākṣasas; it was created by the gods themselves. And for whom, O Lord of Ramā, is this a reproach? (36)
"All the gods are dependent on others; what can we do, and where can we go?
O Lord of Gods, there is no refuge for the gods whose minds are deluded. (37)
And this is neither a *sāttvika* illusion, nor a *rājasa*, nor a *tāmasa* one—by which the head of the Lord of Māyā, the Teacher of the World, has been severed by you today. (38)
Then, seeing the gods led by Śiva lamenting, Bṛhaspati, the foremost knower of the Vedas, spoke as follows to pacify them: || 39 ||
O illustrious ones, what is the use of weeping or even crying out?
A remedy must be devised here that is entirely within the scope of the intellect. (40)
O Lord of Gods, both destiny and human effort are equal;
yet a means must be employed, for it is through that means that destiny bears fruit in every way.
Indra said:
"I consider destiny alone to be supreme; fie upon useless human effort!
Even the head of Viṣṇu was severed while the gods were looking on. (42)
Brahmā said:
Whatever has been brought about by Time must necessarily be experienced, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious; who indeed can transcend destiny? (43)
The embodied being is undoubtedly the experiencer of pleasures and pains;
just as my head was formerly severed by Śambhu through the power of time.
In that very same way, the falling of the *liṅga* occurred due to the curse of Mahādeva;
likewise, today the head of Hari has fallen into the salt waters.
The lord of Śacī experienced a thousandfold loss of fortune as well as suffering,
a fall from heaven, and likewise a dwelling in the Mānasa lake within a lotus.
These illustrious ones are the experiencers of suffering; by whom in this world is suffering not experienced? Therefore, O noble ones, you should indeed abandon grief. (47)
"Let them meditate upon Mahāmāyā, the eternal goddess of knowledge;
she, the supreme Prakṛti beyond the guṇas, will accomplish our task. (48)
The knowledge of Brahman, the sustainer of the world and likewise the mother of all, by which this entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is pervaded. (49)
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to the gods, the Creator indeed commanded the Vedas,
which stood before him embodied in form for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
Brahmā said:
"Let them praise the supreme goddess, the eternal Brahma-vidyā, whose limbs are hidden, the great Māyā, who accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings. (51)
Having heard those words of his, the Vedas, beautiful in all their limbs, praised that Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) who dwells in the world and is accessible through knowledge. 52.
The Vedas said:
"Obeisance, O Goddess Mahāmāyā, auspicious one who brings about the creation of the universe;
O Nirguṇā, Sovereign of all beings, Mother, beloved of Śaṅkara! (53)
You are the earth of all beings, as well as the life-breaths of those possessing life;
you are intelligence, prosperity, beauty, forbearance, peace, faith, wisdom, fortitude, and memory.
You are the half-mora in the Udgītha, as well as the Gāyatrī, the Vyāhṛti,
Jayā, Vijayā, Dhātrī, Lajjā, Kīrti, Spṛhā, and Dayā.

O Mother, we praise you, who are skilled in the arrangement of the three worlds, endowed with the essence of compassion, the mother of all people, the auspicious knowledge, the benefactress of all the world, the most excellent one, proficient in the seed-syllable of speech, and the destroyer of worldly existence. (56)
Brahmā, Hara, Śauri, Sahasranetra, Vāk, Agni, and Sūrya are the lords of the worlds;
yet they exist because of you, and thus are not supreme, since you are the mother of all things mobile and immobile.
O Mother, when you desire to create this entire universe, you bring forth the gods headed by Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra;
remaining one in form, you cause them to perform the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world].
Indeed, O Queen, there is not even the slightest trace of saṃsāra in you in any way whatsoever.
In all the worlds, no one is capable of knowing your form, nor is there any man here fit to recount the number of your names;
for that man who is unable to measure even a small drop of water [is unfit].
How could one whose mind is fixed on the truth be skillful in discerning the near shore and the far shore? 59.
O Blessed One, not even one among the gods understands your infinite majesty; you alone here are the singular mother of the world.
How is it that you alone create this entire universe as if in sport?
O Goddess, the authoritative proof in this matter is established by the words of the Vedas.
Alas, you are indeed effortless, yet the cause of all the worlds; O Blessed One, your wondrous conduct pains our minds.
How can one describe the power of your qualities, which are beyond the reach of all the Vedas, since even you yourself do not know your own supreme nature?
O Mother, do you not know of the falling of the one who has conquered Madhu upon his crown?
O Śivā, have you learned something that makes you wish to know the power of Madhujit?
Or is it, O Mother, that this multitude of my sins is so powerful?
Where could there be any evil for you, who are so skilled in worshipping the lotus-feet of the Lord?
And why is this equanimity of yours so extremely harsh toward the host of gods?
The destruction of Hari’s head is considered here to be a source of great wonder;
O Mother, you are a source of great suffering, skilled as you are in cutting off one's progeny.
We do not know how the delay in the loosening of the crown occurred. || 63 ||

O Goddess, having recognized this fault produced by all the gods, have you cast some evil deed committed against Viṣṇu into your heart? Or has some pride born of battle arisen in Viṣṇu that he seeks to sever with great speed? O Mother, we truly do not understand the intent behind your playful manifestation here.

Or rather, O Bhavānī, did Viṣṇuśīrṣa now undergo disappearance by you, after he had performed terrible penance at a most beautiful sacred site and obtained a boon from the Blessed One, only to be defeated in battle by the Daityas?
Or what amusement could there be in seeing Vāsudeva with his head severed? || 65 ||
O Primordial One, why are you angry with the daughter of the Ocean? Why do you look upon her who is bereft of a protector?
You must forgive this offense committed by one born from your own portion.
Having raised him up, gladden me; make me rejoice. || 66 ||
These gods, preeminent in their duties and renowned for their power, constantly bow down to you;
O Goddess, rescue the gods from the ocean of sorrow by raising up the Lord, the sovereign of all.
O Mother, we do not know where Hari has gone;
indeed, there is no other means for our survival today,
just as nectar alone is capable of the act of sustaining life.
Likewise, O Goddess, you are the giver of life to the world. 68.

Sūta said: Thus praised then by the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and the chanters of the Sāmaveda, the Great Goddess Maheśvarī, the supreme Māyā who transcends all qualities, became gracious.
Then a beautiful, incorporeal voice, situated in the sky, spoke to the gods with auspicious words that bring joy to all people.
"O gods, do not worry; remain at ease, O immortals.
I have been praised by the Vedas as desired, and I am satisfied—of this there is no doubt. (71)
Whatever man in the world of mortals praises this hymn of mine with constant devotion, he shall attain all his desires. (72)
Any man who constantly listens to this hymn of mine with devotion at the three times of day shall be freed from suffering and become happy.
This is indeed declared in the Vedas and is equal to the Veda itself.
Let them hear the reason today as to why it has entered the mouth of Hari;
for how can an action without a cause come to pass here in this world? (74)
Viṣṇu, seeing his beloved daughter of the ocean standing nearby,
smiled upon beholding her beautiful face there.
She realized: "Surely Hari knows; why does the Lord laugh at me?
For what reason has my face been seen by Hari as deformed? (76)
How could laughter arise today even without a cause?
I suspect that another woman of excellent complexion has been made his rival wife by him. (77)
Then Mahālakṣmī became filled with anger and possessed the quality of darkness (tamas);
at that time, the power of darkness (tāmasī śakti) entered her body.
At a certain time, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods' work,
a most terrible tamasic power entered his body.
Then, her body possessed by the quality of darkness (tamas), she became exceedingly enraged and spoke these words slowly: "May this head of yours fall! (80)
Due to her feminine nature, her emotional state, and the influence of the time, she uttered that curse—which destroys one's own happiness—without due reflection. (81)
"However, the suffering arising from a rival wife is even greater than widowhood"—thinking thus in her mind, she spoke because of the influence of her tamasic power. (82)
Untruthfulness, rashness, deceit, folly, excessive greed, impurity, and mercilessness are the faults inherent in the nature of women. (83)
Today I shall restore that Vāsudeva with his head as he was before;
by the power of my curse, his head has been submerged in the salt ocean.
Furthermore, O best of gods, there exists some other cause;
a great task for you shall come to pass, of this there is no doubt.
Long ago, the mighty-armed Daitya Hayagrīva, who was exceedingly famous,
performed most rigorous penance on the banks of the Sarasvatī.
I [meditated upon] my single-syllable mantra, which consists of the seed-syllable of Māyā;
remaining without food, with self conquered, and entirely free from all enjoyments. || 87 ||
Meditating upon me as the Tāmasī Śakti, adorned with all ornaments,
he performed such extremely severe penance for a thousand years.
Then, having assumed a dark (tāmasa) form, I arrived there; as soon as he saw me before him, he meditated upon her exactly as she had been visualized.
Standing there upon a lion, I spoke to him with compassion:
"Choose a boon, O illustrious one; I shall grant it to you, O observer of noble vows."
Having heard these words of the goddess, the Dānava, filled with love, then quickly performed a circumambulation and prostration. || 91 ||
Having seen my form, his eyes blossoming with love and his own eyes filled with tears of joy, he then offered praise to me.
Hayagrīva said:
Salutations to the Goddess Mahāmāyā, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction;
O Śivā, who is skillful in bestowing grace upon devotees, the giver of desire and liberation! 93.
You are the cause of the five elements— earth, water, fire, air, and ether—
and you are the cause of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound.
The nose, the tongue, the eye, the skin, and the ear as the sense organs, and the other organs of action—all this, O Maheśvarī, arises from you. 95.
The Goddess said:
"Tell me what boon you desire; I shall grant whatever you wish for.
I am well-pleased with your devotion and your wonderful austerity. (96)
Hayagrīva said:
"O Mother, act in such a way that death may not come to me;
let me become an immortal yogin, invincible even by gods and asuras. (97)
The Goddess said:
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain.
Since such is the natural order in this world, how could it be otherwise? (98)
"Having thus made this resolve regarding death, O best of Rākṣasas, choose a boon that is desired by you, after indeed reflecting upon it in your mind. (99)
Hayagrīva said:
"O Mother of the Universe, my death shall come from Hayagrīva and from no one else;
fulfill this desire that is in my heart. (100)
The Goddess said:
"Go home, O illustrious one, and rule your kingdom as you please;
surely no death shall befall you except at the hands of Hayagrīva. (101)
Having thus granted him the boon, she likewise vanished; and he too, having attained supreme joy, went to his own abode.
That evil-minded one oppresses the sages and the Vedas in every way;
there is no one today in the three worlds who can slay him.
Therefore, having extracted this horse's beautiful head,
Tvaṣṭṛ shall join it to the body of Viṣṇu here, who is now headless.
Then the Lord Hayagrīva will slay that Asura,
the most wicked and cruel Dānava, out of a desire for the welfare of the gods.
Sūta said:
Having thus addressed the gods, Śarvāṇī then became silent.
The gods, being exceedingly pleased at that time, spoke to that divine architect.
The gods said:
"O Viṣṇu, perform the task of the gods by joining [yourself] to the head;
the Daitya Hayagrīva shall slay the foremost of the Dānavas."
Sūta said: Having heard their words, Tvaṣṭṛ, filled with great haste,
quickly severed the horse-head with a sword in the presence of the gods.
By him, the horse's head was quickly joined to the body of Viṣṇu;
through the grace of Mahāmāyā, Hari became Hayagrīva.
In that much time, the Dānava, arrogant with pride, was slain by him with force in battle through his vigor as the enemy of the gods. 110.
Those men on earth who hear this auspicious narrative become liberated from all suffering; of this there is no doubt. (111)
And the sacred life-story of Mahāmāyā, which destroys sins and brings about all prosperity for those who read or hear it. || 112 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Hayagrīva Incarnation," in the first book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Madhu and Kaiṭabha’s Preparation for Battle.
The sages said:
"O gentle one, regarding that battle of Śauri in the great ocean which was described by you..."
Together with Madhu and Kaiṭabha, for five thousand years. || 1 ||
Why were those two Dānavas born from that single ocean of water—
possessing great heroism, difficult to assail, and exceedingly hard for even the gods to conquer?
How were those two demons born, and how were they slain by Hari?
O highly wise one, relate that most wonderful deed.
We are all desirous of hearing, and you are a speaker of great learning;
by fate, this very conjunction of us two has come to pass here.
Association with a fool is more difficult to endure than even poison;
association with a wise person is considered equal to the essence of nectar. || 5 ||
All animals live, they eat and they urinate; they perceive the forms of sense objects and experience the wonderful pleasure of sexual union. (6)
Their knowledge of existence and non-existence is neither discriminative nor liberating;
they should be known as equal to beasts who have no reverence for hearing [the teachings]. (7)
Certain animals, such as deer, experience the pleasure of hearing;
yet even those without ears, such as serpents, were bewildered by the inhalation of that sound.
Indeed, for the five senses, hearing and seeing are auspicious;
from hearing comes the cognition of an object, and from seeing comes the delight of the mind.
"O highly fortunate one, listening has been declared to be of three kinds—sāttvika, rājasa, and likewise tāmasa—as described by the wise with certainty. (10)
The Vedic scriptures and so forth are sāttvika; literature is rājasa;
and accounts of war and the exposing of others' faults are tāmasa. (11)
The wise and learned have declared the sattvic [nature] to be threefold:
namely, the superior, the middling, and likewise the inferior. (12)

Having reached a definitive conclusion, it has been understood by the wise that the highest [type of gift] bestows the fruit of liberation, the middling bestows heaven, and the lowest is said to bestow worldly enjoyments.

Literature is indeed of three kinds; it is remembered as the best when directed toward one's own wife, middling when directed toward a courtesan, and likewise the lowest when directed toward another's married wife. (14)
The threefold tamasic [killing] should be known by the wise who perceive the scriptures:
that which is fighting against an assassin is declared to be the best. (15)
Furthermore, the middling [type] occurs due to enmity with the enemies of the Pāṇḍavas;
the lowest, however, occurs without cause during disputes and quarrels.
Therefore, O high-minded one, listening to this Purāṇa is the primary means;
it increases the intellect, is meritorious, and consequently destroys all sins. (17)
Therefore, O one of great intelligence, relate that auspicious ancient narrative which was heard by me previously from Dvaipāyana and which accomplishes every purpose. (18)
Sūta said:
You are blessed and highly fortunate, and I too am blessed upon this earth,
since you possess the inclination to hear and I indeed the inclination to narrate.
And in ancient times, when the three worlds had dissolved and become a single ocean, while Janārdana, the God of gods, was reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa; (20)
The two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, born from the wax of Viṣṇu’s ears,
were those two Daityas of great strength who grew up in the waters of the ocean.
Playing there, they remained moving here and there;
once, those two of great body were absorbed in play within the great ocean.
The two brothers, standing together as one, fell into anxiety in their hearts:
"An effect cannot arise without a cause; this is the universal law. (23)
An object to be supported cannot exist in any way whatsoever without a support;
yet this relationship of support and supported does not appear within the sphere of the mind. (24)
"Where does this water, so pleasant in form and so vast, abide?
By whom was it created, and how did it come to be? We two are submerged, yet we remain standing within the water. (25)
"How were we two born, or by whom were we both produced? Where are our parents?"—such knowledge we two do not possess, even though we desire it. (26)
Sūta said:
Thus desiring [to fight], the two of them went forth, yet they reached no certain conclusion.
Then Kaiṭabha spoke there to Madhu, who was standing by him in the water: ||| 27 ||
Kaiṭabha said:
"O Madhu, O brother, you possess great and unwavering power to remain here in these waters; indeed, I consider that to be my reason [for staying]."
By her this water is pervaded, and it remains supported by her;
she alone is the supreme goddess and likewise the cause of both of us. (29)
While those two Asuras were thus awakened and overcome with anxiety,
they then heard a most enchanting seed-syllable of speech in the sky.
Then they both took it up and practiced it with firm diligence.
At that time, they beheld an auspicious flash of lightning rising into the sky.
They deliberated there: "This mantra is undoubtedly present here;
likewise, this visualization with attributes has indeed been perceived in the sky. (32)
Having reflected thus, they became abstinent from food, self-conquered, one-pointed in mind, and composed, devoted solely to recitation and meditation.
In this manner, a great penance was performed by those two for a thousand years;
consequently, that supreme Śakti became pleased with them.
Seeing those two Dānavas exhausted and resolved upon performing austerities,
an incorporeal voice spoke for the sake of showing them favor.
"O Daityas, choose a boon that you desire and which is highly esteemed;
speak it, for I am indeed well-pleased by your ascetic penance. (36)
Sūta said:
Having heard those words, the two Dānavas then spoke:
"O Goddess, O lady of virtuous vows, grant us this boon: death at our own will. (37)
The voice said:
"O two Daityas, by my grace, let your desired death come to pass;
you two brothers shall be invincible by gods and Daityas alike—of this there is no doubt. (38)
Sūta said:
Having thus been granted boons by the Goddess, the two Dānavas, arrogant with pride,
sported in the ocean accompanied by hosts of aquatic creatures.
After some time, O brahmins, the two Dānavas by chance beheld the Lord Prajāpati Brahmā seated upon his lotus throne.
Seeing them, those two of great strength, desiring battle, were filled with joy; they then said to him there, "O observer of noble vows, grant us a fight! (41)
If not, then leave this lotus and go wherever you wish without delay;
for if you are weak, where else is there a suitable and auspicious seat?
"This place is to be enjoyed by heroes; you are a coward, so leave it at once!
Hearing these words of theirs, the Lord of Creatures fell into deep anxiety. (43)
And having seen those two powerful heroes, the ascetic stood then, overcome with anxiety, reflecting in his mind, "What shall I do? (44).

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Preparations for Battle between Madhu and Kaiṭabha," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Regarding the awakening of Viṣṇu,
Sūta said:
Having beheld those two powerful ones, Brahmā then reflected upon a means [to subdue them].
One who is learned in all treatises [should employ] means beginning with conciliation, bribery, and sowing dissension, up to and including war.
I do not truly know the strength of these two as it really is;
indeed, when their strength is unknown, war is by no means recommended. (2)
If I were to offer praise today for these two wicked ones who are intoxicated with pride, my own weakness would surely be exposed by me. (3)
If even a single one of them will slay [him] once his weakness has been revealed, then giving [the secret] today is certainly not appropriate; or else, how can I effect a division among them? (4)
Today I awaken Viṣṇu, Janārdana, who has been sleeping upon Śeṣa;
he is the four-armed one of great prowess, and he shall be the destroyer of my suffering.
Having thus reflected in his mind, the lotus-born Brahmā, seated upon the stalk of a lotus,
went for refuge to Viṣṇu, the destroyer of suffering, with his mind.
He praised Hari, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, who was motionless in his yogic sleep, with auspicious words of address in order to awaken him.
Brahmā said:
O Lord of the distressed, O Hari, O Viṣṇu, O Vāmana, arise, O Mādhava! O Hṛṣīkeśa, who removes the suffering of devotees, O Abode of All, O Lord of the Universe! 8.
O Inner Controller, O immeasurable Self, O Vāsudeva, Lord of the universe, whose mind is one-pointed in the destruction of wicked enemies, you who bear the discus and the mace! 9.
O Omniscient One, Lord of all worlds, endowed with all powers!
Arise, arise, O Lord of gods; O destroyer of suffering, protect me! 10.
O Sustainer of the Universe, O Wide-Eyed One, whose name is meritorious to hear and chant;
O Source of the World, Formless One, the Cause of creation, preservation, and destruction! (11)
"O Great King, these two Daityas, arrogant with pride, desire to kill me;
O Support of All, how is it that you do not know that I have fallen into distress? (12)
If you disregard me, who am afflicted by extreme suffering and have come to you for refuge, then your status as the Protector, O Mahāviṣṇu, would become devoid of foundation. (13)
When the Blessed Lord Hari, overcome by yogic sleep, did not wake even though praised in this manner, Brahmā then reflected.
"Surely Viṣṇu, overcome by Śakti, has fallen under the power of sleep; that righteous soul does not wake up. What shall I do now, being so distressed? (15)
"Both these Dānavas, intoxicated with pride, have arrived intent on killing me;
what shall I do, where shall I go? There is no refuge for me anywhere. (16)
Having thus reflected in his mind and reached a firm resolve, he,
with his heart fixed in one-pointed concentration, praised that Yoganidrā.
Having reflected even thus in my mind, I consider my own power sufficient for his protection—by which power indeed Viṣṇu was rendered unconscious and devoid of movement. (18)
Just as the sun does not perceive the qualities such as sound and the rest here,
so too Hari, with his eyes closed in sleep, does not perceive them.
Since he does not abandon sleep even though praised in many ways, I think that sleep is not under his control; rather, he has been brought under the sway of sleep.
It is said that whoever comes under another's control is indeed that person's servant;
therefore, this Yoganidrā is the mistress of Hari, the Lord of Lakṣmī.
Since even the Lord of the Sindhu was brought under her control, surely this entire world has been brought under the power of the Blessed Lady. 22.
I am Viṣṇu, as well as Śambhu, Sāvitrī, Ramā, and Umā;
we are all under her control—of this there is no doubt.
Even Hari lies down helplessly like any other ordinary person;
when he is thus overcome, what can be said of other great-souled ones? 24.
Today I truly marvel at Yoganidrā, by whom Janārdana—
the eternal Vāsudeva— has been released so that he may engage in battle.
Having formed this thought, Brahmā, then situated upon the lotus stalk,
praised that Yoganidrā who was established within the limbs of Viṣṇu.
Brahmā said: O Goddess, you are indeed the cause of this universe;
this has been known by me through the words of all the Vedas, O Mother.
That even Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person and the creator of discernment for all the worlds, has today been brought under the power of sleep. (27)
O Mother, who knows the playful sport of your delusive charm?
I am a fool, and this Hari lies here helpless;
such is your nature, O abode of the minds of all living beings!
The most learned among millions of wise men [is the knower] of the Guṇa-less [Brahman]. || 28 ||
The Sāṃkhyas speak of the Puruṣa and that Prakṛti which is devoid of the nature of consciousness and is the creator of the world;
are you such? How is it that today, O Abode of the World, you have been made devoid of consciousness? (29)
You perform a drama of manifold kinds through your qualities;
no one understands the application of the methods of your activity.
The hosts of sages meditate upon you constantly at the three times of day.
Having conceived the name "Sandhyā," you have manifested these qualities, O Bhavānī.
For you are always the intellect that awakens all worlds; and you, O Goddess, are Śrī, the eternal bestower of happiness upon the gods;
likewise, you are indeed fame, intelligence, fortitude, and splendor.
O Mother, there is faith and delight in all people. || 31 ||
Indeed, having fallen into this miserable state, I have obtained no authority through hundreds of further conjectures;
and it is true that you are the mother of all the worlds here.
Hari, bestowing sleepiness upon him, beheld this here.
O Goddess, you are difficult even for those learned in the Vedas to comprehend; indeed, even the Veda does not know you in your entirety,
since this Śruti, while attaining its origin from you, [remains incomplete].
All this work of yours is indeed directly perceived. || 33 ||

The wise one alone on earth knows your entire conduct; neither I, nor Hari, nor Bhava, nor the gods, nor others, nor even the sages, nor my own sons are capable of knowing it. Thus, your greatness is indeed difficult to describe in all the worlds. (34)
O Goddess, if in sacrifices the knowers of the Vedas do not utter "svāhā" for you when the oblation has been offered,
they do not constantly receive their share of the sacrifice.
Among the gods as well, you alone are the bestower of sustenance.
O Blessed One, we were indeed first protected by you from the fear arising from the enemies of the gods; likewise now,
O Goddess, granter of boons, I am afraid and have come to you for refuge.
Having beheld the terrible Kaiṭabha along with Madhu.
"Viṣṇu does not know this suffering of mine now; I know that you have brought my body-branch under your own control.
Either release the Primal God or slay the two lords of the Dānavas; O lady of great majesty, do whatever pleases you. (37)
O Goddess, those who do not know your supreme power meditate even upon Hari and Hara with dull minds;
O Mother, today the manifest proof has been known by me.
That even Viṣṇu lies down utterly helpless before it. || 38 ||
"O Blessed One, even the Goddess born from the ocean was not able to awaken Hari today, though she followed her husband's will; I believe that even Ramā herself has been forcibly subdued by you."
She was put to sleep and did not wake, as if rendered powerless.
Blessed indeed are those on earth who, having abandoned the worship of other deities, are devoted to your feet and absorbed in you;
O Goddess, they perform your worship entirely and with great intensity.
Having indeed recognized her as the mother of all beings, the wish-fulfilling cow.
Where have those qualities of Viṣṇu— wisdom, beauty, fame, auspicious conduct, and virtue— gone now, having abandoned him?
For here, this very Hari has been made a captive by sleep.
By the power of you alone, O Blessed One, who transcend the human state.
You alone are the power of all worlds, possessing every majesty;
indeed, everything created by you is merely a manifestation of existence.
You sport within the net of delusion fashioned by yourself.
Just as an actor indeed sports in his own performance in a drama. || 42 ||
Viṣṇu was manifested by you at the beginning of the first age, and indeed the stainless power was granted for the sake of protection;
the entire world has been saved, and today [the enemy] has been rendered helpless.
Whatever pleases you, O Mother, that you shall surely do.
O Blessed One, if you have no desire to destroy me after having created me here, then show mercy and abandon your silence;
why indeed have these two been manifested in the form of Time (Death), or do you wish to mock me, O Bhavānī? (44)
I have understood your wondrous activity: having made this entire world, you sport as one who is independent;
indeed, you likewise cause everything, including me, to dissolve within you.
O Bhavānī, what is there to marvel at in your desire to slay him? || 45 ||
O Mother, O Ambika of the world, grant my death this very day if you wish; yet the grief born of my passing does not trouble me here.
For you yourself first ordained that he be slain by the Daitya, and thus the greatest infamy remains: "He died after being struck down. (46)
"Arise, O Goddess! Assume a wondrous form here; either destroy me or these two, as you desire, O playful child!
Otherwise, awaken Hari, for he would surely slay these two—he by whom this entire range of tasks was indeed to be accomplished through you."
Sūta said: Thus praised then by the Creator (Brahmā), the goddess Tāmasī emerged from the body of Hari and stood at his side.
Having abandoned all her limbs for Viṣṇu of incomparable splendor,
that Yoga-nidrā then emerged for the destruction of those two.
When Janārdana was born with his body quivering,
Dhātṛ then attained supreme joy upon seeing Hari.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Awakening of Viṣṇu," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Determination of the One to be Worshipped.
The sages said:
"O highly fortunate one, there is a great and most wonderful doubt here regarding this narrative."
This has indeed always been determined by the wise through the Vedas, the Shastras, and the Puranas.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—these three gods are eternal;
O great-minded one, there is nothing higher than them in this cosmic egg.
Brahmā indeed creates the worlds, Viṣṇu protects the entire universe, and Rudra withdraws it at the time of dissolution; these three are the cause here.
There is one single form, the three gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
joined with the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas, they are the performers of their respective tasks.
Among them, Hari is the most excellent, Mādhava, the Supreme Person;
he is the primordial god, the Lord of the World, and capable in all undertakings.
No one else is capable [of subduing] Viṣṇu, who possesses incomparable splendor;
how then was that Lord made to sleep, rendered helpless by his own yogic power (yogamāyā)?
Where has his consciousness gone, and from where does his movement while living arise?
O illustrious one, this is a great doubt; explain it as it truly is.
O observer of noble vows, tell me: what was that power previously mentioned by which the Lord Viṣṇu was conquered? From where was it born, how did it become powerful, and what is that power? (8)
He who is the Lord of all, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world, the Supreme Self, supreme bliss, whose very form is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
How could he—the doer of all, the sustainer of all, the creator, free from passion, omnipresent, and pure—who is independent and higher than the highest, have been led away by sleep? (10)
O scorcher of foes, this doubt that has arisen within us is indeed a matter of wonder;
O Sūta, disciple of Vyāsa, O high-minded one, sever it with the sword of knowledge.
Sūta said:
Who in the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, can pierce this doubt?
Even the eternal sons of Brahmā, the sages, are surely bewildered by it.
"Nārada and Kapila are the best of sages regarding this question; O highly fortunate ones, what can I say concerning this difficult investigation? (13)
Among the gods, Viṣṇu is declared to be all-pervading and the protector of all,
from whom this entire universe, including all that is mobile and immobile, has arisen as the Virāṭ.
Having bowed down to the supreme deity, they all together worshipped Nārāyaṇa,
Hṛṣīkeśa, Vāsudeva, and Janārdana.
Likewise, some [saw] Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, the moon-crested one, the three-eyed, five-faced, trident-handed, bull-bannered Lord. || 16 ||
Likewise, in all the Vedas, he is celebrated by the name Tryambaka—
the one with matted hair, the five-faced one, who bears half of Gaurī’s body.
The god who delights in dwelling on Kailāsa, who is endowed with all powers,
who is accompanied by a multitude of spirits, and who is the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Likewise, those learned in the Vedas, O highly fortunate ones, praise the Sun with various hymns every day at dawn, at dusk, and at midday.
Likewise, in all the Vedas, the worship of the Sun is supreme;
"Paramātman" (the Supreme Self) is the renowned name of that Great Soul. (20)
Agni is praised everywhere in the Vedas by those most learned in the Vedas;
so too is Indra, the lord of the three worlds, and Varuṇa as another.
Just as the Gaṅgā flows through many currents,
even so Viṣṇu is proclaimed among all the gods by the great seers.
Indeed, only three means of valid cognition have been taught by the most learned:
perception, inference, and verbal testimony as the third. (23)
Others say there are exactly four, along with those joined by analogy; others of great intelligence say there are five, including those joined by presumption. (24)
The seven wise ones who know the ancient lore declare that this supreme Brahman is difficult to comprehend by means of these very measures.
In this matter, one should exercise deliberation through both the intellect and the scriptures, having investigated again and again with reasoning that is characterized by certainty. (26)
A wise person who constantly follows the path of the virtuous should always reflect upon consciousness through direct perception and also by means of illustrative examples. (27)
Even the learned speak thus, as it is celebrated in the Purāṇas:
the power of creation resides in Druhiṇa (Brahmā), and the power of preservation in Hari (Viṣṇu).
In Hari resides the power of withdrawal; in the Sun is the power of illumination;
and in Śeṣa as well as in the Tortoise is the power of supporting the earth.
That primordial power (sādyā śaktiḥ), which has evolved and is established in everything—
just as the power of combustion resides in fire and the power of impulsion in the wind.
Even Śiva becomes a corpse when deprived of Kuṇḍalinī;
for whoever is devoid of power is considered by the wise to be incapable.
In this same way, O one of great asceticism, [he perceived] everywhere among all beings, both stationary and moving,
from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, within this cosmic egg.
But that which is devoid of power is contemptible, whether it be a mere object or a moving or unmoving being;
one who is powerless [is so] regarding victory over enemies, as well as in walking and eating. (33)
Thus, that all-pervading power is discerned as Brahman;
it should always be properly meditated upon and investigated with wisdom by various means. (34)
In Viṣṇu there is the sāttvika power; though devoid of it, he performs no action. In Druhiṇa (Brahmā) there is the rājasa power; indeed, devoid of it, he would not be a creator.
And in Śiva there is the *tāmasī* power; by that he is the agent of dissolution.
Thus everything should be inferred by the mind, having reflected upon it again and again. (36)
Śakti creates the universe; she indeed protects it in its entirety;
by her will, she destroys this world of the moving and the unmoving. (37)
Neither Viṣṇu, nor Hara, nor Śakra, nor Brahmā, nor Pāvaka,
nor Sūrya, nor Varuṇa is capable of accomplishing their respective tasks in any way whatsoever.
For joined with her, those gods perform their respective duties;
she alone is perceived directly in all causes and effects. (39)
She is said by the wise to be twofold: with attributes (saguṇā) and without attributes (nirguṇā).
She who possesses attributes is to be served by those possessed of passion, while she who is without attributes is to be served by those free from passion.
She is the untroubled mistress of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
when worshipped according to the prescribed rites, she grants all desired objects.
Foolish people, always veiled by illusion, do not know her;
yet some men, even though they know, delude others as well. (42)
Driven by the Kali age, these dull-witted "scholars," for the sake of their own bellies, promote various heretical doctrines individually. (43)
In this Kali age, O highly fortunate ones, various distinctions have arisen; in no other age are there such dharmas that are outside the Veda in any way whatsoever.
That Viṣṇu performs fierce penance for many years;
Brahmā, Hara, and the three gods meditate upon some indeterminate, eternal Reality.
Desiring desire eternally, those three— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— indeed always perform various sacrifices.
They indeed constantly meditate with their minds upon the supreme goddess Śakti, who is called Brahman and is of the nature of the Supreme Self, regarding her as eternal and everlasting. 47.
Therefore, power should always be cultivated by the wise who have reached firm resolve;
O best of sages, the definitive conclusion of all scriptures must be understood. 48.
This was heard by me from Kṛṣṇa; he, however, learned it from Nārada;
and he too [learned it] from his father, who had received it from the words of Viṣṇu. || 49 ||
The wise should neither listen to nor consider the words of others;
rather, those learned ones who have reached firm resolve should always cultivate their own power alone. 50.
Even the exertion of one who is powerless should be observed directly;
therefore, indeed, it is power alone that must be recognized in all beings. (51)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Determination of the Object of Worship," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Hari’s Slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Sūta said:
When sleep had departed from the body of that Teacher of the World,
From the eyes, mouth, nose, arms, heart, and likewise from the chest. || 1 ||
Having emerged, that supreme power of darkness stood in the sky;
then the Lord of the World arose, yawning again and again.
Then he saw Prajāpati standing there, terrified with fear;
and the one of great splendor spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Lotus-born Lord, why have you come here, having abandoned your ascetic penance?
Why are you so distressed by anxiety, your mind overwhelmed by fear?"
Brahmā said: "O Lord, the two Daityas Madhu and Kaiṭabha, born from the wax of your ears,
have approached me in their terrible forms and great strength to slay me."
"O Lord of the World, I have come into your presence out of fear of those two;
O Vāsudeva, protect me today, for I am terrified by fear and deprived of my senses. (6)
Viṣṇu said:
"Stay today; you have become fearless, yet I shall indeed slay those two fools who, their life-span exhausted, have come before me for battle."
Sūta said: While the Lord of Gods was speaking thus, those two exceedingly powerful Dānavas, searching for Aja and intoxicated with pride, arrived there.
O best of sages, those two, free from fever and intoxicated with pride, remained there in the water without support and spoke to Brahmā.
"What is the point of arriving here after having fled?
Fight! We shall both kill each other right before his very eyes. (10)
"Afterwards we shall slay him as he lies upon the coils of the serpent;
you, however, engage in battle today, or say, 'I am your slave. (11)
Sūta said:
Having heard those words, Viṣṇu Janārdana spoke to them both: "O foremost of Dānavas, fight with me as you desire."
"I shall indeed take away the pride of you two who are intoxicated;
come, O illustrious and mighty ones, if you have faith."
Sūta said:
Having heard those words, both of them, their eyes agitated with anger,
became intent on battle while remaining in the water without any support.
Madhu, enraged there, set out quickly to engage in combat with Hari, while Kaiṭabha remained standing as before.
A hand-to-hand struggle took place between the two of them like that of two intoxicated wrestlers;
when Madhu grew weary, Kaiṭabha then engaged in combat.
Furthermore, Madhu and Kaiṭabha fought again and again with their arms in hand-to-hand combat against the all-powerful Viṣṇu, both of them blinded by passion.
At that time, Brahmā, the spectator, and the Goddess, who was situated in the intermediate space, did not feel any exhaustion;
however, Viṣṇu fell into a state of fatigue.
When five thousand years had passed while they were fighting,
Hari reflected upon the cause of their deaths.
"I have indeed fought for five thousand years;
the two terrible Dānavas are not weary, yet I am exhausted—this is truly marvelous. (20)
"Where has my strength and heroism gone, and why are these two limbs free from disease?
What is the cause here that must be reflected upon and considered by the mind? (21)
Seeing Hari thus absorbed in thought, the two of them, intoxicated with pride and filled with joy, spoke to him like clouds with deep resonance: 22.
O Viṣṇu, if you have no strength, or if you are weary from battle, speak;
I am truly your servant, having placed my joined palms upon my head. (23)
O high-minded one, if you are capable, do not refuse to fight today;
having slain you, we shall slay even the four-faced Puruṣa.
Sūta said:
Having heard their speech in that great ocean, the high-minded Viṣṇu spoke these gentle words, preceded by conciliation.
Hari said:
"Heroes do not strike one who is exhausted, terrified, disarmed, fallen, or likewise a child; this is the eternal dharma. (26)
For five thousand years, I have indeed waged war here;
yet I am alone, while you two brothers are both powerful and equal in strength.
"You both have rested repeatedly in the midst of the battle;
having thus taken rest, I shall fight—of this there is no doubt. (28)
"Wait here for a moment, you two who are so powerful and intoxicated with pride;
having rested, I shall engage in battle according to the path of justice. (29)
Sūta said: Having heard his words, those two best of Dānavas, now confident and having resolved upon battle, stationed themselves there at a distance.
Seeing them from a great distance, the four-armed Vāsudeva reflected in his mind upon the cause of their death.
Through reflection, knowledge arose in both of them who had received boons from the Goddess;
thus, they did not wither even when facing their desired death.
"I have fought in vain; this exertion of mine has gone to waste.
Having reached such a firm conclusion, how can I continue to fight? (33)
And if the battle is not fought, how will these two demons—who constantly cause suffering and are arrogant due to their boons—avoid destruction? (34)
A boon was granted by the Blessed One, yet it is difficult to fulfill;
for even one who is suffering does not desire death at will. (35)
"Even one seized by disease or even one who is wretched does not desire to die;
how then could these two, intoxicated with pride, wish for death? (36)
Indeed, today I take refuge in that Vidyā, the Śakti who grants all desires;
for without her, whose favor is perfectly serene, desires are not fully accomplished.
While reflecting thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu beheld Śivā, the enchanting Yoganidrā, stationed in the sky.
With palms joined in reverence, the immeasurable soul, a knower of yoga, praised that Bestower of Boons,
the Sovereign of the World, there for the sake of their destruction.
Viṣṇu said:
Salutations, O Goddess Mahāmāyā, you who cause the creation and destruction [of the world],
who are without beginning or end, O Caṇḍī, O Śivā, bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation!
I do not know your form, whether it possesses attributes or is devoid of them; O Goddess, how could I know your deeds, which are beyond all counting? (41)
Today I have experienced your power, which is exceedingly difficult to achieve;
for though I was absorbed in sleep, I have become unconscious. (42)
Although I was awakened again and again by Brahmā with great effort,
I did not wake up at all, for my six senses were completely contracted.
O Mother, by your power I attained a state of unconsciousness;
released by you, I have awakened and have fought many battles.
"I am exhausted, yet those two excellent ones, granted boons by you, are not weary;
they have come to slay Brahmā, those two Dānavas arrogant with pride. (45)
O giver of honor, when I was challenged at will to a duel by those two,
a most terrible battle was fought by me with them in the great ocean.
At the time of my death, you granted me a boon; therefore, that was known as a great marvel. Having understood this, I have today come to you for refuge—you who grant refuge. (47)
"O Mother, grant me your assistance; I am exhausted by the work of war.
Those two, arrogant because of your boon, are causing affliction to the gods. (48)
"The two sinners are intent on killing me; what shall I do, and where shall I go?"—having been addressed thus, the goddess then spoke with a smile. (49)
To Vāsudeva, the eternal Lord of the World, who was bowing down, he said:
"O God of gods, O Hari, O Viṣṇu, engage in battle yourself once again! (50)
"Having deceived these two heroes, they must be slain while rendered bewildered;
I shall surely delude the two Dānavas with my sidelong glance. (51)
"Go quickly, O Nārāyaṇa, [and deliver] those two who are deluded by my māyā.
Sūta said:
Having heard those words of hers, which were imbued with the essence of affection, Viṣṇu...
Having reached the field of battle, he stood there in that great ocean;
then those two heroes of great strength arrived, desiring combat.
Seeing Viṣṇu standing there, the two became filled with joy and said:
"Stay, stay, O Great Desire! O Four-armed One, engage in battle! (54)
Having realized today that victory and defeat are surely dependent on fate,
the strong man attains victory through fate, and even the weak man conquers through fate.
A high-souled person should by no means give way to joy or sorrow;
indeed, in the past, many Daityas were conquered by the enemy of the Dānavas.
"And now, having fought with us, he has been defeated.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, those two mighty-armed ones stood ready for battle. (57)
Seeing them, Viṣṇu, whose deeds are marvelous, quickly struck them with his fist;
those two, intoxicated by their great strength, likewise struck Hari with their fists.
Thus a most terrible battle arose between them;
then Nārāyaṇa, seeing those two of great prowess engaged in combat, [acted].
Hari cast a piteous glance directly at the Goddess.
Sūta said:
Having beheld Viṣṇu in such a state, filled with the essence of compassion...
As she, with her eyes exceedingly copper-red, gazed at the two Asuras, she struck them with side-long glances as if with other arrows of love. (61)
Beholding the side-long glances of the Goddess, which were accompanied by gentle smiles and imbued with sentiments of love, the two wicked ones became utterly infatuated.
Thinking it to be a special distinction, and deeply tormented by the arrows of desire,
they stood there gazing at that goddess of radiant luster.
Hari also perceived what the Goddess intended to do there;
having recognized that they were both deluded, the Blessed One, the most skilled in discerning what must be done, [acted].
Smiling, he spoke to them gently in a voice as deep as a thundercloud:
"O heroes, choose a boon that is desired by you both."
"Highly pleased, I shall indeed grant you both a battle;
for many Dānavas have been seen by me in combat in the past. (66)
No one like you two has ever been seen or even heard of;
therefore, I am truly pleased with your peerless strength and prowess.
"And I shall grant the desired wish of you two brothers, O mighty ones.
Sūta said:
Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, they were filled with pride and afflicted by love.
Beholding Mahāmāyā, who brings joy to the world,
those two lotus-eyed ones, afflicted by desire, spoke to Viṣṇu.
"O Hara, we two are not beggars; what do you wish to give here?
O Lord of Gods, grant us equally; we two are givers, not beggars. (70)
O Hṛṣīkeśa, request the boon desired by your heart;
we are pleased with you because of this battle and your wonderful deeds, O Vāsudeva.
Having heard those words of theirs, Janārdana replied: "May both of you be pleased with me today; both of you are to be slain by me."
Sūta said:
Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, the two Dānavas were greatly astonished;
thinking themselves deceived, they stood there filled with grief.
Having reflected upon this with their minds, those two Dānavas, seeing that everything was composed of water and that the earth was devoid of dry land, spoke to Viṣṇu.
O Hare, O Janārdana, this boon which was previously granted by you—O Lord of Gods, you are true to your word; grant that desired boon.
"O Madhusūdana, slay us in this vast, waterless region!
We two are to be killed by you; O Mādhava, let your word be true. (76)
Then, remembering that wheel, Viṣṇu, the Lord Hari, spoke to them while smiling:
"O illustrious ones, today I shall slay you both on a vast, waterless plain."
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods, having made his thighs exceedingly broad,
displayed them there upon the water where there was no water.
"O two Dānavas, let water be released here upon my head;
today I shall become true to my word for both of you. (79)
Having heard those truthful words and reflected upon them with their minds,
the two of them increased their bodies to a thousand yojanas.
The Blessed One then doubled their hips; they were amazed as they placed their heads upon those most wonderful hips.
Then, when the wheel had been severed by the powerful Viṣṇu,
their two heads were violently dragged over the hips.
Then the two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, became lifeless;
at that time, the entire ocean was indeed pervaded by their fat.
From that, the name "Medinī" arose for the earth on all sides;
for that reason, O lords of sages, clay is not to be eaten.
Thus everything that I was asked by you has been told with complete certainty:
the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), should always be served by the wise. 85.
The Supreme Śakti is to be propitiated by all the gods and demons alike;
there is nothing higher or more exalted than her in the three worlds. (86)
Truth, truth, and again truth is the definitive conclusion regarding the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras:
the Supreme Power (Parā Śakti), whether devoid of attributes (nirguṇā) or endowed with attributes (saguṇā), is to be worshipped.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha by Hari," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Bestowing of Boons by Śiva.
The Sages said:
O Sūta, previously it was told by you that [this was] spoken by Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor.
Having composed the entire auspicious Purāṇa, he taught it to Śuka.
But how was Śuka produced by Vyāsa after he had performed austerities?
Tell me all of this in detail, exactly as you heard it from Kṛṣṇa.
Sūta said:
I shall proclaim the birth of Śuka from Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī;
how that sage Śuka, the foremost among yogins, was born in person.
On the most delightful peak of Mount Meru, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī,
performed extremely severe penance, having resolved to obtain a son.
Desiring a son, that treasury of asceticism meditated upon the supreme Mahāmāyā while reciting the single-syllable mantra of speech, which he had heard from Nārada.
"May this son of mine be equal in prowess to Agni, the Earth, Vāyu, and the intermediate space," he thought.
Having ceased from food, that lord remained for a hundred years,
propitiating Mahādeva as well as Sadāśiva.
Having reflected again and again that power is everywhere worshipful,
one who is powerless is censured in the world, while the powerful is fully honored.
On that mountain peak, truly wonderful with its groves of karṇikāra trees,
all the deities and sages preeminent in austerity sport.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and likewise the two Aśvins,
as well as the sages and others who are most eminent in the knowledge of Brahman, dwell there.
There, upon the peak of the Golden Mountain, which resounded with the sounds of music,
the righteous Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, performed austerities.
Then, by his splendor, the entire universe, including all things moving and stationary, was pervaded;
the matted locks of the wise son of Parāśara became the color of fire.
Then, perceiving his splendor, the Lord of Śacī became afraid;
seeing Turāsāha thus terrified by fear and exhausted by fatigue.
The Blessed Lord Rudra spoke thus to Maghavan as he stood there;
Śaṅkara said:
"O Indra, why are you afraid today? What is your sorrow, O Lord of the Gods? (14)
One should never harbor resentment toward ascetics;
for the sages practice penance knowing me to be endowed with power. (15)
"But these ascetics do not desire harm at all.
Having spoken these words, Śakra said to him whose banner is the bull: 16.
"Why does Vyāsa perform penance? What is the purpose in his mind?
Śiva said:
"The son of Parāśara is performing difficult penance because he desires a son."
"Having been born for a full hundred years, I now give this auspicious son [to you].
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to Vāsava, Rudra, with a joyful countenance out of compassion, [bestowed him].
Having approached the sage, the Teacher of the World said to him:
"Arise, O son of Vāsavi! A virtuous son shall be born to you. (19)
O sinless one, this son of yours shall always be composed of all splendor, a man of knowledge, a bringer of fame, and beloved by all people here. (20)
"He shall be full of virtuous qualities and possessed of true prowess.
Sūta said:
Having heard those gentle words, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana then [proceeded].
Having paid homage to the trident-bearer, he went to his own hermitage;
having reached that very hermitage quickly, he was distressed by the toil of many years.
Desiring to produce fire, he churned the secret fire-drill together with its base;
as he was performing the churning, a great burden of anxiety then arose in his mind.
He appeared suddenly at the birth of the high-souled one;
his emergence was like that from churning, through the conjunction of the churning-stick and the fire-drill.
Just as it was for Pāvaka, how can there be the birth of a son for me? That which is known as the "son-producing fire" (putrāraṇi) does not exist for me today. (25)
How can I make my beloved—who is young, endowed with beauty, born of noble lineage, and devoted to her husband—like a chain bound to my feet? (26)
She was skilled in the procreation of sons and always established in devotion to her husband;
though she was a devoted wife, capable, and beautiful, she was nonetheless full of desire. (27)
She is eternally of the nature of bondage and bestows the pleasure of her own will;
even Śiva remains forever joined with the noose of his beloved. (28)
"And how shall I manage this household life, which is so difficult to maintain?"—
while he was thinking thus, the celestial Ghṛtācī appeared in her divine form.
Having come within the range of his vision, she stood nearby in the sky;
and he beheld that excellent Apsaras standing close by, with her tremulous side-glances. (30)
With his limbs overwhelmed by the five arrows, he quickly took up his vow and then reflected: "What shall I do now in this crisis? (31)
When the state of passion, so difficult to overcome, has arisen before me regarding this Dharma, if I were to accept her who has come here for the sake of deception, [I would be lost]. (32)
"Having performed most terrible asceticism here for a full hundred years, those great-souled ascetics will laugh at me as I am distraught. (33)
Having seen the apsaras, how did that great ascetic become helpless?
Let there be even censure, provided it results in incomparable bliss. (34)
It is declared to bestow happiness upon those born into the householder stage of life, to grant sons, and likewise to bestow heaven; and for the wise, it likewise bestows liberation.
That will certainly not happen through this celestial maiden;
for I previously heard a story from Nārada concerning how King Purūravas was brought to ruin by the power of Urvaśī. (36)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Granting of Boons by Śiva," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Regarding the birth of the Buddha,
the sages asked: "Who was this King Purūravas, and who was Urvaśī, the daughter of the gods?"
How did that high-souled king come to encounter such hardship? || 1 ||
O Lomaharṣaṇaja, tell us now the entire narrative;
we all desire to hear the nectar falling from the lotus of your mouth. (2)
O Sūta, your speech, which is full of aesthetic flavor, is sweeter even than nectar; we are all not satiated by it, just as the immortals are never satiated by the celestial ambrosia.
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages, to this divine and enchanting story;
I shall relate it according to my understanding, as I heard it from the most excellent Vyāsa.
The beloved wife of the Guru was well-known by the name Tārā;
she was endowed with beauty and youth, possessed of lovely limbs, and intoxicated with passion.
Once, when the moon had gone to the abode of the sacrificer, that beautiful woman,
endowed with exceptional beauty and youth, was seen by the Moon.
Then the moon became afflicted by desire for her whose face was like the moon;
and she too, beholding the moon, became tormented by passion.
Filled with mutual love and afflicted by the god of desire,
Tārā and the Moon became intoxicated with passion, tormented by the arrows of Kāma.
Intoxicated with passion and filled with mutual longing,
those two continued to take delight there for several days.
But Bṛhaspati, afflicted by grief, sent a disciple to his home to bring Tārā back; however, she did not return, having been brought under control [by another].
When the moon turned back toward his pupil again and again, Bṛhaspati became enraged and went there in person. || 11 ||
Having gone there to the abode of Soma, the noble-minded Vācaspati,
filled with anger yet smiling, addressed the Moon who was intoxicated with pride.
What deed, indeed, censured by dharma, was committed by you, O Moon, for what reason was my wife Sundarī protected by you? (13)
"O King, I am your preceptor and you are my patron in every respect;
O fool, how could you have enjoyed the wife of your guru, or was she protected? (14)

The killer of a Brahmin, the stealer of gold, the drinker of liquor, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—these are indeed the perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin), and the fifth is he who associates with them. || 15 ||
"You are burdened with great sins, of evil conduct, and utterly contemptible;
you are not worthy of the abode of the gods, unless this woman has been enjoyed by you. (16)
"Release this woman with dark-cornered eyes; I shall take her to my own home.
Otherwise, I will proclaim you as a wicked soul, a stealer of the preceptor's wife. (17)
To him who was speaking thus— the preceptor filled with anger and distressed by the pain of separation from his beloved— the Lord of Rohiṇī replied.
Indu said:
"Brahmins who are free from anger are difficult to propitiate when they are angry;
they are worthy of worship when they know the treatises on dharma, but otherwise they should be avoided. (19)
That woman of excellent complexion will surely come to your house;
meanwhile, the young girl remains right here—what loss is there for you in this matter, O sinless one? (20)
For she remains here by her own will, desiring happiness;
after staying for a few days, she will depart according to her own desire.
Furthermore, you yourself previously cited the opinion of the Dharmaśāstra:
"A woman is not defiled by her conduct, nor is a Brahmin by his Vedic rites. (22)
Thus addressed by Śaśin, the Guru there became exceedingly distressed;
overcome with anxiety and afflicted by love, he went quickly to his own home. (23)
After staying there for a few days, the teacher, distressed with anxiety,
then went quickly to the home of that lord of medicinal herbs.
Held back by the gatekeeper at the entrance, the Moon stood there filled with anger;
he did not enter, and Bṛhaspati became exceedingly enraged.
