"This unrighteous man, having entered into discipleship with me, has forcibly seized my preceptor’s wife as if she were his mother; he must now be disciplined by me. (26)
Standing outside at the doorway, he spoke these words in anger:
"O dull-witted one, O evil-doer, O lowest of gods, why do you lie there in the palace?"
"Give me my beloved quickly; otherwise, I shall cast a curse upon you.
If you do not give me my dear one, I will surely reduce you to ashes. (28)
Sūta said:
Having heard such cruel words and others like them from Bṛhaspati,
the Lord of the Twice-born quickly went out from his residence.
Soma said to him, laughing: "Why do you speak so much? This dark-eyed woman, endowed with all auspicious marks, is not suitable for you. (30)
"O twice-born one, take another woman who is of similar appearance but of ugly form;
such a woman of excellent complexion is not suitable for the house of a beggar. (31)
"Passion is said to belong to a woman for a lover who resembles her;
you, O dull-witted one, do not know the definitive conclusions of the science of love. (32)
"Go wherever you wish, O evil-minded one; I will not give up this woman of desire.
Do whatever you can do, for this woman of excellent complexion must not be given away."
"O Teacher, since you are afflicted by desire, your curse cannot afflict me;
I will not give up my beloved wife—do as you wish. (34)
Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus by Śaśin, the worshipful one was filled with resentment and fell into deep thought;
overcome with anger, he went swiftly to the abode of the Lord of Śacī.
Seeing his preceptor standing there afflicted by grief, Śatakratu honored him with water for the feet,
the arghya offering, water for sipping, and other rites, and then sat down respectfully before him.
The most noble one questioned the preceptor who remained in that state:
"O illustrious one, what is your concern? O great sage, you are afflicted by grief. (37)
"By whom have you been insulted—you who are my preceptor and in my kingdom?
This entire army, along with the lords of the worlds, is under your command. (38)
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Śambhu and whatever other most excellent gods there may be, will provide assistance; what cause for concern is there? Speak now! (39)
The Guru said:
"My wife Tārā, who has beautiful eyes, was carried off by the Moon;
that evil-minded one does not give her back, even though he has been entreated again and again. (40)
"What shall I do, O Lord of the Gods? You alone are my refuge.
Grant me your assistance, O Lord of Devas; I am distressed, O Śatakratu! (41)
Indra said:
"Do not grieve, O knower of dharma; I am your servant, O observer of noble vows.
I shall surely bring back your wife, O high-minded one. (42)
If, after I have dispatched a messenger, he does not give [it] up due to his arrogance,
then I shall wage war, surrounded by the armies of the gods.
Having thus consoled his preceptor, Śakra dispatched a messenger who was eloquent in speech,
wonderful, and a bearer of news to Soma.
Having gone swiftly to the world of the Moon, that wise one spoke these words with his voice to the Lord of Rohiṇī.
"O illustrious one, I have been sent by Śakra with the desire to speak to you;
O high-minded one, I shall relate that which was told by my lord. (46)
"O highly fortunate one, you are a knower of dharma and you understand policy, O observer of noble vows!
Your father Atri is a righteous soul; you ought not to do anything blameworthy. (47)
A wife must be protected by all beings according to their ability and with diligence;
for her sake, quarrels will surely arise—of this there is no doubt. (48)
Just as you would, so too should he make an effort to protect his wife;
O treasury of nectar, consider all beings as yourself. (49)
Those twenty-eight auspicious women, the daughters of Dakṣa, are your beloveds;
O treasure-house of nectar, how can you desire to enjoy the wife of your guru?
"These charming women, Menakā and the others, dwell forever in heaven;
enjoy them at your will according to your desire, and abandon even your preceptor’s wife. (51)
If the lords were to perform loathsome acts out of pride, and the ignorant were to follow them, then there would be a destruction of dharma. || 52 ||
Therefore, O illustrious one, release the beautiful wife of your preceptor, so that a quarrel caused by you may not arise among the gods today. (53)
Sūta said: Having heard the words of Śakra, Soma, somewhat agitated with anger,
then spoke this reply in a mocking tone to the messenger of Śakra.
Indu said:
"O mighty-armed one, you are a knower of dharma and yourself the sovereign of the gods;
even your priest is such as he, and the intellect of you both is identical. (55)
Many people are skilled in giving instruction to others;
however, one who acts for themselves when the time for action has arrived is always rare to find. (56)
And men accept the treatise composed by Bṛhaspati;
what contradiction is there here, O Lord of Gods, for those who desire to enjoy a woman? (57)
For the powerful, everything is their own; for the weak, nothing is so.
The notions of "one's own" and "another's" are merely the delusion of those with dull minds. 58.
Tārā is devoted to me, though not as she is to her guru;
how can she, being thus devoted, be abandoned according to dharma and justice? (59)
But how could the commencement of a household occur while she was detached?
For when she became detached, she desired the wife of her younger brother. (60)
"I will not give up the beautiful woman; go, O messenger, and speak for yourself.
You are the Lord, O Thousand-eyed One; do whatever you wish."
Sūta said:
Thus addressed by the Moon, the messenger went into the presence of Śakra and reported to Indra everything that had been said by the cool-rayed one.
Having heard that, Turāṣāṭ also became filled with anger;
the powerful lord then made preparations for his army in order to assist his preceptor.
But Śukra, having heard of the conflict, departed from there out of hatred for his preceptor;
he spoke these words to the Moon: "Do not give [him to me]. (64)
"O high-minded one, O worthy sir, if a battle should take place between you and Indra, I shall provide you assistance through the power of my mantras. (65)
But Śaṅkara, having heard of that violation of the preceptor’s wife and regarding Bhṛgu as an enemy of his teacher, then rendered him assistance.
Then a battle between the gods and the Dānavas quickly took place;
indeed, it lasted for many years, like that of the Asura Tāraka.
Having witnessed the battle fought between the gods and the asuras, the Grandfather (Brahmā) mounted upon a swan and went quickly to that place for the sake of pacifying the distress.
Then he said to the lord of the night (the moon): "Release my preceptor's wife;
otherwise, having summoned Viṣṇu, I shall bring about his destruction. (69)
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, restrained Bhṛgu, saying:
"O high-minded one, has an unjust disposition arisen in you due to the fault of association? (70)
Then Bhrigu forbade that lord of medicinal herbs:
"Release the wife of your guru today; I have been sent to you by my father. (71)
Sūta said:
Having heard those wonderful words of Bhṛgu,
the Moon (King of the Twice-born) gave back to his preceptor his beloved and auspicious wife, who was pregnant.
Having obtained his beloved, the preceptor went joyfully and delightedly to his own home;
thereafter, the gods and the demons each departed toward their respective abodes. (73)
Brahmā reached his own abode, and Śaṅkara likewise reached Kailāsa;
and Bṛhaspati, having obtained his beautiful wife, was deeply satisfied.
Then, after some time, Tārā gave birth to an auspicious son on a favorable day and under an auspicious constellation, who was equal to the Lord of Stars (the Moon) in his virtues.
Seeing that a son had been born, the preceptor,
with a heart full of joy, performed all the rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarma) according to the prescribed rules.
O best of sages, having heard of the birth of his son,
the high-minded Candra dispatched a messenger to his preceptor.
This son of mine was not born from your seed;
how then did you perform the rites such as the birth-ceremony (jātakarman) and others according to your desire?
Having heard those words of the messenger, Bṛhaspati said:
"My son is my equal; there is no doubt in this matter. (79)
Once again, a dispute arose; the gods and demons assembled, and having come for the sake of battle, their gathering took place.
Thereupon Brahmā himself, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) desiring peace, arrived there and restrained those who were stationed at his mouth and were intoxicated with the madness of battle.
The righteous-souled one asked Tārā, "O auspicious one, whose son is this?
O lady of excellent hips, tell the truth so that this distress may be appeased. (82)
Though feeling bashful and with her face cast down, that woman of excellent complexion, with her dark-cornered eyes, spoke to him softly; then, as if saying "of the moon," she departed within.
Soma took that son with a joyful inner soul;
he gave him the name Budha and returned once more to his own home.
Brahmā went to his own abode, as did all the gods together with Indra;
everyone, including all the people who had been spectators, departed in every direction just as they had come.
This account of the Buddha’s birth and his time in the preceptor’s household has been told, just as it was previously heard by me from Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī. (86)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Birth of the Buddha," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 11 ||
The Praise of Sudyumna.
Sūta said:
Thereafter Purūravas was born of Ilā; I shall relate this to you.
The son of Budha was exceedingly righteous, a performer of sacrifices, and devoted to the giving of gifts.
A king named Sudyumna, truthful in speech and having conquered his senses,
mounted a horse from the Sindhu region and went hunting in the forest.
Accompanied by a few ministers, Cārukuṇḍala appeared,
having fastened his Ājagava bow and a marvelous multitude of arrows.
Wandering through that forest region, he killed ruru deer,
hares, boars, rhinoceroses, and likewise gayals.
Slaying śarabhas, buffaloes, sambhara deer, and wild cocks— pure animals fit for sacrifice— the king entered Kumāravana.
At the base of Mount Meru, there was a divine place, adorned with rows of Mandāra trees,
strewn with Aśoka creepers, and perfumed by Bakula flowers.
It was covered with groves of *sāla*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, and *campaka* trees, as well as *panasa*,
*āmra*, *nīpa*, and *madhūka* trees, and was adorned with pavilions of *mādhavī* creepers.
It was adorned with pomegranates and coconuts, beautified by groves of plantains,
and completely covered with creepers of jasmine, mālatī, and kunda flowers.
The forest, filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, resounded with the whistling of *kīcaka* reeds; it was made delightful by the humming of bees and brought all happiness.
Seeing this, King Sudyumna, surrounded by his attendants,
was filled with joy upon beholding the trees in full bloom, adorned with the warbling of cuckoos.
Having entered there, the royal sage instantly attained womanhood;
the horse also became a mare, and that king was overcome with anxiety.
Thinking "What is this? and being tormented by anxiety as he reflected again and again, Sudyumna, filled with shame, experienced even greater suffering. (12)
"What shall I do? How can I go home while endowed with this female form?
How shall I rule the kingdom, for by whom have I been deceived? (13)
The sages said:
O Sūta, O Lomaharṣaṇa, this wonder has been told by you—
that King Sudyumna, who was like a god, attained womanhood.
Tell me what that cause was in that charming forest; what was done by that king? O observer of noble vows, speak of it in detail.
Sūta said: Once, Sanaka and the other ṛṣis approached to see Giriśa, illuminating the quarters with a light that dispelled the darkness.
And at that time, Mahādeva Śaṅkara was there with his consort, intent on play; and Śivā, the beloved, was without clothes.
Seated on her husband’s lap and sporting with him,
the beautiful goddess Ambikā, seeing them, was utterly ashamed to be naked.
Rising from her husband's lap and taking a garment, she put it on;
overcome with shame and trembling, that highly proud woman stood there. (19)
Even the sages, having observed the dalliance of those two,
turned back and quickly departed for the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Seeing the amorous woman filled with shame, the Lord Hara said:
"Why are you so overcome by modesty? I shall provide you with happiness."
O fair-faced one, from this day forward, whatever man should enter this forest out of delusion, he shall indeed become a woman.
Those people who anywhere know that the forest was thus cursed by him avoid, in this world, desire for that forest which is so full of faults. (23)
But Sudyumna, entering that place out of ignorance along with his ministers, likewise attained womanhood together with them; of this there is no doubt. (24)
Overcome with anxiety, that royal sage did not go home out of shame;
he wandered here and there outside that forest region.
The message was delivered by that great-souled one; while wandering there, the youthful Budha, son of Soma, arrived at that place in the form of a woman.
Seeing that lovely and charming woman surrounded by her female attendants, and endowed with all the arts of coquetry and amorous expression, the blessed Lord Budha desired her.
She too desired that beloved Budha, the son of Soma, as her husband;
thus, a union was brought about between them through their mutual love.
He begot upon her, Ilā, a son named Purūravas,
the son of Soma, who was a supreme universal monarch.
That young woman, dwelling in the forest and overcome with anxiety, gave birth to a son;
she then called to mind her own family preceptor, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages.
Then, seeing that condition of Sudyumna, he was filled with compassion and propitiated Mahādeva Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
The Blessed One, being pleased with him, granted his desired boon;
Vasiṣṭha then requested manhood for the beloved king.
Śaṅkara, making his own word true, said:
"For one month he shall indeed be a man, and for one month a woman, O King. (33)
Having thus obtained the boon, the king returned once more to his own home;
that righteous soul governed the kingdom through the grace of Vasiṣṭha as well.
While remaining in the female state he stayed in the palaces, and in the male state he ruled the kingdom;
yet the subjects were distressed by him and did not welcome the lord of the earth.
When his son Purūravas had reached youth in due time,
the king bestowed upon him the kingdom and established his own authority, and then departed for the forest.
Having gone to that delightful forest, which was filled with various kinds of trees,
he received from Nārada the unsurpassed nine-syllabled mantra.
With his mind overflowing with love, he recited the mantra intensely;
then the virtuous goddess Tāriṇī, the auspicious one, became fully satisfied.
Mounted upon a lion, she stood before him, possessing a divine and enchanting form;
she was intoxicated by the drinking of wine, her eyes rolling with exhilaration.
Having beheld her of divine form, his eyes overwhelmed with love, he bowed his head in devotion and praised the Mother of the Universe with joy. (40)
He said:
"O Blessed One, your divine form, which accords with the welfare of all the worlds, has been beheld by me in its full manifestation."
O Mother, I bow to your lotus feet, which are served by the hosts of gods and which bestow both all desires and liberation.
Who on earth knows you, O Mother, in this mortal body,
wherein even all the sages and gods are utterly deluded;
yet you possess this entire sovereignty and compassion for the wretched?
O Goddess, upon merely seeing all this, I am indeed filled with wonder.
Śambhu, Hari, the lotus-born Brahmā, Indra, the Sun, Kubera, Agni, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Soma—
even the Vasus do not know your power.
How could a man devoid of qualities perceive your qualities?
O Mother, Viṣṇu of immeasurable luster knows you directly as the Sāttvika one, born from the ocean, and the bestower of all goals;
but who, O Ambikā, can truly know you as the Rājasa Umā, or even as the Tāmasa one? Indeed, no one knows you as you truly are—devoid of all attributes (nirguṇa).
Where am I, of such dull intellect, and where is this incomparable power of yours?
Where is this exceedingly skillful grace of yours toward me? I recognize that your conduct is endowed with compassion.
And you show compassion toward those servants who are devoted to you with sincere intent. || 45 ||
Even though you dwell in the forest, this Hari does not act with joy; nor does Madhusūdana,
for the Primordial Being has indeed placed his feet upon fire for your sake.
Having performed [the preliminary rites], he makes his two hands auspicious and pure with water.
Aho! The ancient Puruṣa Hari, like an Aśoka tree, joyfully desires an excessive trampling of his feet by a man;
yet you, being angry, perform that very act upon him as he bows at your feet.
Having seen her husband, who is praised by all the gods, afflicted by the god of love... || 47 ||
O Goddess, you always dwell upon his chest, which is as vast and profoundly tranquil as a couch,
well-adorned and as dense with beauty as a flash of lightning.
Why is it that even this Lord of the World does not become your vehicle? || 48 ||
O Mother, if you abandon Madhusūdana out of anger, he will indeed become powerless even though he has been worshipped;
for people abandon a man before their very eyes if he is peaceful, devoid of fortune, and utterly lacking in virtues.
Are not the hosts of gods, beginning with Brahmā, truly young women who take refuge day and night at your lotus feet?
I believe they have indeed been made men by you alone.
How can I describe your power, O you of infinite valor?
I have the thought that you are neither neuter nor male; O Goddess, whether you possess attributes or are indeed without attributes,
I bow to you constantly, truly filled with devotion.
I desire unwavering devotion toward you, my mother. || 51 ||
Sūta said:
Having thus offered praise, the protector of the earth then sought refuge;
the Goddess, being thoroughly pleased, granted him union with her own self (sāyujya).
Then, by the grace of that goddess, Sudyumna attained the supreme and stable state, which is difficult even for sages to obtain. (53)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Praise of Sudyumna," in the first book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The narration of the life of Purūravas and Urvaśī.
Sūta said:
When Sudyumna had gone to heaven, Purūravas ruled the kingdom.
He was endowed with virtues and handsome in form, and was devoted to pleasing his subjects.
In the delightful city of Pratiṣṭhāna, he who knew all dharmas and was devoted to protecting his subjects ruled a kingdom honored by all. || 2 ||
His counsel was well-guarded, as was his supernatural insight regarding the future;
likewise, he possessed constant power of energy and supreme sovereign power.
All means, such as conciliation and bribery, were under the control of that king;
indeed, he ruled his kingdom while establishing the castes and stages of life in their respective duties.
That king performed various sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
and then that lord of men gave pure gifts.
Having heard of his physical beauty, noble qualities, magnanimity, virtue, wealth, and prowess,
Urvaśī became subject to his charm and desired that lord of men.
Scorched by the curse of Brahmā, she descended to the world of mortals;
considering him a virtuous king, that proud woman chose him as her husband.
Having made such an agreement, that excellent woman remained there, saying:
"O King, O giver of honor, please protect these two lambs that have been entrusted to you."
"Clarified butter is my constant food, O King, and nothing else;
nor do I look upon you, O Great King, when you are naked, except during sexual intercourse."
"O King, if this bond of speech should be broken, then I shall depart, leaving you behind; I tell you this truly. (10)
And the king accepted what was spoken by his beloved;
she remained bound by her speech, desiring to grant a blessing in exchange for a curse.
Then that king, infatuated by pride for Urvaśī, abandoned his religious duties and other obligations, and remained immersed in pleasure for many groups of years.
But the lord of the earth, having become single-minded and absorbed in her thought, being utterly deluded and deprived of her, was unable to endure even a moment without her. (13)
Thus, at the end of the years, the Lord of the Gods, Pākaśāsana, residing in heaven,
seeing that Urvaśī had not arrived, spoke to the Gandharvas.
"O Gandharvas, all of you together must bring Urvaśī here, having indeed carried her away from the palace of that king at the appointed time. (15)
"My place does not shine at all when it is bereft of Urvaśī;
by whatever means possible, bring that beloved woman here. (16)
Having been addressed thus, those Gandharvas, led by Viśvāvasu,
then departed as a profound darkness set in.
Seeing him sporting there, the two divine calves, though aged,
cried out as they were being carried away through the sky.
Hearing that cry, which was like the wailing of her two sons, Urvaśī became enraged and said to the king: "This condition was established by me. (19)
"O King, I have been lost to you through your lack of trust; my two horses were seized by thieves. These two are like sons to you—why do you remain here, equal to a woman? (20)
I have been deceived by that bad leader, a eunuch who fancies himself a hero;
even my two rams, who were always dearer to me than life itself, have departed today. (21)
Seeing her lamenting in this manner, the king, utterly bewildered, the lord of the earth, went quickly after her while still naked. || 22 ||
There, in the king’s palace, the Gandharvas illuminated the place with lightning;
the king was seen by her as he stood naked, while she was desirous of departing.
Having abandoned them at Uraṇa, all the Gandharvas departed on the road, O King;
the monarch, exhausted and naked, took hold of the two boys and went toward his own home.
Then, seeing that Urvaśī had departed, he lamented, overcome with extreme grief;
seeing his husband naked, that woman of excellent complexion had gone away. (25)
Crying out, the king himself wandered from land to land,
his mind fixed on her, overwhelmed, grieving, helpless, and deluded by passion.
Wandering indeed over the entire earth, that best of kings beheld her at Kurukṣetra; seeing her, with a joyful countenance, he spoke these well-spoken words.
"O cruel wife, wait, wait! You ought not to abandon me—me, who am devoted to you, your beloved, under your control, and innocent. (28)
O Goddess, this body, having been carried far away by you, falls here;
O lady of excellent thighs, since it has been abandoned by you, wolves and crows devour it. (29)
To the king who was thus lamenting— distressed, miserable, exhausted, afflicted by desire, and utterly helpless— Urvaśī spoke.
Urvaśī said:
"O tiger among kings, you are a fool; where has your wisdom gone?
There can never be friendship with women, O ruler of the earth, for they are like wolves. (31)
O King, one should never place trust in women or thieves;
go home, enjoy happiness, and do not set your mind on despair.
Thus enlightened, the king did not understand, being utterly deluded;
constrained by his attachment to his wanton wife, he fell into supreme misery. (33)
Sūta said:
Thus has the entire great life-story of Urvaśī been fully recounted;
it was expanded in the Veda, and has now been told by me in brief.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Life Story of Purūravas and Urvaśī," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 13.
Vyāsa’s Description of the Duties of a Householder.
Sūta said:
Having seen her with dark-cornered eyes, Vyāsa became lost in thought.
"What shall I do? This celestial maiden, an Apsaras, is not suitable for me. || 1 ||
Seeing Vyāsa reflecting in this manner, the Apsaras then became terrified, thinking, "May he not cast a curse upon me."
Then, having assumed the form of a female parrot, she emerged, overwhelmed by fear;
Kṛṣṇa, however, was filled with wonder as he gazed upon that bird.
Upon merely seeing Vyāsa, Kāma became attached to his body;
his mind was filled with great wonder, and he was amazed in every limb.
But even while restraining his mind with great fortitude, that sage Vyāsa was unable to control his mind as it continued to flow outward.
Although his mind was repeatedly captivated by Ghṛtācī,
the mind of Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor was not at all disturbed, owing to his spiritual cultivation.
As that sage was performing the churning with the desire to produce fire,
his semen suddenly fell into the fire-drill itself.
Having thus meditated upon that inconceivable descent, he churned the churning-stick;
from it was born Śuka, enchanting in the form of Vyāsa.
That child born of that forest grew up producing wonder,
shining with brilliance through his offerings, like a kindled fire at a sacrifice.
But Vyāsa, beholding his son, was filled with the utmost wonder; reflecting, "What is this?", he realized it was indeed due to the granting of a boon by Śiva.
Though born from the interior of the fire-drill (araṇī),
Śuka became like a second fire, blazing exceedingly with his own splendor in the form of radiant energy.
Then Vyāsa beheld his son, who was joyful and endowed with divine splendor, like another Gārhapatya fire.
O ascetics, having then arrived at the mountain, he bathed him within the Gaṅgā;
and a rain of flowers fell from the sky upon the child.
Vyāsa performed the birth rites and other ceremonies for that great-souled one;
the celestial drums resounded and throngs of Apsaras danced.
The lords of the Gandharvas, desiring to behold him, sang with joy—
Viśvāvasu, Nārada, Tumburu, and Śuka— at the time of Śuka’s birth.
Seeing the divine son of Vyāsa, born from the womb of the fire-drill (araṇi), all the gods and the Vidyādharas likewise praised him with joy.
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of Śuka, a staff, a beautiful black antelope skin, and likewise a divine water-pot fell from the intermediate space onto the earth.
Immediately upon birth, that boy grew up exceedingly radiant;
Vyāsa, who was well-versed in the rules of learning, performed his initiation ceremony (upanayana).
As soon as that high-souled one was born, the Vedas, along with their secret portions and their compendiums,
approached him just as they had his father.
Since the form of a female parrot was seen at the time of Ghṛtācī’s birth,
that best of sages gave his son the name Śuka.
Then, having appointed Bṛhaspati as his preceptor, the son of Vyāsa performed the vows of celibacy according to the prescribed rites.
Having studied all the Vedas along with their secret doctrines (Upanishads) and compendiums,
as well as all the treatises on Dharma, Śuka remained in the preceptor’s house.
Having given the sacrificial fee to his guru, the sage, having completed his studies,
then returned to the presence of his father, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
Seeing that Śuka had arrived, Vyāsa rose up with affection and agitation; he embraced him repeatedly and kissed his head.
Vyāsa inquired after his welfare and his pure studies;
then, having comforted him, he established Śuka there in that auspicious hermitage.
Then Vyāsa, possessing great speed, reflected upon the marriage of Śuka; he asked a lovely maiden, the daughter of a sage. (26)
Vyāsa said to his son Śuka: "O sinless one, you have studied the Vedas and all the Dharmaśāstras; O high-minded one, now take a wife. (27)
"Having entered the householder's state, O son, worship the gods and the ancestors; having obtained beautiful wives, release me from my debts. (28)
"For one without a son there is no destination, neither heaven nor anything else.
Therefore, O illustrious son, enter the householder's stage of life today."
"O son Śuka, having established me in the householder's life, make me happy;
O high-minded son, fulfill my great hope."
"O Śuka, having performed most terrible austerities, you have been born without a womb;
O highly wise one, possessing a divine form, protect me, your father. (31)
Sūta said:
When his father had spoken thus and approached him, Śuka, who was detached, then spoke to that man who was intensely attached, his own biological father.
Śuka said:
O Knower of Dharma, O Vedavyāsa of great intelligence, what is it that you say? Instruct me, your disciple, according to the truth; I shall fully carry out your command.
Vyāsa said:
"O son, for your sake I have performed penance for a hundred years;
and you have been obtained through great hardship and by the propitiation of Śiva."
"Having petitioned the king, I shall give you wealth;
O highly wise one, enjoy happiness after attaining excellent youth. (35)
Śuka said:
"Tell me, father, what is that happiness in the world of men which is free from affliction?
For the wise do not call that happiness which is pierced by suffering. (36)
"O highly fortunate one, having made myself a woman, I shall become subject to her control;
for what happiness is there for one who is dependent on another, especially for one conquered by a woman? (37)
One who is constrained by iron, wood, and the like might perhaps at some time be released;
but one who is bound by sons and wife shall never be liberated.
The body of women arises from feces and urine, and likewise they are composed of that;
O best of Brahmins, what wise man would desire to find pleasure therein? (39)
"I am not born from a womb, O brahmin-sage; what kind of inclination could there be for a womb in me?
I do not desire even in the future to arise from a womb. (40)
Why should I desire the pleasure of the vulgar, having abandoned the wonderful bliss of the Self?
For one who delights in the Self does not again become excessively greedy. (41)
First, the Vedas were studied by me and then expanded;
they consist of violence, have fallen [from their true purpose], and promote the path of ritual action.
Even Bṛhaspati, the preceptor, has fallen into the ocean of worldly existence;
with his heart seized by ignorance, how is he capable of delivering others? (43)
Just as a physician afflicted by disease treats the illnesses of others, so too is this householder a guru to me who seeks liberation; it is a mere mockery.
Having prostrated before my guru, I have come into your presence;
protect me, who am terrified by the serpent of saṃsāra, through the awakening to reality. (45)
In this most terrible saṃsāra, wandering is like the rotation of the celestial sphere,
and there is no rest anywhere, just as for the sun day and night.
O Father, what happiness is there in saṃsāra other than the investigation into one's own true nature?
For the foolish, however, the notion of happiness is like the pleasure of insects among lechers.
Among those who have studied the Vedas and Shastras yet remain attached to worldly existence, there is no one more foolish than them; their nature is equal to that of dogs and pigs.
Having attained a human birth which is difficult to find, and having studied the Vedas and the scriptures, if one is still bound in saṃsāra, what man could possibly be liberated? (49)
There is nothing more wonderful or marvelous anywhere in this world than this:
that a man attached to children, wife, and home is proclaimed a wise scholar. (50)
The man who is not oppressed by the three qualities of illusion within saṃsāra—
he is truly wise, he is intelligent, and indeed he has reached the further shore of the scriptures.
What is the use here of useless study that only results in firm bondage?
One should quickly study that alone which can liberate one from the fetters of worldly existence.
Because it seizes a person, it is therefore proclaimed as "home" (gṛha). Where is there happiness in a prison? Therefore, O father, I am afraid. (53)
Those who are ignorant, of dull intellect, and those who have been robbed by fate—
they, having attained a human birth, enter again into bondage.
Vyāsa said: A house is not a prison, nor is it the cause of bondage;
he who is liberated in mind is released even while living as a householder.

A householder who has acquired wealth through righteous means, who performs the rites prescribed in the Vedas according to rule and sequence, who is truthful in speech and pure, shall be liberated even while performing ancestral offerings (śrāddha). 56.
The celibate student, the ascetic, the forest-dweller established in his vows, and the householder always wait upon the householder when the midday mealtime has passed. || 57 ||
Those established in dharma who dwell in the householder stage of life assist others through faith, the giving of food, and likewise through pleasant speech.
No duty superior to the householder’s stage of life has been seen or indeed heard of,
even by learned teachers such as Vasiṣṭha and others who have relied upon it.
O illustrious one, what is impossible for one who performs the rites prescribed in the Vedas?
Whatever he desires—whether heaven, liberation, or a noble birth—that shall come to pass. (60)
"Those who know the Dharma understand that one should go from stage to stage;
therefore, having established the sacred fire, perform your duties without sloth. (61)
O son, O knower of dharma, having duly gratified the gods, the ancestors, and human beings, and having procreated a son, you have fulfilled your duties in the householder stage of life.
Having abandoned your home and gone to the forest, you shall perform the highest vow;
having entered the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), you shall thereafter take up renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
O illustrious one, it is certain that the five senses, together with the mind, are intoxicating; for one who lacks self-restraint, they lead to a miserable end. (64)
Therefore, O high-minded one, one should take a wife for the sake of conquering that [sensual desire];
in old age, one should practice austerity—such is the word proclaimed in the scriptures. (65)
The highly fortunate Viśvāmitra, having performed extremely difficult austerities for three thousand years, remained without food with his senses fully subdued.
And the one of great splendor, being infatuated by Menakā, remained in the forest;
from his seed, the auspicious daughter Śakuntalā was born.
Having seen Kālī, the daughter of the fisherman, my father Parāśara,
afflicted by the arrows of desire, took hold of that maiden while staying upon the boat.
Brahmā too, seeing his own daughter and being tormented by the five-arrowed god of love, ran toward her; but he was stopped by Rudra, who rendered him unconscious.
Therefore, O auspicious one, you too should follow my beneficial advice:
choose a maiden born of noble lineage and take refuge in the path of the Vedas. (70)

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of a Householder by Vyāsa," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of Śuka’s Detachment:
"O Father, I shall not build a home, which always bestows suffering;
it is like a snare, a constant bondage for all embodied beings. (1)
O dear one, where indeed can happiness be seen for those who are distressed by anxiety over wealth?
For greedy people, when they are destitute, are surely tormented even by their own kin. (2)
Even Indra is not as happy as a mendicant who is free from desire; for when the splendor of the three worlds exists, who else in this saṃsāra could be so? (3)
Seeing the ascetic performing his austerities, Maghavan became distressed;
the lord of heaven created many kinds of obstacles for him. (4)
Even Brahmā is not happy, nor is Viṣṇu, despite having obtained the enchanting Lakṣmī;
he constantly experiences distress due to battles with the asuras.
The glorious Lord of Ramā himself performs great efforts and practices difficult austerities; who indeed possesses abundant happiness? (6)
I know that even Śaṅkara is always miserable,
constantly performing ascetic penance and perpetually engaged in battle with the Daityas.
Even a wealthy man who is greedy does not sleep happily at any time;
O dear one, how then can a poor man obtain happiness? (8)
O illustrious one, even though you know that a son is born of your own prowess,
you would still consign him to this most terrible cycle of existence, which is ever fraught with suffering.
O Father, there is the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, and likewise the suffering in death;
furthermore, there is the suffering in dwelling within the womb, which consists of feces and urine.
Therefore, the suffering arising from craving and greed is excessive;
O giver of honor, the pain of begging is even greater than death. (11)
Brahmins subsist on the wealth of gifts received, not by the power of their own intellect;
the hope of others is the supreme misery, and death occurs day after day.
Having studied all the Vedas and the Shastras in their entirety,
the wise should go to the wealthy and offer praise with their whole being.
What concern does one who shares a single womb have for leaves, roots, fruits, and the like?
For he is fulfilled by contentment through whatever means available. (14)
When there is a large family consisting of wife, sons, and likewise grandsons, there is great suffering for the sake of supporting them; O Father, where is that wonderful happiness? (15)
"O Father, teach me the Yoga-śāstra, the science of knowledge that produces happiness; I never take delight in the entire section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa). (16)

Tell me the means for the destruction of karma—namely, that which is currently being performed (*prārabdha*), that which has been accumulated (*sañcita*), and likewise that which is present (*vartamāna*)—so that this threefold root of action may perish. (17)
"A woman always drinks blood like a leech;
yet the fool, deluded by her emotional gestures, does not realize this. (18)
Wealth takes away one's vigor; a mind full of riches is led astray by crooked speech; and a beloved woman carries off everything one possesses—what other thief is like her? 19.
Deceived by the Creator, the fool takes a wife for the sake of destroying the pleasure of sleep; it leads only to suffering, not to happiness. (20)
Sūta said:
Having heard such words from Śuka, Vyāsa fell into great anxiety, wondering without doubt, "What shall I do? (21)
Tears born of sorrow flowed from his eyes;
a trembling came over his body, and likewise his mind fell into exhaustion.
Seeing his father grieving, dejected, and overwhelmed by sorrow,
he spoke to his father Vyāsa with eyes wide open in amazement.
Oh, how formidable is the power of illusion (māyā), which deludes even the wise—the omniscient author of the Vedānta, who is equal to the Vedas! 24.
I do not know what that illusion is, nor what it is so exceedingly difficult to overcome, which deludes even the wise Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī. (25)
Even he who was the speaker of the Purāṇas, the author of the Mahābhārata,
and the divider of the Vedas, has fallen into delusion.
I go for refuge to that Goddess who indeed deludes the entire world, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and others; what more can be said of her? (27)
Is there anyone in the three worlds who is not deluded by this Māyā, by which even the ancient gods such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara have been led into delusion? (28)
"Oh, what strength! Oh, what heroism has been displayed by the Goddess! By her very illusion, the omniscient Lord, the Sovereign, has been brought under her control. (29)
The authors of the Purāṇas have declared that Vyāsa was born from a portion of Viṣṇu;
yet even he was submerged in the ocean of delusion, like a merchant whose ship has been wrecked.
Today he sheds tears, helpless like an ordinary man;
oh, how difficult it is to abandon this power of illusion, even for the wise! (31)
Who is this? Who am I? How and of what nature indeed is this delusion here?
Within this body composed of the five elements, there arises the mental impression of "father" and "son."
Truly powerful is this illusion, which deludes even the masters of illusion;
overcome by it, even Kṛṣṇa acts like a weeping brāhmaṇa.
Sūta said:
Having mentally bowed to that Goddess, the cause of all causes, the mother of all the gods beginning with Brahmā, and likewise their sovereign; (34)
Born from the fire-drill, he spoke these auspicious and reasoned words to his father Vyāsa, who was dejected and submerged in an ocean of grief.
O illustrious son of Parāśara, you who are yourself the bestower of enlightenment upon all—why do you grieve like an ignorant, ordinary man, O Lord? (36)
Today I am your son; I do not know who I was or who you were in my previous birth, O illustrious one—this is but a delusion regarding this Great Soul. (37)
Exercise fortitude and awaken; do not set your mind on despondency.
Recognizing this as a snare of delusion, O high-minded one, abandon your grief. (38)
Hunger is relieved by food, not by the sight of one's son; thirst is quenched by drinking water, never by the gaze of a child. (39)
The nose finds pleasure in fragrance, the ear in hearing, and the pleasure of women surely in a woman; I am your son—what can I do for you? (40)
Ajīgarta, for his part, gave even his own son to King Hariścandra—
who desired an animal for a sacrifice— by means of a price in every respect.
Wealth is the means for happiness, and from wealth comes the accumulation of pleasure;
earn wealth if you have greed—if I am your son, what can I do? (42)
Awaken me with your wisdom, for you are a knower of destiny, O high-minded sage; so that I may be utterly liberated from the fear of dwelling in a womb.
O sinless one, birth as a human being here in this land of action is difficult to obtain;
even there, the status of a Brahmin in an excellent family is indeed difficult to attain. (44)
The thought "I am bound" does not depart from my mind;
it remains settled in the web of worldly tendencies and continues to grow. (45)
Sūta said:
Thus addressed then by his son of immeasurable intellect, Vyāsa replied to Śuka, who was tranquil and whose mind was set upon the fourth stage of life (the saṃnyāsa āśrama).
Vyāsa said:
"Recite it, O fortunate son; this Bhāgavata was composed by me—a auspicious Purāṇa, equal to the Vedas, which is neither too extensive nor too brief."
In that very place, there are twelve chapters endowed with five characteristics;
this is my considered view as the ornament of all the Purāṇas. (48)
O high-minded one, recite here that Bhāgavata by which the knowledge and discernment of existence and non-existence arises merely through hearing it. (49)
"To Viṣṇu, who lies upon the leaf of the banyan tree in the form of a child—by whom, as the conscious Self (cidātman), have I been fashioned with the nature of a child? (50)
"For what purpose, by what substance, and how shall I know everything?"—
to the high-souled Mukunda who was reflecting thus, [he spoke].
By that half-verse, the Blessed One spoke what grants all goals:
"All this indeed is I; there is nothing else that is eternal. (52)
Viṣṇu had previously recognized those words even within his own mind;
he reflected in his heart, "By whom was this truthful speech uttered? (53)
"How shall I know whether the speaker is a woman, a man, or a neuter?"—
with these thoughts, he took the Bhāgavata to heart.
Repeating [the name] again and again with his mind fixed upon that very [name],
he lay upon a banyan leaf, filled with anxious thought.
Then the blessed Śāntā appeared, four-armed,
auspicious, and bearing as her excellent weapons the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
The goddess was clad in celestial garments and adorned with divine ornaments, accompanied by her peerless female companions who were her own manifestations.
Before that Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor,
Mahālakṣmī appeared, her face auspicious, offering a gentle smile.
Sūta said:
Seeing her thus situated within his heart, the lotus-eyed one was struck with wonder that she, so beautiful, remained there in the water without any support.
Rati, Bhūti, as well as Buddhi, Mati, Kīrti, Smṛti, Dhṛti;
Śraddhā, Medhā, Svadhā, Svāhā, Kṣudhā, Nidrā, Dayā, and Gati. || 60 ||
Contentment, nourishment, forbearance, modesty, yawning, and languor— these are the powers (śaktis) who stand on all sides, each separately, at the flank of the Great Goddess.
All of them bore excellent weapons, were adorned with various ornaments,
garlanded with mandāra flowers, and resplendent with pearl necklaces.
Having seen her and beholding them as well within that single vast ocean of water,
Janārdana became filled with wonder in his heart.
Having perceived the illusion, the Soul of All, filled with great wonder, reflected:
"From where have all these women come, and from where have I come to lie upon this banyan bed? (64)
"In this terrible single ocean, how has the banyan tree arisen?
By whom have I been placed here, having been made into a child of auspicious form? (65)
"Is this my mother, or is she Māyā, or some other inexplicable being?
By whom has she been shown to me today, and for what reason? (66)
What should I say here, or should I go anywhere at all? I shall remain established in silence, unwearied, out of my childlike nature. (67)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Śuka’s Dispassion," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 15 ||
Having seen that god lying on a banyan leaf, Vyāsa, filled with wonder, spoke these words with a smile: "O Viṣṇu, why indeed are you amazed? (1)
By the power of Mahāśakti, you previously forgot me;
even as the dissolution occurs at the time of creation, having come into being again and again.
That supreme Śakti is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), whereas I, likewise, am possessed of qualities (saguṇa); know that the power which is indeed characterized by sattva is my own Śakti.
From the lotus of your navel, Brahmā shall arise as the Lord of Creatures;
endowed with the quality of passion (rajas), he shall be the creator of all the worlds.
Then, having applied himself to austerity and attained unsurpassed power,
he will turn the three worlds red with passion.
Having produced the five elements along with their qualities, the Great-minded One [created] the sense organs and the lords of the senses, preceded by the mind, on all sides.
He will then bring about creation; therefore, O highly fortunate one, he is called the Creator, while you indeed are the Protector of this universe.
And from the middle of his two eyebrows, Rudra will emerge out of anger;
having performed most terrible penance, he shall obtain the power of tamas.
O Mahāmati, at the end of the kalpa he too shall be the destroyer;
for that reason I have approached you—know me to be of the nature of sattva.
"O Madhusūdana, I shall always remain in your presence;
indeed, I shall eternally make my dwelling within your heart. (10)
Viṣṇu said:
"O Goddess, O lady of excellent hips, I previously heard half of this verse with clear syllables. By whom was that supreme, auspicious secret spoken?"
Tell me that, O lady of excellent hips; this is my doubt, O fair-faced one:
how it is that a poor man remembers wealth again and again. (12)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, Mahālakṣmī, her face beaming with a smile and possessing a lovely laugh, spoke these words with supreme affection.
Mahālakṣmī said:
Listen to my words, O Śauri; I am possessed of attributes and have four arms. You do not know me as I truly am—devoid of attributes, yet the abode of all attributes.
O illustrious one, you should know that it was revealed by her;
understand that the Bhāgavata is meritorious, the essence of the Vedas, and the bringer of auspiciousness. (15)
O destroyer of enemies, O observer of noble vows, I consider this to be the great compassion of the Goddess, by which this supreme secret was spoken for your benefit.
This must always be guarded in the mind and never forgotten;
for it is the essence of all scriptures, revealed by the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā). 17.
There is nothing further to be known that exists within the three worlds;
you are indeed dear to the Goddess, and for that reason these words were spoken to you. (18)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the goddess Mahālakṣmī, the four-armed one (Viṣṇu) held them constantly in his heart, considering them to be the unsurpassed mantra.
After some time,
Brahmā, born from that navel-lotus, terrified by the fear of the Daityas, went for refuge to Hari.
Then, having waged a great battle and slain those two, Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu recited half a verse in clear syllables.
Seeing Vāsudeva engaged in silent recitation, the divine Lord of Creatures,
the lotus-born one, was filled with supreme joy and questioned the Lord of Kamalā.
"O Lord of Gods, what are you chanting? Is there indeed someone superior to you, O Lotus-eyed One, by performing which you are pleased, O Lord of the Universe? (23)
Hari said:
"O illustrious one, reflect upon that power which resides in both me and you, characterized as the cause of action; she is the Blessed Śivā."
Upon whose support the entire world rests here in this great ocean—she who is the Great Power (Mahāśakti), possessing form, immeasurable, and eternal. (25)
She by whom this entire universe, both moving and unmoving, is emitted—she, when pleased, becomes the bestower of boons for the liberation of men. 26.
That knowledge is the supreme, eternal cause of liberation;
it is that very same [knowledge] which is the cause of bondage in saṃsāra, she who is the Mistress of all mistresses.
O Brahman, know that I am this entire universe, which has arisen from her power of consciousness (cicchakti); O sinless one, you must never entertain any doubt about this. (28)
That which was indeed proclaimed by her in half a verse is the Bhāgavata;
it shall likewise become extensive at the beginning of the Dvāpara age.
Vyāsa said:
It was first grasped by Brahmā within the lotus-navel of Viṣṇu,
and he spoke it to his son Nārada, who possesses immeasurable intelligence.
Indeed, this was formerly given to me by the sage Nārada;
it has been completed by me in its full extent of twelve books.
Therefore, O illustrious one, recite this Purāṇa which is equal to the Veda, endowed with the five characteristics, and containing the supreme life-story of the Goddess. (32)
Endowed with the essence of the knowledge of reality, it is the most excellent of all, equal in merit to the Dharmaśāstras, and augmented by the meaning of the Vedas. (33)

It contains the account of the slaying of the demon Vṛtra, is endowed with various narratives and stories, is a treasury of the knowledge of Brahman, and is a means of crossing the ocean of saṃsāra. || 34 ||
Accept it, O illustrious one, for you are most wise and worthy;
[I give] this meritorious Purāṇa named Bhāgavata, O bull among men. (35)
Make a compendium of the eighteen thousand verses—divine, the destroyer of ignorance, and the awakener of the sun of knowledge. (36)
This [work] bestows happiness, peace, and fortune; it grants long life and auspiciousness;
and for those who hear or recite it, it increases sons and grandsons. (37)
This righteous disciple of mine, born of Lomaharṣaṇa,
shall recite the auspicious ancient compendium together with you.
Sūta said:
Thus it was spoken by him to his son, and indeed it was told to me;
I have received that entire Purāṇa in its most extensive form.
Having studied the Purāṇa, Śuka remained in the auspicious hermitage of Vyāsa;
yet that righteous-souled one found no peace, like another son of Brahmā.
Devoted to solitude, he appears as if impaired or empty;
yet he is neither excessively attached to eating nor devoted to fasting. (41)
Seeing Śuka absorbed in thought, Vyāsa spoke to his son:
"What, my son, do you constantly contemplate? Why are you so anxious, O giver of honor? (42)
"You sit constantly devoted to meditation like a poor man burdened by debt. What anxiety could there be for you, my son, while I, your father, am still alive? (43)
Enjoy happiness as you desire and cast off the grief within your mind;
contemplate the knowledge taught in the scriptures and direct your intellect toward higher realization.
If there is no peace in your mind at my words, O you of noble vows,
then go, my son, to Mithilā, which is protected by Janaka.
O illustrious one, that righteous king named Janaka, the ruler of Videha and an ocean of truth, will destroy your delusion. (46)
"Go to that king, my son, and dispel your own doubt;
ask him, my son, about the duties of the social classes and stages of life exactly as they are. (47)
That royal sage was liberated while living, pure, with his mind fixed on the knowledge of Brahman;
he spoke the truth, was exceedingly peaceful, a yogi who was always fond of yoga.
Sūta said:
Having heard those words of Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor,
Śuka, who was born from the fire-drill and possessed great luster, replied.
"O virtuous-souled one, this appears to me now as a mere deception in my mind:
that one who is liberated while living and free from the body should rule a kingdom with such joy. (50)
"O father, this King Janaka, though ruling the kingdom of Videha, appears like the son of a barren woman; what is this wonderful doubt of mine? (51)
"O King, I wish to see the monarch of Videha, that best of rulers;
how he remains in this world like a lotus leaf upon the water. (52)
"O dear one, this great doubt revolves within me regarding Videha:
O best of speakers, is liberation for him something other than that of the Buddhists? (53)
How might that which has been eaten become uneaten, and how might that which has been done become undone?
O Great-minded One, how should one abandon the worldly engagement of the senses? (54)

The mother, the son, as well as the wife and the unchaste sister—how could there not be distinction and non-distinction [between them], and if such were the case, how could there be liberation? || 55 ||
If the tongue perceives pungent, alkaline, sharp, astringent, and sweet [flavors], it enjoys unsurpassed pleasures. (56)
O Father, when there is a thorough comprehension of cold, heat, pleasure, pain, and so forth, what kind of liberation could that be? This doubt of mine is truly extraordinary.
How can a king, remaining engaged in the affairs of others, not always bring about the thorough understanding of enemies and friends, which results in enmity or affection? (58)
How can one regard a thief and even an ascetic as equal?
If the intellect were not impartial, then what kind of liberation would it be? (59)
"I have never before seen any king who was liberated while living;
O father, I have great doubt as to how a monarch could be liberated while remaining at home. (60)
Having heard of that king in such a manner, a great desire to see him has arisen;
for the sake of dispelling my doubt, I shall go toward Mithilā.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Vyāsa’s Instruction to Śuka," in the first book of the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Śuka’s Entrance into the Royal Palace.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to his father, the son Śuka fell at his feet.
With palms joined in reverence, the high-minded one, desiring to depart, spoke these words. || 1 ||
I take my leave of you, O illustrious one; your word must be heeded by me. I wish to see the Videha kingdom protected by Janaka.
"How indeed does Janaka rule the kingdom without punishment?
For if there were no punishment, the world would not abide in righteousness. (3)
Punishment, ordained by Manu and others, is always the cause of dharma;
O father, how does it function? This is a great doubt of mine.
Yet this mother of mine appears to be barren; such is her behavior.
O illustrious one, O scorcher of foes, I ask you this and shall now depart.
Sūta said: Seeing that Śuka was desirous of departing, the son of Satyavatī embraced his son— who was wise, firm, and free from desire— and spoke to him.
Vyāsa said:
"May it be well with you, O Śakra; may you live long, O high-minded son.
Having granted me this true word, go, my dear, as you please. (7)
"Having gone back, you must return again to my unsurpassed hermitage;
you must not go anywhere else at all, my son, under any circumstances. (8)
"I live happily, my son, having beheld your lotus-like face;
not seeing it, I fall into misery. You are my very life-breath, my son."
"O son, having seen your father and dispelled all doubt,
come here and dwell in happiness, devoted to the study of the Vedas."
Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus, he saluted his noble elder and performed a circumambulation;
then he set forth with great speed, like an arrow released from a bow.
Beholding various countries and people devoted to wealth, as well as forests, trees, and fields bearing fruit. (12)
He saw ascetics performing austerities, priests engaged in initiation,
and forest-dwelling yogis devoted to the practice of yoga who had retired to the woods.
Seeing the various types of religious paths— those of the Śaivas, Pāśupatas, Sauras, Śāktas, and Vaiṣṇavas— the sage was filled with great wonder.
Having crossed over Mount Meru in two years, the great-minded one reached the Himalayas in another year and proceeded toward Mithilā.
Having entered the middle of Mithilā, he beheld every supreme prosperity,
and all the subjects were happy, well-established in virtuous conduct.
"O Kṣatriya, you have been forbidden from this place; who are you that has come here?
Tell me, what is your business?"—though questioned thus by him, he did not speak. (17)
Having emerged from the city gate, he stood motionless like a pillar;
filled with wonder and laughing loudly, he remained there without uttering a single word.
The doorkeeper said:
"Speak, O Brahmin! Are you mute? For what purpose have you come here?
It is my conviction that no business can be accomplished without movement."
"O twice-born one, you must always enter this city by the king's command;
however, entry here is by no means permitted for one whose family and character are unknown."
"You truly shine with splendor; you are a Brahmin, the foremost knower of the Vedas.
Tell me your lineage and your purpose; go as you wish, O giver of honor. (21)
Śuka said:
"That purpose for which I came here has been accomplished by your word;
yet, to see the city of Videha, where entry is difficult to obtain—"
"O evil-minded one, this is my delusion; having crossed over the two mountains, I have arrived here while wandering, desiring to see the king. (23)
"I have been deceived by my own father; to whom can this blame be given?
O illustrious one, have I been deluded on this earth by my past actions? (24)
In this world, the hope for wealth is the cause of a man’s wandering;
I have no such hope, yet I have come here indeed through delusion. (25)
"There is constant happiness for one who is free from hope, provided he does not sink into delusion.
O illustrious one, I am free from hope, yet I am submerged in this ocean of delusion. (26)
Where is Mount Meru, and where is this Mithilā? And yet, I have arrived here on foot.
What is the fruit of my exertion? I have surely been deceived by Fate.
Indeed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, that which has been commenced must be experienced;
effort always compels it to take effect in every way.
There is no sacred ford nor any Veda here for the sake of which I have exerted myself;
a king named Videha has been born who does not enter the city. (29)
Having spoken thus, he quickly ceased and remained as if silent;
for the gatekeeper recognized that this was some eminent twice-born man who possessed spiritual knowledge.
With conciliatory words, the steward spoke to that sage who stood there:
"Go, O best of the twice-born, wherever you desire to go for your purpose. (31)
"O Brahmin, it was my transgression that I prevented you;
that must be forgiven, O illustrious one, for forgiveness is the strength of those who are liberated. (32)
Śuka said:
What fault is there in this for you, O Kṣattṛ? You are always dependent on others;
a servant must perform the master’s business as is appropriate.
Nor is there any fault in the king in this matter, since I have been protected by you;
the wise must always take full cognizance of thieves and enemies. (34)
"The fault is entirely mine that I have come here;
for visiting another's house is a cause of one's own degradation. (35)
The doorkeeper said:
"O twice-born one, what is happiness and what is suffering? What is the duty for one desiring auspiciousness?
Who is the enemy and who is the benefactor? Tell me all of this today. (36)
Śuka said:
In all the worlds, everywhere there are two kinds of people:
those possessed of passion and those free from passion; furthermore, the minds of these two are likewise twofold.
The dispassionate person is of three kinds: known, unknown, and middling;
and the passionate person is said to be of two kinds: the fool and the clever. (38)
Cleverness is said to be of two kinds: that born of scripture and that born of intellect.
Furthermore, intellect in this world is entirely of two types: the reasonable and the unreasonable. (39)
The doorkeeper said:
"O learned one, O best of the twice-born, you have said, 'I am not a knower of the meaning';
therefore, O most excellent man, tell me all that in detail and according to the truth today. (40)
Śuka said:
He who possesses attachment within this worldly existence is certainly called "one who is attached";
for him there is manifold suffering, and likewise, various kinds of pleasure. (41)
Having obtained wealth, sons, a wife, honor, and likewise victory, one experiences great suffering at every moment if these are not obtained. (42)
A means for his happiness must be devised; that which accomplishes happiness is what ought to be done.
He who creates an obstacle to happiness is to be known as his enemy. (43)
A friend who always brings about happiness for one possessed by passion is rare;
a fool is never free from delusion, for he is deluded everywhere. 44.
For one who is detached from the world and attached to the Self, happiness consists in the practice of solitude, the constant reflection upon the Self, and the contemplation of the Vedānta. (45)
Indeed, all this—this discourse on saṃsāra and the like—is suffering.
For that wise man who desires what is auspicious, there are many enemies. (46)
Lust, anger, and negligence are remembered as his various enemies;
contentment alone is his friend, and no other exists in the three worlds. (47)
Sūta said:
Having heard those words and considering that brahmin to be a man of wisdom,
the Steward (Kṣattṛ) led him into an exceedingly beautiful inner chamber.
He beheld the city, crowded with people of the three social orders, rich with various commodities in the market-stalls, and filled with those engaged in buying and selling. (49)
It was filled with passion and hatred, agitated by desire, greed, and delusion; it was crowded with quarreling people, yet exceedingly full of wealth. (50)
Beholding the three worlds, he entered the royal palace;
having arrived, that one of supreme splendor was like a second sun.
And having been barred right there by the doorkeeper like a log of wood,
he remained at that very gate, contemplating only liberation.
The great ascetic, viewing shade and sunlight with equanimity,
remained in solitary meditation like an immovable pillar.
Having approached after a moment, the king’s minister, with palms joined in reverence,
then led him into the second courtyard of the royal palace.
There, having shown him that divine, enchanting forest of flowering celestial trees and having performed the rites of hospitality, [he spoke]. (55)
There were courtesans devoted to the service of the king,
skilled in singing and instrumental music, and proficient in the science of erotics.
Having assigned those [attendants] for the service of Śuka, the best of ministers,
the son of Vyāsa, then departed from that residence and remained there.
He was honored by those women with supreme devotion according to the prescribed rites,
and he was thoroughly gratified with various kinds of food appropriate to the time and place.
Then the women dwelling in the inner apartments, deluded by passion, showed him the delightful grove of the harem.
Seeing him—young, handsome, lovely, soft-spoken, and charming—all of them were infatuated with him as if he were another god of love. (60)
Thinking him to be a sage who had conquered his senses, they all then attended upon him; however, the pure-souled son of Aṛaṇi conceived a motherly affection for them.
Delighting in the self and having conquered anger, he neither rejoiced nor was he distressed;
even while observing their transformations, he remained established in his own natural state.
To him, the women gave a most delightful bed, well-prepared,
furnished with the finest coverlets, and provided with various articles of utility.

Having performed the washing of his feet and holding *kuśa* grass in his hand, he remained vigilant; having observed the evening twilight devotions (*paścimā saṃdhyā*), he devoted himself entirely to meditation.
Having remained in meditation for one watch, he slept immediately thereafter;
having slept there for two watches, Śuka then arose.
During the final watch of the night, he devoted himself solely to meditation;
having bathed and performed his morning rites, he sat once more in concentrated composure.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of Śuka’s Entrance into the Royal Palace," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 17.
The Description of Janaka’s Instruction.
Sūta said:
Sūta said: Having heard that he had arrived, the pure king, accompanied by his ministers and placing the family priest at the head, went out to meet the son of his preceptor.
Having properly performed the rites of hospitality and offered an unsurpassed seat,
the king inquired after his welfare, having presented him with a milch cow.
And he indeed accepted that honor from the king according to the prescribed rites;
having announced his own well-being, he inquired after the king's welfare.
Having made inquiries regarding his welfare, the king questioned the peaceful Śuka, son of Vyāsa, as he sat upon a comfortable seat.
"O illustrious one, for what reason have you come to me, who am free from desire? Tell me, O best of sages, what is the purpose of your arrival? (5)
Śuka said:
"O great king, as instructed by Vyāsa, take a wife;
for among all the stages of life (āśramas), the householder's stage is the most excellent."
Thinking that even the command of my guru was a mere word not to be accepted,
he told me, "There is no bondage [in this]," yet I did not do that again.
Perceiving him to be thus of a doubting mind, that best of sages spoke these truthful words: "Go to Mithilā; do not grieve."
There resides a patron of sacrifices, King Janaka, who is liberated while living;
known throughout the world as Videha, he protects his kingdom free from all thorns.
By ruling his kingdom in such a manner, a king is not bound by the snares of illusion;
why then, O son, scorcher of the foe, do you fear living on forest fare?
Behold that tiger among kings; abandon the delusion within your mind.
O highly fortunate one, take a wife, or else question that lord of the earth.
"The king will explain the doubt born in your mind.
Having heard those words of his, O son, come to me with speed.
"O Great King, by your command I have arrived at your city;
O Indra among kings, I am desirous of liberation—tell me, O sinless one, what my duty shall be. (13)
Tell me, O Indra among kings, whether austerity, pilgrimage, vows, sacrifice, Vedic study, visiting sacred fords, or knowledge is the cause for liberation. (14)
Janaka said:
Listen to what must be done by a Brahmin who has taken refuge in the path of liberation:
having been initiated, he should first dwell with a preceptor for the purpose of studying the Vedas.
Having studied the Vedas and Vedāntas and having given the teacher’s fee,
the sage, having returned home, should dwell in the householder stage of life together with his wife.
But one who conducts himself according to justice, being contented, free from desire, and cleansed of impurity, performing rites such as the Agnihotra, truthful in speech, and pure— (17)
Having established his son and grandson [in the household], he should dwell in the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) stage of life;
having conquered the six enemies through austerity and having settled his wife upon his son, [he should proceed]. 18.
Having duly internalized all the sacred fires within himself, the knower of dharma,
being weary of worldly life and having attained pure dispassion, should dwell in the fourth stage of life.
"Only one who is dispassionate has the qualification for renunciation, and never otherwise;
this Vedic statement is the truth, and not otherwise—this is my conviction. (20)
Indeed, forty-eight purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are taught in the Vedas;
among those, forty are prescribed for the householder by the great-souled ones. (21)
And eight qualities, beginning with tranquility and self-restraint, are prescribed for one who desires liberation;
"one should go from stage to stage" is the instruction of the learned. (22)
Śuka said:
"When detachment has arisen in the heart and knowledge and realization have come into being, one must necessarily dwell in the stages of life or in the forests. (23)
Janaka said:
"The senses are powerful, O giver of honor; when not restrained, they repeatedly produce various disorders in one who is immature."
Having become an ascetic, how could one act upon the desire for food, the desire for pleasure, or the desire for sleep when such transformations arise within one's son? (25)
The web of latent impressions (vāsanā) is indeed difficult to digest and does not come to rest;
therefore, for the sake of its pacification, one should gradually renounce it.
One who has fallen asleep while standing falls indeed upwards; one who was lying down does not fall downwards.
But one who has fallen away after having renounced the world finds the path no more.
Just as an ant climbs from the root to the branch,
moving slowly and steadily on foot, it reaches the fruit with ease.
The bird flies swiftly, casting aside all fear of obstacles;
the ant, having rested when weary, proceeds with ease.
But the mind is a powerful desire, unconquerable by those who have not disciplined themselves;
therefore, it must be conquered gradually, following the sequence of the stages of life (āśramas).
Even while established in the householder stage of life, one who is peaceful, wise, and self-possessed should neither rejoice nor grieve; he should remain equanimous toward gain and loss.

Performing actions that have been destroyed and abandoning that which is accompanied by anxiety, one who is satisfied with the attainment of the Self is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter. || 32 ||
Behold, O sinless one, how even while established in kingship, I am liberated while living;
I wander according to my will, and nothing whatsoever arises for me.
O sinless one, just as I shall be while enjoying various pleasures and performing manifold duties, so too shall you become liberated. 34.
Indeed, it is said: "How can that which is visible and invisible be bound?
The five elements are the visible objects, and likewise their qualities. (35)
The Self is accessible through inference and is never perceptible;
O Brahmin, how can it be bound, being changeless and stainless? (36)
But the mind, O twice-born one, is the cause of great joys and sorrows;
when this [mind] becomes pure, indeed, everything becomes pure. (37)
Wandering through all sacred fords and bathing again and again, everything is in vain as long as the mind has not become pure. (38)
Neither the body, nor the individual soul, nor the senses, O scorcher of foes, but the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings. (39)
The Self is eternally pure and liberated; it is never bound at any time. Bondage and liberation reside in the mind; when that [mind] is stilled, they come to rest.
Enemy, friend, and neutral—all these distinctions exist within the mind;
how could division arise in the state of oneness, given that it is only through dualistic perception? (41)
The individual soul is always Brahman; I am He—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
It is only the notion of difference that persists while one remains in the cycle of worldly existence.
O illustrious one, this is ignorance, and knowledge is that which brings it to an end;
both knowledge and ignorance must always be discerned by the wise. (43)
For how can shade be known without the heat of the sun, and likewise, how indeed can one know wisdom without ignorance? 44.
The qualities (guṇas) operate within the qualities, and likewise do the elements;
the sense organs function upon the objects of the senses—what fault of the Self (ātman) is there in that? 45.
O sinless one, the boundaries have been established in all the Vedas for the sake of protecting everything; otherwise, there would be the destruction of dharma, as among the followers of Sugata.
When Dharma is destroyed, the conduct of the social classes (varṇas) perishes as it is transgressed;
therefore, may there be auspiciousness for those who proceed by the path ordained by the Vedas. 47.
Śuka said:
O King, a doubt remains within me and does not depart at all, as I listen to what has been told by you, O lord of men. (48)
For in the Vedic laws there is violence, and that is indeed full of unrighteousness;
alas, O King, how can the dharma declared in the Vedas be the bestower of liberation? (49)
But by direct perception, O lord of men, there is the practice of drinking soma, as well as the slaughter of animals and the eating of their flesh. (50)
Likewise, in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the direct consumption of wine is prescribed;
similarly, gambling and various types of vows have been declared.
Indeed, it is heard that in former times there was a supreme king named Śaśabindu,
who was a performer of sacrifices, eternally devoted to dharma, generous, and an ocean of truth.
He was the protector of the bridges of dharma and the teacher of those who had gone astray;
by him, many sacrifices were performed with abundant sacrificial fees.
From the hides, a mountain was produced equal to the Vindhya range;
furthermore, from the flooding of the water of the clouds, the auspicious river Carmaṇvatī was born.
That king also has gone to heaven, and his fame remains unshakable on earth;
yet, despite such religious duties and the Vedas, my intellect does not incline toward them.
Through association with women, a human being always attains pleasure in worldly enjoyment;
in its absence, there is extreme suffering—how, then, can one be liberated while living? (56)
Janaka said: "In sacrifices, violence is directly perceived, yet it is proclaimed to be non-violence;
for it is determined that violence exists only through the application of limiting conditions (upādhi), and not otherwise. (57)
Just as smoke arises in fire through contact with fuel, so indeed does the state of being smokeless manifest in that same fire when separated from it. 58.
And likewise, O best of sages, know that non-violence as it is declared in the Vedas;
for even that is indeed violence for those possessed by passion, while it is not considered such for those free from desire. (59)
The wise who are learned in the Vedas declare that action which is free from passion and likewise devoid of egoism is "unperformed. (60)
O best of the twice-born, for householders, even that very act of violence which occurs in sacrifice—if it is performed without attachment and likewise free from egoism—is [meritorious]. (61)
O highly fortunate one, that alone is the path for those seeking liberation who have conquered their own selves.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Janaka’s Instruction to Śuka," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 18.
Description of Śuka’s marriage and other ceremonies.
Śuka said:
"O Great King, this doubt exists within my heart."
Abiding in the midst of illusion, how could he be free from longing? || 1 ||
Having acquired knowledge of the scriptures and engaged in the inquiry into the eternal and the non-eternal, if the mind does not abandon delusion, how can that man be liberated? (2)
Indeed, knowledge derived from the scriptures is not capable of cutting away the internal darkness,
just as darkness is not destroyed by the mere report of a lamp having been lit.
Non-malice toward all living beings must always be practiced by the wise;
O tiger among kings, how can that be achieved by a householder? (4)
Your desire for wealth is not stilled, nor is your desire for the pleasures of sovereignty;
and since you still seek victory in battle, how can you be one liberated while living? (5)
You have the notion of "thief" toward thieves and the notion of "sage" toward ascetics;
you still possess the distinction between self and other—how then, O King, can you be one who is "bodiless"? (6)
O King, you perceive the pungent, sharp, astringent, and sour tastes as both auspicious and inauspicious;
yet your mind delights in the auspicious ones, not so in the inauspicious.
O King, waking, dreaming, and deep sleep indeed occur for you according to their respective times; but how is it, O monarch, with the fourth state?
The infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants—all are indeed under my control;
I am the master of them all, yet you do not acknowledge this, nor do you think so.
O King, you always eat sweets with joy and likewise with a clear mind;
O best of monarchs, where else have you seen such equanimity as between a garland and a serpent? (10)
But one who is liberated, O King, regards a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal;
possessing the realization of the single Self everywhere, he acts for the benefit of all living beings.
Today my mind finds no delight anywhere in home, wife, or other such things; it is my resolve that I shall wander alone, utterly free from desire. (12)
Free from attachment, free from the sense of "mine," peaceful, subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits,
I shall wander like a deer— beyond dualities and without possessions.
"O King, what use have I for a house, wealth, or even a beautiful wife, when my mind is detached from passion and I have transcended the qualities? (14)
You are conceived in various forms, agitated by manifold passions;
this hypocrisy of yours indeed appears as you declare, "I am liberated. (15)
Sometimes there is anxiety born of enemies, and sometimes anxiety born of wealth;
sometimes there is anxiety born of the army—O King, when will you be free from anxiety? (16)
Even those Vaikhānasa sages who are moderate in diet and firm in their vows become deluded in this worldly existence, even though they know its unreality.
O Lord of the Earth, you should know that for those born in your lineage, the name "Videha" shall never at any time be anything other than "Kuṭila. (18)
