A Vidyadhara who is a fool, a sun that is blind from birth, and one named Lakṣmīdhara who is poor—for these, their names are meaningless. (19)
Those kings born in your lineage whom I have heard of in the past were renowned by the name "Videhas," but not on account of their actions.
O King, in former times there was a king named Nimi in your lineage;
that royal sage [summoned] the sage Vasiṣṭha, his own preceptor, for the sake of a sacrifice.
Then the sage invited him and said to the king:
"I have indeed now been invited by Devendra for the sake of a sacrifice."
"Having completed his sacrifice, I shall indeed fulfill yours as well;
therefore, O Indra among kings, prepare the necessary materials gradually. (23)
Having spoken thus, the sage then departed for the sacrifice of Mahendra;
Nimi, having appointed another as his preceptor, performed an excellent sacrifice.
Hearing that, Vasiṣṭha became exceedingly enraged and cursed the king again:
"O violator of your preceptor, let your body fall this very day!"
The king also cursed him, saying, "Let this [curse] fall upon you as well.
I have heard that both of them fell due to their mutual curses.
And how was the preceptor himself cursed by Videha, O Indra among kings?
This appears to me in my mind like a source of diversion, O best of monarchs. (27)
Janaka said:
"What you have spoken is true; there is nothing false in this opinion of mine.
Nevertheless, listen, O best of Brahmins: my guru is highly honored by me."
Having abandoned the company of your father, you wish to go to the forest;
there, you will undoubtedly have a close association with the deer. (29)
The great elements are everywhere; where will you find non-attachment? You always have anxiety for the sake of food; O Sage, how can you be free from anxiety? (30)
Just as you have anxiety even in the forest regarding your staff and deerskin,
so too do I have anxiety regarding the kingdom, whether I am contemplating it or not.
"You have indeed come to a distant land, afflicted by conceptual construction (vikalpa).
I have no conceptual doubt; I am entirely free from conceptual construction."
"O Brahmin, I sleep happily and I eat happily in every way;
because of the realization that 'I am not bound,' O Sage, I am always happy. (33)
But you are always miserable, bound by the suspicion that "I am bound.
Abandoning this suspicion, become happy and composed. (34)
"This body is mine, this bond is mine"—such is bondage; "it is not mine"—this is liberation.
Likewise, there is the firm conviction that wealth, home, and kingdom are not mine. (35)
Sūta said:
Having heard those words, Śuka became delighted in mind;
taking leave of him, he went quickly to the excellent hermitage of Vyāsa.
Seeing his son approaching, Vyāsa also attained great joy;
having embraced him and smelled the crown of his head, he inquired after his welfare once more. (37)
He remained there in that delightful hermitage by his father’s side, composed in mind,
perfected in the study of the Vedas, and an expert in all the śāstras.
Having seen the condition of the high-souled Janaka while he was established in his kingdom,
he attained supreme peace while remaining at his father’s hermitage.
The fortunate daughter of the Pitṛs, a beautiful woman named Pīvarī,
Śuka indeed made his wife, even though he was established on the path of Yoga.
He begot upon her exactly four sons:
Kṛṣṇa, Gauraprabha, Bhūri, and Devaśruta.
Having produced a daughter named Kīrti, the powerful son of Vyāsa gave her to the high-souled Aṇuha, the son of Vibhrāja.
The son of Aṇuha was the illustrious and powerful Brahmadatta, a knower of Brahman and protector of the earth, born from the daughter of Śakra. || 43 ||
After some time, having there obtained supreme knowledge and the unsurpassed path of yoga through the instruction of Nārada, [he attained his goal]. (44)
Then, having entrusted the kingdom to his son, he went to Badarikāśrama;
through the instruction on the seed-syllable of Māyā, his knowledge became unimpeded.
By the grace of Nārada, Śuka immediately attained that which bestows liberation; having abandoned all attachment to his father on the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, he was born [into that state]. (46)
Having resorted to vast meditation and remaining turned away from all attachments,
he flew up from the mountain peak and attained supreme perfection.
Moving through the sky with great splendor, he shone like the sun when the peak of the mountain was split in two by Śuka’s flight. 48.
Many portents arose, and Śuka ascended into the sky like the wind in the atmosphere, being praised by the celestial sages.
Shining exceedingly with splendor like a second sun,
Vyāsa, however, overcome by the pangs of separation, cried out repeatedly, "O son!"
Having gone to the mountain peak where Śuka was staying,
he then perceived Vyāsa, who was weeping piteously and overcome with exhaustion.
Then the witness residing in all beings gave his response;
even today, on that mountain peak, an echo clearly arises.
Beholding Vyāsa weeping, filled with grief, crying out "O son! O son! and overwhelmed by separation; || 53 ||
Śiva, having arrived there, enlightened the son of Parāśara:
"O Vyāsa, do not grieve; your son is the foremost among those who know yoga."
"He has attained the supreme goal, which is difficult for those of undisciplined self to reach;
therefore, O Aśoka, you who know what is sorrowless, you should not feel grief for him. (55)
"O sinless one, great fame has arisen for you because of that son.
Vyāsa said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Master of the World, my grief does not depart; what shall I do? (56)
"My eyes are not yet satiated today, longing for the sight of my son.
Mahādeva said:
"You shall see the most beautiful shadow of your son standing by your side. (57)
"O tiger among sages, O scorcher of foes, abandon your grief upon seeing her.
Sūta said: Then Vyāsa beheld the radiant shadow of his son.
Having granted him the boon, Hara vanished right there;
when Mahādeva had disappeared, Vyāsa returned to his own hermitage.
Even by the separation from Śuka, he was tormented and exceedingly distressed.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Śuka’s Marriage and Other Rites," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Birth of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Others.
The Sages said:
"O best of gods, Śuka indeed attained supreme perfection."
What did Vyāsa do after that? Tell us that in detail.
Sūta said: Those who were the disciples of Vyāsa, devoted to the study of the Vedas,
all departed previously to the surface of the earth after receiving his command.
Asita Devala, Vaiśampāyana, Jaimini, and Sumantu—all those whose wealth is asceticism—have likewise departed. || 3 ||
Having beheld these [disciples] and his son who had departed to the other world,
Vyāsa, overcome with grief, set his mind upon departing.
Vyāsa remembered in his mind that auspicious daughter of a Niṣāda,
his mother, who was on the banks of the Ganges, liberated yet filled with grief.
Having remembered Satyavatī, the sage Vyāsa, endowed with great splendor, left that best of mountains and returned to his own birthplace.
Having reached the island, he then asked, "Where has that lovely-faced maiden gone?
The Niṣādas told him, "The girl has been given to the king."
The King of the Dāśas, having honored Vyāsa with affection and having greeted him with a welcome,
spoke while joining his palms in reverence.
The king of the fishermen said:
"O sage, today my birth has become fruitful and our lineage has been purified,
since the sight of you— one who is difficult even for the gods to behold— has occurred."
"O best of the twice-born, tell me the purpose for which you have come;
O Lord, even my wife, wealth, and sons are at your disposal."
On the delightful bank of the Sarasvatī, Vyāsa established a circle of hermitages;
endowed with austerity, he remained right there, composed in meditation.
The two sons of Śāntanu of immeasurable luster were born of Satyavatī;
considering them to be his brothers, Vyāsa lived happily dwelling in the forest.
The king’s first-born son was Citrāṅgada, who was handsome, a scorcher of his enemies, and endowed with all auspicious marks. || 13 ||
A second son was born named Vicitravīrya;
he too was endowed with all virtues and increased the happiness of Śantanu. (14)
The first of his sons was Gāṅgeya, a great hero superior in strength;
likewise, two other sons of great might were born to Satyavatī. (15)
Seeing those sons endowed with all auspicious marks, the high-minded Śāntanu considered himself invincible even to the gods and other beings. (16)
Then, after some time had passed, the righteous Śāntanu, by the turn of time, cast off his body like a living being discards worn-out clothing.
When the king had passed away according to the law of time, Bhīṣma performed all the funeral rites and various kinds of charitable gifts in accordance with the prescribed rules.
Then the valiant one established Citrāṅgada on the throne;
he himself did not exercise sovereignty, and for that reason he became known as Devavrata.
But Citrāṅgada, the son of Satyavatī, was powerful, heroic, pure, and though intoxicated by his own prowess, he caused suffering to others. (20)
Then once, the mighty-armed one, surrounded by a great army,
roamed through the forest regions, slaying the deer and ruru antelopes that were fit for slaughter.
But the Gandharva Citrāṅgada, seeing that king traveling on the road,
ascended from the surface of the earth while seated in his excellent celestial chariot and approached him.
O ascetics, a great battle took place there between those two of equal prowess at the great site of Kurukṣetra for three years.
Slain in battle by the Gandharva, Bhīṣma swiftly reached the world of Indra; hearing this, he then immediately performed the funeral rites for him.
Gāṅgeya, though filled with grief, was surrounded by his ministers and installed the one named Vicitravīrya as the lord of the kingdom.
Later, having been urged by her ministers and by high-souled gurus,
and seeing her own son established in the kingdom, she was stricken with grief for her son.
Satyavatī, the woman of excellent complexion, became exceedingly pleased;
and Vyāsa, having heard that his brother had become king, was filled with joy. (27)
Having reached the prime of youth, the auspicious Bhīṣma, son of Satyavatī,
also gave thought to the marriage of his younger brother.
The King of Kāśī had three daughters endowed with all auspicious marks;
they were placed by that king in a svayaṃvara for the purpose of marriage.
Kings and princes by the thousands were summoned;
being duly honored, they assembled for the sake of the Svayaṃvara according to her wish.
There, the immensely powerful and heroic Bhīṣma,
having crushed the entire circle of kings with a single chariot, forcibly carried them away.
Having conquered all those kings and taken them with him, that radiant great chariot-warrior reached the city called Gajāhvaya by the strength of his arms.
Thinking of them as his mother, his sister, and his daughter,
he brought together three beautiful-eyed maidens.
Having quickly informed Satyavatī and summoned the twice-born,
he hurriedly questioned the astrologers who were learned in the Vedas regarding an auspicious day.
Having prepared the wedding requisites, when he indeed caused his own righteous brother Vicitravīrya to marry them; 35.
Then Jyeṣṭhā also, the beautiful-eyed daughter of Jahnu, bashful with her dark-cornered eyes, spoke thus to the three [others].
"O son of Gaṅgā, best of the Kurus, knower of dharma, lamp of your lineage!
At the svayaṃvara, King Śālva has been chosen by me in my heart. (37)
"I have indeed been chosen by that king, whose heart is filled with love.
O scorcher of foes, act now in a manner befitting this family. (38)
Therefore, I was previously chosen by him, and you are the best among the upholders of dharma;
you are powerful, O son of Gaṅgā, so do as you wish. (39)
Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus by that maiden there, the joy of the Kurus questioned the elderly brahmins, his mother, and likewise his ministers.
Having ascertained the opinion of all, Gāṅgeya, the foremost knower of dharma, said to the maiden, "Go, O lovely-faced one, according to your pleasure. (41)
Then, dismissed by him, she went to the abode of Śālva;
that woman of excellent limbs spoke to the king what was desired by her heart. (42)
"I have been released by Bhīṣma according to dharma because my mind was set on you;
I have come here, O Great King, so accept my hand today. (43)
"O best of kings, I shall become your lawful wife for all time;
you were thought of by me first, and I by you—of this there is no doubt. (44)
Śālva said:
"O lady of beautiful hips, you were seized by Bhīṣma while I was looking on;
since you have been placed upon his chariot by him, I shall not take your hand."
"What wise man would accept a maiden who is the leavings of another?
Therefore, I shall not accept her, for she has been abandoned by Bhīṣma as if she were my own mother. (46)
Weeping and lamenting, she was abandoned by that high-souled one;
returning again to Bhīṣma while weeping, she spoke as follows. || 47 ||
"O hero, Śālva will not accept me once I have been released by you; therefore, take me!
O illustrious one, you are a knower of dharma, for otherwise I shall surely die. (48)
Bhīṣma said:
"O lady of excellent complexion, how indeed can I take you when your mind is set elsewhere?
O beautiful woman, go quickly and without anxiety to your own father. (49)
Thus addressed by Bhīṣma, she indeed departed for the forest;
she performed austerities at a secluded and most purifying sacred site (tīrtha).
That king had two wives who were exceedingly beautiful and wealthy:
Ambālikā and Ambikā, both auspicious daughters of the King of Kāśī.
That mighty King Vicitravīrya took delight with those two women in various diversions, both in the palace and likewise in the groves.
O Indra among kings, having spent nine years enjoying delightful pleasures,
he met his death once again, seized by consumption (rājayakṣman).
When her son had died, Satyavatī was then overcome with extreme grief;
she caused the funeral rites for her son to be performed by the ministers.
Then, in private, she, being exceedingly distressed, said these words to Bhīṣma:
"O illustrious one, son of your father Śantanu, rule the kingdom! (55)
"Take your brother's wife and protect the lineage so that it does not come to ruin, just as the lineage of Yayāti did not. (56)
Bhīṣma said:
"O mother, you have heard the vow which was made by me for the sake of my father:
'I shall not rule the kingdom, nor shall I take a wife. (57)
Sūta said:
Then she became overcome with anxiety, thinking, "How shall the lineage continue?
For there is no happiness for me from idleness now that a kingless state has arisen. (58)
The son of Gaṅgā said this to her: "Do not worry, O beautiful lady;
provide a field-born son for Vicitravīrya. (59)
"Summon a man of noble birth from among the twice-born and unite him with your daughter-in-law;
for there is indeed no fault in this, even according to the Veda, when it concerns the preservation of the family. (60)
"O lady of pure smiles, having thus produced a grandson, give me the kingdom;
for I shall indeed uphold his command. (61)
Having heard those words of his, he went in his mind to Vyāsa Dvaipāyana, the sinless sage who was his own son born of a maiden.
As soon as he was remembered, the ascetic Vyāsa arrived;
having offered salutations to his mother, the radiant sage then stood before her.
Honored by Bhīṣma and respected by Satyavatī as he desired, the one of great splendor remained there like a second smokeless fire. || 64 ||
The mother said to that sage, "Now produce a handsome son for me from the field of Vicitravīrya, born of your own seed. (65)
Having heard his mother’s words, Vyāsa regarded them as the speech of a trustworthy person;
saying "So be it," he remained there and reflected upon the time of her season.
And when Ambikā, a woman in her courses, had bathed and attained union with the sage, she gave birth to a blind son of great strength. (67)
Seeing that her son was blind from birth, Satyavatī was also distressed;
she spoke to her second daughter-in-law, saying, "Produce a son immediately."
Then, when her season had arrived, Ambālikā united with Vyāsa;
thus, that woman conceived a child in the night.
That son Pāṇḍu, though born, was not considered fit for the kingdom;
therefore, at the end of the year, he sent his bride back once again for the sake of obtaining sons.
Then, having summoned Vyāsa, the best of sages, and having made her request to him,
she sent him at night to her excellent bedchamber.
The bride did not go there; instead, a maidservant was sent by her.
And from that maidservant, Vidura—the auspicious portion of Dharma—was born.
Thus were those three sons, Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the others, generated by Vyāsa as great heroes for the sake of protecting the lineage. (73)
All this has been narrated to you regarding the origin of his lineage;
O sinless ones, the lineage was protected by Vyāsa, who knew the dharma of brothers.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Others," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Origin of the Scent of Butter-Milk.
The sages said:
These words of yours concerning the cause of the embryo are truly wonderful.
A doubt has arisen here among all of us ascetics. || 1 ||
O wise one, Vyāsa’s mother was known by the name Satyavatī;
she was married in former times by King Śāntanu.
How was her son Vyāsa born, while she remained in her own home as a virtuous woman; and how was such a woman chosen again by King Śantanu?
O observer of noble vows, tell me the truth regarding how both sons were born from her;
O illustrious one, relate this most purifying story in detail.
"Tell us again of the birth of Vyāsa and likewise of Satyavatī;
for all these sages, firm in their vows, desire to hear it once more. (5)
Sūta said:
Having prostrated before the Supreme Power, the primordial Śakti who bestows the four goals of human existence,
I shall relate this auspicious ancient narrative.
By the mere utterance of which eternal perfection is attained—
even by means of a pretext, and especially in the case of the Vāgbhava seed-syllable.
For the sake of accomplishing all desired aims, the Goddess who bestows wished-for objects should be remembered in every way, with one's whole being, and by all means. 8.
There was a righteous and illustrious lord of the Cedi country named Rājoparicara, who was true to his word and a worshiper of the twice-born.
Pleased by his ascetic penance, Indra, desiring to do what was pleasing to him, gave him that beautiful and auspicious crystal celestial chariot.
Mounted upon that, the lord of the earth traveled everywhere by means of his divine [chariot];
because he was situated above the ground, that Vasu became known as Uparicara.
That king was renowned throughout all the worlds and ever devoted to righteousness;
his wife was a beautiful woman of noble form named Girikā.
And he had five sons of great heroism and immeasurable luster,
who were established as kings in various regions by that ruler of the earth.
Girikā, the wife of Vasiṣṭha, presented her desires at the proper time;
having bathed at the arrival of her season, she was pure for the rite of procreation.
On that day, the ancestors said to him, "Slay the deer.
Having heard that, he reflected upon his wife who was likewise in her season.
Having resolved that the father’s word must be carried out as a command of a guru,
the king went hunting while keeping Girikā in his mind.
While staying in the forest, that royal sage remembered his beloved wife in his mind—
she who was exceedingly endowed with beauty, like another goddess Śrī herself.
As he remembered that amorous woman, his semen was discharged;
the king, however, caught it as soon as it fell upon a banyan leaf.
"How might this semen, which has been shed in vain, not be lost?"—
thinking thus, the king then resolved upon his course of action once he recognized the time of her season.
"My vigor is in every way unfailing; of this there is no doubt.
I shall send this to my beloved"—thus he resolved in his mind. (20)
Having observed the time for the queen's conception,
he consecrated his semen with mantras and placed it within the fold of a banyan leaf.
Addressing the hawk standing at his side, the king said to the twice-born man:
"O illustrious one, take this and go quickly to my home."
O gentle one, taking this for the sake of my beloved, carry it home;
give it quickly to Girikā, for today is indeed her season.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, that best of kings gave the leaf to the hawk;
having seized it, he who was most skilled in flight quickly soared into the sky.
Then another hawk saw that bird coming, having caught the sky-faring hawk in the hollow of its beak as it was moving through the air. (25)
Perceiving it to be food, he quickly rushed toward the bird;
then, both of them engaged in a beak-duel in the sky.
As they were fighting, their semen fell into the waters of the Yamunā;
from that, those two birds emerged at will once the seed had fallen into the vessel.
At that time, a certain Apsaras named Ādrikā approached a Brāhmaṇa who had arrived there, intent upon his twilight prayers.
While she was sporting in the water, she became submerged;
then that woman of excellent complexion seized the foot of the twice-born man.
Then, devoted to breath-control (prāṇāyāma), he saw her moving at will and cursed her: "Since you have caused an obstacle to my meditation, become a fish! (30)
Cursed by that foremost of Brahmins, she became a dweller of the Yamunā;
indeed, the excellent Apsaras Adrikā took the form of a beautiful fish.
Then, that seed, fallen from the talons of the hawk,
was swiftly seized by the daughter of Vasava, who had assumed the form of a fish along with the mountain.
Then, after some time had passed, when the tenth month had arrived, the fisherman caught that beautiful female fish.
That fisherman quickly tore open her belly;
from that belly emerged a pair of human-shaped beings.
Seeing this wonder—the handsome young boy and the fair-faced maiden—he was then filled with the utmost amazement. (35)
He reported to the king that two sons had been born from the fish;
the king, filled with wonder, took up that auspicious son.
That king named Matsya was righteous and true to his promise;
he was the son of Vasu, possessed of great splendor, and equal to his father in prowess. (37)
Kālikā was swiftly given by Vasu to the one who lives by the water;
she became renowned by the names Kālī and Matsyodarī. (38)
Known by the name Matsyagandhā, that auspicious daughter of Vasu was born into the clan of a fisherman; she grew up in the house of the fisherman.
The sages said:
The excellent Apsaras Adrikā was cursed by the sage and became a fish;
she was torn open by a fisherman, died, and was then devoured. (40)
Tell me further, O Sūta, what happened to that Apsaras? How did the end of her curse come about, and how did she attain heaven? (41)
Sūta said:
When she had been cursed by the sage, she became filled with wonder;
then, like one distressed and weeping, she offered praise to the brahmin.
Then the compassionate Brahmin spoke to that weeping woman:

This meritorious history was thus proclaimed by the best of sages.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Devavrata," in the second book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Devavrata’s Vow.
The Sages said: O Sūta, the origin of the Vasus has been told by you, along with the cause of their curse.
Thus was the birth of Gāṅgeya narrated by Lomaharṣaṇa.
O knower of dharma, how did the virtuous Satyavatī, the mother of Vyāsa by name, become the auspicious Gandhavatī and obtain Śantanu as her husband?
Tell me that in detail: how was the daughter of the fisherman sustained by the king, the most excellent in righteousness? O you of noble vows, dispel my doubt.
Sūta said:
There was a royal sage named Śantanu who was constantly devoted to hunting;
he went to the forest, indeed slaying deer, buffaloes, and ruru antelopes.
For exactly four years, the king, sporting happily with his son,
attained bliss just as Hara does with Kumāra.
Once, while shooting arrows and slaying wild boars with his sword,
he reached a forest at the Kālindī, the best of rivers.
The lord of the earth smelled an unsurpassed, indescribable fragrance;
seeking its source, he then wandered through that forest.
This enchanting fragrance is not that of the mandāra, nor of musk; it is not of the campaka, nor of the mālatī, nor of the ketakī.
Nor has such a pure wind ever blown before;
from where does this wind come, which truly intoxicates my sense of smell? (9)
Thinking thus, Śantanu, deluded by his craving for the fragrance and following the wind, wandered through the forest region.
He beheld a beautiful woman standing on the riverbank; she was lovely to behold, yet devoid of ornaments, well-composed, and dressed in soiled garments.
Having seen that woman with dark-cornered eyes, the lord of the earth was struck with wonder;
he reached the firm conviction: "This is the fragrance of her body. (12)
That form was wonderful and exceedingly beautiful; likewise, the fragrance was esteemed by the entire world;
and her age was such that it was the auspicious bloom of fresh youth.
Upon seeing it, the king was indeed struck with wonder. || 13 ||
Who is she, and from where has she now arrived? Is she a celestial nymph, or perhaps a human woman, or indeed the daughter of a Gandharva or the maiden of a Naga?
I know not how he could have known the fragrant, lovely woman.
When the king, having thus reflected in his mind, could not reach a decision himself,
he then fell under the sway of desire while remembering Gaṅgā.
And he questioned his beloved who was standing on the bank.
"Who are you, my dear? Whose daughter are you? Why are you standing here in this desolate place, O fair-limbed one?
Tell me, O lovely-eyed one, are you married or are you unmarried? (16)
"O lotus-eyed one, having beheld you— my beloved and so enchanting— I have conceived love for you. Tell me, my dear, where are you going and what do you intend to do?"
And what else? All of this [I shall tell] to you in detail. || 17 ||
Thus addressed by the king, the lotus-eyed woman with beautiful teeth spoke to him with a smile:
"O King, know me to be the daughter of a fisherman."
And the maiden who remained obedient to her father's command. || 18 ||
"O King, I shall steer this boat here upon the water solely for the sake of the Dharma;
my father has gone home today as he pleases."
I speak the truth before you, O Lord of Wealth.
Having spoken thus, the young woman fell silent; the king, overcome by desire, addressed her:
"O heroine of the Kurus, make me your husband."
Surely your youth should not pass away in vain.
I have no second wife indeed;
O deer-eyed one, become my lawful wife.
I am your slave, always remaining under your command.
O beloved, the passion of my mind torments me.
"My beloved wife has departed, leaving me behind; no other has been chosen by me, O lovely one, and I am desolate.
Having beheld you, who are most beautiful in every limb—"
For my mind, once born, is indeed powerless. || 22 ||
Having heard the king's exceedingly charming words, which were like the taste of the flavor of nectar, the fisherman’s daughter,
endowed with a virtuous disposition, spoke to him.
Having summoned great fortitude, Sugandhā addressed the king.
O King, what you have said regarding me, I consider to be exactly so; yet know this according to your word:
I am not independent, O Kāma.
"Go quickly and ask my father, the giver, for that."
I am not a wanton woman, nor even the daughter of a fisherman;
I always abide under the authority of my father.
If that renowned father of mine grants permission, [then I shall go].
Take my hand; I am under your control. || 25 ||
O King, why does passion afflict you as it does me, who am in the bloom of youth?
For even in that state, she must indeed be protected.
Fortitude consists in adhering to the successive traditions of one's family conduct. || 26 ||
Sūta said:
Having heard her words, the king, deluded by lust,
went to the house of the fisherman's lord in order to beg for her hand.
Seeing the king approaching, the fisherman was filled with great astonishment;
having prostrated before the king, he spoke with palms joined in reverence. (28)
The fisherman said:
"I am your servant, O protector of the earth; my purpose has been fulfilled by your arrival. Grant me your command, O great king, as to why you have come here. (29)
The king said:
"O sinless one, I shall make this daughter of yours my lawful wife, if she is given to me by you; I tell you this truly. (30)
The fisherman said: "O King, if you desire my jewel of a daughter, she must be given;
I shall bestow her upon you, for she is never to be withheld."
"O Great King, her son shall be the lord of the earth after you;
he alone must be consecrated in every way, and no other son of yours. (32)
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of the fisherman, the king became overwhelmed with anxiety;
keeping the son of Gaṅgā in his mind, the monarch then said nothing.
Afflicted by desire and overcome by anxiety upon reaching home, the lord of the earth neither bathed nor ate; having returned to his palace, he did not even sleep.
Then, seeing him distressed with anxiety, his son Devavrata approached the protector of the earth and asked the cause of his dissatisfaction.
"Who is this invincible enemy of yours? I shall bring him under your control.
O tiger among kings, what is your anxiety? Speak the truth, O best of monarchs. (36)
O King, what is the use of that son being born who does not understand suffering and does not destroy it?
He has come merely to incur a debt.
This arises from a previous birth; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 37 ||
Having renounced the kingdom at his father's command, Rāma, the joy of the Raghus and son of Daśaratha,
departed for the forest accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and Jānaki.
Indeed, together with Mount Citrakūṭa. || 38 ||
O King, he was the son of King Hariścandra, renowned by the name Rohita;
he was then purchased by his father and brought to the marketplace.
He was surely delivered as a slave into the house of a Brahmin. || 39 ||
Likewise, the eldest son of Ajīgarta, renowned by the name Śunaḥśepa,
was purchased by his father and subsequently bound to the sacrificial post.
He was subsequently rescued by the son of Gādhi. || 40 ||
It is well known that the head of his mother was previously severed by the son of Jamadagni at his father's command;
and even such an improper act was performed by him.
And the most weighty permission of the guru has been granted. || 41 ||
"O King, this body of yours is [weak]; indeed, I am not capable [of this]. Tell me, what shall I do?
While I am present, you need not grieve; I shall accomplish this impossible task. (42)
"Tell me, O King, what is your anxiety?
Taking up my bow, I shall ward it off this very day,
provided that my body may find its purpose through this deed."
May your desire to act be unfailing.
Fie on that son who, though capable, does not fulfill the desired purpose of his father;
what is the use of such a son being born, however much he may be desired?
For he indeed shall dispel the anxiety of his father. || 44 ||
Sūta said: Having heard these words of his son, King Śāntanu,
feeling ashamed in his mind, quickly spoke to that son.
The king said:
"O son, my anxiety is great, for you are my only child—brave, exceedingly powerful, proud, and one who never turns his back in battles. (46)
"O father, for me who has but one child, this life is indeed in vain;
if you should die somewhere in battle, what shall I do, left without support? (47)
"This is my great anxiety; therefore, I am distressed today.
I have no other concern, my son, which I might speak of before you. (48)
Sūta said:
Having heard that, the son of Gaṅgā then questioned the elder ministers:
"The king does not speak to me today, being overwhelmed with shame. (49)
"Having inquired today of the king regarding the news of his wealth, you all must speak the truth to me with certainty; I shall do everything accordingly, free from anxiety. (50)
Having heard that, they went to the king and, having ascertained the cause, reported it;
and Gāṅgeya, having understood the matter, reflected upon it.
Accompanied by them, he then went quickly to the house of the fisherman;
bowing low with affection, the son of Jahnavī spoke this: || 52 ||
Gāṅgeya said:
"Give this slender-waisted daughter of yours to my father today; I entreat you.
Let this daughter of yours be my mother, and I shall be her slave, O scorcher of foes."
The fisherman said: "O illustrious prince, accept her as your wife;
let it be that no son of hers shall become king while you are still living. (54)
Gāṅgeya said:
"This daughter of the fisherman is not my mother; I shall certainly not rule the kingdom.
Her son will, in every way, rule the kingdom—of this there is no doubt. (55)
The fisherman said:
"I know that your son will indeed be powerful;
it is certain that he too will surely seize the kingdom by force. (56)
Gāṅgeya said:
"I shall certainly not take a wife in any way whatsoever;
this is my truthful word, dear father, for I have taken a vow of Bhīṣma."
Sūta said: Having heard that vow thus made, the fisherman gave Satyavatī, who was beautiful in all her limbs, to that king.
By this method, Satyavatī was chosen by him as his beloved;
however, O best of kings, he did not know of Vyāsa’s previous birth.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Devavrata’s Vow," in the second book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Birth of Yudhiṣṭhira and the Others.
Sūta said:
Thus, it is said, Satyavatī was chosen by Śantanu.
And two sons were born to her, who also died under the power of time.
Born from the seed of Vyāsa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra was indeed blind;
for upon seeing the sage, the lustful woman closed her eyes.
Since the princess became white in complexion upon seeing Vyāsa, Pāṇḍu was undoubtedly born from the wrath of Vyāsa. (3)
Vyāsa was gratified by that maidservant, who was skilled in the arts of love;
meanwhile, Vidura was born as a portion of Dharma, truthful and pure.
Although he was the younger, Pāṇḍu was established in the kingdom by the ministers;
however, because of his blindness, Dhṛtarāṣṭra was not appointed to office.
With Bhīṣma’s consent, the mighty Pāṇḍu obtained the kingdom;
then the wise Vidura was appointed to the task of counsel.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra had two wives: Gāndhārī, the daughter of Subala, is remembered as the first, and the second was a Vaiśya woman, well-established in the duties of a householder.
Likewise, two wives of Pāṇḍu are mentioned by those who recite the Vedas:
Śaurasenī and Kuntī, as well as Mādrī, who was born in the Madra country.
Gāndhārī gave birth to one hundred most beautiful sons;
the Vaiśya woman also gave birth to one beloved and dear son, Yuyutsu.
But Kuntī, while still a maiden living in her father’s house, first gave birth to the charming Karṇa from Sūrya; later, she became the wife of Pāṇḍu.
The sages said:
"O Sūta, O best of sages, what is this strange thing you speak?
A son was previously begotten by Pāṇḍu, and she was married by him."
Tell me in detail how Karṇa was born from Sūrya through a maiden;
and how, moreover, that maiden was born and subsequently married by Pāṇḍu.
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, when Kuntī, the daughter of Śūrasena, was still in her childhood,
she was requested by King Kuntibhoja as a bride.
That girl of lovely smiles was adopted as a daughter by Kuntibhoja and was assigned to serve the illustrious sage.
The sage Durvāsas arrived and stayed during the Cāturmāsya;
Kuntī performed service for him, and the sage attained great satisfaction.
He gave her an auspicious mantra by which, when invoked, the god himself would come and fulfill her desire as she wished.
After the Sage had departed, Kuntī remained in her house for the sake of making a decision; she reflected in her mind, "Which god should I invoke? (17)
Then the risen sun, the maker of day, was seen by her;
having uttered a mantra, she then summoned the one of fierce rays.
Having assumed a most beautiful human form from the maṇḍala,
he then descended from the sky into the vicinity of that temple.
Seeing the god approaching like the sun, the beautiful Kuntī was greatly amazed;
trembling, that passionate woman immediately became subject to the impurity of her menses.
Standing with palms joined in reverence, the beautiful-eyed lady spoke to the Sun: "I am well-pleased by your sight today; please depart for your own orb."
Sūrya said:
"O Kuntī, how is it that I have been summoned by you through the power of a mantra?
Why do you not accept me, even though I have come before you after being invoked? (22)
"O lady with dark-cornered eyes, I am afflicted by desire; favor me with your affection!
I have been brought under your power by a mantra; lead me away for our dalliance," he said. (23)
Kuntī said:
"I am a maiden, O knower of dharma; I bow before you, the witness of all.
Even to you, I am not to be spoken of ill, for I am a girl of noble family, O observer of excellent vows. (24)
Sūrya said:
"Great is my shame today if I go in vain;
I shall incur the reproach of all the gods, there is no doubt that I shall go [to hell]. (25)
O Kuntī, I shall today curse that brahmin who imparted this mantra, and I shall also curse you most severely if you do not serve me.
"O fair-faced one, let the duty of a maiden remain firm for you; indeed, people shall not know [of it]. Furthermore, a son equal to me shall be born to you. (27)
Having spoken thus to Kuntī, who was single-mindedly focused on him and deeply abashed, the Lord of Gods, Taraṇi, granted her most desired boon and departed after she had eaten. (28)
The fair-hipped woman, staying in a well-guarded chamber, conceived a child;
she alone was her nurse and beloved, for neither mother nor any other person was there.
But a son, exceedingly charming, was born secretly in the house,
endowed with a most beautiful armor and two earrings.
Then, like a second sun or another Kumāra,
the nurse took her by the hand and spoke to her who was deeply abashed.
"O lady with thighs like the trunk of an elephant, what anxiety do you harbor today? I am here.
Thus Kuntī spoke these words as she released her son from the basket. (32)
"What shall I do? Afflicted by my daughter, I must abandon you, who are as dear to me as my own life.
Unfortunate as I am, I forsake you, who are endowed with every auspicious mark. (33)
May that very Ambikā, the Goddess who possesses both qualities and the absence of qualities, the Sovereign of all,
and the Mother of the universe, grant her breast-milk.
O Kātyāyanī, bestower of desires!
When shall I behold my beloved’s lovely lotus-face, which is worthy of being cherished as my very life?
Having abandoned you, the son of the Sun, in the lonely forest like a wicked, wanton woman.
In a previous birth as well, the Mother of the three worlds was neither propitiated nor meditated upon, nor were Her bliss-bestowing lotus feet contemplated.
May it be for the long-term welfare of the goddess Śivā;
therefore, O son, I am perpetually unfortunate,
having abandoned you again in the forest.
"O beloved, I shall repent for the sin that I myself committed, which I have now recalled through my intellect. (35)
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to her son, Kuntī, being afraid of being seen by people, placed him— already contained within a basket— into the hands of a nurse.
Having bathed, Kuntī then remained in her father’s house;
meanwhile, the basket was carried away and indeed reached Adhiratha.
He was indeed requested as a son by the wife of the charioteer;
thus Karṇa, a powerful hero, was born and raised in the house of the charioteer.
Kuntī was a maiden married by Pāṇḍu at her svayaṃvara;
and the other wife was Mādrī, the auspicious daughter of the King of Madra. (39)
While sporting in the forest on a hunt, the mighty Pāṇḍu killed a sage who was enjoying himself in the woods, mistaking him for a deer.
Then Pāṇḍu was cursed by that enraged sage:
"If you engage in sexual union with a woman, then your death shall be certain. (41)
Thus cursed by the sage, Pāṇḍu was overcome with grief;
abandoning the kingdom, he lived in the forest, deeply afflicted by sorrow.
O best of sages, Kuntī and Mādrī, his two wives, went together and joined him, having taken refuge in the dharma of chaste women for the sake of service. (43)
Staying on the banks of the Gaṅgā and in the hermitages of sages, Pāṇḍu performed difficult austerities while listening to the treatises on dharma.
Once, while a discourse was underway concerning the Dharma,
the king heard well-articulated words spoken by a sage.
O scorcher of foes, there is no way for one who has no son to go to heaven;
therefore, by whatever means possible, one should bring about the birth of a son.

The son born of a portion [of the body], the son of an appointed daughter, the son born of the wife, the golaka, as well as the kuṇḍa, the son received with a pregnant bride, the maiden-born son, the purchased son, and likewise the one obtained in the forest; 47.
One given by someone else is for one who is incapable; those who take wealth [as payment] are considered sons of the lowest kind.
It is certain that each subsequent type of son is inferior to the preceding one. (48)
Having heard this, he then spoke to the lotus-eyed Kuntī:
"Go to the ascetic sage and quickly procreate a son. (49)
"By my command, there shall be no fault in you; for I have heard that in former times, a son was begotten by the high-souled king Saudāsa upon Vasiṣṭha. (50)
To him Kuntī spoke these words: "O Lord, I possess a mantra that grants all desires; it was given to me long ago by Durvāsas and bestows success in every way. (51)
"O King, whichever deity I invite with this mantra, that one, being thus invited, shall certainly come to my side in every way. (52)
At her husband’s word, she there recalled the supreme dharma of the gods;
having united with him, she gave birth to her first son, Yudhiṣṭhira.
Vṛkodara was the son of Vāyu, and Jiṣṇu was the son of Śatakratu;
thus, three sons of great strength were born to Kuntī year after year. (54)
Mādrī said to her husband Pāṇḍu, "O best of beings, grant me a son!
O great king, what shall I do? O Lord, destroy my sorrow. (55)
Requested by her husband, the compassionate Kuntī gave him the mantra;
Mādrī, for her part, remained faithful to her husband through the succession of their one son.
Then, remembering the two Aśvin deities, the daughter of the King of Madra,
that woman of excellent complexion, gave birth to two sons, Nakula and Sahadeva.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, those five Pāṇḍavas, born from the field [of Kuntī] and being sons of gods, were born in that forest at intervals of one year each.
Once, having seen Mādrī in a secluded hermitage, Pāṇḍu, overcome by intense passion and driven to a state of ruin, seized her.
Although she forbade him repeatedly with cries of "No! No! No! Do not!", he nonetheless embraced his beloved; then, by fate, he fell to the surface of the earth.
Just as a creeper clinging to a tree falls when the tree is cut down,
so did that young woman fall, weeping profusely.
Then Kuntī returned, weeping along with the children;
likewise, the highly fortunate sages returned upon hearing that tumultuous noise.
When Pāṇḍu had died, all the sages of rigid vows performed the funeral rites according to the rules along with the sacred fires and cremated him on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Placing her two infant sons before Kuntī and prioritizing righteousness, Mādrī—out of a desire for truth and in accordance with the conduct of virtuous women—agreed to go along with him. (64)
Having performed the offering of water and other rites, the sages dwelling there escorted Kuntī, together with her five sons, to Hastināpura.
And having learned that she had arrived, Gāṅgeya, Vidura, and all the others came together there to the city of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. || 66 ||
And all the people asked, "Whose sons are they, O lady of beautiful countenance?
Then Kuntī, having learned of Pāṇḍu’s curse, was overcome with grief.
Then all those gods, who were the sons of the deities born of the Kuru lineage, were summoned by Kuntī for the sake of gaining their confidence; thus she spoke to them. (68)
Having arrived in the sky, they then said to us: "O sons, our sons have indeed been honored by Bhīṣma with these words; O sons, you too are honored by the gods. (69)
Having taken those sons and their bride, Bhīṣma and the others all went to Nāgapura; with joyful hearts, they protected them according to their needs.
Thus were the sons of Pṛthā born and then protected by the son of Gaṅgā.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Yudhiṣṭhira and Others," in the second book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The narrative of the Pāṇḍavas and the description of the vision of those who had died.
Sūta said:
Draupadī was the wife of the five; she was honorable and devoted to her husbands.
She shall have five sons who will be exceedingly handsome, surpassing their fathers. || 1 ||
Likewise, Arjuna’s wife was the auspicious Subhadrā, the sister of Kṛṣṇa,
who had previously been carried off by Jiṣṇu with the consent of Hari.
Born from her was the great hero Abhimanyu, who was slain on the field of battle; it is said that the sons of Draupadī were also killed there.
Abhimanyu’s excellent wife, the exceedingly beautiful Vairāṭī, gave birth to a son at the end of his lineage; the infant died from the fire of Śaṅkara’s arrow. || 4 ||
But that son of his sister’s son was himself restored to life by Kṛṣṇa through his wondrous power and majesty, after having been consumed by the fire of the son of Droṇa’s arrows.
Because he was born as an excellent son when his lineage had become extinct,
he became renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Parīkṣit.
When his sons had been slain, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, exceedingly distressed and tormented by the arrows of Bhīma’s words, remained within the kingdom of the Pāṇḍavas.
And Gāndhārī likewise remained there, deeply afflicted by grief for her sons;
the distressed Yudhiṣṭhira performed service for them both day and night.
Vidura, whose soul was exceedingly devoted to dharma, enlightened him whose eye is wisdom;
then, with Yudhiṣṭhira’s permission, he remained by the side of his brother.
The righteous son of Dharma also attended upon his father,
as if making him forget the sorrow arising from grief for his son.
Just as that old man heard him, so did Bhīma, provoked to extreme rage,
strike him with his iron mace while making it heard to the people standing there.
All your sons have been slain by me in battle, you wicked and blind man; likewise, the heart-piercing blood of Duḥśāsana has been drunk by me most excessively.
"This shameless man eats the morsel given by me like a crow or even like a dog; that person lives in vain. (13)
Day after day, that righteous-souled man would cause such harsh words to be heard,
while consoling him by saying, "This man is a fool."
Having remained right there for eighteen years in a state of distress,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra requested the son of Dharma to depart for the forest.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra entreated the son of Dharma:
"Today I shall offer the funeral oblation for my sons according to the prescribed rites. (16)
Vṛkodara performed the funeral rites for all of them here, but he did not perform them for my sons, remembering our former enmity. (17)
"If you give me wealth after performing my funeral rites, I shall go to the forest to perform austerities that yield the fruit of heaven. (18)
Addressed in private by Vidura, the pure King Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma,
set his mind upon giving wealth to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who was seeking it.
Having summoned his own ministers, the lord of the earth said:
"O highly fortunate ones, I shall give wealth to my father who desires the funeral oblation."
Having heard those words of his eldest brother of immeasurable splendor,
the mighty-armed Māruti, filled with indignation, spoke regarding the seizure of this [monkey].
O illustrious one, why should wealth be given for the benefit of Duryodhana?
Even a blind man attains happiness; what folly can exceed this? (22)
"Because of your evil counsel, we have now encountered suffering in the forest, and the highly fortunate Draupadī has been brought here by that evil-minded one. (23)
O observer of noble vows, by your grace we have lived in the palace of Virāṭa, and all of us, possessed of immeasurable prowess, have entered into service under the King of Matsya. (24)
If you, the eldest, had not played [for stakes], how could this destruction have occurred?
Having slain the Māgadha, I became the cook for Virāṭa.
"How could the mighty-armed Jishnu, the son of Vasava, become Bṛhannalā, a dancing master for a boy, having assumed the dress of a woman? (26)
My hands, adorned with the Gaṇḍīva bow, have been made beautiful by bracelets;
having assumed this human form, what sorrow could there be beyond this? (27)
Seeing the braid fashioned upon her head and likewise the collyrium in her eyes, I shall take up my sword and swiftly cut them off; otherwise, there is no peace for me.
And without having consulted the protector of the earth, I cast fire into the house;
that sinful-souled Purocana, who desired to burn us, has himself been consumed by the flames. (29)
O lord of men, all the Kīcakas were slain by me without even asking you;
yet all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with their wife were not slain in such a manner.
O Indra among kings, your foolishness has resulted in the Gandharvas being released and Duryodhana and the others—your enemies—being bound in fetters at will. (31)
"O protector of the earth, though urged by you in every way, I do not wish to give wealth today for the sake of Duryodhana's benefit. (32)
Having spoken thus and Bhīma having departed, the King, the son of Dharma, surrounded by the three,
bestowed very abundant wealth upon Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, performed the funeral rites for his sons according to the prescribed rules and bestowed gifts upon the Brahmins.
Having performed all the funeral rites for the deceased, the king, accompanied by Gāndhārī,
Kuntī, and Vidura, quickly entered the forest.
Having been fully understood by Sañjaya, that high-minded one departed;
and though she was being restrained by her sons, the daughter of Śūrasena went forth.
Bhīmasena, lamenting along with the other Kauravas,
turned back from the banks of the Gaṅgā and all returned to Hastināpura.
Having gone to the auspicious hermitage of Śatayūpa on the bank of the Jāhnavī,
they constructed huts there with grass and performed austerities with concentrated minds.
When six years had passed for those ascetics who had departed, Yudhiṣṭhira, out of longing for his younger brothers, spoke this: (39)
"In a dream, I saw Kuntī, weak and dwelling in the forest;
my mind is now born with the desire to see my mother as well as my two fathers. (40)
And the high-souled Vidura and the highly intelligent Sañjaya—if this pleases you all, let us depart; such is my thought. (41)
Then all those brothers, as well as Subhadrā, Draupadī, the highly fortunate daughter of Virāṭa, and the citizens, [departed]. || 42 ||
Having arrived at the hermitage of Śatayūpa together with all the people, all those Pāṇḍavas, eager for a sight [of him], beheld him.
When Vidura was not seen, Dhṛtarāṣṭra then asked about his duty:
"Where is that wise Vidura? To him, the son of Ambikā replied. (44)
Free from passion, the steward wanders about, devoid of desire and without possessions;
dwelling in some solitary place, he meditates within upon the Eternal.
On the second day, while proceeding toward the Gaṅgā, King Yudhiṣṭhira beheld Vidura in the forest, emaciated by asceticism and firm in his vows.
Upon seeing him, the protector of the earth said, "I, Yudhiṣṭhira, salute you.
Having heard this, the sinless Vidura stood as if he were a pillar.
In an instant, the wonderful splendor that had issued from the mouth of Vidura merged into the mouth of Yudhiṣṭhira, because they were both portions of Dharma.
Then the steward (Kṣattṛ) gave up his life, and Yudhiṣṭhira grieved excessively;
the king made an effort for the purpose of cremating his body. 49.
As the king was listening, an incorporeal voice then spoke:
"This man is dispassionate; he is not worthy of being cremated. Go as you please, O lord of the earth."
Having heard this, all those brothers bathed in the pure waters of the Gaṅgā and went to Dhṛtarāṣṭra to inform him of everything in detail.
All the Pāṇḍavas remained there in that hermitage together with the citizens;
there, the son of Satyavatī and Nārada also arrived.
Other sages and great-souled beings had also come to Dharmanandana;
then Kuntī spoke to Vyāsa, who was seated there with his auspicious appearance.
"O Kṛṣṇakarṇa, my son was seen by me as soon as he was born; my mind suffers exceedingly. O one whose wealth is austerity, show him to me! (54)
"You are capable, O illustrious one; fulfill my desire, O Lord.
Gāndhārī said:
"O sage, I did not see Duryodhana when he went to the battlefield."
"O best of sages, show me that son of mine along with his younger brother—
Abhimanyu, the great hero who is dearer to me than my own life," Subhadrā said. (56)
"O Omniscient One, O Wealth of Austerity, I desire to see them; show them to me today.
Sūta said:
Having heard such words, the son of Satyavatī [replied].
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), that best of sages meditated upon the eternal Goddess when the time for twilight had arrived at the Ganges.
Having bathed in the waters of the holy river and summoned all of them, led by Yudhiṣṭhira, he offered praise to the Mother of the Universe.
To her who is primordial nature, whose delight is the Puruṣa, who possesses qualities as well as being beyond qualities,
the goddess of gods, whose form is Brahman, and who dwells on the Island of Jewels (Maṇidvīpa).
When there was neither Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor Īśvara, nor Vāsava, nor the Lord of Waters;
when there was neither the Lord of Wealth, nor Yama, nor Pāvaka—then you existed, O Goddess; I bow to her.
I am neither water, nor air, nor earth, nor space; nor am I their qualities, nor the sense organs,
nor the mind, nor the intellect, nor the sun, nor the moon.
At that time, O Goddess, you were she; I bow to her. || 62 ||
Having concentrated this world of living beings within the mind and having withdrawn the sheath of the subtle body through its qualities into meditative absorption,
you remain established in that absorption for the duration of a kalpa, independent of any external self.
There is no one at all who has attained discernment. || 63 ||
"This world prays for the sight of the dead once again;
O Mother, I am not able [to grant this], so show me quickly those people who have died."
Sūta said:
Thus praised then, the Goddess Māyā Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī summoned all the kings from heaven and revealed herself to them. 65.
Having seen Kuntī, Gāndhārī, Subhadrā, and the daughter of Virāṭa,
all the Pāṇḍavas rejoiced upon seeing their own people returned.
Then they were dismissed by that Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor,
who, having called to mind the Goddess Mahāmāyā, [made them vanish] like a rising magical illusion.
Then, having taken leave, all the Pāṇḍavas and the sages departed;
meanwhile, the king reached Nāgapura, recounting the story of Vyāsa along the way.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Pāṇḍavas and the Description of the Vision of the Deceased," in the second book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Ruru’s Life.
Sūta said: Then, on the third day, that king Dhṛtarāṣṭra—
Burned by a forest fire in the woods, he was accompanied by his wife and joined by Kunti.
Having departed on a pilgrimage to sacred fords and left the lord of the earth behind, Sañjaya heard from Nārada that King Yudhiṣṭhira had fallen into distress. || 2 ||
Then, when the thirty-sixth year had passed following the destruction of the Kauravas,
all the Yādavas met their end at Prabhāsa due to the curse of the Brahmins.
Having drunk the wine and become intoxicated, those high-souled ones fought with one another and met their destruction while Rāma and Kṛṣṇa looked on. || 4 ||
The lotus-eyed Lord Hari, Kṛṣṇa Rāma, abandoned his body, struck by the hunter’s arrow while fulfilling the curse. || 5 ||
Having heard that news of Hari’s abandonment of the body, Vasudeva then purified his mind by fixing Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī within it and gave up his own life-breaths.
Then Arjuna, having gone to Prabhāsa in great distress,
performed the funeral rites for all of them there according to what was appropriate.
Then, having observed the body of Hari and prepared a pile of wood,
the king had him cremated along with his eight wives.
Having cremated the body of Rāma along with Revatī in the fire,
Arjuna went to Dvārakā and caused the people to depart from the city.
Then that city of Vāsudeva was flooded by the ocean;
Arjuna, having taken all the people with him, departed at that time.
Then, on the road, the wives of Kṛṣṇa were plundered by thieves and Ābhīras;
all their wealth was seized, and Arjuna became devoid of luster.
Then, having arrived at Indraprastha, Vajra was made king by the son of Pārtha, who possesses immeasurable splendor; he was the son of Aniruddha, known by that name.
The suffering was told to Vyāsa, and by him that great chariot-warrior was addressed:
"O high-minded one, when you and Hari shall become [incarnate] once again..."
"Then, in a future age, your splendor shall become exceedingly fierce.
Having heard those words, Arjuna, the son of Pṛthā, went to the city of the Nāgas.
Distressed, he related the entire account to Dharmarāja, having heard of Hari’s abandonment of his body as well as the destruction of the Yādavas. (15)
The king set his mind on going toward the Himalaya mountains,
having installed the son of Uttara in the kingdom for thirty-six years.
Having ruled the kingdom in Hastināpura for thirty-six years, the king went forth to the forest together with Draupadī and his brothers. (17)
Having gone to the Himalayas, those six sons of Pṛthā gave up their lives;
Parīkṣit, the royal sage, was likewise exceedingly righteous toward all his subjects.
And that lord of kings protected [the earth] for sixty years without weariness;
he became devoted to hunting and went to a great forest.
At midday, the king himself, the son of Uttara, being thirsty, exhausted, and hungry, was searching for the wounded deer.
Oppressed by the heat, the king beheld a sage nearby;
seeing the sage absorbed in meditation, the thirsty king asked for water.
Remaining silent, he said nothing; then the king, afflicted by thirst, took up the dead snake with the tip of his bow and became enraged.
But with his mind possessed by Kali, he placed a serpent around his neck;
even when the serpent had been thus fastened, that best of sages said nothing.
Even having returned to his own home, the king did not waver from his state of meditative absorption;
his son, born of a cow, was exceedingly radiant and a great ascetic.
Then, while playing near the edge of the forest, Mahāśakta heard his friends say to his son: "Now your father’s head is upon your neck."
"O Lord of Sages, has some person killed and captured a snake?
Upon hearing those words of theirs, he then became exceedingly enraged. (26)
Taking water quickly in his hand, he angrily cursed the king:
"By him my father's throat was today besmeared with a dead serpent. (27)
Within seven nights, Takṣaka shall bite that sinful man;
then the disciple of the sage approached the king who was staying in his palace.
He reported the curse that had been delivered by the son of the sage;
and the son of Abhimanyu, having heard the curse indeed given by the twice-born one, [acted accordingly].
Realizing that it was unavoidable, he spoke to the elder minister:
"I have undoubtedly been cursed by one in the form of a brahmin out of hatred for me. (30)
"What should be done by me? O ministers, devise a remedy for this;
for those who expound the Vedas say that death is indeed unavoidable. (31)
Nevertheless, the effort prescribed by the scriptures must be performed in every way by the wise;
for some learned men who advocate skillful means have declared this. (32)
Through wise means, tasks are accomplished, and not by any other way;
indeed, the powers of gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs are difficult to fathom.
"What would have been the use of those well-prepared jewels if the wife of the sage, who was bitten by a snake and had died, had not been restored to life? (34)
Having given half of his lifespan to that excellent Apsaras, the sage said: "The wise should never place their trust in what is destined to be. (35)
"Let the ministers indeed observe a direct example in this matter:
is any man whatsoever seen anywhere, either in heaven or on earth? (36)
He who, having fixed his mind on the divine, remains free from worldly exertion,
becomes a detached ascetic and wanders in every way for the sake of alms.
Whether invited at will into the house of householders, or otherwise, whether obtained by chance, or even if thrown into the mouth by someone; 38.
And without effort, how could it enter his stomach? Effort must be exerted in endeavor; for even if success does not come, [the attempt itself is not in vain]. (39)
Then the wise man should take refuge in his mind, thinking, "It was destiny that stood thus.
The ministers asked: "Who was the sage who, having given half of his own life, restored his beloved to life? (40)
"How did she die, O Great King? Tell us that in detail.
The King said:
"The wife of Bhṛgu was a beautiful woman of excellent form named Pulomā. (41)
In that lineage was born the highly renowned sage named Cyavana;
and to Cyavana and Śaryāti was born a beautiful daughter named Sukanyā.
From her was born a glorious son, renowned by the name Pramati;
and the beloved wife of Pramati was the famous Pratāpinī.
A son named Ruru was born, who was likewise a supreme ascetic;
and at that time, there was a certain famous man named Sthūlakeśa.
He became endowed with ascetic power, righteous in soul, and esteemed for his truthfulness. In the meantime, the venerable Menakā, an excellent Apsaras, [arrived]. (45)
The most beautiful woman in the three worlds sported on the riverbank;
having conceived a child from Viśvāvasu, that lady of excellent complexion departed.
Having gone to the hermitage of Sthūlakeśa, the excellent Apsaras released the maiden, who was the most beautiful in the three worlds, upon the riverbank. (47)
Seeing the helpless girl, the best of sages, Sthūlakeśa, took her in; he nurtured her and gave her the name Pramadvarā.
In due time, she reached her youth, endowed with all auspicious marks;
and when Ruru saw that young woman, he was indeed pierced by the arrows of love.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Ruru’s Life Story," in the second book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The description of Parīkṣit’s dwelling in a guarded chamber.
Parīkṣit said:
"Afflicted by desire, that sage Ruru went and slept in his own hermitage."
The father asked that dejected one: "O Ruru, why are you despondent? (1)
Afflicted by excessive desire, he said to him: "In the hermitage of Sthūlakeśa, there is a maiden named Pramadvarā; she shall become my wife. (2)
Having gone there quickly, Pramati, having bewildered the great sage Sthūlakeśa and made him well-disposed, begged for that beautiful-faced woman.
Sthūlakeśa gave his word, "I shall give her on an auspicious day," and the two of them prepared the necessary materials for the wedding in the forest.
Pramati and Sthūlakeśa, those two great-souled ones, were staying nearby in the penance grove, intent upon marriage. || 5 ||
At that moment, a beautiful-eyed maiden, sporting in the courtyard of the house, touched with her foot a serpent that was fast asleep.
Then, having been bitten by the serpent, that beautiful woman died;
and upon seeing Pramadvarā dead, a great clamor arose.
All the sages gathered there cried out, overcome with grief;
seeing her fallen upon the ground, her father was exceedingly distressed.
Ruru wept for her who was lifeless yet blazing with splendor;
having heard that cry, he then arrived to see her.
There he beheld a beautiful woman fallen down as if still alive,
and he saw Sthūlakeśa weeping along with other excellent sages.
Ruru went outside his place and wept, overwhelmed by separation:
"Alas! By fate, this most extraordinary serpent has been sent! (11)
"This is indeed the cause of my suffering, intended to destroy my happiness;
what shall I do, where shall I go? My beloved, dearer than life itself, is dead. (12)
Separated from this beloved woman, I truly have no desire to live;
for I have not yet embraced that lady of beautiful limbs, nor have I kissed her face.
The taking of hands was not attained by me, unfortunate as I am, in any way;
likewise, the offering of parched grain into the fire was not performed with her.
Fie on this human state! May my life-breaths depart this very day;
for death does not come at will to one who is suffering. (15)
How then can that divine happiness desired on earth be attained?
I shall leap into a terrible lake; I shall throw myself into the fire. (16)
"I shall eat poison; having placed a noose around my neck, I shall give up my life.
Having lamented thus, Ruru then reflected further in his mind. (17)
Standing on that riverbank, he reflected upon a means [to end his life]:
"What fruit would there be for me in death? Self-destruction is difficult to overcome. (18)
My father would be grieved and my mother would be exceedingly sorrowful;
yet, the gods might be pleased by seeing me having renounced my life according to their will. (19)
Everyone would be filled with joy at my passing; of this there is no doubt.
What benefit could possibly be rendered to a beloved one in the world beyond? (20)
Even if she were to die by her own hand upon my death, or even if she were tormented by the pain of separation,
that beloved would not belong to me in the next world, for I am a self-killer.
"For this reason, there would be no fault in me if he were dead, but certainly not if he were alive.
Having reflected thus, Ruru bathed there, sipped water, and stood purified.
Having taken water in his hand, that sage spoke these words:
"Whatever merit has been performed by me, such as the worship of the gods and other good deeds... (23)
If the Gāyatrī has been consecrated, then the gurus have been honored with devotion, the oblation offered, the recitation performed, the penance accomplished, and all the Vedas studied. 24.
"May Ravi, propitiated by him, restore my beloved to life;
if my dear wife does not live, then I shall give up my life. (25)
Having spoken thus and propitiated the deities, he threw that water upon the ground.
While he was lamenting in this manner, his wife spoke to him in her distress. (26)
Then the divine messenger approached Ruru and spoke these words.
The divine messenger said: "O Brahmin, do not act rashly; how can the beloved be restored to life once she is dead?"
"The life of this fair-hipped daughter of a Gandharva and an Apsaras has come to an end; she died while still unmarried. O you of lovely limbs, desire another. (28)
"Why do you weep, O one of very poor intellect? What pleasure do you have with her?
Ruru said:
"O messenger of the gods, I shall certainly not choose any other woman. (29)
"Whether he lives or does not live, I must die now.
Having understood his obstinacy, the messenger of the gods was filled with joy. The king said: [30]
He spoke these words, which were truthful, real, and exceedingly captivating:
"O best of Brahmins, hear the means that was ordained by the gods in the past. (31)
"By the gift of half your life, restore Pramadvarā to life at once.
Ruru said:
"I shall give half my life to the maiden; of this there is no doubt. (32)
"Today let my beloved rise up, her life-breaths restored.
Then Viśvāvasu arrived there by means of a celestial chariot.
Having quickly learned that his daughter Pramadvarā had died from the world of heaven,
O best of men, the king of the Gandharvas and the excellent messenger of the gods [then appeared].
Approaching Dharmarāja, they addressed him with these words:
"O Dharmarāja, she is the wife of Ruru and likewise the daughter of Viśvāvasu. (35)
"O son of the Sun, the maiden Pramadvarā, who was bitten by a serpent, has now died; she shall live for half the lifespan of Ruru, who was himself desirous of death. (36)
"Let the slender-limbed girl arise by the power of her observance of vows.
Dharma said: "O messenger of the gods, if you desire the maiden who is the daughter of Viśvāvasu," (37)
"Arise with half of my life; go and restore Ruru.
The king said:
"Having been addressed thus, he then went and restored Pramadvarā to life. (38)
The divine messenger, acting with haste, delivered her to Ruru;
then, on an auspicious day, she was married by Ruru according to the prescribed rites. (39)
In this way, by means of the application of skillful methods (upāya), she who was dead was then restored to life;
indeed, one must employ skillful methods in every respect as sanctioned by the scriptures. (40)
"By means of gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs, one's life may be protected according to the prescribed rules.
Having spoken thus to his ministers and having appointed excellent guardians, the king—
Then, having had an excellent seven-storied palace constructed,
the son of Uttara ascended it at that very moment along with his ministers.
Heroes who possessed jewels and mantras were stationed there for protection;
then the king dispatched the sage Gauramukha.
For the sake of winning favor from his servant, he said "Forgive me" again and again;
meanwhile, for the purpose of protection, he dispatched Brahmins who were masters of perfected mantras here and there.
The minister’s son remained there and stationed elephants;
no one at all was allowed to ascend that well-guarded palace.
Even the wind did not move there; it was warded off at the entrance.
And the king, remaining stationed there, provided all kinds of food, both solid and soft.
Having performed his daily rites, such as bathing and the twilight prayers, right there,
the king remained in that place and carried out all his royal duties.
Having consulted with his ministers and even counting the days,
there was a certain Brahmin named Kaśyapa, the best among counselors.
And he heard that the curse had been incurred by the high-souled king;
then Kaśyapa, that best of the twice-born who was desirous of wealth, reflected upon it. (49)
"I shall go to where the king, cursed by the twice-born, resides. Having thus resolved, the brahmin departed from his own home onto the road.
Kaśyapa, the best of sages, was a learned knower of mantras who desired wealth. || 51 ||

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of King Parīkṣit’s Residence in a Secret Chamber," in the second book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Sūta said: On that very day, Takṣaka by name [approached] that best of kings for the purpose of his death.
Knowing he had been cursed, Puruṣottama quickly departed from his home.
Takṣaka emerged onto the road in the guise of an old Brahmin;
he saw Kaśyapa walking along the path toward the king.
That serpent questioned the Brahmin, the master of mantras:
"Where are you going in such haste, and what task do you wish to accomplish? (3)
Kaśyapa said: "Takṣaka will burn the best of kings, Parīkṣit;
therefore, I am going there in haste to make the king free from fever."
"O best of Brahmins, I indeed possess a mantra that destroys poison;
I shall certainly restore him to life now, for he must live. (5)
Takṣaka said:
"O Brahmin, I am that serpent; I shall consume that lord of the earth.
Turn back, for you are not capable of treating one bitten by me."
Kaśyapa said: "O serpent, I shall undoubtedly restore to life the king who has been bitten by you and cursed by the twice-born, by the power of my mantras, if you so desire."
Takṣaka said:
"O sinless Brahmin, if you wish to live after I have bitten the best of kings, then display the power of the strength of your mantras before me."
"And today I shall indeed burn this banyan tree with my venomous fangs.
Kaśyapa said:
"O best of serpents, I shall restore to life that which has been bitten or even burnt by you."
Sūta said:
A serpent bit the tree and reduced it to ashes;
he then spoke again to Kaśyapa, "O best of the twice-born, bring this back to life."
Having seen the tree reduced to ashes by the serpent’s poisonous fire, Kaśyapa gathered all the ashes together and spoke these words: || 11 ||
Behold today the power of my mantra, O best of serpents! O you of great venom, I shall restore this banyan tree to life even as you watch.
Having spoken thus, Kaśyapa, the best among those who know the mantras, took water and sprinkled that heap of ashes with that very water consecrated by mantras.
From the sprinkling of that water, a beautiful banyan tree grew as before;
seeing that the mountain had come back to life, Takṣaka was filled with wonder.
The Naga said to Kaśyapa: "For what purpose is this exertion of yours?
I shall fulfill that desire; speak, O Vāḍava, what you wish. (15)
Kaśyapa said:
"O serpent, thinking the king to be a seeker of wealth, I departed from my home after having cursed him; however, I have now come to benefit that best of kings through my knowledge. (16)
Takṣaka said:
"O best of Brahmins, take as much wealth from the king as you desire;
I shall give it to you. Go to your own home, for by this I shall have my wish fulfilled. (17)
Sūta said:
Having heard those words of his, Kaśyapa, the knower of the supreme truth, reflected in his mind again and again: "What shall I do? (18)
If I were to take the wealth and go to my own home again, I would have no reputation in the world due to my reliance on greed. (19)
If that best of kings lives, my fame shall be unshakable;
there will be manifold acquisition of wealth, and merit shall arise from his living. (20)
Fame should certainly be protected; fie on wealth that is devoid of fame!
In former times, Raghu gave away his entire possessions to a brahmin for the sake of glory. (21)
How could I neglect King Hariścandra, who is being consumed by the fire of grief, for the sake of my own fame, as was done extensively by Karṇa? 22.
O Queen, as long as I live today, there will be happiness for all people;
in a kingless state, the destruction of the subjects will surely come to pass—of this there is no doubt. (23)
"If the king dies, I shall incur the sin of destroying the subjects, and there will be infamy among the people due to my greed for wealth. (24)
Having reflected thus in his mind and performed meditation, that most wise Kaśyapa perceived that the king’s life had come to an end.
Having perceived through meditation that the king’s death was imminent, the righteous-souled Kaśyapa went home, taking wealth from Takṣaka.
Having turned Kaśyapa back, the serpent, desiring to kill the king on the seventh day, went quickly to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
At the edge of the city, he heard that Parīkṣit was staying in a palace,
being diligently guarded at will by means of jewels, spells, and medicinal herbs.
Then the Naga, overcome by anxiety and distressed by the fear of the Brahmin’s curse, reflected through his yogic power: "How may I enter the house? (29)
How shall I deceive this wicked-acting king—this fool who has been destroyed by the Brahmins' curse, this rogue who caused suffering to the Brahmins? (30)
"Born as one of the Pāṇḍava lineage, no one could possibly be such as this, by whom a dead snake was placed around the neck of an ascetic. (31)
Having committed a censurable deed and knowing the course of death,
the king stationed guards in his palace and ascended to the upper story.
"The king has cheated death and now lives free from anxiety;
how shall I consume him, though urged by the words of the Brahmins? (33)
The dull-witted man does not realize that death is indeed irreversible;
therefore, having stationed his guards, he now rejoices while mounted upon his palace.
If death has indeed been ordained by Fate of immeasurable splendor, how could it be averted even by millions of efforts? (35)
And the king, the heir of the Pāṇḍava, though knowing that [his father] had met his death, remained unperturbed in his station, fixing his mind upon living. (36)
A king ought to perform meritorious acts such as giving charity in every way;
for by means of righteousness, disease is destroyed and one’s lifespan becomes eternal. || 37 ||
Having performed the funeral rites for one who has not been killed, one should carry out the rituals of bathing, giving gifts, and so forth;
[only] in this way does death lead to the heavenly realm, whereas otherwise it leads to hell. (38)
The sin committed by him through the oppression of the twice-born, as well as that of the king, and the terrible curse of the Brahmins, indeed manifested when death was near. (39)
There was no brahmin by his side who could awaken him;
for death, ordained by the Creator, is altogether and in every way unavoidable.
Having reflected thus, that serpent sent those excellent serpents, who were standing near his own snakes,
after having made them wear the garb of ascetics.
Then the Naga Takshaka, having taken fruits, roots, and other offerings for the king,
himself entered into the midst of a fruit in the form of an insect.
Then those nāgas emerged quickly, taking fruits with them;
having reached the royal palace, they stood near the mansion.
Seeing the ascetics, the guards asked about their intentions;
they replied, "We have come today from the penance grove to see the king."
We have arrived here with Atharvan mantras to nurture this heroic son of Abhimanyu, a sun to his lineage and beautiful to behold. (45)
"Announce to the king that the sages have arrived for an audience;
having performed our ablutions and given him sweet fruits, we shall depart. (46)
In the lineage of the Bharatas, gatekeepers have never been seen;
nor indeed has it ever been heard that ascetics were forbidden from having an audience with the king. (47)
"Let us go to that place where King Parīkṣit is;
having honored him with blessings and received his permission, we shall depart. (48)
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of those ascetics, the guards,
regarding them as Brahmins, replied to them as if following the king's command.
"O Brahmins, it is our thought that you should not have an audience with the king today;
tomorrow, all the ascetics must come here to the king's palace."
O best of sages, this palace is without stairs for the Brahmins;
it was undoubtedly constructed by the king out of fear of the Brahmins' curse. (51)
Then the Brahmins said to them: "Let the well-guarded attendants cause the fruits, roots, and water, as well as the blessings of the Brahmins, to be presented to the king."
