Having gone, those people informed the king that the ascetics had arrived;
the king said, "Bring indeed whatever fruits, roots, and so forth there may be."
"Ask the ascetics about your business; you may come again tomorrow morning. Offer my salutations to them, for there shall be no audience with me today. (54)
Having gone there and gathered whatever fruits, roots, and other provisions there were,
they presented them to the king with great respect.
When those elephants, disguised in the form of Brahmins, had departed, the king took the fruits and spoke thus to his ministers: || 56 ||
"Let my friends eat all these fruits today; as for me, O brahmins, I shall eat this one great fruit offered by you. (57)
Having spoken thus and given that fruit to his friends, the son of Uttara,
the king himself took the ripe fruit in his hand and split it open.
When the fruit was split open by the king, a tiny worm appeared therein;
it had black eyes and copper-colored limbs, and it was seen by the monarch himself.
Seeing him, the king then spoke to his astonished ministers:
"The sun is setting; today I have no fear from poison."
"I accept that curse; let this worm bite me.
Having spoken thus, that lord of kings placed it upon his neck. (61)
When the lord of day had set, Kīṭaka was then seized by the throat;
he became Takṣaka, terrifying and appearing like Death itself.
The king was enveloped by it and the lord of the earth was bitten;
the ministers were struck with amazement and wept, being deeply distressed. || 63 ||
Beholding that serpent of terrible form, they fled, afflicted by fear; all the guards cried out, and a great tumult of "Alas! Alas! arose.
Enveloped by the coils of the serpent and having lost much of his manliness, the king said nothing; nor did the son of Uttara move.
A terrible, venomous flame of fire rose up from the mouth of Takṣaka and,
blazing forth, quickly rendered the king lifeless.
Having swiftly taken the life of the king, Takṣaka departed into the sky;
the people here saw him as he was setting the world ablaze.
Deprived of life, the king fell like a tree consumed by fire;
and all the people cried out upon seeing the lord of men dead.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Death of Parīkṣit," in the second book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Serpent Sacrifice.
Sūta said:
Having observed that the young king was indeed lifeless, and his son as well...
And all the ministers performed the rites for the sake of the next world.
They placed the lord of the earth— whose body had been burnt on the bank of the Gaṅgā and was mostly reduced to ashes— upon a funeral pyre prepared with aloe-wood.
And for him who had died an untimely death,
his domestic priests performed the funeral rites according to the prescribed rules with Vedic mantras.
They gave gifts to the Brahmins—cows, gold as was appropriate, various kinds of food, and diverse garments. || 4 ||
At that very moment, the ministers placed the infant son, who increased the joy of the people,
upon that auspicious throne.
The people of the city and the countryside made that infant their king,
naming him Janamejaya, for he was endowed with the marks of royalty.
The nurse instructed him in all the royal insignia;
growing day by day, he became possessed of great intelligence.
And when the eleventh year had arrived, the family priest imparted to him the knowledge appropriate for him, and he received that appropriate knowledge.
Kṛpa imparted the complete and well-refined science of archery (dhanurveda) to him,
just as Droṇa did for Arjuna and Bhārgava did for Karṇa.
Having attained knowledge, he became powerful and difficult to overcome;
he reached the further shore of both the science of archery and the Vedas, and was a knower of the supreme truth.
Skilled in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras, truthful, and having conquered his senses,
that righteous-souled one ruled the kingdom just as Dharmaputra did in ancient times.
Then, it is said, the king named Suvarṇavarman, the lord of Kāśī,
gave his auspicious daughter Vapuṣṭamā to the son of Parīkṣit.
Having obtained her, whose outer corners of the eyes were dark, Janamejaya rejoiced, just as a king of old did upon obtaining the beloved daughter of the King of Kāśī. 13.
Vicitravīrya rejoiced with Subhadrā just as Arjuna did;
the protector of the earth sported in the forests and groves.
Just as Śatakratu is with Śacī, who has eyes like lotus petals,
so too did his subjects become well-pleased and cherished in happiness.
The ministers, skilled in action, performed all their duties in every respect.
At that very time, however, there was a sage named Uttaṅka.
Harassed by Takṣaka, he went to Hastināpura, reflecting, "Who could provide redress for this enmity? (17)
Thinking him to be the son of Parīkṣit, he approached that king:
"O best of kings, you do not distinguish between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done at this time."
Today you do what ought not to be done, and you indeed do not do what ought to be done;
why then do I entreat you today, when you are devoid of resentment and lacking in effort? (19)

[To one who] was ignorant of enmity and unacquainted with the sacred texts, and possessed of childish behavior, Janamejaya said: "What enmity was not known by me? What retaliation was not performed by me? (20)
"Tell me that, O illustrious one, so that I may do what must follow.
Uttaṅka said:
"O King, your father has been slain by the evil-minded Takṣaka."
"Summon your ministers and ask them about the destruction of your father.
Sūta said:
Having heard those words, the king questioned his most excellent ministers.
They said, "He was indeed bitten by a serpent and died due to the curse of a brahmin.
Janamejaya said:
"In this case, the curse by the sage was surely the cause of the king's death. (23)
"But what was Takṣaka's fault? Tell me, O best of sages.
Uttaṅka said:
"Having been given wealth by Takṣaka, Kaśyapa was dissuaded [from going]. (24)
"O King, was that Takṣaka not your enemy and the slayer of your father?
O King, in former times the wife of Ruru was bitten by a serpent and died. (25)
But the beloved, though unmarried by the sage, was restored to life by Ruru;
and there he made an exceedingly terrible vow.
"Whichever snake I see, that one I shall surely slay with my weapon.
Having thus made this vow, Ruru then stood with weapon in hand.
O King, he roamed the earth here and there, slaying snakes;
one day, in the forest, he encountered a terrible Dundubha snake afflicted by old age.
Seeing him, he raised his staff and approached to kill him;
the enraged Brahmin struck him, and then the ḍuṇḍubha spoke to him.
"I have done you no wrong, O Brahmin; why indeed do you strike me?
Ruru said:
"My beloved, dearer to me than life itself, was bitten by a serpent and has died."
"O serpent, this vow was made by me while I was in distress.
The *ḍuṇḍubha* said:
"I do not bite you; indeed, there are other serpents who bite. (31)
"You ought not to harm me by means of your body.
Uttaṅka said:
"Having heard that captivating human voice spoken by the serpent... (32)
Ruru asked, "Who are you, and why have you come to this state of a water-snake?
The serpent replied, "O Brahmin, I was formerly a Brāhmaṇa; my friend, O sage, was named Khagama."
That brahmin, the best among the upholders of dharma, truthful and with senses conquered, was deceived by me through folly because I made him believe a blade of grass was a snake. (34)
Having been brought to extreme fear while staying in the Agnihotra house,
I was cursed by him as he was terrified, agitated, and trembling violently.
"O dull-witted serpent, you by whom I have been provoked!
This best of the twice-born was excessively propitiated by me, yet he has been treated thus by you, O serpent. (36)
Then, having attained some degree of calm after that anger, Ruru said to me:
"He shall be released from this curse; he will become a serpent. (37)
"He spoke these words to me: 'Surely you are the son of Pramati.
I am that serpent Ruru; now listen to my supreme words. (38)
Non-violence is the supreme duty of Brahmins; there is no doubt about this.
A wise Brāhmaṇa must practice compassion toward all beings. (39)
"O best of Brahmins, violence is not considered sacrificial except in the context of a sacrifice.
Sūta said:
Then that Brāhmaṇa Ruru was released from his birth as a serpent.
Having brought about the end of his curse and abandoned all violence, he married the young woman; she who had died was restored to life once more.
Remembering the enmity, you have carried out the slaughter of all the serpents;
yet now, having cast aside that enmity, you behave toward the snakes with kindness.
Free from anger toward those who killed his father, O best of the Bharatas,
his father died in the intermediate space (antarikṣa), deprived of ritual bathing and the giving of gifts.
O Indra among kings, perform his deliverance by slaying the serpents;
for he who does not avenge his father's enmity is dead even while living. (44)
"O best of kings, your father shall remain in an evil state as long as you do not perform a sacrifice by making your mother the sacrificial victim. (45)
"O Great King, remembering the enmity toward his father, he performed a snake-sacrifice.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of his, King Janamejaya then—
Extremely distressed, he shed tears from both eyes and said:
"Fie upon me, the evil-minded one who vainly indulges in pride! (47)
"Since my father, tormented by serpents, has met a terrible fate, I shall today commence a sacrifice and perform the funeral rites for my father. (48)
Having undoubtedly slain the serpents in the blazing fire, the king summoned all his ministers and spoke these words. (49)
"Let the best of ministers prepare the sacrificial materials as is appropriate, after having measured out an auspicious site on the bank of the Gaṅgā with the most excellent brahmins. (50)
"O ministers, being composed, construct for me today a beautiful pavilion with a hundred pillars, and indeed, let an altar for the sacrifice be prepared. (51)
As a constituent part of that, the extensive Sarpa-satra (Serpent Sacrifice) was indeed to be performed;
Takṣaka was the sacrificial animal there, and the great sage Uttaṅka was the Hotṛ priest.
"Let the Brahmins—who are all-knowing and masters of the Vedas—be summoned quickly.
Sūta said:
Then the wise ministers acted according to the king's words.
While all the preparations for the sacrifice were being made and the altar of the sacrifice was being extended, Takṣaka went there as the oblation was being offered.
Afflicted by fear toward Indra, he said, "Save me!
Having comforted him who was terrified by fear and having seated him upon his own throne, [Indra spoke]. (55)
He granted him complete fearlessness, saying, "O serpent, be free from fear.
Knowing that he had sought refuge with Indra, the sage likewise granted him protection from fear.
Uttaṅka, having become anxious, sent an invitation including Indra;
at that time, the descendant of the Yāyāvara lineage was summoned by Takṣaka.
The righteous-souled sage named Āstīka, the son of Jaratkāru,
arrived there and, though still a youth, offered praise to Janamejaya.
Seeing that boy so highly learned, the king honored him;
having honored him, the king gratified him with his desired objects.
But that illustrious king chose instead, "May this sacrifice cease";
for he was bound by truth, and thus he was entreated by him once again.
He brought the fire-sacrifice for the serpents to an end at the word of the sage,
and had Vaiśampāyana recite the Bhārata in detail.
Even after hearing this, the king did not attain peace;
the monarch questioned Vyāsa, "How may my peace be restored? (62)
My mind is burning intensely; tell me, what shall I do? My father, the son of a Pārtha and a daughter, has died like one who is truly unfortunate.
O illustrious Vyāsa, for Kṣatriyas, death in battle is preferable;
whether it be death on the battlefield or at home according to the prescribed rites.
"My father did not die; he died helplessly in the intermediate space.
O son of Satyavatī, tell me the means for pacifying this situation. (65)
So that my father, who has fallen into an evil state, may quickly go to heaven.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Serpent Sacrifice," in the second book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 11.
Regarding the discourse between the listener and the speaker,
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, [spoke].
There, in that assembly, he spoke these words to the king.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the ancient, secret, and wonderful Purāṇa named Bhāgavata, which is meritorious, auspicious, and filled with various narratives. (2)
O King, that which was previously taught by me to my own son Śuka,
I shall now indeed cause you to hear, for it is my supreme secret.

It is said that by hearing this work, which is extracted from all the scriptures, one obtains the cause of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; it is eternally auspicious, bestows happiness, and is a source of excellence.
Janamejaya said:
Whose son is this Āstīka, and for what purpose has he come to cause an obstacle?
O Lord, what is his motive here in the protection of the serpents?
O highly fortunate one, relate this narrative in detail;
likewise, O observer of noble vows, speak at length concerning the entirety of the Purāṇas.
Vyāsa said:
The peaceful sage Jaratkāru did not enter the householder stage of life;
while in the forest, he beheld his own ancestors hanging in a pit.
Then they said to him: "O son, take a wife, so that we may indeed attain supreme satisfaction;
for when you, our son, are endowed with virtuous conduct, we shall surely go to heaven, freed from all suffering. (8)

He then said to them: "When I obtain a wife who is of equal status, unsolicited, and exceedingly submissive, then I shall undertake the building of a house; this I speak as the truth, for such was the command of my ancestors."
Having spoken thus to them, the twice-born Jaratkāru departed for the sacred fords;
at that very moment, the serpents were cursed by their mother, saying, "Fall into the fire!"
The two wives of the sage Kaśyapa, Kadrū and Vinatā,
having seen the horse on the chariot of the Sun, spoke to one another.
Having seen him, Kadrū then said this to Vinatā:
"O blessed lady, what is the color of this horse? Speak the truth without delay. (12)
Vinatā said:
"This king of horses is indeed white; or what do you think, O auspicious one? You too tell me its color, and then let us make our wager. (13)
Kadru said:
"O lady of pure smiles, I consider this horse to be black in color;
come with me, O beautiful one, for the sake of becoming my slave. (14)
Sūta said:
And Kadrū spoke to all her sons, the serpents who remained under her control:
"Make as many dark-colored young snakes as there are hairs on the horse's body."
Some there said, "No," and he then cursed them:
"At the sacrifice of Janamejaya, you shall indeed go into the fire."
Others, the serpents, made the horse variegated with colored coils;
having entwined his tail, they did so out of a desire to please his mother.
The two sisters, having gone together, beheld the horse;
seeing that brindled horse, Vinatā was exceedingly distressed. (18)
Then her son Garuḍa, possessed of great strength, arrived;
seeing his mother distressed, that devourer of serpents questioned her.
"O Mother, why are you so deeply distressed? To me, you appear as if weeping, even though I, your son, am alive, as are the others and the charioteer of the Sun. (20)
"You are suffering; therefore, fie upon the life of you both, O lovely-eyed one!
What is the use of a son being born if the mother is in great distress? (21)
"Tell me the reason, O mother; I shall free you from your distress.
Vinatā said:
"O son, I am a slave to my co-wife. Why should I speak in vain, being as I am wounded? (22)
"O son, she says this to me today, and because of that I am sorrowful.
Garuḍa said:
"I shall indeed carry her to wherever she is eager to go."
"Do not grieve, O auspicious lady; I shall make you free from anxiety.
Vyāsa said: Having been addressed thus, Vinatā then went to the side of Kadrū.
To dispel her state of servitude, even the mighty Garuḍa carried her along with her son and indeed went to the further shore of the ocean.
Having gone there, Garuḍa said to her: "Speak, O Mother; salutations to you!
How may my mother be released from this state of servitude without a doubt? (26)
Kadrū said:
"O son, having brought the nectar from the world of the gods by force, deliver it to my sons immediately; release your mother, the weak one. (27)
Vyāsa said:
Having been thus addressed, the mighty one, that best of birds, went swiftly to the world of Indra;
having fought a battle, he quickly seized the jar of nectar.
Vainateya brought the nectar and presented it to his mother;
by that act, Vinatā was undoubtedly liberated from her state of servitude.
When the serpents had gone to bathe, Indra took back the nectar;
thus Vinatā was forcibly released from her state of servitude by the power of her husband.
The kuśa grass spread there was licked by those named pannagas;
merely by the touch of the tips of the kuśa, those double-tongued beings became fully equipped with their characteristic traits.
And those Nāgas, headed by Vāsuki, who had been cursed by Mātṛkā,
went in grief to Brahmā for refuge and spoke of their fear born of the curse.
To them the Blessed One Brahmā said: "O Jaratkāru, the great sage, bestow upon him the sister of Vāsuki who bears the same name as he. (33)
The son who is born of her shall be the protector of the snakes;
his name shall be Āstīka, of this there is no doubt. (34)
Having heard those auspicious words of Brahmā, Vāsuki went to the forest and,
with humility, gave his daughter to him.
Knowing her to be of the same name, the sage Jaratkāru said to him:
"If she should do anything displeasing to me, then I shall abandon her. (36)
Having made such a vow of silence, the sage himself took her;
and Vāsuki, having granted his wish, departed for his own abode.
Having constructed a bright leaf-hut in the great forest, Jaratkaru,
the scorcher of foes, lived happily with her, taking his delight.
Once, having finished his meal, that best of sages fell asleep;
there stood his sister, the fair-complexioned one, belonging to Vāsuki.
"O beloved, you must not awaken me by any means whatsoever.
Having spoken thus to that fair-toothed woman, the sage then fell asleep.
The sun has reached the mountain of setting and the time of twilight has arrived;
what shall I do? I find no peace, lest he, having been awakened, should abandon me once again.
Fearing the loss of religious merit, Jaratkaru thought:
"If I do not wake him, this time for the twilight prayers will pass in vain. (42)
Abandoning [the body] is better than the destruction of Dharma, for death is nonetheless certain;
indeed, the loss of Dharma leads men once again to hell. (43)
Having reflected thus, that young woman awakened the sage:
"The time for twilight has arrived; arise, arise, O observer of noble vows! (44)
Rising up in anger, that sage said to her, "I am going;
you, however, who have interrupted my sleep, go to your brother's house."
Trembling, she then spoke these words when addressed by the sage:
"O you of immeasurable luster, how can that purpose for which I was given away by my brother be fulfilled? (46)
The sage Jaratkāru, free from agitation, replied, "It exists.
Then she, having been abandoned by the sage, went to the abode of Vāsuki.
Questioned by her brother, she spoke these words exactly as her husband had told her:
"Having said 'I am here,' that best of sages abandoned me and departed. (48)
Having heard that the sage was indeed truthful in speech, Vāsuki placed his full trust in him and took refuge with his sister.
Then, after some time, that young son of a sage was born;
O best of the Kurus, he became renowned by the name Āstīka.
Therefore, O best of kings, this sacrifice of yours has been protected by that sage of purified soul for the sake of guarding his maternal kin. (51)
Well done, O Great King!
You have honored this sage, who was born in the Yāyāvara lineage and is the son of Vāsuki’s sister. (52)
May it be well with you, O mighty-armed one! You have heard the entire Bhārata;
many gifts have been given by you, and likewise the sages have been honored. (53)
O best of kings, despite your virtuous deeds, your father has not attained the heavenly realm, nor has your entire lineage been purified by you.
O King Janamejaya, out of devotion, construct a spacious sanctuary for the Goddess,
by which indeed all success shall be yours.
Worshipped with supreme devotion, Śivā is always the bestower of everything;
she indeed brings about the increase of the lineage and ensures that the kingdom remains forever stable. (56)
O best of kings, having performed the Devīmakhayajña according to the prescribed rites,
listen to the supreme Purāṇa named Śrīmadbhāgavata.
I shall cause you to hear this most purifying story,
which enables one to cross over the ocean of worldly existence, which is divine, and which is composed of various aesthetic flavors.
O King, there is nothing else on earth to be heard beyond this Purāṇa;
and there is nothing to be worshipped other than the lotus feet of the Goddess.
They are fortunate, they are wise, and they are blessed, O best of kings, in whose hearts the Goddess always dwells amidst a flood of love. (60)
O Bhārata, those people on earth who have never propitiated the Great Illusion, the Mother Ambikā, are seen to be deeply afflicted with suffering.
O King, what person would not serve her, when all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, are always intent upon her worship? (62)
Whoever should hear this constantly shall obtain all desires;
it is that unsurpassed [teaching] which was proclaimed by the Blessed Lady to Viṣṇu.
O King, through hearing that, peace shall arise in your mind;
and from hearing the Purāṇa, an inexhaustible heaven shall accrue for your ancestors.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Discourse Concerning the Listener and the Speaker," in the second book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 12.
Description of Bhuvaneśvarī.
Janamejaya said:
O Blessed One, you have described the great sacrifice known as Ambā.
Who was she? How did she arise? Where? From what cause? And what were her qualities? (1)
What kind of sacrifice is it for her, and what is its nature?
O ocean of compassion, you are omniscient; please explain the procedure according to the rules.
O Brahmin, O protector of the earth, tell me in detail the origin of the universe exactly as it was described and in its true nature, for you know everything.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—these three gods, who are the agents of creation, preservation, and destruction, have been heard by me to be endowed with attributes (saguṇa). || 4 ||
"O son of Parāśara, tell me: are those great-souled ones independent, or are they dependent on others? I wish to hear this now. (5)

Are you subject to the nature of death or not? Are you of the form of existence, consciousness, and bliss? Are you joined with the objective elements and so forth, or are you free from the threefold sufferings? (6)
Are those mighty lords of the gods subject to the power of time or not?
How indeed were they born, and from what cause? Such is my doubt. (7)
O Sage, are their bodies indeed possessed of joy and sorrow, endowed with sleep and laziness,
and composed of the seven constituent elements, or is it otherwise?
By what substances are they composed, and by what qualities and sense faculties?
What is their enjoyment like, and likewise, what is the measure of their lifespan?
O Brahmin, tell me also their place of residence and their splendor; I wish to hear this narrative in detail.
Vyāsa said:
O King, O high-minded one, you have now posed a difficult burden of questions, namely:
"From what did the origin of Brahmā and the others arise? (11)
"O King, listen! When I previously questioned that sage Nārada about this very matter, he was struck with wonder and, rising up, replied as follows."
And at one time, I beheld the sage Nārada, who was peaceful, omniscient, and the foremost among those who know the Vedas, standing on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having seen him, I became joyful and fell at the feet of the Sage;
commanded by his splendor, I sat down upon an excellent seat near him.
Having heard this auspicious news, I questioned that son of Brahmā,
who was seated on the secluded bank of the Ganges where the sand is fine.
O Sage of great intellect, who is declared to be the supreme creator of this vast cosmic egg? Tell me that according to the prescribed method.
O best of sages, O most excellent of the twice-born, tell me from what this universe has arisen, and whether it is impermanent or eternal.
Is this [world] created by a single agent, or by many agents, or otherwise, as having no agent at all? To me, this appears to be a contradiction regarding the nature of an effect. (18)
Thus, rescue me now as I am submerged in a multitude of doubts, creating millions of conceptual constructions within this vast cycle of worldly existence. (19)
Some, considering him the cause of all causes, call him Śaṅkara,
Sadāśiva, and Mahādeva, who is devoid of both dissolution and creation.

To Hara, who delights in the self, the lord of gods, who consists of the three qualities yet is stainless, the eternal savior from worldly existence, and the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction. || 21 ||
Others praise this Viṣṇu, the Lord and Master of all, the unmanifest Supreme Self endowed with all powers. || 22 ||
[He meditated upon] Hari, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, the peaceful one, the origin of all, facing every direction, the all-pervading refuge of the universe, without beginning or end.
And others likewise call him Dhātṛ, the cause of creation;
he alone is the knower of all and the impeller of all beings.
The four-faced Lord of the gods, born from the navel-lotus,
the all-pervading creator of all worlds, who dwells in Satyaloka.
Others, the exponents of the Vedas, proclaim him to be Dineśa, the Lord of All;
they praise and sing his praises tirelessly at both evening and morning.
And likewise, they worship Vāsava, the performer of a hundred sacrifices,
the thousand-eyed god of gods, the formidable lord of all, in the sacrifice.
The lord of sacrifice, the lord of the gods, the lord of the three worlds, the husband of Śacī;
the enjoyer of sacrifices, the drinker of Soma, and the beloved of those who drink Soma.
Likewise Varuṇa and Soma, Pāvaka and Pavana, Yama, Kubera the giver of wealth, and others as well as the Lord of the Gaṇas. (29)

And Heramba, who has the face of an elephant and accomplishes all undertakings; the supreme one who grants success through mere remembrance, who fulfills desires, bestows boons, and moves at will. (30)
Some teachers proclaim Bhavānī as the bestower of all goals—the primordial Māyā, the Great Power, Nature (Prakṛti) who follows Puruṣa. (31)
She has attained oneness with Brahman, she is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and end [of the world],
and she is the mother of all beings as well as of the gods.
Without beginning or end, full, pervading all living beings,
the sovereign of all worlds, devoid of qualities yet possessing qualities, the auspicious one.
The Vaiṣṇavī, the Śāṅkarī, the Brāhmī, the Vāsavī, and likewise the Vāruṇī;
the Vārāhī, the Nārasiṃhī, and the wonderful Mahālakṣmī. (34)
And [he praised] the single Mother of the Vedas, the stable Knowledge of the two Lords,
which destroys all suffering and grants all desires through mere remembrance.
She bestows liberation upon those seeking release and grants desires to those who seek fruits;
she is of a nature transcending the three qualities (guṇas) and is the cause of the expansion of the qualities.
Therefore, those seeking rewards meditate upon her as both possessing attributes (saguṇā) and devoid of attributes (nirguṇā);
for she is indeed stainless, formless, untainted, and beyond all qualities.
The lords of sages proclaim that Brahman is formless and all-pervading;
in some places within the Vedas and Upaniṣads, it is described as consisting of light.
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, and likewise a thousand eyes;
he has a thousand hands and ears, a thousand mouths, and a thousand feet.
The supreme space of Viṣṇu’s foot is thus proclaimed;
the wise declare it to be the Virāj, free from passion (viraja), and tranquil.
Likewise, other knowers of antiquity proclaim him to be the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama);
yet others say that he is never even one alone, for he is the Lord and Master.
Some maintain that this entire cosmic egg is without a Lord;
they hold that this inconceivable world was never produced by a Creator.

This [world] is always without a lord and arises from its own nature; it is eternally of such a kind. That person (puruṣa) is declared to be a non-agent, and so too is that primordial matter (prakṛti).
Thus speak the Sāṅkhya sages, Kapila and others;
from these arise multitudes of doubts, as well as others. (44)
O Lord of Sages, what can I do, for my mind is afflicted by conceptual construction?
When I wish to speak of dharma and adharma, my mind does not become steady. (45)
What is dharma and what is adharma? No sign whatsoever is perceived.
The gods are born from the quality of goodness (sattva) and are established in truth and dharma.
They are being oppressed by sinful Dānavas; where, then, is the establishment of dharma?
The Pāṇḍavas, born of my lineage, are established in dharma and always follow right conduct. (47)
Having encountered manifold sufferings therein, what possible standing can there be for Dharma?
Therefore, O father, my heart trembles excessively in this state of uncertainty. (48)
Make my mind free from doubt, for you are capable, O great sage;
protect me, O sage, with the boat of knowledge from the ocean of saṃsāra.
Sinking and rising again, submerged in the turbid waters of delusion.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of Bhuvaneśvarī," in the third book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 1 ||
The Description of the Destinations of Brahmā and Others.
Vyāsa said:
O mighty-armed one, O best of the Kurus, as for that which you have asked me—
Nārada spoke those answers, having been questioned by me, O Lord of Sages.
Nārada said:
O Vyāsa, what shall I tell you today? Formerly, this doubt arose excessively in my heart, as I was tormented by the essence of uncertainty.
Having gone to my father Brahmā, who dwells in his own abode and possesses immeasurable splendor,
I asked him that same excellent question which you have today asked of Vyāsa.
O Father, O All-pervading Lord, from where has this entire universe arisen?
Was it properly created by you, or was it indeed created by Viṣṇu? (4)
O Soul of the Universe, O Lord of the World, tell me the truth:
who is to be propitiated at will, and who is the sovereign most excellent of all? (5)
Tell me all that, O Brahmin; sever my doubts, O sinless one, for I am submerged in this cycle of existence which is of the nature of suffering and like an illusion.
A mind oscillating with doubt finds no peace anywhere—
not in sacred fords, nor in the gods, nor in other spiritual practices.
O scorcher of foes, without knowing the supreme reality, how can there be peace?
The mind, scattered in many directions, does not attain stability in one place. (8)
Whom shall I remember? Whom shall I worship? To whom shall I go? Whom shall I honor?
Whom shall I praise? O God, I do not know You, the Lord of all lords.
Then Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, replied this to me: "O son of Satyavatī, since you have asked this most difficult question. (10)
Brahmā said:
"O son, what shall I say? This most excellent question is difficult to understand; it is impossible for you to resolve, O illustrious one, and even for Viṣṇu, despite his certainty."
O high-minded one, no one who is possessed by passion knows this in this world;
only one who is dispassionate, free from desire, and devoid of envy understands it.
In ancient times, when a single ocean had arisen and all things mobile and immobile had perished, and only the primary elements remained, I was born from the lotus.
I did not see the sun, nor the moon, nor trees, nor mountains;
having entered into the pericarp, I then fell into deep reflection.
"Why have I arisen in this great ocean of water?
Who is my protector, lord, creator, or destroyer at the end of the age? (15)

And yet, when this earth is not clearly perceived as the support for this water, how could the lotus have arisen—given that its existence is well-established through both conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and etymological derivation (*yoga*)? (16)
Today I see that mud which is indeed the root of this lotus;
the earth will exist there as its root—of this there is no doubt. (17)
While searching the earth there in the waters of the north for as long as a thousand years, when he did not find her, then—
Then an incorporeal voice arose in the sky, saying, "Perform penance!
Thereupon, I performed penance for a thousand years upon that lotus.
Then, the voice "Create! arose once more and was heard by me there;
hearing it, I became bewildered, thinking, "Whom shall I create? What shall I do? (20)
Then the two terrible Daityas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, also arrived;
I was terrified by them in the abode of the sea for the sake of battle.
Then, grasping the Nāla reed, I descended into the middle of the water;
there, I beheld a most wonderful man.
With a body dark as a rain cloud, wearing yellow garments, four-armed,
reclining upon Śeṣa, the Lord of the World is adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
I beheld that Great Viṣṇu, resplendent with his weapons such as the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa.
Beholding him lying upon the coils of the serpent, overcome by yogic sleep, motionless, and unshakable. || 25 ||
O Nārada, a wonderful thought arose in me: "What shall I do?
Then I remembered the Goddess, who was praised by me in her form as Sleep.
Having emerged from her body, that auspicious goddess stood in the sky;
her form was inconceivable, and she was adorned with divine ornaments.
Quickly leaving Viṣṇu’s body, she shone, stationed in the sky; Janārdana, the one of immeasurable soul, rose up, released by her.
He waged a supreme battle for five thousand years;
then the two Daityas were beheld and struck down by Hari.
Having made his lap pure, he struck us both right there;
Rudra arrived at that very spot where we two were standing.
Beheld by us three, the goddess Manoharā remained composed;
having been praised as the supreme Śakti, she spoke to us who stood before her.
Then, having gladdened them with purifying glances of compassion,
the Goddess said:
"O lords of the quarters, perform your respective duties without indolence."
Having slain these two great asuras who were distinguished by their power over creation and maintenance,
dwell in your own abodes, free from all anxiety.
"Create all four kinds of beings by means of your own powers.
Having heard her words— which were elegant, pleasant, and gentle— Brahmā spoke.
We said to her: "We are powerless; how can we manage these subjects?
O Mother, the earth is not vast, for water is spread everywhere. (35)
"Neither the elements, nor the qualities, nor the subtle essences, nor the senses [are the cause].
Having heard these words of ours, Śivā became smiling-faced. (36)
Instantly, a beautiful celestial chariot arrived there from the sky;
he said, "O gods, enter this at your pleasure, free from fear."
"Today, in this celestial chariot, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa shall show you a marvel.
Having heard her words, we replied, "So be it," and once again—
Having ascended, we are seated upon a celestial chariot adorned with jewels,
well-covered with strings of pearls and resounding with the tinkling of networks of small bells.
There, in that delightful place resembling the abode of the gods, the three of us entered without hesitation;
then, seeing us seated there, the goddess [observed] that we had conquered our senses.
Indeed, by his own power, he caused that celestial chariot to ascend into the sky.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Destiny of Brahmā and Others," in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 2 ||
Brahmā spoke regarding the sight of the Goddess by Hara and the other gods while stationed in their celestial chariots: "That chariot, swift as thought, has gone to another place."
We did not see water there; we were filled with wonder at that time. || 1 ||
The trees were beautiful, laden with all kinds of fruit, and adorned with the warbling of cuckoos; so too were the earth, the mountains, the forests, and the groves, according to one's desire.
Women and men, as well as animals, excellent rivers, ponds, wells, lakes, pools, and mountain springs; || 3 ||
In front [of him was] a delightful city, adorned with divine ramparts,
provided with a sacrificial hall, and resplendent with various mansions.
Then, upon seeing that city, a recognition arose within us:
"This is heaven! By whom was this wonder created? (5)
We saw the king, who resembles a god, as he was going out for a hunt in the forest,
and we also saw Ambikā seated upon her celestial chariot.
In an instant, the celestial chariot, impelled by the wind, moved through the sky;
and in a mere moment, it arrived at another delightful region.
And there we beheld the most excellent Nandana grove;
the fragrant [goddess] stood there, taking refuge in the shade of the Pārijāta tree.
A four-tusked elephant stood nearby her,
and there were hosts of Apsarases, including Menakā and others.
There, hundreds of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and likewise Vidyādharas sport in various ways accompanied by singing and dancing.
In the midst of the Mandāra grove, they sang and took their pleasure;
there the Lord Śatakratu was seen together with Paulomī.
But we were filled with wonder upon seeing those dwellers of heaven at that time— Varuṇa,
the lord of aquatic creatures, Kubera, Yama, Sūrya, and Vibhāvasu.
Seeing the gods stationed there, we were filled with wonder;
at that moment, the king emerged from that well-adorned city.
Unshakable like the king of the gods, he stood upon the earth borne by men; yet we, situated in our celestial chariot, were shaken as it moved swiftly along.
Then, having beheld the divine Brahma-world, which is saluted by all the gods,
Hara and Keśava were filled with wonder upon seeing Brahmā there.
In that assembly hall, all the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs appeared in personified forms, as did the oceans, rivers, mountains, and serpents and uragas. || 16 ||
The four-faced one said to me, "Who is this eternal Brahmā?
To them I replied, "I do not know the Lord, the Master of Creation. (17)
"Who am I? Who is this? Or for what purpose is this delusion of mine, O Lords?
Then, in an instant, that celestial chariot, swift as thought, moved away rapidly.
He arrived at the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, which was frequented by hosts of yakṣas, delightful with groves of mandāra trees, and filled with the warbling of parrots and cuckoos.

When that celestial chariot, resonant with the sounds of lutes, drums, and other musical instruments— providing comfort and auspiciousness— arrived, at that very moment [he departed] from his beautiful home.
The Blessed Lord Śambhu emerged, mounted upon his bull, three-eyed,
five-faced, ten-armed, and adorned with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Clad in a tiger skin with an elephant hide as an upper garment,
his two great heroic rear-guards were Gajānana and Ṣaḍānana.
The two sons, traveling together with Śiva, shone brilliantly;
as did all those excellent leaders of the Gaṇas, beginning with Nandin. (23)
Uttering cries of "Victory!", they proceeded behind Śiva;
seeing that other Śaṅkara there, O Nārada, they were filled with wonder.
O Sage, filled with doubt because of my mothers, I remained there;
then, in an instant, from that mountain peak, a celestial chariot [arrived] with the speed of the wind.
I reached the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, the palace of the Beloved of Ramā;
and there, O son, I beheld an inconceivable splendor.
Then Viṣṇu was filled with wonder upon seeing that supreme city;
meanwhile, the lotus-eyed Hari proceeded toward the front of the palace.
Having the luster of an atasi flower, clad in yellow garments, four-armed, mounted upon the king of birds, and adorned with divine ornaments. || 28 ||
Then, being fanned by the auspicious chowries of Lakṣmī and his beloved,
we all gazed upon that eternal Viṣṇu and were filled with wonder.
Standing upon that excellent seat, they remained gazing at one another;
then the celestial chariot suddenly shook with the speed of the wind.
The ocean of nectar was reached, possessing great waves of sweet water, teeming with hosts of aquatic creatures and resplendent with surging billows. || 31 ||
It was exceedingly beautified by trees such as the Mandāra and Pārijāta;
it was furnished with various carpets and adorned with diverse and wonderful paintings.
It was adorned with strings of pearls and embellished with various other garlands;
it was further graced by trees known as Aśoka and Bakula, as well as Kurubaka and others.
It was enclosed on all sides by gentle *ketakī* and *campaka* trees,
resounded with the cries of cuckoos, and endowed with divine fragrance.
Adorned with the exceedingly wonderful sounds of humming bees,
upon that island was a most enchanting couch in the form of Śiva.
Exceedingly adorned with jewels and resplendent with various gems,
it was seen by us from afar while staying in our celestial chariot, beautifully decorated.
Covered with various carpets and adorned with rainbows,
that excellent woman sat upon that most noble couch.
Wearing red garlands and garments, anointed with red perfumes and unguents,
her lovely eyes were deep red, and she possessed a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
With a most beautiful face, adorned with red lips,
she surpassed ten million Ramās in splendor, her entire form resembling the orb of the sun.
Holding a boon-granting noose, a goad, and the gesture of fearlessness, the illustrious Bhuvaneśvarī was seen;
never before beheld, that beautiful lady was adorned with a smile. 40.
Attended by flocks of birds intent on the recitation of the syllable *hrīṃ*, she is ruddy-hued, the embodiment of compassion, a maiden in the bloom of youth. (41)
Richly adorned with every elegant ornament, her lotus-face bears a gentle smile;
the pair of her rising, full breasts has surpassed the buds of the lotus.
She was adorned with ornaments studded with various clusters of gems,
and graced by golden armlets, bracelets, and a crown.
Her lotus-face is adorned with earrings shaped like golden *śrīcakra*s;
she is Hṛllekhā Bhuvaneśī, by those devoted to the recitation of her names. (44)
The Great Goddess, the Sovereign of the World, is eternally praised by her circles of female companions and is surrounded by celestial maidens beginning with Hṛllekhā.
Surrounded by goddesses such as Anaṅgakusumā and others, the Goddess stands upon the king of yantras, situated in the center of the hexagon. (46)
Having seen her, we who were standing there were all struck with wonder;
"Who is this lovely woman, and what is her name? We do not know, though we remain here. (47)
The beautiful woman with a thousand eyes, endowed with a thousand hands and a thousand faces, shines from afar, beyond all doubt. (48)
"She is neither an Apsaras nor a Gandharvī, and she is certainly not a celestial maiden"—having fallen into this doubt, O Nārada, they remained there. (49)
Then the Blessed Viṣṇu, having seen that sweetly smiling woman and having formed a resolution in his mind through his own higher knowledge, spoke to the Mother.
This Blessed Goddess is indeed the cause of us all;
she is the Great Knowledge, the Great Illusion, the Full, the Imperishable Nature.
The Goddess is difficult for those of small intellect to know; she is attained through yoga and is hard to conceive by those of evil intent.
She is the will of the Supreme Self, the desire itself, and her nature is both eternal and non-eternal.

The Goddess Śivā, the sovereign of the universe, who contains the Vedas within her and possesses wide eyes, is difficult to propitiate for those of meager fortune; she is the primordial sovereign of all. (53)
Having withdrawn the entire universe and having placed the subtle bodies (liṅgas) of all living beings within her own body, she sports during the dissolution.
For this [city], containing all seeds, now shines, O gods;
behold, its manifestations stand by its side by the tens of millions in successive order. (55)
Richly adorned with divine ornaments and anointed with divine fragrant unguents, they were all intent on serving while Brahmā and Śaṅkara looked on. (56)
We are blessed, highly fortunate, and have now fulfilled our purpose,
since we have obtained this very vision of the Blessed Lady herself here.
This is the supreme fruit of the austerity previously performed with great effort;
otherwise, how could we have obtained this vision with such devotion? (58)
Those who possess a mass of merit, those who are generous, and those who are ascetic behold her;
the passionate do not at all behold the Goddess, the Blessed Śivā. (59)
This very primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), eternally united with the Puruṣa, indeed manifests the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) for the sake of the Supreme Self. 60.
He is the seer of this entire visible universe, including the gods and the two deities;
for him, Śivā, the sovereign of all, is the cause of everything through her Māyā.
Where am I, or where are all the gods, and the celestial women such as Rambhā and others?
We cannot possibly equal even a hundred-thousandth part of her in any way. (62)
This is indeed that excellent woman who was seen in the great ocean;
as a young girl, the great goddess used to joyfully swing me about.
On a bed made of banyan leaves, or on a firm and stable couch, having placed the big toe of one foot in the hand and resting it upon the lotus-face; 64.
Licking his lips and playing with various childish antics, the one of tender limbs was sporting while seated within the fold of a banyan leaf. (65)
Singing and swinging [me] about due to her childhood nature while I stood there—
this very person has been recognized by me with absolute certainty, as soon as she came into my sight.
Granted, she is our mother; listen, for I shall tell you this:
having experienced it before, recognition has now arisen within me. (67)

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Vision of the Goddess by Hara and the Other Devas Seated in Their Celestial Chariots," in the Third Skandha of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Brahmā said: "The hymn to the Goddess was composed by Viṣṇu. Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Janārdana, Viṣṇu, spoke again.
"Let us go to her side, bowing down again and again. || 1 ||
This very Mahāmāyā is the bestower; she will indeed grant boons to us.
Having attained her presence, let us praise her fearlessly at her feet.
If the attendants stationed at the gate do not prevent us,
we shall remain there and, with concentrated minds, recite a hymn of praise to the Goddess.
Brahmā said:
When these words were spoken by Hari, they became exceedingly joyful and well-composed;
they were truly delighted and prepared to go near him at their pleasure.
Having said "Om," all three quickly descended from the celestial chariot and went out to the gate, their minds filled with great apprehension.
Then, seeing them all standing at the door, the divine Bhagavatī smiled and quickly transformed those three into bearers of female forms.
"We are young women, beautiful and adorned with lovely ornaments; filled with great wonder, we have come once again into his presence. (7)
Seeing us standing there at her feet in the form of women,
she of the beautiful limbs gazed upon us with eyes filled with love.
Having prostrated before that Great Goddess, we stood in her presence,
beholding one another, in female form and adorned with beautiful ornaments.
Gazing upon the footstool adorned with various jewels,
which shone like ten million suns, we three remained there.
There, thousands of female companions were dressed in red garments;
likewise, there were auspicious women dressed in blue garments and others in yellow garments.
All the goddesses, auspicious in form and adorned with variegated garments and ornaments, shone resplendently at her side, intent indeed upon her service. 12.
Other women sang and danced, and they attended upon him,
filled with joy as they played lutes, flutes, and musical instruments.
Listen, Nārada, I shall tell you of the wonder that was seen there:
indeed, within the mirror of her toenails, the lotus-feet of the Goddess were reflected.
The entire cosmic egg, including all things mobile and immobile therein—myself, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Vāyu, Agni, Yama, and Ravi [are all contained within it]. || 15 ||
Varuṇa, Śītagu, Tvaṣṭṛ, Kubera, and Pākaśāsana;
likewise the mountains, oceans, rivers, Gandharvas, and Apsarases. || 16 ||
Viśvāvasu, Citraketu, Śveta, Citrāṅgada, as well as Nārada, Tumburu, and likewise Hāhā and Hūhū. (17)
The Aśvins, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, and the Siddhas, as well as the Pitṛs;
all the Nāgas beginning with Śeṣa, along with the Kinnaras, Uragas, and Rākṣasas. || 18 ||
Vaikuṇṭha, the world of Brahmā, and Kailāsa, the best of mountains—
all that entire universe was seen by us situated within the space between his fingernails.
There is the lotus born of my navel; there I abide as the four-faced one, as the Lord of the World reclining upon Śeṣa, and likewise as Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Brahmā said:
Thus was it seen by me there, situated upon the nail of his lotus-foot;
then, having beheld it, I was struck with wonder and became filled with doubt, wondering, "What is this? (21)
Viṣṇu was filled with wonder, and Śaṅkara likewise remained so;
they then regarded that goddess as the mother of the universe.
Then, as he beheld various kinds of dwellings upon that auspicious island consisting of nectar, a full hundred years passed by.
Then the goddesses, adorned with various ornaments and appearing joyful, regarded us who were standing there as if we were their friends.
We too were utterly deluded by its extreme loveliness; beholding those enchanting sights, we all became joyful in heart. (25)
Once, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, abiding in a youthful state, praised that great goddess, the divine Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī.

The Blessed Lord said: Salutations to the Goddess, to Prakṛti, and to the Ordainer; constant salutations to her who grants auspiciousness and desires, and salutations again and again to Vṛddhi and Siddhi. || 27 ||

Salutations to her whose form is truth, consciousness, and bliss; salutations again and again to you, Bhuvaneśī, the creator of the fivefold cosmic functions and the forest-fire that consumes the cycle of worldly existence. || 28 ||
Salutations again and again to her whose form is the support of all, who is immutably established;
salutations again and again to Hṛllekhā, who has become the meaning of the half-measure. || 29 ||
O Mother, today I have realized that all this is established within you; both its origin and its dissolution proceed from you,
and your power to bring it forth possesses far-reaching majesty.
Now she has truly been known as one who consists of all the worlds. || 30 ||
Having expanded everything without exception— the entire modification of the existent and non-existent—
you manifest it in its entirety to the Puruṣa at the proper time,
by means of both the sixteen and the seven principles.
It is indeed like a magician’s trick, spoken for our mere entertainment. || 31 ||
Without you, nothing pertaining to the objective world shines forth;
you abide pervading everything in its entirety.
Without power, even a person is incapable of worldly activity.
She is censured by wise people, O Mother. || 32 ||
You constantly gladden the entire universe with your own powers, and you manifest everything through your splendor; indeed,
O Goddess, you shall consume all by your force at the time of the cosmic dissolution.
Who indeed knows, O Goddess, the true nature of your activity and of Bhava?
O Mother, we have been your saviors from Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and indeed you have shown these worlds to be well-spread out;
they have been led to the abode of happiness and to the highest pinnacle.
O Bhavānī, that vision of yours possesses great power.
O Mother, neither I nor Brahmā knows [your nature];
for who else indeed can know your inconceivable conduct?
How many worlds are there here, O you of great power?
O Bhavānī, in this collection of compositions created by me today. || 35 ||
In this world, O Goddess, we have seen only Hari, Śiva, and the lotus-born Brahmā of renowned power;
do they not exist in other worlds?
O Goddess, what can we understand of your vast and glorious power?
O Mother, having prostrated before your lotus feet, I beg this much:
may this form of yours always dwell within my heart,
and may your very name reside eternally within the cavity of my mouth.
May there always be the sight of your two lotus feet.

"I am your servant, always to be cherished by you; indeed, I contemplate you in my mind as my mistress. O Goddess, may this relationship between us be perpetual, like that of a mother and her son for the sake of our welfare. (38)
You know the entire manifold of the world in its totality; you have reached the ultimate limit of omniscience.
O Mother of the World, what need is there for a common person to report anything to you?
If you act as has been stated, it will be in accordance with your own intention.
"Brahmā creates, Viṣṇu protects, and Umāpati is the agent of destruction— this is the common renown among people.
Is this also true, O Goddess, or is it indeed by Your will?"
O Unborn One, we are capable of doing this, being endowed with your power. || 40 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, it is not the Earth that sustains the world;
rather, it is Your power of support (Ādhāra-śakti) that indeed sustains everything. O Giver of Boons, even the sun shines because it is endowed with Your radiance.
You, O Viraja, shine forth as all this entire universe.

"By your power, I am indeed Brahmā, the supreme Lord; yet we are all subject to birth and are not eternal. What other gods, headed by Indra, could be eternal? You alone are the eternal Mother, the ancient Prakṛti. (42)
If you, O Ancient Puruṣa, show compassion,
I know that today I am forever in your presence; otherwise, I am the all-pervading, beginningless Lord, free from desire.
The cognition of the universal self is always of the nature of darkness (tamas). || 43 ||
You alone are indeed the wisdom of wise men;
you alone are truly the power of those who possess power at all times.
You are the very form of fame, beauty, fortune, purity, and contentment.
In the world of humans, renunciation alone is the bestower of liberation. || 44 ||
You are Gāyatrī, the first digit of the Veda; you alone are the divine Svāhā and Svadhā, the half-mora endowed with qualities. You are ordained as the sacred tradition itself, the Nigama.
For the constant restoration of the gods and those born before them. || 45 ||
Indeed, you fashion this entire phenomenal world solely for the sake of liberation for those who have indeed entered into the state of individual souls,
for they are but portions of You, the faultless One who is without beginning or end.
For they are like the widespread waves of the full ocean. || 46 ||
When the individual soul understands that "this entire activity is yours alone; you withdraw it all," this is well known—
just as a drama performed by an actor ceases when the internal stage-setting is dissolved.
O you of renowned power, you cease once your task has been accomplished.
You alone are my savior from the ocean of existence filled with delusion; O Mother, I constantly come to you, the dispeller of great suffering.
Protect me indeed during this false and ultimately futile time, fashioned by passion and other afflictions, which brings forth manifold miseries. (48)
Homage to the Goddess Mahāvidyā! I bow at your feet;
O auspicious one, bestower of all goals, grant me the constant illumination of knowledge. (49)
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Hymn to the Goddess Composed by Viṣṇu," in the Third Book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Praise Offered by Hara and Brahmā.
Brahmā said:
When Viṣṇu, the god of gods, Janārdana, had finished speaking thus and become silent, [Hara spoke].
Śaṅkara, known as Śarva, spoke while standing bowed before him.
Śiva said:

"O Goddess, if Hari is your source of manifestation, and likewise the Lotus-born (Brahmā) is your origin, then am I not also endowed with your excellent qualities? O Śivā, you are skilled in the creation of all the worlds."
You are the earth, the water, the wind, as well as space; you are likewise the quality of fire,
O Mother, and again those very organs of perception.
You are intellect, mind, and also the ego-sense. || 3 ||
Those who do not know and speak otherwise—
that the entire world was created by Hari, Hara, and the King—
are indeed always created by you alone.
They fashion the world with all its moving and unmoving beings. || 4 ||
If the world were produced from earth, air, ether, fire, water, and so forth, along with their objects and qualities,
then how is it that today it remains so clearly manifest?
O Mother, [this world] prevails through a mere fraction of you, who are nectar itself.
You are all this, both the moving and the unmoving, fashioned in the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
through your playful curiosity for various guises and pastimes, O Mother, you cease and you delight according to your own will.
O Mother, when I, Hari, and the lotus-born Brahmā desire to create the entire world,
we do so by receiving the dust of your lotus feet.
Having attained that, we indeed acted then.

O Mother Ambikā, if your mind were not always moist with compassion, how could I— who am composed of the quality of darkness (tamas)— and even the Lotus-born Brahmā, who arises from the quality of passion (rajas), have been brought into being?
Is Hari, whose nature is goodness, not perfectly established? || 8 ||
O Mother, if your mind were not partial,
how could this world have been fashioned in such manifold ways,
filled with ministers, kings, and servants?
It was crowded with both those possessing great wealth and those who were destitute.
Indeed, Hari, Hara, and Dhruva are always capable of manifesting, protecting, and withdrawing [the world] only by relying upon your qualities; they are so, respectively, through you.
They are indeed fashioned as the cause of the three worlds. || 10 ||
Indeed, while traveling through the worlds on my path, I, Hari, as well as the Lotus-born One seated in his celestial chariot, have thoroughly observed them.
Tell me, by what means do you and the others become new? || 11 ||
O Mother of the World, you create and protect the universe by your own power; how much more do you wish to destroy? You always delight your husband, the Supreme Puruṣa.
O Auspicious One, we truly do not know your course.
O Mother, grant us the service of Your lotus feet, and always [grant] to us young women the status of bhāgavatas;
for having attained manhood, where else could we clearly find happiness if we were deprived of Your lotus feet? (13)
O Mother Śivā, having obtained this human body, there is no desire in me at all to dwell anywhere in the worlds apart from your lotus feet.
Having indeed attained lordship over the three worlds.
O fair-toothed one, even having attained the state of a young woman in your presence, I do not have the slightest pleasure;
for where does masculinity lead to happiness, if your feet are not within the range of one's vision? (15)
O Mother, may this stainless fame of mine always prevail throughout the three worlds;
having attained the state of a young woman, [may it worship] your lotus feet.
This destruction of saṃsāra has been familiarized by you. || 16 ||
Who on earth, having abandoned service at your feet, would desire a thornless kingdom? For this very moment, it is said, attains the duration of an entire Yuga.
If your lotus-like feet are not near me. || 17 ||

O Mother, those stainless sages who are devoted to austerity have indeed been deprived by fate of the worship of your lotus feet; thus, an insult has been inflicted upon them regarding their spiritual power. 18.

O Unborn One, neither by austerity, nor by self-restraint, nor by meditative concentration, nor even by sacrifices performed according to rule, does liberation from the ocean of worldly existence occur as it does through service to the pollen of Your lotus feet. 19.
O Goddess, show mercy if you have compassion for me;
tell me the wondrous, unblemished mantra,
for by reciting it I shall indeed become happy.
And the nine-syllable mantra is most clear and unsurpassed. || 20 ||
Although I attained it in my first birth, that nine-syllable mantra does not manifest to me now;
O Mother, tell me the mantra today, and rescue me, rescue me from the ocean of worldly existence, O Savior!
Thus addressed by Śiva of wondrous splendor,
the goddess Ambikā then uttered clearly the nine-syllable mantra.
Having taken it, Mahādeva attained supreme joy;
bowing at the feet of the Goddess, Śiva remained right there.
Then Śaṅkara remained there, reciting the nine-syllable mantra which bestows both desires and liberation, joined with its seed-syllable and uttered auspiciously.
Seeing Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, situated in that manner,
I stood at his feet and spoke to that Mahāmāyā.
The Vedas were not capable of encompassing you in this manner here, for they did not describe you as the complete sustainer of all people;
you are the Goddess who has become the very essence of the oblations in all sacrifices.
At that time, O Mother, you indeed became omniscient throughout the three worlds. || 26 ||
"I am the creator; I alone fashion this entire, most wonderful universe.
Who else in this threefold world, among all things moving and unmoving, is a man as capable as I?
I am truly blessed here, there is no doubt, for I am Brahmā, transcending the worlds."
"I am in this vast ocean of worldly existence due to the onset of pride. || 27 ||
Today, by your grace, I have become skilled in speaking the truth, thinking with the pride of having received the pollen from your lotus feet that "I am indeed blessed.
Therefore, I entreat you, O Sovereign Goddess, who are expert in destroying the fear of worldly existence and the bestower of liberation.
Having cast off the great fetter of suffering created by delusion, make me endowed with devotion to you. 28.
Therefore, having been born from this immeasurable lotus manifested by you, how could I not be truly liberated? Indeed,
I am surely your obedient servant and your devotee.
O Śivā, protect me, who am submerged in delusion within the ocean of worldly existence. || 29 ||
Those men who do not know speak of me as their Lord and my holy conduct;
those priests here who desire heaven offer sacrifice.
They do not indeed know your power as they wish. || 30 ||
I was created by you for the purpose of performing the ritual of creation; having fashioned the primordial emanation into fourfold divisions,
I alone know this— O Master of Illusion— who else could have known it?
Forgive this offense of mine, born of egoism.
Those fools who, though established in meditative absorption, exert themselves in the eightfold path of yoga,
do not truly know that which bestows liberation.
It was once uttered by me under the guise of my mother. || 32 ||
Having abandoned those who are deluded regarding the supreme investigation and the enumeration of the principles— that very state—
have you not become utterly bewildered in the ocean of existence, O Bhavānī?
You alone are indeed the bestower of liberation from saṃsāra.
Do those by whom the supreme realization of reality was experienced by the primordial beings abandon even this:
a conduct that is pure for merely half a moment, and the names Śiva, Ambikā, Śakti, and Īśa? (34)

Are you not capable of creating the universe instantly by a mere glance? Having fashioned me as Brahmā at the beginning of creation merely for your own diversion, you surely perform all this [creation] by dividing everything into four parts. (35)
Was Hari not your protector? Was he not likewise protected by you from Madhu and Kaiṭabha in the midst of the ocean?
And was Hara not withdrawn by you at the proper time?
How was he born from the middle of my eyebrows? || 36 ||
Your birth has never been seen or heard of anywhere;
whence could your origin be? No one here knows it. Indeed, you are today the sole Śakti, O Bhavānī.
Therefore, you have been awakened by all [the Buddhas] acting independently. || 37 ||
Joined with you, O Mother, I am capable of cutting; joined with you, Hari is capable of protecting;
and joined with you alone here, Hara is capable of striking down.
"Today, all those separated from you have lost their patience. || 38 ||
Just as I am Hari and Śaṅkara, have others not likewise been born here, do they not exist now, or will they not come to be?
Who would not be bewildered by this, O You who are so exceedingly wonderful?
In this diversion, which is a source of dispute for those of limited intellect. || 39 ||
Today the Lord is indeed a non-doer, manifest beyond the qualities (guṇas), devoid of desire, free from limiting adjuncts (anupādhi), and eternally without parts;
nevertheless, Your Lordship has granted me this diversion.
"Those who know the ritual procedure say that one sees clearly in this manner. || 40 ||

When this distinction between the seen and the unseen has been thoroughly investigated regarding the objects of knowledge, there is no other third person superior to you; indeed, there is none at all.
The word of the Veda must never be considered false;
this contradiction has been deeply suspected by me in my heart. (42)
That Brahman which the Vedas declare to be indeed one without a second—is that you, or is it he? Dispel this doubt. (43)
Without doubt, my mind does not function without hesitation;
this small intellect is submerged in this investigation of duality and unity. (44)
You ought to dispel my doubt with your own mouth;
for through the enjoyment of my merit, this meeting with your feet has been attained by me.
"Are you a male or are you a female? Tell me in detail;
having known you as the Supreme Power, I shall be liberated from the ocean of worldly existence. (46)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Hymn Composed by Hara and Brahmā," in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Instruction Given by the Illustrious Goddess to Brahmā.
Brahmā said:
Thus questioned by me, who was bowed down with humility, the Goddess—
That primordial, blessed goddess indeed spoke these gentle words.
The Goddess said:
There is always and eternally only oneness between me and this [universe], and no duality;
he who is that, I am she, and I am she, he is that—any perceived difference exists only through the delusion of the mind.
He who knows the subtle difference between us two is indeed wise;
liberated from saṃsāra, he is released—of this there is no doubt. || 3 ||
Brahman alone is indeed non-dual, eternal, and everlasting;
yet it assumes the state of duality when time is designated as being about to arise.
Just as a lamp appears in two ways due to its connection with an adjunct—
like a shadow in the middle of a mirror or a reflection— so it is with us two.
O Unborn One, at the time of differentiation, You indeed manifest for the sake of creation;
this distinction between the visible and the invisible exists in every way when duality is present.
I am neither woman nor man, nor am I neuter at the dissolution of creation;
when creation exists, this distinction arises, being again imagined by the intellect.
I am intellect, I am fortune, as well as fortitude, fame, and memory;
I am faith, intelligence, compassion, modesty, hunger, thirst, and likewise forbearance.
Beauty, peace, thirst, sleep, lassitude, the decay of old age, knowledge, ignorance, longing, desire, power, and even weakness. (9)
I am fat, marrow, and skin; I am sight and speech, both true and false. I am the supreme, the intermediate, and the visionary [levels of speech], as well as the various channels (nāḍīs).
"O Lotus-born One, know this to be my firm conviction: 'What indeed exists in saṃsāra that is separate from me? Everything is indeed I. (11)
"Tell me, what is it that is devoid of these certain forms of mine?
Therefore, O Creator, I have indeed become expanded within this creation. (12)
"Surely among all the gods, I exist under various names;
indeed, I manifest in the form of Śakti and exercise my prowess. (13)
Gaurī, Brāhmī, Raudrī, Vārāhī, Vaiṣṇavī, Śivā, Vārūṇī, Kauberī, Nārasiṃhī, and Vāsavī. (14)
When all tasks have arisen, I enter into them;
having indeed made him the instrumental cause, I perform all those works.
As there is coldness in water, heat in fire, light in the sun,
and frost in the lord of the night, so do I manifest according to my will.
"O Creator, once abandoned by me, surely not even a living being in this world would be able to move; I declare this certainty unto you. (17)
It is said that Śaṅkara was abandoned by me because he was unable to slay the Daityas;
for the world calls a man who lacks power "weak" indeed. (18)
Indeed, people do not say that one is devoid of Rudra or devoid of Viṣṇu;
rather, they all declare him to be the lowest of men who is devoid of Śakti. 19.
One who has fallen, stumbled, been terrified, become tranquil, or fallen under the power of an enemy is called "incapable" in the world; no one is said to be anything other than Rudra.
Know that power (śakti) is the cause of that, just as you desire to create;
and when you are joined with power, then you shall become the creator of everything.
Likewise Hari, likewise Śambhu, likewise Indra, and then Vibhāvasu;
Śaśin, Sūrya, Yama, Tvaṣṭṛ, Varuṇa, and Pavana as well. (22)
The earth is stable and capable of supporting [the world] only when it is endowed with power;
otherwise, it would be unable to sustain even a single atom. (23)
Likewise, Śeṣa, Kūrma, and all the other elephants of the quarters, being joined with me, are indeed capable of accomplishing their respective tasks. (24)
I drink up all the water, I withdraw the fire, and today I paralyze the wind; I can act in whatever way I desire.
O Lotus-born One, one should never at any time entertain doubt regarding the non-existence of any of the principles (tattvas). || 26 ||
Perhaps it would be a prior absence (prāgabhāva) or indeed a posterior absence (pradhvaṃsābhāva), just as the absence of a jar exists in clay lumps or in potsherds. || 27 ||
If one were to investigate where the earth has gone such that it no longer exists here today, it should be understood that only its atoms remain. (28)
It is intended to be described through seven divisions: as eternal, momentary, empty, permanent and impermanent, possessed of an agent, and preceded by the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). || 29 ||
"O Aja, take hold of the Great Principle (mahat-tattva); from that, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) arises.
From that, fashion all beings just as before. (30)
May you depart to your own abodes; having prepared them, may you dwell there, and being inspired by the divine, may you each perform your respective duties. (31)
"O Creator, accept this Śakti, who is beautiful and sweetly smiling;
she is the excellent Mahāsarasvatī by name, endowed with the quality of Rajas. (32)
She was divine, wearing white garments, adorned with celestial ornaments,
seated upon an excellent throne, and accompanied by her consort for the sake of sport.
"This excellent woman shall be your constant companion;
do not disregard my sovereignty by regarding it as less venerable than this beloved one. (34)
Go now, indeed, with her quickly to Satyaloka;
produce forthwith all four kinds of seeds.
And let the linga-sheaths, together with those living beings and their respective karmas, continue to exist as they were established in time; you must arrange them just as before.

The entire world, including all moving and non-moving beings, is produced by the causes known as time, karma, and inherent nature; it is endowed with its own inherent nature and qualities, just as before. (37)
Viṣṇu must be honored by you and worshipped at all times;
because his nature is primarily characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva), he is always superior in every respect.
Whenever there shall be a task for you that is difficult to accomplish,
Hari indeed will take an incarnation upon the earth at that time.
Furthermore, having taken on a human body elsewhere among the animal species,
Janārdana will indeed bring about the destruction of the Dānavas.
This Bhava shall also be your companion, possessed of great strength;
having created all the gods, sport as you please. (41)
Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas, all of you being well-composed, shall perform sacrifices according to the prescribed rules with various offerings and sacrificial fees.
"O gods, by the mere utterance of my name in all sacrifices and rituals, you shall indeed always remain satisfied and content. (43)
Śiva, who possesses the quality of tamas, is indeed to be honored in every way;
he should be worshipped with diligent effort in all sacrificial rites.
Furthermore, whenever fear of the Daityas arises for the gods,
my Śaktis will then manifest in beautiful forms and take them away.
Vārāhī, Vaiṣṇavī, Gaurī, Nārasiṃhī, and Sadāśivā—perform these and other tasks for me, O Lotus-born One! || 46 ||
O Lotus-born One, always reciting this nine-syllable mantra together with the visualization of the seed-syllable, accomplish all your tasks. 47.
"O high-minded one, know this indeed to be the supreme among mantras;
it should always be held in your heart for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. (48)
Having spoken thus to me, the Mother of the World, with a pure smile, said to Hari:
"O Viṣṇu, go; take this enchanting Mahālakṣmī. (49)
"She shall always reside upon your chest; of this there is no doubt.
For your pleasure, I have given you this auspicious Śakti, the bestower of all goals. (50)
"You must never treat her with contempt; she is always to be honored.
Indeed, this union known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa has been ordained by me. (51)
All sacrifices for the sake of livelihood have been performed by me for the gods in every way;
one should always conduct oneself with the three [means] without opposition and with detachment.
And you shall be the Creator, and Śiva; these gods shall arise from my qualities.
They will all be worthy of honor and worship by everyone, of this there is no doubt. (53)
Those men of deluded minds who shall create division will go to hell because of that division; of this there is no doubt.
He who is Hari is Śiva himself, and he who is Śiva is Hari himself;
a person who maintains a distinction between these two shall go to hell.
In the same way, Druhiṇa is to be known; there is no need for deliberation here.
There is another distinction of qualities; listen, O Viṣṇu, as I tell you.
Let the quality of sattva be primary for you in the contemplation of the Supreme Self;
even as secondary qualities, the qualities of rajas and tamas are well known. (57)
Always remaining endowed with the quality of passion (rajas), sport together with Lakṣmī amidst the various transformations and manifold diversities.
The seed-syllable of speech (Vāgbīja), the Kāmarāja, and the third, the Māyā-bīja—this mantra, O Beloved of Ramā, which bestows the supreme goal, has been given by me to you. (59)
Having taken it up, recite that [mantra] constantly and dwell at ease;
O Viṣṇu, you have no fear of death, nor any fear arising from Time.
"As long as this abode of mine remains firmly established, I shall withdraw everything—the entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving. (61)
"Then you, sirs, will surely be absorbed within me.
This mantra, which grants both desires and liberation, should always be remembered. (62)
It should be performed in conjunction with the Udgītha by one desiring auspiciousness;
and having caused Vaikuṇṭha to be built, O Puruṣottama, one should dwell there.
"Dwell as you desire, contemplating me, the eternal one.
Having spoken thus to Vāsudeva, she, the supreme Prakṛti consisting of the three guṇas, [vanished]. (64) Brahmā said:
The goddess Nirguṇā spoke these immortal words to the god Śaṅkara:
"O Hara, accept Gaurī, the enchanting Mahākālī. (65)
Having caused Kailāsa to be built, dwell there at your pleasure;
let the quality of tamas be your primary attribute, while the qualities of sattva and rajas remain secondary.
For the sake of destroying the demons dwelling there, they performed penance to suppress the qualities of passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas),
as well as for the purpose of remembering the Supreme Self.
O sinless ones, you must always assume the peaceful qualities of all beings;
for in every way, you three possess the [three] guṇas and are the agents of creation, preservation, and destruction.
There is no entity whatsoever in this saṃsāra that is devoid of these [qualities];
indeed, whatever object is perceived in saṃsāra consists of the three guṇas. (69)
In this world, there has never been, nor will there ever be, an object of perception that is devoid of qualities;
for that Supreme Self is devoid of qualities and can never be perceived as an object.
O Śambhu, at the time of the dissolution, I am both with attributes and without attributes, O Supreme Śaṅkara; I am always the cause, and never the effect.
Indeed, she possesses qualities because of her causality, yet she is devoid of qualities in the presence of the Puruṣa;
likewise, the Great Principle (mahattattva), the ego (ahaṅkāra), and the qualities such as sound and the rest [are likewise]. (72)
They transmigrate day and night in the form of cause and effect.
But since the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) has arisen from that, I am the cause, O Śivā.
And my ego (ahaṅkāra) must perform its function; it is established as possessing the three qualities (triguṇa).
From the ego arises the principle of Mahat, which is celebrated as the intellect (buddhi). 74.
For the principle of Mahat is the effect, while the ego (ahaṅkāra) is indeed the cause;
for the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi) always arise from the ego.
The five elements are the cause of all that arises;
likewise, there are exactly five organs of action and five organs of perception.
There are exactly five great elements (mahābhūtas) and the mind as the sixteenth;
this group consists of sixteen principles, comprising both the effect and the cause.
The Supreme Self is the primordial Person; He is neither effect nor cause.
Thus, O Śambhu, is the origin of all when the First Being comes into existence.
In brief, I have described to you their origin there;
O best of beings, go now by celestial chariot for my sake.
"Upon being in a difficult situation, I shall grant you my vision through remembrance;
