O gods, I, the eternal Supreme Self, am always to be remembered. (80)
"By the mere remembrance of both of us, the accomplishment of the task will undoubtedly occur.
Brahmā said this,
and having spoken thus, he dismissed us after bestowing upon us well-consecrated powers.
Then Mahālakṣmī was sent forth from that place for Viṣṇu, Mahākālī for Śiva, and Mahāsarasvatī for me.
Having reached another place, we became men, reflecting upon that true nature and its most wonderful power. (83)
Having reached that celestial chariot, the three indeed ascended it;
neither was that island there, nor was that goddess, nor likewise the ocean of nectar.
Indeed, that celestial chariot was seen by us there once more, and not otherwise.
Having reached that vast celestial chariot,
we arrived in the presence of the Lotus-born One,
where those two who were difficult to overcome had been slain in the great ocean.
By Murāri, those two known as Madhu and Kaiṭabha [were slain]. || 85 ||

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction Given by the Śrī Devī to Brahmā," in the Third Skandha of the Śrī Devī Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Determination of Reality.
Brahmā said:
"Such is the power of that Goddess as she was seen by me and by Viṣṇu."
O highly fortunate one, even by Śiva, those various goddesses were addressed individually.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his father, Nārada, the best of sages,
being exceedingly pleased, questioned the Prajāpati with these words.
Nārada said: O Grandfather, tell me of that primordial, indestructible Person who is devoid of qualities, infallible, and immutable— of whom you have both seen and experienced the presence.

O Father, O Lotus-born One, the Śakti has been observed as possessing the three qualities (triguṇā); what is her nature when she is devoid of qualities (nirguṇā)? Tell me her true form, and that of the Puruṣa as well.
And for the sake of which I performed great penance on Śvetadvīpa,
I have beheld the high-souled Siddhas and ascetics who are free from all anger.
"O Lord of Creatures, that Supreme Self has not yet been attained by me; it has not come within the range of my vision. For this reason, intense austerity was performed by me again and again. (6)
O father, you have seen the beautiful power endowed with qualities;
tell me, what are those two like who are devoid of qualities and without qualities?
Vyāsa said: Thus questioned by Nārada, his father Prajāpati,
the Grandfather, spoke these truthful words with a smile.
Brahmā said:
O sage, the form of the one devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) cannot come within the range of vision;
since that which is visible is perishable, how can the formless be seen?
The power (Śakti) is devoid of qualities and difficult to attain, and likewise the Person (Puruṣa) is devoid of qualities;
yet they are both accessible through knowledge and are to be meditated upon by sages. 10.
Know that Prakṛti and Puruṣa are without beginning or end and are eternally present;
they are to be approached with trust, never with distrust.
Know that consciousness which exists in all beings is of the nature of the Supreme;
it is the eternal, all-pervading light within various manifestations, O Nārada. (12)
O highly fortunate one, know that both of these are all-pervading and omnipresent;
there is not a single thing in this world of transmigration that is devoid of them.
Those two are always to be meditated upon within the body, eternally united and imperishable;
both are of one form, consisting of consciousness, devoid of qualities, and stainless.

That which is Śakti is the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and that which is the Supreme Self is considered to be Śakti; there is no difference whatsoever between these two, and no one knows this subtle truth except Nārada. || 15 ||
O Nārada, even after studying all the scriptures and the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches,
one does not know the subtle difference between those two without renunciation.
The entire universe, both stationary and moving, is created by the ego;
O son, how could it ever be devoid of that, even in hundreds of kalpas? (17)
O son of great intelligence, how can one who possesses qualities perceive that which is devoid of qualities with the eye? And as for that which possesses qualities, reflect upon it with the mind.
O best of sages, when the tongue and the eye are covered by bile,
one perceives the bitter taste and the color, yet not as they truly are.
How can a mind enveloped by qualities know that which is devoid of qualities?
And how could that [mind], which arises from egoism, be free from it? (20)
As long as there is no cessation of the qualities (guṇas), how can there be the vision of that [Reality]?
One perceives it in the mind when one is devoid of egoism (ahaṅkāra). || 21 ||
Nārada said: O Lord of the gods, tell me in detail the true nature of the three qualities (guṇas), for the ego (ahaṅkāra) indeed possesses a threefold form according to their nature. (22)
O Puruṣottama, please describe the distinct forms of the sattvic, the rājasic, and likewise the other, the tāmasa.
O Lord, tell me that knowledge by knowing which I may be completely liberated;
[tell me] the characteristics of the qualities (guṇas) as they are extensively detailed according to their divisions.
Brahmā said: O sinless one, there are three powers belonging to these three; I shall describe them to you:
the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and another, the power of objects (artha-śakti).
The power of knowledge belongs to the Sāttvika, the power of action to the Rājasa, and the power of material substance to the Tāmasa; thus have the three been described to you. (26)
I shall describe their functions; listen, O Nārada, according to the truth:
from the material power of Tamas, there arises sound and touch.
Form, taste, and smell are declared to be the subtle elements (tanmātras).
Space has sound as its sole quality, and wind likewise has touch as its quality. (28)
Fire has the single quality of beautiful form, and water consists of the quality of taste;
earth is to be known as having the quality of smell—these, O Nārada, are the subtle elements. (29)
When these ten, joined together and endowed with the power of their respective substances,
are produced from the tamasic ego, that is the creation which follows its own course.
Now hear from me the products of the Rajasic power of action:
the ear, the skin, the mouth, the eye, and the nose as the fifth. (31)
These are the organs of knowledge, and likewise the organs of action, which are five: speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals.
Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, samāna, and udāna—these five winds combined together are called the rājasa creation. || 33 ||
These means of accomplishment (sādhana) indeed consist of the power of action (kriyā-śakti);
their material cause (upādāna), it is said, is the persistence of consciousness (cid-anuvṛtti). || 34 ||
Endowed with the power of knowledge and born from the quality of sattva, they are the quarters, Vāyu, Sūrya, Varuṇa, and the two Aśvins. (35)
For the five sense organs, there are five presiding deities:
Candra, Brahmā, Rudra, and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña) as the fourth. || 36 ||
Thus, for that which is called the internal organ—namely the intellect (buddhi) and so forth—four presiding deities have indeed been declared as its adhidaivata. (37)
Together with the mind, these indeed constitute fifteen;
this is the creation of the sattvic being, proclaimed as the "sāttvika" creation. (38)
The Supreme Self has two forms, distinguished as gross and subtle;
they declare that form which is consciousness and formless to be its primary cause.
For the practitioner, however, the gross form is taught for the purpose of meditation and so forth;
this subtle body alone is proclaimed to belong to the Puruṣa. (40)
Indeed, my own body is called the Sūtra;
I shall now describe the gross body of Brahmā, the Supreme Self.
Listen with diligence, O Nārada, for by hearing this one is completely liberated:
those subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) which were previously described as being merely of the nature of the [five] elements.
Having indeed quintuplicated those very [elements], there arises the manifestation of the five gross elements;
listen now as I truly explain this process of quintuplication. (43)
First, having taken up the subtle element of taste even within the mind, one should likewise imagine it in such a way that it becomes water.
Having divided the portions of the remaining beings individually,
he should then mix those portions into the water, which has been made into a substance consisting of essence.
Then, when the differentiation of the elements and consciousness have been revealed, the doubt "I am that" arises due to the entry of consciousness [into the body]. (46)
Because he is perceived through that very distinction by way of such conceit, the Lord is called Ādinārāyaṇa and Bhagavān. (47)
Then, when the differentiation of the elements had become solidified and attained clarity,
they grew by means of the qualities (guṇas) in this manner, through the successive increase of each quality.
The quality of space is one alone, which is sound and nothing else;
and the qualities of wind are proclaimed to be two: sound and touch. (49)
Sound, touch, and form—these three are the qualities of fire;
sound, touch, form, and taste—these four indeed belong to water.
Touch, sound, taste, form, and smell are the qualities of earth;
thus, through the union of these combined elements, the creation of the cosmic egg is said to occur.
All living beings, having come together, are born from a portion of the cosmic egg;
indeed, eighty-four lakh species of living beings have been proclaimed.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Exposition of Reality," in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Brahmā spoke on the description of the qualities, forms, and configurations:
"O dear one, this creation has now been told to you, concerning which I was questioned by you just now."
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the true nature and configuration of the qualities (guṇas). || 1 ||
Sattva should be known as having the nature of joy, for joy arises from happiness;
likewise, it consists of straightforwardness, truthfulness, purity, faith, forbearance, and fortitude. (2)
Compassion, as well as modesty, tranquility, and contentment—through these, a constant and unwavering conviction in the existence of the *sattva* arises. (3)
Likewise, the white-colored being always brings joy in the Dharma;
it constantly generates true faith and wards off false faith.
Faith is said to be of three kinds by the sages who perceive the truth: the sattvic, the rājasic, and likewise the tāmasic. (5)
The red-colored *rajas* is said to be wonderful yet unpleasant;
because it leads to the conjunction with suffering, its nature as displeasure is indeed certain. (6)
Furthermore, aversion, as well as malice, envy, and arrogance;
longing, as well as sleep, and faith—therein lies that which is characterized by rajas.
Pride, intoxication, and likewise arrogance are indeed born from *rajas*;
therefore, *rajas* should be recognized by the wise through these characteristics. (8)
Darkness is said to be black in color; it causes delusion and produces despondency, as well as laziness, ignorance, sleep, wretchedness, and fear.
Furthermore, there is dispute, wretchedness, crookedness, and anger;
as well as partiality, extreme atheism, and the observation of others' faults. (10)
The wise should recognize that as characterized by darkness (tāmasa) in every respect;
it is joined with dark faith and results in the affliction of others. (11)
A person desiring their own welfare should always manifest *sattva*, restrain *rajas*, and suppress *tamas* at will. 12.
Furthermore, because they mutually overcome one another, these elements oppose each other;
likewise, all being dependent on one another, they do not remain without a support.
Sattva is never found alone anywhere, nor are rajas and tamas;
they are always combined, and for that reason they are known as being mutually dependent.
I shall now describe their expansion through mutual union;
listen, O Nārada, for by knowing this one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence. (15)
No doubt should be entertained here regarding the words spoken by me after I have understood them;
for that which is known is experienced once the fruit has been realized.
O Mahāmati, through hearing, seeing, and the experience of mental formations, that which is fully understood does not arise again.
The sacred ford was heard of as pure, and royal faith arose within him;
he indeed went to that ford and saw it exactly as he had heard.
Having bathed there, he performed his duties and gave gifts worthy of a king;
covered by the quality of passion (rajas), he remained there for some time.
Not liberated from passion and hatred, shrouded by desire and anger,
he returned once more to his home and remained just as he was before.
O Lord of Sages, that holy place was indeed heard of but not experienced by him;
since he did not attain its fruit, know it, O Nārada, to be as if unheard.
O best of sages, know that the power of the sacred ford (tīrtha) lies in its sinlessness,
just as in this world the fruit of agriculture is the eating of prepared food.
Those other transformations of the sinful body, such as desire and anger, as well as greed, delusion, thirst, hatred, passion, and pride; (23)
O Nārada, malice, envy, impatience, and lack of peace—these are evils;
as long as they have not departed from the body, a man remains possessed by evil.
If, once the sacred rite has been performed, these [vital breaths] do not depart from the body,
then it is merely fruitless labor, just like that of a farmer.
The field was oppressed by labor; the plowed earth was very difficult to manage;
the seed sown was of great value; thus, the livelihood is said to be beneficial. (26)
Having exerted himself day and night for the sake of protection, he was eager for the fruit;
yet, having fallen asleep at the proper time during the winter in the forest, he was greatly afflicted by tigers and other predators. (27)
Just as everything was devoured by locusts and once again rendered hopeless, so too, O son, is the toil of visiting sacred fords: it causes hardship but yields no fruit.
O Nārada, his sattva became intensely dominant and increased through the study of the scriptures; as its fruit, detachment arose toward objects characterized by tamas.
It indeed forcibly overcomes both rajas and tamas;
rajas has become predominant and is active through its connection with greed.
In that same way, it indeed overcomes both [rajas and sattva] when tamas is likewise predominant;
having become thus intensified through the conjunction with delusion (moha), it increases further. || 31 ||
Both that *sattva* and *rajas*, having come together, also overcome [the *tamas*];
today I shall explain in detail how indeed they overcome it.
When sattva has indeed increased and the intellect is established in dharma,
one no longer thinks of external objects arising from rajas and tamas.
He accepts wealth that has arisen from virtuous beings and not otherwise;
he desires wealth acquired without effort, as well as righteousness and sacrifice. || 34 ||
Then he indeed directs his desire toward sattvic enjoyments alone;
not toward rajasic ones for the sake of liberation, and how much less so toward tamasic ones? (35)
Having thus first conquered rajas, there follows the conquest of tamas;
then, O son, sattva alone becomes stainless.

When passion (rajas) has indeed increased, having abandoned the eternal duties (sanātana-dharma), one performs actions contrary to dharma after having acquired a passionate form of faith (rājasī śraddhā). || 37 ||
From rajas arises the increase of wealth, and likewise enjoyment is rajasic;
by means of that, sattva emerges, and there is also the suppression of tamas. (38)
When darkness had increased and become overwhelming,
there was no faith in the Veda, nor likewise in the Dharmaśāstra.
Having acquired a tamasic form of faith, he brings about the loss of wealth;
he practices malice everywhere and does not attain peace.
Having conquered both *sattva* and *rajas*, the wrathful, evil-minded,
and deceitful one conducts himself according to his own whims amidst the various states of existence.
The quality of passion does not exist alone, nor does darkness;
the qualities, possessing the nature of pairs, exist by depending upon one another.
Without rajas, sattva would not exist; nor does rajas ever exist without sattva. And these two do not function without tamas either, O bull among men. (43)
But darkness (tamas) is never devoid of those two [rajas and sattva] alone;
indeed, all the qualities (guṇas), possessing the nature of pairs, exist within various effects.
All of them exist dependent upon one another and do not remain separated, for they are mutual progenitors since they possess the nature of procreation. || 45 ||
Sometimes sattva gives rise to rajas and tamas; at other times, rajas indeed gives rise to both sattva and tamas. (46)
Sometimes, however, darkness produces both goodness and passion;
thus they produce one another, just as a lump of clay produces a jar.
Established in the Buddha, those qualities mutually awaken one another's desires, just as Devadatta, Viṣṇumitra, Yajñadatta, and others [do]. (48)
Just as a woman and a man form a couple with one another, so too do the qualities (guṇas) enter into a state of union with one another. 49.
Sattva is the pair of rajas; rajas is the pair of sattva.
Both of these, sattva and rajas, are known to be the pair of tamas.
Nārada said:
"Having heard this unsurpassed account of qualities and forms as told by my father, I myself then questioned the Grandfather."

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Forms, Configurations, and Other Attributes of the Guṇas," in the third book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Characteristics of the Guṇas.
Nārada said:
"O dear one, you have indeed described the characteristics of the guṇas."
I am not satiated, even as I drink the sweet nectar flowing from your mouth. (1)
Please describe the thorough knowledge of the qualities exactly as they are,
by which I may attain supreme peace in my mind.
Vyāsa said:
Thus questioned by his son, the high-souled Nārada,
the creator of the world, who had arisen from the quality of passion (rajas), spoke.
Brahmā said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe the qualities;
though I do not know them perfectly, I shall speak to you according to my understanding.
Sattva alone is never perceived anywhere;
indeed, due to their mutual intermingling, it is their state of mixture that appears.
Just as a certain excellent woman, adorned with all ornaments and endowed with graceful gestures and expressions, brings pleasure to her husband through desire; || 6 ||
That very same [woman] brings joy to her parents as well as to her circle of kinsmen;
yet it is she alone who produces sorrow and delusion among her co-wives.
Thus, by that very *sattva* which has been brought to the state of femininity,
the activity of *rajas* and *tamas* is produced in a different manner.
Indeed, through the passion (rajas) created by woman and likewise through darkness (tamas),
and from their mutual conjunction, it appears otherwise.
O Nārada, because they abide in their own essential natures, no contrary species are ever perceived anywhere through yoga.
Just as a beautiful woman, adorned with youth, endowed with modesty and sweetness, is likewise possessed of discipline. || 11 ||
She was knowledgeable in the rules of the science of love (kāmaśāstra) and esteemed even in the science of duty (dharmaśāstra);
bringing delight to her husband, she became a source of sorrow for her co-wives.

Abiding in the nature of delusion and suffering, it is called "abiding in existence" (sattvasthā) by people; likewise, when that existence undergoes transformation, it indeed appears as another state of being.
For that very army, possessing such qualities, brings happiness to the virtuous who are oppressed by thieves, yet it is painful and delusive for the bandits.
They naturally avoid erroneous perception, just as when a foul day has arisen, shrouded by dense, great clouds. || 15 ||
Accompanied by lightning and thunder, enveloped in darkness, and raining down as it drenches the earth—that indeed is described as having the form of darkness (tamas). || 16 ||
That which is indeed a most grievous day for farmers becomes, conversely, a source of happiness for those who possess seeds and farming implements. (17)
And for those unfortunate householders whose houses are not well-concealed, and who have taken up grass and wood for their dwellings, it is a source of particular suffering. (18)
They say that for women whose husbands are away, even all the qualities inherent in their own nature appear as if they were perverted, causing delusion. (19)
Furthermore, O son, listen as I describe their characteristics:
Sattva is light, illuminating, stainless, and always pure. (20)
When the limbs are indeed light, as are the senses such as the eyes,
and when the mind is likewise pure, it does not grasp those objects.
At that time, the quality of *sattva* indeed becomes predominant within the body;
furthermore, *rajas* manifests as yawning, stiffness, drowsiness, and restlessness. (22)
When that [passion] has become intense in the body of anyone whatsoever, he seeks to engage in strife or likewise to go to another village. (23)
When that [mind] of a restless person is thus excessively engaged in dispute, then desire, which is an obscuration, becomes darkness (tamas). // 24 //
Then his limbs quickly become heavy and obstructed;
his senses and mind are vacant, yet he does not desire sleep at all. (25)
"O Nārada, the characteristics of the qualities (guṇas) should be understood here in this way.
Nārada said:
"O Grandfather, the three qualities have been described as having distinct characteristics. (26)
How is it that they perform their task eternally in a single location, having indeed united with one another, though they are supposedly distinct enemies? (27)
"Tell me, how do they perform their function while remaining in one place?
Brahmā said:
"Listen, my son, I shall explain; their qualities function like lamps. (28)
And just as a lamp performs its function of revealing objects—wherein the wick, the oil, and the flame are mutually contradictory [yet act together]—so too [is the nature of the cognition]. (29)
For in that way, oil is indeed incompatible with fire when they come together;
oil is opposed to the wick, and fire is likewise opposed to each other.
"Remaining together, they manifest the various categories of objects.
Nārada said:
"Thus, O son of Satyavatī, have the qualities born of Prakṛti been described. (31)
"Indeed, the cause of the universe has been told by me previously exactly as I heard it.
Vyāsa said:
"Thus everything was then told to me in detail by Nārada."

The entire definition of the qualities (guṇas) and their effects, categorized individually, as well as the Supreme Śakti who is to be worshipped and by whom all this is pervaded, [have been explained]. (33)
Indeed, she is always both with attributes and without attributes according to the difference in her effects;
the Puruṣa, however, is the non-agent, complete, desireless, supreme, and immutable.
This Mahāmāyā creates the universe, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
she is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Sūrya, Candra, and the Lord of Śacī.
The two Aśvins, the Vasus, Tvaṣṭṛ, Kubera, the Lord of the Waters (Varuṇa), Vahni (Agni), Vāyu, as well as Pūṣan, Senānī, and Vināyaka. || 36 ||
All are endowed with power and capable of performing their own tasks;
otherwise, they would indeed be powerless, unable even to move.
And she alone, O King, is the cause and the supreme sovereign of the universe;
propitiate her, O ruler of the earth, and perform a sacrifice, O lord of men. (38)
One should perform worship with supreme devotion according to the prescribed rite for her alone:
as Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, and likewise Mahāsarasvatī. (39)
She is the sovereign of all beings, the cause of all causes;
she bestows all desires and goals, is peaceful, pleasant to serve, and endowed with compassion. (40)
By the mere utterance of her name, she bestows the fruits of one's desired objects;
she was formerly propitiated by the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. (41)
Even that name which was uttered, though indistinctly, in the course of conversation by various ascetics who had conquered their selves and were seekers of liberation— (42)
It grants all desired objects, even those that are entirely difficult to obtain, when one sees a tiger or other such beasts in the forest and cries out "Ai! Ai! in distress from fear. (43)
It has been stated that even [the mantra] devoid of the *bindu* indeed bestows one's desired object;
in this regard, O best of kings, the example of Satyavrata himself is seen.
And this is directly perceived by us in the assemblies of brahmins who are sages of purified souls; it is illustrated by the wise as his [the Buddha's] example. (45)
O King, everything that was being told by me has been heard by you in full detail:
there was a twice-born man named Satyavrata, who was illiterate and a great fool.
Having heard the syllable from Kolamukha and having himself uttered it, though devoid of the *bindu*, that best of the wise was born through that incidental occurrence. (47)
Then, upon the utterance of the syllable *ai*, the Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, being moistened with compassion, became pleased and made him a king of poets.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Thorough Knowledge of the Guṇas," in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 9 ||
The Description of the Narrative of Satyavrata.
Janamejaya said:
"Who was this Brāhmaṇa named Satyavrata, O best of the twice-born?"
In which country was he born, and what was he like? Tell me this.
How was that sound heard by him, and how was it uttered again?
And what kind of supernatural power (siddhi) arose for that brahmin at that very moment? || 2 ||
How was that Bhavānī, the omniscient one who abides in all things, satisfied? Tell this delightful story in detail today.
Sūta said:
Thus questioned then by the king, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī,
spoke these most noble, flavorful, and pure words.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall relate this auspicious ancient tale which was formerly heard by me in the assemblies of sages, O best of the Kurus.
Once, O best of the Kurus, while performing a pure pilgrimage to sacred fords,
I arrived at the purifying Naimiṣa forest, which is frequented by sages.
Having bowed down to all the sages, I remained there in that excellent hermitage where the sons of Brahmā,
who were liberated while living and observers of great vows, resided.
While that very conversation was underway in the assembly of brahmins, Jamadagni, remaining seated there, questioned the sages in this manner: || 8 ||
Jamadagni said:
"O illustrious ascetics, there is a doubt in my mind;
indeed, within the assemblies of sages, I shall become free from doubt. (9)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Indra, Varuṇa, Anala, Kubera, Pavana, Tvaṣṭṛ, Senānī, and Gaṇādhipa; || 10 ||
The Sun, the Aśvins, Bhaga, Pūṣan, the Lord of Night (the Moon), and likewise the planets—who among these is most worthy of worship, bestowing the fruits of one's desired objects? (11)
"Let the sages—who are all-knowing and firm in their vows—speak quickly: is he always easy to serve, easily satisfied, and a bestower of honor? (12)
When this question had been asked, Lomaśa spoke these words there:
"O Jamadagni, listen now to that which has indeed been asked by you."
She is the most worthy of being served by all who desire welfare;
she is the supreme primordial nature, omnipresent, and eternally auspicious. 14.
She alone is the mother of the gods and of the great-souled ones beginning with Brahmā;
she is indeed the primordial root-nature of the tree of saṃsāra.
When remembered and invoked, the Goddess indeed grants one's desire;
when served, she is always moist with compassion for the sake of bestowing boons.
I shall proclaim this auspicious history; let the sages listen to how it was indeed obtained by a twice-born man through the mere utterance of syllables.
In the land of Kosala, there was a certain twice-born man renowned as Devadatta;
being childless, he performed a sacrifice for the sake of a son according to the prescribed rites.
Having established himself on the bank of the Tamasā and constructed an excellent pavilion,
he summoned the twice-born who were learned in the Vedas and skilled in the performance of sacrificial rites.
Having constructed an altar according to the rules and established the sacred fires,
that best of the twice-born performed the Putreṣṭi sacrifice there in accordance with the prescribed rites.
He appointed the best of sages, Suhotra, as the Brahmā priest;
Yājñavalkya as the Adhvaryu; and Bṛhaspati as the Hotṛ.

Having duly appointed Paila as the Prastotṛ priest and Gobhila as the Udgātṛ priest, as well as other sages as the members of the assembly, he bestowed wealth upon them according to the prescribed rites.
The Udgātṛ, the most excellent singer of Sāmans, sang the Rathantara hymn, endowed with the seven musical notes and accompanied by modulations of tone.
Then, as he repeatedly exhaled, his voice broke;
Devadatta became enraged and spoke secretly to Gobhila.
"You are a fool; today you have caused a break in my voice while I was engaged in a rite for personal desire, performing a sacrifice for the sake of a son. (25)
Then Gobhila, being greatly provoked, said to Devadatta:
"Your son shall be a fool, deceitful, and devoid of knowledge of the sacred sounds. (26)
The inhalation and exhalation within the bodies of all living beings is indeed difficult to perceive;
O high-minded one, there is no fault on my part here regarding this breaking of my voice. (27)
Having heard those words of the high-souled Gobhila,
Devadatta, fearing the curse, spoke to him in great distress.
O best of Brahmins, why are you angry with me in vain, for I am innocent?
For sages are indeed free from anger and are always bestowers of happiness. (29)
O best of Brahmins, for such a slight offense, why have I been cursed by you?
I was already childless and deeply distressed; now I have been made even more tormented. (30)
Those who know the Vedas understand that it is better to have no son at all than a foolish one;
nevertheless, a foolish Brāhmaṇa is indeed despised by all.
Like a beast and like a Śūdra, he is indeed unfit for all ritual acts.
"O best of the twice-born, what shall I do here with such a foolish son? (32)
As is a Śūdra, so is a foolish Brāhmaṇa; there is no doubt in this matter.
He is unworthy of worship, unworthy of gifts, and censurable in all ritual acts. || 33 ||
Even while residing in the country, a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of the Vedas should be regarded by the king as a Śūdra and made to pay taxes.
In rites for the ancestors and in rites for the gods, that twice-born man who is a fool should not be seated on the seat by one desiring the fruit of the rite. (35)
A king should regard him as equal to a Śūdra and not employ him in any duties;
however, a Brāhmaṇa devoid of Vedic knowledge may be made a farmer by a twice-born man.
A Śrāddha should indeed be performed even with a bundle of Kuśa grass in the absence of a Brāhmaṇa;
however, a Śrāddha must never be performed by a foolish Brāhmaṇa.
One should not give food in excess of what is needed for sustenance to an unwise person;
the giver falls into hell, and the recipient even more so. (38)
Fie upon the kingdom of that king in whose land ignorant people—even foolish Brahmins—are honored with gifts, respect, and the like! (39)
Whether in sitting, in worship, or in giving, where there is not even an atom's worth of difference between a fool and a scholar, that distinction must indeed be understood by the wise.
A wise man should never, under any circumstances, dwell in that land where fools are highly esteemed for their acceptance of gifts, honors, and patronage. 41.
The prosperity of the wicked serves only to benefit the wicked;
though the neem tree is rich with fruit, it is enjoyed only by crows. 42.
When a Brahmin learned in the Vedas has eaten his meal, he indeed performs the study of the Vedas;
it is said that his ancestors then sport joyfully in heaven. (43)
"O best among the knowers of the Vedas, you have indeed been liberated by Gobhila from that which is most contemptible in this world:
the state of being the son of a fool, which is worse than death. (44)
"O illustrious one, have mercy regarding the mitigation of this curse!
You are capable of uplifting the wretched; I fall at your feet. (45)
Lomaśa said:
Having spoken thus, Devadatta fell at his feet,
praising him with an exceedingly dejected heart, wretched and with eyes full of tears.
Then Gobhila, seeing him there with a dejected mind, [spoke]; for great men, though their anger lasts but a moment, are indeed most sinful when provoked to wrath for an entire kalpa.
Water is cold by its very nature; it becomes hot through contact with fire or sunlight, yet it quickly returns to being cool once those [causes] are removed. (48)
The compassionate Gobhila said to the deeply distressed Devadatta:
"Though your son has become a fool, he will indeed become a learned man. (49)
Having thus been granted the boon, that bull among brahmins was then delighted;
having completed the sacrifice, he duly dismissed the brahmins according to the prescribed rites.
After some time, his wife Rūpamatī,
who was virtuous and like Rohiṇī herself, conceived a child in due season, just as Rohiṇī did.
The twice-born performed the rites beginning with the conception ceremony (garbhādhāna) according to the prescribed rules,
as well as the rite for ensuring the birth of a male child (puṃsavana) and the decoration of the womb.
The parting of the hair ceremony was performed according to Vedic injunctions;
and considering the sacrifice to have been fruitful, he joyfully gave gifts.
On an auspicious day, when the moon was in conjunction with Rohiṇī, Rohiṇī gave birth to a son;
on that day, at an exceedingly favorable moment, he performed the birth rites for him.
Having performed the ceremony for beholding his son, he also performed the naming rite;
the knower of ancient lore gave the son the name Utathya.
And in his eighth year, on an auspicious day during a favorable month,
his father performed the rite of initiation for him according to the prescribed rules.
The teacher taught the Vedas to him while he remained established in his vow;
however, Utathya did not speak at all, remaining then like one who was bewildered.
Though instructed in many ways by his father, the rogue did not retain the knowledge;
he remained utterly like a fool, and so his father then grieved for him.
Thus constantly practicing, he reached the age of twelve years,
yet he did not know how to perform the rite of the twilight prayers (sandhyā-vandana) according to the prescribed rules.
The news that he had become a fool spread extensively throughout the worlds—among all the brahmins, the ascetics, and others as well. (60)
O Sage, wherever that brahmin went, the world laughed at him;
then his father and mother censured him, severely rebuking that fool.
Then, though censured at will by the people, his parents, and his kinsmen,
the brahmin attained a state of world-weariness and departed for the forest.
"A blind husband is better than a son who is a fool; a lame husband is likewise better.
Having been told this by his parents, he indeed entered the forest.
Having constructed an unsurpassed hut at a beautiful spot on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
and having resolved upon a forest-dwelling way of life, he remained there with a concentrated mind.
Having made a supreme vow, I do not speak untruth;
for he remains in that delightful hermitage, devoted to the vow of celibacy.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Satyavrata," in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 10 ||
The Description of the Narrative of Satyavrata.
Lomaśa said:
He knew nothing of the study of the Vedas, nor likewise of their recitation.
Neither meditation nor the propitiation of deities is of any avail in that regard. || 1 ||
That brahmin did not know the *āsana*, nor again the *prāṇāyāma*; he did not know *pratyāhāra*, nor the cause which is *bhūtaśuddhi*.
He did not know the mantra-pilings to be recited, nor the Gāyatrī;
he likewise knew nothing of the rules for purification, bathing, or sipping water (ācamana). || 3 ||
That sage knew nothing of the Prāṇāgnihotra, nor of the offering of oblations, nor of guests; he likewise knew nothing of the twilight prayers, the sacrificial fuel, or the fire-oblation.
Having risen in the morning, he performed whatever dental cleansing and bathing there was at the Ganges, just like a Śūdra, devoid of mantras.
Just as one who has taken wild fruits by chance even at midday does not know the distinction between what is fit and unfit to be eaten, so too is the rogue.
He spoke the truth while remaining there and never again uttered a falsehood;
therefore, the people gave that twice-born man the name Satyatapas.
One should not do what is harmful to anyone, nor should one ever do what is improper; reflecting thus, one sleeps peacefully right there, free from fear.
"When will my death come? I live in misery in the forest; fie upon the life of a fool! Death by force is surely better. (9)
"I have been made a fool by fate; there is no other cause for this in my case. Having obtained an excellent birth, it has now become useless for me. (10)
Just as a barren woman may be beautiful, or as a tree may be fruitless, or as a cow may yield no milk, so have I been rendered fruitless. (11)
"Why do I blame destiny? Surely it is my own karma that is thus; for I did not give a book, having had one made, to a high-souled Brahmin. (12)
"Indeed, in a previous birth, pure knowledge was not bestowed upon me by you;
therefore, by that karma, I have become a rogue and the lowest of the twice-born. (13)
I did not perform austerities at sacred fords, nor did I serve holy men;
I did not honor the twice-born with wealth, and therefore I have been born with a wicked mind.
The sons of sages, who have reached the further shore of the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, are present here;
yet I have become utterly deluded by some stroke of fate. (15)
I do not know how to perform penance; what effective means can I employ?
This resolve of mine here is surely in vain; indeed, my fortune is not auspicious.
I consider destiny alone to be supreme; fie upon human effort, which is useless!
An undertaking accomplished with labor becomes successful in every way only through destiny. (17)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and indeed the deities headed by Śakra—all are subject to the power of Time; for Time is indeed insurmountable. (18)
Engaging in such reflections day and night, the twice-born remained there in that hermitage on the pure banks of the Jahnavī.
Having become dispassionate, that twice-born man remained in that hermitage;
peaceful, he spent his time in the solitary forest.
While he remained thus in the forest of pure waters for fifteen years at his pleasure,
he knew neither propitiation, nor recitation, nor even the mantra.
He indeed spent a great deal of time in the forest.
The world knows his vow alone to be extensive; indeed, even though the sage speaks the truth, his entire lineage of names has perished,
yet his fame has spread at will among all people.
This man is devoted to truth and never speaks falsely.
Once, while sporting on a hunt, Niśaṭha the Niṣāda arrived there, bearing bow and arrow;
sporting in the vast forest, his body was like that of Yama.
He was of cruel appearance and exceedingly skillful in the act of killing.
Pierced by that arrow drawn back too far by the Kirāta archer,
the boar fled, overwhelmed with fear.
He fled and went into the presence of the sage. || 24 ||
When he, trembling and with his body drenched in blood, entered the circle of the hermitage,
Time itself became exceedingly moist with compassion.
The sage arrived there and beheld him in distress.
Seeing the boar rushing forward with its body drenched in blood and suddenly pierced, the sage trembled violently,
overcome by compassion.
Then he uttered the seed-syllable of Sarasvatī.
Never known before and likewise never heard, it has indeed come forth from his mouth by fate;
that deluded man did not recognize the seed.
Today that high-souled sage has fallen into grief on my account. || 27 ||
Kola entered that circle of hermitages and,
having gone into a thicket, remained hidden and concealed; finding no way forward, his heart was filled with profound despondency.
Trembling because of being afflicted by arrows. || 28 ||
Then, in an instant,
he arrived at that spot being sought after, bearing a bow drawn to its limit, his body appearing exceedingly terrifying.
It is said that the king of the Niṣādas was indeed Kāla himself. || 29 ||
Seeing the sage named Satyavrata, who was seated there upon a mat of kusha grass and was peerless,
the hunter bowed down and stood before him.
Kola asked, "O Lord of the twice-born, where has he gone?"
I know your renowned vow of excellent conduct;
therefore, I ask you today: my entire family is afflicted by hunger and pierced by my arrows.
"I have indeed come wishing to support [you]," he said. || 31 ||
"O best of Brahmins, this is the livelihood ordained for me by the Creator; there is no other, I speak the truth.
One must indeed properly maintain one's family in this world."
By some means, whether auspicious or inauspicious. || 32 ||
Speak the truth today, for you are one whose vow is truth: your dependents are suffering from hunger;
where has that boar gone, pierced by my arrow?
I ask you, O Brahmin; tell me quickly.
Thus questioned, that high-souled sage, though immersed in reflection, readily agreed:
"May my vow of truthfulness not be broken today."
What indeed is the point of merely uttering the word "not seen"?
The boar here has gone with its body pierced by arrows;
how can I speak today of what is false or true? Afflicted by hunger, it seems to be questioning me.
Having seen him, he will surely kill even a boar.
Truth is indeed not truth where there is violence; rather,
even untruth accompanied by compassion is truth,
since it brings about what is beneficial for human beings in this world.
That alone is the truth; it is not otherwise. || 36 ||

"How can there be benefit for both who are so opposed? What answer could there be that is not false?"—pondering thus in this dilemma of dharma, O Vāḍava, he found no words to speak as was appropriate. (37)
Seeing the boar struck by the arrow and filled with compassion, Śivā was pleased by the words uttered at that moment from her own seed.
And he bestowed upon him that knowledge which is difficult to attain.
Through the utterance of the seed-syllable, the entire Vidyā of the Goddess manifested;
and just as it had been before, Vālmīki indeed became a poet.
The twice-born man, whose nature was righteousness and who was devoted to compassion, spoke this single verse to the hunter standing before him with his bow drawn, for he desired the truth. (40)
She who sees does not speak; she who speaks does not see.
Oh, hunter seeking your own ends, why do you ask again and again? 41.
Having been addressed thus by him at that time, that killer of animals,
losing all hope for the boar, returned once more to his own home.
A brahmin was born, a poet like another Prācetasa;
he was a twice-born man renowned throughout all the worlds by the name Satyavrata.
Then that learned and highly renowned twice-born man on the surface of the earth chanted the seed-syllable of Sarasvatī according to the prescribed rites.
On every festival day, the Brahmins always sing of his glory,
and the sages indeed praise his exceedingly extensive narrative.
Having heard that, he went to his hermitage and approached his home; by him who had previously abandoned him, he was now brought back home and treated with great honor.
Therefore, O King, the primordial Śakti, the supreme goddess who is indeed the cause of the worlds, should always be served and worshipped with devotion. (47)
O great king, perform her sacrifice according to the Vedic injunctions;
it was declared of old as a certainty that it eternally grants all desires. (48)
When remembered, worshipped with devotion, meditated upon, uttered, and praised, she grants all desired objects; therefore, she is celebrated as Kāryadā (the Giver of Success).
O King, having seen those who are afflicted by disease, miserable, hungry, destitute, and deceitful, this power must be exercised in every way by the wise. (50)
People who are distressed, as well as fools, those constantly oppressed by enemies, slaves, those who obey orders, the base, the incapacitated, and the agitated; || 51 ||
Those who are insatiable regarding food and enjoyments, always afflicted, with uncontrolled senses,
excessive in craving, powerless, and perpetually oppressed by distress.
Likewise, [he saw those] endowed with wealth, increasing in sons and grandsons,
with bodies nourished by enjoyments, and devoted to the recitation of the Vedas.
Then [he saw] heroes endowed with royal fortune who had brought people under their control,
who were never separated from their kinsmen, and who were marked by all the auspicious signs.
The wise should investigate through both positive and negative concomitance;
for it was by these means that the auspicious Goddess, the bestower of the fruits of all goals, was not worshipped.
And because Ambikā was thus constantly propitiated by these men, they have all become happy in this worldly existence; of this there is no doubt. (56)
Vyāsa said:
Thus, O King, I heard there in the assembly of sages from the mouth of Lomaśa this excellent majesty of the Goddess, exactly as it is.
Having reflected thus, O Indra among kings, one should always perform worship with supreme devotion and love for the Goddess, O bull among men. (58)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Satyavrata," in the third book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 11 ||
Description of the Ritual for the Sacrifice to Ambā.
The King said:
"Tell me correctly the ritual for the sacrifice to that goddess in its entirety."
"O Mistress, having heard this, I shall indeed act according to my ability, unwearied. || 1 ||
The ritual procedure for worship, the mantras, and the materials for the fire-oblation without doubt; the number of Brahmins required, and likewise the sacrificial fees. || 2 ||
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall describe the sacrifice of the Goddess according to the prescribed rules;
it should always be understood as being threefold, performed through rites seen in the sacred ordinances.
It is of three kinds: sattvic, rājasic, and likewise another, tāmasa.
That which is sattvic is declared for sages; that which is rājasic is remembered for kings.
I shall describe to you in detail that which is tamasic among the Rākṣasas, devoid of qualities among the wise, and consisting of knowledge among those who are liberated.
They know that sacrifice to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika) wherein the place, the time, the materials, the mantras, the Brahmins, and the faith are all characterized by purity.
O King, if there be purity of substance, purity of action, and purity of mantra, then the fruit becomes complete; it is not otherwise.
A meritorious deed performed with wealth acquired through unjust means brings no fame in this world, nor does it yield its fruit in the next world. (8)
Therefore, one should always perform virtuous deeds only with wealth acquired through righteous means; for such actions lead indeed to fame, to the next world, and to happiness.
O Indra among kings, it was witnessed by you directly how the Pāṇḍavas performed the Rājasūya,
the best of sacrifices, which was completed with excellent sacrificial fees.
There, Hari Kṛṣṇa himself, the high-minded lord of the Yādavas,
resides, as do Brāhmaṇas of perfected knowledge such as Bhāradvāja and others.
Having completed the sacrifice perfectly within a single month by the Pāṇḍavas, they instead encountered a far greater hardship: the terrible forest exile.
The oppression of the princess of Pañcāla, as well as the defeat at dice, the forest exile of great hardship—where has the fruit born of sacrifice gone? (13)
And servitude was performed for Virāṭa by all those great-souled ones;
and Draupadī, the most excellent of women, was tormented by Kīcaka.
Where have the blessings of the twice-born with pure hearts gone?
And where has devotion to Vāsudeva gone in that moment of crisis? (15)
At that time, the daughter of Drupada, a virtuous woman of excellent complexion, was not protected by anyone when her hair was seized at the appointed hour. (16)
What indeed is there to be considered here as the cause of this deficiency in dharma, while Keśava, the lord of gods, and Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, are present? (17)
If it were said that "it must come to pass," then the arrival of that [result] would be fruitless;
likewise, the Vedic mantras and others would undoubtedly be rendered false. (18)
Every means of accomplishment is fruitless and every method is useless; yet that which is destined to happen will surely come to pass, regardless of the words used to describe it.
Even the sacred tradition would become mere exegesis; all ritual actions would be purposeless;
asceticism for the sake of heaven would be in vain, as would the duties of the social classes.
If what is destined were already accomplished within the heart, all means of knowledge would be useless;
therefore, both must be considered: destiny and the means. (21)
If, when a rite has been performed, the result turns out to be contrary [to what was expected], then the wise—the crowns of the learned—should infer some deficiency in the performance. (22)

That ritual action has been declared in many ways by learned practitioners of rites, again according to the differences among performers, the differences among mantras, and likewise the differences among substances. (23)
Just as in the past Viśvarūpa was chosen as his preceptor by Maghavan,
that deed was performed by him in a contrary manner for the sake of his mother's welfare.
Having repeatedly said "May it be well with the gods and the Dānavas," he ensured the protection of the Asuras who belonged to his mother's side.
Seeing the Daityas exceedingly well-nourished, Maghavan then became enraged;
Hari swiftly severed their heads with his thunderbolt.
In this very case, there is no doubt that the failure of the ritual action resulted from the difference in the performers;
otherwise, the action would have been successfully performed even by the King of Pañcāla through his wrath alone.
For the destruction of Bhāradvāja and for the production of a son,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna was born from the middle of the sacrificial altar, as was Draupadī.
Formerly, when Daśaratha also performed a sacrifice for the sake of sons,
four sons were born to him who had been childless.
Therefore, O best of kings, an action performed with proper reasoning will always grant success; if performed without reasoning, it will always have the opposite effect.
Just as the Pāṇḍavas obtained a contrary result at their sacrifice due to some deficiency in its performance, so too were they defeated at the game of dice.
Likewise, O King, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, is a speaker of truth;
and so too is the virtuous Draupadī, as well as his other auspicious younger brothers.
Whether a deficiency has arisen in the sacrifice due to the use of inferior materials, or whether some defect has occurred because of the actions of those possessed by pride; 33.
O Great King, that sacrifice which is characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva) is indeed remembered as difficult to attain;
for this great sacrifice was ordained specifically for the Vaikhānasa sages.
Those ascetics who always partake of sattvic food—which is righteously acquired, forest-grown, fit for sages, and well-prepared—[attain the highest state]. (35)

O King, those sacrifices which always have the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) as their focus, which are performed without a sacrificial post (viyūpa), preceded by mantras, and characterized by an abundance of faith, are remembered as the supreme Sāttvika sacrifices. (36)

The sacrifices of the Kṣatriyas and the Vaiśyas are characterized by passion (rājasa), involve abundant materials, include sacrificial posts, are well-prepared, and are indeed accompanied by pride. (37)

Those sacrifices of the Dānavas which are characterized by darkness (tāmasa), accompanied by anger, increasing intoxication, full of resentment, and refined cruelty, have been described by the great-souled ones as such. || 38 ||
For the sages who desire liberation, who are dispassionate and great-souled,
sacrifice performed in the mind is traditionally taught as being endowed with all means of accomplishment.
In all other sacrifices, there might be something deficient—whether in terms of the ritual materials, the faith, the performance, or even the officiating Brahmins. (40)
Through all the means of place, time, distinct substances, and rituals, when these are complete, one indeed does not become something else; rather, the mind itself becomes so.
First, however, the mind must be purified, freed from all qualities;
when the mind is pure, the body is indeed pure—of this there is no doubt. (42)
When the mind has become pure, having abandoned the objects of the senses, then it shall possess the authority for that sacrifice. || 43 ||
Then, having constructed a pavilion extending for many yojanas, he erected it with massive, smooth pillars made from sacrificial trees.
And there, one should mentally conceive of a bright sacrificial altar;
likewise, the sacred fires should indeed be established mentally according to the prescribed rite. (45)
Having likewise performed the selection of the Brahmins—the Brahmā, Adhvaryu, Hotṛ, and Prastotṛ—in accordance with the prescribed rules; 46.
The Udgātṛ, the Pratihartṛ, and the other members of the assembly, as well as the best of the twice-born, are to be honored with effort according to the rules, even with the mind alone. (47)
Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, samāna, and udāna—
these five fires are to be established upon the altar according to the prescribed rite.
Then the Gārhapatya fire was the prāṇa, the Āhavanīya fire was the apāna, the Dakṣiṇāgni fire was the vyāna, and the Āvasathyaka fire was the samāna. || 49 ||
For these fires are remembered as being most fierce when offered by the assembly;
and the substance should be conceived by the mind as being devoid of qualities, supremely pure.
At that time, the mind itself was the Hotṛ priest and likewise the sacrificer;
it was also the supreme deity of the sacrifice—the attributeless and eternal Brahman. (51)
The power that bestows the fruit is devoid of qualities; she is eternally auspicious, granting detachment.
She is the support of all, consisting of the knowledge of Brahman, and remains pervading everywhere. 52.
With that as his objective, the twice-born one should offer that substance into the fires of the vital breaths;
thereafter, O Lord, having made the mind supportless, he should likewise offer the vital breaths.
One should offer oblations into the eternal Brahman through the path of the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī,
[offering] the Great Goddess Maheśvarī, who is one's own self, directly and by means of one's own experience.
Through the yoga of concentration alone, one should meditate with an undisturbed mind upon the Self abiding in all beings, and all beings within the Self. (55)
When the self of beings sees her, then he sees that auspicious one;
having seen her, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, he becomes a knower of Brahman.
Then, O protector of the earth, everything consisting of illusion and the like is burnt away;
however, only the *prārabdha* karma remains as long as the body persists. (57)
Then he becomes liberated while living; upon death, he shall attain liberation.
O dear one, he who worships the Mother of the Universe has accomplished all that was to be done. 58.
Therefore, with every effort, the illustrious Bhuvaneśvarī should be meditated upon;
she should also be heard and reflected upon in accordance with the words of the Guru. (59)
O King, a sacrifice performed in this manner bestows liberation; there is no doubt about this.
Other sacrifices, however, being characterized by desire, lead only toward decay.
"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma according to the rule"—this, the wise declare, is the instruction of the Veda. (61)
When their merit is exhausted, they enter the world of mortals according to their mental disposition;
therefore, the mental sacrifice is indeed superior and it is truly inexhaustible.
This sacrifice is not fit to be performed by a king who desires victory;
for previously you performed the snake-sacrifice, which was characterized by darkness (tamas).
O King, the enmity of the wicked-souled Takṣaka has been avenged,
for it was on his account that millions of other serpents were slain by you in the fire.
"O best of kings, perform today the sacrifice to the Goddess, which was formerly performed by Viṣṇu at the beginning of creation, according to the prescribed rites and in its full extent. (65)
"Act accordingly, O Indra among kings; I shall declare the ritual procedure to you.
There are Brahmins, O Indra among kings, who are knowers of the ritual and most learned in the Vedas. (66)
Those who know the ritual procedures for the seed-syllables (bīja) of the goddesses and are experts in the path of mantra will become the officiating priests;
you yourself shall indeed be the patron of the sacrifice.
Having performed the sacrifice according to the injunctions and having bestowed the merit earned from the rite,
O great king, deliver your father who has fallen into an evil state.
O sinless one, the sin born from insulting a brahmin is difficult to overcome and leads to hell;
likewise, the fault arising from a curse was incurred by your father.
Likewise, although the king met with an untimely death by the bite of a serpent,
his passing occurred in the interval [of the ritual] rather than upon the ground where the kusha grass was spread.
O best of the Kurus, the death of your father occurred there in that palace, devoid of battle or the merit of bathing and giving gifts in the Ganges.
O best of kings, all these things are miserable and lead to hell;
yet the one cause for that [liberation] has not arisen, being exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Wherever the vital breath (prāṇa) may be situated, if one recognizes that the time [of death] has arrived,
then even in the absence of spiritual practices and despite being in extreme distress, one is inevitably liberated.
When one indeed attains world-weariness with a pure mind, [one realizes]: "The body consists of the five elements; what sorrow-giving thing is there in this? (74)
"Let it fall today as it pleases; I am liberated, devoid of qualities, and immutable.
These principles are by nature subject to destruction; what cause for lamentation is there in that? (75)
I am indeed Brahman, not a transmigrating being; I am eternally liberated and eternal.
My connection with the body is brought about by karma. (76)
All those [karmas], both auspicious and otherwise, are liberated through connection with a human body, because of the attainment of pleasure and pain. || 77 ||
"Thus liberated from this terrible and most fearful peril of saṃsāra"—while thinking in this way, he was devoid of bathing and giving gifts. (78)
If he should meet death [at that moment], he would be liberated from the suffering of birth;
this is declared to be the supreme state, difficult to attain even for yogins. (79)
O tiger among kings, having heard the curse uttered by the twice-born,
your father conceived an attachment to his body and did not attain detachment.
"My body is free from disease and my kingdom is rid of all thorns;
how can I live according to my desire? Let them indeed bring the knowledge of mantras. (81)
At that time, the king likewise employed medicine, jewels, mantras, the supreme yantra, and even ascended to the palace.
Neither was bathing performed, nor was charity given, nor was the Goddess remembered; nor indeed was there sleep upon the ground, considering fate to be supreme. (83)
In the great and terrible ocean of delusion, he died like one struck by a serpent in his own palace,
having committed a sin born of insulting an ascetic through the influence of the Kali age.
"By these very actions, hell will certainly come to pass;
therefore, O best of kings, deliver that father from his sin. (85)
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor, Janamejaya became afflicted with great sorrow, his throat choked with tears. 86.
"Fie on this life of mine today, for my father remains in hell!
Therefore, I shall do that by which the son of Uttarā may go to heaven this very day. (87)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Sacrifice to Ambā," in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 12.
Description of Viṣṇu’s performance of the sacrifice.
The King said:
"O Grandfather, how was the sacrifice performed by Hari in the past?"
By the powerful Viṣṇu, in the form of the cause of the universe.
O high-minded one, who were the assistants there? Which Brahmins, those conversant with the essence of the Vedas, served as the officiating priests? Tell me that, O scorcher of foes.
"Having heard of the sacrifice performed by Viṣṇu for Ambikā, I shall, with a concentrated mind, perform a sacrifice according to the rites prescribed by the sacred ordinances. (3)
Vyāsa said:
O King, O highly fortunate one, listen to this most wonderful account in detail,
of how the sacrifice was performed by the Blessed One according to the prescribed rites.
When they had been dismissed by the Goddess after she had bestowed those three powers upon them,
those men became lords of the city of Kāñcī and ascended an excellent celestial chariot.
Having reached the terrible great ocean, those three foremost of gods established themselves upon the earth they had brought forth and created dwelling places for their residence.
Then the immovable foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) was released by the Goddess herself;
supported by that, the earth, endowed with fatness (medas), became established.
Because of its connection with the fat (medas) of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, it is known as Medinī;
because it supports (dhāraṇa), it is called Dhārā; and because of its vast extent (vistāra), it is Pṛthvī.
And the earth, because of its great magnitude, was supported upon the head of Śeṣa;
and all the mountains were made extensive for the purpose of providing support.
Just as an iron nail is driven into wood, so were those mountains made for you;
O great king, they are called "Mahīdhara" (the mountain) by wise people.
Mount Meru, made of gold and extending for many yojanas, was fashioned with peaks of jewels, appearing most wonderful and beautiful. || 11 ||
Marīci, Nārada, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Dakṣa, and Vasiṣṭha—these are the renowned sons of Brahmā. (12)
Kaśyapa was born from Marīci; thirteen daughters were born to Dakṣa.
From them, indeed, gods and Daityas were produced in great numbers. (13)
Thereupon, the creation of the earth proceeded in great detail,
divided in many ways according to the different species of humans, cattle, serpents, and so forth.
From half of Brahmā’s body, Svāyambhuva Manu was born;
likewise, from his left side, the woman Śatarūpā was produced. (15)
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were his two sons;
he also had three daughters of excellent form who were exceedingly beautiful. (16)
Having thus brought forth creation, the Lord born from the lotus fashioned the enchanting world of Brahmā upon the summit of Mount Meru.
The Lord Viṣṇu [resides in] Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme abode of Ramā’s lover,
a most beautiful place of play situated above all the worlds.
Śiva also established the supreme abode known as Kailāsa;
having reached it, he sported with his hosts of spirits according to his pleasure.
Heaven, known as Triviṣṭapa, is fashioned upon the summit of Mount Meru;
that abode of the Lord of the Gods is resplendent with various jewels.
From the churning of the ocean, the Pārijāta, the best of trees, was obtained;
likewise the four-tusked elephant and the wish-fulfilling Kāmadhenu cow.
Likewise, the horse Uccaiḥśravas and the Apsarases beginning with Rambhā—
all that was born was taken up by Indra as the ornament of heaven.
Dhanvantari and Candramas emerged from the ocean;
these two gods, surrounded by many hosts, shine resplendently while stationed in heaven.
Thus, O best of kings, the threefold creation arose, fashioned in various ways through the distinctions of gods, animals, humans, and so forth. (24)
Indeed, living beings joined with karma arise through four types of birth: from eggs, from sweat, from sprouts, and from a womb. (25)
Having thus accomplished the creation, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara all engaged in their respective pastimes in their own abodes as they desired.
When the creation had thus proceeded, the Lord,
the Sovereign Acyuta, sported there in his own world together with Mahālakṣmī.
Once upon a time in the past, Viṣṇu was residing in Vaikuṇṭha;
he then remembered the island situated in the ocean of nectar, adorned with jewels.
Where, having seen Mahāmāyā, the auspicious mantra was attained;
by remembering that supreme Śakti, [the demon] was brought to the state of womanhood. (29)
The Lord of Ramā set his mind upon performing a sacrifice;
having ascended from that world, he summoned Maheśvara.
Brahmā, Varuṇa, Śakra, Kubera, Pāvaka, Yama, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Dakṣa, Vāmadeva, and Bṛhaspati. || 31 ||
He prepared an exceedingly extensive collection of materials for the sake of the sacrifice,
endowed with great magnificence, characterized by purity (sattva), and captivating to the mind.
There he had a spacious pavilion constructed by artisans,
and he chose twenty-seven officiating priests of excellent vows.
He caused the sacrificial hearth (citi) to be constructed as well as very extensive altars (vedīs);
the Brāhmaṇas recited the mantras endowed with the seed-syllables (bīja) of the Goddess.
They offered their oblation according to the rules in the sacrificial fire duly prepared;
and when the extensive homa had been performed, an incorporeal voice spoke.
Then, addressing Viṣṇu with a melodious voice and sweet syllables, she said:
"O Viṣṇu, O Hari, may you always be the most excellent among the gods."
"Honorable, worthy of worship, and capable even among the gods—all beings, beginning with Brahmā and including Indra, shall worship you. (37)
"O Lord, men everywhere on earth shall become powerful through devotion;
and you indeed shall be the bestower of boons upon all those among mankind. (38)
You are the granter of desires to all the gods, the supreme Parameśvara;
you are the foremost among all sacrifices and are to be worshipped by all performers of sacrifice.
People will worship you, and you shall become the bestower of boons;
moreover, the gods, being greatly oppressed by the Dānavas, will take refuge in you.
And you, O Supreme Person, shall become the refuge of all in all the Purāṇas and in the Vedas that are spread abroad. (41)
You are indeed most worthy of worship; your fame shall surely spread.
For whenever there is a decline of dharma upon the earth, [you shall arise].
Having swiftly descended with a portion of that [essence], you must protect the Dharma;
your incarnations will become well-known throughout the earth according to your respective parts. (43)
O Mādhava, they shall indeed be worthy of honor by the high-souled ones on earth throughout all your incarnations in various wombs.
O Madhusūdana, you shall become renowned throughout all the worlds;
in all your incarnations, Śakti shall be your constant companion.
By a portion of myself, she will exist as Vārāhī and Nārasiṃhī, manifesting in many ways through various different forms. (46)
O Viṣṇu, O Mādhava, you are always joined by those women who bear various weapons, possess auspicious forms, and are adorned with all ornaments, as they perform the works of the gods.
"You shall accomplish all of that through the granting of boons by me;
you must never, even with the slightest trace of pride, hold them in contempt. (48)
They are to be worshipped with effort and honored in every way;
indeed, those Śaktis in the land of Bhārata grant all desires. (49)
They shall be honored among men in the form of images;
and through them, O Lord of Gods, your fame shall spread throughout all the worlds. (50)
They are renowned throughout all seven continents on the circle of the earth;
and indeed, O highly fortunate one, men on the circle of the earth [will honor] you.
O Hari, those possessed by desire will constantly worship for the sake of their wished-for objects,
offering various gifts to the images while filled with diverse emotions.
They shall worship you with mantras declared in the Vedas as well as by the chanting of your names;
O Madhusūdana, your greatness shall be manifest in the world of mortals and in heaven.
"O Lord of the gods, through worship by human beings, it shall attain growth.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus granted these boons, Vāṇī, who was born from the ether, became silent.
The Blessed One, the Lord Hari, having duly completed the sacrifice, became joyful in spirit, as if from hearing [the praises]. || 55 ||
Then, having dismissed those gods, the sons of Brahmā, and the sages,
the one whose banner is Garuḍa departed for Vaikuṇṭha together with his attendants.
Then all the gods returned to their respective abodes,
while the sages, filled with wonder, conversed with one another.
Then, being greatly delighted, they went at their pleasure to their own purifying hermitages.
Having heard that most lucid voice born of the sky, which was delightful to the ears of all, a spirit of devotion toward Prakṛti arose in everyone.
Then all the hosts of twice-born ones and sages, filled with devotion, performed her worship according to the rites prescribed in the Agamas, O lords of sages, for she is the granter of all desires.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Viṣṇu’s Performance of the Sacrifice for Ambikā," in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 13.
Janamejaya said: "O twice-born one, I have indeed heard in detail about the sacrifice prepared by Hari for the purpose of war between Yudhājit and Vīrasena."
Likewise, tell me in detail the greatness of the Mother.
"Having heard the life-story of the Goddess, O best of Brahmins, I shall indeed perform an unsurpassed sacrifice; through your grace, I shall become purified. (2)
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the supreme life-story of the Goddess;
I will relate the history and the Purāṇa in great detail.
Among the Kosalas, there was a preeminent king born of the Solar dynasty;
the son of Puṣya, possessed of great splendor, was known as Dhruvasandhi. || 4 ||
Virtuous in soul, true to his promise, and devoted to the welfare of the social orders and stages of life,
he, pure in his vows, ruled the kingdom in the prosperous city of Ayodhyā.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other twice-born men likewise lived according to dharma in that kingdom, each established in his own respective occupation.
In his kingdom, there were no thieves, backbiters, or rogues anywhere;
indeed, no men who were hypocrites, ungrateful, or foolish ever dwelt there.
O best of the Kurus, while the king was living in this manner,
he had two wives endowed with beauty who provided him with the enjoyment of his desires.
Manoramā was his lawful wife, beautiful and exceedingly wise;
Līlāvatī was his second wife, and she too was endowed with beauty and virtue.
She lived with her two co-wives in the houses and in the groves,
on pleasure-mountains, by the long ponds, and in various palatial mansions.
At an auspicious time, Manoramā gave birth to an excellent son named Sudarśana, who was endowed with the marks of royalty.
Līlāvatī, his beautiful wife, also gave birth after one month to a handsome son on an auspicious lunar fortnight and on a favorable day.
There, the king performed the birth-rites and other ceremonies for the two;
delighted by the birth of his sons, he bestowed gifts upon the Brahmins.
The king, O monarch, bestowed equal affection upon those two sons;
that ruler never made any distinction in his friendship toward them.
The best of kings, that scorcher of foes, full of affection, performed the tonsure ceremony for the two of them according to the prescribed rite and in accordance with his means. (15)
Having had their tonsure ceremony performed, the two lovely sons, playing about and delighting the people, captivated the king's heart at will. (16)
Of those two, Sudarśana was the elder, the auspicious son of Līlāvatī;
the one named Śatrujit was indeed full of sweet and flattering speech.
He was a source of joy to the king, possessed of pleasant speech and handsome appearance;
he was indeed beloved by the subjects as well as by the ministers.

In that same way, the king felt affection for him because of his possession of virtuous qualities; however, he did not feel such affection toward Sudarśana due to his own dull-wittedness and ill fortune.
As time passed in this manner, that best of kings, Dhruvasandhi,
who was ever devoted to hunting, went into the midst of the forest.
Slaying ruru deer, kambu deer, boars, gavayas, hares, buffaloes, sharabhas, and rhinoceroses, the king sported in the forest. (21)
While the king was sporting there in that terrible and most dreadful forest,
a highly enraged lion emerged from a thicket.
First pierced by the king with a stone-tipped arrow, the lion fell under the sway of anger;
seeing the monarch before him, he roared with a sound like the thundering of clouds. (23)
Raising his tail and spreading his great mane, he,
filled with extreme rage, leapt up into the air from the sky to slay the king.
Then the king, seeing [him], swiftly grasped a sword in his hand and, taking a shield in his left, stood like another lion. (25)
All his servants also, filled with rage and impelled by intense anger, individually discharged arrows at the lion.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and the combat was terrible;
then a fierce lion sprang upon the king. (27)
Seeing him falling, the king struck him with his sword;
he too, having arrived there, was torn apart by the king's cruel claws.
Struck by his claws, the king fell down and indeed died;
then the soldiers cried out and struck him with their arrows.
The lion died right there, and the king likewise died; the soldiers and the chief ministers arrived at that spot and reported this. (30)
Having heard that the king had passed away to the other world, those excellent ministers went to the edge of the forest and performed the funeral rites.
Vasiṣṭha performed all the rites for the next world right there, according to the prescribed rules, which bring about happiness in the afterlife.
The subjects, the ministers, and the great sage Vasiṣṭha held a consultation among themselves regarding how to make Sudarśana the king.
"The son of a lawful wife, peaceful, and a man endowed with auspicious marks—he is indeed worthy of the royal throne," so said the best of ministers. (34)
Vasiṣṭha also spoke in the same manner: "This son of the king is indeed worthy;
though he is but a child, he is a righteous king and deserves the royal throne here. (35)
When the counsel had been formulated by the elder ministers, a king named Yudhājit,
the lord of Ujjayinī, heard of it and arrived there with great speed.
Upon hearing that his son-in-law had died, Līlāvatī’s father then went there in haste, desiring the welfare of his daughter's son.
Likewise, Vīrasena arrived with the desire for Sudarśana's welfare, as did the king who was the lord of Kaliṅga and the father of Manoramā. (38)
Both those kings, accompanied by their armies and overcome with trepidation,
held counsel with their chief ministers for the sake of the kingdom.
Then Yudhājit asked: "Of these two sons, who is the elder? The elder indeed shall obtain the kingdom, and never the younger. (40)
Vīrasena, the son of his lawful wife, spoke there, saying:
"O King, according to what I have heard from those learned in the scriptures, he is indeed worthy of the kingdom. (41)
Yudhājit spoke again: "This one is the eldest by virtue of his qualities;
he is endowed with the marks of royalty in a way that Sudarśana is not. (42)
A great dispute has arisen here between these two greedy kings;
who would be capable of dispelling the doubt in such a dire crisis? (43)
Yudhājit said to his ministers: "You are indeed intent on your own self-interest;
having made Sudarśana the king, you surely wish to enjoy the wealth. (44)
I have understood this deliberation of yours through your gestures;
therefore, Śatrughna, accompanied by his army, is approved by me for your royal throne.
While I am alive, who indeed would make the younger son king, bypassing the elder who is worthy of virtue and accompanied by an army? (46)
"Surely I shall wage war; by the edge of my sword, that earth shall be split in two—what need is there for you to speak further on that matter? (47)
Having heard that, Vīrasena spoke to Yudhājit:
"O wise one, there are two boys of equal intelligence; what difference is there between them? (48)
While those two kings remained thus disputing,
the subjects and the sages became anxious in their minds.
And the vassal lords, intent on causing distress, assembled with their armies, eager for mutual conflict and remaining vigilant. (50)
For the Niṣādas, who were residents of Śṛṅgaverapura, arrived there to seize the royal property, having heard that the lord of the earth had died. 51.
Hearing that the two young sons were engaged in mutual combat,
thieves arrived there from various regions and even from other lands.
A great crush occurred there when the battle was joined;
Yudhājit and Vīrasena both became desirous of combat.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Preparation for Battle between Yudhājit and Vīrasena," in the third book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 14.
Vyāsa said: When the battle between those two kings had commenced and they had taken up their weapons for the combat, Manoramā set out toward the hermitage of Bhāradvāja.
Then, between the two who were under the sway of anger and greed, there arose a tumultuous conflict.
That king, the conqueror of Pṛthulabāhu in battle, stood in the field with his bow held firm;
joined by his own forces, vehicles, and other resources, the monarch was resolved upon combat.
