O Vīrasena, here in this battle, that king, equal in splendor to the Lord of the Gods, has stood firm according to the duty of a warrior for the sake of his daughter’s son, accompanied by his army. (3)
Seeing Yudhājit standing firm in battle, the king released a shower of arrows upon him,
just as a cloud laden with lightning hurls torrents of rain upon a mountain.
Filled with wrath, he was one whose valor was rooted in truth. || 4 ||
Vīrasena covered him with swift, straight-flying arrows sharpened on stone,
and he [the opponent] cut those stone-tipped shafts with his own arrows.
By that very [means], they were released and fell with great force.
An exceedingly fierce battle took place between the elephants, chariots, and horses, watched by throngs of gods, men, and sages;
immediately, the sky became covered by vast flocks of birds.
And by those such as vultures of desire, who wish to eat flesh.
There, a wondrous and terrible river of blood flowed forth from the very throngs of elephants, heroes, and horses;
it was terrifying to the eyes of the men who fell within its path.
It is as one desires for those of evil nature when [the moon] is in the path of the Sun's son (Saturn). || 7 ||
Human heads, covered with hair, lie scattered upon the broken sandbanks and shine just like gourd-pots placed there by children born of the Sun’s daughter who desire to play. (8)
I think that a vulture circles above the hero who has died, fallen from his chariot onto the earth, for the sake of his flesh;
yet even this living soul, beholding its own beautiful body—
Alas, even though he is utterly helpless, he longs once more to enter.
Even when slain in battle, that best of men, mounted upon a magnificent celestial chariot, speaks his desired words to the divine maiden seated on his lap:
"Behold now this body of mine upon the earth..."
O lady with thighs like the trunk of an elephant, your beloved has fallen, struck by an arrow. || 10 ||
One enemy, having been slain by his foe, ascended into the sky and reached a celestial chariot where he was united with a divine maiden; meanwhile,
[the other] offered his beloved’s body into the fire.
The weak woman, having become strong, seized her own beloved.

In battle and in death, those two noble warriors, slain by each other’s weapons, have gone together to the celestial realm; there indeed they strike at one another with supreme missiles, agitated by their quarrel for the sake of a single apsaras.
A certain young man, having obtained a celestial maiden who was indeed preeminent in beauty and endowed with virtues, being filled with devotion,
then began to proclaim his own extensive qualities.
And he, absorbed in yoga, imitated her in the giving of love. || 13 ||
The dust of the earth spread far and wide, reaching even into the sky; it made the night and completely shrouded the sun.
That very dust suddenly sank into the ocean of blood.
The sun also appeared, endowed with exceeding splendor. || 14 ||
It is said that someone who had gone to the sky, having encountered a celestial maiden of lovely countenance who was full of devotion,
did not accept her, fearing the destruction of his vows.
This word of mine, though seemingly favorable, will indeed go in vain.
When that battle had commenced, Yudhājit, the lord of the earth,
struck Vīrasena with fierce and most terrible arrows.
Slain, that lord of the earth fell to the ground with his head severed;
his entire army was shattered and fled in the four directions.
Having heard that her father had been slain at the forefront of the battle,
Manoramā then became terrified with fear, recollecting the enmity toward her father.
"The evil-minded Yudhājit will surely kill my son in battle out of greed for the kingdom; that wicked soul," she thought, becoming consumed by anxiety. (19)
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? My father has been slain in battle;
my husband too has died this very day, and here is my infant son. (20)
Greed is exceedingly wicked; by it, who has not been brought under its sway? Possessed by that, what sin would even the best of kings not commit? (21)
A person possessed by greed slays his father, mother, brothers, teachers, kinsmen, and relatives; there is no doubt about this.

Afflicted by craving, he indeed consumes what is unfit for consumption, likewise engages in sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached, and furthermore, abandons the Dharma out of greed. (23)
"I have no companion here in this city who possesses great strength, upon whose support I may rely while protecting my auspicious son. (24)
Now that my son has been killed, what shall I do again, O King?
There is no protector for me in this world by whom I might truly be established in security. (25)
That co-wife, Līlāvatī, will always be full of enmity toward my son; she will never be compassionate toward him. (26)
"If Yudhājit arrives, there will be no escape for me;
knowing my son to be a child, he will today lead me away to prison. (27)
For it is heard that in former times, while still in his mother’s womb, the infant was cut into seven pieces by Indra; subsequently, those seven were each cut into seven more.
Having entered his mother's womb and placed a small thunderbolt in his hand,
those Maruts became forty-nine in heaven.
"In the past, I heard that poison was given by a co-wife to the king's wife, another co-wife, with the intent of destroying her fetus. (30)
But after the boy was born, poison indeed entered his body;
because of that, he became famous on the circle of the earth by the name Sagara.
While her husband, the king’s wife Kaikeyī, was still alive,
Rāma, the eldest son, was exiled and King Daśaratha died.
Those ministers, however, were powerless; though they desired my son Sudarśana to become king, they have indeed fallen under the control of Yudhājit.
I have no brother so heroic who might liberate me from this bondage;
indeed, through the turn of fate, I have encountered great suffering. (34)
"Effort must be made by all means, for success indeed arises from destiny;
therefore, I shall today, with great haste, devise a means for the protection of my son. (35)
Having reflected thus, that young woman [considered] Vidalla, who was exceedingly proud and skillful in all affairs, as well as Cintya, the most excellent of the chief ministers. (36)
Having summoned him to a private place, she, deeply distressed, weeping and with a dejected mind, spoke to him while holding the boy by the hand. (37)
"My father has been slain in battle, as has this young son;
the powerful King Yudhājit remains—tell me, what should be done? (38)
Vidalla said to her, "You must certainly not remain here; we shall go as we please to the forest, or indeed back to Vārāṇasī. (39)
There dwells my illustrious maternal uncle, who is exceedingly powerful;
known as Subāhu, he shall be your protector.
With a mind eager for the sight of Yudhājit, you must go out from the city, mount a chariot, and depart; there is no doubt about this. (41)
Having been addressed thus by him, that queen went toward Līlāvatī and said, "O Sulocanā, I am going today to see my father. (42)
Having spoken thus, she then mounted the chariot accompanied by Sairandhrī and Vidalla,
and departed from the city.
For she was terrified, distressed, and piteous, overwhelmed with grief for her father upon seeing King Yudhājit, her father, lifeless. (44)
In need of purification, hurried, trembling, and overwhelmed with fear, the queen reached the bank of the Bhāgīrathī after two days. (45)
There, the Niṣādas plundered them; taking all their wealth and even seizing their chariot, those deceitful bandits departed. (46)
Weeping, carrying her son, beautifully dressed and charming,
she went out to the bank of the Ganges, supported by the hand of Sairandhrī.
And having quickly climbed onto a boat out of fear, she, overwhelmed by terror,
crossed the holy Bhāgīrathī and went to Mount Trikūṭa.
Having reached the hermitage of Bhāradvāja in haste and filled with fear,
she beheld the ascetics there and then became free from fear.
Then the sage asked her: "Who are you? Whose wife are you?
How have you come here with such difficulty? Tell me the truth, O lady of pure smiles. (50)
"Are you a goddess or a human woman? Having a young son in the forest, O lady with beautiful thighs and lotus-like eyes, why do you appear like one fallen from her kingdom? (51)
Thus questioned by the sage, that woman of excellent complexion said nothing;
weeping and tormented by grief, she instead commanded Vidalla.
Vidalla said this to him: "This is the lawful wife of Dhruvasandhi, that best of kings; her name is Manoramā. (53)
The king of the Solar dynasty, who possessed great strength, was slain by a lion;
this son belongs to that monarch and is named Sudarśana.
Her father, being exceedingly righteous, died in battle for the sake of his daughter's son;
terrified by fear, she has arrived in this lonely forest.
"O best of sages, O highly fortunate one, this princess has a young son; having come to you alone for refuge, please be her protector. (56)

The merit gained from protecting one who is distressed is declared to be greater than that of a sacrifice; it is remembered as yielding even more exceptional fruit when protecting one who is terrified and miserable.
The sage said:
"Dwell here without fear, O auspicious one; protect your son, O lady of virtuous vows.
You must not entertain any fear arising from enemies, O large-eyed one. (58)
"Protect your beloved son; he shall become your king.
Neither suffering nor grief shall ever arise for you in this regard. (59)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by the sage, the queen became composed;
free from sorrow, she then dwelt in the hut provided by the sage.
Accompanied there by Sairandhrī and joined by Vidalla,
that charming woman lived on, protecting Sudarśana.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Departure for the Hermitage of Bharadvāja with Manoramā," in the Third Book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 15.
The Description of the Dialogue between Yudhājit and Bhāradvāja.
Vyāsa said: Then the mighty Yudhājit, having returned from battle to Ayodhyā, spoke.
And he questioned Manoramā with the intent to kill Sudarśana.
He sent forth his servants, repeatedly asking, "Where has he gone?
Then, on an auspicious day, he installed his grandson upon the throne.
And he was consecrated by the ministers and by Vasiṣṭha with auspicious Atharvan mantras, using full jars filled with water.
O best of the Kurus, a great festival indeed took place in the city, accompanied by the sounds of kettledrums and conchs, as well as the blasts of trumpets.
Ayodhyā was as if filled with joy by the recitations of the Vedas from the brahmins, by the hymns of the bards, and by the most auspicious shouts of victory.
Crowded with joyful and well-fed people and resounding with the sounds of hymns and musical instruments,
that city shone like something newly created under that new ruler of the earth.
Some virtuous people, remaining at home, were indeed filled with grief as they thought of Sudarśana: "Where has that son of the king gone today? (7)
Where has that most excellent and beautiful woman gone, accompanied by her son?
Her father was slain in battle by an enemy out of greed for the kingdom.
Thinking thus, those virtuous ones of even-mindedness remained there in distress, subject to the will of Śatrujit.
Yudhājit also, having installed his grandson according to the prescribed rites and having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers, set out toward his own city.
Having heard that Sudarśana was staying there in the hermitage of the sages,
he, desiring to kill him, went quickly to Mount Citrakūṭa.
Placing at their head the heroic Niṣāda chief named Bala,
they quickly went to the one called Durdarśa, the lord of Śṛṅgaverapura.
Hearing that he was approaching accompanied by an army, Manoramā, whose young son she bore, became exceedingly distressed with fear.
Afflicted with extreme grief and with tearful eyes, she said to the sage:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? Yudhājit has arrived. (14)
"My father was slain by him, and my grandson has been made king;
now he approaches here with a great force, desiring to kill my son. (15)
O Lord, I have heard before that the Pāṇḍavas were indeed staying in the forest,
together with the princess of Pañcāla, in a holy hermitage of sages at that time.
Those five Pārtha brothers have gone out on a hunt;
Draupadī remains there in that auspicious hermitage of the sages.
Dhaumya, Atri, Gālava, Paila, Jāvāli, Gautama, Bhṛgu, Cyavana, one of the Atri lineage, Kaṇva, Jatu, and Kratu. || 18 ||
Vītihotra, Sumantu, Yajñadatta, Vatsala, Rāśāsana, Kahoḍa, Yavakrī, Yajñakṛt, and Kratu. (19)
These and other auspicious sages, such as Bhāradvāja and others,
all devoted to the recitation of the Vedas, remained established in their hermitage.
O sage, Yājñasenī, her every limb beautiful, remained there in the hermitage surrounded by maidservants and protected by the sages, free from fear.
Meanwhile, the five heroic sons of Pṛthā, the scorchers of their enemies, bearing bows and arrows, proceeded from forest to forest in pursuit of deer.
Meanwhile, the illustrious Lord of Sindhu, accompanied by his army,
arrived near the hermitage while on the road upon hearing the sound of the Vedic recitation.
Hearing the sound of the Vedas from the sages of purified souls,
the king quickly descended from his chariot, desiring a vision of them.
When he went forth from there accompanied by his two servants,
he beheld the sages established in their exertion and engaged in the recitation of the Vedas.
Then, with his palms joined in reverence, King Jayadratha stood before his lord and entered the hermitage frequented by sages.
Then, desiring to see the king seated there, the women and the wives of the sages approached and asked the king, "Who is this? (27)
Among them, the noble-limbed Yājñasenī arrived;
she was seen by Jayadratha, appearing like another goddess Śrī in her beauty. (28)
Beholding her, with dark-cornered eyes like another celestial maiden, the king asked Dhaumya: "Who is this dark-complexioned woman of beautiful countenance? (29)
Whose wife is she, whose daughter, and by what name is this woman of excellent complexion?
Endowed with beauty and grace, she is like Śacī descended to the earth. (30)
Like a young clove-creeper situated in the midst of a barberry forest,
this beautiful woman, though surrounded by a multitude of ogresses, truly shines like a plantain tree.
"Speak the truth, O illustrious one! To whom does this beloved woman belong?
She shines like a queen; she is not the wife of a sage, O twice-born one. (32)
Dhaumya said: "O Indra among the kings of Sindhu, Draupadī, the beloved wife of the Pāṇḍavas, who possesses auspicious marks and is a princess of Pañcāla, dwells here in this excellent hermitage."
Jayadratha said:
"Where have the five Pāṇḍavas gone now, those renowned heroes? Do those mighty warriors dwell here in the forest, free from sorrow? (34)
Dhaumya said:
"The five Pāṇḍavas, mounted on their chariots, have gone out for the sake of hunting;
those kings will return at midday having taken deer."
Having heard those words of his, that king rose up;
having gone into the presence of Draupadī and bowed down, he spoke as follows.
"Is it well with you, O lady of beautiful limbs? Where have your husbands gone?
It has been eleven years now that they have supposedly remained in the forest."
Draupadī, however, then said to him: "May it be well with you, O prince!
Rest in the vicinity of the hermitage; the Pāṇḍavas will arrive in a moment. (38)
While she was speaking thus, that heroic king, overcome by greed, disregarded the best of sages and carried off Draupadī. (39)
The wise should never place their trust in anyone under any circumstances;
by doing so, one encounters suffering, as the case of Bali clearly demonstrates.
The illustrious son of Vairocana was most virtuous and true to his promise;
he was a performer of sacrifices, a donor, a refuge for others, and highly esteemed by the righteous. || 41 ||
Nowhere was the grandson of Pralhāda devoted to unrighteousness;
indeed, he performed ninety-nine sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Viṣṇu, whose form is pure being, is always to be served even by yogis;
for the sake of accomplishing the work of the gods, the Lord, though changeless, [assumes forms]. (43)
And from Kaśyapa was born Viṣṇu as the deceptive Vāmana;
by means of a trick, he seized the kingdom and the earth together with its oceans.
At that time, King Bali, the son of Virocana, became truthful in speech;
however, I have heard that Viṣṇu employed a stratagem for the sake of Indra. (45)
Why does no one else act in this way, as he who has taken the form of a being, having assumed the shape of a dwarf, desires to bring about the downfall of the sacrifice? (46)
Indeed, one should never trust anyone at any time;
for if greed arises in the mind, O Lord, what fear can there be for the evildoer? (47)
"Stricken by greed, living beings indeed commit sins;
O Sage, no one at any time has any fear of the next world. (48)
On account of taking what belongs to others through thought, deed, or speech, men whose minds are utterly destroyed by greed fall [into hell]. (49)
Having constantly propitiated the gods, men desire wealth;
yet the gods, even if they were to place it in their hands, are not able to bestow it directly.
The wealth of another is brought [to them], and they bestow what is desired, whether by means of trade, gifts, theft, or even force. (51)
Having taken up much grain, clothing, and other goods for the purpose of selling them, the Vaiśya worships the gods, thinking, "May there be great prosperity for me. (52)
O scorcher of foes, do you have no desire for the wealth of others here through trade? Yet, when the time for purchase arrives, you even long for it at a high price. (53)
For in this way, O Brahmin, all living beings constantly exist intent upon seizing the property of others; how, then, can there be any trust? 54.
Vain is the pilgrimage, vain is the gift, and vain indeed is the study;
for those shrouded by greed and delusion, that which has been performed becomes as if unperformed.
Therefore, O illustrious one, send him back toward his home;
O best of the twice-born, I shall dwell with my son like Jānaki.
Having been addressed thus, that powerful sage Bharadvāja went to King Yudhājit and spoke these words to the king.
"Go, O King, to your own city as you desire, O best of monarchs! This Manoramā, who has young children and is deeply afflicted by grief, does not come. (58)
Yudhājit said:
"O Sage, O gentle one, abandon your obstinacy and release this beautiful woman;
I will not let her go, for today I shall take her back by force. (59)
The sage said:
"If you have the power, take me away today by force from my hermitage,
just as Viśvāmitra formerly took the cow of the sage Vasiṣṭha."

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between Yudhājit and Bhāradvāja," in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 16 ||
Following the account of Viśvāmitra, comes the description of how the prince obtained the seed of desire.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the sage, the lord of the earth there—
Having summoned the elder minister, he questioned him with vigilance.
"O Subuddhi, O observer of noble vows, tell me what must be done by me here today? Shall I take that eloquent woman and her son by force, according to my desire? (2)
Even a minor enemy should not be neglected by one who desires complete well-being; for like pulmonary consumption, once it has grown, it leads to death. (3)
There is neither army nor warrior here who might restrain me;
having seized him, I shall surely slay that enemy of my grandson right there.
"The kingdom shall become free of thorns; today I shall strive by force, thinking that once Sudarśana is slain, he will surely be without fear. (5)
The Pradhāna said:
"O King, you must certainly not commit such a rash act; you have heard the words of the sage.
O noble one, he has related the example of Viśvāmitra."
Long ago, the illustrious and highly renowned Viśvāmitra, the son of Gādhi and best among kings, while wandering about, arrived at the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
Having paid homage to him, the powerful King Viśvāmitra,
that best of monarchs, sat down upon a seat provided by the sage.
Invited by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha for a meal,
the highly illustrious king, the son of Gādhi, remained there together with his army.
Having eaten all that which was brought by Nandinī, including the various kinds of food and edibles,
the king along with his army enjoyed the desired meal there.
Having recognized that power of Nandinī, the king,
the ruler of the earth, requested Nandinī from Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O Sage, O scorcher of foes, I shall give you a thousand cows with udders as large as jars;
give me the cow Nandini, for that is what I request."
Vasiṣṭha said: "O King, this is the sacrificial cow; I will not give her up under any circumstances. Let these thousand cows of yours remain yours."
Viśvāmitra said:
"I shall give you ten thousand or even a hundred thousand, whatever your heart desires;
O virtuous one, give me Nandini, or else I shall take her by force. (14)
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O King, take Nandinī by force today as you please;
however, O King, I will not give her to you from my own house of my own free will. (15)
Having heard that, the king commanded his mighty servants:
"Take away the cow Nandini, you who are firmly established in the pride of your strength. (16)
The servants seized her, having forcibly overpowered and restrained her;
trembling, Surabhi spoke to the sage with tearful eyes. || 17 ||
"O sage, why do you abandon me, who am well-restrained? I am emaciating myself.
The sage replied to her: "I shall not abandon you, O you who yield such excellent milk. (18)
"O auspicious one, this king leads me away by force, for he has been honored by me today;
what can I do, since I truly do not wish to abandon you even in my mind? (19)
Thus addressed by the sage, the cow became filled with anger;
she immediately let out a lowing sound, a cruel and most dreadful noise. (20)
Then, from that body, most terrible Daityas emerged, clad in armor and equipped with weapons, crying out, "Stay! Stay! (21).
The entire army was slain by them, and Nandinī was set free;
King Viśvāmitra departed alone, deeply distressed. (22)

Alas! That wicked man, his soul exceedingly dejected, censuring the great strength of the Kṣatriyas and considering the power of a Brāhmaṇa to be difficult to overcome, has now settled himself in ascetic penance.
Having performed severe austerities for many years in the great forest,
Gādheya attained the status of a rishi after once again abandoning the kṣatriya way of life.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, do not engage in this extraordinary enmity;
indeed, battle with ascetics will surely bring about the destruction of your lineage. (25)
O best of kings, go today to Vraja and console that preeminent sage, the treasure-house of asceticism;
and let Sudarśana also remain here as he pleases.
"This boy is a child and destitute; what harm can he do to you, O King?
This state of enmity toward a helpless, weak infant is in vain. (27)
Compassion should be practiced toward all; this world is subject to destiny.
O best of kings, what is the use of envy? Whatever is destined to be, that shall come to pass.
O King, by the turn of fate, there is no doubt that even a thunderbolt acts like a blade of grass;
and at some time, through the power of destiny, even a blade of grass acts like a thunderbolt. (29)
A hare kills a tiger, and likewise a mosquito [kills] an elephant;
O wise one, abandon this rashness and do my beneficial word.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, Yudhājit, the best of kings,
bowed his head to that sage and departed for his own city, O King.
Manoramā also became healthy while remaining there in that hermitage;
she nurtured her son Sudarśana, who was firm in his vows.
From then on, that boy grew day by day,
playing fearlessly with the sons of sages, auspicious in every way.
At one time, Vidalla arrived there;
the son of the sage addressed him from nearby, saying, "O eunuch! (34).
But Sudarśana, having heard that, clearly grasped the single syllable accompanied by the nasal *anusvāra*, and he recited it again and again. (35)
Then the boy, having mentally grasped that seed-syllable known as Kāmarāja,
recited it repeatedly, holding it in his heart with great reverence.
O Great King, due to past cultivation, that wonderful being known as Kāmarāja was indeed thus seized by that boy through his very nature. (37)
Then, in his fifth year, he received that unsurpassed mantra,
which was devoid of seers and meters and stripped of meditative visualization and ritual placement.
Constantly reciting it with his mind, even while playing or sleeping,
he did not forget that mantra, knowing for himself that it was the very essence.
When his eleventh year had arrived, that prince, the son of the king,
was initiated by the sage and likewise instructed in the Vedas.

Likewise, through the power of his mantras and other means, he thoroughly practiced the science of archery along with its auxiliary branches, the treatises on ethics, and all branches of knowledge according to the prescribed rules. (41)
Once, he too beheld the Goddess directly in person,
clad in red garments, red in complexion, and with all her limbs adorned in red ornaments.
Seeing the wonderful Vaiṣṇavī Śakti seated upon her vehicle, Garuḍa,
the prince’s face became bright with joy.
Then, staying in that forest, he who knew the true essence of all branches of knowledge lived on the riverbank, attending upon his mother.
And a bow was obtained, as well as arrows sharpened on stone;
a quiver and armor were given to him by Ambikā in the forest. (45)
At that time, there was the daughter of the King of Kāśī,
the divine Supriyā, known by the name Śaśikalā, who was endowed with all auspicious marks.
He heard that the prince Sudarśana was staying in the forest,
endowed with all auspicious marks, a hero like another Kāma.
Having heard from the mouth of a bard about Prince Susaṅgata,
she indeed desired him in her mind and resolved in her intellect to choose him as her husband.
In the middle of the night, the Mother of the World, having approached her in a dream and consoled her as she stood there composed, spoke these words.
"Choose a boon, O fair-hipped one! Sudarśana is my devotee;
by my word, O beautiful woman, let him be the granter of all your desires."
Thus Śaśikalā, having seen that enchanting form in her dream and remembering the words of her mother, the beautiful woman rejoiced greatly. (51)
Having risen up filled with joy, she was questioned again and again by her mother; yet the young girl, overcome with extreme bashfulness, did not speak the cause of her delight.
Having laughed and fallen into a state of joy, remembering the dream again and again,
she then spoke at length to another friend regarding the events of her dream.
Once, that large-eyed lady, accompanied by her friends, went to a beautiful pond-grove for the sake of recreation, which was adorned with campaka trees. (54)
While gathering flowers, the young woman standing beneath a campaka tree saw a brāhmaṇa approaching on the path in great haste.
Having bowed to that brahmin, the dark-complexioned woman spoke these sweet words:
"O illustrious one, from what region have you come? (56)
The twice-born said:
"O child, my arrival from the hermitage of Bhāradvāja has surely occurred due to the exigency of some business; tell me, what do you ask? (57)
Śaśikalā said:
"O highly fortunate one, what indeed is there to be described in that hermitage? Is there something truly transcendent of the world, especially worthy of being beheld? (58)
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O lady of beautiful hips, the illustrious King Sudarśana, the son of Dhruvasandhi, dwells there;
that best of men abides with a name truly meaningful."
To me, her eyes appear utterly fruitless, O lady of beautiful thighs, since they have not beheld the handsome prince. (60)
I believe that all virtues were placed together in one place by the Creator,
who, out of curiosity, wished to behold the very mine of virtues.
This prince is worthy to become your husband;
this union was ordained as if between a gem and gold.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Prince’s Attainment of the Seed-Syllable of Kāma," following the narrative of Viśvāmitra, in the third book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 17.
The sending of a message by Śaśikalā to her mother.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words, the dark-complexioned woman (Śyāmā) became filled with love.
Having spoken thus, the composed Brahmin departed from that place.
But she, due to her former passion, was deeply immersed in love and exceedingly restless;
she felt as if struck by the arrows of Kama once that best of Brahmins had departed.
Then, afflicted by desire, she spoke to her friend who was compliant with her wishes:
"And a transformation has arisen in my body following that which I heard. (3)
The wicked god of love torments this prince of noble birth, who is ignorant of the experience of passion; what shall I do, and where shall I go? (4)
Or perhaps he was seen by me in dreams, like another five-arrowed god of love;
my tender heart, distressed by separation, is tormented exceedingly.
O beautiful lady, this sandalwood paste clinging to my body appears like poison;
this garland is like a serpent, and the rays of the moon are like fire.
Neither in a palace nor in a forest, neither by a pond nor on a mountain; neither by day nor by night do I find happiness through the means of pleasure.
Neither bed nor betel, neither song nor instrumental music delights my mind today; my eyes are not yet satiated.
Today I shall go to that forest where that rogue dwells;
for I am terrified of family dishonor and likewise dependent upon my father.
"My father does not hold a svayaṃvara today; what shall I do?
I shall surely grant my desire to Prince Sudarśana. (10)
There are hundreds of other rulers of the earth possessed of abundant prosperity;
yet they do not seem delightful to me today, for even this man, though deprived of his kingdom, is esteemed by me.
Vyāsa said:
Sudarśana was alone, destitute, and devoid of strength;
dwelling in the forest and subsisting on fruits, she remained firmly established in his heart.
Through the recitation of the seed-syllable Vāk, this success also presented itself to her;
she too, being entirely intent on meditation, recited that supreme mantra. (13)
In his dream, he beheld that goddess Viṣṇumāyā,
the indivisible Mother of the Universe, the unmanifest Ambikā who bestows all prosperity.
The Niṣāda, the governor of Śṛṅgaverapura, approached him and gave him an excellent chariot equipped with all necessary implements.
Knowing that the prince was victorious, he then gave him a gift consisting of a chariot yoked with four horses and adorned with excellent banners.
He too accepted him with affection as a well-established friend,
and he properly honored Śambara with wild roots and fruits.
When that lord of the Niṣādas had departed after having been treated as a guest,
those sages, filled with joy, spoke to one another among themselves.
"O Prince, you shall certainly obtain the kingdom in every way; in just a few days, through your majesty, you will attain it without hindrance—of this there is no doubt. (19)
The goddess Ambikā, the bestower of boons who deludes the universe, is pleased with you;
moreover, your assistance is perfectly secured, so do not worry, O observer of noble vows!
To Manoramā, those sages of strict vows spoke thus:
"O lady of pure smiles, today a son shall become the lord of the earth for you."
That slender-limbed woman said to them: "May your words bear good fruit;
O Brahmins, this man is your slave—what wonder is there in that, given his proper service? (22)
He has no army, no ministers, no treasury, and no ally whatsoever; by what means is my son worthy to obtain the kingdom here? (23)
"By your blessings, this son of mine shall surely become a lord of the earth;
of this there is no doubt, for you are the most excellent among those who know the mantras. (24)
Vyāsa said:
Mounted upon his chariot, wherever that wise Sudarśana goes,
he appears with his splendor as if surrounded by an entire Akṣauhiṇī army.
O King, there is no other power for the seed-mantra than this;
such indeed is the case for one who recites it with total devotion and joy. (26)
Having obtained from a true guru the wonderful seed-mantra known as Kāmarāja, he who recites it while pure and tranquil shall attain all desires. (27)
O best of kings, there is nothing on earth or even in heaven that is difficult to obtain, nor anything unattainable for one who is devoted to Śivā. (28)
They are dull-witted and most unfortunate, pursued by diseases, those in whose hearts there is no faith in the worship of the Mother and other such practices. (29)
She who was proclaimed at the beginning of the age as the mother of all the gods is renowned by the name Ādimātā (the Primordial Mother), O best of the Kurus.
Intellect, fame, fortitude, prosperity, power, faith, understanding, and memory—indeed, she shines forth perceptibly before all living beings. (31)
Indeed, those men who are deluded by illusion do not know; those who rely on fallacious reasoning do not worship the auspicious Goddess, the Sovereign of the Universe. 32.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Śambhu, Vāsava, Varuṇa, Yama, Vāyu, Agni, Kubera, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, the two Aśvins, and Bhaga; || 33 ||
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts—all meditate upon that Goddess, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction. || 34 ||
What wise man indeed would not serve that supreme power?
That auspicious Goddess, the bestower of all goals, was known by Sudarśana. 35.
She is indeed Brahman itself, exceedingly difficult to attain, whose nature consists of both knowledge and ignorance;
she is the supreme power accessible through yoga and beloved by those seeking liberation.
Who is capable of knowing the true nature of the Supreme Self without her, she who, having created the threefold creation, reveals it to the Universal Soul? (37)
But Sudarśana, reflecting upon that goddess in his mind,
remained in the forest, having indeed attained a happiness greater than the acquisition of a kingdom.
Candrakalā too, being excessively tormented by the arrows of love, constantly maintained a distressed body through various remedies. (39)
Then her father, Subāhu, having learned that his daughter was seeking an excellent husband,
diligently arranged a svayaṃvara for her.
The self-choice marriage (svayaṃvara) is proclaimed by the learned to be of three kinds; it is indeed suitable for kings for marriage, but it is said that it is not for others.
One was the self-choice marriage by desire (icchā-svayaṃvara), and the second was that which is called a wager (paṇa);
just as the bow of Tryambaka was indeed broken by Rāma.
The third, known as the bride-price of valor, is proclaimed for heroes;
there, the best of kings held a svayaṃvara based on personal choice.
The platforms were constructed by artisans and provided with beautiful coverings;
likewise, the assembly pavilions were well-constructed in various shapes.
When such an extensive and magnificent preparation for the wedding had been made, the sorrowful and beautiful-eyed maiden spoke to her friend Śaśikalā: (45)
"Go to my mother in private and speak these words of mine:
'I have chosen the auspicious son of Dhruvasandhi as my husband in my heart. (46)
"I shall choose no other boon except for that Sudarśana;
he, the son of a king established by the Goddess, shall be my husband. (47)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, that friend went quickly and spoke these sweet words in private to her mother, the daughter of Vidarbha, who was herself eloquent of speech. (48)
"Listen, O auspicious one, and now act with haste for her benefit regarding that which your virtuous daughter, being distressed, has spoken to you through my mouth. (49)
"In the holy hermitage of Bhāradvāja, there is the son of Dhruvasandhi;
he has been chosen by me as my husband in my heart, and I shall choose no other king. (50)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of her daughter, and now that her husband had returned home, the queen then reported her daughter's speech exactly as it was. (51)
Having heard those words, King Subāhu was amazed and laughed repeatedly;
he spoke these truthful words to his wife, the princess of Vidarbha: || 52 ||
O fair-browed one, you know that this boy has been exiled from the kingdom to the forest;
he indeed dwells alone with his mother in the desolate wilderness.
For his sake, King Vīrasena was slain by Yudhājit;
O lovely-eyed one, how could such a penniless husband be suitable for you? (54)
Speak these words to your daughter, even if they are unpleasant at times:
"Kings of firm resolve will come to the svayaṃvara. (55)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Sending of a Message by Śaśikalā to Her Mother," in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Dialogue with the King.
Vyāsa said:
Having placed her young daughter upon her lap, she was thus addressed by her husband.
Having comforted her who possessed a pure smile, he spoke these gentle words.
"O fair-toothed one, why do you speak such unpleasant words to me in vain?
By these words, O lady of noble vows, your father suffers great distress. (2)
Sudarśana was exceedingly unfortunate, fallen from his kingdom, without refuge,
deprived of both army and treasury, and abandoned by his kinsmen.
Having reached the forest with his mother, he is emaciated, subsisting on fruits and roots;
this bridegroom is indeed unfit for you, being a forest-dweller and unfortunate.
"O daughter, there are other princes who are wise, handsome, and highly esteemed; they are worthy of you and adorned with royal insignia."
His beloved brother indeed rules the kingdom among the Kosalas;
he is endowed with beauty and possessed of all auspicious marks.
Moreover, O fair-browed one, hear another reason as it was heard by me:
King Yudhājit is constantly desirous of his death. (7)
Having made a great conflict and slain King Vīrasena, he consulted with his ministers and established his own daughter's son upon the throne.
Desiring to kill Sudarśana upon his arrival at the hermitage of Bhāradvāja,
he was later restrained by the sage and returned to his own abode.
Śaśikalā said:
"O Mother, even though he dwells in the forest, that prince is truly my desired object;
and by the very word of Śaryāti, Sukanyā is devoted to her husband. (10)
And how, having attained Cyavana, she became devoted to the service of her husband;
for the service of the husband grants women both heaven and liberation. (11)
"Surely that which is performed without guile brings happiness to a woman;
for the Blessed One has granted me an unsurpassed boon in a dream. (12)
Without him, how could I resort to another prince?
For Sudarśana has been inscribed by the Goddess upon the wall of my heart. (13)
"Abandoning that beloved and charming husband, I shall do nothing else.
Vyāsa said:
Thus was the princess of Vidarbha then rebuked by her with many illustrative examples.
She related everything to her husband—the words spoken by their daughter, which she had received before the day of the wedding and which were consistent with what she had heard. (15)
There, Śaśikalā quickly dispatched the twice-born one, saying:
"Go to Sudarśana in such a way that my father does not know. (16)
"O Lord, speak swiftly on my behalf to Bhāradvāja’s hermitage:
'A svayaṃvara has been prepared by my father at his own expense for my sake. (17)
"Kings accompanied by armies will indeed come in great numbers;
yet you have been chosen by me in my heart with every form of affection. (18)
Commanded by the Blessed Lady in a dream, O god-like one, I would rather consume poison or leap into a blazing fire. (19)
"Even if urged by my parents, I choose no other than you;
in thought, deed, and word, you alone have been chosen as my husband by me. (20)
"By the grace of the Blessed Lady, happiness shall come to us both;
you must come here as well, making destiny your supreme strength. (21)
Upon whom the entire world, including all things mobile and immobile, depends;
that which has been commanded by the Blessed Lady shall not prove false. (22)
O Brahmin, that son of a king, under whose control all the deities beginning with Śaṅkara abide, must be spoken to by you in private.
"O sinless one, you must perform that task for me as it ought to be done.
Having spoken thus and given him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), she employed the sage for her purpose.
Having gone there and quickly reported everything, the twice-born Sudarśana returned;
and having understood that, he then made the firm resolve to depart.
Urged by that sage, he performed [the rites] with the highest reverence.
Vyāsa said:
To her son who was prepared to depart, Manoramā spoke.
Trembling, afflicted by extreme suffering, struck with terror, and with eyes full of tears, she asked:
"O son, where are you going today to the assembly of kings? (27)
Alone and having incurred enmity, what are you contemplating regarding the svayaṃvara? King Yudhājit will come here desiring to kill you. (28)
"You have no other companion; therefore, my son, do not go.
I am a mother with only one son, exceedingly wretched, my sole support and without any refuge. (29)
O highly fortunate one, you ought not to leave me despondent today;
for that king by whom your father was slain has also arrived there.
"Yudhājit will kill you there while you are alone.
Sudarśana said: "What is destined to happen must indeed happen; there is no need for deliberation in this matter. (31)
"And by the command of the Mother of the World, I am going today to the svayaṃvara;
do not grieve, O auspicious one, for you are a Kṣatriya woman, O fair-faced lady. (32)
"By the grace of the Blessed Lady, I am constantly free from fear.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, Sudarśana mounted his chariot, desiring to depart.
Having seen her son, Manoramā blessed him with benedictions:
"May Ambikā protect you from the front; may Pārvatī protect you from behind. (34)
May Śivā protect you now on both sides; may Pārvatī protect you everywhere at present;
may Vārāhī protect you on difficult paths; may Durgā protect you whenever there are obstacles; and may the Supreme Goddess Kālikā protect you in terrible conflict. (35)
In that pavilion, during the svayaṃvara, may Mātaṅgī, who is likewise gentle, and Bhavānī,
the liberator from worldly existence, protect you in the midst of the kings.
May Girijā protect you in mountain fastnesses, Cāmuṇḍā in courtyards, and the eternal Kāmagā in the forests. (37)
O scion of the Raghus, may the power of Viṣṇu protect you in dispute;
O gentle one, may Bhairavī protect your feet when meeting with enemies. (38)
May the Mistress of the World, the Great Illusion, the Sustainer of the Universe, whose form is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, protect you at all times and in all places. (39)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to him, his mother, trembling and overwhelmed with fear, said,
"I will certainly come along with you."
"Indeed, I cannot endure to remain here even for half a moment without you;
take me along with you, my child, wherever your mind is set upon going. (41)
Having spoken thus, the mother then departed accompanied by her nurse;
all the brahmins, having been granted blessings, went forth filled with joy.
Then Rāghava arrived at Vārāṇasī in a single chariot;
he was recognized there by Subāhu and honored with offerings and other marks of respect.
For the sake of his settlement, he gave him a house as well as food, drink, and so forth; and having given leave to a servant, he provided him for the purpose of personal attendance.
Then indeed, the kings who were lords of various lands assembled;
Yudhājit also arrived, accompanied by his grandson.
The lord of Karūṣa, as well as the king who was the ruler of Madra, the heroic Sindhu-rāja, and the warrior who was the lord of Māhiṣmatī; || 46 ||
The Pāñcāla, the Parvatīya, the exceedingly powerful Kāmarūpa, the Kārṇāṭa, the Coladeśīya, and the mighty Vaidarbha. || 47 ||
At that time, sixty-three akṣauhiṇīs were assembled in total;
the city was surrounded on all sides by the troops stationed everywhere.
These and many other kings, accompanied by excellent elephants, assembled there out of a desire to witness the svayaṃvara.
Then, having gathered together, those princes said to one another:
"The prince Sudarśana has indeed arrived, free from all anxiety. (50)
"Having mounted his chariot alone with his mother, the high-minded scion of Kakutstha has arrived here for the sake of marriage; what indeed should be done now? (51)
Having abandoned these princes along with their armies and weapons, why will that princess choose this mighty-armed man? (52)
Then Yudhājit, the best of kings, spoke to those lords of the earth:
"I shall slay him for the sake of the maiden; there is no doubt in this. (53)
Then the ruler of Kerala, the best among those skilled in ethics, said to him:
"O King, no war should be waged here; the choice at the svayaṃvara is voluntary."
There is no taking by force here, nor is there a bride-price or a svayaṃvara; here, the choosing is according to the maiden's own wish—what kind of dispute could there be in this? (55)
O best of kings, previously you unjustly exiled him from his kingdom; yet now, O powerful one, you have bestowed the kingdom upon your grandson. (56)
"This is the illustrious descendant of Kakutstha, the son of the lord of Kosala;
how will you kill this prince who is innocent? (57)
"O best of kings, you will surely reap the fruit of this misconduct;
for there is, O long-lived one, a ruler of this world who is the Lord of the Universe. (58)
Dharma triumphs, not adharma; truth triumphs, not falsehood.
O Indra among kings, show honor [to the virtuous] and indeed abandon your sinful intent. (59)
Your daughter's son has arrived, and he too is endowed with beauty;
being possessed of a kingdom and likewise illustrious, how could you not choose him?
Other princes are indeed more powerful, yet at the maiden's svayaṃvara, she will now choose him. (61)
Since [the matter] has been decided in this way, let the kings speak whatever they wish; however, one who possesses true knowledge should not harbor mutual hostility in this matter. 62.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Dialogue with the King," in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 19 ||
Vyāsa said: While the king, the lord of Kerala, was speaking thus to his father, Śaśikalā addressed him with these words.
The illustrious King Yudhājit also replied. || 1 ||
O protector of the earth, this is indeed the proper course of conduct that you,
whose word is truth and whose senses are conquered, have spoken here in the assembly of kings.
"O upholder of the lineage, while worthy suitors exist, this jewel of a maiden is being offered to an unworthy man; O protector of the earth, does this course of action please you? (3)
How indeed could a jackal deserve to enjoy the portion of a lion?
Likewise, how can this Sudarśana deserve such a jewel of a maiden? || 4 ||
The power of Brahmins indeed lies in the Vedas, while the power of kings arises from the bow;
O Great King, what else is unjust? This is what I say here now.
Just as a bride-price (śulka) is prescribed for kings in marriage,
let only the powerful take it, and never one who is weak.
Therefore, having made the maiden the prize, let a policy be adopted here;
otherwise, there will surely be a quarrel among the kings.
When such a dispute had arisen among the kings there,
Subāhu, the best of monarchs, was summoned into the midst of the assembly.
Having summoned all the kings, those seers of truth said to him:
"O King, you must exercise prudent policy with composure regarding this marriage."
"O King, tell me with a composed mind what you intend to do;
to whom, O monarch, does the giving away of your daughter appeal in your heart? (10)
Subāhu said:
"Sudarśana was indeed chosen by my daughter as her heart's desire;
though I dissuaded her most earnestly, she did not heed my words."
"What can I do? My daughter's mind does not remain under my control;
likewise, Sudarśana has arrived alone and undisturbed. (12)
Vyāsa said:
Having summoned Sudarśana, all the kings, being alert and composed, spoke to him as he arrived alone and tranquil. (13)
"O illustrious prince of noble vows, by whom were you summoned, that you have come here alone to this assembly of kings? (14)
"Indeed, you have no army, no ministers, no treasury, and no great force; for what purpose have you come? Tell me the truth, O high-minded one. (15)
In this assembly, kings desirous of war stand ready with their armies for the sake of the maiden; what do you intend to do here? (16)
Your brother Subala, the hero, has arrived with the desire to seize [the prize], and the mighty-armed Yudhājit has also come to provide assistance. (17)
"Go or stay, O Indra among kings; what has been spoken is according to the truth.
Since you are devoid of an army, O observer of noble vows, do as you wish. (18)
Sudarśana said:
"I have no strength, no allies, no treasury, and no refuge in a fortress;
I have no friends, no affection, and no kings to protect me. (19)
Having heard of the svayaṃvara here, I have come desiring to see it;
I have been impelled by the divine Goddess in a dream, of this there is no doubt. (20)
"Nothing else is intended by me today; the Goddess of the Universe has spoken to me, and whatever she has ordained shall come to pass today—of this there is no doubt. (21)
O Lords of the World, there is no enemy whatsoever here in this cycle of existence for me today, as I behold everywhere Bhavānī, the Mother of the Universe.
O princes, whoever shall act as an enemy toward me, the Great Vidyā shall be his punisher; I do not recognize him as an enemy.
O best of kings, that which is destined to be will surely come to pass and not otherwise; what anxiety, then, should be felt here? For I am entirely subject to fate.
O best of kings, among gods, humans, and all living beings at all times, devotion toward him is produced by that very [cause] and not otherwise.
O lords of kings, whatever that woman desires to do to a king, she accomplishes; or if she wishes to make a man penniless, what concern is it of mine? (26)
Without that supreme power, even the gods such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are not able to move; what then is my concern, O kings? (27)
Whether I am capable or incapable, whatever I may be,
by his command I have arrived this very day at the svayaṃvara.
She may do whatever she wishes; what indeed is the use of my worrying?
No doubt should be entertained in this matter; I tell you this as the truth. (29)
"O kings, I have not even an atom of shame here regarding victory or defeat;
rather, it is the Blessed Lady who has shame, and I am entirely dependent upon her. (30)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, the best of kings,
those lords of men who knew how to reach a decision, looked at one another and spoke.
"O virtuous one, what you have said is true; it can never be false.
Nevertheless, the lord of Ujjayinī desires to kill you. (32)
"O high-minded one, compassion was not ordained for your sake; we speak to you so that you may reflect with your mind, O sinless one, and do what is right. (33)
Sudarśana said:
"What more can I say, O best of kings, after having spoken these words? You, my compassionate friends, have indeed spoken the truth. (34)
Death cannot be avoided by anyone, nor for anyone, at any time;
this entire world, both mobile and immobile, is subject to destiny. (35)
This living being (jīva) is not independent; it is always subject to its own karma.
That karma has been declared by the wise who perceive reality to be of three kinds. (36)
Accumulated, present, and the third, the commenced—this entire world is pervaded by time, karma, and inherent nature. || 37 ||
A god is not able to slay a human being without the arrival of the appointed time;
it is eternal Time that kills, with the [god] acting merely as the instrument. || 38 ||
Just as my father, the subduer of enemies, was slain by a lion,
so too was my maternal grandfather Yudhājit killed in battle.
Even one who exerts millions of efforts may be slain by the turn of fate;
yet a man might live for thousands of years without any protection at all.
O righteous ones, O kings, I am never afraid of Yudhājit;
considering destiny alone to be supreme, I remain always composed.
I perform the constant and perpetual remembrance of the Blessed Lady;
she, the Goddess who is the mother of the universe, will bring about my welfare. 42.

For one must experience what was previously acquired, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious; for those who understand this, what cause for grief can there be in the experiencing of their own past deeds? (43)
Having experienced suffering through the connection with the fruits of one's own karma, the mindless person of small intellect indeed harbors enmity toward the instrumental cause. 44.
I do not perceive enmity, sorrow, or fear in that way;
having arrived here at this assembly of kings, I am free from apprehension.
Desiring to witness the unsurpassed svayaṃvara alone,
I have arrived here by the command of Caṇḍikā, for that which was destined to happen has now come to pass.
Restrained, I know no authority other than that of the Blessed Lady; whatever happiness or suffering is brought about by her will come to pass, and not otherwise. (47)
"May Yudhājit obtain happiness; I have no enmity toward you, O best of kings.
He who shall harbor enmity toward me will receive the fruit accordingly. (48)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by him, those kings remained there, satisfied;
and he too, having reached his own hermitage, became well-established.
On the following day, at an auspicious time, the kings were indeed summoned by King Subāhu into his own beautiful pavilion.
And the kings, adorned with auspicious ornaments, sat upon couches prepared and furnished with divine coverings. || 51 ||
Wearing divine attire like immortals in celestial chariots,
they stood there resplendent, desiring to witness the svayaṃvara.
Thus all were lost in thought: "When will she come?
When will she choose that most fortunate and best of kings, whose merit is renowned? (53)
When Sudarśana happens by fate to be adorned here with a garland, there will surely be a dispute among kings; of this there is no doubt. (54)
While the kings were thus reflecting, seated upon their thrones,
a very great sound of musical instruments arose in the royal pavilion.
Then the Lord of Kāśī spoke to his daughter, who had bathed and was well-adorned,
wearing a garland of madhūka flowers and clothed in silken garments.

To her, who was adorned with wedding ornaments, who resembled the daughter of the ocean (Lakṣmī), who was dressed in fine garments, and who was lost in thought, he spoke these words preceded by a smile. (57)
"Arise, O daughter of noble nose! Taking hold of my auspicious garland by the hand, go now into the midst of the pavilion and behold the assembly of kings. (58)
O slender-waisted one, choose that best of kings who dwells in your heart—one who is virtuous, endowed with beauty, and of noble birth. (59)
"O slender-limbed one, behold all the lords of various lands seated upon the prepared couches; choose according to your pleasure. (50)
Vyāsa said:
To her father who was speaking thus, the young girl, who herself spoke with moderation, addressed these words— graceful and consistent with dharma.
Śaśikalā said:
"O father, I shall certainly not come within the range of sight of kings who lust after me; other women go to such rulers. (62)
"O dear one, I have indeed heard this statement in the Dharmaśāstra:
'Only one husband should be looked upon by a woman, and no other.'"
The virtue of chastity has departed from her who goes to many men;
seeing her, they all imagine, "May she become mine. (54)
When she comes to the pavilion at the svayaṃvara having taken up the garland, she then becomes like an ordinary woman, like another unchaste wife. (65)
Just as a courtesan, having gone to the marketplace and observed the men standing there, reflects upon the knowledge of their merits and defects within her own mind; (66)
"Just as a courtesan, being fickle by nature, looks upon a lover in vain, so shall I go to the pavilion and act like a prostitute. (67)
"I shall not now perform the religious duty practiced by these elders;
rather, firm in my vow, I shall observe the vow of devotion to my husband according to my desire. (68)
Having first approached them all equally and having formed many intentions, she chooses but one; in that same way, how indeed shall I choose today? (69)
"O father, O best of kings, Sudarśana was previously chosen by me with my whole soul; I do not wish to act otherwise than that. (70)
O King, if you desire my welfare, bestow the gift of your daughter upon Sudarśana on an auspicious day according to the rites of marriage. (71)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Words of Śaśikalā to Her Father," in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The maiden’s statement to her father regarding the marriage with Sudarśana;
Vyāsa said:
Subāhu, having heard that, then considered what she had said to be appropriate.
He quickly became overcome with anxiety, wondering, "What should be done after this? (1)
The mighty rulers of the earth, accompanied by their armies and retinues, having assembled and seated themselves upon thrones, were eager for battle. || 2 ||
If I say to them all, "She has not come now," then those evil-minded ones, filled with anger, might kill me. (3)
Neither do I possess such strength of an army, nor such a wondrous strength of fortresses, by which I might venture here to challenge all these kings.
Likewise, Sudarśana was alone, without companions, penniless, and a mere child;
"What should be done? I am utterly submerged in an ocean of suffering. (5)
Thus lost in thought, the king went into the presence of the monarchs;
having prostrated before them, the king, bowing low with humility, then spoke to them.
"What should be done, O kings? My daughter does not enter the pavilion at will, even though she has been urged many times by her mother and by me as well. (7)
I prostrate with my head at your feet; I am now the servant of these kings. Having accepted this honor and the rest, please return to your homes today.
"I give many jewels, garments, elephants, and chariots; having accepted these today and shown me favor, let them depart for their own homes."
If my young daughter, being distressed, dies while not under my control, then I shall suffer great grief; therefore, I am consumed by anxiety. (10)
O noble ones, you who are compassionate, highly fortunate, and possessed of great power—
what need have I for that dull-witted and ill-behaved daughter?
"I am indeed to be favored by you; I am your slave in every way. You must always regard my daughter as your own daughter. (12)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of Subāhu, none of the kings spoke;
Yudhājit, his eyes copper-red with anger, addressed him with fury.
"O King, you are a fool; why do you speak thus after having committed such a highly censurable act? Why was this svayaṃvara performed out of delusion when danger was present? (14)
"All the kings have assembled here, summoned by you to the svayaṃvara;
how is it that today those monarchs are fit to go back to their own homes? (15)
"Having disregarded all other kings, why do you wish to give your daughter to Sudarśana? What could be more ignoble than this? (16)
"O King, a person desiring what is auspicious should first deliberate before acting; yet that deed was undertaken by you without such knowledge."
Having abandoned these kings who are equipped with armies and vehicles,
why do you now desire to make Sudarśana your bridegroom?
"I shall kill you, O most wicked one, and likewise Sudarśana later;
today I will give my daughter to your grandson"—this was his firm resolve. (19)
While I am present, who else is there who would wish to abduct the maiden?
How insignificant is Sudarśana today—he is penniless, powerless, and but a child. (20)
"Previously, at the hermitage of Bhāradvāja, I was released by me for the sake of the sage;
today, however, I shall by no means release the life of this child. (21)
Therefore, having deliberated upon this matter together with your daughter and your wife,
grant my beloved daughter of beautiful eyebrows to my grandson.
"Having given this beautiful daughter, become our kinsman; one who desires constant welfare must always seek a high-status alliance. (23)
Having given away your auspicious daughter, who is as dear to you as life itself, to Sudarśana—who is alone and without a kingdom—what happiness do you hope to obtain? (24)
Having considered family, wealth, strength, appearance, kingdom, fortress, and friends, a daughter should be given [in marriage]; otherwise, one does not attain happiness.
Reflect deeply upon the Dharma and the eternal principles of statecraft;
perform your duties as is appropriate, and do not let your mind turn otherwise.
"You are my dear friend; for your own benefit, I tell you this:
O King, bring your daughter to the pavilion, surrounded by her companions. (26)
Even when she chooses someone other than Sudarśana, there shall be no conflict for me; let your desired marriage take place.
All other kings are of noble lineage, possessed of armies, and equal [to him].
What kind of opposition could there be, O best of kings, if he were to choose him? (28)
"Otherwise, I shall today forcibly seize this auspicious maiden.
O best of kings, do not enter into a conflict that is so difficult to resolve. (29)
Vyāsa said:
Commanded by Yudhājit and filled with grief, Subāhu went to his home sighing; overcome by sorrow, he spoke to his wife. (30)
"O daughter, you who are well-versed in the true dharma, tell me what should be done by me when this quarrel has arisen; I am at your mercy, O fair-eyed one. (31)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard her husband’s words, she went and spoke to her son:
"O child, your father, the king, remains even now afflicted by extreme sorrow."
"O fair-hipped one, a conflict among the kings has indeed arisen today for your sake;
choose another king, O lady of beautiful form, with the exception of Sudarśana. (33)
"O child, if you forcibly choose Sudarśana, the powerful Yudhājit will surely slay both you and me. (34)
And that powerful King Sudarśana, intoxicated by his own strength, shall afterwards become your second husband when the quarrel occurs. (35)

"Therefore, O fawn-eyed one, if you desire happiness for me or for yourself, abandon Sudarśana and choose another excellent king. Thus was she exhorted by her mother, and afterwards the king also exhorted her.
Having heard the words of both, the fearless maiden spoke;
the maiden said:
"O best of kings, you have spoken the truth, and you know my vow. (37)
"O protector of the earth, I choose no one else anywhere except for Sudarśana; O Indra among kings, do you perhaps fear other monarchs and thus feel cowardly? (38)
"Having given me to Sudarśana, dismiss me outside the city;
he will place me upon his chariot and depart from your city. (39)
But that which is destined must indeed come to pass later, and it cannot be otherwise;
O best of kings, you should not entertain any anxiety regarding what is destined.
"What is destined to happen will surely come to pass; there is no doubt about this in any way.
The King said:
"O daughter, those possessed of intelligence should never act with recklessness. (41)
"Those who know the Vedas understand that one should not oppose many;
how then shall I give away my daughter after having betrothed her to the king's son? (42)
What improper act would kings endowed with excellent qualities not perform?
If it pleases you, my child, I shall establish the wager. (43)
Just as Janaka previously acted during Sītā’s svayaṃvara,
so too did he hold the bow of Śiva, having made it the stake.
In the same way, O slender-limbed one, I shall today perform that which is difficult to achieve, so that when it has been done, the dispute among the kings will indeed come to rest. (45)
"He who shall protect you according to your desire—whether it be Sudarśana or anyone else who is more powerful—he shall become your husband. (46)
Having fulfilled his wager, he will certainly choose you in every way;
if this is done, the dispute among the kings will be pacified. (47)
"After that, I shall arrange your marriage with ease.
The maiden said, "I do not sink into doubt at all, for this is an act of a fool. (48)
Sudarśana was previously held in my heart and not otherwise;
O Lord of the Earth, the mind alone is the cause of merits and sins. (49)
"O Father, having mentally chosen him, how could I choose another?
O Great King, once the wager has been made, I am indeed under the control of all. (50)
If there be one protector, or two, or even many, what should be done then, my dear, when a dispute has arisen? (51)
Therefore, I do not set my mind upon a task that is founded on doubt;
do not worry, O Indra among kings, give me to Sudarśana.
Having performed the marriage according to the prescribed rite, Caṇḍikā will bestow well-being;
by the mere chanting of her name, the flood of suffering shall go to its dissolution.
"Remembering that supreme power, perform your duty without indolence;
go now and speak to the kings with palms joined in reverence. (54)
"Tomorrow all the kings must come here to the svayaṃvara," having said this, you should quickly dismiss the entire circle of monarchs. (55)
"O King, perform my marriage ceremony this very night according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas;
having given him suitable wedding gifts, dismiss him. (56)
"The son of Dhruvasandhi will surely take me away;
perhaps those kings, becoming enraged, will prepare for battle. (57)
Then the goddess will come into being; she will provide us with assistance, and that prince as well will engage in battle with them.
If he should die by fate in battle, I too shall surely perish.
May it be well with you; stay at home, having given me up along with my army. (59)
"I alone shall go with him, desiring to sport with him.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of hers, that king made his resolve.
Having gained confidence, he resolved to act accordingly.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Maiden’s Account to Her Father Regarding Marriage with Sudarśana," in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Marriage of Sudarśana and Śaśikalā.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of his daughter, he whose soul was blameless...
Having approached the kings, the monarch said:
"O kings, you may depart for your camps as you please;
indeed, I shall arrange the wedding tomorrow."
"May all, being well-pleased with me, accept these foods and drinks offered by me;
for tomorrow there shall indeed be a ceremony here in this pavilion."
Having assembled here with everyone, this must be carried out in unison.
"My daughter has not come to the pavilion today;
what shall I do here, O kings?
Having comforted my daughter in the morning, I shall lead her [to you]."
Therefore, let the kings depart from that camp.
The wise do not engage in conflict with their own dependents;
for compassion must always be shown toward one's offspring. Having established that [compassion], I shall bring you here, O destroyer of enemies.
Let the kings go to their daughters as they please.
Or, having reflected in my mind upon the wish-granting bazaar, I shall perform the marriage ceremony tomorrow morning,
having assembled here with all the kings gathered together.
The svayaṃvara (self-choice marriage) should be held with the consent of all. || 5 ||
Having heard this and knowing his words to be true,
those kings departed for their own abodes after establishing a guard around the city.
And they performed the rites prescribed for midday.
At the time of the wedding, Subāhu, accompanied by noble men, performed the necessary rites;
having summoned his daughter to a well-guarded chamber in the house, together with priests who were the most eminent among those learned in the Vedas.
Having performed the ritual acts such as bathing for the bridegroom, and likewise having adorned him for the wedding,
he should be led into the house where the altar has been prepared.
The lord of the earth performed his worship.
O lord of men, having offered him a seat, water for rinsing the mouth, the arghya offering, two garments, a cow, and two earrings according to the prescribed rites;
He of undiminished courage desired the taking of a son.
With an undaunted mind, he accepted everything; then the anxiety of Manoramā subsided,
for she had obtained a maiden with beautiful hair who was like a daughter of the Nidhi spirits.
At that time, he considered himself to be unsurpassed.

Then, having been well-honored with gifts of ornaments and garments, all those ministers— filled with joy and free from fear— led that most excellent of men into the interior of the marriage pavilion.
Having completed her adornments according to the prescribed rites, those women, skilled in ritual, placed the princess upon a magnificent vehicle and led her into the presence of the bridegroom.
Indeed, in a pavilion provided with four pillars. || 12 ||

Having established the sacred fire and offered oblations according to the rules, the domestic priest summoned those two, who had already performed the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony, during that interval.
The bride and groom were filled with intense love. || 13 ||
Having performed the ritual scattering of parched grain according to the rules and having circumambulated the sacrificial fire,
they both performed there whatever was appropriate.
The entire ritual procedure arising from one's family and lineage. || 14 ||
The king of men gave to Sudarśana two hundred well-adorned chariots yoked with horses, equipped with a multitude of arrows.
In marriage, the wedding gifts should be well-honored. || 15 ||
He gave one hundred and twenty-five elephants, rutting and adorned with gold, their bodies resembling mountain peaks, to the prince.
Then the king, filled with affection, gave [it]. || 16 ||
The king presented to the bridegroom a hundred female slaves adorned with gold and a hundred very beautiful female elephants.
He was delighted at every moment during the time of the wedding. || 17 ||
Furthermore, he gave away another thousand servants,
fully equipped and adorned with all kinds of weapons, as well as jewels and garments appropriate for them.
Divine, variegated, and likewise extraordinary. || 18 ||
Furthermore, he gave him delightful, long, and variegated dwelling-houses;
and he bestowed two thousand most beautiful, excellent horses born in the Sindhu region.
He assigned three hundred very beautiful camels capable of bearing heavy loads,
and indeed two hundred of the finest wagons.
To him he gave [a vessel] filled with the juices of grain.
Having bowed before the beautiful princess, he spoke these words with palms joined in reverence:
"I am your servant, O most excellent princess."
Therefore, tell me whatever is in your mind.
She too spoke those pleasing words:
"May it be well with you, O King; may there be prosperity for your lineage. I have been honored by you on account of my son."
Since his own excellent daughter was bestowed [upon him]. || 22 ||
O King, I am neither the daughter of a bard nor a princess of Magadha; why then do I praise you here as my own most venerable kinsman?
For today my son has been made equal to Mount Sumeru.
By the supreme sovereign, his kinsman. || 23 ||
Oh, how truly wonderful and supremely pure is the conduct of you, O King! What more can I say?
That for my son, who has been deprived of his kingdom today—
You have bestowed your most excellent and worshipful daughter. || 24 ||
Indeed, for the sake of dwelling in the forest, he— bereft of wealth, deprived of his father, and without an army—
has abandoned all these lords of the earth.
To him who is free from the desire for eating fruits. || 25 ||
Furthermore, the king gives his daughter to one of equal wealth, family, and strength;
no one [would give her] to me, the daughter of a king, if I were destitute of means.
One should give a girl who is endowed with good qualities and beautiful in form. || 26 ||
Having established enmity with all the most excellent kings who were endowed with great strength,
my daughter Sudarśanā was then offered to me.
How can I describe this fortitude of yours? || 27 ||
Having heard these words, the king was delighted;
with palms joined in reverence, he spoke again:
"Accept my well-known kingdom."
And today I become the commander-in-chief. || 28 ||
If not, then having accepted half of that, enjoy the fruits of sovereignty here together with your sons,
after abandoning your residence in Vārāṇasī.
Therefore, I have no dwelling in either the forest or the city. || 29 ||
"Kings are indeed full of wrath; having gone there, I shall first employ conciliation,
and thereafter the other two means."
I shall not engage in battle unless challenged. || 30 ||
Victory and defeat depend on fate; nevertheless, victory belongs to righteousness even when unrighteousness has been practiced— such is said of those kings who were indeed unrighteous.
How indeed will that which was never thought of come to pass?
Having heard his meaningful speech,
Manoramā, regaining her composure from him, spoke these beneficial words to him.
She is filled with joy in every way and is serene. || 32 ||
O King, may it be well with you; rule your kingdom, casting aside all fear along with your sons.
Surely my son too, having obtained the kingdom—
It shall circulate here in the city of Sāketa.
"Dismiss us so that we may go to our own home;
Bhavānī will provide for your welfare.
O King, no anxiety whatsoever exists within me."
She was indeed meditating upon the Supreme Mother.
The night passed away with various words and phrases, both savory and like nectar in their mutual conversation;
then, having learned that the marriage had been performed, the kings arrived at dawn filled with rage and spoke thus as they stood outside the city. (35)
This very day, having slain that bearer of the king's disgrace and likewise that boy who is indeed unfit for marriage,
let us seize that Śaśikalā and the royal fortune of the king.
Having incurred shame, how could we go to our own home? || 36 ||
"Let them hear the sounds of trumpets being played; indeed, the sounds of the mṛdaṅgas overwhelm the blasts of conchs.
And hearing the various strains of song and the resonance of the Vedas, we believe that the king has performed the marriage ceremony here. (37)
Having deceived us with their words, they have duly performed the grasping of the hand according to the marriage rite;
now, alas, let them consider what must be done today!
And let the kings support one another's intentions. || 38 ||
While the kings were speaking thus, the king of incomparable majesty, having performed the marriage ceremony for the maiden,
went quickly to invite the monarchs.
The Lord of Kāśī, together with his friends of renowned power. || 39 ||
And seeing the Lord of Kāśī approaching, the kings then said nothing at all; out of anger, they remained standing there observing a vow of silence.
Having gone there and prostrated, he spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"All the kings must come to my house for the sake of a meal. (41)
"This king has been chosen by my daughter; what can I do, whether it be beneficial or harmful?
You must act for his welfare, for the great are indeed compassionate. (42)
Having heard those words of his, the kings, overwhelmed with anger, replied:
"We have already eaten; O king, go to your own home. (43)
Perform all your duties as you wish; well done!
Let all the kings today indeed depart for their respective homes.
Having heard that, Subāhu also went home filled with apprehension, wondering, "What will the best of kings do when they are agitated and possessed by anger? (45)
When he had departed, the kings again made an agreement:
"Having blocked the path and slain Sudarśana, we shall seize the maiden. (46)
Some said, "Alas, what have we to do with that king?
Having seen all this spectacle, we shall go back just as we came. (47)
Having spoken thus, all those kings took their leave and departed;
Subāhu, having returned to his own home, performed his subsequent duties.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Marriage of Sudarśana and Śaśikalā," in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Goddess’s Praise by Subāhu.
Vyāsa said: Having then duly offered him foods worthy of honor, he [said]:
And for six days, the king fed him with devotion. || 1 ||
Having thus performed all the marriage rites and bestowed the wedding gifts, the king then deliberated with his ministers.
Having heard from the messengers that the road had been blocked,
King Subāhu, of immeasurable splendor, became despondent.
Then Sudarśana, firm in his vows, said to his father-in-law:
"Dismiss us quickly; we shall depart without hesitation."
"O King, having gone to the holy hermitage of Bhāradvāja, you must by all means deliberate there with concentrated minds regarding a place to dwell."
O sinless one, you should not entertain even the slightest fear of kings;
Bhavānī, the mother of the world, will surely provide me with assistance.
Vyāsa said:
Having understood the intention of his son-in-law, that best of men (the king) dismissed him after giving him wealth; he too then departed in haste.
Possessed by great strength, that best of kings proceeded onward;
Sudarśana, surrounded there, moved along the path without fear.
Surrounded by chariots, the hero, the joy of the Raghus, seated upon his chariot with his wife, beheld the armies of the kings as he proceeded.
Subāhu, too, having seen them, became overcome with anxiety;
he joyfully sought refuge in Śivā within his heart according to the prescribed rites.
Free from fear and devoid of sorrow, he recited the supreme one-syllable mantra, the King of Desire (Kāmarāja), together with his newly wedded wife.
Then all the rulers of the earth, having raised a great clamor,
rose up accompanied by their armies, desiring to kill the maiden.
Upon seeing them, the King of Kāśī indeed became desirous of killing them;
however, he was then strongly restrained by Rāghava, who wished for victory.
There too, conchs, kettledrums, ānakas, and dundubhis resounded as Subāhu and the kings, desiring to slay one another, [prepared for battle].
Śatrujit, however, stood there well-prepared with the intent to slay;
Yudhājit, for his part, became fully equipped to assist him. || 15 ||
And some spectators then stood with his armies;
Yudhājit, having gone forward, approached Sudarśana.
Accompanied by Śatrujit, the younger brother set out to slay his elder brother;
overwhelmed with rage, they mangled one another with floods of arrows. (17)
