A very great crush occurred there among the excellent archers;
then the Lord of Kāśī, quickly surrounded by a vast army, [advanced]. || 18 ||
She went quickly for the sake of assistance to her blameless son-in-law.
Thus did that fierce and hair-raising battle proceed. (19)
Suddenly the Goddess appeared, seated upon a lion,
bearing various weapons, beautiful, and adorned with excellent ornaments.
Clad in divine garments and adorned with a beautiful garland of Mandāra flowers,
those kings, upon seeing her, were then struck with the utmost wonder.
"Who is this woman mounted upon a lion, and from where has she arisen?
Thus Sudarśana, having beheld her, spoke to Subāhu.
Behold, O King, this Great Goddess of divine appearance who has arrived;
she has surely manifested out of compassion to bestow grace upon me. (23)
"O Great King, I have become fearless even from fearlessness;
Sudarśana and Subāhu, having beheld that lady of beautiful countenance," (24)
Delighted by the sight of her, they both offered their salutations;
at that moment, the lion roared and those terrified of the elephant trembled.
Violent winds blew and the quarters became most dreadful;
then Sudarśana spoke to his own commander-in-chief.
Go quickly along the path where the kings are stationed;
what can those angry kings of wicked intent do? (27)
"For our protection, the divine lady has indeed come to us;
therefore, you must proceed safely on this path crowded with kings. (28)
"I remember that the Great Goddess has arrived for the sake of protection.
Having heard those words, the commander-in-chief proceeded by that path.
But Yudhājit, becoming violently enraged, said to those lords of the earth:
"Why do you stand here paralyzed by fear? Slay [them] along with the maiden! (30)
And disregarding all of us, who are superior in strength, that child, being himself weak, has taken the maiden and departs swiftly and fearlessly. (31)
"Are you afraid because you see a woman seated upon a lion? O noble ones, she must certainly not be ignored; she must be slain here by those who are composed. (32)
"Having killed him, we shall take the girl with her beautiful ornaments;
this jackal does not deserve to seize what was given by a lion. (33)
Having spoken thus, Yudhājit, accompanied by his army and joined by Śatrughna,
arrived there desiring to fight, overwhelmed with rage.
Drawing his bow back to his ear, he quickly released arrows that were polished by smiths, whetted on stone, and furnished with matching feathers.
Desiring to kill him, that one of very dull intellect then [attacked] Sudarśana from above;
but Sudarśana, in an instant, cut those arrows down as they fell with his own shafts.
When the battle had thus commenced, Caṇḍikā became exceedingly enraged;
then Goddess Durgā discharged arrows toward Yudhājit.
Then the auspicious Mother of the World, assuming various forms and bearing various weapons, arrived there and created a tumultuous uproar.
There Śatrujit was slain, and King Yudhājit as well;
both fell from their chariots, and at that moment a cry of victory arose.
All the kings, beholding her and the death of their maternal uncle as well as their nephew in battle, were struck with supreme amazement.
Subāhu, too, seeing their death in battle,
was exceedingly delighted and praised Durgā, the destroyer of the suffering of those in distress.
Subāhu said: "Salutations to the Goddess, the mother of the universe; constant salutations to Śivā. Salutations again and again to you, the divine Durgā, the granter of desires. (42)
Salutations to Śivā, to you who are Peace; salutations to Vidyā, the bestower of liberation.
O Mother of the World, O Sustainer of the World, salutations to Śivā, the pervader of the universe. 43.
O Goddess, even as I reflect with my intellect upon your course, I truly do not know it; for you are indeed devoid of qualities (nirguṇā), while I am possessed of qualities (saguṇa).
How can I praise the Mother of the Universe, whose power is so manifest?
[She is] the supreme Śakti, intent on destroying the suffering of her devotees. || 44 ||

You are the goddess of speech, omnipresent indeed; you are the intellect, knowledge, thought, and the very goal of every living being. Why do I praise you? For you are the controller of all minds; indeed, how can one's own true nature ever be praised? || 45 ||
Even Brahmā, Hara, and Hari— those foremost of gods— have indeed failed to reach the end of Your qualities while praising them incessantly;
how then can I, O Mother, whose mind is full of distinctions, ever encompass You with my virtues?
Oh, it is impossible for one who is unknown to be capable of recounting your life story! || 46 ||
Oh, how association with the virtuous does not fulfill one's desire,
even when it is undertaken incidentally, since the purification of the mind has indeed been accomplished through this union with my son-in-law!
Indeed, this wonderful vision of you has been attained by me.
Even Brahmā, Hara, Hari, the gods led by Indra, and the sages who have realized the truth of reality, always long for that vision of yours,
O Mother, which is so difficult for me to attain today.
And this is attained even without self-restraint, tranquility, and the like, as well as meditative concentration. || 48 ||
Where am I, of such dull intellect, and where is your swift glance?
Where is this, O Bhavānī, your peerless medicine for worldly existence?
For you, O Goddess, are surely always known to be endowed with compassionate love.
She is devoted to compassion for her devotees and is worthy of worship by the supreme classes of beings. || 49 ||
O Goddess, how can I describe this deed of yours,
that Sudarśana has been protected here in this perilous situation,
and that these two very powerful enemies have been swiftly slain by you today?
The supreme and most holy life-story of the one who is compassionate toward his devotees. || 50 ||
"O Goddess, this is not surprising; when the matter is considered, you indeed protect everything in its entirety, both the stationary and the moving.
And by you, out of compassion, the enemy was struck down and saved."
This son of Dhruvasandhi is now well protected. || 51 ||
O Bhavānī, this life-story was composed by you for the sake of making your own fame exceedingly radiant for a devotee intent on service;
otherwise, how could you have so graciously accepted my daughter?
In battle, he shall be skillful and of irreproachable character. || 52 ||
You are capable of destroying the fears of birth, death, and the like; what wonder is there in this regarding the desire of your devotee?
O Mother, you are sung of as boundless by those who are devoted.
You are devoid of both sin and merit, and you possess both qualities and their absence.

O Goddess, Sovereign of the World, by the sight of you I have become a man of merit, one who has achieved his life’s purpose; I am blessed in birth, O Mother! Indeed, I knew neither your seed-mantra nor your worship, yet today your majesty and manifest power have been realized by me.
Vyāsa said: Thus praised, the auspicious Goddess, with a gracious countenance, then spoke to the king: "O you of noble vows, choose a boon."

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Hymn to the Goddess by Subāhu," in the Third Book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 23 ||
The Description of the Goddess’s Majesty.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of Bhavānī, that best of kings—
There, Subāhu, filled with devotion, spoke these words.
Subāhu said:
On one side is the kingdom of the world of the gods and the circle of the earth;
on the other side is the sight of you—these two are never equal.
"There is nothing in the three worlds equal to this sight for me; O Goddess, what boon shall I ask for? I have achieved my purpose upon the earth. (3)
O Mother, I desire to ask for this cherished boon:
may my devotion to you always remain unwavering and eternal. (4)
"O Mother, you must always remain here in this city;
established here as Śakti, you shall indeed abide by the name Durgādevī. (5)
And you must always provide protection for this city,
so that it may remain free from disease, just as Sudarśana was saved from the hosts of enemies.
Likewise, O Ambikā, you must provide protection here for Vārāṇasī,
so that the city may remain well-established and firmly situated upon the earth.
O Goddess, treasure-house of compassion, you must remain here in this fortress;
this boon should be granted to me by you—what else could I possibly ask for? (8)
Grant me all various desires and slay my enemies;
and always bring about the destruction of those who are inauspicious for the world.
Vyāsa said: Thus entreated by him who was distressed by difficulties, the goddess Durgā, the destroyer of the suffering of distress,
stood before that king and, having praised him, spoke to him.
Durgā said:
"O King, my permanent residence shall always be in Muktipurī for the protection of all the worlds, as long as the earth endures. (11)
Then Sudarśana, having arrived there filled with joy,
bowed down with supreme devotion and praised the Mother of the Universe.
Oh, what compassion! What can I say? You have indeed saved me, though I am devoid of devotion;
for every person is compassionate toward their devotees.
Your vow is the protection of those whose devotion has been liberated.
O Goddess, I have heard that you create the entire phenomenal world; you protect what you have created yourself;
and when the time for withdrawal arrives, you consume it all.
In this matter, my protection of you is indeed nothing extraordinary.
"What shall I do for you? Speak, O Goddess, what task must be done, or where should I go? Grant me leave at once;
I am bewildered as to my duty by your command."
I go, I stay, I dwell, O Mother. || 15 ||
Vyāsa said:
To him who was speaking thus, the goddess, filled with compassion, replied:
"Go to Ayodhyā, O illustrious one, and rule a kingdom worthy of your lineage."
I am always to be remembered by you and worshipped with diligence;
O best of kings, I shall eternally bestow welfare and sovereignty upon you.
On the eighth, the fourteenth, and especially on the ninth day,
my worship must be performed according to the rite of offering oblations (bali).
"O sinless one, my image should be installed by you in the city;
it must be worshipped with effort and devotion three times a day. (19)
In the autumn season, a great worship of me must always be performed according to the Navarātra rite and with a spirit of devotion.
A great festival should be celebrated in the months of Caitra, Āśvina, Āṣāḍha, and Māgha;
O Great King, worship should be performed especially during Navarātra. (21)
O tiger among kings, those endowed with devotion to me should always perform [this rite] on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, as well as on the eighth day, by the wise.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess Durgā, the destroyer of the suffering of those in distress, vanished;
she was then bowed to and praised at great length by Sudarśana.
Seeing her vanish, all those kings approached him and bowed down, just as the gods bow before Śakra.
Subāhu also, having bowed to him, stood before him filled with joy;
then all the kings spoke to the lord of Ayodhyā.
"You are our lord and teacher, and we are always your servants;
O best of kings, rule the kingdom in Ayodhyā and protect us. (26)
O Great King, by your grace, I have beheld the auspicious Viśveśvarī, Bhavānī, the primordial Śakti who bestows the fruits of the four goals of human existence. (27)
Blessed are you, you have accomplished your purpose, and you possess great merit upon the earth, since for your sake the eternal Goddess has manifested herself. (28)
"O best of kings, we all do not know the power of Caṇḍikā; we are always enveloped in darkness and deluded by her illusion. (29)
Always delighting in the thought of wealth, wives, and sons, they are submerged in the terrible great ocean agitated by the fish of desire and anger. (30)
We ask you, O illustrious one; you are omniscient, O high-minded one!
What is this power, from where was it born, and what is its influence? Tell us that.
O descendant of Kakutstha, you are a boat for us in this saṃsāra; since virtuous ones are exceedingly compassionate, therefore tell us the supreme majesty of the Goddess.
O best among the foremost of men, we wish to hear everything regarding that goddess—her power, her true nature, and her origin; please tell us.
Vyāsa said:
Thus questioned by them at that time, the king who was the son of Dhruvasandhi reflected in his mind upon the Goddess and, filled with joy, spoke to them.
Sudarśana said:
O protector of the earth, what can I say of her supreme conduct?
Even Brahmā and the hosts of gods, together with Śiva, do not know it.
O protectors of the earth, she is the primordial Great Lakṣmī of all, the most excellent and supreme power; she is of the nature of sattva and is intent upon the protection of the world.
She who takes the form of *rajas* during creation, the form of *sattva* during preservation, and the form of *tamas* during dissolution—she is always considered to consist of the three *guṇas*. (37)
The supreme power is devoid of qualities (nirguṇā) and bestows the fruits of all desires;
for she, O best of kings, is indeed the cause of all beings, beginning with Brahmā. (38)
O kings, she who is devoid of qualities is impossible for yogis to know in any way;
she who possesses qualities is easy to serve and should always be meditated upon by the wise. (39)
The kings said:
"Though you reached the forest while still a child, you were surely afflicted by fear;
how was it that you recognized the Goddess, the supreme and most excellent Śakti? (40)
And how was she worshipped, O King, and how was she honored, that she, being pleased, rendered assistance with great haste? (41)
Sudarśana said:
"O kings, in my childhood I obtained her most esteemed seed-mantra; I remember reciting daily that which is known as the seed-mantra of Kāma. (42)
Described by the sages, that auspicious Ambikā was recognized by me;
I remember her day and night with supreme devotion as the highest. (43)
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words of his, the kings, intent on devotion and regarding her as the supreme power, departed toward their own homes.
Subāhu went to Kāśī after taking leave of Sudarśana;
and the righteous Sudarśana also departed from the land of Kosala.
But when the ministers heard that Śatrujit had been killed in battle and Sudarśana had been conquered, they were filled with affection for the king. || 46 ||
Hearing that the king was approaching, the people residing in Sāketa set out to meet him, bringing various offerings with them. || 47 ||
Likewise, all the subjects, with various gifts in their hands, having given Dhruvasandhi’s son, departed joyfully. || 48 ||
Then Sudarśana, accompanied by his wife, having reached Ayodhyā and honored all the people, went to the royal residence.
He was being praised by bards, honored by his ministers,
and showered with parched grain and flowers by young maidens.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Goddess by Sudarśana," in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 24 ||
Description of the Installation of the Goddess.
Vyāsa said:
Having gone to Ayodhyā, that best of kings, surrounded by his friends, entered the palace of the king.
Śatrujit, having bowed down, spoke to his mother, who was overwhelmed with grief. || 1 ||
"O mother, your son was certainly not slain by me in battle, nor was your father Yudhājit; I swear this by your feet. (2)
Those two were slain in battle by Durgā; indeed, there was no fault of mine in this matter.
Against events that are destined to happen, no remedy exists.
O proud lady, you should not grieve here for your deceased son;
living beings, subject to the power of their own karma, experience pleasant and unpleasant enjoyments.
"O Mother, I am your slave; just as Manorama is mine, so too are you, O knower of dharma—there is not even the slightest difference between us. (5)
One must inevitably experience the results of actions performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
therefore, you should never grieve over pleasure or pain.
In times of suffering, one should view others as even more afflicted than oneself; in times of happiness, one should view others as even more joyful.
One should not surrender oneself to grief and joy as if they were two enemies.
"All this is dependent on destiny and never dependent on oneself;
therefore, a wise man should not wither away his soul through grief. (8)
Just as a wooden puppet moves by the efforts of actors and others,
so the embodied soul, subject to its own karma, functions everywhere.
O mother, having gone to the forest, my mind was not troubled by sorrow;
reflecting upon my own past deeds, I knew that they must be experienced.
My maternal grandfather has died right here, and my mother, overcome with grief and seized by fear, has taken me and departed for the dense forest. (11)
Robbed by thieves on the road, she was likewise stripped of her clothes;
all her provisions were taken away, and she, with her young son, was left without refuge. (12)
Taking me with her, my mother arrived at the hermitage of Bhāradvāja;
so too did this Vidalla and the frail nurse-maid.
Nourished on all sides by sages and sage-wives endowed with compassion with fruits and wild rice, we three remained there.
At that time there was indeed suffering, but today there is happiness upon the arrival of wealth;
yet in my mind, there has never been any enmity nor any envy at any time. (15)
O scorcher of foes, eating wild rice (nīvāra) is superior to enjoying royal luxuries; one who aspires for such [royal] things goes to hell, whereas one who eats wild rice never does. 16.
A wise man should practice righteousness, having truly conquered the group of his senses, so that he does not go to hell. 17.
O Mother, human birth in this auspicious land of Bhārata is difficult to obtain; indeed, food and other comforts may be found in all [other] wombs. (18)
Having obtained this human body, which bestows heaven and liberation upon men and is difficult to attain in other wombs, one must perform the means for achieving dharma. (19)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by him, Līlāvatī was then deeply abashed;
casting aside her grief for her son, she spoke to him with eyes full of tears.
"O son, I am guilty; I was made so by my father Yudhājit, who indeed killed your maternal grandfather and seized his kingdom. (21)
I was not able to prevent him then, nor my son;
whatever deed was done by him alone, there is no fault of mine, O son. (22)
Those two died solely because of their own actions; you are not the cause of their death, nor am I.
I do not grieve for that son, but I always grieve for his deeds.
"O son, you are my auspicious one; Manoramā is my sister.
I have not the slightest anger or sorrow toward you, my son. (24)
"O highly fortunate one, rule the kingdom; protect the subjects, O observer of noble vows! By the grace of the Blessed Lady, this realm has been obtained free from all thorns. (25)
Having heard those words of his mother and having bowed to her, the prince went to the beautiful palace where Manoramā had previously resided.
Having gone there, he dwelt there after summoning all his ministers; then he questioned the astrologers regarding an auspicious hour and day.
Having likewise caused a beautiful golden lion-throne to be made, I shall always worship the Goddess as she sits upon that lion-throne. (28)
Having seated the Goddess, the bestower of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, upon her throne,
I shall thereafter rule the kingdom just as it was ruled by Rāma and the others.
The Goddess should always be worshipped by all city-dwellers;
she is the venerable Śiva-śakti, the bestower of the fulfillment of all desires and aims. (30)
Thus addressed, those ministers indeed carried out the king's command;
they had a most beautiful palace constructed by artisans.
Then, having had an image fashioned on an auspicious day and at a favorable moment,
the king summoned brahmins learned in the Vedas and established it.
Having performed the oblation according to the rules and having worshipped the deity,
the wise king installed her in the temple of the Goddess.
O King, a festival took place there with the sounds of musical instruments,
the Vedic chants of the Brahmins, and various kinds of songs.
Vyāsa said:
Having installed the goddess Śivā according to the rules by those who recite the Vedas, the king performed various kinds of worship with great ritual precision. (35)
Having performed the rites of worship and regained his ancestral kingdom,
the king became renowned as the goddess Ambikā among the people of Kosala.
Having obtained the entire kingdom, the king—
victorious through the true Dharma and exceedingly righteous— brought all the neighboring kings under his control.
Just as Rāma was in his own kingdom, and as Raghu was in that of Dilīpa, so too did the people experience happiness, and the moral boundaries likewise remained intact. (38)
Likewise, the dharma of those belonging to the various castes and stages of life became four-footed;
on the surface of the earth, the minds of no one took delight in unrighteousness. (39)
In every village, all the lords of men constructed palaces,
and then the worship of the Goddess was joyfully established throughout the Kosala lands.
Subāhu, moreover, having had a beautiful image of Durgā fashioned in Kāśī, installed it in a temple with devotion. || 41 ||
There, all the people, devoted to loving devotion,
performed her worship according to the prescribed rites, just as they do for Viśveśvara.
Then she became renowned as the goddess Durgā upon the surface of the earth;
O great king, her devotion increased in every land.
At that time, Bhavānī became an object of worship for everyone in every way, throughout the world of Bhārata and among all social classes. 44.
O King, they all became devoted to Śakti and full of pride;
then, intent on recitation and meditation, they offered hymns of praise as prescribed in the Āgamas.
During all nine nights, all the people, devoted to the Goddess, performed worship, oblations, and sacrifice according to the prescribed rules.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Installation of the Goddess," in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 25 ||
Description of the Worship of the Virgin (Kumārīpūjā).
Janamejaya said:
"O best of the twice-born, when the Navarātra has arrived, what should be performed?"
Please explain the ritual procedure according to the rules, especially for the autumn season.
O Great-minded One, what indeed is the fruit, and what rite should be performed therein?
O best of the twice-born, please tell me this in detail out of compassion. (2)
Vyāsa said: Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the auspicious Navarātra vow;
it should be performed according to the prescribed rites, especially during the autumn season. (3)
And likewise, it should be performed with love during the spring;
for indeed, among all people, there are two seasons known as the fangs of Yama. || 4 ||
Autumn and spring, known by those names, are difficult for living beings to traverse here;
therefore, one who desires well-being everywhere should perform this rite with diligent effort.
Only two seasons are exceedingly terrible for men, causing disease;
both spring and autumn alone bring about the destruction of all.
Therefore, O lord of men, the wise should perform the worship of Caṇḍikā there with devotion during the auspicious months of Caitra and Āśvina.
Having reached the new moon day (amāvāsyā), one should prepare auspicious materials;
on that day, one should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) and observe the practice of eating only once.
The pavilion should be constructed on level ground in an auspicious location, measuring sixteen cubits in size and provided with pillars and banners.
Then, one should have the ground smeared with white clay and cow dung;
in its center, a bright, level, and stable altar (vedikā) should be constructed.
The excellent site for the pedestal should be four cubits in length and one cubit in height;
one should then arrange various ornate arches and a canopy.
Then, at night, he addressed the twice-born who were experts in the true nature of the Goddess,
devoted to right conduct, self-controlled, and masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
On the first day of the lunar fortnight, one should perform the morning bath according to the prescribed rules,
whether in a river, a stream, a lake, a pond, a well, or even at home.
Every morning, having first performed the formal invitation of the twice-born,
one should then perform all the rites beginning with the offering of water for the hands (arghya) and water for the feet (pādya), preceded by the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Garments, ornaments, and other such items should be given according to one's own capacity; when wealth is available, one should never practice stinginess regarding the expenditure.
When the Brahmins have been satisfied, the task shall be entirely accomplished.
For the recitation of the Goddess, nine, five, three, or even one Brahmin is prescribed. (16)
Then, one should select a peaceful Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of reciting the Pārāyaṇa;
the rite of Svastivācana should be performed according to the rules of the Vedic mantras.
Having placed a lion-throne upon the altar, provided with a silken cloth,
the goddess Ambikā should be installed there, endowed with four hands and her weapons.
Adorned with jewel ornaments and radiant with pearl necklaces,
wearing divine garments, she was gentle and endowed with all auspicious marks.
The eternal Śivā, holding a conch, discus, mace, and lotus, seated upon a lion, or even with eighteen arms, should be installed. (20)
In the absence of an image, one should likewise install a yantra conjoined with the nine-syllable mantra for the purpose of worshipping the pedestal, and place a water-pot (kalaśa) there at its side.
It was joined with five sprouts, well-consecrated with Vedic mantras,
filled with water from an excellent holy ford, and endowed with gold and jewels.
Having arranged the requisites for worship on all sides,
he should indeed cause the sounds of songs and musical instruments to be made for the sake of auspiciousness.

O King, worship performed on the first lunar day (Pratipad) when it is conjoined with the asterism Hasta and falls on a Nandā tithi is excellent; when conducted according to the rules, it grants the desires of men.
Having first established the restrictive observance (niyama), one should afterwards perform the worship,
either by means of fasting, eating only at night, or consuming a single meal.
"O Mother, I shall observe the unsurpassed vow of Navarātra;
O Goddess, Mother of the World, grant me your entire assistance. (26)
A restraint (niyama) should be observed according to one's capacity for the sake of the vow;
afterwards, worship should be performed according to the rules, preceded by mantras. || 27 ||
With sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, and with fragrant flowers— mandāraka, rāja-aśoka, campaka, and karavīra— (28)
One should worship the Mother of the Worlds with *mālatī* flowers, *brahmakā* flowers, and auspicious *bilva* leaves, along with incense and lamps, according to the prescribed rite. (29)
And there, indeed, an offering (arghya) should be presented with various kinds of fruits:
coconuts, citrons, pomegranates, and plantains.
O lord of men, one should perform the gift of food with devotion, using oranges, jackfruits, and likewise auspicious fruits that are fully ripe. (31)
Those who consume meat must perform the slaughter of animals;
the offering of buffaloes, goats, and boars as a sacrificial gift (bali) is especially recommended.
O sinless one, animals slain before the Goddess go to the imperishable heaven; for there is no violence born of the animal in that act of killing performed for her sake.
In the definitive conclusion of all scriptures, non-violence is declared to be the essence of sacrifice;
for animals released for the sake of the deities, the attainment of heaven is certain.
For the purpose of the fire sacrifice (homa), a triangular pit (kuṇḍa) must be prepared;
or else, an auspicious triangular sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should be made according to the prescribed measurements. || 35 ||
Worship should be performed daily at the three times of day with various enchanting offerings,
and a great festival should be celebrated with songs, instrumental music, and dance.
One should always sleep upon the ground and worship young maidens with divine garments and ornaments, as well as with food that is like nectar.
One should worship them daily, one by one, or again by increasing by one; likewise, one may worship two, three, or even nine of each.
Indeed, worship should be performed according to one's means;
O King, one must never practice stinginess regarding wealth during a sacrifice performed according to one's capacity.

O King, a girl who has reached only one year of age should not be employed in the ritual of worship; however, a young girl who possesses supreme knowledge of enjoyments such as perfumes and the like [may be used]. (40)
She who is two years old here is called Kumārikā;
Trimūrti is three years old, and Kalyāṇī is four years old. (41)
Rohiṇī is known to be five years old, and Kālikā six years;
Caṇḍikā is seven years old, and Śāmbhavī eight years.
Durgā should be nine years old, and Subhadrā ten years old; beyond that age, she must not be made [as an image], for it is censured in all ritual matters. (43)
With these names, worship should be performed according to the prescribed rite;
I shall now describe the fruits of always worshipping these nine.
When the Kumārī is worshipped, she brings about the destruction of suffering and poverty;
she indeed effects the destruction of enemies, the increase of wealth and longevity, and the growth of strength. (45)

From the worship of the Trinity (Trimūrti), there shall arise longevity, the fruits of the three aims of life (trivarga), the acquisition of wealth and grain, and the increase of sons, grandsons, and progeny. (46)
One seeking knowledge, one seeking victory, a king seeking sovereignty, and one seeking happiness should always worship Kalyāṇī, the granter of all desires. (47)
One should worship Kālikā with devotion for the sake of destroying enemies;
and one who desires sovereignty and wealth should fully worship Caṇḍikā. (48)
One should worship the consort of Śambhu constantly for the purpose of enchanting kings, for the destruction of suffering and poverty, and for victory in battle. (49)
For the sake of destroying cruel enemies, as well as for accomplishing fierce rites,
one should worship Durgā with devotion for the happiness of the next world.
For the sake of accomplishing one's desired aims, one should always worship Subhadrā;
for the destruction of disease, a person should worship Rohiṇī according to the prescribed rites.
Devoted to worship, one should perform the rite with the mantra "śrīrastu," or else with mantras associated with Śrī, or even with seed-mantras (bījamantra). 52.
I worship that Kumārī who, even in play, creates the principles (tattvas) of Kumāra as well as the gods beginning with Ka.
I worship the triple-formed Śakti, who, through the qualities of sattva and the others, possesses various forms and pervades the three periods of time. 54.
She who eternally brings about auspiciousness for her devotees and is incessantly worshipped—I worship that auspicious goddess, the granter of all desires, with devotion. (55)
I worship Rohiṇī, that goddess who causes the seeds accumulated in previous births to sprout for all living beings.
I worship that Kālikā who, at the time of the end of the aeon, impels the entire universe, including all things moving and unmoving, toward its dissolution.
I worship that Caṇḍikā, the remover of fierce sins. || 58 ||
I worship that Goddess Śāmbhavī, the bestower of happiness, whose arising without a cause has been proclaimed by me. (59)
I worship that Durgā, who always protects her devotee from misfortune, who destroys all difficulties, and who is difficult for even all the gods to comprehend.
She always brings auspiciousness to her devotees when she is worshipped;
I worship the goddess Subhadrā, the destroyer of misfortune. (61)
With these mantras, wise men should always worship the maidens with garments,
ornaments, garlands, and various kinds of perfumes.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of the Virgin," in the Third Book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 26 ||
Description of the Greatness of the Worship of the Goddess.
Vyāsa said:
One should avoid a girl who has missing limbs, one afflicted with leprosy, or one marked by sores.
Her limbs were radiant with fragrance, and she was born of a noble lineage. || 1 ||
One should abandon a girl who is blind from birth, squint-eyed, one-eyed, deformed, excessively hairy, diseased, or marked with red flowers and the like.
One who is emaciated, one who has recently given birth, a *golaka* (a son born to a widow), and one born of a maiden— these should always be avoided in all rites such as worship and the like.
One should properly honor a maiden who is healthy, beautiful in her limbs, lovely, free from blemishes, and born of a single lineage.
A Brāhmaṇī is for all undertakings; one born of a royal lineage is for the sake of victory;
one born of a Vaiśya lineage or indeed a Śūdra lineage is considered suitable for the sake of profit. || 5 ||
Those born of Brahmā are to be honored by Brāhmaṇas; those born of the lineage of Brahmā are to be honored by Kṣatriyas;
those born of the three [other] classes are to be honored by Vaiśyas; and all four are to be honored by those born from the feet.
And one should always worship the bamboo images produced by artisans according to the rules,
with devotion and in accordance with the Navarātra ritual.
If one is unable to perform worship regularly during the Navarātra,
especially on the eighth day, one must always perform the worship [at that time].
Formerly, on the eighth lunar day, Bhadrakālī, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
manifested as a most terrible Yoginī together with ten million [other] Yoginīs.
Therefore, worship should always be performed especially on the eighth day with various kinds of offerings, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
One should gratify the Mother of the World with offerings of milk-rice, meat, oblations, feasts for Brahmins, and gifts of fruits and flowers.
O King, for those who are unable to observe the fast throughout the entire Navarātra vow,
three days of fasting have been prescribed, which grant the same fruit as described.
Likewise, on the seventh, eighth, and ninth [lunar days], by performing the three-night rite with a spirit of devotion, the entire fruit is obtained through worship.
That vow is declared to be complete through worship, fire-offerings (homa), as well as the honoring of young maidens, and by providing meals for Brahmins. || 14 ||
Whatever other vows and various kinds of gifts there may be on this earth, they are not at all equal to this Navarātra vow. (15)
It constantly bestows wealth and grain, grants the increase of happiness and progeny,
and likewise bestows long life, health, heaven, and liberation.
Whether a man seeks knowledge, wealth, or a son,
he should duly perform this auspicious vow which bestows good fortune.
A seeker of knowledge indeed attains all branches of learning through the accomplishment of this vow;
a king fallen from his throne always regains his kingdom. 18.
Those who certainly did not perform the supreme vow in a previous birth become afflicted by disease, impoverished, and deprived of sons. (19)
If there be a woman who is barren, or a widow destitute of wealth, one should infer in that case: "She has not performed this vow. || 20 ||
How can he who has not performed the Navarātra vow on this earth, even after attaining great prosperity, rejoice likewise in heaven? (21)
He by whom Bhavānī is worshipped with tender bilva leaves mixed with red sandalwood shall become a king upon the earth.
He by whom the eternal Śivā— the remover of suffering and affliction, the bestower of perfection, and the most excellent in the world— has not been propitiated,
remains shrouded in misery and beset by enemies upon this earth.
Surely that person becomes poor in this world. || 23 ||

Why do human beings not worship that Caṇḍikā, whom Viṣṇu, Indra, Hara, Brahmā, as well as Agni, Kubera, Varuṇa, and the Sun-god meditate upon, being delighted by the fulfillment of all their aims? (24)
By the power of Manu, the gods and likewise the ancestors are satisfied with the names Svāhā and Svadhā;
that name which the lords of sages joyfully carry in pairs during all sacrifices through their sacred utterances. (25)
By whose will the Lord of Creatures creates this universe, and by whom Hari performs his various incarnations;
indeed, Śambhu surely reduces the world to ashes—how then can a human being not worship her, the bestower of happiness? (26)
Indeed, in all the worlds, there is not a single god, man, bird, or serpent who is bereft of her;
certainly, among the Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and Nāgas as well, [there is none].
He who is endowed with the power to move according to his will. || 27 ||
Who would not serve that auspicious Caṇḍī, who grants all desires and goals?
And who, desiring the fourfold aims of life, would not observe her vow? 28.
One who is joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) should observe the Navarātra vow;
he is liberated from all sins—no deliberation is required here. || 29 ||
Formerly, O best of kings, there was a certain merchant in Kosala who was miserable, destitute of wealth, deeply distressed, and burdened with a family.
He had many offspring who were tormented by hunger;
however, his young children obtained some food in the evening. (31)
Then, though hungry himself, that performer of duties ate the food of another;
there he maintained his family with complete composure.
Always delighting in the Dharma, peaceful, of virtuous conduct, and truthful in speech;
free from anger, steadfast, devoid of pride, and without malice. (33)
Having daily worshipped the deities, as well as the ancestors and guests,
the merchant would then take his meal once the circle of those dependent on him had eaten.
As time passed in this manner, one named Suśīla, who was truly endowed with virtues,
being afflicted by poverty and overcome by intense hunger, questioned a peaceful brahmin.
Suśīla said:
O Bhūdeva, O high-minded one, having shown compassion, tell me today with certainty how the destruction of poverty may come about. (36)
O giver of honor, I have no desire for wealth, nor do I wish to become wealthy;
O best of the twice-born, I ask you this only for the sake of maintaining my family. (37)
"My son is a young child who cries out intensely for food;
there is only that much food in the house, so I give him but a single handful. (38)
"Since that fool was sent away from my house by me while weeping, for that reason I am burning intensely; what can I do without wealth? (39)
"I have a daughter for whom a marriage is required, yet I possess no wealth; what shall I do?
For one who has exceeded ten years of age, even the time for giving her away in marriage is passing away. (40)
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, I grieve; you are omniscient, O ocean of compassion!
Tell me of some austerity, charity, or vow, as well as the recitation of mantras. (41)
"O twice-born one, may I obtain only as much wealth as is required for me to maintain my circle of dependents; indeed, I do not pray for more. (42)
"By your grace, may my family become happy here in this world;
therefore, O illustrious one, act accordingly after reflecting with your wisdom. (43)
Vyāsa said: O best of kings, having been thus questioned by him, that brahmin of rigid vows, being exceedingly pleased, spoke to that vaiśya.
O best of Vaiśyas, perform today the auspicious Navarātra vow,
including the worship of the Goddess, the fire-oblation, and likewise the feeding [of the deities].
Perform today, according to your ability, the complete study of the Vedas, as well as the recitation of mantras, fire offerings, and so forth; thus your purpose will be accomplished.
O Vaiśya, there is no other vow on the surface of the earth superior to this one called Navarātra; it is indeed purifying and likewise bestows happiness. (47)
The Navarātra vow always bestows knowledge and liberation, increases the continuity of happiness, and fulfills desires while destroying enemies. 48.
Deprived of his kingdom and separated from Sītā, Rāma,
indeed afflicted by grief, performed this vow in Kiṣkindhā.
Although Rāma was scorched by the fire of separation from Sītā,
the Goddess was indeed worshipped according to the rules through the Navarātra vow.
Having built a bridge across the great ocean and slain the immensely powerful Kumbhakarṇa, the lord of Mandodarī, he then reached Vaidehī.
Having slain his son Meghanāda and having installed Vibhīṣaṇa as king,
he subsequently returned to Ayodhyā and obtained a kingdom free from all thorns.
O best of men, by the power of this Navarātra vow, happiness was attained on the surface of the earth by Rāma of immeasurable splendor. (53)
Vyāsa said: O King, having heard these words of the Brahmin, that Vaiśya took him as his preceptor and received the excellent mantra known as Māyābīja.
He recited [the mantra] with supreme devotion throughout the nine nights without weariness,
and he worshipped [the deity] respectfully with various kinds of offerings.
Devoted to the seed-syllable of Māyā for nine years,
at the end of the ninth year, on the Mahāṣṭamī day, Maheśvarī [appeared].
When midnight had arrived, he gave a direct vision and,
by granting various boons, made him successful in his purpose.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Worship of the Goddess," in the third book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 27 ||
The Description of Rāma’s Life Story.
Janamejaya said:
How was that vow, which bestows happiness upon the Goddess, performed by Rāma?
How did he then fall from his kingdom, and how was Sītā subsequently abducted?
Vyāsa said:
In ancient times, there was a glorious King Daśaratha, the sovereign of Ayodhyā;
he was a sustainer of the solar dynasty and a worshiper of the gods and Brahmins.
Four sons were born to him, renowned throughout the worlds,
known by the names Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and Bharata.
All were dear to the king and equal in their qualities and appearance;
Rāma was known as the son of Kausalyā, and Bharata as the son of Kaikeyī.
Two beautiful twin sons were born to Sumitrā;
indeed, they were born as youths already bearing bows and arrows.
The sons, having received their sacraments, increased the happiness of the king;
then Kauśika, having arrived, made a request to the joy of the Raghus.
For the sake of protecting the sacrifice, he gave that son Rāma, sixteen years of age,
along with Lakṣmaṇa, to that Kauśika.
Having met the sage on the path, those two of beautiful appearance proceeded;
on the way, the demoness Tāṭakā, who was terrible to behold, was slain.
By Rāma alone, with a single arrow, the protection of the sacrifice was secured there, and the wicked Subāhu, who had always caused suffering to the sages, was slain.
Then Mārīca, nearly dead, was cast away by the force of the arrow;
having thus performed this great deed for the protection of the sacrifice.
Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Kauśika all went to Mithilā;
Ahalyā was liberated from her curse, and that woman was rendered free from sin.
They both went with the sage to the city of Videha;
there, he broke the bow of Śiva which had been staked by Janaka.
Then he married Sītā, the daughter of Janaka born from a portion of Ramā;
likewise, the king gave his other daughter, Ūrmilā, to Lakṣmaṇa.
Thus both brothers,
Bharata and Śatrughna, who were virtuous and possessed auspicious marks, obtained the two daughters of Kuśadhvaja as wives.
O King, in this manner the marriage rites of those four brothers took place in Mithilā according to the prescribed rules and rituals. (15)
Then, seeing his son fit for the kingdom, King Daśaratha set his mind upon bestowing the burden of sovereignty upon his own descendant, Rāghava.
Seeing that the preparations had been made, Kaikeyī requested from her husband, who was under her control, the two boons previously promised to her. (17)
He gave the kingdom to his high-souled son Bharata,
and likewise to Rāma, he granted a forest dwelling for fourteen years.
At her word, Rāma, accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
went to the Daṇḍaka forest inhabited by rākṣasas.
King Daśaratha, tormented by separation from his sons and recollecting his former curse, gave up his life, he whose soul was immeasurable. (20)
Seeing his father dead on account of his mother, Bharata did not accept the prosperous kingdom out of a desire to do what was pleasing to his brother.
While dwelling at Pañcavaṭī in the forest, Rāma made Śūrpaṇakhā, the younger sister of Rāvaṇa, deformed, as she was excessively afflicted by lust.
But upon seeing her with her nose cut off, the night-stalkers, Khara and the others,
waged an incomparable battle against Rāma of immeasurable splendor.
Seeking the welfare of the sages, Rāma, whose prowess is truth, slew Khara and the other Daityas who were endowed with exceeding strength. (24)
Having gone to Laṅkā, Śūrpaṇakhā, being defiled, reported to Rāvaṇa the slaughter of Khara and Dūṣaṇa by the descendant of Raghu.
Having heard of that destruction, the wicked one, overcome by anger,
mounted his chariot and then went to the hermitage of Mārīca.
Having fashioned a golden deer, Rāvaṇa dispatched that illusory and impossible creature in order to entice Sītā.
Then, having become a golden deer with most wonderful limbs, that master of illusion moved powerfully nearby, coming within the range of Sītā’s vision.
Seeing him, Janaki, impelled by fate, spoke to Raghava as if she were a woman who had her husband under her own control: "O beloved, bring the hide. (29)
Then Rāma, without further deliberation, stationed Lakṣmaṇa there and,
taking up his bow with an arrow, followed the tracks of the deer.
Sāraṅga, too, being an expert in millions of illusions, upon seeing Hari,
became visible and invisible at will and then departed into the depths of the forest.
Realizing that it was within his grasp, Rāma, drawing his bow with fury once more,
struck the artificial deer with an exceedingly sharp arrow.
Struck by him with great force, that deceitful, perishable, and wicked one, deeply afflicted by pain, cried out: "Alas, Lakṣmaṇa! I am slain! (33)
Then that tumultuous noise was heard by Jānakī;
thinking it belonged to Rāghava, she spoke dejectedly to her husband’s elder brother.
"Go quickly, Lakṣmaṇa! This descendant of Raghu has been slain. He is calling out to you, O son of Sumitrā; provide him assistance at once. (35)
Thereupon Lakṣmaṇa said to Sītā: "O Mother, even for the sake of Rāma's life, I will not go today, leaving you here in this hermitage without a companion."
"O daughter of Janaka, Raghava’s command is for me to remain here;
fearing to transgress it, I do not leave your side. (37)
"O lady of pure smiles, having seen Raghava far off in the forest, that master of illusion indeed abandoned you; I cannot find even a single step [of his path]. (38)
"Be firm; I do not think it is possible to kill Rāma now that he has been hurled down.
I shall not depart, having disregarded the words spoken by Rāma. (39)
Vyāsa said: Then,
impelled by fate, the weeping Sudatī spoke these cruel words to the auspicious Lakṣmaṇa, who was free from cruelty.
"O Saumitri, I know him;
he is full of affection for me and has been sent here by Bharata himself on my account. (41)
O lowest of deceivers, I am not such a wanton woman as to desire to make you my husband out of passion once Rāma is dead. (42)
If Rāma does not come, I shall give up my life;
without him I cannot live, being utterly distressed and deeply afflicted by sorrow.
"Go, or stay, O son of Sumitrā; I do not know what you desire. Where has your friendship toward your elder brother, who is devoted to dharma, gone today?"
Having heard those words of hers, Lakṣmaṇa, with a dejected mind and his throat choked with emotion, then spoke to that daughter of Janaka.
"O daughter of the Earth, why do you speak such exceedingly cruel words to me? What do you say?
For with my intellect, I know that what you speak will surely come to pass as a great misfortune for you. (46)
Having spoken thus, O Lord of the Earth, the hero departed, leaving her while weeping bitterly; afflicted with grief, he went on, looking toward his elder brother.
Then, after Lakṣmaṇa had departed, Rāvaṇa, assuming a deceptive form and donning the garb of a mendicant, entered that hermitage.
Considering him to be an ascetic, Jānakī respectfully offered him water for the feet and forest produce,
and presented alms-food to the evil-minded Rāvaṇa.
That evil-minded one questioned her with a previously humble and gentle voice: "Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, staying all alone in the forest, my dear? (50)
"O lady of beautiful thighs, who is your father, who is your brother, and who is your husband?
O woman of excellent complexion, why do you stand here alone like one bewildered? (51)
"O beloved, why are you in this desolate forest? You are worthy of a palace;
with a splendor equal to that of a celestial maiden, you are like the wife of a sage in this hermitage. (52)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words and realizing by divine fortune that the ascetic was the husband of Mandodarī, the daughter of Videha then replied.
The illustrious King Daśaratha had four sons;
the eldest among them is my husband, renowned by the name Rāma. (54)
Now, having been exiled by the king because of a boon granted to Kaikeyī,
Rāma shall dwell here for fourteen years together with Lakṣmaṇa.
"I am the daughter of Janaka, renowned by the name Sītā;
having broken the bow of Śiva at my will, I was married to Rāma. (56)
"By the strength of Rāma's arms, we dwell here in the forest without fear;
however, having sighted a golden deer, my husband has gone out to kill it. (57)
Lakṣmaṇa, too, having heard the cry again, has now gone after his brother;
indeed, I dwell here without fear due to the strength of their arms. (58)
"I have related all this account concerning my dwelling in the forest;
they will surely come here and perform worship for you according to the prescribed rites. (59)
Since you are a Yati whose very nature is Viṣṇu, you have been worshipped by me;
yet you have established a hermitage in this terrible forest within the race of Rākṣasas.
Therefore, I question you: speak the truth before me.
Who are you that have come to the forest in the form of a triple-staffed ascetic? (61)
Rāvaṇa said:
"O lotus-eyed one, I am the illustrious Rāvaṇa, lord of Laṅkā and husband of Mandodarī;
it was for your sake, O lady of beautiful form, that I assumed this appearance."
"O lady of beautiful hips, I have indeed come here at the instigation of my sister, having heard that the two brothers Khara and Dūṣaṇa have been slain in Janasthāna. (63)
Accept me as your king, O lady, abandoning that human husband who has been stripped of his kingdom, deprived of his fortune, powerless, and dwelling in the forest. (64)
"Clearly become my principal queen above Mandodarī;
I am your slave, O slender-limbed one—be my mistress, O beautiful lady. (65)
"Victorious over the world-protectors, I fall at your feet;
take my hand today, O Jānakī, and make me your protector."
"O weak one, your father was previously entreated by me on your behalf. Janaka spoke thus to me: 'A wager has been made by me. (67)
Out of fear of Rudra’s bow, I did not attend the svayaṃvara;
meanwhile, my mind remained fixed there, submerged and distressed by separation. (68)
"O lady with dark-cornered eyes, having heard that you are staying here in the forest, I have come, deluded by my former passion; make my exertion fruitful. (69)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Life of Rāma," in the Third Book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 28.
Vyāsa said: Having heard those wicked words, Jānakī was overwhelmed with fear; [then followed] the consolation of Rāma’s grief by Lakṣmaṇa.
Trembling, she steadied her mind and spoke these words.
O descendant of Pulastya, why do you speak such improper words, deluded as you are by passion?
I am certainly not a wanton woman, but one born of Janaka’s lineage.
"Go to Laṅkā, O Ten-faced one; Rāma will surely slay you there.
For my sake, death will come to you in that place—of this there is no doubt. (3)
Having spoken thus, she went to the leaf-hut near the fire, saying "Go, go!
to Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the world cry out.
Then, assuming his own form, he went near the hut and forcibly seized that young girl as she wept, overwhelmed by fear.
Crying out "Rāma, Rāma! and "Lakṣmaṇa" again and again, the wicked man seized her, placed her upon a chariot, and departed in haste.
As he was proceeding, his path was blocked by Jaṭāyu, the son of Aruṇa;
a most fierce battle then took place between the two of them there in the middle of the forest.
Having slain him and seized her, that wicked-minded lord of the rākṣasas departed;
she, O dear one, was crying out in Laṅkā like a female osprey.
She was placed in the Aśoka grove together with the rākṣasīs;
indeed, she did not waver from her own conduct despite [attempts to sway her] by means of conciliation, gifts, and other [strategies].
Rāma, having killed that deer, departed contentedly taking it with him;
then, seeing Lakṣmaṇa approaching, he asked, "What have you done, O younger brother? (10)
"Having abandoned your beloved wife all alone, for what purpose have you come here?
Hearing the voice of the sinner, Rāghava spoke this.
But the son of Sumitrā, tormented by the word-arrows of Sītā, spoke these words:
"O Lord, I have arrived here through the turn of time; of this there is no doubt. (12)
Then, having gone to the leaf-hut and searched, the two of them, seeing it empty, were deeply distressed;
both exerted themselves to make an effort to search for Jānaki. (13)
Searching for him, they arrived at the place where that bird had fallen—
Jaṭāyu, who lay fallen upon the surface of the earth with only his life remaining.
Rāvaṇa said: "Today that daughter of Janaka was carried off by me;
that evil-souled one was restrained by me, and I, in turn, was cast down in battle. (15)
Having spoken thus, he departed his life; he was indeed consecrated with funeral rites by Rāghava, and after performing the post-mortem ceremonies, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa departed from there.
Having caused Kabandha to be slain, that Lord liberated him from his curse;
then, at his request, Rāghava formed a friendship with Hari.
And having slain the heroic Vālin, Rāma gave the excellent kingdom of Kiṣkindhā to Sugrīva, who had formed an alliance with him for the sake of their common purpose.
Right there, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, he remained for the months of the rainy season,
contemplating in his mind his beloved Jānakī, who had been carried away by the ten-faced Rāvaṇa.
Afflicted by the pain of separation from Sītā, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa:
"O son of Sumitrā, the daughter of Kaikeyī has attained her full desire."
"Janaki has surely not been found; I shall certainly not live without her. I will not return to Ayodhya without the daughter of Janaka."
The kingdom is lost, I dwell in the forest, my father is dead, and my beloved has been carried away;
that evil-minded one torments me, so what can fate do against me now? (22)
For the destiny of living beings is indeed difficult to discern, O younger brother of Bharata; what will be our fate, dear one, which will bring such great suffering? (23)
Having obtained birth in the lineage of Manu, both were indeed princes who,
due to their past actions, became subjects of extreme suffering in the forest.
Having renounced all enjoyments, you too have gone forth with me;
yet by the turn of fate, O son of Sumitrā, you must endure this insurmountable suffering.
In my family, there has never before been a man who experienced suffering equal to mine;
neither has there ever been one so destitute, powerless, and afflicted, nor will there ever be.
"What shall I do today, O son of Sumitrā? I am submerged in an ocean of sorrow, and for me, who am indeed without a companion, there appears to be no means of crossing over. (27)
O hero, there is neither wealth nor power; you alone are my companion.
O younger brother, with whom shall I direct my anger today regarding this enjoyment brought about by my own actions?
The kingdom, which was like the throne of Indra, has gone from my hand;
now residence in the forest has been attained—who knows what is ordained by Fate? (29)
And due to her youthful nature, Vaidehī departed from us both;
led away by wicked fate, that dark-complexioned woman has been brought to a most miserable state.
How could the dark-complexioned Śyāmā experience suffering in the house of the Lord of Laṅkā, she who is devoted to her husband, virtuous in character, and deeply full of affection for me? (31)
And yet, O Lakṣmaṇa, that Vaidehī would not come under his control;
how could the daughter of Janaka be like a wanton woman of noble form? (32)
"O younger brother of Bharata, Maithilī would rather give up her life under my guardianship than fall under the power of Rāvaṇa; this is certain. (33)
O hero, if Jānakī is dead, I shall undoubtedly give up my life;
if that dark-eyed woman is dead, O Lakṣmaṇa, what is the use of my body?
To Rāma, the lotus-eyed one, who was thus lamenting,
the righteous Lakṣmaṇa spoke, consoling him with truthful words.
"Take heart, O mighty-armed one, casting aside all despondency here;
having slain that lowest of Rākṣasas, I shall bring back Vaidehī."
Those who remain equal in adversity and prosperity through their fortitude are the wise;
the small-minded, however, become submerged in distress even when they possess great wealth.
Both union and separation are dependent upon destiny;
what then is the nature of sorrow in that regard, whether with respect to the body or the self? (38)
Just as there was the loss of the kingdom and dwelling in the forest, and just as the abduction of Vaidehī occurred,
so too shall our reunion come about when the time is right.
The cessation of the experience of pleasures and pains must occur somewhere;
it cannot be otherwise, O Knower of Janaki. Therefore, abandon your grief now.
There are many monkeys who will go in the four directions;
it is said that they will bring back news of the purity of Janaka’s daughter.
Having ascertained his location on the road and gone there, I shall exert my prowess,
slay that evildoer, and bring back Maithilī.
Or else, having summoned Bharata along with his army and his younger brother, we shall slay the enemy; why do you grieve in vain, O elder brother? (43)
In former times, all the quarters were conquered by Raghu alone with a single chariot;
O Raghava, how can you, born of that lineage, deserve to grieve?
"I alone am capable of conquering all the gods and asuras;
how much more so, with my companions, can I defeat Rāvaṇa, that disgrace to his lineage? (45)
Or, O descendant of Raghu, having brought Janaka to our aid,
I shall slay the evil-doing Rāvaṇa, that thorn in the side of the gods.
"Suffering follows immediately after happiness, and happiness follows immediately after suffering;
like the rim of a wheel, O descendant of Raghu, they do not exist as one alone. (47)
He whose mind is exceedingly timid at the arising of pleasure and pain is submerged in an ocean of sorrow and shall never be happy. 48.
O descendant of Raghu, in ancient times Indra indeed fell into calamity;
Nahuṣa was then installed by all the gods in the place of Maghavan.
And Indra, having abandoned his own station out of fear, remained for many groups of years in the midst of a lotus pond, living in concealment.
When time had turned again, Nahuṣa returned to his own place; however, due to the curse, he fell to the earth in the form of a serpent.
Desiring Indrāṇī and having insulted the Brāhmaṇas,
that lord of the earth was born with a serpent's body due to the wrath of Agastya.
Therefore, O Raghava, one should not give way to grief when misfortune occurs;
rather, having resolved the mind upon effort, a wise man should indeed remain steadfast.
O illustrious one, you are omniscient; O Lord of the world, you are capable.
Why do you indulge in such excessive grief within yourself like an ordinary man? (54)
Vyāsa said:
Thus enlightened by the words of Lakṣmaṇa, the joy of the Raghus abandoned his excessive grief and became free from his feverish distress.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Consolation of Rāma’s Grief by Lakṣmaṇa," in the Third Book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 29.
Vyāsa said: When the two of them had thus made this agreement and became silent, the Goddess granted a boon to Rāma.
Then the venerable sage Nārada arrived from the sky.
Then, playing a great lute adorned with the scales and notes of music,
he approached him while singing the Bṛhadratha Sāman.
Seeing him, Rāma rose and then gave him an auspicious bull; the one of immeasurable splendor also offered him a seat, water for his hands, and water for his feet. || 3 ||
Having performed the highest worship, Hari stood with palms joined in reverence; then, having received instructions from the sage, he sat down near him.
Then, as Rāma sat with his younger brother, his mind filled with sorrow,
Nārada, the best of sages, affectionately inquired after his welfare.
O Raghava, how is it that you are afflicted by grief like an ordinary man?
I know that Sita has been carried off by the evil-minded Ravana.
Having gone to the abode of Surasā and having heard that the daughter of Janaka had been carried off by the descendant of Pulastya out of delusion and ignorance of his own death, I [proceeded].
O descendant of Kakutstha, O lord of men, your birth was indeed for the sake of the destruction of Paulastya,
and the abduction of Maithilī occurred for this very purpose.
In a previous birth, the daughter of a sage,
the ascetic Vaidehī of pure smiles, was seen by Rāvaṇa in the forest while she was performing penance.
O Raghava, when she was requested by Ravana, "Become my wife," he was indeed rebuffed by her;
nevertheless, he seized her hair with force.
O Rāma, at that moment the ascetic woman, being greatly enraged and desiring to cast off her body defiled by his touch, severely cursed Rāvaṇa. (11)

"O evil-souled one, for the sake of your destruction, I shall become an excellent woman not born from a womb upon the surface of the earth; having abandoned [this] body, I shall even cast it off. (12)
This very [woman], born from a portion of Ramā, was seized by that Rākṣasa like a serpent or a garland out of haste,
for the sake of the destruction of his own lineage.
And your birth, O descendant of Kakutstha, was for the destruction of him [Rāvaṇa] by the immortals;
you who, though unborn, were born from a portion of Hari into the lineage of Aja.
Take heart, O mighty-armed one; there she remains, helpless—that virtuous Sītā, devoted to righteousness, meditating upon you day and night. (15)
Having placed the milk of the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhenu into a vessel, Maghavan himself sent it for him to drink; and he drank it as if it were nectar. || 16 ||
From drinking the milk of a fragrant cow, she became free from the suffering of hunger and thirst;
with eyes like lotus petals, she was seen by me as she remained there. || 17 ||
O Raghava, I shall now tell you the means for his destruction;
with faith, perform a vow this very month of Āśvina.
O Rāma, fasting during the nine nights and the thorough worship of the Blessed Lady,
performed according to the rules of recitation and fire-offerings, brings about all accomplishments.
Having offered a sacrifice to the Goddess with domestic animals that have been slaughtered,
and having performed a fire-oblation consisting of one-tenth [of the offerings], you will become empowered.
This was formerly practiced by Viṣṇu, as well as by Mahādeva and Brahmā;
likewise it was performed by Maghavan while he was dwelling in the midst of heaven.
O Rāma, this auspicious Navarātra vow should be performed by one who is happy;
indeed, it must especially be performed by a man who has fallen into distress.
O descendant of Kakutstha, this was undoubtedly performed by Viśvāmitra, as well as by Bhṛgu, Vasiṣṭha, and Kaśyapa. (23)
"This great vow was undertaken by my preceptor after his wife was abducted;
therefore, O Indra among kings, you too must act for the sake of Rāvaṇa's destruction."
This unsurpassed vow was formerly undertaken by Indra for the destruction of Vṛtra,
and it was also undertaken by Śiva for the destruction of Tripura.
O high-minded descendant of Kakutstha, perform this vow diligently and according to the rules on Mount Meru, as it was performed by Hari for the destruction of Madhu.
Śrī Rāma said:
Who is that goddess? What is her power? From where was she born? What is her name?
O ocean of compassion, you are omniscient; tell me duly what the vow is. (27)
Nārada said:
Listen, O Rāma, to the Goddess who is eternally constant, the primordial and everlasting power; when worshipped, she grants all desires and destroys all suffering. (28)
O descendant of Raghu, she is the cause of all beings, beginning with Brahmā;
without her power, no one would be capable of even a single movement. (29)
That power of protection belonging to Viṣṇu is my father’s power of agency;
that power of destruction belonging to Rudra is another supreme power, Śivā.
Whatever object there may be, whether existent or non-existent, anywhere within the three worlds—the power that belongs to all of that, from what could its production arise? (31)
When there was neither Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor Rudra, nor the Sun; when none of the gods beginning with Indra existed, nor the earth, nor the mountains. || 32 ||
Then, at the beginning of the age, that primordial nature (prakṛti), which is full and devoid of qualities (nirguṇā), indeed sports while united with the supreme Puruṣa, O auspicious one.
Having subsequently become possessed of attributes (saguṇā), she creates the three worlds after first emanating Brahmā and the other gods, bestowing upon them all their respective powers (śaktis).
Knowing that, a living being is liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra;
that is to be known as the supreme knowledge (vidyā), which is the source of the Vedas and the cause of their manifestation. (35)
Indeed, it is said that her names are innumerable, devised by Brahmā and others according to her qualities and functions; what more can I say? (36)
O descendant of Raghu, when joined with the vowels beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', as well as with the consonants, there come to be innumerable names.
Rāma said:
"O brahmin-sage, tell me the procedure for this vow in brief;
endowed with faith, I shall perform the worship of the Goddess Śrī this very day."
Nārada said:
"O Rāma, having prepared a seat in a level place and having installed Jagadambikā, observe nine fasts according to the prescribed rules. (39)
"O Lord of the Earth, I shall be the preceptor in this rite;
I am exerting my efforts for the purpose of performing the divine task. (40)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words and considering them to be true, the powerful Rāma had an auspicious pedestal constructed and installed the goddess Ambikā Śivā.
When that month of Āśvina had arrived, Hari, observant of his vow, performed her worship according to the prescribed rites on that excellent mountain.
Devoted to fasting, Rāma performed the supreme vow; there he duly offered oblations, presented sacrificial offerings, and performed worship.
Out of love, the two brothers observed the vow approved by Nārada;
for on the eighth day at midnight, that goddess, the Blessed One, indeed [manifests].
Mounted upon a lion and duly worshipped, she granted her vision there;
standing upon a mountain peak, she addressed Rāghava and his younger brother with these words.
Pleased by this [prayer] uttered with a spirit of devotion as deep as a thundercloud, the Goddess said:
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, I am gratified by your vow. (46)
"Choose whatever boon you desire that dwells in your mind;
for you, O sinless one, have been born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa in the lineage of Manu."
In the past, having assumed the form of a fish and slain the terrible Rākṣasa, you were indeed entreated by the gods for the very purpose of slaying Rāvaṇa. || 48 ||
Desiring the welfare of the gods, you indeed protected the Vedas;
having assumed the form of a tortoise, you supported Mount Mandara.
Having churned the boundless ocean, you nourished the gods and the waters;
having assumed the supreme form of a boar, you supported the earth with the tip of your tusk. 50.
O Rāma, you have maintained this resolve and you slew Hiraṇyākṣa;
formerly, having assumed the body of a man-lion, you killed Hiraṇyakaśipu.
O Rāghava, O Rāma, having protected Prahlāda, you slew [Hiraṇyakaśipu];
in former times, assuming the form of a dwarf, you deceived Bali.
Having become the younger brother of Indra at will, you have accomplished the task of the gods;
as the son of Jamadagni, you are united with a portion of Viṣṇu.
Having brought an end to the kṣatriyas, he gave gifts of land to the twice-born;
likewise, O descendant of Kakutstha, you have now been born as the son of Daśaratha.
Requested by all the gods who were being severely oppressed by Rāvaṇa, those monkeys—
who are portions of the gods and exceedingly powerful— will indeed be your allies.
O tiger among men, these [brothers] shall indeed be endowed with my power;
and this younger brother of yours, a portion of Śeṣa, shall be the destroyer of Rāvaṇa’s offspring.
O sinless one, you must have no doubt in this matter;
you should perform its service there with great faith during the spring season.
Having slain the wicked Rāvaṇa, rule the kingdom as you please for eleven thousand years upon the surface of the earth.
"O best of the Raghus, having ruled the kingdom, you shall go again to the third heaven.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess vanished, and Rāma was delighted in his heart. (59)
Having completed that vow, he set out on his journey on the tenth day,
after performing the worship of Vijayā and giving various gifts in abundance.

Accompanied by the strength of the monkey army and his younger brother, the Lord of Śrī—his every desire fulfilled and impelled by the manifest supreme power—reached the shore of the ocean; having constructed a bridge, he of celebrated fame slew Rāvaṇa, the enemy of the immortals.
The man who listens with devotion to this supreme life-story of the Goddess,
having enjoyed abundant pleasures, attains the highest state.
There are many other Purāṇas that are extensive and numerous;
it is my conviction that none of them are equal to this Śrīmad Bhāgavata. (63)
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Boons upon Rāma," in the Third Book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 30 ||
The Questions of Janamejaya.
Janamejaya said:
O son of Vasava, best of sages, storehouse of all knowledge, O sinless one!
O Lord, enhancer of our lineage, I wish to ask you a question.
The glorious and powerful Vasudeva, son of Śūrasena,
is he of whom I have heard that Hari attained the state of being his son.
He who was worthy of worship even by the gods and known by the name Ānakadundubhi—how could he, being devoted to righteousness, be bound in the prison of Kaṃsa? (3)
What offense did he commit against his wife Devakī?
Furthermore, why was the destruction of Devakī’s six children carried out?
Why indeed was it that Vāsudeva, the Lord Hari, born into the lineage of Yayāti, took birth in a prison cell because of that Kaṃsa?
And how was the Blessed One, the Lord of the Sātvatas, led to Gokula? Why did He undergo another birth while His parents remained in fetters? (6)
And why were Devakī and Vasudeva, the aged parents of Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable splendor, not liberated by this Hari? (7)
While he who is capable of creating the universe remained within the womb of Janaka, what was their past karma? That is difficult even for great-souled ones to discern.
Where indeed was the birth of Vāsudeva, the Supreme Self?
Who were his sons, and who were those women who were crushed by Kaṃsa?
O sinless one, tell me how she emerged from the stone, became eight-armed in the sky, and how there came to be a household life for Hari who has many wives.
I have heard reports concerning his affairs there and his very abandonment of the body;
that which I have heard seems to bewilder my mind.
Relate accurately the life-story of Vāsudeva,
as well as that of the two ancient gods, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the best of sages.
The two high-souled sons of Dharma, those two sages, performed supreme austerity for many years in the holy hermitage of Badarikāśrama.
Without food, with self-conquered minds, free from desire, and having mastered the six qualities,
those two portions of Viṣṇu performed supreme penance for the stability of the world.
For the two of great strength, Jiṣṇu and Kṛṣṇa, are indeed the partial incarnations (aṃśāvatāra) of those two;
they are well known and proclaimed by all-knowing sages such as Nārada and others. (15)
How did those two gods, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, who possessed existing bodies, pass into another body; and how [did they become] Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna again?
How did those two best of sages, who performed fierce austerities for the sake of liberation and had attained yoga and great penance, obtain their two bodies? (17)
A Śūdra who is steadfast in his own duty becomes a Kṣatriya at the end of the body;
indeed, a Śūdra who dies while possessing auspicious conduct shall become a Brāhmaṇa.
The Brahmin, free from desire and peaceful, is liberated from the disease of worldly existence;
yet this appears otherwise to those two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Those two Kṣatriyas had their selves withered by asceticism;
by what action or, again, by what curse did they become pacified? (20)
O Sage, tell me the reason why these two Brahmins were born as Kṣatriyas;
for it has been heard that the destruction of the Yādavas was caused by a Brahmin’s curse.
Indeed, even for Kṛṣṇa, the destruction of his lineage occurred solely through the curse of Gāndhārī;
and how was Pradyumna carried away by Śambara? (22)
While Vāsudeva, the god of gods and Janārdana, was present,
the abduction of his son from the lying-in chamber was an exceedingly difficult feat.
How was that not known by Vāsudeva, who possesses divine vision, from within the fortress of Dvārakā, specifically from the invincible palace of Hari? 24.
"O Brahman, O Lord, this is a great doubt; please resolve it without uncertainty:
how is it that the wives of Vāsudeva were plundered and carried off by bandits? (25)
O best of sages, O Brahmin, now that the God of gods has ascended to heaven, how is it that a doubt arises which causes my mind to waver? (26)
How could Janārdana Śauri, an emanation of Viṣṇu who has come forth to remove the burden of the earth, abandon the kingdom of Mathurā out of fear? (27)
O virtuous one, having gone to Dvāravatī with his army and his circle of friends, this incarnation of Hari was indeed proclaimed for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth. (28)
"For the destruction of the evil-minded and for the establishment of dharma, why were those thieves not struck down by Vāsudeva? (29)
Were those thieves, by whom the wives of Vāsudeva were abducted and plundered, not recognized again by him who is truly omniscient? (30)
The slaying of Bhīṣma and Droṇa was indeed intended for the removal of the earth's burden;
moreover, the high-souled Pāṇḍavas, who are devoted to righteousness, have been duly honored. (31)
The devotees of Kṛṣṇa, who were of virtuous conduct and led by Yudhiṣṭhira,
performed the Rājasūya, the king of sacrifices, according to the prescribed injunctions.
Having given various sacrificial fees to the Brahmins with great devotion,
O Sage, the sons of Pāṇḍu, who were portions of the gods and devoted to Vāsudeva, [departed].
How did they come to experience such terrible suffering, and where has their merit gone? What was that most dreadful sin by which they are perpetually tormented? (34)
And the highly fortunate Draupadī, born from the center of the sacrificial altar, was a virtuous woman born of a portion of Ramā, likewise endowed with devotion to Kṛṣṇa. || 35 ||
How did she repeatedly encounter such terrible and incomparable suffering?
She was seized by her hair and violently tormented by Duḥśāsana. || 36 ||
But while she was in her menses, she was led into the assembly by a frightened servant girl wearing a single garment;
she then became a maidservant to Matsya in the city of Virāṭa. (37)
Then she was violated by Kīcaka, weeping like a female osprey;
then she was abducted by Jayadratha, crying out in extreme distress.
They were later liberated by the powerful and high-souled Pāṇḍavas;
what was that evil committed in a previous birth because of which they were so tormented? (39)
"O Mahāmati, tell me today how those ancestors of mine experienced many sufferings after performing the Rājasūya, the best of sacrifices. (40)
They have indeed encountered this great suffering due to what was done in their previous births;
how can there be such a great doubt regarding those who possess a divine portion? This is truly my concern. (41)
By the sons of Kuntī, who knew the world to be perishable, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others were slain through deceit for the sake of gaining wealth, despite their own virtuous conduct. (42)
Impelled by the high-souled Vāsudeva, the Supreme Lord Hari, they brought about the destruction of their own lineage for the sake of terrible sin. (43)
Better for a virtuous man is wandering for alms, better is living on wild grains (nīvāra), and better is living by one's craft than by slaying warriors out of greed. (44)
O best of sages, the lineage that had been severed by you has now been preserved by quickly procreating sons from Golaka who shall be destroyers of their enemies. (45)
How is it that, in such a short time, the son of Virāṭa’s daughter placed a serpent around the throat of the ascetic—how truly wonderful! (46)
No one born of the Kṣatriya lineage hates a Brāhmaṇa;
O Sage, what was done by your father to that ascetic who was engaged in silence? (47)
My mind is now distressed by these and other doubts;
O virtuous father, make it steady, for you are omniscient, O ocean of compassion. (48)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Question of Janamejaya," in the fourth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
An Exposition on Karma as the Cause of Birth and Other Phenomena.
Sūta said:
Thus questioned, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī and knower of the Purāṇas, [replied].
Then indeed [he begat] Janamejaya, the son of Parīkṣit, who was peaceful.
He who was skilled in speech spoke these words that dispel doubt.
Vyāsa said:
