"O King, what is there to be said? The course of karmas is profound."
It is indeed difficult for the gods to comprehend, so what need is there to mention human beings, when this universe consisting of the three qualities has arisen? (3)
The birth of all beings occurs through karma alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
Living beings are without beginning or end, arising from the seed of karma.
They are born and die again and again in various wombs;
however, a conjunction with a body never occurs when one is devoid of karma.
This [world] is indeed enveloped by auspicious, inauspicious, and mixed karmas;
for those who are wise and knowers of reality have declared them to be of three kinds.
Indeed, there is a threefold nature of actions in this body: those that have been accumulated, those that have begun to bear fruit, and those that are currently manifesting.
O lord of men, Brahmā and all others are subject to its power;
likewise, pleasure and pain, old age and death, joy and sorrow, and so forth [depend upon it].
Desire, anger, and greed—all these qualities reside within the body;
they prevail over everyone, O lord of men, being subject to destiny.
For states such as passion and hatred indeed prevail even in heaven, among gods, humans, and likewise among animals. (10)
All these transformations are indeed joined with the body, either through the persistence of former enmity or again through the bond of affection. (11)
The birth of all living beings does not occur without karma;
by karma the sun revolves, and the moon suffers from the disease of waning.
And Rudra likewise became Kapālī solely through his action; of this there is no doubt.
This cause known as action exists, being without beginning or end.
Therefore, in this world, the entire universe—both the stationary and the moving—is eternal;
here, the sages are always immersed in the investigation of the permanent and the impermanent.
They do not know what this truly is—whether it is eternal or indeed non-eternal;
for while Māyā exists, the world appears as eternal.
How can the absence of an effect be asserted when the cause exists in every way?
For indeed, Māyā is eternal and is the cause of all things at all times. (16)
Therefore, the wise should always contemplate that the seed of karma is impermanent;
O King, the entire world wanders about, constrained by karma.
O Indra among kings, by his own will, Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor may take birth in various wombs and in those composed of various dharmas.
How is it that, throughout many ages and various low births, you have abandoned residence in Vaikuṇṭha and manifold enjoyments of happiness? (19)
Who, being terrified, would desire to dwell in a chamber of excrement and urine, or engage in the play of gathering flowers, sporting in water, or sitting in comfort? (20)
Having abandoned residence in the inner chamber, what wise person would desire even a divine bed fashioned from soft cotton wool? (21)
Having abandoned dwelling with face cast down, what wise man would desire song, dance, and instrumental music accompanied by various emotional expressions? (22)
Who, having abandoned residence in hell, would even contemplate it with their mind, after having renounced the taste born of the ocean, which is so difficult to abandon? || 23 ||
What wise man would desire to drink the essence of feces and urine?
There is no hell in the three worlds greater than dwelling in the womb. (24)
Fearing that [death], sages perform difficult austerities;
abandoning enjoyments and sovereignty, the wise go to the forest. (25)
Who would wish to serve that which terrifies the deluded soul?
Within the womb, worms sting, and the digestive fire burns from below. (26)
O King, what pleasure is there in that minced meat wrapped in omentum? Better is dwelling in a prison cell; better is bondage with fetters. (27)
The dwelling in a womb is never auspicious for even a brief moment;
dwelling in the womb for ten months is a source of great suffering. (28)
Likewise, there is suffering in the exit through the most dreadful mechanism of birth;
then, in childhood, there is suffering joined with the state of being mute and ignorant. (29)
Overpowered by the sensations of hunger and thirst, dependent on others, and extremely distressed, the mother was then consumed with anxiety for her hungry, crying child. (30)
Desiring to drink the medicine, she recognized the intense agony of disease;
indeed, various kinds of sufferings arise in childhood. (31)
What happiness have the wise seen that they desire birth at will, even after abandoning the constant bliss of battle with the immortals? (32)
And what fool would wish to do that which causes exhaustion and destroys happiness?
O best of kings, all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, are entirely [averse to it]. (33)

Through the ripening of performed actions, beings experience pleasure and pain; for embodied beings— whether humans, gods, or animals, O best of kings— one must inevitably experience the results of whatever action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, one has committed.
Through austerity, charity, and sacrifice, a human being may attain the status of Indra;
yet when his merit is exhausted, even Śakra falls—of this there is no doubt. (35)
By means of the incarnation of Rāma, the gods attained the state of monkeys;
likewise, for the sake of assisting Kṛṣṇa, the gods attained the state of Yādavas.
Thus, in age after age, Viṣṇu, being strongly impelled by Brahmā, performs numerous incarnations for the sake of protecting dharma.
O King, in this manner, other wonderful incarnations of Hari occur again and again in various wombs, like the wheels of a chariot.
The task of slaying the Daityas must be performed by Hari himself;
indeed, the Great-Souled One shall take birth on earth through a portion of his own portions. (39)
Therefore, I shall fully relate the auspicious narrative of Kṛṣṇa’s birth;
that very Lord Viṣṇu has descended into the lineage of Yadu.
O King, the powerful Vasudeva was a portion of the sage Kaśyapa; due to the influence of a previous curse, he lived the life of a cowherd.
O lord of the earth, O ruler of the world, Kaśyapa had two wives, Aditi and Surasā, who were present here [in this state] due to a curse. (42)
O bull of the Bharata race, it is heard that both Devakī and Rohiṇī were sisters,
and that Varuṇa had pronounced a great curse upon them out of anger.
The king said:
"What offense was committed by Kaśyapa, because of which the great ṛṣi was cursed?
O high-minded one, tell me how he was born together with his wife. (44)
And how was the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu born there in Gokula—he who dwells in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, the unassailable Lord of Ramā? (45)
At whose command does the Lord act—he who is the immutable master, Nārāyaṇa, the best of gods, the beginning of the ages, and the sustainer of all? || 46 ||
How is it that he, having abandoned his celestial abode, undergoes birth among humans as if possessed by karma?
Why does this happen? In this matter, I have a great doubt.
Having obtained a human body, however, one performs a mockery by manifesting various kinds of dispositions within that human birth, which is otherwise base.
Desire, anger, intolerance, grief, enmity, and affection; pleasure, pain, fear, as well as dejection and even straightforwardness—these at times [afflict] men. (49)
Misdeed and good deed, as well as speech and killing, nourishing and moving, burning and reflection, and boasting—these [are the functions of the senses]. (50)
Greed, hypocrisy, delusion, deceit, and grief—these and other such states indeed arise within the human condition. (51)
How does that Blessed One Viṣṇu, who by his own nature bestows imperishable happiness, take human birth, driven by various such dispositions?
O Lord of Sages, having attained a human birth on this earth, what is the happiness [therein]?
For what reason indeed does Hari himself undergo dwelling in a womb? (53)
There is the suffering of the womb, the suffering of birth, and likewise again the suffering of childhood;
in youth there is the suffering born of desire, and in the householder's state it is exceedingly great. (54)
O best of the twice-born, he encounters these miseries in the human world;
how then does that Blessed Viṣṇu take incarnations again and again? (55)
Indeed, even after attaining the incarnation as Rāma, Hari, who is born from Brahmā,
experienced great suffering during his exceedingly harsh forest exile.
The sorrow born of separation from Sītā, the repeated battles,
and even the abandonment of his beloved were experienced in this manner by that great-souled one.
Likewise, in the Kṛṣṇa incarnation as well, there was birth in the protection-chamber,
the journey to Gokula, and furthermore, the herding of cows.
How did the Blessed One experience the slaying of Kaṃsa with great hardship, his subsequent return to Dvārakā, and the various miseries of worldly existence? (59)
Who that is wise and liberated from sufferings would wait by his own will?
O Omniscient One, sever my doubt for the sake of the peace of my mind. (60)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Determination that Karma is the Cause of Birth and Other States," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Vyāsa said: There were indeed many reasons for Hari’s descent here, including the bestowal of a curse by Aditi upon Aditya.
And also in the partial incarnations of all the gods.
Listen to the cause of the incarnation of Vasudeva according to its true nature,
as well as the cause of the incarnations of Devakī and Rohiṇī.
Once, the illustrious Kaśyapa brought a cow for the sake of a sacrifice;
though entreated in many ways, he did not give up that excellent cow.
Then Varuṇa, having gone there, bowed down to Brahmā, the lord of the world,
and with a distressed soul and full of humility, spoke of his own suffering.
"What shall I do, O illustrious one? He will not give me a cow.
I have already cast a curse upon him: 'Become a cowherd among mortals! (5)
Both wives there shall likewise become exceedingly sorrowful,
because the dear children here weep, deprived of their mother and deeply afflicted.
Therefore, on this earth, she will become one whose children die at birth;
moreover, she will dwell in a prison and be greatly afflicted by suffering.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the Lord of the Fish, the Lotus-born Prajāpati summoned the sage there and spoke to him.
O illustrious one, why were the cows of the world-protector taken by you and not returned? Why do you commit such injustice? (9)
O illustrious one, knowing what is right, how could you have committed the injustice of seizing another's wealth? O high-minded one, you are all-knowing. (10)
Oh, how great is the power of greed! It does not release even the greatest person from itself—this greed which surely leads to hell, is a mine of sin, and is utterly disagreeable. (11)
Even Kaśyapa was not able to abandon him; what could I do? For greed has always been more powerful than that, and it has indeed taken hold of me. (12)
Blessed are those peaceful sages who have conquered greed itself—
those forest-dwellers devoted to tranquility who turn their backs on receiving gifts.
In this cycle of existence, greed is always a powerful, impure, and base enemy;
even Kaśyapa was of wicked conduct and his affection was formed by that evil-souled one.
Then Brahmā also cursed that Kaśyapa, the best of sages,
even though he was his own most beloved grandson, for the sake of preserving the bounds of propriety.
Having indeed obtained birth on earth through a portion [of yourself] in the lineage of Yadu,
you shall act as a cowherd there, accompanied by two wives.
Vyāsa said:
Thus was Kaśyapa cursed by Varuṇa and Brahmā for the purpose of descending as partial incarnations and for the removal of the earth’s burden.
Likewise, Diti was cursed by Aditi, who was intensely tormented by grief:
"Indeed, seven sons shall be born to you, but as soon as they are born, they shall perish. (18)
Janamejaya said: O Sage, why was Diti, the sister of Indra and mother of the gods, cursed?
O best of sages, tell me the cause of that curse, for I am filled with grief. (19)
Sūta said:
Thus questioned by the son of Parīkṣit, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī,
being well-composed, replied to the king with these words concerning the cause.
Vyāsa said: O King, there were two excellent daughters of Dakṣa, Diti and Aditi,
who became the beloved wives of Kaśyapa, O you of wide strides.
When Maghavan became the son of Aditi, being exceedingly heroic,
then Diti, through her vital power, desired such a son.
O giver of honor, you whose side-glances are like those of a great serpent, grant me a son who is as powerful as Indra, a hero, most righteous, and preeminent in valor. (23)
The sage said to her, "O beloved, be composed at my word;
at the conclusion of your vow, you shall have a son equal to Indra."
Having promised "So be it," she undertook the highest vow,
bearing the most beautiful embryo infused by the sage.
Devoted to a vow of subsisting on milk, the fair-complexioned woman made her bed upon the ground; purified and engaged in meditative concentration, she remained there.
Thus born and fully developed, when the embryo became exceedingly powerful,
Diti, seeing her own limbs blazing with a brilliance like that of the bright moon, was filled with grief.
"A son equal to Maghavan and possessed of great strength shall be born;
meanwhile, it is said that my son Diti's will be devoid of splendor. (28)
Thus lost in thought, the proud woman spoke to her son Indra:
"A very powerful enemy has today arisen within the womb of Diti."
"O beautiful one, having reflected upon it, devise a means today for the destruction of the enemy;
the very birth of this embryo must be destroyed. (30)
Beholding that dark-eyed woman who has assumed the status of a co-wife, anxiety—which destroys the very vitals of happiness—torments my heart. (31)
An enemy who has grown powerful, like the disease of consumption (rājayakṣmā), can never truly be destroyed;
therefore, a wise person should indeed strike down an adversary while he is still in the sprout stage. 32.
"O Śatakratu, this embryo in my womb is like an iron spike driven in; by whatever means possible, cause it to fall today! (33)
O highly fortunate one, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me, you must destroy Diti’s embryo by means of conciliation, bribery, or force. (34)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard his mother’s words, Śakra, the lord of the immortals, reflected upon them in his mind and then went into the presence of his other mother.
O King, that evil-minded one bowed at the feet of Diti with humility;
he spoke with courtesy, yet his words were sweet on the surface but poisonous within. (36)
Indra said:
"O Mother, you are engaged in a vow, your body is emaciated and exceedingly weak;
I have arrived here for the sake of service—tell me, what must be done? (37)
"O devoted wife, I shall perform the massaging of your feet;
for by serving one's elders, one obtains merit and an imperishable state. (38)
"I have no difference toward you; I swear this truly by the Sun," having said this, he touched his feet and became intent on massaging them. (39)
Having obtained the pleasure of being massaged, the beautiful-eyed woman, exhausted and emaciated by her vows, fell asleep— she who was supremely virtuous and full of trust.
Seeing her fallen under the power of sleep, he entered her body,
assuming an exceedingly subtle form, with weapon in hand and composed in mind.
By the power of his yoga, he quickly entered her womb;
then the Lord of the World cut the fetus into seven pieces with his thunderbolt.
And then the boy wept as if struck by a thunderbolt;
he spoke these gentle words to Maghavan: "Do not weep."
Furthermore, O King, those seven fragments were each cut into seven parts; thus, there came to be forty-nine Maruts.
Then, having awakened and realized that her pregnancy had been brought about in such a way by Indra through deceitful means, the fair-toothed woman became deeply distressed and grew furious.
Having learned that her sister had done this, Aditi, who was devoted to the observance of truthful vows, then became enraged and cursed both Maghavan and him.
"Just as my fetus was cut out by your son through deceit, so may his sovereignty over the three worlds come to destruction. (47)
Just as my embryo was caused to fall by Guptā through her evil deed, so too was my son slain by the wicked-acting Aditi. || 48 ||
"May her sons perish again and again as soon as they are born;
let her dwell in prison, deeply afflicted by grief for her children. (49)
"And in another birth as well, she shall have her offspring die.
Vyāsa said: Having then heard this curse uttered, the son of Marīci—
Filled with affection, he spoke these words as if to pacify her:
"Do not be angry, O auspicious lady; your sons are exceedingly powerful. (51)
All the gods shall become the Maruts, the friends of Maghavan;
this is your curse, O lady of beautiful thighs, to take place in the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age.
Having obtained a human birth by means of a portion [of her merit], that beautiful woman shall experience [the consequences];
for a curse was also pronounced upon her by Varuṇa, who was greatly distressed.
"By the application of the curses of both, she shall become human.
Vyāsa said:
The goddess, consoled by her husband, then became satisfied.
Then that woman of excellent complexion spoke some unpleasant words.
Thus, O King, has the cause of her former curse been told to you.
O best of kings, Aditi was born as Devakī through her own partial incarnation.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Bestowal of a Curse upon Aditi by Diti," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Regarding the description of the condition of the lowest world,
the King said:
"O illustrious one, O high-minded one, I am filled with wonder having heard this narrative."
This cyclic existence is of the nature of evil; how may one be liberated from this bondage?
Even the heir of Kaśyapa, while possessing the sovereign power of the three worlds, performed such a deed; who would not commit what is loathsome?
Having entered the womb, he indeed committed the terrible act of killing the child,
having made a miraculous oath with his mother under the pretext of serving her.
The Teacher, the protector of the Dharma, and even the Lord of the three worlds—having performed such an act, who would not consider it improper? (4)
O Teacher of the World, my grandfathers performed an exceedingly terrible and wondrously wicked deed in battle on Kurukṣetra. (5)
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, and even Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma—
all were impelled by Vāsudeva through a contrary force.
How could those of great intelligence, who understand the worthlessness of saṃsāra and are devoted to the principles of dharma, have performed such a censurable act even for the sake of the gods? (7)
"O best of Brahmins, what is determined to be the final authority regarding dharma?
Having heard this narrative, my mind has become wavering. (8)
If the word of a trustworthy person is a means of valid cognition, who is that trustworthy person?
For a person possessing another body is in every way attached to sense objects and full of passion. (9)
Passion and hatred will surely arise without doubt from the loss of wealth;
out of hatred, one must speak untruthful words for the sake of achieving one's own purpose.
For the sake of destroying Jarāsaṃdha, Hari, who possesses the form of pure being and is all-knowing, assumed the guise of a Brāhmaṇa through a stratagem.
Who then is an authoritative person, and what is the proof, even if one possesses such a form of being?
Arjuna likewise is [unreliable] in this matter concerning the performance of the sacrifice.
What kind of sacrifice has this been made? For what purpose has it been performed, devoid of tranquility—either for the sake of the state of the next world, or for fame, or indeed otherwise? (13)
"Truth is the first foot of Dharma—this is the word of the Śruti;
likewise, purity is the second, and compassion is the third foot. (14)
The knowers of the Purāṇas indeed declare that charity is the fourth foot;
how could Dharma remain well-regarded here in this world if it were deprived of them? (15)
How can an action performed devoid of dharma yield its fruit?
It is not perceived that anyone’s mind is ever firmly established in dharma. (16)
And when Viṣṇu, the Lord, became Vāmana for the sake of the six purposes—that form of Vāmana by which King Bali was deceived. (17)
He was the performer of a hundred sacrifices, the protector of Vedic injunctions, most righteous, charitable by nature, truthful, and one who had conquered his senses. || 18 ||
Suddenly cast down from his position by the all-powerful Viṣṇu—who among those two was victorious, O Kṛṣṇa: the mighty one or Vāmana? (19)
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, this great doubt exists within me regarding one who knows the art of deception; having been deceived by a deceiver, tell me the truth. (20)
"You are the author of the Purāṇas, a knower of Dharma, and possessed of great intelligence.
Vyāsa said:
"O King, victory indeed belongs to Bali, by whom the earth was given away. (21)
O King, O lord of men, he who was renowned by the name Trivikrama became Vāmana for the purpose of deception; this dwarf-form was assumed by him.
Hari has once again attained the very office of gatekeeper;
O King, there is nothing other than truth that is the root of dharma.
O King, it is indeed true that for embodied beings, [the truth] is difficult to accomplish with all one's soul;
O Monarch, Māyā is powerful, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), and multiform.
Since this universe has been created by that [Brahman] which is variegated by the three qualities (guṇas), O King, how could truth ever be pierced through by one who is deceitful? (25)
And this eternal state was produced by the mixed [caste];
the Vaikhānasa sages are free from attachment and do not accept gifts.
In this world, those who are endowed with truth, free from passion, and devoid of longing exist;
they are created as such for the purpose of providing an illustration. (27)
O King, everything else is variegated by these three qualities;
O best of kings, there is not a single statement in the Purāṇas or the Vedas [to the contrary]. (28)
In this world, regarding the Dharmaśāstras and the Aṅgas composed by those possessed of qualities,
one who possesses qualities may perform them, but one devoid of qualities certainly does not.
All those qualities are mixed together; they do not exist in isolation from one another.
No one's mind remains steady in the faultless and stable Dharma.
O Great King, for one who is indeed deluded by illusion regarding the arising of existence,
the senses are turbulent and the mind is likewise attached to them.
Impelled intensely by those qualities, it produces various states of being—
the living beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, both stationary and moving.
O King, all are under the power of Māyā; she sports here with them, deluding everyone and constantly transforming the world.
O King, a man who has business to attend to first becomes untruthful;
when a man, contemplating the objects of the senses, does not obtain them, [he falls into falsehood]. (34)
For that purpose, one resorts to deception; through deception, one engages in evil.
Desire, anger, and greed are exceedingly powerful enemies. (35)
Living beings who have fallen under its sway do not know what has been done or left undone;
even when wealth is present, a powerful egoism arises.
From egoism arises delusion, and from delusion comes death itself;
therein many volitions arise, and from them, conceptual constructions are produced. (37)
Envy, malice, and likewise hatred arise in the mind; as do hope, thirst, wretchedness, hypocrisy, and an unrighteous disposition. (38)
These states arising from delusion prevail over living beings:
sacrifices, gifts, sacred fords, vows, and likewise restraints. (39)
But a person who is overcome by egoism performs [actions] day after day;
everything done out of a sense of "I" will indeed not result in purity. (40)
Action performed out of passion and greed is devoid of purity in all its parts;
indeed, the wise must first examine the purity of the materials used. (41)
Wealth acquired without malice is commended for righteous deeds;
whatever auspicious act a man performs with wealth acquired through malice [is rendered fruitless]. (42)
O best of kings, that [result] may indeed be reversed at the time of fruition;
however, he whose mind is exceedingly pure shall partake of the fruit correctly.

But when that [rite] is joined with such a defect, the performers of the rituals—the preceptor, the officiating priests, and all others—shall not obtain the fruit corresponding to the truth of the rite. (44)
Then those of pure mind shall obtain the full fruit, provided there is purity of place, time, action, substance, and agent. (45)
Then he enjoys the full fruit of his actions through the mantras, aiming for the destruction of his enemies as well as his own supreme prosperity. (46)
In the same way, he performs good deeds, yet it may indeed turn out otherwise;
for a man who is constantly attached to his own self-interest does not distinguish between what is auspicious and what is inauspicious. (47)
One who is always dependent on fate would perform only evil deeds and never what is virtuous;
for all the gods are born of Prajāpati, as are the asuras who arise from him. 48.
All of them are intent on their own self-interest and are mutually antagonistic;
all these gods, though born of the principle of goodness (sattva), are declared in the Vedas to be human.
Those born from *rajas* and characterized by *tamas* are proclaimed to be the animals;
there is constant mutual enmity between them and those born from *sattva*.
What is surprising here regarding the emergence of innate enmity among animals?
The gods are likewise always intent on malice and create obstacles to ascetic penance.
Dissatisfied, intent on hatred, and mutually antagonistic—this is the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) that arises from egoism (ahaṅkāra), O King. 52.
But how, O King, does one become free from passion and hatred? (53)
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Sustenance of the Lower World," in the Fourth Book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Story of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Vyāsa said:
Now, O best of kings, what is the use of speaking further regarding this worldly existence?
But someone whose soul is devoted to Dharma may occasionally develop a mind free from malice.
O King of kings, the entire universe, including all things mobile and immobile, was shrouded by passion and hatred even in the first age; how much more so today, when it is corrupted by the Kali age?
O King, even the gods are full of envy and malice, and are constantly engaged in deceitful acts; what then can be said of humans and animals? (3)
"To be intent on malice toward one intent on malice is considered equal [to him];
likewise, to harbor hatred toward one who is non-malicious and peaceful is known as wickedness. (4)
If there should be any ascetic who is peaceful and devoted to recitation and meditation,
Maghavan indeed becomes the supreme creator of obstacles for his recitation.
For the virtuous, the Kṛtayuga is ever manifest; for the wicked, it is always the Kali age.
For those of middling character, however, the Kṛta and Tretā ages are traditionally held to exist through their ritual actions and yogic practices.
At some time, someone may become a follower of the true dharma;
otherwise, indeed, all people in other ages are solely devoted to their respective dharmas.
O King, latent impression (vāsanā) is the cause in all established states of dharma;
indeed, when that is defiled, dharma itself becomes defiled.
Impure latent impressions must certainly be destroyed by all means;
therefore, Dharma is remembered as the son born from the heart of Brahmā.
The Brāhmaṇa was endowed with truth and always delighted in the Vedas and dharma;
indeed, ten daughters of Dakṣa were chosen by that high-souled one.
Through the marriage rite performed correctly by the sage who was a householder,
Dharma, the best among the truthful, begot sons upon those wives.
O King, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nara, and likewise Nārāyaṇa—
being constantly devoted to the practice of yoga, Hari became Kṛṣṇa.
And Nara and Nārāyaṇa themselves performed supreme austerity,
having gone to the snowy mountain at the sacred ford of Badarikāśrama.
Those two ancient and best of sages, the foremost among ascetics,
were chanting that supreme Brahman on the vast bank of the Gaṅgā.
The two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, portions of Hari, were situated there and performed supreme austerity for a full thousand years.
The entire world, including all things mobile and immobile, was scorched by the ascetic heat of Nara and Nārāyaṇa; at that time, Śakra fell into a state of agitation.
Overcome with anxiety, the thousand-eyed Indra reflected in his mind:
"What should be done? These two sons of Dharma are ascetics absorbed in meditation. (17)
"How can an obstacle be created for him, who is about to take my most excellent and highly perfected seat, so that his asceticism may not indeed come to fruition? (18)
Having generated desire, anger, and even most cruel greed, with this as his aim, the Thousand-eyed One mounted his excellent elephant. (19)
Desiring to create obstacles, he went swiftly to Gandhamādana;
having arrived there at that holy hermitage, Śatakratu beheld those two.
"With bodies blazing from asceticism like two risen suns, are these indeed Brahmā and Viṣṇu, or are they the two manifest fires? (21)
"What will these two sages, sons of Dharma, accomplish through their asceticism?"—
thinking thus, the Lord of Śacī beheld them and then spoke.
"O illustrious sons of Dharma, what task is there to be done?
Speak, for I have come as a seer to grant you an excellent boon."
"Though it is something that should not be given, I shall grant it, for I am indeed pleased by your asceticism.
Vyāsa said:
Standing before them, Śakra spoke thus again and again.
The bull [Śiva] did not see the two sages, who were established in meditation with firm minds;
thereupon, he indeed created a deluding illusion that was terrifying.
He terrified him by conjuring up wolves, lions, and tigers, and by repeatedly producing rain, wind, and fire. (26)
Śakra, having employed a deluding illusion, terrified those two;
yet, even though they were brought under his control by fear, those two sons of Dharma did not succumb, O sage.
Having seen Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Śakra returned to his own abode; they were so captivated by the granting of the boon that they did not even fear Agni and Vāyu.
Even when threatened by tigers, lions, and other predators, they did not stir from their own hermitage;
indeed, no one at all was able to disturb their meditation.
Indra, too, having gone to his abode, reflected in distress:
"These two best of sages have been shaken by fear and greed."
They meditated upon the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), the primordial power (Ādiśakti), the eternal one, the sovereign of all worlds, the supreme and wondrous Prakṛti. || 31 ||
Who in this world, even among those skilled in many illusions, is capable of meditating upon Him, from whom all illusions—indeed, those created by both gods and asuras—have their root? (32)
How can they be able to cause harm when they meditate, free from all impurity?
[They meditate upon] the seed-syllable of speech (vāgbīja), the seed-syllable of desire (kāmabīja), and likewise the seed-syllable of illusion (māyābīja). || 33 ||
No one at all was able to afflict him whose mind was thus [steadfast];
yet Śakra, deluded by Māyā, again sought a counter-measure against him.
Desiring to act, he summoned Kāma and Vasanta and spoke these words:
"O Manobhava, go now accompanied by Vasanta and Rati."
Accompanied by Apsarases, he went swiftly to Gandhamādana,
where the two ancient and most excellent sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, resided.
While the two were performing austerities, staying in seclusion at the hermitage of Badarī,
Manmatha went there into their presence and [assailed them] with his arrows.
Make my mind, which is afflicted by desire, accomplish its task now;
having deluded it and driven it away, strike it quickly with your arrows.
"O illustrious one, bring under your control even the sages and the two sons of Dharma.
For who in this entire world—whether god, demon, or human—is beyond your reach? (39)

He who, having fallen under the power of your arrow, does not succumb even when severely struck—be he Brahmā, I (Śiva), the Lord of the Mountain-born (Pārvatī), Candra, or Agni—is utterly deluded. (40)
O Kāma, what count can there be of the prowess of your arrows? This host of courtesans has been sent by me to assist you. (41)
The enchanting Rambhā and others will come to that very place;
among them, Tilottamā alone is capable of accomplishing the task.
You alone are capable of fulfilling this desire; what doubt could there be when we are united?
Accomplish the task, O illustrious one; I shall grant you your wish.
The two ascetics were excessively enticed by me with boons, yet they did not waver from their place; remaining peaceful, this labor of mine has gone in vain.
Thus, having terrified those two ascetics greatly by means of his illusory power (māyā), he remained there; nevertheless, intent on protecting their bodies, they did not rise from their places.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, the Mind-born (Kāma) spoke to Śakra:
"O Vāsava, today I shall accomplish for you the task desired by your mind."
If those two sages were then to meditate upon Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Brahmā, or Divākara, they would come under our control. (47)
I am not able to subjugate a devotee of the Goddess by any means whatsoever, for he constantly contemplates the great seed-syllable Kāmarāja within his mind. (48)
If those two ascetics have taken refuge in that goddess Mahāśakti with a spirit of devotion, then indeed they shall not fall within the range of my arrows.
Indra said:
"Go there, O highly fortunate one, along with all those prepared for the task; you shall accomplish my most difficult mission, which will bring about unsurpassed benefit. (50)
Vyāsa said:
Thus commanded by him, they all set out with great effort for the place where those two sons of Dharma were performing difficult austerities.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Nara and Nārāyaṇa," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Apsarā’s Petition in the Presence of Nārāyaṇa.
Vyāsa said:
First, the spring season arrived there on that best of mountains.
All the trees were in full bloom, resplendent with swarms of bees.
Mango trees, beautiful *bakula* trees, lovely *tilaka* trees, auspicious *kiṃśuka* trees, as well as *sāla*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, and *madhūka* trees, all appeared in full bloom. || 2 ||
The enchanting warbling of cuckoos arose from the tops of the trees,
and all the flowering creepers embraced the best of mountains.
Living beings, filled with love for their own wives and afflicted by passion,
became exceedingly intoxicated and devoted to mutual play.
Gentle, fragrant, and pleasant to the touch, the southern winds blew;
even the senses of the sages became agitated.
Then Kāma, filled with passion and fulfilling his five arrows,
quickly made his dwelling there at the Badarikāśrama.
Rambhā, Tilottamā, and others, being experts in song, went to that excellent hermitage and performed singing endowed with proper scales and modulations.
Having heard that sweet singing, the warbling of cuckoos,
and the humming of swarms of bees, those two lords of sages were awakened.
Seeing the king of seasons out of its proper time and the forest in full bloom,
the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa there became filled with anxiety.
Has the end of winter arrived today without the passing of time? For all living beings appear agitated and afflicted by excessive passion. (10)
"How has this reversal of the law of time become so difficult to overcome today?
Nārāyaṇa said to the man, his eyes wide with wonder. (11)
Nārāyaṇa said:
"Behold, brother, these trees appear truly in full bloom;
they resound with the warbling of cuckoos and are adorned by swarms of bees. (12)
O Sage, the lion of spring has arrived, tearing apart the formidable elephant of the cold season with its hooves and claws— the blossoming palāśa flowers.
The slender one has hands like red Aśoka flowers, O divine sage, and feet like Kiṃśuka blossoms;
she has hair like blue Aśoka flowers, is dark-complexioned, and her face is like a blooming lotus. 14.
She had eyes like blue lotuses, breasts like the fruits of the *bilva* tree,
teeth like blossoming *kunda* flowers, and was adorned with *mañjarī* blossoms upon her ears.
Her lips are like the bandhujīva flower, her teeth are bright white, and she possesses the voice of the male cuckoo; she is auspicious, clad in garments of kadamba flowers, and beautiful.
With a mass of *barhi* feathers for her hair-tuft, the sound of cranes for her anklets, the *vāsantī* flower for her girdle, and the gait of an intoxicated swan, she was thus adorned. (17)
O Brahmin, the splendor of spring has arrived at Badarikāśrama, adorned with rows of hair-like buds placed upon the garments of the putrajīva trees.
"Why has she arrived at this improper time? This now causes me wonder.
O celestial sage, consider well; she must surely be an obstacle to my ascetic penance. (19)
It is heard that the song of celestial women, which destroys meditative concentration,
was indeed performed by Indra for the purpose of breaking our asceticism.
"How else could the king of seasons produce delight out of season?
This appears to be an obstacle ordained by the enemy of the asuras, who is filled with fear. (21)
Fragrant, cool, and captivating breezes blow;
there is no other cause for this here than the performance of a hundred sacrifices.
While the eminent brahmin, the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa, was speaking thus,
all those led by Manmatha then came within the range of his vision.
The Blessed One, Nara, and likewise Nārāyaṇa, beheld them all;
both of them became filled with wonder in their minds.
Manmatha, Menakā, Rambhā, Tilottamā, Puṣpagandhā, Sukeśī, Mahāśvetā, and Manoramā. || 25 ||
[He saw] Pramadvarā and Dhṛtācī, who were skilled in song and possessed lovely smiles;
and Candraprabhā and Somā, adorned with the warbling of cuckoos. || 26 ||
Vidyunmālā, Ambujākṣī, and Kāñcanamālinī—
these and other women of beautiful form were then seen by the two of them nearby.
Seeing those sixteen thousand and fifty [women], they both became amazed at that vast army of Kama.
Then all those celestial courtesans, adorned with divine ornaments and enriched by divine garlands, stood bowing before him.
Under the pretext of singing, they all sang that which is exceedingly rare on earth—divine, remaining as it was, and increasing passion and the like. (30)
Then the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu—Nara and Nārāyaṇa—heard [them].
Having heard them, the sage Nārāyaṇa spoke there to them with affection.
"Please sit here comfortably; I shall provide you with wonderful hospitality.
O slender-waisted ladies, you have arrived from heaven in the capacity of guests. (32)
Vyāsa said:
At that time, the sage Nārāyaṇa became filled with pride;
surely she had been sent by Indra with the intent to create an obstacle.
"Who are all these wretched women? Indeed, I shall create new ones today.
By means of the power of my asceticism, I shall show them forms of divine beauty. (34)
Having reflected thus in his mind, he struck the thigh with his hand and,
with great speed, produced a woman beautiful in every limb.
Then they beheld the auspicious Urvaśī, born from the thigh of Nārāyaṇa, standing there; seeing her, they were struck with the utmost wonder.
And for the sake of serving them, the sage, remaining unperturbed, then suddenly manifested an equal number of exceedingly beautiful women.
Singing and laughing, with various offerings in their hands,
all those women bowed down to the sages, standing before them with palms joined in reverence.
Having beheld that power of asceticism which causes such wonder.
For the celestial maidens were utterly infatuated as they themselves enchanted [the couple];
with the beauty of their lotus-faces radiant with joy, and the lovely creepers of their own limbs bristling with horripilation, they spoke to the two of them. (39)
Beholding your great austerity and likewise your fortitude, how could we children possibly offer praise? We have been consumed by the arrow smeared with the poison of your sidelong glances.
Or is there no distress in the minds of your honors regarding that? 40.
O sages, you two are known to be the supreme portions of Nṛhari, gods who are eternally the repositories of tranquility, self-restraint, and other virtues;
our coming here was not for the sake of service, nor out of desire.
It was solely for the purpose of performing the task of Hari, the performer of a hundred sacrifices. || 41 ||
By what fortune has this meeting with you two been brought about for us? Indeed, that accumulated merit is not known to us.
Your hearts are set upon your own kin; yet toward one like us who has committed an offense, you have shown compassion free from resentment. (42)
The wise and high-souled ones do not at all waste their ascetic merit upon a curse that yields only trivial results.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus heard the words of the celestial maidens who were bowed with humility, those two best of sages spoke.
Delighted, with serene countenances, having conquered desire and greed,
their limbs adorned by the splendor of their own ascetic fervor, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the two sons of Dharma, spoke.
"Let them speak their desired wishes; with satisfied minds, we shall grant them. || 44 ||
"Let them go to heaven, taking with them this large-eyed Urvaśī;
let this charming young girl go today as a gift. (45)
"Born from the thighs, we two have been given by us for the gratification of Maghavan;
may it be well with all the gods, and let them depart as they please. (46)
Henceforth, no one should cause any obstacle to the ascetic practices of anyone.
The goddesses said:
"O illustrious one, where shall we go? We have reached your lotus feet, O Nārāyaṇa, best of gods, with supreme devotion and joy. (47)
O Lord Madhusūdana, if you, whose eyes are like lotus petals, are pleased and grant the boon we desire, we shall speak that which is wished for in our hearts. (48)
O Lord of Gods, O scorcher of foes, become our husband;
O Lord of the Universe, we shall serve you with affection. (49)
Furthermore, there are other beautiful-eyed women created by you, such as Urvaśī and others; let them indeed go to heaven at your command. (50)
"O best of ascetics, let sixteen thousand women remain here— half of that number— and we shall serve you both here."
"O Lord of Gods, grant my desire; O Mādhava, be true to your word!
For the shattering of hope is proclaimed to be the greatest injury to women. (52)
And by the sages who know the Dharma and perceive the truth, those who were overwhelmed with love have been brought here from heaven through the power of their good fortune. (53)
"O Lord of Gods, you ought not to abandon me; you are capable [of granting my wish], O Lord of the World.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"Indeed, for a full thousand years I have performed penance here."
How then can I, who have conquered my senses, bring about the downfall of this lovely-limbed woman?
I have no desire for sensual pleasure or for happiness that destroys the dharma of bliss.
"How could a wise man take pleasure even in the commonality shared with animals?
The Apsarases replied:
"Among the five [objects], beginning with sound, the pleasure of touch is the best. (56)
Indeed, there is no other happiness whatsoever that has the essence of bliss as its root;
therefore, O Great King, by all means do as we say. (57)
Having attained abundant happiness, dwell on Gandhamādana;
for if you desire it, there is no other peak superior to Gandhamādana.
"Enjoy yourself here in this auspicious place, having obtained all these celestial maidens. (59)

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Apsarases Making Their Petition in the Presence of Nārāyaṇa," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Whirlpool of Egoism.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, the powerful son of Dharma [Yudhiṣṭhira]—
He reflected in his mind: "What should be done by me now? (1)
Today, through this association, I shall become an object of ridicule among the hosts of sages;
that this suffering has been obtained due to egoism requires no further deliberation, for it is the very root of the destruction of dharma, namely, the first-born: self-conceit. (2)
Since silence has been declared by the great-souled ones to be the root of the tree of saṃsāra, having seen [him] approaching, I remained there having composed myself in silence. || 3 ||
Because I indulged in a multitude of courtesans, I have become a vessel for suffering;
likewise, women were produced by me through the destruction of dharma.
Those excellent women, afflicted by desire, have set themselves to obstruct me;
today I am indeed like a spider caught in its own web.
"I am bound here by very firm [bonds]; what should be done after this?
If, casting aside anxiety, I abandon these weak women... (6)
Having been cursed, they shall all fall, their desires shattered;
released from this, I shall wander in solitude performing supreme austerity.
"Therefore, having aroused anger, I shall abandon the host of beautiful women.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus reflected in his mind, the sage Nārāyaṇa then— || 8 ||
He reflected in his mind upon the means for generating happiness:
"This second great enemy, anger, is the cause of torment. (9)
Even more prevalent in the world than desire, and more terrible even than greed, one overcome by anger commits violence that destroys life. (10)
It brings suffering to all beings and serves as a long pond for the pleasure-garden of hell;
just as fire produced by friction burns down a tree, so does it consume them.
"Likewise, the fierce anger born within the body consumes the body itself.
Vyāsa said:
While his brother was thus reflecting with a distressed mind... (12)
Nara, the younger brother of Dharmasuta, spoke these truthful words:
Nara said, "O illustrious Nārāyaṇa, O high-minded one, restrain your anger. (13)
"Resorting to a state of tranquility, destroy that supreme egoism;
for in the past, it is said that our ascetic power was destroyed by the fault of egoism. (14)
And a most wonderful battle took place between those two beings and the asura Prahlāda for a thousand divine years.
O best of gods, we have experienced much suffering there;
therefore, O Lord of Sages, abandon your anger and become peaceful. (16)
Quiescence is proclaimed by the sages to be the root of austerity.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, the son of Dharma became tranquil.
Janamejaya said:
O best of sages, this doubt was [raised] by the high-souled Prahlāda.
How was war fought in ancient times by a peaceful devotee of Viṣṇu?
And how did the two sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, engage in battle? (18)
How did the meeting between those two ascetics, the sons of Dharma, both of whom were perfectly tranquil in mind, and the son of the Daitya come about?
How was that battle waged by him with those two great-souled ones?
For Prahlāda too was exceedingly righteous, wise, and devoted to Viṣṇu.
Likewise, Nara and Nārāyaṇa were ascetics established in goodness;
yet, through that [power], enmity arose between them.
At that time, in both austerity and dharma, there was indeed nothing but mere exertion;
for where was recitation, and where was the practice of penance even in the former Satya Yuga?
The mind, enveloped by anger and egoism, has not been conquered by such as these;
for neither anger nor envy exists without the sprout of egoism. (23)
It is said that desire, anger, and the like arise from the ego (ahaṅkāra);
yet, having performed most rigorous penance for thousands of millions of years, [they were subdued].
Once the sprout of egoism has arisen, everything becomes entirely futile;
just as when the sun has risen, that which consists of darkness no longer remains. || 25 ||
Likewise, merit does not remain at the tip of the sprout of egoism;
even the illustrious Prahlāda fought with Hari. (26)
Then indeed all the merit performed on this earth would have been rendered futile, had the peaceful Nara and Nārāyaṇa abandoned their supreme asceticism. 27.
When they have already engaged in battle, where is there peace or further merit?
For if egoism were invincible against two such beings endowed with strength, [what could be done]? (28)
O Sage, what can be said of those like me regarding the destruction of ego?
There is no one in the three worlds who has completely abandoned ego. (29)
That which has not been, will not be, and does not exist—by him it is abandoned in every way;
thus one who is bound by iron shackles as well as those made of wood is liberated.
But one bound by egoism is never liberated;
the entire world, both moving and stationary, is enveloped by egoism. 31.
For one indeed wanders in this saṃsāra, which is defiled by excrement and urine;
how then can there be knowledge of Brahman in this saṃsāra enveloped by delusion? (32)
O observer of noble vows, the doctrine of the Mīmāṃsakas indeed appears highly esteemed;
yet even great men, O sage, are always bound by desire, anger, and other such passions. (33)
"O best of sages, what talk can there be for those like me in this Kali age?
Vyāsa said:
"O Bhārata, how indeed can an effect be distinct from its cause?"
Just as a bracelet and an earring are essentially identical to gold, so too is the entire universe, including all moving and non-moving beings, born from the ego (ahaṅkāra). 35.
A cloth is said to exist by virtue of its threads; how could it exist when separated from them?
All things, both stationary and moving, are fashioned from the three qualities of Māyā. (36)
What lamentation can there be for that which extends even to a blade of grass?
Even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are deluded by egoism. (37)
O best of kings, even the most supreme and wise sages, such as Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, and others, wander within this profound ocean of saṃsāra.
Overcome by these, they wander again and again in this cycle of existence;
O best of kings, there is no embodied being in the three worlds who is not so.
Freed from these qualities of illusion, peaceful and established in the bliss of the Self, he is liberated from desire, anger, greed, and delusion born of egoism. (40)
O best of kings, they do not release any embodied being, even after one has studied the Vedas and Shastras and reflected upon the Puranas. (41)
Having performed pilgrimages, giving, meditation, and the worship of the gods, one who is attached to sense objects performs all such actions like a thief. (42)
O descendant of Kuru, possessed by lust, delusion, and pride, he does not reflect beforehand, even during the Kṛta, Tretā, or Dvāpara ages.
Even dharma is pierced here; what then can be said of the Kali age?
There is constant rivalry and malice, along with greed and indignation at all times.
Such is the nature of this saṃsāra; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Those who have cast away envy and are truly virtuous are rare in this world. (45)

"Those who have conquered anger, who have conquered resentment, and who remain established in the meaning of the examples—the King said: 'They are blessed; they have performed meritorious deeds; they are free from intoxication and delusion. (46)
Those who have conquered their senses and follow virtuous conduct have already conquered the three worlds;
yet, remembering the sin of my high-souled father, I am consumed with grief.
Indeed, a dead snake placed around the neck of an ascetic brings no sin;
therefore, O best of sages, what can he do before me? (48)
I do not know what will happen next due to the confusion of my intellect;
the fool perceives only the honey and does not see the precipice at all. (49)
He performs censurable deeds and does not fear the hells.
Tell me in detail how that battle occurred in the past. (50)
And just as [the battle] was fierce between Prahlāda and Nara-Nārāyaṇa,
tell me how Prahlāda indeed departed from Pātāla.
At the great and holy pilgrimage site of Sārasvata, in the sacred hermitage of Badarikāśrama,
dwell the peaceful Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the two ascetics and best of sages.
O giver of honor, for what reason did you two engage in such a battle?
Hostility between people arises either for the sake of wealth or for the sake of a wife. (53)
Why did those two, who are free from worldly desire, engage in this great battle?
And why did even the righteous-souled Prahlāda, having recognized the two as eternal gods, [join them]? (54)
How did he wage war against the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa?
O Brahman, I wish to hear the reason for this in detail.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Revolving of Ego," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of Prahlāda’s Pilgrimage.
Sūta said:
Thus was the brahmin questioned at that time by King Pārīkṣita.
Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, related everything in detail.
The righteous Janamejaya, too,
having perceived the wickedness of mind of the son of Vairāṭī, attained a state of supreme world-weariness.
He constantly set his mind upon the deliverance of that very person who,
through the sin of insulting a Brahmin, had indeed gone to the realm of Yama.
O lords of sages, because he protects his own father from the hell named Punnāma and others, the name "putra" (son) becomes meaningful for him.
Having heard that the king had been bitten by a serpent and likewise died upon his palace roof,
[it was known] that this son of Uttara was devoid of ritual bathing and charity due to the curse of a brahmin.
Having heard of his father's fate, that illustrious King Pārīkṣita became filled with world-weariness; he was deeply distressed and overwhelmed by fear.
Then the blameless one questioned the sage Vyāsa, who had arrived at his home,
regarding this story of Nara and Nārāyaṇa which he had completely forgotten.
Vyāsa said: O King, when that fierce Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain,
his son named Prahlāda was then consecrated in the kingdom.
While that lord of the Daityas, who worshipped gods and Brahmins,
was ruling, kings on earth performed sacrifices with great faith.
The Brāhmaṇas perform austerities and religious duties and undertake pilgrimages;
the Vaiśyas remain established in their respective vocations, and the Śūdras are devoted to service.
Then, established in Pātāla by Nṛsiṃha, that king of the Daityas ruled right there, devoted to the protection of his subjects. || 11 ||
Once, the son of Bhṛgu, known as Cyavana, a man of great asceticism,
went to the Narmadā river to bathe at the holy site of Vyāhṛtīśvara.
Having seen the great river Revā, he then descended into it;
as he was crossing over, a serpent terrifying with its venom seized him.
Seized and terrified, that best of sages remembered Viṣṇu, Janārdana, the God of gods, within his mind while in Pātāla.
When the lotus-eyed Lord was remembered, the great serpent became free from poison;
Cyavana felt no suffering even as he was being led to the subterranean realm.
Abandoned by the double-tongued [serpent] who was despondent and full of apprehension, the sage might curse me in his anger, thinking, "This ascetic is a great man. (16)
Honored by the daughters of the Nāgas, that best of sages wandered about;
then he entered the great city of the Nāgas and the Dānavas.
Once, that king of the Daityas, Prahlāda, who was devoted to righteousness, beheld the son of Bhṛgu wandering in that excellent city.
Having seen him, the lord of the Daityas then honored the sage and asked:
"Tell me, what is the reason for your coming to Pātāla?"
"O best of the twice-born, tell me truly:
have you been sent by Indra, who is filled with hatred for the Daityas and desires to see my kingdom? (20)
Cyavana said:
"O King, what have I to do with Maghavan, since I was sent back? While performing the duty of a messenger, I have arrived here in your city."
"Know me to be that son of Bhṛgu, Svanetra, who is devoted to dharma. O Lord of Daityas, do not entertain any suspicion regarding me, for I have been sent by Vāsava. (22)
O best of kings, having arrived at the Narmadā at a holy ford for the purpose of bathing,
I descended into the very river and was seized by a great serpent.
That serpent became poisonless as if from the mere remembrance of Viṣṇu;
indeed, I was liberated by that Nāga through the power of that remembrance.
"O Indra among kings, by coming here I have obtained the sight of you. O Lord of Daityas, you are a devotee of Viṣṇu; therefore, consider me as one devoted to Him. (25)
Vyāsa said: Having heard those gentle words of Hiraṇyakaśipu’s son, he,
with great affection, inquired about various sacred fords (tīrthas).
Prahlāda said:
O best of sages, which sacred places on earth are meritorious?
Likewise, tell us in detail those in the netherworld (pātāla) and in the sky.
Cyavana said:
"O King, for those pure in mind, speech, and body, there is a sacred ford at every step;
however, for those with defiled minds, even the Gaṅgā is worse than the land of Kīkaṭa."
If first the mind becomes pure and freed from evil, then indeed all sacred fords become purifying. (29)
For along the entire course of the Ganges' bank dwell cities,
as well as cow-pens, mines, villages, and all other types of settlements.
O best of Daityas, there are also the dwellings of the Niṣādas, as well as others such as the Kaivartas, Hūṇas, Vaṅgas, and Khasas— those who are Mlecchas.
O Lord of Daityas, people always drink the water of the Gaṅgā, which is eternally equal to Brahman; they bathe there at their own will during the three periods of the day.
In that regard, O noble one, not even a single person becomes pure of soul;
what then is the fruit of the sacred ford for those whose selves are afflicted by sense objects?
O King, reflect upon this: the mind alone is the cause here, and nothing else.
One who desires purity must constantly cultivate the purity of the mind. (34)
One who dwells at a sacred ford (tīrtha) becomes a great sinner through self-deception;
the sin committed right there leads to infinite [retribution].
Just as a ripe *indravāruṇa* fruit does not become sweet, so too, O father, one whose inner disposition is corrupt is not purified even by ten million pilgrimages to sacred sites. (36)
One who desires what is auspicious must first purify the mind;
when the mind is pure, the purity of the ritual substance follows, and not otherwise. (37)
In that very way, there shall be purity of conduct, and thereby the sacred site (tīrtha) becomes perfected;
otherwise, however, everything performed becomes useless at that very moment.
Having gone to a sacred ford, one should always avoid contact with those of inferior caste.
Compassion for all living beings must be practiced through both action and thought.
If you ask, O Indra among kings, I shall describe to you the unsurpassed sacred site (tīrtha). 39.
First is the meritorious Naimiṣa, then Cakratīrtha and Puṣkara; indeed, there is no counting the number of other holy fords on the surface of the earth. (40)
"And there are many purifying places, O best of kings.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words, the king prepared to go to Naimiṣa.
With a mind overflowing with joy, he indeed urged the Daityas forward.
Prahlāda said:
"Arise, O highly fortunate ones; we shall go today to Naimiṣa."
"We shall see the lotus-eyed, yellow-robed, and infallible one.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by that devotee of Viṣṇu, all those Dānavas then—
Together with him, those mighty Daityas and Dānavas emerged from Pātāla with supreme joy, having come together.
Having reached the Naimiṣa forest, they joyfully performed their ablutions;
there, Prahlāda, accompanied by the Daityas, wandered among the sacred fords.
O best of kings, he beheld the highly meritorious Sarasvatī with its pure waters at that sacred ford belonging to the high-souled Prahlāda.
Having bathed in the waters of the Sarasvatī, his mind became serene;
there, O Lord of Daityas, he duly performed auspicious acts such as bathing and giving gifts. (47)
With a heart exceedingly serene, he performed [his rites] at that most purifying sacred ford.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Prahlāda’s Pilgrimage," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Viṣṇu’s Arrival during the Battle between Prahlāda and Nārāyaṇa.
Vyāsa said:
While performing the rites for the sacred bathing place there, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu—
Then he saw before him a very large nyagrodha tree with a vast shade. || 1 ||
Then he saw other arrows of various kinds—
fierce, whetted on stone, blazing with great luster, and furnished with vulture feathers.
He reflected in his mind: "Whose arrows are these here in this holy hermitage of sages, at this most purifying sacred ford?"
While he was reflecting thus, he then beheld the two sons of Dharma, sages wearing black antelope skins and bearing heavy masses of matted hair.
In front of them were held two bright bows endowed with auspicious marks—
the Śārṅga and the Ājagava— as well as two inexhaustible great quivers.
Then the lord of the Daityas beheld there the two highly fortunate rishis, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, established in meditation, along with the two sons of Dharma.
With eyes red with anger, the protector of the asuras spoke to them both:
"Why have you begun this deceit that destroys righteousness? (7)
Indeed, neither has it been heard nor ever seen in this saṃsāra that there was such a practice of severe austerity as well as the wielding of a bow.
This is a contradiction; how is it appropriate for that which is dear to Kali to exist in the first age? For a Brāhmaṇa, asceticism is proper; what then is the purpose of carrying a weapon?
Where is this wearing of matted hair upon the body, and where these quivers that are mere mockery?
It is fitting for you two, who possess divine natures, to practice righteousness.
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words of his, O Bhārata, Nara spoke:
"O Lord of Daityas, what is this anxiety of yours here? Why do you both engage in fruitless asceticism?"
Whatever one who possesses capability might do would surely succeed;
for we two, O dull-witted one, are world-renowned as being capable in these two tasks.
"You possess prowess in battle and in asceticism; what, then, will you do?
Go by whatever path you desire; why do you boast here? (13)
The splendor of Brahman is difficult to propitiate; you do not know this, being utterly deluded.
Those living beings who desire happiness should not engage in disputes with Brahmins. (14)
Prahlāda said:
"You two ascetics are of dull intellect; you are falsely deluded by pride while I, the lord of the Daityas and upholder of the bridge of dharma, am present. (15)
"Furthermore, it is not fitting for unrighteous conduct to be practiced in this sacred place.
O ascetic, what power do you have in battle? Show it now! (16)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, the man replied to him:
"If such is your mind, then fight with me today."
Today I shall shatter your head, O lowest of asuras!
(After this, you shall never again have any desire for battle.)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, the lord of the Daityas then became enraged.
The powerful Prahlāda then made this vow:
"By whatever means possible, I shall conquer both of them. (19)
"Nara and Nārāyaṇa are self-controlled sages endowed with ascetic power.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken these words, the Daitya took up his bow.
Having swiftly drawn his bow, he made the sound of the bowstring;
Nara also took up his bow and [prepared] sharp arrows whetted on stone.
O King, out of anger, he repeatedly hurled [them] at Prahlāda.
The king of the Daityas, having swiftly approached, cut those arrows with shafts made of refined gold;
seeing his own discharged arrows severed, Nara, filled with rage, quickly released others.

The lord of the Daityas, having cut those [arrows] with arrows of fierce velocity, struck that lord of sages in the chest; Nara, also enraged, struck the lord of the Daityas on the arm with five swift arrows.
The gods, together with Indra, remained in their celestial chariots in the sky there to witness the battle between those two,
and the prowess of Nara as he stood firm in combat.
And they praised the Lord of the Daityas once again. || 25 ||
The lord of the Daityas, having taken up his bow, rained down arrows like a cloud pouring forth water;
he took up the immeasurable Śārṅga bow.
He released arrows with sharp, golden shafts.
O King, a tumultuous battle took place between those two, the god and the daitya, as they both sought victory;
while stationed in the path of the sky, they rained down [missiles].
With joyful hearts, they offered divine flowers. || 27 ||
The lord of the Daityas became enraged at Hari and released arrows of exceedingly fierce velocity;
the son of Dharma then swiftly cut them down with very sharp shafts discharged from his bow.

Then Prahlāda showered Nārāyaṇa— the hero, the son of Dharma, the eternal one who stands firm— with exceedingly sharp arrows. Nārāyaṇa, for his part, [struck] him with arrows whetted on stone and released with great force.
He struck with great force at the lord of the Daityas standing before him;
meanwhile, a gathering of those desiring to witness the spectacle took place in the sky.
While the gods and the dānavas were raising shouts of victory,
the sky was then shrouded by the rain of arrows from both sides.
Even by day, there was a great darkness resembling night;
the gods and the Daityas, being utterly amazed, spoke to one another.
"Indeed, a most terrible battle, never seen before, is taking place today;
the celestial sages, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, and Pannagas [are watching]. (33)
The Vidyādharas and Cāraṇas were filled with supreme wonder;
the two sages, Nārada and Parvata, remained there for the sake of witnessing the spectacle.
Nārada said to Parvata: "Such a thing has never occurred before, nor did the battle with the demon Tāraka or the demon Vṛtra. (35)
Such was the battle waged by Hari against Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
for Prahlāda was a powerful hero who [even] confronted Nārāyaṇa himself.
He engaged in a battle equal to that of the Siddha of wondrous deeds.
Vyāsa said:
Day after day, and likewise night after night, he did this again and again. (37)
Then those two, the Daitya and the ascetic, engaged in a supreme battle;
Nārāyaṇa, however, cut asunder Prahlāda’s bow.
With one swift arrow he took up another bow,
while Nārāyaṇa, with speed, released another shaft.
At that very moment, the light-handed one cut the bow in the middle;
whenever the Daitya’s bow was cut, he took up another.
But Nārāyaṇa, provoked to anger, swiftly cut it asunder with his arrows;
when his bow was severed, the lord of the Daityas took up a mace.
Exceedingly enraged, he swiftly struck the son of Dharma between the arms;
as he was approaching, the powerful sage [struck him] with nine arrows.
He cut the terrible iron club with ten arrows and struck him;
then the lord of the Daityas took up a firm mace made entirely of iron.
Standing firm like a mountain with a steady mind, he swiftly struck Lord Nārāyaṇa on the knee with his mace out of rage.
The exceedingly powerful son of Dharma quickly released his feathered arrows;
then the Blessed One shattered the firm mace of the lord of the Daityas.
The spectators stationed in the sky were filled with supreme wonder;
then Prahlāda, the slayer of enemy heroes, took up his spear.
Enraged, he forcefully hurled it with all his might at the chest of Nārāyaṇa;
seeing it rushing toward him, [Nārāyaṇa] effortlessly struck it down with a single arrow. || 47 ||
Having quickly divided him into seven parts, he struck him with those seven;
that supreme battle between the two lasted for a hundred divine years.
O King, a wonder was born there in that hermitage for everyone;
then, the four-armed one clad in yellow garments arrived with speed.
And there Gadādhara went to the hermitage of Prahlāda—
the four-armed beloved of Ramā, bearing the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Seeing him arrived there, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu bowed with supreme devotion and, with palms joined in reverence, replied: || 51 ||
Prahlāda said: O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Mādhava, who are affectionate toward your devotees,
why did I not defeat these two ascetics in battle?
"O Lord, I have waged war for a full hundred years."
"Why have these two not been conquered by the gods? This is my great wonder.
Viṣṇu said:
"These two are perfected beings (siddhas) and portions of myself; what cause for wonder is there in this, O noble one?"
The two ascetics, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, who have conquered their own selves, have not been defeated; you have been defeated.
Go now to Vitala, O King, and offer me unwavering devotion. (54)
"O high-minded one, do not create enmity with these two ascetics.
Vyāsa said:
Thus commanded, the king of the Daityas set out together with the asuras.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa once again became engaged in ascetic penance.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Viṣṇu’s Arrival during the Battle between Prahlāda and Nārāyaṇa," in the fourth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Cause of Bhṛgu’s Curse.
Janamejaya said: "O son of Parāśara, there is a great doubt here regarding this narrative."
Nara and Nārāyaṇa were peaceful, portions of Viṣṇu, and rich in asceticism.
Resorting to sacred fords, endowed with goodness, always subsisting on forest fare,
those two high-souled sons of Dharma were ascetics established in truth.
How did they become possessed by passion and fight with one another in battle? Why did they engage in combat, having abandoned their unsurpassed asceticism? (3)
O sages, how is it that they both abandoned the bliss of peace and engaged in battle for a full hundred divine years together with Prahlāda?
O sage, how did those two wage war with Prahlāda?
O illustrious one, tell us the cause of that conflict.
The beloved woman is gold; she is indeed the effect and the cause of the body.
How did the thought of war arise in those two who were so detached from it,
and for what reason did they perform such ascetic penance?
O scorcher of foes, for the sake of delusion, for the sake of enjoying pleasures, or for the sake of heaven,
those two performed exceedingly intense penance that yields all fruits.
"What wonderful fruit was obtained by the two sages of tranquil mind?
Their bodies were emaciated by asceticism and repeatedly subjected to battle. (8)
For a full hundred divine years, they were oppressed by toil—
not for the sake of sovereignty, nor for wealth, nor for wives, nor for homes.
For what purpose was this battle waged by him with those two high-souled ones?
Why would a man who is free from worldly desire engage in such a conflict? (10)
Knowing that the body is in every way a source of suffering and that dharma is eternal,
the person of sound intellect always performs actions here that grant happiness.
O knower of dharma, these two do not cause suffering; this is the eternal state.
They are the two sons of Dharma, portions of Hari, omniscient and adorned with every excellence.
How did you two engage in this war, which is a source of suffering and a destroyer of dharma, having abandoned the practiced asceticism that is a garden of happiness and yields great fruit? 13.
O Kṛṣṇa, even a fool does not desire a terrible conflict;
I have heard that King Yayāti fell from heaven.
Felled to the surface of the earth by the sin arising from egoism,
he was a performer of sacrifices, a giver of gifts, and a righteous lord of the earth.
He was struck down by Vajrapāṇi with a mere utterance of words;
it is certain that no battle occurs without egoism. (16)
"What is the fruit of that battle which destroys the merit of the sage?
Vyāsa said: "O King, the root of saṃsāra is indeed proclaimed to be threefold."
Since egoism has been [identified] by all-knowing sages in their determination of the Dharma, how indeed could it be fit to be abandoned by a sage who still possesses a body? (18)
It is certain that an effect cannot exist without a cause;
likewise, austerity, charity, and sacrifices originate from the quality of goodness (sattva). 19.
O highly fortunate one, strife arises from the *rājasa* or the *tāmasa* [qualities];
O Indra among kings, even the slightest action never occurs anywhere without egoism (*ahaṅkāra*).
Whether auspicious or inauspicious, even the very certainty of their arising proceeds from ego; there is nothing else on the surface of the earth that causes bondage. (21)
How could that by which this universe was created be devoid of it?
For Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu—these are all possessed of egoism (ahaṅkāra). || 22 ||
What then can be said of other sages, O lord of the earth?
This entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, wanders about enveloped in egoism.
Rebirth and repeated death—all follow the power of karma for gods, animals, and humans in this cycle of existence, O Lord of the Earth. (24)
The revolving [of the wheel] is always remembered as being like a chariot wheel, not for the sake of all purposes;
for who among men can know the number of even Viṣṇu’s incarnations? (25)
In this vast cycle of existence, among the highest and lowest wombs,
Nārāyaṇa, Hari himself, assumed the form of a fish.
In age after age, Vāsudeva Janārdana, the Lord of the World, appears as Kāmaṭha, Saukara, Nārasiṃha, and Vāmana. (27)
O great king, in the seventh Vaivasvata Manvantara, the Lord Hari, constrained by destiny, performs innumerable incarnations.
O great king, listen now to the truth regarding the incarnations he indeed assumed during the Manvantaras; for due to the curse of Bhṛgu, Viṣṇu, the lord and best of gods, [took these forms].
The Lord of All has indeed performed many incarnations.
The King said: "O Illustrious One, this doubt arises within my heart. (30)
O Grandfather, how was the Lord Viṣṇu cursed by Bhṛgu? And what displeasure was done to that sage by Hari, O Sage? (31)
"Out of anger for which Viṣṇu, who is worshipped by the gods, was cursed by Bhṛgu?
Vyāsa said:
"Listen, O King, I shall explain the cause of Bhṛgu’s curse. (32)
Formerly, when King Hiraṇyakaśipu, the descendant of Kaśyapa, was ruling,
a mutual conflict was waged between him and the gods.
When that king was slain, the entire world became agitated;
then King Prahlāda arose.
Prahlāda, the subduer of enemies, oppressed the gods;
then a terrible battle took place between Śakra and Prahlāda.
For a full hundred years, O King, he performed deeds that caused wonder in the world;
a fierce battle was waged with the gods, and Prahlāda was defeated.
Having attained supreme detachment and realized the eternal Dharma,
O King, Bali established Virocana’s son in the kingdom.
Having obtained the kingdom, the illustrious Bali waged war against the gods; he went to the Gandhamādana mountain to perform austerities. || 38 ||
Since a most terrible mutual battle had arisen,
the Daityas were then defeated by the gods and by Indra of immeasurable splendor.
O King, having been deprived of their kingdom by Viṣṇu acting as their ally,
the defeated Daityas then sought refuge with Kāvya.
"O Brahmin, why do you, being so powerful, not provide us assistance? For we are unable to remain here; indeed, we shall enter the netherworld. (41)
"O best among those who know the mantras, if you are not my helper to protect me," Vyāsa said;
having been addressed thus, the compassionate sage Kāvya spoke to the Daityas.
"Do not fear, O Asuras; I shall sustain you with my own splendor.
Indeed, I shall always provide you assistance through mantras as well as medicinal herbs. (43)
"I shall do it; let them be full of enthusiasm and free from their feverish anxiety.
Vyāsa said:
Then those Daityas became fearless, having taken refuge with Kāvya.
The news was indeed heard by all the gods through the mouths of their spies;
having consulted there with one another and with Śakra, those gods [acted]. 45.
Greatly agitated, they performed a mantra through the power of Kāvya’s incantations:
"Let us go quickly to fight, before they indeed cause us to fall. (46)
"Having forcibly slain them, we shall send the survivors to Pātāla.
Then the gods, enraged and with weapons in hand, went after the Daityas. || 47 ||
Commanded by Hari, they went toward those Dānavas together with Viṣṇu;
but being struck down, those Daityas became terrified and oppressed by fear.
They sought refuge with Kāvya and cried out, "Protect us! Protect us!
Seeing those mighty Daityas thus oppressed by the gods, Śukra [spoke].
"Have no fear," the Lord spoke these words by the power of his mantras and herbs;
having seen Kāvya, all the gods abandoned them and indeed departed.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Cause of Bhṛgu’s Curse," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Killing of Śukra’s Mother.
Vyāsa said:
When the gods had thus departed, Kāvya replied to them.
O best of Dānavas, listen to that which was previously spoken by Brahmā.
Janārdana Viṣṇu, intent on the destruction of the Daityas, will slay them;
having assumed the form of a boar, he will kill them just as Hiraṇyākṣa was slain.
Just as Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by him in the form of Nṛsiṃha, so shall he, having exerted his full effort, slay all; it cannot be otherwise.
The power of my mantra does not manifest correctly enough for me to conquer Hari;
you yourselves are capable of conquering him, O gods, protected as you are by me.
Therefore, wait for some time, O best of Dānavas;
today I shall indeed depart to Mahādeva for the sake of counsel.
"O best of Dānavas, having obtained the mantras from Mahādeva, I shall now return; I will bestow them upon you according to their true purpose."
The Daityas said:
"O best of sages, having been defeated, how shall we be able to remain on earth? We are powerless even to wait for such a length of time. (7)
All the powerful ones have been slain, and only a few Dānavas remain;
it is no longer appropriate for them to stay in battle in such a way that brings ease.
Śukra said:
"Until I have brought the knowledge of mantras from Śaṅkara,
you must remain engaged in austerity and endowed with tranquility."
The wise have declared that conciliation, bribery, and the other [stratagems] are appropriate for the occasion,
once the place, time, strength, power, and force have been understood by the heroes and the learned.
Service toward enemies should be performed at the proper time by those desiring their own welfare;
however, when the time for the increase of one's own power arrives, they should be destroyed by the wise. (11)
Therefore, having today employed discipline preceded by conciliation and indeed through artifice,
remain in your own dwellings, awaiting my return.
