"O Dānavas, having obtained the mantras from Mahādeva, I shall return;
then, relying on the power of the mantras, we shall fight the gods once again. (13)
Having spoken thus to them, O great king, Bhṛgu, the best of sages, made his resolve and departed for Mahādeva in order to obtain the mantra. (14)
The Dānavas sent Prahlāda into the presence of the gods—
he who was truthful in speech, composed, and a source of confidence for the deities.
But Prahlāda, O King, together with the asuras, bowed down with humility and spoke these words full of modesty to the gods. (16)
"Having laid down our weapons and likewise cast off our armor, O gods, we shall practice austerities, clothed in bark garments. (17)
Having heard those words of Prahlāda, which were spoken with truth,
the gods then desisted from their attack, freed from anxiety and filled with joy.
When the Daityas had laid down their weapons, the gods then turned back; full of confidence, they went to their own homes and remained there, well-settled and intent on their pleasures.
Resorting to hypocrisy, the Daityas, appearing as ascetics endowed with austerities,
took up residence in the hermitage of Kaśyapa, desiring the arrival of Kāvya.
Then Kāvya, having gone to Kailāsa and bowed down to Mahādeva, was asked by the Lord, "What is your business? and the master replied. (21)
"O Lord, I desire those mantras which do not exist with Bṛhaspati, for the defeat of the gods and the victory of the asuras. (22)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, the omniscient Śaṅkara-Śiva reflected in his mind: "What should be done after this?"
Now, with a mind intent on hostility toward the gods, this son of Kavi has arrived here for the sake of counsel and for the victory of those Daityas. (24)
Thinking, "The gods must be protected by me," Maheśvara Śaṅkara spoke to him regarding that most fierce and difficult vow.
If you drink the smoke of chaff for a full thousand years with your head hanging downwards—
may it be well with you— then you shall obtain the mantras.
Thus addressed, he bowed to the Lord and spoke these words:
"O God, O Lord of the Suras, commanded by you, I shall indeed perform the vow. (27)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to Śaṅkara, Śukra undertook an excellent vow;
devoted to inhaling smoke, he became tranquil, having resolved upon the meaning of the mantra.
Then the gods, having recognized that Kāvya was devoted to his vows,
while the Daityas were intent on deceit, became absorbed in consultation.
Having deliberated thus with their minds, O King, they all prepared for battle and,
taking up their weapons, went to that place where those foremost of Dānavas were.
Then, seeing them approaching, armed and clad in armor,
those Daityas became agitated with fear on all sides toward the gods.
Afflicted by fear, they suddenly rose up in their armor and spoke these truthful words to the gods who were arrogant with pride: || 32 ||
"When the preceptor has laid down his weapons and is in a state of fear, having previously granted him protection, the gods have come with the intent to kill us. (33)
O gods, where has your truth gone, and where is the dharma taught by the Vedas?
Those who have laid down their weapons must not be slain, nor those who are terrified and have come for refuge. (34)
The gods said:
"Kāvya has been sent by you for the sake of counsel and through deception;
indeed, your ascetic power was known by him, and therefore we shall certainly fight."
"Let them be ready for battle, enraged and with weapons in hand;
an enemy must be struck at his weak point—this is the eternal law. (36)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words and deliberated among themselves, all the Daityas, overwhelmed by fear, set out to flee. || 37 ||
Terrified, the Dānavas went for refuge to Kāvya’s mother;
seeing them deeply distressed, she then granted them fearlessness.
Kāvyamātā said:
"Do not fear, do not fear! Cast away your fear, O Dānavas! As long as you remain in my presence, there ought to be no cause for dread. (39)
Having heard those words, the Daityas stood there free from distress;
indeed, the Asuras remained in that excellent hermitage unarmed and unperturbed.
Seeing those gods in flight, the Dānavas who followed in their wake attacked them by force, without considering the relative strength of the two sides. || 41 ||
All the gods arrived there, intent on slaying the Daityas;
though restrained by Kāvya (Śukra), they nevertheless struck those staying in the hermitage.
Seeing the gods being slain, Kāvya’s mother trembled violently and said to all those who were asleep, "I shall indeed put them to sleep by means of my ascetic power. (43)
Having spoken thus, the instigated Sleep approached them and fell upon them;
including Indra, the gods fell under the power of sleep and remained as if mute.
Seeing Indra overcome by sleep and dejected, Viṣṇu said:
"Enter me; may it be well with you; I shall lead you away, O best of gods. (45)
Having been addressed thus, Purandara then entered Viṣṇu;
protected by Hari, he became fearless and free from sleep.
Seeing Śakra there free from distress because he was protected by Hari, Kāvya’s mother then became enraged and spoke these words: || 47 ||
"O Maghavan, by the power of my asceticism, I shall indeed devour you along with Viṣṇu while all the gods look on; such is the power of my asceticism! (48)
Vyāsa said: When the two gods, Viṣṇu and Indra, were thus addressed by her through that yogic knowledge,
those two high-souled ones became overcome and rendered motionless.
Then the gods, seeing those two so greatly oppressed, were struck with wonder;
they uttered cries of "kilakila," yet their minds were filled with dejection.
Seeing the gods crying out, the Lord of Śacī said to Viṣṇu:
"O Madhusūdana, I am being especially overwhelmed by you."
O Viṣṇu, O Lord, slay her by force before she consumes us;
O Mādhava, do not hesitate regarding this wicked woman who is arrogant because of her asceticism. 52.
Thus addressed by Śakra and the renowned [Viśvakarman],
Lord Viṣṇu Mādhava then quickly called to mind his discus, casting aside all compassion.
As soon as it was remembered, the discus, following the will of Viṣṇu, arrived;
and urged by Śakra, he, filled with rage, held it in his hand for the purpose of slaying.
Having seized that discus in his hand, he swiftly severed her head;
seeing her slain, Śakra then became filled with joy. || 55 ||
The gods were exceedingly satisfied; crying out "Victory! Victory to Hari!", they all praised him with joy, their distress having vanished.
At that very moment, Indra and Viṣṇu were born with pained hearts,
fearing the unavoidable curse of Bhṛgu resulting from the killing of a woman.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of Śukra’s Mother," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 11 ||
The Description of Jayantī’s Co-residence with Śukra.
Vyāsa said:
Having witnessed that terrible slaughter, the venerable Bhṛgu became enraged.
Trembling and afflicted by extreme sorrow, he spoke to Madhusūdana.
Bhṛgu said:
O Viṣṇu, O high-minded one, though you knew it was wrong, you have committed a sin;
this killing of a woman of the brahmin caste was impossible for you to even contemplate in your mind.

You are declared to possess the quality of goodness (sattva), while Brahmā is remembered as having the quality of passion (rajas); likewise, Śambhu is said to have the quality of darkness (tamas). How is it that this is considered the reverse?
How have you become possessed by tamas? Why was such a highly censurable deed committed?
O Viṣṇu, why was a woman—who ought not to be slain—killed by you when she was innocent?
I curse you, O man of evil conduct; what else can I do for you?
O sinful one, I have been rendered helpless by you on account of Śakra.
I do not curse Śakra in that manner; rather, I curse you, O Madhusūdana!
You are always intent on deceit, born from the womb of a worm, and evil-minded.
And those sages who call you "sāttvika" are indeed fools;
for you, O Janārdana, are manifest before my eyes as one of tamasic conduct.
May there be incarnations in the world of mortals arising from my curse;
O Janārdana, endure the suffering of birth from a womb as a result of your own sin.
Vyāsa said: Then, when dharma had been repeatedly destroyed by that curse,
he was born here among human beings for the sake of the welfare of the world.
The king said:
"The wife of Bhūgu was slain there by the discus of immeasurable splendor;
how then did the state of householdership arise again for that high-souled one?"
Vyāsa said:
Having thus cursed Hari in anger, Bhṛgu, who knew his purpose, quickly took that head and swiftly joined it back to the body; then he spoke.
"O Goddess, today I shall restore you to life, slain as you are by Viṣṇu, if indeed the entirety of dharma is known or even practiced by me. (12)
If I speak the truth, may I live by that truth;
let all the deities behold my great splendor and power.
"Sprinkling you with cool waters, I restore you to life by the power of my asceticism, provided that truth, purity, and the Vedas constitute the strength of my penance. (14)
Vyāsa said:
Sprinkled with water, the goddess was then instantly restored to life;
the wife of Bhṛgu, possessed of a radiant smile, rose up filled with supreme joy. (15)
Then, seeing her as if she had just awakened from sleep, all beings praised her from every direction, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! (16).
Thus was that woman of excellent complexion brought back to life by that Bhṛgu;
seeing this, the gods, including Indra, were struck with the utmost wonder.
Indra then said to the gods: "Now that Śukrācārya has been restored to life by the sage, what will he do, he who is a knower of mantras after having performed such severe penance?"
Vyāsa said:
O King, sleep has departed from the body of the lord of the gods,
and distress has arisen within him as he recalled the account of Kāvya and the exceedingly terrible purpose of the mantra.
Then Śakra, having reflected with his mind upon his daughter Jayantī,
spoke these words preceded by a smile to the girl of beautiful limbs.
"Go, my daughter; you have been given by me to the ascetic Kāvya. Propitiate him, O slender-limbed one, and bring him under your control for my sake. (21)
"Having propitiated the sage with various services pleasing to the mind,
go quickly to that excellent hermitage and remove my fear.
Hearing her father's words, she, the beautiful one, went there.
The large-eyed woman saw him drinking smoke in the hermitage.
Then, beholding his body and remembering the words of his father,
he took a plantain leaf and fanned that sage.
Having quickly brought pure, cool, and well-perfumed water, he prepared it for drinking with the highest devotion. (25)
When the sun was at its zenith, that slender-limbed woman, remaining steadfast in her virtue, herself created shade with a cloth parasol.
Having brought divine fruits that were ripe and sweet, he placed them before the sage, prepared for him to eat.
Then, for the successful completion of his daily rites, he held at the tip [of his hand] green kuśa grass, a span in length and resembling parrots.
She prepared a bed strewn with sprouts for the sake of his sleep;
and while that sage was there, she stood respectfully and fanned him gently.
At that time, Jayantī, fearing the sage’s curse, did not display any gestures of coquetry (*hāva*), emotional expressions (*bhāva*), or anything else that might produce a transformation in him.
The slender-limbed woman offered praise to that high-souled one with well-spoken words that were both favorable and truly heart-warming.
When he had awakened, she took water and held it for him to sip;
constantly doing what was pleasing to his mind, she then moved about.
Indra, too, being clever, dispatched servants there,
desiring indeed to learn news of that self-controlled sage.
Thus, for many years, she remained devoted to her service—
unchanging, having conquered anger, and dedicated to the life of celibacy.
When a full thousand years had passed, Maheśvara was thoroughly pleased;
Hara, with a joyful mind, invited Kāvya to choose a boon.
Īśvara said:
"O Brahmin, O descendant of Bhṛgu, whatever little exists that you perceive, and whatever is not to be spoken of to anyone— " (36)
By virtue of your all-surpassing power,
you will undoubtedly become invincible to all beings, the lord of creatures, and the best among the twice-born.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus granted these boons, Śambhu vanished on that very spot.
Then Kāvya, beholding Jayantī, spoke these words: || 38 ||
"Who are you, whose daughter are you, O fair-hipped one? Tell me, what do you intend to do? For what purpose have you arrived here? O lady of beautiful thighs, tell me your business. (39)
"What do you desire? Shall I perform today even that which is difficult to accomplish, O fair-eyed one?
I am pleased by what you have done; choose a boon, O lady of virtuous vows. (40)
Then Jayantī, with a joyful countenance, spoke to the sage:
"O Blessed One, you ought to know what I intend to do through my ascetic penance. (41)
Śukra said: "I already know this; nevertheless, tell me what you desire in your heart.
I shall accomplish it in every way, O auspicious one, for I am pleased with your service."
Jayantī said: "O Brahmin, I am the daughter of Śakra; I have been entrusted to you by my father.
O Sage, I am Jayantī by name, the younger sister of Jayanta. (43)
"I am filled with desire for you, O Lord; fulfill my wish now.
O illustrious one, I shall enjoy your company in accordance with dharma and with love. (44)
Śukra said:
"O fair-hipped one, O beautiful woman, remain here with me for ten years,
invisible to all beings, and enjoy yourself as you please."
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus and returned home, the descendant of Bhṛgu took the hand of Jayantī in marriage and lived with that goddess for ten years.
The Lord, concealed by his illusory power (māyā), remained invisible to all beings;
yet the Daityas, hearing that he had arrived accompanied by his mantra and having accomplished his purpose, [were alarmed].
Desirous of seeing him, they joyfully went to his house;
however, they did not see him rejoicing, united with Jayantī.
Then they all became dejected and their efforts were frustrated;
overcome by anxiety and deeply distressed, they gazed at him again and again.
But not seeing him, as he had vanished, those foremost of Daityas returned the way they had come to their own homes, overcome with anxiety and afflicted by fear.
Knowing that he was thus enjoying himself, Śakra spoke to his preceptor Bṛhaspati: "O highly fortunate one, what should be done after this?"
"Go today, O Brahmin, and entice the Dānavas with your power of illusion;
having reflected well with your intellect, O giver of honor, accomplish our task. (52)
Having heard those words of Kāvya, which were delightful and well-composed,
and having understood their intent, the Guru assumed that very form and went to the Daityas.
Having gone there, he summoned the Dānavas with great devotion;
all those Asuras arrived and beheld Kāvya before them.
Having bowed down, they all stood there, utterly deluded, considering it to be the work of Kāvya; they did not recognize the guru’s māyā, which had manifested in the form of Kāvya.
The preceptor, in the form of Kāvya, spoke to them through his concealed power of illusion:
"Welcome! I have arrived for the benefit of you, my sacrificers."
I shall awaken you to the knowledge obtained through non-deception;
Śambhu, gratified by my ascetic penance, has done so for the sake of your welfare.
Having heard that, those best of Dānavas became joyful in mind;
considering their preceptor’s task accomplished, they rejoiced, being utterly deluded.
Filled with joy, free from fear and devoid of distress, they prostrated themselves;
having cast off all dread of the gods, they all remained in a state of perfect well-being.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of Jayantī’s Dwelling with Śuka," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 12.
The Description of the Deception of the Daityas by the Preceptor in the Form of Śukra.
The King said:
What was done by the preceptor while he existed subsequently in the form of Bhṛgu?
Indeed, by means of his guile alone, through the office of priest held by that wise one, [he overcame] the Daityas. || 1 ||
The preceptor of the gods, an inexhaustible treasury of all branches of knowledge and the very son of Aṅgiras—how could such a sage be a practitioner of deceit? (2)
In all the treatises on Dharma, truth has been declared by the sages to be the cause of righteousness, by means of which even the Supreme Self is attained.
If even Vācaspati speaks falsely toward the Dānavas, who then will be a speaker of truth in this world as a householder? (4)
There is no food greater than nourishment, even within the vast resources of the entire universe;
O sage, why then do sages engage in falsehood for its sake? (5)
In the absence of learned authorities (śiṣṭas), has the authority of verbal testimony (śabdapramāṇa) not been destroyed?
Or, how can there be the quality of being unobjectionable (avigītatva) regarding a teacher who is engaged in deceitful actions?
The gods are said by the sages to have arisen from sattva, human beings from rajas, and animals from tamas at the time of their creation.
If even the preceptor of the immortals were himself a speaker of falsehood, then who could be a speaker of truth? Especially one who is a king and of a tamasic nature.
Where does that Dharma abide? This is my own doubt. What is the destiny of all living beings when the three worlds are illusory?
Hari, Brahmā, the beloved of Śacī, and other foremost of the gods—all are skilled in the art of deception; what then can be said of human beings?
All the gods and the sages whose wealth is austerity are consumed by desire and anger, their minds struck down by greed, and they are all skilled in deceit. (11)
Vasiṣṇṭha, Vāmadeva, Viśvāmitra, and likewise the Guru—these were devoted to sin; what, then, O giver of honor, is the destiny of dharma here?
Indra, Agni, the Moon, and Brahmā are all lusting after the wives of others;
O Sage, tell me, where in these worlds does true nobility reside? (13)
O sinless one, whose word should be accepted as authoritative advice?
At that time, all those gods and sages were overcome by greed.
Vyāsa said:
Is it Viṣṇu, or Śiva, or Brahmā, or Maghavan, or Bṛhaspati? For one who possesses a body is indeed subject to power only when joined with the transformations [of nature]. (15)
Viṣṇu is possessed of passion, Śiva is possessed of passion, and even Brahmā is joined with passion;
O lord of men, what indeed is there that one who possesses passion would not do?
Even though he possesses passion, through his cleverness he appears like one who is bodiless (videha). || 16 ||
Even he, when a crisis arrives, is indeed constrained by his own qualities;
for how can an effect exist without a cause? (17)
Indeed, for all beings beginning with Brahmā, the qualities (guṇas) alone are the cause;
their bodies arise from the twenty-five principles and not otherwise. (18)
O King, those subject to the law of death will die in due time; what doubt can you have in this matter?
For all refined people are perfectly clear in their instructions to others. (19)
For when one's own duty has presented itself, there is a general failure [to perform it] due to desire, anger, greed, malice, egoism, and envy. (20)
O Great King, what embodied being is capable of abandoning them again? This cycle of worldly existence is traditionally held to be always of such a nature.
Indeed, the world consisting of good and evil cannot possibly arise otherwise;
for at times the Lord Viṣṇu performs severe ascetic penance.
Sometimes the Lord of the Gods performs various sacrifices,
while at other times the Supreme Lord is delighted by the theater of the goddess Ramā.
It is said that the youthful and all-pervading Lord sports in Vaikuṇṭha under their control;
once, he engaged in a most terrible battle with the Dānavas.
Afflicted intensely by those arrows, that ocean of compassion sometimes achieves victory, and at other times, even he suffers defeat through the power of fate. (25)
Overcome by pleasure and pain, he certainly becomes thus; there is no doubt.
At times, indeed, he lies upon Śeṣa, enveloped in yogic sleep.
At the appointed time, the Soul of the Universe awakens, awakened by His own nature—He who is Śarva, Brahmā, Hari, and likewise Indra and all the other gods. (27)
Indeed, the sages move about through their own emanations during the duration of their lives;
for when the end of the night has arrived, the world of both the stationary and the moving beings [awakens].
O King, there is no doubt that nothing ever dies at any time;
O Ruler of the Earth, it is only at the end of their own lifespan that those beginning with the lotus-born Brahmā meet their destruction.
Furthermore, the gods such as Viṣṇu, Hara, and Śakra attain their power;
therefore, an embodied being experiences states such as desire and the like.
O King, you should never feel astonishment at this;
for this cycle of worldly existence, O Monarch, is fraught with uncertainty due to desire, anger, and other such passions.
Rare is the person who, being liberated from that [bondage], knows the ultimate truth;
he who fears this worldly existence does not even take a wife.
Freed from all attachments, he wanders about without fear;
therefore, the wife of Bṛhaspati was recovered by the Moon once again.
A wife may be bestowed by one's gurus, or likewise by a younger brother;
thus, in this wheel of worldly existence, one is enveloped by passion, greed, and other such afflictions.
And having entered the state of a householder, how may a man become liberated?
Therefore, with every effort, one should abandon the notion that worldly existence possesses any essence. (35)
One should propitiate Maheśānī, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
by her māyā and its qualities, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is concealed.
O King, everything wanders like one who is insane or like one intoxicated by wine;
and by the propitiation of her alone, all virtues are crushed.
The wise man should resort to liberation; there is no other path beyond this, as long as Maheśānī, when propitiated, does not bestow her grace.
Until then, how could there be happiness? For who else is endowed with compassion?
Therefore, one should worship this ocean of mercy with sincerity and without guile. (39)
But he who, having attained this rare human birth, does not serve the Great Goddess—by whose worship alone one attains liberation while living—is truly lost. (40)
We know that the universe, enveloped by ego and endowed with the three qualities, has fallen downward from the top of the ladder.
Otherwise, how could one be liberated even when bound by falsehood?
Therefore, having abandoned everything, the Goddess of the World should be served by all. 42.
The King said:
"O Grandfather, tell me what was done there by the preceptor and by the one assuming the form of Kāvya; and when did Śukra arrive?"
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall tell you what was then done by the high-souled preceptor,
who assumed the form of Kāvya and remained concealed.
Instructed by their preceptor, the Daityas, regarding Śukra as their own teacher,
placed their supreme trust in him and then became entirely devoted to him.
Thinking him to be Bhṛgu, they sought refuge with him for the sake of knowledge, utterly deluded;
they were deceived by their preceptor through greed—for who does not become deluded? (46)
Then, when the full period of ten years had elapsed,
Kāvya, having sported with Jayantī, reflected upon his sacrificial patrons.
"Indeed, they stand waiting, watching my path with hope;
I shall go and see those sacrificers who are overcome with great fear. (48)
Thinking, "May there be no fear of the gods for those devotees of mine," he resolved upon an intellect and spoke to Jayantī.
"O fair-eyed one, my sons go only unto the gods;
today your agreement has reached its completion, for this ten-year period has come to an end. (50)
Therefore, O goddess of slender waist, I shall go to see my patrons;
I will return to your presence immediately thereafter.
"So be it," replied Jayantī, the most knowledgeable in dharma;
"Go as you wish, O knower of dharma, for I shall not cause your dharma to be violated. (52)
Having heard those words, Kāvya departed from there in haste;
he then beheld Vācaspati standing by the side of the Dānavas.
He was gentle in appearance, wearing a deceptive form, and by means of guile he awakened them to the Jaina doctrine which he himself had composed, as well as his intent to revile the sacrifice. (54)
O enemies of the gods, I speak the truth for your own benefit:
non-violence is the supreme dharma; indeed, even those who attack as aggressors must not be killed.
For in the Veda, the slaughter of animals has been shown by twice-born ones who are devoted to enjoyments;
yet for those intent on the taste of the tongue, non-violence alone is considered the supreme goal.
Hearing his guru uttering such words as well as those devoted to the Vedas and the Shastras, that son of Bhrigu was filled with wonder.
He reflected in his mind: "My preceptor is indeed hateful toward me;
surely my patrons have been deceived by this rogue—of this there is no doubt. (58)
Fie on greed, the seed of evil and the powerful gateway to hell, by which even a teacher, impelled by that wickedness, speaks untruth! (59)
Even he whose word is authoritative is a bearer of heresy;
he is the preceptor of all the gods and the promulgator of the Dharmaśāstras.
What does one whose mind is defiled by greed not obtain?
Even another, even a guru, has thus become a pseudo-scholar of heresy. (61)
"Having adopted all the behaviors of an actor, this best of the twice-born deceives even me, as well as the utterly deluded Daityas who are unworthy of sacrifice. (62)

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Deception of the Daityas by the Preceptor in the Form of Śukra," in the Fourth Book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Vyāsa said: [This is] the pacification of Śukra’s anger by Prahlāda.
Having reflected thus in his mind, he spoke to them as if smiling.
"Have the Daityas been deceived by my own form; what indeed is the use of a preceptor? (1)
I am Kāvya, and this is my preceptor, who accomplishes the work of the gods.
By this you have been deceived, O sacrificers of mead; of this there is no doubt.
"Do not believe her words; this noble lady is a deceiver, acting out of pride."
Follow me; abandon this Bṛhaspati as one who is to be sacrificed for. || 3 ||
Having heard his words and having seen those two again as being identical, [he reflected].
They were filled with supreme wonder, certain that "this is Kāvya."
Seeing them so greatly agitated, the Guru spoke these words.
"This Bṛhaspati, appearing in my form, is surely deceiving you, O Gurus. || 5 ||
I have come to deceive you for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
O best of Daityas, do not place your trust in his words.
I have obtained the knowledge of Śambhu; I shall teach it to you.
I shall surely bring victory for the gods; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus heard these words of the preceptor Kāvya Rūpadhara, they—
They heaved a great sigh, certain that this was indeed Kāvya.
It is said that there the Dānavas were awakened in many ways by means of poetry.
Deluded by the illusion of the Guru, they did not realize [the truth] due to the passage of time.
Having thus made their resolution, they then spoke to the descendant of Bhṛgu.
This preceptor of ours is righteous in soul, possessed of wisdom, and devoted to our welfare.
For ten years, this descendant of Bhṛgu has constantly ruled over us.
"Go! You speak like a deceiver; you are not even our guru. || 11 ||
Having spoken thus to the descendant of Bhṛgu, the foolish woman reviled him again and again.
Having prostrated and saluted their preceptor with affection, they received him. ||12||
But Kāvya, seeing them absorbed in that [state], became enraged and then uttered a curse.
Awaken those Daityas, considering them to have been utterly deceived by their preceptor.
Because they have been awakened by me, they will indeed not accept my word.
Therefore, having indeed lost your consciousness, you shall surely meet with defeat.
Indeed, you shall surely reap the fruit of your contemptuous disregard in a very short time.
Then all his deceit will be fully recognized. ||15||
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, that descendant of Bhṛgu, filled with wrath, departed quickly.
Bṛhaspati, having attained joy, remained there with a concentrated mind.
Then the preceptor, having learned that those Daityas had indeed been cursed by Bhārgava, [acted accordingly].
Having abandoned his own true form and assumed another, he departed with speed.
Having gone there, he then said to Śakra, "The task has certainly been accomplished by me."
Those Daityas were cursed by Śukra and abandoned by me again and again.
She has surely been rendered supportless; therefore, O best of gods, exert yourselves!
O illustrious one, they were rendered by me as targets for battle, having been consumed by my curse.
Having heard these words of the Guru, Maghavan attained great joy.
And all the gods rejoiced, having honored Bṛhaspati.
Having deliberated among themselves once more, they set their minds upon battle.
All the gods went forth together, facing toward the Dānavas.
Having perceived the gods to be prepared, exerting effort, and possessed of great strength;
And when their preceptor had vanished, they became filled with anxiety.
Then, deluded by his illusion, they spoke thus to one another.
That great-souled one, who was to be propitiated, has departed with an angry mind. ||23||
The wicked preceptor, a scholar of deceit, has departed after having deceived [us].
He generally seduces the wives of his brothers; he is filthy within but pure without.
What shall we do, and where shall we go? How can this poem, once provoked to anger, be appeased?
Let us make him our ally, with his heart gladdened and his mind joyful.
Having reflected thus, they all gathered together, trembling with fear.
Placing Prahlāda at their head, they went again to the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Then they bowed down at the feet of that sage who maintained silence.
Then Bhārgava, his eyes bloodshot with rage, spoke to them.
I have awakened you, who were deluded by the great illusion.
At that time, he did not accept the appropriate, beneficial, and pure words of the officiating priest.
Then I was disregarded by you all, who had fallen under his control.
Surely I have now reaped the fruit born of my own contempt, brought about by those intoxicated with pride.
Go there, you who have fallen from the path of truth, to where that one of deceitful form resides.
I am a deceiver seeking the purpose of the gods' work; for I am not a deceiver like him.
Vyāsa said:
As Śukra was speaking these words in a faltering voice, [the king said:]
Then Prahlāda, having grasped his feet, spoke to him.
Prahlāda said:
O descendant of Bhṛgu, today you have come upon us who are unworthy of sacrifice and likewise afflicted.
O Omniscient One, you ought not to abandon our sons, who are devoted to your welfare.
But while you had gone for the sake of counsel, that evil-minded actor—
We have been deceived by him through his sweet words, which were full of hatred for you. || 33 ||
One who possesses tranquility does not become angry at a fault committed through ignorance.
O Omniscient One, you know that our hearts are inclined toward you.
"Knowing our disposition through our asceticism, O high-minded one, abandon your anger."
All sages say that virtuous people have but momentary anger. || 35 ||
Water is cold by its very nature, yet it becomes hot through contact with fire and the sun.
It becomes hot through union and, through separation, it attains coolness. || 36 ||
Anger, which is indeed like a caṇḍāla, must be abandoned in every way by the wise.
Therefore, O observer of noble vows, abandon your anger and grant me your favor.
If you do not abandon your anger, you will abandon us who are deeply afflicted by sorrow.
"O highly fortunate one, abandoned by you, we shall go to the netherworld. (38)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of Prahlāda, Bhārgava [beheld] with the eye of knowledge.
Having looked at them and become well-disposed, he spoke to them as if smiling.
One should neither fear nor go to the netherworld of the Dānavas.
"I shall indeed protect you, my sacrificers, with unerring mantras."
Today I speak what is beneficial and true; listen to that with certainty.
O knowers of dharma, you have heard my words, which were formerly heard from Brahmā.
Inevitably, auspicious and inauspicious states of being arise.
No one on the surface of the earth is capable of making the divine decree otherwise.
Today, without a doubt, you have become weak due to the power of time.
"Even though you have been defeated by the gods but once, you shall nevertheless enter Pātāla."
"The time for the transition has indeed arrived," Brahmā declared.
"The entire kingdom has been enjoyed by you in its fullness and all its prosperity. (44)
Having ascended to the heads of the gods for ten full ages.
And by the turn of fate, the powerful three worlds were enjoyed by you.
That same kingdom shall come into being once again during the reign of Sāvarṇika Manu.
Your grandson Bali, the conqueror of the three worlds, shall obtain the kingdom.
When it was taken by the god Viṣṇu in the form of a dwarf.
And at that very moment, your grandson was addressed by the god Jiṣṇu: ||47||
By whom the kingdom was seized from Bala for the sake of accomplishing the gods' desire.
And you shall become Indra at the beginning of the Sāvarṇika Manvantara.
Bhārgava said:
Thus addressed by Hari, O Prahlāda, your grandson has now [spoken].
Invisible to all beings, he moves about in secret like one who is afraid.
Once, Vāsava assumed the form of a donkey and [approached] this Bali.
O Śatakratu, staying in an empty house, he was indeed terrified with fear.
And then Bali was questioned in many ways by that Vāsava.
For what purpose, O foremost of Daityas, did you assume the form of a donkey?
You are the enjoyer of all the worlds and the ruler of the Daityas.
O best of Rākṣasas, you have no shame in assuming the form of a donkey.
Having heard those words of his, Bali, the king of the Daityas, then [acted].
He spoke these words to Śakra: "O Śatakratu, what cause for grief is there here?"
Just as Viṣṇu, possessed of great splendor, assumed the forms of a fish and a tortoise. ||53||
Likewise, by the power of time, I have come to exist in the form of a donkey.
Just as you are situated, merged within the lotus, so too are you possessed by the sin of killing a Brahmin.
For I am thus afflicted today, standing here while assuming the form of a donkey.
O Pākaśāsana, for one who is subject to destiny, what is sorrow and what is happiness?
Time indeed brings about whatever it desires, in whatever manner.
Bhārgava said:
Thus, those two, Bali and the Lord of Devas, having made this supreme agreement, [proceeded].
They attained awakening at will and went to their respective places.
Thus has this superior power of destiny been fully explained by me to you. (57)
The entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans, is dependent upon destiny.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 14 ||
The Departure of the Dānavas for Rasātala at the Word of the Goddess.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the high-souled Bhārgava, [the Dānavas departed].
But Prahlāda, the son of the king, became exceedingly joyful.
Realizing that destiny was all-powerful, Prahlāda said to them:
"Even if war is waged, victory will never be achieved."
Then those victorious Dānavas, arrogant with pride, said:
"War must indeed be waged; do we not know what destiny is? (3)
O Lord of Asuras, for those who make no effort, destiny is indeed paramount;
by whom has it been seen, where has it been seen, of what nature is it, and by whom was it created? (4)
Therefore, O best of Daityas, we shall now wage war, relying upon our strength; you are omniscient and possess great intelligence, O high-minded one.
Thus addressed by them at that time, O King, Prahlāda— the slayer of powerful enemies— then became the commander-in-chief and challenged the gods to battle.
Seeing those asuras assembled for battle there,
all the gods, having gathered their equipment, fought against them.
Then a terrible battle took place between Śakra and Prahlāda;
it lasted for a full hundred years, causing wonder among the sages.
O King, while that great battle was underway, the Daityas led by Prahlāda, protected by Śukra, then achieved victory.
At that very moment, at the word of his preceptor, Indra mentally recalled the goddess Śivā— the supreme bestower of liberation who destroys all suffering.
Indra said:
"Victory to you, O Goddess Mahāmāyā, wielder of the trident, O Mother!
You who hold the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and sword in your hands, and who bestow fearlessness! (11)
Salutations to you, O Sovereign of the World, O Leader who reveals the Power (Śakti)!
O Mother, whose essence consists of the ten principles, you who are the very nature of the Great Bindu! 12.

O you who are in the form of Mahākuṇḍalinī, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss; O you who are the knowledge of Prāṇāgnihotra, salutations to you whose essence is the flame of the lamp.
O Mother, who resides within the five sheaths, whose nature is the Brahma at the tail [of the Śiva-liṅga], the digit of bliss, worshipped by all the Upaniṣads! 14.
O Mother, be gracious; be well-disposed toward us. O Janani, protect us who are of little strength and have been defeated by the Daityas.
O Goddess, you are our refuge-giver, the ultimate authority in this world; endowed with all prowess, you are capable of pacifying our suffering. (15)
Those who meditate become exceedingly happy; likewise, others are freed from sorrow and fear, though they remain beset by suffering;
and those seeking liberation are devoid of pride and released from attachment.
The virtuous cross over the waters of the ocean of saṃsāra. || 16 ||
O Goddess, Mother of the Universe, you whose power is renowned, you who have arisen with majesty that dispels the distress of the afflicted for the sake of protection; indeed,
you take the form of Time (Kāla) to withdraw this entire world.
O Mother, who indeed—being of dull intellect—can know your life-story? || 17 ||
Brahmā, Hara, the one whose chariot is drawn by green horses (Viṣṇu), Hari, Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Agni, and Vāyu—
even the sages of great majesty are not capable of knowing him.
Whose incomparable power even the Vedas and Agamas proclaim.

Blessed indeed are those great souls devoted to you, who are freed from the suffering of saṃsāra and immersed in an ocean of bliss; whereas those devoid of the sentiment of devotion, O Umā, never cross the ocean of worldly existence with its waves of birth and death. 19.
Those fortunate ones who, being fanned with white whisks, sport while mounted upon palanquins—
it is said that you were indeed honored by them in a previous life.
I think thus with various offerings. || 20 ||
Those who, mounted upon excellent elephants, attended by throngs of graceful women, and accompanied by submissive vassal lords, travel while being honored;
For I believe that you were indeed honored by them. || 21 ||
Vyāsa said: Thus praised by Maghavan, the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Universe,
then suddenly manifested, mounted upon a lion and possessing four arms.
The goddess, with beautiful eyes, bore the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
she was clad in red garments and adorned with divine garlands and ornaments.
The goddess, with a gracious countenance, spoke to those gods in a gentle voice:
"O gods, cast away your fear; I shall indeed now provide for your welfare."
Having spoken thus, that exceedingly beautiful goddess, mounted upon her lion,
went swiftly to where the intoxicated Daityas were located.
Having seen the Goddess standing before them, all of them, led by Prahlāda, spoke to one another in fear: "What should be done here now? (26)
It is said that the goddess Caṇḍikā, the slayer of Mahiṣa and the destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, has indeed arrived here before Lord Nārāyaṇa.
"Ambikā will slay us all; there is no doubt in this, for by her with a sidelong glance, Madhu and Kaiṭabha were previously slain. (28)
Seeing them thus distressed with anxiety, Prahlāda said to them:
"O lords, O best of Dānavas, you must fight; you must not flee. (29)
Then Namuci spoke to them as they were intent on fleeing: "The Mother of the World, truly enraged, will slay you here with her weapons. (30)
"O illustrious one, act in such a way that no suffering arises;
having praised her with her permission, let us go this very day to Pātāla. (31)
Prahlāda said:
I praise the Goddess Mahāmāyā, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction;
the power who is the mother of all, and the granter of fearlessness to her devotees. (32)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, Prahlāda, the devotee of Viṣṇu and knower of the supreme truth,
then praised the Mother of the worlds with his palms joined in reverence.
Salutations to her whose form is *hrīṃ*, who is the substratum of all, in whom the entire world of moving and non-moving beings appears like a snake upon a garland. (34)
From you proceeds this entire universe, both the stationary and the moving;
others are merely instrumental causes, created by you as their agents. (35)
Salutations to the Goddess Mahāmāyā, who is remembered as the mother of all.
What difference is there for you between the gods, the Daityas, and those created by yourself? (36)
What difference can there be for a mother between sons, whether they be wicked or virtuous? Likewise, you must not now make any distinction between us gods. (37)
O Mother, such indeed are your sons, the Dānavas;
for you are proclaimed in the Purāṇas as the mother of the entire universe. (38)
They too are surely intent on their own self-interest, just as we are;
there is no difference between the Daityas and the Suras—this distinction arises from delusion. (39)
O Queen of the Gods, we are attached day and night to the enjoyment of wealth, wives, and other such things;
the gods are exactly the same—what, then, is the difference between asuras and gods? (40)
"We too are indeed the descendants of Kaśyapa and born from him;
O Mother, how has this outbreak of hostility arisen toward you now? (41)
O Mother, source of all things, you have not acted in such a manner;
for you must indeed maintain equanimity toward both the gods and us.
Since all gods and demons have arisen from the intermingling of the *guṇas*, how can those embodied beings, though endowed with the *guṇas*, be immortal? (43)
Desire, anger, and greed reside within all bodies; they are always active therein, so what person could possibly remain free from conflict? (44)
"Indeed, this mutual conflict was devised by you out of curiosity; we believe it was surely done through division, with a desire to witness a battle. (45)
Otherwise, O sinless one, what kind of conflict would there be among brothers?
Indeed, O Cāmuṇḍā, if you do not wish to witness this quarrel; || 46 ||
O knower of dharma, I know the dharma and I also know Śatakratu;
nevertheless, O Goddess, there is always a quarrel between us for the sake of enjoyment. (47)
O Mother, there is no teacher whatsoever in this world other than you;
for what wise person, even if full of desire, would be able to carry out the word of another? (48)
At one time, this ocean was churned by the gods and the asuras;
indeed, Viṣṇu brought about a division under the guise of the nectar and the jewels.
By you, that Śauri, the teacher of the world, was appointed to the office of protector;
by him, out of greed, Lakṣmī herself—the beauty of the gods—was seized.
Likewise, Airāvata was taken by Indra, and Pārijāta as well as Kāmadhuk;
Uccaiḥśravas was taken by all the gods—all this indeed being by the will of Viṣṇu.
"Having committed such an injustice, the gods have become virtuous; indeed, the gods are unjust—behold, you must observe the true characteristic of Dharma!"
Surely the gods were established by Viṣṇu, who is full of great pride.
"Surely the Daityas have been defeated; behold now the characteristics of dharma!
Where is dharma, and what is dharma like? Where is duty, and where is goodness? (53)
And before whom shall I proclaim my established doctrine of Mīmāṃsā?
[There are] logicians who know the arguments of reasoning, those who know the ritual injunctions, and proponents of the Vedas. (54)
Those whose nature is inert dispute that the universe has a creator;
for if indeed there were a creator in this vast cycle of existence— || 55 ||
What kind of mutual contradiction exists there regarding a single action? Why is there no consensus on the Veda, and likewise again among the various Śāstras? (56)
Furthermore, even the words of those who know the Vedas do not constitute a single consistent statement,
because the entire world, both stationary and moving, is intent upon its own self-interest.
No one in this world has been free from desire, nor will anyone ever be;
even Śaśinātha, having learned of it, forcibly took the wife of his preceptor.
Likewise, although Indra knew Gautama’s certainty regarding the Dharma, his elder brother forcibly enjoyed his younger brother’s wife while she was pregnant. (59)
The child was cursed while still in the womb and likewise made blind;
furthermore, the head of Rāhu was forcibly severed by Viṣṇu with his discus.
O Mother, at that time, though he was free from fault, that grandson of yours—valiant, devoted to righteousness, and dedicated to his vows of truth—was at the mercy of desire. (61)
A performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, peaceful, all-knowing, and a worshiper of all—him [Viṣṇu], who was skilled in deception, having assumed the form of a dwarf; || 62 ||
It is said that in former times Bali was deceived and his entire kingdom was seized;
nevertheless, the wise declare that the gods are established in righteousness.
Having attained victory through their discourse on Dharma, they even utter flattering words;
knowing this, O Mother of the World, do as you wish.
"All the Dānavas have come for refuge; either slay them or protect them.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"All of you go to Pātāla, or dwell there as you desire. (65)
"O Dānavas, all of you act without fear and free from resentment;
time must be awaited by you, for it is the cause of both good and evil. (66)
For those who are intent on complete detachment, there is happiness everywhere and at all times;
yet even in the sovereignty of the three worlds, there is no happiness for those whose minds are possessed by greed.
Even when accomplished, there is no complete happiness for those who still possess desire, even through the fruits [of their actions].
Therefore, abandoning this earth, let them go today to the surface of the great earth (the netherworld).
"Placing my command before them, may you all be freed from defilement.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the Goddess, they replied, "So be it," and [went] to Rasātala.
Having bowed down, all the Dānavas departed, protected by Śakti;
then the Goddess vanished, and the gods went to their own abode.
Then all those gods and dānavas remained there, having abandoned their enmity.
Whoever hears this entire narrative or recites it [attains merit]. (71)
Completely liberated from all suffering, he goes to the supreme state. || 72 ||

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Departure of the Dānavas for Rasātala through the Words of the Goddess," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Various Incarnations of Hari.
Janamejaya said:
O best of sages, [tell me] of Hari, the performer of wondrous deeds, [and how he was born] from the curse of Bhṛgu.
O Lord, how were the incarnations born, and in which Manvantara did they occur?
O knower of dharma, O Brahmin, tell me in detail the narrative of Hari’s descent, which destroys sin and brings all happiness when heard.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall describe the incarnations of Hari according to which Manvantara and in which Yuga they occurred, O lord of men.
O King, I shall now describe to you in brief all those forms in which Nārāyaṇa indeed performed his various deeds.
During the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara, Dharma himself appeared;
he became known on the surface of the earth as Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the two sons of Dharma. || 5 ||
Then, in this second age known as the Vaivasvata,
Hari again took the incarnation of Dattātreya, becoming the son of Atri.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— these three most excellent gods—
became sons to that Atri, having been chosen by his wife.
Anasūyā was the wife of Atri and the most excellent among virtuous women;
by her prayers, the three gods attained the state of being her sons.
Brahmā became Soma-rūpa, Dattātreya was Hari himself, and Durvāsas was Rudra; they all attained the state of being your sons.
The incarnation of Nṛsiṃha, however, occurred for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods;
he was born in the fourth age, possessing a captivating dual form.
For the complete slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Blessed Lord Hari assumed the form of a Man-Lion (Nārasiṃha), which struck wonder into the gods.
Likewise, in the excellent Tretā Yuga, for the purpose of subduing Bali,
the Blessed One assumed the form of a dwarf from the sage Kaśyapa.
Having deceived the king at the sacrifice,
he who assumed the form of a dwarf seized his kingdom and established Bali in the netherworld (pātāla).
Then, in the nineteenth age known as Tretā, the Lord Hari was born as the son of Jamadagni, the mighty one named Rāma.
The glorious slayer of the Kṣatriyas, truthful in speech and having conquered his senses,
gave the entire earth to the high-souled Kaśyapa.
O King of kings, that which is known as Paraśurāma is indeed an incarnation of Hari of wondrous deeds; it has been described as the destroyer of sins. (16)
In the Tretā Yuga, in the lineage of Raghu, two sons of Daśaratha were born on earth as Rāma—the portions of Nara and Nārāyaṇa—possessing great strength. (17)
In the twenty-eighth yuga, during the Dvāpara age, Arjuna and Śauri were praised;
Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna were born on earth for the purpose of removing the burden of the world.
They waged a most terrible great battle at Kurukṣetra;
thus indeed, O King, are the incarnations of Hari in age after age.
Many things indeed come to pass according to the nature of Prakṛti;
the entire threefold world is under the control of this Prakṛti. (20)
Just as she desires, so does she cause this world to revolve incessantly;
for the sake of the Puruṣa’s pleasure, she creates the entire universe.
For in the past, having created this world of moving and non-moving beings, the Blessed One— He who is the beginning of all, omnipresent, difficult to know, supreme, and immutable— [remained].
Supportless, formless, and desireless, yet higher than the highest—she who shines forth in three ways through limiting adjuncts is the supreme Prakṛti. 23.
Through her union with the time of emanation, that auspicious Śivā then appears as if divided;
she creates the universe at will and, as the granter of desires, she protects it.
At the end of the kalpa, she who deludes the universe in her three forms indeed withdraws everything;
joined with her, Brahmā creates, and Viṣṇu protects, accompanied by her.
Joined with her, Śiva as Rudra withdraws the world at will;
and she, O descendant of Kakutstha, formerly gave birth to that best of kings.
And he stationed them in various places for the sake of the victory of the Dānavas;
thus, indeed, in this saṃsāra, they are possessed of both pleasure and pain.
All living beings are governed by the laws of destiny and ritual injunctions. || 28 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Various Incarnations of Hari," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 16.
Janamejaya said:
"The courtesans were described by you as being at the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa."
Afflicted by love and longing for the one peaceful Nārāyaṇa, they were overcome with passion. || 1 ||
O King, at that time the sage Nārāyaṇa became desirous of cursing them,
but he was then restrained by his brother Nara, who was a knower of dharma.
O Sage, what was done by that sage when the calamity had arrived,
brought about by those women who were intensely intent upon the objects of desire?
And when he was again entreated with many supplications by Śakra, who had brought her forth,
what did that Jiṣṇu do when requested for the sake of marriage?
O Grandfather, I desire to hear this life-story of Nārāyaṇa which bestows liberation; tell it to me in detail. (5)
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, knower of dharma; I shall tell you in detail how it was for that great-souled son of Dharma. I shall speak to you at length.
When Hari was seen by Nara desiring to pronounce a curse,
the sage Nārāyaṇa then restrained him, having consoled him.
Then that great sage, a practitioner of austerities and a delighter of Dharma, his anger having subsided, spoke these sweet words preceded by a smile. (8)
"In this birth, O fair-limbed one, I have made a firm resolve:
neither of us two shall by any means enter into marriage."
Therefore, out of compassion for me, let them go to the third heaven;
for those who know the Dharma do not indeed cause the breaking of another's vow.
In this erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), the permanent emotion (sthāyībhāva) is traditionally held to be love (rati);
O fair-eyed ones, how can I establish a connection [to this rasa] in the absence of that? 11.
It is certain that an effect cannot exist without a cause;
thus, it has been stated by the poets in the treatises that the stable emotion (sthāyībhāva) is indeed the aesthetic flavor (rasa).
"Blessed am I on this earth, handsome in all my limbs and fortunate, since I have become the object of your genuine affection. (13)
"Out of compassion, you must protect my vow;
O illustrious ladies, I shall become your husband even in another birth."
In this twenty-eighth Dvāpara age on the surface of the earth, I shall manifest in every way as large-eyed women for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods. (15)
Then, you ladies, having taken birth separately as my wives,
shall become the daughters of kings and attain the status of consorts.
Having thus consoled them and promised to take them under his protection, the Blessed Lord Hari dismissed them;
and they departed, their distress gone.
Thus dismissed by him, those women then went to heaven and related the entire reason once more to Śakra.
Having heard from them the account of his deeds in detail,
Maghavan praised that high-souled one upon seeing the women, who were like Urvaśīs.
Indra said: "Oh, what fortitude this sage possesses, as well as his desire and the power of his asceticism, by which,
through his own penance, he has fashioned Urvaśīs of such beauty!"
Having praised him thus, the king of the gods then became serene in soul;
and Nārāyaṇa, the righteous one, likewise became intent upon ascetic penance.
Thus, this entire wonderful account of the sage has been related in its entirety— the story of Nārāyaṇa and of the great sage Nara.
For those two heroes, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna,
were born here, O best of the Bharatas, by the power of Bhṛgu’s curse, for the purpose of removing the earth's burden.
The King said:
"Tell me in detail the life and deeds of the Kṛṣṇa incarnation;
O giver of honor, there is a doubt in my mind—dispel it. (24)
O sage, how did Devakī and Vasudeva come to share in suffering, they who had obtained as their sons the two immensely powerful ones, Hari and Ananta?
Bound in shackles by Kaṃsa and oppressed for many years,
they were those whose son was Hari himself, who had been propitiated through their ascetic penance.
He was born in Mathurā; how did he go to Gokula? Having slain Kaṃsa, how did he make his residence in Dvāravatī? || 27 ||
Having abandoned his own prosperous and purifying land, which was served by his ancestors and others, how did that Hari go to another region among the non-Aryans? (28)
And how was the lineage of Hari destroyed by the curse of the twice-born, after the eternal Vāsudeva had accomplished the removal of the earth's burden? (29)
Hari swiftly cast off his body and went to heaven;
and the earth became distressed by the burden of the most wicked. || 30 ||
They were slain by Vāsudeva and by Pārtha of immeasurable deeds;
how was it that those by whom the wives of Hari were plundered were not struck down? (31)
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and King Bāhlika;
then Vairāṭa, Vikarṇa, and King Dhṛṣṭadyumna. || 32 ||
All the kings, beginning with Somadatta, have been slain in battle;
their burden has been removed, but why was that of the thieves not taken away? (33)
O best of sages, how did the wives of Kṛṣṇa—who were devoted to their husbands—attain such suffering at the end? This doubt revolves within my mind. (34)
But how did the righteous-souled Vasudeva, tormented by grief for his son, abandon his life and meet with an untimely death? || 35 ||
O best of sages, how did those Pāṇḍavas— who were ever devoted to dharma and always intent upon Kṛṣṇa— come to experience such suffering?
And how did the highly fortunate Draupadī become a partaker of suffering, she who was born from the center of the sacrificial altar and is said to have arisen from a portion of Lakṣmī? (37)
Then that young woman, afflicted by the onset of her menses and tormented by Duḥśāsana’s seizing of her hair, was brought into the assembly hall.
Then, while staying in the middle of the forest, she was oppressed by the King of Sindhu;
likewise, she was also oppressed by Kīcaka and wept bitterly.
His five sons were indeed slain by the son of Droṇa while at home;
the son of Subhadrā, though but a child, was struck down in battle. (40)
Likewise, six sons of Devakī were slain by Kaṃsa;
though Hari was capable [of preventing it], he did not alter destiny. 41.
Likewise, there was the curse upon the Yādavas, their destruction at Prabhāsa, the terrible ruin of the lineage, and the plundering of their wives. (42)
Indeed, service was constantly performed by Viṣṇu, Īśvara, and Nārāyaṇa himself, like that of a servant, for Ugrasena.
O illustrious one, this is my doubt regarding that sage Nārāyaṇa:
how he maintains a state of equality toward all living beings in his daily conduct at all times. (44)
How is it that states such as joy and sorrow are common to all? How could the nature of the Lord Hari be otherwise? (45)
Therefore, relate in detail the great life-story of Kṛṣṇa—
the deeds performed on the surface of the earth by Hari, who is beyond the mundane world.
O best of sages, when their lives were exhausted, the Daityas were slain with great effort; where else, O most excellent one, has the power of sovereignty been so celebrated by Hari?
"Indeed, during the abduction of Rukmiṇī, Vāsudeva took her and fled; he acted like a thief at that time."
Having abandoned the prosperous and esteemed region of Mathurā out of fear of Jarāsandha, he made his way to Dvārakā. (49)
At that time, the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign, was not recognized by anyone.
O Brahmin, tell me the reason why he remained hidden from Vraja.
O son of Vāsavi, O illustrious one, dispel these and many other doubts today; for you, O best of the twice-born, are omniscient. (51)
O Gopīs, thus one doubt does not depart from my heart:
Is the state of having five husbands for the princess of Pañcāla not loathsome in this world? (52)
For the wise declare that the conduct of the virtuous is indeed the authority;
how then could they, despite being capable, have resorted to the way of beasts? (53)
Or what was done by Bhīṣma on the surface of the earth in the form of a god?
For he protected his lineage only after producing those two "golakas" (testicles). || 54 ||
"Fie upon the determination of dharma as it has been fully demonstrated by the sages—that which consists of procreating a son by whatever means possible! (55)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Granting of Boons to the Celestial Women," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 17.
Vyāsa said: O King, listen; I shall relate the great life-story of Kṛṣṇa. Regarding Brahmā, Viṣṇu spoke these words.
The cause of the descent and the wonderful life-story of the Goddess. || 1 ||
Once, Dhara, overcome by her burden, weeping, and exceedingly emaciated,
assumed the form of a cow and, miserable and terrified, went to the celestial realm.
Then Śakra asked her, "O Vasundharā, what fear exists for you today? By whom indeed are you oppressed, and what is your sorrow? (3)
Having heard that, she then said: "Listen, O Lord of Gods, to all of this;
you ask me about my sorrow, yet I am overwhelmed by a heavy burden, O Giver of Honor. (4)
Jarāsandha, the great sinner, is my lord among the Māgadhas;
likewise Śiśupāla, the king of Cedi, and the powerful King of Kāśī. || 5 ||
And Rukmī, the powerful Kaṃsa, and the exceedingly strong Naraka; Śālva, the lord of Saubha, the cruel Keśin, Dhenuka, and Vatsaka.
All the kings were devoid of righteousness, mutually antagonistic, of sinful conduct, intoxicated by pride, and like the very embodiment of Death.
O Śakra, O Lord, I am oppressed by them; overcome by this burden, I have no strength left.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? A great anxiety has taken hold of me. (8)
"I have been oppressed by the boar-form Viṣṇu, the all-powerful one;
O Śakra, know that through Hari I have gone from sorrow to even greater sorrow. (9)
For I was indeed abducted by the wicked Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Kaśyapa, and submerged in that great ocean.
Then, although he was slain by Viṣṇu in the form of a boar,
I was uplifted by the Varāha, established, and made firm.
Otherwise, O Lord of Gods, I would remain comfortably established and sleeping at ease in the netherworld;
I am not able today to bear the burden of these evil-minded ones.
At the outset, the wicked Kali, the twenty-eighth [yuga], shall arrive;
then, O Śakra, being tormented, I shall quickly go to the netherworld (rasātala).
Therefore, O Lord of the gods of gods, become the one who carries me across this ocean of the form of suffering; take away my burden; I bow at your feet.
Indra said: "O Ilā, what shall I do for you today? Go to Brahmā for refuge;
I will come there, and he will remove your suffering. (15)
Having heard that, the Earth then went quickly to the world of Brahmā;
Śakra also followed behind her, preceded by all the gods.
Seeing Surabhī arrived there, O great king, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), having recognized the Earth through meditation, spoke to her as she stood before him.
"Why do you weep, O auspicious lady? Tell me now, what is your sorrow?
By what evil-doer have you been oppressed? Speak, O Earth! (18)
Dharā said:
"This wicked Kali is approaching; I am afraid of him.
O Lord of the World, the subjects there will become practitioners of sinful conduct. (19)
The kings were of wicked conduct and hostile toward one another;
they were all engaged in the work of thieves, being Rākṣasas full of enmity. || 20 ||
"Having slain those kings, O Grandfather, take away my burden today;
O Great King, I am oppressed by the weight of these sovereigns' armies. (21)
Brahmā said:
"O Goddess, I am not capable of thus relieving your burden.
Let us go to the abode of Viṣṇu, the god of gods, the wielder of the discus."
That Janārdana will surely remove your burden;
previously, I too reflected upon your task after careful deliberation.
"Go there, O best of gods, where the god Janārdana resides.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the author of the Vedas placed the gods and the Earth in front of him.
Mounted upon a swan, the four-faced one went to the abode of Viṣṇu;
with his mind inclined toward devotion, he praised him with Vedic hymns.
Brahmā said: You are the thousand-headed one, the thousand-eyed, and the thousand-footed;
you are the primordial Veda-Purusha, the eternal God of gods.
O Lord, O Master of Ramā, whatever immortality has been granted by you to us in the past, the future, and the present; [27]
Such is your greatness; who in the three worlds does not know it?
You are the creator, the protector, and the destroyer; you are the refuge of all, O Lord.
Vyāsa said:
Thus praised, the Lord Viṣṇu, whose banner is Garuḍa and whose heart is pure, was pleased and granted his vision to Brahmā and the others.
With a gracious countenance, Hari asked the gods a welcome and then inquired in detail about the reason for their arrival.
Bowing down and recollecting the suffering of the Earth, the Lotus-born One said to him:
"O Viṣṇu, O Janārdana, the removal of the burden must be performed by you."
Having taken incarnation upon the earth when the end of the Dvāpara age has arrived,
O ocean of compassion, slay the wicked kings and remove the burden of the world.
Viṣṇu said:
"In this matter, I am not independent, nor are Brahmā or Śiva;
neither is Indra, Agni, Yama, Tvaṣṭṛ, Sūrya, or Varuṇa."
Under the power of Yogamāyā, all this— both the stationary and the moving,
from Brahmā down to a blade of grass— is strung together by the thread of the *guṇas*.
O observer of noble vows, just as she previously desired to act according to her own will, so does she now act with great satisfaction; we are all likewise under her control.
"If indeed I were truly independent, let them reflect with their intellects:
from where did I come to have the body of a fish or a tortoise in the great ocean? (36)
What enjoyment, what fame, what happiness, what merit, and what fruit can there be for me, who have entered this lowly womb among the animal species? (37)
"O Grandfather, how could I have been Kola, or Nṛsiṃha, or Vāmana? And why would I have become the son of Jamadagni? (38)
"What cruel deed have I committed upon this earth, that I must once again fill all the lakes with my own blood? (39)
How then, having become the son of Jamadagni and the best of the twice-born, could you slaughter Kṣatriyas in battle, even those still in the womb, with such mercilessness? (40)
Then, O Lord of Gods, having become Rāma, he entered the Daṇḍaka forest on foot,
clothed in bark garments, with matted hair and wearing a deerskin.
For, without companions and without provisions, I wandered shamelessly there in that terrifying, desolate forest while engaged in the hunt. || 42 ||
Concealed by illusion at that time, he did not perceive the golden deer;
having left Jānakī in the hut, he went out following its tracks. (43)
And Lakṣmaṇa also, though repeatedly forbidden by me, abandoned her and departed following my path, deluded by worldly qualities.
Then, assuming the form of a monk through his deceptive appearance,
the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa swiftly abducted Jānakī, who was emaciated by grief.
Afflicted by grief, I wept there in forest after forest;
and for the sake of my purpose, I established a friendship with Sugrīva.
Vālin was slain through injustice and was indeed restrained by a curse;
nevertheless, having made the monkeys his allies, he set out for Laṅkā once again. 47.
"I am bound by serpent-nooses, as is my younger brother Lakṣmaṇa;
seeing us both fallen and unconscious, the monkeys were struck with amazement. (48)
Then, it is said, the two brothers were released by Garuḍa after he arrived;
great anxiety arose within me as to what destiny would do.
"The kingdom has been seized, we dwell in the forest, our father is dead, and my beloved has been taken away;
even this painful battle is being forced upon me—what, then, will he do hereafter? (50)
O gods, first there was the great suffering of living in the forest without a kingdom, even though I was accompanied by a princess, yet remained destitute of wealth.
Not even a single cowrie was given to me by my father when I departed for the forest;
I went out on foot, without a companion and destitute of wealth. (52)
Thus, for fourteen years,
I spent my time in the great forest, abandoning the duty of a Kshatriya and living by the livelihood of a hunter.
By fate, victory was obtained in battle and that great asura was slain;
furthermore, Sītā was recovered and I likewise reached Ayodhyā.
Having ruled over Kosala, he enjoyed for some years the complete sovereignty and the pleasures arising from worldly existence. (55)
Previously, while I was still ruling and had already attained the kingdom, I abandoned Sītā in the forest out of fear of public scandal. || 56 ||
Furthermore, he experienced the difficult-to-endure suffering born of separation from his beloved;
for that daughter of the Earth had subsequently gone to Pātāla after piercing through the earth. (57)
Thus, even during the incarnation as Rāma, I experienced continuous suffering while dependent on another; indeed, who could then be truly independent? (58)
"By the power of my past deeds, heaven was attained by me along with my brothers;
what indeed can be said of one who is dependent on another, O wise one? (59)
"O Lotus-born One, observe: I am indeed dependent on another;
so too are you, Rudra, and all the other supreme gods. (60)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Words of Viṣṇu to Brahmā," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 18 ||
Description of the Goddess’s speech to the gods.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu spoke again to Prajāpati.
All people, deluded by Māyā, do not know the true reality.
Enveloped by illusion, we do not remember the Teacher of the World—the Supreme Person, peaceful, consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and immutable. || 2 ||
"Deluded by the thoughts 'I am Viṣṇu,' 'I am Brahmā,' and 'I am Śiva,' we do not know, O Creator, the supreme and eternal Reality. (3)
Deluded by the Māyā of the Supreme Self, I always remain under His control, like a wooden puppet in the hands of a magician. || 4 ||
That wonderful manifestation of his was seen by you in that same way;
and it was also seen by me, joined with existence at the beginning of the kalpa, in the ocean of nectar.
Then, on the island of jewels, at the Mandāra tree in the circle of the rāsa dance,
she was seen there in that assembly, yet not even heard by word.
Therefore, let the gods today remember that supreme, auspicious Śakti—the primordial Māyā of the Supreme Self, who bestows all desires. (7)
Vyāsa said: Having been addressed thus by Hari, the gods, headed by Brahmā,
mentally remembered the Goddess, the eternal Yogamāyā, the sovereign of the world.
As soon as she was remembered, the Goddess then granted her a direct vision;
holding a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, the Goddess was as red as a hibiscus flower.
Seeing her, the gods were overjoyed and praised that Sudarśanā.
The gods said:
"Just as a thread comes from a spider or sparks from fire, so has this world emerged from her; to her we bow."
We meditate upon that Consciousness, the sovereign of the worlds and an ocean of compassion, by whom this entire universe of moving and unmoving beings is fashioned through the power of Māyā. 11.

We remember that Goddess who is the very nature of consciousness—through whose ignorance arises worldly existence and through whose knowledge comes the destruction of existence; may she inspire us. 12.
May we know Mahālakṣmī, may we meditate upon the All-Powerful One;
may that Goddess inspire us. 13.
O Mother, we bow before you; O remover of the world's suffering, be gracious! O peaceful one, grant us peace; O you who are moist with compassion, perform this task!
Destroy the host of the enemies of the gods and take away their burden.
O Maheśvarī, O Bhavānī, grant welfare to the virtuous through your greatness.
O lotus-eyed one, if you never show compassion toward the gods,
why is your patience capable of striking them with swords and arrows on the front lines of battle?
Indeed, it was by you yourself that this form of a Yakṣa was described.
O Fire, hold a blade of grass and burn it with your desire for [my] feet.
Kaṃsa, Kuja, the son of the Yavana king, Keśin, Bārhadratha, Baka, Bakī, Khara, Śālva, and the foremost of others—
whatever other kings exist on earth, you [should know them].
Having slain him, O Mother, quickly take away the burden of the world. || 16 ||
O lotus-eyed one, those who were not indeed slain by Viṣṇu, nor even after being challenged by Śaṅkara or Purandara,
are now gazing intently at your face which bestows happiness.
In battle, they were struck down by his arrows as if in mere sport.
Without Śakti, even the gods headed by Hari and Hara [would be powerless].
O Goddess of gods, even the lords are not able to waver from you;
for who, even if he were the infinite Lord himself, could support the earth without your sustaining power, O you who wear the crescent moon as your crest-ornament? (18)
Indra said:
"Without speech, Hari is indeed capable of creating this entire universe; how much more so, then, is he capable of protecting it even when deprived of Ramā?"
Is the Lord Īśvara, who is capable of withdrawing [the world] yet is abandoned by Umā, your master? Or are those lords of creatures (prajeśas), together with her, your masters? || 19 ||
Viṣṇu said:
Neither Druhiṇa nor I am ever capable of creating the three worlds; nor is the Lord [Śiva] so, for he is devoid of your power.
O sinless one, you indeed appear here as the sovereign power to act and to sport, for you are truly the Mistress of all glory. (20)
Vyāsa said: Thus praised, the Goddess then spoke to those lords of the gods:
"Tell me now, free from anxiety, what task must be done; I shall perform it."
"O best of gods, I shall accomplish even that which is impossible in this world if it is desired by you; tell me your sorrow and that of the earth. (22)
The gods said:
"O Earth, you have come before us gods, overcome by the burden of [the weight of] beings;
weeping and trembling, you are oppressed by wicked kings. (23)
O Goddess of the World, O Śivā, the removal of her burden must now be carried out;
this alone is the desired task of the gods at present.
O Mother, in the past you slew the exceedingly powerful Dānava who had assumed the form of a buffalo, along with his millions of followers. (25)
Likewise, Śumbha and Niśumbha, as well as the other, Raktabīja;
and the two of great prowess, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, and likewise Dhūmralocana. || 26 ||
Durmukha, Duḥsaha, and the exceedingly powerful Karāla, as well as many other cruel ones, have been struck down by you alone. || 27 ||
In that very same way, slay all the enemies of the gods and the lords of the earth;
bear the unbearable burden of the earth caused by wicked kings.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, the goddess Ambikā, who is auspicious, then summoned the gods.
Smiling, the goddess with the corners of her eyes darkened by collyrium spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The illustrious goddess said: "O gods, this descent of my portions was previously conceived by me. (29)
"And so that there may be a removal of the burden of wicked kings, I must slay all those lords of the Daityas who have become rulers of the earth. (30)
The illustrious ones, such as Māgadha and others, whose splendor has become dimmed according to their own power,
shall also descend to the surface of the earth by means of your own portions.
"O gods, the burden must be removed by those endowed with my power;
Kaśyapa, the progenitor of the gods, shall do so together with his wife."
Formerly, in the lineage of the Yādavas, there will be Ānakadundubhi;
likewise, due to the curse of Bhṛgu, the immutable Lord Viṣṇu himself [will be born].
There, Hari will exist as a portion of myself, born as the son of Vasudeva; at that time, I too shall manifest in Yaśodā in Gokula.
"O best of gods, I shall perform every task for the gods;
I will bring Viṣṇu, who has been cast into prison, to Gokula. (35)
And I shall transfer the remainder from Devakī’s womb into Rohiṇī;
nourished by my power, those two shall bring about the destruction of the wicked.
At the end of the Dvāpara age, it is certain that even Arjuna, who is a direct portion of Indra, will bring about the destruction of the forces of wicked kings according to their desire.
The great king Yudhiṣṭhira will be a portion of Dharma;
Bhīmasena a portion of Vāyu; and the two Yamas (Nakula and Sahadeva) will also be portions of the Aśvins. (38)
Now the son of Gaṅgā, a portion of Vasu, will cause the destruction of your forces;
therefore, depart this day, and let the earth be well-settled.
"O best of gods, I shall surely effect the removal of the burden;
by my own power, I shall act as nothing more than the instrumental cause for them—of this there is no doubt. (40)
"I shall bring about the destruction of the Kṣatriyas at Kurukṣetra.
Envy, jealousy, the mind, thirst, possessiveness, pride, and longing—these [are my attendants]. (41)
Through the faults of ambition, lust, and delusion, the Yādavas will perish;
and by the curse of a Brāhmaṇa, the destruction of the lineage shall come to pass. (42)
The Blessed One too shall cast off this body by means of a curse;
you also, along with your own limbs, are the companions of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
"May they flourish together with their women in Mathurā and in Gokula.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess Yogamāyā, who belongs to the Supreme Self, vanished.
All the gods indeed departed for their own abodes;
and Dharā also became well-established, being gratified by her words.
O Janamejaya, the earth became endowed with medicinal herbs and creepers;
the subjects became happy, and the twice-born attained great prosperity. All the sages were contented and became devoted to righteousness.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Goddess’s Words to the Devas," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The description of the commencement of the narrative of the Kṛṣṇa incarnation.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O Bhārata, I shall likewise relate the descent of the burden.
At Kurukṣetra and at Prabhāsa, it was destroyed by Yogamāyā. || 1 ||
The birth of Viṣṇu, who possesses immeasurable splendor, occurred in the Yadu lineage through the power of Bhṛgu’s curse and by the force of Mahāmāyā.

"It is my conviction that this manifestation of Viṣṇu on the surface of the earth, a yoga brought about through his illusory power (māyā), was intended for the purpose of lifting the burden of the world."
O King, what is surprising about this? That Goddess Māyā, composed of the three qualities (guṇas), incessantly makes even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the gods dance; how much more so others?
The suffering arising from dwelling in the womb, joined with feces, urine, and sinews, was fully brought about by Viṣṇu through his effortless play. || 5 ||
Formerly, even during the incarnation as Rāma, the gods were made into monkeys;
it is known to you how Viṣṇu was deluded by the noose of suffering.
O lord of men, by the very firm noose of "I" and "mine," even yogins who are free from attachment—whether desiring worldly enjoyment or seeking liberation—are bound. (7)
