They worship that very Goddess, the Sovereign of the Universe, the Auspicious One, by whom even a minute fraction of a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of devotion [is bestowed]. (8)
Having obtained her, what person would not become liberated? Who would not serve her, who bestows the three worlds upon the very mouth by the mere name "Bhuvaneśī"? (9)
"O King, know that because there is no one to whom the words 'Protect me' can be addressed, she is burdened by debt; her two forms are knowledge and ignorance. (10)
By knowledge a living being is liberated, but by ignorance one is bound again;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—all are subject to her control. (11)
All the incarnations are indeed as if restrained by ropes;
yet at times, he enjoys happiness in Vaikuṇṭha and in the Ocean of Milk.
Sometimes Hari engages in battle with the more powerful Dānavas, and sometimes he indeed performs extensive sacrifices.
And sometimes, O observer of noble vows, he performs intense austerity at a sacred ford;
and sometimes he lies upon his bed, having resorted to the yoga of sleep.
The Blessed Lord Madhusūdana is never independent;
nor are Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, Varuṇa, or Yama. || 15 ||
Kubera, Agni, Ravi, and Indu, as well as other foremost of gods,
the sages beginning with Sanaka, and others such as Vasiṣṭha and his peers.
All are eternally subject to the mother, just as a man is subject to his wife; like oxen pierced by a nose-rope, they move about following her will.
In the same way, all the deities are constrained by the noose of Time, as are states such as joy and sorrow, and conditions such as sleep, drowsiness, and lassitude. (18)
O King, for all embodied beings at all times, those residing within the body are called by the authors of the texts "immortals," "those free from decay," and "gods. (19)
Neither by name nor by meaning are they surely such things anywhere as those entities called arising, persistence, and destruction which [you claim] exist incessantly. (20)
How can they be called immortals, and how, moreover, can they be called ageless? Or how is it that these best of the wise are overcome by suffering? (21)
How can the gods be addressed [with such words], and how can there be sport in the midst of calamity?
In this world, arising and destruction are seen in an instant; of this there is no doubt. (22)
Furthermore, there is no comparison for these [beings]—the aquatic creatures, insects, and mosquitoes—at the end of their lifespan, they are known to die like mortals. (23)
Then there were humans with a lifespan of a hundred years, and likewise gods who were immortal; therefore, Brahmā is remembered as being beyond that.
Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā indeed arise in succession;
they likewise perish in succession, yet they increase more and more as time goes on.
"Surely for all embodied beings there is destruction and, upon death, rebirth;
O King, they revolve like a wheel—of this there is no doubt. (26)
A living being enveloped by the net of delusion is never liberated;
as long as illusion exists, the net of delusion does not perish. (27)
O King, at the time when they are about to arise, the birth of all occurs;
likewise, at the end of the kalpa, the destruction of Brahmā and the others takes place in due order. (28)
O King, he who perceives the sign at the time of another's destruction shall surely cause that person's death;
for what has been ordained by destiny cannot otherwise come to pass. (29)
Whether it be the suffering of birth, death, old age, and disease, or even happiness itself—let that indeed come to pass exactly as it may; there is no other certainty in this world. (30)
The two gods, the Moon and the Sun, are the manifest bestowers of happiness upon all;
their affliction arising from their enemies never perishes. (31)
The son of the Sun is dull-witted, and the Moon is subject to waning and possessed of a spot;
behold, O King, the thread of destiny which is difficult to resist even for the great. (32)
The creator of the Vedas, the progenitor of the world, and the bestower of intelligence— the four-faced Brahmā himself—
fell into a state of dejection upon seeing his daughter Sarasvatī.
Even Śiva’s wife Satī died; having cremated her body, he, the remover of the suffering of people, became tormented by grief and afflicted by desire.
O King, Śiva, his body scorched by the fire of passion, fell into the Kālindī; because of the heat of his body, even she became dark-watered.
Afflicted by desire and sporting about, he went naked to the forest of Bhṛgu; having arrived there, he was severely cursed by Bhṛgu because he was so overcome by lust.
"O shameless one, let your linga fall this very day! she cried out loudly; and for her pleasure, she drank from the pool of nectar constructed by the Dānavas.
And even Indra, having become a bull, attained the state of a vehicle on earth for Viṣṇu himself—the primordial being of all worlds and the possessor of discernment. (38)
Where has his omniscience gone, and where has his sovereign power departed, since the knowledge of the golden deer was apparently not realized by Hari? (39)
O King, behold the power of illusion; for Rāma, deluded by desire, being tormented by separation, wept, deeply distressed. (40)
Then that fool, weeping most bitterly, asked the trees: "Where has Janaka’s daughter gone? Has she been devoured, or by whom has she been carried away? (41)
"Lakṣmaṇa, I shall die, distressed by the sorrow of separation from my beloved;
and you too, O younger brother, will die because of my grief in the forest. (42)
Knowing of our death, my mother will perish;
and how can Śatrughna, afflicted by extreme grief, continue to live? (43)
Sumitrā, emaciated by the calamity of her son, might give up her life;
meanwhile, Kaikeyī, having attained her desire, would be fulfilled along with her son.
"Alas, Sītā! Where have you gone, leaving me behind, you who were so afflicted by love? Come, come, O fawn-eyed one; revive me, O slender-waisted one! (45)
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? My life is dependent upon you.
O daughter of Janaka, comfort me, your beloved, for I am wretched. (46)
While Rāma, of immeasurable splendor,
was thus lamenting and wandering from forest to forest, he did not see the daughter of Janaka.
Rāma, the lotus-eyed one who is the refuge of all the worlds,
has gone for protection to the monkeys, deluded by his own illusory power.
Having made the monkeys his allies, he bound the abode of Varuṇa;
he slew the heroic Rāvaṇa, as well as Kumbhakarṇa and Mahodara.
And having brought Sītā back from there, Rāma had her undergo a divine ordeal;
for although he was omniscient, he considered her to have been abducted by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa.
"What can I say, O Great King, regarding the great power of yogic illusion (yogamāyā), by which this entire universe is indeed deluded and made to wander? (51)
Thus, in various incarnations here, Viṣṇu, having come under the power of a curse,
performs diverse activities, for he is always subject to destiny.
I shall relate to you the deeds of Kṛṣṇa as well—
his manifestation in the world of men for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
In ancient times, there was Madhuvana on the beautiful bank of the Kālindī;
there dwelt the powerful Dānava Lavaṇa, the son of Madhu.
O illustrious one, that sinful man, who brought suffering to the twice-born and was arrogant due to the granting of a boon,
has indeed been slain by Lakṣmaṇa’s younger brother.
Then, having slain that one intoxicated with pride in battle,
Śatrughna established the most beautiful city named Mathurā.
Having installed his two lotus-eyed sons there in the kingdom, that wise destroyer of enemies, when the time had come, departed for heaven.
O King, when the solar dynasty had come to an end, the Yādavas took possession of that Mathurā,
which bestows liberation, just as Yayāti’s son did in former times.
There was a heroic king named Śūrasena who ruled over the lands of Mathurā and Śūrasena. O King, he enjoyed those territories. (59)
Born there as a portion of Kaśyapa due to the curse of Varuṇa,
he was then the highly renowned Vasudeva, the son of Śūrasena.
After his father died, Mādhava then devoted himself to the livelihood of a Vaiśya;
Ugrasena became king, and Kaṃsa was his great son.
Then Aditi was born as Devakī, the daughter of Devaka,
having indeed followed Kaśyapa due to a curse from Varuṇa.
She was given to Vasudeva by the high-souled Devaka;
when the marriage had been performed there, a voice then arose in the sky: || 63 ||
"O Kaṃsa, O fortunate one, your eighth son, born from the womb of Devakī, shall be glorious and will be your slayer. (64)
Having heard those words, the exceedingly powerful Kaṃsa was struck with wonder;
considering that voice of the deity to be true, he fell into deep reflection.
Thinking, "What shall I do?", he then reflected:
"If I kill her, my own death will surely come this very day immediately. (66)
"There is no other means in this matter that brings the fear of death;
how can I kill this venerable paternal aunt? he thought. (67)
He reflected again: "Alas, my sister is facing death!
Even by means of sin, a wise man must protect his body. (68)
Purification from sin always occurs through expiation;
likewise, even by the wise, the protection of life must be ensured despite the presence of sin. (69)
Having reflected thus in his mind, the wicked Kaṃsa quickly took up a sword and,
having seized that woman of beautiful hips by her hair, dragged her away.
Drawing his sword from its scabbard, the evil-minded man, desiring to kill her, dragged away that newly wed bride while all the people looked on. (71)
Seeing her being struck, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose;
the heroes following Vasudeva stood with their bows raised for battle.
"Release her! Release her! they cried to him, those men of wonderful courage; then, out of compassion, they set free Devakī, the mother of the gods.
Then a terrible battle took place between those heroes on one side,
aided by Vasudeva, and the high-souled Kaṃsa on the other.
While that terrible and hair-raising battle was thus proceeding,
the elder members of the Yadu clan, the best of their kind, restrained Kaṃsa.
O hero, this daughter of your paternal aunt is both venerable and innocent;
she must not be slain by you, O hero, during the celebration of the wedding festival. (76)
"O hero, the killing of a woman is unbearable, it destroys fame, and is the worst of sins;
it must not be committed by a wise man even at the mere mention of it by others. (77)
"O Lord, why might this harmful speech not have been uttered by some hidden enemy of yours or his? (78)
O King, an enemy who understands the power of illusion has uttered words intended to destroy your fame and that of Vasudeva’s household. (79)
"O hero, having become one who speaks the language of spirits, you are afraid; this is merely a stratagem devised by your enemy for the purpose of destroying the very root of your fame. (80)
A father’s sister must not be killed at the time of marriage;
O Great King, this was destined to happen—how else could it have been? (81)
When, despite being exhorted in this manner by them, he did not desist,
then Vasudeva, who was skilled in policy, addressed him in reply.
"O Kaṃsa, I speak the truth today: the three worlds are supported by truth;
I shall give you all the sons of Devakī, even those yet unborn."
"O Lord, if I do not give you every son as soon as he is born, then may my ancestors fall into the terrible Kumbhīpāka hell. (84)
Then, having heard those truthful words, the citizens standing before him spoke in haste to Kaṃsa, saying "Excellent! Excellent! again and again. (85)
The high-minded Vasudeva never speaks falsely anywhere.
O illustrious one, release Keśin, as well as the sin of killing a woman.
Vyāsa said:
Thus enlightened by the high-souled elders of the Yadu clan,
Kaṃsa abandoned his anger and remained there, having approved of their truthful words.
Then the kettledrums resounded and musical instruments made their sound; a cry of "Victory! arose from everyone there in that assembly.
Having propitiated Kaṃsa and secured the release of Devakī,
the highly illustrious son of Śūra then departed for his own home, followed by his kinsmen.
Free from fear and full of vigor because of his newlywed bride. || 89 ||

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Commencement of the Narrative of the Kṛṣṇa Incarnation," in the fourth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Kaṃsa’s Slaying of Devakī’s First Son.
Vyāsa said:
Then, when the time had arrived, Devakī, who possessed a divine form, [gave birth].
Having united with Vasudeva according to the prescribed rites, she conceived a child.
Then, when the tenth month was complete, Devakī gave birth to an excellent son,
endowed with perfect form and limbs, for the first time.
Then the highly fortunate Vasudeva, approved by his truthful words and because of his realization, spoke to Devakī, the mother of the gods.
"O fair-thighed one, you know my vow regarding the offering of my own daughter;
O illustrious lady, you were then released by me through that oath. (4)
"O lady with beautiful hair, I shall give this son to my brother's grandson—for the sake of destroying the wicked Kaṃsa; what can fate do against that?"
Indeed, the ripening of diverse karmas is difficult to understand for those who have not disciplined themselves.
Indeed, for all living beings who follow the noose of time,
their own performed karma— whether auspicious or inauspicious— must be experienced.
"In this matter, the *prārabdha* (commenced karma) ordained by fate for the living being must be experienced in every way.
Devakī said: "O Lord, the karma performed previously must necessarily be experienced by men in every way. (7)
O King, does that [sin] not indeed come to an end through pilgrimages, austerities, or gifts? For the procedure for expiation has been recorded in the treatises on Dharma. (8)
For the destruction of sins accumulated in the past, great-souled ones [perform this];
even a killer of a Brahmin, a thief of gold, a drinker of liquor, or one who violates the teacher’s bed [is purified].

Since purification is attained from whatever [sin] once a twelve-year vow has been performed, one should carry out the expiation exactly as prescribed by Manu and others according to the injunctions. (10)
O sinless one, having acted thus, a man may or may not be released from sin;
for are those sages who perceive the truth not of censurable speech? (11)
Yājñavalkya and all the other founders of the Dharmaśāstras [have said this];
O Lord, if such is your certainty, then it must surely come to pass.
Then Āyurveda would be entirely false, as would all forms of mantra-lore;
and all human effort would be in vain if everything were thus ordained by fate. (13)
That which is destined to be, simply comes to be; yet ritual activity is purposeless.
The Agniṣṭoma and other such rites, though certainly the means for attaining heaven, are in vain.
Whenever that is so, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is indeed explained in vain; for if that means of valid cognition is false, how could there not be the destruction of Dharma? (15)
When effort is exerted, success is established by direct perception itself;
therefore, one should here employ the mental elaboration fashioned by the mind. (16)
"Just as this young child, my little son, attains safety, so too must a falsehood be uttered by one who desires his own welfare. (17)
The wise do not voice any criticism regarding that.
Vasudeva said:
Listen, O highly fortunate lady; I tell you this truth.
Indeed, effort must be exerted, for the fruit follows from the power of destiny;
those who know the ancient lore declare that there are three kinds of actions here in this world. (19)

O slender-waisted one, it is declared here in the Purāṇas and the Āgamas that the accumulated and worn-out karmas of living beings have been exhausted, while those that are currently operative (prārabdha) remain.
O lady of beautiful thighs, whatever various deeds—both auspicious and inauspicious—of embodied beings exist here in the present, these constitute the seeds. (21)
Arising from many births, they remain in every way until their time;
then, having abandoned the previous body, the living soul follows under the power of karma.
Indeed, one attains either heaven or even hell by virtue of one's own deeds;
having obtained a divine body or a body for torment born of wealth.
He enjoys various pleasures, whether in heaven or in hell;
and when the time for his rebirth arrives at the end of those enjoyments, (he departs).
Together with the subtle body (liṅgadeha), that which is designated as the "living soul" (jīva) is born; at that very moment, from the accumulated karmas, it is again [bound] by karmas. (25)
He indeed joins that very time with the actions performed in the past—both auspicious and inauspicious—which are to be experienced by means of this body. (26)
O fair-eyed one, those actions already commenced must be experienced by the living being;
however, O beautiful lady, those that are currently underway are destroyed through expiation.
Likewise, accumulated [karmas] are quickly exhausted by performing what is appropriate; the destruction of prārabdha-karmas occurs through experience alone, and not otherwise. (28)
Therefore, you must by all means give this boy to Kaṃsa;
my word cannot be false, for it would be defiled by the censure of the world. (29)
In this impermanent cycle of existence, for the great-souled ones who take the Dharma as their essence, both birth and death are indeed subject to destiny. (30)
Therefore, grief should not be felt by an embodied being, for it is indeed useless;
he whose truth has departed, O lovely one, his life is in vain.
"Since this world has perished, how can there be a next world?
Therefore, O fair-browed one, give me a son; I shall deliver him to Kaṃsa. (32)
"O Goddess, because of this truthful spreading [of the grass], auspiciousness will come before you;
O beloved, men must perform virtuous deeds both in happiness and when suffering exists. (33)
"O Goddess, by virtue of protecting the truth, only auspiciousness shall come to pass."
Vyāsa said:
When her beloved had spoken thus, the wise Devakī, overcome with grief and trembling,
gave him her newborn son.
The righteous Vasudeva also, taking his infant son,
went to the abode of Kaṃsa, being praised by the people along the way.
The people said:
"O people, behold Vasudeva, so high-minded!
In accordance with his own word, he is now departing, taking the child with him. (36)
Desiring today to give [him] to Death, Satyavān, free from malice, shall make his life fruitful; let them behold this wondrous dharma! (37)
"He who goes even to Kaṃsa, the embodiment of Time, to give him his son.
Vyāsa said:
"O King, being thus praised, he arrived at the abode of Kaṃsa."
Kaṃsa gave him that superhuman boy as soon as he was born;
Kaṃsa, too, was struck with wonder upon seeing the fortitude of that great-souled one.
Taking the boy, he spoke these words preceded by a smile:
"O son of a hero, you are blessed today, for you are known as such through the offering of your son. (40)
"This eighth one mentioned by your speech is certainly not my death;
this child must not be killed by me. Let him go to your house as you desire. (41)
"O high-minded one, you must give me the eighth son.
Having said this, the wicked man quickly gave the infant to Vasudeva.
"Let this child go home safely," the king declared;
then Śauri, taking him with joy, went to his own house. (43)
Kaṃsa also said to his ministers: "Why should I kill this infant in vain? It has been prophesied that my death shall come from the eighth son of Devakī. (44)
"Therefore, why should I first commit this sin by killing the child?
Having said, "Excellent, excellent! those best of ministers then remained silent. (45)
Dismissed by Kaṃsa, they went toward their own homes;
when they had departed, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived.
Then the fierce son performed the rites of rising to greet him, offering the arghya and pādya;
the king inquired after his welfare and the reason for his arrival there.
Then Nārada spoke these words to him with a smile:
"Kaṃsa, Kaṃsa, O fortunate one, I have gone to the Golden Mountain."
There, Brahmā and the other gods, being composed in mind, performed a mantra;
[they prayed that] the best of the gods [should be born] in Devakī, the wife of Vasudeva.
"Viṣṇu will take birth here for the purpose of slaying you;
why then was your son not killed by you, who are well-acquainted with statesmanship? (50)
Kaṃsa said:
"I shall kill my eighth [child], for it has been declared by the gods to be my death.
Nārada said:
O best of kings, you do not understand the auspicious and inauspicious principles of statecraft. 51.
Do you not know the power of illusion belonging to the gods? What more need I say?
Even a minor enemy must not be disregarded by a hero who desires his own welfare. (52)
In the act of gathering, however, all of them are indeed considered to be of the eighth [inferior] rank;
yet this abandonment of the Immortal has been carried out by you, even though you are aware [of the truth].
Having spoken thus, the illustrious Nārada, who beholds the gods, departed quickly.
When Nārada had gone, Kaṃsa then summoned the boy and dashed him against a stone; yet that dull-witted one attained happiness.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Kaṃsa’s Slaying of Devakī’s First Son," in the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 21.
The Description of the Descent of Portions of the Gods and Dānavas.
Janamejaya said:
"O Grandfather, what sin was committed by that boy?"
For as soon as he was born, he was likewise slain by that evil-minded one. || 1 ||
Even Nārada, the best of sages, possessed of knowledge and devoted to dharma—
the foremost among the knowers of Brahman— how could he have committed such a sin?
The wise declare that both the doer and the instigator of a sin are equally guilty of that sin;
how then did the sage then incite the wicked Kaṃsa?
I have a great doubt in this matter; tell me everything in full detail: by what ripening of karma did the boy meet his death? (4)
Vyāsa said:
Nārada, who was always eager for spectacle and fond of quarrels,
came for the sake of the gods' mission and performed all of this.
That sage never had the thought of speaking falsely;
he was a speaker of truth, devoted to his duties, and pure. || 6 ||
In this way, six children were born to him and struck down as soon as they were born; through the power of the curse, six fetuses perished together upon their formation.
Listen, O King, I shall explain to you the cause of their curse.
During the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, there were six sons of Marīci who possessed great strength.
And seeing Brahmā intent on violating his own daughter, those who were experts in dharma laughed at him in the presence of his wife Ūrṇā.
Then Brahmā cursed them, saying, "Go down and enter the womb of Daityas.
O lord of the people, those six embryos were then born as the sons of Kālanemi.
O King, in another incarnation, those sons of Hiraṇyakaśipu were born endowed with knowledge due to the fear of their previous curse.
In that birth, being composed, they performed peaceful austerities;
Brahmā became pleased with them and granted boons to the six embryos.
Brahmā said:
"O dear sons, you were previously cursed by me while I was filled with anger.
Now I am pleased with you, O highly fortunate ones; tell me the boon you desire."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of Brahmā, they were all delighted in their minds; intent upon accomplishing their purpose, they spoke to Brahmā according to their desire.
The embryos said:
"O Grandfather, you are pleased today; grant us our desired boon:
that we be unslayable by all the gods, by humans, and by great serpents. (15)
"O Grandfather, let there not be slaughter by the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and their lords.
Vyāsa said: Then Brahmā spoke to them, "All this shall come to pass."
"O highly fortunate ones, let truth alone prevail for you; there is no doubt.
Having granted this boon, Brahmā departed, and they were then filled with joy.
O best of the Kurus, Hiraṇyakaśipu, filled with rage, said to them:
"Since, O sons, you have abandoned me and instead gratified the Grandfather (Brahmā), [you shall suffer the consequences]. (18)
Because they were excessively entreated with a boon, they have become powerful;
since affection has been abandoned by you, I therefore forsake you.
"Go to the netherworld, you who are renowned on earth as the Six Embryos;
remain in the netherworld, overcome by sleep, for many years. (20)
Then, year after year, Kālanemi shall again and again become Kaṃsa, your father, within the womb of Devakī.
"That most cruel one shall slay them as soon as they are born.
Vyāsa said: Thus were they cursed by him, again and again, while still in the womb.
Released from his curse, he slew the six embryos who were the sons of Devakī;
the seventh portion remaining there was situated within the womb of Devakī.
And that embryo was caused to fall away by means of yoga and yogic power;
having forcibly performed the transference, he placed it within the womb of Rohiṇī.
Having fallen in the fifth month, he then became famous throughout the world;
Kaṃsa also learned there that Devakī’s fetus had been aborted.
Upon hearing that pleasant news, that evil-minded one attained joy;
for in the eighth pregnancy of Devakī, the Blessed Lord, the Master of the Sātvatas, was [to be born]. (26)
He dwelt there for the sake of the gods' mission and to relieve the earth's burden.
The King said:
Vasudeva was then a portion of Kaśyapa, and Śeṣa was his other portion. (27)
O best of sages, you have thus described the portion of Hari;
now tell us of those other portions of the gods who were born there.
Vyāsa said: Those who were the portions of the gods and the asuras, renowned upon the earth—
I shall declare them to you; listen to them in brief:
Vasudeva was a portion of Kaśyapa, and Devakī was likewise Aditi.
Baladeva is a portion of Ananta; and among those present here, he who is the illustrious son of Dharma is known as Nārāyaṇa.
Vāsudeva was an incarnation of that [portion] while the Sage was still present;
and Arjuna was indeed an incarnation of his younger brother, Nara.
Yudhiṣṭhira was a portion of Dharma, Bhīma was a portion of Vāyu, and the two sons of Mādrī, who possessed great strength, were declared to be portions of the Aśvins. (33)
Karṇa is said to be a portion of the Sun, Vidura is remembered as a portion of Dharma;
Droṇa was a portion of Bṛhaspati, and his son was born from a portion of Śiva.
Samudra is declared to be Śantanu, and Gaṅgā is considered his wife by the wise; Devaka, however, is described in the Āgama as the lord of the Gandharvas.
Vasubhīṣma and Virāṭa are remembered as the Marudgaṇa;
Haṃsa, the son of Ariṣṭa, is proclaimed as Dhṛtarāṣṭra. || 36 ||
The host of Maruts is said to be Kṛpa, and likewise Kṛtavarman is another;
Duryodhana is a portion of Kali, and know Śakuni to be Dvāpara.
The son of Soma, known as Suvarcas, is declared to be Somapra;
Dhṛṣṭadyumna is a portion of Pāvaka, and Śikhaṇḍin is likewise a Rākṣasa.
Pradyumna is proclaimed to be a portion of Sanatkumāra;
Drupada is a portion of Varuṇa, and Draupadī is born from a portion of Ramā.
The five sons of Draupadī are remembered as being born from portions of the Viśvedevas.
Kuntī is Siddhi, Mādrī is Dhṛti, and the daughter of the king of Gāndhāra is Mati.
Likewise, all the wives of Kṛṣṇa are remembered as celestial courtesans;
and all the kings, as well as the Asuras, were incited by Śakra. || 41 ||
Śiśupāla is declared to be a portion of Hiraṇyakaśipu;
likewise, Jarāsaṃdha is Vipracitti, and Śalya is Prahlāda. (42)
Likewise, Kālanemi, Kaṃsa, Keśin, Hayaśiras,
Ariṣṭa, and Bali’s son Kakudmin were slain at Gokula.
Anuhlāda became Dhṛṣṭaketu, Bhagadatta became Bāṣkala, Lamba became Pralamba, and that Kharas became Dhenuka. (44)
The two Daityas Vārāha and Kiśora, who were exceedingly fierce,
were born as wrestlers known as Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika.
Likewise, Diti’s sons were Ariṣṭa and the elephant named Kuvalaya;
Bali’s daughter was the famous Bakī, and his younger brother is remembered as Baka. (46)
Yama, Rudra, as well as Kāma and Krodha as the fourth—by their respective portions the exceedingly powerful son of Droṇa was born. (47)
Formerly, during the partial incarnations, all the Daityas and Rākṣasas were born as portions of the gods for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth. (48)
O King, this descent of portions of the gods and the asuras has been told to you; it is proclaimed in the Purāṇas, O ruler of men. (49)
When the gods, headed by Brahmā, went to Hari for the sake of a boon,
Hari indeed granted them two locks of hair, one white and one black.
Then Kṛṣṇa was dark-complexioned and Saṅkarṣaṇa was white;
for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden, those two were born as manifestations of portions of the gods.
He who hears this account of the partial incarnations with a spirit of devotion,
being liberated from all sins, rejoices surrounded by his own kinsmen.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Partial Incarnations of the Devas and Dānavas," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Vyāsa spoke these words of Yogamāyā to Kaṃsa regarding the six sons of Devakī who had been slain by the son of Ugrasena:
And when the seventh embryo had fallen due to the words of Nārada. || 1 ||
And for the sake of protecting the eighth embryo,
the king, reflecting upon his own death, made an unremitting effort.
At that time, Hari entered the womb of Devakī through his partial incarnation (aṃśa),
having arrived with Vasudeva in due order.
Thus, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, the goddess Yogamāyā entered into Yaśodā according to her will.
Rāma, the son of Rohiṇī, was born in Gokula,
for that beautiful woman remained there, agitated by fear of Kaṃsa.
Then Kaṃsa placed Devakī, who is praised by the gods,
in prison and appointed servants for her protection.
But Vasudeva, bound by the cords of love for his beloved and reflecting upon the birth of a son, entered [the city] together with his wife.
Viṣṇu, having entered the womb of Devakī for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods,
was praised by the hosts of immortals and grew up in due order.
Then, when the tenth month had arrived, in the auspicious month of Śrāvaṇa,
on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, conjoined with the Prajāpatya (Rohiṇī) asterism.
But Kaṃsa, overwhelmed by fear, said to all the Dānavas:
"Devakī must be guarded by you within the inner chamber of her womb."
"The eighth child in Devakī’s womb will become my enemy;
that boy, though appearing as death itself, must be protected with great effort. (11)
"Having killed this boy, I shall sleep happily in my palace;
for when the eighth son is destroyed, suffering—devoid of cessation—is brought to an end. (12)
Let all of you stand bearing swords and spears, holding bows, free from sleep and drowsiness, with your eyes fixed everywhere. (13)
Vyāsa said:
Having thus commanded the hosts of Asuras, the emaciated one, overwhelmed by extreme fear, quickly went to his own abode; the Dānava found no peace.
At midnight, Devakī spoke there to Vasudeva: "What shall I do, O Great King? The time for my delivery has arrived. (15)
Many terrifying guardians stand here;
furthermore, a compact was previously made by me together with Nanda’s wife.
"O proud lady, you must send your son to my palace;
there I shall indeed protect him with all my heart. (17)
"I shall give you an offspring for the sake of convincing Kaṃsa;
what must be done here, O Lord, now that this crisis has arisen? (18)
O Śauri, how could you possibly effect a reversal of my lineage?
Stay far away today, O beloved; my shame is exceedingly difficult to overcome. (19)
"O Lord, turning my face away, what else could I do?
Having spoken thus to that illustrious one, who was honored by the gods, Devakī—
There, at midnight, she gave birth to an exceedingly wonderful boy;
seeing that auspicious child, Devakī was filled with amazement.
The highly fortunate woman, her body overflowing with joy, said to her husband:
"Behold the face of your son, O beloved; for it is indeed difficult for you, O Lord, to obtain. (22)
"Today this brother’s son, appearing in the form of Death, will slay him.
Vasudeva, saying "So be it," took his son by the hand.
And he beheld the face of that son of wondrous deeds;
having gazed upon his son’s face, Śauri became overcome with anxiety.
"What shall I do? How can there be no suffering for me on his account?"—while he was thus distressed by anxiety, an incorporeal voice spoke.
Addressing Vasudeva with clear syllables in the sky, she said:
"O Vasudeva, take him and lead him to Gokula with all haste."
Likewise, all the guards have been rendered unconscious by me with sleep;
the eight door-panels and the chains have been opened.
"Having released him in the house of Nanda, you must bring back the Yogamāyā.
Upon hearing this, Vasudeva went to that prison cell.
Seeing the door opened, O King, he quickly took him and departed swiftly, unobserved by the gatekeepers. (29)
Having reached the bank of the Kālindī and seeing the flood with certainty,
that best of rivers immediately became waist-deep at that very moment.
By the power of his yogic illusion, Ānakadundubhi crossed over;
having gone to Gokula at midnight on a deserted path, Śauri [arrived].
Standing at the gate of Nanda, beholding the manifestation known as "beastly" (paśu),
Yaśodā, born from a womb, was conceived right then and there.
The goddess, born from a portion of Yogamāyā, possessing the three qualities and divine form,
was taken by him with his lotus-like hands as that divine girl was born.
Having arrived there, the goddess, assuming the form of Sairandhrī, gave [the child];
Vasudeva, having placed his son into the lotus-like hand of Sairandhrī, [departed].
Taking that girl with a joyful heart, he went quickly;
then, having gone to the prison, he placed the daughter upon Devakī’s bed.
Having cast it down, he stood at the side, overcome with anxiety and afflicted by fear;
then the girls, who had regained their senses, wept with a loud voice. || 36 ||
Hearing that weeping in the night, the king’s servants arose;
having gone to him in great haste and extreme agitation, they spoke to the lord of the earth. (37)
"A son has been born to Devakī; come quickly, O high-minded one! Having heard those words of theirs, the lord of the Bhojas departed at once.
Seeing the door closed, he then called out to Vasudeva.
Kaṃsa said:
"O high-minded Vasudeva, bring the son of Devakī here."
"And death shall be my eighth conception; therefore, I shall slay that enemy Hari.
Vyāsa said: Having heard Kaṃsa’s words, Vasudeva’s eyes became terrified with fear.
Taking that daughter by the hand, he quickly gave her [to him] as if weeping;
then, upon seeing the girl, the king was struck with the utmost wonder. (41)
"The speech of the gods and the words of Nārada have proven false;
how could Vasudeva, even when situated in a crisis, utter an untruth? (42)
"All my guards are undoubtedly on their guard;
how then could a maiden enter here at will, and where indeed has that son gone? (43)
"No doubt should be entertained here; the course of time is treacherous.
Having reflected thus, the wicked man seized that young girl by her feet.
That merciless defiler of his lineage dashed her against a stone;
the young girl, escaping from his hand, went into the expanse of the sky.
Then, assuming a divine form, she spoke to him in a gentle voice:
"O wicked one, what is gained by killing me? A powerful enemy has been born for you. (46)
"He, who is difficult to propitiate, will destroy you, the lowest of men, in every way.
Having said this, that auspicious maiden, capable of going anywhere at will, departed for the sky.
Kaṃsa, however, overcome with astonishment, then went to his own home; having summoned all the Dānavas, he spoke these words: || 48 ||
"Overcome with rage and afflicted by fear, let all the Dānavas, including Baka, Dhenuka, Vatsa, and the others, go forth for the successful accomplishment of my purpose. (49)
"Wherever infants are born, they must be killed;
let this Pūtanā, the slayer of children, go today to Nanda’s cowherd settlement. (50)
By my command, Dhenuka, Vatsaka, Keśin, Pralamba, and Baka slaughtered the infants there as soon as they were born.
"Let all remain right there, desiring to carry out my business," having thus commanded the Asuras, the wicked Kaṃsa went to his own home.
Overcome by anxiety and deeply dejected in spirit, he reflected upon that once again.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Words of Yogamāyā to Kaṃsa," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Vyāsa said: In the morning, at the house of Nanda, there arose a great festival celebrating the birth of a son, which dispelled the queen’s sorrow for Kṛṣṇa.
Then, what was reported by Kaṃsa, even from the mouths of his spies? || 1 ||
He knows that Vasudeva’s wife and all his cattle and servants are staying there in Nanda’s cowherd settlement.
O descendant of Bharata, filled with apprehension because of that,
Nārada also previously explained the entire reason regarding Gokula.
Those in Gokula such as Nanda and others, their wives who were born from portions of the gods,
and Devakī, Vasudeva, and the rest— all of them were indeed his enemies.
O King, having been thus enlightened by the words of Nārada, that lowest of his clan,
Kaṃsa— the perpetrator of supreme evil— became filled with rage.
There, Pūtanā was slain by Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable splendor,
as were Baka, Vatsāsura, and the exceedingly powerful Dhenuka.
Having heard that Pralamba had been slain by him and likewise that Govardhana had been held up,
Kaṃsa considered his own death to be certain.
When Keśin had been thus slain, Kaṃsa, realizing this,
became exceedingly dejected and quickly set about inviting them both under the pretext of a bow-sacrifice.
Then the cruel one, whose mind was wicked, dispatched Akrūra to bring back Rāma and Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable prowess for the purpose of killing them.
Having placed the two cowherds upon the chariot, the son of Gāndinī came from Gokula to Mathurā, where he remained indeed by the command of Kaṃsa.
Then, having arrived there, they both broke the bow;
thereafter, they killed the washerman at their will, as well as the elephant, Cāṇūra, and Muṣṭika.
Then Hari slew both Śala and Tośala;
the Lord of Gods effortlessly seized Kaṃsa by the hair and killed him.
Then, having liberated his parents, the destroyer of enemies made them free from suffering;
he gave that kingdom to Ugrasena.

There, the high-minded Vasudeva caused the two of them to undergo the formal investiture of the sacred thread (vratibandha) according to the prescribed rites, preceded by the tying of the girdle of muñja grass.
Then, having been initiated, the two went to the abode of Sāndīpani;
and after mastering all branches of knowledge, they returned once more to Mathurā.
Twelve years old, accomplished in learning, and possessed of great strength, the two heroic sons of Ānaka-dundubhi resided in Mathurā. (16)
But Jarāsandha of Magadha, distressed by the slaughter of his son-in-law,
assembled a host of troops and came to the city of Mathurā.
Having encountered him in battle, he was defeated seventeen times by Kṛṣṇa, who had made up his mind while residing in Madhupurī.
And later, impelled by him, that hero named Kālayavana, the lord of all the Mlecchas and a source of terror to the Yādavas, [arrived]. || 19 ||
Having heard that the Yavana was approaching, Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of Madhu, summoned all the best of the Yadus as well as Rāma and spoke to them.
"Great fear has arisen here for us from the exceedingly powerful Jarāsaṃdha;
O illustrious one, what should be done, for the Yavana is indeed approaching? (21)
One must protect one's life even by abandoning home, strength, and wealth;
indeed, that country where one dwells in happiness is one’s ancestral land.
Granted that one who desires happiness should act in accordance with his family tradition, even if it causes constant anxiety, he should nevertheless remain near mountains and oceans. (23)
The wise should dwell where there is no fear of enemies;
Hari himself rests upon the serpent Śeṣa as his bed while sleeping in the ocean.
And likewise, the destroyer of Tripura remains on Kailāsa out of fear;
therefore, we, tormented by our enemies, must not remain right here.
"We shall all go together to Dvāravatī;
today Garuḍa has described to us that beautiful city of Dvāravatī. (26)
"On the bank of the Sindhu, near Mount Raivata, she is enchanting.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those truthful words, all the foremost of the Yādavas [acted accordingly].
Together with their families and their vehicles, they resolved to depart;
likewise, there were wagons, camels, mares, and buffaloes.
Having filled [their carts] with wealth, they all set out from the city,
placing Rāma and Kṛṣṇa at their head, accompanied by all their attendants.
Placing all their subjects at the forefront, all those best of the Yadus set forth;
indeed, after some days, they reached the city of Dvāravatī.
Mādhava indeed caused the restoration of the ruins to be carried out by artisans,
having established those two, Bala and Keśava, there among the Yādavas.
Having arrived at Mathurā with speed, they settled in that deserted city;
then, the powerful lord of the Yavanas reached that very place.
Having learned that he had arrived, Kṛṣṇa went out from the city;
Janārdana stood before that Yavana on foot.
The glorious Madhusūdana, wearing yellow garments, laughed;
he saw that lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa walking before him.
The wicked Yavana, though himself a foot-soldier, followed closely behind at a place where the mighty royal sage Mucukunda was fast asleep.
The blessed Lord Hari proceeded there together with Kālayavana;
and having looked upon Mucukunda, Viṣṇu vanished right there.
Right there, a Yavana arrived and saw him as if he were asleep;
thinking him to be Vāsudeva, he struck the king with his foot.
Awakened, the immensely powerful Mucukunda, his eyes red with rage, consumed him with fire;
having burnt him, he then beheld the lotus-eyed one.
Having bowed down to Vāsudeva, the lord of the virtuous gods, he set out for the forest;
accompanied by Baladeva, Kṛṣṇa went to Dvārakā. (39)
Having installed Ugrasena as king, he lived according to his pleasure;
he took Rukmiṇī at will from the svayaṃvara of Śiśupāla.
By means of the Rākṣasa form of marriage, Hari performed the rite of taking wives;
then he took Jāmbavatī, Satyā, and the beautiful Mitravindā.
Janārdana also married Kālindī, Lakṣmaṇā, Bhadrā, and the auspicious Nāgnajitī, having brought them together individually.
O protector of the earth, Rukmiṇī gave birth to eight most beautiful wives and a son, Pradyumna, who was lovely to behold. (43)
Madhusūdana performed for him the birth-rites and other ceremonies;
he had been carried away from the lying-in chamber by the powerful Śambara.
The boy was led back to his own city and handed over to Māyāvatī;
Vāsudeva, seeing that his son had been taken away, was overcome with grief.
With a heart full of devotion, he sought refuge in the Goddess, by whom the Daityas, beginning with Vṛtrāsura, were slain as if in mere sport. (46)
Then he directed his supreme mindfulness toward Yogamāyā with most noble words, syllables, and auspicious hymns of praise.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Mother, you were propitiated by me through intense penance in a previous birth, and you were worshipped with flowers and other offerings.
O Mother, has your state of devotion toward me been forgotten by the son of Dharma in the midst of the Badarī forest? (48)
Has my infant been carried away from the lying-in chamber by someone of wicked intent, or perhaps out of curiosity? Surely it is for the purpose of robbing me of my honor today.
O Mother, it is indeed fitting that you feel shame for your devotee. || 49 ||
The city is exceedingly difficult to traverse and well-guarded;
even there, my residence is said to be in the middle part,
and within the inner apartments, the lying-in chamber is indeed concealed.
The child has indeed been carried away; yet it is solely due to my own fault.
I have not gone to the enemy's city, nor have the Yādavas;
the city of Rākṣāvatī is indeed protected by the best of heroes.
O Mother, this is merely your own illusion, whose power is manifest.
"By what deceiver has my child been carried away? (51)
O Mother, I do not know your well-guarded conduct; who else could know it, for I am but a dull-witted being of little knowledge?
Where has he gone, that he was not seen by my soldiers?
O Mother, this curtain has been fashioned by me for you. || 52 ||
It is no wonder that you, by means of your illusory power, brought this child from your mother’s womb to me at the halfway point;
for it is well known that Rohiṇī gave birth to the wielder of the plow.
Standing at a distance, she was devoted to her husband, even though she was without her mate.
You perform the creation, the protection, and likewise the destruction of the worlds, again and again, incessantly through your qualities;
O Mother, who can know your conduct, which brings an end to all suffering?
For the most part, all of this has been entirely ordained by you.

Having produced the joy arising from the birth of a son and then, it is said, bestowed upon us the burden of suffering born of separation, you indeed sport with those most graceful pastimes; otherwise, how could my delight in obtaining a son be anything but in vain? (55)
His mother weeps bitterly like a female osprey;
she who is always by my side spreads sorrow for me. Alas, O Lalitā of immeasurable power, you do not perceive this!
O Mother, you alone are the refuge for those afflicted by the cycle of existence.
O Goddess, the wise declare that the birth of a son is the boundary of happiness and his loss is the boundary of suffering;
O Mother, what shall I do when the first has already perished?
O Mother, today my heart seems to burst within me because of my son.
I perform sacrifices for your satisfaction, as well as vows and divine worship; you are the destroyer of all suffering.
O Mother, if this son of mine lives here, show yourself quickly!
You are indeed forbearance for the destruction of all sorrow.
Vyāsa said: Thus praised then by Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds, the Goddess,
appearing visibly before him, spoke to that teacher of the world.
The illustrious Goddess said:
"Do not grieve, O Lord of Gods; this curse of yours is ancient.
By its power, your son was forcibly carried away by Śambara."
Therefore, in the sixteenth year, having slain that Śambara by force, your son will return through my grace; of this there is no doubt.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess Caṇḍikā, of fierce prowess, vanished;
and the Blessed One, too, having abandoned grief for his son, became happy.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Dispelling of Kṛṣṇa’s Sorrow by the Goddess," in the fourth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 24.
Regarding the statement that Parāśakti is omniscient,
the King said:
"O best of sages, a doubt arises in me because of your words."
And having observed the arising of suffering within the Blessed One, who is a portion of Viṣṇu. || 1 ||
How was the powerful Vāsudeva, born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa,
carried away as a child even from the chamber of birth by Hari?
Then, having entered a well-guarded lying-in chamber in the beautiful city of Sugupta, how was that infant seized by that Daitya? (3)
"It was not known by Vāsudeva; this is a wonder to me.
O son of Satyavatī, a great marvel arises in my mind."
O Brahmā, tell me the reason for that which was not understood by Keśava,
who remained there in the lying-in chamber, regarding the abduction of the infant from the maternity room.
Vyāsa said:
O King, the power of Māyā is mighty, deluding the intellects of men;
it is renowned in the world as Śāmbhavī—who indeed does not fall into delusion?
Having attained human birth, all humans indeed possess human qualities born of the body; at that time, they are neither gods nor asuras.
Hunger, thirst, sleep, fear, lassitude, delusion, sorrow, doubt, joy, pride, as well as old age and death. (8)
Ignorance, languor, lack of pleasure, envy, malice, intoxication, and fatigue—these states arising from the body prevail, O lord of men. (9)
Just as Rāma did not perceive the golden deer standing before him,
so too he did not perceive the abduction of Jānaki and the death of Jaṭāyu.
On the day of his consecration, Rāma did not know of his exile to the forest;
likewise, Rāma was unaware of his father’s death due to his own grief.
Wandering from forest to forest like one ignorant,
he did not find Jānakī, who had been forcibly carried away by Rāvaṇa.
Having made the monkeys his allies and having slain the son of Śakra by force,
he built a bridge across the ocean and crossed over that lord of rivers.
He dispatched those elephant-like monkeys in all directions;
he engaged in a terrible battle and met with suffering on the field of combat.
The mighty Rāma, the joy of the Raghus, was bound by a serpent-noose, and subsequently experienced liberation from Garuḍa. || 15 ||
Enraged, the joy of the Raghus slew the mighty Kumbhakarṇa in battle, as well as Meghanāda and Nikumbha.
Janārdana did not know that Jānakī was beyond reproach;
therefore, he caused her to undergo the divine ordeal by entering the blazing fire.
Furthermore, due to public censure, the son of Daśaratha abandoned his beloved Sītā, whom he considered blameless, thinking her to have been defiled. (18)
Rāma did not recognize his two sons, Kuśa and Lava;
however, the sage declared them to be his two immensely powerful sons.
Rāghava did not know that Jānakī had gone to the netherworld; filled with rage, he prepared to kill his brother.
The slayer of Khara did not even perceive the arrival of Time;
having assumed a human body, he performed human actions.
In the same way, one should not entertain any doubt regarding human states;
for previously, the joy of the Yadus arrived at Gokula out of fear of Kaṃsa.
Later, out of fear of Jarāsandha, Hari went to Dvārakā;
there Kṛṣṇa committed an unrighteous act by abducting Rukmiṇī. (23)
And knowing the eternal dharma,
Kṛṣṇa grieved for the child Śiśupāla, who had been forcibly abducted by Śambara.
Then, recognizing him as his son, he rejoiced, filled with both joy and sorrow;
for it was by Satyabhāmā’s command that he had indeed fought while in heaven.
He who, displaying his own subjection to women for the sake of a footstool, defeated Śatakratu and seized the Kalpavṛkṣa tree from Indra.
To protect the pride of the proud Satyabhāmā, the Lord Hari assumed various forms;
having tied Hari to a tree, Satyā presented her husband to Nārada.
Then, having given the golden [coins], the beautiful woman released Kṛṣṇa;
she did so after seeing her sons, headed by Pradyumna, who possessed many virtues.
The distressed Jāmbavatī entreated Kṛṣṇa for an auspicious offspring;
having resolved to perform penance, Kṛṣṇa went to the mountain.
Where the sage Upamanyu, a devotee of Śiva and a scorcher of foes, resides;
there Hari, having taken Upamanyu as his preceptor, received the Pāśupata initiation.
Desiring a son, he took them up and became one with shaven head and a staff;
there he performed fierce penance for one month, subsisting on fruits.
Hari, intent on meditation upon Śiva, muttered the Śiva-mantra;
in the second [month], Hari remained standing on one foot, subsisting only on water.
In the third [period], subsisting on air alone, he remained fixed on the tip of his big toe;
then, in the sixth [period], the Lord Rudra was pleased by his state of devotion.
And there Soma, the bearer of the lunar digit, granted his vision;
he arrived mounted upon his bull, surrounded by the gods led by Indra.
Accompanied by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and personally attended by Yakṣas and Gandharvas,
Śaṅkara spoke to Vāsudeva, awakening him to consciousness.
"I am pleased, O Kṛṣṇa, by your fierce austerity, O high-minded one! I grant you your desired boons; speak, O delight of the Yādavas! (36)
"When I am seen, who am the fulfiller of desires, no trace of desire shall remain.
Vyāsa said:
Having seen that Śaṅkara was pleased, the Blessed Lord, the son of Devakī, [spoke]. (37)
Filled with love, he fell at his feet like a staff;
the Lord of Gods then offered praise with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The eternal Vāsudeva stood before Śambhu;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O God of gods, O Lord of the world, O destroyer of the suffering of all beings! (39)
O source of the universe, O destroyer of the enemies of the gods, O creator of the three worlds, salutations to you!
O blue-throated one, salutations to you; salutations again and again to you, the wielder of the trident.
Salutations to you, the beloved of Śailajā and the slayer of the sacrifice;
O observer of noble vows, by the sight of you I am blessed and my purpose is fulfilled.
My birth has become fruitful by bowing to your lotus feet;
for I am bound by the snares consisting of women in this worldly existence, O Teacher of the World. (42)
O Three-eyed One, O Destroyer of Suffering, I have today come to you for refuge for the sake of protection; having attained this human birth, I am weary. (43)
Protect me now, who have come to you for refuge and am terrified of worldly existence;
O burner of passion, I have encountered great suffering while dwelling in the womb.
From birth, I experienced the fear of Kaṃsa in Gokula; thus was I born as Nanda the cowherd, a servant obeying the commands of the cowherds. (45)
With his hair covered in cow-dust, wandering in the dense Vṛndāvana and terrified by the fear of the Mleccha king, he returned once more to Dvāravatī.
O Lord, having abandoned his auspicious ancestral land of Māthura which is difficult to attain, he was bound by the curse of Yayāti; out of fear, O Lord, it was surrendered to him.
And although I possessed a well-nourished kingdom, being devoted to the protection of dharma,
I indeed acted as a servant to Ugrasena at all times.
"O Śambhu, this king of the Yādavas was indeed appointed by our ancestors;
yet household life is painful, subject to women, and a destroyer of dharma. (49)
In this state of perpetual dependence, news of liberation is difficult to find;
having seen the sons of Rukmiṇī, my wife Jāmbavatī [is now mine]. 50.
O destroyer of Madana, he urged me toward asceticism for the sake of a son;
indeed, today I have performed this penance with desire for the sake of a son.
O Lord of Gods, O Teacher of the World, shame comes upon me in making this request;
for who, having propitiated you—the Lord of Gods, the bestower of liberation, and the one who is affectionate toward his devotees—[would seek anything further]? 52.
The fool begs from you, who are gracious, for a fruit that is trivial and perishable;
such is this one whose soul is deluded by illusion—he begs for the happiness of a son, O All-pervading Lord. (53)
O Śambhu, Lord of the World, though impelled by my beloved, I know you to be the giver of liberation;
yet, O Śambhu, I know this worldly existence to be a source of suffering that yields only pain. (54)
Though it is impermanent and subject to destruction, I nevertheless do not desist;
for by a curse, I, an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa, have been born upon the circle of the earth. (55)
"Bound by the snare of illusion, he experiences manifold suffering to endure.
Vyāsa said:
To Govinda, who had spoken thus, Maheśvara replied. (56)
"O destroyer of enemies, you shall have many sons;
there will be sixteen thousand and five hundred women [in your harem]."
"In each of them there will be ten sons of great strength";
having said this, the lovely Śaṅkara quickly ceased speaking.
The goddess Girijā spoke to Madhusūdana as he bowed before her:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed lord of men, in this cycle of worldly existence... (59)
"O Janārdana, you shall become the foremost householder in this world; then, at the end of a hundred years, due to the curse of a brahmin... (60)
Furthermore, due to the curse of Gāndhārī, the destruction of your lineage will come to pass;
your sons, deluded by that curse, shall slay one another in battle.
All the Yādavas and others likewise shall go to their destruction;
you too, along with your younger brothers, shall cast off this body and indeed go to heaven.
O Lord, you should not grieve regarding what is to come;
there is no remedy for events that are destined to happen. (63)
In this matter, you should certainly never grieve; such is my constant opinion.
O Madhusūdana, by the curse of Aṣṭāvakra, she has become your wife.
"O Kṛṣṇa, upon your death, they will fall into the hands of thieves.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, Śambhu vanished along with Soma and the host of gods.
Then, having bowed to Upamanyu, Kṛṣṇa also departed for Dvārakā;
for although Brahmā and others, O King, are indeed supreme lords, [they remain subject to him]. (66)
Nevertheless, with their inner selves agitated by the union of the waves of illusion, all remain dependent upon it, like wooden puppets. (67)
In whatever manner their past-life karma exists, in that very manner Māyā, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, incessantly impels them.
There is never any partiality or cruelty in the Blessed Lady;
the Sovereign of the World strives solely for the liberation of living beings. (69)
If she were not to create this world of moving and non-moving beings, then,
in the absence of Māyā, all that exists would eternally remain merely inert matter.
Therefore, relying upon compassion, the Goddess constantly performs all that pertains to the world, living beings, and so forth, and she impels it incessantly. (71)
Therefore, one must certainly not entertain any doubt regarding this delusion beginning with Brahmā;
for all gods and demons fall within the scope of Māyā and are subject to Māyā.
That very Goddess of the gods is independent, wandering and acting according to her own will;
therefore, O King, that Great Sovereign (Maheśvarī) should be served with one's whole being. 73.
There is nothing superior or more excellent than this in the three worlds;
for the remembrance of the feet of the Supreme Śakti is indeed the fruition of birth.
May there never be birth in that family where the Goddess is not the deity;
I am the Goddess, I am none other, I am Brahman itself, and I am not subject to sorrow.
Thus, having learned of this eternal Mother of the World from the mouth of the Guru through the study of Vedānta and other means, one should contemplate her as non-different [from oneself]. (76)
One should constantly meditate with a one-pointed mind upon her whose form is the Self;
by that, one is swiftly liberated, and not otherwise even by tens of millions of ritual acts.
Śvetāśvatara and all the other sages, whose inner dispositions were stainless, realized the nature of the Self within their hearts and were liberated from the bonds of worldly existence. 78.
In the same way, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others, as well as Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and the rest,
worship her alone, who is of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Thus, O sinless King, I have told you everything that was requested by you, who are terrified by the phenomenal world;
what more do you wish to hear?
O King, I have thus related to you this unsurpassed narrative, which removes all sins, is meritorious, ancient, and most wonderful. (81)
Whoever should constantly hear this Purāṇa, which is equal to the Vedas, shall be liberated from all sins and honored in the world of the Goddess. (82)
Sūta said:
This fifth Purāṇa, truly known by the name Śrīmad Bhāgavata, was heard by me in detail as it was being narrated by Vyāsa. (83)

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Omniscience of the Supreme Śakti," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 25 ||
Description of the Power of Yogamāyā.
The Sages said: O Sūta, you have narrated this great and supreme account.
The divine life-story of Kṛṣṇa, which destroys all sins. || 1 ||
O illustrious one, O high-minded one, as this narrative of Vāsudeva is being told in detail, a doubt arises within us.
Having gone to the forest, Vāsudeva performed difficult austerities;
as an incarnation of a portion of Viṣṇu, he offered worship to Śiva.
And furthermore, the granting of boons by the goddess Pārvatī, the mother of the world, who is the full manifestation and an emanation of the venerable Goddess Śrī; || 4 ||
How is it that those two were fully honored even by the Lord Kṛṣṇa?
Or is there some deficiency in him? Such is my doubt.
Sūta said:
Listen, O highly fortunate ones, to the cause therein which was heard by me from Vyāsa; I shall relate this narrative endowed with the qualities of Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard the account in detail, the son of Vairāṭī’s son, being wise, then asked again, having fallen into a state of great doubt. || 7 ||
Janamejaya said:
O son of Satyavatī, I have heard the supreme cause correctly;
nevertheless, the activity of my mind does not relinquish its doubt.
O illustrious one, this is a marvel that Śambhu was propitiated by Viṣṇu, the god of gods, after he had performed most rigorous penance.
How did Hari, who is the soul of all, the Lord of all, the master who bestows all perfections,
perform such terrible penance like an ordinary being?
Kṛṣṇa is capable of creating the world, likewise capable of protecting it, and even capable of destroying it; why then did he perform such severe austerity?
Vyāsa said:
"O King, you have spoken the truth; Vāsudeva Janārdana, the slayer of the Daityas, is capable in all undertakings for the sake of the gods."
Nevertheless, the Supreme Lord, having assumed a human body,
performed human activities based upon the system of castes and stages of life.
The honoring of the elderly, prostrating at the feet of the guru, service to the Brahmins, and likewise the propitiation of the deities; || 14 ||
In sorrow there is the onset of grief, and in joy the swelling of delight;
there is wretchedness, various censures, and the pursuit of desire among women. (15)
For desire, anger, and likewise greed arise from time to time;
so how can there be freedom from qualities in a body composed of the qualities? (16)
Due to the fault arising from the curse of Saubalī, as well as that arising from the curse of the Brāhmaṇas, there was the destruction of the Yādavas and the liberation of Kṛṣṇa’s body. || 17 ||
O lord of men, likewise there was the abduction and plundering of his wives;
and while Arjuna discharged his weapons, there was cowardice shown toward the robbers. (18)
The ignorance regarding the abduction of Pradyumna and Aniruddha from their home—such indeed is the human-like activity displayed in this human body. (19)
In this incarnation as a partial manifestation of Viṣṇu, and likewise in Vāsudeva, who was born from a portion of the sage Nārāyaṇa,
what is surprising about his service to Śiva?
For he is the Lord of all, the God who is even the cause of Viṣṇu;
he is the master of the state of deep sleep (suṣupti), and he is worshipped by Viṣṇu.
Since Kṛṣṇa and others are but portions of Him, why is He not worshipped by them?
The Lord Brahmā is the syllable *A*, and Hari Himself is the syllable *U*. (22)
The syllable *ma* is the Lord Rudra, and the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) is Maheśvarī;
by virtue of each succeeding one, the state of being supreme is declared by the wise. (23)
Therefore, in all the scriptures, the Goddess is remembered as the most supreme;
she is eternally established in the half-mora (ardhamātrā), and she is especially that which is not to be uttered.
Rudra is even superior to Viṣṇu, while Viṣṇu is superior to Brahmā;
therefore, one should have no doubt regarding Kṛṣṇa’s worship of Śiva. (25)
By the will of Brahmā, for the purpose of granting a boon,
there emerged from his mouth a second one named Rudra, who was a portion of Mūlarudra.
He too is worthy of worship by all; what need is there to mention Mūlarudra?
O Śivā, its excellence is traditionally held to arise from the presence of the Devī-tattva.
Thus the incarnations of Hari manifest age after age through the power of his yoga-māyā; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
She who, with her hidden nature, perfectly creates, sustains, and destroys the universe by the mere movement of the lashes of her eyes—
she herself constantly subjects Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva to various incarnations, treating them as mere instruments in her manifold manifestations.
She was also commissioned by her to depart from the lying-in chamber,
and she was concealed in the palace of the King of the Cowherds; she was then brought to Mathurā and assigned her duties.
Indeed, his heart was filled with fear at the abduction of Śrī Dvārakā. || 30 ||
Having created sixteen thousand women who were most highly esteemed for their eightfold qualities and possessed of their own artistic skills,
he brought Kāma under the sway of their charms.
For even by her, the infinite Blessed One has been made a slave.
Even a single young woman is capable of binding a man with a bond of very firm iron;
what then need be said of sixteen thousand five hundred women?
They bind him very tightly, like a parrot that has been captured. || 32 ||
At that time, Hari—filled with joy and having come under the influence of Satrājit’s daughter—reached the abode of the Lord of the Gods after a conflict with Maghavan;
there, the Lord of Trees (the *kalpavṛkṣa*), having been sported with, became an ornament for his beloved’s dwelling.

He who, having conquered Śiśupālaka and others, desired to perform the rites prescribed by the Creator for one who has abducted the daughter of Bhīma, took her as his lawful wife by his own power—what kind of rite was that which he devised for the abduction of another’s wife? (34)
Under the sway of egoism, a living being performs both auspicious and inauspicious deeds, being utterly deluded by the snare of ignorance born of delusion, which brings about his downfall. (35)

For this entire world of moving and non-moving beings has arisen from ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra), which is fierce, born of primordial nature (prakṛti), and the root of Hari, Hara, and the other gods. (36)
When the lotus-born one becomes completely free from egoism, then he is liberated; otherwise, he remains a performer of the karma of saṃsāra.
One who is freed from that is indeed liberated, while one who has fallen under its control is bound.
Neither woman, nor wealth, nor home, nor sons, nor siblings [can liberate him]. (38)
O King, the bondage of living beings is indeed the ego;
"I am the doer," "this task was performed by me," so thinks the powerful one. (39)
"I shall do it," "I am doing it"—thus the living being binds itself;
for an effect can never occur without a cause. (40)
Just as a jar is not seen to have been produced without a lump of clay, so too Viṣṇu, endowed with egoity, is the protector of the universe. (41)
Otherwise, how could a human being ever cease to be submerged in the ocean of anxiety? It is only when one becomes liberated from egoism that this occurs. || 42 ||
How could one of pure intention sink into the currents of worldly incarnation?
Egoism is the root of delusion, and from it arises this cycle of existence (saṃsāra). || 43 ||
For those devoid of egoism, there is neither delusion nor worldly existence.
The Puruṣa is said to be of three kinds: the Sāttvika, as well as the Rājasa, [and the Tāmasa]. (44)
But the tamasic [nature], O great king, is threefold among Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others—O Indra among kings, it always exists in these three, such as Kāma, Īśa, and the rest. (45)
Egoism has always been proclaimed by the sages who perceive the truth;
by that very egoism these beings are bound, of this there is no doubt. (46)
Deluded by Māyā, the dull-witted speak thus:
"Viṣṇu creates his numerous incarnations according to his own will. (47)

Even a dull-witted person does not set his mind upon dwelling in the womb, which is a dense thicket of suffering and extreme confinement; how much less, then, could the wise Lord, the Wielder of the Discus, do so?
Indeed, Madhusūdana has truly entered by his own will into the wombs of Kausalyā and Devakī, which are filled with the impurity of excrement; so they say. 49.

Having abandoned the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, what happiness indeed can there be in dwelling within a womb—a place that gives rise to millions of anxieties, is fraught with suffering, and is comparable to poison? (50)
Having performed austerities, having conducted sacrifices, and having given gifts many times,
they do not desire those worlds from which there is dwelling in a womb, which brings such great suffering.
If that Lord Viṣṇu, Janārdana,
were truly self-dependent, how could he have become one who delights in dwelling in a womb, if he possessed such self-dependence?
Know, O Great King, that this world— consisting of gods, humans, and animals, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass— is under the control of Yogamāyā.
Those such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the rest, who are bound by the strings of Māyā,
wander about and fall into bondage through their own play, like a spider.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Power of Yogamāyā," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Origin of Mahiṣāsura.
The King said:
"This power of the Mistress of Yoga has been described by you in great detail."
"Speak of his deeds, O Lord; I have a great curiosity to hear them."
Who indeed would not desire to hear of the power of Mahādevī, who knows that this entire world, including all things moving and stationary, has arisen from her? || 2 ||
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King of great intelligence; I shall explain it to you in detail.
One should not speak this to one who lacks faith or is not tranquil, for such a person is dull-witted.
O protector of the earth, in former times there occurred a terrible battle between the armies of the gods and the dānavas, when the lord of the earth was the king named Mahiṣa.
O Indra among kings, one named Mahiṣa went to the Golden Mountain and performed supreme and fierce penance that caused wonder even to the gods.
O Great King, as he meditated upon the deity within his heart for a full ten thousand years,
Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, was pleased with him.
Having arrived there, the four-faced one, mounted upon a swan, spoke these words:
"Choose a boon, O righteous-souled one; I shall grant you whatever you desire. (7)
Mahiṣa said: "O God of gods, O Lord Druhiṇa, I desire immortality;
O Grandfather, act in such a way that there may be no fear of death."
Brahmā said: For one who has been born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain.
Indeed, for all living beings, death and birth are inevitable in every way.
O bull among the Daityas, all living beings, as well as the great mountains and the oceans, are entirely subject to destruction by time.
O Lord of the Earth, having abandoned one place at the time of death,
tell me, O virtuous one, what boon you have in mind.
Mahiṣa said:
"O Grandfather, neither from gods, nor from humans, nor from Daityas shall I meet death;
nor is there death for me from men—what woman will slay me? (12)
"Therefore, O Lotus-born One, surely bring about my death at the hands of that passionate woman;
for how else will this weak woman be able to kill me? (13)
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of Daityas, at some time or other, your death by a woman is certain;
O illustrious Mahiṣāsura, your death shall not be at the hands of men."
Vyāsa said: Having thus granted him the boon, Brahmā departed for his own abode;
and that best of Daityas also reached his own place, filled with joy.
The king said:
Whose son is this buffalo, and how was he born so exceedingly powerful?
And how did that great-souled one obtain the form of a buffalo?
Vyāsa said:
O great king, there were two sons of Danu, renowned throughout the circle of the earth;
Rambha and Karambha were those two foremost of Dānavas. (17)
O Great King, those two sons performed penance for the sake of obtaining a son for many groups of years, according to their desire, in the holy waters of Pañcanada.
Karambha, submerged in water, performed supreme austerity;
having reached the Rasālavaṭa tree, Rambha attended upon the sacred fire.
When Rambha became intent upon the practice of the five fires,
the Lord of Śacī, perceiving his distress, rose up against the two Dānavas.
Having gone there to Pañcanada, he indeed assumed the form of a crocodile; Vāsava, however, then seized him by the feet.
And the slayer of Vṛtra struck down that wicked Karambha;
hearing that his brother had been killed, Rambha fell into a state of supreme rage. || 22 ||
Filled with rage, he quickly seized his own head by its mass of hair with his left hand and, having severed it, desired to offer it into the fire.
Having seized that fierce, supreme sword with his right hand, he cuts off the head; meanwhile, he is awakened by the fire.
And it was said: "O Daitya, you are a fool; you wish to cut off your own head.
Self-destruction is extremely difficult to accomplish; how can you be intent on performing it? (25)
Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever dwells in your mind.
Do not die; for what purpose will death serve you today? (26)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those well-spoken words of the Fire-god,
Rambha then spoke these words, casting aside her mass of hair.
"If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, grant me my desired boon:
may we have a son who is a conqueror of the three worlds and a crusher of enemy forces. (28)
He shall be invincible in every way by gods, dānavas, and humans; capable of assuming any form at will, possessed of great heroism, and honored by all the worlds. (29)
Pāvaka said to him, "So be it; your desire shall be fulfilled.
O illustrious one, your son shall live; desist now from death."
O Rambhā, upon whichever woman you shall fix your mind, O illustrious one, a son endowed with superior strength will be born to her. (31)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by the Fire-god, Rambha, that best of Dānavas, listened to those heart-pleasing words, bowed down, and departed from that Fire-god.
Seeing that delightful place, surrounded by yakṣas and endowed with splendor,
the best of the Dānavas then conceived a desire for his queen.
When Mātā was filled with passion and had left behind all other women,
she approached him swiftly, full of desire and joy.
Rambha also departed, impelled by destiny;
she, however, became pregnant through his seed. || 35 ||
Then, taking her, he entered the enchanting netherworld (pātāla),
protecting his beloved— who was indeed consented to— against the buffaloes.
Once, another buffalo, afflicted by lust, rushed toward her;
the Dānava himself then approached to slay him. (37)
Having approached for the sake of self-protection, he struck the buffalo;
he too, deluded by passion, quickly struck him back with his two horns.
Struck violently in the heart by his two sharp horns, he fell swiftly to the ground and died, unconscious. || 39 ||
When her husband had died, that wretched woman, afflicted by fear, fled in great haste;
having reached that banyan tree with speed, she sought refuge with the Yakṣas. (40)
But behind her went a buffalo there, tormented by desire;
full of lust and intoxicated by the pride of his strength and valor, he pursued her with longing. (41)
Seeing her weeping bitterly, distressed, and overcome with fear, the yakṣas, upon observing him rushing toward her, came forward to protect her. (42)
A terrible battle took place between the yakṣas and the enemy of horses (Garuḍa);
struck by an arrow, he quickly fell to the surface of the earth. 43.
Having brought the dead Rambha, who was most dear to them, those Yakṣas placed him upon the funeral pyre for the purification of his body.
Then, seeing her husband placed upon the funeral pyre,
that queen resolved to enter the fire along with her husband.
Though being restrained by the yakṣas, that virtuous woman entered the fire, which was filled with garlands of flames, taking her beloved husband with her. (46)
The mighty Mahiṣa rose up from the midst of the funeral pyre,
and Rambha too, out of affection for his son, emerged after assuming another body.
This Raktabīja was born as a buffalo of great strength;
he was then consecrated in the kingdom by the best of the Asuras as Hayāri.
Thus that powerful Mahiṣa was born as Raktabīja;
he was incapable of being slain by gods, daityas, or humans, O best of kings. (49)
Thus, O King, has the birth of that great-souled one been told;
likewise, the granting of the boon has been related in its entirety with full detail.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Origin of the Asura Mahiṣa," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
In the *Bhagavatīmāhātmya*, regarding the mobilization of the Daitya army,
Vyāsa said:
"Thus that Dānava named Mahiṣa, arrogant because of the boon [he had received],"
Having obtained the kingdom, the one of great strength brought the entire world under his control.
He protected the earth, bounded by the oceans, which he had acquired by the strength of his own arms—
ruled under a single umbrella, free from fear, and devoid of any host of enemies.
His general was Cikṣura, who was of great heroism and fierce with pride;
likewise, Tāmra, the lord of wealth, was surrounded by ten thousand troops.
Asiloman, likewise Udarka, the one named Biḍāla, and Bāṣkala;
then Trinetra, and likewise Kālabandhaka, who was arrogant in his strength. (4)
Then all these Dānavas, accompanied by their armies, stood covering the earth— which was prosperous and girt by the ocean— exactly as they desired.
All the ancient protectors of the earth were made to pay tribute;
those who were fierce in their strength and established in the dharma of the Kṣatriyas were slain.
O great king, throughout the entire circle of the earth, the Brāhmaṇas became subject to Mahiṣa and were made to surrender their shares of the sacrificial offerings.
Having established that kingdom under a single umbrella, Mahiṣāsura,
arrogant due to the granting of the boon, set his mind upon conquering heaven.
Hayāri, however, dispatched a messenger to the Lord of Śacī;
the king of the Daityas quickly summoned that bearer of the message and spoke to him.
Go, O hero, O mighty-armed one; perform the duty of a messenger for me, O sinless one.
Having gone to heaven, speak fearlessly to Śakra in the presence of the gods.
"O Thousand-eyed One, abandon heaven and go wherever you wish without delay;
or else, O Lord of Gods, perform service for the high-souled Mahiṣa. (11)
That king will surely protect you once you have come to him for refuge;
therefore, O Lord of Śacī, seek refuge with Mahiṣa.
Otherwise, O slayer of Bala, quickly take up your vajra for battle;
you have been defeated by us before, and I know your prowess. (13)
O paramour of Ahalyā, O leader of the hosts of gods, your strength is known.
Fight or go wherever your mind delights! 14.
Vyāsa said:
O best of kings, having heard those words of his, Śakra, filled with anger, then spoke these words to him with a smile.
