"I do not know, O dull-witted one, why you, arrogant with pride, have become so;
I shall provide the medical treatment for this disease of yours, my master. (16)
"From now on, I shall proceed with the total uprooting of this very root.
Go, messenger, and speak these words of mine before him. (17)
Messengers must not be killed by the cultured; therefore, I release you.
O son of Mahiṣī, if you desire battle, come quickly!
"O enemy, your strength has been recognized; you are but a dull-witted form made of straw.
With my two horns, I shall fashion a very firm bow. (19)
Your pride arises from the strength of your horns; the cause is known to me.
Having severed your tusks, I shall take away that strength.
"O lowest of buffaloes, it is because you are so excessively filled with strength that you have become arrogant with power; you are skilled in striking, but not in battle. (21)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by the lord of the gods, that messenger departed in haste;
he went to the intoxicated Mahiṣa, and having bowed down, replied.
The messenger said:
"O King, that lord of the gods does not disregard you at his pleasure;
surrounded by the divine army, he considers his own strength to be complete. (23)
"What was said by that fool—how can I say anything else?
A servant must speak what is both pleasing and true in the presence of his master. (24)
"O Great King, the auspicious maxim that 'one who desires welfare should speak what is pleasant and true in the presence of a master' remains ever vigilant. (25)
If you speak only what is pleasant, your purpose will not be achieved;
nor should one who desires welfare ever utter harsh words.
Just as words issue from the mouths of enemies like poison, [so too should one guard against them].
O Lord, how is it that such words issue forth from the mouths of your servants? || 27 ||
O Lord of the Earth, my tongue is never capable of uttering such words as those which were spoken by him here. (28)
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words of his, which were full of reason, Mahiṣāsura, who feeds on grass, became intensely overcome with anger.
With eyes bloodshot with rage, he summoned the Daityas,
placing his tail upon his back and discharging urine.
"O Daityas, this lord of the gods is in every way desirous of battle; indeed, make preparations for force, for this lowest of gods must be conquered. (31)
Who could be a hero in my presence, even if there were tens of millions of such as him?
I do not fear Kāma alone; I shall slay him today by all means.
This Śara is surely superior in strength even among those ascetics who have attained peace;
for he is a deceiver, a libertine, and a stealer of others' wives—the very one who creates such power.
Intoxicated by the power of the Apsarases, this wicked man creates obstacles to asceticism;
he is a sinner who strikes at vulnerabilities and is a constant betrayer of trust.
By him Namuci was slain after having made an alliance with that evil-minded one,
who, being terrified, first employed various oaths and deceitful stratagems.
Viṣṇu, however, is a teacher of deceit, a fraud, one who makes false oaths;
he assumes various forms at will, is a strengthener of force, and is a scholar in hypocrisy. || 36 ||
By whom Hiraṇyākṣa was struck down after he had assumed the form of a boar, and by whom Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain as Nṛsiṃha; || 37 ||
O sons of Danu, I shall certainly not be subject to their power;
I do not place my trust in the gods at any time or in any place.
"What can Viṣṇu do to me, or even the more powerful Indra?
Or even Rudra—he is not capable of countering me on the field of battle. (39)
"I shall seize the triple heaven after conquering Indra, Varuṇa, and Yama, as well as Kubera and Agni, and having defeated both the Moon and the Sun. (40)
"Today we shall all become partakers of the sacrificial portions and drinkers of Soma;
and having conquered the host of gods, I shall sport with the Dānavas. (41)
O Dānavas, by virtue of the boon granted to me, I have no fear of the gods;
I shall not die at the hands of men; and what can a woman do to me? (42)
"And having summoned the most excellent Dānavas from the mountains of the netherworld, let my swift messengers appoint them as commanders of my army. (43)
"Alone, I am capable of conquering all the lords of the gods;
having summoned you for the sake of splendor, I shall lead you to the assembly of the deities. (44)
"Indeed, with my two horns and my two hooves, I shall strike down the gods;
by the power of the granted boon, I have no fear of the deities. (45)
"I am invincible by the hosts of gods, asuras, and likewise by humans;
therefore, prepare yourselves today for the conquest of the world of the gods."
"Having conquered the abode of the gods, I shall sport in the Nandana grove, wearing garlands of Mandāra flowers and accompanied by celestial women. (47)
Sprinkled with the milk of the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhenu, they were delighted by the drinking of nectar;
they were accompanied by the songs, dances, and rhythmic movements of gods and gandharvas. || 48 ||
Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Ghṛtācī, Tilottamā, Pramadvarā, Mahāsenā, Miśrakeśī, and Madotkaṭā. (49)
Vipracitti and the others, who are experts in dance and song,
will delight you all with various indulgences in wine.
"Let everyone be ready today; let the departure for the battle with the gods be approved, after performing the most excellent auspicious rites. (51)
And for the protection of all, having summoned the best of sages, Bhārgava, and having honored and established that supreme preceptor at the sacrifice— 52.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus instructed the lords of the Daityas, O King, the evil-minded Mahiṣa then departed quickly for his own abode, filled with joy.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Mobilization of the Daitya Army," in the Glorification of the Blessed Goddess, within the fifth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Consultation with the Gods, including Indra and others, who were afflicted by fear.
Vyāsa said:
After the messenger had departed, the Lord of the Gods (Indra) likewise summoned the deities.
He spoke these words to Yama, Vāyu, Dhanādhyakṣa, Varuṇa, and Agni.
The lord of the Daityas named Mahiṣa, the son of Rambhā, was possessed of great strength;
intoxicated by the pride and arrogance of having received boons, he was skilled in a hundred illusions.
O gods, his messenger has arrived today, sent by that greedy one who desires heaven; he spoke these words to me: || 3 ||
"O Śakra, abandon the abode of the gods; go wherever you wish, O Vāsava, or else perform service to the high-souled Daitya Mahiṣa. || 4 ||
That compassionate lord of the Dānavas will provide for your livelihood;
he never becomes angry with those who are submissive and serve him as his subjects.
Otherwise, O Lord of Gods, prepare the army yourself for battle;
once I have departed, that lord of the Daityas will swiftly approach.
Having spoken thus, that messenger of the wicked-minded Dānava departed.
"O best of gods, consider what must be done next; reflect upon the task at hand."
O gods, even a weak enemy must not be disregarded by one who is powerful,
especially one who is constantly industrious, strong, and arrogant of his own strength.
One must indeed exert effort according to one's intellect and according to one's strength;
for victory or defeat is surely dependent upon destiny.
There is no compromise here; compromise with a wicked person is useless. The virtuous should always act only after deliberating again and again.
Furthermore, no vehicle should now be used again in haste;
instead, swift messengers who can enter easily should be dispatched as observers. (11)
Perceptive of gestures, unattached, free from desire, and truthful in speech, they [reported] the mobilization of the army, the departure, and the exact number of the forces as they truly were. (12)
Having ascertained the nature of the heroes, let them come with haste,
once they have understood the strength and weakness of that lord of the Daityas and his army.
"Therefore, I shall quickly undertake either an expedition or the fortification of our stronghold.
Indeed, a wise person should always act after due deliberation;
an action performed impulsively will result in misery in every respect. (14)
Therefore, the wise should always act with deliberation so as to bring about happiness in every way;
in this matter, it is not right to employ any stratagem of division among the Dānavas under any circumstances.
Therefore, let spies indeed go forth for this task while their minds are focused;
having ascertained their strengths and weaknesses, and having subsequently deliberated upon the course of policy.
Those who know the rules should carry out their duties according to the injunctions toward those intent on performing their tasks;
otherwise, a task performed contrary to the rules yields an opposite result. (17)
"In every respect, that must surely remain unknown, like an untested medicine.
Vyāsa said:
Having reflected thus, they all [appointed] a spy who understood the nature of the task. (18)
The Lord of the Gods dispatched him, O King, for the sake of gaining certain knowledge.
The messenger, having gone quickly and approached the Sovereign of the Suras, [reported]. (19)
Then he reported the strength and weakness of his entire army;
having learned of that force and its preparations, Turāṣāṭ was greatly amazed.
Having summoned his domestic priest, the lord of the thirty gods quickly urged the deities and composed a mantra, being the best among those who know mantras.
He spoke to the best of the Aṅgirasas as he sat upon an excellent seat.
Indra said:
"O teacher of the gods, O learned one, tell us what ought to be done."
"You are omniscient; when this task has arisen, you are our refuge today.
There is a Dānava named Mahiṣa, possessed of great heroism and filled with pride. (23)
Desirous of battle, he approaches surrounded by many dānavas;
therefore, you who are skilled in mantras must now take countermeasures there.
"Among them, you, Śukra, are likewise my remover of obstacles, being well-restrained.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words, Bṛhaspati spoke to Turāsāha (Indra).
Having reflected in his mind upon his desire, intent on accomplishing his task, the Guru said:
"Be composed, O Lord of the Gods; take courage, O noble one. (26)
When misfortune arises, one must certainly not abandon fortitude;
for victory and defeat, O Lord of the Gods, are always dependent upon destiny.
Therefore, O Śatakratu, a wise person should always remain firm by relying on fortitude; for one who truly understands, existence itself must necessarily come to pass.
One must exert effort in every way according to one's own human capacity;
for even the sages are always devoted solely to effort for the sake of liberation.
Knowing that everything is dependent on destiny, yet remaining devoted to yoga and meditation,
one should therefore always exert effort in worldly conduct.
Whether there be happiness or not, what lamentation can there be regarding destiny? Without human effort, one might never attain success. (31)
Even if human effort has been exerted, if success does not arise, it would not bring as much joy as one might wish, being like the union of a blind man and a lame man. (32)
There is no blame for him regarding that embodied being who is subject to fate;
for the accomplishment of the task depends neither on the army, nor on counsel, nor even on deliberation.
"Neither in the chariot nor in the weapon is there any certainty, O Lord of the Gods; everything is subject to destiny.
The powerful man encounters suffering, while the weak enjoys happiness. (34)
The wise man sleeps hungry, while the foolish man may possess enjoyments;
the coward achieves victory, and the hero suffers defeat. (35)
But since this worldly existence is dependent on destiny, what cause for lamentation is there?
O Lord of the Gods, one should certainly apply oneself to effort; yet that which is destined to be must come to pass. (36)
One should not dwell upon those two, whether they bring suffering or happiness;
rather, in times of suffering one should look for those who suffer more, and in times of happiness one should look for those who are happier.
One should not surrender oneself to joy and sorrow as if they were two enemies;
rather, the wise should maintain steadfastness whenever joy or sorrow arises. (38)
The kind of suffering that arises from a lack of fortitude does not exist when there is fortitude; indeed, the capacity for endurance during times of both pleasure and pain is difficult to find. (39)
Where, through the certainty of the intellect, neither joy nor sorrow arises—what is suffering, or whose is the suffering? I am eternally devoid of qualities and immutable. (40)
I am beyond the twenty-four [tattvas]; what sorrow or what pleasure can there be for me?
Hunger and thirst belong to the vital breath (prāṇa), while grief and fainting belong to the mind (manas).
Old age and death belong to the body; Śiva is free from the six waves [of worldly existence].
Grief and delusion are attributes of the body—what concern is there for me in reflecting upon them? (42)
I am not the body, nor am I its possessor;
I am distinct from the seven, the one, the sixteen, and so forth, and I am eternally blissful. (43)
"I am neither nature nor its transformation; what sorrow can there be for me forever?"—thinking thus, O Lord of the Gods, become mentally free from the sense of "mine. (44)
O Śatakratu, this is your first means for the destruction of suffering:
possessiveness is the supreme misery, while freedom from possessiveness is the highest happiness. (45)
O Lord of Śacī, there is no state of happiness greater than contentment;
unless, indeed, one possesses the knowledge that destroys the sense of "mine-ness. (46)
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, one must practice detachment regarding that which is destined to be;
for indeed, the destruction of prārabdha-karmas is not observed through mere enjoyment. (47)
Whatever is destined to happen, that indeed comes to pass; what concern is there for pleasure or pain, O best of beings, whether with all the gods as allies or even with your own intellect? (48)
Happiness leads to the exhaustion of merit, O worthy one, while suffering leads to the exhaustion of evil;
therefore, the wise should always rejoice in the exhaustion of happiness. (49)

Alternatively, O Great King, having consulted with your ministers today, exert yourself according to the prescribed rites; when such effort has been made, whatever is destined to happen will come to pass.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Consultation with the Preceptor of the Gods by Indra and the Other Deities Afflicted by Fear," in the fifth book of the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Defeat of the Daitya Army.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard this, the thousand-eyed one spoke again to Bṛhaspati.
I shall indeed undertake preparations for battle for the destruction of the enemy of horses.
Without exertion, there is neither kingdom, nor happiness, nor indeed fame;
the timid praise neither the one devoid of effort nor the one possessed of effort.
Knowledge is the ornament of ascetics, while contentment is indeed the ornament of the twice-born;
for those who desire prosperity, exertion and the destruction of enemies are their ornaments.
O best of sages, just as the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, Namuci, and Bala were slain through exertion,
so shall I slay this Mahiṣa.
O Lord, you are my strength; the thunderbolt is my supreme weapon;
and Hari as well as the imperishable Lord of Umā are surely my allies.
"O virtuous one, recite for me the mantras that destroy demons; O giver of honor, today I shall make an effort to station my army and direct it against Mahiṣa."
Vyāsa said:
Having been thus addressed by the king of the gods, Vācaspati then spoke these words with a smile to the lord of the gods, who was flushed with the passion for battle.
Bṛhaspati said:
"I do not urge you forward, nor do I restrain you;
for victory here is uncertain, as is defeat for one who fights according to his own desire."
O Lord of Śacī, there is no fault whatsoever in this matter of what must come to be;
whether it be happiness or sorrow, it shall occur as it has been ordained.
O Vāsava, you indeed know that which was experienced by me in the past during the abduction of my wife—a future suffering as well as happiness that I did not fully comprehend at the time. || 10 ||
"O crusher of enemies, my wife has been carried off by the Moon, who acted as my friend while staying at my hermitage; thus has come upon me this sorrow that robs one of all happiness. (11)
O Lord of the Gods, I am known throughout all the worlds as being possessed of intelligence;
where did that intelligence of mine go when my wife was forcibly abducted?
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, wise men should always employ skillful means; for the accomplishment of one's purpose is always certainly dependent upon destiny.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those truthful and meaningful words of his preceptor, the Lord of Śacī went for refuge to Brahmā, and having bowed down, he spoke these words. (14)
O Grandfather, O Lord of the Gods, the Daitya named Mahiṣa, desiring to seize my heaven, is making a great exertion of force. (15)
And all the other Dānavas, possessed of great heroism and skilled in battle, having assembled with that army, stood there desiring to fight. || 16 ||
Therefore, being deeply afraid, I have come here into your presence;
you are omniscient and possessed of great wisdom, so you ought to grant me your assistance. (17)
Brahmā said:
"Let us all go today to Kailāsa with haste, placing Śaṅkara and Viṣṇu, the best among the strong, at our head. (18)
Then, having assembled and deliberated upon a plan, and having considered the place and the time, the battle must be waged by all the hosts of gods together. (19)
A man who acts with rashness, without discerning his own strength and weakness and abandoning discrimination, meets with a downfall. (20)
Vyāsa said: Having heard that, the thousand-eyed Indra departed from Kailāsa,
placing Brahmā in front and accompanied by the guardians of the worlds.
Having gone there, he praised Maheśvara, Śaṅkara, with Vedic mantras;
and having made him gracious before him, he departed toward the city of Viṣṇu.
Having praised that Lord of the Gods of gods, he declared his own purpose:
the fierce fear arising from Mahiṣa, who was arrogant due to the granting of boons.
Having heard that, Viṣṇu spoke to the gods out of fear:
"We shall wage war and slay this invincible one. (24)
Vyāsa said:
Having thus made this resolution, the gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and Īśvara—
mounted their respective vehicles and departed.
Brahmā is mounted upon a swan; Viṣṇu has Garuḍa as his vehicle;
Śaṅkara is mounted upon a bull; and Vṛtrahā (Indra) is seated upon an elephant.
Skanda with his peacock vehicle and Yama with his buffalo vehicle—once the gods had assembled their forces, they set forth. (27)
Just then, the arrogant army of the Daityas, led by Mahiṣa, arrived;
thereupon, a tumultuous battle took place between the armies of the gods and the Dānavas.
With arrows, swords, as well as spears, clubs, battle-axes, maces, sharp-edged spears, tridents, discuses, pikes, and javelins; || 29 ||
With mallets, javelins, and most terrible plows,
as well as with various other weapons, they struck one another.
His commander-in-chief, Cikṣura, who was mounted upon an elephant and possessed great strength,
struck Maghavan with five of those arrows.
Turāṣāṭ, being skillful, also swiftly cut down those arrows with his own arrows and struck him in the heart with a crescent-headed shaft.
Struck by the arrow, the commander fell into a swoon upon his elephant;
he then struck the elephant on its trunk with a blow like a thunderbolt.
Struck by that thunderbolt, the elephant was broken and fled toward the army.
Seeing this, the king of the Daityas became enraged and then spoke to the one named Biḍāla.
Go, O hero of mighty arms, and slay Indra who is arrogant with pride;
having struck down Varuṇa and the other supreme gods, come back to my presence. (35)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, the exceedingly powerful one named Biḍāla mounted an intoxicated elephant and went to the lord of the gods.
Seeing him approaching, Vāsava, filled with rage, struck him with sharp arrows possessing a luster like that of venomous serpents. || 37 ||
Having swiftly cut down those arrows with his own shafts released from his bow,
he quickly struck Vāsava with fifty stone-tipped arrows.
Likewise, Indra also, filled with wrath, cut those arrows and struck him with sharp shafts possessing a luster like that of venomous serpents. || 39 ||
Having swiftly cut down those arrows with his own arrows discharged from his bow,
he struck the elephant on its trunk with a mace.
Slain by his own hand, the Naga repeatedly uttered cries of distress;
turning back, he swiftly struck the army of Daityas, which was overcome with fear.
But the Dānava, seeing the elephant turn back and depart from the battle,
quickly entered a beautiful chariot and went swiftly against the gods in the fray.
Turāṣāḍ, seeing him returned once more standing upon his chariot,
struck him with sharp arrows possessing a luster like that of venomous serpents.
Enraged, that one of great strength also unleashed a fierce shower of arrows;
a tumultuous battle ensued there between those two who were desirous of victory.
But Indra, seeing him so powerful, his senses agitated by anger,
placed Jayanta at his front and fought in conjunction with him.
Jayanta, however, struck that asura, who was arrogant with pride, between the breasts with five sharp arrows drawn with great force.
Struck by that arrow, he fell down upon the chariot;
having carried him past the chariot, the charioteer departed from the field of battle. (47)
When that Daitya named Biḍāla had thus departed, rendered unconscious, there arose a great shout of victory and the sound of kettledrums. (48)
All the gods, greatly delighted, praised that Lord of Śacī;
the lords of the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
Hearing the cry of victory raised by the gods, Mahiṣa became enraged;
he dispatched Tāmra, the destroyer of great pride, to that very place.
But Tāmra, having encountered many [enemies] on the field of battle,
quickly unleashed a shower of arrows, like a cloud-charged sky over the ocean.
Then Varuṇa, raising his noose, departed in haste;
and Yama, mounted upon his buffalo and taking up his staff, went forth.
There, a terrible battle took place between the gods and the dānavas with arrows,
swords, maces, spears, and axes.
Struck by the staff raised in Yama’s hand,
the mighty-armed Tāmra did not waver from the field of battle at that time.
Drawing his bow with force and discharging sharp, stone-tipped arrows,
Tāmra swiftly struck Indra and the other gods upon that field of battle.
Those gods also, enraged, struck the Dānavas with divine arrows, whetted and sharpened on stone, crying out, "Stay! Stay! || 56 ||
Struck by those gods, the Daitya fell into a swoon upon the field of battle;
a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the Daitya army, overcome with fear.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Defeat of the Daitya Army," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Battle between Mahiṣāsura and the Gods headed by Indra.
Vyāsa said:
When the Daitya Tāmra had fainted, Mahiṣa, filled with rage, [attacked].
Having raised his heavy mace, he indeed approached the gods.
Let all the gods stay today; I shall indeed slay them with my mace, for they are all merely crows, eternally devoid of strength as they please.
Having spoken thus, he, arrogant with pride, approached the one mounted upon the elephant and swiftly struck the mighty-armed one on the base of his arm with a mace.
He too, with a terrible thunderbolt, swiftly cut down that mace;
desiring to strike, he quickly rushed toward Mahiṣa.
Even Hayāri, seizing his radiant sword in fury,
advanced toward the immensely powerful Indra as if intending to strike him.
And between those two there occurred a battle that brought fear to all the worlds;
with various weapons therein, it caused wonder even to the sages.
Then the Daitya quickly employed the deluding Śāmbarī illusion,
which indeed bewilders all people and even infatuates the sages.
There, crores of buffaloes of that same appearance and possessing that same prowess were seen, all armed with weapons, slaughtering the army of the gods.
Seeing that illusion created by the Daitya there, Maghavan was struck with wonder and became exceedingly agitated with fear at that deluding magic.
Varuṇa was also greatly terrified, as were Kubera,
Yama, Agni, Sūrya, and the Moon, all afflicted by fear.
All the gods became bewildered and intent on flight;
they rose up and performed the remembrance of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa. || 11 ||
Thereupon, as soon as they were remembered, the supreme gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva— arrived,
mounted respectively upon a swan, a Tārkṣya bird, and a bull, bearing excellent weapons and desiring to rescue her.
Seeing that enchanting woman, Śauri then released his blazing Sudarśana; by its very splendor, that illusion was brought to dissolution.
Beholding them there— those who cause the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world— the buffalo,
desiring to fight, took up an iron club and rushed forward.
The great hero named Mahiṣa, as well as Senānī, Cikṣura,
Ugrāsya, and Ugravīrya, all ran forth, desiring battle.
Asiloman, Mātṛnetra, Bāṣkala, and Andhaka—these and many others, desiring battle, went forth. || 16 ||
Equipped with armor, holding their bows, and mounted upon chariots, those men, arrogant with pride,
surrounded all the gods like wolves surrounding a fine calf.
Then the Dānavas, arrogant with pride, unleashed a rain of arrows, and the gods likewise did so, each desiring to slay the other. || 18 ||
Andhaka, having approached Hari, released five arrows sharpened on stone—drawn back to his ear, possessed of great power, and smeared with poison. (19)
Then Vāsudeva, the destroyer of enemies, with his own swift arrows, cut down those shafts before they had even reached him; he then released five more.
A battle took place between those two, Hari and the Daitya,
with arrows, swords, discuses, clubs, maces, spears, and axes.
The tumultuous battle between Maheśa and Andhaka, which caused the hair to stand on end,
continued for fifty days between them.
Likewise between Indrā and Bāṣkali, and between Mahiṣāsura and Rudra; likewise between Yama and Atrinetrī, and between Mahāhanu and Dhaneśa. || 23 ||
The battle between Asiloman and Varuṇa was exceedingly fierce;
the Daitya struck Garuḍa, the vehicle of Hari, with a mace.
With his limbs exhausted by the blow of the mace, he stood there sighing;
Śauri quickly comforted him with his right hand.
The Lord of Gods steadied the mighty Vainateya;
drawing his bow Śārṅga, he released many arrows.
Janārdana, desiring to kill Andhaka out of anger, [discharged his arrows], but the Dānava also cut those shafts with his own sharp arrows. || 27 ||
In anger, he struck Hari with fifty arrows sharpened on stone;
Vāsudeva, for his part, quickly evaded those excellent shafts.
He released with great force the thousand-spoked Sudarśana discus;
the Sudarśana, once released, was warded off from afar by his own discus.
And he roared, O great king, as if to confound the gods,
upon seeing that the discus of the Lord who bears the Śārṅga bow had become fruitless.
All the gods fell into grief, while the Dānavas rejoiced; Vāsudeva also, seeing the gods overwhelmed by sorrow, acted with speed.
Grasping his mace Kaumodakī, Hari rushed toward the Dānava;
with great force, he struck that master of illusion on the head.
Struck by the mace, he fell to the ground in a deep swoon;
seeing him fallen in that manner, the enemy of the horses (Garuḍa) became exceedingly enraged.
He approached the Lord of Ramā, terrifying him with his exceedingly loud roars;
Vāsudeva, too, saw him approaching, filled with wrath.
Making a fierce sound from the bowstring, he brought joy to the gods;
the Blessed One swiftly unleashed a shower of arrows upon Mahiṣa.
He too, with a flood of arrows, cut down those shafts discharged into the sky;
O King, a battle ensued between them that struck fear into one another.
Keśava struck him on the head with his mace;
struck on the crown of his head by that mace, he fell to the earth in a deep swoon.
A great and most terrible cry of "Alas! Alas! arose in his army;
casting aside his pain, that Daitya rose up again after a moment. (38)
Seizing an iron club, he struck Madhusūdana on the head;
struck by that club, Janārdana fell into a swoon.
Garuḍa swiftly bore him away, unconscious, and departed from the battlefield;
when the Lord of the World had turned back, the gods, led by Indra, [returned].
Afflicted by great suffering, they fell into fear and cried out upon the field of battle;
seeing the gods thus lamenting, Śaṅkara, the wielder of the trident, then [acted].
Approaching the buffalo with speed, he, filled with rage, struck him;
then the buffalo clearly discharged a spear at the chest of Śaṅkara.
And that evil-minded one roared, having deceived him with the trident;
yet Śaṅkara, though struck upon his chest, felt no pain at that time.
With eyes red with anger, he struck him with his trident upon seeing Śaṅkara closely engaged in combat with the wicked-souled Mahiṣa.
Just then, Hari regained consciousness after the fainting spell caused by the blow;
meanwhile, Mahiṣa beheld that both Hari and Śaṅkara had arrived.
Desirous of battle, those two great heroes, excellent wielders of the discus and the trident, became filled with wrath upon seeing that he had approached them. (46)
Then that mighty-armed one, assuming the form of a buffalo and lashing his formidable tail, went forward to face him for the sake of battle. 47.
He let out a terrifying roar, frightening even the immortals;
shaking his horns with his massive body, he was like a formidable rain-cloud.
With his two horns, he hurled extremely formidable peaks from the mountain;
and seeing those two of great prowess, the two best of gods confronted the Dānava.
They both rained down a terrible shower of arrows upon the Dānava; seeing Hari and Hara thus discharging that shower of arrows, Hari [intervened].
He hurled a formidable mountain peak, having covered it with his tail;
and seeing the mountain rushing toward him, the Blessed Lord, the protector of the Sātvatas, [acted].
With his discus, he quickly struck him with arrows that split [the enemy] into a hundred pieces;
struck by Hari’s discus in battle, that king of the Daityas fell into a swoon.
And in an instant, he truly rose up, assuming a human form—the most terrible Dānava, resembling a mountain, with a mace in his hand. (53)
He roared loudly at Meghanāda, terrifying even the immortals;
hearing that, the Blessed Viṣṇu blew his resplendent conch, Pāñcajanya.
He swiftly filled [the air] with a harsh-sounding roar;
by that sound of the conch, the Dānavas were terrified with fear, while the gods and the sages rich in asceticism became joyful. || 55 ||

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between Mahiṣāsura and the Gods headed by Indra," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of Taking Refuge in Śaṅkara.
Vyāsa said:
Then, seeing the Asuras dejected in mind, Mahiṣa—
Having abandoned that buffalo form, he became this king of beasts.
Having let out a most terrible roar and spreading his great mane,
he fell upon the army of the gods, terrifying them with the sight of his claws.
Having made the Garuḍa drenched in blood with blows from his claws,
the lion struck Viṣṇu on the arm with a blow from his claw.
Vāsudeva, too, seeing him, raised his discus with great speed;
filled with wrath and desiring to slay him, Hari quickly attained his desire.
Just as he struck that enemy with his discus with great speed,
even so did that exceedingly powerful Śṛṅgin strike Hari with his two horns.
Struck on the chest by the two horns, Vāsudeva became overwhelmed and,
intent on flight, departed swiftly for his own realm.
Seeing that Hari had departed as he desired, Śaṅkara too was filled with fear; considering him to be invincible and supreme, he went to Mount Kailāsa.
Brahmā also fled quickly to his own abode out of fear;
the mighty Maghavan, seizing his thunderbolt, stood ready for battle.
Varuṇa stood firm, grasping his spear and summoning his fortitude;
Yama too, taking up his staff, remained vigilant and intent on the battle.
Then the lord of the yakṣas became intent on battle at will;
Pāvaka, taking up his spear, set his mind on fighting there. (10)
The lord of the stars, Sūrya, and [the moon], both standing together,
beheld that foremost of Dānavas and resolved upon battle.
In the meantime, the enraged army of the Daityas approached,
discharging nets of arrows resembling cruel serpents.
Having assumed the form of a buffalo, the king then stood there;
a tumultuous roar arose from the warriors of the gods and the dānavas.
In that most terrible battle between the armies of the gods and the dānavas, the striking of the bowstring and the clapping of hands became like the roar of thunderclouds.
The immensely powerful Dānava, intoxicated with pride, hurled mountains and mountain peaks with his two horns and struck down the hosts of gods.
Overcome with rage, that most extraordinary buffalo struck the gods with blows from his hooves and by whirling his tail. || 16 ||
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, were seized by fear as they stood ready;
upon seeing Mahisha, Maghavan became intent on flight. || 17 ||
When Śakra, the lord of Śacī, had departed after completely abandoning the battle, Yama, the lord of wealth, Varuṇa, and all the others fled, overcome with fear. || 18 ||
Mahiṣa, considering himself victorious, then went to his own home,
having obtained Airāvata, the elephant left behind by Indra as he departed.
Likewise, having taken Uccaiḥśravas from the Sun and the milch-cow Kāmadhenu,
he, surrounded by his own army, quickly set his mind on going to heaven.
Having gone swiftly to the abode of the gods, that Mahiṣāsura seized the sovereignty of the deities, which had been abandoned by the gods who were overcome by fear.
The Dānava sat down upon the delightful throne of Indra;
he then established the other Dānavas in the positions belonging to the gods.
Having thus waged that most terrible battle for a full hundred years, the Dānava, intoxicated with pride, attained his heart's desire: the station of Indra.
Nirjarā had departed from heaven, and because of that, everyone was greatly afflicted;
thus they wandered for many years within the mountain caves.
Then, O King, all of them, being exhausted, went for refuge to Brahmā—the Lord of Progeny, the Master of the World, whose form is passion (rajas) and who possesses four faces. (25)

The lotus-seat, which is the womb of the Vedas and is frequented by sages born of his own lineage—such as the peaceful Marīci and others who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences—is served [by him]. (26)
Terrified by fear, the Kinnaras, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Uragas, and Pannagas praised the God of gods, the Teacher of the World.
The gods said:
O Creator, why is this? Having beheld us gods, you—the lotus-born one who removes all suffering—do not show compassion toward us?
They were oppressed by the lord of the asuras, defeated in battle,
fallen from their positions, and made to dwell in mountain caves.
O Father, why do you, free from greed, abandon your sons even when they are beset by hundreds of offenses and leave them in extreme distress?
For you today neglect those gods who are devoted to your lotus feet, yet are miserable, being oppressed by the Daityas.
He has enjoyed the sovereignty of the immortal realm;
he appropriates from the brahmins even the sacrificial oblations that are their due;
and this evil-souled one partakes of the flowers of the most excellent celestial tree.
He serves that Earth, who has become a treasure-store of the ocean.
Or what shall we say regarding the wondrous task of the gods? O Lord of Gods, you know the conduct of the enemies of the gods;
through your knowledge, you are aware of every undertaking without exception. Therefore, O Lord, we bow at your feet.

Wherever the gods have gone, that wicked-minded one of evil conduct and sinful intent surely inflicts suffering upon them; O Lord of Gods, you are our protector—O All-pervading One, grant us well-being! 32.
If we are not tormented by this great forest fire,
to which performer of peace rites of infinite splendor, the lord of subjects and beloved of the gods, shall we go for refuge?
Who else but the primordial Creator, Śiva, is auspicious? || 33 ||
Vyāsa said:
Having praised him thus, all the gods bowed down to that Prajāpati;
with their palms joined in reverence, they all had deeply dejected faces.
Seeing them thus afflicted, the Grandfather of the World then spoke in gentle words, as if generating comfort within them.
Brahmā said:
"O gods, what shall I do? This Dānava is arrogant because of the boon he received;
he is to be slain by a woman, not by a man—what, then, should be done in this matter?"
"O gods, let us all go today to Kailāsa, the best of mountains, placing Śaṅkara, who is skilled in all affairs, at our head. (37)
"Then let us go to Vaikuṇṭha, where the Lord Janārdana resides; having met there, we shall deliberate especially upon the task of the gods. (38)
Having spoken thus, Brahmā, for the sake of accomplishing his task, mounted his swan and,
placing the gods behind him, departed toward Kailāsa.
In the meantime, Śiva also, having quickly perceived through meditation that the Lotus-born was approaching along with the gods, went out from his own abode.
Having seen one another, they both offered a deep salutation;
and being bowed down by all the gods, they became greatly satisfied.
Having provided separate seats for the gods, the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain sat down upon his own seat once they were seated.
Having exchanged greetings regarding his welfare with Brahmā, the omnipresent Lord whose emblem is the bull asked the reason for the gods' arrival at Kailāsa.
Śiva said:
O Brahmin, what is the reason for your arrival here, along with the gods headed by Indra?
O illustrious one, please tell me the cause of this.
Brahmā said:
O Lord of the gods, the inhabitants of heaven have been oppressed by Mahiṣa;
including Indra himself, they wander through mountain fastnesses, terrified with fear.
Mahiṣa has become a consumer of the sacrifice, and likewise other enemies of the gods;
the guardians of the worlds have been oppressed, and they have today come to you for refuge.
"O Śambhu, I have brought you to this abode because of the gravity of the task;
O Lord of the Gods, now perform whatever is appropriate for the sake of the gods."
"O Creator of beings, the burden of all the gods rests upon you.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words, Śaṅkara, as if smiling, [replied]. (48)
With gentle words, Śiva spoke to the Lotus-born One:
"O Lord, this task was already accomplished by you alone through your granting of boons in the past. (49)
And what further should be done by the gods regarding this useless matter?
Such a one is powerful and heroic, a source of fear to all the gods. (50)
What excellent woman is capable of slaying him who is intoxicated with pride?
Neither my wife nor yours ought to go to battle. (51)
Having gone there, O illustrious lady, how did those two fight again? For the highly fortunate Indrāṇī is indeed not skilled in combat.
"What other person is capable of slaying that wicked one who is arrogant with pride?
It is my opinion that this very day I shall go to the god Janārdana. (53)
Having praised him, let us urge him very swiftly for the sake of the gods' mission;
for Viṣṇu is the foremost among those of supreme intelligence in accomplishing all purposes.
Having united with Vāsudeva, one must indeed deliberate upon what is to be done;
through his power and intellect, he will provide the means for accomplishment.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Rudra, Brahmā and the other foremost of the gods rose up,
saying "So be it," and departed quickly along with Śiva.
All of them, delighted at seeing auspicious omens that portended the success of their mission, proceeded toward the city of Viṣṇu on their own vehicles.
Auspicious, calm, and fragrant winds blew, foretelling good fortune; and everywhere along the path, birds uttered auspicious cries. (58)
The sky became stainless and the directions likewise pure;
as the gods proceeded there, everything appeared as if auspicious.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Defeated Deities Seeking Refuge in Śaṅkara," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Emergence of the Goddess’s True Form.
Vyāsa said:
Then, having swiftly reached Vaikuṇṭha, the beloved abode of Viṣṇu, they...
They beheld it, rich in every beauty and resplendent with celestial mansions.
It was auspicious and bliss-bestowing, endowed with lakes, ponds, and rivers, and resplendent with the warbling of swans, cranes, and ruddy geese. || 2 ||
It was covered with *campaka*, *aśoka*, *kahlāra*, *mandāra*, and *bakula* trees,
and joined by *mallikā*, *tilaka*, *āmra*, *atimukta*, *kurabaka*, and other species.
It was endowed with divine groves, resonant with the warbling of cuckoos, beautified by peacocks delighted in their dance, and made charming by the humming of bees.
He was accompanied by his attendants, such as Sunanda, Nandana, and others, who were devoted to him with devotion,
as well as by devotees whose mental activities were focused on no other than him.
It was joined by auspicious palaces, studded with jewels, adorned with gold, decorated with various ornaments, reaching to the clouds, and shining brilliantly.
It was constantly delighted by singing celestial gandharvas, by dancing throngs of apsaras, and by enchanting kinnaras with lovely voices.
And the abode of Hari was adorned by sages who were likewise peaceful, devoted to the recitation of the Vedas, and praising him with Vedic hymns.
Having reached the abode of Viṣṇu, they saw the two gatekeepers of auspicious form,
Jaya and Vijaya, standing there holding golden staffs, and spoke to them.
Let even one person go between the two and announce those who have assembled—
the gatekeepers, Brahmā, Rudra, and the others— who are longing for a vision of Viṣṇu.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words, Vijaya went into the presence of Viṣṇu and,
having prostrated before all the assembled gods, spoke to them with haste.
Vijaya said:
"O God of gods, O Great King, O Beloved of Ramā, O Slayer of the enemies of the gods!
O Lord, all the deities have arrived and are indeed standing at the gate. (12)
Brahmā, Rudra, as well as Indra, Varuṇa, Pāvaka, and Yama—
the immortals, desiring a vision of you, praise you with Vedic utterances.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of Vijaya, Viṣṇu, the Lord of Ramā,
emerged quickly from his house with even greater festive joy.
Having gone there and seen the gods standing at the gate, emaciated by fatigue and distressed, Hari gladdened them with a gaze inclined toward affection.
All those gods bowed down to Janārdana, the God of gods,
and they praised the slayer of the enemies of the gods with words established in the Vedas.
The gods said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, author of creation, preservation, and destruction;
O great king, ocean of compassion, protect us who have come to you for refuge! 17.
Viṣṇu said: "Let all you immortals enter; may it be well with you. For what purpose have you gathered and come here to these seats? (18)
"Why have you become so distressed with anxiety, dejected, and downcast in spirit?
Together with Brahmā and Rudra, tell me quickly what must be done. (19)
The gods said:
"O great king, we have been oppressed by Mahiṣa, a man of sinful deeds—unconquerable, exceedingly wicked, arrogant because of a boon, and a sinner. (20)
He enjoys the sacrificial portions offered by the Brahmins,
while the gods wander through mountain fastnesses, overcome with fear.
O Madhusūdana, because of the boon granted by the Lord, he is difficult to conquer;
therefore, recognizing the gravity of this task, we have come to you for refuge.
O expert in the illusions of the Daityas, you are capable of rescuing [us];
O Kṛṣṇa, crusher of the Dānavas, devise a means for his destruction. (23)
"The Creator indeed granted him a boon, saying, 'You are truly unslayable by men.
What woman could there be, even one so young, who might slay such a rogue in battle?"
"Whether Umā, Māyā, Śacī, or Vidyā—who among them is capable of slaying this most wicked Mahiṣa, even by virtue of the power of his boon? (25)
Having reflected with your intellect upon everything that is the cause of this death,
O Mountain, you who are kind to your devotees, perform the task of the gods.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words, Viṣṇu spoke to them as if smiling:
"A battle was fought by us in the past, yet even so, he did not die."
If that woman of excellent hips were born today through the combined splendor and perfection of form of all the gods, she would surely slay him by force in battle.
"A woman fashioned from portions of our own power would indeed be capable of slaying the enemy of horses, who is arrogant because of his boon and skilled in a hundred illusions. (29)
And let our women likewise pray for portions of that splendor,
so that by those produced portions of splendor, there may arise a mass of radiance.
We all, led by Rudra, give her all our divine weapons, including the trident and whatever others there may be. (31)
A woman bearing all weapons and endowed with all splendor shall slay that wicked, sinful man who is arrogant with pride.
Vyāsa said:
When the Lord of Gods had spoken thus, a mass of splendor, exceedingly unbearable, manifested itself from the mouth of Brahmā.
Red in color, of auspicious form, with the luster of a ruby;
somewhat cool and likewise warm, adorned with a network of rays.
It was seen by Hari and by the high-souled Hara;
O great king, those two of wide stride were filled with wonder.
From the body of Śaṅkara, however, there issued forth a great wonder:
it was silver-colored, intense, difficult to behold, formidable, and vast. || 36 ||
It was terrifying to the Daityas and a source of wonder to the gods;
it was of a terrible form, resembling a mountain, like another manifestation of the quality of darkness (tamas).
Then, from the body of Viṣṇu, there appeared another mass of splendor,
dark blue, endowed with the quality of sattva, and possessed of great radiance.
Then, from the body of Indra, there emerged a radiant form of variegated appearance, difficult to approach,
a perfectly formed splendor consisting of all qualities.
From the bodies of Kubera, Yama, and Agni,
as well as from that of Varuṇa, a great splendor issued forth on all sides.
And from the bodies of other gods as well, there emerged a mass of great splendor, exceedingly brilliant and intensely radiant. || 41 ||
Seeing him, all the gods, led by Viṣṇu, were struck with wonder;
he was a mass of splendor, most divine, like another Himalaya mountain.
While the gods were watching there, a most excellent woman, beautiful and inspiring wonder, arose from a mass of radiant energy.
She is Mahālakṣmī, composed of the three qualities (triguṇā), born from the bodies of all the gods;
she has eighteen arms, is beautiful, possesses three colors, and is the enchantress of the universe.
With a white face, black eyes, and sprout-like lips deeply reddened, she was lovely, with copper-colored palms, adorned with divine ornaments. (45)
The goddess has eighteen arms and is adorned with a thousand arms;
she has arisen from a mass of splendor for the destruction of the asuras. (46)
Janamejaya said:
O Kṛṣṇa, O God, O highly fortunate one, O omniscient best of sages,
tell me in detail the origin of that body.
Is the splendor of all of them unified as one, or does it exist separately? And are her limbs indeed composed of all that splendor? (48)
Those limbs which are produced through the division of distinct parts—such as the distinctions of the mouth, nose, and eyes—are nevertheless of a single nature throughout. (49)
O Vyāsa, tell me that in detail— the origin of the limbs of the body—
and how it was that a limb of that deity became so wonderful through his splendor.
I desire to hear from the lotus of your mouth all that has been given—weapons, ornaments, and so forth—and exactly how each was bestowed. (51)
O Brahman, I am not satiated as I drink the nectar-like essence of the life-story of Mahālakṣmī, which has issued from the lotus of your mouth. 52.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the king, the son of Satyavatī spoke sweet words, as if pleasing the monarch.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O illustrious King; I shall describe to you in detail, according to my understanding, O best of the Kurus, the origin of her body. 54.
Neither Brahmā, nor Hari directly, nor Rudra,
nor Vāsava is ever capable of describing that form according to its true nature.
How can I know the form, the nature, or the origin of the Goddess? I say that she has arisen as a mere verbal designation.
She exists eternally at all times for the sake of accomplishing the purposes of the gods;
though she is of one form, she manifests in various forms according to the gravity of the task.
Just as an actor on the stage assumes various forms, even though his own nature remains single, for the sake of pleasing the world. (58)
In the same way, for the sake of the work of the gods, she— though formless by her own play—
manifests many forms, both with attributes and devoid of attributes.
Indeed, names arise according to their functions and actions;
there are very many secondary names as well, which are endowed with the meanings of verbal roots and specific qualities. (60)
O lord of men, I shall indeed describe that according to my understanding,
just as her form, born of splendor, was enchanting to the mind.
And by that splendor of Śaṅkara, his lotus-like face became exceedingly great,
white in color and auspicious in form.
Her hair became glossy through that southern splendor;
its tips were curved, it was exceedingly long, cloud-colored, and captivating.
By the fiery splendor [of that gaze], her three eyes were produced, adorned with the three colors:
black, red, and white.
The two eyebrows of the goddess, curved, glossy, and dark-hued,
have become radiant with luster like the two bows of Kāma at twilight.
And by the power of fire, his two ears became excellent;
neither too long nor too short, they were like the swings of the god of love. (66)
His nose, possessing the form of a sesame flower, was exceedingly beautiful;
it became endowed with a glossy complexion through the splendor of the Giver of Wealth.
O King, his teeth have become peaked, smooth, even, resembling the tips of kunda flowers,
and possessed of a beautiful luster through the splendor of Prajāpati.
Her lower lip became intensely red through the power of Aruṇa, while her upper lip likewise became beautiful through the power of Kārttikeya. (69)
The eighteen arms took on the form of Viṣṇu’s splendor,
and the fingers became red in color through the splendor of the Vasus.
From gentle splendor was born her pair of excellent breasts;
likewise, from the splendor of Indra was born her waist, endowed with the three folds.
Then his shanks and thighs were produced from the splendor of Varuṇa;
that broad hip was born from the splendor of the Earth.
In this way, O King, that woman of auspicious form, beautiful and possessed of a most melodious voice, was born, having arisen from a mass of splendor.
Seeing her, whose every limb was exquisite, with beautiful teeth and lovely eyes,
all the gods who had been oppressed by Mahiṣa attained great joy.
Viṣṇu said to all the gods: "O gods, let all auspicious ornaments and weapons be bestowed upon her right now. (75)
"Let all of you, with haste, produce from your own weapons various armaments endowed with splendor and present them today to the Goddess. (76)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Goddess's Own Form," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Minister of Mahiṣa describes the news of the Goddess.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of Viṣṇu, all the gods were then greatly delighted.
And they quickly gave them ornaments, garments, and their own weapons.
And Kṣīroda gave him a divine necklace, red, subtle, ageless, stainless, and beautifully adorned; he was pleased with him. || 2 ||
He gave him a divine crest-jewel with a radiance equal to ten million suns,
as well as two bright earrings and bracelets for his arms.
With his senses and mind pleased, Viśvakarman gave her divine armlets and bracelets resplendent with various jewels.
Tvaṣṭṛ gave her two beautiful, sweet-sounding anklets, spotless and adorned with jewels, which shone like the sun upon her lovely feet.
Likewise, the great ocean gave her a beautiful neck-ornament and radiant jeweled rings of every kind.
Likewise, let Varuṇa bestow the Vaijayantī garland, which is composed of unfading lotuses, rich in fragrance, and followed by bees.
Then Himavat, being well-pleased, gave various jewels and a beautiful, golden-hued lion as a vehicle.
Adorned with divine ornaments, that excellent and auspicious lady shone resplendent;
mounted upon a lion, she of beautiful form was endowed with all auspicious marks.
Viṣṇu, having produced from his discus a wheel with a thousand spokes,
brilliantly radiant and capable of destroying the heads of the enemies of the gods, gave it to her.
Having produced from his own trident that supreme spear, Śaṅkara gave it to the Goddess— it was the cutter of the enemies of the gods and the destroyer of fear.
And Varuṇa, with a gracious soul, produced from his own conch a most auspicious, resonant, and brilliantly shining conch and gave it to him. || 12 ||
Then Hutāśana, with a gracious soul, bestowed upon her the Śakti weapon, the Śataghnī, and the Sumanojavā, which were destroyers of the Daityas.
And Māruta gave her a quiver full of arrows and a bow of wondrous appearance, which was difficult to draw and possessed a harsh sound.
Indra produced a most formidable vajra from his own vajra and gave it [to him];
he also quickly took from Airāvata a beautiful bell that produced a fine sound. (15)
Yama gave him at will the staff born from the rod of Time (Kāladaṇḍa),
by which he brought about the end of all beings when the time had arrived.
Brahmā, filled with joy, gave her a divine water-pot filled with the waters of the Gaṅgā, and Varuṇa likewise gave her his noose.
Then Kāla gave him a sword and a shield, O lord of men;
and Viśvakarman then gave her a sharp axe.
Dhanada gave a golden drinking vessel filled with wine,
and Varuṇa gave a divine, enchanting lotus to the Goddess.
Tvaṣṭṛ, with a gracious soul, gave her the mace Kaumodakī, which resounded with the sound of a hundred bells and was the destroyer of the enemies of the gods.
Tvaṣṭṛ gave the Mother of the World missiles of many forms as well as an impenetrable armor; and the Sun-god gave her his own rays.
Seeing her equipped with weapons and adorned with ornaments, those gods were filled with wonder;
they praised that auspicious goddess, the enchantress of the three worlds. (22)
The gods said: Salutations to Śivā, the auspicious one; salutations again and again to Peace and Nourishment.
Salutations to the Blessed Goddess, to Rudrāṇī; salutations eternally. (23)
Salutations again and again to you, Kālarātri, Ambā, and Indrāṇī;
salutations again and again to you, Siddhi, Buddhi, Vṛddhi, and Vaiṣṇavī. || 24 ||
I bow to that supreme Goddess who, though situated within the earth, is not known by the earth, and who, dwelling within it, governs the earth. 25.
We praise the auspicious Śivā, who, though known as abiding within Māyā, is not born of Māyā; remaining within, she impels that very Māyā, the impeller. 26.
"O Mother, do what is auspicious; protect us who are tormented by our enemies!
Slay the wicked enemy of horses, who is deluded by his own power! (27)

Wicked, deceitful, and terrible, he was to be slain by a woman; arrogant due to the boon he had received, he was a source of suffering for all the gods and assumed various forms as a hundredfold enemy. (28)
O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, you alone are the refuge of all the gods;
O Goddess, protect us today from the oppressed by the Dānava; salutations be unto you! (29)
Vyāsa said: Thus praised then by the gods, the Great Goddess, the bestower of all happiness,
spoke these auspicious words preceded by a smile to them.
The Goddess said:
"O gods, cast away your fear of the dull-witted Mahiṣa;
today itself in battle I shall slay him, who is arrogant due to his boon and utterly deluded. (31)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to the gods, the goddess laughed very loudly with a beautiful voice:
"How strange is this world in saṃsāra, filled with wandering and delusion! (32)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others, as well as Indra and the other gods,
were indeed trembling with fear because of Mahiṣa.
"O best of gods, oh, how terrible is the power of destiny! It is difficult to overcome; Time is the creator of sorrows and the sovereign lord of pleasures. (34)
Even though they are capable of creation, preservation, and destruction,
when they are tormented by afflictions and oppressed by Mahiṣa, they become bewildered.
Having thought thus, the goddess let out a smile accompanied by a loud, most terrible laugh, a sound that struck fear into the Dānavas. (36)
Upon hearing that wondrous sound, the earth there trembled;
all the mountains shook, and the powerful ocean was agitated.
Mount Meru trembled and all the directions were filled with the sound;
hearing that great roar, the Dānavas were then struck with fear.
"Victory! Protect us! the gods said to her, filled with supreme joy;
and Mahiṣa, hearing that sound, became enraged, intoxicated by his pride.
Suspecting it to be his own voice, he asked those Daityas, "What is this?
and commanded, "Let messengers go quickly to ascertain the source of this sound."
"By whom has this most fierce sound, which causes pain to the ears, been produced? Is it a god or perhaps a dānava who is the maker of this noise? (41)
"Let them seize that evil-souled one and bring him here into my presence;
I shall slay this man of wicked conduct who roars with the arrogance of pride. (42)
I lead to the abode of Yama those whose lifespan is exhausted and who possess dull intellects;
the gods, utterly defeated and overcome by fear, no longer roar at will. (43)
"The Asuras are not under my control; whose foolish deed is this?
Let them come to me in haste, having learned the cause of this sound. (44)
"I shall go and slay that wicked one, whose efforts are in vain.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by him, those messengers [approached] the Goddess, who was beautiful in all her limbs.
Divine, with eighteen arms, adorned with all ornaments, endowed with all auspicious marks, bearing excellent weapons, and beautiful. || 46 ||
Beholding her holding a cup in her hand and repeatedly drinking the honey-wine, they became terrified with fear and departed in great alarm and apprehension. (47)
They quickly informed Mahiṣa of the reason for their arrival.
The messengers said:
"O Lord of the Daityas, a certain mature woman is seen there. (48)
Adorned with ornaments on every limb and graced by all kinds of jewels, she was neither human nor asura; she possessed a divine form that was captivating to the mind. 49.
Mounted upon a lion, bearing weapons, and possessing eighteen excellent arms,
that woman utters a roar and appears intoxicated with pride.
"Granted, we know her to be devoted to drinking liquor and not to have a husband;
yet the gods stationed in the intermediate space praise her with great joy. (51)
"Victory to you! "Protect us! "Slay the enemy!"—O Lord, I do not know who that woman of beautiful hips is, or whose wife she may be. (52)
"For what purpose have you come here, and what does Sundarī intend to do? We are not at all able to look upon her, being overwhelmed by her splendor. (53)

Abounding in the sentiments of love, heroism, and humor, and endowed with the sentiments of wrath and wonder—having seen such a woman as this, they have come together without even speaking to her. (54)
"O King, what should we do hereafter by your command?
Mahisha said:
"Go, O hero, my best minister, accompanied by troops, as commanded by me. (55)
Win over that fair-faced woman by means of conciliation and the other expedients; if that woman does not come here even through these three methods beginning with conciliation, [then take action].
"Without killing that woman of beautiful hips, bring her to my presence;
I shall joyfully make that lady with eyebrows like a swan's the chief queen. (57)
If that deer-eyed woman comes filled with affection, act so that my desire is fulfilled without any interruption of the aesthetic flavor (rasa). 58.
"Today I am infatuated by hearing of the excellence of her beauty.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these charming words of Mahiṣa, the best of ministers [replied]. (59)
Accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots, he proceeded swiftly according to his desire;
having gone a great distance and halted, he spoke to that high-minded woman.
Bowing with humility, the minister, speaking gently with sweet words, said:
"Who are you, O lady of sweet speech, and what is the purpose of your coming here? (61)
"O highly fortunate one, my lord asks you through my mouth:
'He is indeed the conqueror of all the gods, yet he is supposedly incapable of being slain by men.'"
O lady of beautiful eyes, that powerful lord of the Daityas, who can always assume any form at will, was made arrogant by the granting of a boon from Brahmā.
"Having heard that you have arrived, beautifully attired and captivating, the king named Mahīṣa, the ruler of the earth, desires to see me. (64)
"Assuming a human form, he will come into your presence;
O lady of beautiful limbs, we consider it as you wish. (65)
"Come then, O fawn-eyed one, to the presence of that wise man;
otherwise, I shall bring that king, who is so devoted to you, here."
O Goddess of gods, I shall act in such a way that he will be entirely under your control according to your heart's desire,
merely by hearing of your beauty.
O lady with thighs like an elephant's trunk, tell me quickly how I should act accordingly.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of News Concerning the Goddess by Mahiṣa’s Minister," in the fifth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Proposal for Marriage with the Goddess by Mahiṣāsura through his Minister.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, that most excellent of women laughed and—
He spoke to him, O great king, with a voice as deep as a thundercloud. || 1 ||
The Goddess said: "O best of ministers, know me indeed as the mother of the gods;
I am renowned as Mahālakṣmī, the destroyer of all the Daityas."
"I was requested by all the gods, who were oppressed by the lord of the Dānavas and excluded from their shares of the sacrifice, for the sake of slaying Mahiṣa. (3)
Therefore, O best of ministers, I have come here today alone, not accompanied by an army, having made an effort to slay him.
O sinless one, because you have welcomed me with affection, preceded by conciliatory words, and addressed me with such sweet speech, I am pleased with you.
Otherwise, I would surely consume you with my gaze like the fire of time;
indeed, to whom would sweet speech not be pleasing? (6)
"Go and speak these words of mine to that wicked buffalo:
'If you have any desire for life, go now to the netherworld.'"
If not, I shall slay you, O wicked evildoer, upon the field of battle;
with your body mangled by my arrows, you shall go to the abode of Yama.
Knowing this compassion of mine, depart quickly;
O fool, once you are slain, the gods will swiftly attain heaven.
Therefore, O dull-witted one, depart alone, abandoning this earth with its oceans,
and quickly go to the netherworld before my arrows fall upon you.
If there is a desire for battle in your mind, then come quickly, O Asura!
I shall send all these heroes of great strength to the abode of Yama.
"O great fool, in age after age, those like you have indeed been slain in countless numbers; likewise, I shall surely slay you on the field of battle. (12)
Make the wielding of your weapons fruitful; otherwise, your labor is in vain.
Therefore, being tormented by desire, fight with me in battle.
Do not be arrogant, O evil-souled one, for I possess a boon from Brahmā;
you fools, you have oppressed the best of the gods because they are invulnerable to women. (14)
"O Dhātu, it was my duty to speak; therefore, having assumed this incomparable female form, I have come to you to slay the truth-slayer who has committed an offense. (15)
"Go as you wish, O fool, even to the netherworld (pātāla) inhabited by serpents, having abandoned the abode of the Brahmins today, since you still have a desire for life. (16)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by the goddess, that best of ministers, endowed with strength, listened to her words pregnant with reason and replied. (17)
"O Goddess, intoxicated by pride, you speak words befitting a common woman.
Where is he, and where are you? How indeed can this battle be possible? (18)
Moreover, this young girl is alone, her youth having just begun, and she is delicate;
while that buffalo is massive in body—indeed, their union is inconceivable. (19)
His army was of many kinds, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots; it was joined by throngs of foot soldiers and resplendent with various weapons.
What effort is required for the king of elephants to crush a *mālatī* flower? Or what effort, O fair-thighed one, to slay a buffalo in battle such as yours? (21)
If I were to speak even a very slight harsh word to you, it would indeed be contrary to the erotic sentiment; for I fear the disruption of the aesthetic flavor (rasabhaṅga).
"Our king, the enemy of the gods, is devoted to you;
therefore, I must speak words that are conciliatory as well as accompanied by offers of gifts. (23)
If not, I shall this very day strike you with an arrow— you who speak falsely, who are clever in false pride, and who are arrogant because of your beauty and youth.
"My lord has been captivated upon hearing of your form, which transcends the world;
therefore, for the sake of his pleasure, you must grant the beloved desire that I shall speak to you."
"The kingdom is yours, all wealth is yours, and indeed, Mahiṣa is your slave.
O large-eyed lady, cast aside this anger that brings death and adopt a favorable disposition. (26)
O beautiful lady, with a spirit of devotion I fall at your feet;
O lady of pure smiles, quickly become the chief queen of the great king. (27)
Through the acquisition of Mahiṣa, you shall obtain the entire, untroubled sovereignty of the three worlds and all the pleasures born of saṃsāra. (28)
The Goddess said:
Listen, O minister, I shall speak the supreme essence of words, reflecting upon wisdom according to the path seen in the scriptures. (29)
"O Mahisha, I have indeed recognized through my intellect that you are the foremost [of demons];
from your speech just now, it is clear that your nature is that of a beast. (30)
How could he whose ministers are like you be considered wise?
Indeed, this union of two such similar natures was brought about by Fate itself. (31)
"O fool, why do you investigate this statement that 'you are of female nature'?
I am not a man; having become of her nature, I am merely wearing a woman's dress. (32)
"Since death was previously requested by your mistress, just as it was by you,
I consider him to be exceedingly foolish and not the most knowledgeable in the sentiment of heroism."
The death of the beloved woman, which brings pleasure to the impotent and causes suffering to the brave,
was requested by that lord Mahiṣa, who possessed such a self-conceited intellect.
Therefore, having assumed the form of a woman, I have come to accomplish my purpose;
how could I fear your words, which contradict the treatises on dharma? (35)
When destiny is adverse, even a blade of grass becomes like a thunderbolt; but if fate is favorable, then even a diamond is like cotton wool.
What is the use of armies or weapons, or what is the use of elaborate fortifications?
For one whose death is imminent, what fruit is there in having an army? (37)
When this connection with a body occurs for the living soul through the conjunction of time,
at that very moment everything— happiness, suffering, and likewise death— is inscribed.
In whatever manner death is ordained by destiny for anyone, it shall occur for that person in that very same way and not otherwise; such is the certainty. (39)
Just as the destruction and arising of Brahmā and the others are ordained according to their time, so it is with you; what need is there to deliberate on others? (40)
Those who are subject to death, being arrogant because of the granting of boons, do not think, "We shall die"; they are fools of dull intellect. (41)
Therefore, go quickly and speak my words to the king:
"Whatever the monarch commands must indeed be carried out by you. (42)
"May Maghavan attain heaven; may the gods be eaters of the oblation.
You all, depart for Pātāla if you desire to live. (43)
O dull-witted one, if the mind of the evil-souled Mahiṣa is otherwise, then fight with me, intent upon death. (44)
You think that the gods, led by Viṣṇu, were broken in battle;
however, destiny was the cause there, namely the boon granted by Prajāpati.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the goddess, the Dānava reflected:
"What should be done by me? Should I go to war or approach the king? (46)
"Commanded here by the king who is indeed afflicted by desire for the sake of marriage, how could I go into the presence of the monarch having made it unpleasant? (47)
This is the correct understanding: that I shall go away from Kali;
I shall quickly inform the king of this exactly as it happened. (48)
Furthermore, that king, the best among the wise, will deliberate with his skillful ministers and then act as the authority regarding what must be done.
"I must not engage in battle with her impulsively;
whether in victory or defeat, it would be displeasing to the king. (50)
"If Sundarī were to kill me, or if I were to kill her again, by whatever means necessary, that king would surely become enraged. (51)
Therefore, having gone to that very place, I shall enlighten that king so that he may act according to his own inclination, just as has been stated by the Queen today.
Vyāsa said:
Having reflected thus, the wise minister went into the presence of the king;
having prostrated before him, he spoke these words with palms joined in reverence. (53)
The minister said:
"O King, the goddess of beautiful form stands upon a lion;
she has eighteen arms, is lovely, and wields supreme, excellent weapons. (54)
I said to her, "O great king, O beautiful lady, accept Mahiṣa;
become the queen of the king, the beloved of the lord of the three worlds. (55)
"You alone shall become his chief queen; of this there is no doubt.
He will be born as one who carries out your commands and will remain under your control. (56)
Having enjoyed the sovereignty of the three worlds for a long time, O lady of beautiful countenance,
may you become a fortunate woman by obtaining Mahiṣa as your husband.
Having heard these words of mine, that large-eyed woman, deluded by the onset of passion and pride, spoke these words to me with a smile: || 58 ||
"Born from the womb of a buffalo, the lowest among animals, I shall offer this victim to the Goddess out of a desire for the welfare of the gods. (59)
"What deluded woman in this world would indeed choose a buffalo as her husband? O dull-witted one, why would someone like me embrace the state of a beast in this life? (60)
The female buffalo makes a loud outcry toward her lord, the male buffalo, as if she possessed horns to join with his; indeed, I am not so deceitful as she.
"I shall wage war in battle and slay you, the enemy of the gods;
or go to the netherworld, O wicked one, if you have any desire for life. (62)
O King, having heard those harsh words spoken by her in her intoxication, I have returned here after reflecting upon them again and again. (63)
It was only out of consideration for the loss of my vigor that I did not engage in battle;
how could I possibly exert myself in vain without your absolute command? (64)
O King, this beautiful woman behaves as if intoxicated by excessive power;
I do not know what destiny awaits her, nor what will come to pass. (65)
In this matter, you alone are our authority; the counsel is exceedingly difficult to fathom.
Whether battle or flight is better, I do not know for certain.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Proposal for Marriage between Mahiṣāsura and the Goddess through the Minister," in the fifth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Words of Dismissal Addressed to the Goddess Made of Copper.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, Mahiṣa, overwhelmed by intoxication, spoke.
Having summoned the elder ministers, the king spoke these words.
The king said:
"O ministers, what must be done? Speak with confidence and do not delay.
Has this illusion, fashioned by the gods like that of Śambara, arrived?"
"You are skilled in this task and discerning in means; tell me, which among the methods beginning with conciliation (sāma) should be employed here?"
The ministers said:
"O best of kings, one should always speak what is true and pleasant;
indeed, after deliberation, wise men should certainly act in a way that is beneficial. (4)
O King, truth may be beneficial yet unpleasant, while that which is pleasant may be harmful;
for just as medicine in this world is unpleasant to men, yet it destroys disease.
O Lord of the Earth, one who hears and reflects upon the truth is difficult to find;
indeed, a speaker of it is also rare, for there are many who speak only pleasant flattery.
O King, how can we speak in this matter, for in this profound inquiry, who in the three worlds knows what is auspicious or even inauspicious? (7)
The king said:
"Let each of you speak today separately according to your own judgment;
for having heard what the disposition of each is like, I shall reflect upon it."
Having ascertained the opinion of many and having deliberated upon it again and again,
that which is beneficial must indeed be performed as the duty by those who are experts in discerning what ought to be done.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, the mighty Virūpākṣa quickly spoke these words, pleasing the lord of the earth.
Virūpākṣa said:
"O King, this wretched woman speaks thus out of pride in her own beauty;
you should understand that these words of hers are merely a means of intimidation."
Who would fear the ill-spoken words of women, intoxicated by the frenzy of battle, when one knows that the behavior of women consists of falsehood and recklessness? (12)
O King, having conquered the three worlds today out of fear for his beloved, even in this state of wretchedness, infamy will surely befall the hero in the world. (13)
Therefore, O Great King, I shall go alone to fight against Caṇḍikā; I will slay her, so be fearless now. 14.
Surrounded by my army, I shall indeed go there and destroy that unbearable Caṇḍikā of fierce prowess with various weapons and missiles. (15)
"Having bound her with nooses made of serpents, I shall bring her to your presence;
she shall be forever under your control. Behold, O King, my power! (16)
Vyāsa said: Having heard the words of Virūpākṣa, Durdhara spoke these words:
"O King, the speech spoken by the wise Virūpākṣa is true. (17)
My words, too, should be heard with gentleness by you, who are wise;
for it is evident even by inference that this fair-toothed woman is overcome by passion. (18)
Granted, such a heroine may indeed be proud of her beauty; yet this woman of noble form desires to bring you under her control by means of intimidation. (19)
This is indeed the *hāva* (coquettish gesture) of proud women; he who knows it is the most skilled connoisseur of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
This is the *vakrokti* (indirect speech) of a loving woman, which is entirely devoted to her beloved. (20)
Only some man, an expert in the science of love, truly knows desire, when it is said: "I shall slay you with arrows on the front line of battle. (21)
This statement, pregnant with reason, should be understood by those most skilled in logic:
it is well known that for proud women, side-long glances are indeed their arrows. (22)
Others consist of handfuls of flowers, and others are suggestive words;
O King, what power do other arrows have against you? (23)
Even among those such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, there is no such power as that by which you said,
"O dull-witted king, I shall slay you with the arrows from my eyes."
"Indeed, that knower of flavors has understood it perversely;
I shall cast your husband upon a bed made of battle. (25)
That speech of hers should indeed be understood as a playful jest involving perverse intent; "I shall render you lifeless"—such were the words she spoke. (26)
"Vigor is said to be one's life-force; without it, there is no other [value].
O King, with these words, which were full of insinuation, the excellent woman chose him. (27)
That indeed should be understood through careful investigation by those expert in the treatises on rasa;
having realized this, O Great King, one should perform [the rite] endowed with rasa. 28.
O King, for her there is no other means than these two—conciliation and bribery;
for even when angry or proud, a woman of self-respect may be brought under control. (29)
With such sweet words as these, I shall bring her into your presence.
O King, what need is there for much speaking? She must be made subject to my will.
"Having gone [there], I shall now always serve you like a maidservant.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words, Tāmra, who was discerning of the truth, [replied]. (31)
He spoke these words, O King: "Listen to what I have said—reasoned, consistent with dharma, flavorful, and endowed with logic. (32)
"O giver of honor, this young woman is neither afflicted by passion nor lacking in devotion; she is discerning, and no words of reproach were ever spoken by her. (33)
O mighty-armed one, it is wonderful here that this single woman of excellent complexion, possessing a wondrous form and captivating the mind, approaches without any support. (34)
A woman with eighteen arms, powerful and auspicious, has never been heard of nor seen by anyone anywhere in the three worlds. (35)
"Even those weapons were held so numerous and powerful;
yet I consider all this to be contrary to the natural order, O King, brought about by Time. (36)
"Indeed, I have seen evil omens in dreams during the night; therefore, I know for certain that a great slaughter has arrived. (37)
