If a woman wearing black garments is seen weeping in the courtyard of one's house even in a dream at the time of dawn, one must contemplate the impending calamity. (38)
Deformed birds shrieked loudly at night in every house;
O King, various portents appeared in every house. (39)
Therefore, I know for certain that there must be some underlying cause why this young woman, having made her resolve, seeks you for battle. (40)
"This is neither human, nor of the Gandharvas, nor likewise of the Asuras;
O Lord, it must be known as an illusion created by the gods, intended to cause delusion. (41)
"You must not yield to cowardice; this is my firm resolve.
You must fight by all means; whatever is destined to happen will happen. (42)
Who knows what the divine will ordain, whether it be auspicious or likewise inauspicious?
Therefore, the wise should remain firm by relying upon fortitude.
O Lord of Men, the life and death of men are dependent on destiny;
no one at all in the three worlds is capable of making them otherwise. (44)
Mahiṣa said:
"Go, O illustrious Tāmra, resolved for battle;
having conquered her by righteous means, bring back that proud woman of beautiful form. (45)
If that woman of yours does not fall under your power in battle, she must be slain; otherwise, she should by all means be honored with great effort. (46)
"You are a hero, O Omniscient One, and an expert in the science of love;
by whatever means possible, that woman of excellent complexion must be won over. (47)
O hero of mighty arms, proceeding swiftly surrounded by a great army, you must go there and investigate the matter again and again. 48.
For what purpose has she come? That reason must indeed be known:
whether it is out of desire or from a sense of enmity, and whose illusion this is.
Having first made a firm determination regarding that, one should ascertain what he intends to do;
thereafter, battle should be waged as is appropriate and according to one's strength. (50)
You must not act with cowardice, nor likewise with cruelty;
for you should adopt whatever disposition she herself possesses. (51)
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words of his, Tāmra, falling under the power of Time,
departed accompanied by his army after bowing down to King Mahiṣa.
As he was traveling on the road, that evil-minded man, seeing dreadful omens that indicated the path of Yama, was struck with both wonder and fear.
Having approached and beheld that goddess seated upon a lion, being praised by all the gods and adorned with all her weapons; || 54 ||
Standing there, bowed down with humility and resorting to a conciliatory disposition, he spoke these words to her in a sweet voice with great modesty. (55)
O Goddess, Śṛṅgin, the lord of the Daityas, is infatuated by the beauty and virtues of your form; moreover, Mahiṣa desires to take your hand in marriage.
O large-eyed one, cultivate an affection for that conqueror of the immortals;
having obtained him as your husband, O lady of delicate limbs, sport in the wonderful Nandana grove.

Having obtained a body beautiful in all its limbs, which is the abode of all happiness, it is the established rule that pleasure should be pursued with one's whole being and suffering should be abandoned. 58.
O lady with thighs like an elephant’s trunk, for what purpose have you taken up these weapons?
Your hands, as delicate as lotuses, are suited only for flowers and balls. (59)
When the bow of her eyebrows is already present, what need is there for a [physical] bow?
When side-long glances are her arrows, what is the use of useless shafts? (60)
A wise person should not engage in war, which brings suffering in saṃsāra;
yet those attached to greed wage war against one another.
One should not even fight with flowers, much less with sharpened arrows;
for whom would the piercing of one's own limbs bring joy? (62)
Therefore, O slender-limbed one, you too ought to show favor;
accept my husband as your lord, he who is worshipped by gods and dānavas.
He will fulfill all your desires and wishes here;
you shall become the chief queen of the king in every respect—of this there is no doubt. (64)
"O Goddess, do as I say; you shall attain supreme happiness.
There is no doubt that you will encounter hardship in battle, yet victory is certain. (65)
O lady of excellent complexion, you know the principles of statecraft exactly as they are;
enjoy the full happiness of sovereignty for tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of years.
"A beloved son shall be born to you, and he too shall become a king;
having sported in his youth, you will attain happiness in old age. (67)

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Words of Tāmraka Expressing His Relinquishment to the Goddess," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Vyāsa spoke these words of difficult-to-sustain awakening in order to bring about the defeat of the Goddess; having heard those words of Tāmra, the Mother of the World—
Laughing, she spoke to him with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Goddess said:
"Go, Tāmra, and speak to that husband of yours, the dull-witted Mahiṣa, who is on the verge of death, afflicted by excessive lust, a fool devoid of wisdom."
"Just as your mother is a mature buffalo that eats grass, I am not like her—I have horns, a long tail, and a large belly. (3)
I do not desire the Lord of Gods, nor Viṣṇu, nor Śaṅkara;
nor Dhanada, nor Varuṇa, nor Brahmā, nor Pāvaka. || 4 ||
"Leaving aside these hosts of gods, for what reason indeed would I choose an animal? It would be in vain; I would incur reproach in the world. (5)
I am not a woman choosing her own husband; my husband is the Lord.
He is the creator of all, the witness of all, indeed the non-doer, free from desire, and steadfast.
Devoid of qualities, free from the sense of "mine," infinite, without support, and without refuge;
omniscient, all-pervading, the witness, perfect, with a perfect intention—He is Śiva.
Capable of enduring all dwellings, peaceful, all-seeing, and the creator of all things—having abandoned that dull-witted Mahiṣa, how could I venture to serve him? (8)
"Once I have awakened, I shall, at my pleasure, make those who fight my vehicle;
or else, I shall indeed make human beings carriers of water."
O sinner, if you have a desire for life, go quickly to the netherworld along with all the dānavas; otherwise, I shall slay you in battle.
Granted that a union between two similar beings may bring happiness in this world;
otherwise, if it is brought about through ignorance, it will result only in suffering. (11)
"You are a fool to say, 'O beautiful woman, accept me as your husband';
where am I, and where is a horned buffalo? What kind of relationship could there be between the two of us? (12)
"Go or fight as you wish; I shall slay you along with your kinsmen.
Otherwise, abandon your share of the sacrifice and the world of the gods, and live in happiness. (13)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, that goddess then roared most wonderfully;
she let out a sound like the end of a kalpa, bringing terror to the Daityas.
The earth trembled and the mountains shook at that sound;
and from the roar, the fetuses of the Daityas' wives were miscarried.
Having heard that sound, Tāmra, his mind then terrified with fear,
fled from there and went into the presence of Mahiṣa.
O King, those Daityas who were in his city also fell into anxiety;
with their ears deafened, they were intent on flight.
Then, with his mane bristling, the lion also roared loudly out of anger;
by that roar, the Daityas clearly fell into a state of fear.
Seeing that Tāmra had arrived, even Hayāri was bewildered;
he deliberated with his ministers as to what should be done hereafter. (19)
O best of Dānavas, either a siege of the fortress must be undertaken, or else, having gone out, war must be fought; or perhaps it would be better if we were to flee. (20)
Those who are intelligent, invincible, and proficient in all the scriptures—indeed, counsel with them should be kept strictly secret for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose. (21)
The kingdom is traditionally held to have its root in the mantra; therefore, if it is to be well-protected, it must be managed in every way by wise ministers who follow virtuous conduct. (22)
If there is a disclosure of the mantra, there will be the destruction of the kingdom as well as of the king;
therefore, one who desires prosperity should keep it secret for fear of such disclosure. (23)

Therefore, in this matter, the ministers should speak words that are reasoned and beneficial, having reflected upon the determination of policy in accordance with the requirements of time and place. (24)
As for this woman who has arrived here, powerful and fashioned by the gods—she is alone and without support; let the reason for this be reflected upon. (25)
This fool seeks war; what could be more astonishing than this?
Who in the three worlds knows whether what is beneficial here is actually its opposite? (26)
Victory does not belong to the many, nor is there defeat for the one;
victory and defeat in battle should always be known as dependent upon destiny.
Those who advocate for skillful means (upāya) ask: "What is this 'destiny' (daiva), and by whom has it been seen?
That which the wise call 'the unseen' (adṛṣṭa) [is nothing more than the result of one's own actions]. (28)
Even if that were true, what proof is there for it? It is merely the resort of the faint-hearted; for nowhere is destiny observed to prevail over capable men. (29)

Exertion and destiny—these two are considered [the factors] for the brave and the cowardly respectively; having reflected upon everything today with the intellect, one's duty must be performed with diligence.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the king, which were pregnant with reason,
the highly illustrious one named Biḍāla spoke thus to the great king with palms joined in reverence.
"O King, this large-eyed woman must be investigated with great care: for what purpose has she arrived here, from where does she come, and whose wife is she? (32)
Having fully understood your death, the gods, having brought forth by their own splendor this lotus-eyed woman, dispatched her with all their soul. (33)
They too all remained there in the sky, concealed, desiring to witness the battle; at the proper time, they will become her allies, eager for combat.
Placing a woman before them, those led by Viṣṇu will indeed slay us all; she, moreover, will kill you in battle.
O lord of men, I have understood this which they intend to do;
however, I possess no knowledge whatsoever regarding what is destined to happen.
"O Lord, I am not able to say, 'You must not fight today';
O Great King, you alone are the authority in this matter ordained by the gods. (37)
For that purpose, we must die incessantly due to the gravity of our duties;
however, you should sport together with him, for this is the duty of those who serve. (38)
O King, there is great deliberation here as to how a single woman seeks battle with us, who are accompanied by armies and proud of our strength. (39)
Durmukha said:
"O King, I know for certain that victory will be ours today in battle;
one must not flee, as it causes the loss of fame for men. (40)
That which was not done even by Indra and the other gods in battle—who indeed, having encountered a woman alone, would flee in disgrace? (41)

Therefore, one must either wage war or face death in battle; victory belongs to the conqueror. Whatever is destined to happen will surely come to pass—what anxiety can there be for one who sees clearly? (42)
In death here there is the attainment of glory, and in life likewise there is happiness;
having considered both in your mind, you must indeed engage in battle today.
In flight there is loss of reputation, and death occurs when one's lifespan is exhausted;
therefore, one should not indulge in grief over life or death in vain.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of Durmukha, Bāṣkala, who was skilled in speech, bowed with joined palms and addressed the king. (45)
Bāṣkala said:
"O King, you should not worry about this task which is dear to cowards;
I alone shall slay Caṇḍī, she of the flickering eyes. (46)
O best of kings, enthusiasm must be cultivated as the stable emotion (sthāyībhāva) of rasa; furthermore, the fearful (bhayānaka) rasa becomes the enemy of the heroic (vīra).
Therefore, O King, casting aside fear, I shall wage a marvelous battle;
O lord of men, I will lead Caṇḍikā to the abode of Yama.
I do not fear Yama, Indra, Kubera, nor even Varuṇa; nor do I fear Vāyu, Agni, Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, the Moon, or the Sun.
"If even a single woman is thus [powerless], how much more so one intoxicated with pride?
I shall slay her with arrows sharpened on stone. (50)
Behold my strength of arms today; sport as you please.
You must not go there with her, even into battle.
Vyāsa said:
While Bāṣkala, arrogant with pride, was thus speaking to the king of kings, Durdhara bowed there to the monarch and spoke these words. (52)
Durdhara said:
"O Mahiṣa, I shall conquer the goddess created by the gods—charming, with eighteen arms, and arrived here for a specific purpose. (53)
"O King, this illusion was indeed created by the gods to frighten you;
recognizing this as a mere terror, abandon the delusion within your mind. (54)
O King, listen now to this policy of statecraft and the duties of ministers:
some are of the nature of goodness (sāttvika), some of passion (rājasa), and others likewise of darkness (tāmasa).
O Lord of the Dānavas, there are three kinds of ministers in the world:
the *sāttvika* ones accomplish the tasks of their master through their own powers. || 56 ||
They perform their own duties without conflicting with the master's business;
they are single-minded, devoted to the Dharma, and proficient in the treatises on counsel. (57)
Those characterized by passion (rājasa) have divided minds and are always intent on their own affairs; they perform the master's work only occasionally, and then by mere chance.
Those characterized by tamas are devoted to greed and always intent on their own interests;
having destroyed the master's work, they accomplish only their own. (59)
At that time, those who have been deceived by others will fall apart;
remaining at home, they will point out their own vulnerabilities to those on the enemy's side.
Constantly causing division among their duties and always sheathed like swords in a scabbard,
they always terrify their master when a conflict arises.
O King, one should never place trust in them;
for by placing trust, there will surely be the loss of one's purpose and always the disclosure of one's secret counsel.
What will the wicked not do when they are trusted—those who are intent on greed, characterized by darkness, devoted to sin, devoid of intelligence, and likewise deceitful? (63)
Therefore, O best of kings, you must not worry in any way; I shall go to the front of the battle and accomplish what needs to be done.
"Having seized that woman of wicked conduct, I shall return in haste;
behold today my strength and fortitude as I perform my master's task to the best of my ability. (65)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Words of Durdhara for Awakening [the Goddess] in Order to Cause Her Defeat," in the fifth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 12.
The description of the felling of Bāṣkala, Durmukha, and the commander of the buffalo army;
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, those two mighty-armed Daityas, Bāṣkala and Durmukha—
Their limbs smeared with the ichor of rut, those two, skilled in all weapons and missiles, went forth.
Having gone there to the battlefield, those two Dānavas, intoxicated with pride, then spoke these words to the Goddess in voices as deep as thunderclouds.
"O Goddess, by that high-souled Mahiṣa the gods have been conquered;
therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, choose him as your husband, the king who is the sovereign of all the Daityas."
Having assumed a human form endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with divine ornaments, he will indeed come to you in secret.
"O lady of pure smiles, you shall obtain every desire for the sovereignty of the three worlds; O beloved, direct your heart's intent toward Mahiṣa. (5)
Having made the Great Hero your husband, you shall indeed obtain the wonderful happiness of saṃsāra and that which is desired by women, O sweet-voiced cuckoo.
The Goddess said:
"O fool, what do you know? This woman is deluded by passion;
being of dull intellect and extreme weakness, she would serve the wicked Mahiṣa."
Noble women consort with one who is their equal in lineage, character, and virtues,
and who excels them in beauty, dexterity, intelligence, moral conduct, patience, and other such qualities.
What woman, afflicted by desire, would resort to one in the form of a beast? Surely this buffalo, the lowest of beasts, has assumed the form of a god. (9)
"O Bāṣkala and Durmukha, go quickly to King Mahiṣa—that Daitya who is like an elephant and possesses horns—and speak my words to him. (10)
"Either go to the netherworld or come and engage in battle with me;
for once the combat has begun, it is certain that the thousand-eyed Indra will be free from fear."
"Having killed you, I shall depart; there is no other way for me to go.
Knowing this, O evil-minded one, do as you wish. (12)
"Without first conquering me, O four-footed beast, you shall never have a place anywhere on this earth, nor in heaven, nor in mountain caves. (13)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by her, those two heroic Daityas, their eyes agitated with anger and bearing bows and arrows, became desirous of battle.
Having let out a very loud roar, that goddess stood there fearless;
and both of them, O best of the Kurus, rained down a fierce shower of arrows.
The Blessed One also, uttering an exceedingly sweet roar for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, released a flood of arrows toward the two Dānavas.
Of those two, Bāṣkala quickly came face-to-face on the field of battle,
while Durmukha remained there as a spectator, standing opposite the Goddess.
Then a terrible battle took place between the goddess and Bāṣkala;
with the blows of arrows, swords, and iron clubs, it struck fear into those of feeble minds. 18.
Then the Mother of the World, enraged upon seeing him intoxicated with the pride of battle,
struck him with five arrows whetted on stone and drawn back to her ear.
The Dānava also cut the goddess's arrows with his own sharp shafts,
and struck the goddess, who was seated upon her lion, with seven more.
She too, having cut through his arrows, struck that wicked man with ten sharp and well-polished shafts, and she laughed again and again. (21)
With a crescent-shaped arrow, he severed his bow;
Bāṣkala, seizing a mace, also advanced to slay the Goddess.
As the Dānava, arrogant with pride, approached with mace in hand,
Caṇḍikā struck him down to the earth with blows from her own mace.
Bāṣkala fell to the ground, but after a moment he rose again;
and he too, of fierce prowess, hurled his mace at Caṇḍikā.
Seeing him approaching, the goddess, enraged, struck Bāṣkala in the chest with her trident; he fell down and died. || 25 ||
When Bāṣkala had fallen, the army of that evil-minded one was broken;
and the gods, stationed in the sky, cried out with joy, "Victory! (26).
When that Daitya had been slain, Durmukha, endowed with great strength,
arrived at the goddess in battle, his eyes bloodshot with rage.
"Stay! Stay, O weakling! he cried again and again, as that illustrious one, equipped with bow and arrows, stood upon his chariot clad in armor.
Seeing him approaching, the goddess sounded her conch shell and made a twanging sound with her bowstring,
inciting that Dānava to anger.
He too quickly released sharp arrows resembling venomous serpents;
Mahāmāyā cut those down with her own arrows and let out a roar.
O King, a tumultuous battle took place between the two of them with the blows of arrows,
spears, and maces, as well as with clubs and javelins.
Then, on the field of battle, a river carrying floods of blood was produced;
the heads that fell upon its banks then shone brilliantly.
Just as, for the sake of crossing over, the leaders of Yama’s servants joyfully brought gourd fruits to those who were eager for new instruction. (33)
Then the battlefield became exceedingly terrible and impassable,
with bodies fallen upon the ground being devoured by wolves and other beasts.
Jackals, dogs, crows, herons, iron-beaked birds, vultures, and hawks devour the bodies of the evil-minded. (35)
A foul-smelling wind blew, arising from contact with the bodies of the dead;
and there arose the "kila-kila" cry of the birds that feed on flesh.
Then the evil-minded Durmukha, deluded by fate, became enraged;
raising his auspicious right hand, he spoke to the goddess with arrogance.
"Go, you fierce woman! I shall slay you this very day, you great fool!
Or else, O lady of lovely thighs, resort to the demon Mahiṣa, who is arrogant with pride. (38)
The Goddess said:
"O Kāma, being deluded and with death at hand, you prattle today as you wish;
this very day I shall slay you, just as this Bāṣkala was slain. (39)
"Go or stay, you fool—if death pleases you!
Having killed you, I shall surely slay this foolish son of the queen. (40)
Having heard those words of hers, Durmukha prepared for death;
he released a terrible shower of arrows toward Caṇḍikā.
She too, having swiftly cut down that shower of arrows with her own sharp shafts,
angrily struck the Dānava, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt struck Vṛtra.
A battle took place between the two of them that was exceedingly fierce—inspiring fear in the timid and increasing the strength of the brave. || 43 ||
The goddess swiftly severed the bow held in his hand;
likewise, with five arrows, she shattered his excellent chariot.
When his chariot was broken, the mighty-armed Durmukha then took up an invincible mace and went toward Caṇḍikā on foot.
That one of great strength dealt a blow with his mace upon the crest of the lion;
yet Hari, though struck, did not waver from his place, despite his own great power.
Seeing him standing before her with a mace in hand,
Ambikā severed his head, including its crown, with a sharp-edged sword.
When his head was severed, Durmukha fell dead upon the ground;
then the delighted gods raised a great shout of victory.
Then, when Durmukha had been slain, the immortals praised that goddess;
remaining in the sky, they rained down flowers and raised shouts of victory.
The sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, along with Vidyādharas and Kinnaras,
rejoiced upon seeing that Dānava slain at the forefront of the battle.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of Bāṣkala and Durmukha, the Commanders of Mahiṣa’s Army," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 13 ||
The Description of the Slaying of the One Named Tāmracikṣu.
Vyāsa said: Having heard that Durmukha had been slain, Mahiṣa was overcome with rage.
He spoke to all the Dānavas repeatedly, asking, "What has happened? (1)
The two heroic Dānavas, Durmukha and Bāṣkala, have been slain in battle by that slender woman;
let them behold this supreme marvel, the working of divine destiny. || 2 ||
For Time is the powerful agent of happiness and suffering for men who are dependent on others, according to their connection with merit and demerit. (3)
"The two foremost Dānavas have been slain; what should be done after this? Let all of you assembled here speak what is appropriate for this critical situation."
Vyāsa said:
O king of kings, while the exceedingly powerful Mahiṣa was speaking thus,
the great car-warrior commander-in-chief named Cikṣura addressed him.
"O King, I shall slay him; what concern is there regarding the injury of a woman?
Having said this, he set out, joined by his own forces and accompanied by chariots.
Having appointed the exceedingly powerful Tāmra as the second rear-guard,
he filled the sky and the quarters with the great roar of his army.
Beholding him approaching, the divine and auspicious Goddess Śivā sounded the conch and the bowstring and made a most wonderful noise with her bells.
Then, at that terrifying sound, all those enemies of the gods, trembling with fear, fled while crying out, "What is this? || 9 ||
But seeing them intent on flight, the one named Cikṣura, becoming exceedingly enraged, said: "What fear has come upon you? (10)
"This very day I shall slay with my arrows this young woman who is arrogant with pride;
O Daityas, remain here at the front of the battle, casting away all fear. (11)
Having spoken thus, the best of the Dānavas, powerful and with bow in hand,
approached the Goddess in battle and spoke these words, free from distress.
"Why do you roar, O large-eyed one, terrifying other men?
I am not afraid, O slender-limbed one, having heard your conduct today. (13)
"O fair-eyed one, having recognized the fault in killing a woman as well as the resulting infamy, my mind remains indifferent. (14)
O beautiful one, the battle of women is waged with side-long glances and gestures;
it is never ordained anywhere for those like you to be fought with weapons. (15)
One should not even fight with flowers, much less with sharpened arrows; for even a petal of the *mālatī* flower causes pain upon the bodies of those such as you.
Fie upon this birth in the world of men for those who subsist by the dharma of the warrior!
This cherished body, so long pampered, must now be cut down with sharp arrows. (17)
This beloved body, nourished by oil massages, flower-scented breezes, and the eating of sweet foods, must be destroyed by the arrows of others.
Having cut his body with sword-blades, a man is born as a Dhanabhṛt;
fie on wealth that gives pain at first—what could it possibly give in the way of happiness later? (19)
Since you too, O fair-thighed one, desire battle as if you were ignorant, what quality do you perceive in combat that makes you renounce the pleasure born of union? (20)
The falling of swords, the blows of clubs, and being pierced by arrows;
at the end of life, there is the funeral rite and being dragged by the mouths of jackals. (21)
Poets and rogues have excessively praised that very thing;
the attainment of heaven for those who die in battle is merely a figurative assertion (arthavāda). || 22 ||
Therefore go, O lady of beautiful hips, wherever your heart finds delight;
or else serve the lord of the earth, the protector, the enemy of horses (Garuḍa), the crusher of the gods' foes.
Vyāsa said:
To that Daitya who was speaking thus, the Mother of the World replied:
"O fool, why do you speak falsely, like a wise scholar? (24)
"You do not know the science of ethics (nītiśāstra), nor the science of inquiry (anvīkṣikī);
you have not served the elders, and you possess no inclination toward dharma. (25)
Since you are intent on serving fools, you yourself are indeed a fool;
you do not know the duty of kings—what are you saying before me? (26)
Having slain Mahiṣa in battle and created a mire of blood,
and having erected a firm pillar of glory, I shall go as I please.
"I shall slay that wicked Dānava, arrogant with pride, who brings suffering to the gods; fight and remain steadfast! (28)
O fool, if you have a desire for life just as this buffalo does,
then let all those Dānavas go to the netherworld.
If the desire for death has arisen in your minds, then wage war with haste;
I shall slay every one of you—this is my firm resolve now.
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words of hers, the Dānava, arrogant in his strength,
released a shower of arrows like another downpour from a cloud.
Then she cut his arrows with her own sharp shafts and struck him with terrible arrows resembling venomous serpents.
A battle took place there between them that was filled with wonder;
then the Mother of the World struck him down from his chariot with her mace.
Struck violently by the mace, that evil-minded one fell into a swoon;
for the duration of two muhūrtas, he remained motionless like a mountain upon the seat of his chariot.
Seeing him thus unconscious, Tāmra, the crusher of enemy forces,
rushed out of impetuosity to fight Caṇḍikā in battle.
Seeing him approaching, Caṇḍikā laughed and said:
"Come, come, O best of Dānavas! I shall lead you to the realm of Yama."
"What is the use of you weaklings who have reached the end of your lives coming here?
What can the foolish Mahiṣa do, remaining alive in his own home? (37)
"What is the use of killing you wretched ones? My own labor would be in vain as long as that wicked, evil-minded enemy of the gods, Mahiṣa, remains unslain. (38)
Therefore, having gone home, you should send the buffalo here;
let that dull-witted one see me standing exactly as I am. (39)
Having heard those words, Tāmra,
with his bow drawn back to his ear, discharged a shower of arrows out of anger toward Caṇḍikā.
The Blessed One Tāmrākṣī also, having drawn her bow,
swiftly released arrows, desiring to slay the enemy of the gods.
The powerful one known as Cikṣura, having cast off his fainting spell, rose up again;
seizing his bow along with an arrow, he stood before him in an instant.
Both the one named Cikṣura and Tāmra, exceedingly fierce and possessed of great strength, those two great heroes fought with the Goddess on the field of battle. (43)
And Mahāmāyā, enraged, rained down a continuous stream of arrows;
she rendered all the Dānavas such that their armor was pierced by shafts.
Struck by the arrows, the Asuras became bewildered with rage;
filled with fury, they hurled nets of shafts toward the Goddess. (45)
All those Rākṣasas, wounded by arrows in that battle, shone like flowering Kiṃśuka trees in a forest during the springtime. || 46 ||
A tumultuous battle took place with Tāmra in that encounter;
the gods who stood as spectators were filled with the utmost amazement. || 47 ||
Taking up a fierce, solid iron mace made of copper, he struck the lion on the head; and he laughed and roared aloud. (48)
Then, seeing him roaring, the goddess, filled with rage,
swiftly severed his head with a sharp-edged sword.
When his head was severed, the powerful Tāmra, though headless and armed with a mace,
wandered for a mere moment and then fell upon the field of battle.
Seeing the copper vessel fallen, the exceedingly powerful one named Cikshura took up his sword and rushed swiftly toward Caṇḍikā.
The Blessed Lady also, seeing that Dānava approaching with sword in hand,
swiftly struck him with five arrows in the battle.
By one [arrow] the sword was felled; by a second, his hand;
and by other arrows, his head was severed from his neck. || 53 ||
Thus those two cruel Rākṣasas, intoxicated by battle, were slain;
their army, its minds terrified, quickly fled in all directions.
And all the gods, seeing those two slain in battle,
joyfully rained down flowers from the sky while uttering shouts of victory.
The ṛṣis, devas, gandharvas, vetālas, siddhas, and cāraṇas cried out again and again, "Victory to the Goddess! O Ambikā! (56)

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of the One Named Tāmracikṣu," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 14.
The Description of the Slaying of those known as Asiloman and Biḍāla.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard that those two had been slain by her, Mahiṣa was filled with amazement.
He dispatched the exceedingly powerful Daityas for the purpose of slaying him.
[He saw] those led by Asiloman and the one named Biḍāla, who were fierce in battle,
accompanied by a great army, armed, and fully equipped with their retinues.
There they beheld the divine goddess seated upon a lion,
possessing eighteen arms and holding a sword and a shield.
Asiloman, having gone before her, spoke to the goddess who was intent on slaying the Daityas, bowing with humility and remaining tranquil, as if smiling. (4)
Asilomā said:
O Goddess, speak the truth; for what purpose have you come here, O beautiful one? Or why do you slay these innocent Daityas?
Tell me the reason today; I shall make an alliance with you, [offering] gold, gems, jewels, and excellent vessels.
"O lady of noble limbs, take whatever you desire and go; do not delay.
For what reason do you wish for battle, which only increases suffering and torment? (7)
The great-souled ones say that war utterly destroys all happiness,
especially for those whose bodies are exceedingly delicate and utterly unable to endure the blows of flowers.
"Why do you endure the falling of weapons? he wondered in amazement; for the fruit of wisdom is peace and the constant enjoyment of happiness. (9)
So why do you wish to engage in battle, which is a cause of suffering? In this cycle of existence, the established rule is that pleasure is to be grasped and suffering is to be abandoned. (10)
That happiness is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by being eternal and non-eternal:
the knowledge of the Self is eternal happiness, while that born of enjoyment is remembered as non-eternal. (11)
That which is of the nature of destruction must be abandoned by those who contemplate the meaning of the Vedic scriptures;
yet, O fair-faced one, you accept the doctrine of the Buddhists.
Nevertheless, having attained youth, enjoy unsurpassed pleasures;
O slender-waisted one, if you have any doubt regarding the next world.
O beautiful lady, remain constantly devoted to the enjoyment of heaven on this earth;
knowing that youth in the body is impermanent, one should perform meritorious deeds.
The wise should always avoid actions that cause suffering to others;
they should practice the pursuit of dharma, artha, and kāma in a manner free from conflict. 15.
Therefore, O auspicious one, you too should always set your mind upon dharma;
O Mother, why do you slay the Daityas when they have committed no offense?
Compassion is his body and truth is proclaimed to be his life-breaths;
therefore, compassion as well as truth must always be protected by the wise.
"O lady of beautiful hips, tell me the reason for your slaying of the Dānavas.
The Goddess said:
"O mighty-armed one, you have asked why I have come here. (18)
Therefore, O Daitya, I shall fully explain the purpose for my slaying; I always wander at all times throughout all the worlds. (19)
Beholding the right and wrong conduct of living beings in the form of a witness, I have never had a desire for enjoyment, nor greed, nor enmity. (20)
I wander here in this saṃsāra for the sake of dharma, protecting the virtuous;
I always steadfastly observe this vow of mine.
The protection of the virtuous must be performed, and those who are wicked must be slain;
likewise, the preservation of the Vedas must be accomplished through various incarnations.
In age after age, I indeed assume those very incarnations;
meanwhile, the wicked Mahiṣa was intent on slaying the gods.
"O Rākṣasa, having learned of this, I have now arrived for the purpose of slaying him;
I shall kill that evil-doer, the mighty enemy of the gods. (24)
"Go or stay as you wish; this truth has been spoken.
Or rather, speak to that evil-minded king, the son of the queen. (25)
"Why do you send others here? Fight yourself! If you, O King, desire to make peace with me, then do so. (26)

"Let all go to Pātāla at their ease, having abandoned enmity. Whatever property of the gods was seized after defeating the deities in battle—having returned that, let them go to Pātāla where Prahlāda resides. (27)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the goddess, Asiloman, standing before her,
affectionately questioned the great hero named Biḍāla.
Asiloma said:
"O you named Biḍāla, you have heard today what has been told by Bhavānī.
This being the case, should war be waged or peace made?"
The one named Biḍālākha said:
"This proud king has no desire for peace, for he knows death is certain in battle.
Having seen others slain, he likewise urges us forward; indeed, who is capable of overcoming destiny?"
"Let the duty of servants here always remain difficult to fulfill— those who are devoid of pride, devoted to commands, and subservient."
Like puppets when the strings are broken,
having gone before him, how could this harsh thing be spoken by you and by me as well?
Then, having given jewels and wealth to the gods, let all of them go from here to the netherworld (pātāla). || 31 ||
For one should speak what is pleasant, even if it be untrue; yet that which is beneficial, though not pleasant, should indeed be spoken.
In this world, truth and pleasantness do not necessarily coincide.
Therefore, silence is established as the proper conduct for the wise.
Furthermore, according to the science of polity (*nītiśāstra*), a king should not be awakened [to his duty] by insignificant words, but rather by heroes. (32)
Surely one should not go there, nor speak for his welfare with earnestness, nor even inquire after him; for once he has departed, the king will be filled with anger. (33)
Having reflected thus, one should engage in battle when life is at risk, considering the service of one's master as supreme and death as being like a blade of grass. (34)
Vyāsa said:
Having reflected thus, those two heroes stood intent on battle, bearing bows and arrows, fully equipped and stationed upon their chariots. (35)
First, the one named Biḍāla discharged seven arrows,
while Asiloman, a master of supreme weapons, stood at a distance as a spectator.
Ambikā likewise cut down those arrows before they reached her with her own shafts,
and she struck the one named Biḍāla with three stone-sharpened arrows.
Having suffered the pain of the arrow, the Daitya fell upon the field of battle;
then, rendered unconscious, the Dānava died quickly by the turn of fate. 38.
Seeing the one named Biḍāla slain in battle by a multitude of spears and arrows,
Asiloman stood with bow in hand, intent on combat.
Raising his left hand, he spoke these measured words to her:
"O Goddess, I know the death of the evil-minded Dānavas."
Nevertheless, I, being subject to another's will, must indeed wage war;
for the dull-witted Mahiṣa does not distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful.
Therefore, I must not speak even beneficial words that are unpleasant in his presence;
rather, I must die according to the dharma of a hero, whether it be for good or for ill.
I consider destiny alone to be supreme; human effort is useless.
The Dānavas, struck by your arrows, fall swiftly to the earth. (43)
Having spoken thus, that best of Dānavas unleashed a shower of arrows;
the Goddess, however, cut them down with her own shafts before they could reach her side.
Then, while being watched by the hosts of immortals, she, her face filled with rage, swiftly pierced Asiloman with other swift-flying arrows.
With his body pierced by arrows, the Dānava indeed shone at will, like a blossoming Kiṃśuka tree with streams of flowing blood. || 46 ||
Asiloma, raising a heavy iron mace with great force,
rushed at Caṇḍikā in anger and struck the lion on its head.
The lion also tore him apart in the middle of his chest with blows from its claws,
disregarding the mace-strike delivered by that powerful one.
Springing up with speed, the most terrible Daitya, mace in hand,
mounted upon the lion's head and struck Ambikā with his mace.
O lord of the people, having evaded that blow,
he severed the head from the neck with a sharp-edged sword.
When his head was severed, the lord of the Daityas fell swiftly to the earth;
a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose within the army of that evil-souled one.
"Victory to the Goddess!"—thus did the gods praise that Mother of the World;
the celestial drums resounded, O King, and the Kinnaras sang.
Seeing the two Dānavas slain and fallen upon the field of battle,
all the soldiers there were forcibly killed by Kesarin.
Some were likewise devoured, and that battle was rendered complete;
some were broken and, being dejected, fled toward Mahiṣa. || 54 ||
O best of kings, Asiloman and Biḍāla were slain; they cried out and wept with cries of "Save us! Save us! (55).
"O King, those other soldiers who were devoured by the lion," saying this, they then committed a slaughter against the king. (56)
Having heard those words of theirs, Mahiṣa then became dejected;
he was overwhelmed with anxiety, despondent, and filled with sorrow. || 57 ||

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of Asiloman and Bidala," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 15 ||
The Awakening of the Goddess by Mahiṣadvāra.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of theirs, the lord of men was filled with wrath.
He spoke swiftly to Dāruka: "Bring me my wonderful chariot."
It was yoked with a thousand donkeys, adorned with banners and flags,
equipped with weapons, brilliant, possessing excellent wheels, and having beautiful poles.
The charioteer also, having brought the chariot, spoke to him with haste:
"O King, this chariot has been brought; it stands adorned at the gate."
Knowing that the chariot, equipped with all weapons and furnished with excellent coverings, had been brought, the exceedingly powerful lord of the Dānavas [prepared himself].
Having assumed a human body and being prepared to go into battle, he reflected thus in his mind upon seeing the goddess Durmukhī: ||| 5 ||
"She will surely be despondent at the sight of the horned buffalo;
for women, beauty and cleverness are likewise dear. (6)
Therefore, having assumed beauty and skill, I shall go toward her,
so that upon seeing me, that young woman will become filled with love.
"May happiness belong to me alone at that very time, and not through the nature of another"—
having thus reflected in his mind, the exceedingly powerful lord of the Dānavas [spoke].
Having abandoned that buffalo form, he became an auspicious man,
bearing all weapons, glorious, and adorned with beautiful ornaments.
Wearing divine garments, lovely as a second god of love with his flower-arrows,
he sat upon his chariot, adorned with armlets and garlands, wielding his bow and arrows.
Surrounded by his army and intoxicated with pride, he approached the goddess,
assuming a charming form that captivated the hearts of proud women.
Then, beholding the lord of the Daityas who had arrived surrounded by many heroes, the Goddess blew her conch shell.
Having heard that sound of the conch which caused wonder among the people,
he approached the Goddess and spoke to her as if smiling.
O Goddess, it is said that every person existing in this wheel of saṃsāra—whether man or woman—desires happiness in every respect. (14)
The happiness born of union for men does not exist here in the absence of union;
union is divided into many kinds, so listen as I describe them to you. (15)
There are manifold divisions arising from the causes of joy and arising from their own nature;
among those, I shall first describe those born of joy according to my understanding. (16)
The union of a son with his mother and father is recorded as the highest;
likewise, the union of a brother with a brother is considered middling for a specific reason. (17)
He is remembered as "Supreme" (uttama) because he is the giver of the highest happiness alone;
and he is "Intermediate" (madhyama) because he is the giver of only limited happiness. (18)
The wise have declared that the association of sailors with those whose minds are clouded by various [passions] and who revolve in worldly attachments is natural. (19)
Because it bestows only very slight happiness, this [lower union] is considered inferior by the wise;
however, the supreme union always bestows happiness within saṃsāra. (20)
The union that is always described as occurring between a man and a woman who are equally beautiful and of equal age is considered the very best. || 21 ||
Because he is the bestower of the very highest bliss, he is of such a nature; likewise, by means of his cleverness, beauty, dress, and so forth, as well as his lineage, conduct, and virtues. (22)
Indeed, mutual excellence is proclaimed between one another;
if you would enter into that union with me, a hero. (23)
You shall attain the very highest bliss, of this there is no doubt;
O beloved, I assume various forms according to my own will.
All the gods, beginning with Indra, have been conquered by me in battle;
whatever divine jewels there are in this palace of mine now, [they were seized]. (25)
Enjoy all of those as you wish, or give them away as you please;
become the chief queen today, O beautiful one, for I am your slave.
"I shall abandon my enmity with the gods at your word, there is no doubt;
I shall indeed act in such a way that you may attain happiness."
"Command me, O large-eyed one; I shall do exactly as you say. My heart has been infatuated by your beauty, O sweet-spoken lady. (28)
"I am afflicted, O lady of beautiful hips; I have indeed come to you for refuge.
Protect me, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, who am tormented by the arrows of desire. (29)
The supreme duty among all duties is the protection of those who have come for refuge.
O lady with dark-cornered eyes, I am yours; O slender-waisted one, I am your servant. (30)
My word is true unto death; I shall not act otherwise.
O slender-limbed one, I bow at your feet, having laid aside my various weapons.
"Have mercy, O large-eyed one; I am tormented by the arrows of desire. O lady of beautiful limbs, from birth until now, I have never practiced wretchedness. (32)
"Having approached the lords beginning with Brahmā, I shall place that [burden] upon you;
for Brahmā and the other gods know my conduct in battle. (33)
"O beautiful lady, look at my face; even I am your servant.
Vyāsa said:
To that Daitya who was speaking thus, the divine Goddess indeed [replied]. (34)
Laughing with a smile, the woman of excellent complexion spoke these words.
The goddess said:
"I do not desire a man other than the Supreme Puruṣa. (35)
O Daitya, if I so desire, I create the entire universe;
that Soul of the Universe beholds me, for I am his auspicious Prakṛti.
"By the power of His very presence alone, consciousness is eternal within me;
though I am insentient, through union with Him, I become possessed of consciousness. (37)
Just as iron acquires consciousness through the proximity of a magnet, so too does the desire for vulgar pleasures never arise in me at any time. (38)
"You are a fool, O dull-witted one, that you desire union with a woman;
a woman is proclaimed to be a chain for the bondage of man. (39)
Even one bound by iron may be released, but one bound by women is never released.
O dull-witted one, do you desire to frequent a latrine? (40)
Bring peace for the sake of happiness; from peace you shall obtain happiness.
Knowing that association with women brings great suffering, why do you become deluded? (41)
Abandon your enmity with the gods and roam the earth as you please;
or go to Pātāla at your will, if there is any desire for life remaining in you.
Or rather, engage in battle, for I am powerful at present;
I have been sent by all the gods, O Dānava, for the sake of your destruction.
I speak the truth: I am pleased by the kindness of speech you have shown me today; go hence alive and at your ease.
The friendship of the virtuous lasts for seven steps; therefore, I relinquish my life.
O hero, if you desire death, then fight as you please! (45)
"O mighty-armed one, I shall kill you; of this there is no doubt.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of hers, the Dānava was deluded by passion. (46)
Then, with gentle speech, he spoke these sweet words:
"O lady of excellent hips, O fair-faced one, I am afraid to strike you."
Having completely conquered Hari, Hara, and the other guardians of the world, he took a woman who was tender, beautiful in all her limbs, and enchanting to men. 48.
"O lotus-eyed one, is it fitting for me to fight with you?
O lady of beautiful limbs, if it pleases you, enter into marriage and accept me."
Otherwise, go to whatever land you desire from which you have come;
I shall not strike you, since you have shown me friendship.
"Beneficial and auspicious words have been spoken; therefore, go as you please.
What beauty would there be for me in the end after killing you, O lovely-eyed one? (51)
The killing of a woman, the killing of a child, and the killing of a Brahmin are difficult to overcome;
O fair-faced one, having taken you, I shall surely go home this very day.
Nevertheless, there would be no fruit for me; how could there be the happiness of enjoyment by force?
O lady of beautiful hair, I speak to you thus, bowing low with humility. (53)
A man would have no happiness without the lotus-face of his beloved;
likewise, a woman would have no such happiness without a man. (54)
In union there is the arising of happiness; in separation, the arising of suffering.
You are lovely, endowed with beauty, and adorned with every ornament. (55)
Is there no cleverness in you, alas, that you do not devote yourself to me?
By whom was this abandonment of enjoyments taught to you? (56)
"O you of sweet speech, you have been deceived here by some enemy;
O beloved, release this obsession and perform what is most auspicious. (57)
"Indeed, when the marriage is performed, there will be happiness for you and for me as well;
Viṣṇu shines with Lakṣmī, and the Self-born One (Brahmā) with Sāvitrī. (58)
Rudra shines with Pārvatī, and likewise the Lord of a Hundred Sacrifices with Śacī;
for what woman, deprived of her husband, can attain eternal happiness? (59)
O lady with dark-cornered eyes, why do you not make him your husband?
O beloved, where has that Kāma gone today, he who [pierced] you with his most tender arrows? (60)
The dull-witted man does not strike at passion with the five arrows of intoxication;
O beautiful one, I believe that even Kāma must be compassionate toward you, just as I am.
Thinking "she is not yet a maiden," he does not discharge his arrows;
or perhaps there is some enmity between the Mind-born [Cupid] and me. (62)
And for that reason, O lady with beautiful eyes, he does not release his arrows at you;
or rather, that god whose banner is a fish has been restrained by my malevolent deities.
Because of those things which destroy happiness, he does not strike you even now;
O fawn-eyed one, having abandoned me, you will later feel remorse.
Like Mandodarī, O slender-limbed one, she first abandoned her auspicious king and then later made that fickle husband her own;
for when she became afflicted by passion, her inner self was agitated by delusion. (65)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Awakening of the Goddess by Mahiṣa," in the fifth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 16.
The description of the life of the princess Mandodarī.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, the goddess questioned the Dānava.
Who was that woman Mandodarī, and who was that king abandoned by her? (1)
"Who was that deceitful king? Tell me that story afterwards."
Furthermore, the suffering obtained by the woman was related in detail.
Mahiṣa said:
There is a country named Siṃhala, renowned upon the surface of the earth.
It was endowed with dense trees and possessed an abundance of wealth and grain. || 3 ||
There, a king named Candrasena reigned, who was devoted to righteousness.
He was a bearer of justice as his rod, peaceful, and devoted to the protection of his subjects.
A speaker of truth, gentle, brave, patient, and an ocean of statesmanship.
He was a knower of the scriptures, an expert in all dharmas, and exceedingly proficient in the science of archery.
His wife was Varārohā, beautiful, fortunate, and auspicious.
She was devoted to virtuous conduct, possessed an exceedingly pleasant countenance, and was entirely dedicated to devotion for her husband.
The beloved wife was named Guṇavatī, endowed with all auspicious marks.
In her first pregnancy, she gave birth to a daughter who was exceedingly beautiful.
And the father was exceedingly delighted, having obtained such a beautiful daughter.
Her father, filled with joy, gave her the name Mandodarī.
Like a digit of the moon, she grew exceedingly more and more day by day.
When a maiden has reached ten years of age and is exceedingly beautiful, [she should be given away]. || 9 ||
And day after day, the king fell into anxiety for the sake of obtaining a boon.
The king of the Madra country was a brave ruler named Sudhanvan.
His son was Atimedhāvin, the highly renowned Kaṃbugrīva.
The Brahmins told the king, "This auspicious boon is suitable for her."
Endowed with all auspicious marks, he has reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge and their meaning.
Then the king asked his beloved queen, Guṇavatī by name.
I shall give my own daughter, who possesses an excellent complexion, to Kaṃbugrīva.
Having heard her husband's words, she respectfully questioned her daughter.
Your father desires to perform your marriage with Kaṃbugrīva.
Having heard that, Mandodarī then spoke these words to her mother.
I will not take a husband; I have no desire for marriage.
Having undertaken the vow of lifelong celibacy, I shall spend my time in every way.
Indeed, I shall always practice intense austerity with complete independence.
O Mother, dependence is the supreme misery in the ocean of worldly existence.
The wise, who are experts in the scriptures, say that liberation comes from sovereignty.
Therefore, I shall become liberated; I have no need for a husband.
While the marriage was taking place, however, in the presence of the sacred fire.
That which is to be spoken must be said; I am always dependent upon the True Dharma.
She shall become a slave to her mother-in-law, her brother-in-law, and their kin, within the house of her father-in-law.
Compliance with those who require expiation is considered more painful than pain itself. || 19 ||
If at some time her husband should resort to another woman or a mistress;
Then there would arise a far greater suffering born of a rival wife. || 5.17.20 ||
Then envy arises toward her husband, and moreover, there will be suffering.
O Mother, where is there happiness in saṃsāra, especially for women? (21)
Of those dependent on their own-nature within this cyclic existence, which has the nature of a dream.
"O Mother, I have heard before that he was the son of Uttānapāda."
The king was the most excellent, knower of all dharmas, and the younger brother of Dhruva.
[He saw] his wife, who was devoted to dharma, virtuous, and entirely dedicated to her husband.
Without any offense, he abandoned his beloved wife in the forest.
Such are the sufferings that exist while the husband is still alive. || 24 ||
If he dies due to the conjunction of time, the woman shall become a vessel of suffering.
Widowhood is the supreme misery, causing grief and torment. || 25 ||
Even when one has become a protector of others, suffering would be even greater at home.
For one consumed by the fire of passion, what happiness can there be arising from union with a husband? || 26 ||
Therefore, it is my opinion that one should never, under any circumstances, become a husband.
When she had spoken thus, the mother, the princess, then said to her husband:
And she, observing the vow of lifelong maidenhood, did not desire a husband.
She was constantly devoted to vows and recitations, always turned away from the cycle of worldly existence.
Perceiving many faults, she does not desire to make him her husband.
Having heard what his wife said, the king remained exactly as he was. || 29 ||
No marriage was performed for his daughter, knowing her to be devoid of any [suitable] disposition.
Thus dwelling in the house, she was protected by her father and mother.
The sprouts of youth have arisen in women, which kindle the fire of desire.
Nevertheless, though she was urged again and again by her female companions, || 31 ||
She who spoke words concerning the goal of knowledge desired to make him her husband.
Once, she went to wander in a garden region abounding in many trees.
With a cheerful countenance, she went forth, attended by a group of maidservants out of affection.
There the slender-waisted woman played; she beheld flowering creepers.
The lovely woman, surrounded by her companions, was gathering flowers.
At that time, by the power of destiny, the lord of Kosala was on that path.
The great hero Vīrasena, who was exceedingly renowned, arrived.
Alone, mounted upon his chariot, and accompanied by only a few attendants. || 35 ||
And his army followed behind him, advancing very slowly.
Then her companion saw the king from a distance.
Thus it was said to Mandodarī: "A man is coming along the path."
Mounted upon his chariot, the long-armed one was handsome, like another Madana.
I believe that some king has arrived here by the power of destiny.
While she was speaking thus, the lord of Kośala arrived there.
Upon seeing her with her dark-cornered eyes, the king was filled with wonder.
Having quickly descended from the chariot, he questioned his female attendant.
Who is this large-eyed girl, and whose daughter is she? Tell me quickly.
Thus questioned, the Sairandhrī, with a pure smile, spoke to him.
First, O hero, speak to me; I ask you, O one of beautiful eyes.
"Who are you? Why have you come here? Tell me now, what is your purpose? (41)
Thus questioned by the Sairandhrī, the lord of the earth spoke to her.
There is a land named Kosala on earth, most wonderful.
And I, O beloved, am his protector, named Vīrasena.
The fourfold army follows behind at will.
Know me to be the lord of Kosala, who has arrived here by mistake of the path.
Sairandhrī said:
O King, she was indeed the daughter of Candrasena, known by the name Mandodarī.
This lotus-eyed woman has arrived at the garden desiring to sport.
Having heard what she had said, the king replied to the female attendant: || 45 ||
"O Sairandhrī, you are clever; awaken the princess."
And I am a king born of the lineage of Kakutstha, O lovely-eyed one. (46)
O lovely one, make me your husband by the Gāndharva rite of marriage.
"O fair-hipped one, I have no wife, even though I am in the marvelous bloom of youth. (47)
Indeed, I desire a woman endowed with beauty, born of a noble family, and full of passion.
Or rather, your father ought to give me [to you] according to the prescribed rite.
And I shall become a favorable husband; of this there is no doubt.
Mahiṣa said:
Having heard these words of his, the Sairandhrī then spoke to her.
Laughing, she who was expert in the science of love spoke these sweet words.
O Mandodarī, the king who has arrived is born of the Solar dynasty.
Moreover, he is handsome, strong, charming, and equal to you in age.
O beautiful one, the king has become entirely filled with affection for you.
O large-eyed one, your father also suffers in every way.
Knowing that the time for your marriage had arrived and that you were possessed by a spirit of detachment, [he spoke].
Thus that king spoke to us, sighing again and again.
"Let these maidservants, devoted to their duties, awaken this daughter."
We are not able to speak to you again, for you are devoted to the way of obstinacy.
Manu has declared that for women, service to their husband is the highest duty. || 54 ||
Indeed, by serving her husband, a woman shall attain heaven.
Therefore, O large-eyed one, perform the marriage ceremony according to the prescribed rites.
Mandodarī said:
I will not take a husband; I shall practice wondrous austerity.
"O young girl, restrain the king; why does he look at me so shamelessly? || 56 ||
The Sairandhrī said:
O Goddess, this desire is difficult to conquer; this time is difficult to transcend.
Therefore, O beautiful one, you ought to carry out my wholesome advice.
Otherwise, it is certain that disaster will surely befall us.
Having heard these words of hers, the maiden then spoke to her friend with her voice.
Whatever may happen, let it happen through the power of destiny; of this there is no doubt.
"O attendant, I shall by no means enter into marriage. (59)
Mahiṣa said:
Having thus understood her persistence, he spoke again to the king.
Go, O King, as you wish; she does not desire a husband who is merely virtuous.
Having heard those words, the king went forth accompanied by his army.
Becoming despondent toward Kośalā, he was devoid of desire for his beloved. || 61 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devī Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 17 ||
The Slaying of the Asura Mahiṣa;
Mahiṣa said:
Her sister was a maiden named Indumatī, who was auspicious.
When his younger sister became beautiful and reached a marriageable age, [he reflected: || 1 ||
Her marriage was performed, and Sūjātā held her own svayaṃvara.
Kings from many countries assembled there in that pavilion.
By her, a certain king was chosen—one who was powerful and endowed with beauty.
Endowed with noble lineage and virtuous conduct, he was possessed of all auspicious marks.
Then, upon seeing that king, who was like a libertine, she became afflicted by desire.
But by the turn of fate, he desired that rogue who was adorned with cleverness.
The slender-limbed maiden said to her father, "O father, perform my marriage."
Having seen Bhadrādhipa here today, a desire has arisen within me.
Candrasena, having heard what his daughter had spoken in private, [acted accordingly].
Even while laughing, he became mentally intent upon that task.
Having summoned him to his palace, the king gave her to him according to the rites of marriage.
He gave him his daughter Mandodarī as well as many other wedding gifts.
Cārudeṣṇa, too, having obtained that beautiful woman, became joyful.
The king also, being satisfied, went to his own home together with his wife.
That tiger among kings sported with his beloved for many days.
It is said that once he was sporting in secret with the wife of a servant.
The maidservant told her that she had likewise seen her husband.
Filled with anger, she gave him a rebuke preceded by a smile.
Once, the king [saw] Rūpavatī in secret, though she was with others.
While she was seen playing and fondling [the child], she felt distress at that very moment.
This rogue was not recognized previously when he was seen at the svayaṃvara.
"What have I done out of delusion that I have been deceived by the king? (12)
"What shall I do today, O tormenting one, shameless, pitiless, and deceitful?"
What joy can there be in such a husband? Fie upon my life today! || 13 ||
From this day forward, I have indeed renounced all worldly pleasure within saṃsāra.
Today I have practiced contentment regarding everything born of mutual enjoyment. || 14 ||
That which ought not to have been done has been performed; it has become a source of suffering for me.
If the abandonment of the body is performed by means of killing, it is exceedingly difficult to overcome.
I shall go quickly to my father’s house; even there, no happiness will be found.
I shall become an object of ridicule for my friends; of this there is no doubt. || 16 ||
Therefore, it is here alone that I shall dwell together with you, endowed with dispassion.
Having again abandoned the pleasure of sensual desires, one should act according to the requirements of the time. ||17||
Mahiṣa said:
Having reflected thus, that woman was utterly devoted to grief and sorrow.
Having abandoned her husband's home, she remained there, experiencing the pleasures born of worldly existence. || 18 ||
Therefore, O auspicious lady, you too, disregarding me, [should disregard] the king.
Afflicted by desire, you will resort to another, a dull-witted and base man. || 19 ||
Follow my truthful word; it is the supreme benefit for women.
Without having performed this supreme act of grief, you will not obtain it; of this there is no doubt.
The Goddess said:
O Madātman, go to Pātāla or engage in battle right now.
Having slain you and all the asuras, I shall proceed according to my pleasure.
For whenever, O Dānava, suffering befalls the virtuous, [then I manifest myself].
Then, for their protection, I shall maintain this body.
And for me, who am formless, there is form; and for me, who am unborn, there is birth.
Know this, O Daitya, to be firmly resolved for the sake of protecting the gods.
I speak the truth; know this: I have indeed been entreated by the gods.
O enemy of horses, for the sake of slaying you, I shall stand firm after having killed you.
Therefore, either fight or go to Pātāla, the abode of the Asuras.
I shall slay you along with all your kinsmen; I tell you this truly. || 25 ||
Vyāsa said:
Thus addressed by that goddess, the Dānava took up his bow.
Desirous of battle, he stood there upon the grounds of the field of combat.
He swiftly released arrows, sharpened on stone and drawn back to his ear.
The goddess cut them down with iron-tipped arrows released in fury. ||27||
A battle that inspired terror broke out between the two of them.
Of the gods and the dānavas, who were each desirous of victory over the other. || 28 ||
Durdhara, arriving in the midst of them, released his stone-tipped arrows.
Provoking those exceedingly cruel beings who were intent on harming the Goddess.
Then the Blessed Lady, enraged, struck him with sharp arrows.
But Durdhara fell to the earth like a mountain peak whose life has departed.
Seeing him slain by her, the three-eyed one, who is a supreme knower of weapons, [was moved].
Having arrived, he struck Parameśvarī with seven arrows.
But the goddess cut down those arrows before they had even arrived with her own shafts.
The Mother of the World struck the three-eyed one with her trident.
But Andhaka, seeing that the Three-eyed One had been slain, quickly approached the bull.
With an iron mace, he swiftly struck the lion on the head.
But the lion, having killed that exceedingly powerful one with a blow of his claws, [departed].
Filled with rage, he swiftly devoured the flesh of Andhaka.
Seeing them slain in battle, the Dānava was filled with amazement.
He swiftly discharged arrows that were exceedingly sharp and keen-edged.
The goddess split those arrows into two with her own stone-tipped shafts before they could reach him.
Ambikā struck the Daitya on the chest with her mace.
Struck by the mace, that harasser of the immortals fell into a swoon.
Having endured the pain, the evil-souled one quickly returned once more. || 37 ||
Filled with rage, he struck the lion on the head with his mace.
The lion also tore that great asura with a strike of its claws.
Abandoning his human form, he too became a lion.
With her claws, she tore apart the lion of the goddess, who was fierce with rut.
And beholding that lion, the queen, filled with rage, [struck him] with iron-tipped [arrows].
He covered him with sharp arrows, like arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Having abandoned that form of Hari, he became an elephant with flowing rut.
Taking a mountain peak in his hand, he hurled it toward Caṇḍikā.
As he was approaching the mountain peak, the goddess [struck him] with arrows whetted on stone.
The Mother of the World laughed and reduced [him] to pieces as small as sesame seeds.
And then, having leaped up, the lion stationed himself upon his head.
He tore apart the buffalo, who was in the form of an elephant, with his claws.
And having abandoned the form of an elephant, she likewise became a female eight-legged lizard.
Desirous of killing [him], he was more terrible and more powerful due to the wrath of Hari.
Seeing that śarabha, the goddess, filled with rage, [struck] him with her sword.
He quickly struck her on the head, and she in turn struck him then.
A battle between the two of them took place, inspiring great terror.
Then, assuming the form of a buffalo, he struck him with his two horns.
The great asura quickly struck with blows from his horns, causing the tail to whirl around.
The one of terrible form and fearsome appearance struck the slender-limbed woman. || 47 ||
Seizing the mountain peaks with his tail, he whirled them about with force.
The evil-minded one sent him forth, laughing with supreme joy.
Intoxicated by his strength, he said to her, "Stay, O Goddess, on the field of battle!"
Today I shall kill you, who are adorned with beauty and youth.
"You are a fool, intoxicated with pride today, that you have entered into combat with me."
Deluded, you act most excessively, falsely, powerfully, and harshly.
Having slain you, I shall destroy the gods who are deceived by your guile.
Those rogues who, placing a woman before them, desire to conquer me; || 51 ||
The Goddess said:
Do not be arrogant, O dull-witted one; stay, stay on the field of battle!
"Having slain you, O best of gods, I shall make them free from all fear."
Having drunk the desired Mādhavī wine today, I shall strike down the lowest of men in battle.
It is a sin that causes suffering to the gods and brings fear to the sages. || 53 ||
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, he took a golden cup filled with wine.
Out of anger, desiring to kill the great asura, she drank [the poison] again and again.
Having drunk the sweet grape-wine, she quickly took up a lotus root.
The goddess pursued the Dānava, gladdening the hosts of deities.
The gods praised her with love and showered a rain of flowers.
"Victory! Live long! they cried, amidst the resounding blasts of kettledrums.
The ṛṣis, siddhas, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and cāraṇas—
Beholding the battle, the Kinnaras stood in the sky, filled with joy.
He too, having repeatedly assumed various kinds of bodies again and again, [attained liberation].
The goddess, skilled in deception, struck down those who were composed of illusion in battle.
And Caṇḍikā also forcibly struck that sinner in the heart with her trident.
With eyes reddened by anger, she struck him with a sharp [weapon]. || 59 ||
Struck, he fell to the earth and remained unconscious for a moment.
Rising up again, he struck Cāmuṇḍā violently with his feet.
Having struck him with blows of his feet, he laughed again and again.
He uttered a terrible sound that caused fear among the gods.
Then the goddess [saw] the supreme thousand-spoked wheel with its beautiful nave.
Placing his hand [upon him], he spoke loudly to the standing Mahiṣāsura.
Behold today the discus of me, blinded by intoxication, which shall sever your throat.
"Stay steady for just a moment and now go to the realm of Yama."
Having spoken thus, the Mother of the World released her terrible discus.
Then, in that battle, the head of the Dānava was severed by a wheel of his chariot.
And warm blood flowed from his throat-tract like [water] from a mountain.
It was as red as ochre and other minerals, like the full, surging torrent of a mountain stream.
The headless trunk of that Daitya, while wandering about, indeed fell upon the earth.
And there arose the cry of "Victory! from the gods, increasing their joy.
Then the exceedingly powerful lion [attacked] those who were intent on flight there.
He devoured the Dānavas in battle like one afflicted by hunger.
And when the cruel Mahiṣa was dead, the Dānavas were tormented by fear.
And those who remained after the slaughter, O King, went to Pātāla.
When he had been struck down, the gods attained supreme joy.
The sages, human beings, and whatever other virtuous ones there are on earth—|| 69 ||
Caṇḍikā too, having abandoned the battle, then took her stand in an auspicious place.
The gods arrived there quickly, desiring to praise her who bestows happiness.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Asura Mahiṣa," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said: Then all the gods, led by Indra, were filled with joy. They offered consolation to the goddesses.
Seeing the buffalo slain, they praised the Mother of the World.
The gods said:
"Brahmā creates this world, Viṣṇu protects it, and Maheśa indeed withdraws it by your power alone at the time of dissolution."
Even the lords do not exist without you; therefore, you alone are the cause of the preservation and destruction of the world. || 2 ||

You are fame, intellect, memory, and movement; you are compassion, mercy, faith, and fortitude; you are the earth, the consort of Kamala, nourishment, art, victory, the daughter of the mountain, and triumph.
You are contentment, you are valid cognition, you are intellect, Umā, and Ramā. (3)
Knowledge, forbearance, beauty, and intelligence— everything in these three worlds is known by you alone;
yet without these powers of yours, it would be impossible to act swiftly.
Or who indeed is capable [of protecting] this dwelling place of all the worlds? || 4 ||
Are you not indeed *dhāraṇā* (the power of retention)? For if you were not, how could even the tortoise and the serpent be capable of supporting the earth?
And if you were not the earth itself, O Mother, how could all this world, burdened with such great weight, remain suspended in the sky? (5)
Or those deluded men who praise the immortals—
Caturmukha, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— as well as Śubhrāṃśu, Vahni, Yama, Vāyu, Gaṇeśa, and the others, [all of whom are merely] through your illusory powers.
But, O Mother, who else besides you has the power to accomplish this task?
O Mother, how indeed did those of small intellect— who, having appointed the gods as the object, offer abundant oblations into the fire in the extended sacrifice—
attain their goal, if you were not present with the cry of "Svāhā"?
Why indeed do they not worship you alone? Therefore, they are deluded.
O Mother, you bestow enjoyments upon all things moving and unmoving in this world; indeed, through your own portions, you grant life itself eternally.
Just as you nourish your own deities here, for that same reason, you protect others as well.

O Mother, skillful men do not, under any circumstances, cut down trees that are barren, leafless, bitter, and useless, even if they are found in the forest for their own amusement; therefore, you likewise protect the Daityas exceedingly.

But as for the fact that you slay your enemies with arrows at the head of the battle, having perceived that they are preoccupied with the amorous sports of celestial nymphs—even while in another body, you take up the essence of compassion; this is your conduct for the fulfillment of their desires.
It is a marvel that these demons of renowned power do not perish even though they are bereft of life-force due to your thought; for whose sake, O Mother, you have undertaken this bodily existence.
The flavor of play is not the cause for you here, nor is any other. || 11 ||
Alas, when the most wicked age of Kali has arrived, men do not worship you; indeed,
they have been deceived by rogues who are experts in the ancient [myths] of Hari and Śaṅkara.
And they have been appointed as devoted to the service of those created by you. || 12 ||
Having known that the gods were under your control and that those on earth who worshiped them with devotion were indeed afflicted by the asuras,
you took up a truly stainless lamp in your hand.
Men fall into a waterless well that is exceedingly terrible.
O Mother, you alone are knowledge that bestows happiness, and you alone are ignorance that bestows misery; you alone are the remover of the pain of birth for men.
Indeed, you are sought after by those of dull intellect who desire liberation, yet you are not worshipped by the ignorant who are intent only on worldly enjoyment, O Mother.
Brahmā, Hara, Hari, and other gods as well constantly worship your lotus feet, which are the refuge of all;
yet those of small intellect do not worship them even with their minds.
Deluded, they constantly fall into the ocean of existence. || 15 ||
O Caṇḍī, by the grace of the dust arising from the lotus of your feet, Brahmā creates the entire universe at the beginning of existence;
Śauri protects it, and Hara indeed destroys it; yet that unfortunate man here does not serve you.
O Goddess, you are the deity of speech; even the foremost of the immortals among gods and asuras are not capable of describing you,
for they lack the power [to do so] unless you dwell within their mouths.
For human beings do not exist at all without that. || 17 ||
Harī, having been cursed at will by the enraged Bhṛgu,
indeed became a fish, a tortoise, and a boar;
thereafter, he who acted with deceit toward the Earth became known as Nṛsiṃha.
O Mother, for those who serve them, how could there be any fear of death?
This famous linga of Śambhu fell to the earth by that curse when Bhṛgu had gone to the forest;
those men on earth who worship that Kapālin—
O Mother, how can there be happiness for them in this world or in the next? || 19 ||

O Goddess, those men who, having resorted to falsehood, worship Gajānana—the lord of the Gaṇas—who was born from Maheśa, do not know you, the Mother of the Universe, the bestower of the fruits of all goals, who is easily accessible through service. 20.
It is wonderful that even the host of your enemies, having been slain in battle with your sharp arrows out of a heart softened by compassion, have been sent to the celestial realm;
for otherwise, they would have fallen into the depths of the most agonizing suffering in the hells accumulated by their own karma. (21)
Even Brahmā, Hara, and Hari—those very gods—do not know your power due to their state of pride;
what other humans would be capable of knowing it, being deluded by your qualities of immeasurable majesty? (22)
Even those sages suffer, for with deluded minds they do not worship your lotus feet, which are difficult to conceive; instead,
they are intent on serving the sun and fire, [failing to grasp] the reality of the supreme goal.
Even by means of hundreds of scriptures, they have not known the essence of the Veda.
I believe that your virtues, whose power is renowned throughout the world,
indeed turn away those who are devoid of a spirit of devotion by means of various scriptures composed according to their own intellects.
Having installed Viṣṇu, Īśa, Bhāskara, Gaṇeśa, and Parā; || 24 ||

O Mother, you do not become angry with those foremost of men who, by means of their own scriptures and through the yoga of devotion to the worship of Hari and Hara, turn their backs on you; rather, you show them compassion and fully extend your power over those experts in the mantras of delusion.
In the fourth age, the power of the fourth quality (guṇa) becomes exceedingly great; by that, the false scriptures are churned away, and indeed,
in the Kali age, skillful poets protect you.
They praise even the hosts of gods fashioned by you. || 26 ||
Sages of extremely pure being meditate upon the supreme knowledge that is perfected through yoga and bestows the fruit of liberation on earth;
they do not experience the suffering within a mother's womb.
Blessed indeed are those men who have merged into you.

The power of consciousness exists within the Supreme Self, by which He too becomes manifest and known throughout the worlds as the performer of the acts of existence; who else, apart from You, has the power to prevail in this?
To act, to sport, and even to move about according to one's own power. || 28 ||
O Mother of the Universe, how could the principles (tattvas), being devoid of consciousness and insentient, be capable of creating the world? Furthermore,
the sense organs exist as mere adjuncts to the qualities and actions.
O Goddess, [these trees], being separated from you, are unable to bestow fruit. || 29 ||

O Mother, would not the gods accept their own portions offered according to the rules even at sacrifices by the sages? What need is there for you, O Svāhā, to be the instrumental cause therein, if you yourself were not present?
Therefore, you yourself indeed protect the entire universe as it were. || 30 ||
All this has been ordained by you from the beginning of existence;
you indeed protect the lords of the directions, headed by Hari and Hara;
