and in due time, you devour even the entire universe—your conduct, O Bhava, is primordial.
Where indeed do those unfortunate men not know [this]? || 31 ||
O Mother, it is said that by slaying the fierce Asura who had assumed the form of a buffalo, this host of gods was protected by you;
what praise, then, can we of dull intellect offer to you, O Mother?
The Vedas did not reach your true nature as it actually is. || 32 ||
Our duty has been accomplished in this world, for that evil-souled enemy, an inconceivable thorn in the side of the universe, has been slain.
Indeed, fame has been established throughout the worlds; yet, O Mother of renowned power, you must still exercise compassion and protect us as well.
Vyāsa said: Thus praised by the gods, the Goddess spoke to them in a gentle voice:
"O best of gods, tell me of any other task that is difficult to accomplish."
Whenever the gods have a task that is exceedingly difficult to accomplish, I should be remembered then; I shall swiftly destroy their calamity.
The gods said:
"O Goddess, everything has been accomplished by you; indeed, our task is now complete, since this enemy of ours, Mahiṣāsura, has been slain. (36)
O Mother, act in such a way that we may always remember Your lotus feet; O Mother of the World, grant us also unwavering devotion unto You. (37)
"Knowing that she always forgives thousands of offenses like a mother, why do people not worship her, the source of the universe? (38)
There are two birds in this body, and between them there is constant friendship;
indeed, there is no third friend who could endure their transgression. (39)
Therefore, what indeed will that evil-souled and unfortunate Jīva do after abandoning you, his friend, among the wombs of gods and humans? (40)
Having obtained this body so difficult to attain, that lowest of men who does not remember you—we speak the truth again and again—with mind, deed, and speech. (41)
Whether in happiness or in sorrow, you are our wonderful refuge;
O Goddess, protect us constantly with all your excellent weapons. 42.
"Otherwise, there is no refuge other than the dust of your lotus feet.
Vyāsa said: Thus praised by the gods, the Goddess vanished right there.
Seeing her emerge, the gods were filled with supreme wonder.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Consolation of the Goddess," in the fifth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 19.
The Description of the Earth’s Happiness Following the Slaying of Mahiṣa.
Janamejaya said:
"O Sage, having then witnessed that wonderful power..."
O best of the twice-born, there is no satiety for me as I listen to the nectar of your speech, born from the lotus of your mouth, which brings supreme peace to the world.
And when Bhavānī had vanished,
what did those gods, led by Indra,
say regarding the supremely purifying life-story of the Goddess?
It is indeed difficult for men of little merit to attain. || 2 ||

Who, having pierced the cavity of his ear with a sharp needle, does not attain satisfaction through this nectar of discourse— by drinking which one attains immortality, yet remains separated from it due to meager fortune?
Fie on those men who do not drink it with reverence! || 3 ||
The playful deeds of the Mother of the World,
which provide protection for gods and great sages,
and serve as a means for men to cross the ocean of worldly existence.
For how could those who are grateful ever abandon [you]? || 4 ||
It should always be drunk by the ears of those who are liberated, those who seek liberation, worldly beings, and those afflicted by disease.
Those who know the Vedas declare it to be the bestower of all goals.
Likewise, O Sage, it is especially for kings who are always devoted to virtue, wealth,
and pleasure that they drink from that [tree], since they are indeed liberated from it.
How is it that one who is devoid of these [qualities] should not drink from them? || 6 ||
Those who in a previous existence worshipped Bhavānī with *satkunda* flowers, campaka blossoms,
or leaves of the *bilva* tree, shall be endowed with enjoyments upon this earth.
Thus it is to be inferred that they become kings. || 7 ||
Those who, having obtained this human body in the land of Bhārata, are devoid of devotion and have not worshipped You,
are destitute of wealth and grain.
Afflicted by diseases and deprived of progeny. || 8 ||
They indeed wander perpetually as slaves, obedient servants who carry only burdens;
day and night they are intent on their own self-interest, never otherwise.
They do not even obtain enough to fill their bellies. || 9 ||
The blind, the mute, the deaf, the lame,
and those afflicted with leprosy who suffer on this earth—
for them, poets should employ inference.
Bhavānī was not constantly propitiated by them.

Those who are endowed with royal enjoyments and full of prosperity, being served by many people, or those who are seen possessed of great wealth—by these it must indeed be inferred that they have been honored by me. (11)
Therefore, O son of Satyavatī, having shown compassion, please narrate the supreme life-story of the Goddess; you are indeed merciful at this time. (12)
Having slain that wicked buffalo, where has that Mahālakṣmī gone—she who was praised and honored by the gods and who is born from the essence of all splendor? || 13 ||
"It has been told to you, O illustrious one: that Mistress of the World (Bhuvaneśvarī) has quickly vanished; she may be established either in heaven or in the world of mortals."
Has she gone to dissolution, or has she taken refuge right there in Vaikuṇṭha? Or is she on the Golden Mountain (Meru)? Tell me now according to the truth.
Vyāsa said: Previously, I described to you the enchanting Maṇidvīpa,
the place of sport always held as the supreme favorite of the Goddess.
There, Brahmā, Hari, and Sthāṇu assumed the state of women;
then, having regained their manhood once more, they performed their respective duties.
In the midst of the ocean of nectar, there is an exceedingly beautiful island;
there Ambikā always sports in various forms.
Praised and worshipped by the gods, that auspicious Śivā went right there,
to where the eternal power of Māyā constantly sports.
Seeing that goddess, the sovereign of all, thus departed,
the gods established a mighty protector of the earth born of the solar dynasty.
[He installed] the heroic lord of Ayodhyā, the king named Śatrughna,
who was endowed with all auspicious marks, upon the splendid throne of Mahiṣa.
Having then bestowed the kingdom upon him, all the gods, led by Indra, departed for their own abodes on their respective vehicles.
O lord of the earth, when those gods had departed, thereupon a kingdom of righteousness prevailed upon the earth and the subjects were likewise made happy.
Parjanya poured rain at the proper time, the earth was covered with the excellence of grain, and the trees, rich in fruits and flowers, were always a source of happiness. (24)
And there were cows abundant in milk, yielding pots of it and granting the desires of men;
and there were rivers flowing on excellent paths, clear, cool, and filled with birds. || 25 ||
The Brāhmaṇas were knowers of the true essence of the Vedas and likewise devoted to the performance of sacrifices;
the Kṣatriyas were endowed with righteousness and intent upon charity and study. || 26 ||
All the kings were constantly devoted to the science of weaponry, intent on protecting their subjects, dispensing justice through lawful punishment, and endowed with tranquility. || 27 ||
Indeed, there was no conflict among any living beings;
the mines yielded wealth for men, and the cow-pens were filled with herds of cattle. (28)
O best of kings, on the surface of the earth, all—the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—became entirely devoted to the Goddess. (29)
Everywhere there were sacrificial posts and enchanting pavilions;
the earth was filled with sacrifices performed by Brahmins and Kṣatriyas. (30)
The women were devoted to their husbands, possessed of good character, and endowed with truthfulness;
the sons were intent on devotion to their fathers and dedicated to righteousness. || 31 ||
Neither heresy nor unrighteousness existed anywhere on the surface of the earth;
there were only the doctrines of the Vedas and the doctrines of the Śāstras, and no other doctrines whatsoever. (32)
There was no quarreling among anyone, nor any wretchedness or unwholesome thought;
everywhere people were happy, and likewise, death occurred only at the proper time. (33)
There shall never be separation from friends nor any calamity;
there shall be no drought, no famine, and no plague that brings suffering to men.
There was neither disease nor stinginess, nor mutual hostility;
everywhere men and women were endowed with happiness and possessed of well-being. (35)
All the people played there like hosts of gods in heaven;
there were no thieves, no heretics, no deceivers, nor any hypocrites. (36)
O King, lord of the earth, at that time there were no backbiters, no lechers, and no arrogant men;
nor were there any sinful people who hated the Vedas.
Always delighting in all dharmas and devoted to the service of the twice-born, the Brāhmaṇas are therefore threefold, according to the threefold nature of the dharma of creation. (38)
There were those of a sattvic nature, those of a rājasic nature, and others who were tāmasa;
all were knowers of the Vedas and skillful, yet the sāttvikas were characterized by the quality of purity (sattva).
Free from accepting gifts and devoted to compassion and self-restraint,
they perform sacrifices with food characterized by *sattva*, being intent upon righteousness.
Neither by means of sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) nor by animal sacrifices at any time [is merit gained], but rather through giving, study, and thirdly, performing sacrifice itself. (41)
O King, those Brāhmaṇas who delight in the three types of ritual acts are indeed Sāttvika;
those who are Rājasa are learned in the Vedas and serve as priests for the Kṣatriyas.

All were devoted to the six duties and ate meat according to the prescribed rules; [they practiced] sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, giving gifts, and likewise receiving them. (43)

Furthermore, the study of the Vedas and likewise their teaching— these six [occupations] belong to those who are characterized by darkness (tamas), joined with anger, and devoted to passion and hatred.
The servants of kings were always devoted to some study;
when Mahiṣa was slain, they all became happy and intent upon the Vedas. (45)
The Kṣatriyas were devoted to their vows and intent upon the duty of giving; they were engaged in protection, while the Vaiśyas followed the occupation of trade. (46)
Others followed the livelihoods of agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and usury;
thus the world rejoiced when Mahiṣa was struck down.
Indeed, there was no distress among the subjects and wealth arrived in abundance;
the cows yielded much milk and were auspicious, and the rivers likewise possessed abundant water. 48.
The trees bore abundant fruit, and the people were free from disease; there were no mental anxieties nor any deceivers anywhere to bring suffering to the subjects. (49)

Those living beings who are devoted to the dharma ordained by the Vedas and whose minds are fixed on serving the lotus feet of Caṇḍikā do not meet their end prematurely; they remain forever endowed with all prosperity and free from disease.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Earth’s Happiness Following the Slaying of Mahiṣa," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Conquest of Heaven by means of Śumbha and Niśumbha.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall recount the supreme life-story of the Goddess.
It bestows happiness upon all living beings and destroys all sins. || 1 ||
Just as Śumbha and Niśumbha, those two exceedingly powerful brothers,
were great heroes who were indeed said to be incapable of being slain by any men.
Surrounded by vast armies, those two heroes were constant sources of suffering for the gods;
they were of wicked conduct, intoxicated with pride, and accompanied by many dānavas. || 3 ||
Indeed, those two were slain by Ambikā in an exceedingly terrible battle,
for the sake of the welfare of the gods, along with all their attendants.
The mighty-armed Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, the exceedingly cruel Raktabīja,
and the one named Dhūmralocana— all these were slain upon the field of battle.
Having slain them, she removed the supreme fear of the gods;
she was praised and worshipped by the deities on the auspicious Hemācala mountain.
The king said:
Who were these two Asuras in the beginning, and how did they become the foremost among the strong?
By whom were they established here, and why did they come to be slain by women?
By what asceticism and by the granting of what boon were these two of great strength born? And how were they slain? Tell us everything in detail.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, to this divine story which destroys all sins,
which is joined with the life-story of the Goddess, and which is auspicious and bestows the fruit of all goals.
Formerly, two asuras named Śumbha and Niśumbha, brothers of auspicious appearance, arrived from the netherworld upon the surface of the earth. (10)
Having reached the prime of youth, they both performed supreme austerity at Puṣkara, the purifier of the world, having renounced food and water.
For ten thousand years, devoted solely to the science of yoga,
they performed supreme austerity, remaining seated together in one place.
Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, was pleased with the two of them;
and the Blessed One arrived there, having mounted his swan-king.
And the Creator of the World, seeing both of them absorbed in meditation, said:
"Arise, O highly fortunate ones; I am indeed pleased with your austerity."
"I grant you both your desired boon and wish; speak here!
Having seen the power of your asceticism, I, the granter of desires, have arrived. (15)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, the two of them became enlightened and composed;
they then performed a circumambulation and offered their salutations.
Having prostrated themselves like a staff, those two of feeble appearance, being distressed, spoke sweet words with voices faltering from emotion. (17)
O God of gods, ocean of compassion, bestower of fearlessness upon devotees;
O Lord Brahmā, if you are pleased with us, O All-pervading One, grant us immortality.
There is no fear whatsoever on the surface of the earth greater than death;
terrified by that very fear, we have come to you for refuge. (19)
Save us, O Lord of the gods of gods, Creator of the world, Treasure of Forgiveness!
O Soul of the Universe, instantly dispel the fear born of death. (20)
Brahmā said:
What is this that you seek to request? It is entirely contrary [to what should be asked]. It is something that cannot be given by anyone to anyone at all in the three worlds.
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain.
Indeed, this boundary was established in the world of old by the Creator of the Universe.
"All living beings must die in every way; there is no doubt about this.
Ask for another desire, and I shall grant whatever you wish. (23)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words and having reflected deeply upon them, the two Dānavas then prostrated themselves and spoke to Brahmā, who stood before them.
O ocean of compassion, grant us our desired boon: invincibility against men, gods and others, humans, beasts, and birds. (25)
"Which powerful woman is there who will bring about our destruction?
You need not fear women at all, even in the three worlds with all that is mobile and immobile. (26)
"O Lotus-born One, the two brothers shall be invulnerable to men;
nor shall they have fear from women, for by their very nature, she is weak. (27)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard their words, Brahmā, with a gracious mind, granted the desired boon and then departed for his own abode.
Then, having departed from that abode, the two Dānavas went to their own home;
having appointed Bhṛgu as their domestic priest, they then performed worship.
On an auspicious day and under a favorable constellation, the sage fashioned a divine and beautiful throne made of gold and bestowed it for the sake of his sovereignty.
He gave the auspicious royal throne to Śumbha, who was the eldest;
at that very moment, the best of the Dānavas quickly arrived to serve him.
The two great heroes, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, brothers proud of their strength,
arrived accompanied by an army and provided with chariots, horses, and elephants.
And one named Dhūmralocana, possessing that same form and fierce prowess,
having heard of King Śumbha, then arrived accompanied by his forces.
Likewise, the heroic Raktabīja, empowered by the strength of a boon,
arrived at that very place accompanied by two akṣauhiṇīs and joined the fray.
O King, there is one cause for this for him who always fights in battle:
the flow of blood from his body when he is struck by weapons. (35)
And when such cruel men, numerous and with weapons in their hands, are born and arise repeatedly upon the earth. || 36 ||
Men born from blood arise with those very forms, those same appearances, and those same prowess; furthermore, they engage in battle. (37)
Therefore, that great Asura Raktabīja, possessed of immense prowess, was exceedingly difficult to conquer in battle and was incapable of being slain by any living beings.
And many other heroes, endowed with the fourfold army, considering Śumbha to be a king, became his servants. (39)
At that time, an innumerable army arose for Śumbha and Niśumbha;
by their great strength, the entire kingdom of the earth was seized. (40)
Then, having formed his military array, Niśumbha, the slayer of enemy heroes,
went swiftly to heaven in order to conquer the Lord of Śacī.
He waged a great battle with the world-protectors on all sides;
Vṛtrahā struck him in the chest with the fall of his thunderbolt.
Struck by the vajra, that younger brother of the Dānavas fell to the ground;
then the army of that great-souled Niśumbha was broken.
Hearing that his brother had fainted, Śumbha, the crusher of enemy forces,
arrived there and struck all the gods with arrows.
A great battle was fought with that Śumbha of unwearied deeds;
indeed, all the gods, including Indra, and all the guardians were utterly defeated. (45)
Then, by virtue of his great strength, he seized that station of Indra,
which was endowed with the wish-fulfilling tree and accompanied by the cow of plenty.
The three worlds and the sacrificial portions were seized by that great-souled one;
having reached the Nandana grove, the great asura became joyful.
By drinking the nectar, the great Asura attained happiness;
having conquered Kubera, he indeed ruled over his kingdom.
Likewise, he established his authority over the sun and the moon;
and having utterly defeated Yama, he seized that very office as well.
Likewise, Niśumbha, endowed with his own strength, exercised the sovereignty of Varuṇa and performed the duties of Agni; he also carried out the work of Vāyu.
Then the gods, shaken off, deprived of their kingdom, and robbed of their splendor,
all abandoned the Nandana grove and departed for the mountain caves.
Deprived of their authority, they all wandered through the lonely forest—
unsupported, without refuge, lusterless, and weaponless.
All the immortal gods, the ministers, and [the hosts] were in the caves of the mountains,
in empty gardens, and in the deep recesses of the rivers.
Deprived of their positions and deprived of their senses, O Great King, those guardians of the world found no happiness at all; for indeed, happiness is subject to destiny.
O lord of men, those who are powerful, highly fortunate, possessed of great knowledge, and endowed with wealth,
nevertheless encounter suffering and wretchedness in due course of time.
This is a marvel, O Great King, the very working of Time itself, which makes a man first a king and then a beggar. (56)
Whether it be a donor or a beggar, one who is strong or likewise weak, a wise man or one who is disabled, a lustful person or even one who is exceedingly timid; (57)
Having performed a hundred sacrifices and attained the supreme throne of Indra, he again encountered the greatest suffering; such is the course of Time.
Time makes a man most righteous and endowed with knowledge;
it makes that very same person exceedingly wicked and utterly devoid of even a trace of knowledge.
One should not feel astonishment in any way regarding the workings of Time;
even for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others, such miserable conduct occurs.
Viṣṇu undergoes birth in wombs such as that of a boar,
and Hara becomes a skull-bearer (Kapālī) solely through the power of time.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Victory over Heaven by Means of Śumbha and Niśumbha," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Goddess’s worship performed by the gods.
Vyāsa said:
All the gods were defeated, and Śumbha ruled the kingdom.
In this manner, O best of kings, a thousand years passed by.
Then the gods, having been deprived of their kingdom, fell into an insurmountable anxiety;
afflicted by grief, they respectfully questioned their preceptor as follows. (2)
"O Guru, tell me what must be done; you are the omniscient Great Sage.
O Illustrious One, there is a means for the cessation of suffering. (3)
Surely the thousands of Vedic mantras are devoted to ritual application;
indeed, they are said to be characterized by the Sūtras as the means for accomplishing desired goals.
Various sacrifices have been proclaimed that bestow the fruits of all desires;
perform them indeed, O sage, for you know their ritual procedures.
Perform today, according to the prescribed rites, that method for the destruction of the enemy as taught in the authentic scriptures, so that our suffering may come to an end.
O descendant of Aṅgiras, you ought to act this very day in such a way that,
according to your wisdom, there may be a rite of exorcism for the destruction of the Dānavas.
Bṛhaspati said: "O Lord of the Gods, all mantras declared in the Vedas have their fruits dependent upon destiny;
they are not independent, nor do they bestow results with absolute certainty. (8)
You are the deities of the mantras, yet you have become the sole vessel for suffering; born as we are through the power of time, what can I do to bring about our deliverance? (9)
In sacrificial rites, Indra, Agni, Varuṇa, and the others are worshipped;
having fallen into calamity, what will you offer-sacrificers do for them? (10)
There is no remedy for events that are destined to happen;
however, one must employ the appropriate means—this is the instruction of the learned.
For some wise men proclaim that destiny is powerful;
those who advocate for means, however, declare destiny to be useless.
Fate and human effort—these two alone are considered the means for men;
one should never remain relying solely upon fate. (13)
Therefore, having reflected again and again with your own intellect, you must devise a means in every way;
for this reason, I speak to you all after having deliberated repeatedly.
Formerly, the Blessed Lady, being pleased, slew the demon Mahiṣāsura;
then, praised by you, the Goddess granted a boon.
"Whenever you encounter calamities arising from fate, O lords of gods, remember me always; for when remembered, I shall surely destroy your misfortune. (16)
"Then, when you wish, I may certainly be remembered by the gods at all times;
being remembered, I shall destroy your greatest calamities. (17)
Therefore, having gone to the most beautiful Himācala mountain,
perform the propitiation of Caṇḍikā with love.
"Those who know the ritual procedures for the seed-syllable of Māyā and are devoted to its preparatory rites—I know through the power of yoga that she will become well-disposed. (19)
"The end of your suffering is seen today; there is no doubt about this.
I have heard that the Goddess always resides upon that mountain. (20)
"Once praised and fully worshipped, she will immediately grant your desired objects. Having made this firm resolve, go indeed to the Himalayas. (21)
"O gods, she will perform all your tasks according to your desire.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, those gods departed for the mountain.
O Great King, all of them remained intent on meditating upon the Goddess in the Himalayas,
constantly chanting the seed-syllable of Māyā with their hearts.
They paid homage to Mahāmāyā, the bestower of fearlessness upon her devotees; filled with supreme devotion, they praised her with hymns and mantras.
Salutations to the Goddess, Sovereign of the Universe, the Mistress of Life, whose form is eternal bliss, who bestows joy upon the gods;
salutations to her who brings an end to the Dānavas, who grants manifold goals to human beings, and whose true nature is accessible through devotion.
Neither can your names nor your form be numbered; no one at all knows such a form as yours, O Goddess who is the very nature of the Vedas.
You alone exist in all things as the embodiment of power (śakti), eternally present at the times of the creation and dissolution of all beings.
You are mindfulness, you are fortitude, and you alone are intelligence; you are old age, nourishment, contentment, steadfastness, splendor, and peace.
You are true knowledge, true prosperity, the goal, fame, and wisdom; you alone are the ancient seed of the universe. (27)
We bow today for the sake of peace to those very forms by which you perform the work of the gods here;
you are forgiveness, yogic sleep, compassion, and eloquence.
She abides within all beings through her auspicious forms. || 28 ||
O Goddess, you have already accomplished the task for the gods at the outset,
for that great enemy, the horse-slayer blinded by pride, has been slain;
you always possess compassion toward all the deities.
The Gītā is well-known in the Purāṇas and the Vedas. || 29 ||
What is there surprising in this, that a mother should joyfully protect and properly nourish her own son,
since you are the progenitor and the helper of the gods?
Perform the entire task with a one-pointed mind. || 30 ||
O Goddess, worshipped by the universe, we do not know the extent or the true nature of your virtues;
yet, considering us merely as objects of your compassion, protect us always from all fears, for you are capable of protecting us. (31)

Though you are capable of slaying enemies even without the discharge of arrows, without blows from fists, without spears or swords, and without pikes or clubs, nevertheless, this playful sport here is for the benefit of the world.
Fools do not know this eternal truth:
that no effect can possibly exist without a cause;
we consider inference to be the valid means of knowledge.
And you alone are the creator of this entire universe. || 33 ||
Aja is the creator, Mukunda is the protector,
and Hara is indeed the destroyer; these three are well-known in the Purāṇas as having been born from you at the beginning of the Yuga.
You alone belong to everyone; for that very reason, you are the Mother.
O Goddess, you were propitiated by the three [gods] in ancient times, and by you the entire fierce power was bestowed upon them;
united with you, they accomplish every desire.
[He performs] the very act of the protection, creation, and destruction of the world. || 35 ||

Are those ascetics not of dull intellect and utterly deluded, who do not take refuge in you—the Mother of the Universe, that supreme knowledge which bestows the fruit of all desires, grants liberation, and whose feet are beautifully praised by the hosts of the wise? (36)
Those who are Vaiṣṇavas, Pāśupatas,
and Sauras surely appear to be hypocrites;
they do not meditate upon you, nor upon Lakṣmī, nor upon Modesty.
Beauty, stability, fame, and even nourishment. || 37 ||
You are served here by Hari, Hara, and others, as well as by the best of gods and the asuras;
yet those men of meager intellect do not worship you on earth.
O Mother, we have indeed been deceived by fate. || 38 ||
Hari himself colors the lotus at the foot of the ocean-born goddess with liquid lac;
even the three-eyed Shiva is intent upon serving the pollen of the tree born from the mountain. (39)

What need is there for the stories of other men? Who does not worship the pair of your lotus feet? Even sages who have abandoned passion and home, whose intellects are perfected, worship you with compassion and patience.
O Goddess, those people who do not delight in worshiping Your feet have indeed fallen into the pit of saṃsāra;
they become afflicted with leprosy, abdominal tumors, headaches, and other ailments.
They were accompanied by the wretchedness of poverty and deprived of floods of happiness. || 41 ||
Those who are skilled in the tasks of carrying loads of wood or gathering fodder, yet are destitute of wealth and wives—
we consider their service to Your feet to be performed by those of small intellect.
In previous births, O Mother, they never once performed [these acts]. || 42 ||
Vyāsa said: Thus praised by all the gods, Ambikā, filled with compassion,
suddenly manifested herself, endowed with beauty and youth.
The goddess wore celestial garments, was adorned with celestial ornaments, was endowed with celestial garlands, and was anointed with celestial sandalwood paste. || 44 ||
Possessing the loveliness that deludes the world and endowed with all auspicious marks, she of peerless form came into the sight of the gods. 45.
Desirous of bathing in the Jāhnavī, that goddess, possessing a divine form and enchanting the entire universe with her beauty, emerged from the mountain cave. (46)
Smiling with affection, she whose voice was as sweet as a cuckoo’s spoke to the gods, who were intent on praising her, in a voice as deep as a thundercloud. (47)
The Goddess said:
"O, O best of gods, who is it that is being praised by you here so intensely?
For what purpose? Tell me your business; why, moreover, are you overcome with anxiety?"
Vyāsa said:
Having heard her speech and being infatuated by the perfection of her beauty,
those best of gods, their hearts filled with enthusiasm born of love, spoke to her.
The gods said:
O Goddess, Sovereign of the Universe, we praise you; prostrated before you, O ocean of compassion, protect us from all miseries—we who are agitated and tormented by the Daityas. (50)
"O Great Goddess, in the past, after you had slain the thorn in our side, Mahiṣa the Asura, you granted us this boon: 'I am to be remembered always in times of distress.'"
"By remembering you, I shall undoubtedly destroy the suffering born of the Daityas;
therefore, O Goddess, you have surely been remembered by us. (52)
Today two asuras of terrible appearance, Śumbha and Niśumbha, have arisen; they are indeed creators of obstacles who cannot be slain by men. (53)
Raktabīja was powerful, as were the two asuras Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa;
by these and other beings of great strength, the kingdom of the gods was seized. (54)
"O lady of beautiful waist, we have no other recourse; you alone are our refuge, O one of great power! Indeed, perform the task for the sake of the suffering gods. (55)
The gods are ever intent upon devotion to your feet; they have been brought to calamity by the exceedingly powerful Dānavas.
O Goddess, make them free from suffering, for you alone, O Mother, are the refuge for those who are afflicted. (56)
O Goddess, you must now perform the protection of the entire world, knowing that this universe was created by you at the beginning of the age;
O Mother, the Dānavas, filled with pride, are causing affliction in the world.
O Mother, filled with the intoxication of their own strength, they act thus. || 57 ||

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of the Goddess Performed by the Gods," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 22 ||
Vyāsa said: Thus was the Goddess then praised by the deities who were tormented by their enemies, as she spoke of her own vow to Sugrīva, the messenger.
He caused a supreme form to manifest from his own body.
When Ambikā indeed emerged from the body of Pārvatī,
she was thereafter celebrated in all the worlds as Kauśikī.
When she had emerged, Pārvatī, through the exchange of bodies, then became black in form; she is celebrated as Kālikā.
Dark as ink, most terrible, and increasing the fear of the Daityas, she is called Kālarātri; she is the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
The supreme form of Ambikā shone forth, captivating the mind,
endowed with every ornament and possessed of the quality of exquisite beauty.
Then Ambikā, smiling, spoke thus to the gods:
"Remain here free from fear; I shall slay the enemies."
Your task must be accomplished by all means; I shall range through the battlefield and slay Niśumbha and the others for the sake of your happiness.
Having spoken thus, that goddess, mounted upon a lion and fierce with passion,
placed Kālikā at her side and went to the city of the enemy.
Having gone there, Ambikā stood in the grove accompanied by Kālikā;
then she sang there in a sweet tone that which deludes even the Deluder of the World.
Hearing that sweet song, the birds and deer fell into a state of enchantment,
while the gods stationed in the sky attained the highest joy.
At that moment, two terrible Dānavas named Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, servants of Śumbha, were sporting there at their own pleasure.
Upon their arrival, they then beheld Ambikā, who possessed a divine form, standing before them as Kālikā accompanied by song.
O best of kings, having seen her of divine form, the two Dānavas were filled with wonder and quickly went to the side of Śumbha.
Having gone to his palace, they approached that lord of the Daityas as he sat there,
and bowing their heads to the king, they addressed him with sweet words.
O King, from the Himalayas, a beautiful woman, enchanting with desire and endowed with all auspicious marks, has arrived mounted upon a lion. 15.
"Such a supreme woman has never been seen nor heard of anywhere on earth, neither in the world of the gods nor in the city of the Gandharvas. (16)
O King, he performs such singing that delights the people;
even the deer stand by his side, enchanted by his sweet voice. (17)
"Let it be known whose daughter she is and for what purpose she has come here;
let her be taken, O tiger among kings, for she is a woman worthy of you. (18)
"Having learned of her, bring that lady of auspicious eyes to our home and take her as your wife;
for it is certain that there is truly no woman of such a kind in this world. (19)
"O King, you have taken all the jewels of the gods;
why then, O best of kings, do you not accept this woman of beautiful limbs? (20)
O King, it is said that you forcibly seized Indra’s majestic elephant Airāvata, the Pārijāta tree, and the horse with seven mouths.
O King, by that power you have seized that divine celestial chariot of Brahmā, adorned with a swan-banner, which is like a jewel and truly marvelous.
O King, the lotus-treasure of Kubera was seized by you, and that bright umbrella of the Lord of Waters was taken by you by force. (23)
Moreover, O best of kings, the noose belonging to Varuṇa, who was conquered by force, has also been seized by your brother Niśumbha at his will. (24)
The ocean gave you a garland of unfading lotuses, O Great King, as well as various jewels out of fear of you. (25)
The power of Death and even the most terrible staff of Yama have been conquered and taken away by you at will; O King, what more can be described? (26)
O King, the wish-fulfilling cow born from the ocean is now held by you;
likewise, Menakā and the other celestial nymphs remain under your control. (27)
"In this way, you have seized all these jewels even by force; why then is this excellent woman, a jewel from the wilderness, not taken? (28)
Furthermore, O Lord of the Earth, all those pure treasures found in households shall arise from her as she becomes a treasure herself. (29)
"O Lord of Daityas, no such beloved woman exists in the three worlds;
therefore, bring her quickly and make that captivating woman your wife. (30)
Vyāsa said: Having heard their words, which were sweet and composed of sweet syllables, he,
with a serene countenance, spoke to Sugrīva who was standing nearby.
"Go, Sugrīva, and perform the duty of a messenger; O wise one, you must speak there in such a way that the slender-waisted lady comes to us. (32)
"Those who are experts in the aesthetic flavor of love (śṛṅgāra-rasa) say that two means should be employed by those who are well-discerning toward beloved women: conciliation and generosity. (33)
Even when a deviation (bheda) is employed, a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa) arises;
however, in the case of suppression (nigraha), there is a disruption of rasa (rasabhaṅga). Therefore, those two have been condemned by the wise. (34)
O messenger, what woman, when afflicted by desire, does not come under control through words characterized by conciliation and generosity, as well as gentle speech mixed with jest? (35)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words spoken by Śumbha, which were very pleasing and eloquent, Sugrīva went swiftly to that place where the Mother of the World resides.
He beheld the lovely Sumukhī seated upon the lion;
having bowed down, he addressed these sweet words to the Mother of the World: || 37 ||
The messenger said:
"O lady of beautiful thighs, Śumbha—the enemy of the gods, handsome in every limb, the lord of the three worlds, a hero, and a conqueror of all—shines as king. (38)
Therefore, I have been sent at will to your presence by that high-souled one, whose mind is intensely distressed and deeply attached to hearing reports of your beauty. (39)
O slender-limbed one, listen to his words preceded by love, just as the lord of the Daityas spoke to you after prostrating himself. (40)
"All the gods have been conquered by me; I am the sovereign of the three worlds.
O beloved, standing here, I always receive the portions of the sacrifice. (41)
"Surely the sky has been stripped of its essence by me and rendered devoid of jewels;
for whatever jewels belonged to the gods, those I have carried away. (42)
"O beautiful lady, I am the enjoyer of all jewels in the three worlds;
all the gods, as well as the Daityas and humans, are under my control. (43)
Having reached Karna through your virtues and entered the interior of his heart, you have made him entirely subject to you; I am but a servant at your disposal—what shall I do? 44.
"Command me, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks; I am your obedient servant.
I am your slave, O fair-limbed one; protect me from the arrows of Love. (45)
"O lotus-eyed one, resort to me, for I am agitated by passion and dependent upon you;
having become the mistress of the three worlds, enjoy unsurpassed pleasures. (46)
"O beloved, I shall be your servant until death;
O lady of noble hips, I am inviolable by gods, asuras, and humans alike. (47)
O fair-faced one, you shall always be endowed with good fortune;
O beautiful lady, sport wherever your heart finds delight. 48.
Having reflected upon these words in her heart, O you who are slow with passion, speak those sweet words that ought to be spoken out of love. (49)
"O lady with tremulous eyes, I shall tell that to Śumbha immediately.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the messenger, she smiled very charmingly.
The goddess, who accomplishes the purpose of the gods, spoke these sweet words to him.
The goddess said:
"I know Niśumbha and the exceedingly powerful King Śumbha. (51)
The conqueror of all gods and the slayer of enemies, the mass of all virtues and the enjoyer of all prosperity. || 52 ||
A donor, exceedingly brave, handsome, with the form of the god of love, endowed with the thirty-two marks, and incapable of being slain by gods or men. || 53 ||
Having learned this, I have come here desiring to see the great Asura;
for even gold comes to a jewel to increase its own luster through the jewel's superior splendor.
I have indeed come from afar to see my own husband there;
I have seen all the gods and the men on earth who bestow honor.
The Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, and others who were exceedingly handsome—all were terrified by the fear of Śumbha, trembling and deprived of their senses. || 56 ||
"Having heard of Śumbha's virtues here, I have come today with the desire to see him. Go, O illustrious messenger, and speak to the mighty Śumbha."
In a secluded place, with gentle speech, speak these words according to my instruction:
"Knowing you to be the best among the strong and the most beautiful among the handsome. (58)
A donor, virtuous, heroic, and proficient in all branches of knowledge;
a conqueror of all the gods, skillful, fierce, and preeminent in his lineage. (59)
O lord of men, I am truly desirous of you as my husband—you who enjoy all jewels, who are self-dependent, and exalted by your own power; I am worthy of you.
O high-minded one, O best of Rākṣasas, they have come here to this city of their own free will; however, I have a certain purpose regarding my marriage.
O King, in my childhood, while playing with my companions in a secluded place by chance, I once observed a certain vow. (62)
Out of pride in the strength of his own body, he said in private before his friends:
"A hero with strength equal to mine will clearly defeat me in battle. (63)
"Having ascertained his strength and weakness, I shall choose that desire.
Upon hearing these words, her friends laughed, their minds filled with astonishment. (64)
What cruel and wonderful vow has she indeed performed so swiftly?
Therefore, O Indra among kings, having recognized such power as mine, you too— (65)
"Having conquered me here by your own strength, do as you desire for yourself.
Either you or your younger brother, having come together onto the field of battle and conquered me in combat here, perform the marriage, O handsome one. (66)

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Goddess’s Narration of Her Own Vow to the Messenger Sugrīva," in the fifth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
In the *Devīmāhātmya*, regarding the dispatching of the messenger Dhūmralocana to the presence of the Goddess,
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the Goddess, that messenger spoke, filled with wonder.
"What do you say, O lady of lovely eyes? For [this] is due to the rashness inherent in the nature of women. (1)
O Goddess, O beautiful lady, how can you wish to conquer in battle him by whom Indra and the other gods, as well as the Daityas and others, have been defeated?
"In the three worlds there is no one who could defeat Śumbha in battle;
who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, to stand before him now in combat? (3)
O beautiful one, one should not speak without having reflected;
rather, speech should be uttered only after assessing the strength of both oneself and the other, and in accordance with the occasion.
Śumbha, the lord of the three worlds, has been infatuated by your beauty;
the king entreats you, so fulfill his desire, my dear.
Abandoning your foolish nature and honoring my words, resort to either Śumbha or Niśumbha; I tell you this for your own benefit.
The erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) should be cultivated with supreme joy by all sentient beings in every way by those who are wise, since it is the most excellent among the nine [sentiments]. (7)
O foolish girl, if you do not come, the lord of the earth, being enraged,
will now send other obedient men by force to take you away.
O lady of beautiful thighs, those Dānavas, arrogant in their strength, will surely drag you by the hair and carry you with force into the presence of Śumbha.
"O slender-limbed one, preserve your own modesty; abandon all rashness.
Go to his side with honor, for you are indeed worthy of respect. (10)
Where is battle with sharpened arrows, and where is the pleasure born from sexual union?
Discerning the essential from the non-essential, follow my wise advice. (11)
"Worship either Śumbha or Niśumbha, and you shall obtain supreme happiness.
The Goddess said:
"O messenger, O illustrious one, it is true; you are indeed skilled in speaking. (12)
"I know for certain that Niśumbha and Śumbha are powerful;
how else could the vow I made in my youth remain unfulfilled? (13)
Therefore, tell me whether Niśumbha or Śumbha is the more powerful;
for without a battle, no one shall become my husband by virtue of his excellence alone.
"O King, having conquered me by force at will, take my hand now;
know me to be a woman who has come here with the desire for battle. (15)
Give battle, for you are capable; practice the duty of a hero!
If you fear my trident, go to the netherworld without delay.
"O messenger, go quickly and say with respect to your husband: 'Since you have abandoned both heaven and earth, yet still possess a desire for life... (17)
Having reflected, that one of great strength will act as is appropriate;
for in this cycle of existence, the duty of a messenger is indeed to speak the truth. (18)
"O knower of dharma, act accordingly toward both the enemy and your husband; do not delay.
Vyāsa said:
Then, having heard those words, which were full of wisdom and consistent with policy—
Then, filled with wonder, the messenger departed, eloquent and endowed with sound reasoning; having gone to the lord of the Daityas, he reflected upon the matter again and again. (20)
Bowing low at his feet, he addressed that king with words consistent with statecraft— gentle, pleasing, and full of courtesy.
The messenger said:
"One must speak what is both true and pleasant; for that reason, O Indra among kings, I am indeed lost in thought. Truly and pleasantly spoken words, it is said, are difficult to find. (22)
The king may indeed become angry in every way with those who speak unpleasantly;
but how could she have arrived here in person, or whose is she, and what is her strength or weakness? 23.
There is nothing within the range of my knowledge; what can I say of her conduct? I saw her desiring battle, arrogant, and speaking harshly.
O Mahāmati, listen well to what was said by her:
"In my childhood, this vow was previously made by me in jest. (25)
"In the presence of my friends, he has declared that in every way he will surely defeat me in battle regarding marriage and will truly humble my pride. (26)
"I shall choose that very Kāma as my husband, for he is indeed equal in power to me;
O best of kings, I must not make that promise false. (27)
"Therefore, O knower of dharma, fight; having conquered me, bring me under your control.
Having heard these words uttered by her, I approached. (28)
"O Great King, do as you wish for your own pleasure;
she has set her mind on battle, equipped with weapons, and moves with the gait of a lion. (29)
"O King, she remains steadfast; let whatever is appropriate be done.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Sugrīva, the lord of men [acted]. || 30 ||
He questioned his heroic brother, who was standing nearby and possessed of great strength.
Śumbha said:
"O brother, O high-minded one, tell me truly—what should be done here? (31)
"There is one noble woman here who desires to fight; she now challenges you.
Either I shall go into battle, or you, endowed with strength, may go. (32)
"Whatever pleases you here, Niśumbha, that must indeed be done by me.
Niśumbha said:
"O hero, neither I nor you shall go to the front of the battle. (33)
O Great King, dispatch Dhūmralocana with haste;
having gone there and conquered her in battle, let him bring back that woman of beautiful eyes. || 34 ||
"Śumbha will come here; let the wedding be prepared.
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words of his younger brother, Śumbha—
In anger, he dispatched Dhūmralocana, who was standing by his side.
Śumbha said: "O Dhūmralocana, go quickly, surrounded by a great army! (36)
"Seize that innocent woman, who is deluded by the pride of her own power, and bring her here—whether he be a god, a dānava, or a man of great strength. (37)
Having become his rear-guard, he must be slain by you with speed;
then, having killed Kālī who stands at his side, take her captive once again. (38)
"Come here quickly after having accomplished this unsurpassed task;
you must protect that virtuous woman while she releases her gentle arrows. (39)
O hero, with great effort, those soft-bodied ones with slender waists and their assistants who bear weapons in battle must be slain. (40)
"In every way she must not be killed; she must be protected with great effort.
Vyāsa said:
Having been thus commanded by the king, Dhūmralocana then departed with speed.
Having bowed to Śumbha, he quickly went forth to battle with his army,
surrounded by sixty thousand of those wicked ones.
Then he beheld the goddess seated in a lovely grove;
seeing her, whose eyes were like those of a young deer, he was filled with humility.
He spoke these gentle words, reasoned and adorned with elegance:
"Listen, O illustrious goddess; Śumbha is distressed by separation from you. (44)
An envoy skilled in statecraft was dispatched by him to your side; anxious for fear of breaking the flow of sentiment, he himself addressed you with conciliatory words. (45)
Having arrived, O lady of beautiful countenance, he spoke words that were contrary [to the truth];
by those words, my husband, the king, became possessed by anxiety of mind.
Śumbha, deluded by passion, became enamored of her who knew the ways of love;
yet that messenger did not understand your words, which were pregnant with reason.
"O proud lady, he who defeated me in battle and spoke those harsh words did not understand that battle is indeed of two kinds. (48)
The [laughter] arising from love and that arising from enthusiasm are intended according to the distinction of the recipient;
O fair-thighed one, yours is remembered as born of love, while that of the enemy is born of enthusiasm. (49)
"O beloved, the first [type] is known to grant happiness, while that born of an enemy is said to cause suffering.
O lady of beautiful hips, I truly know your heart's desire. (50)
"The state of passion for sexual union revolves within your heart.
Having thus recognized me as one who knows that, the lord of men [sent me] to your presence. (51)
Today Śumbha has dispatched you, surrounded by a great army;
O highly fortunate one, listen to my gentle words. (52)
Worship Śumbha, the lord of the three worlds and the destroyer of the pride of the gods;
becoming his beloved chief queen, enjoy unsurpassed pleasures. (53)
"The mighty-armed Śumbha, who knows the power of desire and its objects, will conquer you; display various gestures of allure, for he too will employ such expressions. (54)
"In this Kali age, she shall indeed be a witness to our jests;
thus, through the union of our agreement, my husband will come to know the supreme truth. (55)
Having conquered you, he will leave you exhausted upon his comfortable bed—your body smeared with blood from the wounds of his nails, and your lower lip bitten by his teeth. (56)
The king will restore you, who are broken and drenched in sweat;
your heart’s desire shall be fulfilled through the pleasure born of battle.
"O beloved, by the mere sight of you, Śumbha has come entirely under your power; therefore, follow my words, which are wholesome, beneficial, and pleasing. (58)
"O highly proud one, you who are worthy of honor, resort to Śumbha, the leader of the Gaṇas;
for those who are fond of combat with missiles are surely of meager fortune. (59)
O beloved, you who are ever fond of amorous play, it does not befit you to leave King Aśoka withered; rather, cause him to blossom by a kick from your foot. (60)
Likewise, cause the bakula and the kurabaka to bloom by sprinkling them with sidhu wine.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Dispatching of the Messenger Dhūmralocana to the Presence of the Goddess," in the Devīmāhātmya of the fifth book of the Śrīmaddevībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Regarding the dispatching of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa for battle with the Goddess,
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken these words, Dhūmralocana fell silent.
Then Kālī, smiling, replied with these charming words. || 1 ||
"You are a buffoon, you wretch; you speak like a stage actor.
You harbor vain desires in your mind while speaking so sweetly. (2)
Strong and endowed with power, you have been sent by that evil-minded one;
engage in battle now, O dull-witted one, and abandon your vain talk.
Having slain Śumbha and Niśumbha, or whoever else among them is more powerful,
the enraged Goddess will return to her own abode by means of the wounds inflicted by her arrows.
Where is that dull-witted Śumbha, and where is she who deludes the entire universe?
Indeed, the act of marriage between these two in this world is utterly improper.
Does a lioness, afflicted by excessive lust, make a jackal her husband? Or does a female elephant, or even a cow, do so with a donkey or a gayal? (6)
Go and speak these true words of mine to Śumbha and Niśumbha:
"Engage in battle; otherwise, depart for the netherworld immediately by force. (7)
Vyāsa said: Having heard the words of Kālikā, that Daitya Dhūmralocana,
his eyes bloodshot with rage, spoke to her, O highly fortunate one.
"Having slain you, who are difficult to behold, in battle, as well as the lion who is arrogant with pride, I shall indeed take her and go before the king every day. (9)
O Kali, I am now afraid of the destruction of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) here;
otherwise, O you who delight in quarreling, I shall slay you today with sharpened arrows.
Kālikā said:
"Why do you boast, O dull-witted one? This is not the way of archers.
Release your arrows according to your own power; you shall go to the assembly of Yama."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words, the Daitya took up his firm bow and rained down volleys of arrows, whetted as sharp as stone, upon that Kālikā.
But the gods, stationed there upon their excellent celestial chariots, with Śakra at their head, praised her and cried out "Victory! to the goddess. (13)
A most terrible battle ensued between the two of them,
fierce with arrows, swords, maces, spears, clubs, and other weapons.
Having first slain the donkeys with the discharge of her arrows, Kālikā shattered that arrayed chariot and laughed again and again.
And mounting another chariot, O Bhārata, he, as if blazing with rage, unleashed a fierce shower of arrows upon Kālikā.
She too swiftly cut down his unerring arrows, while Kālikā released other arrows of fierce velocity upon the Dānava.
By those arrows, his thousands of rear-guards were struck down;
and having slain the charioteer and the mules, he shattered the chariot with great force.
She immediately severed that bow with arrows resembling serpents;
she brought joy to the gods and likewise produced a sound like the blast of a conch shell.
Deprived of his chariot, the enraged Dhūmralocana seized a firm iron-bound mace and approached the seat of the chariot.
Rebuking Kālī with his voice, Karāla, who resembled Time itself, said:
"O you of ugly form and tawny eyes, I shall slay you this very day! (21)
Having spoken thus, when he suddenly approached and hurled his iron club,
Ambikā instantly reduced him to ashes by her mere roar of "Hum."
Seeing the Daitya reduced to ashes, the soldiers, overwhelmed with fear, immediately fled, crying out "Alas, O Father! along the way.
Seeing that Dānava Dhūmralocana slain, the gods,
standing joyfully in the sky, released a rain of flowers.
Then, O King, the battlefield became terrible with slain Dānavas, horses, donkeys, and likewise elephants.
Vultures, crows, ravens, hawks, cranes, and jackals danced and shrieked over the fallen spirits upon the battlefields. (26)
Ambikā, having abandoned that battlefield and gone a great distance to another place,
uttered a fierce blast upon her conch shell that struck fear into all.
Hearing that sound of fear while staying in his palace,
Śumbha then saw the Dānavas returning, broken and drenched in blood.
And those with hands and feet severed, even those placed upon stretchers,
with their backs, hips, and necks broken, crying out many times— (29).
Having observed this, Śumbha and Niśumbha asked, "Where has Dhūmralocana gone?
Why have they returned defeated? And why was that fair-faced woman not brought back? (30)
"O dull-witted ones, tell me where the army has gone;
who is this whose conch-blast is heard today, increasing our fear? (31)
The Gaṇas said:
"All the forces have been struck down and Dhūmralocana has been slain;
Kālikā has performed superhuman deeds upon the field of battle."
The sound of Ambikā’s conch resounded, pervading the sky;
it brought joy to the hosts of gods and caused grief among the Dānavas. || 33 ||
O Lord, when all [the enemies] had been struck down by that lion,
the chariots were shattered and the horses destroyed by the falling of his arrows.
Seeing the entire army shattered and Dhūmralocana struck down, the gods stationed in the sky, filled with joy, rained down a shower of flowers.
"We have reached the certainty that victory will not be ours;
O Indra among kings, deliberate with your ministers who are most skilled in counsel. (36)
This is a marvel, O Great King, that the Mother of the World, being alone and devoid of an army, stands ready for battle with you all. (37)
"A young woman, fearless and alone, mounted upon a lion and fierce with passion—this appears instantly as a wondrous and marvelous marvel, O Great King. (38)
O Great King, having deliberated upon peace, war, maintaining the status quo, or even retreat, perform your duty as you see fit. (39)
In his presence there is no strength; nevertheless, O scorcher of enemies, all the gods will surely become rear-enemies in times of distress.
At that time, Hari and Śaṅkara were known to be standing near him;
today the world-protectors remain present nearby, stationed in the sky. (41)
O scorcher of enemies, the hosts of rākṣasas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and likewise humans,
as well as their companions, are to be understood as being present at that time.
By our own intelligence, it is known in every way to be thus:
there is no hope for Ambikā’s assistance, nor any hope for that task to be accomplished. (43)
"One alone is capable of destroying the entire world, including all things moving and stationary;
what need is there to mention all the dānavas? This is certain. (44)
Knowing this, O illustrious one, act as you please;
followers should speak words that are beneficial, truthful, and measured. (45)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of theirs, Śumbha, the crusher of enemy forces,
summoned his younger brother and questioned him while staying in private.
"O brother, this very day Dhūmralocana has been slain by Kālikā;
his entire army has been destroyed, and the assembled hosts have been routed. (47)
Ambikā, intoxicated with pride, indeed utters the sound of a conch;
the course of time is in every way difficult to comprehend even for the wise.
Grass indeed acts like a thunderbolt, and a thunderbolt itself acts like grass;
the strong may become weak—such is the course of destiny.
I ask you, O illustrious one, what should be done hereafter? Ambikā is surely not to be enjoyed; she has come here for a certain reason.
"O hero, it is fitting that you either flee or speak quickly regarding battle;
for I know you to be swift when faced with a crisis of duty. (51)
Niśumbha said:
"O sinless one, neither flight nor taking refuge in a fortress is appropriate;
for you, O blameless one, fighting alone is in every way the highest good."
Accompanied by my army and relying upon my preeminent warriors, I shall go to battle;
having slain that woman, I will swiftly return with this [city] devoid of strength.
Or rather, if by the power of destiny it should turn out otherwise,
then after I have died, you must deliberate upon this again and again.
Having heard these words of his, Śumbha spoke to his younger brother:
"Stay here; let Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa both go forth accompanied by an army."
It is not appropriate to release the elephant here for the sake of catching a hare;
the two great heroes Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa are entirely capable of killing her.
Having spoken thus to his brother and addressed those two of great strength, King Śumbha spoke these words to Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, who stood before him.
"Go, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, both surrounded by your own armies, to quickly slay that shameless woman who is arrogant with pride. (58)
"Then, having seized and slain Kālikā, who has tawny eyes, in battle, come back, O highly fortunate ones, after having accomplished this most important task. (59)
If that Ambikā does not come even when seized, being full of pride,
then she must be slain with exceedingly sharp arrows upon the field of battle.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Dispatching of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa to Fight with the Goddess," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 25 ||
The description of the Goddess’s name as Cāmuṇḍā due to the slaying of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
Vyāsa said:
Thus commanded, the two heroes Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, who were possessed of great strength, [acted].
Accompanied by a great army, they both proceeded swiftly to the field of battle.
Seeing the goddess, who acts for the welfare of the gods, stationed there,
those two of great prowess then spoke words imbued with conciliation.
O foolish girl, do you not know Śumbha, the crusher of the hosts of gods, and Niśumbha, who possesses great heroism and is arrogant from his victory over Indra? 3.
"O lady of excellent limbs, you are alone, joined only by Kālikā and the lion;
yet, O evil-minded one, you wish to conquer Śumbha, who is endowed with all forces. (4)
There is no one, whether woman or man, who can grant you wisdom;
even the gods are merely inciting you toward your own destruction.
O slender-limbed one, reflect and then perform the task [of assessing] the strength of yourself and your opponent;
you vainly harbor pride because of your eighteen arms.
"What is the use of these many useless arms, or what is the use of weapons that only cause exhaustion, in the presence of Śumbha—the conqueror of the gods who is preeminent in battle? (7)
O you who severed the trunk of Airāvata and caused the destruction of elephants, O victor over the hosts of gods, accomplish the desire of our hearts. (8)
O beloved, you vainly indulge in pride; follow my pleasing words.
O large-eyed one, this is for your own benefit, bestowing happiness and destroying suffering.
Those who bring suffering must be abandoned from afar by the wise; those who bestow happiness should be cultivated by those proficient in the true principles of the scriptures. (10)
O cuckoo of fourfold speech, behold the great power of Śumbha, which brings immense glory through the crushing of the hosts of gods before their very eyes. (11)
Indeed, to abandon direct perception and rely on inference alone is futile;
a wise person does not engage in an action that is accompanied by doubt. (12)
"Śumbha is the supreme enemy of the gods, invincible in battle;
therefore, the gods, oppressed by the lord of the Daityas, urge you to come here. (13)
Therefore, O lady of pure smiles, you have been deceived by those affectionate words;
the gods' instruction, which was intended to accomplish their own purpose, has resulted in your sorrow. (14)
Having set aside a friend for worldly affairs, one should rely upon a friend of the Dharma.
The gods are intent on their own self-interest; I have spoken this truth to you. (15)
Worship Śumbha, the lord of the gods, the conqueror and sovereign of the worlds—
he who is clever, handsome, heroic, and an expert in the science of love.
By the command of Śumbha, you shall attain sovereignty over all the worlds.
Having made a firm resolve, serve your husband, who is excellent. || 17 ||
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Caṇḍa, the Mother of the World roared with a sound as deep as a thundercloud and spoke again.
"Go away, you wretch! Why do you speak such false and deceitful words?
Having abandoned Hari, Hara, and the others, why would I worship Śumbha as my husband? (19)
"I must not have any husband, nor should I have anything to do with a husband;
listen, for I alone am the mistress of all beings. (20)
Many Śumbhas have been seen by me, and Niśumbhas by the thousands;
hundreds of Daityas and Dānavas were previously slain by me. (21)
Before me, hosts of gods have perished age after age;
likewise, the multitudes of Daityas shall surely meet their destruction once again today.
"The very time that brings about the destruction of the Daityas has arrived here;
you are exerting yourself in vain for the protection of your own progeny. (23)
O high-minded one, engage in battle for the sake of upholding the dharma of heroes;
death is inevitable and difficult to avoid, but fame must be preserved by great souls. (24)
"What business do you have with Niśumbha and the evil-minded Śumbha?
Having attained the supreme dharma of heroes, go to heaven, the abode of the gods. (25)
Śumbha, Niśumbha, and all your other kinsmen here will now follow behind you as your attendants. (26)
"Today I shall gradually bring about the destruction of all the Daityas.
Cast off your despondency, O dull-witted one; engage in battle, O lord of people! (27)
"I shall now slay you, your brother, as well as Śumbha, Niśumbha, and Raktabīja who is intoxicated with pride. (28)
Having slain all other Dānavas on the field of battle, I shall go to my own place; stay or depart quickly.
"Take up your weapon, you who are nourished in vain! Now engage in battle with me! Why do you utter false words that are entirely pleasing only to cowards? (30)
Vyāsa said:
Thus incited by her, the two Daityas, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa,
filled with rage and proud of their strength, swiftly produced a terrible twang of their bowstrings.
She too sounded her conch, filling the ten directions;
and the powerful lion, becoming enraged, let out a roar.
At that sound, Śakra and the other immortals rejoiced,
as did the sages, yakṣas, gandharvas, siddhas, sādhyas, and kinnaras.
There, a fierce battle broke out between Caṇḍikā and Caṇḍa, terrifying the cowards, fought with arrows, swords, maces, and other weapons. (34)
The Goddess cut down the fierce, released arrows with her own sharp shafts;
she, in turn, discharged fierce arrows like venomous serpents.
Then, in that battle, the sky was covered with arrows,
like locusts appearing at the end of a cloud that portends fear for the farmers.
Even though he was shaven-headed, he fell swiftly upon the soldiers in battle;
enraged and exceedingly terrible, he indeed released a rain of arrows.
Seeing that great mass of arrows, Ambikā there became exceedingly enraged;
through her anger, her face became like a dark cloud. (38)
Then Kālī, whose eyes were like plantain flowers and who was frowning with a knitted brow,
swiftly emerged from the surface of her forehead.
Clad in tiger-skin garments, cruel, with an elephant-hide upper garment, wearing a garland of severed heads, terrible, and possessing a belly like that of a dried-up well. (40)
Holding a sword and a noose, she is exceedingly terrifying and inspires fear;
bearing a skull-topped staff, she is fierce like another Kālarātri.
With her wide face, repeatedly flicking her tongue,
she of the broad hips struck the demon soldiers with great force.
Having seized those great heroes with her hands, she, filled with fury,
cast the Daityas into her mouth and slowly crushed them with her teeth.
Seizing by the hand elephants equipped with bells, he placed them in his mouth;
having devoured them along with their riders in battle, he let out a loud, boisterous laugh.
In the same way, having cast down horses, camels, and charioteers together with their drivers into his mouth, he chews them most terrifyingly with his teeth.
Seeing the army being slaughtered, the two great asuras Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa covered the Goddess with an incessant shower of arrows.
Fierce as the shadow of the fierce-rayed sun, he violently hurled at the Goddess the discus—the weapon of the wielder of the discus—and roared again and again. (47)
Seeing him roaring and that Sudarśana discus, which was as radiant as the sun, Kālī severed that brilliantly shining weapon with a single arrow.
The fierce Caṇḍī struck him with sharp arrows whetted on stone;
severely afflicted by the goddess’s shafts, he fell unconscious upon the earth.
Seeing his brother fallen, Muṇḍa, afflicted by grief,
then rained down a shower of arrows upon Kālikā out of anger.
Caṇḍikā, by means of arrows released with force from her reed-stalk weapons, instantly reduced that most terrible shower of arrows discharged by Muṇḍa to pieces as small as sesame seeds.
He struck him again with a crescent-shaped arrow;
that one of great prowess fell upon the earth, deprived of his pride.
Then a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the host of Dānavas;
all the immortals, free from distress, rejoiced as they stood in the sky.
Recovering from his swoon, Caṇḍa seized a massive club and swiftly struck Kālikā on her right arm.
Having evaded that blow from the mace, Kālikā swiftly bound the great asura with a noose of arrows released through the power of a mantra.
Then, seeing his younger brother forcibly bound, Muṇḍa rose up and,
having equipped himself well, approached with a firm spear held in his hand.
Then, seeing the Dānava approaching, Kālī quickly and forcefully bound her second brother very tightly.
Seizing those two of great prowess, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, like two rabbits,
she approached Ambikā while letting out a massive laugh.
Having arrived, she then said to her: "O dear one, take these two animals;
they are two Dānavas, invincible in battle, brought here for the sake of the sacrifice of war."
Then, seeing those two brought before her like two wolves,
Ambikā Caṇḍikā spoke these words full of sweetness to Kālikā.
"Do not strike, do not release [your weapon], O four-armed one who delights in battle!
You must swiftly accomplish the task of the gods. (61)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of hers, Kālikā spoke to her again,
while the sacrifice of battle was highly renowned and the sacrificial post of the sword was firmly established.
"I shall perform a ritual slaughter so that no violence occurs," having said this, the goddess then [struck] the heads of those two with her sword. (63)
Kālī swiftly cut [them] apart and joyfully drank the blood;
seeing the two Daityas thus slain, Ambikā spoke with delight.
"The task of the gods has been accomplished by you; today I grant you an auspicious boon.
Since Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa have been slain by you, therefore, O Kālikā, your name shall become renowned upon the earth as Cāmuṇḍā. (65)

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Goddess’s Name as Cāmuṇḍā through the Slaying of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 26 ||
The Description of the Dialogue between Śumbha and Niśumbha in the Presence of the Goddess by Means of Raktabīja.
Vyāsa said:
Having seen those two Dānavas slain, the remaining soldiers...
Then, having fled from there, they all went toward the king. || 1 ||
Some with their limbs pierced by arrows, others likewise with their hands severed,
and with bodies streaming with blood, they advanced toward the city while wailing.
Having gone there, they all repeatedly raised a tumultuous cry toward the lord of the Daityas:
"Protect us! Protect us, O Great King! Kālikā is devouring us this very day! (3)
By her, the two great heroes Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, the tormentors of the gods, were slain;
all the soldiers were devoured, and we have been routed, overcome with fear.
O Lord, the battlefield was made terrifying by Kālikā through the fallen elephants,
heroic horses, and the Dāseraka foot-soldiers.
A canal was made that carried a flood of blood, with flesh for its mud,
hair for its moss, and adorned by the broken wheels of chariots.
Abounding with fish whose fins and tails are severed, and provided with heads and gourd-fruits,
she indeed brings fear to the timid while increasing the joy of the gods.
"Protect your family, O Great King; go quickly to Pātāla!
The enraged Goddess will bring about your destruction immediately; of this there is no doubt. (8)
O Lord of the Danujas, the lion also devours the Dānavas in battle;
likewise, the goddess Kālikā slays them in many ways with her arrows.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too, together with your brother Śumbha, have set your mind on death through falsehood, being of a provoked disposition.
What will this cruel woman do, this destroyer of her family, for whose sake, O Great King, you desire to slay your kinsmen? (11)
O Great King, victory and defeat in this world are dependent on destiny;
a wise man should not inflict great suffering for the sake of a small gain.
Behold the wondrous work of Fate, O Lord, upon which the entire world depends:
all the Rākṣasas have been slain by this one woman alone. 13.
"You are indeed the conqueror of the world-protectors, accompanied by your army at this very moment; yet a single young girl requests you for battle—how truly astonishing! (14)
Formerly, you performed austerities at Puṣkara, the abode of the gods;
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, arrived there to grant you a boon. || 15 ||
"O Great King of noble vows, you were told by Dhātṛ: 'Choose a boon.
At that time, it is said, you requested immortality from Brahmā. (16)
"May there be no death for me from gods, Daityas, or humans; nor from serpents, Kinnaras, or Yakṣas, nor even from any word denoting a masculine gender. (17)
Therefore, O Lord, this excellent woman has arrived desiring to kill you;
O Indra among kings, do not engage in battle, but reflect upon this now with your intellect. (18)
For this goddess is considered Mahāmāyā, the supreme Prakṛti;
O Indra among kings, at the time of the end of the kalpa, she is the bringer of universal destruction.
The auspicious Goddess, the sovereign of the gods and the progenitor of the worlds, possesses the three qualities; she is of the nature of *tamas* and is endowed with all powers. (20)
Invincible, imperishable, eternal, omniscient, and ever-arisen;
she is Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, the twilight prayer (sandhyā), and the abode of all the gods. || 21 ||
She is without attributes and yet possesses attributes; she is perfected, the bestower of all perfections, and imperishable.
She is Gaurī, who grants bliss to bliss itself and bestows fearlessness upon the gods.
Knowing this, O Great King, abandon your state of enmity toward her;
seek refuge, O Lord of Kings, and the Goddess will protect you. (23)
Become her obedient servant and restore your own lineage to life;
let those Daityas who remain after the slaughter become long-lived.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, Śumbha, the destroyer of the hosts of gods,
spoke these truthful words, which were endowed with the qualities of the best of heroes.
Śumbha said:
"O dull-witted ones, keep silent! You have been defeated on the field of battle.
Go quickly to the netherworld; the hope for life is very strong."
The entire world is subject to destiny; what concern is there for my victory? For even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, are just as subject to destiny as we are.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and this Rudra, as well as Yama, Agni, Varuṇa,
Sūrya, Candra, and Śakra— all these are indeed subject to the power of destiny.
What concern, then, is there for me, who am dull-witted? Whatever is to be, will be; let my effort be such as the destiny itself requires. (29)
Having investigated in every way, the wise never grieve;
the men of knowledge do not abandon their own duty here out of fear of death. (30)
Happiness, suffering, as well as the lifespan, life, and death of men—when the time has arrived, all these come about entirely as ordained by destiny. (31)
Brahmā falls at his own appointed time, as does Viṣṇu, the lord of Pārvatī;
at the end of their lifespan, all the gods, including Indra, go to destruction.
Likewise, I too am now entirely subject to the power of time;
through the fulfillment of my own duty, I shall go either to destruction or to victory.
"Even though I have been challenged by this weak woman for battle, how could I live for a hundred autumns as one intent on flight? (34)
Today I shall engage in battle; let whatever happens here happen—whether victory or death, I accept it however it may be.
"Those who speak of effort and know what has been said understand that the statement of the learned—that destiny is false—is consistent with reason. (36)
Without effort, desires are certainly not fulfilled;
only the faint-hearted prattle that "whatever is destined to be, will be. (37)
The foolish, not the wise, proclaim that the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is powerful; what proof is there for its existence? How can that which is unseen be seen? (38)
Even if the unseen were seen, it would still be this same terror of fools;
this is merely the mind's fixation on suffering without any basis.
Seated near the millstone, she remained there as a grinder of flour;
yet without exertion, flour can never be produced in any way whatsoever. (40)
When effort is exerted, a task invariably reaches completion;
however, if there is a deficiency in that effort, the task may not even come to fruition.
Having understood the place and the time, as well as one's own strength and the enemy's force, the task is indeed accomplished; such is the word of Bṛhaspati.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus resolved, the lord of the Daityas dispatched the great asura Raktabīja,
surrounded by a vast army, into the battle.
Śumbha said:
"O mighty-armed Raktabīja, go to the field of battle!
O illustrious one, wage war according to the strength you possess. (44)
Raktabīja said: "O Great King, you need not entertain even the slightest anxiety;
I shall slay her and bring her under your control. (45)
Behold my skill in battle! Where is this young girl, beloved of the gods?
Having conquered her by force in combat, I shall make her your slave. (46)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, O best of the Kurus, the great asura Raktabīja mounted his chariot and departed, surrounded by his own army.
Surrounded by multitudes of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry,
he mounted his chariot and went forth to the Goddess who was situated upon the mountain.
Beholding him arrived, the Goddess sounded her conch shell, which struck fear into all the Daityas and increased the joy of the gods. (49)
Hearing the fierce sound of the conch, the exceedingly swift Raktabīja approached Cāmuṇḍā and spoke these gentle words.
Raktabīja said:
"O girl, why do you terrify me, thinking me to be a coward? O slender-limbed one, do you not know Dhūmralocana by the sound of his conch?"
"I am Raktabīja by name; I have come here to your presence.
O cuckoo, if you desire battle, be ready; I have no fear."
"Behold my strength today, O beloved; those cowards whom you have seen—I am not among their ranks. Fight as you wish! (53)
In the past, you have served the elders and studied the treatises on ethics; furthermore, you have acquired knowledge of worldly affairs or participated in the assemblies of the learned. (54)
"O beautiful one, if you possess knowledge of the science of literature and ritual, then listen to my words, which are wholesome, true, and supported by valid cognition. (55)
