Indeed, among the nine sentiments, only two have attained preeminence in the assemblies of learned men: the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) and the sentiment of peace (śānta). || 56 ||
Of these two, the erotic sentiment alone is established first in the state of the King;
indeed, Viṣṇu dwells with Lakṣmī, and the four-faced Brahmā with Sāvitrī.
Indra lies with Śacī, and Śaṅkara with the Daughter of the Mountain;
the tree with its creeper, the deer with the doe, and the pigeon with the female pigeon. (58)
Thus, all living beings are intensely addicted to union; so too are those other men who are timid and have not attained the power of enjoyment. (59)
Those who act thus are indeed fools, deceived by fate;
being ignorant of the true essence of worldly existence, they are cheated by those intent on deception.
For they are devoted to the aesthetic flavor of tranquility through their skill in sweet conversation; where is knowledge, and where is dispassion, while the god of love reigns supreme? (61)
"In greed, in invincible anger, and in delusion which destroys the intellect—therefore, O auspicious lady, you too must make yourself beautiful and captivating. (62)
"Whether it be Śumbha, the conqueror of the gods, or the exceedingly powerful Niśumbha.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, that Raktabīja ceased speaking as he stood before him.
Upon hearing this, Cāmuṇḍā, Kālikā, and Ambikā likewise laughed.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between Śumbha and Niśumbha in the Presence of the Goddess via Raktabīja," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Dialogue between Śumbha and Niśumbha in the Presence of the Goddess by means of Raktabīja;
Vyāsa said:
O Lord of the People, having laughed, the Goddess then spoke to him.
With a voice as deep as a thundercloud, he spoke these words, which were full of logical reasoning. || 1 ||
O dull-witted one, I have already told you what was appropriate and beneficial to say before a messenger; why do you boast now? (2)
"If there should be anyone in the three worlds who is my equal in beauty, strength, and prosperity, him I shall choose as my husband. (3)
"Speak to Śumbha and Niśumbha; a vow was made by me long ago.
Therefore, fight me, and having conquered me, perform the marriage according to the prescribed rites."
Indeed, you have come here by his command for the sake of accomplishing his purpose;
either wage war or go to the netherworld with your husband.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the goddess, that Daitya, filled with indignation,
swiftly loosed terrible arrows upon the lion.
Seeing those arrows resembling serpents in the sky, Ambikā,
by virtue of her lightness of hand, instantly cut them down with sharp shafts.
With other arrows released from Ambikā’s bow— drawn back to the ear and sharpened on stone— he struck the great asura Raktabīja.
Struck by the goddess’s arrow, the wicked one fell into a swoon upon his chariot;
and when Raktabīja had fallen, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
All the soldiers cried out and said, "We are slain!
Then, hearing that most dreadful tumultuous roar, Śumbha [acted].
He indeed gave orders for the mobilization of all the Daitya armies.
Śumbha said:
"Let all the Dānavas set forth, including the Kāmbojas, surrounded by their own forces. (11)
"Others too are exceedingly powerful heroes, especially the Kālakeyas.
Vyāsa said:
Thus was the entire fourfold army commanded by Śumbha.
He emerged, possessed by intoxication, into the arena of battle against the goddess;
and seeing that Dānava Bala approaching, Caṇḍikā [observed him].
The Mother of the World quickly and repeatedly made a terrifying and fearsome sound with her bell,
and she produced the twang of her bowstring and the blast of her conch.
By that roar, Kālī became wide-mouthed;
and hearing that terrible sound of the Goddess, her vehicle, the lion, [also reacted].
That powerful one also roared, producing a most wonderful fear;
hearing that sound, the Dānavas were overcome with rage.
In that very long and fierce battle, which caused the hair to stand on end, all those of great strength hurled their weapons at the goddess.
The powers of the gods, beginning with Brahmā, went to Caṇḍikā;
each deity assumed his own form, along with his respective ornaments and vehicle.
Then goddesses of such forms proceeded to the field of battle:
Brahmāṇī, mounted upon a swan and holding a rosary and a water-pot; || 19 ||
The power of Brahmā has arrived, known as Brahmāṇī;
likewise Vaiṣṇavī, mounted upon Garuḍa and bearing the conch, discus, and mace.
Padmahastā arrived, adorned with yellow garments;
Śāṅkarī, however, was mounted upon a bull and bore an excellent trident. || 21 ||
The goddess Kaumārī, who bears the crescent moon, is auspicious and adorned with a serpent-bracelet; she is mounted upon a peacock, holds a spear in her hand, and possesses a beautiful countenance.
Desirous of battle, Indrāṇī arrived, appearing in the form of Kārttikeya; she possessed a beautiful countenance and was mounted upon a magnificent white elephant.
Abounding in intense wrath, Vārāhī, who is considered to be seated upon a mature corpse, went forth facing the battle in the form of a boar, holding a vajra in her hand. (24)
Nārasiṃhī, assuming a body similar to that of Nṛsiṃha, and Yāmyā, mounted upon a buffalo, holding a staff in her hand and inspiring fear. (25)
Then Śucismitā, appearing like Yama in battle, arrived;
likewise did the spear Vāruṇī and Kauberī, who was fierce with intoxication.
Such beings, of such forms, arrived surrounded by their respective armies;
seeing them come, the Goddess experienced great joy. (27)
The gods rejoiced in their own state, while the Daityas fell into fear;
there, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, was surrounded by them.
Having arrived at the battlefield, he spoke thus to Caṇḍikā:
"Let the asuras be slain quickly for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods. (29)
Having slain both Niśumbha and Śumbha, as well as whatever other Dānavas remained,
and having destroyed the entire host of Daityas, she rendered the world free from fear.
Let the Śaktis gather at their respective abodes;
let the gods be partakers of the sacrifice, and let the Brāhmaṇas be devoted to the ritual.
May all living beings, both mobile and immobile, be satisfied;
likewise, may calamities and epidemics be pacified once again. (32)
"May the clouds rain abundantly in due season, and may agriculture likewise yield great fruit.
Vyāsa said:
While Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods and benefactor of the world, was speaking thus—
From the body of Caṇḍikā, however, there emerged a wondrous power (śakti),
terrifying, exceedingly fierce, and roaring with the sound of a hundred jackals.
Then, with a smiling face, she of terrible form said to the five-faced one:
"O God of gods, go quickly toward the lord of the Daityas."
O Śaṅkara, enemy of Kāma, act as a messenger; speak on my behalf to Śumbha, who is agitated by passion, and to Niśumbha, who is arrogant with pride. (36)
"Leaving Triviṣṭapa, go quickly indeed to Pātāla!
O gods, may you attain happiness in heaven; may Turāṣāṭ regain his auspicious throne. (37)
May the deities attain the celestial realm and their sacrificial shares, provided that your desire for life remains very great. (38)
"In that case, go quickly to Pātāla where the Dānavas dwell;
or else, relying on your strength, if you desire battle, then come for death. (39)
"Then let my auspicious attendants come and be satisfied with your flesh.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of hers, the wielder of the trident (Śiva) acted with haste.
Having gone there, he spoke to Śumbha, the king of the Daityas, as he sat in the assembly hall.
Śiva said:
"O King, I am the messenger of Ambā; I am Hara, the destroyer of Tripura. (41)
Having come here to your presence to accomplish every benefit for you, I have abandoned both heaven and earth; therefore, you all depart quickly.
Wherein Prahlāda and Bali, the best among the strong, dwell in Pātāla;
or, if you desire death, then come quickly!
"In battle, I shall indeed swiftly slay all of you," thus spoke the great queen for the sake of your welfare.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus caused the excellent Daityas to hear those words of the Goddess, which were like nectar and conducive to their welfare, the wielder of the trident returned.
By her, Śambhu was impelled to act as a messenger to the Dānavas;
thus she became renowned throughout the entire three worlds as Śivadūtī.
Having heard those words of the goddess, which were as difficult to accomplish as those spoken by Śaṅkara, they also quickly went forth for battle, armored and with weapons in hand. || 47 ||
Having swiftly arrived at the battlefield against Caṇḍikā,
the Dānavas struck her with sharp arrows, whetted on stone and drawn back to their ears.
Kālikā moved about there, rending those Dānavas with her tridents and maces, splitting them apart with her spears, and devouring them as she went.
And there on the field of battle, Brahmāṇī deprived the mighty Dānavas of their lives by hurling water from her water-pot.
Māheśvarī, mounted upon her bull, struck down the Dānavas in battle with her trident of extreme velocity and cast them to the ground. || 51 ||
By the falling of her discus and the falling of her mace, Vaiṣṇavī quickly deprived the Dānavas of their lives and stripped them of their heads.
Aindrī struck them to the ground with a blow from her thunderbolt,
while the preeminent Daityas were crushed by the impact of Airāvata’s trunk.
Vārāhī, filled with wrath, struck down hundreds of Daityas and Dānavas with blows from her snout and by the falling of the tips of her tusks.
Tearing apart the foremost of the Daityas with her fierce claws, the Nārasiṃhī roamed the battlefield devouring them and roared again and again. (55)
Śivadūtī caused them to fall to the ground with her loud bursts of laughter;
then Cāmuṇḍā and Kālikā, acting with great haste, devoured them.
And Kaumārī, stationed upon a peacock, struck down the enemies in battle with arrows whetted on stone and drawn back to her ear, truly for the benefit of the gods.
Vāruṇī cast the Daityas, bound by her noose, down upon the surface of the battlefield;
they fell there unconscious and deprived of their senses. || 58 ||
Thus, the army of Dānavas, though possessing great vigor and prowess, was crushed by the host of Mothers and became intent on flight. || 59 ||
A great roar arose there from that ocean of forces;
then the gods showered flowers upon the Goddess and her hosts.
Hearing that terrible roar and the sound of "Victory!",
and seeing the Daityas fleeing, Raktabīja quickly became enraged.
Then, beholding the gods roaring in that manner, the mighty and radiant Daitya Raktabīja advanced toward the battle.
Armed and seated upon his chariot, making a wondrous sound with his bowstring,
he then approached the Goddess, his eyes raised and blood-red with rage.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between the Goddess and Raktabīja," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Departure of Niśumbha for Battle with the Goddess.
Vyāsa said: This boon, which had been granted to that Dānava by Śiva, was now [fulfilled].
O King, listen to that which is most wonderful; I shall now relate it to you.
Whenever a drop of blood falls from his body onto the ground,
Daityas arise, identical in form and equal in prowess to him.
"May the innumerable, highly valiant Dānavas born of blood prevail"—thus was an exceedingly wonderful boon granted by Rudra. (3)
Proud because of that boon and filled with wrath,
he swiftly approached the battle to slay the Goddess together with Kālī.
Having seen the Vaiṣṇavī power seated upon Garuḍa,
the lord of the Daityas struck that lotus-eyed goddess with his spear.
She warded off the mace with her own spear, and that spear, joined with power,
struck the great asura Raktabīja with her discus.
From his body struck by the wheel of the chariot, much blood flowed forth,
like streams of red chalk from the peak of a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Wherever drops of blood fell upon the ground at that time,
from those very forms arose thousands of men.
Aindrī struck the terrible demon Tamasura with her thunderbolt;
possessed by wrath, she also struck Raktabīja, and blood flowed forth.
Then, from that blood, many Raktabījas were born;
they possessed his vigor, bore his form, carried weapons, and were fierce in battle.
Enraged, Brahmāṇī struck him violently with the staff of Brahmā, and Māheśvarī tore the Dānava apart with her trident. || 11 ||
Nārasiṃhī pierced that great asura with blows from her claws;
enraged, she struck that lowest of Rākṣasas with a blow from her snout.
And Kaumārī likewise struck him on the chest with her spear;
he too, enraged, pierced them with a shower of sharp arrows.
Struck by blows from clubs and spears, all the Mothers individually pierced him with showers of arrows, provoked as they were by his assault.
Caṇḍikā cut his weapons apart with her own sharp arrows;
and the goddess, being exceedingly enraged, struck him with other shafts.
From his body flowed blood in many streams,
and from that, thousands of heroes resembling him appeared.
The world was pervaded by the Raktabījas, born from floods of blood, who were fully armed, equipped for battle, and engaged in a truly marvelous conflict. (17)
Seeing those Raktabījas striking them repeatedly, the gods became terrified; dejected and overcome by grief, they trembled with fear. || 18 ||
How will the thousands of Daityas meet their destruction today—those Dānavas of massive bodies and great prowess, born from blood? (19)
"There is only one Caṇḍikā here, as well as Kālī and the Mothers;
all the Dānavas must be conquered by these—this is indeed a difficult task. (20)
Whether it be Niśumbha or Śumbha, surrounded by a host of forces, will suddenly come forth in battle; from that, a great calamity will arise. || 21 ||
Vyāsa said: When the gods, agitated by fear, fell into great anxiety,
then Ambikā spoke to the lotus-eyed Kālī.
O Cāmuṇḍā, quickly and most urgently open your mouth wide;
swiftly drink the blood produced by the falling of my weapon! 23.
"Roam through the battlefield today at will, devouring the Dānavas;
I shall slay them with sharp arrows, as well as with maces, swords, and clubs. (24)
"Act accordingly, O large-eyed lady, so that not even a single drop of that blood shall fall upon the ground right now. (25)
As they are being devoured then, no other Daityas shall be born;
thus their destruction will surely come to pass, and not otherwise.
"I shall slay the Daitya; you, meanwhile, drink quickly all his blood while striving for the destruction of the enemy. (27)
"Having thus brought about the destruction of the Daityas and having bestowed the entire stable kingdom of the gods' abode upon Indra, we shall depart as we please. (28)
Vyāsa said: Thus addressed by Ambikā, the goddess Cāmuṇḍā, of fierce prowess,
drank all the blood produced from the body of Raktabīja.
Ambikā quickly struck him with a sword and a mace,
and the slender-waisted Cāmuṇḍā devoured the fragments of his body.
Enraged, he too struck Cāmuṇḍā with blows from his mace;
nevertheless, she quickly drank the blood and devoured him.
Those other cruel ones born of blood, the mighty Raktabījas—they too were all struck down, devoured, and stripped of their blood. || 32 ||
All the artificial asuras were devoured; but even that one who was a natural asura was struck down and slain, his body cut into many pieces with a sword.
When the fierce Raktabīja was slain, the other Dānavas who were in the battle fled from there, trembling with fear. || 34 ||
Crying out "Alas! Alas!", they spoke to Śumbha while overcome with agitation;
their bodies were drenched in blood, and they were deprived of their weapons and consciousness.
O King, that Raktabīja was struck down by Ambikā;
Cāmuṇḍā, moreover, drank all the blood from his body.
And whatever other heroic dānavas there were, all were slain by the lion with its exceedingly swift mount, while others were devoured by Kālī.
O King, we have come to tell you of your deeds in battle and likewise of the most wonderful conduct of the Goddess in the conflict. (38)
O Great King, I am invincible in every way by the Daityas and Dānavas, and by the Gandharvas, Asuras, Yakṣas, Pannagas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas. (39)
O great king, other goddesses led by Indrāṇī arrived there in great numbers,
fighting with their mounts and weapons.
By them, with their excellent weapons, the entire army of the Dānavas was destroyed;
even Raktabīja, O king of kings, was swiftly struck down.
Even a single queen is difficult to withstand, how much more so when accompanied by them? Even a lion of immeasurable luster slays Rākṣasas in battle. (42)
Therefore, having deliberated with your ministers, let that which is appropriate be carried out;
hostility with her is not fitting, for peace alone brings happiness. (43)
It is entirely a marvel that a woman slays the Rākṣasas;
even Raktabīja was slain, and his blood was drunk by her.
Other Daityas were struck down in battle by Ambikā, O King,
and all their flesh was indeed devoured by Cāmuṇḍā on the field of war.
"O Great King, it would be better to go to the netherworld or even to serve her; however, you must not engage in battle with Ambikā."
This is no ordinary woman, for she is the accomplisher of the gods' purpose;
she has arisen as this powerful goddess, Māyā, consuming [all things]. 47.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these truthful words of theirs, Śumbha, deluded by fate and desiring to die, replied thus with his lips quivering: || 48 ||
Śumbha said:
"Go to Pātāla for refuge, you who are overcome by fear;
I myself, fully prepared, shall slay both them and those women this very day. (49)
Having conquered all the gods in battle and established a most prosperous kingdom,
how can I, agitated by fear of a woman, enter the netherworld?
Having slain all the attendants headed by Raktabīja in battle,
why should I depart for the sake of saving my life, abandoning such vast fame?
Death, ordained by Time, is indeed unavoidable for all living beings;
who would abandon that fame so difficult to attain, which is acquired through birth, out of fear of it? (52)
"Niśumbha, I shall go mounted upon my chariot to the field of battle;
having slain her, I will return, or else I will not return at all. (53)
But you, O hero, accompanied by your army, become my rear-guard;
swiftly lead that woman to the abode of Yama with your sharp arrows. 54.
Niśumbha said: "Today I shall go and slay that wicked Kālikā;
I will return quickly after having seized that Mother Ambikā."
"Do not worry, O Indra among kings, on account of this wretched woman. Where is this young girl, and where is the strength of my arms that brings the entire universe under its control? (56)
"O brother, casting aside this great distress, enjoy unsurpassed pleasures;
I shall bring back that proud woman together with her pride, according to your desire. (57)
O King, while I am here, it is not right for you to go into battle;
having gone myself, I shall indeed bring the glory of victory for your sake.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to his elder brother, the younger one, arrogant of his strength, mounted a massive chariot, armored and surrounded by his own forces. (59)
Having performed auspicious rites for the battle, praised by bards and panegyrists, and equipped with weapons and his retinue, he proceeded swiftly and with great speed.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Departure of Niśumbha for Battle with the Goddess," in the fifth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The narration of the news by the Rākṣasas who had returned from battle to Śumbha.
Vyāsa said: Having made his resolve for either death or victory, Niśumbha—
Exerting himself, powerful and heroic, he approached the Goddess in battle. || 1 ||
Śumbha also arrived there, surrounded by his own army;
the king, an expert in the delights of battle, became a spectator of the fight.
Then the gods stationed in the sky, enveloped by masses of clouds,
as well as the hosts of Yakṣas together with Indra, remained there desiring to witness the battle.
Then Niśumbha, having entered the battle and taken up his Śārṅgaka bow,
unleashed a shower of arrows, terrifying the Mother of the World.
Seeing Niśumbha discharging nets of arrows in battle,
Caṇḍikā took up her excellent bow and laughed repeatedly with a loud voice.
The goddess said to Kālikā: "Behold the foolishness of these two;
O Kālikā, they have now come here into my presence for the sake of death."
Having witnessed the terrible slaughter of the Daityas as well as the destruction of Raktabīja,
these two, deluded by my māyā, have conceived hope for victory.
For this hope is indeed powerful; it never leaves a man, even when he is broken, stripped of strength, ruined, deprived of his wings, and senseless. (8)
Bound by the snares of desire, these two, Śumbha and Niśumbha, have come together for battle; O Kālī, they must be slain by me in the fray.
"These two, deluded by fate, have arrived with death at hand;
today, while all the gods look on, I shall slay them."
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to Kālikā, Caṇḍī swiftly covered Niśumbha, who stood before her, with a multitude of arrows drawn back to her ear.
The Dānava also cut her arrows with his own sharp shafts;
a most terrifying battle took place between the two of them.
Shaking the masses of his mane,
the powerful lion plunged into the ocean of the army, just as an elephant enters a lake.
With his claws and bites, he devoured the Dānavas standing before him,
their limbs shattered like elephants intoxicated with rut.
While the army was thus being crushed by Kesarin,
Niśumbha then rushed forward, having drawn his excellent bow.
Other lords of the Daityas, many in number, also approached to slay the Goddess, enraged, with their fangs bared and eyes bloodshot. (16)
Thereupon Śumbha, surrounded by his army, arrived with speed,
having slain Kālikā out of anger, in order to seize the Mother of the World.
Having arrived there, he beheld Ajāmbikā standing before him—
fierce with the sentiment of wrath, yet beloved and endowed with the sentiment of love.
Beholding her, who possessed wide-reaching eyes, was the most beautiful woman in the three worlds,
had lovely blood-red eyes, and likewise eyes reddened with anger— 19.
Abandoning the desire for marriage and likewise casting hope for victory far away,
he stood with his bow strung, having made a firm resolve to die.
To that Dānava, the Goddess spoke these words preceded by a smile,
while those Daityas were listening on the summit of the battlefield.
"Go away, you commoners, either to the netherworld or into the ocean, having abandoned your weapons right here and fixed your hope for life! (22)
Or else, let all those whose lives were taken by me through envy and malice on the field of battle, having attained the bliss of heaven, sport there free from all distress. (23)
Cowardice and heroism do not exist at all;
indeed, I grant the gift of fearlessness, so let everyone go as they please.
Vyāsa said: Having heard her words, Niśumbha, arrogant with pride,
took up a sharpened sword and a shield adorned with eight moons.
Running swiftly with his sword, he struck the lion, who was fierce with intoxication,
on the head with great force, while whirling the Mother of the World.
Then the goddess, having deceived him with her own mace so that he would not strike with his sword,
struck him on the base of the arm with an axe at that time.
Struck by the sword at the base of his arm, that Mahāmada then suppressed the pain and once more struck Caṇḍikā.
She too let out a terrible sound from her bell that struck fear into men;
desiring to slay Niśumbha, she drank the liquor again and again. (29)
Thus, a battle occurred between the gods and the dānavas, who were each desirous of victory over the other, and it was exceedingly terrifying.
Carnivorous birds, cruel dogs, and jackals, as well as vultures, herons, and crows, danced with great delight. || 31 ||
The battlefield shone, crowded with the fallen bodies of many excellent warriors, drenched in streams of blood, and strewn with the carcasses of elephants and horses. 32.
Seeing the Dānavas fallen, Niśumbha, filled with extreme rage,
quickly approached Caṇḍikā, taking up a terrible mace.
Intoxicated with pride, he struck the lion on the head with his mace;
having struck it, he smiled and struck the goddess once more.
Then the Goddess, seeing Niśumbha standing before her, striking out in a state of extreme rage, spoke these words: || 35 ||
The Goddess said:
"Wait, O dull-witted one, until I drive this sword into your neck; because of this, you shall go to the abode of Yama. (36)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess Caṇḍikā, composed in mind, swiftly severed the head of Niśumbha with her sword.
With his head severed by the Goddess, the exceedingly dreadful trunk wandered about,
mace in hand, terrifying the hosts of deities.
The goddess severed his feet and hands with her sharp arrows;
then that sinner, resembling a mountain, fell lifeless upon the earth. 39.
When that Daitya Niśumbha of terrifying prowess had fallen, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among his army, which was trembling with fear.
Abandoning all their weapons, the soldiers, drenched in blood, went toward the royal palace while all of them raised a tumultuous cry. (41)
Seeing them arrived, Śumbha, the destroyer of enemies, asked: "Where is that Niśumbha? How were you defeated and why have you fled?
Hearing those words of the king, they, bowing down deeply, spoke.
O King, your brother lies slain at the forefront of the battle.
The heroes who were struck down by her, as well as their followers and subordinates—we have all come to relate this entire account to you. (44)
Niśumbha has been slain there by that Caṇḍikā;
indeed, O King, this is not the time for battle for you on the field of war today.
Reflecting upon this, consider that some supreme woman has surely arrived here for the sake of the gods' mission, in order to destroy the race of the Daityas. (46)
She is not merely an ordinary woman; she is the unsurpassed goddess Śakti, whose conduct is inconceivable and who is difficult to be known even by the gods.
Assuming manifold forms and highly skilled in the root of illusion,
the auspicious Goddess bears diverse ornaments and carries all weapons.
She is profound and her conduct is hidden, like another Kālarātri;
she has reached the further shore of the shoreless, she is full, and endowed with all auspicious marks. || 49 ||
The gods stationed in the intermediate space, free from fear from any quarter, praised that most wonderful Śrī Devī as she was performing the work of the gods.
Fleeing is the highest duty; by all means, one must protect the body.
For when this body is protected, our happiness will surely be attained in due time.
O King, victory in battle shall be yours; of this there is no doubt.
Time makes one strong at one moment and weak at another. (52)
Indeed, having made him powerful once more, Time establishes him for victory;
for at some point in time, Time makes the giver a beggar.
In the course of time, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, or even the Lord of Pārvatī will surely make a giver of wealth into a beggar. (54)
Indra and all the other gods are themselves subject to time alone as their master;
therefore, wait for the right time, for your fortune is now adverse.
O King, he stood face-to-face with both the gods and the Daityas as the cause of their destruction; indeed, there was but one destiny for them all, for Time, it is said, has no alternative.
One must understand his activity, even though he assumes various forms:
sometimes there is the birth of men, and likewise sometimes their dissolution. (57)
Time is one cause of origination, and another is the cause of destruction;
O Great King, all the gods, including Indra, are manifest before your very eyes.
Those Asuras who were previously made to pay tribute by Kāla when he was face-to-face with them, have today been rendered powerless by that very same Kāla when he turned his back on them.
Time indeed brings about both the auspicious and the inauspicious, utterly destroying them;
herein neither Kālī nor the eternal gods are the cause. (60)
O King, reflect upon this and do as seems best to you;
for this is the time, and there is no other reason for it, whether for us or for the Dānavas. (61)
Śakra, having gone before you, was defeated in battle and rendered weaponless;
likewise were Viṣṇu, Rudra, Varuṇa, Dhanada, and Yama.
In the same way, O Indra among kings, having observed that the world is subject to time, go quickly to the netherworld (pātāla); living there, you shall attain well-being.
But when you have died, O Great King, your enemies, filled with joy and singing auspicious songs, will roam everywhere.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Report to Śumbha by the Rākṣasas Returned from Battle," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Now the thirty-first chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, Śumbha, the lord of the Daityas, then [spoke].
With eyes agitated by anger, he spoke quickly to the soldiers. || 1 ||
Śumbha said:
"O wretches, why do you speak such foul words? Having killed my ministers and brothers, how can I, devoid of shame, continue to live and wander about?"
Time is the most powerful agent of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds;
what concern is it to me, when even that irresistible Lord is formless?
Let whatever happens happen; let him do whatever he does.
I have no anxiety whatsoever regarding either death or life. (4)
Even that time cannot be altered in any way when it is so perceived;
nor does the rain-cloud ever fail to pour down in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Sometimes, during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, Māgha, or Phālguna, it rains suddenly out of season; therefore, this [rain] is not the primary one.
Time is merely a pretext, for destiny is indeed more powerful;
everything is ordained by destiny and cannot be otherwise—this is the truth.
I consider destiny alone to be supreme; fie upon useless human effort! For even Niśumbha, the conqueror of all the gods, has been slain by her.
When even that great hero Raktabīja has met his destruction, then why should I abandon my fame and cling to the hope for life? (9)
When the time arrives, measured by two parārdhas, Brahmā himself,
the creator of the world and the self-sovereign Lord, meets his end with speed.
Indeed, during a single day of Brahmā, which consists of a thousand cycles of the four yugas,
five and nine Indras respectively fall from their celestial abodes, and likewise, they are born again.
In the same way, Viṣṇu prepares for death when the three qualities [predominate];
likewise, Śaṅkara attains peace when two qualities [predominate].
O fool, what anxiety is there regarding death, which is fixed and ordained by fate? Even the destruction of the earth, of the mountains, and of the sun and moon [is certain]. (13)
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain.
Since this body is impermanent, one’s enduring fame alone must be protected. 14.
"Let my chariot be prepared quickly; I shall go to the field of battle.
Let there be either victory or death this very day, as ordained by fate. (15)
Having spoken thus to his soldiers, Śumbha quickly mounted his chariot and departed for the place where Ambikā was stationed on the Himālaya.
His fourfold army,
consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, accompanied by many weapons, set out from there.
Having gone there, Śumbha beheld the Mother of the Universe seated upon Mount Acala— she who fascinates the three worlds, the beloved one, riding upon a lion.
Richly adorned with all kinds of ornaments and endowed with all auspicious marks, she was being praised by gods dwelling in the sky, as well as by gandharvas, yakṣas, and kinnaras. (19)
She was being honored with flowers born from the mandāra trees,
while she herself made the sound of conchs and the charming resonance of bells.
Upon seeing her, Śumbha, deluded by passion and struck by the five arrows of Love, fell into a state of infatuation and reflected thus in his mind: ||21||
"Oh, how perfect is this form! Oh, how wonderful is this marvelous skill!
Her limbs are so delicate and exceedingly slender, yet she has manifested youth all at once.
It is a marvel that this young girl is entirely devoid of any amorous passion. (23)
Equal in beauty to Kāmakāntā and endowed with all auspicious marks, who is this Ambikā? Indeed, she destroys even those of great strength. (24)
"What means should be employed here by which she might come under my control? Neither mantras nor other methods are effective in the presence of this swan-eyed woman. (25)
"For she consists entirely of mantras; she is enchanting, intoxicated with pride, and beautiful. How might this woman of excellent complexion come under my control? (26)
"It is not proper for me to go to the netherworld from this battlefield; moreover, this one of great strength cannot be subdued by means of conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension. (27)
"What should be done, and where should one go, when such a crisis has arisen? Death is not the best course here, for it would destroy the reputation earned through my wife. (28)
Death in battle has been declared by the sages to be a source of auspiciousness, provided it occurs while two warriors of equal strength are indeed fighting. (29)
This woman, created by fate, the most excellent among hundreds of women, has arrived here; she is an exceedingly powerful woman who will bring about the destruction of our lineage in every way. (30)
"Why should I now employ conciliatory words in vain? For she has come here for the purpose of killing me; would she be appeased by conciliation? (31)
She cannot be moved by gifts, being adorned with various weapons; and sowing dissension is likewise fruitless, for she is entirely under the control of all the gods. (32)
Therefore, death is better than fleeing from battle;
let there be either victory or death today, according to the proper way.
Vyāsa said:
Having reflected thus, Śumbha took recourse in the quality of goodness (sattva);
becoming firmly resolved for battle, he spoke to her who stood before him. 34.
"O Goddess, fight today, O beloved; this exertion of yours is in vain.
You are indeed foolish among women, for this is never the proper conduct. (35)
The eyes of women are their arrows; their eyebrows alone are the bow;
their gestures and expressions are the weapons; and the wise man is the target. (36)
In this [kingdom], armor is body-unguent and the chariot is the fulfillment of one's desires;
the sound of the kettle-drum is but soft conversation, and never anything else. (37)
For women, wielding other weapons is undoubtedly a mockery;
O beloved, modesty alone is their ornament, and never indeed audacity.
A noble woman engaged in combat appears as if she were coarse;
how indeed could her breasts, which ought to be concealed, endure the drawing of a bow? (39)
Where is slow movement, and where is running while wielding a mace?
Here, Kālikā is the bestower of intelligence, and Cāmuṇḍā is the supreme mistress.
Seated in the midst of the mantra of Caṇḍikā, Śivā is of harsh voice in her fondling;
the king of beasts, who strikes fear into all living beings, stands as her vehicle.
O woman of excellent complexion, since you have abandoned the sound of the lute and taken up the sound of the bell, everything regarding beauty and youth is now in opposition [to your purpose].
"If you have a desire for combat, O beautiful woman, then become deformed:
have protruding lips, malformed nails, be cruel, and have eyes the color of a crow."
With long legs, protruding teeth, and the appearance of a cat's eyes—assuming such a form, remain firm in battle. (44)
"Speak harsh words, and then I shall fight;
seeing such a woman with beautiful teeth as this, my hand does not feel at ease. (45)
"O fawn-eyed one, resembling the beloved of Kāma, I shall slay you in battle!
Vyāsa said:
Having seen him speaking thus, afflicted by lust, the Mother of the World [spoke]. (46)
With a smile, she spoke these words, O best of the Bharatas.
The Queen said:
"Why do you despair, O dull-witted one, deluded as you are by the arrows of desire? (47)
"I am standing here as a mere spectator, O fool;
engage in battle with Kālikā or with Cāmuṇḍā on this battlefield suited for you. (48)
"Strike me as you please; I do not venture to fight with you.
Having spoken thus, the Goddess addressed Kālikā in a sweet voice. (49)
"Kill him, O Kālikā, cruel one, you who delight in battle with such a misshapen form!
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, Kālikā, impelled by Time and possessing the form of Time, [acted].
Seizing her mace, she stood in the battle with swift exertion;
between them there occurred a most terrifying combat.
While all the gods and the high-souled sages were looking on,
Śumbha then raised his mace and struck Kālikā in battle.
Kālikā struck the king of the Daityas violently with her mace;
Caṇḍī shattered his gold-glittering chariot with that very mace.
Having killed the donkeys, she of the dreadful voice quickly struck Dāruka;
he, filled with rage, took up a heavy mace and stood on foot.
Then, laughing, he struck between Kālikā’s two arms;
having thus evaded the blow of the mace, he quickly seized his sword.
He severed his left arm, which was still grasping a weapon and smeared with sandalwood paste;
with his arm lopped off and deprived of his chariot, he leaped forward, mace in hand.
Then, having arrived shortly thereafter, Kālī struck Kālikā; with her sword, she [severed] her right arm.
Laughing, she indeed cut off his arm along with the mace;
enraged, he rushed forward with speed to deliver a kick to her feet.
Kālī, acting with haste, severed his feet with her sword;
even though his hands and feet were cut off, he remained there, crying out, "Stay! Stay! (59).
Running, he went quickly as if terrifying Kālikā;
seeing him approaching, who was like a lotus, Kālikā— || 60 ||
He violently severed the head from the neck, which flowed with a torrent of blood;
once the head was cut off, it fell to the ground like a mountain.
His vital breaths quickly departed, having emerged from his body;
seeing the Daitya fallen and lifeless, the gods, together with Indra, [rejoiced].
Then they praised that goddess Cāmuṇḍā as well as Kālikā;
auspicious winds blew there, and the quarters became exceedingly clear.
The fires for the oblation became auspicious, with their flames turning to the right;
and those Daityas who remained after the slaughter bowed down to the Mother of the World.
Having cast aside their weapons, O King, they all departed for Pātāla.
Thus, this entire supreme account of the Goddess’s deeds has been narrated to you. 65.
The slaying of Śumbha and his followers, as well as the protection of the gods—human beings on earth recite this entire narrative. (66)
And those who always listen with devotion indeed become successful;
one without a son obtains sons, and one without wealth obtains great riches.
The sick person is freed from disease and shall obtain all desires;
he who recites this auspicious life-story shall have no fear of enemies.
The man who constantly hears and recites it becomes possessed of liberation. || 68 ||
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Slaying of Śumbha," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 31 ||
Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
Janamejaya said:
"O Sage, the greatness of Caṇḍikā has been fully described by you."
By whom was she previously propitiated through the practice of the three modes of conduct? || 1 ||
To whom did she become gracious and grant her boons? By whom was this great fruit obtained? O treasury of compassion, tell us how one propitiates the Goddess who fulfills all desires. (2)
O Brahman, O highly fortunate one, tell me in detail the method of worship, as well as the ritual for adoration, and furthermore, the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa).
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the king, Kṛṣṇa, the son of Satyavatī, being pleased, replied to the monarch regarding the worship of Mahāmāyā.
Vyāsa said:
Formerly, in the Svārociṣa Manvantara, there was a king named Suratha, who was supremely noble and devoted to the protection of his subjects. ||5||
He was a speaker of truth, devoted to his duties, and a worshiper of the brahmins;
he was constantly intent on devotion to his guru and remained faithful to his own wife.
Generous, ethical, and non-opposing, he was the sole master of the science of archery;
while he was thus protecting the kingdom, the Mlecchas dwelling in the mountains [attacked].
Having forcibly become enemies and having assembled a fourfold army consisting of elephants,
horses, chariots, and infantry, they were intoxicated with pride.
The destroyers of Kolā arrived, intent on seizing the earth;
Suratha, taking his army with him, appeared before them face to face.
A terrible battle took place between him and those most cruel [foes];
the force of the Mlecchas was small, while the king's army was wonderful.
Nevertheless, though he was victorious in battle, by fate the king was defeated;
broken, he reached his own city, which was well-guarded and adorned with fortifications. (11)
The wise king, skilled in statecraft, became despondent upon seeing his principal ministers had taken refuge with the side of the enemy, and he began to reflect.
Having occupied a vast position fortified by moats and difficult to assail, one should wait for the [right] time; or is battle considered better? (13)
"Those ministers who have fallen under the power of the enemy are indeed unfit for counsel.
Thus the king reflected in his mind, "What shall I do? (14)
Perhaps those of sinful conduct, relying on others, will seize me and hand me over to their enemies; what then will happen? (15)
One should never place trust in those of evil intent;
what indeed can those men do who are under the sway of greed? (16)
A man possessed by greed always hates his brother, father, friend, well-wisher, kinsman, as well as his teacher, the venerable one, and the twice-born. ||17||
Therefore, I must not place any trust whatsoever now in this circle of ministers, who are exceedingly wicked and have taken refuge with the side of the enemy.
Having reflected thus in his mind, the king, deeply dejected,
mounted his horse alone and departed from that city.
Then, having gone out alone and entered a dense forest, the wise man reflected: "Where should I go next? (20)
Having learned that the excellent hermitage of the sage Sumedhas was located at a distance of only three yojanas, the king went to the ascetic’s abode,
which was filled with many trees and situated upon a riverbank.
It was free from enmity, filled with wild beasts, and adorned with the songs of cuckoos. ||22||
Abounding in the sounds of students engaged in study, surrounded by hundreds of herds of deer,
rich with well-cooked wild rice, and filled with trees bearing beautiful flowers and fruits.
Always bringing delight to living beings by the sweet fragrance of the sacrificial smoke, it was pervaded by the sound of the Vedas and was more enchanting even than heaven. 24.
Having seen that hermitage, the king became filled with joy;
casting off his fear, he set his mind on taking rest in the brahmin’s hermitage. 25.
Having tethered his horse to a tree, he proceeded with humility,
seeing that sage seated there, taking refuge in the shade of a *sāla* tree.
Seated upon a deer-skin, peaceful, exceedingly emaciated by asceticism, upright, teaching his disciples, and perceiving the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras; ||27||
Free from anger, greed, and the like; transcending the pairs of opposites; devoid of envy; devoted to self-knowledge; truthful in speech; and endowed with tranquility. (28)
Beholding him, the king then fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff,
his eyes filled with tears of water and his heart overflowing with love.
"Arise, arise; may it be well with you," the sage then said to him.
Then, urged by his teacher, the disciple gave him a grass mat (bṛsī).
Having risen and seated himself before her by her command, King Sumedhas performed the offering of water for the hands and feet and other honors according to the prescribed ritual.
He asked him there: "From where have you come? Who are you, and why are you so absorbed in anxiety?
Tell me freely the cause that has arisen here."
"Tell me the purpose of your arrival; speak the matter that is in your mind. I shall fulfill your desired wish, even if it be impossible for you. (33)
The king said:
"I am a king named Suratha, defeated by my enemies;
having abandoned my kingdom, home, and wife, I have come to you for refuge. (34)
"O Brahman, whatever you command, I shall carry out with devotion;
there is no other protector for me on the surface of the earth but you. (35)
I have terrible fear of my enemies; today I have come into your presence.
Save me, O tiger among sages, you who are compassionate toward those who seek refuge! 36.
The sage said:
"Dwell here without fear, O Indra among kings; indeed, no enemies shall come against you here, for by the power of your asceticism, they will surely be overcome. (37)
"O best of kings, one must not practice violence here; one should sustain life through the forest-dweller's way by means of the recommended wild grains, fruits, and roots. (38)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, that king, free from fear,
then dwelt right there in the hermitage, pure and subsisting on fruits and roots.
Once, while taking refuge in the shade of a tree there, that king,
afflicted by anxiety and with his heart set on returning home, began to reflect.
My kingdom has been seized by enemies—Mlecchas who are ever devoted to sin;
the worlds are being oppressed by those of wicked conduct and shameless character.
All the elephants and horses will become weak and deprived of food;
they will be tormented by the enemy—of this there is no doubt. (42)
All those servants of mine who were formerly protected by me have now fallen under the control of my enemies and have become truly miserable.
"Indeed, my wealth has been spent by others of very wicked conduct, intent on improper expenditures, upon gambling, liquor, female slaves, and the like. (44)
Those evil-minded Mlecchas, though my ministers, will exhaust the treasury through calamities; they are not skilled in the giving of gifts to worthy recipients. 45.
While the king remained at the foot of the tree, absorbed in such thoughts,
a certain merchant, likewise overcome by distress, arrived there.
Seen by the king in front of him, he was seated there at his side;
the king asked him, "Who are you, and from where have you come to the forest? (47)
"Who are you, and why are you so dejected, green-hued, and afflicted by grief?
Speak the truth, O illustrious one; friendship is said to be formed by walking seven steps together. (48)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the king, that best of men sat down, became composed, and, considering it a meeting with a holy man, spoke to him. (49)
The Vaiśya said:
"I am a Vaiśya by birth, well-known by the name Samādhi;
I am wealthy, skilled in dharma, truthful in speech, and free from malice. (50)
Cast out by my sons and wife— who were wicked and greedy for wealth—
and having abandoned my Maya, so difficult to relinquish, under the pretext of being a "miser," I was forsaken by my own kin and quickly reached this forest. (51)
"Who are you? You appear to be fortunate; tell me now, my dear.
The king said:
"I am a king named Suratha, and I have been oppressed by bandits. (52)
"I have arrived here, deprived of my kingdom and deceived by my ministers;
by good fortune, O best of men, you have been met by me here as a friend. (53)
We shall dwell happily here in this forest of auspicious trees;
abandon your grief, O one of great intelligence, and be at ease, O best of the world. (54)
"And stay here with me at your pleasure and in happiness.
The Vaiśya said:
"My family, deprived of me and without support, is suffering greatly."
And it shall become afflicted by anxiety, tormented by disease and grief. 55 ||
"O King, my mind, distressed by the thought that there is neither happiness in the body of my wife nor happiness in the body of my son, finds no peace. (56)
"When shall I see my son, my wife, my home, and my own kin?
O King, my mind is not at ease; it is deeply agitated by thoughts of my household. (57)
The king said:
"O high-minded one, having seen those sons and others who have cast you out—being of wicked conduct and utterly foolish—what happiness will there be for you today? (58)
A benefactor is the best enemy; where are friends who cause suffering?
Therefore, having made your mind firm, sport with me. (59)
The Vaiśya said:
"O King, my mind is not steady today; it is deeply distressed by anxiety for this family, which is so difficult for the wicked-hearted to abandon. (60)
The king said:
"The sorrow born of my kingdom indeed torments my mind as well.
Today let us question the peaceful sage, who is the medicine that destroys grief. (61)
Vyāsa said:
Having thus resolved their minds, the king and the Vaiśya,
filled with humility, went to the sage to inquire about the cause of their grief.
Having gone there and prostrated before that unsurpassed seer as he sat properly, the king—himself seated, peaceful, and having attained tranquility—spoke to him. (63)
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 32 ||
Then the thirty-third chapter.
The King said:
"O Sage, this Vaiśya has now become my friend in the forest."
Cast out by his sons and wife, he has arrived here and attained union with me.
Due to separation from his family, he is exceedingly sorrowful and dejected;
likewise, at this moment, he finds no peace for me either.
"O high-minded one, I am afflicted with grief by the sorrow of having lost my kingdom. ||1||
And this causeless anxiety does not depart from my heart:
"Have my horses grown weak? Or have the elephants fallen under the power of the enemy? (2)
Likewise, the class of servants will become miserable without me;
moreover, the enemies, through their great strength, will exhaust the treasury in an instant.
As I was reflecting in this way, sleep came easily upon my body;
for I knew that this entire world is indeed false, just like a dream.
O Lord, even though I know this, my mind is deluded and does not become steady:
"Who am I? Who are these horses and elephants? Are they mine, or are they my brothers?"
Neither sons nor friends cause me such pain as this suffering;
yet, even though I know it is but an illusion, my mind remains thus afflicted.
Delusion does not depart at all; what is the cause of this wonder?
O Lord, you are omniscient and the destroyer of all doubts. (7)
"O ocean of compassion, tell me the cause of this delusion of mine.
Vyāsa said:
Thus questioned then by the king, Sumedhas, the best of sages, [replied]. (8)
He spoke to him that supreme knowledge which destroys grief and delusion. The sage said:
"Listen, O King, I shall explain the cause of bondage and liberation. (9)
She is renowned here as Mahāmāyā to all living beings;
[so too are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśāna, Indra, Varuṇa, and Vāyu. || 10 ||
All the gods and humans, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas; various trees and creepers, as well as beasts, wild animals, and birds. || 11 ||
And they are all subject to Māyā, being the vessel for both bondage and liberation;
by her this entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, has been created. 12.
He surely remains under its control, bound by the snare of delusion;
what are you, one among men, a kṣatriya defiled by passion? (13)
For she constantly deludes even the minds of the wise;
for even Brahmā, Śiva, Vāsudeva, and others remain subject to her influence, despite their possession of knowledge. (14)
They too, deluded by passion, wander about in the world.
O King, in former times, during the Satya Yuga, Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa himself—
Having reached Śvetadvīpa, he performed extensive penance for ten thousand years in order to attain proficiency in the knowledge of Brahman.
Then, contemplating that which is beyond this for the sake of imperishable bliss,
even Brahmā went to a certain solitary place of supreme wonder.
O Indra among kings, that Vāsudeva Hari once remained in ascetic penance for the sake of dispelling delusion, while his mind was directed toward another place.
Rising from that place, O king of kings, he departed with a desire to see another;
the four-faced one likewise emerged from the dry land.
Having met on the way, the four-faced and the four-armed ones asked one another, "Who are you? Who are you? indeed.
Brahmā said to that god, "I am indeed the creator of the universe.
Viṣṇu said to him, "O fool, I, the infallible one, am the creator of the universe;
how insignificant you are, being devoid of power and dependent upon the quality of passion (rajas)."
Know me as the eternal Vāsudeva, who indeed rests within all beings.
Having fought a most terrible battle, you have been protected by me this very day, for you came to me for refuge, oppressed by the two Dānavas. (23)
"Those two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, have indeed been slain by me.
Why do you boast, O dull-witted one? Abandon this delusion at once! (24)
"In this vast expanse of saṃsāra, there is no one superior even to me.
The sage said:
While Brahmā and Viṣṇu were thus speaking to one another, [the Lord appeared]. (25)
With their lips quivering and their eyes bloodshot, they became trembling;
while they were thus disputing, [the sword] suddenly appeared before them. (26)
In the midst [of it], there was a vast, long, and wonderful linga, white as nectar;
then, suddenly, an incorporeal voice spoke there from the sky.
Having awakened those two illustrious ones who were disputing with one another, [he said]:
"O Brahmā, O Viṣṇu, do not engage in mutual dispute. (28)
"Whoever goes from the bottom to the very top of this liṅga, remaining fixed above it, shall indeed always be the superior one between you two. (29)
"Let one go now to the netherworld and the other to the sky;
my word must be carried out, abandoning this useless dispute. (30)
"In this dispute between the two of us here, an arbiter must always be appointed.
The sage said:
"Having heard that divine speech, they both prepared themselves and exerted their efforts. (31)
They went to worship the foremost Liṅga of wondrous appearance;
Viṣṇu descended to the netherworld (Pātāla), while Brahmā ascended to the very heavens.

In order to increase his own greatness, Viṣṇu went toward the Great Liṅga to measure it; however, he became exhausted after traveling only a short distance, for the Liṅga was exerted by its entire essence.
He did not reach the end of the liṅga, but turned back and went to dry land;
then Brahmā went further upward and found a fallen ketaka petal.
Having received it from the head of Śiva and returned filled with joy,
Brahmā quickly approached Viṣṇu with a *ketakī* petal.
Having shown it to be false, he, deluded by pride, said:
"This ketaki petal was taken from the top of the linga. (36)
"It has been brought for recognition and for the pacification of your mind.
Having heard those words of Brahmā and having seen the ketaka petal, [he was filled with joy].
Hari replied to him: "Who now is the witness?
[Tell me of one who is] a speaker of truth, wise, of virtuous conduct, pure, and impartial. (38)
He becomes a witness in every instance when a dispute arises.
Brahmā said:
"Who is the witness now who has arrived from a distant land at this moment? (39)
"That which is true, these words of hers, this Ketakī flower shall declare.
Having spoken thus, the Ketakī was clearly dispatched there by Brahmā. (40)
He quickly spoke these words and awakened the wielder of the Śārṅga bow:
"Brahmā has arrived, having taken me who was stationed upon the head of Śiva. (41)
"O Viṣṇu, you should never entertain any doubt in this matter;
for my word is authoritative, and Brahmā has indeed reached the further shore of it."
Having heard the words of Ketakī, "He has come taking me, who was offered by the devotees of Śiva," Hari spoke as if smiling: 43.
"Mahādeva is my authority, if he should speak these words.
The Rishi said:
Having heard those words of Hari, the eternal Mahādeva [spoke]. 44.
Enraged, he said to the Ketakī: "O speaker of falsehood, do not speak!
You were encountered by me as I was passing through the midst [of the forest] and fell from my head. (45)
"Indeed, you who speak falsely have been abandoned by me forever.
Then Brahmā, overcome with shame, bowed down to Madhusūdana.
From that day forth, O King, the Ketakī was indeed abandoned by Śiva among all flowers;
thus, know the power of Māyā, which causes delusion even for the wise. What need is there to speak of other living beings regarding such bewilderment?
For the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, the Lord of Ramā [assumed the form] of all the gods.
Hari, the Lord Mādhava, who takes incarnations in various wombs, swiftly deceives the Daityas by casting off all fear of sin. (49)
Having abandoned the bliss of happiness, the omnipresent Lord engaged in battle with the Daityas;
surely this is the power of Māyā, even in Mādhava, the teacher of the world. 50.
O King, what need is there to speak of anyone else regarding the task of the gods for the Omniscient One?
For even the minds of the wise are surely drawn toward the Supreme Nature.
O Lord of the Earth, she forcibly draws [beings] away and delivers them to delusion;
by this Blessed Lady all this world, both moving and unmoving, is pervaded. (52)
"She alone is the giver of delusion and the giver of knowledge; she is always the bestower of both bondage and liberation.
The King said:
"O Blessed One, tell me her true nature and her supreme power. (53)
[He is] the cause of origination, the support, and that which is supreme.
The sage said:
"And there is never any origination for her, O King, because she is beginningless. (54)
That supreme goddess is eternal and the cause of all causes;
she exists within all beings as power, O King, through her entire self.
A living being is entirely devoid of power, like a corpse;
for the power of consciousness (cicchakti) exists in all beings, and that alone is its true form.
The manifestation and disappearance of the gods occur for the accomplishment of their tasks;
O lord of the people, when both gods and men offer praise to her, [these things happen]. 57.
The goddess Ambikā appears for the destruction of the suffering of living beings;
she assumes various forms and is endowed with manifold powers. 58.
The Supreme Goddess manifests by her own will for the sake of accomplishing her tasks;
that Goddess is not subject to fate, O King, unlike all the other gods.
It is never subject to the power of time, but proceeds according to human effort;
the Puruṣa is the non-agent and the witness, while this entire world is the object of perception. 60.
She alone is the mother of all that is visible, the Goddess whose nature is both being and non-being;
she, as the one, delights the Puruṣa by performing the drama of the cosmic egg.
When the Puruṣa is colored [by her], she withdraws everything with extreme velocity;
by her, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are made the instrumental causes.
These beings have been fashioned for their respective tasks and impelled by you through your divine play;
having projected a portion of yourself into them, they have been made exceedingly powerful.
To them were given the horse, the spear, Gīḥ, Lakṣmī, and likewise Girijā;
those lords of gods meditate upon her and worship her with supreme joy.
Having known the power that is the sovereign of all, the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction—
this entire supreme majesty of the Goddess has been recounted to you.
O King, according to my own understanding, I do not know its end.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 33 ||
Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter.
The King said:
"O Blessed One, tell me correctly the procedure for her propitiation."
"Tell me the ritual for worship, the mantras, and likewise the ritual for the fire-oblation (homa).
The Sage said:
"Listen, O King, I shall explain her auspicious ritual for worship."
It bestows desires and liberation upon men, grants knowledge, and destroys suffering. ||2||
First, having performed the ritual of bathing, the man, being pure and wearing white garments,
should sip water for purification (ācamana) with a restrained mind and prepare his own auspicious sanctuary.
Then, having established an excellent seat upon the consecrated ground,
he sat there according to the prescribed rite and, filled with joy, performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times.
Having properly arranged the articles of worship according to one's capacity,
one should then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and carry out the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
One should perform the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) after sprinkling the ritual materials with mantras;
then, having determined the auspicious time, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the prescribed rule.
In an auspicious copper vessel, one should draw a six-pointed yantra with white sandalwood paste, and outside of that, an eight-pointed one.
Then, one should write down the seed-syllables (bījas) of the nine-syllabled mantra,
having performed the consecration of the yantra according to the injunctions prescribed in the Vedas.
Or one should fashion an image made of metal and perform worship with the mantras proclaimed by Śiva;
O protector of the earth, one should diligently perform the worship of the Blessed Lady.
Having performed the worship according to the rules as prescribed in the Āgamas, one should, with a concentrated mind,
constantly recite the nine-syllable mantra preceded by meditation.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with a tenth part [of the total], and the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of that;
likewise, one should cause the feeding of Brahmins to be performed with a tenth part of that.
One should daily recite the three Caritras and perform the ritual dismissal;
likewise, the Navarātra vow must be observed according to the prescribed injunctions.
O lord of men, one who desires auspiciousness should observe the fast of Navarātra during the bright fortnight of both Āśvina and Caitra.
A very extensive fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with mantras to be recited, using well-prepared milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with sugar, clarified butter (ghṛta), and honey. 14.
Or it should be performed with goat meat, or likewise with auspicious bilva leaves,
or with red flowers of the hayāri plant, or with sesame seeds mixed with sugar.
On the eighth, the fourteenth, and especially on the ninth day, the worship of the Goddess must be performed, as well as the feeding of Brahmins. (16)
The poor man obtains wealth; the sick man is liberated from disease;
and the childless man obtains virtuous sons who remain under his control. ||17||
A king fallen from his kingdom regains a universal empire;
one oppressed by enemies slays the foe through the grace of Māyā. (18)
The seeker of knowledge who performs worship with his senses restrained obtains blameless and auspicious learning; of this there is no doubt. (19)
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, one who worships the Mother of the Worlds with devotion shall become a partaker of all happiness. || 20 ||
Any group of men and women who performs the Navarātra vow,
being ever devoted with faith, attains their desired fruit.
He who, endowed with devotion, performs the auspicious Navarātra vow during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, shall attain all his desires. ||22||
Having constructed the maṇḍala according to the rules, one should prepare the place of worship;
there, one should install the water-pot (kalaśa) according to the ritual procedure of the Vedic mantras.
Having fashioned a very beautiful yantra, one should place it upon the water-jar (kalaśa),
after having sown beautiful barley grains arranged around its sides.
Having fashioned a canopy above, covered with garlands of flowers,
and well-provided with incense and lamps, the temple of Caṇḍikā should be prepared.
Worship should be performed there three times a day according to one's capacity;
one must not practice stinginess regarding wealth in the worship of Caṇḍikā.
With incenses, lamps, excellent food offerings, and numerous fruits and flowers;
likewise with songs, instrumental music, the recitation of hymns, and the complete chanting of the Vedas.
A festival should be celebrated there accompanied by various musical instruments,
and the worship of young maidens should be performed according to the prescribed rites.
With sandalwood, ornaments, garments, and various kinds of food, as well as with fragrant oils and garlands that are pleasing to the mind. (29)

Having performed worship in this manner, one should carry out the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the rules of the mantra-vidhi on either the eighth or the ninth lunar day, following the prescribed ritual.
Afterwards, on the tenth day, one should feed the Brahmins and perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa);
kings, filled with devotion, should give gifts according to their capacity.
Thus, the man who performs the Navarātra vow with devotion, or the woman—whether she be a married wife or a widow devoted to her husband—who does so with devotion; || 32 ||
In this world, one who is devoted to this vow obtains the pleasures desired by the mind;
at the end of the body, such a person attains the supreme abode.
In another birth, devotion to Ambikā becomes unfailing;
having attained birth in an excellent family, he indeed becomes one of virtuous conduct.
The Navarātra vow has been proclaimed as the most excellent among all vows;
it is the supreme worship of Śivā that bestows all happiness. (35)
By this method, O King, propitiate Caṇḍikā;
having conquered his enemies, he shall obtain an unsurpassed and unshakable kingdom. (36)
Furthermore, O King, you will obtain supreme happiness in this body within your own home, having regained your sons and wife; of this there is no doubt. (37)
"O best of Vaiśyas, you yourself must now propitiate the Goddess Māyā, the Sovereign of the Universe, the bestower of desires, who effects both creation and dissolution. (38)
And having returned home, you will be honored by your own kinsmen, and you shall again obtain worldly happiness according to your desires. (39)
Your residence will be in the auspicious world of the Goddess; of this there is no doubt.
Those by whom the Blessed Lady has not been propitiated are destined for hell.
In this world, O King, men become afflicted by extreme suffering, tormented by various diseases, and defeated by their enemies. (41)
For they were without wives and without sons, afflicted by craving and of rigid intellect;
[they worshipped] with bilva leaves, karavīra flowers, śatapatras, and campakas. ||42||
Those by whom the Mother of the worlds has been worshipped become exceedingly graceful;
they are performers of merit who are devoted to Śakti and to devotion. ||43||

Those men who have worshipped Bhavānī with mantras recited from the Vedas become lords of speech, possessing human dignity, enriched with wealth, power, and happiness, and becoming the receptacles of all multitudes of virtues; they become the foremost among the ornaments of kings in this world. (44)
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 34 ||
Now begins the thirty-fifth chapter.
Mahiṣa said:
Having heard these words of his, the Vaiśya and the king were indeed distressed.
Having prostrated before the Sage with affection, they bowed down deeply with humility. ||1||
With eyes wide open with joy, those two, skilled in speech,
spoke with palms joined in reverence, tranquil and with hearts inclined toward devotion.
O Blessed One, today we two have been purified, made peaceful,
and freed from our wretchedness and grief by your eloquent speech, just as Bhagīratha was by the Gaṅgā.
In this world, there arise virtuous ones who are intent on benefiting others;
delighting in their genuine qualities, they bring happiness to all embodied beings. (4)
"O highly fortunate one, through the power of past merit, this auspicious body has been obtained by us both; it is the destroyer of great suffering. (5)
On this earth there are many men who are solely intent on their own self-interest;
those who are skilled in accomplishing the welfare of others are rare, appearing only here and there like you.
"I am suffering, O best of sages, and this Vaiśya is also deeply distressed;
both of us, scorched by the cycle of worldly existence, have come with joy to your hermitage. (7)
O wise one, by the mere sight of you, the suffering born of our bodies and minds has now departed from both of us simply upon hearing your words. (8)
"O Brahmin, ocean of compassion, by the nectar-like essence of your well-spoken words, we two have become blessed and have fulfilled our purpose; we have been purified by your grace. (9)
"O holy one, take our hands; lead us across the ocean of worldly existence. Knowing that we are submerged and exhausted, do so now by granting us the sacred mantra. (10)
Having performed extensive austerities and propitiated the Goddess who bestows happiness,
we shall obtain her vision once more and return to our own abode.
Having received the nine-syllable mantra of the Goddess from your mouth, [we shall proceed].
And we two shall perform remembrance of you, fasting and firm in our vows.
Vyāsa said:
Thus urged by those two, Sumedhas, the best of sages, gave them the auspicious mantra preceded by the seed-syllable of meditation. 13.
Having obtained the mantra from the sage and having consulted together, the two—
the Guru and the King— went to an excellent riverbank.
Having taken their seats in a solitary and secluded place,
those two of steady wisdom sat down, their bellies exceedingly lean;
intent upon the recitation of mantras, they were peaceful and devoted to the study of the three codes of conduct.
For one month they remained there, devoted entirely to meditation.
By that very month-long vow, an unsurpassed affection arose for them,
and their intellect became firmly fixed upon the lotus feet of Bhavānī.
Once, having gone to the feet of that high-souled sage and performed their salutations, they returned and stood upon a seat of kusha grass.
They were never at any time intent on any other task;
they were constantly devoted to the meditation on the Goddess and always engaged in the recitation of mantras.
When the full year had thus passed,
O King, they both abandoned their diet of fruits and subsisted on leaves instead.
For one year, the Vaiśya and the king performed austerities there,
subsisting on dry leaves, self-controlled, and devoted to recitation and meditation.
When two full years had passed, they once beheld a captivating vision of the Blessed Lady within a dream.
Once, even in a dream, the king beheld the Mother of the World, the Goddess clad in red garments and adorned with beautiful ornaments. 23.
Having seen the goddess in their dream, the two became filled with joy;
then, when the third year had arrived, they subsisted on water alone.
Having done this for three years, the Vaiśya and the king, longing for a vision [of the deity], then began to reflect thus in their minds. (25)
The sight of the Goddess, which grants peace to men, has not been obtained;
we two, deeply afflicted and miserable, shall give up our bodies. (26)
Having reflected thus in his mind, the king fashioned a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that was triangular,
very stable, pleasing, and one cubit in measurement.
Having established the sacred fire, the king and likewise the Vaiśya, being exceedingly devoted,
dwelt in a cave and repeatedly cut off their own flesh.
Likewise, the Vaiśya also then cast his own flesh into the blazing fire; and those two, having exerted themselves, offered an oblation of blood to her. (29)
Then the Blessed Lady, having granted them a direct vision,
spoke to those two who were deeply distressed, seeing them overwhelmed by an excess of love.
The illustrious Goddess said: "Choose a boon, O King, whatever is desired in your heart;
I am pleased today by your penance, for you are considered by me to be a devotee. (31)
Then the Goddess said to the Vaiśya: "O high-minded one, I am pleased.
What is your desire? I shall grant it today; quickly pray for whatever is in your heart. (32)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words, the king, filled with joy, spoke to her:
"Give me back today my own kingdom, for the strength of my enemies has been destroyed by force. (33)
Then the Goddess said to him: "Go, O King, to your own home;
your enemies, their strength exhausted, shall depart defeated. (34)
But the ministers, having assembled, will fall at your feet and say:
"O illustrious one, rule the kingdom in your own city as you please. (35)
O King, having ruled a vast kingdom for ten thousand years,
at the end of his life he will take birth from the Sun and become a Manu.
Vyāsa said:
The pure Vaiśya, with his palms joined in reverence, spoke this to her as well:
"I have no need for a house, nor indeed for a son or wealth. (37)
O Mother, everything that causes bondage is clearly perishable like a dream;
grant me pure knowledge, which bestows liberation and destroys bondage. (38)
In this essence-less cycle of existence, the foolish and the vulgar sink;
the wise cross over here, and therefore they do not desire worldly existence. 39.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard that, Mahāmāyā spoke to the Vaiśya standing before her: "O best of Vaiśyas, you shall attain knowledge; of this there is no doubt. (40)
Having thus granted the boon to them, he vanished right there;
and when she had become invisible, the king [beheld] that best of sages.
Having prostrated and mounted his horse, he set his mind on departing;
at that very moment, his ministers and subjects arrived there before the king.
Endowed with humility, they bowed down and, standing with palms joined in reverence, said to him:
"O King, all those enemies of yours have been slain in battle because of their own sins."
"O King, remaining in your city, rule your kingdom free from all thorns.
Having heard those words, the king bowed to that best of sages.
Having taken his leave there, he departed surrounded by his ministers;
and having reached his own kingdom, he rejoined his wife, kinsmen, and relatives.
Then he ruled over the entire earth, girdled by the oceans;
even as a Vaiśya, having attained knowledge, he became entirely free from attachment.
There, having been released from bondage,
he spent his time wandering among the sacred fords (tīrthas) while singing the praises of the Blessed One’s virtues.
Thus has been told to you this most wonderful life-story of the Goddess,
and how the two— the king and the merchant— attained the fruit of their propitiation exactly as it was.
The slaying of the Daityas has been proclaimed, as well as her auspicious manifestation;
such is the power of that Goddess, who bestows fearlessness upon her devotees. (49)
The man who constantly hears this supreme narrative truly attains the wonderful happiness of worldly existence. (50)
This wonderful narrative is truly purifying upon hearing; it bestows knowledge, liberation, fame, and likewise happiness. (51)
It bestows all goals upon men, is encompassed by all dharma, and is considered the supreme cause of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. ||52||
Sūta said:
Being questioned by King Janamejaya,
Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī and knower of the truth of all matters, spoke this divine compendium (Saṃhitā).
The compassionate Lord Kṛṣṇa, the sage, recounted the life-story of Caṇḍikā, which concerns the slaying of the demon Śumbha.
Thus, O lords of sages, the essence of the Purāṇas has been recounted to you.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter in the fifth book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 35 ||
The fifth skandha of this Devībhāgavata has been proclaimed by the wise Vyāsa in two thousand and ninety verses (2090). ||5||
This fifth section is concluded:
the description of the contemplation of various stratagems by Indra, the king of the gods, for the purpose of breaking the ascetic penance of Triśiras.
The sages said:
O Sūta, O Sūta, O highly fortunate one! Your words are sweet like nectar;
we are not satiated by drinking this auspicious work composed by Dvaipāyana.
Furthermore, we wish to ask you about an auspicious ancient narrative, which is recounted even in the Vedas—a delightful, well-known story that destroys all sins. (2)
The powerful son of Tvaṣṭṛ, renowned as the Asura Vṛtra—
how was he slain in battle by the high-souled Vāsava?
Tvaṣṭṛ was indeed a partisan of the gods, and his son, who was even more powerful and born of Brahman, was slain by Śakra; why was this so? || 4 ||

The gods are said to be born of the quality of goodness (sattva), humans are known to be of the nature of passion (rājasa), and animals are declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa) by those who proclaim the Purāṇas and Āgamas. || 5 ||
Indeed, a great contradiction appears here with the performer of a hundred sacrifices;
for by means of deceit, the powerful Vṛtra was struck down by Śakra.
Viṣṇu is the impeller therein; he is the supreme upholder of *sattva*.
That Lord, the Blessed One, entered into the midst of the thunderbolt by means of a disguise.
Having thus made a pact and being addressed with these words, that one of great strength abandoned the truth and was struck down by the two monkeys with the foam of the water.
"O charioteer, what is this rash act committed by Indra with his horse?
Even great beings, when deceived by delusion, fall prey to evil intentions. (9)
O best of gods, those who act unjustly fall far from excellence;
it is through being endowed with right conduct that the gods have attained the status of the learned (śiṣṭa).
Such being the case, what kind of cultured status can there be for one who possesses such distinguished qualities, when Śakra again killed the trusting Vṛtra by means of a stratagem? (11)
"Has the fruit of sin arising from the slaughter of a Brahmin not been obtained by us?
Furthermore, what was previously stated by you—that the slaying of the demon Vṛtra was performed [by Indra]? (12)
"Even that [account] of the illustrious Goddess deludes our minds here.
Sūta said:
"O sages, listen to the account concerning the slaying of the demon Vṛtra."
Just as Indra experienced suffering arising from the act of killing,
so too was Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, questioned in former times.
I shall relate what was said by King Pārīkṣita as well.
Janamejaya said:
"O Sage, how was Vṛtrāsura formerly slain by Maghavan?"
Having obtained Viṣṇu as his ally through a virtuous stratagem,
for what reason and by what cause was that Daitya slain by the Goddess?
O bull among sages, how could the killing of one be accomplished by two?
I desire to hear this, for my curiosity is indeed great. (17)
"Who among men would not become detached from worldly things upon hearing the life-story of the great?
