O Mother, please narrate the account of your own glory as it relates to the slaying of the demon Vṛtra."
Vyāsa said:
"O King, you are blessed; such an intellect as yours has arisen, being so deeply devoted to hearing the Purāṇas."
Having drunk the nectar, those best of gods indeed become free from thirst regarding all drinks for all time. || 19 ||
O King of illustrious fame, when a listener hears the stories with a single-minded focus day after day, his state of devotion increases ever further.
Then the speaker, with a joyful mind, says: || 20 ||
The battle between Vāsava and Vṛtra, which is well-known in the Veda as well as in the Purāṇa,
resulted in suffering being experienced by the Lord of the Gods in that very same way.
Having slain the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, he remained entirely free from sin.
O King, what is so wonderful here that Triśiras was slain by Hari and Vajrabhṛt through a ruse, or that Vṛtra was likewise struck down?
Even the sages were deluded by the power of their *māyā*.
And, fearing sin, they indeed censured him incessantly. || 22 ||
Even Viṣṇu, though his very form is the essence of goodness, always slew the Daityas through deceit, having fallen under the delusion of desire;
who else is there capable of conquering that Blessed Goddess even with the mind?
He was capable of [worshipping] Bhavānī, who deludes all people. || 23 ||
By which [power] even the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the friend of Nara, the infinite one, was immediately directed here into thousands of yugas within the wombs of fish and other such forms.
Sometimes it performs actions that are prescribed or prohibited. || 24 ||
Falling under the delusion that "this body, this wealth, this house, these kinsmen, my sons, and my wife are mine," everyone performs meritorious deeds and likewise accumulates a heap of sins.
For he has been rendered distraught by the exceedingly powerful qualities of Māyā. || 25 ||
O King, no man whatsoever who understands the nature of the higher and the lower is ever capable of destroying delusion;
for he remains fundamentally deluded by those very three.
Having brought his self under control, he [dwelt] extensively upon the surface of the earth. || 26 ||
Then Viṣṇu and Vāsava, utterly deluded by that illusion and intent on accomplishing their own ends, slew Vṛtra through a stratagem.
Therefore, O lord of the earth, I shall fully relate the account of the cause of the ancient enmity between Vṛtra and Vāsava.
Tvaṣṭṛ was indeed Prajāpati, the best of gods and a great ascetic;
he was the performer of the gods' tasks, skillful and dear to the Brāhmaṇas. || 29 ||
Out of hatred for Indra, he indeed created a son named Triśiras,
who was renowned by the name Viśvarūpa and was enchanting in appearance.
With his three excellent and captivating faces, he shone brilliantly;
with those three mouths, the sage accomplished the three distinct tasks.
With one mouth he studied the Vedas, with another he drank wine,
and with the third he simultaneously gazed upon all the directions.
Having renounced his worldly enjoyments, Triśiras performed most difficult austerities;
as an ascetic, gentle and self-controlled, he took refuge in dharma alone. (33)
The practice of the five fires at the proper time, standing on the tips of one's feet, and dwelling in the midst of water during the late autumn and winter seasons; || 34 ||
Without food, having conquered his self and renounced all possessions, that wise man performed austerities difficult for those of dull intellect to perform. (35)
And seeing him performing penance, the Lord of Śacī fell into distress; Śakra there became despondent, thinking, "May this man not become [the Indra]. (36)
Having seen the ascetic power, heroism, and truthfulness of that one of immeasurable splendor, Indra,
the subduer of Pāka, fell into deep anxiety day and night.
"As he grows stronger, this three-headed one will destroy me;
a wise person must by no means neglect an enemy whose power is increasing. (38)
Therefore, a means must now be employed for the destruction of my asceticism;
for desire is the enemy of austerities, and indeed, through desire, austerity perishes. (39)
"Thinking thus in his mind, 'In this very way it must be done today so that he becomes attached to enjoyments,' the wise Balamardana [acted]. (40)
He commanded the Apsarases— Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Ghṛtācī, and Tilottamā— to entice the son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
Then Śakra summoned those women who were proud of their beauty and said to them:
"All of you, do what is pleasing to me now that this task has arisen. (42)
"Since today a great and invincible enemy of mine is performing austerities, go quickly and entice him; do what must be done without delay."
"By means of various amorous costumes and gestures arising from the body, entice me—blessings be upon you—and pacify my fever. (44)
"O illustrious ones, knowing his power of asceticism, I am unwell;
today that powerful one will take my seat without delay. (45)
"O powerless ones, quickly dispel the fear that has come upon me;
together, assist me now that this task has arrived. (46)
Having heard those words, the women bowed before him and said:
"O Lord of Gods, do not fear; we shall strive to entice him."
O one of great splendor, you must act in such a way that no fear arises from him, by means of enticing that sage with dance, song, and diversions. (48)
"O Lord, having deluded the sage with side-long glances and various gestures of the limbs, we shall bring that greedy man under our control and subjugate him. (49)
Vyāsa said:
Having thus addressed Hari, the women went into the presence of Triśiras,
displaying various gestures appropriate even to the treatises on love.
Singing with various rhythmic patterns and dancing before the sage,
those excellent women attempted to entice him by manifesting diverse emotions.
That mass of asceticism did not perceive the deceptive charms of women;
having brought his senses under control, he remained as if mute, blind, and deaf. (52)
For some days those women remained in that excellent hermitage,
performing elaborate displays of singing, dancing, and other arts that were exceedingly enchanting.
When the sage Triśiras did not waver from his meditation at will,
the goddesses turned back and again approached Śakra.
Then all of them, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the king of the gods;
they were exhausted, miserable, terrified by fear, and their faces were exceedingly pale.
O God of gods, O Great King, the utmost effort has been made;
yet that invincible one cannot be shaken from his fortitude, O Lord.
"O Indra, subduer of Paka, another means must be devised by all means;
our strength is of no avail against this ascetic who has conquered his senses. (57)
By good fortune we have not been cursed by this great-souled sage, who indeed blazes with ascetic power like a fire. (58)
Having dismissed the Apsarases, Śakra, dull-witted and evil-minded as he was, brooded upon an improper means for his destruction. (59)
Having cast aside both worldly shame and his intense fear of sin,
O Lord of the Earth, he formed a wicked intent to kill him.
The description of the birth of Vṛtra following the slaying of Triśiras.
Vyāsa said:
Then that lord of the gods, having succumbed to greed—
Having attained [his seat] and being established upon his elephant-throne,
he of wicked mind then beheld the sage of immeasurable prowess facing toward Triśiras. || 1 ||
Beholding him seated firmly upon his seat, having conquered speech and come under the power of perfect concentration,
radiant with splendor like the sun or fire;
The lord of the gods fell into the greatest calamity. || 2 ||
Alas, how can I slay this sage who is indeed renowned for his sinless mind? He is an enemy whose power of asceticism is fully kindled.
How can one who desires a seat here remain indifferent? || 3 ||
Having reflected thus, he released toward the sage established in austerity his supreme weapon, the thunderbolt—
a swift missile resembling the moon and the sun.
The Lord of the hosts of gods himself [confronted] Triśiras.
Struck by that blow, the ascetic indeed fell to the surface of the earth and died,
like the peak of a mountain shattered by a thunderbolt.
And it fell upon the earth, a wondrous sight to behold. || 5 ||
Having slain him, the Lord of the Gods attained joy, while the sages standing there cried out, "Alas, alas!
with sounds of intense distress, exclaiming, "What has been done by the sinful Indra?"
The lord of Śacī, a treasure-house of asceticism, was slain by that evil-minded, wicked soul without cause; indeed,
this is surely the fruit of his own violent deed.
Let the sinner incur the consequence arising from the act of killing.
Having swiftly struck him down, the king of the gods quickly departed for his own palace;
though slain, that great-souled one still shone resplendent.
Like one still living, he was a treasury of splendors.
Seeing him fallen upon the ground as if still alive, the slayer of Vṛtra was overcome with anxiety, his limbs utterly distressed, wondering: "How could this man live again?"
Having reflected deeply in his mind and beholding the carpenter standing before him, Maghavan spoke words appropriate to his own purpose.
"Carve it; cut off its heads and do as I say!
Let this one of great splendor not live, for he shines as if he were alive himself. (11)
Having heard these words of his, the carpenter spoke in reproach.
The carpenter said:
"Your great shoulder shines intensely; the axe will not pass through."
Therefore, I shall not perform this despicable deed;
for you have committed an act censured by you yourself and condemned by the virtuous.
"I am indeed afraid of sin, as if it were the killing of one already dead.
This sage is already as good as dead; what is the use of cutting off his head? (14)
"O Pākaśāsana, tell me, what fear has arisen within you here?
Indra replied, "This body appears with a clear form, as if it were still alive. (15)
"Therefore I am afraid; may this enemy of mine not live as a sage.
Takṣaka said:
"O learned one, are you not ashamed here of this cruel deed? (16)
"Having killed this son of a seer, do you have no fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin?
Indra said:
"I shall indeed perform an expiation later for the destruction of my evil deed. (17)
"An enemy must be slain by all means, even by deceit, O Great-minded One.
The carpenter said:
"O Indra, struck by greed, you commit a sin here."
“Without him, how shall I commit sin? Tell me, O Lord.
Indra said:
“I shall indeed always grant you a share in the sacrifices.”
"Men will offer the head as your portion in the sacrifice;
for this price, cut off his heads and do what pleases you."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Mahendra, the carpenter was filled with joy;
indeed, with a very firm axe, he cut off his heads.
When the three heads were severed and fell upon the ground,
thousands of birds quickly flew forth from them.
Then, kalaviṅkas, tittiris, and likewise kapiñjalas,
each separately, rushed forth swiftly from his mouth.
From that mouth by which he used to study the Vedas and likewise drink the Soma,
it is said that Kapiñjala birds emerged instantly.
Because he gazed at all directions at will as if drinking them in,
from him were born there the partridges (tittiras), possessed of fierce splendor.
That mouth of Triśiras which drank liquor, O King, is said to have produced sparrows; thus those birds emerged from him.
O King, having seen those egg-born beings thus emerged from them, Śakra rejoiced in his mind and returned once more to the third heaven.
When Śakra had departed, O Lord of the Earth, the carpenter also went quickly to his own home;
having obtained a supreme share of the sacrifice, he attained great joy.
Then Indra, having returned to his own home and slain the mighty enemy,
considered himself to have accomplished his purpose, disregarding the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having heard that his most righteous son had been slain, Tvaṣṭṛ became exceedingly enraged in his mind and spoke these words: || 30 ||
"Since you have slain my innocent son, a sage, I shall therefore produce another son for the purpose of slaying you. (31)
"Let the gods behold my heroism as well as the power of my asceticism;
let that evil-souled one recognize everything—the great fruit of his own actions. (32)
Having spoken thus, Tvaṣṭṛ, overwhelmed with anger, then offered oblations into the fire with mantras proclaimed in the Atharvaveda for the purpose of producing a son.
When the oblation had been performed for eight nights, a man resembling fire suddenly emerged from the blazing sacrificial fire.
Seeing that son before him, endowed with splendor and strength, appearing as if he were a blazing fire manifested from the speed of Agni, Tvaṣṭṛ—
Tvaṣṭṛ, looking at his son standing before him, spoke these words:
"O enemy of Indra, increase by the power of my ascetic heat."
When these words were spoken by Tvaṣṭṛ, who was blazing with anger,
he grew in size, reaching up to the heavens, with a splendor equal to Vaiśvānara.
Born with the form of a mountain, like Time or Death itself, and possessing sovereign power, he said to his extremely distressed father, "What shall I do? (38)
"O Lord of noble vows, tell me what task I should perform for you;
why are you so distressed by anxiety? Tell me the cause of your grief. (39)
"I shall destroy your grief today; this is the vow I have undertaken. Why, then, should my father be further distressed by your birth? (40)
I shall drink up the ocean this very instant, I shall pulverize the mountains,
and I shall today restrain the rising sun of fierce radiance.
I shall instantly slay Indra along with the gods, or Yama, or any other deity;
I shall even uproot the entire earth and cast it into the ocean.
Having heard these pleasing words of his son, Tvaṣṭṛ,
being exceedingly delighted, replied to that son who was like a mountain.
"O son, because you are now able to protect [the world] from evil (vṛjina),
therefore your name shall be known as Vṛtra."
O highly fortunate one, your brother was an ascetic named Triśiras;
he indeed possessed three heads that were full of vigor. (45)
He was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, proficient in all branches of learning,
and was mostly established in ascetic penance that inspired wonder throughout the three worlds.
But today he has been struck by Śakra with the blow of his thunderbolt;
and suddenly, without any offense, their heads have been severed. (47)
Therefore, O tiger among men, slay Śakra, who has committed a crime—he who is devoid of shame, evil-minded, deceitful, and burdened by the sin of ten thousand Brahman-murders. 48.
Having spoken thus, Tvaṣṭṛ, overwhelmed with grief for his son,
then fashioned various divine weapons.
And he gave him, for the sake of slaying the thousand-eyed one, powerful weapons indeed,
headed by swords, spears, maces, javelins, and lances.
Likewise, he held the Śārṅga bow and arrows, a mace, and a sharp-edged spear,
as well as the divine thousand-spoked discus, equal in splendor to Sudarśana.
And two divine, inexhaustible quivers, and a most beautiful armor;
a chariot resembling a cloud, firm, capable of bearing great weight, and swift.
O King, having prepared all the equipment for battle and given it to his son,
Tvaṣṭṛ, filled with wrath, dispatched him.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Vṛtra Following the Slaying of Triśiras," in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Vṛtra’s Instruction by Tvaṣṭṛ for the Purpose of Worshipping Brahmā.
Vyāsa said:
Having had rites for his well-being performed by Brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas, Vṛtra—
The immensely powerful one, mounted upon his chariot, went forth to slay Śakra. || 1 ||
At that very time, the cruel Rākṣasas, who had previously been defeated by the gods,
assembled for the sake of service, having learned that Vṛtra possessed great strength.
But the messengers of Indra, seeing that he had arrived for battle,
came with speed and reported the news of his activities to him.
The messengers said:
"O Lord, your enemy named Vṛtra is quickly approaching here;
he is powerful, mounted upon a chariot, and is said to have been created by Tvaṣṭṛ."

Indeed, out of anger and tormented by the thought of having slain his son, he acted without reflection for the purpose of your destruction; he was accompanied by the Rākṣasas, who were difficult to withstand.
Exert yourself, O illustrious one; a terrible and most dreadful sound, resembling Mount Meru and Mandara, is now approaching swiftly.
In the meantime, the hosts of gods, being greatly terrified there,
approached and spoke to the Lord of the Gods as he was listening to the messenger's words.
The Gaṇas said:
"O Maghavan, ill omens are appearing in the abode of the gods;
there are many cries of birds foreboding fear."
Crows, vultures, hawks, herons, and other such dreadful birds are crying out with distorted sounds and vomit upon the palace.
The birds are crying out loudly with "cī-cī-kū-cī" sounds,
and streams of water are falling down from the eyes of the mounts.
O illustrious one, a very great and terrible sound of weeping rakshasis is heard upon the roof of the palace even at night. (11)
O giver of honor, banners fall swiftly even without wind;
great portents arise in the heavens, on the earth, and in the intermediate space.
Women wearing black garments wander from house to house;
with distorted faces, they cry out, "Go away! Go quickly from this house! (13)
At night, in their own homes, rakshasis, becoming extremely distressed and terrifying them, cut the hair of their beloveds while they were sleeping in their dreams.
O Lord of Gods, such portents as earthquakes and meteors occurred, and jackals howled in the courtyards of the palace during the night. (15)
And webs of lizards appear in every house; there are ill omens everywhere, such as the twitching of limbs and so forth. (16)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, the Lord of the Gods fell into reflection;
he summoned Bṛhaspati and questioned him regarding what was in his mind.
Indra said:
"O Brahmin, why indeed do such terrible omens appear? Fierce winds blow, and fireflies fall from the sky. (18)
O illustrious one, you are omniscient and capable of destroying obstacles;
you are wise, a knower of the true principles of the scriptures, and likewise a preceptor of the deities.
O knower of rites, perform a propitiatory rite that brings about the destruction of my enemies;
let it be performed in such a way that no further suffering may befall me. (20)
Bṛhaspati said:
"O Thousand-eyed One, what shall I do? A wicked deed has been committed by you today.
Having slain an innocent sage, what fruit have you acquired? (21)
The fruit of merit and sin is exceedingly fierce and comes swiftly;
therefore, one who desires prosperity should indeed perform an action only after careful deliberation. (22)
One should never perform an action that causes suffering to others; a living being who is intent on tormenting others finds no happiness. (23)
"O Śakra, out of delusion and greed, the murder of a Brahmin was committed by you just now;
the fruit of that sin has suddenly arrived. (24)
This one known as Vṛtra has been born invincible to all the gods;
surrounded by many Dānavas, he comes here to slay you.
And having taken all his divine weapons, equal to the thunderbolt and given by Tvaṣṭṛ, O Vāsava, he has arrived. || 26 ||
The invincible and powerful one, mounted upon his chariot, will arrive bringing about the destruction of the Lord of the Gods; he shall be his death.
A great clamor arose then as the Lord of Speech spoke thus;
the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, and sages whose wealth is their austerity [were all present]. (28)
Abandoning their abodes, all the immortals fled;
seeing that great marvel, Śakra became lost in thought.
Then he commanded his servants for the mobilization of the army:
"Bring the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the Divākaras! (30)
Having ascended their celestial chariots, Pūṣan, Bhaga, Vāyu, Kubera, Varuṇa, and Yama— the best of the gods— stood equipped with their weapons.
"Let them assemble with haste; the enemy is approaching now!
Having thus commanded, the Lord of the Gods mounted his excellent elephant. (32)
Having placed Bṛhaspati at their head, they departed from their own abode;
likewise, all the gods mounted their respective vehicles.
Having resolved to fight, they set out with weapons in hand;
then Vṛtra, joined by the Dānavas, reached Mount Mānasottara.
Indra also came to that delightful mountain, the abode of deities adorned with trees, and waged war upon Mānasottara.
On the mountain, accompanied by the gods and preceded by Vācaspati,
there then occurred a fierce battle between Vṛtra and Vāsava.
With maces, swords, iron clubs, nooses, arrows, spears, and axes,
he fought for a hundred autumns with a human-sized body.
He became a source of terror to men and to the sages of purified souls;
first Varuṇa was broken, and then indeed the host of Vāyu.
Yama, Vibhāvasu, and Śakra—all of them departed from the battle upon seeing the gods, led by Indra, intent on flight. || 39 ||
Vṛtra also went with joy to his father Tvaṣṭṛ, who was staying at the hermitage; having prostrated before him, he said, "Father, my task has been accomplished."
All the gods, including Indra, were utterly defeated while standing in the midst of battle; they fled and went to their own abodes, just as deer and elephants flee from a lion.
"O Lord, Indra has come on foot, while this supreme elephant Airāvata was brought by me; please accept this best of elephants. (42)
"They were not killed by me because killing those who are terrified is improper;
command me again, dear father, what desired task shall I perform for you? (43)
All the gods fled, terrified by fear and exhausted with fatigue;
even Indra, struck with dread, abandoned Airāvata and fled away. || 44 ||
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his son, Tvaṣṭṛ spoke, filled with joy:
"Today I have become a father; my life has borne fruit. (45)
"O son, I have been purified by you; the fever of my mind has departed.
My mind has become steady upon seeing your wonderful prowess. (46)
Listen, my son, I shall speak; attend now to what is for your benefit.
O fortunate one, perform penance with mindfulness and a steady posture. (47)
O Pākaśāsana, you must never place trust in anyone;
for he is your enemy, a master of deceit, and an expert in various forms of dissension. 48.
Through austerity, prosperity is attained; through austerity, supreme sovereignty;
through austerity, there shall be an increase in strength, as well as victory in battle. (49)
Having propitiated the god Druhiṇa and obtained an unsurpassed boon,
slay Śakra, who is evil-doing and enveloped by the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Becoming attentive and steady, worship Śaṅkara, the giver;
being satisfied, the four-faced one will grant you your desired boon. (51)
Having gratified Brahmā, the source of the universe, who possesses immeasurable splendor,
and having attained invincibility, slay Śakra, who has committed an offense.
"O son, enmity born from the slaughter of my son dwells within my mind;
I find no peace, nor do I sleep in comfort. (53)
"Since my innocent son has been slain by a sinner, O Vṛtra, I find no happiness; you must deliver me from this grief."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his father, Vṛtra was then filled with anger;
taking leave of his father, he went joyfully to perform penance.
Having reached the auspicious and holy celestial river on Mount Gandhamādana,
he bathed, prepared a seat of kuśa grass, and remained there with his posture steady.
Having renounced both food and the drinking of water, devoted solely to the practice of yoga,
he sat upon a firm seat, meditating on the Creator of the Universe within his mind.
Knowing him to be performing austerities, Maghavan, the subduer of Pāka, became anxious with thought and dispatched Gandharvas to create obstacles. (58)
And [he saw] yakṣas, pannagas, serpents, and kinnaras of immeasurable luster;
vidyādharas, apsarases, and numerous messengers of the gods.
Those deceitful ones employed various skillful means to obstruct his austerities;
yet the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, that supreme ascetic, did not waver from his meditation.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of Vṛtra’s Instruction by Tvaṣṭṛ for the Purpose of Brahmā’s Propitiation," in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Viṣṇu’s Seeking Refuge with the Gods, Including Indra, when Brahmā was the Leader.
Vyāsa said: Those gods who had come to obstruct his ascetic penance turned back and departed.
Despairing of the successful completion of their task upon seeing him so firm in resolve. || 1 ||
When a full hundred years had passed, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
arrived there with speed, mounted upon his swan and possessing four faces.
Having arrived, he said this to him: "O son of Tvaṣṭṛ, may you be happy! Abandoning your meditation, choose a boon; I shall grant you whatever you desire."
"I am pleased with you today because of your asceticism, having seen you so exceedingly emaciated.
Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—that which is desired by your heart."
Vyāsa said:
Then Vṛtra, having heard before him those exceedingly clear words from the Creator of the Universe— words whose flavor was like nectar—
suddenly abandoned his state of meditative absorption and rose up, his eyes brimming with a multitude of tears born of joy.
Having bowed his head at the feet [of Brahmā] out of affection, he stood before the Creator with palms joined in reverence;
bowing low with humility, he spoke to that bestower of boons—who was pleased by his asceticism—with words faltering from love and with great modesty.
O Lord, today I have attained the station of all the gods, for the vision of you, which is so difficult to obtain, has swiftly come to pass.
O Protector, there remains a desire in my devoted mind that is yet hard to achieve.
I declare that to you, O Lotus-seated One; you know the true state of things.
"May death not come to me by means of iron, wood, dry or wet bamboo, or by other weapons;
may my prowess increase exceedingly in battle, so that I shall be invincible even to the gods with their hosts. (8)
Vyāsa said: Thus entreated, Brahmā spoke to him as if smiling:
"Arise, go; may it be well with you; your desire shall always be fruitful."
"Your death shall not come by means of anything dry, nor by anything moist, nor by stone, nor by wood; I speak this truth to you. (10)
Having thus granted the boon, Brahmā departed for the supreme realm;
Vṛtra, having obtained that boon, went to his own home filled with joy.
The high-minded one related that granting of the boon before his father;
and Tvaṣṭṛ, being delighted, then beheld his son who had obtained the boon.
May it be well with you, O highly fortunate one! Slay Śakra, my enemy;
having slain him, come back, [you who are] the slayer of Triśiras and the destroyer of the wicked. (13)
"O Lord of the Thirty-three, having attained victory in battle, become [my] sovereign;
dispel my immense anxiety arising from the loss of my son. (14)

By carrying out the command of one who is living, by providing abundant food on the anniversary of his death, and by offering funeral cakes at Gayā—through these three acts, a son truly fulfills the duty of a son. (15)
Therefore, my son, you ought to destroy this excessive grief of mine;
for Triśiras never departs from my mind.
He was virtuous, truthful, an ascetic, and the most learned in the Vedas;
yet he was slain by that evil-minded man without any offense having been committed.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, the exceedingly invincible Vṛtra swiftly mounted his chariot and departed from his father’s house.
Having caused the sound of war-drums and the blast of conchs to be made,
he, intoxicated with pride, set out on his march.
Accompanied by his ministers, he set forth, speaking thus:
"Having slain Śakra, I shall seize the kingdom of the gods, free from all thorns."
Having spoken thus, he quickly went forth, surrounded by his own army,
terrifying Amarāvatī with the great roar of his troops.
O descendant of Bharata, perceiving that he was approaching, Turāṣāṭ also, trembling with fear, quickly mobilized his army.
Having swiftly summoned all the world-protectors, that subduer of enemies,
possessing great splendor, shone brightly as he urged them all toward battle.
Then, having formed the Gṛdhra array, the subduer of Pāka took his stand;
thereupon Vṛtra, the crusher of enemy forces, arrived there with great speed.
Then a tumultuous battle took place between the god and the Dānava,
Vṛtra and Vāsava, both desiring victory over one another in that conflict through their minds alone.
Thus, while the mutual battle was blazing and inspiring intense fear,
the gods perceived their own intent, and the Daityas attained supreme joy.
With tomaras, bhindipālas, swords, axes, and spears, the gods and daityas struck one another with their respective excellent weapons. (27)
While that fierce and hair-raising battle was thus proceeding,
Vṛtra, filled with rage, suddenly seized Śakra.
Having opened his mouth and cast Śatakratu inside, Vṛtra stood there, O great king, filled with joy as he recollected their former enmity. (29)
Then, while Śakra was being swallowed by Vṛtra, the gods were thrown into confusion; overcome with supreme distress, they cried out "Alas, Śakra! again and again.
Perceiving that Śakra’s mouth was open, all the inhabitants of heaven, dejected and with distressed minds, bowed to Bṛhaspati and said: || 31 ||
"What should be done, O best of the twice-born? You are our supreme preceptor.
Śakra was seized by Vṛtra, but he was protected by the other deities. (32)
"What can we all do without Śakra? We are all devoid of prowess. O Lord, perform a malevolent rite quickly for the sake of releasing Śakra. (33)
Bṛhaspati said:
"O gods, what must be done? Vāsava has been cast into the mouth;
though struck down by Vṛtra, he remains alive within the belly of his enemy."
Vyāsa said: All the gods, overcome with anxiety upon seeing Indra thus treated, reflected and swiftly made an effort for his liberation.
The great beings created a yawning spell (jṛmbhikā) that destroys enemies;
then, as he yawned, his mouth became wide open.
Then, as Vṛtra was yawning,
the slayer of Bala emerged from his mouth, having withdrawn even his own limbs.
From that time forward, yawns remained present among living beings in the worlds;
and all the gods rejoiced upon seeing Śakra emerged.
Then a battle commenced between them that struck fear into the worlds;
it lasted for ten thousand years, being fierce and hair-raising.
On one side all the gods stood ready for battle,
while on the other side the powerful son of Tvaṣṭṛ advanced in the conflict.
When Vṛtra, who was protected by his boon, grew powerful in battle,
Śakra was then defeated and overwhelmed by his splendor.
Then Maghavan suffered in battle upon suffering defeat;
and the gods fell into despair upon seeing Śakra vanquished. 42.
All the gods, led by Indra, fled, abandoning the battlefield;
for Vṛtra, having arrived with great speed, had seized the abode of the gods.
That Dānava forcibly enjoys all the celestial gardens;
even Airāvata, that best of elephants, has been seized by the Daitya. (44)
And all the celestial chariots were seized, O lord of the people;
furthermore, Uccaiḥśravas, the best of horses, then came under his control.
The wish-fulfilling cow, the Pārijāta tree, and likewise the host of Apsarases—
these were indeed taken as mere jewels by that son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
All the gods, fallen from their positions and dwelling in mountain fastnesses,
suffered misery, having been deprived of their sacrificial shares and their celestial abode.
Having attained the status of a god, Vṛtra became intoxicated with pride;
and Tvaṣṭṛ, having obtained exceeding happiness, rejoiced together with his son.
O Bhārata, having consulted with the sages, the gods, overcome by fear and delusion when that [threat] had arrived, deliberated, "What should be done? (49).
The gods, accompanied by Śakra, went to Mount Kailāsa;
bowing deeply to Mahādeva with palms joined in reverence, they spoke.
O God of gods, Mahādeva, ocean of compassion, Maheśvara!
Protect us who are terrified by fear and utterly defeated by Vṛtra. (51)
"O Lord, that powerful deity has seized the abode of the gods;
O Śambhu, tell us truly today, O Śiva: what should be done after this? (52)
"What shall we do, and where shall we go, O Maheśvara? Having fallen from our place, O Īśvara, we find no means for the destruction of our suffering. (53)
"O Lord of Beings, O Treasure of Compassion, grant us your assistance; we are distressed!
O All-pervading One, slay Vṛtra, who is arrogant with pride due to the power of the boon he received. (54)
Śiva said:
"Placing Brahmā at our head, we all went to the abode of Hari;
having approached that Viṣṇu, we deliberated upon the plan for his slaughter. (55)
He is Vāsudeva, Janārdana— the capable, the knower of deception, the powerful, the most intelligent, the refuge, and the ocean of compassion.
"Without that Lord of the Gods of gods, the accomplishment of our purpose will not occur;
therefore, you must go there for the sake of accomplishing all our tasks. (57)
Vyāsa said:
Having reflected thus, all those gods— Brahmā, Śakra, and Śaṅkara—
went to the abode of Viṣṇu, the refuge who is affectionate toward his devotees.
Having gone to the abode of Viṣṇu, the gods praised the Supreme Lord Hari,
the teacher of the world, with the Puruṣasūkta as declared in the Vedas.
The Lord of the World, that husband of Kamalā, became manifest before them; and having honored all the gods, he stood before them and spoke thus.
"O Lords of the World, accompanied by Hara and Brahmā, why have you come? O best of gods, tell me the reason for all of your arrival."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Hari, the gods did not speak to the Lord of Ramā;
for the most part, they all remained absorbed in thought with their palms joined in reverence.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gods, led by Brahmā and including Indra, seeking refuge in Viṣṇu," in the sixth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Praise Offered by the Gods for the Propitiation of the Goddess.
Vyāsa said:
Having observed them all thus distressed with anxiety, the knower of the truth of all matters—
O Lord of the Earth, Mādhava spoke to those who were agitated by the weight of their love.
Viṣṇu said: "O gods, why have you resorted to silence? Speak the reason;
whether it be good or bad, having heard it, I shall strive to prevent it."
The gods said:
"O Lord, what exists in the three worlds that is unknown to you? You know every matter; why do you ask again and again? (3)
In former times, Bali was bound by you and Śakra was made the lord of the gods;
having assumed the form of a dwarf, the three worlds were traversed with your strides.
O Viṣṇu, the nectar has been brought by you and the Daityas have been struck down;
you are the lord of all the gods in warding off every calamity.
Viṣṇu said:
"O best of gods, you need not fear; I know a highly esteemed means. I shall declare it for his destruction, by which happiness will come to pass."
I must certainly accomplish your welfare by myself,
whether through intelligence, strength, wealth, or by whatever means possible.
Indeed, four expedients beginning with conciliation have been taught by those who perceive reality; they are to be employed toward friends and especially toward enemies. (8)
A boon was granted to him by Brahmā, who had been propitiated through his ascetic penance;
and by the power of that granting of the boon, he attained invincibility.
Invincible to all beings, he was fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ;
thereafter, that conqueror of enemy cities attained growth through his strength.
"O gods, this enemy is difficult to subdue; he cannot be brought under control except through conciliation and deception.
Having enticed him, he should be brought into our power, and thereafter he must be slain. (11)
"Go, all you gandharvas, to where he who is more powerful resides; employ conciliation toward him, and then you shall conquer him."
Having come together, having made an oath, having inspired confidence through an agreement, and having established friendship, a powerful enemy must indeed be slain. (13)
Remaining invisible, I shall enter his thunderbolt, that supreme weapon;
and I, O best of gods, shall provide assistance to Śakra.
"And wait for the appointed time, O gods, only when his life has entirely expired; his death will not come about otherwise. (15)
"Go forth with the sages, O Gandharvas disguised by deceit;
establish friendship with Indra by granting his word. (16)
He must be deceived in such a way that he gains confidence;
I shall enter while remaining concealed within this firm, covered shield. (17)
Indra will slay his trusting enemy, and not otherwise;
for having committed a sin for the sake of that trust, Śakra followed behind him.
Then, with my assistance, he shall strike down the sinner with his thunderbolt;
there is no fault in this when one employs deceit against a deceitful enemy.
"One who is powerful is not to be slain otherwise according to the code of heroes;
having assumed the form of a dwarf, this Bali was deceived by me. (20)
And having assumed the form of Mohinī, all the Daityas were deceived;
you all together [approached] the divine Goddess Śivā.
"Go for refuge with your hearts through hymns and mantras, O best of gods;
that Yogamāyā will provide assistance to you. (22)
We ever revere the Goddess, the supreme Sāttvika Prakṛti,
the bestower of perfection and the fulfiller of desires, who is difficult to attain by those of unrefined self.
Indra too, having propitiated her, will slay the enemy in battle;
she, the enchanting Mahāmāyā, will delude the Dānava.
Deluded by Māyā, Vṛtra will become easy to defeat;
when the Supreme Mother is propitiated, everything shall be accomplished. || 25 ||
The attainment of one's heart's desire will not happen for anyone;
she is the inner controller, the cause of all causes.
Therefore, O best of men, with the highest reverence, worship that Prakṛti, the mother of the universe,
through pure (sāttvika) dispositions for the destruction of your enemies.
In former times, having also engaged in a most terrible battle for five thousand years, I slew Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Then, being praised by me, the supreme Prakṛti became exceedingly pleased;
at that time, those two Daityas were deluded and slain by me through a stratagem.
"O mighty-armed ones, you two Dānavas who are arrogant with pride, having been thus deceived, act accordingly by devoting yourselves to Prakṛti with sincere intent. (30)
"In every way, that best of goddesses will accomplish the success of your task, O supreme gods. Thus did the powerful Viṣṇu grant them his counsel.
They went to the peak of Mount Meru, adorned with Mandāra trees;
there the gods, having performed meditation, recitation, and austerity, took their place in a secluded spot.
They praised the Mother, the sustainer of the worlds, the agent of creation and destruction,
the cow of plenty for her devotees, and the destroyer of the afflictions of saṃsāra.
The gods said:
O Goddess, be gracious; protect us gods who are tormented and oppressed in battle by the demon Vṛtra.
Those who are intent on destroying the suffering of the wretched have always attained your lotus feet as their refuge within the reality of the ultimate truth.
O Mother of all the universe, protect us as if we were your own sons fallen into this peril from our enemies;
O Mother, there is nothing in the three worlds unknown to you.
Why do you disregard the gods who are tormented by the asuras? || 35 ||
This entire triple world was created by you alone;
Brahmā, Hari, and Paśupati arise from your latent impressions.
They perform all their respective duties under your control; they are not independent.
They sport at will by means of the movement of their knitted brows. || 36 ||
A mother protects her sons from humiliation even when they are wretched and have committed manifest offenses; this is the way of conduct established by you alone.
O Goddess, ocean of the essence of compassion, why do you not protect us, who are without offense and have taken refuge at your feet? (37)
"Surely these people have attained their status by worshipping my feet; having abandoned devotion, they are merely greedy for wealth, power, and sensual enjoyment.
They are not even within the range of my side-long glances. If you think thus, it is not so.
The manner [of conduct] is also observed in the son and in the progenitor as well. || 38 ||
O Mother, no fault appears to us in our hearts that we have abandoned your worship and become immersed in worldly power;
rather, it is the delusion created by you that prevails over us. Therefore, O you whose very nature is compassion, why do you not show us mercy?
O Mother, previously in battle, you indeed slew the exceedingly powerful lord of the Daityas who had assumed the form of a buffalo;
he who was a source of terror to all the worlds for our sake.
O Mother, why do you not dispel Vṛtra, who causes such fear? || 40 ||
Śumbha, who was likewise exceedingly powerful, and his younger brother Niśumbha—those two brothers and their followers have been slain and destroyed.
Therefore, slay the wicked and mighty Vṛtra; drench him with compassion and utterly delude him so that he may no longer exist.
O Mother, protect today the gods who have been excessively tormented by the asura and overwhelmed with fear;
there is no one else in the worlds who can destroy the affliction of the deities.
He who, by his own power, should utterly consume the entire web of afflictions. || 42 ||
If your compassion for Vṛtra is indeed renowned, nevertheless,
quickly slay this wicked one who causes suffering to the people;
O Bhavānī, purifying us with your arrows, deliver us from sin.
If not, will he whose mind is wicked surely not go to darkness? 43.
Those enemies of the gods, who were brought to the celestial grove after being slain in battle by your arrows— and who were indeed purified thereby—
were they not saved from the fear of falling into hell by you, whose heart was moist with compassion?
Why indeed do you not slay Vṛtra, even though he is an enemy? || 44 ||
We know that this enemy of yours, though a servant, does not generally afflict us, for he is indeed evil-minded;
but what of him who is your own here on earth— he would surely [afflict] even the immortals?
Or would it not rather afflict those who are devoted to your lotus feet? || 45 ||
O Mother, how can we perform your worship today, O Mother, since even the flowers and other offerings have been fashioned by you?
For we and all the mantras are but the form of the Supreme Śakti.
Therefore, we have surely prostrated ourselves at your feet. || 46 ||
Blessed indeed are those men who with devotion worship the lotus-feet of yours, which serve as a boat in the waters of the ocean of existence,
and which even yogis constantly remember with their minds.
Those seeking liberation are free from passion, transformation, and delusion. || 47 ||
Those performers of sacrifice, though they are knowers of all the Vedas, surely and constantly remember you indeed at the time of the oblation—
Svāhā, the producer of satisfaction for the lords of the immortals.
Furthermore, [he gave] the *svadhā* offering for the assembly of ancestors, which is the cause of their satisfaction. || 48 ||
You are intelligence, you are splendor, and you are renowned as peace; you alone are the wisdom that clarifies the meaning for men.
Having created all power within these three worlds, you always bestow it upon those who worship you out of compassion. 49.
Vyāsa said: Thus praised by the gods, the Goddess then became manifest before their eyes—
slender, assuming a beautiful form, and adorned with all ornaments.
Her four arms shine with a noose, a goad, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness;
her beautiful waist is bound by a girdle consisting of a network of tinkling bells.
The beloved woman has a voice like that of a cuckoo, her bracelets and anklets jingle, and she is resplendent with a jeweled crown set with crescent moons. || 52 ||
With a gentle smile upon her lotus-like face, adorned with three eyes,
she possesses a radiance equal to the color of a cluster of pārijāta flowers.
Clad in red garments and anointed with red sandalwood paste, the Goddess has a countenance gracious with favor; she is an ocean of the essence of compassion. (54)
She is enriched with every graceful ornament, the supreme friction-stick for the fire of all duality;
she is all-knowing, the creator of all, and whose very form is the substratum of everything.
Established by all the Vedāntas and consisting of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss,
the gods prostrated before that Goddess as she stood before them.
To them, as they bowed down, the Mother said: "Tell me, what is your task?
The gods said:
"Delude this enemy Vṛtra, who causes extreme suffering to the gods. (57)
Act so that the gods may have confidence in you who are thus deluded;
bestow strength upon your weapon, by which the enemy shall be slain. (58)
Vyāsa said:
Having said, "So be it," the Blessed Lady vanished right there;
the gods, filled with joy, departed for their respective abodes.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Praise Offered by the Gods for the Propitiation of the Goddess," in the sixth book of the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The description of the slaying of Vṛtra by Chadmendro through the medium of foam, preceded by the remembrance of the Supreme Power.
Vyāsa said: Thus, having obtained boons, the gods and the sages rich in asceticism—
Having consulted together, they all went to the excellent hermitage of Vṛtra;
there they beheld Vṛtra, blazing as it were with splendor.
Then the sages, approaching Vṛtra as he seemed about to burn the three worlds and swallow the immortals, spoke these pleasing words to him.
For the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods' work, [he is] endowed with the power of time and consists of the essence of rasa.
The sages said:
"O Vṛtra, O Vṛtra, O highly fortunate one, O terrifier of all the worlds! (3)
Indeed, this entire Brahmāṇḍa is pervaded by you;
as for that enmity of yours toward Śakra, it is a destroyer of happiness.
"Surely this desire of yours brings suffering and greatly increases anxiety;
for neither you nor Indra yourself sleep in contentment. (5)
One who is afflicted by anxiety sleeps happily, for there is no fear arising from enemies in either case;
yet, while you two were fighting, a great deal of time has passed here.
All beings—gods, asuras, and humans alike—are afflicted;
in this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), the established rule is that pleasure is to be grasped and suffering is to be abandoned.
It is the certain conclusion that there is no happiness for one who has created enmity; heroes who delight in battle praise such deeds, but not the wise.
War, though cleverly adorned with passion, is a destroyer of the objects of the senses;
one should not fight even with flowers, much less with sharpened arrows.
In battle, there is doubt regarding victory; the certainty is the strike of the arrow.
This entire universe, as well as victory and defeat, is dependent upon destiny.
Knowing that these two are dependent on destiny, one should never engage in combat;
likewise, eating at the proper time, bathing, and sleeping upon a bed are all subject to fate.
A wife devoted to service is the means of happiness in this world;
what happiness is there for one fighting in battle amidst the terrifying shower of arrows? (12)
In a battle that is exceedingly fierce with the falling of swords, yet which bestows happiness upon one's enemies, it is clear that through death one attains the bliss of heaven. (13)
Having cut his body and endured agony at the hands of jackals, Karata, and others, he heard words that were intent on seduction, urging him on but devoid of meaning. (14)
What dull-witted person would desire the attainment of heavenly bliss hereafter?
O Vṛtra, let there be eternal friendship between you and Śakra.
"You and Śakra shall obtain uninterrupted happiness, as shall we all—the ascetics and the Gandharvas—in our own hermitage. (16)
"We shall go to a state of happy dwelling now that your enmity has been stilled, O steadfast one, even as this battle between you two continues day and night. (17)
All the sages, gandharvas, kinnaras, and men are being oppressed;
we desire friendship with all those who wish for peace. (18)
"O Vṛtra, let the sages, you, and Śakra indeed attain happiness; we shall remain neutral for the sake of establishing friendship between you two. (19)
"Having made him take an oath here, let us unite with one another in mutual affection.
Śakra, however, having taken the oaths as prescribed in your presence, [proceeded]. || 20 ||
Your mind shall now indeed be filled with joy;
for the earth is surely supported by truth, and the sun by truth. (21)
This sun shines according to the proper season, and the wind blows by means of truth;
even the ocean does not overstep its bounds because of truth alone.
Therefore, let there be friendship today according to our mutual pleasure;
let us share a bed, play, water-sports, and comfortable seating together. (23)
"Having entered into friendship, you both must by all means perform this task.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of the great seer, the high-minded one spoke to them. (24)
"Surely these venerable ascetics are worthy of my respect;
you sages are by no means speakers of falsehood. (25)
Those of virtuous conduct and great tranquility do not know the cause of deception;
[they do not deceive] one who has committed enmity, the deceitful, the arrogant, the lustful, or one whose luster has faded.
A wise person should never form a friendship with one who is shameless;
for this man is shameless, ill-behaved, a slayer of a Brahmin, lecherous, and deceitful. (27)
One should never place trust in such a person;
you are all skillful and are not always inclined toward malice.
But because the minds of those who speak excessively are not tranquil, the sages who lack higher knowledge said:
"A living being is indeed the experiencer of what has been done, both auspicious and inauspicious. (29)
Having committed an act of treachery, how could one whose consciousness is destroyed attain peace? Those who commit betrayal of trust certainly go to hell. (30)
Indeed, the betrayer of trust surely incurs suffering;
there is atonement for those who kill Brahmins, and there is atonement for those who drink liquor. (31)
O Omniscient One, tell us the rule regarding those who betray trust and even those who commit treachery against friends, exactly as it is firmly established in your mind. (32)
"At that very moment, it is said, there would be a truce between the two.
Vṛtra said: "Neither with the dry, nor with the wet, neither with stone, nor with wood [shall I fight]."
"O illustrious ones, neither by the thunderbolt, nor by day, nor by night, shall I be slain even by Śakra together with the gods, O best of Brahmins. (34)
"In this way, an alliance with Śakra pleases me, and not otherwise.
Vyāsa said:
Then the sages, showing due respect, said to him, "So be it. (35)
Having brought the Lord of the Gods there, they made him hear the covenant;
Indra also, his fever of anxiety gone, took the oaths there.
Having indeed made the Fire-god his witness in the presence of the sages,
Vṛtra then gained confidence through his words.
He became devoted to companionship with Śakra like a friend;
sometimes both were in the Nandana grove, and sometimes in Gandhamādana.
Once, they wandered about joyfully on the shore of the ocean;
when this agreement had been made, Vṛtra became exceedingly delighted.
Śakra, desiring to kill him, pondered upon the means;
Maghavā, seeking a vulnerability, became exceedingly anxious at that time. (40)
As he was reflecting in this manner, time passed;
Vṛtra gained supreme confidence in Śakra, despite his extreme ferocity.
In this manner, after some years had passed,
Indra too reflected in his mind upon the means for the death of Vṛtra.
Once, Tvaṣṭṛ spoke to his son Vṛtra, who was confident in his power over the subduer of Pāka (Indra):
"O illustrious son Vṛtra, listen to my beneficial words. (43)
One should never place trust in someone with whom enmity has been established; Maghavan has established enmity with you and is always intent on finding fault with others.
Intoxicated by greed, delighting in hatred, taking pleasure in the suffering of others, lustful for the wives of others, that man of sinful intellect was a deceiver. (45)
Seeking out vulnerabilities, intent on treachery, deceitful, and arrogant with pride,
he entered the mother's womb and indeed caused the destruction of the fetus.
Seven times, seven times he cried out, yet remained unafflicted;
therefore, my son, one should never place trust in anyone under any circumstances.
"What shame is there for one who has committed sin, O son, if he commits it again?
Vyāsa said:
Thus was he enlightened by his father with words full of reason. (48)
At that time, Vṛtra, whose death was indeed imminent, did not perceive it;
however, he once beheld that great asura on the shore of the ocean.
When the twilight hour had arrived, at a moment that was exceedingly terrible,
Indra then reflected upon the boon granted by those high-souled ones.
This terrible twilight prevails; it is neither night nor day.
This one must be slain by me today by force alone, without a doubt.
Having reflected thus in his mind— that he had arrived alone in this desolate place at a time appropriate for such a moment— he remembered the imperishable Hari.
There the Blessed One, the invisible Supreme Person, arrived;
having entered into the center of the thunderbolt, the Blessed Lord Hari remained stationed there.
Then Indra quickly set his mind upon the slaying of Vṛtra;
reflecting thus in his mind, "How shall I kill the enemy in battle? (54)
"If I do not slay the exceedingly powerful Vṛtra today by deceiving him, he will remain invincible in every way against all the gods as well as the Dānavas. (55)
"It would surely not be for my welfare to protect the enemy by any means.
Then he saw a mass of foam upon the ocean that resembled a mountain. (56)
"This is neither dry nor moist, and likewise this is not a weapon";
thus Śakra indeed then took up the foam of the waters as if in play.
Endowed with supreme devotion, he called to mind the Supreme Śakti;
as soon as she was remembered, the Goddess then caused her own portion to be placed within the foam.
There he fashioned a thunderbolt covered with hair and joined with a lion;
then Śakra hurled that thunderbolt, covered in foam, at him.
He suddenly fell down instantly like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt;
and Vāsava, his heart filled with joy, became overjoyed when he was thus slain.
And the sages praised Mahendra with various hymns;
Vāsava, his enemy slain, was delighted in spirit along with the deities.
He worshipped the Goddess, by whose grace the enemy was slain;
he then propitiated her with various kinds of hymns as well. 62.
In the celestial garden, Hari constructed a palace for Parāśakti,
and Vāsava installed an image made of rubies.
All the gods performed a great worship three times a day;
from that time forward, Śrī Devī became the family deity of the gods.
Vāsava worshipped Viṣṇu, the most excellent in the three worlds;
then, when the immensely powerful Vṛtra, the terror of the gods, had been slain.
A propitious wind blew and the deities rejoiced when he,
along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kinnaras, had been slain.
Thus Vṛtra was suddenly slain by Śakra, who, through that [power], produced foam joined with the entry of supreme power (parā-śakti) and caused him to be deluded by her.
Therefore, the Goddess is celebrated in the worlds as "the slayer of Vṛtra," and because she was slain by Śakra, she is called "Slain by Śakra. (68)

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of Vṛtra, Preceded by the Remembrance of the Supreme Power by Indra through a Deceitful Means via a Bubble," in the sixth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The description of the consecration of Nahuṣa in the position of the Lord of the Gods immediately after Indra’s entry into the lotus-stalk:
Vyāsa said—
Then, seeing him fallen, Viṣṇu departed for the city of Viṣṇu.
But fearing in his mind the danger arising from the killing of him, [he remained there].
Indra, too, terrified with fear, then departed for the city of Indra;
and the sages became agitated with fear once their enemy was slain.
"What sin have we committed that he has been deceived?
The title of 'sage' has become meaningless through his association with the Lord of the Gods. (3)
It is said that Vṛtra gained confidence because of our words;
through association with those who betray trust, we too have become betrayers of trust. (4)
"Shame on this possessiveness, which is the very root of evil and the cause of such misfortune, that we have deceived the Asura by resorting to guile and oaths! (5)
The composer of the incantation, the provider of the idea, the instigator of evildoers, and likewise the partisan—each of these shall certainly partake in the sin. (6)
Even Viṣṇu committed a sin when he provided assistance;
for by him, assuming a form of pure being, Vajra was entered and cast down.
Surely a living being intent on his own self-interest feels no dread of sin;
by Hari, through his attachment to a deer, an evil deed was committed in every way. (8)
Of all things, there are only two that have reached their end;
they are the first and the fourth, which are difficult to obtain even within the three worlds.
Wealth and pleasure are the two praised goals, approved and dear to all;
as for the verbal dispute over "dharma" and "adharma," this is merely the hypocrisy even of the great. (10)
The sages, having thus repeatedly caused mental anguish,
returned to their own hermitages dejected and with their efforts frustrated.
But Tvaṣṭṛ, O Bhārata, having heard that his son had been slain by Indra,
wept, tormented by grief, and again fell into despair.
Having gone to where he had fallen and beheld the Tathāgata,
he performed the funeral rites according to the prescribed rules for the sake of the next world.
Having bathed, offered water for him, and performed the funeral rites, he,
afflicted by grief, cursed that most sinful slayer of his friend, the lord of the Śakas.
"Just as my son was slain by you after you enticed him with many oaths, so may Indra too experience great suffering ordained by fate. (15)
Having thus cursed the Lord of the Gods, Tvaṣṭṛ, accompanied by ascetics,
ascended the peak of Mount Meru and performed a most difficult penance.
Janamejaya said:
Having slain the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, what state did the Lord of the Gods then attain? Was it happiness or indeed sorrow that he experienced first? Tell me that, O Grandfather. (17)
Vyāsa said:
"What do you ask, O highly fortunate one? What kind of doubt is yours?
Whatever action has been performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, must necessarily be experienced. (18)
Whether by the strong or the weak, whether little or much has been done, it must certainly be experienced in every way by gods, asuras, and humans alike. (19)
Thus did Hari grant this counsel to Śakra, the slayer of Vṛtra;
then Viṣṇu entered the thunderbolt and became his ally.
O lord of men, in this worldly existence, Vāsudeva was not a helper in times of distress in any way; indeed, all one’s own kin are likewise so during such times.
When fate turns its face away, no one is a helper—not father, nor mother, nor wife, nor even a brother born of the same womb. (22)
Whether it be a servant, a friend, or even one's own biological son, when destiny turns adverse, no one comes to one's aid. (23)
The enjoyer of both sin and merit becomes the doer in every respect;
having slain Vṛtra, they all departed, and the Lord of Śacī was left devoid of luster.
All the gods then spoke softly to him, saying, "O Brahmahetu, who indeed, having made oaths and given a word of truth, would [then act otherwise]? (25)
He sought to kill the sage who had placed his full trust in him and had entered into friendship with him,
even in the assembly of the gods, in a beautiful garden, and at a gathering of the Gandharvas.
Indeed, his story spread everywhere:
"What evil deed was committed today by Śakra as he sought to slay him? (27)
Vṛtra, having been deceived by the sages through trickery while he was trusting, abandoned the authority of the Vedas and accepted the Buddhist doctrine. (28)
Since this Śaṅkha has been slain through excessive rashness after being deceived, who indeed, having given his word, would then act contrary to it? (29)
"Even without Śakra or Hari, this one has been struck down"—such and other stories like these circulated extensively among the assemblies. (30)
Indra also heard various reports that were detrimental to his own fame; for "cursed be the wretched life of one whose reputation has been destroyed in the world. (31)
Seeing him walking on the road, even an enemy would have a smiling face;
yet even the royal sage Indradyumna fell away due to the destruction of his fame.
Why is this evildoer not cast down from heaven?
Indeed, even for a minor offense, King Yayāti fell.
The king attained the state of a crab for eighteen yugas;
meanwhile, due to the severing of the head of Bhṛgu’s wife, the Lord Hari, the infallible Acyuta, [remained in his vow].
Due to a Brahmin’s curse, he was born in the wombs of animals such as crocodiles;
and Viṣṇu, having become a dwarf, went to the house of Bali for the sake of begging.
What further suffering does a man of evil deeds encounter after death?
Even Rāma experienced much sorrow born of separation from Sītā during his forest exile. (36)
O descendant of Bharata, he experienced terrible suffering due to the curse of Bhṛgu;
likewise, even Indra incurred great fear arising from the murder of a Brahmin.
He found no peace in his home, though it was endowed with every prosperity;
seeing him deprived of his assembly hall, Paulomī spoke to Vāsava.
"Sighing, terrified by fear, deprived of consciousness and bewildered—O Lord, why are you afflicted by fear today? Your terrible enemy is dead. (39)
What anxiety exists for you, O beloved slayer of enemies? Why do you grieve, O Lord of the World, sighing like an ordinary man? (40)
"There is no other powerful enemy by whom you would be filled with anxiety.
Indra said:
"There is no enemy more powerful than this for me; likewise, I have neither peace nor happiness. (41)
"O Queen, out of fear of killing a Brahmin, I am constantly afraid even in my own home;
neither the Nandana grove, nor the blissful [state], nor the nectar, nor the forest is as secure as home. (42)
Likewise, there is the singing of the Gandharvas and the dancing of the Apsarases;
yet you are not a woman who brings happiness, nor are the celestial damsels.
Neither the wish-fulfilling cow nor the celestial tree bestows such happiness;
what shall I do, where shall I go, and where will my peace arise? (44)
"Thus absorbed in thought, O beloved, I find no happiness within myself.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken these words to his deeply distressed beloved, Śakra—
Slowly he emerged from his dwelling for the excellent Mānasa lake;
afflicted by fear and emaciated by grief, he entered the stalk of a lotus.
The lord of the gods was no longer recognized, for he was overwhelmed by impurities;
concealed, he dwelt within the waters like a writhing serpent.

Then, when the Lord of the Gods had perished—stricken by the fear of the murder of a Brahmin, rendered helpless, afflicted with anxiety, and his senses impaired—Turāṣāṭ (Indra) was distressed. || 48 ||
Then the gods became afflicted with anxiety, and portents appeared;
the sages, Siddhas, and Gandharvas were also greatly distressed by fear.
The entire world was without a king and overwhelmed by calamities;
then a drought occurred, and the earth lost its splendor.
The rivers had their currents cut off and the lakes were indeed devoid of water;
even so, when the state of being without a king arose, the deities and the sages likewise [perished].
After deliberating, all the inhabitants of heaven made Nahuṣa their Indra;
and having attained kingship, Nahuṣa, though most righteous, fell under the power of passion (rajas).
Struck by the arrows of the five-arrowed god [Kāma], he became attached to the objects of the senses;
surrounded by Apsarases, O Bhārata, he sported in the celestial gardens.
Having heard of the virtues of Śakra’s wife, that king desired her and said to the sages, "Why indeed does Indrāṇī not come to me? (54)
"O all you immortals, I have been made into Vāsava here by you;
therefore, O gods, send Śacī at your pleasure for the sake of my service. (55)
O sages, O immortals, if you would do what is pleasing to me in every way, then today I am Indra of the gods and likewise the lord of the worlds. (56)
"Let Śacī come quickly today to my abode.
Having heard these words of his, the gods and the celestial sages likewise [responded]. (57)
Having gone there, overcome with anxiety, they bowed down and said to Paulomī:
"O wife of Indra, the evil-doing Nahuṣa desires you here."
Enraged, he said this to us: "Send Śacī here!
We replied, "What can we do? We are subject to her, by whom this Indra was indeed made [king]. (59)
Having heard that, the dejected goddess said to Bṛhaspati:
"O Brahmin, protect me from Nahuṣa; I have come to you for refuge."
Bṛhaspati said:
"O Goddess, you must not fear Nahuṣa, who is deluded by sin.
O child, I shall not surrender you, forsaking eternal dharma."
That lowest of men who abandons one who has come for refuge and is in distress shall go to hell until the dissolution of all beings.
Be at ease, O lady of broad hips; I will never forsake you.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Consecration of Nahuṣa in the Position of Devendra Following Indra’s Entry into the Lotus-stalk," in the sixth book of the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Indrāṇī’s Vision of Śakra.
Vyāsa said:
Then Nahuṣa, having heard that she had sought refuge with her preceptor, [acted accordingly].
Afflicted by the arrows of Smara, he quickly became enraged at that descendant of Aṅgiras.
"I have heard that this fool, the son of Aṅgiras, while guarding Indrāṇī in her house, has said: 'Indeed, this [Indra] must be slain by me. (2)
Seeing him thus enraged, the gods, led by the sages,
then spoke these terrible words to Nahuṣa with conciliatory intent.
"Restrain your anger, O Indra among kings; abandon this sinful intent, O Lord!
For in the treatises on dharma, they censure the violation of another's wife."
While her husband was still alive, Śakra’s wife was ever virtuous; how then could she, so fortunate and devoted to her husband, take another as her lord? (5)
O Lord, you are now the ruler of the three worlds and the teacher of Dharma;
if one such as you were to practice unrighteousness, the subjects would surely perish.
In every way, it is the duty of the master to preserve the conduct of the virtuous;
moreover, there are hundreds of courtesans here who are equal to Śacī.
Delight is declared by the great-souled ones to be the cause of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra); however, a loss of rasa arises when force is employed.
O best of kings, if the love between both is equal,
then indeed the attainment of happiness arises for both.
Therefore, abandon this intent to violate another’s wife;
establish yourself in righteousness, O Lord of Gods, for you have attained the unsurpassed state.
Supernatural power is diminished by sin, whereas it increases greatly through merit;
therefore, O King, abandon evil and cultivate a virtuous mind.
Nahuṣa said:
"O deities, when Gautama’s wife was enjoyed by Śakra and Soma by Vācaspati, where were you all stationed then?"
It is said that men are indeed capable when it comes to instructing others; however, a man who is both a practitioner and a teacher is rare to find. (13)
"Let that goddess come to me; it will be for your great benefit.
O gods, from her alone shall supreme happiness arise. (14)
"Otherwise, I shall not be satisfied; I tell you this truly.
Let them bring her here quickly, whether by means of persuasion or even by force. (15)
Having heard these words of his, the gods and the sages,
being greatly terrified, spoke to Nahuṣa who was afflicted by passion.
"We shall bring Indrāṇī to your presence through conciliation," having said this, they then departed for the abode of Bṛhaspati.
Vyāsa said:
Having gone there, the gods, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the son of Aṅgiras:
"We know that Indrāṇī has sought refuge in your house."
"She must be given to Nahuṣa today, since he has been made Vāsava;
let this beautiful woman of excellent complexion choose him as her husband. (19)
Having heard those terrible words, Bṛhaspati said to the gods: "I shall not abandon Paulomī, for she is virtuous and has come to me for refuge. (20)
The gods said:
"Another means must be employed by which he may be propitiated today;
otherwise, filled with anger, he will become difficult to appease. (21)
The preceptor said:
"Having gone there, O King, Śacī should entice the monarch greatly with her words; let the young woman make an agreement: 'I shall worship my husband once I know him to be dead.'"
"While my beloved Indra is alive, how can I make another my husband?
I must go in search of that great-souled one. (23)
"Thus, having made this agreement and having deceived the king, let her exert effort toward bringing back my husband at my word. (24)
Having reflected thus, all those dwellers of heaven, led by Bṛhaspati,
went together to Nahuṣa along with the wife of Indra.
Seeing them arrived, the artificial Indra then said;
and beholding her, he rejoiced with joy and, being delighted, spoke to her.
"O beloved, today I am Vāsava; O fair-eyed one, accept me!
As the lord of all the worlds, I have been ordained by the gods as one worthy of worship. (27)
Thus addressed, she spoke to the king, trembling and filled with shame:
"O King, O Lord of the Gods, I desire a boon from you that has been obtained. (28)
Wait for a short while until I reach a decision;
the doubt as to whether Indra exists or does not exist remains fixed in my heart. (29)
Therefore, having made a firm resolve within myself, I shall attend upon you;
until then, O Indra among kings, please forgive me—I speak this truth to you.
"Indeed, it is not known whether Śakra has perished or where he has gone.
When addressed thus by Indrāṇī, Nahuṣa became delighted. (31)
Having said "So be it," he joyfully dismissed that goddess;
once released by the king, the virtuous lady went quickly and spoke to the gods.
"Exert yourselves today and make an effort for Indra's arrival!
Having heard those words of Indrāṇī, which were full of flavor and pure, the gods [acted].
O best of kings, with one-pointed minds they deliberated for the sake of Śakra;
having gone to the abode of Viṣṇu, they praised the Supreme Lord.
Distressed, those experts in speech addressed these words to the primordial god, the lord of the world, who is compassionate toward those who have come for refuge: || 35 ||
O God of gods, Vāsava, the lord of the Suras, afflicted by the sin of Brahman-slaughter, remains invisible to all beings, staying somewhere in secret.
O Lord, when the Brahmin has been slain by your own intellect, how can there be the sin of killing a Brahmin?
O Blessed One, you are his refuge, and you are likewise ours as well. (37)
"Save us who have fallen into supreme distress; point out the path of liberation to him.
Having heard the piteous words of the gods, Viṣṇu spoke.
"Let him perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice for the removal of Śakra’s sin;
purified by the meritorious Horse-sacrifice, the Subduer of Pāka shall be cleansed. (39)
Furthermore, being satisfied by the horse-sacrifice, the Goddess Śrī Jagadambikā will grant him the sovereignty of the gods, free from fear from any quarter.
It will undoubtedly destroy sins such as the killing of a Brahmin;
by the mere remembrance of it, the entire web of sins perishes. (41)
What need is there for the horse sacrifice performed for the sake of pleasing her?
Let Indrāṇī constantly perform the worship of the Blessed Lady.
"May this propitiation of Śivā be a source of happiness;
for even Nahuṣa was indeed deluded by the Māyā of the Mother of the World. (43)
O gods, he will swiftly meet his destruction through his own committed sin;
yet Turāṣāṭ, having been purified by the Aśvamedha sacrifice, shall also regain his power.
"He shall attain his own unsurpassed seat in no long time.
Having heard those auspicious words of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor, they [departed].
They went incessantly to that place where the subduer of Pāka (Indra) resided;
having consoled Śakra, the gods, led by Bṛhaspati, [approached him].
They caused the entire great sacrifice, the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha), to be performed,
having distributed the sin of Brahmin-slaughter among trees and rivers.
The omnipresent Lord cast it upon the mountains, upon the earth, and indeed among women;
having released it among all beings, the sinless Pākaśāsana was cleansed of his taint.
Free from fever, he remained once more in the water awaiting his time;
invisible to all beings, he stayed within the lotus stalk.
The gods, having performed that wonderful deed, departed for their own abodes;
but Paulomī, distressed and overwhelmed by separation, spoke to her father-in-law.
"Even though my husband has performed the sacrifice, why is Purandara invisible?
O Lord, tell me the means by which I may see my beloved. (51)
Bṛhaspati said:
"Worship the goddess Paulomī, the blessed Śivā;
the goddess will show you a husband who is free from all taint."
The Mother of the World, having been propitiated, will restrain Nahuṣa;
and Ambikā, having deluded the king, will cause him to fall from his station.
Thus addressed by him at that time, O King, that daughter of Puloman duly received from her guru the mantra of the Goddess along with its ritual application.
Having received the lore from her guru, the goddess duly propitiated the goddess Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī with auspicious offerings of oblations, flowers, and worship.
Having renounced all other enjoyments and equipment, wearing the garb of an ascetic woman and longing for the sight of Priyadarśana, she performed worship of the Goddess.
After some time, the goddess, assuming a gentle form, riding upon a swan, and bestowing boons, appeared visibly before him in person.
Resembling ten million suns in brilliance, as cool as ten million moons,
possessing a luster equal to ten million flashes of lightning, she is endowed with the four Vedas.
Holding a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons with her own arms,
she wears a pure pearl necklace that hangs down as far as her feet.
With a face graced by a serene smile and adorned with three eyes,
she is the mother of all beings from Brahmā down to a worm, an ocean of the nectar of compassion.
The Supreme Goddess is the mistress of infinite millions of cosmic eggs; she is endowed with gentle and infinite graces and is resplendent with two breasts.
She, the sovereign of all, omniscient, and of the nature of the immutable and imperishable,
being pleased, spoke to her— the wife of Śakra— who had exerted herself with effort.
Greatly gladdened by his voice, which was as deep as a thundercloud, the goddess said: "O lady of beautiful hips, beloved of Śakra, choose a boon, whatever you desire. (63)
"I grant [this] today; I am pleased, having been most thoroughly honored by you. I have come as a giver of boons; my appearance is not something that occurs spontaneously. (64)
"Indeed, it is obtained through heaps of merit accumulated over many millions of births.
Having been told this, the goddess then spoke to her as she stood bowed before her. (65)
O Mother, I desire a vision of you— the blessed Goddess, the supreme sovereign, and the consort of Śakra— so that my husband may obtain what is most difficult to attain.
[He granted] the destruction of fear from Nahuṣa and likewise the restoration to his own station.
The Goddess said:
"Go, O illustrious one, together with this female messenger to Lake Śrīmanasa. (67)
Where my immovable form, known as Viśvakāmā, is situated,
there you shall see Śakra, distressed and overwhelmed by fear.
"In how much time, moreover, shall I delude the king?
Be at ease, O large-eyed one; I shall accomplish what you desire. (69)
"I shall cause the king, who is deluded, to fall from his celestial throne.
Vyāsa said:
Taking that wife of Śakra, the goddess's messenger departed with great haste.
The Supreme Goddess brought her husband into her presence;
seeing her husband, the Lord of the Gods, who had remained hidden, the young woman was filled with joy upon beholding the boon she had desired for so long. (71)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Indrāṇī’s Vision of Śakra," in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Nahuṣa’s Fall from Heaven.
Vyāsa said:
Having beheld her of wide, sidelong glances, filled with grief in that secluded place, [Nahuṣa spoke].
Then Ākhaṇḍala, filled with wonder, spoke to his beloved wife.
"How have you come here, O lovely one, and how indeed was I recognized by you? I am difficult for all beings to perceive when I am present, O fair-faced one. (2)
Śacī said:
"O God, by the grace of the Goddess, you have been recognized here today;
and again, by her grace, O Lord of Heaven, I have attained you."
A royal sage named Nahuṣa has been established upon your throne;
he, along with the gods and the sages, constantly harasses me. (4)
"O lady of beautiful limbs, make me your husband, Turāsāha, the lord of the gods.
Thus did Sin speak to me; "What shall I do, O crusher of Bala? (5)
Indra said:
"O lady of beautiful limbs, I am established here awaiting my time by chance;
likewise, O auspicious one, you too should make your own mind perfectly steady. (6)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by her husband, who was praising her excessively,
that goddess, sighing, trembling, and deeply distressed, spoke to Śakra.
O illustrious one, how can this evil-minded man remain at ease, arrogant because of the boon he has received, now that he is intoxicated with pride and will bring me under his control?
And all the gods and sages, agitated by fear of him, said to me:
"O lady of excellent hips, resort to that king of the gods who is afflicted by love."
But Bṛhaspati, O Śatrughna, is a mere Brahmin devoid of strength;
how could he, though always a follower of the gods, be capable of protecting me? (10)
Therefore, O Lord, there is great anxiety; I am not a woman who can act according to her own will. Being without a protector, what shall I do when destiny has turned adverse? (11)
I am not an unchaste woman, nor am I a wanton; my mind is solely devoted to you as a most faithful wife.
Yet I have no refuge there who might protect me in my distress. (12)
Indra said:
