"I shall tell you a means today; perform it, O lady of beautiful countenance, and your character will be preserved in this time of distress. (13)
A woman protected by another will not be devoted to her husband;
even with millions of means, her mind is pierced by passion and she is exceedingly fickle. (14)
For it is virtue alone that always protects women from evil;
therefore, O lady of pure smiles, remain steadfast by adhering to virtue. (15)
But when the wicked King Nahuṣa forcibly draws you toward him,
then, having made an agreement, you must deceive the monarch with the elephant.
"O Madālasā, go to him in private and say:
'O Lord of the World, come to me by means of this divine rishi-yāna. (17)
"Thus, being pleased, I shall come under your control"—speak these words to him, O lady of beautiful hips, for you will then be utterly infatuated. (18)
Blinded by lust, that king will compel the sages to draw his chariot;
inevitably, the ascetic will consume the monarch with a curse.
The Mother of the World will undoubtedly grant you her assistance;
for one who remembers the feet of the Mother of the World, there shall never be any calamity. (20)
If that [desire] should arise, it too must be known as leading to one's own welfare;
therefore, with every effort, [one should worship her] who dwells on Maṇidvīpa.
"Worship the Mistress of the World (Bhuvaneśānī) according to the words of your preceptor.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by him, Śacī went toward Nahuṣa.
Having said "So be it," she was filled with great confidence and made an effort toward her future task;
beholding her, Nahuṣa was delighted and spoke these words. (23)
Welcome, O lovely one, by means of your truthful words; I am at your disposal.
By truth, I am your slave, for your word has been fulfilled.
"Since you have come near me, O lady of measured speech, I am pleased; you should feel no shame. Worship me, who am devoted to you, O lady of the beautiful smile. (25)
"Tell me what must be done, O large-eyed one; I shall do what is pleasing to you.
Śacī said:
"O artificial Indra, everything that needed to be done for me has already been accomplished by you. (26)
"O Lord, I have a desire; listen now, O All-pervading One, in your heart.
O Auspicious One, fulfill my wish, for from this moment forth I am under your control. (27)
"I speak of mental resolve; you ought to perform that here.
Nahuṣa said, "O moon-faced one, tell me what must be done; I shall fulfill your desire. (28)
"O fair-browed one, tell me; I shall grant you even that which is unobtainable.
Śacī said: "How can I speak, O Indra among kings? I have no confidence in you. (29)
"Take an oath, O Indra among kings, regarding that which I shall do for your pleasure;
for kings who are true to their word are indeed rare upon this earth. (30)
"O King, having realized that you are restrained by truth, I speak this later:
O ruler, once my desire is fulfilled, I shall always remain under your control. (31)
"I shall indeed become Turāṣāṭ; this word of mine is the truth.
Nahuṣa said:
"O beautiful one, your word must certainly be carried out."
"I swear by my own merit earned through sacrifices and gifts.
Śacī said: "Indra’s bay horses are his vehicles, as are his elephant and his chariot. (33)
Garuḍa belongs to Vāsudeva, and likewise Mahiṣa to Yama;
the bull belongs to Śaṅkara, and the lord of the female swan (Hamsa) to Brahmā.
A peacock is for Kārttikeya, but a mouse is for the elephant-faced one;
O Lord of the Gods, I desire indeed an unprecedented vehicle for you.
O Great King, let the sages of rigid vows carry you—[you] whom neither Viṣṇu, nor Rudra, nor the Asuras, nor the Rākṣasas can carry. 36.
"O King, let us all go by palanquin; for this is my desire.
O Lord of the Earth, I truly know you to be superior even to all the gods. (37)
"Therefore, I desire an increase in your splendor, remaining unwearied.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of hers, he who was weak in wisdom laughed. (38)
But at that moment, deluded by the Great Goddess through her power of enchantment,
the king spoke these words while praising the beloved of Vāsava.
Nahuṣa said:
"O slender one, you have spoken the truth; this vehicle is indeed pleasing to me. O lady with beautiful hair, I shall carry out your word in every way."
For he who makes sages his vehicles does not become one of little vigor;
O lady of pure smiles, having mounted a vehicle, I shall come to you.
The seven ṛṣis and all the celestial ṛṣis will speak of me,
having recognized that I am capable throughout the three worlds and preeminent in ascetic power.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, he, being well-pleased, dismissed that beloved of Hari;
then, filled with longing, he summoned all those sages and spoke to them.
Nahuṣa said:
"O Brahmins, today I am Indra, endowed with all powers;
let you, free from pride, perform your duties here."
"The throne of Indra has been obtained by me, yet Indrāṇī does not come to me;
though summoned, she gives birth to me and speaks these words out of affection. (45)
O Lord of Gods, O Sovereign of the Suras, approach me by means of the chariot of the Muni;
O God of Gods, O Great King, O Bestower of Honor, do what is pleasing to me.
O best of sages, this task of mine is exceedingly difficult to accomplish;
nevertheless, you who are compassionate must perform it by all means. (47)
"Desire for Śakra’s wife consumes my mind; O sirs, grant me refuge today and perform a marvelous deed! (48)
Having heard his discourteous words, the supreme sages, headed by Agastya, accepted them out of their magnanimity and compassion. (49)
When the words of that [sage] were accepted by the sages who perceive the truth,
the king— whose mind was fixed on Paulomī— attained great joy.
Having ascended a beautiful palanquin, he stood there filled with haste;
having urged on his divine steeds, O serpent, he said, "Serpent! Serpent! (51)
Afflicted by lust, that fool then touched with his foot the head of the sage Agastya,
the best of ascetics and the husband of Lopāmudrā.
Though struck by the arrows of the five-arrowed god (Kāma), he lashed with his whip the one who had devoured Vātāpi and dried up even the ocean.
His mind captivated by Indrāṇī, he addressed the sage, saying, "Crawl like a serpent!
Enraged and remembering the lash-stroke [he had previously received], the sage cursed him.
"O man of evil conduct, become a great serpent of terrifying form in the forest for many thousands of years, where there shall be great suffering. (55)
By means of your valor you shall wander again and regain heaven;
upon seeing the one named Yudhiṣṭhira, your liberation will come to pass.
Having heard the answers to the questions from the mouth of Dharmaputra,
Vyāsa then said:
"Thus cursed, that royal sage, having praised that best of sages..."
He fell suddenly from heaven and assumed the form of a serpent;
then Bṛhaspati went swiftly toward Lake Mānasa.
He related the entire account in detail to Indra;
having heard that—beginning with the king's fall from heaven—Maghavan [Indra] [was moved].
O Great King, Vāsava remained right there filled with joy;
and the gods and sages, seeing Nahuṣa fallen upon the earth, rejoiced.
They all went to that very place where Indra was situated at the lake;
then all the gods, together with the sages, comforted him.
They respectfully brought the Lord of Śacī to heaven;
then all those sages and gods approached Śakra who had arrived there.
Having seated him on the throne, they subsequently bestowed the auspicious consecration;
Indra too, having reached his own seat in the abode of the gods together with Śacī.
He sported with her, who was filled with love, in the delightful Nandana grove.
Vyāsa said:
"In this manner, Indra experienced such extremely terrible suffering."
Having slain the asura Kāmarūpa Viśvarūpa, O King, that great sage regained his own place once again through the grace of the Goddess. (65)
O King, all this unsurpassed narrative concerning the slaying of the demon Vṛtra, about which I was questioned by you, has now been related to you in its entirety.
Whatever kind of action one performs, one shall obtain a corresponding fruit;
whatever action has been committed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, must necessarily be experienced.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Nahuṣa’s Fall from Heaven," in the sixth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Janamejaya said: O Brahmin, you have narrated the life-story of Śakra, whose deeds are marvelous; now describe the profound course of karmas.
Likewise, the loss of one's position and the attainment of suffering have been specifically described. || 1 ||
In this [work], the greatness of the God of Gods has been described exceedingly;
yet even here I have a doubt, namely that Śakra too was a performer of great penance.
Having attained lordship over the gods, he experienced unbearable suffering;
yet, by performing a hundred sacrifices, he attained the unsurpassed station.
Having attained the status of Lord of the Gods, how did he fall from his position?
O ocean of compassion, explain all of this, including the underlying cause.
O best of sages, you are omniscient and the originator of the Purāṇas;
there is nothing that should remain unsaid to great beings, especially when a disciple is endowed with faith.
"Therefore, O illustrious one, dispel my doubt.
Sūta said:
Thus questioned by the king, the son of Satyavatī [then spoke].
To him, whose soul was exceedingly serene, Vyāsa spoke the subsequent reply in due order:
"Listen, O best of kings, to this most wonderful cause. (7)
The movement of karma has been declared as threefold by the best among the knowers of reality,
distinguished as the accumulated (sañcita), the present (vartamāna), and the commenced (prārabdha).
It is taught that the previously accumulated karma produced over many births is threefold: sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasic. (9)
O King, whether auspicious or inauspicious, that which has been accumulated over a long period—whether well-done or ill-done—must necessarily be experienced. (10)
Even in hundreds of millions of kalpas, there has been no complete exhaustion of the accumulated karmas of living beings throughout birth after birth. (11)
And that action which is being performed is called "present";
having obtained a body, one indeed performs either auspicious or inauspicious deeds. (12)
Furthermore, from among those [atoms] that have been accumulated, how much indeed is gathered together at the time of the commencement of the body; it is as if Time impels that [matter]. (13)
Prārabdha karma is to be understood as that which must be exhausted through experience; indeed, living beings must experience the fruits of their prārabdha—of this there is no doubt. (14)
O Indra among kings, it is certain that actions performed in the past—whether inauspicious or auspicious—must necessarily be experienced as their results. (15)
O Great King, among gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras,
karma alone is indeed the cause for the commencement of a body.
Upon the exhaustion of karma, there is the destruction of birth for living beings; of this there is no doubt.
[This applies even to] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and likewise Indra and the other gods. (17)
Dānavas, Yakṣas, and Gandharvas—all are indeed subject to the power of karma;
otherwise, O King, how could there be such a connection with a physical body? (18)
For that which is the cause of the experience of pleasure and pain for an embodied being, [is the ripening] of those karmas accumulated over many lifetimes. (19)
In the interim, momentum arises for someone due to the ripening of time; by the power of that prārabdha, he performs merit in whatever manner it may be.
O King, a human being commits evil, as do the gods and others;
likewise, O King, both Nārāyaṇa and A-ra are born of dharma.
Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna were born as portions of Nārāyaṇa according to their desire;
this is indeed the ancient foundation proclaimed by the sages.
He who possesses great wealth should be known as having a portion of the gods;
for no one who is not a seer composes poetry, nor does anyone who is not Rudra worship Rudra. (23)
O Lord of the Earth, neither one who lacks a portion of the gods, nor one who is not Viṣṇu, becomes a lord of the earth;
[one attains this] from Indra, Agni, Yama, Viṣṇu, and Kubera.
Having taken sovereignty, power, anger, and prowess, the body is surely fashioned; such is the certainty. (25)
Whoever in this world is powerful, fortunate, or possessed of enjoyments,
whether learned or generous, is proclaimed to be a portion of the gods.
In this very way, O lord of the earth, these Pāṇḍavas have been described by me;
and Vāsudeva also is a portion of the gods, possessing splendor equal to Nārāyaṇa.
The body of living beings is surely a vessel for pleasure and pain;
the embodied soul shall accordingly experience pleasure or pain immediately thereafter. (28)
There is no embodied being who possesses any autonomy; for everyone is always subject to destiny.
Helpless indeed, one undergoes birth, death, suffering, and happiness. (29)
Those Pāṇḍavas, who were born in the forest, have returned once more to their own home;
subsequently, by the strength of their own arms, they performed the Rājasūya, the supreme of sacrifices.
Furthermore, they reached the forest dwelling, which causes supreme and manifold suffering;
for Arjuna performed austerities that are indeed difficult for those who have not conquered their senses.
The gods, being satisfied, granted another auspicious boon: "Where has the merit produced by the human body gone? Where has the merit born of dwelling in the forest gone? (32)
The fierce austerity performed by Arjuna in his human body at the Badarikāśrama indeed became fruitful within that very body. || 33 ||
In connection with the bodies of living beings, the course of karma is profound;
it is difficult to understand in every respect even for the gods, so what need be said of human beings? (34)
Vāsudeva, having been born in the extremely cramped prison,
was taken by Vasudeva to the cowherd settlement of Nanda Gopa.
O descendant of Bharata, he remained there for exactly eleven years;
then, returning again to Mathurā, he forcibly slew the son of Ugrasena.
He liberated his parents, who were deeply distressed,
from their bonds and established King Ugrasena in the city of Mathurā.
Out of fear of the Mleccha king, he went again to Dvāravatī;
Kṛṣṇa performed all that great manly effort under the power of destiny.
Having performed many deeds in Dvāravatī, Janārdana abandoned his body at Prabhāsa along with his family and ascended to heaven. || 39 ||
Sons, grandsons, friends, brothers, and sisters-in-law—all the Yādavas at Prabhāsa met their destruction due to the curse of the Brahmins. (40)
Thus, O King, has this profound course of action been explained to you;
even Vāsudeva met his end by the arrow of a hunter.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Profound Course of Actions," in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Establishment of the Duties of the Ages.
Janamejaya said:
The birth of the two Kṛṣṇas has been narrated for the purpose of removing the burden [of the earth].
O best of the twice-born, this doubt dwells within my heart.
At the end of the Dvāpara age, the Earth, exceedingly distressed and oppressed by a heavy burden, took refuge with Brahmā in the form of a cow.
Requested by the Creator, Viṣṇu, the Lord and husband of Kamalā,
[appeared] for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth and for the protection of the virtuous.
O Blessed One, O Janārdana, O All-pervading Lord, quickly take birth in the house of Vasudeva along with the gods in the land of Bhārata.
Thus entreated by the Creator, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī,
together with Rāma, indeed became incarnate for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth.
Having slain numerous wicked ones here, and having recognized all those of evil conduct and sinful-minded kings, how much of the burden has been removed?
Bhīṣma was slain, Droṇa was slain, as were Virāṭa and Drupada;
Bāhlīka, Somadatta, and Karṇa Vaikartana likewise.
How was it that those wicked ones who remained upon the surface of the earth were not destroyed, by whom all wealth was plundered and the wives of Hari were carried away? (8)
The Ābhīras, Śakas, Mlecchas, and Niṣādas by the millions—what was that "removal of the burden" accomplished by the wise Kṛṣṇa? (9)
O illustrious one, this doubt does not depart from my mind;
for in this Kali age, all people appear to me as being resolved upon evil. (10)
Vyāsa said:
O King, whatever kind of beings arise in a particular age due to the influence of time, it cannot be otherwise; the nature of the age (yuga-dharma) is surely the cause in this matter.
Those living beings who were devoted to the essence of dharma existed indeed in the Satya Yuga;
those who were devoted to the essence of both dharma and artha existed indeed in the Tretā Yuga. || 12 ||
In the Dvāpara age, people were devoted to dharma, artha, and kāma; indeed, in this Kali age, all become intent upon artha and kāma alone.
But the dharma of the age, O Indra among kings, does not undergo reversal again;
for Time is the maker of both dharma and indeed adharma.
The king said:
O highly fortunate one, where do those beings who lived in the Satya Yuga, devoted to righteousness and partakers of merit, reside today? (15)
O Grandfather, tell me where those excellent sages abide who, in the Tretā or Dvāpara ages, perform acts of charity and religious observances. (16)
Where will those most sinful revilers of the gods go—those shameless ones of wicked conduct who exist here in this Kali age, as they did in the first age? (17)
Explain all of this in detail, O Mahāmati;
I am desirous of hearing in every way this determination of the Dharma. (18)
Vyāsa said:
O King, those men who indeed exist here in the Kṛta Yuga,
having performed meritorious deeds, go to the worlds of the gods.
O best of kings, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are devoted to their own duties indeed go to worlds won by their actions.
Truthfulness, compassion, as well as generosity, fidelity to one's own wife, absence of malice toward all beings, and equanimity toward all creatures. (21)
Having established this common dharma once again in the Satya Yuga, other castes, such as washermen and the like, attain heaven through their righteous conduct.
Likewise, O King, in the Tretā age, in the Dvāpara age,
and in this Kali age, sinful men go to hell.
They remain there for as long as the duration of a yuga;
then they are born again on earth as human beings in the world of men.
O King, when there is the beginning of the Satya Yuga and the end of the Kali Yuga,
it is said that meritorious men are born from heaven.
When the beginning of the Kali Yuga coincides with the end of the Dvāpara Yuga,
all sinful men become human beings on earth once again after emerging from hell.
Thus, the conduct of the age was never otherwise;
therefore, Kali is the defiler, yet the people therein remain as they were.
Sometimes, by the turn of fate, a reversal occurs among living beings; those who are virtuous in the Kali age may appear during the Dvāpara age.
Likewise, some in the Tretā age and some in the Satya age—those who were wicked in the Satya age become so again in the Kali age. (29)
By the power of their performed actions, they encounter miseries;
and again, due to the nature of the age, they perform similar actions.
Janamejaya said: O highly fortunate one, tell me all the duties of the ages (yugas) without omission;
I wish to know exactly what kind of dharma prevails in each one.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O tiger among kings; I shall tell you an illustration:
for even the minds of the virtuous wander due to the influence of the age (yuga).
O Indra among kings, just as your mind was directed toward the contempt of Brahmins by Kali, O King, despite being a high-souled knower of dharma. (33)
Otherwise, why would a Kṣatriya king born of the lineage of Yayāti have placed a dead snake around the neck of an ascetic? (34)
O King, all the power of the age must be understood by one who possesses discernment;
for indeed, with diligent effort, one must especially perform deeds of dharma.
"O King, in the Kṛtayuga, the Brāhmaṇas were masters of the Vedas, devoted to the worship of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), and longing for a vision of the Goddess. (36)
Those who are devoted to the Gāyatrī and the Praṇava, those who perform meditation on the Gāyatrī, those intent on the recitation of the Gāyatrī, and those who recite only the Māyā-bīja; || 37 ||
In every village, all were eager to build temples for Parāmbā;
they were devoted to their own duties and endowed with truthfulness, purity, and compassion. || 38 ||
There, the Kṣatriyas were devoted to the duties prescribed by the three Vedas, proficient in the knowledge of reality, and intent upon the protection of their subjects. (39)
O King, in that meritorious Satya Yuga, the Vaiśyas were devoted to agriculture, trade, and the tending of cattle, while the Śūdras were intent on service.
In the supreme age (Kṛtayuga), all castes were devoted to the worship of Parāmbā;
likewise, in the Tretāyuga, the establishment of Dharma was slightly diminished. || 41 ||
And in the Dvāpara age, the condition of the Kṛta age is especially diminished.
O King, those who were formerly Rākṣasas are recorded as being Brāhmaṇas in the Kali age. 42.
Those devoted to heretical sects are generally deceivers of people; they are all speakers of untruth and are devoid of the Vedic dharma. (43)
Some will be hypocritical, clever at worldly affairs, conceited, and devoid of the Vedas;
others will be intent on serving Śūdras while promoting various false doctrines. || 44 ||
O King, as the Kali age increases, there arise those who revile the Vedas, who are cruel, fallen from the Dharma, and excessively talkative. 45.
There would be a total destruction of Dharma, which is rooted in truth; likewise, the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras would become devoid of Dharma. (46)
In the Kali age, there will be sinners who speak untruths and those of mixed castes;
Brahmins will be devoted to the duties of Śūdras and intent upon accepting gifts.
O King, in the Kali age, women will indeed have grown to such a state that they act according to their own desires, being possessed by lust, greed, and delusion.
O King, they are wicked, speakers of falsehoods, always delighting in afflictions, constant deceivers of their own husbands, and experts in preaching dharma. (49)
In this Kali age, women indeed become such and even most sinful;
however, O King, through purity of food, purity of mind arises. (50)
O best of kings, when the mind is pure, there is the manifestation of Dharma;
through the fault of confusion in conduct, confusion of Dharma arises. (51)
When the confusion of dharma arises, there will surely be a confusion of castes;
so it shall be in the Kali age, O King, when all dharma has been abandoned. (52)
This news regarding the duties of one's own caste is not found anywhere;
even great men who know the dharma, O King, commit unrighteousness. (53)
This very nature of Kali must be avoided by no one;
therefore, in this regard, for men who are by nature doers of evil, [this is the case]. (54)
"O Indra among kings, there can be no atonement through ordinary means.
Janamejaya said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, expert in all the śāstras! (55)
In this Kali age, which abounds in unrighteousness, what will be the destiny of men?
If there exists a remedy for this, please tell it to me out of compassion. (56)
Vyāsa said:
O great king, there is only one means for this and no other;
for the sake of dispelling all defects, one should meditate upon the lotus feet of the Goddess.
Indeed, there are no sins so great as the power she possesses; since there is nothing that the Goddess cannot burn away with her wrath, O King, whence can there be any fear?
If even that which is uttered playfully, though involuntarily, bestows this or that [blessing], neither Hara nor the others are capable of knowing its full extent. 59.
The recollection of the names of the illustrious Goddess is indeed the atonement for sins;
therefore, O King, out of fear of the Kali age, a man should dwell in a sacred field.
One should constantly practice the recollection of the names of the Supreme Mother;
even after cutting through, piercing, and slaying all beings and this entire world. (61)
He who bows with devotion to the Goddess is not defiled by sins;
O King, this secret of all the scriptures has been declared by me. (62)
Having reflected upon this in its entirety, take refuge in the lotus feet of the Goddess;
all people mutter the Gāyatrī known as Ajapā.
They do not know my greatness or the vast power of my illusion;
all the Brahmins chant the Gāyatrī within their hearts. (64)

They do not know the greatness [of the Lord], nor the vast power of Māyā. O King, all that was asked by you regarding the establishment of the duties of the Yugas has been fully explained; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Establishment of the Duties of the Ages," in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 11 ||
The Description of Hariścandra’s Affliction by the Disease of Dropsy.
The King said:
"O best of sages, tell me of the meritorious holy places (tīrthas) on earth."
The sacred fields as well as the rivers are accessible to both men and gods. || 1 ||
And what kind of fruit is obtained from bathing and giving gifts at various sacred fords (tīrthas),
as well as the specific rules and observances for the pilgrimage to those sacred sites.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O King, I shall describe various sacred fords (tīrthas), and among those fords, the excellent paths of the goddesses.
Among rivers, the Jāhnavī is the most excellent, as are the Yamunā, the Sarasvatī,
the Narmadā, the Gaṇḍakī, the Sindhu, the Gomatī, and likewise the Tamasā.
The Kāverī, the Candrabhāgā, the auspicious and holy Vetravatī,
the Carmaṇvatī, the Sarayū, the Tāpī, and likewise the Sābhramatī.
These have been described, O King, as well as hundreds of others;
among them, those flowing to the ocean are meritorious, while those not reaching the sea possess little merit.

Those rivers that flow into the ocean and carry all their waters at all times become "menstruating" (rajasvalā) for two months beginning with Śrāvaṇa; all of them are in that state during that period.
Likewise, by means of the rain, there arise rivers carrying village water,
as well as Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, and the most purifying Dharmāraṇya.
Prabhāsa, Prayāga, and Naimiṣa forest,
as well as the renowned Arbuda forest and likewise the purifying mountains.
Śrīśaila, Sumeru, and Mount Gandhamādana; and the sacred lakes, most famous of all, such as Mānasa. || 10 ||
Likewise, there is the most excellent Bindusaras, the purifying lake named Acchoda;
and likewise, there are the meritorious hermitages of the sages whose souls are purified.
The sacred hermitage of Badarikāśrama is ever-renowned and famous,
where those two sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, performed their austerities.
The hermitage called Vāmana-āśrama and likewise Śatayūpa-āśrama became widely renowned by the names of those who performed penance there.
Thus, O lord of the earth, there are indeed innumerable meritorious places upon the surface of the earth that have been celebrated by the sages as purifying. (14)
O King, in all these places there dwell shrines of the Goddess that,
by their very sight, remove sin, and they abide there according to fixed rule.
O King, I shall first describe those holy places, as well as certain gifts, vows, and sacrifices, in their proper sequence.
O Lord of the Earth, ascetic practices and meritorious deeds are dependent;
they depend upon the purity of material substances, the purity of ritual actions, and the purity of the mind.
For holy fords, austerities, and vows are indeed purifying;
yet at times there may be purity of substance, and at other times purity of action. (18)
O King, purity of mind is difficult for all to attain at all times;
for the mind, O King, is fickle and clings to manifold objects. (19)
O King, how can that which rests upon various states of being become pure?
For there are desire, anger, greed, egoism, and likewise pride. (20)
For these indeed cause all obstacles to asceticism, sacred fords, and vows:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses. || 21 ||
O King, the observance of one's own duty bestows the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites;
[yet this is lost] through the abandonment of obligatory rites on the road and through the defect of contact with others.
Visiting sacred fords is useless; only sin remains.
For sacred fords wash away, in every way, the impurity born of the body.
O King, they are indeed not capable of washing away the mind;
if they were capable, then everyone dwelling on the banks of the Gaṅgā would be so.
How could sages who were joined with malice ever have the Lord as their meditated object?
For it is said that those such as Viśvāmitra and others were humble like Vasiṣṭha.
All are always devoted to passion and hatred and are agitated by desire and anger;
the sacred ford consisting of purity of mind is more purifying than the Gaṅgā and other such sites.
If, by the power of destiny, one should wash away internal impurity—especially through association with the virtuous, O King—for one who is established in knowledge. (27)
Neither the Vedas, nor the scriptures, nor vows, nor austerities;
neither sacrifices nor gifts are the cause of the purification of the mind. (28)
Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā and an expert in Vedic knowledge,
though he was free from passion and hatred, once resided at will on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
The great battle between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha, known as Āḍībaka, arose from mutual hatred; it was rendered futile and caused amazement among the gods. (30)
There, Viśvāmitra was born as Baka, a supreme ascetic;
however, he was cursed by Vasiṣṭha on account of Hariścandra.
Kauśika also cursed Vasiṣṭha, causing him to assume the body of a crane;
due to that curse, those two sages of pure luster were born as cranes.
They reached the shore of Lake Mānasa and engaged in a fierce battle with blows from their claws and beaks.
For as long as ten thousand years,
those two sages, filled with rage and intoxicated with pride, fought one another like two lions.
The king said:
"How did those two tigers among sages, those ascetics devoted to dharma, come to harbor mutual enmity? For what reason did it arise? (35)
For what reason did those two of great intelligence bestow curses upon one another—curses that cause mutual affliction and bring suffering to human beings? (36)
Vyāsa said: In ancient times, Hariścandra, the son of Triśaṅku, was the best of kings; he belonged to the solar dynasty and was the elder brother of Rāmacandra.
Childless and desiring a son, that royal sage promised Varuṇa a difficult-to-perform human sacrifice as a great ritual. 38.
Varuṇa was pleased when that sacrifice was duly performed;
the king’s wife, who was most beautiful, conceived a child. (39)
Seeing his wife pregnant with longing, the king was filled with joy; he performed according to the prescribed rites the ceremonies for the consecration of the embryo.
The woman gave birth to a son endowed with all auspicious marks;
O lord of the people, the king attained great joy there at the birth of his son.
He performed the supreme rites of consecration, beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman),
and gave gold and milch cows especially to the Brāhmaṇas.
When the birth festival had fully concluded at home,
O great king, the Lord of the Sea arrived there, wearing the guise of a brahmin.
Then, having been honored by the king and provided with a seat according to the prescribed rites, Varuṇa, when asked about his business, spoke these words to the monarch: "I am Varuṇa. (44)
"O Indra among kings, perform a sacrifice after making your son the most pure sacrificial animal; be true to your word, for a solemn vow has been made by you. (45)
Having heard those words, the king was overwhelmed and deeply distressed by grief;
steadying his sorrow, the monarch spoke to Varuṇa with his hands joined in reverence.
"O Lord, I shall perform that sacrifice in every way according to the prescribed rites;
I shall make my promise to you true. (47)
O best of gods, after a full month has passed, the lawful wife shall be purified;
once the wife is purified, that animal sacrifice must be performed.
Vyāsa said:
When these words had been spoken by the king, Varuṇa went to his own home;
the king became satisfied, yet at the same time somewhat anxious with thought.
When the month was complete, Pāśī again came to the king’s palace for the sake of testing him,
having become a brahmin well-attired and speaking elegantly.
When that best of gods had been honored and was seated comfortably, the king, endowed with humility,
then spoke these words pregnant with reason.
"O mistress, how can I bind this unrefined son to the sacrificial post?
Having consecrated him and made him a Kṣatriya, I shall perform the supreme sacrifice. (52)
O Lord, if you take pity upon me, your wretched servant, know that an uninitiated child has no entitlement anywhere. (53)
Varuṇa said:
"O Indra among kings, you deceive me after having first made an agreement. I know that your affection for your son is difficult to relinquish, for you have no other offspring. (54)
"O protector of the earth, I shall go home at your gentle word;
after waiting for some time, I will return to your house. (55)
O dear one, you must then act in accordance with truthful speech;
otherwise, I shall release my wrath, accompanied by a curse, upon you. (56)
The king said:
"O Lord of aquatic creatures, at the conclusion of the Samāvartana rite,
I shall perform a sacrifice according to the prescribed rules, offering my son as the sacrificial animal."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the king, Varuṇa, with a pleased mind, said "So be it" and departed quickly; the king, however, became well-composed.
His son, known by the name Rohita, grew up prosperous, becoming clever and an expert in all branches of knowledge. (59)
By him, the entire cause of the sacrifice was understood in full detail;
then, perceiving his own impending death, he too became terrified with fear.
Having fled, that hero went into a mountain cave;
overcome by fear, he remained there in a place inaccessible to the king.
Then, when the time had arrived, Varuṇa, desiring to perform a sacrifice, went to the king's palace and said to that protector of the earth: "O lord of the people, perform the sacrifice."
With a withered face and agitated senses, the king said to him:
"O best of gods, what shall I do? My son has gone somewhere."
Hearing those words of the king, the lord of aquatic creatures became enraged and,
out of anger, severely cursed that king for being a speaker of untruth.
"O King, let the disease known as *jalodara* (ascites) afflict your body, since you have deceived me by acting as a pseudo-scholar. (65)
Having thus uttered the curse, the Holder of the Noose (Varuṇa) then departed for his own abode;
the king remained in his palace, overcome with anxiety and afflicted by disease.
When the king was severely afflicted by a disease born of a curse,
then the son also heard that his father was tormented by illness.
The traveler said: "O prince, your father is indeed deeply distressed by a disease of dropsy born of a curse. (68)
O evil-minded one, your life is ruined today;
you were born in vain, since you have abandoned your father in his distress and reached this mountain cave. (69)
"O lowest of sons, what fruit of birth have you obtained with this body? Having made the giver of your body miserable, you remain here. (70)
It is the settled conviction that a virtuous son must sacrifice his life for the sake of his father;
for your sake, the king, afflicted by grief as if by disease, is weeping. (71)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those truthful words from the traveler, which were consistent with dharma,
he then set his mind on going to see his father who was afflicted by grief.
Then, O descendant of Bharata, Vāsava, assuming the form of a Brahmin, approached him and spoke these beneficial words in private, as if out of compassion.
"You are a fool, O prince; you vainly set your mind on going.
You do not realize that today your father is filled with agony. (74)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of Hariścandra’s Affliction by the Disease of Dropsy," in the sixth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 12 ||
The description of the battle between Āḍībaka, together with the description of the majesty of the Goddess.
Indra said:
"The king previously performed a rash act, namely the sacrifice that was described."
Having made his beloved son a sacrificial animal, he promised him to Varuṇa.
"O highly intelligent one, once you have departed, your pitiless father, having bound you again to the sacrificial post and treated you as a beast, will slaughter you while tormented by grief. (2)
Thus forbidden by Śakra of immeasurable splendor, his son remained right there,
utterly deluded by the illusion of Māyeśī.
But when, having heard again and again that his father was afflicted by disease,
he set his mind on departing, Indra forbade him.
Hariścandra, afflicted by extreme sorrow, questioned his preceptor Vasiṣṭha, who was seated nearby in private— the omniscient one ever intent on his welfare.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, what shall I do now? I am cowardly and overwhelmed by distress.
Protect me, whose mind is sorrowful and who is afflicted by the fear of a great disease. (6)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O King, there is a praised remedy for the destruction of disease;
thirteen kinds of sons have been described in the Compendium of Dharma (Dharmasaṃgraha).
Therefore, having adopted a purchased son, perform the most excellent sacrifice;
give the wealth as prescribed and bring back that best of the twice-born.
"O King, when the sacrifice has been performed in this manner, there will be a destruction of the disease, and Varuṇa too, with a gracious soul, will become well-disposed. (9)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, the king spoke to his minister:
"O highly intelligent one, search with great effort throughout the realms."
Sometimes, a father seeking wealth out of greed gives away his own son, saying,
"Bring him back once you have given me the money," even as he continues to entreat him.
The young brahmin must by all means be brought here for the sake of the sacrifice;
you must not entertain a pitiable thought on my account.
"You must request a son from some Brahmin scholar;
for the sake of the sacrifice, you must indeed provide him with wealth, for he is to be the sacrificial animal. (13)
Thus urged by him for the sake of his duty, the minister searched throughout the city— village by village and house by house.
While he was searching in this manner, there was a certain sick man in his kingdom who was poor and had three sons; he was known by the name Ajīgarta.
Then that best of ministers, having given the requested wealth, brought his son Śunaḥśepa, the middle one, at that time.
Having brought Śunaḥśepa, the son of a brahmin who was fit for sacrifice, the minister, intent on his duty, presented him to the king. (17)
The king, exceedingly delighted, summoned from all sides Brahmins who were most proficient in the Vedas and had them prepare the materials for the sacrifice.
But while that sacrifice was underway, the great sage Viśvāmitra,
seeing Śunaḥśepa bound, then forbade the king.
"O King, do not act rashly; release this young brahmin boy.
I entreat you, O long-lived one: happiness shall be yours today. (20)
"This Śunaḥśepa is crying out; his piteous state distresses me as well. Be compassionate, O Indra among kings; O King, do my bidding. (21)
In former times, those kṣatriyas who were devoted to compassion, desirous of heaven, and pure in their vows, gave up their own bodies for the protection of another's body. || 22 ||
For the sake of protecting your own body, you are killing the son of a brahmin by force;
do not commit this sin, O Indra among kings, but be compassionate toward the child.
"O King, you yourself know that affection for one's body is equal toward all;
therefore, release this child if my word is authoritative to you. (24)
Disregarding the words spoken by Vyāsa, the king, being greatly afflicted by grief,
did not release [the child]; and the sage, an ascetic who was exceedingly enraged, [cursed] him.
Then the compassionate Kauśika, the foremost knower of the Vedas, gave instruction to that Śunaḥśepa, as well as the mantra of the Holder of the Noose (Varuṇa).
Śunaḥśepa, too, being emaciated by the slaughter, repeatedly cried out that mantra with a plaintive voice, intensely remembering Varuṇa. (27)
Recognizing that the son of the sage was indeed praising him, the Lord of the Sea,
an ocean of compassion, came there and released Śunaḥśepa.
Having freed the king from disease, Varuṇa went to his own abode;
Viśvāmitra, however, made that son released from death.
The king did not carry out the word of the high-souled Kauśika;
that son of Gādhi held resentment toward the king in his mind.
At one time, the king went to the forest mounted on a horse;
desiring to kill a boar, he was at the bank of the Kauśikī at midday. (31)
Deceived by Viśvāmitra, who had assumed the guise of an old Brahmin, he was asked for his entire possession; he gave him his wonderful kingdom.
Since that Hariścandra, performing the sacrifice, was being greatly oppressed,
Vasiṣṭha spoke to Kauśika when he arrived in the forest by chance.
O lowest of Kṣatriyas, evil-minded one, you who wear the dress of a Brāhmaṇa in vain! O hypocrite, you who follow the conduct of a crane, why do you carry such pride in vain? (34)
"O rogue, why have you brought this best of kings—who was performing a sacrifice for me as well—into such extraordinary suffering without any fault on his part? (35)
"Since you are intent upon deceitful meditation, therefore you shall indeed become a crane (baka).
Thus cursed by Vasiṣṭha, Kauśika spoke to him again: || 36 ||
"You too, O long-lived one, shall become a crane; for I am indeed Baka.
Vyāsa said:
Thus, having mutually given each other curses, the two were tormented by anger.
Born from eggs, the two sages were born as a male and female crane;
having built a nest upon a single tree, that one assumed the form of a crane. (38)
Viśvāmitra remained there at the divine Mānasa lake,
while Vasiṣṭha made an excellent nest upon another tree.
Assuming the forms of vultures, they stood intent on mutual hatred;
day after day, filled with rage, they engaged in combat.
Causing suffering to all the worlds, both of them cried out intensely,
striking one another with blows from their beaks and wings, as well as with the wounds of their claws.
Drenched in blood, they struck each other like two flowering *kiṃśuka* trees;
thus did those two sages, assuming the forms of birds, [fight] for many years.
"O Great King, while they remained there, restrained by the noose of the curse," the king asked,
"How were the two best of sages, Vasiṣṭha and Kauśika, released from the curse? (43)
"Tell me that, O brahmin-sage, for my curiosity is great.
Vyāsa said:
"Seeing both of them engaged in combat, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds," ||| 44 ||
There the Creator of the World arrived, surrounded by all his unblinking attendants who were intent on compassion; having comforted them both and turned them away from the battle, he spoke.
He released the curse that had been cast upon them by one another;
then all the gods and the Lotus-born Brahmā departed to their own respective abodes.
The powerful Viśvāmitra, mounted upon a swan, went swiftly to Satyaloka;
Vasiṣṭha also departed quickly and returned to his own hermitage.
Then, having formed a mutual affection based on the instruction of Prajāpati,
Maitrāvaruṇi likewise engaged in this causeless battle.
O King, who indeed in this world—whether a human, a god, or even a demon—is capable of enduring mutual suffering equal to that which Kauśika has experienced? (49)
Having achieved victory over the ego, one shall always partake in happiness;
therefore, O King, purity of mind is difficult to attain even for the great. (50)
That [knowledge] must be accomplished with effort; everything else—pilgrimage, charity, austerity, truth, and whatever else is a means for achieving dharma—is useless without it. (51)
Faith is said here to be threefold— sāttvika, rājasa,
and likewise tāmasa— in all bodies among embodied beings regarding their religious duties and actions.

The *sāttvikī* [devotion] is difficult to find in the world; it always bestows the fruit as described. That which is joined with ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is said to be *rājasī*, bestowing half of that fruit.
But that which is characterized by darkness (*tāmasī*), O King, yields no fruit and does not bring fame;
it belongs to those people who are overcome by desire and anger, O best of monarchs.
Having rendered that mind free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) through hearing the scriptures and other means, [one should practice].
He should always dwell at sacred fords and other such places, devoted to the worship of the Goddess.
Afflicted by the fear of the defects of the Kali age, he would utter the names of the Goddess with his speech, praise her virtues, and meditate upon her lotus feet.
For one who acts in this manner, there is never any fear of the Kali age;
even a person burdened by sin is liberated from saṃsāra without effort.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Goddess, Together with the Description of the Battle between Āḍībaka," in the sixth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 13.
The Description of the Name "Maitrāvaruṇi" of Vasiṣṭha.
Janamejaya said:
How did that sage come to be called by the name Maitrāvaruṇi?
Of Vasiṣṭha, O highly fortunate one, the son of Brahmā. || 1 ||
"O best among speakers, tell me the reason for his name: did he acquire it through his actions, or likewise through his qualities? Tell me the origin of that name."
Vyāsa said: Listen, O best of kings, how Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā,
having cast off his body due to the curse of Nimi, was born again with great splendor.
O King, because it belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa, that name became renowned everywhere in this world as "Maitrāvaruṇi."
The king said:
"Why was that righteous-souled sage, the son of Brahmā, cursed by the king?
It is a marvel that such an exceedingly terrible curse from the king has fallen upon the sage."
O Sage, what did that king say to the sinless sage?
O knower of dharma, tell me the reason for that curse from its very root.
Vyāsa said:
"O King, I have already explained to you the definitive cause:
this cycle of worldly existence is indeed pervaded by the three qualities of Māyā."
Let the king practice dharma and let the ascetics perform penance;
yet, pierced by the faults of all, that [dharma] would not shine brightly here. (8)
Even kings and sages, overcome by desire and anger and possessed by greed and ego, perform penance that is difficult to practice.
O King, the Kṣatriyas perform sacrifices, being enveloped by the quality of passion (rajas);
but among the Brāhmaṇas as well, O King, there is no one at all who is endowed with the quality of goodness (sattva).
That Nimi was cursed by the Ṛṣi, and the sage was cursed in turn by him;
both, by the power of destiny, fell from sorrow to even greater sorrow.
O King, the purity of material objects, the purity of ritual action, and the radiant purity of the mind are difficult for living beings to attain within this world composed of the three gunas.
This power of the Supreme Śakti cannot be transgressed by anyone anywhere;
she who desires to bestow grace upon someone liberates that person in an instant. (13)
Even great beings such as Hari, Brahmā, and Hara are not liberated;
yet even commoners, such as Satyavrata and others, are liberated.
No one in the three worlds knows her heart;
nevertheless, it is certain that she remains subject to her devotees.
Therefore, devotion to that [Lord] should be cultivated for the sake of eradicating faults;
yet if that devotion is joined with passion, hypocrisy, and the like, it will lead to destruction. (16)
Born in the Ikṣvāku lineage was a lord of men named Nimi,
who was handsome, endowed with virtues, a knower of dharma, and a delighter of the world.
He was truthful, devoted to charity, a performer of sacrifices, wise, pure, the twelfth son, intelligent, and intent upon protecting his subjects. (18)
He established a city named Jayantapura in the vicinity of Gautama’s hermitage for the welfare of the Brāhmaṇas.
A passionate thought arose in that Buddhist:
"I shall perform a sacrifice with many rituals over a long period of time, accompanied by sacrificial fees. (20)
Having consulted his father, King Ikṣvāku,
the monarch had the sacrificial materials prepared as prescribed by the high-souled ones for the performance of the sacrifice.
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Vāmadeva, Gautama, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Ṛcīka, Pulaha, and Kratu. || 22 ||
He invited the sages who were all-knowing and masters of the Vedas,
as well as ascetics who were experts in the science of sacrifice and most proficient in Vedic knowledge.
The king, having gathered the necessary materials and honored his own preceptor,
Vasiṣṭha, spoke with humility, being himself a knower of dharma.
"O tiger among sages, may I perform a sacrifice; O treasure of compassion, please officiate as the priest.
You are my guru and the knower of all things; perform my rite now. (25)
All the sacrificial implements have been brought and well-prepared;
my mind is resolved to undertake the initiation for five thousand years.
In this sacrifice, having propitiated the Goddess Śrī Jagadambikā,
I perform this sacrifice according to the prescribed rites for the sake of her pleasure.
Having heard those words of Nimi, Vasiṣṭha said to the king:
"O best of kings, I was previously chosen by Indra for the sake of the sacrifice."
Intent on performing a sacrifice to the Supreme Power (Parāśakti),
that lord Indra underwent initiation lasting for five hundred years.
Therefore, O King, wait for this interval until the sacrifice to Indra is completed here, after you have performed the task of the Lord of Heaven.
"I shall come, O King; meanwhile, please wait.
The king said:
"Other sages have been invited by me for the sake of the sacrifice. (31)
"All the requisites have been gathered; O Guru, how shall I protect them?
O Brahmin, you are the best among those who know the Vedas and are the preceptor of the Ikṣvāku lineage. (32)
"Why, having abandoned my task today, are you so intent on departing so quickly?
O best of the twice-born, it is not fitting for you to leave my sacrifice. (33)
With his mind agitated by greed, he set out out of a desire for wealth;
though forbidden by the king, the preceptor went to the sacrifice of Indra.
The king, having become despondent, paid honor to Gautama;
he performed sacrifices on the slopes of the Himalayas near the ocean.
Abundant sacrificial fees were given to the Brahmins during the performance of the sacrifice;
O King, Nimi underwent initiation there for five thousand [years].

The officiating priests (ṛtvijas), honored at will with wealth and cattle and filled with joy, [were dismissed] upon the completion of the sacrifice of Śakra, which lasted for five hundred years. (37)
Vasiṣṭha arrived, desiring to see the king’s sacrificial session;
having arrived, he stood there for the purpose of seeing the monarch.
Then the king, having fallen fast asleep, was completely overcome by slumber;
he was not awakened by his servants, nor did the king come to the sage. (39)
Then, due to that insult and because Nimi was nowhere to be seen there, the anger of Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, was aroused and he became enraged. (40)
Overcome by anger, he uttered a curse upon that king:
"Since you have abandoned me, your guru, and have made another your own preceptor," (41)
"O dull-witted king, you have become initiated by force through your contempt for me;
therefore, even though I have forbidden it, you shall become bodiless. (42)
"Let this body of yours fall; become bodiless, O lord of the earth!
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words spoken by him, the king's attendants... (43)
They immediately awakened the sage and said that he was provoked to anger;
the king, freed from all taint, approached him while he was still enraged.
He spoke words that were gentle, pregnant with reason, and logical:
"O knower of dharma, it is not my fault; you have gone forth, agitated by thirst. (45)
O best of the twice-born, having abandoned me while I am performing a sacrifice— even though I entreated you most earnestly— you feel no shame for having committed such a loathsome deed.
O best of Brahmins, being content and knowing the certainty of dharma,
you are truly the son of Brahmā himself, the most eminent knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
"You do not understand the subtle and difficult-to-traverse course of the dharma of Brahmins;
having recognized my own fault in you, you wish to reproach me falsely. (48)
Anger must be abandoned by the virtuous, for it is worse than a caṇḍāla;
overcome by useless wrath, you have cast this curse upon me. (49)
"And may this body of yours also fall today, filled with anger.
Thus was the sage cursed by the king, and the king likewise by the sage.
Having incurred curses from one another, the two of them became sorrowful;
Vasiṣṭha, however, being afflicted by extreme anxiety, went to Brahmā for refuge.
He reported the great curse imposed by the king.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"I have been cursed by the king, saying: 'Let this body of yours fall today! (52)
"O Father, what can I do? Tell me now, what is the cause for the birth of another body—the misery arising from the fall of the physical form? (53)
"O Father, let my union with this body be restored as it was before; whatever knowledge existed in this body, let that same knowledge remain there. (54)
"O Great King, you are capable; you ought to show favor.
Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, Brahmā spoke to that son.
"Entering the splendor of Mitra and Varuṇa, remain steadfast;
therefore, you shall be born not from a womb at the proper time—of this there is no doubt. (56)
Having regained a body once more, you will be endowed with righteousness;
as the self of all beings, a knower of the Vedas, you will be at will omniscient and honored by all.
Thus addressed by his father, he then departed for the abode of Varuṇa,
having affectionately circumambulated and bowed down to his grandfather.
Then Vasiṣṭha, having abandoned his unsurpassed body, entered the bodies of Mitra and Varuṇa by means of a portion of his vital breath (jīva). 59.
Once, O King, the beautiful Urvaśī, surrounded by a group of her female companions, came to the abode of Varuṇa by chance.
O King, having seen that celestial nymph endowed with beauty and youth,
the two gods then became overcome with desire and spoke to her.
"Helpless and agitated, we two choose you, O lady of faultless limbs, who are beautiful in every part of your body and as enchanting as a celestial maiden. (62)
"Dwell at your pleasure in this place, O lady of excellent complexion.
Having been addressed thus by those two, the goddess remained there, constrained.
Having made her disposition firm in the house of Mitra and Varuṇa, that goddess of beautiful appearance remained there, having assumed their nature.
By chance, however, their semen fell into an uncovered jar;
from that, O King, were born two sages who were exceedingly beautiful.
There, Agasti was the first and Vasiṣṭha was the other;
those two best of sages were ascetics born from the seed of Mitra and Varuṇa.
But the first, Ikṣvāku, who was a great ascetic even as a mere child when he reached the forest,
chose that boy Vasiṣṭha as his domestic priest.
O King, for the sake of the welfare of this lineage, he protected it;
moreover, having recognized him as a sage, he became filled with affection. 68.
Thus has all this been told, as well as the cause regarding Vasiṣṭha, and how [the two sons] attained another body due to a curse within the lineage of Mitrāvaruṇa. (69)

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Name Maitrāvaruṇi of Vasiṣṭha," in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 14 ||
In the *Devīmahimna*, there is a description of various states of being.
Janamejaya said:
"Indeed, you have related the attainment of a body by Vasiṣṭha."
Tell me how Nimi again obtained a body. || 1 ||
Vyāsa said:
O lord of men, Vasiṣṭha regained his body once more;
however, Nimi did not regain his body in the same way after the curse.
When he had been cursed by Vasiṣṭha, all those brahmins who had been chosen as officiating priests (ṛtvij) for the sacrifice by the king deliberated together.
"Alas, what must be done by us? The righteous lord of the earth has been consumed by a curse while still engaged in the initiation for this sacrifice that remains incomplete."
"What should be done? This task has indeed turned out contrary to our expectations;
because the event was inevitable, we were powerless to prevent it."
Then, by means of various kinds of mantras, they maintained his body— belonging to that great-souled one—
and kept it slightly endowed with breath.
Being worshipped repeatedly with various perfumes and garlands,
he was established as changeless and well-honored through the power of mantras.
And when the sacrifice was completed there, O King, all the gods assembled and, being praised by the officiating priests, became well-pleased.
Addressed by the sages with hymns of praise, they spoke to themselves in disillusionment:
"O protector of the earth, O observer of noble vows, we are now pleased; choose a boon."
O royal sage, by means of this sacrifice, an excellent birth is ordained—whether as a divine body or a human body, whichever is desired in your mind. (10)
"Let your proud priest remain at his pleasure in the world of mortals.
Having been addressed thus, the soul of Nimi, being satisfied, spoke to them.
I have no desire for this body, which is ever-perishing;
my dwelling, O best of gods, is in the perception of all living beings.
"I move about as the wind within the eyes of all beings.
When he had spoken thus, the gods there said to Nimi, "Show us yourself."
O Great King, pray to the Goddess Śivā, the Sovereign of All;
being satisfied by this sacrifice, she will fulfill your desire.
Thus addressed by the gods, he prayed to the deity with various kinds of divine hymns and with devotion, his voice faltering.
Then that goddess, being pleased, granted a direct vision;
she appeared in a form radiant with beauty and resembling ten million suns.
Upon seeing her, everyone was overjoyed and felt in their hearts that they had accomplished all that was to be done.
When the deity was pleased, O King, the monarch chose a boon.
"Grant me that stainless knowledge by which liberation may be attained, and may my dwelling be in the eyes of all living beings. (18)
Then the Goddess of gods, the Mother of the World, being pleased, spoke:
"May your knowledge become stainless, [only] due to the remainder of your prārabdha karma. (19)
He shall also become the dwelling place for all beings within their eyes;
it is by your very power that the eyes of embodied beings close in a blink.
Due to your dwelling here, human beings and animals will become blinking, while the gods shall once again become unblinking. (21)
Having thus granted him the boon, the illustrious goddess Varadā then took leave of all the sages and vanished right there.
When the goddess had vanished, all the sages remaining there reflected upon the matter and, according to the prescribed rite, withdrew Nimi’s body.
Having established the fire-drill there, those great-souled ones then churned it with mantras for the sake of a son for Nimi, by means of mantras and burnt offerings.
Then, while the fire-drill wood was being rubbed in the forest, a son appeared, endowed with all auspicious marks, like a second Nimi in person. || 25 ||
Because he was born from the churning of the Araṇī wood, he is remembered as Mithi;
because he was born from Janaka, he became known as Janaka.
Since Nimi was born in Videha, therefore the kings who arose in his lineage are celebrated as the Videhas.
Thus King Janaka became renowned as the son of Nimi;
by him was built a captivating city on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Mithilā is well-renowned, endowed with gate-towers and watchtowers, filled with wealth and grain, and adorned with marketplaces and halls. || 29 ||
All those kings who were in this lineage were likewise Janakas;
they were all renowned as wise men and are celebrated as the Videhas.
O King, this supreme narrative of Nimi has been told to you;
I have related in detail how he attained bodilessness due to a curse.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, the cause of Nimi’s curse has been explained by you;
yet having heard it, my mind has fallen into doubt and is exceedingly restless. (32)
How was the sage Vasiṣṭha—the most excellent of Brahmins, the domestic priest of the king, and the son of the Lotus-born—cursed by the king? (33)
"Knowing him to be both a preceptor and a Brahmin, Nimi did not show forbearance;
having performed the auspicious sacrificial rite, how has he come to such anger? (34)
Having understood the true knowledge of Dharma, how could one born of the Ikṣvāku lineage fall under the sway of anger and curse his guru, a brāhmaṇa? (35)
Vyāsa said:
O King, forgiveness is extremely difficult for living beings who have not conquered their own selves;
one who possesses forgiveness is rare in the world, especially one who is highly capable.
May he become an ascetic sage who has renounced all attachments, a conqueror of sleep and hunger, and one firmly established in the practice of yoga. (37)
Lust, anger, greed, and egoism as the fourth—these enemies residing within the body are difficult to discern; therefore, they are to be regarded as such in every respect. (38)
Never before in the cycle of existence has there been such a man, nor does one exist now, nor will there ever be anyone who could conquer these enemies. (39)
Neither in heaven, nor on the earth, nor in the world of Brahmā, nor in the abode of Hari,
nor on Kailāsa, is there anyone such as this who could conquer these enemies.
Even the sages, the sons of Brahmā, and other supreme ascetics are pierced by the three qualities; how much more so, then, for human beings on earth?
Kapila was a knower of Sāṃkhya, devoted to the practice of Yoga, and pure;
yet even by him, through the power of destiny, the sons of Sagara were indeed consumed by fire.
Therefore, O King, since the three worlds have arisen from this ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra), how could they be separated from it, given the relationship between cause and effect? (43)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śaṅkara are pervaded by the three qualities;
they manifest within bodies, and their dispositions are each distinct.
And what need is there to speak of human beings when it comes to abiding solely in goodness?
O King, the intermixture of the qualities (guṇas) is established everywhere.
Sometimes there is an increase of *sattva*, sometimes indeed of *rajas*,
sometimes an increase of *tamas*, and at other times there is an equilibrium of all three.
This Supreme Self is devoid of qualities, untainted, supreme, and immutable;
it is imperceptible to all beings, immeasurable, and eternal. || 47 ||
In the same way, the supreme power, which is devoid of qualities and established in Brahman—the very foundation of all beings—is difficult to be known by those of small intellect. (48)
For the Supreme Self and the individual self, as well as their power, are indeed always one;
by knowing that their nature is non-different, one is liberated from all defects. (49)
"Liberation arises from the knowledge of that alone"—this is the drumbeat of the Vedānta.
He who knows this is liberated from this transmigratory existence consisting of the three qualities (guṇas). 50.
Knowledge is said to be of two kinds; the first is declared to be verbal, which arises from the understanding of the meaning of the Vedas and scriptures through the application of the intellect. (51)
In that regard, many conceptual constructions arise, fashioned by the mind;
some are fashioned by fallacious reasoning, while others are fashioned by sound reasoning. From such discursive thoughts arises delusion, and from delusion comes the ruin of the intellect.
The destruction of knowledge in living beings is proclaimed to result from the derangement of the intellect;
but the second kind of knowledge, called experience, is difficult to attain, O King. (52)
That is attained by the knower only when there is attachment [to the means];
O Bhārata, the accomplishment of the task does not arise from the mere knowledge of the words.
Therefore, a superhuman experiential knowledge is not possible;
for verbal cognition is indeed incapable of cutting away the darkness residing within.
Just as darkness is not dispelled by the mere report of a lamp, so too is that action which does not lead to bondage; that is true knowledge which leads to liberation. 55.
Other action leads to weariness; other knowledge is mere skill in crafts; while good character consists in the welfare of others, the absence of anger, forbearance, and fortitude. (56)
And contentment is the brilliantly radiant fruit of the ripening of knowledge;
whether by means of knowledge, austerity, or the practice of yoga, O King. (57)
Without [subduing] the enemies such as desire and the rest, there is never any destruction [of suffering].
The mind, however, is fickle and extremely difficult to grasp due to its passionate nature;
under its sway, every living being in the three worlds is of one of three kinds.
States such as desire, anger, and the like are proclaimed to be born of the mind.
They truly do not exist at all when the mind has been conquered;
therefore, O King, forbearance was not practiced by Nimi toward the sage.
Just as in former times Yayāti was cursed by Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, even though he had committed an offense against him, that best of kings, Yayāti, [remained steadfast]. (60)
The king did not curse the sage out of anger; rather, he had taken upon himself old age.
One person may be gentle, while another may be cruel, O King. (61)
O King, since there is a difference in their natures, whose fault can be imputed here?
Formerly, the Haihayas [slew] the Bhārgavas, their family priests, out of greed for wealth. (62)
Overwhelmed by rage, they cut down all the Brāhmaṇas from their very roots,
casting behind them the sin arising from the slaughter of a Brāhmaṇa.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Various States of Being," in the section on the Greatness of the Goddess within the sixth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 15.
The description of the slaughter of the Bhṛgus along with the Haihayas' seizure of their wealth.
Janamejaya said:
"In whose lineage were those Kṣatriyas, the Haihayas, born?"
And those who, disregarding the murder of a Brahmin, slew the descendants of Bhṛgu.
O Grandfather, tell me what is the cause of their enmity;
how do those most excellent beings give way to anger without any apparent provocation?
Why did enmity arise between them and the family priests?
For such enmity among Kṣatriyas cannot be caused by a trivial reason. (3)
Otherwise, how could they have slain the blameless Brāhmaṇas who are worthy of worship? And why were those powerful Kṣatriyas not afraid of sin?
"O bull among Kṣatriyas, why would he kill the Bāḍavas for such a slight offense?
I have a doubt, O best of sages; you ought to tell me the reason. (5)
Sūta said:
Thus questioned then by that king, the son of Satyavatī,
being exceedingly pleased, spoke after recollecting the story in his mind.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O son of Parikṣit, to this ancient account of the Kṣatriyas,
which is truly wonderful and was fully understood by me in the past.
There was a lord of the earth named Kārtavīrya of the Haihaya lineage;
he was Arjuna, possessed of a thousand arms, powerful, and devoted to righteousness.
He became a disciple of Dattātreya, like an incarnation of Hari;
he was a perfected one (siddha) who grants all aims, devoted to Śakti, and indeed the sacrificial priest for the Bhrigus.
A performer of sacrifices, most righteous, and always devoted to charity,
he gave wealth to the Bhṛgus after having performed numerous sacrifices.
Through the gift of that king, those twice-born ones became wealthy Bhṛgus; enriched by an abundance of excellent horses, they became renowned throughout the earth. (11)
O King, after that tiger among kings, Kārtavīryārjuna, had ascended to heaven,
the Haihayas became destitute of wealth after a long period of time.
O King, once a financial need arose for the Haihayas;
they went to those Bhṛgus as supplicants for wealth.
Having established the discipline, the Kṣatriyas requested much wealth;
yet, afflicted by excessive greed, they did not give it, saying, "There is none, there is none! || 14 ||
Some Bhṛgus buried their excellent wealth in the ground,
while others gave it to the twice-born, perceiving danger from the Kṣatriyas.
Having hidden their wealth in another place, the Brāhmaṇas, overwhelmed by fear, all abandoned their hermitages and departed, driven by thirst for sustenance. || 16 ||
Seeing the supplicants in distress, they, deluded by greed, gave nothing;
having fled, they all went and took refuge in mountain fastnesses. (17)
Then, O dear one, those Haihayas, the bulls among Kṣatriyas, being distressed by the gravity of their situation, went to the hermitages of the Bhṛgus for the sake of wealth. (18)
Then, seeing that the Bhrigus had departed and their houses were empty,
the Haihayas dug the earth there intensely for the sake of wealth.
All the Kṣatriyas, emaciated by their labors, beheld the wealth acquired through digging that had been found in the house of a Bhṛgu. || 20 ||
Wherever abundant wealth was produced from the surface of the earth,
at that time even the houses of the Brahmins standing on your side [received it].
Having pierced through the wealth, the Haihayas beheld it out of a desire for riches;
all the Brahmins cried out in distress and, being terrified, sought refuge. || 22 ||
As the many houses of the Brahmins were being searched,
they angrily struck with arrows those Bāḍavas who had come seeking refuge.
They went through mountain fastnesses where the Bhṛgus were stationed;
cutting [the embryo] even from the womb, they wandered over this earth.
They slaughtered all the Bhṛgus they encountered with sharpened arrows— slaying them from children to the elderly— and committed further sins by showing no mercy to others.
While the Bhārgavas were being thus uprooted from here and there,
the Haihayas violently seized the fetuses of the women and killed them.
Those women wept as much as they desired, like distressed female ospreys, for their fetuses had been torn out by the Kṣatriyas of sinful resolve. (27)
Other sages dwelling at sacred fords also spoke to those arrogant men:
"O Kṣatriyas, let go of this fear-inspiring anger toward the Brāhmaṇas. (28)
"This reprehensible deed you have undertaken is improper—that these bulls among Kṣatriyas should slay the fetuses of the wives of Bhṛgu. (29)
One may experience the fruit of extremely intense merit and sin right here in this world;
therefore, one who desires prosperity should abandon despicable actions.
Then the enraged Haihayas spoke to those sages who were devoted to compassion:
"You are all virtuous men, yet you do not understand the nature of sinful deeds. (31)
All the wealth of their high-souled ancestors was seized by these men,
who were experts in deception, like highway robbers who deceive their victims on the road.
These are deceivers, hypocrites, and those who act like herons;
yet, when a great task arose, they were entreated with humility.
Though entreated even with the promise of increasing the fee by a quarter, the brahmins did not give what was requested;
stubbornly declaring "there is nothing," they looked upon their distressed patrons with indifference.
For what reason was the wealth obtained from Kārtavīrya not protected? Why were no sacrifices performed with it, nor was abundant charity bestowed upon supplicants? (35)
Brahmins should never accumulate wealth;
rather, they should sacrifice according to the rules, give gifts, and enjoy their sustenance as they please.
O twice-born ones, danger from thieves regarding wealth has been declared, as well as danger from the king;
there is most terrible danger from fire, and likewise great danger from rogues. (37)
By whatever means possible, he abandons wealth that protects him;
or else, having died, he goes to an evil rebirth, leaving behind his property. (38)
Thus we, full of humility, requested an increase by a quarter;
nevertheless, our priests, clouded by greed, did not grant it. (39)
Giving, enjoyment, and loss—such is the course of wealth;
indeed, giving and enjoyment belong to the virtuous, while loss belongs to the sinful. (40)
Neither a giver nor one who enjoys, but a miser intent on guarding his wealth—such a man, a deceiver who partakes in suffering, must be punished in every way by the king. (41)
Therefore, we are all prepared to slay these deceitful gurus, the lowest of Brahmins; the high-souled ones should not be angry.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken these reasoned words and thus comforted those sages,
they then wandered about, searching for the wife of Bhṛgu in many places.
Afflicted by fear, the wives of Bhrigu, weeping, trembling, and exceedingly emaciated, took refuge with Himavat, the lord of mountains. || 44 ||
Thus those brahmins, afflicted by the Haihayas who were greedy for wealth,
were slaughtered at will by those furious evildoers.
Greed alone, residing within the bodies of men, is the great enemy;
it is declared to be the source of all suffering, the giver of misery, and the destroyer of life. (46)
For he is indeed the root of all evil, always possessed by craving;
he is a creator of discord among the three castes and likewise the cause of all suffering.
Out of greed they indeed abandon dharma as well as their family tradition;
they kill their mother, brother, father, and likewise their kinsmen. 48.
Overcome by greed and deluded by sin, what improper and wicked act would one not commit against a teacher, a friend, a wife, a son, or even a sister? (49)
From anger, from desire, and from egoism, greed alone is the great enemy;
one gives up even one's life through greed—how much more so that which is not covered? (50)
O Great King, your ancestors, who were knowers of dharma and established on the path of the righteous—
both the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas— met their destruction through greed.
Wherein were Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, and Bāhlika;
Bhīmasena, the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira), as well as Arjuna and Keśava. || 52 ||
Nevertheless, they waged a most fierce battle against one another;
driven by greed, they caused a great slaughter of their own kin here on earth.
Droṇa has been slain, Bhīṣma has been slain, and likewise the sons of the Pāṇḍavas;
brothers, fathers, and sons—all have indeed been killed in battle.
Therefore, what indeed might a man not do when overcome by greed?
By the Haihayas, whose minds were possessed by sin, all the Bhṛgus were slaughtered.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaughter of the Bhṛgus along with the Seizure of Wealth by the Haihayas," in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 16.
In the context of the origin of the Haihayas, there is a description of the dialogue between Ramā and Viṣṇu.
Janamejaya said:
"How did all those women [cross] over the ocean of suffering of the Bhṛgus?"
Furthermore, the lineage of those Brāhmaṇas became firmly established as the Muktāvaṃśa. || 1 ||
Tell me, what deed was accomplished by the Haihayas after they killed even those brāhmaṇas?
Speak of that act performed by the kṣatriyas who were possessed by greed and followed sinful conduct.
O Brahmin, there is no satiety for me as I drink the nectar of your discourse,
which purifies men, bestows happiness, and yields fruit in the world beyond.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall relate the sin-destroying story of how those women were liberated from that insurmountable suffering.
O King, when the wives of the Bhṛgus went to the Himavat mountain,
terrified by fear and their hopes shattered, having been severely oppressed by the Haihayas.
Having installed an earthen image of Gaurī there on the bank of the river,
they devoted themselves to fasting and made a firm resolve regarding death.
Having gone there in a dream, the goddess then said to those most excellent women:
"Among you, a man with thighs like an elephant's will be born to one of you."
"Pervaded by a portion of my power, he shall accomplish your task.
Having thus commanded, Parāmbā subsequently vanished.
Then all those excellent women woke up and attained great joy;
among them, one clever woman was exceedingly agitated by fear.
When that Brāhmaṇa woman was seen by the Kṣatriyas intent on flight, she bore the embryo with one thigh for the sake of the lineage's prosperity.
Overwhelmed and struck with terror by that splendor, they then fled in great haste, crying out, "Seize her! Kill her! The woman, though pregnant, is escaping quickly! (11)
Speaking thus, they arrived with swords in hand;
seeing them approach, she, afflicted by fear, wept.
For the sake of protecting the fetus, she cried out, overcome by extreme fear;
hearing her mother weeping, distressed, and as if deprived of life, [the child spoke]. (13)
Supportless and wailing, she was intensely tormented by the Kṣatriyas, like a pregnant doe seized by a lion. || 14 ||
Then the boy, becoming enraged, quickly emerged from her thigh—she whose eyes were filled with tears and who was trembling—just as a second sun might burst forth. (15)
Stealing away the sight of the Kṣatriyas by his splendor,
that auspicious boy caused everyone to regain their vision instantly upon seeing him.
The Kṣatriyas wandered through mountain fastnesses like those born blind;
they all pondered in their minds, "What is this now? (17)
That we were all born deprived of sight due to the vision of a child is the power of this Brāhmaṇī; great indeed is the strength of her vow of chastity.
"Having achieved their goals in an instant, what will those who are now suffering do?"—thinking thus in their minds, they became sightless and without refuge. (19)
The Haihayas, deprived of their senses, sought refuge with the Brāhmaṇī;
trembling with fear, they bowed down to her with their palms joined in reverence.
And those bulls among Kṣatriyas, agitated by fear, spoke to her for the sake of seeing her:
"Be gracious, O blessed mother; we are indeed your servants. (21)
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, these Kṣatriyas of sinful intent who committed offenses have all become sightless upon seeing you, O slender-limbed one. (22)
