O beautiful lady, we do not see your face at all, like those born blind;
wonderful is your ascetic power and vigor—what can we, evildoers, do? (23)
We have come to you for refuge; O giver of honor, grant us eyesight!
You ought to show compassion, for this blindness is more terrible than death. (24)
Furthermore, by granting us our sight, make the kṣatriyas your servants;
and having desisted from our evil deeds, let us go together.
Henceforth, such an act must never be performed again;
for we are indeed the servants of all the Bhārgavas. (26)
Whatever sin has been committed out of ignorance, that must now be forgiven by you;
henceforth, there shall be no enmity anywhere between the Bhṛgus and the Kṣatriyas. (27)
"The Haihayas must act with integrity and behave properly toward you by means of oaths;
remain with your sons, O lady of beautiful hips, for we are bowed down before you. (28)
"Be gracious, O auspicious lady; we shall never harbor enmity toward you.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, the brahmin woman was filled with wonder. (29)
To those who were prostrate, distressed, and deprived of sight, he spoke, consoling them:
"O Kṣatriyas, I have indeed not accepted your gaze. (30)
"It is not out of anger that I speak; hear now the true reason:
this descendant of Bhṛgu, born from your thigh, has surely become angry with you today. (31)
Therefore, your eyes have been paralyzed by that wrathful one,
who, having learned that his own kinsmen— even those still in the womb— had been slain by the Kṣatriyas.
O sons, when you, out of a desire for wealth, killed even the unborn embryos of the Bhṛgus— who were sinless ascetics devoted to the Dharma— then [the curse was incurred].
Then this embryo was carried by me in my thigh for a hundred years;
and by him, the entire Veda with its six auxiliary limbs was instantly mastered.
Even while remaining in the womb, that boy desires to kill him, surely inflamed by anger on account of his father’s murder, for the sake of increasing the lineage of Bhṛgu.
"By the grace of the Blessed Lady, this boy has been born to me;
by his divine splendor, your eyes have been robbed of their sight. (36)
Therefore, request my son Aurva today with humility;
for he, being pleased by your prostration, will restore your sight.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of hers, the Haihayas praised him;
filled with humility, they bowed down to that best of sages, the thigh-born one.
Then, being satisfied, he spoke to those wise ones:
"O kings, go to your own homes; you have fulfilled my command."
Those events ordained by the gods are inevitable;
a wise person should not feel grief on this account. (40)
As before, may all the sages attain their desires as they please;
free from anger, may they go to their abodes at their ease.
Thus instructed by him, the Haihayas, having regained their sight,
took leave of Aurva and returned to their homes as they pleased.
O protector of the earth, the Brāhmaṇī took that divine son and went to her own hermitage; there, unwearied, she nurtured the radiant child.
Thus has the destruction of the Bhṛgus been told to you, O King, as well as the sin indeed committed by the kṣatriyas who were possessed by greed. 44.
Janamejaya said:
"I have heard of the great and terrible deed of the Kṣatriyas;
in this matter, greed alone was the cause, and it brought suffering to both sides. (45)
O son of Vāsavi, I wish to ask something regarding a doubt:
how did those sons of kings become known on earth by the name Haihayas? (46)
Let the Yādavas be as they wish, and likewise the Bhāratas from Bharata;
however, there was a certain king of the Haihayas established in their lineage.
Therefore, O ocean of compassion, I wish to hear the cause:
how were those Haihayas born as Kṣatriyas, and by what deed? (48)
Vyāsa said:
O King, listen in detail to the origin of the Haihayas,
an ancient and most meritorious narrative that destroys all sins.
O King, at one time there was a very handsome son of the Sun,
renowned as Revanta, who was beautiful and possessed immeasurable splendor.
Having mounted the beautiful Uccaiḥśravas, the jewel among horses,
the son of the Sun went to Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Viṣṇu.
When he arrived mounted on a horse, desiring a vision of the Blessed One,
that son of the Sun was seen by Lakṣmī while still standing upon his horse.
Seeing the divine horse and her brother born from the ocean, Ramā was struck with wonder by his beauty and stood there with her eyes transfixed.
The Lord Viṣṇu, seeing him approaching mounted on a beautiful horse, affectionately questioned Ramā.
"O lady of beautiful limbs, who is this approaching like another god mounted on a horse, O lovely one, whose body is the very splendor of Love, enchanting the three worlds? (55)
Then Lakṣmī, gazing [at him] with her mind fixed on him through the turn of fate,
did not say anything at all, even though she was questioned again and again.
Vyāsa said:
Seeing her mind attached to the horse, utterly deluded by passion,
gazing with supreme love, fickle-eyed and unsteady— (57)
The Lord, enraged, said to her: "What do you see, O fair-eyed one?
Deluded upon seeing Hari, you do not speak even when questioned. (58)
"Since you take delight everywhere, you shall therefore become 'Rama';
and because of your fickleness, you shall be called 'Cañcala'—of this there is no doubt whatsoever. (59)
Just as an ordinary woman is surely fickle, so too you, O auspicious lady, have never been steady at all. (60)
O fair-thighed one, if you, standing near me, become deluded upon seeing the horse,
then become a mare in this most dreadful world of mortals.
Thus cursed by Hari due to the turn of fate, the goddess Ramā wept,
trembling, terrified, and deeply distressed.
Having bowed her head to the god, her own husband, the sweet-smiling Ramānātha, full of humility, spoke to him with apprehension. (63)
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Keśava, mine of compassion!
O Govinda, why do you bestow a curse upon me for such a slight offense? (64)
O Lord, never before have I seen such anger as this from you;
where has your innate affection for me gone, which is not subject to destruction? (65)
The vajra-strike should indeed be directed at an enemy, never against a friend.
I am always worthy of your favor; why have I been made an object for your curse? (66)
O Govinda, I shall give up my life today before your very eyes;
how could I live, deprived of you and tormented by the fire of separation? (67)
"O Lord of Gods, grant me grace from this most terrible curse.
O All-pervading One, bestower of happiness, when shall I be released and reach your presence? (68)
Hari said:
"O beloved, when you shall have a son on earth equal to me, then, O slender-limbed one, having obtained me, you will become happy. (69)

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Dialogue between Ramā and Viṣṇu," in the context of the origin of the Haihayas, in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 17.
A Description of the Propitiation of the Goddess through Lakṣmī by the Grace of Śiva.
Janamejaya said:
Thus was the daughter of the ocean cursed by the Blessed One out of anger.
How was that mare born, and what was done by Revanta? || 1 ||
In what land did the ocean-born goddess, assuming the form of a mare, remain all alone like a young woman whose husband has gone abroad? || 2 ||
"O venerable one, for how long was Ramā separated from her husband? How long did she remain in the lonely forest, and what did she do there? (3)
When did the daughter of the ocean obtain a union with Vāsudeva?
And how was a son obtained by her while she was separated from Nārāyaṇa?
O Noble Lord, relate this account in detail;
O Best of Brahmins, I am desirous of hearing this unsurpassed narrative.
Sūta said:
O brāhmaṇas, having been thus questioned by the son of Parīkṣit, Vyāsa then related this story in great detail.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall relate a auspicious ancient narrative (paurāṇikī), which is purifying, pleasant, and composed of clear syllables for the ears. (7)
But Revanta, seeing that his beloved had been cursed by the god, fled far away in fear after bowing down to the Lord of the worlds. || 8 ||
Seeing the anger of the Lord of the World, he hurried to his father and reported to Bhāskara the story concerning the curse.
Distressed, that lotus-eyed goddess Ramā bowed down to the Lord of the Universe; having been commanded, she reached the world of mortals.
Assuming the form of a mare, she went quickly to that very place where Sūrya’s wife had formerly performed a most severe penance.
At the confluence of the Kālindī and Tamasā, to the north of Suparṇākṣa,
in that place which grants all desires and is adorned with most delightful forests.
Remaining there, she meditated with a single-minded focus upon Mahādeva Śaṅkara, the bestower of desired boons, the wielder of the trident and the moon-crested one.
Five-faced and ten-armed, bearing half of Gaurī’s body, with a complexion as white as camphor, blue-throated, and three-eyed. (14)
The god wears a tiger skin and has an elephant hide as his upper garment;
he is adorned with a garland of skulls and has a serpent as his sacred thread.
Having assumed a charming female horse form, Ramādevī, the daughter of the Ocean,
performed difficult penance at that sacred site.
Meditating upon the Supreme God and having fully resorted to dispassion,
a thousand divine years passed there, O lord of the earth.
Then the three-eyed Mahādeva, the bull-mounted Lord Maheśāna, being pleased, became manifest together with Pārvatī. || 18 ||
Having arrived there with his retinue, Śambhu spoke to that beloved of Hari,
who was performing penance and had assumed the form of Aśvinī, O highly fortunate one.
"O auspicious one, O Mother of the World, tell me why you are performing penance;
your husband is the bestower of all goals and the creator of all worlds. (20)
"O Goddess, why do you praise me today, abandoning Hari, the Lord of the Universe, Vāsudeva, the Master of the World, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation? (21)
The word spoken in the Vedas must be followed: for women, the husband is a deity; they must never, under any circumstances or at any time, direct their affection toward another.
Service to the husband is the eternal dharma of women; regardless of his character, he must be served in every way by those desiring their own welfare. (23)
"Nārāyaṇa alone is indeed always worthy of being served by all;
O Daughter of the Ocean, having abandoned that Lord of the gods of gods, why do you meditate upon me?"
Lakṣmī said:
O Āśutoṣa, O Maheśāna, O Śiva, I have been cursed by my husband;
O Lord of Gods, O Ocean of Mercy, deliver me from this curse. (25)
Thus it was said by Hari to Śambhu: "O Śambhu, when I was entreated by you, Viṣṇu, filled with compassion, granted the cause for both curse and favor. (26)
When you have a son, then there shall be liberation from the curse,
and your residence shall be in Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Kamalā.
Having been told this, I have come to this penance grove to perform austerities;
I have propitiated you, O God, the bestower of all goals. (28)
O God of gods, how can I obtain a son without a husband? For he remains in Vaikuṇṭha, having abandoned his innocent and beloved wife.
"O Lord of Gods, O Śaṅkara, if you are pleased with me, grant me a boon;
for there is certainly never any duality in your disposition. (30)
O Hara, beloved of Girijā, I have realized this before my husband:
you who are here are he who was there, and he who was there is you; of this there is no doubt. (31)
"O Śiva, having realized our oneness, I have performed this remembrance for you; otherwise, O Auspicious One, a fault would accrue to me by my taking refuge in you."
Śiva said:
"O Goddess, O beautiful one, daughter of the ocean, how was the identity between me and that Hari truly known by you? Tell me the truth."
Even the gods and sages, as well as the wise who know the truth of the Vedas, do not understand this oneness; they are indeed afflicted by fallacious reasoning.
Many of my devotees likewise revile Vāsudeva, while many devotees of Viṣṇu are intent upon reviling me. (35)
O Goddess, these things occur especially in the Kali age due to the division of time.
How was this known by you, O auspicious one, for it is difficult to be understood by those who have not disciplined their souls? (36)
"In every respect, however, the state of oneness between Hari and me is difficult to attain.
Vyāsa said:
Thus was that beloved of Hari questioned by the gratified Śambhu.
Having learned of his situation,
Ramā, with a very cheerful countenance, began to speak to Śiva there.
Lakṣmī said:
O Lord of the gods, once I saw Viṣṇu in solitude, intent on meditation, performing penance while seated in the lotus posture.
Then, filled with wonder, I questioned that god, my husband, having recognized him as awakened and very gracious, and having approached him with humility. (40)
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, O Lord, when I emerged from the ocean while it was being churned by all the gods and daityas, beginning with Brahmā; || 41 ||
At that time, I observed them all with the desire for a husband,
and having reached the firm conclusion that you are the best among all the gods, you were chosen by me.
"Whom do you meditate upon, O Lord of All? This is a great doubt of mine.
You are dear to me, O Slayer of Kaiṭabha; tell me what is in your mind. (43)
Viṣṇu said:
Listen, O beloved, I shall describe that supreme god whom I meditate upon in my heart— the Great Lord who is easily pleased, the beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Sometimes the God of gods, of immeasurable prowess, meditates upon me;
and I, in turn, meditate upon Śaṅkara, the Lord of gods and destroyer of Tripura.
I am the dear life-breath of Śiva, and Śaṅkara is likewise mine;
there is no difference between us two, whose minds are mutually attached.
"Those who hate Maheśvara surely go to hell;
O large-eyed one, they are my devotees—this I tell you as the truth. (47)
Thus was it spoken by Viṣṇu, the powerful God of gods,
when he was questioned by me in private, O beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Therefore, knowing you to be the beloved of Viṣṇu, I have meditated upon you;
O Maheśāna, act in such a way that there may be a reunion with my beloved.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Śrī, Maheśvara,
who is skilled in speech, comforted her with affectionate words and replied according to the truth.
"Be at ease, O lady of broad hips; I am pleased with your asceticism.
You shall be reunited with your husband, of this there is no doubt. (51)
Right here, the Blessed Lord of the World, urged by me, will come in the form of a horse to fulfill your desire. (52)
In that manner, I shall impel that god Madhusūdana so that he,
intoxicated with pride, will come to you in the form of a horse.
"O fair-browed one, you shall have a son on earth equal to Nārāyaṇa;
he shall become a protector of the world, honored by all people. (54)
O highly fortunate lady, having attained that state, you shall go to Vaikuṇṭha together with that husband of yours, O goddess, and you will become his beloved. (55)
"This son of yours shall become renowned by the name Ekavīra;
through him, the Haihaya dynasty will spread across the earth. (56)
But you have forgotten the Supreme Goddess who dwells within your heart;
blinded by pride and intoxicated in mind, this is the fruit you reap for that.
Therefore, O daughter of the ocean, for the sake of pacifying that fault, take refuge with your whole being in the Supreme Deity who dwells within the heart.
"Otherwise, O best of steeds, how could your mind go [to that place]?
Vyāsa said:
Having thus granted the boon to the Goddess, the Blessed Lord, the husband of the Mountain-born One, [departed]. (59)
Śiva himself, together with Umā, vanished from sight;
and she too, the lotus-seated one of beautiful limbs, remained right there.
She meditated upon the supremely beautiful lotus-feet of the Goddess,
the circle of whose toenails was polished by the crest-jewels of the gods and asuras.
And with a voice faltering with love, she praised him again and again, awaiting her husband, Hari, who had assumed the form of a horse. (62)

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Propitiation of the Goddess through Lakṣmī by Means of Śiva's Grace," in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 18.
The Description of the Departure for Vaikuṇṭha in Her Own Form Immediately After the Birth of the Son.
Vyāsa said:
Having granted her the boon, Śambhu quickly departed for Kailāsa.
Delightful, frequented by hosts of gods, and adorned by apsarases. || 1 ||
Having gone there, he dispatched the group Citrarūpa, who was skilled in action,
to Vaikuṇṭha for the sake of accomplishing Lakṣmī’s purpose.
Śiva said:
O Citrarūpa, go to Hari and speak these words on my behalf,
so that he may make his distressed wife free from sorrow.
Having been addressed thus, Citrarūpa then departed in haste for Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme abode, which was surrounded by hosts of Vaiṣṇavas.
It was filled with various groves of trees, adorned with hundreds of ponds,
and frequented by swans, kāraṇḍava ducks, peacocks, parrots, and cuckoos.
It was joined with lofty palaces, adorned with banners,
filled with the arts of dance and song, and provided with mandāra trees.
It was adorned with Bakula, Aśoka, Tilaka, and Campaka trees,
and filled with the warbling of birds that brought delight to the ears.
Having gazed upon the palace of Viṣṇu, he bowed down and spoke to the two gatekeepers named Jaya and Vijaya, who both stood there with canes in their hands.
Citrarūpa said: "O, announce quickly to Hari, the Supreme Soul,
that a messenger has arrived here, sent by the trident-bearing Śiva."
Having heard those words of his, the supremely intelligent Jaya went to Hari,
prostrated before him, and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
"O God of gods, O Beloved of Ramā, O Keśava, the mine of compassion!
A messenger of Śaṅkara has arrived and stands here at the gate. (11)
"Command whether he is to be admitted or not, O Lord whose banner is Garuda;
for although he bears a variegated form, I do not know the gravity of his purpose. (12)
Having heard this, Hari, who understood the cause, said to Jaya:
"Bring in here the servant of Rudra who is established in his vow."
Having heard this, Jaya quickly went to that most wonderful servant of Śaṅkara and summoned him, saying, "Come! (14).
Then Citrarūpa, having been introduced by Jaya, prostrated himself like a staff before Viṣṇu and stood with his palms joined in reverence. || 15 ||
Seeing him, the Lord whose banner is Garuḍa was filled with wonder at Śambhu’s servant, who possessed a wondrous form and was full of humility.
Smiling, the Lord of Ramā questioned that Citrarūpa: "O sinless one, is all well with the God of gods and his family?"
"Tell me, for what purpose have you been sent here? What is the business of Hara, or has some task arisen concerning the gods? (18)
The messenger said:
O Garuḍa-bannered Lord, what is unknown to you here in this world? For you know the three periods of time regarding that which I am indeed declaring. (19)
"I have been sent here by Bhava; O Janārdana, being well-acquainted with you, I speak these words to you at the command of Hara, O Lord. (20)
He said this: "O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, your wife Kamalālayā is performing austerities at the confluence of the Kālindī and the Tamasā."
The Goddess, assuming the form of a mare, is the bestower of the accomplishment of all goals;
she is worthy of being meditated upon by hosts of gods, humans, yakṣas, and kinnaras. (22)
Without her, no man whatsoever can truly partake in happiness;
O lotus-eyed Hari, what joy do you obtain by abandoning her? (23)
O Lord of the World, even one who is weak protects his wife, and even one who is destitute does so;
O All-pervading One, why has the Mistress of the Universe been abandoned without any fault? (24)
O Teacher of the World, he whose wife [is such] experiences suffering in saṃsāra;
fie upon his life in this world, for it is despised by the circles of his enemies! (25)
Having seen you today utterly separated from Rāmā and exceedingly distressed, those enemies,
their desires fulfilled, will laugh at you day and night.
"O Lord of Gods, delight in Ramā; take her onto your lap—she who is endowed with all auspicious marks, possessed of excellent character, and beautiful in form. (27)
Be happy having obtained that beloved woman of lovely smiles;
for I remember the suffering born of separation from my own beloved without being afflicted by it. (28)
O Viṣṇu, when my wife Satī died at Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
O lotus-eyed one, I then experienced unbearable suffering.
Afflicted by the pain of separation from her, I felt grief in my mind, thinking: "In this saṃsāra, may there never be another man like me. (30)

After a long time, having performed a penance that was exceedingly difficult to accomplish, I have once again obtained the daughter of the mountain, she who had been consumed by wrath at the sacrifice.
"O Hara, what happiness have you attained by abandoning your beloved and remaining alone for a period of a thousand years?"
"Go, console that illustrious lady, and bring her back to your own home;
let no one in this world become liberated from this cycle of existence while she, Ramā, remains there."
Assuming the form of a horse, you must consort with that lotus-dwelling goddess;
having fathered a long-lived son, O venerable one, bring back that woman of pure smiles.
Vyāsa said:
O Bhārata, having heard those words of Citrarūpa,
Hari said "So be it" to that messenger and dispatched him to Śaṅkara.
Then, after the messenger had departed, the Blessed Lord, filled with desire, quickly assumed a charming horse-form and went there from Vaikuṇṭha.
Where that daughter of the ocean, having assumed the form of a mare, was performing penance,
Viṣṇu reached that place and beheld her standing there in the form of a horse.
She too, beholding her husband Govinda in the form of a horse, recognized him; and having seen him, that virtuous woman stood there, filled with wonder and her eyes brimming with tears.
The union of those two, both afflicted by the god of love, took place there at the world-renowned and purifying confluence of the Kālindī and the Tamasā. (39)
Then that mare, the beloved of Indra, became pregnant;
she gave birth right there to a beautiful child who was preeminent in his virtues. (40)
The Blessed One, smiling, spoke these words to her that were consistent with the agreement:
"Cast off this body of a Vāḍava today; become now as you were in your former body. (41)
"O fair-eyed one, having assumed our own Vaikuṇṭha forms, we two shall depart; let this son born of you remain here with you."
Lakṣmī said:
"O bull among the gods, how can I depart, leaving behind my own son born of my own body? Indeed, affection for one's own offspring is very difficult to abandon. (43)
O immeasurable soul, what will be the fate of this child here on the riverbank—helpless, incapable, and small of body in this desolate place? (44)
O Lord, O lotus-eyed one, how could my mind be capable of departing, leaving behind my son who is without refuge, even though he is capable and compassionate? 45.
Then both Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa became endowed with divine bodies; seated upon an excellent celestial chariot, they were praised by the gods in heaven.
Desiring to depart, Kamalā said to her husband, the Lord of Kamalā:
"O Master, take this son; I am not able to abandon him. (47)
"O Lord, my son is as dear to me as my own life, and he resembles you in beauty, O Madhusūdana; taking him with us, we shall go to Vaikuṇṭha. (48)
Hari said: "O beloved, O fair-faced one, you should not give way to despondency;
let him remain here in comfort, for protection has been provided for him by me."
"O lady of beautiful thighs, there is a certain great and wonderful task to be performed;
listen, for I shall tell you today how to bring about the liberation of my son. (50)
The son of Yayāti, renowned on earth by the name Turvasu, was given a very famous name by his father: Harivarma.
That king, desiring a son, is now performing penance at the Pāvana Tīrtha;
a hundred years have passed while he was engaged in his ascetic practice.
O Kamalālayā, this son was created by me for his sake;
having gone there now, O fair-browed one, I shall urge the king to action.
"O passionate woman, I shall give my son to that man who desires a son;
having taken him, the king will deliver the boy to his own home. (54)
Vyāsa said:
Having thus consoled his beloved Padmā and having performed protective rites for the child,
he ascended an excellent celestial chariot and departed together with his beloved.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Departing for Vaikuṇṭha in Her Own Form after the Birth of the Sons," in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Narrative of Ekavīra.
Janamejaya said:
"There is a great doubt here regarding how he was thus a mere infant as soon as he was born."
By whom was he released, and by whom was he seized—this man alone in the desolate forest? (1)
O son of Satyavatī, what has become of that child who was seized by violent beasts such as tigers and lions while still very young? (2)
Vyāsa said:
When Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa departed from that place,
at that very moment a Vidyādhara named Campa arrived there.
O King, mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot together with his beloved,
who was languid with passion, he sported at will according to his desire.
Beholding that unsurpassed child lying alone upon the ground, resembling a son of the gods and sporting at his ease; (5)
Quickly descending from the celestial chariot, Campaka seized that child with speed and attained great joy, like a man of wealth who has found a treasure.
Taking that child, who was like the god of love, just born and enchanting, Campaka gave him to Queen Madanālasā.
Taking the infant with love, her hair standing on end and filled with wonder,
she pressed him firmly against her heart and kissed his face.
O descendant of Bharata, he was embraced and kissed by her with affection; and that slender woman placed him upon her lap as if he were her own son.
Having joyfully ascended the celestial chariot with those two seated on his lap,
the fair-limbed lady, languid with passion, smiled and questioned her husband.
"Whose child is this, O beloved, and by whom was he abandoned in the forest?
This son has been given to me by the Lord with his own hand, O Three-eyed One. (11)
Campaka said:
"O beloved, having gone today, I shall quickly question Śakra, who is all-knowing,
as to whether this child is indeed a god, or a Dānava, or even a Gandharva."
Therefore, being commanded, I shall bring back this son from the forest;
indeed, no task whatsoever must certainly be undertaken by me without first consulting him.
Having spoken thus and taken her, Campaka then went swiftly to the city of Śakra by means of that celestial chariot, his eyes wide with joy.
Having bowed with affection at the feet of the Lord of Śacī, Campaka presented the boy and, standing with palms joined in reverence, spoke.
O God of gods, at this most purifying sacred ford at the confluence of the Kālindī and the Tamasā, I have obtained this boy who possesses the splendor of the god of love.
"Whose lovely child is this, and why was he abandoned, O Lord of Śacī?
If it is your command, O Lord of Gods, I shall take this child as my son. (17)
The boy was exceedingly handsome, the beloved son of his mistress;
yet, according to all the treatises on dharma, he is declared to be an adopted son.
Indra said:
"O highly fortunate one, this son of Vāsudeva, who had assumed the form of a horse, is this Haihaya, a scorcher of foes born of Lakṣmī. (19)
It is said that the Blessed One brought forth this boy for a specific purpose, surely to be given to King Yayāti’s son. (20)
Impelled by Hari, that most righteous king will come today to that delightful sacred site for the sake of his son.
Therefore, go to that very place taking the auspicious boy with you, before the king, urged by Hari, arrives to seize him.
"Go there and release him; do not delay, O best of men!
If the king does not see the boy, he will become distressed. (23)
Therefore, O Campaka, release him; let the king obtain this son.
By the name Ekavīra, he shall become renowned upon the surface of the earth.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, O lord of the earth, Campaka, filled with haste, went to that place taking his son.
He released the boy at the very place where he had previously been standing;
then, ascending his own celestial chariot, he departed for the circle of his own hermitage.
At that very moment, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the teacher of the world, mounted an excellent celestial chariot together with Lakṣmī and went toward the king.
Then Viṣṇu was seen by that king as he was descending from his excellent celestial chariot;
the king rejoiced at the sight of Hari.
He indeed fell upon the ground like a staff. || 28 ||
"Rise, my child! Hari said, comforting his own devotee as he fell to the ground.
Eager and filled with devotion, he then began to praise Vāsudeva, who stood before him, making his voice resonant.
O God of gods, Lord of all the worlds, ocean of compassion, Teacher of the world, Lord of Lakṣmī!
That vision of You which is indeed very difficult to obtain, unattainable even by practitioners of yoga—[that has been granted] to me, the dull-witted. (30)
Those who are free from longing are detached from sense objects; to them indeed belongs your vision.
O Blessed One, O Infinite One, O God of gods, I am one whose hope is supreme, yet I am not worthy of your vision.
Thus praised by that king, Viṣṇu spoke to him with words consisting of nectar:
"O King, choose whatever is desired by your mind; being pleased by your austerity, I shall grant it to you."
Then the king, having prostrated at his feet,
spoke to Viṣṇu who stood before him: "Indeed,
this penance has been performed by me for the sake of a son."
O Murāri, grant me a son who is equal to yourself.
Having heard the king's request, the Primordial God, whose word is never in vain, said to that monarch:
"O son of Yayāti, go to that sacred ford at the confluence of the Kalindakanyā and the Tamasā."
Today, my son of immeasurable power, born of my own seed and begotten by Lakṣmī, has been released by me right there according to your wish.
Now, O King, accept this which has been performed for the sake of your praise. || 35 ||
Having heard Hari’s exceedingly sweet words,
the king became satisfied in his heart; and Hari, having thus granted the boon, departed.
And he went to the world of Vaikuṇṭha, accompanied by Ramā. || 36 ||
When Hari had departed, that son of Yayāti, King Yadu, accompanied by his charioteer,
proceeded with great affection to where his son was, having heard these words of Janārdana.
Having gone there, he saw that most enchanting child playing on the ground;
having placed [the child] in his mouth with one hand...
His big toe is smooth, and he is without a second being [to equal him]. || 38 ||
Beholding that son, who was the very embodiment of Love, born from Kamalā as a portion of Nārāyaṇa,
and possessed of the power of Hari, he named him Harivarma.
His lotus-like face became fully blossomed with joy. || 39 ||
Taking [him] with great speed by his lotus-like hands,
his body became submerged in an ocean of love;
having smelled the crown of his head, he was filled with joy.
The king rejoiced and embraced his son.
Beholding his exceedingly charming face, he spoke to him with a throat choked by tears:
"You have been bestowed upon me by Lord Janārdana, for a mother, fearing the suffering of her son, has indeed surrendered you."
O son, for your sake I performed a most difficult penance for a full hundred years;
by that very act, the beloved of Ramā was pleased.
You have been granted for the arising of happiness within saṃsāra. || 42 ||
Your mother Ramā, having abandoned you, her own son, for my sake, has gone away together with Hari;
blessed indeed is she who holds you laughing upon her lap.
Having made you her son, she would have a joyful countenance. || 43 ||
"O son, Lakṣmīdhara himself has made you the very form of a ship for the ocean of saṃsāra.
Having spoken thus to his son, the king joyfully took him by the hand and went home.
Hearing that the king had arrived near the city, all the ministers of the monarch,
along with the people and the family priests, went into the presence of the king, bringing offerings with them.
The bards, singers, and chroniclers quickly came before the king;
having reached the city, the king saw them assembled in front of him.
And having comforted the people with his words and his gaze. || 46 ||
Honored by the citizens, the king entered the city together with his son;
the monarch proceeded along the roads while parched grain and flowers were scattered all around him.
Accompanied by his ministers, he joyfully took his son with both hands from their prosperous home and then installed that charming son upon the throne.
And [he saw] one who had just given birth, resembling the god of love. || 48 ||
Taking her newborn son, that blameless queen asked the king:
"O King, from where indeed has this son of noble birth come?"
One whose form is equal to that of the God of Love has been obtained by you. || 49 ||
"By whom was this given? Tell me quickly, my beloved; my heart has been struck by this son.
Then the king, filled with joy, spoke:
O beloved, for my son has indeed been taken by Rāmeśa. || 50 ||
"O lady of tremulous eyes, this portion of Janārdana, born from Kamalā and possessed of undiminished strength, has been bestowed upon you.
Having accepted him, the queen attained great joy.
And the king celebrated a wonderful festival. || 51 ||
And indeed, he gave gifts to beggars;
many songs and musical instruments resounded as the king celebrated a festival for his son.
He bestowed upon him the renowned name Ekavīra.
Having attained happiness, he, whose valor was equal to that of the lord of the gods, rejoiced with joy;
[he beheld] a son in Hari who was endowed with beauty and virtues worthy of himself.
Having attained [this], he is liberated from the debt to his lineage. || 53 ||
Thus, having obtained that son— who was endowed with the full multitude of virtues and entrusted to him by the Lord of all the gods— the king,
attended by his wife amidst various pleasures and diversions, [reigned].
He, whose majesty was equal to that of Śakra, lived in his own home. || 54 ||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Ekavīrā," in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Vyāsa said: At that time, the king performed the purificatory rites for the princess Ekāvalī, beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman).
Day by day, the boy, being well-nurtured, quickly attained growth.
Having obtained through that high-souled one the happiness born of worldly existence arising from a son, the king considered his three debts to have been discharged.
In the sixth month, having performed the annaprāśana for him according to the prescribed rite,
and likewise in the third year, the excellent cūḍākaraṇa ceremony should be performed.
Having honored the Brahmins with various riches and diverse wealth, he also gratified the cows and other beggars with manifold gifts.
And in his eleventh year, having performed the ceremony of tying the girdle of muñja grass for him,
the king caused him to study the science of archery.
Seeing that his son had mastered the Vedas and was proficient in the duties of kings,
the lord of men resolved to consecrate him.
On a day joined with the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism and the Sun, the best of kings respectfully had the requisites prepared for the consecration.
Having summoned the twice-born who were knowers of the Vedas and experts in all the scriptures,
he performed the consecration of his own son according to the prescribed rites.
Having brought water from sacred fords and from the oceans,
the king himself performed the consecration according to the prescribed rites on an auspicious day.
Then, having given wealth to the brahmins and entrusted the kingdom to his son,
that king, desiring heaven, quickly departed for the forest.
Having made the king his sole hero and having honored his ministers,
the self-controlled monarch then entered the forest together with his wife.
Having established his third hermitage on the peak of Maināka, the king,
subsisting daily on leaves and fruits, meditated upon Pārvatī.
Having acted thus, that king, having died together with his wife at the end of his allotted time, went to the world of Vāsava by virtue of his meritorious deeds.
Having heard that his father had reached the world of Indra, the Haihaya then performed the funeral rites prescribed by the Vedas.
Having performed all the subsequent rites for his father,
the wise son of the king ruled the kingdom bestowed by his father with great approval.
Then Ekavīra, the knower of dharma, having obtained unsurpassed sovereignty,
enjoyed various pleasures, highly honored by his ministers.
One day, the powerful king, accompanied by the sons of his ministers, went to the bank of the Jāhnavī mounted upon a horse. (17)
He beheld delightful trees, filled with the warbling of cuckoos,
laden with flowers and fruit, and graced by swarms of bees.
He saw the divine hermitages of the sages, resounding with the sound of the Vedas,
their skies filled with the smoke of burnt offerings, and crowded with young fawns.
He saw rice fields where the grain was fully ripened and well-guarded by cowherd girls,
as well as delightful groves containing gardens of blossoming lotuses.
He gazed upon the lovely priyāla trees, campakas,
breadfruit trees, bakulas, tilakas, nīpas, and mandāras, all in full bloom.
As he went along, he passed by *śāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, as well as *jambū*, mango, and *kadamba* trees, and saw a hundred-petaled lotus in full bloom in the waters of the Ganges.
The lord of the earth saw a lotus exceedingly rich in fragrance, and then,
at the southern side of that water-born flower, he beheld a lotus-eyed woman.
She was golden-hued with beautiful hair, a neck like a conch shell, and a slender waist;
she had lips like the bimba fruit, was lovely, and her breasts were slightly budding.
The king beheld a maiden with a beautiful nose and lovely limbs, who had abandoned her companion—a woman overwhelmed and tormented by grief—as she was weeping. (25)
Beholding her with tearful eyes, weeping like a female osprey in a lonely place,
the king asked the maiden for the cause of her grief.
"Tell me after hearing [me]: who are you, whose daughter are you, O fair-faced one? Are you a Gandharva woman or a daughter of the gods? Why do you weep, O beautiful one? (27)
"How is it that you, O young girl, are left all alone? By whom were you abandoned, O one with a voice like a cuckoo?
Where has your husband gone, O beloved, or where is your father? Tell me now. (28)
"O lady with brows like a young deer, tell me today what is your sorrow in my presence;
O slender-waisted one, I shall utterly destroy your suffering in every way. (29)
O slender-limbed one, no one at all causes me excessive distress in my kingdom;
O beloved, there is no fear of thieves, nor likewise any fear of Rākṣasas.
While I rule as king, no terrible portents shall appear upon the earth;
there shall be no fear from tigers or lions, nor shall anyone experience any fear whatsoever.
"Speak, O lady of beautiful thighs! Why do you lament here on the bank of the Jāhnavī?
You are without protection; tell me, what is your sorrow? (32)
"O beloved, I shall destroy the most violent suffering of living beings upon the surface of the earth, both that caused by fate and that caused by men; this is my wonderful vow. (33)
"O large-eyed one, speak; I shall do what you desire," when these words were spoken by the king, she, having heard them, spoke with a gentle voice.
Listen, O Indra among kings, I shall tell you the cause of my grief:
how can a living being, free from calamity, weep, O lord of the earth? (35)
O mighty-armed one, I shall tell you the reason why I weep:
in a land other than your own kingdom, there is a most righteous king. (36)
O Great King, there was a monarch named Raibhya who was deeply distressed by being childless;
his wife was well-known by the name Rukmarekhā. (37)
Beautiful, clever, virtuous, and endowed with all auspicious marks, she, being childless and sorrowful, spoke thus to her beloved again and again: (38)
"O Lord, what is the use of my life? Fie upon my life, which is in vain on this earth—for I am barren, devoid of happiness, and childless! (39)
Thus urged by his wife, the king then summoned Brahmins who were experts in that matter and performed an excellent sacrifice according to the prescribed rites.
Then, desiring a son, he gave abundant wealth as prescribed;
while the ghee was being offered in great measure into the exceedingly radiant fire, [a voice emerged].
A maiden of beautiful limbs and auspicious marks appeared;
she had lips like the *bimba* fruit, fine teeth, lovely eyebrows, and a face resembling the full moon. (42)
She has a golden luster, beautiful hair-ends, and soft palms that are red;
her eyes are deeply crimson, she is slender, and the soles of her feet are intensely red.
Then that Hotrā, who had arisen from the sacrificial fire, was accepted by him;
taking hold of that woman of slender waist, the Hotṛ spoke to the king. (44)
"O King, accept this daughter of mine, endowed with every auspicious mark, who was born like a single-stringed necklace from the sacrificial fire while the oblation was being poured. (45)
And she shall become a daughter renowned in the world by the name Ekāvalī;
O protector of the earth, be happy with this daughter who is equal to a son.
"Be satisfied, O Indra among kings; she has been given by Lord Viṣṇu.
Having heard the words of the priest and having seen that auspicious maiden, the king [was pleased]. (47)
Greatly delighted, the king accepted the highly esteemed Hotrā who had been given;
having taken her, the monarch bestowed that fair-faced woman upon his wife.
Having addressed Rukmarekhā, he said, "O fortunate lady, accept this daughter.
Having obtained that lovely girl with eyes like lotus petals, she [accepted her]. (49)
The queen rejoiced with great joy upon obtaining her son as she desired;
she performed the auspicious rites, such as the birth-ceremony (jātakarma) and others. || 50 ||
Then, having duly completed that entire sacrifice arising from the birth of his son, the king gave auspicious sacrificial fees to the twice-born.
Having given gifts and dismissed the best of brahmins, the lord of the earth attained great joy;
day by day, she of the dark-cornered eyes shone intensely with the increase of her sons.
The king’s wife, accompanied by her son, attained supreme joy;
on that day, a festival arose for him on account of the birth of his son.
Indeed, the daughter became beloved for the sake of her son and ministers;
and I am the minister’s daughter, O Subuddhi, fashioned by the god of love for the king. (54)
And there was one named Yaśovatī, whose age was equal to mine;
I was made her companion by the king for the sake of playing with her. (55)
She became her constant companion, filled with love day and night;
wherever she saw fragrant lotuses, there she beheld Ekāvalī.
There that young woman finds delight; she would find no happiness elsewhere.
For even lotuses grow only on the far bank of the Ganges.
O King, having enjoyed herself there together with me and her companions, she went away;
I have informed you, O King, that your daughter has departed from Kamalākara.
Looking back from afar, she departed into the desolate forest;
then her father, having constructed reservoirs, restrained her within his home.
Then, even after seeing the lotuses in bloom, covered with bees,
the young woman still went forth, her mind still attached to the lotus.
Then the king dispatched guards armed with weapons; thus,
that slender maiden, accompanied by her friends and protected by such a guard,
used to come and go daily to the waters of the Ganges for the sake of sport.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Princess Ekāvalī," in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Queen’s Dream for the Sole Hero of the Haihayas, who was released from his single-string necklace by Yaśovatī.
Yaśovatī said:
"Having risen at dawn, the slender-limbed woman set out accompanied by her friend."
She was being fanned with yak-tail whisks and guarded by many guards.
Accompanied by those who were well-armed and fully armored, that woman of excellent complexion arrived here at the auspicious Nalinī lake for the sake of sport, O Indra among kings.
I too have come here to the bank of the Gaṅgā together with her,
accompanied by celestial nymphs, as she plays with lotuses.
And likewise, Ekāvalī and I were engaged in play when suddenly a powerful Dānava arrived.
Known as Kālaketu, he was accompanied by many Rākṣasas who held in their hands iron clubs, swords, maces, bows, arrows, and javelins.
And he beheld a single-stringed necklace, radiant with beauty and youth,
playing with beautiful lotuses like the wife of Kāma herself.
I said, "O King, who is this Daitya who has arrived?
O lotus-eyed one, let us go into the midst of the guards. (7)
Having reflected thus, O Prince, my friend and I, out of fear, quickly went right into the midst of the armed soldiers.
But Kālaketu, seeing that enchanting woman and afflicted by passion, seized a heavy mace and rushed forward. || 9 ||
Having put the guards at a distance, he seized the lotus-eyed woman—
trembling with fear, shivering, and crying out, her slender-waisted form.
Although I said to the Dānava, "Abandon her;
take me," he, afflicted by lust, did not take me, but instead took her and departed.
Crying out "Stay! Stay!", the guards restrained that mighty one and engaged in a battle that caused great wonder.
Cruel Rākṣasas, with weapons in their hands on all sides, also fought together with the guards, having exerted themselves for the sake of their master’s cause. || 13 ||
Then a battle took place with Kālaketu in that conflict;
having slain all the guards, the one of great strength seized her.
Accompanied by the army of Rākṣasas, he set out toward the city,
beholding that young woman weeping as she was seized by the Dānava.
I followed behind her to the place where my friend had been led,
crying out so that she might see me as I pursued her step by step.
Seeing that I had arrived, she then became somewhat composed;
I went near her and addressed her again and again. (17)
Having reached me, O King, she was afflicted with extreme sorrow, overwhelmed by trembling and perspiration;
clasping my neck, she wept, deeply distressed.
That Kālaketu spoke these words to me with affection:
"Console your frightened friend, whose eyes are tremulous. (19)
"O beloved, today I have reached this city which is equal to the world of the gods;
indeed, I am your slave through our love. Why then do you weep so despondently? (20)
"Tell this to your friend today; be at ease, O fair-eyed one.
Having spoken thus, he placed me beside his friend in that excellent chariot.
Accompanied by a vast army, his face like a blooming lotus, the wicked one went swiftly to his own charming city.
Having likewise established Ekāvalī and me in a white house,
she appointed crores of Rākṣasas for the purpose of guarding the residence.
Then, on the second day, O King, he spoke to me in private:
"Awaken this young friend of mine, who is grieving and distressed by separation."
"O fair-hipped one, become my wife; enjoy happiness as you desire.
O moon-faced one, the kingdom is yours; I am forever your servant. (25)
"Having heard those harsh words spoken by me repeatedly, I am unable to speak anything pleasant; you, O Lord, must say this to her."
When these words were spoken, the wicked one, whose mind was pierced by passion,
spoke with humility to his beloved friend, the slender-waisted woman.
"O slender-waisted one, you have cast a spell upon me;
therefore, O beloved, my heart has been stolen by you and has come under your control. (28)
"Therefore, it is certain that I have been made your slave today;
favor me, who am utterly helpless and tormented by the arrows of love. (29)
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, youth passes away; it is fleeting and difficult to obtain again.
O auspicious one, make it fruitful by embracing me, your husband. (30)
Ekāvalī said:
"I was previously intended by my father to be given to a prince;
however, O illustrious one, that Haihaya was chosen by me in my heart. (31)
"How can I resort to another lover, abandoning the eternal Dharma?
Having cast aside the duty of a maiden, do you now claim to know the definitive conclusions of the scriptures? (32)
To whomever the father may give her according to his desire, that girl shall obtain him as her husband;
for a maiden is always dependent, never possessing independence.
Although addressed thus by her, that sinner did not desist, being deluded;
he did not release the large-eyed woman, nor likewise me who stood at his side. (34)
In an opening of the netherworld, his city was situated in an extremely perilous place;
it was a fortress guarded by Rākṣasas, adorned and surrounded by moats.
There my dear friend, who is as beloved to me as life itself, remains afflicted by suffering;
therefore, separated from her, I cry out here in great distress. (36)
Ekavīra said:
"How have you arrived here from that city of that evil-minded one?
Great is my wonder in this matter; tell me the truth, O fair-faced one. (37)
And the statement spoken by you appears doubtful, O beautiful lady;
it now seems to me that she was conceived as your father for the sake of the Haihayas. (38)
"I am a king named Haihaya; there is no other lord of the earth.
Was that beautiful-eyed friend of yours mentioned for my sake? (39)
O fair-browed, beautiful lady, you ought to dispel this doubt of mine;
I shall bring her back after slaying that lowest of Rākṣasas.
"O lady of virtuous vows, if you know it, show me his location;
or has it been reported to the king, or perhaps to his father, who is deeply distressed? (41)
Does he whose beloved daughter she is not know that she has been abducted? Why was no effort made by him for her sake to bring about her release? (42)
Knowing his daughter has been taken captive, how can the king remain so composed? Is he powerless, or what is the reason? Tell me quickly. (43)
"O lotus-petal-eyed one, by describing your superhuman qualities, you have stolen my heart; indeed, O friend, I have been brought completely under the sway of desire. (44)
"When shall I see that beloved woman after having released her from this great peril?"—thus does my heart today form an exceedingly intense longing. (45)
Tell me the means of reaching that city which is so exceedingly difficult to access;
tell me how you yourself have come here from that perilous place.
Yaśovatī said:
"O Lord of the People, out of my youthful nature, I obtained from a perfected Brahmin this mantra of the Blessed One, preceded by the meditation upon the seed-syllable. (47)
O King, while staying there, I reflected in my mind:
"I shall constantly propitiate Caṇḍikā, whose prowess is fierce. (48)
That Goddess, when served according to one's desire, will bring about both bondage and liberation;
she is the Power who is compassionate toward her devotees and capable in every accomplishment.
She who creates the universe by her power and likewise protects it, withdraws it at the end of the aeon; she is formless and without support.
Having thus reflected in his mind upon the Goddess Śivā, the Sovereign of the Universe,
he meditated within his heart on her, who was clad in red garments, gentle, and possessed of deep red eyes.
Recalling her form in my mind and intent upon the muttering of the mantra,
I worshipped the Goddess for one month with meditative concentration.
In a dream, Caṇḍikā, gratified by my devotion, came to me and addressed me with nectar-like words, asking, "Why are you asleep? (53)
"Arise and go quickly to the beautiful bank of the Gaṅgā;
that preeminent king of the Haihayas will arrive there. (54)
The one hero with mighty arms, the crusher of all enemies,
was given by Dattātreya my mantra, the supreme one known as Mahāvidyā.
He was granted [this boon], and he too constantly attends upon me with extreme devotion;
his mind is perpetually attached to me, and he is ever intent on my worship.
Meditating on me alone among all beings, he dwells with me as his supreme goal;
that high-minded one will surely bring about the destruction of your suffering.
Moving about there, your son shall become your protector;
having slain that terrible Rākṣasa, he will liberate you, O proud lady.
O Ekāvalī, that auspicious prince, Ekavīra, who is proficient in all the scriptures, should subsequently be made your husband by you.
Having spoken thus, the goddess vanished; at that very moment, I indeed awoke.
I then related the account of the dream as well as the worship of the goddess.
Upon hearing this, that lotus-eyed woman became serene of countenance;
especially delighted, she spoke to me with a pure smile. (61)
Go there with haste and perform my task, O beloved;
the blessed Satyavākya will bring about our liberation.
Thus commanded by that friend who was filled with affection,
O King, I then considered it appropriate to depart from that place.
Then, O prince, by the grace of Mahādevī, I was swiftly set in motion; I attained knowledge of the path and swift speed.
All this cause of my suffering has been told;
O hero, tell me exactly who you are and whose son you are. (65)

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Goddess’s Dream," in the sixth book of the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses, concerning the release of the single-string necklace by Yaśovatī for the sole hero of the Haihayas. || 22 ||
The Description of the Marriage of Ekavīra and Ekāvalī.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard her words, the powerful son of Ramā [Kṛṣṇa]—
With his lotus-like face in full bloom, O lord of the people, he spoke to her.
The king said:
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, regarding the account you asked for in clear words:
I am a Haihaya, the son of the daughter of Sindhu, known by the name Ekavīra. || 2 ||
"Surely my mind has been made dependent upon you by you;
what can I do, and where can I go, being so intensely tormented by separation? (3)
First, you described that form which transcends all the worlds;
by that, my mind, struck by the arrows of desire, has become utterly distraught. (4)
Then her virtues were described, and by them her heart was captivated once again; as for the words you spoke further, because of them I was filled with wonder.
The words of Ekāvalī were spoken by me in the presence of the Dānava: "The Haihaya has been chosen; I have made the firm resolve that I will choose no other than him. (6)
"O slender-limbed one, by those words you have now made me her servant;
O lady with beautiful hair, tell me, what shall I do for the two of them? (7)
I do not know the location of that evil-minded Rākṣasa; O fair-eyed one, there is no way for me to go to that city.
"Tell me, O large-eyed one, you are capable of leading me there;
quickly bring that beautiful friend of yours to where she stays. (9)
Having slain that cruel Rākṣasa, I shall now liberate your beloved princess, who is helpless and tormented by grief.
Having quickly freed her from suffering, I shall lead you to your city;
and I shall bestow this maiden, Ekāvalī, upon your father.
"Afterwards, that king, the scorcher of his enemies, will perform the marriage of his daughter;
thus shall your heart's desire be fulfilled, O Priyaṃvadā, and it will also be pleasing to me. (12)
"He shall now become complete through your means;
show him the city quickly and behold my prowess."
"Just as I slay the man of evil conduct who carries off another's wife, so do that which you are capable of doing to please me, O woman of excellent complexion. (14)
"Show me today the way to that city which is so difficult to reach.
Vyāsa said: Having heard those pleasing words, Yaśovatī was delighted. (15)
He spoke with respect to that son of Ramā regarding the means of departure:
"O Indra among kings, receive this mantra which bestows success through the Blessed Goddess."
Today I shall show him that city protected by the Rākṣasas;
be ready, O highly fortunate one, to go with me.
Accompanied by a great army,
the mighty hero Kālaketu, surrounded by powerful Rākṣasas, will engage in battle there.
Therefore, having received the mantra, go there with me;
I shall show you the way to that city of the evil-minded one. (19)
"Having slain that evildoer, quickly deliver my friend!
Hearing those words, the hero swiftly took up his mantra. (20)
From the auspicious Dattātreya, the best among the wise, whom she had obtained through divine providence,
she received the great mantra of Yogeśvarī known as Trilokītilaka.
By that [means], omniscience was born and likewise all conduct [was perfected];
together with her, he quickly went to his city, which was so difficult to reach.
The king was accompanied by Yaśovatī and a great army, and was protected by fierce Rākṣasas as Pātāla is guarded by serpents.
Beholding him approaching, his messengers, overcome with fear, ran to the side of the swift Kālaketu while crying out. (24)
Thinking him suddenly to be a Rākṣasa deluded by lust, they spoke to him as he stood near Ekāvalī, performing many acts of humility. (25)
The messengers said:
"O King, the woman Yaśovatī, the companion of Kāminī, is approaching together with her army and accompanied by the prince. (26)
"O Great King, is it perhaps Jayanta, or is it Kārtikeya?
He is surely approaching, intoxicated with power and accompanied by his army. (27)
Be prepared, O Indra among kings; the battle has arrived.
Fight with the son of a god, or else abandon the lotus-eyed woman. 28.
"The army is far from here, at a distance of only three yojanas;
O protector of the earth, prepare yourself and quickly sound the kettledrum! (29)
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words of theirs, the Rākṣasa, overwhelmed with rage,
dispatched many other Rākṣasas, well-armed and accompanied by troops.
"Go forth, all you Rākṣasas, facing forward with weapons in hand!
Having thus commanded them, Kālaketu, filled with affection, questioned them.
"O slender-limbed one, who is this person approaching—your father or some other man—who has come near you while you are helpless and deeply distressed? (32)
"O slender-waisted one, speak the truth for my sake: has your father arrived, distressed by separation, accompanied by his army, to take you away? (33)
"Having fully understood your father's intent, I shall not engage in battle;
rather, having brought him home, I shall offer him worship with jewels, garments, and auspicious horses. (34)
I shall by all means provide hospitality to whoever arrives at my house;
however, if another should arrive after him, I shall slay him with sharpened arrows. (35)
"It is said that this great-souled one has been brought by Time for the sake of death;
therefore, O large-eyed lady, tell me who this dull-witted man is who approaches? (36)
Not knowing me to be invincible, in the form of Time, and possessed of great strength, Ekāvalī said:
"O illustrious one, I do not know who this is that approaches so swiftly. (37)
While you were held in captivity, was there no one known by name who could have been my protector?
Neither this man is my father, nor my brother; yet there is someone else of great strength. (38)
"For what purpose has he come here? I do not know the certainty.
The Daitya said:
"O Yaśovatī, these messengers, who are your friends, speak thus. (39)
Having brought that hero here, she exerted herself with the thought, "She has arrived";
but O beloved, where has that clever friend gone in the matter of deciding the course of action? (40)
"There is no other enemy whatsoever who could be a match for me.
Vyāsa said:
In the meantime, other messengers indeed arrived there.
They, hurried and terrified, spoke thus to Kālaketu as he sat in his house:
"O Great King, are you at ease while the army has arrived in your vicinity? (42)
"Depart quickly from the city, surrounded by a great army.
Having heard these words of theirs, the exceedingly powerful Kālaketu [set forth].
Mounting his chariot,
the powerful and pre-eminent hero, though alone, swiftly departed from his own city, suddenly mounted upon his horse.
Arriving there, agitated by separation from his beloved, a battle took place between the two of them like that between Vṛtra and Vāsava. || 45 ||
When that battle was then raging, terrifying to the cowardly, with various weapons and missiles discharged so as to set the horizons ablaze; (46)
The son of the daughter of the ocean struck the Daitya with his mace;
deprived of life, he fell upon the earth like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
All the Rākṣasas, oppressed by fear, fled away;
then Yaśovatī, having gone there with speed, [approached] Ekāvalī at that time.
Greatly amazed and exceedingly joyful, she spoke these sweet words:
"Come, friend! That Dānava has been struck down by the prince. (49)
Having fought a most terrible battle with the wise Ekavīra, that king now remains in his camp, overcome by exhaustion. (50)
Desiring a sight of you, having heard of your beauty and virtues, that king—equal to the god of love—waits; behold him, O lady with curved outer corners of the eyes! (51)
I previously described you before him on the bank of the Jāhnavī;
consequently, he has become filled with perfect passion and is now distressed by separation.
"The prince desires to see you, who are so beautiful.
Having heard her words, she set her mind on going. (53)
Deeply ashamed and filled with fear, she thought: "How shall I look upon his face? For as a maiden, I am utterly helpless. (54)
Thinking, "He is seizing me, overcome by passion," Yaśovatī, agitated with anxiety, set out from there in a palanquin carried by men.
Seeing that large-eyed woman arrive at the military camp, exceedingly soiled and wearing filthy garments, the prince spoke: (56)
"O slender-limbed one, grant a vision to my thirsty eyes!
Seeing him afflicted by desire and her shrouded by a weight of bashfulness, [he spoke]. (57)
Yaśovatī, who was skilled in policy and knew the path of the virtuous, said to him:
"O Prince, her father also desires to give her to you."
"O Indra among kings, this union with you will surely come to pass through your power; wait for the right time and lead her to her father's presence. (59)
"It is certain that he will give her away after performing the marriage rites.
Believing her words to be true, he set out accompanied by his army. (60)
Accompanied by the two loving women, he went to his father’s hermitage;
having heard that the princess had arrived there, he was filled with love.
Surrounded by his ministers, he quickly went forward to meet him;
after many days, that daughter was seen wearing soiled garments.
The story of Yaśovatī was then related in detail;
having met Ekavīra, she respectfully brought him to her home.
On an auspicious day, he caused the marriage to be performed according to the prescribed rites;
then, having honored him according to the rules, he bestowed wedding gifts upon him.
He sent forth his daughter accompanied by Yaśovatī;
thus, when the marriage was completed, the son of Ramā was filled with joy.
Having reached his home, he enjoyed many pleasures together with his beloved. A son named Kṛtavīrya was indeed born to her;
his son was Kārtavīrya. Thus has this lineage been recounted by me.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Marriage of Ekavīra and Ekāvalī," in the sixth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Conception of the Embryo for the Purpose of Producing a Son by the Command of Ambikā.
The King said:
"O Blessed One, from the lotus-face of Your Honor has issued forth the nectar of divine narrative."
I do not attain satiety, even while drinking as if it were nectar itself. || 1 ||
This wonderful narrative has been told by you to me;
the detailed account of the origin of the Haihayas is truly marvelous.
I have a great curiosity here regarding Viṣṇu, the Lord of Kamalā,
the God of gods, the Master of the world, and the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction.
How did that very Lord Hari, the infallible Supreme Person who is independent, become dependent by having entered the state of a horse? (4)
O Brahmin, you ought to sever this doubt of mine now;
you are omniscient, O best of sages, so tell me this wonderful account. (5)
Vyāsa said: Listen, O King, I shall declare the resolution of this doubt,
just as it was heard by me previously from Nārada, the best of sages.
The mind-born son of Brahmā was an ascetic named Nārada;
he was omniscient, all-pervading, tranquil, beloved by all the worlds, and a seer.
And once that best of sages, wandering this earth while playing his great lute endowed with perfect notes and melodies, [arrived there].
Singing the various numerous varieties of Sāmans, such as the Bṛhat and Rathantara, he attained the immortal Gāyatra and then reached my hermitage.
Śamyāprāsa is a great and most purifying holy ford (tīrtha) on the Sarasvatī;
it is the abode of the foremost sages and likewise bestows happiness and knowledge.
Seeing that son of Brahmā of great splendor arrive, I rose from my seat and performed all the rites of hospitality, beginning with welcoming him and honoring him.
Having performed the rites of offering water for honor and water for the feet, I sat down nearby the sage of immeasurable splendor as he remained seated upon his throne.
O King, having seen Nārada— restful, tranquil, and one who has reached the further shore of knowledge— I asked him that very same question which you have now asked me.
O Sage, in this essence-less cycle of existence, what happiness do living beings possess?
Having reflected thoroughly, I do not perceive any at all, anywhere, or at any time.
Born on an island, I was abandoned by my mother at that very moment;
without any refuge, I grew up in the forest according to the force of my past karma.
"O divine sage, for many years I performed severe austerities on the mountain, and with the desire for a son, I worshipped Śaṅkara. (16)
Then I obtained a parrot, the best among those possessed of knowledge;
I thoroughly taught him the essence of the Vedas from the very beginning. (17)
O virtuous one, having been awakened by your words, he abandoned me as I wept, distressed by separation, and went from this world to another world, departing for some unknown place.
Then, tormented by grief for my son, I abandoned the great mountain Meru and,
keeping my mother in my mind, arrived at Kurujāṅgala.
With limbs exceedingly emaciated by affection for his son and filled with grief, he knew this worldly existence to be false, yet remained bound by the snares of illusion. (20)
Then, having learned that his auspicious mother Vāsavī had been chosen by the king,
he remained right there, establishing a hermitage on the beautiful bank of the Sarasvatī.
Śāntanu attained the heavenly realm, while his widowed mother remained,
virtuous and protected by Bhīṣma, accompanied by her two sons.
Citrāṅgada was made king by the wise son of Gaṅgā;
in time, even that brother of mine, who possessed a splendor equal to Kāma, died.
Then his mother Satyavatī, submerged in an ocean of grief,
wept bitterly and piteously for her deceased son Citrāṅgada.
"O illustrious one, having learned that she was suffering, I arrived there;
she was consoled extensively by me and by the high-souled Bhīṣma. (25)
Furthermore, the other heroic lord of the earth, Vicitravīrya,
was indeed made his brother by Bhīṣma, who had turned away from ruling over women.
Having defeated the lords of the earth, Bhīṣma brought back and offered two beautiful daughters of the King of Kāśī to him by his own power. (27)
At an auspicious time, a marriage was arranged for Satyavatī with my brother Vicitravīrya; at that, I became happy. (28)
Furthermore, that brother of mine, though young, died while severely afflicted by consumption;
being childless and a wielder of the bow, my mother became deeply distressed. (29)
Then, having seen their husband dead, the two daughters of the King of Kāśī,
both devoted to the dharma of faithful wives, became sisters.
They said to their weeping mother-in-law, who was deeply distressed:
"We two shall go into the fire together with our husband."
"O mother-in-law, having gone with your son to heaven and then to the Nandana grove, we two shall sport happily together, united with our husband. (32)
Then, at the word of Bhīṣma, the two daughters-in-law were dissuaded from that great undertaking by their mother, who relied upon her affectionate disposition.
After Gāṅgeya had consulted with my mother and they had performed all the funeral rites for me, I was summoned to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
As soon as I was remembered, O Mother, having understood the state of mind within your heart, I arrived with great speed at the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
Then, having bowed my head to my mother and standing with palms joined in reverence,
I spoke to her, whose limbs were scorched and emaciated by grief for her son.
"O ascetic mother, by whom was I summoned in your mind?
Command me in some great task; I am your servant, what shall I do? (37)
O Mother, you are my supreme sacred ford, and you are celebrated as the highest deity.
Having arrived here just as I was thinking of you, tell me what pleasing task I may perform for you.
Vyāsa said:
O sage, when I had spoken thus and stood there before my mother,
she then spoke these words to me while looking toward Bhīṣma who was nearby.
"Your son, your brother, has died today, afflicted by consumption;
because of that, I have become sorrowful here through fear of the extinction of our lineage. (40)
Therefore, O wise one, you have been summoned by me today through my meditative concentration,
in accordance with the opinion of Gāṅgeya, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of Pārāśarya.
Establish the family that has perished for the sake of Śantanu’s name;
O Kṛṣṇa, protect me quickly from this sorrow arising from the extinction of our lineage. 42.
"The two daughters of the King of Kāśī are the wives of your younger brother, the virtuous Vicitravīrya, who are adorned with beauty and youth. (43)
"O wise one, unite with those two and procreate a son;
protect the Bharata lineage, for there is never any fault in this. (44)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of my mother, I became indeed distressed with anxiety;
with a heart overwhelmed by shame, I spoke to her, bowing down with humility. (45)
O Mother, having recognized that the violation of another's wife is a most sinful deed, how can I perform it with devotion while correctly knowing the path of dharma?
Likewise, the wife of a younger brother is proclaimed to be like a daughter;
having studied the Vedas, how could I commit such an act of transgression? (47)
The protection of one's family must never be carried out through unjust means;
for the ancestors of those who commit such evil deeds do not cross over from the cycle of existence.
How could he who is the instructor of the worlds and the originator of the Purāṇas, having known [the situation], perform such a marvelous and censurable deed? (49)
For I was repeatedly addressed by my mother as she wept bitterly in my presence—she who was consumed by grief for her son and desirous of preserving our lineage. (50)
"O son of Parāśara, my dear child, there is no fault in you for these words of mine;
for the speech of elders is to be accepted as truth by men, even if it contains a flaw. (51)
"Without even deliberating on what ought to be done, act according to the authority of the conduct of the virtuous.
Follow my word, my son; there is no fault in you, O giver of honor. (52)
Having brought about the birth of a son, make your mother happy, especially since she is tormented and submerged in an ocean of grief, O son. (53)
Having heard her speaking thus, the son of the celestial river,
who was an expert in discerning the subtle points of dharma, then spoke to me.
O sinless Dvaipāyana, you should not entertain any further doubt in this matter;
accepting your mother’s word, sport as you please.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his and likewise the request of my mother,
I then became free from hesitation regarding that loathsome task.
I approached Ambikā with joy during her fertile period at night;
however, she was deeply distressed in mind because I was a contemptible ascetic. || 57 ||
At that time, during our first encounter, I cursed that woman of beautiful hips:
"Since you closed your eyes, your son shall be born blind. (58)
On the second day, O best of sages, he was questioned again by his mother in private: "O son, will there be a son born from the womb of the daughter of the King of Kāśī? (59)
Thereupon, with my face bowed down in shame, I said to my mother:
"O Mother, by my very curse, your son shall indeed be blind."
O sage, rebuked there by her with harsh words, he said: "How is it, my son, that you have cursed him? Your son shall become blind. (61)

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Conception of the Embryo for the Procreation of Sons by the Command of Ambikā," in the sixth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Vyāsa’s Description of His Own Delusion.
Vyāsa said: Having heard such words from me, Vāsavī became terrified.
Dāśeyī, being deeply distressed for the sake of her son, said this to me: || 1 ||
O son, Ambālikā, the daughter of the King of Kāśī, is a blessed bride;
she is the wife of Vicitravīrya, now a widow filled with grief.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and radiant with beauty and youth,
form an attachment to her and, having done so, procreate a highly esteemed son.
A blind man must not hold the office of king; therefore, O giver of honor, at my word, procreate a charming son upon the princess.
Having been addressed thus by my mother,
O sage, I remained there in the city called Hastināpura until the daughter of the King of Kāśī reached her season.
Then, at her mother-in-law's command, that woman of beautiful hair, feeling ashamed, came into my presence within the private bedchamber.
Seeing me, with matted hair, self-controlled, an ascetic devoid of passion, her face broke into sweat; she became pale and deeply despondent.
Then, seeing that amorous woman standing by my side at night, trembling, I became enraged and spoke to her with anger.
"If, upon seeing me, you become pale in color due to pride, then your son shall be pale, O slender-waisted one. (9)
Having spoken thus, he remained there that very night together with Ambālikā;
having eaten that night, he departed after taking leave of his mother.
Then, in due time, two sons were born to them who were blind and pale;
they became renowned as Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu.
Seeing her two sons in such a state, my mother became despondent;
then, at the end of a year, she summoned me and spoke to me thus.
"The two sons born of Dvaipāyana are not such as to be fit for the kingdom;
therefore, procreate another son for me who is pleasing and captivating. (13)
"So be it," she was told by me; then my mother, filled with joy, when the time had come, prayed to Ambikā for the sake of a son. (14)
"O daughter of beautiful countenance, embrace Vyāsa and give birth to a wonderful son, the founder of the Kuru lineage and one worthy of sovereignty. (15)
Then the bride, filled with shame, said not a word;
at her mother's command, I went to the bedchamber at night. (16)
A maidservant of Vicitravīrya, endowed with beauty and youth,
and adorned with various ornaments and garments, was sent there by Ambikā.
Her body reddened with sandalwood paste, adorned with flower garlands, endowed with graceful gestures, possessing beautiful hair, and walking with the gait of a swan, she arrived. (18)
Having seated me upon the couch, she remained there filled with love;
O sage, I then became delighted by her playful charm.
O Nārada, during the night, I sported with her intensely out of love; being well-pleased, I granted her a boon once again.
O fortunate lady, a son shall be born to you who is endowed with all auspicious marks,
handsome, a knower of all dharmas, truthful, and devoted to tranquility.
At that time Vidura was born, and thus three sons were mine;
O virtuous one, my illusory power (māyā) increased through these offspring born in another's field.
Having seen his three sons—desirous, powerful, and esteemed for their prowess—he forgot the separation involving Śuka, which was the cause of his grief. (23)
O Brahmin, Māyā is powerful and indeed difficult to abandon for those of unrefined self;
she is formless and without support, yet she deludes even the wise. 24.
Bound by affection for my mother and likewise constrained by my sons,
O best of sages, my mind found no peace in the forest.
The mind became like one mounted on a swing; at times it was in Hastināpura, and again on the banks of the Sarasvatī, having no stability in any one place. (26)
Once, while reflecting upon knowledge, it indeed dawned upon his mind:
"Who are these sons? Where is this delusion? They are not worthy of the funeral rites for my deceased father."
"How indeed could sons born of infidelity bring me happiness?
For powerful illusion spreads delusion within the mind. (28)
"O Sage, knowing that I have fallen into this blind well of delusion in vain," I once, being well-composed, felt remorse in secret. (29)
Then the powerful Pāṇḍu, approved by Bhīṣma, obtained the kingdom;
at that time, my mind became serene on account of having sons. (30)
He had two beautiful wives, Kuntī and Mādrī;
Kuntī was the daughter of Śūrasena, and the other was the daughter of the King of Madra.
Having received that curse from the twice-born, Pāṇḍu, accompanied by his two wives,
fell into despondency, abandoned the kingdom, and went to the forest.
Then, hearing that my son was staying in the forest, grief entered me;
I went to that place where he was dwelling together with his two wives.
Having consoled Pāṇḍu in the forest, I returned once more to the city called Gajāhvaya;
after addressing Dhṛtarāṣṭra, I went to the bank of the Brahmajā river.
Having fathered five sons born of his wife by means of dharma from Vāyu, Śakra, and the two Aśvins while in the forest hermitage, he [bequeathed] those five Pāṇḍavas.
Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, and likewise Arjuna—
these sons of Kuntī are proclaimed to have been born from Dharma, Vāyu, and the Lord of the Gods (Indra), respectively.
Once, in private, the lord of the earth embraced Mādrī, who was the mother of Nakula and Sahadeva, the two sons of the King of Madra. (37)
Having died by the curse of the sages, he was consecrated in the mouth of the fire;
there, the virtuous Mādrī, having become a chaste wife, entered along with her husband.
Then Kuntī stood with her sons in the blazing fire;
