the sages likewise beheld the daughter of Śūrasena accompanied by her sons.
They brought that sorrowful woman, deprived of her husband, to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura);
she was then entrusted to the high-souled Bhīṣma and Vidura.
Having heard that the sons of Pāṇḍu were protected by Bhīṣma, I, being tormented by the happiness and suffering of others, reflected upon them. (41)
Thus, with affection, Vidura and the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra [consoled him],
as did his sons, Duryodhana and the others, though they were cruel-minded.
Having come together in one place, they displayed a wondrous conflict;
then Dronācārya arrived there and was honored by Bhīṣma.
When Karna was a newborn infant abandoned by Kunti, he was settled in that city for the purpose of teaching her sons.
Protected by his charioteer Adhiratha on the riverbank,
Karṇa became the beloved of Duryodhana and likewise the most heroic of men.
Mutual hostility arose among Bhīma, Duryodhana, and the others;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, however, reflected upon the suffering of those sons and himself.
He established a residence for the high-souled Pāṇḍavas in the city of Vāraṇāvata solely for the purpose of pacifying the conflict. 47.
Right there, Duryodhana, out of malice, had divine houses made of lac constructed by sending his friend Purocana.
O best of sages, having heard that the Pāṇḍavas, together with Pṛthā, were burned in the house of lac, I am submerged in an ocean of calamity because they are my grandsons. (49)
Afflicted with intense grief, seeing [them] day and night in the empty forest,
I beheld the Pāṇḍavas, emaciated by suffering, in Ekacakrā.
Then, with a joyful mind upon seeing the sons of Pṛthā,
I quickly dispatched them toward the city of Drupada.
Afflicted by grief, emaciated, and wearing the garments of Brahmins and deer skins, they went there and then took their places in the assembly hall.
Having displayed his prowess and conquered the daughter of Drupada, the victorious one performed the marriage with the proud maiden five times, according to the word of his mother.
Having witnessed their wedding, O sage, I was then exceedingly joyful;
thereafter, we arrived at the city called Nāga accompanied by Pāñcālī.
O best of the twice-born, the son of Vasudeva indeed prepared Khāṇḍavaprastha as a dwelling for the Pāṇḍavas by the arrangement of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
There, the sacrificial fire was gratified by Viṣṇu along with Jiṣṇu;
the Rājasūya sacrifice was performed, and at that time, I became joyful.
Then, having seen their wealth as well as the assembly hall constructed by Maya,
Duryodhana became deeply distressed and commenced a game of dice.
Śakuni is an expert at foul gambling, while the son of Dharma is unskilled at dice;
thus the kingdom and all wealth have been seized, and Yājñasenī has been subjected to suffering.
Those Pāṇḍavas were exiled to the forest for twelve years together with the princess of Pañcāla; because of that, great sorrow has been produced within me. (59)
"O Nārada, thus I have been deeply immersed in this worldly existence consisting of pleasure and pain, solely through delusion, even though I knew the eternal Dharma. (60)
"Who am I? Whose daughter am I? Who are these [people]? Who is my mother? And what is happiness?
For my heart wanders day and night due to delusion. (61)
What shall I do? Where shall I go? Satisfaction is not attained;
my mind is mounted upon a swing here, flickering and unable to become steady. (62)
O best of sages, you are omniscient; dispel my doubt.
Act in such a way that I may become happy and free from the fever of anxiety.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Vyāsa’s Description of His Own Delusion," in the sixth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 25 ||
The Description of the Introduction to Damayantī’s Marriage.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of mine, Nārada, the knower of the supreme truth, [spoke].
And having smiled, he spoke to me as I was asking about the cause of his delusion.
Nārada said:
O son of Parāśara, knower of the Purāṇas, what do you ask for the sake of certainty?
In this worldly existence, there is no embodied being who is free from delusion.
Brahmā, Viṣṿu, as well as Rudra, Sanaka, and Kapila—
all are enveloped by Māyā and wander upon the path of worldly existence.
People know me as a man of wisdom, yet I am deluded like everyone else in the world;
listen to my former history, which I shall relate with complete certainty.
O son of Vāsavi, such great suffering as was previously experienced by me was brought about by my own delusion for the sake of a wife.
Once, I, Parvata, descended from the world of the gods to the surface of the earth to behold the excellent land of Bhārata.
Wandering together upon the earth, they beheld the circle of sacred fords (tīrthas),
purifying places, and the auspicious hermitages of sages.
Having previously sworn an oath to one another from the world of the gods,
they indeed deliberated and firmly resolved upon this agreement.
However, the nature of one's mental fluctuations—whether they be auspicious or inauspicious—must be spoken of as they arise; they should never be concealed.
Whether it be a desire for food, a desire for wealth, or even a desire for pleasure—whatever resides in one's heart should be communicated to another. (10)
Having thus made this agreement, we two have come from the heavenly realm to the world of mortals;
with one mind, having become sages, we wander according to our will. (11)
Thus wandering in this world, when the end of summer had arrived,
they reached the delightful city of Sañjaya once again, O King.
Having been worshipped with devotion by him and highly honored by the king,
they remained there in the house of that high-souled one for the duration of the Cāturmāsya.
The four months of the rainy season are always difficult to traverse on the road; therefore, it is the settled conclusion that the wise should remain in one place during this time. 14.
A twice-born man may travel abroad for eight months at any time due to the necessity of his duties;
however, one who desires happiness should not go on a journey during the rainy season.
Having thus reflected in his mind, they then remained in the house of Sañjaya,
honored by the high-souled king and provided with hospitality.
The daughter of that lord of the earth was renowned as Damayantī;
she, possessing beautiful teeth and being exceedingly lovely, was commanded for the purpose of serving [him]. (17)
The princess, possessing discerning wisdom and large eyes, being diligent in her efforts, performed service to both of them at all times. (18)
At the proper time, she gives water for bathing, delicious and abundant food, mouth-fresheners, and whatever else is desired.
The maiden also provided both of them with whatever desires they mentally longed for, including fans,
seats, beds, and other such desired objects.
Thus, while being well-honored, we two remained indeed in the king’s house,
devoted to the study of the Vedas and engaged in Vedic observances.
Holding the lute in my hand and having perfected the most excellent notes,
I sang the Gāyatra Sāman, which is sweet-sounding and a tonic for the ears.
But having heard that enchanting song of the Sāmaveda, the princess became filled with passion for me; she was full of affection and confident.
Day by day, her passion for me has increased to the highest degree;
likewise, my mind has become filled with longing for her who is full of affection. (24)
Filled with affection, that maiden never made even the slightest distinction between me and him regarding food and other such matters, nor did she show any difference in her service.
She provided hot water for my bath and cool water for Parvata;
likewise, she prepared curd for me and buttermilk for Parvata as well.
She prepared a bright bed and covering for my sake with such supreme affection as she had never shown even toward Parvata. (27)
The beautiful woman gazed at me with love, and not at the mountain;
then, having observed her such behavior, Parvata understood the cause of her affection.
Filled with wonder, he reflected in his mind, "What is this?
and asked me in private, "O Nārada, tell me everything exactly as it is."
The princess, filled with joy, feels great love for you; full of affection, she bestows upon you all kinds of food and delicacies from every side. (30)
This difference regarding me does not produce doubt in this matter;
rather, the daughter of Sañjaya considers you in every way to be her husband.
I also recognize such a disposition in you by your physical characteristics; the cause of your affection is known through the expressions of your eyes and face. (32)
"Speak the truth; you must not utter a false word, O Sage.
Remember now the agreement made by us two when we departed for heaven."
Nārada said:
When I was thus persistently questioned by Parvata regarding this cause, I was overcome with shame; yet, being thus addressed, I spoke again.
"O Parvata, this large-eyed lady is intent on making me her husband;
likewise, my own heart is especially inclined toward her. (35)
Having heard those truthful words, the sage Parvata was filled with anger and spoke these words to me, saying "Fie! Fie! again and again.
"Since I have been deceived by you after first making oaths, become one with the face of a monkey due to my curse, O betrayer of friends! (37)
Thus cursed by that enraged high-souled one, I suddenly became cruel and possessed the face of a monkey. (38)
Even I did not show forgiveness toward that son of my sister;
in great anger, he was indeed cursed by me: "May you certainly have no place in heaven."
"O Parvata, since you have cursed me for such a trivial offense, therefore, O dull-witted one, your own residence shall indeed be in the world of mortals. (40)
But Parvata departed from that city deeply dejected;
at that very moment, I too became possessed of a monkey's face.
Seeing me, a fierce monkey, the princess became embarrassed;
she grew deeply despondent, longing to hear the lute.
Vyāsa said:
"O Brahmin, what happened after that? How were you released from the curse? You were born again with a human face; tell me this according to the facts. (43)
"Where did Parvata go again, and where did your meeting take place? When, where, and how did it all happen? Tell me everything in detail. (44)
Nārada said:
O highly fortunate one, what can I say of the great deeds of Māyā?
I am deeply distressed there on that mountain now that she has departed in anger.
Furthermore, the princess became exceedingly devoted to serving me;
then, when Parvata had departed as he pleased, I remained right there in that very residence.
Afflicted by sorrow, wretched, and with a face like that of a monkey, I was especially tormented by anxiety, reflecting: "What might happen to me? (47)
Then, seeing his daughter whose youth was slightly manifest, Sañjaya at that time asked his minister regarding the marriage of the princess.
"The time for my daughter's marriage has now arrived;
tell me of a suitable prince who is highly esteemed as a bridegroom. (49)

"I shall now indeed perform the marriage of my daughter according to the prescribed rites with one who is endowed with the qualities of physical magnificence, who is heroic, and born of a noble family. (50)
But Pradhāna said, "O King, there are indeed many princes on earth who are worthy of your daughter and endowed with all virtues. (51)
O Indra among kings, having summoned that prince in whom you take delight, give him your daughter along with abundant wealth consisting of elephants, horses, and chariots. (52)
Nārada said: Having learned of her father’s intention, Damayantī, skilled in speech, then spoke to the king as he sat in private through the mouth of her nurse.
The nurse said: "O Great King, your daughter Damayantī has spoken thus to me:
'O nurse, speak to my father on my behalf, words full of comfort. (54)
Then I chose the wise Nārada, who was endowed with great majesty;
for I, infatuated by passion, desired him alone and no one else was dear to me.
"O father, fulfill my desire; let there be a marriage with the sage.
O knower of dharma, I shall choose no other husband than Nārada. (56)
I am indeed great in the ocean of sound, which is devoid of crocodiles, consists of the essence of rasa, is free from salt, is filled with bliss, and is bereft of the timiṅgila fish. || 57 ||

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Introduction to Damayantī’s Marriage," in the sixth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 26.
The Description of Nārada’s Marriage with Damayantī through Illusion.
Nārada said:
Having heard those words of his daughter from the mouth of the nurse, the king then...
He spoke to his wife Kaikeyī, the beautiful-eyed one who was standing nearby.
The king said:
"O beloved, you have heard those words spoken by the nurse:
'This Nārada, though a sage with the face of a monkey, has been chosen at will.'"
"What is this that has been thought by my daughter? It is an act devoid of sense.
How could I give my daughter to this one who has the face of a monkey? (3)
"Where is that ugly monk, and where is my daughter Damayantī? This matter is inverted; it must never be permitted. (4)

"O lady of beautiful hair, restrain that daughter of yours by force in private; use skillful means to turn this innocent girl away from her devotion to the sage, in accordance with the teachings of the elders."
Having heard these words of her husband, the mother then said to her:
"What is this beauty of yours? And where is that sage, he who has the face of a monkey and is destitute?"
"How is it that you, a clever nun, have fallen into delusion? You possess a body as delicate as a creeper, while this one has a frame as coarse as ashes. (7)
O sinless one, how is it fitting for you to have news from the mouth of a monkey? O lady of pure smiles, what pleasure could there be in a contemptible man? (8)
"Let the prince be your husband; do not persist in this futile obstinacy.
Your father will fall into sorrow upon hearing these words from the mouth of the nurse."
Seeing the delicate mālatī creeper entwined with a rough babbūla tree, whose mind—even that of the wise—does not succumb to sorrow? (10)
On this earth, who—even a fool—would give tender betel leaves for the sake of eating to a servant? (11)
Beholding you with your hand clasped in the presence of Nārada while the wedding was taking place, whose heart would not burn? (12)
Therefore, conversation with Kumukha does not produce pleasure;
how then can you spend your time with him until death? (13)
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of her mother, the slender-limbed Damayantī,
deeply distressed and having made a firm resolve regarding me, spoke to her mother.
What is the use of a face and beauty for a fool, and what is the use of wealth? What is the use of a kingdom for one who is unrefined and ignorant of the path of aesthetic flavor? 15.
Even the female deer in the forest are blessed, for they surrender their lives when bewildered by his roar; fie upon the foolish men on this earth! 16.
O Mother, that knowledge consisting of the seven notes which Nārada knows— indeed,
no other man besides Śiva knows it, for he is truly unique.
Dwelling with a fool is death at every moment;
a man who is handsome and wealthy but devoid of virtue should always be abandoned. 18.
Fie on that friendship toward a foolish king who is filled with vain pride!
It is far better to have it toward a mendicant who recognizes virtue, for such friendship brings happiness through its very words. (19)

One who knows the notes (*svara*), understands the scales (*grāma*), and possesses the various distinctions of the knowledge of melodic modulations (*mūrcchanā*)—such a person is difficult to find, even if he is weak, provided he knows the eight aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*). (20)
Just as the Gaṅgā and the Sarasvatī lead to Kailāsa, so too does one who is proficient in the knowledge of the Svaras lead to Kailāsa. 21.
He who knows the resonating sound, even though he be a human, is a god;
but he who does not know its sevenfold division, even if he be the king of the gods, is a beast.
He who does not experience joy upon hearing the path of the *mūrcchanās* and *tānas* should be known in every way as a beast; for deer are not beasts.
Better is a venomous serpent that, upon hearing a captivating sound, attains joy even though it lacks ears; fie upon those humans who possess ears! 24.
Even a child, upon hearing a song of beautiful melody, becomes joyful in mind; yet those elders do not recognize it—fie upon them! (25)
Alas, does my father not know the virtues of Nārada? There is no second master of the Sāman hymns equal to him in the three worlds. (26)
Therefore, he was surely chosen by me before our meeting;
later, under the influence of a curse, he became this mine of virtues with the face of a monkey.
Whom do these horse-faced Kinnaras not delight? For what is the use of an excellent face if it is not endowed with the knowledge of song? 28.
"O mother, speak to my father: 'This best of sages has been chosen;
therefore, casting aside your insistence, give me to him with joy. (29)
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of her daughter, the queen informed the king;
she understood that Sundarī was insistent upon [giving] her daughter to the sage Nārada.
"O Indra among kings, perform the marriage with Damayantī on an auspicious day;
for that omniscient sage has already been chosen by her in her heart. (31)
Nārada said:
Thus urged by the queen, Sañjaya, the lord of the earth,
then performed the entire marriage ceremony according to the prescribed rules.
Having thus taken a wife, O scorcher of enemies,
he remained right there with a mind burning day after day.
When the princess came into my presence for the sake of service,
I, who have the face of a monkey, was then tormented by grief.
But Damayantī, seeing me, her lotus-face blossomed with joy; she never felt any sorrow because of my monkey-like face. (35)
As time passed in this manner, the sage Parvata suddenly arrived before me while traveling to visit many sacred fords (tīrthas).
Honored by me with great respect and worshipped according to the prescribed rites,
he became truly distressed upon seeing me seated on the divine throne.
To me, his maternal uncle—who was emaciated, distressed, married, monkey-faced, and deeply afflicted by anxiety—the compassionate Parvata spoke these words: || 38 ||
"O Nārada, best of sages, you have been cursed by me out of anger;
listen now as I perform the atonement for that curse. (39)
O Nārada, by my merit, may you become handsome-faced;
having seen the princess, compassion has now arisen in my heart. (40)
Nārada said: Having made my mind inclined [toward him] and having heard his speech,
I immediately bestowed a favor upon him at that very moment to counteract that curse.
"O nephew, may you too have access to the abode of the gods;
now, Parvata, this favor for the curse has been granted at your will. (42)
Nārada said:
"I was born with a beautiful face while he was looking on at his word.
Then the princess, being well-pleased, quickly spoke to her mother. (43)
A son of beautiful countenance has been born to you, and a son-in-law of great luster;
by the word of Parvata, the sage’s curse has been released today. (44)
Having heard those words spoken by the queen to the king,
Sañjaya then went there with joy to see the sage.
Then, the high-souled king, being well-pleased, bestowed upon me and my nephew a great amount of wealth as a marriage dowry.
All this ancient conduct has been related to you, as well as the power and majesty of Māyā, exactly as it was experienced by me. (47)
O illustrious one, in this unreal saṃsāra created by the qualities of Māyā, there is no embodied being who is happy—none has been so in the past, nor will there be one in the future. (48)
By whom have all these mighty ones been conquered: lust and anger, as well as greed, envy, possessiveness, egoism, and pride? (49)
O Sage, these three qualities— sattva, rajas, and tamas— are indeed the cause in every respect for the arising of the bodies of living beings.
O Vyāsa, at one time while I was traveling through the forest with Viṣṇu,
I was turned into a woman in an instant by his playful jesting.
Having attained the status of the king's consort, she was utterly deluded by the power of Māyā;
indeed, many sons were born to her in the palace of that monarch.
Vyāsa said:
O virtuous one, having heard your words, this doubt has indeed arisen:
"O sage, how did you, who possess such great wisdom, come to attain womanhood? (53)
And how was this man born? Tell me everything without omission. How were the sons born by you, and in whose king's house did they truly come forth?
Relate this great and wonderful deed of Māyā, by whom all this—both the stationary and the moving—is deluded. (55)
I do not reach satiety while listening to the nectar of your discourse, which contains the true essence of the meaning of all philosophical systems and destroys all doubts. (56)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Nārada’s Marriage with Damayantī," in the sixth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Nārada Attaining His Sisterhood.
Nārada said:
Listen, O best of sages, as I relate this virtuous tale.
The power of illusion is extremely difficult to comprehend, even for sages who are the most proficient in yoga.
The entire world, both moving and unmoving, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is deluded by Māyā through her unconquerable and inscrutable power.
Once, indeed, desiring a vision of Hari of wondrous deeds, I went from Satyaloka to the enchanting Śvetadvīpa.
Playing a great lute adorned with proper tuning and notes,
he sang the Gāyatra Sāman endowed with the seven musical notes.
I have beheld the God of gods, who holds the discus and the mace;
whose chest is illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, who is dark as a rain-cloud, and who possesses four arms.
Clad in yellow garments, adorned with a crown and armlets,
he was sporting with the playful Lakṣmī, filled with joy.
Having beheld me, the goddess Kamalā— endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament— vanished from my presence.
She was the most excellent and beloved of women, proud of her beauty and youth;
she was very dear to Vāsudeva and possessed the luster of the finest gold.
Having gone inside the house and seen the daughter of the Ocean provided with various condiments,
I questioned the God of gods, the wearer of the forest garland, the Lord of the universe.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Padmanābha, slayer of the enemies of the gods!
Why did she flee upon seeing me approaching so close?
"I am neither a libertine nor a rogue; I am an ascetic, O Teacher of the World! I have conquered my senses, subdued my anger, and mastered illusion, O Janārdana. (11)
Nārada said:
Having heard those words somewhat filled with pride, Janārdana,
smiling, spoke to me in a voice as sweet as the sound of a lute.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Nārada, such conduct as this must never be adopted by a woman who, in the absence of her husband, should ever remain in the presence of another man."

O learned one, Māyā is exceedingly difficult to conquer even for yogis who have mastered their vital breaths, for those learned in Sāṃkhya, for ascetics who abstain from food, and for those who have subdued their senses. (14)
O tiger among sages, as for those words you have just spoken, "I have conquered Māyā, O knower of song"—this should never be said by you. (15)
Neither I, Śiva, nor Brahmā am capable of conquering that Unborn One;
even the sages beginning with Sanaka are unable—what of you, and who else is fit for victory? (16)
Whether one possesses a divine body, a human body, or even the body of an animal—how could such a person conquer that Unborn One? (17)
How can a man, even if he is a knower of the Vedas, a knower of yoga, omniscient, and one who has conquered his senses, be able to conquer that Māyā when he is joined with the three? (18)
Time indeed, though devoid of form, is the creator of forms;
under its power stands every embodied being—whether wise, foolish, or middling.
Time makes even one who knows the Dharma deficient at times;
whether by its own nature or through karma, its movement is difficult to comprehend.
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu ceased; with a mind full of wonder, I addressed that eternal Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World.
O Lord of Ramā, what is the nature of that Māyā? Furthermore, what is it like?
How great is its power? Where is its location? Upon what does it rest? Tell me this.
"I desire to see that illusion; show it quickly, O Upholder of the Earth! I wish to know it thoroughly; grant me your favor, O Lord of Māyā. (23)
Viṣṇu said:
She consists of the three qualities (guṇas), she is the support of all, omniscient, and honored by all;
invincible and manifold in form, she stands pervading the entire universe.
If there is a desire to see [him] in your mind, O Nārada, mount Garuḍa; accompanied by me today, let us both go elsewhere now. (25)
"I shall show you my illusory power (māyā), which is difficult to conquer for those who have not mastered their own selves.
Having seen it, O son of Brahmā, do not set your mind on despair. (26)
Having spoken thus, the God of gods remembered the son of Vinatā;
and as soon as he was remembered, Garuḍa arrived in the presence of Hari.
Seeing that the Garuḍa had arrived, Janārdana mounted him;
having placed me upon his back, he prepared with all due respect for the journey.
The son of Vinatā, possessing the speed of the wind, was moved from Vaikuṇṭha by Kṛṣṇa, who desired to go to the forest.
The great divine forests, lakes, and rivers, as well as cities, villages, mines, and the like, along with hamlets, market towns, and cow-pens; (30)
He saw the delightful hermitages of the sages, most enchanting ponds,
vast pools, and lakes adorned with lotuses.
And having observed herds of deer and wild boars as well,
we two, seated upon Garuḍa, went to the vicinity of Kānyakubja.
There he beheld a beautiful, divine lake adorned with lotuses,
teeming with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and graced by ruddy geese.
It was adorned with various kinds of blossoming lotuses,
possessed pure and sweet water, and resounded with the humming of swarms of bees.
Beholding that most wonderful lake, which rivaled the milk-ocean and possessed especially sweet water, the Blessed One said to me: || 35 ||
The Blessed Lord said: "Behold, O Nārada, this deep lake resounding with cranes,
covered everywhere with lotuses and filled with clear water."
"Having bathed here, we shall go to Kānyakubja, the most excellent city.
Having said this, he quickly took me down from Garuḍa and set me ashore. (37)
Smiling there, the Blessed One took hold of my forefinger;
praising the lake further, the Lord led me to the shore. (38)
Having rested on the charming bank, which was pleasant with its lush shade, he said to me, "O sage, perform your ablutions in this pure water. (39)
"Afterwards, I shall make the waters of this most sacred tank as pure as the hearts of the virtuous. (40)
"Especially with the fragrant pollen of lotuses"—
having been addressed thus by the Blessed One, I set aside my lute and deer-skin.
Having resolved to bathe, he went to the bank filled with love;
having washed his feet and hands and tied his topknot, he took hold of *kuśa* grass.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and become pure, I bathed in that water;
while bathing in that delightful water, I was watched by Hari.
Having abandoned his masculine form and attained an unsurpassed female state,
Hari took my lute as well as my auspicious black antelope skin.
Having swiftly mounted Garuḍa, he went to his own home in an instant;
then I attained womanhood, adorned with beautiful ornaments.
At that very moment, the memory of his former body arose in his mind;
he forgot that Lord of the World, and thus a great forgetfulness occurred once again.
Having assumed the form of Mohinī, I emerged from the pond outside and beheld that lake of pure water, frequented by lotuses.
"What is this?"—thus I repeatedly felt wonder in my mind.
While I was reflecting in this way, he who had assumed the form of a woman [spoke]. (48)
Suddenly, King Tāladhvaja appeared within the range of vision there,
seated upon his chariot and surrounded by multitudes of elephants, horses, and chariots.
Seeing me there, adorned with divine ornaments, the king—himself a youth, decked out in finery like the god of love incarnate—[was struck with wonder]. (50)
Filled with supreme wonder at the woman whose face was like the full moon, he asked: "Who are you, O auspicious one? Whose daughter are you—of a human or of a god? (51)
O beloved, how can this young girl, adorned with beauty and youth, be alone—whether she belongs to a human, a Gandharva, or a serpent? 52.
"Whether you are married or a maiden, tell the truth, O fair-eyed one!
What do you see in this pond, O lady with beautiful hair and slender waist? (53)

"O enchantress of the mind, speak what you desire to do amidst the warbling of the cuckoos! O lotus-eyed one, O slender-waisted lady, surely having made me your most excellent husband, enjoy all the pleasures desired by your heart together with me. (54)

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Nārada’s Attainment of His Own Wifehood," in the sixth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The description of Nārada’s restoration to his true form:
Nārada said:
"Having been addressed in this way by that king Tāladhvaja at that time,"
Having reflected deeply in his mind, O lord of the people, he spoke to him.
"O King, I do not know for certain whose daughter I am, nor where my parents are, or by whom I was placed in this lake. (2)
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How may my merit increase?
O Indra among kings, I am without support; I ponder what ought to be done. (3)
"O King, destiny alone is supreme; here, there is no human effort on my part.
You are a knower of dharma, O protector of the earth; do as you wish. (4)
"I am dependent upon you, O King; I have no protector at all—not a father, nor a mother, nor a dwelling place, nor kinsmen. (5)
Having been addressed thus by me, that king became afflicted with passion;
gazing upon me, the large-eyed one, he spoke to his servants as follows.
"Bring a chariot for Nara, beautiful and drawn by four horses;
let it be draped in silken cloth for her to ascend."
It was provided with soft coverings, adorned with nets of pearls,
square, spacious, fashioned from gold, and auspicious.
Having heard those words of his, the servants, moving with haste,
brought for my sake a divine palanquin wrapped in cloth.
Then, desiring to do what was pleasing to him, I ascended that [chariot];
having brought me to his home, that lord of the earth was then filled with joy.
Then, according to the marriage rites, on an auspicious day and at a favorable moment, the king married me there in the presence of the sacrificial fire.
I became his beloved, dearer to him than even his own life;
thus, the name Saubhāgyasundarī was bestowed upon me there.
Delighting with me, the lord of the earth attained happiness through various enjoyments and diversions as prescribed in the treatises on love. (13)
Having abandoned his royal duties, he was devoted to play day and night; addicted to the arts of desire, he did not perceive the passing of time.
In delightful gardens, in ponds and in houses, in palatial mansions, on choice mountains, and in excellent long lakes.
Intoxicated by the liquor of Varuṇī, while wandering in the beautiful forest,
he abandoned all his duties and became entirely subject to his intoxication.
I am Vyāsā, who became deeply attached to him and was overcome by the savor of our play;
I did not remember my former body, nor my male state, nor my birth as a sage.
"This man is my very husband; I am his beloved wife among wives, the crowned queen who understands the arts of pleasure—my life has become fruitful. (18)
While he was thinking thus, she remained under his control, bound to him by love day and night,
though she was intent on play and greedy for pleasure.
The realization of Brahman and the eternal knowledge of Brahman were forgotten;
she remained with her mind entirely absorbed in the thorough study of the Dharmaśāstras.
O Sage, as I dwelt there in this manner for twelve years, being intent on the play of desire, those years passed away like a single moment.
When I became pregnant, the king then attained great joy;
he performed the sacramental rites for the fetus according to the prescribed rules.
The king asked about my pregnancy longing again and again, seeking to please me;
yet, though the king was exceedingly pleased in mind, I did not speak, being overcome by shame.
Then, when the tenth month was complete, a son was born to me on an auspicious day endowed with the strength of the planets, lunar mansions, ascendant, and stars.
In the king's palace, there was a great festival celebrating the birth of a son;
the king became supremely delighted by the birth of his child. || 25 ||
At the end of the period of birth-impurity, the king beheld his son and attained great joy;
O scorcher of foes, I was the beloved wife of that lord of the earth. (26)
Then, at the end of two years, I indeed conceived again;
a second son was born, endowed with all auspicious marks. (27)
Then the king gave the name Sudhanvan to that son;
and, urged by the Brahmins, he gave the name Vīravarman to the eldest.
In this way, twelve sons were born who were honored by the king; at that time, I was deluded by my affection for them and my constant fondling and nurturing of them. (29)
Furthermore, eight sons were born to me in due course of time, possessing beautiful forms;
thus, my life as a householder became complete, having attained the means of happiness.
In due time, the king performed for them marriages as was appropriate;
thus, with daughters-in-law and sons, their retinue became great.
Then, born from their grandsons and others, those [beings] as well were filled with the essence of play; endowed with various flavors, they greatly increased delusion. (32)
Sometimes there was happiness and sovereignty, and sometimes there was extraordinary suffering caused by disease among his sons, which brought torment to his body.
At times, however, a most terrible mutual conflict arose between the sons and the daughters-in-law, from which great suffering was born.

O best of sages, I am deeply immersed in this terrible world consisting of pleasure and pain, which is intensely characterized by false conduct, produced by mental constructs, and utterly trivial. (35)
My former knowledge has been forgotten, and likewise my knowledge of the scriptures has vanished; in the absence of women, I have become entirely absorbed in household chores. (36)
But egoism, once arisen, greatly increases delusion:
"These sons of mine are powerful; these daughters-in-law are born of noble families. (37)
"These sons of mine, well-armored, play within my dwellings;
oh, among women in this world, I am indeed most exceedingly blessed! (38)
"I am Nārada; indeed, I have been deceived by the Lord's illusory power (māyā).
Never before has such a thing even been conceived by me in my mind. (39)
"I am the wife of a king, of virtuous conduct, with many sons, and devoted to my husband;
indeed, I am blessed in this world"—thus was I deluded by Kṛṣṇa. (40)
Then, O giver of honor, a certain great king who was the ruler of a distant land became an enemy toward her husband.
Having assembled his army, complete with chariots and elephants,
he arrived at the city of Kānyakubja and contemplated war.
The city was surrounded by that king together with his army;
then my sons and grandsons emerged from the city.
A tumultuous battle was waged there by him with those sons;
all his sons were slain in the fray by the enemy through the power of time.
The king, having been defeated in battle, returned once more to his own home;
meanwhile, I heard that my sons had died in that most terrible conflict. (45)
Having slain my sons and grandsons, that king, endowed with great strength, departed;
then I, weeping, went there to the field of battle.
Seeing those sons and grandsons fallen, she, afflicted by grief, lamented, "O long-lived one, I am submerged in an ocean of sorrow. (47)
"Alas, my sons! Where have you gone today? Alas, I am destroyed by this evil-minded, most powerful, irresistible, and exceedingly sinful fate! (48)
In the meantime, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana,
having assumed the form of an exceedingly handsome elderly brahmin, arrived there.
Well-attired and a knower of the Vedas, he approached me at my will;
on the field of battle, he spoke to me as I was weeping in extreme distress. (50)
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O slender-limbed one, why do you despair? This delusion has been manifested by your infatuation regarding the warbling of the cuckoo, which consists of husband, son, and home. (51)
"Who are you? Whose daughter are you? And who are these people? Reflect upon your own supreme state.
Arise, O fair-eyed one; abandon your weeping and become composed. (52)
O beloved, perform the ritual bathing and the offering of sesame seeds for your sons who have departed to the other world, indeed for the sake of preserving the bounds of dharma.
The bath at a sacred ford must by all means be performed, and never at home;
such is the determination of the Dharmaśāstras regarding deceased kinsmen. (54)
Nārada said:
Having been thus addressed and enlightened by that aged brahmin,
I then arose, accompanied by the king and surrounded by my kinsmen.
The Blessed One, the creator of all beings, appeared before me in the form of a brahmin;
I then departed quickly for that most purifying sacred ford.
There, at that Puṃstīrtha lake, the Lord Hari, the Blessed Viṣṇu, Janārdana in the form of a brahmin, took me with compassion and said: || 57 ||
"Perform your bath in this purifying pond, O lady who moves like an elephant!
Cast off your grief; the time for the funeral rites of your sons has arrived, and [your mourning] is now useless. (58)
Tens of millions of sons born in birth after birth have died, as have fathers, husbands, brothers, and sisters-in-law. (59)
For whom should you feel sorrow regarding this delusion born of the mind—this vain, dream-like source of affliction for embodied beings in this world? (60)
Nārada said: Having heard these words of his, I entered that sacred ford known as Puruṣa, desiring to bathe there, having been impelled by Viṣṇu.
Merely by bathing at the sacred fords, even for a moment, a man was instantly reborn;
Hari stood upon the bank with his own body, holding a lute in his hand.
And having emerged upon the shore, O best of the twice-born, I beheld that lotus-eyed one;
then, O most excellent of brahmins, recognition arose within my mind.
"I had intended to go there, yet here I have come; deluded by Māyā, I have attained the state of a woman along with Hari. (64)
While I was thus absorbed in thought, Hari said to me:
"Nārada, come! What are you doing staying in the water? (65)
Then, remembering that most terrible state of womanhood, I was struck with wonder: "By what cause has this male state been restored once again? (66)

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Nārada’s Re-attainment of His Original Form," in the sixth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Preeminence of Māyā.
Nārada said:
Upon seeing me, the brahmin Nārada, that lord of the earth was struck with wonder.
Where has that wife of mine gone, and from where has this best of sages come? || 1 ||
There the king lamented again and again, "O beloved!
Where have you gone, abandoning me as I wail in separation? (2)
"O lady of broad hips, without you my life, my home, and my kingdom are in vain, O lotus-petal-eyed one; what shall I do, O lady of pure smiles? (3)
My vital breaths do not depart from me now because of separation from you;
indeed, the duty of affection has departed, since the maintenance of life exists only because of you.
I lament, O large-eyed one; give me a dear reply.
Where has that affection for me gone, which existed at our first meeting? (5)
Has she of the beautiful brows submerged herself in the water? Has she been devoured by fish and turtles? Or has she been swiftly seized by Varuṇa due to my misfortune? (6)
"Blessed are you, O lady of beautiful limbs, who have been reunited with your sons;
for you, O speaker of nectar-like words, possess a natural affection toward your children. (7)
It is not right that you have now gone to the third heaven, abandoning me,
your wretched husband who laments, while you yourself are constrained by affection for your son.
"O beloved, both [my son and you] have departed; you are as dear to me as my own life.
Nevertheless, O dear one, death does not come to one who is so deeply afflicted by grief."
What shall I do? Where shall I go? Rāma is no longer upon the earth.
Only the joy of the Raghus knows the sorrow born of separation from Rāma.
By cruel fate, an inversion has occurred here on earth:
the death of a husband and wife who were entirely equal in mind has been brought about separately. (11)
Indeed, a benefit for women has been ordained by the sages, as it is stated in the treatises on dharma: that they should enter the fire together with their husband.
As the king was thus lamenting, the Blessed Lord Hari then restrained him with words endowed with reason.
The Blessed One said: "Why do you despair, O Indra among kings? Where has your beloved wife gone?
Have you not heard the scriptures, and have you not taken refuge in the wise? (14)
Who am I? Who are you? What is our union? And what is your separation like?
In this worldly existence, which is like a flowing current, human beings are carried away as if upon a boat. || 15 ||
Go home, O best of kings; what is the use of your weeping in vain?
For men, union and separation are always dependent upon destiny. (16)
O King, this union with her has been brought about for you here;
you have enjoyed the company of this large-eyed, beautiful woman of slender waist. (17)
Her parents were not seen by you when she was found in the lake; what happened through that chance occurrence like the "crow and the palm fruit" has simply passed away.
Do not grieve, O Indra among kings, for time is indeed difficult to overcome;
having encountered the turn of time, enjoy the pleasures in your home as you did before.
That woman of excellent complexion has departed just as she came;
go there as you were before and accomplish your task, O Lord. (20)
"O lord of the earth, by weeping today, the beloved woman will not return;
you grieve in vain, so now become absorbed in yoga. (21)
Enjoyment comes under the power of time and likewise departs again;
one should not feel grief here on this fruitless path of worldly existence.
Union with happiness does not last in one place, nor does union with suffering;
rather, there is a constant wandering between pleasure and pain, like the rotation of a waterwheel. (23)
O King, having made your mind steady, rule your kingdom as you please;
or else, entrusting it to your heir, retire to the forest now.
The human body of living beings is difficult to obtain and is momentary in its destruction;
once it has been attained, one must by all means accomplish the realization of the Self.
O King, the tongue, the generative organ, and taste exist in animal wombs;
however, knowledge exists only in the human body and not in other base wombs.
Therefore, go home and abandon the grief arising from your beloved;
this is but the illusion of the Blessed One by which the entire world is deluded.
Nārada said:
Having been addressed thus by Hari, the king bowed to the Lord of Kamalā,
performed the ritual of bathing thoroughly, and went to his own palace.
Having bestowed the kingdom upon his own grandson and attained a profound sense of world-weariness,
the king went to the forest and attained the knowledge of reality.
When the king had departed, I beheld the Lord Adhokṣaja;
laughing at me again and again, that Lord of the World spoke to me.
"I have been deceived by you, O Lord; the great power of your illusion has been recognized.
I remember all my conduct while I was in a female body, and everything that was done by me. (31)
Speak to me, O Lord of the gods of gods; having entered the lake, my previous knowledge has vanished simply by bathing—how is this so, O Hari? (32)
"O Teacher of the World, having obtained a woman's body, I have been deluded, like Pulomā who obtained Vāsava as her husband, the best of kings. (33)
O Lord of Gods, that very mind is that consciousness, and that ancient body is the subtle body (liṅga); O Hari, how then can there be a destruction of memory?
O Lord, this is a great wonder to me regarding the destruction of my knowledge;
O Beloved of Ramā, tell me today the supreme cause of it. (35)
Having obtained a female body, I have indeed enjoyed pleasures many times; I constantly drank liquor and ate food in a manner contrary to the prescribed rules. (36)
At that time, I did not clearly know that very thing—that I am Nārada;
today I know everything as it truly is, whereas at that time it was not so distinct.
Viṣṇu said: Behold, O Nārada of great intelligence, this play of Māyā;
for within the bodies of all living beings, there are indeed manifold variations of conditions.
Waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth state are the conditions of embodied beings;
likewise, when another body is attained, what kind of doubt could there possibly be? (39)
A sleeping man does not know, nor does he hear, even though he speaks;
yet, having awakened again, he knows everything without exception. || 40 ||
The mind is agitated by sleep, and the occurrences of dreams arise;
indeed, there are manifold varieties of mental distinctions and numerous mental states. (41)
"The elephant is coming to kill me; I am not able to flee.
What shall I do? There is no place for me where I might go with speed. (42)
In a dream, he sees his deceased grandfather come to his own home; he imagines union with him, conversation, and eating together. (43)
Indeed, one who has awakened knows the pleasure and pain seen in a dream;
having remembered it all, he even explains it to people in detail. (44)
Even in a dream, one does not know with certainty that "this is an illusion";
likewise, the manifestation of māyā is indeed difficult to comprehend.
"O Nārada, I do not know the further shore of this most difficult-to-traverse [ocean] of qualities; indeed, neither Śambhu nor the Lotus-born knows it, nor does Māyā herself. (46)
Who else, moreover, being dull-witted due to pride, would have been capable of knowing this?
In this world, no one at all could possess a complete understanding of the qualities of Māyā. (47)
The entire world, both stationary and moving, is produced by the three qualities (guṇas);
without the qualities, this saṃsāra does not exist in the slightest degree.
I am characterized by the quality of sattva, yet endowed with rajas and tamas;
O Lord of the World, I am never devoid of these three qualities.
Likewise, Brahmā, your father, is proclaimed here as one whose nature is primarily rajas;
he is indeed joined with tamas and sattva, and is not abandoned by those two qualities.

Śiva is likewise characterized by darkness (tamas) as his primary quality, yet he is enveloped by passion (rajas) and goodness (sattva); indeed, I have never heard of anyone who is entirely devoid of the three qualities.
Therefore, O Lord of Sages, one should not give way to delusion in this saṃsāra—
which is fashioned by illusion, essence-less, shoreless, and exceedingly difficult to navigate.
Māyā has been seen by you this very day, and indeed many enjoyments have been experienced;
O illustrious one, why do you ask about her wondrous conduct?
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Preeminence of Māyā," in the sixth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Greatness of the Blessed One.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O great king, as I speak in clear syllables.
Indeed, I have heard from Nārada the greatness of Māyā. || 1 ||
Furthermore, having heard that account concerning the origin of the female body from that sage, I questioned Nārada, the sage who knows all things best.
"Tell me, Nārada, what was said by Hari afterwards?
And where did Mādhava, the Lord of the World, go along with you? (3)
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus at that most enchanting lake, the Blessed One mounted Garuḍa and set his mind on going to Vaikuṇṭha.
The Beloved of Ramā said to me: "O Nārada, go wherever you wish;
or come to my world—do as you please."
Having taken leave of Madhusūdana, I departed for the world of Brahmā;
and at that very moment, the Blessed Lord, the Ruler of the Gods, mounted upon Garuḍa, also departed.
Having instructed me as he pleased, he quickly departed for Vaikuṇṭha;
then, after Janārdana had gone, I went to the abode of the ancestors.
Reflecting upon all suffering and most wonderful happiness,
he went and bowed to his father, remaining before his father for as long as he stood there.
Having been questioned thus by his father, O Sage, he looked at me who was distressed with anxiety and said,
"O Brahmin, where have you gone, O fortunate one? Why are you so distressed with anxiety, my son?"
"O best of sages, I do not see your mind at all composed today;
have you been deceived by someone, or have you seen some great wonder? (10)
"O son, why do I see you so dejected and deprived of consciousness?
Nārada said:
"Thus questioned by his father, he was then seated upon a grass mat (bṛsī)."
I told him my own story, arising from the power of illusion:
"O father, I have been deceived at will by the all-powerful Viṣṇu."
Although I have been made to assume the state of a woman for very many years, I have experienced great suffering arising from grief for my son. (13)
Awakened by him with the nectar of gentle words,
I bathed once again in the lake and was born as the man Nārada.
O Brahmin, what was the cause that I fell into such delusion then? My previous realization was forgotten, as I was suddenly made one with that [state]. (15)
O Brahmā, I do not know this power of Māyā, which is so difficult to overcome;
it has clearly become the root of delusion that destroys true knowledge. (16)
Everything, both auspicious and inauspicious, has been experienced and correctly understood by me.
Tell me, O father, how you conquered that; explain the means to me.
Nārada said:
After I had thus petitioned the Creator with affection,
my father, the son of Vāsavi, smiled and spoke to me.
Brahmā said:
"She is difficult to conquer by all the gods, by the high-souled sages, by ascetics endowed with knowledge, and by yogis who subsist on air. (19)
I am not able to know that immensely powerful Māyā in every respect;
neither Viṣṇu nor Śambhu, the Lord of Umā, is able to know it.
That Great Māyā, which effects creation, preservation, and destruction, is difficult to comprehend;
she is veiled by causal factors such as time, karma, and inherent nature.
"Do not grieve, O wise one, regarding that great power of illusion;
nor should you feel any astonishment, for we have all been utterly deluded. (22)
Nārada said:
Having been addressed thus by my father, O Vyāsa, I took leave of him and,
freed from pride, arrived here while beholding various excellent holy places.
Therefore, O best of beings, you too should cast aside the delusion born of the destruction of the Kauravas; remain seated comfortably in this place and bide your time.
One must inevitably experience the results of actions performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
having made this firm resolve in your heart, go about as you please.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, O King, Nārada departed after awakening me;
I, meanwhile, reflected upon those words that had been spoken by the sage at that time.
Standing on the bank of the Sarasvatī during the excellent Sārasvata Kalpa,
this Bhāgavata was composed by me for the purpose of passing the time.
O King, this Purāṇa is supreme, the destroyer of all doubts, endowed with various narratives, and grounded in the authority of the Vedas. (28)
O best of kings, you must not entertain any doubt in this matter whatsoever;
it is just as if some magician were to hold a wooden Pāñcālī puppet in his hand.
Having brought her under his control, he makes her dance at will according to his own desire;
in the same way, Māyā makes the world—both the stationary and the moving—dance.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, including gods, asuras, and humans,
it is endowed with the five senses and follows the lead of the mind and consciousness.
O King, the three qualities (guṇas) are in every way the cause of all things;
it is a certainty that an effect is inseparably joined with its cause. || 32 ||
These qualities, arising from Māyā, possess distinct and diverse natures;
for they are threefold, being calm, terrible, and deluded. (33)
A person is eternally endowed with that [Self]; how could he ever be devoid of it?
In this world, a cloth never exists when separated from its threads. || 34 ||
Likewise, O lord of men, it is certain that one who is devoid of these three qualities— whether a divine being, a human, or an animal— is not a true possessor of a body.
Devoid of qualities, he would not exist, just as a jar is nothing without clay;
likewise, these three—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—are the substrata of the qualities.
At times they are endowed with joy, and again they are likewise endowed with displeasure;
thus they become possessed of sorrow due to the conjunction of the qualities (guṇas). || 37 ||
Sometimes Brahmā, abiding in the state of sattva, is then peaceful and possessed of meditative concentration;
endowed with joy toward all beings, he is united with knowledge. || 38 ||
Furthermore, when devoid of *sattva* and enveloped by the quality of *rajas*, he then becomes terrible in form and filled with dissatisfaction everywhere. (39)
When the Creator (Brahmā) is predominantly possessed by the quality of darkness (tamas), then, being filled with despondency, he becomes deluded; it is not otherwise.
Mādhava, too, should always be entirely established in goodness (sattva), so that he may become peaceful, full of joy, and endowed with knowledge. || 41 ||

That very Lord of Ramā, though dependent on the qualities (guṇas), becomes joined with displeasure due to the predominance of rajas; he is formidable toward all beings, yet remains subject to the gunas.
Even Rudra, when joined with *sattva*, becomes full of joy and peaceful; yet, when enveloped by *rajas*, he too becomes terrible and devoid of joy. (43)
Even he, being possessed of the quality of tamas, becomes deluded and filled with despondency.
If Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others are thus dependent upon these qualities, [what need be said of others? (44)
Likewise, those born of the solar dynasty and those born of the lunar dynasty, as well as the fourteen Manus and others who are proclaimed in every age; (45)
What need is there to speak of others, O best of kings, in this world of saṃsāra?
This entire universe, including gods, asuras, and humans, is subject to illusion (māyā).
Therefore, O King, you must never entertain doubt in this matter:
an embodied being, subject to illusion (māyā), acts under its influence, following its power. (47)
And that Māyā is always dependent upon and impelled by Him, even within the Supreme Reality which is of the nature of pure consciousness; thus, it is always active among living beings.
Then [he beheld] that Supreme Goddess, the Mistress of Māyā, the Blessed One whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, who is distinguished by her power of illusion. || 49 ||
One should meditate upon her, worship her, bow down to her, and also recite her mantra;
by that, she becomes compassionate and surely liberates the embodied soul.
She indeed withdraws her own māyā by bestowing self-experience;
for māyā is the world, and its mistress is the Sovereign Goddess (Īśvarī). 51.
Then the goddess Bhuvaneśī, the beauty of the three worlds, was proclaimed;
O Lord of the Earth, if the mind were always attached to her form, [then it would be well]. (52)
O King, what could possibly arise there from illusion, whether it be real or unreal?
Therefore, for the purpose of dispelling illusion, there is indeed no other deity whatsoever.
But without the Goddess, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, darkness would not be capable of destroying the mass of darkness; indeed, it would have no power at all. (54)
But the light of the sun, the moon, lightning, fire, and so forth [are not self-luminous];
therefore, one should know the Mother, the Mistress of Māyā, as consciousness that is self-luminous.
One should propitiate [the Lord] with great devotion for the sake of turning away from the qualities of Māyā.
Thus has the account beginning with the slaying of the demon Vṛtra been correctly narrated by me. (56)
O tiger among kings, what else do you wish to hear that was asked?
O you of noble vows, this first half of the Purāṇa has been narrated to you. (57)
In this [work], the greatness of the Goddess has been established in detail;
this secret of the Illustrious Mother must not be given to just anyone.
It should be given to one who is devoted, peaceful, and intent on devotion to the Goddess;
and to a disciple, or an eldest son, who is endowed with devotion to the Guru. (59)
This Purāṇa is the essence of all narratives, equal to the entirety of the Vedas, and permeated by authoritative evidence; whoever reads it with supreme devotion or hears it here with faith—
That man indeed becomes possessed of wealth and possessed of knowledge in this world. || 60 ||
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Blessed Goddess," in the sixth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Dakṣa Prajāpati.
Sūta said:
Having heard this divine narrative from the ascetic, the king was filled with joy.
The righteous son of Parīkṣit questioned Vyāsa once again.
Janamejaya said:
O Lord, I am desirous of hearing in every way the detailed account of the lineage of the kings of the solar dynasty as well as that of the lunar dynasty.
O sinless, omniscient one, tell us the story that destroys all evil—
the life-stories of kings from both lineages— in great detail.
For I have heard that they were all devotees of the Supreme Power;
who could remain detached while listening to the life-story of a devotee of the Goddess? (4)
Thus questioned by the royal sage, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī and best of sages,
spoke to him with a serene countenance.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O great king, as I speak at length concerning the origins of the lineages of the Moon and the Sun, as well as those of others.
From the lotus of Viṣṇu’s navel, indeed, Brahmā with four faces came into being;
having performed austerities and propitiated the Great Goddess, who is so difficult to attain.
Having been granted a boon by her, the Creator, the Grandfather of the worlds, prepared to create the universe;
yet he was unable to effect a creation consisting of human beings.
Having reflected in his mind in many ways for the sake of creation, the four-faced one did not quickly attain expansion, even though it had been fashioned by that Great-Souled One.
The Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) created seven sons from his mind:
Marīci, Aṅgiras, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulaha, Kratu, and Pulastya; these seven are renowned as his mind-born sons.
Rudra was born from his wrath, while Nārada emerged from his lap; likewise, Dakṣa arose from his thumb, as did others such as Sanaka and the rest, who were born of his mind.
From the left thumb was born the wife of Dakṣa, beautiful in all her limbs;
she is renowned in the Purāṇas by the name Vīriṇī, O lord of the earth. (12)
She was named Asiknī, in whom Nārada was born—
that foremost of celestial sages, the son of Brahmā born of his mind, who could fulfill every desire.
Janamejaya said:
O Brahmin, regarding the words spoken by you here— how the great ascetic Nārada was born from Dakṣa through Vīriṇī— I have a doubt.
How was the sage Nārada born from Vīriṇī, the wife of Dakṣa;
for he was the son of Brahmā, a knower of dharma, and the best among ascetics.
This wonderful account of Nārada’s birth from Dakṣa’s wife has been related by you; tell it to me again in full detail.
How was his former body released from the curse of whom, O high-minded one?
And for what reason, O sage, was this birth undertaken by the all-knowing Nārada? (17)
Vyāsa said: At the beginning, Dakṣa was commanded by Brahmā for the purpose of creation;
he was urged by the Self-born One to produce offspring for the sake of great increase.
Then the powerful Prajāpati Dakṣa begot five thousand sons, even more mighty, upon Vīriṇī.
Seeing all those sons of his desiring to increase their progeny, the celestial sage Nārada, impelled by Time, spoke these words with a smile: || 20 ||
Without knowing the extent of the earth, how will you, desiring to create progeny, not become objects of ridicule for the worlds? Of this there is no doubt. (21)
Having indeed ascertained the dimensions of the earth, one should undertake the effort;
once it is performed, it attains success—of this there is no doubt. || 22 ||
"Alas, you are indeed foolish, since without knowing the surface of the earth, you are prepared to create subjects; how will success come to pass? (23)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by Nārada, those Haryaśvas, through the power of destiny, suddenly spoke to one another: "The sage has indeed spoken correctly."
"Having ascertained the measure of the earth, we shall create subjects with ease.
Having reflected thus, they all set out to examine the world. (25)
In order to fully explore the entire earth according to the words of Nārada,
some went at their pleasure toward the east, and others likewise toward the south.
In the west and the north, they were everywhere filled with zeal;
seeing his sons thus gone, Dakṣa was indeed deeply afflicted by grief.
Having made his resolve for the sake of the subjects, he caused others to be born;
those sons also became intent there upon making an effort for the welfare of the people.
Seeing them, the sage Nārada spoke those words he had previously uttered:
"Alas, you are indeed childish, since you have set out for the earth without knowing its true nature."
But for what reason did the subjects proceed to establish authority?
Having heard the words of the sage and considering them to be true, they were nonetheless bewildered. (30)
All the brothers set out just as before;
seeing his sons thus departed, Dakṣa was overcome with anger.
Out of anger arising from grief for his son, Dakṣa cursed Nārada, saying: "Since my daughter has been destroyed by you, therefore you shall meet with destruction. (32)
"O evil-minded one, because of this sin, go to dwell in a womb! Become my son at your pleasure, since you have caused the downfall of my sons. (33)
Thus cursed, the sage Nārada was then born from Vīriṇī;
furthermore, we have heard that he subsequently begot sixty daughters upon Vīriṇī.
Abandoning grief for her sons, Dakṣa, the knower of the supreme dharma,
gave thirteen of them to the high-souled Kaśyapa.
O King, he gave ten to Dharmasoma, twenty-seven to Bhṛgu, two to Ariṣṭanemi, and four to Bhṛgu. (36)
And there were two daughters of Aṅgiras, likewise belonging to Aṅgiras;
their sons and grandsons were the gods and the Dānavas as well. (37)
Born endowed with strength, they were mutually antagonistic;
all possessed passion and hatred and were hostile toward one another. Enveloped by delusion, they were indeed heroic and exceedingly deceitful. (38)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of Dakṣa Prajāpati," in the seventh book of the *Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses, within the description of the Lunar and Solar Dynasties. || 1 ||
O illustrious one, relate to me in great detail the genealogy of kings,
specifically that of those born of the solar lineage who were especially knowers of dharma, beginning with the description of King Śaryāti.
Listen, O Bhārata, I shall describe the expansion of the solar dynasty (Ravivaṃśa) exactly as it was previously heard by me from Nārada, the best of sages.
Once, the illustrious sage Nārada, wandering at his own will, arrived at a holy hermitage on the auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī.
Then, having bowed his head at his feet, he stood before him;
thereafter, having respectfully offered him a seat and performed the rites of hospitality, [he waited].
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, he spoke these words:
"O best of sages, I am indeed purified by the arrival of one so worthy of worship."
O Omniscient One, relate the narrative joined with the deeds of kings—
those kings who are proclaimed as belonging to this seventh family of Manu.
O Brahmin, their birth was incomparable and their conduct most wonderful; I am desirous of hearing the detailed account of the Solar dynasty.
"O best of sages, explain this to me, both in brief and in detail.
Thus was Nārada, the knower of the supreme truth, questioned by me, O King.
Addressing him with joy, he spoke laughingly and with delight;
Nārada said:
"Listen, O son of Satyavatī, to the unsurpassed lineage of kings."
It is purifying, pleasing to the ear, and endowed with righteousness, knowledge, and other virtues;
formerly, Brahmā, the creator of the world, was born from the lotus of his navel.
Thus he is celebrated and proclaimed in the Purāṇas as Viṣṇu;
he is omniscient, the creator of all, self-existent, and possessed of all powers. (11)
In ancient times, having performed austerities for ten thousand years, that Soul of the Universe,
desiring to create, meditated upon Śivā and attained unsurpassed power.
He produced mind-born sons endowed with auspicious marks;
among them, Marīci became foremost in the work of creation.
His son was the highly renowned Kaśyapa, esteemed by all;
he indeed had thirteen wives who were the daughters of Dakṣa.
All the gods, as well as the Daityas, Yakṣas, Pannagas, beasts, and birds, have arisen from him; therefore, the creation belongs to Kaśyapa.
Among the gods, he was renowned as Sūrya, named Vivasvat;
his son was the famous King Manu Vaivasvata. (16)
His son was Ikṣvāku, the increaser of the solar dynasty;
Manu had nine sons, with Ikṣvāku as the first-born.
O Indra among kings, listen once more with a focused mind to their names:
Ikṣvāku, Nābhāga, Dhṛṣṭa, and Śaryāti. (18)
Nariṣyanta, Prāṃśu, Nṛga, Diṣṭa as the seventh, Karūṣa, and Pṛṣadhra—these nine are remembered as the sons of Manu. (19)
Ikṣvāku was born as the first son of Manu;
he had a hundred sons, the eldest of whom was the self-controlled Vikukṣi.
Listen briefly to the expansion of the lineage of the nine heroic sons of Manu, who were born during the interval of Manu's reign.
The son of Nābhāga was the powerful Ambarīṣa, who was a knower of dharma, true to his word, and devoted to the protection of his subjects. (22)
From Dhṛṣṭa was born the Kṣatriya lineage known as Dhārṣṭaka, which became Brahman-like; they were entirely devoted to the duties of Brahmins and were utterly devoid of cowardice in battle. || 23 ||
Śaryāti had a son, widely renowned by the name Ānarta,
and likewise a daughter named Sukanyā, who was endowed with beauty and charm.
The beautiful daughter was given by the king even to the blind Cyavana;
indeed, by her virtue of character, the sage became one with beautiful eyes.
"We have heard that he was ordained by the two Aśvins, the sons of the Sun.
Janamejaya said:
"O Brahmin, this great doubt has been raised by you in the course of this narrative. (26)
That the king gave his daughter Sulocanā to a blind sage—whether she be ugly, devoid of virtues, or lacking auspicious marks. || 27 ||
"When a daughter becomes a king, he gives her away to one who is blind;
knowing him to be blind, why did that best of kings give his beautiful-faced daughter? (28)
"O Brahman, tell me the cause; I am always worthy of your favor.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of King Janamejaya, the son of Parīkṣit...
Dvaipāyana, with a serene soul, spoke to him as if smiling.
Vyāsa said:
"There was a glorious king named Śaryāti, the son of Vaivasvata."
He had four thousand women as his wives;
they were princesses, beautiful in form and endowed with all auspicious marks.
All the wives were full of love for the king, dear to him, and highly esteemed;
they had one daughter, indeed, a beautiful girl named Sukanyā.
Beloved by her father and all her mothers, she of the lovely smile was near the city at a lake resembling Lake Mānasa.
And there was a flight of stairs leading down to a path filled with clear water,
teeming with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and graced by *cakravāka* birds.
It was crowded with gallinules and cranes, filled with flocks of all kinds of birds,
endowed with five types of lotuses, and well-frequented by bees.
And on its sides it was covered with trees, surrounded by auspicious footstools—adorned with *sāla*, *tamāla*, *sarala*, *punnāga*, and *aśoka* trees. (36)
It was adorned with banyan, holy fig, and kadamba trees, and shone with groves of plantains, as well as with citron, pomegranate, date, and jackfruit trees.
It was surrounded by *kramuka* trees, coconut palms, *ketaka* flowers, and golden trees,
as well as by clusters of white *yūthikā* and groups of *mallikā* jasmine.
It was surrounded by rose-apple, mango, and tamarind trees, as well as karañja and kuṭaja;
it was adorned with palāśa, nimba, khadira, bilva, and āmalaka trees.
There was the warbling of cuckoos, resplendent with the cries of peacocks,
in that auspicious region nearby, which was surrounded by groves of trees.
The descendant of Bhṛgu, Cyavana, a peaceful ascetic and established sage,
perceiving that place to be secluded, performed austerities with a concentrated mind.
Having assumed a firm posture, maintaining silence, and having conquered his breath,
he restrained his senses and abandoned food, becoming a treasury of asceticism.
Deprived of water for drinking and other necessities, he remained meditating upon the Supreme Mother;
O King, he became covered with anthills and entwined by creeping vines.
O King, after a long time, he was completely covered by ants;
thus that wise man was enveloped on all sides like a lump of clay.
Once, O King, that protector of the earth, surrounded by a circle of amorous women, came to this excellent lake to sport. || 45 ||
Accompanied by a multitude of beautiful women, King Śaryāti became absorbed in play within the pure waters of a lotus pond.
Having reached the forest, Sukanyā, fickle and like a flickering flame, sported surrounded by her companions, gathering flowers with a joyful mind. || 47 ||
Adorned with all ornaments and with anklets tinkling on her feet, she approached the anthill of Cyavana as she was walking about. || 48 ||
Seated near an anthill, absorbed in play,
she saw two lights within its opening like fireflies.
Thinking, "What is this?", the slender-waisted woman resolved to extract it;
taking up a sharp thorn, she acted with haste. (50)
The sage beheld that young woman standing nearby, making her efforts;
with her beautiful hair, she moved about like a beloved of the God of Love.
Beholding that fair-toothed woman there, the storehouse of asceticism, Bhārgava, with a constricted throat, addressed that auspicious lady, saying, "What is this? (52)
"Go far away, O large-eyed one; I am an ascetic, O lovely-faced one.
Do not pierce this anthill today with your thorn, O slender-waisted one. (53)
Therefore, even though this was being proclaimed, she did not hear it at all;
saying, "What indeed is this?", she pierced his eyes.
Impelled by fate, the princess broke through [the wall] and departed;
while playing, she was filled with apprehension, wondering, "What have I done? (55).
With his eyes thus pierced, he became exceedingly wrathful;
afflicted by the pain, he indeed experienced intense torment. (56)
At that very moment, the soldiers experienced a total obstruction of feces and urine,
especially the king along with his ministers on all sides.
Then, when the excrement and urine of all elephants, camels, horses, and living beings were thus obstructed, Śaryāti became distressed.
The soldiers told him of the obstruction of his feces and urine;
the king reflected upon the cause of this arising of suffering.
Then the king, having reflected, spoke to his soldiers and his own people; returning home afflicted with anxiety, he asked, "By whom has this evil deed been committed? (60)
On the western side of the lake, in the midst of a forest, the great ascetic Cyavana,
a practitioner of penance, performs difficult austerities there.
"Someone has committed an offense against that ascetic who possesses a radiance like fire;
therefore, it is certain that this suffering has arisen for everyone. (62)
I believe that some person has done wrong to the high-souled Bhārgava, who is especially aged in asceticism, venerable, and most excellent.
Whether known or unknown, this is the supreme fruit of that [merit]:
that such an insult was committed against that ascetic by certain wicked ones.
Thus questioned, those soldiers, afflicted by pain, said to him:
"We do not know of any harm done by us through thought, word, or deed."
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of King Śaryāti," in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Householder Life of Cyavana and Sukanyā.
Vyāsa said:
Thus the king, agitated by anxiety, questioned them all.
He questioned his circle of friends both with gentleness and even with severity.
Seeing the people being oppressed and her father likewise distressed,
Sukanyā reflected upon Śūlabheda and spoke these words.
"O father, while I was playing there in the forest, I saw an ant-hill covered with creepers; it was very firm and possessed two openings. (3)
There, O Great King, I saw two glowing lights like fireflies; when pierced by a needle, I suspected them once again to be fireflies.
"O father, I indeed saw a needle soaked in water at that time, and a faint sound of 'Alas! Alas! was heard from within the anthill. (5)
Then, O King, filled with wonder and the doubt "What is this?",
I did not know what it was that I had pierced in that anthill.
Having heard Sukanya’s gentle words and realizing that it was an offense against the sage, King Śaryāti quickly went to the anthill.
There he saw Cyavana, advanced in asceticism and deeply distressed,
violently tearing apart the anthill that completely covered the sage’s body.
Having prostrated himself on the ground like a staff before that descendant of Bhṛgu, the king,
filled with humility, praised him and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
O highly fortunate one, O Brahmin, a misdeed was committed by my daughter while she was playing; since it was done by a young girl out of ignorance, you ought to forgive her.
"For I have heard that sages are indeed free from anger; therefore, you too ought to forgive this young girl now. (11)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, and seeing the king deeply distressed and bowed down in humility, Cyavana spoke these words.
Cyavana said:
"O King, I never indeed harbor even the slightest anger;
it was not by me alone that you were cursed today when your daughter was mistreated."
"O lord of the earth, pain has arisen in my eyes today, though I am innocent; by that sin, I know you are suffering. (14)
Having committed a supreme offense against a devotee of the Goddess, what person could obtain happiness, even if Śiva himself were his protector? (15)
"What can I do, O protector of the earth, being blind and overcome by old age?
And who, O King, will provide service for one who is sightless? (16)
The king said: "Many servants will serve you incessantly;
forgive them, O tiger among sages, for ascetics are indeed possessed of little anger. (17)
Cyavana said:
"O King, I am blind and without attendants; how shall I be able to perform austerities?
What will your servants do for my benefit? (18)
If you would grant me forgiveness, O King, then follow my word:
give me a lotus-eyed maiden for the purpose of serving me.
"O Great King, O high-minded one, I shall be pleased with this daughter of yours;
I will perform penance, and she will serve me. (20)
If this is done, there will be happiness for me and it will surely be so for you as well;
O Indra among kings, when I am satisfied, there is no doubt that the soldiers will also be satisfied. (21)
"O King, having reflected in your mind, perform the gift of your daughter;
there is no fault whatsoever in this, for I am an ascetic firm in my vows. (22)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of the sage, Śaryāti became anxious with thought;
"Shall I give her, or shall I not give her? he said nothing at all, O Bhārata. (23)
"How can I be happy after giving this daughter of mine, who resembles a celestial maiden, to one who is blind, old, and ugly? (24)

What man of small intellect and sinful nature would, for the sake of his own happiness, deprive his daughter of the worldly pleasures she seeks, even though he knows the distinction between good and evil? (25)
Having obtained Cyavana, that fair-browed woman, afflicted by the arrows of the five-arrowed god [Kāma], how will she spend her time having obtained a husband who is blind and aged? (26)
In youth, desire is difficult to conquer, especially for one so beautiful;
having obtained a husband equal to herself, how much more so now that he is old and blind? (27)
Having approached the ascetic Gautama while endowed with beauty and youth,
the fair-complexioned Ahalyā was quickly deceived by Vāsava.
And having been cursed by her husband, she later realized the perversion of dharma;
therefore, let my own suffering be the consequence, for I will not give away this virtuous maiden. (29)
Having reflected thus, Śaryāti went to his own home dejected; taking his ministers with him, he, being deeply distressed, held a consultation.
"O ministers, speak now: what must I do at this time? Should my daughter be given to the Brahmin, or should I simply endure this misery? (31)
"Deliberate together on how there might truly be welfare for me.
The ministers said: "O Great King, what can we say in this most difficult crisis? (32)
"How can this most beautiful girl be given to an unfortunate Sukanya?
Vyāsa said:
Then, seeing their father overwhelmed with anxiety, the ministers [spoke]. (33)
But Sukanyā, perceiving his inner feeling, smiled and said this:
"Father, why are your senses so agitated with anxiety today? (34)
"Indeed, you are distressed in countenance and agitated by grief on my account;
I shall go there and console that sage who is afflicted by fear. (35)
"O father, I shall indeed make him pleased by the gift of my own self.
Having heard these words spoken by Sukanyā, the king—
With a serene soul, he spoke to her while his ministers listened:
"How, my daughter, can you, a weak woman, perform service for a blind man in the forest? (37)
"How will you perform for one afflicted by old age, and especially for one prone to anger, an act resembling pleasure with this blind form? (38)
