Out of a desire for happiness, I give my daughter to one whose body is seized by old age; a father must give his daughter to one who possesses the strength of youth and knowledge. (39)
"To one who is prosperous with wealth and grain, never to one who is destitute.
Where is your beauty, O large-eyed lady, and where is that old forest-dweller? (40)
"How can I give my daughter to such an unworthy suitor, whose dwelling is always fixed in a charming hut? (41)
O lotus-petal-eyed one, how can I possibly conceive of you?
It would have been better for me to meet my death, as well as that of my soldiers. (42)
"O lady with the voice of a cuckoo, this gift does not please one who is blind;
destiny must indeed come to pass, yet I shall not abandon my fortitude. (43)
"Be steadfast, O lady of beautiful hips; I shall never give myself to a blind man.
Let my kingdom remain or perish, and likewise let this body of mine go as it may. (44)
"O girl, I will not give you to that blind man," [said the father].
Having heard those words of her father, Sukanyā then spoke to him.
With a serene face and words full of great affection, Sukanyā said:
"O Father, you need not worry for me; give me to the sage now. (46)
"May there be happiness for all the worlds through my deed;
being well-pleased, I shall serve my supremely purifying husband. (47)
And with supreme devotion, in this lonely forest, I, devoted to the dharma of a virtuous wife, shall conduct myself in a manner most worthy of respect toward my aged husband. (48)
"O father, I have no desire for enjoyments; my mind is at peace, O sinless one.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of hers, the ministers were filled with wonder. (49)
And the king, filled with supreme joy, went into the presence of the sage;
having arrived and bowed his head to him, he spoke to that one whose wealth is asceticism.
"O Lord, O Master, accept my daughter for the sake of service according to the prescribed rites.
Having spoken thus, the king gave his daughter in marriage according to the wedding ceremony.
Having accepted the maiden, the sage Bhārgava became pleased;
he did not accept the dowry being offered by the king.
He chose the maiden herself for his own service;
when that sage was pleased, happiness then arose for the soldiers.
And at that very moment, the king experienced supreme joy when he gave his daughter away and departed for his home.
Then the fair-limbed daughter formed a plan and spoke to the king;
Sukanyā said:
"O father, take my garments and my ornaments."
Give me bark for my lower garment and an excellent deerskin;
having assumed the attire of the sages' wives, I shall devote myself to ascetic practice.
"O father, I shall act in such a way that your imperishable fame shall exist upon the surface of the earth, as well as in heaven and in the netherworld. (57)
For the sake of happiness in the next world, I shall practice [virtue] day and night, having given myself—a beautiful young woman—to a blind old man. (58)
You should not entertain any anxiety regarding the destruction of your virtue, just as Arundhatī was the lawful wife of Vasiṣṭha on this earth. 59.
In that very same way I shall become; there is no need for deliberation on this point, just as the virtuous Anasūyā is renowned on earth as the wife of Atri.
"In that very way, O daughter, I shall become a bringer of fame for you.
Having heard the words of Sukanyā, the king, who was a supreme knower of dharma, [replied]. (61)
Having given away the deerskin, he wept immediately upon seeing his daughter of lovely smiles,
who had cast off her ornaments and garments and was wearing the dress of a sage.
With his face turned pale, the king remained right there;
all the queens, seeing their daughter clad in bark garments and deerskins, [were struck with grief]. (63)

Afflicted by intense grief, they wept and became as if trembling. Having taken leave of her, O King, the protector of the earth, surrounded by his ministers, departed for his own city, leaving behind his daughter who was overwhelmed with sorrow. 64.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Domestic Life of Cyavana and Sukanyā," in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Words of Awakening Addressed to Sukanyā by the Two Aśvinīkumāras.
Vyāsa said:
When the king had departed, that young woman remained devoted solely to the service of her husband.
And she became thus devoted to dharma in the service of the sacred fires.
Taking sweet fruits and various kinds of roots,
that young woman, devoted solely to the service of her husband, gave them to the sage.
Having quickly bathed her husband with warm water and wrapped him in a deerskin, she placed him upon an auspicious seat of *bṛsī* grass.
Having first arranged sesame seeds, barley, and kuśa grass, as well as a water-pot, he said to him: "O best of sages, perform your daily rites."
Having raised him up and taken him by the hand once her daily rites were completed,
the young woman seated her husband upon a grass mat or a spread of straw.
Thereafter, having brought back ripe fruits,
the princess fed Cyavana with well-prepared food made of wild rice (nīvāra).
After her husband had eaten and was satisfied, she respectfully offered him water for sipping;
thereafter, filled with devotion, she gave him betel nuts and leaves.
Having seated him, who was holding a mouth-perfume, upon a beautiful throne and having received his command regarding the body, she then performed the ritual preparation.
Having herself prepared food from fruits and returned to his presence, she spoke with affection: "O Lord, what do you command? (9)
"If you so desire, I shall massage your feet today.
Thus she became constantly devoted to service, intent solely upon her husband.
At the conclusion of the evening fire-oblation, that beautiful woman, having gathered fruits,
offered them to the sage— fruits that were both sweet and soft.
Then, filled with love, she ate the remaining food at his command;
having prepared a very soft bed, she joyfully laid him down upon it.
While her beloved was asleep, the slender-waisted woman, who was fond of his happiness,
then performed the massaging of his feet, inquiring about the dharma of noble women.
Having massaged his feet at night, she, devoted with deep affection,
perceived that the sage was asleep and lay down near his feet.
Seeing him established in purity, the beautiful woman then served her husband, creating a cool breeze with a palm-leaf fan.
In the winter, having prepared a stock of wood and set a blazing fire before him, he repeatedly asked him, "Are you well? (16)
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, the beloved wife, having provided water, a vessel, and earth for the purpose of purification, roused her husband.
Having placed him at a distance from her spot and gone far away, she remained steady;
then, perceiving that her husband had performed his purification, she went back and took hold of him again.
Having brought him to the hermitage, she calmly seated him on an auspicious seat and washed his feet according to the prescribed rite with earth and water.
Having offered the vessel for sipping water, she brought the tooth-stick;
and having presented the tooth-wood as prescribed, the princess [waited]. (20)
Having brought pure, auspicious, and warm water for the purpose of bathing, she, filled with affection, asked: || 21 ||
"What do you command, O Brahmin? The cleaning of the teeth has indeed been performed.
Hot water is well-prepared; perform your bath with the appropriate mantras. (22)
This is the time for the fire-oblation (homa), and the morning twilight (sandhyā) is now beginning;
having performed the forest-dwelling rites according to the rules, perform the worship of the deities.
Thus the blameless maiden, having obtained an ascetic as her husband,
constantly attended upon him with affection, through austerity and self-restraint.
Always performing service to the sacred fires and her guests, that lady of auspicious countenance joyfully propitiated Cyavana. (25)
Then, at a certain time, both the Aśvins, the sons of the Sun, arrived while playing in the vicinity of Cyavana’s hermitage.
Having bathed in the water, the two sons of the Sun beheld that maiden, beautiful in all her limbs, returning toward their own hermitage as she was walking along.
Seeing her, who resembled a celestial maiden, the two Nāsatyas, utterly infatuated, approached her with respect and, having run toward her, spoke.
"Wait a moment, O lady of excellent limbs, O you who walk with the gait of an elephant, so that we may question you!
We have arrived as the sons of gods; tell the truth, O lady of pure smiles. (29)
"Whose daughter are you? Who is your husband? And how have you come to this garden all alone to bathe in this lake, O lovely-eyed one? (30)
"O lotus-eyed one, you shine like a second Śrī with your radiance; O beautiful lady, we wish to know the truth—please tell us. (31)
O beloved with tremulous eyes, your two tender feet, standing uncovered upon the ground, cause pain to my heart even as they move.
"O slender-limbed one, you are worthy of a celestial chariot; why do you travel here on foot?
Why are you wandering through this forest without any covering? (33)
"Accompanied by a hundred female slaves, how have you come forth?
Are you a princess or an apsaras? Tell the truth, O lovely-faced one. (34)
Blessed is your mother from whom you were born, and blessed is that father of yours;
O sinless one, they are not even able to describe the good fortune of your husband.
O Sulocanā, this ground is indeed more worthy than even Devalikā;
today your moving foot sanctifies the surface of the earth.
The deer in the forest who behold you at their pleasure possess good fortune;
likewise, all other birds and this exceedingly pure earth do so as well. (37)
Enough with your excessive praise; speak the truth, O fair-eyed one! Who is your father, who is your husband, and where is he whom you so earnestly desire to see? (38)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, the princess, the daughter of a king and exceedingly beautiful, being overcome with shame, spoke to them, O sons of gods. (39)
"Know me here to be the daughter of Śaryāti, the virtuous and beloved wife of the sage Cyavana, given by my father to you both as you pleased. (40)
"O gods, my husband is blind and very old;
he is an ascetic, and with a joyful heart, I serve him day and night. (41)
"Who are you two, and why have you come here? Your husband remains in the hermitage; having gone there, make the hermitage pure this very day."
Having heard those words, O lord of men, the two Dasras said to her:
"How is it, O auspicious lady, that you too were given by your father to an ascetic? (43)
You shine in this forest region like the lightning-flash Saudāminī;
indeed, O radiant lady, no one equal to you has been seen even among the gods.
"You are worthy of divine garments; you do not shine when covered in deerskins.
Adorned with all ornaments, you possess a mass of dark, curling locks. (45)
Alas! How perverse is the ill-conceived act of Fate, that you, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, languish here in this forest,
O beloved with wide eyes, while your husband is blind!
Having approached the sage who was severely afflicted by old age. || 46 ||
O you who are skilled in beautiful dancing, having attained this fresh youth, you do not shine at all with these futile vows;
for the arrows of the Mind-born God have been swiftly and firmly aimed at you.
In whom do they fall? Such is your husband. || 47 ||
O lady with long, dark eyes, you have been made the wife of a blind man by a creator of dull intellect;
surely you do not deserve this.
O fair-eyed one, you must instead take another as your husband. || 48 ||

O lotus-eyed one, your life is indeed in vain, for having obtained a husband who is a sage with sightless eyes, we do not consider your dwelling in the forest or your wearing of the excellent antelope skin to be at all fitting. (49)
Therefore, O lady of faultless limbs, you who possess beautiful eyes, choose one of these two with focused attention;
O proud woman, why do you waste your youth?
O beautiful one, you are serving the sage in vain. || 50 ||
Why do you serve that one who is devoid of fortune and abandoned by both nourishment and protection,
having forsaken the Sage who is the source of all happiness?
O lady of faultless limbs, choose one of the two.
O beloved, enjoy your renowned pastimes in the Nandana and Caitraratha groves;
for how can one spend time as a blind old man?
O proud lady, you will discipline me who am devoid of pride.
You are a princess, endowed with auspicious marks, and you understand the nature of wandering in this worldly existence; yet,
deprived of fortune, you are here in this desolate forest.
How do you spend your time in vain? || 53 ||
Therefore, O sweet-voiced one with a lovely face and wide eyes, resort to him for the happiness of both; and you,
O slender-waisted one who have lived in the abode of the gods, enjoy the pleasures of life.
"O daughter of the king of men, quickly abandon this aged sage!"
O lady of beautiful hair, O fawn-eyed one, what happiness is there for you here in this lonely forest with an old man—
this service to one who is blind and your own youthful age?
"O daughter of a king, what do you consider to be suffering? || 55 ||
O moon-faced one, you are exceedingly delicate;
fetching fruit and water is not suitable for you. (56)

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Words of Enlightenment Spoken by the Aśvinīkumāras to Sukanyā," in the seventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Promise Made by the Aśvins for Cyavana to Drink Soma.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of theirs, the princess trembled.
Maintaining her composure, she, who was wont to speak with moderation, addressed them there.
"You two gods, sons of the Sun, omniscient and honored by the immortals, ought not to speak thus to me, who am virtuous and of righteous character. (2)
"O best of gods, I was given by my father to a sage who follows the path of yoga;
how can I go upon that path frequented by throngs of unchaste women? (3)
This sun, the witness of the deeds of all the world, was born from Kaśyapa; you ought not to speak in such a manner.
How could a woman of noble family, knowing the determination of dharma, abandon her husband and resort to another man in this worthless cycle of existence?
"Go as you please, O gods; I shall cast a curse upon you, you sinless ones.
I am Sukanyā, devoted solely to my husband Śaryāti."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard her words, the two Nāsatyas were greatly amazed;
suspecting fear on the part of the sage, they spoke to her again.
"O Princess, O woman of excellent complexion, we are pleased with your righteousness.
Choose a boon, O lady of beautiful hips; we shall grant it for your welfare. (8)
"Know for certain, O young woman, that we two are the foremost physicians of the gods;
we shall make your husband young and endowed with beauty. (9)
"Therefore, O wise one, choose one of us three as your husband from among those who possess identical forms and bodies. (10)
Having heard those words of Tārā, she was struck with wonder; she then went to her own husband and related the marvelous speech uttered by those two.
Sukanyā said:
"O Lord, O descendant of Bhṛgu, two divine sons of the Sun have arrived at Cyavana’s hermitage; I have seen those two Nāsatyas with their celestial bodies. (12)
Beholding me, whose every limb was beautiful, both became overcome with desire;
they spoke these words: "O Lord, your husband is in the prime of youth. (13)
"We shall indeed make the sage possessed of divine form and sight;
listen now to the condition for this that is spoken by me. (14)
"And we shall create for you a husband whose form is composed of equal parts;
from among us three, choose one as your husband. (15)
Having heard that, I have come here to ask you about this wonderful matter;
O virtuous one, tell me what must be done in this crisis of affairs.
Even the divine illusion is difficult to discern; I do not know the deception of those two.
O Omniscient One, whatever you command, that which is desired by you, I shall perform.
Cyavana said:
"Go today, O beloved, O lady of virtuous vows; at my word, bring the two Nāsatyas, the best of divine physicians, quickly to my presence."
"Let her word be carried out quickly; no hesitation should be made here.
Vyāsa said:
Thus authorized, she went there and spoke these words.
"O best of gods, Nāsatyas, let it be done quickly according to our agreement.
Having heard those words of hers, the two Aśvins arrived there.
They said to that princess, "Let your husband Cyavana enter the water quickly for the sake of his beauty"; thereupon, he entered the water.
The two Aśvins also subsequently entered that excellent lake;
then, at that very moment, those three emerged from the lake,
possessing identical forms, divine bodies, and appearing as youths exactly alike.
They were richly adorned with divine earrings and possessed symmetrical limbs. || 23 ||
They all spoke together: "O lady of excellent complexion, O auspicious one with a stainless face, choose us as your husband, for we are desired by you. (24)
"O fair-faced one, choose whichever among them you feel greater affection for.
Vyāsa said:
Having seen them all identical in form and likewise equal in age, she— || 25 ||
Seeing those three, who were like sons of gods, possessing identical voices and identical attire and having similar appearances, she fell into a state of doubt.
Not knowing her husband correctly, she became deeply distressed and reflected:
"What shall I do? These three are equal; I do not know whom I should choose. (27)
"These are indeed the sons of gods; I have fallen into danger.
This is a complete magical illusion (indrajāla) devised here by the two gods."
"What must I do here now that death has arrived?
I shall by no means choose another husband, having abandoned my lord. (29)
Thinking in his mind, "Some modern person has become a god"—this is my conviction—[he meditated] upon the supreme Śivā, the Sovereign of the Universe. (30)
The slender-waisted woman meditated upon the divine Goddess and praised her;
Sukanyā said, "O Mother of the World, I have come to you for refuge, being deeply afflicted by sorrow. (31)
Protect my virtue today; I bow at your feet.
O Goddess born from the lotus, salutations to you! O beloved of Śaṅkara, salutations! (32)
Obeisance to you, O Lakṣmī, beloved of Viṣṇu; O Sarasvatī, mother of the Vedas!
This entire world, both stationary and moving, has been created by you.
Behold this with an undistracted mind and consume it likewise for the peace of the world;
you are the highly esteemed mother of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
O giver of intellect to the ignorant, you are always the bestower of liberation to the wise;
you are the command, the perfect primordial nature (prakṛti), and one whose appearance is dear to Puruṣa. 35.
You bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon living beings of pure soul;
yet you willfully grant suffering to the ignorant, while serving as the means for the happiness of virtuous beings.
O Mother, you grant success to yogis, and furthermore, you bestow victory and fame;
I have attained a state of supreme wonder and have come to you for refuge. (37)
"O mother, show me my husband; I am submerged in an ocean of grief.
A deception has been practiced upon me by the two gods; utterly deluded, whom shall I choose? (38)
"O omniscient one, show my husband after you have recognized my vow of fidelity.
Vyāsa said: Thus praised then by her, the gods as well as Tripurasundarī [responded]. (39)
Then, having determined in her mind, that virtuous woman quickly bestowed upon his heart a knowledge that brings about happiness, [selecting] those who possessed similar age and form.
Having carefully observed them all, the young woman chose her own husband;
when Cyavana was chosen, the two gods became satisfied.
Beholding the dharma of Satī,
those two supreme gods, being delighted by the grace of the Blessed Lady, joyfully granted her a boon.
Having addressed the sage, both were eager to depart quickly;
meanwhile, Cyavana had regained his eyesight, his wife, and his youth.
Delighted, the one of great splendor spoke these words to the two Nāsatyas:
"O best of gods, this service has been rendered to me by you both."
What can I say of the happiness attained in this unsurpassed cycle of existence? Having obtained a wife with beautiful hair-ends, my suffering has increased day by day. (45)
To one who was blind, very old, and destitute in the forest, you two gave back his eyes, as well as youth and wonderful beauty. (46)
Having thus completed this work, I speak something to be of benefit;
for he who would not assist his benefactor and friend in any way whatsoever [is unworthy]. (47)
"Fie upon that man, O two gods, who would become a debtor on this earth!
Therefore, I now wish to grant you whatever you desire. (48)

"For the sake of liberating yourselves from debt and for the sake of the New One, O Lords of the Gods, I shall grant you whatever you have requested, even that which is unobtainable by gods or asuras. (49)
"Speak what is intended by your minds; I am pleased with your virtuous deed.
Having heard the sage’s words, the two of them consulted with one another.
They spoke to that best of sages, who was standing there together with Sukanyā:
"O Sage, by the grace of our father, everything we desired in our minds has been attained. (51)
"We have a longing to drink the Soma together with the gods. Thus addressed by the Lord, the two physicians were forbidden from taking up the sacrificial cups.
When Śakra performed a sacrifice for Brahmā on the Golden Mountain (Meru),
therefore, O knower of dharma, you too, O ascetic, if you are capable— || 53 ||
"This task must indeed be performed, for it is desired and highly approved by us both.
Having understood this, O Brahmin, act accordingly, you who drink the soma. (54)
"There is a thirst that is very difficult to satisfy; it will come from you.
Having heard those words, Cyavana spoke softly to the two of them.
"That I, being endowed with beauty and possessed of youth, have been made old by you two, yet have obtained a wife. (56)
"Therefore, out of affection, I shall make you both drinkers of Soma while the King of the Gods looks on; I speak this truth. (57)
Having heard these words regarding King Śaryāti of immeasurable splendor during his extensive sacrifice, the two of them departed for heaven, filled with joy. (58)
Having taken her, Cyavana went to the circle of the hermitage.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Promise Made by the Aśvins through Cyavana for the Drinking of Soma," in the seventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
A description of Cyavana’s efforts to secure for the Aśvins the right to drink the Soma;
Janamejaya said:
"How did Cyavana make those two physicians drinkers of the Soma?"
And how did the word of that great-souled one become true?
"What is the strength of a human compared to the strength of the King of the Gods?
Those two physicians, who were drinkers of the Soma juice, were forbidden by him. (2)
O Lord, you who are established in Dharma, tell me that wonder in detail;
I am desirous of hearing the life-story of Cyavana today in every respect.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O great king, to the most wonderful account of Cyavana at that sacrifice of Śaryāti on earth, O Bhārata.
Having obtained the beautiful Sukanyā, Cyavana, resembling a celestial being,
sported with a tranquil soul like another god with a divine maiden.
Then once, the beloved wife of Śaryāti, being deeply distressed with anxiety,
spoke these words to her husband while trembling and weeping.
"O King, your daughter was given by you to a blind sage in the forest;
whether she is dead or alive, she must certainly be seen by you."
"Go, O Lord, to the hermitage of the sage with respect to see him;
what will that Sukanyā do now that she has obtained such a husband? (8)
"O royal sage, I am utterly consumed in my heart by grief for my daughter;
bring that large-eyed girl, emaciated by her ascetic penances, into my presence."
I see my daughter in every respect as one with emaciated limbs, clad in bark garments;
having obtained a blind husband, that slender-waisted woman is now a partaker of sorrow.
Śaryāti said:
"O large-eyed one, O lady of beautiful hips, let us go today with reverence to see Sukanyā,
the beloved daughter of that sage who is firm in his vows."
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to the woman who was overwhelmed with grief, Śaryāti mounted his chariot and departed quickly for the hermitage of the sage.
Having gone near the hermitage, the lord of the earth beheld that sage,
endowed with fresh youth and resembling a son of the gods.
Beholding him with the form of an immortal, the king was struck with amazement:
"What despicable deed, censured by the world, has been committed by my daughter? (14)
That aged sage has been slain by her, and another husband—though utterly tranquil and exceedingly poor—has been chosen at will by her, afflicted as she was by passion. (15)
This flower-bowed god (Kāma) is difficult to withstand, especially during youth;
by her, a very great stain has been cast upon the human race. (16)
Fie upon the life in this world of him whose daughter is indeed contemptible;
for a daughter leads to suffering for embodied beings through all manner of evils. (17)
I have indeed committed an improper act for the sake of achieving my own purpose;
for I gave away my daughter with all my heart to one who is old and blind. (18)
"A daughter must indeed be given by her father to a worthy suitor with his whole heart;
for such a fruit has been obtained as was surely sown by me. (19)
If I were to kill my daughter today—she who is ill-behaved and a doer of evil—the sin of killing a woman would be difficult for me to overcome, especially since she is my own daughter. (20)
The renowned lineage of Manu has been defiled by me;
public scandal is powerful, and the chain of affection is difficult to cast off. (21)
When that king was submerged in an ocean of anxiety, wondering "What shall I do?",
his father, overwhelmed with worry, was by chance seen by Sukanyā.
Having seen him, Sukanyā went quickly to her father;
having arrived, she questioned the king with a heart overflowing with love. (23)
"O King, why do you reflect with a face agitated by anxiety upon seeing this young, lotus-eyed sage seated here? (24)
"Come, come, O tiger among men! Pay homage to my husband.
Do not give way to despair now, O best of kings, O man! (25)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his daughter, Śaryāti, afflicted by anger,
then spoke these words to his daughter standing before him.
The king said:
"O daughter, where is the sage Cyavana, the aged, blind, and most excellent ascetic?
Who is this youth intoxicated with pride? I have a great doubt in this matter. (27)
"O sinful woman, perpetrator of evil deeds, why was the sage slain by you? O destroyer of your lineage, this husband was chosen out of lust as if he were a mere newcomer. (28)
Thus, afflicted with anxiety, I do not see him staying in the hermitage;
what evil deed has been committed, that which is indeed the conduct of an unchaste woman? (29)
"I am now submerged in an ocean of grief caused by you because of my wicked conduct, having seen this divine person and not having seen the sage Cyavana. (30)
Having heard her father's words, she laughed and quickly spoke to him;
then, taking her father with her, she respectfully brought him into the presence of her husband.
O dear one, that sage Cyavana is undoubtedly your son-in-law;
he has been made so beautiful and lotus-eyed by the two Aśvins.
When the two Nāsatyas arrived here at my hermitage by chance, they surely restored Cyavana to such a state out of compassion. (33)
"I am not your daughter, O father; I would not be such an evildoer as you imagine me to be, O King, deluded by the uncertainty of outward appearance. (34)
"O King, O father, bow down to the sage Cyavana of Bhrigu's lineage;
inquire of him the entire reason, and he will explain it to you in detail. (35)
Having heard these words of his daughter, Śaryāti then went there in haste,
prostrated before the sage, and questioned him with reverence.
The king said:
O Bhārgava, tell me quickly and appropriately your own history;
how were your eyes restored, and where did your old age go again? (37)
"A great doubt has arisen in me upon seeing this exceedingly beautiful form;
O Brahman, tell me in detail, for by hearing it I shall attain happiness. (38)
Cyavana said: "O best of kings, both the Nāsatyas, the physicians of the gods, have arrived here; they have rendered assistance out of compassion. (39)
I have granted a boon to those two for the sake of their service:
"In the sacrifice of the king, you both shall become drinkers of the Soma juice. (40)
"In this way I have attained youth, and likewise my eyes are clear;
be at ease, O Great King, and sit upon this auspicious throne. (41)
Thus addressed by the brahmin, that lord of the earth, together with his wife,
sat down comfortably and engaged in auspicious conversation with the high-souled sage.
Then, consoling that king, he said to the descendant of Bhṛgu:
"O King, I shall perform the sacrifice for you; prepare the necessary materials."
"I have promised them that you two shall be made drinkers of the Soma;
therefore, O best of kings, this must be done by you at your very extensive sacrifice. (44)
"I shall indeed restrain the enraged Indra by means of my own splendor and strength;
O King of kings, I shall cause you to drink the Soma at your Soma sacrifice. (45)
Thereupon, O great king, Śaryāti, the lord of the earth, being exceedingly gratified, honored those words of Cyavana.
Having honored Cyavana, the king,
together with his wife and exceedingly delighted, returned toward the city while conversing about the sage.
On an auspicious day suitable for sacrifice, Śaryāti, possessing the fulfillment of all desires,
had an excellent sacrificial ground constructed.
Having brought together the venerable sages headed by Vasiṣṭha,
Cyavana, the descendant of Bhṛgu, caused that lord of the earth to perform the sacrifice.
When that sacrifice had been spread out, all the gods together with Indra arrived there, and the two Aśvins also came to attend for the sake of the Soma. || 50 ||
Indra, however, became apprehensive upon seeing those two Aśvins there; he questioned all the gods, "Why have these two arrived? (51)
During the king’s extensive sacrifice, the immortals did not say there, "O King, why have these two physicians, who are unworthy of the Soma, been brought here?"
Then Cyavana took the Soma for the two divine Aśvins;
Śakra tried to stop him, saying, "Do not take the draught for these two! (53)
There Cyavana said to him: "O Lord of Śacī, tell me the truth: why are these two sons of Ravi, the Nāsatyas, not worthy of being planets?"
The son and the lawful wife of the Sun were not born of a mixed union;
by what fault, O Lord of the Gods, are these two excellent physicians unworthy of the Soma? (55)
"O Śakra, a decision must be made here at this sacrifice by all the deities.
I shall cause Soma to be accepted [as the victim], so that those two shall become drinkers of Soma through my act. (56)
"O Maghavan, that king has indeed been impelled by me for the sake of a sacrifice;
for this purpose I shall act, O Lord—my word is true. (57)
O Śakra, they have assisted me and likewise granted me new youth;
therefore, I must by all means perform a return service for them.
Indra said:
"These two Nāsatyas have been made physicians and are censured by the gods;
neither of these two is worthy of the Soma—do not take a draught for them. (59)
Cyavana said:
"O paramour of Ahalyā, restrain your anger today, for it is useless.
O slayer of Vṛtra, are the two Aśvins, the sons of the gods, not worthy of the Soma?"
When the dispute had thus arisen,
O King, no one spoke a word to him; then Bhārgava, possessing the brilliance of a fierce flame, addressed those two.
He caused it to be gathered together by the power of his asceticism.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Efforts of Cyavana and the Aśvins for the Purpose of Attaining the Right to Drink Soma," in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Revata’s Journey to the World of Brahmā for the Sake of Obtaining a Wife from Revatī;
Vyāsa said: O Indra among kings, when the planet had been given away, Vāsava became exceedingly enraged.
There he spoke to Cyavana, demonstrating his own power.
"O wretched Brahmin, you ought not to transgress this boundary!
I shall slay you, my enemy, like another Viśvarūpa. (2)
Cyavana said:
"O Maghavan, do not despise these two high-souled ones on account of their beauty, wealth, or splendor,
for they have made me like another celestial being."
"O Lord of the Gods, how could any other deities accept the offering except for you?
Know that even the two Aśvins are gods, O scorcher of foes. (4)
Indra said:
"The two physicians do not deserve to receive a portion of the sacrifice at all.
If you wish to give it, O dull-witted one, I shall cut off your head this very moment. (5)
Vyāsa said:
But disregarding those words of Vāsava, the descendant of Bhṛgu seized the planet, as if severely rebuking him.
When the two of them had taken up the soma vessel out of thirst,
the god Indra, the slayer of Bala, observed this and spoke these words.
If you yourself cause Soma to be seized for this purpose,
I shall strike you with my thunderbolt, as if against another Viśvarūpa.
Thus addressed by Vāsava, the exceedingly arrogant Bhārgava,
filled with great indignation, duly received the Soma from the Aśvins.
Indra also, out of anger, hurled at him his own weapon, the thunderbolt,
which possessed a brilliance equal to ten million suns, while all the gods looked on.
Then, beholding the thunderbolt hurled [at him], Cyavana, by means of his ascetic power,
paralyzed the vajra of Śakra, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
With that magical spell, the mighty-armed one, the best of sages, prepared here to slay Indra; he offered the famous oblation into the fire with the mantra.
There, by the power of Cyavana’s asceticism, a *kṛtyā* was produced—
a powerful, cruel, and massive-bodied great asura.
In this world, intoxication is indeed a most terrible and fearsome thing for living beings;
within the body, it is like a mountain, possessing sharp fangs and being utterly terrifying.
His four long fangs were each a hundred yojanas in length,
while his other teeth were ten yojanas long.
His two arms were as massive as mountains, long, and fierce in appearance;
his tongue was terrifying and cruel, licking the very sky.
Her neck was like a mountain peak, hard and extremely terrifying;
her claws resembled those of a tiger, and her hair was exceedingly fearsome. (17)
His body was the color of collyrium, and his face was terrifying;
his two eyes were like forest fires—frightening and exceedingly fearsome.
One jaw of his remained on the earth and one went to heaven;
such was the great-bodied being named Mada who was thus born.
Upon seeing him, all the gods were suddenly seized by fear;
even Indra, trembling with terror, set his mind not upon battle.
The Daitya also stood with his mouth wide open, holding the thunderbolt;
with a terrible gaze, he seemed to devour the three worlds as the sky was filled [with his form].
Desiring to devour him, he rushed furiously toward Śatakratu;
and all the gods, standing there, cried out, "Alas! We are destroyed! (22)
But Indra, his arm paralyzed, though desiring to release the thunderbolt from his side,
was unable to hurl the weapon at him, O subduer of Pāka.
Seeing him who resembled Time (Death) himself, the Lord of the Gods, Vajrahasta,
remembered there in his mind his preceptor, who was well-versed in the sacred commitments (samaya).
Upon being remembered, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati arrived quickly;
the preceptor, seeing that great occasion which resembled a calamity.
Having reflected upon the matter with his mind, he said to the Lord of Śacī: "O Vāsava, this one cannot be overcome by great mantras; he must be struck down by you with the thunderbolt. (26)
The Asura named Mada, possessed of great strength through the power of the sage Cyavana’s asceticism, emerged from the sacrificial pit. (27)
"For this enemy is indeed unavoidable by you, by the gods, or likewise by me;
O Lord of Gods, seek refuge with the high-souled Cyavana. (28)
He will surely ward off the magical spell (kṛtyā) wrought by himself;
for those devoted to Śakti are never able to restrain the wrath of Śakti.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by his preceptor, Śakra then approached the sage;
bowing with his head bent low, he spoke to him while filled with fear.
Forgive me, O tiger among sages; pacify the Asura who has risen up. Be gracious, O Omniscient One; I shall do as you command.
"O Bhārgava, from this day forward these two Aśvins shall be worthy of the Soma;
O Brahmin, this word is true, be gracious unto me. (32)
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, this effort of yours is indeed in vain;
yet I know, O knower of dharma, that you will not act in vain. (33)
"These two Aśvins, the drinkers of Soma, shall indeed always be created by you;
and the fame of Śaryāti shall become vast. (34)
O best of sages, whatever deed has been performed by me in every way should be understood as being for the sake of testing you and for the manifestation of your prowess. (35)
O Brahmin, show me favor; restrain this arrogance that has arisen.
Let what is auspicious for all the gods be further established once more.
Thus addressed by Śakra, Cyavana, the knower of the supreme truth,
withdrew his ascetic power and the anger that had arisen from the conflict.
Then Bhārgava, having consoled the distressed Deva,
divided his pride among women, drink, gambling, and hunting.
Having dispelled the pride of the Lord of the Gods, consoled him who was terrified with fear,
and restored all the deities to their places, he brought that sacrifice to a halt.
Then the Bhārgava, whose very soul was dharma, caused the consecrated Soma to be drunk by the high-souled Vāsava and the two Aśvins.
Thus, O King, by the power of his asceticism, Cyavana ordained that those two noble Aśvins, the sons of the Sun, should become drinkers of the Soma juice in every respect.
That lake also became famous, adorned with sacrificial posts;
and the hermitage of the sage became renowned throughout the entire earth.
Śaryāti also became highly satisfied with that deed;
having completed the sacrifice, he returned to his city surrounded by his ministers. || 43 ||
The powerful son of Manu, who knew the dharma, ruled the kingdom.
Ānarta was his son, and from Ānarta, Revata was born.
Having constructed the city of Kuśasthalī within the inner ocean,
that subduer of enemies took up residence there and enjoyed the territories of Ānarta and other regions.
To him were born a hundred sons, with Kakudmin as the eldest and most excellent;
and a daughter named Revatī, who was beautiful and possessed of auspicious marks.
When she had become fit for choosing a husband, King Revata,
the lord of kings, then reflected upon princes born of noble lineage.
And having taken refuge on the mountain named Raivata, that powerful lord of men, the ruler of the earth, governed the kingdom among the Ānartas. || 48 ||
Having reflected thus in his mind, the king thought: "To whom should my daughter be given?
I shall go and ask Brahmā, the omniscient one who is worshipped by the gods. (49)
Having reflected thus, the protector of the earth took his daughter Revatī and went quickly to the world of Brahmā, desiring to question the Grandfather.
Wherein the gods and sacrifices, as well as the meters and mountains, the oceans, and the Siddhas and Gandharvas assuming divine forms, are stationed. || 51 ||
The sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Pannagas, and Cāraṇas likewise—
all those ancient ones— stood with palms joined in reverence, offering hymns of praise.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Revata’s Journey to the World of Brahmā for the Sake of a Boon from Revatī," in the seventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Ikṣvāku Lineage.
Janamejaya said: "O Brahmin, this great doubt exists within my mind."
The king himself, accompanied by Revatī, went to the world of Brahmā.
Formerly, I heard this entirely from Brahmins during the course of a conversation:
"A Brahmin who knows Brahman and is tranquil shall attain the world of Brahman. (2)
How did the king himself, accompanied by Revatī, go from the world of mortals (bhūrloka) to that Satyaloka which is so difficult to attain? This is my doubt. (3)
"One who has died attains heaven; this is the conclusion in all the scriptures.
But how can there be a journey to the world of Brahmā with a human body?
And how does one’s transition from heaven lead to birth again in the world of men? (4)
O learned one, you ought to sever this doubt of mine now,
as to how the king went there desiring to question Prajāpati.
Vyāsa said: O King, upon the summit of Meru all the worlds are established—
the world of Indra, the world of Agni, and the city of Saṃyaminī.
In the same way, Satyaloka and Kailāsa likewise exist there;
furthermore, Vaikuṇṭha is also there, which is called the station of Viṣṇu.
Just as Arjuna, the son of Pṛthā and wielder of the bow, went to the world of Śakra;
there, the son of Kuntī remained for five years in that abode of the gods.
Indeed, with his very human body, he stood in the presence of Vāsava;
likewise, other kings as well, headed by Kakutstha, were there.
Afterwards, the exceedingly powerful Daityas also went to the world of the gods;
having conquered Indra’s abode, they remained there according to their desire.
In ancient times, King Mahābhiṣa, a self-ruling sovereign, went to the world of Brahmā;
there, the king beheld the most beautiful Gaṅgā as she was approaching.
"O King, her garment was carried away by the wind through fate;
then, while she was thus somewhat naked, that beautiful woman was seen by the king. (12)
Afflicted by desire, he smiled, and she indeed laughed slightly;
then, seen by Brahmā, the two were cursed and born upon the earth.
Even in Vaikuṇṭha, all the gods were oppressed by the Daityas and Dānavas;
they went to Hari, the Lord of the Universe and husband of Kamalā, and offered him praise.
No doubt should be entertained here in any way, O best of kings;
all worlds are accessible to human beings, O lord of men. (15)
"O lord of men, for ascetics who have certainly performed meritorious deeds, it is the very presence of their merit alone that is the cause for going there, O King. (16)
In the same way, for those sacrificers whose souls were purified by sacrifice—Janamejaya said:
"Reva took the daughter Revatī, who possessed beautiful eyes. (17)
After he had gone to the world of Brahmā, what did that king do?
What was commanded by Brahmā, and to whom was his daughter given? (18)
"O Brāhmaṇa, relate all of that to me now in detail.
Vyāsa said: "Listen, O protector of the earth; it is said that there was once a king named Revataka."
When he had gone to the world of Brahmā to inquire about his daughter’s husband,
he remained for a moment in the celestial music, having found an opportunity.
Listening with a joyful heart in the assembly along with his daughter, he was not satiated;
and when the musical performance there had concluded, he bowed down to the Supreme Lord.
Having shown him his daughter, he declared his own intention.
The king said:
"O Lord of Gods, choose a boon; this girl is my daughter. (22)
"To whom should it be given by me, O Brahmin? It is for this reason that I have come to question you. I have observed many princes of noble birth. (23)
My fickle mind does not find satisfaction in anything;
therefore, O Lord of the gods, I have come here to question you. (23)
Therefore, O Omniscient One, command a suitable bridegroom for the prince—one who is of noble birth, powerful, and endowed with all auspicious marks. || 25 ||
"Instruct the prince, who is a giver and of virtuous character.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the king, the Creator of the World [then spoke].
Seeing the reversal of time, Brahmā spoke these words to him with a smile: "O King, those boons which you have held in your heart, O Prince... (27)
All of them, along with their fathers, grandsons, and kinsmen, have been swallowed by Time;
today itself is the twenty-seventh [cycle], and the Dvāpara age has begun.
All those born of that lineage have died, and the city has been plundered by the Daityas;
indeed, a king born of the Lunar dynasty now rules there. (29)
It is said that there was a king known as Ugrasena, the lord of Mathurā,
born in the lineage of Yayāti, who ruled over the region of Mathurā.
Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena, a hater of the gods and possessed of great strength,
being a portion of a Daitya, even he cast his father into prison.
Intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty over kings, he himself ruled the kingdom;
and the Earth, oppressed by an excessive burden, went for refuge to Brahmā.
Overwhelmed by the burden of the army of wicked kṣatriyas,
the best of the gods declared that an incarnation of a portion [of themselves] must take place there.
Vāsudeva, the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa,
who is that sage Nārāyaṇa, was born from Devakī, who possessed a divine form.
The eternal son of Dharma performed difficult penance on the sacred bank of the Gaṅgā at Badarikāśrama, accompanied by Nara. (35)
Having descended into the Yadu clan, he is renowned as Vāsudeva;
by him, O best of beings, that sinful Kaṃsa was slain by Kṛṣṇa.
Having slain his wicked son, the kingdom was indeed given to Ugrasena; meanwhile, Kaṃsa’s father-in-law, the sinful and mighty Jarāsandha, [remained a threat]. || 37 ||
Having arrived at Mathurā, that mighty Jarāsaṃdha joyfully engaged in battle out of anger; however, he was defeated by Kṛṣṇa in the conflict.
Then he dispatched the Yavana king with his army for battle;
having heard that the great hero, the lord of the Yavanas, was approaching with his forces. (39)
Kṛṣṇa, however, having abandoned Mathurā, went to the city of Dvāravatī;
Kṛṣṇa, together with assembled artisans, [reconstructed] that city which had been destroyed.
The powerful Vāsudeva, having first carried out the restoration of the dilapidated city, caused it to be made rich with fortifications and adorned with marketplaces and workshops;
he also brought King Ugrasena under his control.
The best of the Yadus established the Yādavas in Dvāravatī;
Vāsudeva, however, remains there even today together with his kinsmen.
Before her stands that renowned Baladeva, the wielder of the plow, the heroic Śeṣa incarnate who bears the club; let him be your chosen husband according to your preference. (41)
Then, quickly bestow the lotus-eyed maiden Revatī upon Saṅkarṣaṇa, that is, Balabhadra, according to the rites of marriage.
O best of kings, having given away your daughter, go to Badarikāśrama to perform penance in that holy place, which delights the gods and grants the desires of men. (43)
Vyāsa said:
Thus commanded by Brahmā, the lotus-born one, O King,
the monarch departed swiftly for Dvārakā accompanied by his daughter.
He gave that maiden, endowed with auspicious marks, to Baladeva;
thereafter, at the turn of time, the king performed intense penance.
Having abandoned his body on the riverbank, he went to the abode of the thirty gods.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, a great marvel has been recounted by you. (46)
But Revata remained there in the world of Brahmā for the sake of his son;
indeed, one hundred and eight yugas passed there.
The maiden has not grown old, nor has the king;
how indeed could their lifespan have been so fully exhausted for such a long time? (48)
Vyāsa said: O sinless one, neither old age nor hunger, nor thirst, nor death, nor fear, nor even exhaustion ever prevails in the world of Brahmā.
The progeny of Śaryāti, having gone to Mount Meru, were slaughtered by Rākṣasas;
terrified by fear, they abandoned Kuśasthalī and fled hither and thither.
And as Manu was yawning, a son of even greater vigor was born;
he became renowned as Ikṣvāku, the founder of the Solar dynasty.
For the sake of his lineage, having received the unsurpassed initiation through the instruction of Nārada, he performed penance while meditating on the Goddess incessantly.
O King, Ikṣvāku was renowned for having a hundred sons;
among them, Vikukṣi was the first, endowed with strength and valor.
In Ayodhyā there dwelt a king renowned as Ikṣvāku;
he had fifty sons, the most powerful of whom were headed by Śakuni. (54)
O King, it is said that those sons of his were appointed by him as the protectors of the northern region, and likewise, they were assigned to the southern region.
Forty-eight [attendants] were stationed by the high-souled one for the sake of protection, while two others stood at his sides for the service of that king. (56)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ikṣvāku Dynasty," in the seventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The description of the birth of Māndhātṛ.
Vyāsa said:
Once, at an Aṣṭakā Śrāddha ceremony, the lord of the earth [Yayāti] addressed Vikukṣi.
The undeluded one commanded: "Bring meat quickly! || 1 ||

Having been respectfully told by Sūta, "Go now to the forest for the sake of sacrificial materials suitable for the śrāddha," that wielder of weapons replied, "So be it," and quickly departed for the forest.
Having gone there, he killed boars, wild pigs, deer, and even rabbits with his arrows;
then, becoming exhausted, he grew hungry.
He forgot the Aṣṭakā festival and gave the rabbit to him in the forest;
he then offered the remaining excellent meat to his father.
Then, seeing the meat brought for sprinkling, the preceptor,
that best of sages, realized it was unfit and became enraged.
"It is the established rule that what remains from a meal should not be sprinkled with water in a *śrāddha* ceremony.
Thus Vasiṣṭha informed the king of the defect in the cooking.
Having learned from his preceptor that such was the deed of his son, the king became enraged due to the violation of the sacred law and banished him from the country.
The son of the king, born with the name Śaśāda, became renowned as Śaśāda; however, due to his father's anger, he went to the forest without any agitation.
Devoted to righteousness, he spent his time subsisting on forest produce;
when his father passed away, that high-souled one obtained the kingdom.
Śaśāda himself ruled as the sovereign of Ayodhyā;
on the banks of the Sarayū, he performed numerous complete sacrifices.
Śaśāda had a son renowned as Kakutstha;
indeed, due to his various names, he was also known as Indravāha and Purañjaya. (11)
Janamejaya said:
O sinless one, how did the change of name of the prince come about?
Tell me the entire cause and by what action it occurred.
Vyāsa said: When Śaśāda had gone to heaven, there was a king named Kakutstha;
that knower of dharma ruled his ancestral kingdom by means of his strength.
In the meantime, all the gods were defeated by the Daityas.
They went for refuge to Viṣṇu, the imperishable lord of the three worlds;
then the eternal Mahāviṣṇu spoke to those gods.
Viṣṇu said:
"O best of gods, let them entreat the king born of Śaśāda to become their rear-guard;
he will indeed slay the Daityas in battle."
The righteous Dhanurdhara will come for the sake of assistance;
by the grace of Parāśakti, his power is incomparable.
At the well-spoken words of Hari, all the gods, including Indra,
went to Ayodhyā, O great king, toward the son of Śaśāda.
The king honored those gods who had arrived according to dharma;
unwearied, he asked them the purpose of their coming.
The king said:
"I am blessed and I am purified; my life has become fruitful, since the gods have come to my home and granted me their great vision. (19)
"O lords of the gods, speak your task; even if it be difficult for humans to accomplish, I shall perform this great work, which is in every way significant for you."
The gods said:
"O Indra among kings, grant us your assistance; become the friend of the Lord of Śacī.
In battle, conquer the lords of the Daityas, who are difficult to defeat even for the thirty gods."
By the grace of the Supreme Power (Parā-Śakti), there is nothing whatsoever that is difficult for you to attain;
impelled by Viṣṇu, we have thus come into your presence. (22)
The king said:
"O best of gods, I shall today become the rear-guard of the gods, provided that Indra, the lord of the deities, becomes my vehicle there. (23)
"I shall now wage war against the Daityas for the sake of the gods;
having mounted Indra, I shall go—this I tell you truly. (24)
Then the gods said to Vāsava: "An extraordinary task must be performed;
O Lord of Śacī, casting aside shame, become the leaf of the king. (25)
Then Śakra, greatly urged by Hari and feeling ashamed,
quickly became a bull, like another great bull of Rudra.
That king indeed mounted him in order to go to battle;
because he stood upon his hump (kakuda), he therefore became known as Kakutstha.
Because he was made the vehicle (vāha) of Indra by that name, he became Indravāhaka;
and because he conquered the city of the Daityas, he became Purañjaya. || 28 ||
Having conquered the Daityas, the mighty-armed one bestowed their wealth upon them;
and having thus questioned the royal sage, a friendship indeed arose between them. (29)
And Kakutstha was a most renowned king; those born of his lineage became the Kākutsthas, kings on earth who were highly celebrated. (30)
Kakutstha had a son of great strength born of his lawful wife;
he was known as Anenas, and his son was the heroic Pṛthu.
He is known as a direct portion (aṃśa) of Viṣṇu and a worshiper of the feet of Parāśakti;
he is to be understood as Viśvarandhi, the son of Pṛthu and lord of men. || 32 ||
His son was the illustrious Candra, remembered as the king who continued the lineage;
his son was Yuvanāśva, radiant and exceedingly powerful.
Śāvanta, the most righteous, was born of Yuvanāśva;
by him the city of Śāvantī was built, which was equal to the city of Śakra.
Bṛhadaśva was the son of the high-souled Śāvant;
his son was Kuvalayāśva, who became a lord of the earth.
The Daitya named Dhundhu was slain by him on the surface of the earth;
consequently, he acquired the highly renowned name "Dhundhumāra. (36)
His son was Dṛḍhāśva, who protected the earth;
the illustrious son of Dṛḍhāśva is celebrated as Haryaśva. (37)
His son was said to be Nikumbha, who became a lord of the earth;
Barhaṇāśva was the son of Nikumbha, and Kuśāśva was indeed his son.
The powerful Prasenajit was the son of Kṛśāśva, whose valor was truth;
his illustrious son was renowned as Yauvanāśva. (39)
The illustrious son of Yuvanāśva, King Māndhātṛ,
was the lord of the earth by whom one thousand and eight palaces were constructed.
O giver of honor, for the sake of pleasing the Blessed Lady,
he was not born from a mother’s womb, but was produced from the belly of Janaka at great sacred fords.
Then the son emerged, having pierced the belly of his father once more.
The king said:
"Has this which you have described never been heard or seen by you? (42)
"O highly fortunate one, the birth of him as it has been described is inconceivable;
tell me today in detail the cause of Māndhātṛ’s birth. (43)
"Just as a son, beautiful in all his limbs, was born from the belly of a king," Vyāsa said: "King Yauvanāśva, who was supremely righteous, was childless. (44)
O King, that monarch had a hundred wives;
the king was consumed by anxiety and reflected constantly upon it. (45)
For the sake of offspring, the sorrowful Yauvanāśva went to the forest;
and that king, despondent, stayed in a holy hermitage of sages. (46)
Distressed, he let out sighs while the ascetics looked on;
and seeing him so sorrowful, O brahmins, they were moved with compassion. (47)
The brahmins said to him: "O King, O ruler of the earth, why do you grieve?
What is your sorrow, O great king? Tell us truly what is in your mind. (48)
"We shall provide every kind of remedy for your suffering.
Yauvanāśva said:
"O sages, my kingdom, wealth, and excellent horses are at your disposal. (49)
I have a hundred pure wives of radiant luster;
moreover, there is no man at all in the three worlds who is more powerful than I. (50)
The vassal lords and likewise the ministers carry out my commands;
O ascetics, I see no other suffering than that which arises from progeny. (51)
"For one without a son there is no destination, neither heaven nor even [the absence of hell].
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, I grieve intensely for the sake of offspring. (52)
May the ascetics, who have mastered the true meaning of the Vedas and Shastras and have exerted themselves in their practice,
examine the sacrifice intended for one desiring progeny and ordain it for me.
"O ascetics, if you have compassion, please perform my task.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the king, their hearts were filled with pity.
Without distraction, they caused the sacrifice dedicated to Indra to be performed;
a water-filled pitcher was then established there by the Brāhmaṇas.
Consecrated with Vedic mantras for the sake of that king’s son,
the king entered the sacrificial hall at night, feeling thirsty.
Seeing the Brahmins lying down, he himself drank the consecrated water that had been prepared by the Brahmins for his wife, sanctified with mantras and drawn out according to the prescribed rite.
O best of kings, the king, afflicted by thirst, drank from it out of ignorance;
seeing that the pitcher was empty of water, O brahmins, they were then filled with apprehension.
Those twice-born ones asked the king, "By whom has the water been drunk?
Having learned that it had been drunk by the king, they recognized the great power of destiny.
Having completed the sacrifice, those sages returned to their homes;
then, by the power of the mantras, the king conceived a child.
Then, in due time, having burst through his right side, he emerged as a son; the ministers of that king brought him forth.
By the grace of the gods, the lord of the earth did not die there;
"Whom shall this prince suck? the ministers cried out intensely. (62)
Then Indra gave him a finger and spoke these words: "Suckle me.
He became the powerful King Māndhātṛ, the lord of the earth. O protector of the land, his birth has thus been recounted to you in detail.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Māndhātṛ," in the seventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Narrative of Satyavrata. Vyāsa said:
That king, true to his promise, became a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Māndhātā, the lord of kings, conquered the entire earth. ||1||
Terrified by fear of him, the Dasyus fled into mountain caves.
Indra clearly bestowed upon him the name Trasadasyu.
His wife was Bindumatī, the daughter of Śaśabindu.
She was devoted to her husband, beautiful, and endowed with all auspicious marks.
In her, O King, Māndhātṛ begot two sons.
Purukutsa, who was well-renowned, and likewise another, Mucukunda.
From Purukutsa was born a son named Araṇya, who was supremely righteous.
And his son was Bṛhadaśva, who was devoted to filial piety. || 5 ||
His son was Haryaśva, who was righteous and a knower of the supreme truth.
His son was Tridhanvan, and Aruṇa was his son.
The illustrious son of Aruṇa was known as Satyavrata.
He became a self-willed wanderer, lustful, dull-witted, and exceedingly greedy.
That evil-souled man, deluded by lust, abducted the wife of the brahmin.
That son of the king created an obstacle to his marriage.
O King, the Brahmins gathered there [approached] King Aruṇa.
Afflicted by intense sorrow, they cried out repeatedly, "Alas! We are destroyed! (9)
The king questioned those distressed brahmins who were residents of the city.
"O brahmins, what inauspicious thing has been done by my son to you?"
Having heard those words of the king, which were preceded by humility, the twice-born ones—
Then the brahmins, having pronounced their blessings, spoke very earnestly to Aruṇa.
The Brahmins said:
O King, it is said that today at your son's wedding, she was indeed struck.
O best among the strong, you have forcibly abducted the daughter of a Brahmin who was already married.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard their truthful words, the most righteous king—
He said to his son: "In vain has your name been given by you of wicked deeds."
Go far away from my house, O dull-witted one of wicked conduct!
O wicked one, you must not remain in my domain under any circumstances.
He spoke repeatedly to his angry father, saying, "Where shall I go?"
Then Aruṇa said to him: "Live together with the dog-cookers (outcastes)."
The act committed by the outcaste was the abduction of the twice-born man’s wife.
Therefore, having formed an association with them, remain as you please.
For one desiring a son does not find it through a son such as you, who brings disgrace to the family.
Go wherever you wish, O evil-minded one; you have brought about the destruction of Kīta.
Having heard the words of his father, the high-souled one who was filled with anger, he [acted].
He departed swiftly from that city and went toward the Śvapacas.
At that time, Satyavrata lived there together with the outcaste dog-cookers (śvapākas).
The glorious one, bearing a bow and arrows, clad in armor, was an abode of compassion. || 19 ||
When he was expelled by his father, the high-souled one who was filled with wrath.
Then that lord of the earth was urged by his preceptor Vasiṣṭha.
Therefore, being devoted to the vow of truth, he became filled with anger toward him.
While Vasiṣṭha, the knower of the treatises on dharma, remained averse to offering any restraint. || 21 ||
Then, for a certain reason, his father, the lord of the earth, [acted].
For the sake of a son, he abandoned the city and went to the forest to perform austerities.
At that time, the subduer of Pāka did not send rain upon that region.
O Indra among kings, for twelve years he was entirely deprived of his kingdom because of that unrighteousness.
Then, O King, Viśvāmitra [left] his wife in that region.
Having renounced all worldly ties, he performed extensive austerities on the banks of the Kauśikī.
The wife of Kauśika indeed became terrified there.
For the sake of supporting her family, the woman of excellent complexion was distressed.
She beheld the children, overcome by hunger, weeping bitterly.
And though she begged for wild grains (nīvāra), that devoted wife fell into great distress.
Afflicted with grief, she reflected as she beheld her children tormented by hunger.
"The king is indeed not in the city today; whom shall I beg, or what shall I do? (27)
I have no protector for my sons, nor is my husband present here with me.
The children are weeping as much as they wish; fie upon my life today indeed! (28)
Deprived of wealth, my husband has abandoned me and gone away to perform austerities.
Though capable, he does not recognize her as one who is suffering and destitute of wealth. || 29 ||
Without my husband, by what means shall I provide for my children?
All my sons will die, severely afflicted by hunger.
But having sold even one son for some amount of wealth, [one may perform it] again.
I protect my other sons; this is the duty ordained for me. || 31 ||
The killing of all [beings] is certainly not appropriate for me in this reversal of circumstances.
For the sake of calculating time, I likewise sell my own son.
Having made her heart hard and having reflected thus in her mind, the virtuous woman [spoke].
Then, bound by a cord of darbha grass around her neck, she emerged with her son.
The sage’s wife, having tied her own middle biological son around her neck, said:
Having taken [the child] for the sake of supporting the remainder [of the family], she departed from her home. || 34 ||
Satyavrata beheld the distressed female ascetic, overwhelmed with grief.
The king, however, asked her: "O beautiful one, what do you wish to do? (35)
Whom are you leading now, having bound this weeping child to your neck?
And for what purpose, O lady of beautiful limbs, tell me the truth before me.
The wife of the sage said:
"I am the wife of Viśvāmitra, and this is my son, O prince."
I shall go, if I so desire, to sell my own legitimate son on this difficult path.
"O King, there is no food anywhere; my husband has gone out somewhere and has not yet returned."
"I am selling it, being afflicted by hunger, indeed for the sake of maintaining my remaining family. (38)
The king said:
"O devoted wife, protect your son; I shall provide for your maintenance."
At that very moment, your husband will return here from the forest. || 39 ||
In the tree near your hermitage, there is food constantly available.
Having bound him, I shall depart; I tell you this as the truth.
Thus addressed at that time by the king, she who was the beloved of Kauśika—
Having created an obstruction for that [enemy], he went to the circle of hermitages.
Due to his throat-tumor, that great ascetic became known by the name Gālava.
Having returned to her own hermitage, she rejoiced, surrounded by children.
But Satyavrata was overwhelmed with devotion and compassion.
And she bore that embryo for the sage Viśvāmitra.
Having slain deer, boars, and likewise buffaloes dwelling in the forest.
Near the forest of Viśvāmitra, he indeed tied the meat to a tree.
Then the wife of the sage took that flesh and gave it to her sons.
Having obtained that unsurpassed food, he attained supreme liberation.
The sage [renounced] Ayodhyā itself, as well as the kingdom and likewise the inner apartments.
When that king had departed to perform penance, Vasiṣṭha protected [the city]. || 46 ||
Satyavrata, whose soul was devoted to righteousness, remained outside the city.
Abiding by his father’s command, he lived in the forest observing the vow of a butcher.
For King Satyavrata, indeed, did so without cause and for no reason whatsoever.
And he constantly harbored even greater wrath toward Vasiṣṭha.
His most righteous and beloved son was being abandoned in the forest by his father.
The sage Vasiṣṭha did not prevent him, for a certain reason.
The completion of the marriage mantras occurs at the seventh step.
Although he was aware of this, that righteous-souled one [proceeded] with the taking of the brahmin's wife.
On a certain day in the forest, the lord of the earth [observed] the absence of deer.
And he saw Vasiṣṭha’s milch-cow in the middle of the forest.
He struck her like a bandit, out of anger and delusion, as he was tormented by hunger.
Having taken that flesh, he tied it to a tree and ate it himself. || 52 ||
Then the noble Ṛṣiṣeṇa fed all his sons at that time.
Suspecting it was a deer and not a cow, she of virtuous vows [remained there].
But Vasiṣṭha, knowing that the milch-cow had been killed, spoke to him in anger:
O evil-souled one, what sin have you committed by killing a cow, like a piśāca? (54)
In this way, let those three cruel spikes fall swiftly upon you.
Due to the killing of a cow, the seizing of food, and likewise because of his father's intense anger. || 55 ||
"You shall indeed become renowned on earth by the name Triśaṅku."
Manifesting himself in the form of a Piśāca to all embodied beings.
Vyāsa said:
Thus was King Satyavrata cursed by Vasiṣṭha at that time.
And remaining in that very hermitage, he practiced intense austerity.
Having received an unsurpassed mantra from a certain son of the Sage,
Meditating upon the Blessed Goddess, the supreme and auspicious Prakṛti.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 10 ||
A description of the instruction in royal policy given to Satyavrata.
Janamejaya said:
"That Triśaṅku, the son of the king, was cursed by Vasiṣṭha."
O one of great intelligence, tell me how he was liberated from that curse. || 1 ||
Vyāsa said: Thus cursed, Satyavrata attained the state of a Piśāca;
remaining in that very hermitage, he became entirely devoted to the Goddess.
Once, having recited the nine-syllable mantra there, the king went to the Brahmins for the sake of the fire-oblation and, having prostrated before them, spoke with devotion: || 3 ||
"O gods of the earth, listen indeed to the words of me who am prostrate before you;
may all of you here act as my officiating priests."
And for every ten parts of the recitation, a fire-offering (homa) must be performed according to the rules by you—
those who know the Vedas and are intent on compassion— for the sake of accomplishing the task.
"O best among the knowers of Brahman, I am Satyavrata, the son of the king;
my purpose must be accomplished by all means for the sake of happiness. (6)
Having heard that, the Brahmins there said to the king's son:
"You have been cursed by your preceptor; you have now attained the state of a Piśāca."
Therefore, you are not worthy of sacrifice because you lack the qualification for the Vedas;
thus, you have attained this state of a Piśāca, which is despised in all the worlds.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of theirs, the king fell into grief:
"Fie upon this life of mine today! What shall I do, staying here in the forest? (9)
Abandoned by my father and severely cursed by my preceptor, fallen from my kingdom and having attained the state of a piśāca, what shall I do? (10)
Then, having made the funeral pyre very large with wood, the prince remembered the goddess Caṇḍikā, contemplating his entry into it.
Having remembered the goddess Mahāmāyā and having prepared a blazing funeral pyre before him,
he bathed and stood with palms joined in reverence at the front, ready to enter.
Having perceived that the lord of the earth desired to die, the Blessed Lady then came through the sky and appeared visibly before him.
Then, having granted him her vision, the Goddess, mounted upon a lion, spoke to that son of the king with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, O Great King.
The Goddess said:
"What have you resolved, O virtuous one? Do not cast off your body in the fire!
Be steadfast, O illustrious one; your father is overcome by old age. (15)
"Having given the kingdom to you, he is indeed going to the forest for asceticism;
cast off your despondency, O hero, O lord of the earth, on the day after tomorrow. (16)
Your father’s ministers will come to take you away;
and by my grace, your father shall consecrate you upon the royal throne.
"Having conquered desire, I shall go to the world of Brahmā"—this was his resolve.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to him, the goddess then vanished right there.
Then the prince was rescued from death by the fire;
having arrived in Ayodhyā at that time, he was [consoled] by the high-souled Nārada.
The entire account was quickly related to the king from the beginning;
then, having heard of his son’s such attempt at death, the king [was moved]. (20)
Feeling dejection in his mind, the righteous king, overwhelmed by grief for his son, lamented in many ways and spoke to his ministers.
"You have learned of my son's most formidable deed;
I, for my part, abandoned my wise son Satyavrata in the forest."
At his command, he who was worthy of sovereignty and a knower of the supreme truth departed immediately;
though devoid of wealth, he remained steadfast in that very realization, endowed with forbearance. (23)
Having been thus cursed by Vasiṣṭha, he was turned into one resembling a Piśāca;
tormented by grief today, he intends to enter the fire.
Having been restrained by the illustrious Mahādevī while he was preparing [to depart], he has remained there once more;
therefore, go quickly to that mighty eldest son.
Having comforted him here with words, let them quickly bring him here and,
having consecrated his own biological son— who is capable of protection— in the kingdom, [let them depart].
"I shall go to the forest; I am at peace, having resolved to practice asceticism.
Having spoken thus, the king sent away all his ministers. (27)
Indeed, with their minds inclined toward joy for the sake of bringing him back,
those ministers went and consoled that prince.
Having brought the high-souled Satyavrata to Ayodhyā with due honor,
the king beheld him looking weak and clad in soiled garments.
Wearing his matted locks, cruel and overcome with anxiety, he thought:
"What harsh deed have I done that my son has been exiled? (30)
"He is worthy of the kingdom and exceedingly wise, knowing the certainty of Dharma"—having reflected thus in his mind, the lord of the earth embraced him. (31)
Having consoled him, he had him sit upon a seat close by;
once his son was seated, the king spoke to him with affection.
With a voice faltering with affection, the king, who was an expert in the treatises on ethics, said:
"O son, you must set your mind upon dharma; those born from my own mouth are to be honored. (33)
Wealth acquired through righteous means should be accepted, and the subjects must always be protected. One should never speak untruth anywhere, nor should one ever deviate from the path. (34)
One should perform what is proclaimed by the cultured; ascetics are to be honored;
cruel bandits are to be slain; and likewise, there must be mastery over the senses. (35)
O son, for the sake of accomplishing his tasks, a king must always act; however, the counsel shared with his ministers must be kept secret under all circumstances. (36)
O son, a wise man should not neglect an enemy, even if he is insignificant, with his whole being;
likewise, he should not place his trust in a minister who is devoted to another or one who is bowing down in subjection.
Spies should be employed everywhere in every way among both enemies and friends;
one's mind should always be fixed on righteousness, and one should give gifts constantly. (38)
One should not engage in empty talk and should avoid the company of the wicked;
various sacrifices should be performed and the great seers should be honored. (39)
One should never place trust in a woman, nor in a man who is dominated by women or addicted to gambling;
one should never show excessive devotion to hunting. (40)
He himself should certainly turn away from gambling, intoxicants, singing, and courtesans, and he should protect his subjects from these. (41)
One should always rise at all times during the Brāhma-muhūrta;
having performed the bath and all other rites according to the prescribed rules.
One who is well-initiated should perform the supreme worship of Parāśakti with devotion;
O son, this worship of the feet of Parāśakti is the fulfillment of the fruitfulness of this birth.
Having performed the great worship once and drinking the water from the feet of the Goddess, one shall never again enter a mother’s womb; this is the certain conclusion.
"O Great Goddess, everything that is seen is she alone; she indeed is both the seer and the witness.
Thus, filled with that state of being, one should remain with a fearless mind. (45)
Having properly performed the daily rites, one should go to the assembly of the twice-born;
having summoned them, the determination according to the Dharmaśāstras should be inquired of.
Having honored the venerable Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and Vedāntas,
one should always give gifts such as cows, land, and gold to those worthy recipients.
No ignorant brāhmaṇa whatsoever is ever to be honored;
never should anything more than mere food be given to a fool. (48)
"O son, you must not commit a transgression of dharma out of greed;
henceforth, you must never again show disrespect toward brahmins. (49)
The Brahmins, the gods upon earth, must be honored with great effort;
for there is no doubt that the twice-born alone are the cause of the Kshatriyas' prosperity. (50)
Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brahmin, and iron from stone;
the all-pervading energy of these subsides within their own respective sources.
Therefore, those born from the mouth [the Brahmins] should be especially honored by a king who desires prosperity in every way, through both gifts and disciplined conduct. 52.
The science of government must always be practiced in accordance with the treatises on Dharma; indeed, the treasury must be filled with wealth acquired through just means. (53)

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction on Royal Policy Given to Satyavrata," in the seventh book of the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Narration of the Story of Triśaṅku:
Thus enlightened by his father, King Triśaṅku bowed down and replied to his father, "So be it," with a voice faltering with affection. (1)
Having summoned Brahmins who were knowers of the mantras and experts in the Vedas and Shastras,
he quickly had the requisites for the consecration prepared.
Having brought together the waters of all the holy fords,
the lord of the people likewise summoned the subjects, the vassals, and the sovereigns.
On an auspicious day, the father duly offered him an excellent seat and,
having consecrated his son Triśaṅku in the kingdom according to the prescribed rites, [departed].
Accompanied by his wife, he entered the third meritorious stage of life and performed difficult austerities in the forest on the banks of the triple-pathed river.
When his time had come, he went to heaven, honored even by the thirty gods;
seated near Indra’s throne, he shone forever like the sun.
The King said: Previously, it was stated by your holiness through the course of our conversation that Satyavrata was indeed cursed by Vasiṣṭha for the killing of a milch cow.
O Lord, there is this doubt: how was he released from the state of a *piśāca* after having been reduced to that condition by his enraged preceptor?
Indeed, one who is possessed by a curse would not be worthy of a lion-throne;
by what other action was he released from the curse by the sage? (9)
Tell me this, O brahmin-sage: what is the cause of my release from the curse?
And how was one of such appearance brought by my father to his own home?
Vyāsa said:
Having been cursed by Vasiṣṭha, he immediately attained the state of a Piśāca;
possessing a hideous form and being exceedingly difficult to overcome, he became a source of terror to all the worlds.
O King, as soon as the Goddess was worshipped with devotion by Satyavrata, she,
being pleased, instantly granted him a divine body.
His state as a piśāca vanished and his sin was utterly destroyed;
through the nectar of her compassion, he became free from evil and endowed with great splendor. (13)
Vasiṣṭha also became serene in soul through the grace of Śakti,
and his father too became filled with affection for him due to that same favor.
When his father had passed away, that righteous king ruled the kingdom and performed various sacrifices to the eternal Goddess of gods.
Then he had a son named Hariścandra, who was most beautiful, endowed with the auspicious marks prescribed in the scriptures, and exceedingly handsome. || 16 ||
Having made his son Triśaṅku the crown prince,
the lord of the earth resolved to enjoy heaven with his human body.
Having gone to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha and having prostrated according to the prescribed rites, the king,
being delighted, then spoke these words with his palms joined in reverence.
