The king said:
"O son of Brahmā, illustrious one, expert in all mantras, O ascetic, you ought to listen with a well-disposed mind to my petition. (19)
A desire has arisen in me today for the happiness of the heavenly world, so that I may enjoy superhuman pleasures with this very body. (20)
One shall dwell together with Apsarases to sport in the Nandana grove, and indeed, the sweet singing of gods and Gandharvas is to be heard. (21)
O great sage, perform for me quickly such a sacrifice that I may dwell in the celestial realm with this very body.
"You are capable, O best of sages; perform my task now.
Having completed the sacrifice, quickly lead me to the celestial realm, which is difficult to attain. (23)
Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, dwelling in heaven with a human body is extremely difficult to attain;
for it is taught that heaven is certain only for one who has died after performing meritorious deeds.
Therefore, O Omniscient One, I am afraid of this desire which is so difficult to attain;
for a dwelling together with the Apsarases while one is still alive is hard to obtain. (25)
"O highly fortunate one, perform sacrifices; when dead, you shall attain heaven.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, the king became exceedingly dejected in mind.
He spoke these words once more to Vasiṣṭha, who had been angered by him previously:
"O Brahmin, if you do not officiate at my sacrifice because of an obsession with pride..."
"Having appointed another as my domestic priest, I shall indeed perform the sacrifice now.
Hearing those words of his, Vasiṣṭha was filled with anger.
And he cursed the king, saying: "O evil-minded one, become a Cāṇḍāla!
With this very body, become a dog-eater immediately! (29)
O destroyer of heaven, most sinful one, defiled by the slaughter of Surabhi, you who have severed the wife of a Brahmin and corrupted the path of dharma! 30.
"O sinful one, there is no way for you to attain the heavenly realm even after death.
Vyāsa said:
O King, having been addressed thus by his preceptor, Triśaṅku at that very moment—
There, with that very body, he took on the form of a dog-cooker (outcaste);
and at that very moment, his earrings turned into stone.
At that time, the fragrance of sandalwood on his body turned into a foul odor;
then, when his divine body had become blue in color, yellow garments appeared upon it.
The body of that high-souled one became the color of gold due to the curse;
O King, this was the fruit resulting from his anger toward a devotee of Śakti.
Therefore, a devotee of Śrī Śakti should never be disregarded;
for Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, was devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī. || 35 ||
Seeing his own censurable body, the king was overcome with grief;
dejected, he did not go home but departed for the forest.
Afflicted by suffering and overwhelmed with grief, Triśaṅku reflected: "What shall I do? Where shall I go? My body is utterly contemptible. (37)
I do not see anything that must be done by which my suffering may come to an end;
if I go home, my son will surely be distressed today. (38)
Even my wife, upon seeing a dog-eater, will not accept me;
furthermore, the ministers will show no respect once they see me in such a state again. (39)
My kinsmen and circle of relatives will no longer associate with me; for one abandoned by everyone, death is surely better than life. (40)
Either by consuming poison today, or by falling into a body of water, or by placing a noose around my neck, I shall abandon this body. (41)
Or, while the fire is blazing, I shall offer my body as an oblation according to the prescribed rites;
or, having undertaken a fast, I shall renounce these life-breaths which have been utterly defiled.
Self-destruction will surely occur birth after birth;
furthermore, the state of being a dog-eater (outcaste) and even a curse may arise from the fault of such killing. (43)
Reflecting further, the king pondered within his mind:
"I must by no means commit suicide at this time."
One's own performed karma must be experienced with this very body in the forest;
through the experience of its ripening, there will be total exhaustion of it in every way. (45)
The exhaustion of prārabdha-karmas cannot occur except through their experience;
therefore, I must here experience the fruits of the deeds I have performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
While staying near the holy hermitage, he likewise engaged in visiting sacred fords, the remembrance of Ambikā, and the service of the virtuous. || 47 ||
Thus, dwelling in the forest, I shall surely bring about the exhaustion of my karma;
perhaps, through the power of fortune, there may even be a meeting with a holy person. (48)
Having reflected thus in his mind and abandoned his own city, the king went to the bank of the Gaṅgā and remained right there, grieving at will.
Then King Hariścandra, having learned the cause of his father’s curse,
became distressed and dispatched his ministers there.
Having gone there quickly, the ministers,
filled with humility, bowed down to him who had the appearance of a dog-eater (cāṇḍāla) and was sighing again and again, and spoke to him.
"O King, know us to be your ministers who have arrived, sent indeed by your son, remaining here at the command of Hariścandra. (52)
The son of the crown prince said: "O lord of men, listen to what he said:
'Bring the king here, honoring my father. (53)
Therefore, O King, come back to your kingdom free from distress;
all your ministers and subjects alike will serve you.
We shall propitiate the Guru so that he may indeed show us compassion; once he is pleased, that one of great splendor will bring an end to our suffering.
Thus, O King, has it been told to you in many ways by your son;
therefore, let the departure for your own home be pleasing to you immediately.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, the king, who was in the form of a dog-cooker (śvapaca),
did not thereafter set his mind on returning to his own home.
Then he spoke these words to them: "Let the ministers go to the city;
having gone to the city, O highly fortunate ones, let them speak my words."
"I shall not come back, my son; rule the kingdom without sloth, honoring the Brahmins and the gods, and performing sacrifices many times over. (59)
"I will not enter Ayodhyā wearing this despised garb of a dog-cooker, which is condemned by the great-souled ones; let everyone go, without delay."
"Having installed my son Hariścandra, who is possessed of great strength, upon the lion-throne, you must carry out the duties of kingship there by my command. (61)
Having been thus instructed, those ministers, overcome with intense distress, wept bitterly;
they then bowed to him and departed quickly from that forest hermitage.
Having arrived in Ayodhyā on an auspicious day,
they then performed the consecration upon the head of Hariścandra according to the prescribed rites.
Having been consecrated by his ministers with the king's command,
the radiant and most righteous prince ruled the kingdom while reflecting deeply upon his father.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Triśaṅku," in the seventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Viśvāmitra’s Consolation for the Purpose of Removing Triśaṅku’s Curse.
The King said: "By the command of the monarch, Hariścandra has been made king by his ministers."
But how was Triśaṅku liberated from that body of a Cāṇḍāla?
Either he died in the midst of the forest or was immersed in the waters of the Gaṅgā;
or else, through the compassion of his preceptor, he was liberated from that curse. || 2 ||
Relate this entire account before me;
I am eager in every way to hear the life-story of that king. (3)
Vyāsa said: Having consecrated his son, the king, with a satisfied mind,
delayed there while contemplating Śivā.
As time passed in this manner, having performed austerities with a concentrated mind,
the sage Kauśika then went there to see his wife, sons, and others.
Having arrived and seen his kinsmen well-established, he attained great joy;
the wise one then questioned his wife, who stood before him with respectful service.
O Sulocanā, how was that time spent by you during the famine?
Tell me, by what means were these children sustained in the absence of food?
"Listen, O beautiful one; I have not come because I am intent upon asceticism.
But what have you done, O lovely and auspicious one, without any wealth? (8)
Having heard of that extraordinary famine, I reflected there and thought:
"I have not come; having considered this, what shall I do being destitute? (9)
O lady of beautiful thighs, I too, tormented by hunger in the forest,
entered a certain dwelling of a Śvapaca with the intent of stealing.
Seeing the dog-cooker asleep and being severely tormented by hunger, he recognized the kitchen and approached it for the sake of food. || 11 ||
When I opened the vessel and took the cooked flesh of the dog's offspring for the purpose of eating it, I was indeed seen by him.
Questioned respectfully, "Who are you, and how have you come to my house at night?
Tell me, for what purpose do you open this chest? (13)
Thus addressed by the dog-eater, I, being severely tormented by hunger, spoke to him with faltering words, O lady of beautiful hair: || 14 ||
"O illustrious one, I am a brahmin and an ascetic, afflicted by hunger;
having fallen into the state of a thief, I see food in this vessel. (15)
"O high-minded one, I have arrived as a thief;
I am hungry, so give me permission, for I shall eat well-prepared meat. (16)
Viśvāmitra said:
Having heard the words of the dog-cooker (śvapaca), he spoke to me with firm resolve: "O foremost of the castes, do not eat me; know this to be the abode of a dog-cooker. (17)
Human birth is indeed difficult to attain, and within that, the status of the twice-born;
and within the state of being twice-born, the status of a Brāhmaṇa is difficult to obtain—do you not know this? 18.
One who desires the world [of higher rebirth] must by all means avoid improper food;
Manu has declared that seven types of outcastes are unfit to be associated with through ritual action. (19)
"O Brahmin, I am to be abandoned by you through my actions as a dog-eater; there is no doubt about this.
O twice-born one, I do not prevent you from eating out of greed, but rather directly [out of compassion]. (20)
"O best of the twice-born, let this fault of the mixture of castes not come upon you.
Viśvāmitra said:
"You speak the truth, O knower of dharma; your intellect is clear, O outcaste. (21)
Nevertheless, O giver of honor, I shall explain the subtle path of dharma in times of distress: the body must be protected by all means. (22)
At the conclusion of a sin, an expiation must again be performed for the sake of purification;
otherwise, through that sin, a miserable rebirth will occur—both when there is no calamity and even when there is a calamity.
For one who dies hungry, there is no doubt that hell awaits;
therefore, he who desires his own welfare must provide for the removal of hunger.
Therefore, O outcaste, I shall protect my body by the practice of theft;
for it has been stated by the wise that whatever sin is incurred through theft during a drought [is equal to the merit gained here]. (25)
"Whatever the rain-cloud does not rain, that shall belong to him"—
when these beloved words were spoken, the rain-cloud suddenly descended.
Desiring showers from the sky as thick as an elephant's trunk,
I was filled with joy upon seeing a cloud raining along with lightning.
Then, having abandoned that house, I departed with supreme joy.
Tell me, O lady of beautiful hips, how was this time spent by you?
"In this wilderness, there is a supreme, cruel being who causes the destruction of living creatures here.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, Priyaṃvadā spoke to her husband. (29)
Listen as I describe how this most terrible time has passed;
O best of sages, when you had departed, a famine arrived.
For the sake of food, all the little sons became exceedingly distressed;
seeing their hungry children, they searched through forest after forest for wild rice (nīvāra).
Overwhelmed by anxious thought, I was deluded; yet at that time, some fruit was obtained.
In this manner, several months were passed subsisting on wild grain (nīvāra). || 32 ||
In the absence of that, O beloved, I further reflected in my mind:
"Indeed, there will be no alms during this famine, nor will there be wild grains (nīvāra) in the forest."
There were no fruits upon the trees, nor were there roots in the earth;
afflicted by hunger, the children wept intensely, overcome with distress. (34)
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? What shall I say to those afflicted by hunger?"—having reflected thus in my mind, I made this resolve: (35)
"I shall give one son today to some wealthy man; having taken his price, with that wealth [I will ransom] the other boys. (36)
"I shall protect those afflicted by hunger; there is no other means for their protection.
Having reflected thus in his mind, he sent this son [of mine]. (37)
"O illustrious one, for the sake of selling him, I, overcome with intense distress and devoid of shame, took hold of this weeping child and went out while he was crying loudly. (38)
Then the royal sage Satyavrata, seeing me on the road in great distress, asked: "Why is this boy weeping? (39)
Then, O best of sages, I spoke these words to him:
"O King, this boy is being led away by me today for the purpose of sale. (40)
Having heard my words, the king, his heart softened with compassion, then said to me: "Go home, taking this young boy with you."
"Meat has been prepared for the princes as their food;
I shall provide it to you constantly until your meeting with the sage. (42)
Day after day, that king, filled with compassion, would place deer and pigs upon this tree, slay them, and then depart. (43)
By him alone, O beloved, were the children protected from the ocean of calamity;
then, for my sake, that king was cursed by Vasiṣṭha.
On a certain day, meat was not obtained by him in the forest;
consequently, he killed Vasiṣṭha’s milch cow, and because of that, the sage became enraged.
The name Triśaṅku was given to that high-souled king by an enraged [sage],
and for the sake of his execution, the king was turned into a Cāṇḍāla.
Therefore, O Kauśika, I have become sorrowful because of his suffering;
for the sake of me, this prince has attained the state of an outcaste. (47)
By whatever means possible, O King, you must indeed provide protection for him through powerful asceticism. 48.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his wife, Kauśika, the best of sages and subduer of enemies, spoke with consoling words to that distressed and longing woman.
Viśvāmitra said: "O lotus-eyed one, I shall release that king from his curse,
for he has rendered you a service by protecting you in the wilderness."
"By the power of my knowledge and asceticism, I shall bring about the destruction of suffering.
Having thus comforted his beloved there, Kauśika, the knower of the supreme truth, [proceeded]. (51)
He reflected, "How might the king's suffering be destroyed?
Having deliberated there, the sage went to where the monarch was.
Triśaṅku, dwelling in a hamlet of outcasts in a wretched state with the appearance of a dog-cooker, was struck with amazement upon seeing the sage approaching. (53)
Then Kauśika, having quickly seized the king by the feet as he fell prostrate upon the earth like a staff, took hold of him by the hand.
Raising him up, that best of the twice-born spoke these words with consolation:
"O protector of the earth, since you have been cursed by the sage on my account..."
"I shall fulfill your desire; tell me, what may I do for you?
The king said:
"Previously, I requested Vasiṣṭha for the purpose of performing a sacrifice. (56)
"O best of sages, perform a sacrifice for me; I shall perform the most excellent rite.
O lord of brahmins, act as you desire so that I may go to heaven. (57)
"O evil-minded one, having become enraged, this Vasiṣṭha has said to me: 'By this very body, you shall go to Śakra’s world, the abode of happiness. (58)
"How indeed can you dwell in heaven with a human body?
Thus was the Blessed One addressed again by me, O sinless one, as I was greedy for heaven.
"Having appointed another as my domestic priest, I shall perform a supreme sacrifice;
then he cursed me: 'Become a Cāṇḍāla, a low-born outcast! (60)
Thus, all this cause arising from the curse has been told;
O Lord of Sages, you are capable of destroying my sorrow.
Having spoken thus, the king, afflicted by the pain of grief, fell silent;
Kauśika, for his part, reflected upon how to avert his curse.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Viśvāmitra’s Consolation for the Removal of Triśaṅku’s Curse," in the seventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 13.
The description of the birth of a son to Śaivyā through the grace of Varuṇa.
Vyāsa said: Having reflected in his mind upon what was to be done, the son of Gādhi, a man of great asceticism, spoke.
Having prepared the materials for the sacrifice, he then invited the sages.
Knowing that sacrifice and having been invited by Viśvāmitra, all those sages did not come, for they had been forbidden by Vasiṣṭha. || 2 ||
Then, having learned of that, the son of Gādhi, dejected and exceedingly distressed,
went to the hermitage where that king was staying.
Kauśika, enraged that all the Brāhmaṇas had not come for the sake of the sacrifice, spoke to him, O best of kings, saying: "They have been prevented by Vasiṣṭha."
Behold the perfection of my ascetic power, O great king, as I shall lead you to the abode of the gods;
I shall fulfill your desire.
Having spoken thus, that best of sages took water in his hand and then bestowed upon him the merit arising from the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra.
Having then bestowed this merit upon the king, he said to that lord of the earth:
"O royal sage, go at your pleasure to the third heaven, unwearied."
O Indra among kings, by means of my merit accumulated over a long time, go joyfully to the city of Śakra; may it be well with you in the abode of the gods.
Vyāsa said:
When the lord of brahmins had spoken thus, Triśaṅku then suddenly flew up like a swift bird by the power of his asceticism.
When the king, having flown up into the sky, went to the city of Śakra,
he was seen there by the hosts of gods as a cruel man wearing the guise of a Caṇḍāla.
He was told by the Lord of the Gods: "Who is this who comes so swiftly through the sky like a god, yet is difficult to discern and has the appearance of a dog-cooker (outcaste)? (11)
Rising up suddenly, Śakra beheld that lowest of men;
recognizing him as Triśaṅku, he rebuked him and spoke with force.
"O dog-cooker, where are you going? You are loathed even in the world of the gods.
Go quickly from there to the earth; it is not fitting for you to remain here. (13)
Thus addressed by Śakra, O crusher of enemies,
the king slipped from heaven and fell down like a god whose merit has been exhausted.
Again the king cried out repeatedly, "O Viśvāmitra!
I am falling; protect me, who am afflicted by suffering and swiftly falling from heaven! (15)
O King, having heard that cry of his as he was falling, the sage Kauśika looked at the monarch and said, "Stay! (tiṣṭha).
At his word, that king remained right there in the sky,
even though he had been moved from the abode of the gods by the power of the sage’s asceticism.
Viśvāmitra, too, having touched water, performed an extensive sacrifice in order to create a new creation and a second heavenly world. (18)
Having thus recognized his exertion, the Lord of Śacī quickly and suddenly went there toward the sage born of Gādhi.
"O Brahmin, what is being done? O virtuous one, why are you so overcome with anger? Enough of this creation, O best of sages; tell me, what may I do for you? (20)
Viśvāmitra said: "O Lord, out of affection, lead back to his own abode King Triśaṅku, who has fallen from your world and is exceedingly distressed. (21)
Vyāsa said:
Having understood his resolve and knowing the fierce power of his asceticism, Turāṣāṭ Vāsava became greatly apprehensive and said, "So be it."
Having restored the king to a divine body and seated him upon an excellent celestial chariot,
Śakra took leave of Kauśika and then departed for his own city.
When Śakra had indeed departed for heaven along with Triśaṅku, Viśvāmitra, having attained happiness, became firmly established in his own hermitage. || 24 ||
Then Hariścandra, having heard that account of Viśvāmitra’s assistance and the fulfillment of his father’s desire for heaven, ruled the kingdom with joy.
The lord of Ayodhyā, filled with affection, engaged in dalliance with his wife,
who was endowed with beauty, youth, and grace.
In the past, that young woman had never been pregnant;
at that time, the king became anxious with thought and was exceedingly distressed. (27)
Having gone to Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage and bowed his head to the sage,
he informed the preceptor of the anxiety born of his childlessness.
"You are indeed an astrologer, O giver of honor, and highly skilled in the science of mantras;
O knower of dharma, devise a means for the continuation of my lineage. (29)
"There is no destination for one who is sonless; you know this, O best of the twice-born.
Why do you remain indifferent, knowing my suffering and being capable [to help]? (30)
"Blessed indeed are these kalaviṅka birds who dote upon their young;
I, however, am unfortunate, for I think of him incessantly, day and night. (31)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, which were mixed with despondency, the sage,
the son of Brahmā, reflected thoroughly in his mind and spoke to him.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Tell the truth, O Great King: in this world of transmigration, there exists no sorrow so extraordinary as the sorrow born of childlessness."
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should diligently propitiate Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures; he will accomplish your task for you.
"There is no god superior to Varuṇa as a bestower of progeny;
worship him, O most righteous one, and the accomplishment of your purpose will come to pass. (35)
Destiny and human effort—both of these must be honored by men;
for without exertion, how can the accomplishment of a task ever come to pass? (36)
However, O best of kings, men who perceive the truth must exert effort according to the proper method; when that is performed, success will follow, and not otherwise.
Having heard these words of his guru Amitatejas,
the king bowed down and departed, having resolved to practice asceticism.
Seated in the lotus posture at an auspicious spot on the bank of the Gaṅgā, the king practiced difficult penance while meditating in his mind upon the Holder of the Noose (Varuṇa).
O great king, as he was thus performing penance, Pracetas appeared before his eyes; out of compassion, his lotus-like face was serene.
The Lord of aquatic creatures spoke these words to Hariścandra:
"Choose a boon, O knower of dharma; I am pleased with your asceticism."
The king said:
"O Lord of Gods, I am childless; grant me a son who bestows happiness.
This endeavor has been undertaken by me for the sake of removing the three debts. (42)
Having heard the bold words of the sorrowful king,
Pāśī then, preceded by a smile, spoke to him as he stood before him.
Varuṇa said:
"O King, if a virtuous son, desired in your heart, should be born, then after that task is accomplished, what further favor will you do for me? (44)
O King, if you, being apprehensive, were to sacrifice me with that very son as the victim in an animal sacrifice, I shall grant you a boon.
The king said:
"O Lord, let there not be fruitlessness for me; O Lord of Waters, I shall perform a sacrifice, making my own son the sacrificial animal. I tell you this truly. (46)
O giver of honor, on this earth there is no suffering more supreme or unbearable than barrenness;
it extinguishes the fire of grief for men. Therefore, grant us an auspicious son. (47)
Varuṇa said:
"O King, your son shall indeed be born according to your desire; go home.
You must fulfill those words of truth which you have spoken in my presence."
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by Varuṇa, Hariścandra went home and related to his wife the account arising from the granting of the boon.
He had a full hundred wives who were exceedingly beautiful;
his chief queen was the auspicious Śaivyā, a lawful wife devoted to her husband.
When the time had passed, that woman of excellent complexion conceived;
the king became joyful upon hearing of her pregnancy longings.
Then the king had the purificatory rites performed according to the rules;
and when the tenth month was complete, she gave birth on an auspicious day.
When the son, who was endowed with the strength of the stars and planets and resembled the son of a god, was born, the king bathed and was surrounded by Brahmins. (53)
He performed the birth rites and other ceremonies, bestowing gifts in abundance;
and there arose in the king an exceeding joy born of the son's birth.
He became exceedingly generous, endowed with wealth and grain, distinguished by his practice of giving, and filled with the sounds of singing and musical instruments. || 55 ||

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Śaivyā’s Son through the Grace of Varuṇa," in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The description of Hariścandra’s contracting of the disease of dropsy.
Vyāsa said:
While that king’s great festival for his son was underway, his palace was filled with joy.
Then the auspicious Pāśī, wearing the guise of a brahmin, arrived there.
Having said "Svasti" to the king, Varuṇa spoke: "Listen, O Lord;
a son has been born to you. Sacrifice to me quickly with him, O King."
"O King, make true your word that was spoken by you previously;
for indeed, through my granting of this boon, your childlessness has come to an end today. (3)
Having heard these words of his, the king fell into deep reflection:
"How can I kill my own son, who has been born with a face as beautiful as a lotus?"
The powerful guardian of the world arrived in the guise of a brahmin:
"One who desires welfare in every way must never show contempt for a god. (5)
Affection for one's son is exceedingly difficult for all living beings to sever at all times; what shall I do, and how may I obtain the happiness that arises from progeny? (6)
Maintaining his composure, the king bowed to him, honored him in return,
and spoke words that were gentle, appropriate, and preceded by humility.
The king said:
"O God of gods, O ocean of compassion, I seek your permission to perform a sacrifice with abundant sacrificial fees according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas."
When a son is born, the father becomes fit for ritual acts after ten days;
the mother becomes pure after a month. This is the reason regarding the couple.
"You are omniscient and possessed of great wisdom; you know the eternal Dharma.
O Lord of Waters, show mercy; O Supreme Lord, forgive us. (10)
Vyāsa said:
Thus addressed, Pracetas replied to that lord of people:
"May it be well with you; I shall depart. Perform your duties, O King."
"I shall return at the end of the month; you must by all means perform the sacrifice, O best of kings, having performed the customary rites for the son's departure."
Having spoken thus with gentle words to the king, the lord of aquatic creatures departed;
King Hariścandra attained great joy once the wielder of the noose had gone. (13)
He gave away tens of millions of cows, their udders like jars filled with gold,
to Brahmins learned in the Vedas, and likewise he gave mountains of sesame seeds.
Having beheld his son’s face, the king attained a most profound happiness; he then performed the naming ceremony according to the prescribed rites and gave him the name Rohita.
When the month was complete, Pāśī then suddenly arrived at the king's house in the guise of a Brahmin, repeatedly saying, "Perform a sacrifice! (16)
Beholding that god, the king was submerged in an ocean of grief;
having prostrated before him and offered hospitality, he spoke with palms joined in reverence.
"By good fortune, O Lord, you have come to my home; it has been purified by you, O Master.
O Lord of Waters, I shall perform the sacrifice according to the rules as desired by you."
"The Vedic scholars say that an animal which has not been castrated is not to be praised;
therefore, once its tusks have grown, I shall perform a great sacrifice for it. (19)
Vyāsa said: Having been addressed thus by him, Varuṇa replied, "So be it," and departed;
then Hariścandra, having attained joy, lived out his life in the householder stage.
Then, knowing that his teeth had grown back, Pracetas, assuming the form of a brahmin,
came to his house saying, "Perform your duty."
The protector of the earth, seeing the Lord of the Waters arrived in the form of a brahmin,
bowed down and honored him with seats and other marks of respect, paying him due homage.
Having offered praise, he spoke these words with his neck bowed in humility:
"I shall duly perform the sacrifice according to my desire, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees."

"Even this child, though his tonsure ceremony has not yet been performed, is not considered [fit] as a 'womb-hair' (garbhakeśa) for the purpose of being made an animal for sacrifice; I have heard this from the mouths of the elders. (24)
"Wait a moment, O Lord of Waters; you know the eternal rule.
Indeed, the sacrifice for a child must be performed in every way at the conclusion of the tonsure ceremony. (25)
Having heard those words of his, Pracetas spoke to him again:
"O King, by saying this over and over again, you are deceiving me."
"O King, do you now possess all the necessary requisites? Bound by affection for your son, you are indeed deceiving him at this moment. (27)
"If you do not perform the sacrifice after having completed the rite of shaving, then, filled with anger, I shall utter a terrible curse. (28)
"Today I depart, O Indra among kings, at your command, O giver of honor;
you who are born of the Ikṣvāku lineage must not make your word false. (29)
Having spoken thus, Pracetas departed quickly from the king’s house;
the king, supremely satisfied, then rejoiced in his palace.
But when the time for the tonsure ceremony had arrived, a supreme festival was underway,
Varuṇa (Pāśī) once again swiftly reached the king's palace.
When the queen, having taken her son onto her lap, was seated in the presence of the king at the time of the ritual, Varuṇa arrived at that very moment.
"Perform your duty!"— thus speaking these clear words to the king,
the illustrious one, assuming the form of a brahmin, appeared like the fire-god Agni in person.
Beholding him, the king became exceedingly overwhelmed;
with palms joined in reverence, he bowed before him out of fear.
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, the king spoke with humility:
"O Master, today I shall perform the work of the sacrifice according to the ritual injunctions."
"There is something more to be said even there; listen with a focused mind, O Lord.
If you deem it appropriate, O Master, I shall speak it before you. (36)
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—these three castes are the twice-born; when they are consecrated by the sacraments, otherwise they are Śūdras—thus the knowers of the Vedas understand. (37)
Therefore, this son of mine, though but a child, behaves today like a Śūdra;
for it is the settled conclusion in the Vedas that one becomes fit for the sacred rites only after being initiated. (38)
The initiation ceremony is traditionally prescribed for kings in their eleventh year;
for Brahmins it is in the eighth, and for Vaiśyas indeed in the twelfth. (39)
O Lord of Gods, if you take pity on me, your wretched servant, then, having brought [an animal], I shall perform an excellent sacrifice with that beast. (40)
"You are a guardian of the world, O knower of dharma, proficient in all scriptures;
you consider my word to be true, so go now to your abode, O Lord. (41)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, the compassionate lord of aquatic creatures replied,
"So be it," and departed quickly with a cheerful countenance, O King.
Then, upon his departure, King Varuṇa became filled with exceeding joy;
having thus obtained the welfare of his son, the king indeed attained great delight.
Then King Hariścandra performed his royal duties;
as time passed, a son was born who reached the age of ten years.
The king, accompanied by learned brahmins as well as his ministers, provided for him the equipment for the sacred thread ceremony in a manner befitting his prosperity. (45)
In the eleventh year from her birth, during the ceremony for binding the sacred thread, the king performed the rites according to the rules,
yet he remained anxious in his mind.
While the task was thus underway and the young boy had been brought forward,
Varuṇa then arrived, wearing the guise of a brahmin.
Beholding him, the king quickly bowed down and stood before him;
with palms joined in reverence and filled with joy, he replied to the supreme god: ||| 48 ||
"O Lord, this son of mine has been invested with the sacred thread and is now fit for the status of a sacrificial animal;
by your grace, the grief born of the reproach of being barren has departed from me. (49)
"I wish to perform a sacrifice with abundant and excellent sacrificial fees;
listen at this time, O knower of dharma, for today I speak the truth. (50)
"At the conclusion of the rite of returning home, I shall fulfill your desire;
having shown compassion toward me, you ought to forgive me for now. (51)
Varuṇa said:
"O King, you are greatly deluding me, being intensely overwhelmed by affection for your son; O high-minded one, you repeatedly form arguments that appear well-reasoned. (52)
"I shall go today, O Great King, impelled by your word;
I will return at the proper time for the rite of my return. (53)
Having spoken thus and having taken leave of Tapa, O lord of the people, Varuṇa departed;
and the king, being delighted, carried out his business accordingly.
Seeing that Varuṇa had arrived and recognizing the timing of the sacrifice, the highly discerning prince then became anxious with thought. || 55 ||
He inquired here and there about the cause of the king's grief;
having learned that it was his own death, O long-lived one, he set his mind upon departing.
Having made a firm resolve and consulted with his ministers and sons,
he departed from that city and went forth into the forest.
When his son had departed, the king then became exceedingly distressed at will;
he dispatched his own messengers with the desire to search for him.
When time had passed in this manner, Varuṇa went to that house, saying to the king who was tormented by grief, "Perform a sacrifice. (59)
The king, having bowed to him, said: "O God of gods, what shall I do?
I do not know where my son has gone today, overwhelmed by fear. (60)
O Lord of aquatic beings, though he was searched for everywhere by my messengers in mountain fastnesses and the hermitages of sages, he was not found.
"Command me, O Great King; what shall I do now that my son has departed?
O Omniscient One, there is no fault here on my part; rather, the fault lies entirely with destiny. (62)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the king, Pracetas became exceedingly enraged;
deceived again and again, he cursed the king out of anger.
"O King, because I have been deceived by you with your words, let this most terrible disease of dropsy afflict you. (64)
Vyāsa said: Thus cursed by the enraged Pracetas, the protector of the earth,
the king, was then afflicted by a disease that brought him great suffering.
Having thus cursed the king, the wielder of the noose (Varuṇa) departed for his own abode;
the king, having contracted a great disease, became exceedingly distressed.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Hariścandra’s Contracting of the Disease of Dropsy," in the seventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 15 ||
The description of Viśvāmitra’s refusal to kill the son of a Brāhmaṇa who had become a sacrificial animal.
Vyāsa said:
After Varuṇa had departed, the king was exceedingly afflicted by disease.
Having encountered suffering after suffering, he was then deeply distressed. || 1 ||
O King, having heard in the forest that his father was afflicted by disease, that prince, constrained by affection, made up his mind to go.
When a year had passed, Śakra came there, knowing that he was desirous of going with reverence to see his father.
Then Vāsava, quickly assuming the form of a brahmin,
skillfully restrained the prince who was intent on departing.
Indra said:
"O prince, you do not know the very difficult principles of royal policy;
therefore, being deluded, you vainly set your mind on going."
O highly fortunate one, your father will have the brahmins, who have mastered the Vedas,
perform a fire sacrifice for you once the sacred fire has been kindled.
For the self, O dear one, is indeed beloved by all living beings;
for its sake, sons, wives, wealth, and so forth, are held dear.
"Having killed you, his beloved son, for the sake of protecting his own body, he will have a fire-sacrifice performed and shall be freed from disease. (8)
Therefore, O prince, you must not go to your father's house;
however, once your father has died, you must certainly go there for the sake of the kingdom.
Having been thus forbidden there by Vāsava, O King,
the prince remained at his will in the middle of the forest for another year.
Hearing that Hariścandra was then in extreme distress, his son,
having resolved upon death, set his mind on departing.
Then the Lord of Snow, having arrived there in the form of a brahmin,
repeatedly restrained his son Rohita with reasoned arguments.
Hariścandra, afflicted by extreme suffering, questioned his own priest Vasiṣṭha regarding a definitive means for the destruction of that disease.
To him the son of Brahmā said: "O best of kings, perform a sacrifice;
through a son purchased by means of a purchase, there shall be liberation from the curse. (14)
"Ten kinds of sons have been declared by Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas;
therefore, O best of kings, bring a son here with wealth and perform the rite. (15)
Varuṇa, being pleased, will also act for our happiness;
out of greed, some twice-born man born in his own kingdom will give up his son.
Thus delighted by Vasiṣṭha, the high-minded king dispatched his chief minister with the desire to search for him.
In the realm of that king, there was a certain twice-born man named Ajīgarta;
he had three sons, and he was especially destitute of wealth.
When that weak brahmin was asked by Pradhāna for the sake of a son, he said, "I shall give a hundred cows; indeed, grant me a son for the sacrifice. (19)
"Śunaḥpuccha, Śunaḥśepa, and Śunolāṅgūla—give me any one of these, and I shall give you a hundred cows. (20)
But Ajīgarta, having heard that and being severely tormented by hunger,
set his mind upon selling whichever one among those sons he might choose.
Considering the eldest to be the one entitled to the inheritance, my mother did not give him [the property]; nor did she give it to the youngest, saying, "This one is mine. (22)
And for the middle one, he gave Śunaḥśepa along with a hundred cows;
the lord of men then brought him and made him the sacrificial animal in the human sacrifice.
Beholding him weeping, distressed, dejected, trembling, and intensely afflicted— bound to the sacrificial post— the sages then cried out in lamentation.
In the human sacrifice, the lord of men prepared the animal for the *śāmitra* rite;
yet the *śamitṛ* priest did not take up the weapon to immolate that child. (25)
"I will not kill the wretched son of a brahmin, who is weeping so piteously,
for the sake of my own greed," he said at that time.
Having spoken thus, O brahmins, that King Ābhāsada ceased from his difficult task and asked, "What should be done? (27)
Then, as Śunaḥśepa was crying out intensely in the assembly hall, a most wonderful sound of "kila-kila" arose from the people who were shouting. 28.
Then Ajīgarta, having risen, spoke to that best of kings:
"O King, I shall perform your task; remain firm. (29)
"Give me double the wage; I shall indeed slaughter the animal.
Desiring wealth, I must perform the sacrificial rite for you today. (30)
"For one who suffers for the sake of wealth, envy is always produced.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, Hariścandra was filled with joy.
He said to him, "I shall give you today a hundred unsurpassed cows.
Upon hearing that, his father prepared to kill his son.
With his mind agitated by greed, he made a firm resolve regarding the slaughter;
and seeing him thus prepared, all the members of the assembly [were moved]. (33)
Afflicted by intense suffering, they cried out and uttered these words: "Alas!
Alas! This is a Piśāca, a great sinner of cruel deeds, disguised in the form of a twice-born. (34)
"Shame on you, O outcaste! You who are a disgrace to your lineage, prepared to kill your own son—what evil deed do you intend to perform? (35)
Having killed your son and acquired wealth, what happiness will there be for you?
For it is declared in the Vedas that a son is indeed born from one's own body as one's very self. (36)
"O Pāpabuddhi, how can you wish to kill yourself?
While such a clamor arose there, the son of Kuśika [Vasiṣṭha]—
Approaching the king, the compassionate Viśvāmitra said to him:
"O King, [look upon] this Śunaḥśepa, who is weeping and deeply afflicted. (38)
Your sacrifice shall be complete and there will be a total destruction of your disease.
There is no merit equal to compassion, and indeed no sin equal to violence. (39)
Reflect upon this exhortation: it is intended to inspire those possessed by passion;
for the sake of protecting one's own body, one cuts down the bodies of others. (40)
O Great King, one who desires auspiciousness in every respect should not perform [such acts];
rather, he should be compassionate toward all beings and content with whatever comes his way. (41)
And by the pacification of all the senses, the Lord of the World is quickly pleased;
O best of kings, one should contemplate all beings as being like oneself. (42)
Life is surely dear to all at all times;
yet you desire to bring happiness to your own body by killing this brahmin. (43)
How could he not wish to protect his body, which is the abode of his own happiness?
O King, you have no enmity with him from a previous birth. (44)
By which you desire to kill this innocent son of a brahmin;
for whoever constantly kills another out of self-interest, even without enmity. (45)
Having encountered him who was his slayer in another birth, he now kills that very person;
his father, a man of most wicked soul, is the one by whom he was delivered over to you.
One's own son, though of evil conduct and wicked intellect due to greed for wealth, is to be desired;
for it is said that many sons should be sought so that at least one might go to Gayā. (47)
One should perform the horse sacrifice or release a dark-colored bull;
and whoever should commit an evil deed in the midst of the country [should be dealt with accordingly].
The king undoubtedly partakes of one-sixth of that sin;
therefore, he who is intent on committing evil must be restrained by the king. (49)
Why did you not forbid him as he was intent on selling his son—the auspicious Triśaṅku’s son, born of the Solar dynasty? (50)
O King, though you are noble, you desire to perform an ignoble deed by releasing the son of the sage and by acting upon my word. (51)
O King, happiness will come to your body through lack of deliberation;
by the power of a curse, your father has fallen into the state of a Cāṇḍāla.
Indeed, by that very act of affection, he was sent by me to the heavenly world in that body; therefore, O King, follow my word.
"Release this poor boy, who is weeping and deeply distressed;
you have surely been entreated by me for this Rājasūya sacrifice. (54)
O best of kings, how do you not perceive the fault arising from the frustration of a prayer? Whatever is requested must always be given in this sacrifice.
"Otherwise, O King, there would be nothing but sin for you; of this there is no doubt.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Kauśika, that best of kings [acted accordingly].
He replied to the great king, Kauśika, the best of sages:
"O son of Gādhi, O sage, I am greatly afflicted by dropsy. (57)
Therefore, I will not release him; ask for something else, O Kauśika.
You must by no means engage in conflict with me regarding this matter.
Having heard those words of the king, Viśvāmitra became exceedingly incensed;
seeing the son of the twice-born so dejected, he was consumed by grief.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Viśvāmitra’s Prohibition Against the Slaughter of the Brahmin’s Son, Who Had Become a Sacrificial Animal," in the seventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 16 ||
The Description of the Bargain between Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra.
Vyāsa said:
Seeing the boy weeping, Viśvāmitra was overcome with compassion.
Having approached the deeply distressed Śunaḥśepa, he spoke these words to him.
"O son of Pracetas, by my command, as you recite this mantra which I have spoken while remembering it with your mind, prosperity shall be yours. (2)
Having heard the words of Viśvāmitra, Śunaḥśepa, overwhelmed with grief,
mentally recited the mantra spoken by Kauśika with distinct syllables.
O King, as he was chanting there, the compassionate Pracetas suddenly appeared, being well-pleased with the boy.
Seeing him arrive, they all were filled with the utmost wonder;
delighted by the sight of him, they praised the god Varuṇa.
Greatly amazed, the king, afflicted by pain, prostrated at his feet;
with palms joined in reverence, he stood before the Lord and offered praise.
Hariścandra said:
O God of gods, ocean of mercy, I am a sinful soul of very dull intellect;
though a wretched offender, I have been purified by the Supreme Lord.
Out of a desire for a son, I, established in suffering, committed an offense against you;
O Lord, please forgive it—what fault can there be in one of such wicked mind?
One who is driven by desire does not perceive a fault; therefore, O God of gods, O Lord, being afraid of hell, I who was desirous of a son deceived you. (9)
"There is no destination for one without a son, nor indeed is there heaven for him.
Frightened by those words, I committed that offense against you. (10)
O Lord, one who possesses knowledge should certainly not contemplate the fault of the ignorant;
I am suffering, overcome by pain, having been deceived by my own son.
"I do not know, O Great King, where my son has gone, O Lord;
having deceived me in the forest, he has fled out of fear of death, O Ocean of Compassion. (12)
Having given wealth, he departed after taking the brahmin boy;
this sacrifice has been commenced by one who purchased a son for your satisfaction.
Having obtained your vision, my wondrous suffering caused by dropsy has now entirely vanished, since you are pleased with me.
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words of the king who was afflicted by disease,
the compassionate Lord of the gods replied to that best of monarchs.
Varuṇa said: "O King, release Śunaḥśepa, who praises me while being greatly distressed.
This sacrifice of yours is now complete; may you yourself be freed from disease."
Having spoken thus, Varuṇa quickly made the king free from pain and well-established once more,
while the members of the assembly looked on.
That twice-born man was liberated from the noose by the high-souled Varuṇa;
then, a cry of "Victory! arose there in the sacrificial pavilion.
The king was immediately delighted, being freed from that most terrible disease;
and Śunaḥśepa, released from the sacrificial post, became exceedingly composed. || 19 ||
The king, endowed with discipline, completed this sacrifice;
then Śunaḥśepa, with palms joined in reverence, spoke thus to the members of the assembly.

O honorable members of the assembly, you who are well-versed in the sacred truths, please deliver a verdict on dharma according to the Vedas and the Shastras, for you are indeed speakers of what is true.
"Whose son am I, O omniscient ones? Who is my father, and who is supreme before me?
According to your word, I go for refuge to him. (22)
When these words were spoken, the members of the assembly said to one another.
The members of the assembly said:
"This is the son of Ajīgarta; to whom else could he possibly belong? (23)
Born from every limb and nurtured by him with devotion—of whom else could this man be the son? Such is the certainty.
Having heard that, Vāmadeva spoke to those members of the assembly:
"It is said that his father has indeed sold his son out of greed for wealth."
"He is undoubtedly the son of King Dhanada;
or rather, he has indeed been liberated from the noose of Varuṇa by him. (26)
The giver of food, the protector from fear, the giver of knowledge, and likewise the giver of wealth—these five are remembered as fathers. (27)
Then some said it was [the son] of the father, others of the king, and still others of Varuṇa; yet in their discussion, they did not reach a definitive conclusion.
When they had thus fallen into doubt, Vasiṣṭha— the omniscient one honored by all— spoke these words to the members of the assembly who were disputing there.
Listen, O fortunate ones, to this conclusion which is in accord with the Vedas:
when this infant son was sold by his father out of a lack of affection... (30)
At that very moment, through the acquisition of wealth, Hariścandra’s connection with him was established; he became his son, indeed purchased. (31)
When he was bound to the sacrificial post by the king, he had no son at all;
however, having praised Varuṇa, he was released by the god who was pleased with him.
Therefore, this highly fortunate one is indeed the son of Pracetas;
whoever praises him with the great mantras, he too, being pleased, bestows [boons]. || 33 ||
Wealth, life-breaths, cattle, sovereignty, and even the desired liberation—
this son of Kauśika has indeed protected [us] from Arishta.
Having bestowed the mantra of great power upon Varuṇa in that extreme distress,
Vyāsa said:
"Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, the members of the assembly said, 'So be it.'"
Then Viśvāmitra, filled with love, took him by the right hand and said, "Come, my son, come to my home. (36)
Śunaḥśepa went quickly with him in great haste, while Varuṇa, his soul satisfied, departed for his own abode. || 37 ||
Then the officiating priests and the members of the assembly likewise departed from their own homes;
the king also became free from disease and was filled with great joy.
He protected his subjects with a very serene mind;
and Rohita, having heard that news concerning Varuṇa, [acted accordingly].
He returned home joyfully from the difficult forest and mountain;
the messengers approached the king and announced that his son had arrived.
Filled with joy, the lord of Kosala went quickly forward to meet him;
seeing his father approaching, he was overflowing with love and great agitation. (41)
Prostrate on the ground like a staff, his face filled with tears from grief, the king also raised him up and embraced him, filled with joy. || 42 ||
Having smelled his son on the head, the joyful lord of the earth asked after his welfare once more, and then placed him upon his lap.
Then he performed an ablution upon his head with the warm tears from his eyes;
and by means of that son, who was exceedingly dear to him, he ruled the kingdom.
He related in detail the account of the human sacrifice;
that best of kings performed the Rājasūya, the most excellent of sacrifices. (45)
Then, having honored Vasiṣṭha, the omnipresent Lord made him his Hotṛ priest;
and when the sacrifice was completed, Vasiṣṭha was exceedingly honored by the Lord of Sacrifice.
The sage Viśvāmitra, accompanied by Vasiṣṭha, went with reverence to the delightful abode of Śakra. || 47 ||
Having met and stood together in the abode of the gods, O best of sages,
Viśvāmitra also questioned Vasiṣṭha, who had been duly honored.
Beholding him in the assembly of the Lord of Śacī, Viśvāmitra, his mind filled with wonder, said: "O best of sages, where did you obtain this great honor from me? (49)
"By whom was this done, O illustrious one? Tell me the truth.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"The powerful King Hariścandra is my patron (yajamāna). (50)
The Rājasūya sacrifice was performed by that king with excellent sacrificial fees;
there is no other king such as he, who is truthful and firm in his vows. (51)
"He was a donor, virtuous in character, and devoted to pleasing his subjects;
at his sacrifice, O descendant of Kauśika, I received honor. (52)
"What more do you ask? I shall tell you the truth, O twice-born one, which is unaltered:
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a king equal to Hariścandra.
He was a speaker of truth, likewise a giver, a hero, and supremely righteous. (53)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, Viśvāmitra became exceedingly enraged;
with eyes bloodshot from anger, he spoke to him as well.
Viśvāmitra said: "Thus you praise a king who is a speaker of falsehood and fond of deceit,
by whom Varuṇa was deceived after having promised him a boon."
O high-minded one, let us make a wager regarding the merit I have earned through my births, as well as through my asceticism and study, or that which belongs to you from your extreme penance. (56)
If I do not immediately make that king highly renowned—though he is a liar, a selfish non-giver, and a great villain—[then my vow would be broken]. (57)
"May all my merit accumulated since birth perish;
otherwise, may all the merit performed by you [perish]—thus do we make our wager. (58)
Having thus made a wager and disputing with one another, those two sages, filled with supreme wrath, then went from their own hermitage to the heavenly realm.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duel between Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra," in the seventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Hariścandra’s Promise to Give Wealth to an Aged Brāhmaṇa.
Vyāsa said:
Once, however, Hariścandra went to the forest for the purpose of hunting.
He saw the young Sundarī, with beautiful eyes, weeping. || 1 ||
Filled with compassion, the Great King questioned that lovely woman:
"O lady with eyes as broad as lotus petals, O fair-faced one, why do you weep? (2)
"By whom have you been so greatly tormented? What is your sorrow? Tell me quickly.
Who are you, in this desolate and terrible place? Who is your husband or your father? (3)
Moreover, O beloved, even the Rākṣasa does not violate another's wife within my kingdom;
therefore, O beautiful one, I shall swiftly slay him who violates you.
"Speak, O lady of beautiful hips; be at ease, O slender-waisted one! That sinful soul does not remain within my domain, O fair-hipped woman. (5)
Having heard these words of his, the woman wiped the tears from the face of that best of kings, Harishchandra, and spoke to him.
The woman said: "O King, the great sage Viśvāmitra, the descendant of Kuśika, is excessively harassing me; for my sake, he performs terrible austerities in the forest."
Therefore, O King, observer of noble vows, I am distressed within your realm;
know me as a beloved woman, longing for my lover and severely tormented by the sage. (8)
The king said:
"Be at ease, O large-eyed lady; you shall have no more sorrow.
I shall ward off that sage who is devoted to asceticism. (9)
Having thus consoled his wife, the king quickly approached the presence of the sage;
bowing down and prostrating with his head, the lord of the earth spoke to him.
"O Lord, why do you subject your body to such extreme suffering through asceticism? For what purpose is this undertaking of yours? Tell me the truth, O high-minded one. (11)
"O son of Gādhi, I shall indeed make your desire fruitful.
Arise, arise quickly; enough of this asceticism beyond this point."
O Omniscient One, you must never perform a most cruel, terrible penance that causes suffering to the world within my domain. (13)
Having thus rebuffed him, King [Daśaratha] went home; that sage Viśvāmitra, the descendant of Kuśika, departed while harboring anger in his mind.
Having gone there, he reflected upon the king's improper conduct and his conversation with Vasiṣṭha regarding the obstruction of asceticism.
Then, with a mind possessed by anger,
he contemplated various ways in his heart to retaliate against the Dānava of terrible form.
Having assumed the form of a boar, that Atikāya Mahākāla sent [the messenger] to that region,
uttering a most dreadful roar.
Then, reaching the king’s grove and terrifying the guards,
he [passed through] clusters of *mālatī* flowers and likewise of *kadamba* trees.
Repeatedly shaking the clusters of jasmine flowers and scratching the earth with his tusk, he uproots the trees.
He planted auspicious and tender Campaka trees, groves of Ketakī, Mallikā shrubs, Karavīras, and Uśīras.
Uprooting mucukundas, aśokas, bakulas, and tilakas as well,
the boar wrought destruction there in the forest.
All the garden guards, weapons in hand, fled;
there the florists, deeply distressed, cried out, "Alas! Alas! (22).
Even though he was being struck with arrows, the boar, who possessed a splendor like that of Time (Kāla), was not at all terrified; instead, he began to afflict the guards. || 23 ||
Then, overcome by extreme fear, they went to the king for refuge;
trembling and agitated by terror, they said to him, "Save us! Save us! (24)
Then, beholding them arrived and afflicted by fear, the king asked: "What is this fear? From what does it arise? Tell me, you who have come together. (25)
O protectors, I do not fear the gods nor the rākṣasas;
tell me before whom this fear has arisen. (26)
And with a single arrow, I shall indeed slay that wretched enemy, that evil-minded villain who has arisen in the world as my foe. (27)
Whether he be a god or even a dānava, I shall slay him with my sharp arrows.
Where does he stand? What is his form? With what strength is he endowed? (28)
The gardeners said:
"O King, there is no god, nor a Daitya, nor a Yakṣa, nor a Kinnara;
rather, some boar of massive body dwells in the forest. (29)
With his snout, he uproots even the most delicate flowering trees;
that entire forest is torn asunder by the boar of exceeding speed.
Though struck by us with arrows, stones, and likewise with clubs, O great king, Hanumān did not fear; he rushed toward us.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard their words, the king, overwhelmed with anger,
mounted his horse and swiftly went toward the grove.
Accompanied by a vast army consisting of elephants, horses, and chariots,
and joined by multitudes of foot soldiers, he set out for that excellent forest.
There he saw a terrifying great boar grunting loudly;
and beholding the forest laid waste, the king became filled with rage.
Having fixed an arrow to his bow and drawn the bowstring,
he swiftly set out to kill that wicked boar.
And beholding the king with bow in hand and agitated by rage, he rushed swiftly toward him, uttering a most dreadful sound. || 36 ||
Beholding that boar with its deformed face approaching, the lord of the earth, desiring to slay it, released an arrow at him. (37)
Then, having evaded that arrow by means of his speed and strength,
the boar emerged with great velocity, having leaped over the king at that time.
Beholding him as he was departing, the king, filled with wrath,
drew his bow with great effort and released sharp arrows.
For a moment coming within the king's range of vision, and for a moment disappearing from sight,
he rushed toward the boar while letting out various kinds of cries.
Highly incensed, Hariścandra pursued the deer, drawing his bowstring while mounted on a horse swift as the wind. || 41 ||
The army went here and there into the interior of the forest,
while the king, all alone, rushed toward a boar that was moving along.
At the time of midday, the king arrived in a secluded forest;
he became exceedingly thirsty and hungry, and his mount was exhausted. (43)
The boar vanished from sight, and the king became overwhelmed with anxiety;
lost on the path in the dense forest, he stood like a wretched man.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? I have no companion in the forest.
Not knowing my own path, where shall I go? he thought. (45)
While the king was thus lost in thought in that forest devoid of people, overcome by anxiety, he beheld a river of very pure water.
Beholding her, the king was delighted; having made the horse drink, he dismounted from the steed and drank the pure, excellent water.
Having drunk water there, the king, the lord of the earth, found comfort;
thus, utterly bewildered by his wandering through the quarters, he set out for the city. (48)
Viśvāmitra, having arrived assuming the form of an aged brahmin, was seen by the king, who bowed with affection to that best of the twice-born. (49)
King Gādhi spoke to that best of kings as he was bowing down:
"May it be well with you, O Great King; for what purpose have you come here? (50)
"O King, being alone in this desolate place, what do you intend to do here?
O best of kings, compose yourself and tell me everything—the reason for your presence. (51)
The king said:
A very large-bodied and powerful boar, having approached the Puṣpaka grove, quickly crushed the delicate flowering trees.
O best of sages, taking my bow in hand to restrain that wicked one, I departed from my own city accompanied by my army.
That wicked sorcerer has gone somewhere out of sight with great speed;
I have followed after him, while my army has vanished somewhere.
"Hungry and thirsty, having been separated from my army, I have come here;
O Sage, I do not know the way to the city nor the path of the army. (55)
"O Lord, show me the way; I am going toward the city.
By the power of my good fortune, you have been found by me here in this desolate forest. (56)
And I am the lord of Ayodhyā and other cities, the highly renowned Hariścandra; I am the performer of the Rājasūya sacrifice and the constant bestower of desired objects.
"O Brahmin, O best of the twice-born, if you have a desire for wealth for the sake of a sacrifice, you must come to Ayodhyā; I shall give you abundant riches. (58)

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Promise to Give Wealth to the Aged Brāhmaṇa through Hariścandra," in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 18.
The Offering of All Possessions to Kauśika and the Description of the Giving of that Dakṣiṇā.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the king, the sage Kauśika—
Laughing, he replied thus to Hariścandra, O King.
"O King, this sacred ford is meritorious, purifying, and destructive of sin;
perform your ablutions here, O illustrious one, as well as the libations for the ancestors."
O lord of the people, this is the most auspicious time here; having bathed at this sacred ford, bestow gifts according to your ability at this exceedingly purifying holy site.
He who reaches a highly meritorious sacred ford and departs without bathing becomes a destroyer of his own soul; thus Svāyambhuva has declared.
Therefore, O King, perform meritorious deeds according to your ability at this best of holy places;
I shall show you the way, and from there you will go to the city.
"O sinless one, O descendant of Kakutstha, I shall come today with you for the purpose of seeing the path, being gratified by your gift."
Having heard those words of the sage, which were adorned with deceit,
the king removed his garments and went to the river to bathe according to the prescribed rites.
Having tied the horse to a tree, deluded by the words of the sage,
he then fell under its power due to the inevitability of their union.
Having performed the ritual of bathing and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, the king said this to Viśvāmitra: "O Lord, I give a gift to you."
"O illustrious one, whatever you desire, that I shall give to you now:
cattle, land, gold, and vehicles such as elephants, horses, and chariots."
"There is nothing that I cannot give; this vow was undertaken by me long ago, even in the presence of the sages during the Rājasūya, the best of sacrifices. (11)
Therefore, O sage, since you have arrived here at this most excellent sacred ford, speak whatever you desire; I shall grant you that which you wish for.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O King, I have previously heard of your vast fame upon the earth, as proclaimed by Vasiṣṭha: 'There is no giver on the surface of the world.'"
Hariścandra, the best of kings and lord of the earth in the solar dynasty—
such a donor as that king has never existed before, nor will there ever be one again.
Just as the son of Triśaṅku was most noble on earth, so am I;
therefore, O King, I entreat you today, for I have a marriage to perform.
"And for the sake of my son, O illustrious one, grant me that wealth.
The king said:
"Perform the marriage, O best of Brahmins; I shall give you what you have requested. (16)
"If you desire wealth or any object of desire, I shall certainly give it to you.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by him, the sage Kauśika, who was intent on deception, [proceeded]. (17)
Manifesting his Gandharva-like power of illusion, the prince Sukumāra displayed it even to the king,
as did a ten-year-old girl.
O best of kings, the duty of these two must also be performed today;
for a householder, the merit derived from marriage is even greater than that of the Rājasūya sacrifice. (19)
"Today itself, you shall have a son born to you by a Brahmin woman.
Having heard those words, the king was deluded by her illusory power.
Having promised "So be it," he did not speak even a single word;
thus shown the way by him, he proceeded toward the city. (21)
Viśvāmitra also, having deceived the king, went to his hermitage;
once the marriage rites were completed, Viśvāmitra then spoke to the king.
"O King, today give whatever gift you desire upon the middle of the altar.
The king said:
"O twice-born one, tell me what is your wish; indeed, I shall grant your desire. (23)
"I am now desirous of fame in this world which is difficult to traverse;
for indeed, the life of one who has attained wealth is truly in vain. (24)
"Pure fame that bestows happiness in the next world has not been acquired.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O Great King, grant me the kingdom along with its appurtenances as a boon. (25)
Rich with elephants, horses, chariots, and jewels, [he stood] in the midst of the most sacred altar.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of the sage, the king was deluded by his illusory power. (26)
Having said "It is given," he [Daśaratha] bestowed the kingdom without reflection and by his own will;
Viśvāmitra, being exceedingly harsh, replied to him, "It has been accepted. (27)
"O Indra among kings, O high-minded one, give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) worthy of being given;
Manu has declared that a gift devoid of a sacrificial fee is fruitless. (28)
"Therefore, for the sake of the fruit of your gift, give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as prescribed.
Thus addressed, the king, being greatly amazed, then spoke to him: || 29 ||
"Tell me, O Master, how much wealth should now be given to you by me?
O holy one, please state the exact measure for the fee as a recompense. (30)
"I shall give this for the fulfillment of my gift; be at ease, O you whose wealth is asceticism.
Having heard that, Viśvāmitra spoke to that lord of the earth: (31)
"Give me now as a sacrificial fee two and a half bhāras of gold.
Having promised him, "I shall give it," the king was greatly amazed. (32)
At that very moment, his soldiers arrived while looking about;
seeing the lord of the earth agitated, they praised him, filled with joy.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard their words, the king, without saying anything good or bad,
went then into the inner apartments while reflecting upon his own past deeds.
"What gift of my entire possessions have I accepted that has been surrendered?
I have been cheated here in the forest by this brahmin, as if by thieves. (35)
I gave him the entire kingdom along with its appurtenances, as well as all my wealth and learning; furthermore, I offered two bhāras of gold and half a bhāra as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
"What shall I do? My mind is bewildered; I did not recognize the deception of the sage.
I have been suddenly deceived by this ascetic Brahmin. (37)
"I do not know the work of destiny; alas, O Fate, what will happen?
Thinking thus, the king, overcome with extreme agitation, reached his home. (38)
Seeing her husband absorbed in thought, the queen asked him the reason: "O Lord, why do you appear dejected? Tell me now, what is your anxiety? (39)
"Your son has returned from the forest; the Rājasūya sacrifice was performed long ago.
Why do you grieve, O Indra among kings? Tell us the cause of your sorrow. (40)
No enemy exists anywhere, whether powerful or weak;
even Varuṇa is well-pleased, for you have accomplished your purpose on this earth. (41)
The body wastes away through anxiety; there is no death equal to anxiety.
O tiger among kings, let it be abandoned; be at ease, O wise one. 42.
Having heard those affectionate words, the lord of men, filled with joy,
spoke somewhat regarding the cause of his reflection, both auspicious and inauspicious.
Overcome by anxiety, that king did not take his meal;
even after lying upon a white bed, the lord of the earth found no sleep.
Having risen in the morning, while the king, distressed by anxiety, was performing his twilight rites and other duties,
Viśvāmitra arrived.
The sage, who had taken away all his possessions, was reported to the king by the guards;
having arrived, he spoke to the king as the latter bowed down to him again and again.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O King, relinquish your own kingdom and give me that which was promised by your word.
O Indra among kings, touch gold and become true to your word this very moment. (47)
Hariścandra said:
"O Lord, this kingdom of mine is now indeed given by me to you;
having abandoned it, I shall go elsewhere. Do not worry, O Kauśika. (48)
"O Brahmin, O Lord, my entire property has been accepted from me according to the prescribed rites.
O twice-born one, I am currently unable to give the gift of gold. (49)
"I shall give you a gift now, as long as my income of wealth lasts;
furthermore, when the time is right, I will then give you a sacrificial fee. (50)
Having spoken thus, the king said to his son and his wife Mādhavī:
"Indeed, this very extensive kingdom has been granted by me to him upon the sacrificial altar."
Having abandoned his three bodies, he surrendered everything to him—the elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as the jewels and gold. || 52 ||
"Having abandoned Ayodhyā, I shall go somewhere into a forest thicket;
let this sage properly take over this kingdom, which is fully endowed with all prosperity. (53)
Having thus addressed his son and his wife, the virtuous Hariścandra departed from his palace,
honoring that best of the twice-born.
Seeing the king departing, both his wife and son, overcome with anxiety and with dejected faces, then followed behind him.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose in the city upon seeing them in such a state;
all the living beings dwelling in the city of Sāketa wailed aloud. (56)
"Alas, O King! What deed has been done? From where has this suffering come?
You have been deceived, O Great King, by Fate, who is truly unwise. (57)
Then all the social orders (varṇas) would suffer distress upon seeing that lord of the earth together with his wife and his high-souled son. 58.
But the city-dwellers, including the brahmins and others, afflicted by grief, censured that brahmin of wicked conduct, saying, "This man is a rogue. (59)
Having emerged from that city, Viśvāmitra approached the king as he was departing and spoke these harsh words to him.
"O lord of men, go after giving me the gold for the sacrificial fee;
otherwise, tell me that I shall not give it, for the gold has already been relinquished by me. (61)
"Take back the entire kingdom if greed still persists in your heart;
O King, if you consider it already given, then give that which was promised. (62)
To Gādheya, who was speaking thus, King Hariścandra, with a deeply distressed soul, bowed down and spoke with palms joined in reverence: || 63 ||

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Offering of All Possessions to Kauśika and the Description of the Bestowal of that Dakṣiṇā," in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Narrative of Hariścandra.
Hariścandra said:
"Without having given you gold, I shall certainly not take my meal."
This is my vow, O best of sages; cast away your despondency, O you of noble observances.
I am a Kṣatriya king born of the Solar dynasty,
the performer of the Rājasūya sacrifice, desired among men.
"O Lord, how can I avoid taking on a form at will?
O best of the twice-born, a debt must certainly be repaid to you. (3)
"Be at ease; I shall give you gold as desired by your heart.
Wait for some time until I have acquired wealth. (4)
Viśvāmitra said:
"O King, how will you obtain wealth from this point forward? Your kingdom has gone, as have your treasury, your army, and the means for achieving your purposes."
"O protector of the earth, your hope for wealth is in vain; what can I do?
O King, how could I afflict you, who are destitute, with greed? (6)
Therefore, O protector of the earth, tell me now: "I will not give it.
Having abandoned my great hope, I shall certainly depart from here. (7)
"Go as you wish, O Indra among kings, accompanied by your wife and sons.
Gold is no longer mine; tell me now what I shall give to you. (8)
Having heard these words of the Brahmin while on his way, the king replied to the sage: "O Brahmin, maintain your composure; I shall grant it to you."
"My body, my wife, and my city are indeed free from ailment;
having purchased that very body, O twice-born one, I shall surely repay your debt. (10)
"O Lord of Brahmins, O Master, look for a purchaser in the city of Vārāṇasī;
I shall enter into servitude there, together with my wife and my son. (11)
"O Sage, O Supporter of the Earth, accept this full two-and-a-half-bhāra measure of gold;
having given it at its value, be satisfied with us all. (12)
Speaking thus, he then departed with his wife and accompanied by his sons,
together with his beloved Umā, to where Śaṅkara himself was dwelling.
And having seen that beautiful city which brings delight to the mind,
he said, "I have achieved my purpose, beholding this city of such great splendor."
Then, having reached the Bhāgīrathī, bathed, performed the libations for the gods and others,
and completed the worship of the deities, he cast his gaze in all directions.
Having entered the divine city of Vārāṇasī, the protector of the earth [thought]:
"This is not for human enjoyment; it is the domain of the wielder of the trident. (16)
Afflicted by grief and deeply distressed, he went on foot together with his wife;
having entered the city, the king then established his trust [in that place]. 17.
Then he beheld the best of sages, a Brāhmaṇa seeking sacrificial fees;
seeing him arrived, he became bowed down with humility.
And having joined his palms in reverence, Hariścandra said to the great sage:
"O Sage, these are my vital breaths, this is my son, and this is my beloved wife. (19)
"O best of the twice-born, take today whatever you have need of;
you should also tell me what other business we may have for you. (20)
Viśvāmitra said:
"The month is complete; may you be blessed. Let the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) be given to me, if indeed your own previous word is remembered as the cause for that."
The king said:
"O Brahmin, even now the month is not yet complete, O you whose power lies in knowledge and austerity;
since only half a day remains, wait for that and nothing else."
Viśvāmitra said:
"So be it, O great king; I shall come again.
If you do not grant [the request] today, I will pronounce a curse upon you. (23)
Having spoken thus, the brahmin departed; then the king reflected:
"How shall I bestow upon him the sacrificial fee that was promised? (24)
Where are my well-nourished friends? Where now is my wealth? Since accepting gifts has become a source of corruption for me, how could I possibly resort to begging? (25)
"The three modes of conduct for kings have been declared with certainty in the treatises on Dharma;
yet, if I were to relinquish my life without having bestowed the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), [I would incur sin]. (26)
By seizing the property of a Brahmin, I shall become a worm, a sinner, and the lowest of the low;
or else I shall go to the state of a ghost—therefore, the sale of oneself is indeed better.
Sūta said:
Then the wife replied to the king, who was agitated, dejected, and brooding with his face cast downward, in a voice faltering with tears.
Abandon your anxiety, O Great King, and uphold your own duty;
for a man who is excluded from truth should be shunned like a ghost. (29)
"O tiger among men, they say there is no higher duty for a person than this: the observance of one's own truth. (30)
The Agnihotra sacrifice, Vedic study, and all rites such as giving gifts—all these become fruitless for that person whose speech is untruthful. (31)
Truth is indeed supremely exalted in the treatises on Dharma for the wise;
likewise, falsehood leads to the crossing over [of the world] for some, but to the downfall of those who have not disciplined their selves. (32)
Having disregarded a hundred horse-sacrifices and even the Rājasūya, that king, after performing [the latter] once, fell from heaven due to his untruthful speech. (33)
The king said:
"This son, who shall increase the lineage, remains but a child.
O lady with the gait of an elephant, speak whatever words you desire to say."
The wife said:
"O King, let there be no falsehood in you; women bear fruit through their sons.
Therefore, having given me away for wealth, bestow me as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) upon the Brahmin. (35)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words, the lord of the earth fell into a swoon;
and having regained consciousness, he lamented, being exceedingly distressed.
"O blessed lady, this is a great sorrow that you speak thus to me;
have my smiles and friendly conversations been forgotten by you, a sinner? (37)
"Alas, alas! O lady of pure smiles, how is it fitting for you to speak such words?
O beautiful woman, why do you utter this speech which is so difficult to hear? (38)
Having spoken thus, that best of kings— who was not steadfast in the face of selling his wife—
fell upon the surface of the earth, utterly overwhelmed by a swoon.
Seeing the lord of the earth lying on the ground, overcome by a swoon, the princess, deeply distressed, spoke these words with great compassion: (40)
Alas, Great King! From whose ill-will has this come upon you, that you, who are worthy of refuge, have fallen to the ground like a beggar? (41)
He by whom wealth was bestowed upon brahmins by the tens of millions—he, that very lord of the earth, my husband, now sleeps upon the ground. (42)
