Alas, what a tragedy! O Fate, what has this king done to you, that he—equal to Indra and Upendra—has been brought to this wretched state? (43)
Having spoken thus, that woman of beautiful hips fell down in a swoon,
utterly overwhelmed by the unbearable and immense burden of grief for her husband.
Seeing this, the child, overcome by hunger and deeply distressed, spoke these words:
"Father, father, give me food! Mother, give me something to eat! (45)
Hunger has become powerful within me; the tip of my tongue is excessively parched. || 46 ||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Legend of Hariścandra," in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
In the meantime, the great ascetic Viśvāmitra arrived,
enraged like the God of Death himself, with the intent of asking for his own wealth from his heart.
Upon seeing him, Hariścandra fell to the ground in a swoon;
having sprinkled water upon the king, he spoke these words to him. (2)
"Arise, arise, O Indra among kings! Give back your own desired sacrificial fee.
For those who harbor a debt, suffering increases day by day. (3)
Then, being refreshed by that water as cold as ice,
the king regained consciousness and looked toward Viśvāmitra.
Then the sage again fell into delusion and became angry;
having consoled the king, that best of the twice-born spoke these words.
Viśvāmitra said:
"Let that sacrificial fee be given to me, if you have regard for steadfastness;
by truth the sun shines, and upon truth the earth stands firm. (6)
Truth has been declared the supreme dharma; heaven is established upon truth.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were once placed upon a scale [and weighed]. (7)
Indeed, a single truth excels a thousand horse-sacrifices;
or rather, what need have I for this that has been said? (8)
"O King, if you do not give me my sacrificial fee, I shall certainly curse you once the sun has set behind the western mountain. (9)
Having spoken thus, the brahmin departed; and the king became afflicted by fear, miserable and destitute on the earth, tormented by the cruel sage.
Sūta said:
In the meantime, a Brāhmaṇa who had mastered the Vedas came out from his own house accompanied by many other Brāhmaṇas.
Then, seeing that ascetic standing there as he approached, the queen spoke these words, consistent with righteousness and purpose, to the king.
Among the three castes as well, the father is called a Brāhmaṇa;
for there is no doubt that the father’s property must be taken by the son. || 13 ||
"Therefore, it is my opinion that he should be entreated for wealth.
The king said, "O slender-waisted one, I do not desire a gift; I am a Kshatriya."
Indeed, begging is not known among Brahmins;
for the Brahmin is the preceptor of all social classes and is always worthy of worship. (15)
Therefore, a preceptor should not be entreated [for wealth] by Kṣatriyas, especially;
for sacrifice, study, and giving are prescribed for the Kṣatriya. (16)
Granting fearlessness to those who have come for refuge and protecting the subjects—this is what must be done; one should not utter such piteous words as "Give [me]! (17).
"O Goddess, the words 'I give' are ever fixed in my heart;
whatever wealth I have acquired from anywhere, I give it to a Brāhmaṇa. (18)
The wife said:
Time makes things even and uneven; time bestows both humiliation and honor. It is time that makes a man either a giver or a beggar. (19)
Behold the workings of Time: the king was cast out from his kingdom and his happiness by a learned Brahmin who, though exceedingly powerful, was provoked to anger. (20)
The king said:
"It would be better for my tongue to be cut in two with a sharp-edged sword than for me, having abandoned pride, to utter the words, 'Give, give! (21)
"I am a Kṣatriya, O illustrious lady; I do not beg for anything at all.
Indeed, I always give away wealth acquired by the strength of my own arms. (22)
The wife said:
"O Great King, if indeed your mind is not inclined to beg,
I have been given to you rightfully even by the gods, including Indra."
O one of great splendor, I am to be instructed by my father and protected by my husband;
therefore, having taken my price, let it be given for the sake of the preceptor. (24)
Having heard these words, King Hariścandra, crying out "Alas! Alas!", lamented, being exceedingly distressed.
And his wife spoke further: "Do as I say;
because you have been consumed by the fire of a brahmin’s curse, you will fall into a low state. (26)

Not for the sake of splendor, nor for the sake of intoxicants, nor for the sake of sovereignty, nor for the sake of enjoyments—therefore, give this for the sake of your guru; make your vow of truthfulness bear fruit.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Legend of Hariścandra," in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 21 ||
The Description of Hariścandra’s Sale of His Wife and Son.
Vyāsa said:
Thus urged again and again by his wife, the king—
He said, "O blessed lady, I, utterly merciless, shall carry out your sale. || 1 ||
I shall do that which even the cruel cannot do,
if your speech shines forth so exceedingly harsh to utter.
Having spoken thus, the king, that best of monarchs, went to the city in great distress; then, having brought his wife down into the arena,
he spoke these words with a throat choked by tears.
O all you citizens, listen to my words! || 4 ||
If anyone has any business with me, let him speak with haste while I still hold my life-breath through this sacrifice for my own life. || 5 ||
The learned men said, "Who are you that has come to sell your wife?
The king replied, "Why do you ask me who I am? O cruel one, I am a non-human being."
"Or perhaps I am a cruel Rākṣasa, and for that reason I commit this sin.
Vyāsa said:
Having suddenly heard those words, Kauśika, who was assuming the form of a Brahmin, [spoke]. (7)
Assuming the form of an old man, he spoke to Hariścandra:
"Hand over a female slave to me; I am a purchaser who provides the wealth. (8)
"I possess incomparable wealth and my beloved wife is delicate;
she is unable to perform household chores, therefore grant her to me. (9)
"I shall take a female slave; how much wealth will you give me?"—when this was said by the brahmin, King Hariścandra [replied]. (10)
His heart was rent with grief, yet he said nothing to him.
The Brahmin said:
"In deed, age, appearance, and character, you are equal to your wife. (11)
"Take this wealth which is appropriate; give me back my weak woman.
For that which is seen in the treatises on dharma regarding the price of a woman and a man—" (12)
Endowed with the thirty-two marks, skillful, and possessed of the virtues of moral conduct—
such women and men [should be given] a crown worth ten million gold pieces, and likewise [a necklace worth] one hundred million.
Having heard these words of his, King Hariścandra was overcome with great sorrow and said nothing at all to him.
Then that brahmin, having placed the wealth upon the bark garment before the king, seized the queen by her hair and dragged her away. || 15 ||
The queen said: "Release me, release me at once, O noble one, so that I may see my son;
O Brahmin, it will be difficult for me to behold him again. (16)
"Behold here, my son, me, your mother, reduced to such servitude!
Do not touch me, O prince; I am no longer to be touched by you now. (17)
Then that boy, suddenly seeing his mother drawn away, ran toward her with tears in his eyes, crying out, "O Mother! (amba).
Then, as he approached pulling at his garment with his hand, his hair still in the form of side-locks,
and stumbling along, the brahmin struck him out of anger, even though he was but a child.
Even while speaking thus, "O Mother," he would not let go of his mother.
The queen said: "O Lord, show me favor; please purchase this boy. (20)
"Even though I have been purchased, I shall not be effective in accomplishing this task without him.
Therefore, O Lord, grant your favor to me, one of such little fortune. (21)
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Let this wealth of yours be taken; let my boy be given to me.
For the fee for a man and a woman has indeed been fixed by those who know the Dharmaśāstras. (22)
Others [offered her] with a value of a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, or ten million;
she was endowed with the thirty-two marks, skillful, and possessed of the virtues of moral conduct.
"A woman's [fine] is declared to be ten million [gold pieces], and likewise a man's is one hundred million.
Sūta said:
"In that very manner, his wealth was again cast upon the cloth before him."
Taking hold of the boy, he bound him together with his mother;
filled with joy, he set out quickly for home along with her.
Having performed a circumambulation, she knelt down in prostration and, distressed and overwhelmed with tears, spoke these words: || 26 ||
If I have given gifts, if I have offered oblations, and if I have gratified the Brahmins—by that merit, may my husband Hariścandra truly be restored to me once again. || 27 ||
Seeing her fallen at his feet—she who was dearer to him than his own life—the king, crying out "Alas! Alas!", lamented with his senses overwhelmed.
How has she become separated from him who was endowed with truthfulness, virtue, and excellence?
For even the shade of a tree never abandons that tree at any time. (29)
Having thus spoken to his wife with these well-connected words, he then said this to his son: "Where will you go, leaving me behind? (30)
"To which direction shall I go? Who will ward off my sorrow?
O twice-born one, I have no grief in the renunciation of the kingdom, nor do I have any grief in dwelling in the forest. (31)
"That my son should be separated from me," said that king; "for in this world, wives are indeed always intended to be enjoyed by their virtuous husbands. (32)
"O auspicious lady, you have been abandoned by me and cast into misery—you who were born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku and were worthy of all the pleasures of sovereignty. (33)
"Having obtained such a husband as me, you have indeed fallen into the state of a slave;
for I am sinking here into a vast ocean of grief. (34)
"O Goddess, who will deliver me through the detailed accounts of ancient legends?
Sūta said:
While that royal sage was looking on, [he was struck] with most cruel lashes of the whip.
Having had them killed, the lord of brahmins proceeded to lead them away;
seeing his wife and son being led away, that king— || 36 ||
Afflicted by extreme sorrow, he sighed hotly again and again and lamented:
"Her whom neither the wind, nor the sun, nor the moon, nor ordinary people [could behold]... (37)
"We saw her formerly as our wife; she has now fallen into slavery. And this man, born of the Solar dynasty, with his delicate fingers and limbs—" (38)
The child has been brought to sale; fie on me, the evil-minded! Alas, my beloved! Alas, my infant! O dear one, this is the misfortune of my ignoble self. (39)
"Having fallen into a state dependent on fate, yet I have not died—fie upon me!
Vyāsa said: Having lamented thus before the king, the brahmin vanished.
Taking with him tall trees, houses, and other such items, he proceeded with great haste;
in the meantime, the best of sages, a man of great asceticism, arrived there.
Accompanied by his disciples, that lord of the Kauśikas was harsh and cruel in appearance.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O King, as for the sacrificial fee for the Rājasūya which you mentioned previously—" (42)
"O mighty-armed one, give her up if truth is held paramount.
Hariścandra said:
"I pay homage to you, O royal sage; please accept this as your own sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). (43)
"O sinless one, regarding that Rājasūya sacrifice which I previously mentioned," Viśvāmitra said:
"From where was this wealth obtained, which is being given for the purpose of the sacrificial fee? (44)
"Tell me this, O Indra among kings: how was the wealth acquired by you?
The king said:
"O illustrious one, O sinless one, what is the use of telling this to you? (45)
"O brahmin of noble vows, my grief increases because of this learning.
The seer said:
"I do not accept what is improper; give me only that which is proper. (46)
"O King, tell me truly how this wealth came to be.
The king said:
"That queen, my wife, was sold by me for ten million [pieces of gold]."
"My son, named Rohita, has been sold for ten billion niṣkas;
O Brahmin, please accept from me eleven crores of gold. (48)
Sūta said:
Perceiving that wealth to have been acquired through the sale of his wife, the enraged Kauśika spoke to the king, who was overwhelmed by grief: (49)
The sage said: "This is not the sacrificial fee for the Rājasūya sacrifice;
produce something else quickly, by which it may become complete. (50)
"O kṣatriya, if you consider this worthy bride of mine to be a suitable sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), then quickly behold my supreme strength. (51)
Of this well-performed austerity of the stainless Brahmin,
and of my own fierce power, as well as of his pure study of the Vedas— 52.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, I shall give you something else; let some time be awaited.
My wife and young son have just now been sold. (53)
Viśvāmitra said:
"O lord of men, only this one-fourth portion of the day that remains is to be awaited by me; you must not speak further."

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Hariścandra’s Sale of His Wife and Son," in the seventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Legend of Hariścandra.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus spoken these cruel and harsh words to the king, [he departed].
Having taken that full amount of wealth, the enraged Kauśika departed.
When Viśvāmitra had departed, the king then fell into grief;
sighing repeatedly, he spoke aloud with his face cast downward. || 2 ||
"Let him who suffers distress because of wealth purchased by me, having become a ghost, speak with haste while the sun still remains in the sky. (3)
Then Dharma arrived in haste, assuming the form of a Caṇḍāla—
foul-smelling, with a deformed chest, bearded, protruding teeth, and devoid of compassion.
Kṛṣṇa was pot-bellied, oily-skinned, and terrifying— the lowest of men—
carrying a staff worn out by his hands and adorned with garlands of corpses.
The Cāṇḍāla said:
"I accept you for slavery, as my need for servants is very great. Tell me quickly, what is the price for this that is being offered to you? (6)
Vyāsa said:
Then, observing him to be such—a man of cruel gaze, utterly pitiless, and speaking with extreme ill-nature—the king asked, "Who are you? (7)
The Cāṇḍāla said:
"O best of kings, I am known here as the Cāṇḍāla Pravīra;
always remain under my command as the remover of the clothes of the dead."
Thus addressed, the king then spoke these words:
"Whether it be a Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya, let him take [it]; this is my intention. (9)
"The highest dharma belongs to the highest, the middle to the middle, and the lowest indeed to the lowest—so say the wise. (10)
The Cāṇḍāla said:
"O best of kings, you have indeed described dharma in this very way;
O King, you have now spoken before me without having reflected upon it. (11)
The man who speaks after having reflected obtains his desired object;
that which was spoken by you, O sinless one, without reflection, is merely common.
"If truth is your authority for you, then you have been captured; of this there is no doubt.
Hariścandra said:
"The lowest of men, by means of untruth, would immediately go to a cruel hell. (13)
"Therefore, it is better for me to be a virtuous outcaste than to be untruthful.
Vyāsa said:
While he was speaking thus, Viśvāmitra, that treasury of asceticism, arrived.
With eyes rolling in anger and indignation, he said this to the lord of men:
"This outcaste has come forward to give you the wealth that was in your mind. (15)
"Why is the entire sacrificial fee not given to me?
The King said:
"O Kauśika, O Blessed One, I know myself to be born of the Solar dynasty. (16)
"And how shall I go to the state of a Cāṇḍāla slave out of desire for wealth?
Viśvāmitra said:
"If you give me the wealth of a Cāṇḍāla born from the sale of yourself..."
"If you do not give it, then I shall undoubtedly curse you;
therefore, give me the wealth of the sacrificial fee from either a Cāṇḍāla or a Brāhmaṇa. (18)
"O King, apart from this Cāṇḍāla, there is no one else who can provide me with wealth;
without wealth, O King, I shall not go—of this there is no doubt. (19)
O King, if you do not give me my wealth this very moment, then when half a ghaṭikā remains of the day, I shall consume you with the fire of my curse.
Vyāsa said: Then King Hariścandra, his life-breath having returned as if from death, spoke the words "Be gracious" and, overwhelmed with emotion, grasped the feet of the seer.
Hariścandra said:
"I am your slave, I am afflicted, I am wretched, and I am especially devoted to you.
Grant me your grace, O brahmin-sage; for this mingling with outcasts is miserable. (22)
With whatever remains of my wealth, O tiger among sages, may I become your submissive servant; may I be your very messenger, following your every wish.
Viśvāmitra said:
"So be it, O great king; become my very servant.
However, O lord of men, my word must always be carried out."
Vyāsa said:
When these words had been spoken, the king, filled with joy,
considered himself born again and spoke to Kauśika.
"I shall always carry out your command; of this there is no doubt.
Give me your orders, O best of the twice-born; what may I do for you, O sinless one? (26)
Viśvāmitra said:
"O Cāṇḍāla, come! What price for my slave will you give me?
Take this slave now, given by me at his price."
"I have no need for a servant; my desire is for wealth.
Vyāsa said:
When he had spoken thus, his own partisan was delighted in heart. (28)
Having arrived quickly into his presence, he spoke to Viśvāmitra.
The Cāṇḍāla said:
"Within the precinct of Prayāga, extending for ten yojanas..."
"O best of the twice-born, having made the earth consist of jewels, I shall give it to you;
by this sale, your distress has been dispelled."
Vyāsa said:
Then the best of the twice-born accepted thousands of jewels given by the Cāṇḍāla, including gold, gems, and pearls.
King Hariścandra likewise remained with an expression free from agitation;
for out of such fortitude, he thought, "Viśvāmitra is indeed my master."
"I must perform exactly that which he shall cause me to do.
Then, suddenly, an incorporeal voice spoke from the sky:
"O highly fortunate one, you are now free from debt; that sacrificial fee has been paid by you.
Thereupon, a rain of flowers fell from the sky upon the head of the king.
"Excellent! Excellent! said the gods, including Indra, who were possessed of great majesty.
Overcome with great joy, the king spoke to Kauśika.
The king said:
"O high-minded one, you are indeed my mother and my father; you are my kinsman.
For your sake I have been liberated, and in an instant I have been made free from debt."
"What shall I do, O mighty-armed one? Your word is beneficial to me.
When these words had been spoken, the sage addressed the king.
Viśvāmitra said: "O King, from this day forward, you must carry out the word of the Cāṇḍāla.
May it be well with you! Having spoken thus to him, he took that wealth and departed. (38)

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Hariścandra," in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 23 ||
The Description of Hariścandra’s Reflection.
Śaunaka said:
What did the king do after he had gone to the house of the Caṇḍāla?
Therefore, O best of charioteers, speak to me who am asking you; for I am in haste.
Sūta said:
When the brahmin Viśvāmitra had departed, the outcaste, his heart filled with joy,
gave those goods to Viśvāmitra and bound the lord of men.
Saying, "You shall go [to hell], you liar! he then struck him with a staff;
his mind was bewildered by the blow of the staff, and his senses were utterly agitated. (3)
Having brought the man, who was afflicted by the pain of separation from his beloved kinsman, to his own hamlet and placing him in fetters, he himself slept soundly, free from anxiety.
Then the king, remaining in fetters while dwelling in the settlement of the Cāṇḍālas,
renounced food and drink and constantly lamented.
Seeing the boy with a dejected face before her, the slender woman, her own face dejected and overcome by sorrow,
will remember me and the king will deliver us both.
Having given away his acquired wealth and the wealth he had promised to the Brahmin,
he will see his weeping son and awaken me as well.
She will likewise console the weeping boy who says, "I am going to my father's side," as he repeatedly calls out, "Father! Father! (8).
That fawn-eyed woman does not know that I have fallen into the state of a Cāṇḍāla;
she knows not of the loss of my kingdom, the abandonment of my friends, or the sale of my wife and son.
And thus this state of being a caṇḍāla—alas, what a succession of miseries!
Living there constantly in this manner, he would remember his beloved wife and his son.
Afflicted by fate, the king passed four days;
then, on the fifth day, the other king was released from his fetters by him.
And he was instructed by a Cāṇḍāla in the removal of the clothes of the deceased, having been repeatedly rebuked with harsh words by that angry man. || 12 ||
And on the southern side of Kāśī, there exists a great cremation ground;
protect it according to the law, for it must never be abandoned by you. (13)
"Take this worn-out staff and go without delay;
proclaim everywhere: 'This is the staff of Vīrabāhu.'"
Sūta said:
Now at a certain time, King Hariścandra, who was a carrier of the clothes of the deceased, went to the cremation ground accompanied by his attendants. (15)
Instructed by a Cāṇḍāla who collected the clothes of the deceased,
the king, commanded by him, went to the cremation ground.
In the southern region of the city, there was a terrifying place, strewn with garlands of corpses, foul-smelling, and filled with much smoke. || 17 ||
The cremation ground was filled with terrifying sounds and crowded with hundreds of jackals;
it was swarming with vultures and jackals and surrounded by packs of dogs. || 18 ||
It was crowded with heaps of bones and filled with a great stench;
it was filled with half-burnt corpses whose rows of teeth were bared. (19)
The body situated thus in the midst of fire appears as if laughing;
it resounds with the various friend-sounds of nectar, tumultuous with a great clamor.
"Alas, my son! Alas, my friend! Alas, my kinsman! O brother, my dear child! Today you are being abandoned by me! Alas, worthy nephew! Alas, maternal uncle! Grandfather! (21)
"O grandfather! O father! O grandson! Where have you gone? Come here, O kinsman!"—with such terrifying cries from all embodied beings was the place filled.
It was filled with the hissing sounds of burning flesh, fat, and marrow, where the terrifying crackling of the fire arose. (23)
That most dreadful cremation ground, appearing like the end of an eon,
was reached by the king, who there lamented thus out of grief.
"Alas, you servants and ministers! Where is that kingdom, so worthy of your lineage?
Alas, my dear young son! Having abandoned me, unfortunate as I am—" (25)
And because of the Brahmin’s anger, you have gone far away;
for without righteousness, no auspiciousness ever arises for human beings. (26)
"Therefore, a man should indeed uphold dharma with great effort.
Thinking thus, he reflected repeatedly on what had been said there by the Caṇḍāla.
With all his limbs smeared with filth, he went about beholding corpses;
appearing like a mere walking stick, he ran hither and thither. (28)
"In this corpse, I shall obtain this price of one hundred [coins] right here;
this is mine, this is the king's, and this is the Caṇḍāla's. (29)
Reflecting thus, the king fell into a difficult predicament;
he took up a patched garment made from a single worn-out cloth with its seams well-knit.
His face, arms, belly, and feet were smeared with the dust of funeral pyre ashes;
his hands and fingers were coated with various kinds of fat, marrow, and grease, as he breathed heavily.
Intent on satisfying his hunger with various kinds of rice and meat, he had the circle of his head adorned by contact with her garlands. (32)
He did not sleep by night or by day, crying out "Alas! Alas! repeatedly;
thus twelve months were passed, which felt like a hundred years.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Hariścandra’s Anxiety," in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 24 ||
The description of Hariścandra taking up the sword at the command of the Cāṇḍāla.
Sūta said:
Once, he went out to play together with the boys.
Not far from Vārāṇasī, there was a young boy named Rohita.
Having finished his play, he then proceeded to take darbha grass—
tender, with small roots and tips— according to his ability.
Having said, "For the sake of noble joy," he should diligently take with both hands sacrificial fuel-sticks possessing the proper characteristics,
as well as the sacrificial grass and the firewood, all of which possess the proper characteristics.
Taking pieces of *palāśa* wood with care for the purpose of the fire-oblation,
he bore the burden upon his head, wearying at every step.
Then, having reached a place of water, the child, overcome by thirst,
set down his burden upon the ground at that watering place.
Having drunk water at his pleasure and rested for a moment,
he set down his burden upon an anthill and proceeded to carry it away.
Then, by the command of Viśvāmitra, a terrifying black serpent,
highly venomous and most formidable, emerged from an anthill.
By him that boy was bitten and fell down at that very moment;
seeing Rohita dead, the boys went to the house of the twice-born.
Hurried and agitated by fear, they said in the presence of her mother: "O servant of the brahmin, your son has gone outside to play. (9)
"Accompanied by us, he was bitten by a snake there and died.
Having heard those words of his, which were like the falling of a thunderbolt, she [then]— || 10 ||
She fell unconscious upon the ground like a severed plantain tree;
then the enraged Brahmin sprinkled her with water.
After a moment she regained consciousness, and the Brāhmaṇa then spoke to her.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Knowing that it is censurable and a cause of misfortune, you [have acted thus] at the onset of night."
"You weep, O wicked woman; is there no shame in your heart?
When addressed thus by the Brahmin, she did not utter a single word in reply. (13)
Afflicted by grief for her son, the wretched woman wept piteously;
her face was filled with tears, she was miserable, soiled, and her hair was disheveled.
Then, enraged, the brahmin spoke to that queen: "Fie on you, wicked woman! Having taken my fee, you are ruining my business. (15)
"If you are incapable, then how was that wealth of mine taken?
Thus she was repeatedly reviled by him with cruel words.
Weeping, she spoke the cause to the Brahmin with a faltering voice:
"O Master, my young son was bitten by a snake and died outside. (17)
"Grant me permission; I shall go to see the child.
O you of noble vows, it has become difficult for me to obtain a sight of him. (18)
Having spoken thus piteously, the young woman wept once more;
then the brahmin, becoming angry, spoke again to the king’s wife.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
O deceitful one of wicked conduct, do you not know that it is a sin for one who, having received wages from his master, ruins his work? (20)
Then he is cooked in hell, beginning with Mahāraurava;
having dwelt in hell for a kalpa, he thereafter becomes a cock.
Or rather, what need have I for this proclamation of my own righteousness, since I am one who is devoted to sin, foolish, cruel, base, untruthful, and deceitful? (22)
That speech would be fruitless toward him, like a seed in saline soil;
come, if you have any fear of the next world. (23)
Having been addressed thus, she, trembling, spoke these words to the brahmin:
"Have compassion for me, O Lord; be gracious and look upon me with a favorable countenance. (24)
"Wait for me for a moment until I have seen my child.
Having spoken thus, she then prostrated with her head at the feet of the twice-born man. (25)
The young woman, afflicted by grief for her son, wept piteously;
then the brahmin, his eyes bloodshot with rage, spoke in anger.
The Brahmin said:
"What business have I with your son? Perform my household chores for me! Do you not know my anger, which yields the fruit of lashes from a whip? (27)
Having been addressed thus, she remained steadfast in her composure and performed her domestic duties;
midnight passed for her while she was engaged in tasks such as massaging his feet.
Then the Brāhmaṇa said to her: "Go now to your son's side;
after performing his cremation and other rites, return again quickly. (29)
Thinking, "May my household duties not be neglected this morning," she then went out alone at night, lamenting.
Seeing her own son dead, she was deeply afflicted by grief, like a doe strayed from the herd, or like a cow deprived of her calf. (31)
Having gone outside Vārāṇasī, he saw in an instant his own son lying on the ground like a beggar upon wood, darbha grass, and straw.
Afflicted by extreme grief, she lamented, uttering a most harsh cry: "Come before me! Why are you angry? Tell me now! (33)
Constantly calling out "O Mother! as she went toward him, she walked with faltering steps and fell upon him, unconscious.
Regaining consciousness once more, she embraced the boy with both arms,
placed her face against his, and then wept with cries of distress.
He struck him on the head and the belly with both hands, crying out:
"Alas, my boy! Alas, my child! Alas, my dear one! Alas, my beautiful youth! (36)
"Alas, O King, where have you gone? Behold this, your own child, dearer to you than life itself, fallen dead upon the ground! (37)
Seeing his face thus, she again hoped for his life;
but perceiving that his face was lifeless, she fainted and fell down.
Taking hold of his face with his hand, he spoke again in this way:
"O child, leave your bed; wake up quickly, for it is terrifying! (39)
Midnight advanced,
resounding with the howling of hundreds of jackals and the cries of throngs of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and ḍākinīs.
"Your friends have departed; why do you remain here all alone?
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the slender woman wept piteously once more.
"Alas, my infant! Alas, my child! O young boy named Rohita!
My son, why do you not give me an answer? (42)
"I am your mother, my child; do you not know me? Look at me!
O son, [I have suffered] from exile from my country, the loss of my kingdom, and being sold by my own husband. (43)
"O son, it is solely because I have seen you that I live as a slave;
for at the time of your birth, the brahmins predicted this regarding your future."
Long-lived, O King of the Earth, he shall be endowed with sons and grandsons;
devoted to valor and charity, he shall be courageous and a worshiper of gurus, gods, and the twice-born. (45)
"One who does what is pleasing to his parents, speaks the truth, and has conquered his senses"—all such qualities as these, my son, have now become untrue. (46)
O son, upon the palm of your hand are a wheel, a fish, an umbrella, the śrīvatsa, a svastika, a banner, a jar, and likewise a fly-whisk.
Furthermore, O son, all those other auspicious marks that were upon your hand have now become fruitless.
Alas, O King, Lord of the Earth! Where is your kingdom? Where are your ministers?
Where is your throne and your parasol? Where is your sword and where is that wealth? (49)
Where is that Ayodhyā? Where are the palaces? Where are the elephants, horses, chariots, and subjects?
O son, having abandoned me, where have you gone, leaving all this behind? 50.
"O beloved! O King, come! Behold this dear son of yours, by whom your chest was smeared with saffron as he played. (51)
By you, in your childhood, that vast expanse was defiled with the dust and mud of your own body, even though it had been anointed with musk.
"O King, the tilaka on your forehead has been displaced by the one resting in your lap—he whose face was smeared with clay and kissed by me out of affection. (53)
Behold that face, once to be kissed by flies, now defiled by worms!
Alas, O King, look at that son lying on the ground, dead like a beggar! (54)
"Alas, O Lord! What deed was performed by me in a previous existence, the end of which fruit of karma I do not perceive here? (55)
"Alas, my son! Alas, my child! My dear one! O handsome youth!
Hearing her lamentation thus, the city guards [approached]. || 56 ||
Awakened and greatly astonished, they quickly went to her side.
The people said:
"Who are you? To which child does he belong? And where is your husband? (57)
"Why do you weep here alone and fearlessly at night?
When she was addressed thus, that slender woman did not say anything in reply. (58)
Questioned once more, she became silent and paralyzed;
afflicted with extreme sorrow, her eyes overflowing with tears of grief, she lamented.
Then, filled with suspicion toward her, their hair standing on end with thrill,
they became terrified and spoke to one another with weapons raised in their hands.
"Surely this is not a woman, since she says nothing at all;
therefore, she must be put to death with effort, for she is a slayer of children. (61)
If she is auspicious, why then does she stand outside at this midnight?
Surely some child has been brought here by her for the purpose of devouring.
Having spoken thus, they quickly seized her by the hair with great force;
others likewise grasped her by her two arms, and some by her throat.
"She will go to Khecarī," so it was said by many with weapons in their hands;
she was dragged away, led to the outcaste settlement, and surrendered to a Cāṇḍāla. (64)
"O Caṇḍāla, we have indeed seen that child-killer outside; let her be executed, let her be executed! Take her quickly to a place outside. (65)
Seeing her, the Cāṇḍāla said: "This woman is world-renowned for her kinship;
she has never before been seen by anyone, even by the children of the world in their various forms. (66)
"Much has been eaten by her, and great merit has been acquired by you;
your fame shall be eternal in the world. Now depart as you please. (67)

The man who kills a twice-born, a woman, a child, or a cow; he who steals gold; he who sets fire to a house, destroys a road, drinks liquor, or violates the bed of his guru—[these are the perpetrators of great sins]. (68)
And even the killing of one who opposes the great multitude bestows merit upon him;
there is no fault found in the killing of such a person, whether he be a twice-born man or a woman. (69)
Saying, "Her execution is fitting for me," he bound her with firm fetters,
then pulled her by the hair and struck her with ropes.
Then he spoke to Hariścandra with harsh words: "O slave, let this wicked-souled woman be executed; do not hesitate! (71)
Having heard those words, which were like a thunderbolt falling at that moment, the king trembled and, fearing the killing of a woman, spoke to the Cāṇḍāla.
"I am not able to do this; give me another task to perform.
Whatever work you have spoken of, even if it be impossible, I shall accomplish it. (73)
Having heard those words spoken by him, the outcaste replied:
"Do not fear; take up your sword, for the slaying of this woman is considered a bestower of merit. (74)
"This [place] causes fear only to the ignorant; it should never be protected.
Having heard those words of his, the king spoke these words: || 75 ||
Women must be protected with great effort and should never be killed;
for the murder of a woman, sin has been proclaimed by the sages devoted to dharma. (76)
A man who kills a woman, whether intentionally or even unintentionally,
is then cooked in hell, beginning with the Mahāraurava.
The Cāṇḍāla said:
"Do not speak thus; take this sharp [sword] which has the brilliance of lightning, by means of which, when one person is led to death, there will be happiness for many. (78)
Indeed, the act of killing her would surely bestow great merit;
for by this wicked woman, many children have been devoured in the world. (79)
"Therefore, let her be executed quickly; the world will then be at peace.
The king replied, "O Lord of the Cāṇḍālas, there is a strict vow regarding the avoidance of killing women. (80)
"Therefore, from birth until death, I shall not make an effort to kill you like a woman.
The Cāṇḍāla said: "O wicked one, what other duty exists besides the service of one's master? (81)
Having received my wages today, why do you neglect your duty?
He who, having taken his master's wages, neglects his master's work [is a transgressor]. (82)
"There is no liberation for him from hell even in ten thousand kalpas.
The king said,
"O Lord of the Cāṇḍālas, grant me some other very terrible thing to obtain."
"Tell me who your enemy is; I shall slay him without a doubt.
Having slain that enemy, I will give the earth back to you. (84)
"O Lord, even if he is joined by gods, serpents, siddhas, and gandharvas, I shall conquer even the lord of the gods by striking him down with sharpened arrows. (85)
Having heard these words of King Hariścandra,
the Cāṇḍāla, filled with rage, spoke to the trembling monarch.
The Cāṇḍāla said:
"This speech is not well-composed, this speech uttered by a slave; having assumed the state of a Cāṇḍāla slave, you speak the words of the gods."
O Dāsa, what more need be said? Listen indeed to my words as I speak them. (87)
O shameless one, if there were even a trace of fear of sin in your heart, for what reason would you have become a slave in the house of a Cāṇḍāla? (88)
"Take this sword and then sever her lotus-like head.
Having spoken thus, the Caṇḍāla then presented the sword to the king. (89)

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Hariścandra Taking Up the Sword at the Command of the Cāṇḍāla," in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 25 ||
In the narrative of Hariścandra, the description of the king’s effort to enter the fire.
Sūta said:
Then the king, standing with his face cast downwards, spoke to the queen.
"O young girl, sit here before me, a sinner. (1)
"I shall cut off your head if my hand is able to strike you.
Having spoken thus, the king raised his sword and went forward to kill him.
The king did not know his wife, and she did not know the monarch;
afflicted by intense grief, she spoke, longing for her own death. (3)
The woman said:
"O Caṇḍāla, listen to my words if you have any regard for them;
my son lies dead not far away, outside the city. (4)
"I shall burn him once I have brought him slain to your presence;
meanwhile, please wait, and afterwards you may have me killed with a sword. (5)
Then, having said "So be it," she was sent toward the boy;
afflicted with extreme sorrow, she went forth, wailing most piteously.
The wife of that lord of men, repeatedly crying out, "Alas, my son! Alas, my child! Alas, my infant! [found] the boy indeed bitten by a serpent. || 7 ||
Emaciated, pale, and soiled, with her hair covered in dust,
she arrived at the ground of the cremation ground, placed the child there, and sat down upon the earth.
"O King, today you see here upon the earth that very young son of yours,
playing with his friends, bitten by a venomous snake and dead.
Hearing those words of lamentation from her, that lord of men—
Having approached the presence of Śava, she then cast her garment over him.
The lord of the earth did not recognize his wife as she wept in that manner— her, who was tormented by his long absence, appearing like a woman born anew.
She too, seeing before her that man with beautiful hair-ends now matted,
resembling the bark of a withered tree, did not recognize the best of kings.
Seeing the boy fallen on the ground, afflicted by a venomous serpent, and endowed with the marks of a lord of men, that king reflected: || 12 ||
His face is auspicious like the full moon, with a prominent nose and free from blemish, beautified by a pair of high cheeks resembling a mirror. (13)
Her hair was dark blue, with curled tips, thick, long, and wavy;
her eyes were like lotuses, and her lips resembled the bimba fruit. (14)
Broad-chested, long-eyed, with long arms and elevated shoulders, he had broad feet, was deep-toned, and possessed slender fingers and a prominent nose. || 15 ||
With feet like lotus stalks, a deep navel, and an uplifted neck—alas, what a tragedy! This child must belong to the lineage of some great king. (16)
"Once born, he was led away by the evil-minded Kṛtānta with his noose of Time.
Sūta said:
"Having thus seen that boy stretched out upon his mother's lap," (17)
When the king regained his memory, he cried out "Alas, alas! and shed tears;
and he said, "My dear child has fallen into this state."
Even though he was brought under the power of the terrible Kṛtānta (Death),
King Hariścandra remained steadfast after having reflected thus.
Then the queen, overcome by great sorrow, spoke these words. The queen said:
"Alas, my child! By whose sin, or by whose ill-will toward you, has this great calamity occurred?"
A terrible suffering has befallen me, the like of which cannot be found;
alas, O Lord, O King, having abandoned me in my extreme misery! (21)
In what place does one rest securely, and for what reason?
[There is] the loss of kingdom, the abandonment of friends, and the sale of wife and son. (22)
"O Creator, what have you done to the royal sage Hariścandra?
Having heard these words of hers, the king was then dislodged from his position.
Having recognized that queen and her son who had met their end, he thought:
"Alas! This woman is my own wife, and this child is also my son. (24)
Having realized this, he fell down, tormented by grief, and indeed swooned;
and she, recognizing him as having reached that state, [acted accordingly].
Fainted and distressed, she fell motionless upon the surface of the earth; then, having regained consciousness, both the lord of kings and his queen together— || 26 ||
Afflicted by a heavy burden of grief and deeply distressed, they both lamented.
The king said:
"Alas, my child! Your face is so delicate, with its curling locks of hair."
As I behold his dejected face, why does my heart not shatter—this one who has come of his own accord, calling out sweetly, "Father! Father!"? (28)
When, out of affection, will I embrace him and say, "O dear child"?
When will the earth be covered by the dust raised by his knees as he crawls along? (29)
"My upper garment, my lap, and likewise my body will become soiled;
my mind has not yet reached its full maturity, O delighter of the heart. (30)
"By him who sold you like a commodity, you have been deprived of your father;
my entire kingdom, along with my great wealth and kinsmen, has gone.
Because of my ill fortune, my son was seen by that cruel man."
I [beheld] the lotus-face of my son, who had been bitten by a great serpent.
"Beholding [him], I am now overcome by terrible poison.
Having spoken thus, he took the boy while his voice was choked with tears. (32)
And having embraced him, he fell down motionless in a swoon.
Then, seeing him fallen, Śaivyā thought thus: || 33 ||
This tiger among men is recognized by his voice alone;
he is Hariścandra, the moon to the minds of the learned—of this there is no doubt. (34)
Likewise, the nose of this high-souled one of renowned fame was prominent and auspicious like a sesame flower, and his teeth resembled flower buds. (35)
"Why has that lord of men come to the cremation ground? Having thus abandoned his grief for his son, she beholds her husband fallen there. (36)
Delighted, astonished, and distressed, tormented by grief for her husband and son,
she gazed [at him] and then fell to the surface of the earth in a swoon.
Regaining her composure, she spoke slowly and with a faltering voice:
"Fie on you! Fie on cruel fate, which is merciless, lawless, and loathsome! (38)
By whom this king, who was like an immortal, was reduced to the state of an outcaste, suffering the loss of his kingdom, the abandonment of his friends, and the sale of his wife and son. (39)
Even though you have brought about this king who was once a Cāṇḍāla,
today I see neither your royal umbrella nor even your lion-throne.
Or even these two yak-tail fans—what is this reversal of fate?
For he, as he goes forth, has been preceded by kings who have become his servants. (41)
They make the surface of the earth free from dust with their own upper garments;
yet here [is this skull], which is joined to another skull and filled with a continuous stream of dripping water.
It was most dreadful, with hair caught within the threads of discarded funeral wreaths,
and adorned with great, dried-up patches where fat had congealed.
It was terrifying with the clashing of ashes, embers, half-burnt bones, and marrow;
it resounded with the cries of vultures and jackals, and was filled with large and small birds.

In that place where the quarters of the sky were turned blue by the smoke-clouds rising from funeral pyres, and where the night-stalkers (rākṣasas) were intensely drawn to the devouring of corpses, [he remained]. 45.
"The king of kings wanders in the impure cremation ground, afflicted by suffering.
Having spoken thus, the princess then embraced the king around his neck. (46)
"Alas! Overcome with grief, she lamented with a piteous voice:
'O King, whether you consider this a dream or reality... (47)
Therefore, let it be told, O illustrious one, for my mind is indeed bewildered;
if, O knower of dharma, there is truly no assistance in dharma even from this [worldly life]. (48)
In that same way, when there is no honoring of Brahmins, gods, and others, and no protection of truth, where is there dharma? Where is truth, uprightness, or compassion? (49)
"Where you, who were devoted to righteousness, have been deposed from your own kingdom.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of hers, he sighed hotly and spoke with a faltering voice.
He told the slender-limbed woman how he had attained the state of a dog-cooker;
she, however, weeping for a long time and sighing hotly in great distress, [spoke]. (51)
The timid man reported the death of his son exactly as it had happened;
hearing those words, the king fell to the ground.
Having brought the dead son and repeatedly licking him with her tongue, Śaivyā then spoke to Hariścandra with a faltering voice: (53)
"Perform the service of your master by having my head cut off;
let there be no treachery toward your lord for you today, O King—be true to your word. (54)
"O Indra among kings, truth is yours, yet malice toward others is a sin.
Upon hearing this, the king fell to the ground in a swoon. (55)
Regaining consciousness in an instant, he lamented, deeply afflicted by grief.
The king said:
"O beloved, how could you have spoken such exceedingly cruel words? (56)
"When it is impossible to speak, how can that task be performed?
The wife said:
"Gaurī has been worshipped by me, as have the gods and the brahmins. (57)
"O Lord, you shall indeed become my husband in another birth.
Having heard those words, the king then fell prostrate upon the ground.
Then, filled with grief, he kissed the face of his deceased son.
The King said:
"O beloved, it does not please me to endure suffering for such a long time. (59)
"O slender-limbed one, I am not my own master; behold my misfortune! If I am not permitted by the Caṇḍāla, I shall enter the blazing fire. (60)
I shall again become a slave to a Cāṇḍāla in another birth;
having fallen into hell, I shall experience terrible suffering. (61)
Having reached the Mahāraurava and Raurava hells, I shall suffer torment;
for one submerged in an ocean of misery, separation from life is better.
Even this one son, who was the sole child destined to continue my lineage, has died through the powerful decree of fate. (63)
"How shall I give up my life, for I am dependent on others and in a wretched state?
Nevertheless, due to the abundance of my suffering, I shall cast off this body of mine. (64)

In the three worlds, there is no such suffering as that found in the Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana), nor in the Vaitaraṇī river; how much less could there be such as that which occurs during the calamity involving one's son?
Therefore, O slender-limbed one, I shall cast myself into the blazing fire with my son’s body; you must now forgive me for this.
"O lotus-eyed one, you must not say anything further;
O slender-limbed lady, listen to my words with an undistracted mind. (67)
"Then, being permitted, go to the house of the Brahmin, O lady of pure smiles, if [the merit of] what was given, what was offered in sacrifice, and if the teachers have been satisfied. (68)
If there is to be a reunion with your own son by you in the next world, how then will this desired object be achieved in this world? (69)
O lady of pure smiles, whatever I have said to you in private while laughing, all of that must be forgiven by me as I depart. (70)
"O auspicious one, that twice-born man must not be treated with contempt by you out of pride because you are the king's wife;
rather, he should be propitiated with every effort, for a husband is like a deity. (71)
The queen said: "O royal sage, I too shall fall here into the fire;
unable to bear the burden of this sorrow, O Lord, I shall indeed go with you. (72)
"It is better for me to go with you; it cannot be otherwise. O giver of honor, I shall experience heaven or hell together with you.
Having heard this, the king then said: "So be it, O devoted wife."

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the King's Resolve to Enter the Fire," in the Hariścandra episode of the seventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Fruit of Hearing the Narrative of Hariścandra.
Sūta said:
Then, having prepared a funeral pyre, the king placed his own son upon it.
Then the king, together with his wife, joined his palms in reverence.
He meditated upon the Supreme Sovereign, the hundred-eyed Mistress of the Universe, who resides within the five sheaths and whose nature is the Brahma at the tail-end [of the Śruti]. || 2 ||
Clad in red garments, an ocean of the essence of compassion, bearing various weapons, the Mother is ever intent upon the protection of the world. (3)
While he was thus reflecting, all the gods, including Indra,
placing Dharma at their head, arrived there with great haste.
Having arrived, they all said: "O King, O Great Lord, listen!
I am Pitāmaha (Brahmā) in person, and Dharma is you yourself."
The Sādhyas along with the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, the world-protectors, the Cāraṇas, the Nāgas, the Siddhas together with the Gandharvas, the Rudras, and likewise the two Aśvins; || 6 ||
These and many others, as well as Viśvāmitra himself—he who desires to establish friendship with the three worlds in accordance with dharma—[are present]. (8)
"Viśvāmitra truly desires to bring about what you wish for. Dharma said:
"O King, do not commit this rash act; I am Dharma who have come to you. (8)
Pleased by your virtues such as forbearance, self-restraint, and courage,
Indra said:
"O illustrious Hariścandra, Śakra has come into your presence."
"By you today, together with your wife and son, the eternal worlds have been won.
Ascend to the third heaven, O King, accompanied by your wife and son. (10)
"Extremely difficult for other men to attain, it was won by him through his own deeds.
Sūta said:
"Then there fell a rain consisting of nectar, which destroys untimely death."
As the child was situated in the midst of the funeral pyre, Indra released from the sky a great rain of flowers and the sound of kettledrums.
The dead son of that high-souled king rose up,
his body delicate, healthy, serene, and with a joyful mind.
Then King Hariścandra, together with his wife, endowed with his own splendor and clothed in divine garlands and garments, embraced his son.
At that very moment he became Indra, and spoke thus to the king: || 15 ||
O highly fortunate one, together with your wife and your son, ascend to the heavenly realm and the supreme goal—
the fruit of your own deeds.
Hariścandra said: "O King of the Gods, without the permission of my master, the dog-cooker,
and without having performed the expiation for him, I shall certainly not ascend to the abode of the gods."
Dharma said:
"Having understood that such suffering was destined for you, I brought myself to the state of a dog-cooker through my own power of illusion, and that settlement of outcasts was shown to you."
Indra said:
"O Hariścandra, ascend to that supreme station on earth which is sought by all men—the station of those men who have performed meritorious deeds. (19)
Hariścandra said:
"O King of the Gods, salutations to you; listen also to these words of mine. The people in the city of Kausala have their minds consumed by grief for me."
"Having cast these aside, they remain; how then shall I go to heaven?
[For there are] the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, the slaughter of a cow, and likewise the killing of a woman. (21)
"Having cast these aside, they remain; how then shall I go to heaven?
[For there are] the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, the slaughter of a cow, and likewise the killing of a woman. (21)
A great sin equal to these is declared to arise from abandoning a devotee;
how could there be happiness for one who abandons a devoted person who should not be forsaken?
Without them I shall not depart; therefore, O Śakra, go to heaven.
If they are to go to heaven together with me, O Lord of the Gods, [then let it be so]. (23)
"Therefore, I too shall go to hell along with them.
Indra said:
"O King, their merits and sins are indeed diverse."
"O King, how can you desire heaven while eating food obtained through communal feasting?
Hariścandra said:
"O Śakra, a king certainly enjoys his kingdom by the power of his subjects. (25)
He performed great sacrifices and carried out works of public utility;
all of that was accomplished by me through their power.
Out of attachment and a desire for heaven, I shall not abandon them;
therefore, O Lord of Gods, whatever good deed I possess— || 27 ||
May whatever has been given, sacrificed, or chanted by them be common to us;
and may the fruit resulting from my own actions be something to be enjoyed over a long period of time.
"By your grace, let there be even a single day with them.
Sūta said:
Having said, "It shall be so," Śakra, the lord of the three worlds, [departed].
With a serene mind, Dharma and Viśvāmitra, the son of Gādhi, all went to the city which was filled with people of the four castes. || 30 ||
In the presence of Hariścandra, the Lord of the Gods spoke:
"Let the people come quickly to the heavenly world, which is so difficult to attain. (31)
"Indeed, all of you have attained this through faith in the Dharma. Hariścandra then addressed all those people residing in the city: || 32 ||
The king, devoted to dharma, said, "Ascend to heaven.
Sūta said:
Having heard those words of Indra and of that monarch, they were filled with joy.
Those people who were weary of worldly existences, having placed the burden upon their own sons,
ascended to heaven with joyful minds.
Then all of them, mounted upon the excellent celestial chariot and possessing radiant bodies,
were filled with joy, as was King Hariścandra.
Having consecrated his son named Rohita upon the throne in the delightful city called Ayodhyā, which was filled with happy and well-fed people, the high-minded one [departed].
Having honored and greeted both his son and his friends, [he spoke of] that vast [attainment] which is obtained through merit and is very difficult even for the gods and others to reach. (37)
Having attained incomparable fame, that lord of the earth took his seat in a celestial chariot that moved at will and was adorned with tiny bells.
Then, having observed him, the illustrious preceptor of the Daityas, who knew the essential truth of the meaning of all scriptures, recited this verse-mantra. (39)
Śukra said:
"Oh, the greatness of endurance! Oh, the great fruit of giving!
Since Hariścandra has attained the same world as Mahendra. (40)
Sūta said:
This entire narrative of the deeds of Hariścandra has been told to you;
whoever, being afflicted by sorrow, hears it, obtains happiness every day.
One desiring heaven shall attain heaven; one desiring a son shall obtain a son;
one desiring a wife shall obtain a wife; and one desiring a kingdom shall obtain a kingdom. (42)

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Fruit of Hearing the Legend of Hariścandra," in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Deeds of Śatākṣī.
Janamejaya said:
"This wonderful narrative of Hariścandra has been recounted."
Of the righteous royal sage who was devoted to Śatākṣī with his whole being. || 1 ||
From where was that goddess Śatākṣī born, the divine and auspicious Śivā?
Tell me the reason for that, O Sage; make my birth meaningful.
For what person of pure intellect, hearing the virtues of the Goddess, would ever reach satiety?
At every step, one enjoys the imperishable fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the auspicious account of the origin of Śatākṣī;
for one who is devoted to the Goddess, there is nothing whatsoever that I may not tell you.
Formerly, there was a great Daitya named Durgama, who was extremely cruel;
born in the lineage of Hiraṇyākṣa, he was the son of Ruru and a great villain.
The Veda is indeed the strength of the gods; when it is destroyed, even the deities will surely perish—of this there is no doubt. Therefore, that must first be undertaken.
Having reflected upon this, he went to the Himalayas to perform austerities;
meditating on Brahmā in his mind, he remained there subsisting only on air.
He performed supreme austerity for a period of a thousand years;
by his splendor, the worlds, including the gods and the asuras, were scorched.
Thereupon, the Lord, four-faced and mounted upon a swan,
with a serene lotus-like countenance, went forth to grant him a boon.
To him who was established in samādhi with eyes closed, the Four-faced One clearly said:
"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever dwells in your mind."
"Today, gratified by your austerity, I have come to grant you a boon.
Having heard this voice from the mouth of Brahmā, he arose from his meditative absorption.
Having worshipped him, he chose a boon: "O Lord of Gods, grant me the Vedas—whatever mantras exist in the three worlds among the Brāhmaṇas and even among the gods. (12)
O Maheśvara, may they be present in my vicinity;
and grant me such strength that the gods may be defeated. || 13 ||
Having heard these words of his and saying, "So be it," that supreme lord of the four Vedas departed for Satyaloka.
From that time forward, the Brahmins forgot the masses of Vedic knowledge, as well as the ritual baths, twilight prayers, daily fire-oblations, ancestral rites, sacrifices, recitations, and so forth.
The surface of the earth was devastated, and a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose;
"What is this? What is this? the Brahmins asked one another. (16)
"Since the Vedas have disappeared, what more must we do than this?"—thus it was when a great calamity, most terrible, had arisen upon the earth. (17)
Due to the absence of sacrificial portions and other offerings, the gods became subject to old age;
then that Daitya besieged the city of Amarāvatī.
Being unable to fight with that asura whose body was like adamant,
the gods then fled and went away somewhere.
Dwelling in mountain fastnesses and in caves upon jeweled peaks,
they remained meditating upon that supreme power, the Mother Beyond (Parāmbikā).
O King, due to the absence of oblations and other rites in the fire, there was also a lack of rain;
and because of the lack of rain, the surface of the earth became parched and devoid of water. (21)
Wells, step-wells, ponds, and rivers have all gone dry;
O King, this drought has lasted for a hundred years.
The subjects died in many ways, as did cows, buffaloes, and other animals; in every house of men, there was a collection of corpses. (23)
When such a calamity had arisen, the Brāhmaṇas, with tranquil minds,
went to the side of the Himavat mountain, desiring to propitiate Śiva.
Day after day they praised the Goddess with offerings of meditative concentration and dhyāna;
abstaining from food and absorbed in her, they took refuge in her alone.
O Great Goddess, show compassion indeed toward these base people, even though they are guilty of every offense; O Mother, this [harshness] is not worthy of you.
O Goddess of gods, O you who exist as the inner controller of all, withdraw your anger;
for this person acts exactly as he is impelled by you. (27)
There is no other refuge for these people; why do you look again and again?
O Maheśvarī, you are capable of doing whatever you desire.
O Maheśānī, deliver us from this supreme calamity!
O Ambikā, without life, how could we possibly endure? (29)
Be gracious, O Great Sovereign; be gracious, O Mother of the Universe!
Salutations, salutations to you, the Mistress of infinite millions of cosmic eggs.
Salutations to her whose form is immutable; salutations again and again to her whose form is consciousness.
Salutations to her who is known through the Vedānta; salutations again and again to the Mistress of the World.
We bow with our whole being to that Goddess, the cause of all, who is made known by all the scriptures through the words "not this, not this."
Thus entreated, the Goddess Bhuvaneśī, the Great Sovereign Pārvatī,
revealed her form consisting of infinite eyes.
Resembling blue collyrium in appearance, with eyes as long as blue lotuses, and possessing breasts that were very firm, symmetrical, high, rounded, full, and dense. (34)
He offered arrow-reeds, fist-reeds, lotuses, flowers, shoots, and roots; vegetables and other items combined with fruits, along with fresh butter.
With her hands she bore away hunger, thirst, and old age,
and she possessed that form which was the essence of all beauty, adorned with loveliness.
Having revealed herself as one who resembles ten million suns and is an ocean of the essence of compassion, that Mother of the World, born from the infinite eyes [of Śiva], appeared. (37)
He released thousands of streams of water upon the worlds;
for nine nights there was a great rain from the waters born of his eyes.
Beholding all those who were suffering, she shed tears from her eyes;
by that, all those worlds and even all the medicinal herbs were gratified.
O King, by those waters, the currents of the rivers and streams were formed;
the gods who had previously remained hidden now emerged outside.
Having assembled together with the gods and the Brahmins, they praised the Goddess:
"Salutations to you, who are to be known through the Vedānta; salutations to you, whose nature is Brahman. (41)
Salutations again and again to you, the creator of the entire world through your own *māyā*;
O Goddess, who are like a wish-fulfilling tree for your devotees, you who assume a physical form for the sake of your devotees. 42.
O eternally satisfied, incomparable Sovereign of the World, salutations to you!
For the sake of our peace, [you have bestowed] this peerless thousand eyes. (43)
O Goddess, since you have been held by me, therefore become Śatākṣī;
O Mother, we are afflicted by hunger and have no power to offer praise.
"O Great Goddess, show mercy; O Ambikā, bring forth even the Vedas!
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, she [placed] the vegetables within her own hands. (45)
Śivā gave various kinds of sweet fruits and roots for the purpose of eating,
as well as various types of food fit for animals.
O King, she granted him a new chariot joined with horses swift as the wind;
from that day forth, she also acquired the name Śākambharī.
Then, when a great clamor arose, the asura named Durgama, awakened by the words of the messenger, set out with his army and weapons to fight.
Accompanied by a thousand akṣauhiṇīs and discharging arrows with great haste,
he besieged that army of the gods which had previously stood before the Goddess.
Likewise, he hemmed in the assembly of Brahmins on all sides;
then a tumultuous roar arose throughout the circle of the gods.
"Save us! Save us!"—thus all the twice-born and the immortals cried out.
Then, from all sides, Śivā [held] a wheel consisting of radiant energy for the sake of the gods.
She herself stood outside for the sake of protection;
then a battle ensued between both the Goddess and the Daitya.
The wondrous solar disc was completely shrouded by a rain of arrows,
brilliantly illuminated by the fire produced from the friction of their mutual shafts.
Then, from the body of the Goddess, intense powers emerged, deafening the quarters of the horizon with the harsh twanging of their bowstrings.
Kālikā, Tāriṇī, Bālā, Tripurā, Bhairavī, Ramā, Bagalā, Mātaṅgī, and likewise Tripurasundarī. (55)
Kāmākṣī, Tulajā Devī, Jambhinī, Mohinī, as well as Chinnamastā, Guhyakālī, and Daśasāhasrabāhukā. (56)
There were thirty-two other powers, and sixty-four supreme ones;
from them, innumerable goddesses emerged, equipped with their weapons.
The battlefield resounded with the sounds of drums, conchs, lutes, and other instruments,
while hundreds of akṣauhiṇīs in the Daitya army were destroyed by the Śaktis.
The commander of the army became the leader at the front, difficult to overcome;
and first, the enemy engaged in battle with the Śaktis.
A great battle took place where a river of blood flowed;
all those akṣauhiṇī divisions were destroyed within ten days.
Then, when the eleventh day, which was most terrible, had arrived, he,
wearing red garlands and garments and anointed with red perfumes and unguents, [appeared].
Having celebrated a great festival, he mounted his chariot for battle;
and with great fury, having conquered all the Śaktis, [he advanced]. 62.
He stationed his own chariot at the front of Mahādevī’s chariot;
then a great battle ensued between both the Goddess and the Daitya.
For the duration of two watches, it caused terror in the heart;
thereafter, the Goddess discharged fifteen exceedingly fierce arrows.
With four [arrows] he struck the four horses; with one arrow, the charioteer;
with two, the eyes; with two, the arms; and with one feathered shaft, the standard. (65)
Jagadambikā pierced his heart with five [arrows];
then, vomiting blood, he died in the presence of the Lord.
His splendor, having emerged, entered the form of the Goddess.
When that one of great heroism was slain, the three worlds became peaceful.
Then Brahmā and all the others, placing Hari and Īśāna at their head, praised the Mother of the Universe with devotion and voices faltering with emotion.
The gods said:
O Supreme Goddess, sole cause of the manifestation and transformation of the world’s delusion;
salutations to Śākambharī, O Śivā; salutations to you, O hundred-eyed one! (69)
Salutations to you, proclaimed by all the Upaniṣads, who destroy the inaccessible Asuras; O Maheśvarī, O Śivā, who abide within the five sheaths.
We worship that Bhuvaneśvarī, whose essential nature is the meaning of the Praṇava, whom the lords of sages meditate upon with a non-conceptual mind. 71.
We bow with all our being to her who possesses a divine form, the mother of infinite millions of universes,
and the progenitor of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods.
Who, even the Lord of All, could bring about weeping upon seeing the wretched, were it not for the compassionate Supreme Goddess, the Mother Śatākṣī? (73)
Vyāsa said: Thus praised by the gods, including the eminent Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others,
and worshipped with various offerings, the Goddess became satisfied at that very moment.
Then that goddess, being pleased, brought forth the Vedas and gave them;
she who speaks with the voice of a cuckoo spoke especially to the Brāhmaṇas. (75)
"This body of mine is excellent and must be especially protected;
for without it, this calamity has just now been witnessed. (76)
I am always to be honored and indeed always to be served by you;
nothing superior to this is taught for the sake of one's welfare.
Indeed, this supreme majesty of mine should be recited at all times;
by that I shall be pleased and likewise remove all calamities.
He who utters my name "Durgā" because I am the slayer of the demon Durga,
and [my name] "Śatākṣī," pierces through illusion and goes forth.
What is the use of much speaking here? I shall state the essence according to reality:
O gods, I am to be constantly served by all the Suras and Asuras alike.
Having spoken thus, the Goddess, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, vanished even as the gods were looking on, thereby producing great satisfaction. (81)
All this supreme and great secret has been told to you;
it must be guarded with effort, for it brings about all auspiciousness. || 82 ||
Whoever listens to this chapter daily, intent on devotion, shall attain all desires and be honored in the world of the Goddess. (83)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Life of Śatākṣī," in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
A description of the performance of penance by the gods seeking to propitiate the Blessed Goddess.
Vyāsa said:
Thus ends the supreme account of the deeds of the kings of the Solar dynasty.
And how much of the lineage of the Somas can possibly be described by me? || 1 ||
By the grace of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), they attained greatness;
O King, know for certain that this is through the grace of the Supreme Power.
Whatever being is possessed of majesty, splendor, or even power,
know that each one of them has arisen from a portion of my supreme Śakti.
These and other kings, O King, were worshippers of the Supreme Power (Parā-Śakti) and became axes for the root of the tree of saṃsāra.
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship Bhuvaneśvarī;
like one seeking grain, one should discard everything else entirely, even as if it were mere straw.
O King, having churned the ocean of the milk of the Vedas, I have obtained this jewel;
through the lotus feet of Parāśakti, I have achieved my life’s purpose.
There is no other deity whatsoever who is seated upon the five Brahmās;
for that very reason, the seat of the five Brahmās was prepared for the Great Goddess.
But that entity which exceeds the five and is called the Unmanifest in the Veda,
in whom [the universe] is woven across and lengthwise— that indeed is Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī.
O Indra among kings, without knowing that [truth], a man shall never be liberated;
only when men shall wrap up the sky like a piece of leather will [liberation be attained].
Then, by not knowing Śivā, there will be no end to suffering;
for this very reason, the followers of the Śvetāśvatara branch declare in the Śruti: || 10 ||
Following the yoga of meditation, they beheld the divine power of the Self, concealed by its own qualities.
Therefore, with every effort for the sake of making one's birth fruitful—
whether out of shame, fear, devotion, or love accompanied by affection—
one should renounce all attachments and restrain the mind within the heart. (12)
"May one become intent upon that and devoted to that"—this is the drumbeat of the Vedānta;
by whatever pretext, even while sleeping, standing, or walking. (13)
One who constantly glorifies the Goddess shall indeed be released from bondage;
therefore, O King, worship the Great Sovereign with every effort.

First, one should meditate upon her in the form of Virāṭ, then in the form of Sūtra, and likewise in the form of Antaryāmin, following the sequence of the steps; thereafter, when the mind has become purified— (15)
Worship that supreme Śakti, whose form is the goal characterized by Being, Consciousness, and Bliss, who is of the nature of Brahman, and who is devoid of the manifestation of the phenomenal world.
The absorption of the mind in her is known as her propitiation;
O King, I have thus related to you the conduct of kings who are devotees of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti). 17.
It is purifying for the righteous, born of the solar and lunar lineages, and for those of noble mind; it bestows fame, awakens the intellect toward dharma, and grants a favorable rebirth.
"This merit-bestowing account has been told; what else do you wish to hear?
Janamejaya said:
"In the past, Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī were bestowed by the Supreme Mother. (19)
Likewise,
it is well known that Gaurī is the daughter of Himavat and Dakṣa, born from the lotus of his navel for the sake of Hara and Hari.
And [it is said] that she is the daughter of the Ocean of Milk, known as Mahālakṣmī;
but how can the other two be daughters, given that they originated from the Root Goddess? (21)
"This appears impossible; there is doubt here, O Great Sage.
You, who are intent on cutting through doubt, sever it with the sword of knowledge. (22)
Vyāsa said: Listen, O King, I shall proclaim a most wonderful secret;
for you, who are devoted to the Goddess, there is nothing indeed that should not be told.
When the Supreme Mother gave the three goddesses to the three gods,
from that time forward those gods performed the tasks of creation.
O King, at one time there arose Daityas named Hālāhalas of great prowess; by them, the three worlds were conquered in an instant.
Proud due to the boon granted by Brahmā, they besieged the Silver Mountain (Kailāsa) with their own armies,
as well as Vaikuṇṭha itself.
The enemy of Kāma and the enemy of Kaiṭabha both made preparations for battle;
for sixty thousand years, there was a most fierce conflict.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the armies of both the gods and the Dānavas;
then, with great effort, those Dānavas were slain by the two of them.
Having returned to their respective abodes, O King, those two conceived pride, thinking, "It was solely because of our own power that they were slain. (29)
Perceiving their arrogance, Mahālakṣmī and Gaurī both feigned laughter; and seeing their laughter, those two [the other pair] likewise laughed at them.
As if possessed by the gods and deluded by the primordial illusion (ādimāyā), they both became exceedingly enraged and uttered words that were difficult to answer,
preceded by insults.
Then, at that very moment, those two deities abandoned them and vanished once again; indeed, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose at that time.
Then, due to the insult to those two powers, Hari and Hara became lusterless, powerless, distracted, and senseless.
Brahmā became anxious with thought: "What is this that has arisen?
How is it that these two foremost among the deities are incapable of performing their duty?"
Why has this calamity arisen so unexpectedly?
Will there be a dissolution of this innocent world? (35)
"I do not know the cause at all; how should a remedy be applied?
Thus, extremely distressed by anxiety, he meditated with his eyes closed. (36)
"O best of kings, knowing then that this had arisen from the provocation of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), the Lotus-born One became vigilant. (37)
Then, for some time, that treasure of asceticism himself performed whatever task was required for those two by means of his own power and influence.
Then, for the sake of their well-being, that righteous-souled one quickly summoned his sons, Manu and the others, as well as Sanaka and the rest. (39)
The storehouse of asceticism spoke these words to them as they bowed before him:
"I am now occupied with my duties; I am not able to perform further penance."
For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), I am burdened by the weight of the universe;
both Śiva and Viṣṇu have been cast down by the wrath of the Supreme Power.
Therefore, endowed with supreme devotion, you should perform most wonderful austerities and then gratify that supreme Śakti.
"O my sons, act in such a way that those two may become endowed with power as they were in their former lives; for in this way, your own glory shall increase. (43)
In whichever family those two Śaktis may be born, that family shall purify the entire world and itself become one that has fulfilled its purpose. || 44 ||
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of the Grandfather, Dakṣa and all the others, their inner selves purified, departed into the forest with the desire to propitiate him. (45)

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Performance of Austerities by the Gods Desiring to Propitiate the Blessed Goddess," in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Devī-pīṭhas.
Vyāsa said:
Then they, taking refuge on the slopes of the Himālaya, stayed in a forest region.
Devoted to the recitation of the seed-mantra of Māyā, they performed austerities with concentrated minds.
O King, as they meditated upon the supreme power for a hundred thousand years,
the Goddess became pleased and granted them a direct vision of herself.

She has four arms holding a noose, a goad, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness; she is three-eyed, completely filled with the essence of compassion, and her form consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Having beheld her, the mother of all beings, the stainless sages offered praise:
"Salutations to you, who possess the form of the universe and whose beautiful body is like that of Vaiśvānara! (4)
Salutations to her whose form is splendor, salutations to her whose body is the subtle self (sutrātman),
in whom all subtle bodies are established as warp and woof.
Salutations to her whose nature is pure wisdom; salutations to her whose form is the unmanifest;
salutations to her whose nature is direct perception; salutations to you, the embodiment of Brahman.
"Salutations to you who possess all forms, whose very embodiment is the essence of all that is perceived.
Having thus praised the Mother of the Universe with a voice faltering with devotion, [he spoke]. (7)
The pure sages, headed by Dakṣa, bowed at her lotus feet;
then that goddess, speaking with the voice of a cuckoo, being pleased, spoke.
"Choose a boon, O highly fortunate ones; I am always considered a granter of boons.
Having heard her words, [they sought] the pacification of the bodies of Hara and Viṣṇu.
O best of kings, they chose the attainment of that power for those two;
then Dakṣa spoke again: "O Goddess, let my birth be in their family. (10)
"O Mother, may there be for you that by which I may become one who has fulfilled his purpose"—thus [he spoke of] recitation, meditation, worship, and various sacred sites. (11)
"Speak to me, O Supreme Goddess, using your own mouth alone. The Goddess said: "The condition of those two has arisen from the slighting of my powers."
"Such an offense must never again be committed by me;
now, by a mere fragment of my grace, health has been restored to their bodies. (13)
And there shall be power for you in the Ocean of Milk within your own home;
two sons will be born there, and they, impelled by me, shall attain [their goals].
The seed-syllable of Māyā is indeed my primary mantra, always dear to me;
or else, my meditation upon the form of Virāṭ stands before you. (15)
Or rather, my entire world is a state of the nature of Truth, Consciousness, and Bliss;
