and I am always to be worshipped and meditated upon by you at all times.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the Goddess who dwells on Maṇidvīpa vanished;
then all the sages, Dakṣa and the others, returned once more to Brahmā.
They respectfully related the entire account to Brahmā;
O King, both Hara and Hari remained at ease, each capable of performing his own respective task.
Then, born by the grace of Parāmbā, they were free from pride;
and after some time, the Śākta festival descended.
O Great King, when Dakṣa’s body [was restored], there was a festival throughout the three worlds;
all the gods were delighted and showered down flowers. (20)
O King, kettledrums struck with drumsticks resounded in heaven, and the minds of the pure-souled virtuous ones became serene. (21)
The rivers flowed along their courses and the sun became brilliantly radiant;
when Maṅgalā was born, auspiciousness arose everywhere.
He gave her the name Satī because of the truthfulness of her supreme consciousness;
then he gave her to Śiva as his own power (śakti).
Furthermore, O King, by a stroke of fate, she was burned in a fire while still a maiden.
Janamejaya said:
"O Sage, this speech you have made heard to me is productive of no benefit."
How was such a great entity consumed by fire, the mere remembrance of whose name removes for men the fear of the fire of saṃsāra? (25)
"By what ripening of karma was that very Manu burnt?
Vyāsa said:
"Listen, O King, to the ancient account concerning the cause of Satīdāya."
Then once, Durvāsas went to Jāmbūnadeśvarī;
having seen the Goddess there, he muttered the seed-syllable of Māyā.
Then the Goddess of Gods, being pleased, [offered] the garland from her own neck,
which was frequented by wandering bees and heavy with the intoxication of nectar.
The sage accepted that gift, which was a manifestation of grace, with his head bowed;
then, departing swiftly by way of the sky, the ascetic went forth.
He went to where Dakṣa, the father of Satī herself, was staying; for the sake of beholding his mother, he prostrated at the feet of Satī.
Questioned by Dakṣa, that sage said: "To whom does this extraordinary garland belong?
O Lord, how was it obtained by you, for it is difficult for men on earth to obtain? (31)
Having heard those words of his, with eyes filled with tears and his heart faltering with love, he spoke of the incomparable grace of the Goddess.
The father of Satī requested that garland from the sage, [saying]:
"In the three worlds, there is nothing that cannot be given to a devotee of Śakti. (33)
With this thought, he offered that garland to Manu;
the garland was taken by Manu upon his head to his own abode.
There, he was placed upon a most beautiful bed for the husband and wife;
at night, intent on bestial acts, he was delighted by the scent of the garland. (35)
O King, because of that sin toward Śaṅkara,
that protector of the earth became one whose mind was filled with hatred for Śiva and likewise for the Goddess Satī.
O King, by that offense, her very body— which was produced from it—
was consumed by the fire of yoga out of a desire to witness the true nature of the dharma of a virtuous wife.
And again, that great light appeared upon the ridge of the Himalayas.
Janamejaya said: When the body of Satī was being consumed by fire, what did Śiva do? (38)
She was dearer to him than his own life, and he was distressed by her separation.
Vyāsa said:
Beyond that, what occurred I am unable to tell you.
O King, the destruction of the three worlds occurred through the fire of Śiva’s wrath;
Vīrabhadra emerged, accompanied by the hosts of Bhadrakālī.
When Vīrabhadra was intent on destroying the three worlds,
the gods, headed by Brahmā, then went to Śaṅkara for refuge.
Even when their entire possessions were lost, the Lord, a treasure-house of compassion,
granted them fearlessness and that mantra through the mouth of the goat.
Having failed to bring that great-souled one back to life, Maheśvara became despondent;
approaching the sacrificial enclosure, he wept, overwhelmed with intense grief.
Seeing that virtuous woman being consumed by fire, he perceived her as the digit of consciousness (citkalā) and placed her upon his shoulder, crying out repeatedly, "Alas, Satī! (44).
With a bewildered mind, Śaṅkara wandered through various lands;
at that time, the gods, headed by Brahmā, fell into unsurpassed anxiety.
But Viṣṇu, acting with haste, raised his bow there and severed Satī’s limbs with arrows; they fell upon their respective places.

In those various locations, Hara assumed diverse forms; and then he spoke to the gods regarding those places where Śivā [was established]: He said to the gods: "In these places, those who [worship] Śivā... (47)
For those who worship with supreme devotion, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain, for there the Supreme Mother is eternally present within their own bodies. 48.
For those mortals who perform the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) in these places, their mantras become effective, especially the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ). || 49 ||
Having spoken thus, O best of kings, Śaṅkara, afflicted by separation from them, passed his time in those places through recitation, meditation, and absorption.
Janamejaya said: O sinless one, what are those places that are seats of the Siddhas?
How many in number are they, and what are their names? Tell these to me. (51)
O Great Sage, O Compassionate One, tell me quickly the names of the goddesses residing there, so that I may become one who has achieved his purpose. 52.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall describe the seats of the gods in their entirety;
by the mere hearing of which a man becomes free from sin. (53)

I shall describe in accordance with reality those various seats (pīṭhas) upon which I am to be worshipped by those desiring spiritual accomplishments (siddhi), and meditated upon by those desiring prosperity.
In Vārāṇasī she is Viśālākṣī, residing in the face of Gaurī;
in the sacred field of the Naimiṣa forest, she is said to be Liṅgadhāriṇī.
Lalitā is said to be at Prayāga; Kāmukī is at Gandhamādana;
Kumudā is said to be at Mānasa, as well as in the south and the north.
The Blessed One fulfills all desires; she is Viśvakāmā, the fulfiller of every wish.
On Mount Gomanta she is the goddess Gomatī, and on Mandara she moves at will as Kāmacāriṇī. || 57 ||
Madotkaṭā is in Caitraratha, Jayantī in Hastināpura;
Gaurī is said to be in Kānyakubja, while Rambhā is on the Malaya mountain. (58)
On Ekāmrapīṭha she is proclaimed as Devī Kīrtimatī;
and in Puṣkara they call her Viśveśvarī and Puruhūtā.
The goddess who bestows the true path is proclaimed to be at Kedārapīṭha;
Mandā is on the back of the Himavat mountain, and Bhadrakarṇikā is at Gokarṇa.
Bhavānī is at Sthāneśvara, Bilvapatrikā at Bilvala,
Mādhavī is said to be at Śrīśaila, and likewise Bhadrā at Bhadreśvara.
Jayā is on Varāhaśaila, Kamalā is in Kamalālaya,
Rudrāṇī is at Rudrakoṭi, and likewise Kālī is at Kālañjara.
The Mahādevī resides in Śālagrāma; Jalapriyā in the Śivaliṅga; Kapilā in the Mahāliṅga; and Mukuṭeśvarī in Mākoṭa.
In Māyāpurī she is Kumārī; in Santāna she is Lalitāmbikā;
in Gayā she is said to be Maṅgalā; and in Puruṣottama she is Vimalā. (64)
Utpalāṣī is at Sahasrākṣa, Mahotpalā at Hiraṇyākṣa,
Amoghākṣī at the Vipāśā river, and Pāṭalā at Puṇḍravardhana.
Nārāyaṇī is on Supārśva, Rudrasundarī on Trikuṭa;
the goddess Vipulā is on Vipula, and Kalyāṇī is on the Malaya mountain. (66)
Sahyādrāvakavīrā resides at Hariścandra, Candrikā at Rāmatīrtha, and Mṛgāvatī at the Yamunā. || 67 ||
Koṭavī is at Koṭatīrtha, Sugandhā is in Mādhava forest,
Trisandhyā is in the Godāvarī, and Ratipriyā is at Gaṅgādvāra.
Śubhānandā is at Śivakuṇḍa, Nandinī is on the bank of the Devikā,
Rukmiṇī is at Dvārakā, and Rādhā is in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
Devakī is in Mathurā, while Parameśvarī is in Pātāla;
likewise, Sītā is at Citrakūṭa, and Vindhyādhivāsinī is in the Vindhya mountains.
Mahālakṣmī is in Karavīra, the goddess Rumā is in Vināyaka;
Ārogyā is in Vaidyanātha, and Maheśvarī is in Mahākāla. (71)
Abhayā is at the Uṣṇatīrthas, Nitambā on the Vindhya mountain,
Māṇḍavī by name at Māṇḍavya, and Svāhā at Maheśvarapura.
Pracaṇḍā is at Chagalaṇḍa, Caṇḍī at Kāmarakaṇṭaka;
Varārohā is at Someśvara, and Puṣkarāvatī is at Prabhāsa. (73)
Devamātā is remembered on the banks of the Sarasvatī; Pārāvārā is on the shore [of that river]; the highly fortunate Mahābhāgā is at Mahālaya; and Piṅgaleśvarī is on the Payoṣṇī.
Siṃhikā is at Kṛtaśauca; in the month of Kārttika, she is Atiśāṅkarī; she is Lolā at Utpalāvartaka, and Subhadrā at the confluence of the Śoṇa.
Mātā is in Siddhavana, Lakṣmī in Bharata’s hermitage, Anaṅgā in Jālandhara, Viśvamukhī in Tārā, and [Tārā] on Kiṣkindha mountain.
Puṣṭi is in the Devadāru forest, Medhā in the region of Kaśmīra; Bhīmā the Goddess is on the Himālaya, and likewise Tuṣṭi is at Viśveśvara.
At Kapālamocana, the mother is Śuddhi; at Kāmāvarohaṇa, she is Dharā; likewise, at Śaṅkhoddhāra, she is named Dhṛti, and at Piṇḍāraka, she is the same.
Kalā is in Candrabhāgā, Acchodā is Śivadhāriṇī, Amṛtā by name is in the Veṇā, and likewise Urvaśī is in Badarī. (79)
In Uttarakuru she is Auṣadhi; in Kuśadvīpa she is Kuśodakā;
on Hemakūṭa she is Manmathā; and on Kumuda she is Satyavādinī.
She is to be worshipped in the Aśvattha tree, she is indeed the treasure in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa;
she is Gāyatrī at the mouth of the Vedas, and Pārvatī in the presence of Śiva.
In the world of the gods she is Indrāṇī; in the mouths of Brahmās she is Sarasvatī;
in the solar orb she is named Prabhā; and among the Mothers she is considered to be Vaiṣṇavī. 82.
Among chaste women, Arundhatī is the foremost; among beautiful women, Tilottamā;
and in the hearts of all embodied beings, she is the power named Brahmakalā.
O Janamejaya, there are these eight hundred sacred seats (pīṭhas);
their attendants, their lords, and the goddesses are proclaimed to be equal in number to them. (84)
The sacred seats (pīṭhas) that constitute the limbs of the Goddess Satī have been described, as well as other principal ones on the surface of the earth that arose incidentally. 85.
Whoever should remember or even hear this supreme hundred-and-eight names shall be liberated from all sins and go to the supreme world of the Goddess. (86)

One should go to all these sacred seats (pīṭhas) according to the prescribed rules for pilgrimage, and having performed the śrāddha rites and other ceremonies, one should offer libations to the ancestors and others.
And one should perform a great worship of the Blessed Lady according to the prescribed rite;
one should repeatedly ask forgiveness from the Mother of the World, the Sustainer of the Universe. (88)
O Janamejaya, one should consider oneself to have accomplished all that was to be done;
thereafter, one should feed all the Brahmins with various kinds of foods, both hard and soft.
O King, [he honored] married women, maidens, young brahmin students, and others;
even those who were cāṇḍālas and the like residing in that sacred field, O Lord. (90)
All of them are remembered as having the form of goddesses; therefore, they are to be worshipped.
One should avoid all such things as accepting gifts from them in those sacred fields.

The best of beings should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) of the mantra according to his capacity, [worshipping] the Goddess of the gods, who dwells upon each respective seat, with the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ). 92.
O King, one should worship incessantly and thus perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa);
a man devoted to the Goddess should not practice stinginess regarding his wealth.
He who performs such a pilgrimage with a delighted mind toward the Illustrious Goddess shall dwell for a thousand kalpas in the most exalted world of Brahmā.
His ancestors dwell there, and he likewise dwells in the city of the Goddess;
finally, having attained supreme knowledge, he becomes liberated from the ocean of worldly existence.
By reciting the name one hundred and eight times, many have attained perfection;
wherever this [mantra] is written, whether in a manuscript or otherwise, it remains present in person.
Indeed, fears such as those caused by malevolent planets and Mārīs do not exist there at all;
prosperity increases constantly, like the ocean on a festival day. (97)
For one who recites the eight hundred names, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain;
devoted solely to the Goddess, he shall surely have accomplished his purpose. (98)
The deities indeed bow down to him, for he is remembered as being of divine form;
he is worshipped in every way by the gods, how much more so by the best of men? 99.
One should recite this supreme eight-hundred-name hymn at the time of a śrāddha ceremony;
then all those ancestors, being satisfied, proceed to the highest state. (100)
O King of kings, a wise man should take refuge in these fields of liberation, which are directly composed of pure consciousness, as well as in the seats of the Siddhas. 101.
O King, everything that was asked by you regarding the Great Lord has been told, including the most profound secrets; what more do you wish to hear? (102)
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Seats of the Goddess," in the seventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 30 ||
In the abode of the Himalayas, regarding the birth of Pārvatī, there is a description of the Goddess’s speech to the gods.
Janamejaya said:
"Upon the crest of the lord of the mountains, the supreme light appeared."
Tell me that which was previously spoken by you in detail.
What wise person, drinking the nectar of the discourse on Śakti, would not become dispassionate?
For those who drink the [ordinary] nectar of immortality there is death, but for one who hears this, there shall be none.
Vyāsa said:
You are blessed, you have fulfilled your purpose, and you have been instructed by the great-souled ones;
you are fortunate that you possess such sincere devotion toward the Goddess.
Listen, O King, to what occurred in the past when Satī’s body was consumed by fire;
Śiva wandered in confusion and eventually came to rest in a certain place.
Free from the appearance of conceptual proliferation, with his mind attained to meditative absorption,
that self-possessed one passed his time meditating upon the very form of the Goddess.
The three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, have become bereft of fortune;
the entire universe, along with its oceans, islands, and mountains, has been deprived of power.
Ānanda has become withered within the hearts of all;
all the worlds are indifferent, their minds shattered by anxiety.
They were then constantly submerged in an ocean of suffering, afflicted by diseases,
due to the adverse behavior of the planets and the deities.
Because of the true nature of the presiding deities of the elements (adhibhūta) and the presiding deities of the divine (adhidaiva), they became kings.
Now, at that very time, there was a great asura named Tāraka.
Having received a boon from Brahmā, the Daitya became the leader of the three worlds;
however, he who is the legitimate son of Śiva shall be your slayer.
Thus, having secured his own death at the hands of the gods of gods, that great asura roared and rejoiced because he would no longer have to face the biological son of Śiva.
Harassed by him and displaced from their own abodes,
all the gods fell into insurmountable anxiety due to the absence of a legitimate son of Śiva.
Śaṅkara has no wife; how, then, can there be the birth of his son? For us who are devoid of fortune, how will our purpose be accomplished? (13)
Thus, all of them, distressed with anxiety, went to the realm of Vaikuṇṭha;
they praised Hari in private, and he spoke a remedy to them.
"Why are you all so anxious? The auspicious Kāmakalpadrumā, the sovereign of the world who dwells on Maṇidvīpa, is awake. (15)
O Lord, we have no indifference toward this matter; it is otherwise.
This very instruction was given by the Mother of the World for our own training. (16)
Just as there is no lack of compassion in a mother toward her child, whether she is fondling or striking him,
so too it is with the Mother of the World, who restrains beings according to their virtues and faults.
A son indeed commits an offense at every step;
who else in this world, save for his mother alone, can endure it? (18)
Therefore, seek refuge in that Supreme Mother without delay;
with a sincere disposition of mind, she will accomplish your purpose.
Having thus instructed all the gods, Mahāviṣṇu,
the lord of the deities, departed quickly accompanied by his wife and the gods.
He went to the great mountain Himavat, the lord of mountains;
and all the gods became engaged in the performance of preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa).
O King, those who were experts in the ritual procedures for the Ambā sacrifice performed the Ambā sacrifice;
all the gods swiftly observed the vows beginning with the third day.
Some were proficient in meditative absorption (samādhi), some were devoted to the recitation of names (nāma-pārāyaṇa);
some were intent on the hymns (sūkta), and others were eager for the complete recitation of the names (nāma-pārāyaṇa). || 23 ||
Some are devoted to the recitation of mantras and perform penances such as the *kṛcchra*;
some are intent on internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), and others are dedicated to ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
With unwearied devotion, they performed the worship of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) through the Hṛllekhā mantra;
in this manner, O Janamejaya, many years passed by.
Suddenly, on the ninth day of the month of Caitra, on a Friday,
that splendor revealed by the Vedas manifested before him.
It was praised from the four directions by the four Vedas personified;
it shone like ten million suns and was as cool as ten million moons.
That supreme light, red in hue and possessing a brilliance equal to ten million flashes of lightning,
could not be grasped either above, nor across, nor in the middle.
That [reality], however, is devoid of beginning and end; it is not joined with limbs such as hands, nor is it in the form of a woman, nor in the form of a man, nor both.
O lord of the earth, their eyes were blinded by that radiance;
yet, when those gods regained their composure and looked again, [they saw it].
At that moment, it appeared in the form of a woman—divine and captivating, a maiden in the bloom of youth with exceedingly beautiful limbs. (31)
Her pair of full, uplifted breasts surpassed the beauty of lotus buds;
her tinkling girdle and anklets resounded with the sound of a cluster of small bells.
Adorned with golden armlets, bracelets, and neck-ornaments,
she shone with a collar fashioned from priceless gems fastened around her neck.
Her hair shone like a cluster of slender ketaka flowers with dark blue bees [as curls], and she was beautiful with the orb of her hips, adorned by a line of body hair. || 34 ||
Her mouth was filled with betel-leaf mixed with pieces of camphor,
and her lotus-face was adorned with shimmering golden earrings.
Her forehead resembles the orb of the eighth-day moon, her eyebrows are long,
her eyes are like red lotuses, her nose is prominent, and her lips are sweet.
Her front teeth are like jasmine buds, she is resplendent with a pearl necklace, her crown is inlaid with jewels, and she is adorned with a crescent moon as an ear-ornament. || 37 ||
She is resplendent with a mass of hair adorned with garlands of *mallikā* and *mālatī* flowers;
she has a dot of saffron upon her forehead and is graced by three eyes.
She has four arms holding a noose, a goad, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness; she is three-eyed, clothed in red garments, and possesses the luster of the pomegranate flower.
She is enriched with every kind of elegant attire, saluted by all the gods, the fulfiller of all hopes, the mother of all, and the enchantress of all. || 40 ||
The gods beheld before them their Mother, whose face was bright with grace, whose lotus-like countenance bore a gentle smile, and who was the very embodiment of sincere compassion. (41)
Beholding that embodiment of compassion, all the gods prostrated themselves;
their voices choked with tears, they were unable to say anything at all. || 42 ||
Having somehow regained their composure and with their necks bowed in devotion,
their eyes filled with tears of love, they praised the Mother of the World.
The gods said:
"Salutations to the Goddess, the Great Goddess; salutations eternally to Śivā.
Salutations to Prakṛti, the Auspicious One; being self-restrained, we bow down before her. (44)
I take refuge in that Goddess Durgā, who is fire-colored, blazing with ascetic power, the daughter of Virocana, and who delights in the fruits of ritual actions.
Homage to you, the one who easily crosses over and causes others to cross over. || 45 ||
The gods generated divine speech; animals of every form speak it.
May that cow-like speech, lowing sweetly and yielding for us refreshment and vigor, come to us with well-offered praise. 46.
We bow to Kālarātri, praised by Brahmā, the power of Viṣṇu, the mother of Skanda, Sarasvatī, Aditi, the daughter of Dakṣa—the purifying and auspicious one. 47.
We know Mahālakṣmī; we meditate upon the All-powerful One;
may that Goddess inspire us. 48.
Salutations to her whose form is the Virāṭ; salutations to her whose embodiment is the Sūtrātman;
salutations to her whose form is the Unmanifest; salutations to the venerable embodiment of Brahman. || 49 ||
We bow to that Bhuvaneśvarī, through whose ignorance the world appears like a snake or a garland upon a rope, and through whose knowledge it attains dissolution. 50.
We bow to her whose referent is the meaning indicated by that word, whose nature is the single essence of consciousness,
whose form is indivisible bliss, and who is the ground of the Vedas' ultimate purport.

We bow to her who transcends the five sheaths, who is the witness of the three states, who is the indicated meaning of the term "thou" (tvaṃpada), and whose nature is the inner self (pratyagātman). || 52 ||
Salutations to her whose form is the *praṇava*, salutations to her whose embodiment is the syllable *hrīṃ*;
salutations again and again to you, compassion itself, whose nature consists of manifold mantras.
Thus praised by the gods at that time, the goddess dwelling on Maṇidvīpa spoke with sweet words, her voice like the song of a cuckoo in rut.
The illustrious Goddess said:
"O wise ones, tell me the purpose for which you have assembled here;
I am always the granter of boons, and I am the wish-fulfilling tree for the desires of my devotees. (55)
"What concern is there for you who are full of devotion while I remain present?
I deliver my devotees from the ocean of the miserable cycle of worldly existence. (56)
"O best of the wise, know this promise of mine to be true.
Hearing these words, which were overwhelmed with love, they became satisfied in their minds. (57)
O King, the fearless and ageless gods spoke of their own suffering.
The gods said: "There is nothing in these three worlds that is unknown to you. (58)
O Supreme Goddess, who are omniscient and the witness of all,
we are oppressed day and night by the lord of the asuras, Tāraka.
O Śivā, his death was ordained by Brahmā through one born from Śiva’s own body;
yet, O Maheśvarī, you know that there is no such thing as a wife of Śiva. (60)
What indeed could be said by vulgar people in the presence of the Omniscient One? This has been declared by way of summary; consider the rest for yourself, O Ambika. 61.
"May your devotion to my lotus feet be unwavering at all times;
this is the primary thing to be prayed for, while another is for the sake of the body. (62)
Having heard these words of theirs, the Supreme Goddess spoke:
"My own power shall become Gaurī in the Himalayas."
She should be given to Śiva; she will accomplish your purpose, provided that you have devotion for his lotus feet with great respect.
For the Himalaya worships me with his mind through supreme devotion;
therefore, taking birth in his house is considered pleasing to me. (65)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those exceedingly gracious words, Himālaya,
his throat and eyes choked with tears, spoke these words to the Great Queen.
"You treat him as most great whom you desire to favor;
otherwise, what difference is there between me—a dull, motionless pillar—and you, whose nature is pure existence and consciousness? (67)

O sinless one, it is impossible for you to become my mother even through hundreds of births, nor by means of the merits of horse-sacrifices and the like, nor by merits born of meditative concentration equal to them. (68)
"Today her fame shall spread throughout the world, for the Mother of the Universe has become his daughter.
Oh, how blessed and fortunate is this Himālaya! (69)
But she in whose womb reside millions of universes—she alone has become his daughter; who indeed on earth could be equal to him?
I do not know what supreme abode has been prepared for our ancestors, in whose lineage there exists one such as I, unfit for the residence of those like them.
Tell me how this was given to me out of compassion and full of love,
and likewise describe my own form as established in all the Vedāntas.
O Supreme Goddess, since you alone are I, please speak of yoga accompanied by devotion and of the knowledge sanctioned by the Vedas. (73)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, Ambā, her lotus-like face serene,
began to speak that secret which had been hidden from the Vedas.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Goddess’s Speech to the Devas Regarding the Birth of Pārvatī in the Abode of Himālaya," in the seventh book of the *Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, consisting of eighteen thousand verses.
The description of the individual and collective aspects of the Goddess;
the Śrī Devī said:
"Let all you immortals listen to my words as I speak."
By the mere hearing of which, one attains the state of my own form. || 1 ||
O Lord of Mountains, in the beginning there was only I, and nothing else whatsoever;
that form of mine is consciousness and awareness, known by the single name of the Supreme Brahman.
Inconceivable, indescribable, incomparable, and free from affliction—
His certain power, established by itself, is renowned as Māyā.
It is not existent, nor is it non-existent, nor does it possess the nature of both due to contradiction;
rather, there is always some entity that is distinct from these [three] characteristics.
Like the heat of fire, like the radiance of the sun, or like the moonlight of the moon—this [nature] is my innate and constant companion. || 5 ||
Within that [state], the actions, individual souls, and times of living beings move about;
they become merged without distinction, just as worldly activities cease during deep sleep.
Through the conjunction with my own power, I have attained the state of being the seed;
yet, due to the obscuration of my own support, I have also come to possess the nature of a defect.

Due to its conjunction with consciousness, it is described as the efficient cause (nimitta), and due to the transformation of the phenomenal world (prapañca), it is called the material cause (samavāyin). || 8 ||
Some call that [nature] austerity (tapas), some darkness (tamas), others the inert (jaḍa);
[others call it] knowledge (jñāna), illusion (māyā), the primary matter (pradhāna), primordial nature (prakṛti), or even the unborn power (ajā-śakti).
Those proficient in the Śaiva scriptures call that state *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), while others who contemplate the true meaning of the Vedas call it *avidyā* (ignorance). 10.
Thus, there may be various names for her in the Vedas and other scriptures;
however, because she is an object of perception, she is insentient, and since she perishes through knowledge, she is therefore non-existent.
Consciousness cannot be an object of perception; if it were an object of perception, it would be insentient.
Furthermore, consciousness is self-luminous and is not illumined by another.
Because of the fault of infinite regress, it is not illuminated by itself either; there would be a contradiction between the object and the agent. Therefore, it is self-illuminating like a lamp. (13)
O Mountain, know that which is manifesting to others to be the illuminator;
for this very reason, the eternity of my nature as established consciousness is proven. (14)
Because the object of perception varies across states such as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, whereas no variation whatsoever has ever been experienced in consciousness itself. (15)
If there is an experience of that [cognition] as well, then the witness by whom it was experienced is precisely what remains here, having previously been of the nature of consciousness.
For this very reason, her eternity has been proclaimed by those learned in the true scriptures;
and her nature as bliss [is established] because she is the object of supreme love. (17)
"May I not cease to be; may I indeed exist"—this [desire] resides in the Self out of love.
Since everything else is illusory, my state of non-attachment is manifest. (18)
For this very reason, I maintain that its indefiniteness is likewise established;
moreover, that knowledge is not an attribute of the Self, for if it were an attribute, the Self would be insentient. (19)
The insentience of knowledge has never been observed, nor is it possible;
likewise, it does not possess the quality of consciousness, for consciousness is not distinct from consciousness. (20)
Therefore, the Self is always of the nature of knowledge and of the nature of bliss;
it is real, complete, unattached, and free from the web of duality. || 21 ||
Furthermore, through his own māyā joined with desire, karma, and so forth, [he arises] from the latent impressions of previous experiences and from the ripening of time and karma. || 22 ||
And due to a lack of discernment regarding reality, he becomes desirous of creation;
this creation, which is not preceded by conscious intent, has been described to you, O Lord of Mountains. (23)
For this which has been described by me as my own extraordinary form is unmanifest, unevolved, and is also called "variegated by Māyā. (24)
He is proclaimed in all scriptures as the cause of all causes, the primordial source of all principles, and whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss. (25)
That which is the condensation of all actions, the substratum of will, knowledge, and action,
and is denoted by the mantra *hrīṃ*— that is called the primordial principle (*āditattva*).
From that, space is produced, consisting of the subtle element of sound; from that, wind arises, whose nature is touch; and then fire, whose nature is form. (27)
Subsequently, water consists of the quality of taste, and from that, the earth consists of the quality of smell;
space has the single quality of sound, and wind is endowed with both touch and sound.
Fire is said by the wise to possess the qualities of sound, touch, and form;
water is traditionally held to have four qualities: sound, touch, form, and taste. (29)
Earth possesses five qualities: sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. From these arose the Great Thread (Mahat-sūtra), which they call the Liṅga.
That is declared to be the essence of all; this is the subtle body of the self. That which is unmanifest is indeed called the causal body, as has been stated previously.
In that [subtle body] resides the form of the seed of the world, from which the emergence of the subtle body (liṅga) occurs;
from that, the gross elements arise by way of the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa).
Five [elements] are produced; their specific types are now described. One should divide each of the previously mentioned elements into two parts. (33)
One should divide each single part of the mountain fourfold;
by joining each [part] with its own second and the other's second, those [parts] become five each.
And its effect is the Virāṭ body; this is the gross body of the Self.
Through the portions of *sattva* residing in the five elements, there arises the manifestation of the ears and the other senses. (35)
O King of kings, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is one among the sense organs; though it is single, it becomes fourfold through the distinction of its functions. (36)
When its function consists of conceptualization and discursive thought,
then it bears the name "mind" (manas);
and when it perceives [objects], it is designated as "intellect" (buddhi).
It is well-ascertained and free from the nature of doubt. || 37 ||
That mind is proclaimed to be of the nature of investigation;
however, through the function of the self consisting of ego-making, it attains the state of ego (ahaṅkāra). || 38 ||
From portions of those [elements], the organs of action are produced in succession;
and from these, when combined individually, the vital breath (prāṇa) becomes fivefold.
Prāṇa is in the heart, apāna is in the anus, samāna resides in the navel, udāna is in the region of the throat, and vyāna pervades the entire body. (40)
There are exactly five organs of perception and five organs of action;
likewise, there are the five vital breaths beginning with prāṇa, together with the intellect and the mind. (41)
This subtle body is what is called my *liṅga*;
O King, the *prakṛti* that is spoken of therein is traditionally held to be twofold.
Māyā, however, consists of the quality of goodness (sattva) and is mixed with the other qualities (guṇas); it is that which protects its own substratum, and thus it is called "māyā. (43)
The reflection of the Lord who serves as the original object within that [intellect] is declared to be the Supreme Lord, who possesses knowledge residing in his own substrate. (44)
He is the omniscient, the creator of all, and the one who bestows grace upon all;
yet, O Lord of Mountains, whatever reflection appears within ignorance [is merely that]. (45)
That very [unmanifest] becomes known as the individual soul (jīva), which is again the locus of all suffering;
thus, it is declared here that for both [the unmanifest and the soul], there are three bodies due to ignorance.
Furthermore, from the identification with the three bodies, there arose again a triad of names:
the Prājña is the causal self (kāraṇātman), while the Taijasa possesses the subtle body (sūkṣmadehin). || 47 ||
The one possessing the gross body is proclaimed as being threefold, known by the names Viśva and so forth; likewise, Īśa is also described by the terms Īśa, Sūtra, and Virāṭ.
The first is known as the individual form (*vyaṣṭi-rūpa*), while the other is remembered as the universal self (*samaṣṭy-ātman*).
For he is the Lord of All in person, desiring to bestow grace upon living beings. (49)
O King, impelled by my power and eternally established within me, he creates the manifold universe again and again as the locus of various enjoyments.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Individual and Collective Aspects of the Goddess," in the Devīgītā, within the seventh book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighteen thousand verses. || 32 ||
The description of the hymn composed by the gods, accompanied by the vision of the Śrīdevī in her form as Virāj.
The Goddess said:
"The entire world, including all moving and non-moving beings, is fashioned by my power of Māyā."
That māyā, moreover, does not exist as something separate from me in the ultimate sense.
From the perspective of conventional discourse, this very [reality] is renowned as "knowledge" (vidyā) or "illusion" (māyā);
however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, it does not exist at all—only the Absolute Reality (tattva) alone exists. (2)
Having created the entire world, O Mountain, I enter into its midst, accompanied by Māyā, karma, and the like, with the vital breath (prāṇa) as my precursor.
If there were no transition to another world, how could it be? For this reason, just as various manifestations of illusion arise, so too do they exist.
Just as the ether within jars and other vessels appears divided due to the difference in their limiting adjuncts,
so too the Sun always illumines objects such as the high and the low.
I am not defiled in that same way; I am never smeared by faults.
It is other people who, through their own intellect, superimpose agency upon me, such as the agency of the intellect and so forth.
The deluded, not the wise, declare that the self is karma;
likewise, this arises from the differentiation of ignorance and from the differentiation of māyā.
The distinction between the individual soul and the Lord is indeed imagined through Māyā alone,
just as the distinction between the space within a jar and the great outer space is imagined.

In the same way, the distinction between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) is imagined; likewise, the multiplicity of individual selves exists only through māyā and not by its own nature.

Likewise, the multiplicity of lords exists through *māyā* and not by way of their own nature; it is differentiated by the diversity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding the aggregates of body, senses, and so forth. (10)

Ignorance alone is proclaimed as the cause of the distinction between the individual soul and [the Supreme], and nothing else, O Mountain, for it is differentiated by the various latent impressions of the qualities (guṇas). 11.
That Māyā is the cause of the differentiation of the Supreme; it is never anything else.
O Supporter of the Earth, all this is woven across and through me.
I am the Lord, and I am the Sūtrātman; I am also the Virāḍātman.
I am Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; I am Gaurī, Brāhmī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
I am the sun, I am the stars, and likewise I am the Lord of the stars;
I am in the form of beasts and birds, and I am the outcaste and the thief.
"I am a hunter, I am one of cruel deeds, I am a man of virtuous deeds, and I am a great person;
even in the form of a woman, a man, or a neuter, I alone am so—of this there is no doubt. (15)
Whatever object whatsoever is seen or even heard anywhere, both internally and externally—I, pervading all that, abide forever. 16.
There is not a single thing, whether moving or unmoving, that has been abandoned by me;
if there were such a thing, it would be empty, for it would be like the son of a barren woman.
Just as a single rope appears as various things such as a snake or a garland, so indeed do I manifest in the forms of Īśa and others; there is no doubt in this. 18.
That which is imagined does not appear apart from its substratum;
therefore, this [world] possesses existence only through my existence, and not otherwise. (19)
Himālaya said:
O Goddess of gods, if you have compassion for me, O Goddess, I wish to see this very body of yours as a collective whole, exactly as you describe it.
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words of his, all the gods, together with Viṣṇu,
rejoiced with delighted hearts, honoring those words.
Then, having understood the intention of the gods, Śivā— the wish-fulfilling cow for her devotees and the fulfiller of the desires of her devotees— revealed her own true form.
They beheld the supreme Virāḍ-form of the Great Goddess, whose head was the sky and whose two eyes were the moon and the sun. (23)
The quarters are said to be his ears, the gods his speech, and Vāyu his breath;
they call the universe his heart, and the earth is remembered as his loins.
The vault of the sky is the navel-lake, the circle of luminaries is the chest, Maharloka is the neck, and Janoloka is remembered as the mouth. (25)
The world of heat (tapoloka) is the forehead, situated below the world of truth (satyaloka);
Indra and the other gods are the arms, and sound is the ear of the Great Lord.
The two nostrils are known as the Nāsatyas and Dasras; the sense of smell is considered by the wise to be the nose.
The mouth is declared to be Agni, and day and night are the two eyelashes.
The abode of Brahmā is the expansion of the eyebrows; water is proclaimed to be the palate;
taste is declared to be the tongue; and Yama is proclaimed to be the fangs. (28)
The teeth of the Great Lord are proclaimed to be the essence of affection, his smile is said to be Māyā, the casting of sidelong glances is creation, and the raised upper lip is his modesty. (29)
Greed is her lower lip, and the path of unrighteousness is her back;
the progenitor who is the creator upon the surface of the earth is her generative organ.
The belly of the Great Goddess Maheśvarī is the oceans, and her bones are the mountains;
her channels are declared to be the rivers, and her hair is celebrated as the trees. || 31 ||
Childhood, youth, and old age are his stages of life; his supreme movement is the wind; the clouds are his hair, and the two twilights are his garments, O All-pervading Lord.
O King, the moon is remembered as the mind of Śrī Jagadambā;
Hari is her power of cognition (vijñāna-śakti), and Rudra is remembered as her internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
For all the classes of horses are situated in the hip region of the All-pervading Lord;
and the great worlds beginning with Atala have come to occupy the portion below his waist. (34)
The foremost of the gods beheld such a great form,
rich with thousands of garlands of flames and licking with its tongue.
Vomiting fire from his eyes with a fierce clattering sound from his fangs, that hero bore various weapons and was the consumer of the *brahmakṣatra* (the priestly and warrior classes). || 36 ||
He has a thousand heads and eyes, and likewise a thousand feet;
he resembles ten million suns and possesses a splendor equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
All the gods beheld that terrifying and most formidable sight, which caused alarm to their hearts and eyes, and they raised a cry of "Alas! (hāhākāra).
With their hearts trembling, they fell into an insurmountable swoon, and even the memory that "she is the Mother of the World" vanished from them. (39)
Then those Vedas that were situated in the four directions of the Great Lord awakened the gods, who had fainted from their swoon, by means of their most formidable [sound].
Then those gods, having regained their composure and obtained that supreme revelation, stood with eyes filled with tears of love and throats choked with emotion. (41)
With voices faltering with tears, they began to offer praise.
The gods said:
"O Mother, forgive our transgression; protect us, the wretched ones born from you. (42)
"O Goddess of gods, restrain your anger; we are filled with fear at the sight of your form. What praise could be offered here by us, mere mortals and non-gods? (43)
Even for himself, that which is his own prowess—both its extent and its nature—is indeed unknowable;
how then could it be an object of perception for those born after him? (44)
Salutations to you, O Sovereign of the World; salutations to you, whose essence is the Praṇava.
Salutations to you, who are perfectly established in all the Vedāntas, and who are the embodiment of the syllable Hrīṃ.
Salutation to that Soul of All, from whom fire has arisen, from whom the sun and the moon have arisen, and from whom all medicinal herbs have arisen. || 46 ||
And since from him the gods, the Sādhyas, and even the birds, as well as the animals and human beings, have come into existence, salutation to that Soul of All. (47)
Salutations again and again to Him from whom proceed the out-breath and in-breath, rice and barley, austerity, faith, truth, as well as celibacy and sacred injunction. 48.
Salutation to that Self of All, from whom there are seven rays of vital breath, seven indeed as fuel-sticks, seven oblations, and likewise seven worlds.
Salutations again and again to Him from whom the oceans, mountains, and rivers flow forth, and from whom all herbs and juices arise.
Salutation to Him, the Soul of All, from whom sacrifice arose, as well as initiation, the sacrificial post, the priestly fees, the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants.
Salutations in front and behind; salutations to you on both sides;
below, above, and in the four directions—O Mother, salutations again and again!
O Goddess of gods, withdraw this extraordinary form;
show us instead that form which is most beautiful of the beautiful.
Vyāsa said:
Seeing the gods thus terrified, the Mother of the World, that ocean of compassion,
withdrew her terrible form and revealed her beautiful one.
Holding a noose, a goad, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, his entire body is delicate;
his eyes are filled with compassion, and his lotus-face bears a gentle smile. || 55 ||
Having seen that beautiful form, they were then freed from fear;
with peaceful minds, they bowed down, their voices faltering with joy. || 56 ||

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Hymn Offered by the Gods Along with the Vision of the Universal Form of Śrī Devī," in the seventh book of the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 33 ||
The description of the praise offered by the gods, accompanied by the vision of the Śrī Devī in her Virāṭ form.
The Śrī Devī said:
"Where indeed are you, so unfortunate, and where is this most wonderful form?"
Nevertheless, out of affection for my devotees, I have displayed such a form.
This form cannot be seen through the study of the Vedas, nor by yogic practices, nor by gifts, austerity, or sacrifice; it is possible only through my grace alone.

Listen to the subject at hand, O Indra among kings: here, the Supreme Self, through association with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), attains the state of being a living being as well as agency and other such qualities. (3)
One performs various actions, which have dharma and adharma as their sole causes; having thereby attained diverse wombs, one is joined with happiness and suffering. (4)
Furthermore, due to the power of that [past] conditioning, always delighting in various actions, it attains various bodies and is joined with pleasure and pain. || 5 ||
Indeed, like a water-wheel, there is never a cessation for this [cycle];
ignorance alone is its root, from which arises desire, and from that, actions.
Therefore, a person should strive with constancy for the destruction of ignorance;
for this indeed is the fulfillment of birth: the eradication of ignorance.

The attainment of the goals of human existence and even the state of liberation while living are accomplished by knowledge alone; indeed, knowledge is the most powerful force capable of destroying ignorance.
O Mountain, neither ritual action nor its resulting practice [is required], because there is no contradiction;
on the contrary, once ignorance regarding the Self has been destroyed, let it be understood that there is no further need for ritual action.
For harmful actions indeed yearn for one again and again;
from that arises passion, from that arises hatred, and from that great misfortune comes to be. (10)
Therefore, a person should acquire knowledge with every effort;
yet, because it is said "even while performing actions here," ritual action is also indispensable.
For liberation arises from knowledge alone; therefore, there should be a combination of the two.
Karma, being beneficial, may serve as an auxiliary to knowledge. (12)

Thus some say; however, due to the contradiction therein, it would not be possible, for the severing of the heart-knot occurs through knowledge, while the arising of karma exists within the heart-knot. (13)
Simultaneity is not possible for those two because of their contradiction;
just as simultaneity is impossible for darkness and light.
Therefore, O Great-minded One, all Vedic rites should culminate only in the purification of the mind; one should perform them with diligent effort. || 15 ||
Tranquility, self-restraint, endurance, and dispassion arise from the quality of goodness (sattva);
ritual actions exist only up to that point, and not beyond it.
At the conclusion of that, the self-possessed one, having renounced everything, should again take refuge with a guru who is learned in the Vedas and established in Brahman, with sincere devotion.
One should constantly listen to the Vedānta without indolence;
one should perpetually contemplate the meaning of such statements as "That thou art. (18)
But the sentence "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) and others reveal the identity of the individual soul and Brahman;
once this identity is known, one becomes fearless and indeed arises in my own form. (19)

First comes the comprehension of the word-meanings, and from that, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning; and the meaning of the sentence is proclaimed by me as being the meaning of that word. (20)
And the expressed meaning of the word *tvam* is the individual soul (*jīva*) alone; of this there is no doubt.
The identity of these two is declared by the wise through the word *asi*. (21)
Because the two literal meanings are contradictory, their identity cannot possibly be established;
therefore, one must employ figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) for those two principles situated in the sacred revelation.
Pure consciousness alone is the objective referent (lakṣya) of those two; thus, the possibility of their identity exists.
Having realized the identity of those two in such a way, one becomes non-dual through non-distinction from oneself.
Just as in the expression "this is that very Devadatta," it is traditionally held that there is metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā);
thus, a person, being devoid of the body characterized by stoutness and so forth, attains Brahman.
The gross body is produced from the fivefold great elements;
it is the locus of experience, joined with old age and disease, and [the seat] of all karmas. (25)
"This [world] appears clearly as something false because it consists of illusion;
O Lord of Mountains, this is that gross limitation (upādhi) of my self. (26)
The wise know that subtle body to be endowed with the organs of knowledge and action, joined with the five vital breaths, and possessed of mind and intellect. (27)

This subtle body (sūkṣmadeha) of the Self, arising from the unquintuplicated elements (apañcīkṛtabhūta), is its second limiting adjunct (upādhi); it is that which makes possible the experience of pleasure and so forth. (28)
O Lord of Mountains, this third [state] is beginningless and indescribable ignorance;
it appears as this body, the causal self of the Atman. (29)
When the dissolution of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) has occurred, the absolute Self alone remains.
Within the three bodies, the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) are always present. (30)
Upon the relinquishment of the five sheaths, Brahman is indeed attained as the tail;
it is my very form that is described by such statements as "not this, not this" (neti neti).
It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come into being, it never ceases to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain. (32)
If one thinks to kill the slayer, or if the slain thinks he has been killed, both of them do not understand; this [Self] neither kills nor is killed. (33)
Smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the secret cave of this living being;
free from desire and with his sorrow dispelled, he beholds that majesty through the grace of the Creator. 34.
Know the self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself;
know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins. (35)
The senses, they say, are the horses; the objects are their paths.
The wise say that the Self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer. (36)
But he who is ignorant, lacks mental control, and is always impure, does not attain that state and instead enters the cycle of worldly existence. || 37 ||
But he who possesses discernment, who is possessed of a controlled mind and is always pure, attains that state from which he is not born again. (38)
But that man who has consciousness as his charioteer and holds the reins of the mind reaches the end of the path—that supreme state which is mine. (39)
Having thus ascertained the Self by means of oneself through both scripture and reasoning,
one should meditate upon Me as being of the nature of the Self, even through profound contemplation (nididhyāsana).
Prior to the practice of yoga, one should contemplate the three syllables within oneself for the purpose of meditating upon the two things expressed by the mantra known as the Goddess-Pranava. (41)
The letter *ha* is the gross body, the letter *ra* is the subtle body, and the letter *ī* is that causal self; the syllable *hrīṃ* is I, the fourth state (*turīya*).
Having thus understood the three seed-syllables in sequence within the collective body as well,
the wise man should contemplate the unity of the collective and the individual.
But before the time of formal meditative absorption (samādhi), having thus cultivated [this practice] with devotion,
one should then meditate upon me, the Goddess, the Sovereign of the World, with the senses withdrawn.
Having made the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal as they move within the nostrils,
one whose desire for sense objects has ceased, who is free from defects, and devoid of envy— (45)
Endowed with sincere devotion, in a cave or in a place free from noise,
one should dissolve the universal self, which is the letter *ha*, into the letter *ra*.
One should dissolve the fiery deity represented by the syllable *ra* into the syllable *ī*;
one should dissolve the *ī* syllable, which is the conscious self (*prājña-ātman*), into the syllable *hrīṃ*.

One should meditate within the crest-lock upon that which is devoid of the relationship between the expressed and the expresser, free from dualistic existence, indivisible, and consisting of being, consciousness, and bliss. (48)
Thus, O King, by means of meditation, that best of men, having directly realized me,
becomes my very self, because there is oneness between the two.
Having perceived me, the Self who is higher than the highest, by means of this yoga-method,
one becomes at that very moment the destroyer of ignorance along with its effects.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Knowledge as the Cause of Liberation," in the Devīgītā, within the seventh book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 34 ||
The description of the hymn composed by the gods, accompanied by the vision of the Śrīdevī in her Virāṭ form.
Himālaya said:
"O Maheśānī, tell me the Yoga that bestows pure consciousness, along with its ancillaries."
By performing that [practice] by which I may become fit for the vision of reality. || 1 ||
The Goddess said:
"There is no yoga on the back of the sky, nor on the earth, nor in the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Those expert in yoga declare that the union of the individual soul (jīva) and the Self (ātman) is yoga. (2)
O sinless one, their six obstacles, which cause hindrances to yoga, have been declared:
they are known as desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy. (3)
By means of the very limbs of yoga, having pierced through those [obstacles], yogins shall attain yoga:
namely, restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), and breath control (prāṇāyāma), followed by that which comes after.
Withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), that which is called concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), together with absorption (samādhi)—
these they call the eight limbs for the practice of yoga by yogins.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion,
straightforwardness, forbearance, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity— these are the ten restraints (yamas).
Austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the deity, listening to the established doctrines, modesty, intelligence, recitation of mantras, and burnt offerings.
O Lord of Mountains, these ten observances have been declared by me:
the lotus posture (padmāsana), the auspicious (svastika), the fortunate (bhadra), and likewise the thunderbolt posture (vajrāsana).
This is declared to be the vīrāsana; thus, in sequence, the five postures [are described].
Having properly placed the auspicious soles of the feet upon the thighs— [this is the vīrāsana]. (9)
Then, one should bind the two thumbs with the hands in reverse order;
this is called the lotus posture (padmāsana), which is heart-pleasing to yogins.
Having properly placed the two auspicious soles of the feet between the knees and thighs, the yogi should sit with an upright body; that they call the Svastika posture. (11)
Having firmly placed the pair of ankles on both sides of the suture,
one should bind the heels beneath the scrotum with those two heels.
This is called the Bhadrāsana, highly honored by yogins.
Having placed the feet successively upon the thighs, with the knees facing outward and the toes turned inward; (13)
One should place the hands as described; this is the unsurpassed Vajrāsana (diamond posture), formed by placing one foot below and likewise resting the thigh upon the other.
The yogi should sit with the body straight; this is called the vīrāsana posture. He should draw in the external air through the iḍā [nāḍī] for sixteen mātrās. (15)
The yogi should retain [the breath] when full for sixty-four measures;
then, slowly and correctly, he should let it pass through the center of the suṣumnā for thirty-two measures.
The best among those who know yoga should exhale through the piṅgalā nāḍī;
those learned in the yoga scriptures call this prāṇāyāma.
In this manner, one should practice the external [breath] for him again and again in succession;
the increase in the measure (mātrā) should be done gradually, properly reaching twelve and then sixteen.
The wise know that [prāṇāyāma] together with recitation, meditation, and so forth, to be "with seed" (sagarbha); others know that which is devoid of these to be "seedless" (vigarbha). 19.
For a person practicing in due order, the emergence of perspiration in the body is considered the lowest [stage];
that accompanied by trembling is the middling; and the abandonment of the ground is regarded as the highest.
The attainment of the highest qualities is held to depend upon the restraint of the senses as they roam unimpeded among their objects. (21)
The forceful extraction [of the breath] from those [locations] is called *pratyāhāra*.
[It is performed] at the thumbs, the ankles, the knees, the thighs, the base of the genitals, and the navel. (22)
In the heart, the neck, and the region of the throat, then in the uvula, in the nose,
between the eyebrows, on the forehead, at the crown of the head, and at the "end of twelve" (dvādaśānta), according to the prescribed rule.
The retention of the vital breath is called *dhāraṇā*, performed with a concentrated mind abiding within consciousness. (24)

Meditation here is said to be the contemplation of one's chosen deities within oneself, and the constant cultivation of equanimity between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman). (25)
The sages have declared that samādhi is characterized by eight limbs;
now I shall describe to you the unsurpassed mantra-yoga. (26)
O Mountain, the universe is said to be the body, consisting of the five elements;
it takes the form of the unity of the individual soul and Brahman through the splendors of the moon, the sun, and fire.
It is held that there are thirty-five million channels (nāḍīs) in the body;
among them, ten are declared to be principal, and from among those, three are established as preeminent.
Here, within the spinal column (merudaṇḍa), the principal [channel] has the form of the tips of the moon and sun;
the white channel Iḍā is situated on the left, having the form of the moon. (29)
That channel which is on the right, known as Piṅgalā, has the form of Śakti; it is directly the embodiment of nectar, having the form of the Sun and the nature of Puruṣa.
That Suṣumnā, consisting of all splendor, is in the form of fire;
in its center, within the place called Vicitra, resides that which consists of will, knowledge, and action.
In the center is the self-manifested liṅga (svayaṃbhūliṅga), possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
above that is the seed-syllable of Māyā, consisting of the soul of Hara along with the bindu and nāda.
Above that, however, is Kuṇḍalī, shaped like a crest and red in form;
she is said to be of the nature of the Goddess, O Lord of Mountains, and non-different from me. (33)
Outside of that, one should contemplate a lotus with four petals beginning with the letter *va* and ending with *sa*, having the appearance of gold, shining like molten gold. (34)
Above that is the unsurpassed Svādhiṣṭhāna, resembling fire, having six petals with the luster of a diamond,
and consisting of the six syllables beginning with ba and ending with la.
The root is the six-cornered base; therefore they know it as the *mūlādhāra*. By the word "self" (*sva*), they know the supreme *liṅga* as the *svādhiṣṭhāna*. (36)

Above that, in the region of the navel, is the Maṇipūra [cakra], which possesses great luster; it has the appearance of a cloud and the brilliance of lightning, and is composed of manifold splendor. || 37 ||
That lotus, being pierced like a jewel, is likewise called a "jewel-lotus" (maṇipadma);
it is endowed with ten petals and is accompanied by the letters beginning with 'ḍa' and ending with 'pha'.
The lotus presided over by Viṣṇu is the cause for the vision of Viṣṇu;
above that is the Anāhata lotus, resembling the rising sun.
It was established upon petals beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ṭha', as well as solar leaves;
in its center stood a Bāṇaliṅga, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns.
There, the unstruck sound (anāhata), consisting of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), is perceived;
that lotus is celebrated by the sages as being called "Unstruck" (anāhata). || 41 ||
That is indeed the abode of bliss, presided over by Puruṣa;
above that is the petal known as Viśuddha, a sixteen-petaled lotus.
Endowed with sixteen vowels, smoke-colored and of great luster, it is called *viśuddha* because it expands from the perception of the world of the *haṃsa* by the individual soul. (43)
The pure lotus is called "Space," most wonderful;
above that is the wheel of command (ājñācakra), supreme and presided over by the Self.
Because the transmission of command occurs there, it is proclaimed as "Ājñā" (the Command).
That most beautiful lotus consists of two petals joined with the letters Ha and Kṣa. 45.
Above that is the one called Kailāsa, and above that is Rodhinī;
thus, O observer of noble vows, the ādhāra-cakras have been described to you.
The place of the *bindu* is said to be ten thousand million *yojanas* above that;
thus has this entire unsurpassed path of yoga been described. (47)
First, one should fix the mind in the foundation (ādhāra) by means of the practice of inhalation (pūraka);
having contracted the power (śakti) located between the anus and the genitals, one should awaken it. (48)
Following the sequence of the differentiation of the *liṅgas*, one should lead [the breath] to the *bindu-cakra*;
one should contemplate that supreme Śakti as having become one with Śambhu. (49)
Therein, having caused that nectar which has arisen—which resembles molten lac—to be drunk by that power (śakti) known as Māyā, which bestows the perfection of yoga; || 50 ||
Having satiated the deities of the six cakras there with a stream of nectar,
the wise one should then bring [the nectar] back to the mūlādhāra by that same path.
Even for one practicing in this manner day after day, all the previously mentioned defiled mantras will certainly attain success; it cannot be otherwise.

Just as those qualities which belong to me, the Goddess and Mother of the World, exist, so too is one liberated from the bonds of existence through [the realization of] the sufferings of old age, death, and the like. (53)
These qualities certainly arise in the best of practitioners and not otherwise;
thus, my dear, has this supreme practice of breath-retention (vāyudhāraṇa) been described. 54.
Now, listen attentively to me regarding that which is called *dhāraṇā*: having fixed the mind upon the Goddess who is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth. (55)
One quickly becomes absorbed in that through the union of the individual soul and Brahman;
or, if the mind is still stained, it may not achieve success quickly. (56)
Then, O Mountain, through the application of its parts, the yogi should practice the yogas upon my own limbs, such as my hands and feet, which are sweet [to the touch].
The mantra-practitioner should stabilize the mind again through mastery over the various states;
with a purified mind, he should fix the mind upon every form.
O Mountain, as long as the mind remains dissolved in the Goddess, who is pure consciousness,
for that long the practitioner should diligently practice the recitation of the desired mantra along with fire offerings.
Through the practice of mantra and yoga, one becomes fit for the knowledge of that which is to be known;
for there is no mantra without yoga, nor indeed is there yoga without mantra.
For the practice of these two is indeed the cause for the perfect realization of Brahman;
just as a jar in a house enveloped by darkness is seen by means of a lamp. 61.
"Thus the Self, veiled by illusion, has indeed been made an object of perception by Manu;
in this way, the entire method of yoga, along with its auxiliary limbs, has now been declared by me. (62)
It is to be known through the instruction of the guru, and not otherwise, even by millions of scriptures. || 63 ||

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Means for Attaining Mantra-Siddhi," in the Devīgītā, within the seventh book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 35 ||
In the Devīgītā, the description of the instruction on the knowledge of Brahman: The Goddess said:
"Thus, one whose self is united with yoga should meditate upon me, who am the form of Brahman."
O King, with sincere devotion, he presented himself before the throne. || 1 ||
Manifest and yet hidden, moving in secret is the name of the great state;
herein all this is deposited—whatever is trembling, whatever breathes, and whatever moves.
Know this as the existent and the non-existent, the most excellent, the supreme beyond consciousness, the highest among all creatures;
that which is luminous and subtler than the subtle.
In whom the worlds and the inhabitants of the worlds are established.
This is that syllable, Brahman; it is Prāṇa, and it is Speech and Mind.
This is the Truth, the Immortal; know this, my dear, as that which is to be pierced.
Taking up the great weapon of the Upaniṣadic bow, one should fix the sharpened arrow of meditation; drawing it back with a mind absorbed in that state, one should aim.
Know that very object to be perceived, O gentle one, to be the Imperishable. || 5 ||
The syllable Om is the bow, the self is indeed the arrow, and Brahman is said to be its target.
One must pierce it with undistracted mind; like the arrow, one shall become absorbed in that.

In whom heaven and earth, as well as the intermediate space and the mind, together with all vital breaths, are woven—know him alone as the Self; abandon other words. He is the bridge to immortality. 7.
Wherein the channels are gathered together like the spokes in the nave of a wheel,
that very one moves within, being born in many ways.
Meditate on the Self as "Om.
May there be well-being for you to reach the further shore beyond darkness.
The Self is firmly established in the divine city of Brahman, in the ether. || 9 ||
Consisting of mind, leading the body of vital breaths, established in food and having fixed its seat in the heart—
the wise behold it through the knowledge of that.
That which shines forth as the immortal form of bliss. || 10 ||
The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.
In the supreme golden sheath is the resplendent Brahman, partless;
that is the pure light of lights, which those who know the Self know.
There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this earthly fire.
Everything shines only after Him as He shines.
By its light all this shines. || 13 ||
Brahman alone is this immortal reality in the east; Brahman is behind, and Brahman is to the south and to the north.
Spread below and above, Brahman alone is this entire universe, the most excellent.
He who has such an experience is one who has accomplished his purpose, the best among men;
having become Brahman, with a serene self, he neither grieves nor desires. (15)
O King, fear arises from a second; in the absence of that, one does not fear.
For me, there is no separation from Him, nor for Him is there any separation from me.
"Know for certain, O Parvata, that I am indeed he;
my presence is wherever a knower of me resides. (17)
I do not dwell at a sacred ford, nor on Kailāsa, nor in Vaikuṇṭha, nor anywhere else;
rather, I reside in the midst of the lotus-heart of those who possess knowledge of Me.
The worship of one who possesses my knowledge even once yields the fruit of ten million of my own worships;
his lineage becomes pure, and his mother has fulfilled her purpose. (19)
The earth is meritorious for one whose mind has its abode in consciousness;
and as for that knowledge of Brahman which you have asked about, O best of mountains. (20)
I have told all of that; indeed, there is nothing further to be said.
This [teaching] is for an eldest son who is endowed with devotion and virtuous conduct.
It should be taught to a disciple who is as described, and never otherwise;
to one who possesses supreme devotion for the Divine, and for the Guru just as for the Divine. (22)
For these truths revealed here shine forth clearly to that high-souled one by whom this knowledge has been taught; he alone is the Supreme Lord. (23)
He who is unable to perform meritorious deeds for another is thereby a debtor to him;
yet he who bestows the birth of Brahman is said to be even greater than one's own parents.
"O Mountain, the birth derived from one's father is lost; such a birth as this has never occurred before.
One should not bear malice toward him," so the Veda has declared. (25)
Therefore, according to the established doctrine of the scripture, the supreme Guru is the giver of Brahman;
when Śiva is angry, the Guru is the protector, but when the Guru is angry, not even Śaṅkara can save one.
Therefore, O Mountain, one should please the glorious Guru with every effort;
one should always be intent upon him through body, mind, and speech. (27)
Otherwise, he would be ungrateful, and for the ungrateful there is no atonement;
this was told by Indra to Atharvan under the condition of cutting off his head.
When he spoke to the two Aśvins, his head was severed by the wielder of the thunderbolt;
seeing that horse-head of his lost, the two physicians, the best of gods, [acted]. (29)
Then, O Lord of Mountains, he joined his own head back together with those two;
thus, O Mountain, Brahma-vidyā is attained through such hardship—
he by whom it is obtained is blessed and has fulfilled his life's purpose.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction on the Knowledge of Brahman," in the Devīgītā of the seventh book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 36 ||
In the Devīgītā, the description of the greatness of devotion:
Himālaya said:
O Mother, tell me of your own devotion, by which knowledge may indeed be attained with ease.
[This] would arise for this person of middling capacity who is not free from passion. || 1 ||
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Mountains, O best of beings, three paths are renowned to me for the attainment of liberation:
the yoga of action, the yoga of knowledge, and the yoga of devotion. (2)
This [practice] is suitable for all three [types of practitioners] and can be performed in every way;
for it is easily accessible, mental in nature, and does not afflict the body, mind, or other faculties. (3)
That devotion is considered to be of three kinds according to the differences in the qualities of men;
[the first] is that which is directed toward the injury of others, preceded by hypocrisy. || 4 ||

The devotion of one who is possessed by stinginess and anger is *tāmasī*; whereas that which is free from harming others and the like, and is performed solely for the sake of one's own welfare, [is *sāttvikī*]. (5)
Constantly desiring [worldly] objects, seeking fame for his heart, and greedy for enjoyments,
he worships me with extreme devotion in order to obtain each respective fruit.
But the vulgar person, through the intellect of duality, perceives me as other than himself;
O Lord of Mountains, his devotion is declared to be of the passionate (rājasa) type.
Action dedicated to the Supreme Lord serves to wash away sins;
because it is prescribed in the Vedas, I must certainly perform it incessantly. (8)
Thus, one whose intellect is resolved yet who relies upon the notion of duality performs action for the sake of pleasure; that devotion, O Mountain, is of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
This devotion to the Supreme is what leads to the attainment of Him, because it relies upon the realization of difference;
for the two types of devotion previously mentioned are not considered to lead to the attainment of the Supreme. (10)
Now, listen to me as I describe supreme devotion:
the constant hearing of my qualities and the perpetual chanting of my names.
May my mind abide steadily upon me, who am a mine of the jewels of virtuous qualities, and may its constant flow be like a stream of oil.
In that state, no cause whatsoever could ever exist;
nor is there any desire for proximity (sāmīpya), equal power (sārṣṭi), union (sāyujya), or co-residence (sālokya). || 13 ||
He never perceives anything whatsoever as superior to service unto Me;
because of the state of being the served and the server, he does not desire liberation therein.
He who, through supreme devotion, meditates upon me alone without sloth,
knows me eternally as non-different from himself, and not as distinct.
But he who contemplates all living beings as being of my own nature experiences love for the Supreme Self just as he does for his own self. (16)
But he who, because of the equality of consciousness, does not make a distinction among those existing everywhere, in all forms, and at all times— (17)
The Lord bows and offers sacrifice even unto the lowest outcaste;
because he is free from all sense of duality, he harbors no thought of malice toward anyone whatsoever.
O Lord, may there be faith in beholding my abodes, as well as faith in beholding my devotees, faith in hearing my scriptures, and faith in the mantras, tantras, and so forth. (19)
His mind is always overwhelmed with ecstatic love, his body is covered in horripilation, his eyes are filled with tears of love, and the sound of his voice is choked with emotion. (20)
He who worships me, the Sovereign, the source of the world, and the cause of all causes, with undivided devotion, O Lord of Mountains— || 21 ||
My divine vows, both daily and occasional, he who performs them constantly with devotion, free from stinginess regarding his wealth, [attains success]. || 22 ||
O Mountain, the desire to witness my festival and the act of performing my festival arise in such a person inevitably from their very nature. (23)
Singing my names aloud, he indeed dances,
free from egoism and the like, and devoid of identification with the body.
Whatever is performed by the force of past karma (prārabdha) shall happen exactly so;
I have no concern even regarding such matters as the preservation of the body.
Thus, that devotion which has been described is known as supreme devotion (parabhakti),
in which nothing whatsoever is conceived apart from the Goddess.
O Supporter of the Earth, when such supreme devotion has truly arisen in one,
at that very moment their dissolution occurs within my form, which is pure consciousness.
That which is the supreme pinnacle of devotion is proclaimed to be knowledge itself;
it is also the limit of detachment, because both of these reside within knowledge. (28)
O Mountain, even for one who has performed devotion, if my knowledge does not arise due to the power of *prārabdha* karma, he goes to Maṇidvīpa.
Having gone there, O Mountain, one experiences all enjoyments even if one does not desire them;
at the end of that, the knowledge of my nature as consciousness shall arise perfectly.
By that [knowledge], one should always be liberated; liberation comes from knowledge and not otherwise.
For whomsoever there is knowledge here and now of the inner Self residing within the heart. || 31 ||
The vital breaths of that person who is dependent on my consciousness do not depart;
he attains Brahman itself, for he who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself. || 32 ||
It is like gold on the neck, hidden by ignorance;
indeed, through knowledge and the destruction of ignorance, that which was already attained is truly obtained.
O Best of Mountains, my body is other than both the known and the unknown;
as it is in a mirror, so it is in the self, as it is in water, so it is in the world of the ancestors.
Just as shadow and sunlight are pure and distinct from one another, even so may my knowledge in this world be free from the state of duality. (35)
But he who, being devoid of passion yet lacking knowledge, should die,
would dwell eternally in the world of Brahmā for as long as a kalpa, and thereafter [attain liberation].
Furthermore, his birth shall take place again in the home of those who are pure and prosperous;
thereafter, he performs spiritual practice, and from that, knowledge indeed arises.
O King, knowledge is attained through many births, not by means of a single birth;
therefore, with every effort, one should apply oneself to the pursuit of knowledge.
Otherwise, there would be a great destruction, and this birth is difficult to obtain again;
even therein, the attainment of the Vedas in the first caste is rare. (39)

The perfection of the six qualities beginning with tranquility, as well as the attainment of yoga, and likewise the meeting with a supreme guru—all of this is indeed difficult to obtain in this world. (40)
Likewise, through the sharpness of the faculties and the refinement of the body, the desire for liberation arises from the merits accumulated over many lifetimes. (41)
Even when the means of accomplishment have thus become fruitful, the birth of that man who does not strive for the sake of knowledge is utterly useless. (42)
Therefore, O King, one should apply effort toward the acquisition of knowledge according to one's ability;
one certainly obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice at every step. (43)
Like clarified butter hidden within milk,
discernment dwells within every being;
it must be constantly churned.
By means of the mind, which serves as the churning-stick. || 44 ||
"Having attained knowledge, one becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose"—this is the drumbeat of the Vedānta.
Everything has been stated in brief; what more do you wish to hear? (45)

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Devotion," in the Devīgītā of the seventh book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 37 ||
In the Devīgītā, the description of the places for the Great Festival Vow (Mahotsava-vrata):
Himālaya said:
