"O Goddess of gods, how many places on the surface of the earth are to be visited?"
These are the principal purifiers and most beloved of the Goddess.
Likewise, whatever vows grant satisfaction and whatever festivals there may be—O Goddess, O Mother, all that is for the sake of the man who has fulfilled his purpose. || 2 ||
The illustrious Goddess said:
"Everything visible is my abode; all times consist of vows, and festivals occur at all times, because I am the one who possesses all forms. (3)
Nevertheless, out of affection for my devotee, I shall say something, little by little;
O King of Mountains, listen attentively to my words.
Kolāpura is a great sacred site where Lakṣmī is ever-present;
it is the second city of the Mother, the supreme abode presided over by Reṇukā.
Tulajāpura shall be the third, as well as Saptaśṛṅga;
likewise, there is the great site of Hiṅgulā and that of Jvālāmukhī.
The supreme abode of Śakambharī, the most excellent abode of Bhrāmarī,
the abode of Śrī Raktadantikā, and likewise the abode of Durgā.
The supreme among all supreme places is the abode of her who dwells on the Vindhya mountain;
the great site of Annapūrṇā is the unsurpassed city of Kāñcī.
The supreme abode of Bhīmādevī, as well as the Vimalā abode, the great Śrīcandralā abode, and the Kauśikī abode; || 9 ||
The supreme abode of Nīlāmbā is on the peak of the Blue Mountain;
likewise, there is the abode of Jāmbūnadeśvarī and the auspicious Śrīnagara.
The great seat of Guhyakālī which is established in Nepal, and that supreme seat of Mīnākṣī which is proclaimed to be in Cidambaram; || 11 ||
Vedāraṇya is a great place presided over by Sundarī;
Ekāmbara is a great place established by Paraśakti.
Mahālasā is the supreme abode, and likewise that of Yogeśvarī;
similarly, the abode of Nīlasarasvatī is renowned among the Cīnas.
At Vaidyanātha, however, the site of Bagalā is considered the most excellent;
at Śrīmacchrībhuvaneśvarī, Maṇidvīpa is remembered as mine. 14.
The yoni-maṇḍala of Kāmākhyā belonging to the illustrious Tripurabhairavī is a jewel among sacred fields on the earth’s surface, consecrated by Mahāmāyā. (15)
There is no place superior to this on the surface of the earth;
for there, every month, the Goddess herself becomes visibly menstruating.
All the deities residing there have attained the nature of mountains;
indeed, even the great deities dwell within the mountains. (17)
The entire earth there is considered by the wise to be the form of the Goddess;
there is no place higher than this Kāmākhyā-yonimaṇḍala. 18.
The supreme abode of the Gāyatrī is said to be the glorious Puṣkara;
Caṇḍikā is at Amareśa, and Puṣkarekṣiṇī is at Prabhāsa.
In the great sacred site of Naimiṣa, that goddess is Liṅgadhāriṇī;
in Puṣkarākṣa she is Puruhūtā, and likewise in Āṣāḍha she is Rati.
At the great site of Caṇḍamuṇḍī, the Supreme Goddess is Daṇḍinī;
at Bhārabhūti she is Bhūti, and at Nakula she is Nakuleśvarī.
Candrikā is remembered as Śāṅkarī on Mount Hariścandra;
she is Triśūlā at Japyeśvara and Sūkṣmā at Āmrātakeśvara.
Śāṅkarī is at Mahākāla, Śarvāṇī is in the one called Madhyama, and that Goddess Mārgadāyinī is in the great field known as Kedāra. (23)
She is known as Bhairavī in the place called Bhairava, and she is remembered as Maṅgalā in Gayā;
she is Sthāṇupriyā in Kurukṣetra, and also in Svāyambhuva and Nākula.
Ugrā shall be at Kanakhala, Viśveśā at Vimaleśvara;
Mahānandā at Aṭṭahāsa, and Mahāntakā at Mahendra. (25)
In Bhīma, Bhīmeśvarī is proclaimed; furthermore, in the place of Vastrāpatha, she is called Bhavānī Śāṅkarī; and in Ardha-koṭika, she is Rudrāṇī.
The large-eyed one is at Avimukta; the highly fortunate one is at Mahālaya;
Bhadrakarṇī is at Gokarṇa; and Bhadrā is at Bhadrakarṇaka.
Utpalākṣī is in Suvarṇākṣa; Sthāṇvīśā is in the place named Sthāṇu;
Kamalā is in Kamalālaya; and Pracaṇḍā is in Chagalaṇḍaka.
At Kuraṇḍala there is Trisandhyā; at Mākoṭa, Mukuṭeśvarī;
at Maṇḍaleśa, Śāṇḍakī; and again, at Kālañjara, Kālī.
Sound is said to reside in Śaṅkukarṇa, and it becomes gross in Sthūlakeśvara;
in the heart-lotus of the wise, the Supreme Goddess is Hṛllekhā.
These places have been declared as most beloved by the Goddess;
O best of mountains, having first heard the majesty of each respective sacred field (kṣetra), [one should visit them]. 31.
Thereafter, one should worship the Goddess according to the prescribed rite;
or else, O best of mountains, all sacred fields (kṣetra) exist within Kāśī.
Therefore, one who is devoted to the Goddess should dwell there constantly,
visiting those sacred places and reciting the mantra to the Goddess without interruption.
Meditating upon her lotus feet, one is liberated from bondage;
whoever recites these names of the Goddess after rising in the morning [shall attain the same]. (34)
O Mountain, sins are reduced to ashes at that very moment;
one should quickly recite these pure verses in front of the twice-born during the time of a śrāddha ceremony.
All his ancestors, being liberated, attain the supreme goal.
Now, O you of noble vows, I shall describe the religious observances (vratas) to you.
Both women and men should diligently perform this vow known as Anantatṛtīyā, also called the Rasakalyāṇinī vow.
The vow known as Ārdrānandakara on the third lunar day, the Friday vow, and likewise the Kṛṣṇacaturdaśī; || 38 ||
There is the vow of the day of Mars (Bhaumavāra-vrata) and likewise the vow of Pradoṣa;
there, the god Mahādeva, having seated the goddess upon a throne, [performs these rites].
At the onset of night, she performs a dance before him together with the gods;
having fasted there at the beginning of the night, during the twilight hour (pradoṣa), one should worship Śivā.
O Mountain, this vow on Monday is especially an antidote and brings delight to that Goddess; it is exceedingly dear to me.
There too, having worshipped the Goddess, one should take a meal at night;
indeed, this vow for two Navarātras is pleasing to me.
O Lord, likewise, he who, free from envy, performs other constant and occasional vows for the sake of pleasing me; || 43 ||
He attains union with me; he is my devotee, he is dear to me.
O Lord, one should also perform festivals, including the joyous festival of the swing.
Just as you would perform the festival of the bed, so too should you perform the festival of the vigil,
the chariot festival for me, and indeed the damana festival.
My devotee should always perform the Pavitrōtsava, which brings joy in the month of Śrāvaṇa, as well as other great festivals in this manner. (46)
One should joyfully feed my devotees, as well as married women, virgins, and young celibates (baṭukas), with one's inner self absorbed in them and regarding them with the same mind as myself. (47)
Free from stinginess regarding wealth, one should worship them with *sumanā* flowers and other offerings;
whoever performs this with devotion every year, unwearied, [attains the fruit]. (48)
He is blessed and has fulfilled his purpose; he is truly a worthy recipient of my affection. Everything that bestows my pleasure has been told to you in brief.
This must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor ever to one who is not devoted.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Great Festival, Vows, and Sacred Sites," in the Devīgītā, within the seventh book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 38 ||
In the Devīgītā, the description of the procedure for the worship of the Śrīdevī:
Himālaya said:
O Goddess of gods, O Maheśānī, O Mother, ocean of compassion!
Now tell me correctly and as it truly is your own ritual procedure for worship.
The illustrious Goddess said:
"O King, O preeminent among mountains, listen with great faith as I shall describe the ritual of worship for Ambikā that is dear to her."
My worship shall be of two kinds: external and internal as well.
The external is also said to be twofold: Vedic and likewise Tantric. (3)
O Supporter of the Earth, the Vedic rite is also twofold according to the distinction of forms;
the Vedic rite should be performed by those who are initiated into the Vedas.
But for those who have received the initiation prescribed in the Tantras, the Tantric [method] should be resorted to;
thus, without knowing the secret of worship, one acts contrarily.
The foolish man who performs [this] falls in every way;
of those [types], I shall first describe that which is declared in the Veda. (6)
O Supporter of the Earth, you have seen my supreme form directly before you—
vast, with infinite heads and eyes, and infinite feet.
One should constantly worship, bow to, meditate upon, and remember that very [Reality] which is endowed with all powers, the impeller, and higher than the highest.
O Mountain, thus has the nature of the first image been described;
one who is peaceful, with a concentrated mind, and free from hypocrisy and egoism— || 9 ||
Be devoted to that, perform sacrifice for that, and go for refuge to that alone;
behold that with your mind, and always chant and meditate upon it.
Resorting to my state of being with undivided devotion joined with love,
worship me alone through sacrifices, austerities, and gifts, and thus fully satisfy me.
"In this way, through my grace, you shall be liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
Those who are intent on me, whose minds are attached to me, are considered the best of devotees. (12)
I promise that I shall deliver you from this state of existence before long,
either through meditation joined with ritual action, or else through devotion and knowledge.
O King, I am attained in every way, but not by mere ritual acts alone;
devotion arises from dharma, and from devotion the Supreme is attained. (14)
That which is declared by the Śruti and Smṛti is proclaimed as Dharma;
that which is taught by other scriptures is called a semblance of Dharma (dharmābhāsa). || 15 ||
The Veda has arisen from me, who am omniscient and omnipotent;
because ignorance is absent in me, the Śruti is not invalid.
And the Smṛtis have emerged only after grasping the meaning of the Śruti;
therefore, the authority of both Manu and others as well as of the Śrutis is accepted. (17)

Sometimes and in certain instances, they speak of a Dharma proclaimed by others through a glance toward the meaning of the Tantras; however, that portion is not at all to be accepted by the followers of the Veda. (18)
Because other authors of treatises arise from ignorance and their teachings are corrupted by the defect of ignorance, their words do not possess authoritative validity.
Therefore, one who desires liberation for the sake of dharma should in every way take refuge in the Veda;
for just as the king’s command in this world is never transgressed.
That command of mine, which is the authority of all, is the Śruti; how could it be abandoned by men?
Indeed, for the sake of preserving my command, the castes of Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas [must uphold it].
Therefore, it should be known that this secret word of mine, the Veda, was created by me;
for whenever there is a decline of dharma, O Supporter of the Earth. (22)
When unrighteousness arose, I then assumed various guises;
it was from this very cause, O King, that the distinction between gods and daityas came into being.
For those who do not practice that Dharma, I have always prepared hells so that terror may arise from merely hearing of them, for the sake of their training. (24)
The king should banish from his own realm those unrighteous persons who, having abandoned the dharma of the Vedas, take refuge in another dharma. || 25 ||
They are not to be conversed with by Brahmins, nor are they to be admitted into the row of eaters by the twice-born;
as for whatever other various scriptures exist in this world, [they are likewise rejected]. (26)
Those [teachings] which contradict the Śruti and Smṛti are entirely of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), namely:
the Vāma, the Kāpālaka, the Kaulaka, and the Bhairava Āgama. (27)
It was brought forth by Śiva for the purpose of deluding [them], and not for any other reason;
[it occurred] due to the curse of Dakṣa, the curse of Bhṛgu, and the curse of Dadhīca.
For the sake of uplifting those excellent Brahmins who have been scorched by being cast outside the path of the Vedas, [this work] is provided always as a gradual series of steps.
The Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Sauras, Śāktas,
as well as the Gāṇapatyas and the Āgamas, were indeed promulgated by Śaṅkara.
In that regard, even those portions not in conflict with the Vedas have indeed been mentioned here and there; for those who accept them, no fault whatsoever ever arises. (31)
In no way may a twice-born man be entitled [to practice] a matter that contradicts the Veda;
however, one who is devoid of entitlement to the Veda may be entitled to that [contradictory matter]. 32.
Therefore, with every effort, one who follows the Veda should take refuge in the Veda;
for knowledge conjoined with dharma reveals the supreme Brahman. || 33 ||
Having renounced all desires, they have come to me alone for refuge;
they are compassionate toward all beings and free from pride and egoism.
With their minds fixed on Me, their lives surrendered to Me, and delighting in discourse concerning My abode—whether they be renunciants, forest-dwellers, householders, or students. (35)
They always worship with devotion the yoga known as the Lordly (aiśvara);
for those who are constantly devoted to it, I [dispel] the darkness born of ignorance. (36)
"I shall destroy [it] by the light of the sun of knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, O Lord of Mountains, is the first [stage] of the Vedic worship. (37)
The essential nature has been stated in brief; now I shall describe that of the second [mudrā].
Whether upon an image, or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or likewise within the orbs of the sun and moon— || 38 ||

Having meditated upon the Goddess, who is higher than the highest, either in water, or in a Bāṇaliṅga, or in a yantra, or on a great cloth-painting, or likewise in the lotus of the heart, [one should worship].
She was endowed with qualities, filled with compassion, youthful, and as red as the rising sun;
she was the ultimate limit of the essence of beauty, beautiful in every limb. (40)
To the Mother who is filled with the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra-rasa), who is always distressed by the suffering of her devotees,
whose face is gracious, and who wears a crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
One should worship her, who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, whose nature is bliss, with ritual offerings according to one's means.
As long as one does not have the qualification for internal worship, one should resort to this external worship; but once that [qualification] has arisen, one should abandon it.
But that worship which is internal is known as the dissolution into consciousness;
consciousness alone is my supreme form, free from all limiting adjuncts.
Therefore, one should fix the mind without support upon consciousness, which is my own form;
for the world, which is beyond the nature of consciousness, is false and composed of illusion.
Therefore, for the destruction of saṃsāra, one should meditate upon her who is the witness and whose nature is the Self, with a mind free from mental constructs (nirmanaska) and joined in yoga.
Henceforth, the expansion of the external worship is described by me;
listen with an attentive mind, O best of mountains. (47)

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Worship of the Goddess," in the Devīgītā, within the seventh book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 39 ||
In the Devīgītā, the description of the procedure for external worship: The Goddess said:
Having risen in the morning, one should meditate upon a radiant lotus on the head.
There, one should remember the venerable Guru in his own form, radiant as camphor.
Having prostrated before the Goddess, who is exceedingly serene, adorned with radiant ornaments, and endowed with power, the wise one should then meditate upon Kuṇḍalinī.
I take refuge in that Woman who is the very form of bliss, who shines forth at the first departure, who becomes like nectar upon the return journey, and who moves within along the path.

Having meditated thus, one should meditate upon me in the center of that crest-lock (śikhā) as having the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss; then, one should complete all the rites such as purification.
Then, having performed the Agnihotra sacrifice for my pleasure, O best of the twice-born,
he should sit upon his own seat at the conclusion of the oblation and perform the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) for worship.
Having first performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa),
one should always perform the placement of the Hṛllekhā-Mātṛkās (hṛllekhāmātṛkānyāsa).
One should place the syllable *ha* at the root-support (*mūlādhāra*), the syllable *ra* at the heart,
likewise the syllable *ī* between the eyebrows, and the syllable *hrīṃ* on the crown of the head.
One should perform all other nyāsas prescribed by their respective mantras;
furthermore, one should conceive of a sacred seat (pīṭha) within one's own body by means of dharma and the other [guṇas].
Then, once [the mind] has been expanded through breath-control (prāṇāyāma), the wise one should meditate upon the Great Goddess within the heart-lotus,
my own abode, seated upon a throne of five corpses.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
these five great spirits (mahāpreta) stand at the soles of my feet.
For these [elements] consist of the five gross elements and also consist of the five states;
but I, being of the nature of unmanifest consciousness, am in every way beyond them.
Thereafter, they always become my seats in the Śakti-tantras;
having meditated thus, one should worship me with mental enjoyments and also perform recitation.
Having offered the recitation (japa) to the Śrī Devī, one should then perform the placement of the arghya vessel;
having arranged the ritual vessels, one should purify the articles of worship.
Having first performed the binding of the directions with that water, with the *manu*, and with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), the preceptor should then pay homage to his gurus.
Having then received his permission at the external seat (bāhyapīṭha),
[I shall manifest] my divine and heart-stealing form residing within the heart.
Then, one should invoke [the deity] upon the pedestal with the vidyā for the stabilization of the vital breath (prāṇasthāpana);
likewise, there should be the offering of the seat, the invocation, the arghya, the water for the feet, and so forth, as well as the water for sipping.
Having offered with devotion to the Goddess a bath, two garments, all kinds of ornaments, and appropriate perfumes and flowers according to one's means (verse 17).
One should properly perform the worship of the enclosures situated within the Yantra;
for those who are unable to do so every time, Friday is prescribed as the specific day.
The deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatāḥ) are to be remembered as having forms like the radiance of Mūladevī;
one should contemplate the three worlds pervaded by the mass of that radiance. 19.
One should worship the Root Goddess together with her retinue,
using fragrant perfumes such as sandalwood and other scents, as well as beautifully scented flowers.
One should satisfy me with food offerings, libations, betel leaves, sacrificial fees, and so forth,
as well as with this thousand-name hymn composed by you.
O Lord, I [protect myself] with the Kavaca-sūkta beginning with "Aham Rudraibhiḥ," with the Atharvaśīrṣa mantras of the Goddess, and with those arising from the Hṛllekhā Upaniṣad.
With the great mantras of the Mahāvidyās, a man, his heart moist with love, should repeatedly please me and ask forgiveness from the Mother of the World. (23)
With all his limbs marked by horripilation and with a voice choked by tears in his eyes, he should repeatedly please me with the sound of dancing, singing, and other such performances. 24.
Since I am indeed to be propounded by the complete study of the Vedas as well as by all the Purāṇas, one should therefore please me with them.
One should constantly offer even one's own entire possession, including one's body;
thereafter, one should perform the daily fire-sacrifice (nityahoma) and [honour] Brahmins and married women.
One should feed the *baṭukas*, the commoners, and others with the thought that they are the Goddess; then, having bowed, one should dismiss them from the heart in reverse order. || 27 ||
O observer of excellent vows, you should perform my entire worship with the *hṛllekhā* mantra;
for *hṛllekhā* is remembered as the supreme leader of all mantras. (28)
I am eternally reflected in the mirror of Hṛllekhā;
therefore, whatever is offered by Hṛllekhā is presented by all the mantras. (29)
Having worshipped the Guru with ornaments and other offerings, one should attain a sense of fulfillment;
whoever thus worships the Goddess Śrīmad-Bhuvanasundarī [attains that same state]. (30)
Indeed, for him nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain anywhere or at any time;
at the end of the body, he certainly goes to my Maṇidvīpa in every way.
He should be known as the very embodiment of the Goddess; the gods always bow down to him.
Thus, O King, I have described to you the worship of the Great Goddess.
Having reflected upon this in its entirety, yet in accordance with your specific qualification, perform my worship; by that, you shall become one who has achieved his purpose.
But this scripture of the Gītā one should never speak to one who is not a disciple; it must not be given to one who lacks devotion, nor to a rogue, nor to one of evil intent. 34.
This disclosure is the unveiling of the Mother’s breasts;
therefore, this must always be guarded with diligent effort. (35)
It should indeed be given to a devoted disciple, or to one's eldest son,
provided he is of good character, well-attired, and endowed with devotion to the Goddess.
One should recite this in the presence of Brāhmaṇas at the time of the Śrāddha ceremony;
then all those ancestors, being satisfied, proceed to the supreme state. || 37 ||
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, that Blessed Lady vanished right there;
and all the gods became joyful from the sight of the Goddess.
Then that goddess Haimavatī was born on Himālaya;
she who became renowned as Gaurī was given in marriage to Śaṅkara.
Then Skanda was born, and by him Tāraka was struck down.
O lord of men, previously, during the churning of the ocean, jewels appeared.
There, the goddess Ramā, having been praised by the gods with devotion for the sake of attaining Lakṣmī and for the purpose of bestowing grace upon them, emerged from that place.
Vaikuṇṭha was given [the boon] by the gods, and by that his peace was restored.
Thus, O King, the supreme majesty of the Goddess has been narrated to you. 42.
This subject concerning the origin of Gaurī and Lakṣmī, which grants all desires, must not be told to anyone else, for it is a secret that has been disclosed [only to you]. (43)
This Gītā is the very secret; it must be guarded with great effort.
O sinless one, everything that you asked has been told by me. It is pure, purifying, and divine. What more do you wish to hear? 44.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for External Worship," in the Devīgītā, within the seventh book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 40 ||
In the context of the description of the universe, there is the narration of the granting of boons by the Goddess to Manu.
Janamejaya said:
[Tell me] that which rests upon the noble accounts of kings born from the lineages of the Sun and the Moon.
The life-story recounted by you has been heard; it is a source of nectar.
Now I wish to hear how that Goddess, the Mother of the World,
is worshipped in whatever form she is adored throughout all the Manvantaras.
In whatever place and by whatever action the Goddess of Devas,
the bestower of fruits, is to be worshipped with the body;
and by whichever seed-mantra she is worshipped in whichever location.
And the description of the Goddess’s universal form (virāṭ-svarūpa) exactly as it is. || 3 ||
O brahmin-sage, tell me all about that meditation by which the mind may attain its own subtle essential nature, so that I may obtain the highest good.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the supreme worship of the Goddess;
by performing it or even by hearing of it, a man attains welfare in this world.
Thus was Nārāyaṇa questioned by Nārada in ancient times;
that which the Lord, the initiator of the practice of yoga, spoke to him [is here].
Once, the illustrious Nārada, wandering this earth,
arrived at the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa and remained there, free from all weariness.
Having bowed to that soul of yoga, the one born from the body of the god Brahmā questioned him regarding this very matter about which you have asked, O sinless one.
Nārada said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, Purāṇa-Puruṣottama, support of the universe, omniscient one, whose noble virtues are worthy of praise! (9)
Tell me, as you desire, that which is the primordial reality of the world;
from where indeed is this born, and upon what is it established?
From where can one reach the end in time, and where does the arising of all fruits occur? By knowing what would this illusion—the ground of delusion—come to destruction? (11)
O Lord, by what worship, by what recitation, or by what meditation within the lotus of one's own heart does illumination arise, like the rising of the sun in the darkness? (12)
O Lord, speak this answer to the question in its entirety and without omission, so that the world may easily cross over the blinding darkness. (13)
Vyāsa said:
Thus questioned by the celestial sage, the ancient and most excellent of sages,
the great yogin Nārāyaṇa, having offered his salutation, spoke these words.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O best of divine sages, to the supreme truth of the universe, by knowing which a mortal indeed is no longer born into the delusion of the world. (15)
Indeed, the Goddess has been declared by me, as well as by the sages, gods, gandharvas, and other wise men, to be the very reality of the universe.
That Goddess creates the world, by her it is maintained, and by her everything is destroyed; thus it is declared through the three qualities (guṇas).
I shall describe the true nature of that Goddess, who is worshipped by the Siddhas and Ṛṣis;
it destroys all sins for those who remember her, and likewise bestows both desired objects and liberation. (18)
The first Manu, Svāyambhuva, was the powerful son of the Lotus-born [Brahmā];
he was the illustrious husband of Śatarūpā and the sovereign lord of all manvantaras.
In former times, that Manu attended upon his father, the god Prajāpati, who is free from all stain, with devotion; then the Self-born One spoke to his son.
"Son, son, you must perform the supreme worship of the Goddess;
by her grace, my dear, the creation of progeny will be accomplished for you. (21)
Thus addressed by the Creator of beings, the powerful Manu Svāyambhuva Virāj then gratified the Goddess, the source of the universe, through austerity.
With a concentrated mind, he indeed praised the Goddess, the Queen of Gods—the primordial Māyā, possessed of all powers, the cause of all causes. (23)
Manu said:
Salutations, salutations to you, O Goddess of gods, the cause of the cause of the universe;
you who hold the conch, discus, and mace in your hands, and who reside within the heart of Nārāyaṇa.
O embodiment of the Vedas, O Mother of the world, O you whose form is the abode of the cause, O knower of the authority of the three Vedas, O Śivā, praised by all the gods! || 25 ||
O Maheśvarī, O highly fortunate one, O Mahāmāyā, O you of great prosperity! O you who dwell as the beloved of Mahādeva, O you who bring delight to Mahādeva! || 26 ||
O beloved of Gopendra, O eldest one, O great bliss, O great festival, O remover of the fear of the Great Plague, salutations to you who are worshipped by the gods and others! 27.
O most auspicious of all that is auspicious, O Śivā, who accomplishes all purposes, O refuge, O Tryambakā, O Gaurī, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you! (28)
For that by which this entire universe is always woven like warp and woof is consciousness—unique, devoid of beginning or end, and a treasury of splendors. (29)
Through his glance, Brahmā always performs the creation of everything, and Hari likewise protects; and by his grace, the Lord of the Universe acts as the destroyer.
Afflicted by the fear arising from Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the Lotus-born Lord was liberated from the ocean of existence caused by those terrible Daityas through her hymn of praise.
You are modesty, fame, mindfulness, splendor, Lakṣmī, and Satī, the daughter of the mountain;
you are the daughter of Dakṣa, the womb of the Vedas, the bestower of perfection, and the eternal grantor of fearlessness.
I shall praise you, I bow to you, I worship you, and I mutter your name;
I meditate upon you, I contemplate you, I gaze upon you, and I shall listen to you—O Goddess, be gracious to me! 33.
Brahmā, the treasure-house of the Vedas; Kṛṣṇa, whose abode is the target; Purandara;
the sovereign of the three worlds; the wielder of the noose; and the supreme lord of aquatic creatures.
Kubera became the lord of treasures, Yama was born as the king of the departed, Nairṛta became the lord of the Rākṣasas, and Soma was born consisting of water.
O Goddess worshipped by the three worlds, O Sovereign of the World, O You whose form is the supreme auspiciousness!
Homage be to You; again and yet again, O Mother of the Universe, salutations, salutations! (36)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Thus praised, the supreme Goddess Durgā, the consort of Nārāyaṇa,
being pleased, O divine sage, spoke these words to the son of Brahmā:
The Goddess said: "Choose a boon, O Indra among kings, son of Brahmā, whatever you desire;
for I am pleased here by this hymn of praise, by your devotion, and by your worship. (38)
Manu said:
"O Goddess, O most excellent among the compassionate, if you are pleased with my devotion, then by your command may the creation of progeny proceed without obstacles. (39)
The Goddess said:
"O King of kings, by my grace, let the creation of progeny indeed proceed for you without obstacle, and may there be ever-increasing prosperity. (40)
Whoever always recites this hymn composed by you with devotion to me, for them there shall indeed be the attainment of knowledge, progeny, fame, and the dawning of splendor. (41)
Wealth and grain arise, and the power of men remains unassailed;
there is victory everywhere, O King, as well as happiness and the destruction of enemies. 42.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having thus granted boons to Manu, the son of Brahmā,
the Goddess vanished even as that wise one was looking on.
Then the powerful king, the son of Brahmā, having obtained the boon, said to Brahmā: "O Father, let a secluded place be granted to me."
"Command me without delay as to that place where, having established myself, I shall create abundant progeny and worship the Lord of Gods with sacrifices. (45)
Having heard these words of his son, the all-pervading Lord Prajāpatipati reflected for a very long time: "How can this matter be accomplished? (46)
As I was engaged in creation, a vast period of time, numbering infinitely, has passed;
the earth, submerged by the waters, has been praised [as the foundation], having become the essence and the refuge of all. (47)
The Blessed One, the primordial Puruṣa, will carry out this task conceived by me, since I have taken refuge in his command as my helper. (48)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Goddess Granting Boons to Manu," in the context of the Cosmology, within the eighth book of the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 1 ||
In the context of describing the universe, regarding the granting of boons by the Goddess to Manu,
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"O scorcher of foes, while the lotus-born one was thus reflecting..."
By the eminent sages beginning with Manu, and by Marīci and the others on all sides.
O sinless one, as Viriñca was thus meditating, a small boar the size of a single finger suddenly emerged from the tip of his nose.
While he was looking on, O Nārada, that being standing in the sky increased in an instant to the size of an elephant; indeed, it was most wonderful.
O Nārada, having seen that boar-form, the Lotus-born Lord reflected upon it along with Marīci and the other chief sages, as well as Sanaka and the others.
"What is this divine being dwelling here under the guise of a pig?
This most wonderful thing has arisen, having emerged from the nose. (5)
"Was it seen as no more than the tip of a thumb, and in an instant became like the king of mountains?
Or was it the Blessed One, or perhaps my sacrifice itself, that has distressed my mind?"
While that Brahman, the Supreme Self, was thus reflecting,
the Blessed Lord, in the form of a boar resembling a mountain, let out a roar.
Making the ends of the quarters resound with the mere sound of his roar, he gladdened Virañci and the assembled best of the twice-born.
Having heard that deep, resonant sound intended to exhaust their own weariness,
those foremost of immortals dwelling in Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka [approached].
O best of the twice-born, they overwhelmed that primordial Puruṣa with excellent hymns consisting of meters, arising from the Ṛg, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas.
Having heard their hymn of praise, the primordial Lord Hari, the Sovereign,
having favored them with a mere glance of compassion, entered into the waters.
As he was entering within, the ocean, tormented by the blows of his cruel mane, then said: "O Lord, protector of those who seek refuge, save me! (12)
Having heard these words spoken by the ocean, the omnipresent Lord Hari,
tearing asunder the aquatic creatures, entered within the waters.
Running hither and thither and searching the earth,
the Lord of All gradually reached the ground, sniffing it again and again.
Then that Lord of the Gods of gods extracted with his tusk that earth which had not been submerged in water and which serves as the refuge for all beings.
Having lifted her up with the tip of his tusk, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Person of Sacrifice,
shone like a world-elephant lifting up a lotus-pond.
Having seen him, Virañci, the lord of the gods, together with Manu and Svarāṭ, praised the Lord of Gods, who had lifted up the earth with his tusks, with these words: ||| 17 ||
Brahmā said:
Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one, destroyer of the afflictions of devotees!
You who have humbled the support of the gods and bestow the fruits of all desires.
And this earth, O King, shines as your domain, like a lotus-pond rich with beautiful petals when upturned by the trunk of a mighty elephant. (19)
And this body of yours truly shines from its contact with the earth,
resembling the body of a lordly elephant with its trunk-tip raised like an uprooted lotus.
Salutations, salutations to you, O Lord of gods, the cause of creation and destruction;
O Lord who has assumed various forms for the sake of destroying the Dānavas! 21.
Salutations be to you in front, and salutations again and again from behind;
O support of all the immortals, O vast effulgence, salutations be to you!
"Empowered by your strength, I and you have been appointed to the creation of beings;
under the authority of your command, I perform and transform the creation. (23)
O Hari, O Lord of Gods, in ancient times, with you as their ally,
all the immortals divided the nectar according to the time and according to their strength.
By his command, Indra obtained the sovereignty over the three worlds;
honored by the hosts of gods, he enjoys abundant prosperity upon the earth. (25)
Having attained the state of fire through its various divisions such as the digestive fire (jāṭhara) and others, it likewise provides nourishment for gods, asuras, and humans. || 26 ||
Then Dharmarāja, the sovereign of the ancestors and the witness of all actions, is the bestower of the fruits of deeds; by your command, O Lord, he is the presiding authority.
Nairṛta, the lord of the Rākṣasas, the Yakṣa who destroys obstacles, and the witness of the actions of all living beings—these are born from you. (28)
Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, guardian of the world, and sovereign of the waters, attained the status of a world-guardian by relying on the power of your command. (29)
Vāyu, the bearer of fragrance and the cause of the vital breath of all beings, has been born by your command as a guardian of the world and a teacher of the universe. (30)
Kubera is the refuge of the livelihood for the yakṣas, including the kinnaras and others;
he is subject to your command and is honored among all the lords of the worlds. (31)
The Lord of all Rudras, the sovereign who brings about the end of even Īśvara, he was born as one to be venerated by the lords of the world and the protector of all the gods. || 32 ||
We pay homage to you, the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, from whose portions all the gods have indeed been born by the thousands. (33)
Nārada said: Thus praised by the Creator of the Universe, the Blessed One, the Primordial Person,
bestowed his grace merely by a glance of his playful look.
Right there, Hari struck with his mace the formidable Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa, a great Asura who had arrived and was obstructing the path.
With his limbs smeared by the mud of that blood, the Lord, the Primordial Person,
the Divine One, playfully raised the earth from the waters with his tusk.
Having established [himself], the Lord of the lords of the world departed for his own abode.
This supreme lifting up of the earth by the Blessed One is truly marvelous.
The man who hears and he who recites this supreme narrative shall be liberated from all sins and attain the state of Viṣṇu. || 38 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Rescue of the Earth," in the eighth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The second chapter, concerning the description of the extent of the universe and the glorification of the lineage of Svāyambhuva Manu, is completed.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Nārada, having established the earth in its proper place, the Lord went to the realm of Vaikuṇṭha; then Brahmā spoke to his own son.
O son of Svayambhū, O mighty-armed one, O best among the radiant!
Abide in your station of earth and create progeny as is fitting.

Worship the Lord of Sacrifice, the Supreme Person, according to the distinctions of place and time, O All-pervading One, with various articles of high and low quality that serve as the means for sacrifice.
Practice the Dharma as taught by the Teacher, which is bound to the system of social classes and stages of life;
by this gradual application, the increase of progeny will come to pass.
Having begotten sons who were preeminent in virtue, fame, and beauty of form, and who were endowed with learning and humility, being the best among those of virtuous conduct; (5)
Having given his daughters in marriage to those who were virtuous and renowned, he remained composed,
having properly concentrated his mind upon the Supreme Being, the Pradhāna-Puruṣa.
Through the yoga of the practice of devotion and by means of service to the Blessed One,
you have attained the desired goal that is ever to be revered by yogins.
Having thus consoled his son Manu, the lotus-born Prajāpati, having appointed him to the creation of progeny, returned to his own abode.
Obeying his father’s command, "Create offspring," Svāyambhuva, the lord of the earth, undertook the creation of progeny.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were the two sons of Manu, possessed of great splendor;
they begot three daughters—listen to their names from me:
the first daughter was Ākūti, and the second was Devahūti.
The third progeny was indeed renowned as the purifier of the world.
He gave Ākūti to Ruci, the middle one to Kardama, and he gave Prasūti to Dakṣa; from them these creatures in the world have descended.
From Ruci was born the blessed Yajña, the primordial Puruṣa;
and from Kardama, upon Ākūti and Devahūtī,
was born that Kapila, the master of Sāṃkhya, the all-pervading one renowned throughout all the worlds.
From Dakṣa, through Prasūti, many daughters were born as progeny;
from their offspring were produced the gods, animals, humans,
and others, all world-renowned and the initiators of creation.
And in the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, the omnipresent Lord Yajña,
surrounded by hosts of gods and Yāmas, protected Manu from the Rākṣasas.
Furthermore, the Lord Kapila, the great yogi, remained in his own hermitage.
To Devahūti, he taught the supreme knowledge that removes all ignorance—
specifically the yoga of meditation, the certainty of spiritual knowledge,
and the Śāstra of Kapila, which destroys all nescience. (17–18)
Having instructed [them], that great yogi departed for the hermitage of Pulaha;
even today, that divine and noble-minded teacher of Sāṃkhya remains there.
By the mere remembrance of his name, both Sāṃkhya and Yoga are perfected.
I bow to that Kapila, the teacher of yoga, the bestower of all boons.
Thus has been told this excellent description of the lineage of Manu’s daughters;
it destroys all sins for those who read or even hear it.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the auspicious lineage of Manu’s sons,
by the mere hearing of which one may attain the supreme state.
[I shall also describe] the arrangement of the continents, regions, oceans, and so forth, which was established by his sons.
"For the sake of establishing worldly conventions and for the attainment of happiness by all beings.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Lineage of Svāyambhuva Manu," in the *Bhuvanakośa-vistāra* (Detailed Description of the Cosmic Egg) within the eighth book of the *Śrīmad-devībhāgavata-mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Regarding the description of the lineage of Priyavrata within the context of the cosmic egg (*bhuvanakośa*),
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "The eldest son of Svāyambhuva Manu was Priyavrata."
He was constantly devoted to the service of his father and dedicated to truth and righteousness.
He married Barhiṣmatī, the beautiful daughter of Prajāpati Viśvakarman, who was equal to him in character and conduct. || 2 ||
Upon her, he begot ten sons endowed with virtues and purified souls,
as well as a daughter, Urjasvatī, who was the youngest.
Āgnīdhra, Idhmajihva, and Yajñabāhu as the third;
Mahāvīra is the fourth, and Rukmaśukraka is the fifth. || 4 ||
Ghṛtapṛṣṭha, Savana, Medhātithi as the eighth, Vītihotra, and Kavi—these ten are the names of the fire-gods. || 5 ||
Among these ten sons, three were free from passion:
Kavi, Savana, and Mahāvīra—these three.
Having fully realized the knowledge of the Self, they were all indeed perpetual celibates; in the stage of life known as the Paramahaṃsa, they lived joyfully, free from all desire.
And by his other wife, three sons were born, renowned as Uttama, Tāmasa, and Raivata. (8)
These sons of great prowess were the lords of the Manvantaras;
that king of kings, Priyavrata, enjoyed this earth.
When the sun shone upon the first division of the earth, his strength and senses remained unimpaired for eleven arbuda years.
It is said that in the second part of that [night] there was the onset of darkness;
thus the king, having observed this situation for a long time with his mind, [reflected]. (11)
"While I rule over the earth, how could darkness manifest?
In this way, I shall ward it off from the earth by the power of yoga. (12)
Having thus resolved, that son of Svāyambhuva,
illuminating [the earth] seven times with his chariot as bright as the sun, departed.
As that king was proceeding, the wheel-rims of his chariot fell upon the earth;
for the sake of the world, they became known as oceans.
Those seven regions born on the earth were divided into continents;
the seven oceans arose as moats from the rims of the wheels of the chariot.
From where they originated, seven islands of the earth are indeed remembered;
namely, Jambūdvīpa, Plakṣadvīpa, and that known as Śālmalīdvīpa. || 16 ||
Kuśadvīpa, Krauñcadvīpa, Śākadvīpa, and Puṣkaradvīpa;
their dimensions increase twofold for each successive one.
And it was arranged all around, in order from the outermost parts:
the salt-water ocean, the sugarcane-juice ocean, the wine-ocean, and the ghee-water ocean.
The Kṣīroda, Dadhimaṇḍoda, and Śuddhoda—
these seven are remembered as the oceans renowned upon the earth at that time.
The first [continent], named Jambūdvīpa, which is surrounded by the salt ocean—
the king appointed his son, named Āgnīdhra, as its ruler.
In this second island, Plakṣadvīpa, which is flooded with sugarcane juice,
was born as its ruler the son of Priyavrata named Idhmajihvaka.
In this Śālmalīdvīpa, which is surrounded by the sea of wine,
Priyavrata appointed Yajñabāhu as its sovereign.
In the most beautiful Kuśadvīpa, which is surrounded by the ocean of clarified butter (ghṛtoda),
there was a king named Hiraṇyaretas, the son born of Priyavrata’s daughter.
In Krauñcadvīpa, the fifth, which is surrounded by the Ocean of Milk,
there was a mighty lord named Ghṛtapṛṣṭha, the son of Priyavrata.
In Śākadvīpa, which is most beautiful and filled with the waters of curd-cream (dadhimaṇḍoda),
there was a preeminent king named Medhātithi, the son of Priyavrata.
In Puṣkaradvīpa, which was filled with pure waters and rivers,
there was a king named Vītihotra, who was esteemed by Janaka.
The powerful lord gave a daughter named Ūrjasvatī to Uśanas;
from her was born the famous daughter of Kāvya, Devayānī. (27)
Having thus divided the seven continents among his sons, Priyavrata,
coming under the sway of discernment, took refuge in the path of yoga.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of Priyavrata," concerning the Geography of the World, in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
In the description of the worlds of the universe, there is a description of the distinctions between the continents and regions. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"O divine sage, listen to the detailed account according to the divisions of the continents and regions."
Of the entire circle of the earth, just as it was fashioned by the gods. || 1 ||
I shall explain it briefly; it is not possible to do so in detail anywhere.
First, Jambūdvīpa is one hundred thousand yojanas in extent.
It is vast and circular in shape like the pericarp of a lotus,
and it contains nine regions, each measuring nine thousand yojanas.
They were completely enumerated by their lengths, surrounded on all sides by eight mountains of elongated form that stood encircling them, and were well-proportioned in every respect.
Two regions, situated to the south and north, should be known as being shaped like a bow;
among them, four are long and Ilāvṛta is square.
Ilāvṛta is the central region,
in whose navel this king of mountains, made of gold, is firmly established, rising one hundred thousand yojanas high.
This very Karṇikāra tree stands upon the head of the earth-lotus,
extending for thirty-two thousand yojanas.
At its base it is sixteen thousand [yojanas], and by that same extent it is submerged in the earth.
To the north of Ilāvṛta are the Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgavān mountains.
Indeed, three mountains are said to be the boundary limits within these three regions:
in the one called Ramyaka and likewise in the second, Hiraṇmaya.
In the third region, Kuruvarṣa, they mark the boundaries;
extending eastward, they likewise reach as far as the salt ocean on both sides.
Each one is successively twice as wide as the preceding one, increasing by a tenth part from each earlier one toward the north. || 11 ||
These very mountains, including the various Nanda and Ananda rivers, decrease in length from Ilāvṛta toward the south; [there stand] Niṣadha and Hemakūṭa.
And the Himālaya—these three are said to be wide at their base, most beautiful, and renowned for reaching a height of ten thousand yojanas. || 13 ||
These three boundary mountains describe, according to their true nature, the divisions of Harivarṣa, Kimpuruṣa, and Bhārata.
To the west of Ilāvṛta is the mountain named Mālyavat,
and to its east is the glorious Gandhamādana mountain.
But these two mountains, Ānīla and Niṣadha, are two thousand yojanas long and have attained a width of two thousand yojanas; they serve as the boundary-forming mountains.
And those two are renowned as the regions of Ketumāla and Bhadrāśva;
likewise, [the mountains] Mandara, Merumandara, and Supārśvaka [are there]. (17)
And the mountain known as Kumuda— these are the foothills of Meru,
extending ten thousand yojanas in both breadth and height on the four sides of Meru.
These supporting pillars, however, are resplendent on all sides;
upon these mountains are found mango and rose-apple trees.
The four mountains Kadamba and Nyagrodha are situated there;
on these kings of mountains stand eleven hundred peaks.
Each of those four lakes has branches extending as far as its width and a circumference of one hundred [yojanas]; their waters consist of milk, honey, sugarcane juice, and pure water.
By touching which, the gods obtain the powers of yoga;
there arise four divine gardens that provide the pleasures of dalliance. (22)
Nandana, Caitrarathaka, Vaibhrāja, and Sarvabhadra—
residing in these, the hosts of immortals are accompanied by throngs of celestial nymphs.
Their greatness sung by hosts of secondary deities,
those noble-minded ones roam about independently, according to their desire and according to their pleasure.
From the summit of the divine mango tree situated upon the lap of Mount Mandara,
which rose eleven hundred [yojanas] high, fruits filled with nectar fell.
The fruits were as large as mountain peaks, delicious, and soft; and from the juice of those fruits as they were being crushed, [a stream flowed].
With a color like that of the Aruṇoda lake, the river Aruṇodā flows forth; its waters are delightful, and it is worshipped by the kings of the gods and the Daityas.
O Great King, there exists the sin-destroying place named Aruṇā;
and they worship that Goddess, who bestows the fruits of all desires. (28)
By means of various offerings and oblations, they attain security and health through her compassionate glance, for she is the destroyer of sins and the bestower of fearlessness. (29)
The first is known on earth as Māyātulānantā, Puṣṭi, Īśvaramālinī, Duṣṭanāśakarī, and Kāntidāyinī.
By the power of her worship, he brought forth gold of the Jambū river.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Divisions of the Continents and Sub-continents," in the Description of the Worlds and Planes, within the eighth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
In the description of the cosmic egg (*bhuvanakośa*), there is a description of the origins and locations of rivers such as the Aruṇodā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "O Nārada, as for that river Aruṇodā which was mentioned by me..."
Falling from Mount Mandara, it would float toward Ilāvṛta in the east.
By the pleasure of Bhavānī, even the wind that carries the fragrance from the bodies of the wives of Yakṣas and Gandharvas— who are female attendants— becomes fragrant.
It perfumes the ground on all sides for a distance of ten yojanas,
due to the falling of the jambu fruits from such a great height.
From the marrow of the bones of elephants as large as the limbs of great tuskers, which were being shattered,
a river named Jambū flowed from Mount Mandara, known as Meru.
Falling upon the surface of the earth, she went to Dakṣiṇelāvṛta;
the goddess, satisfied by the taste of the jambū fruit, is known as Jambvādinī.
She is one whose feet are to be worshipped by the people there— by gods, nagas, rishis, and rakshasas— and she is honored and compassionate toward all living beings.
She is the purifier of sinners, the destroyer of diseases for those who remember her,
the remover of obstacles when praised, and she is worthy of honor by the gods.
Kokilākṣī, Kāmakalā, Karuṇā, Kāmapūjitā, Kaṭhoravigrahā, Dhanyā, Nākimānyā, and Gabhastinī. (8)
These names should always be recited at will by men;
[this earth] which exists on the bank of the river Jambū, situated upon its shore.
Intermingled with the juice of the Jambu fruit and through the conjunction of wind and sun,
it became the various and magnificent ornaments for the women of the Vidyādharas and the immortals.
And Jāmbūnada gold is said to be fashioned by the gods;
it is that gold which the wise, as well as lustful women, always desire.
They fashion crowns, waist-bands, armlets, and other ornaments;
this is declared to be Mahākadamba, situated on Mount Supārśva. || 12 ||
The five streams that are recorded as issuing from its hollows fall here upon the summit of Mount Supārśva and reach the earth.
Those five streams of honey overflow into the western region of Ilāvṛta;
and as they are enjoyed by the gods, they bear the fragrance of their mouths.
The wind, carrying its fragrance for a hundred yojanas, blew from all sides;
she is the great goddess Dhāreśvarī, who accomplishes the tasks of her devotees. 15.
Worshipped by the gods, possessed of great energy, having the form of Time and a massive face,
she dwells as the mistress of the forest and the planets, bestowing the fruits of karma.

The Goddess, the sovereign of all the gods, is to be worshipped with these names: Karāladehā (She of the Terrifying Body), Kālāṅgī (She of the Black Limbs), and Kāmakoṭipravartinī (She who Moves to the Pinnacle of Desire). 17.
Thus, from the branches of that banyan tree named Śatabala which grows upon the Kumuda mountain,
rivers flow downward from its trunk into the summit of Kumuda.
Through offerings of milk, curd, honey, ghee, molasses, food,
garments, and the like, as well as beds, seats, ornaments, and so forth, they all become granter of every desire.
To the north of Ilāvṛta, they flood it on all sides;
beneath that is the goddess Mīnākṣī, who is served by gods and asuras.
Clad in blue garments, with a fierce countenance and blue locks of hair,
she is the bestower of fruits and the granter of boons to the celestial hosts of the gods.
Exceedingly proud and exceedingly worthy of worship, she moves with the gait of an elephant in rut;
she intoxicates with passion, she is fond of honor, and she is the ender of those who seek honor.
She who bears the onset of Māra, she who is worshipped by Māra, she who destroys Māra;
she who is enriched with the splendor of the excellent peacock, and she who is the womb of the one whose vehicle is the peacock. 23.
By these names and words, that fish-eyed Goddess, who bestows honor upon those who recite and remember her and who dwells with the Lord, is to be worshipped. (24)
For those people whose minds were intent on drinking the water of those rivers,
the signs of old age— such as wrinkles and grey hair— would never appear.

Fatigue, perspiration, and other such foul odors; the delusions of old age, disease, and death; cold, heat, wind, discoloration, and the accumulation of afflictions to the mouth—[all these arise]. (26)
No calamities shall arise, and there shall be happiness for as long as one lives;
indeed, that happiness shall be continuous and unsurpassed. (27)
Thereafter, I shall describe the arrangement of that mountain Sumeru, which is indeed named Suvarṇamaya, as well as its individual peaks.
Like twenty petals surrounding a pericarp, all those mountains here have become filaments at the base of Mount Meru. (29)
And they were prepared all around for those who heard their names:
Kuraṅga, Kuraga, Kusumbha, and Vikaṅkata. (30)
Trikūṭa, Śiśira, Pataṅga, Rucaka, Niṣadha, Śinīvāsa, Kapila, and Śaṅkha. || 31 ||
Vaidūrya, Cārudhi, Haṃsa, Ṛṣabha, Nāga, Kālañjara, and Nārada—these constitute the twenty. || 32 ||

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Source and Location of Rivers such as the Aruṇodā," in the Description of the Cosmic Egg (Bhuvanakośa) within the eighth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 6.
In the description of the cosmic egg (bhuvanakośa), there is a description of the mountains, rivers, and seasons.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: To the east of Mount Meru are two mountains at a distance of eighteen yojanas.
It is one thousand [yojanas] in length, and two thousand [yojanas] wide in the north. || 1 ||
Jaṭhara and Devakūṭa—these two are the best of mountains;
to the west of Meru are these two mountains, and Pavamāna is another.
Those two, Pāriyātra and [Vindhya], are renowned for their height and extent; Kailāsa and Karavīraka are likewise famous, situated to the south of Meru.
In the east, there are two great kings of mountains, extending eastward and shaped like a wheel;
likewise, to the north of Meru, there are the two mountains Triśṛṅga and Makara.
And surrounded by these eight mountain ranges, Mount Sumeru,
the golden mountain, shines brilliantly like the sun.
Indeed, on the summit of Meru is the city of the Lotus-born Lord;
it is fashioned in the center with an extent of ten thousand yojanas.
The high-souled wise ones, who know the higher and the lower, describe the city as being made of gold and perfectly square.
Beyond that city of the worlds of the eight lords,
there are other cities of renowned golden form, situated according to their respective directions.
According to their respective forms, they were constructed measuring one thousand five hundred [yojanas];
there are nine cities on Mount Meru: Manovatī and Amarāvatī, and so forth.
Tejovatī, Saṃyamanī, and likewise Kṛṣṇāṅganā;
Śraddhāvatī, Gandhavatī, and another, Mahodayā.
And Yaśovatī [is the consort] of Brahmā, Indra, Agni, and the others respectively;
and there itself is the sacrifice-mark of the all-pervading Lord Viṣṇu.
And, O Nārada, from the center of the opening above the egg, which has been pierced by the nail of the big toe of his left foot, he enters into heaven.
O Lord, this Gaṅgā, whose waters are filled with the remover of the sins of all worlds, descends and enters here at the crown of your head.
And this very foot of the Blessed One is renowned throughout the worlds;
yet, after a long time of a thousand yugas, it [shall manifest].
Having reached the summit of heaven, the goddess, the sovereign river of the gods,
arrived at that place renowned throughout the three worlds known as Viṣṇupada.
There dwells Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, who is supremely purifying,
bearing the pollen from the lotus-bud of the pair of feet of the Blessed Lord.
Even today that royal sage remains there, having taken refuge in the immovable path;
there, the high-minded Seven Sages, who are cognizant of his power, dwell.
Those who desire the welfare of the entire world perform circumambulations;
this is the ultimate perfection that bestows success upon those who practice austerity. 18.
And they honor her with their heads, which are adorned with masses of matted hair.
Then, from the station of Viṣṇu, the Goddess [descends] with many thousands of crores.
Descending through the path of the gods crowded with celestial chariots,
she fell, flooding the lunar orb, toward the abode of Brahmā.
O Nārada, being divided fourfold in the world of Brahmā,
that goddess has spread out in the four directions under four names.
And Sītā, along with the Alakanandā, followed that very lord of rivers and streams by their names: Caturbhadrā (or Cakṣurbhadrā).
And from the abode of Brahmā and from the peaks of the mountains, the celestial river named Kesara flows forth as the Sītā. (23)
Having fallen here upon the summit of Gandhamādana, this sin-removing river flows through the middle and reaches the eastern region of Bhadrāśvavarṣa.
That river of heaven, worshipped by the gods, flows into the salt ocean;
then, from the peak of Mālyavat, a second [river] issues forth.
Then, becoming Vegavatī, she arrived at Ketumāla;
as the celestial river named Cakṣu, she reached the western quarter.
Having entered the lord of rivers, that Gaṅgā, who is worshipped by the gods,
then became known by the name of the third stream, O Nārada.
The auspicious Cālakanandā indeed flows from the south of the lotus-born Brahmā;
having traversed forests and mountain peaks, she has arrived here.
Having reached Hemakūṭa, the best of mountains, she emerged from there as well;
becoming exceedingly swift, another [stream] came here to Bhārata.
That third best of rivers reached the southern ocean;
for men traveling there to bathe in it, at every step—
Indeed, the fruit of the Rājasūya, Aśvamedha, and other sacrifices is not difficult to attain;
thereafter, the fourth stream flows again from the mountain like a bee.
Named Bhadrā, the Gaṅgā, the purifier of the three worlds, having flowed forth and satiated the Northern Kurus, reached the ocean.
Indeed, O Nārada, there are many other male and female rivers as well, arising from Mount Meru and Mandara in every single region.
Even there, they indeed declare Bhārata-varṣa to be the field of action (karmakṣetra),
while the other eight regions are bestowers of celestial happiness upon the earth.
O Nārada, these are the places of enjoyment for those who have gone to heaven while their residue of merit remains;
there, the men have a lifespan of ten thousand years, possess bodies as firm as adamant, and resemble gods. (35)
The men were appointed in groups of ten thousand;
they were exceedingly contented with great gentleness, endowed with excellent wives, and filled with happiness.
Indeed, even women conceive when their lifespan is short by only one year;
for time always remains equal to that of the Tretā Yuga. (37)

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Description of Mountains, Rivers, and Continents," in the Description of the Cosmic Egg (Bhuvanakośa), within the eighth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 7.
In the description of the cosmic egg (*bhuvanakośa*), the description of the regions of Ilāvṛta and Bhadrāśva:
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"In those regions, the lords of the gods [are always worshipped] with the hymns previously mentioned."
They worship the Great Goddess through recitation, meditation, and absorption. || 1 ||
The forest groves there are adorned with rows of blossoms from all seasons,
where the splendor of fruits and sprouts shines without interruption.
In those excellent forest regions, on the ridges of the rain-bearing mountains, and in all the mountain valleys containing masses of pure water; (3)
In those very [waters], which were intermingled with garlands of blooming lotuses and filled with the warbling of flocks of swans and cranes; || 4 ||
And they sport with various diversions such as water-games in the pleasure-pavilions of beautiful women with graceful eyebrows. (5)
The inhabitants there dwell here at their own will together with young women;
and even during the nine years, the Blessed One, the Primordial Person, remains here.

Known as Nārāyaṇa, he whose sole gaze is fixed on the essence of favoring the worlds— while they worship the Goddess, he too is worshipped by all; through his own emanation and through sacrifice, he, being composed, makes his presence known.
In Ilāvṛta, however, the Lord Bhava, born from the lotus-eyed one,
dwells eternally alone together with his consort.
No one else at all gains entrance into that sacred field;
due to the curse of Bhavānī, any man there clearly becomes a woman.
The Lord of Gods, being surrounded by countless crores of his own Gaṇas who were the lords of Bhavānī, was worshipping the god Saṅkarṣaṇa.
By means of his own self through the yoga of meditation, and out of a desire for the welfare of all beings,
he [perceived] that fourth form of his own nature, which was characterized by darkness (tāmasī).
And with one-pointed mind, he approaches the unborn Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the Great Person."
Salutation to the infinite and unmanifest one, who is the enumeration of all virtues. || 12 ||
I worship the lotus feet of Bhajanīya,
the supreme refuge of all fortune,
who fully nurtures the beings cherished by his devotees.
O Bhava, I seek refuge in you, the Lord who brings an end to worldly existence.

For one whose vision is not stained even in the slightest by observing His illusory powers, qualities, actions, or activities—just as one does not become bound by the anger of the Lord when He is not provoked—who that desires to conquer his own self would not revere Him? 14.
Appearing like an unreal phantom through illusion,
like a drunken woman with eyes wide from sweet liquor,
the serpent maidens were not able to offer him worship out of modesty.
Those whose senses were overwhelmed by the touch of his feet. || 15 ||
That which the seers call his restraint of abiding and birth— devoid of the three [qualities] and infinite—
is not known by anyone, as if it were a perfected goal that remains somewhere.
The circle of the earth [is situated] upon the thousand abodes of the head. || 16 ||
Of whom, it is said, there was today the Great Lord, unborn, whose body consists of the qualities (guṇas), who is the abode of supreme knowledge;
by whose own threefold splendor I am pervaded on all sides.
I create the Vaikārika, the Tāmasa, and the Aindriya [forms].
We abide under the control of that Great Soul,
like birds bound by a string;
our senses are great, yet they are distorted and characterized by darkness.
"Let us all create that by whose grace this [universe] exists. || 18 ||

This person, deluded by the heavy weight of worldly existence, does not easily understand the means of deliverance from this illusion— a product of karma— which has been fashioned [by the Lord] at some point in time.
Salutation to You, whose nature is both dissolution and emergence.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Thus the Lord Rudra,
with his mind fully concentrated upon the goddesses, worshipped the Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa in Ilāvṛta.
In that very same way, this son of Dharma was named Bhadraśravas;
the men who were the lords of his family were also called Bhadrasevakas.
In the region of Bhadrāśva, that famous image of Vāsudeva was [installed],
distinguished by the form of a horse and marked with the footprints of Hayagrīva.
Restrained by the supreme enclosure of meditative concentration,
those who chant that very form likewise attain it.
The Bhadraśravas said: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, to Dharma, the purifier of the self; obeisance!
"Aha! How wonderful is the Blessed One’s marvelous activity!"
Indeed, while this person slays, the world looks on and does not see; for while they meditate, they do not perceive that they are practicing forbidden acts,
living on by having carried off their own sons and fathers.
The poets declare the universe to be perishable,
and the wise who know the inner self perceive it as such; yet even they are deluded by Your power of illusion.
I bow to that Unborn One, whose deed is most wonderful.
The activity of the origin, maintenance, and cessation of the universe is indeed accepted by You as being performed even though You are a non-agent;
this is not surprising in You, who are both the cause and the effect.
And [it exists] in the universal self and as something distinct in reality. || 26 ||
At the end of the age, he who has the body of a man-lion retrieved the Vedas, which had been obscured by darkness,
from the subterranean realm for the sake of the poet who entreated him.
Salutation to you, whose efforts are rendered futile. || 27 ||
Thus they praise the Lord of Gods, Hayaśīrṣa Hari;
those named Bhadraśravas describe his virtues as well.
Whoever reads or causes others to hear this account of their deeds shall cast off the cloak of sin and go to the world of the Goddess. (29)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Varṣas of Ilāvṛta and Bhadrāśva," in the Description of the Cosmic Egg (Bhuvanakośa) within the eighth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 8 ||
In the description of the cosmic egg (*bhuvanakośa*), regarding the description of the regions of Harivarṣa, Ketumāla,
and Ramyaka, Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "And in Harivarṣa, the Lord Nṛhari is the destroyer of sins."
He, whose self is united with yoga, remains active, bestowing grace upon his devotees. || 1 ||
Beholding that beloved form of his, the highly fortunate Asura, endowed with devotion and knowing the truth of His qualities, offers praise.
Prahlāda said:
Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Narasiṃha; obeisance to you, the splendor of splendors! Manifest, manifest! O you with adamantine fangs, rend, rend the latent impressions of karma!
Tamo grasa grasa oṃ svāhā! May fearlessness abound within my self. Oṃ kṣauṃ.
May there be well-being for the universe; may the wicked be appeased; may all beings contemplate one another with auspicious intent;
and may the mind take refuge in the auspiciousness of Adhokṣaja.
Let our intellect also be made to enter [into this], even though it is without cause.
If we should have attachment toward house, wife, children, wealth, or kin, may it instead be toward those dear to the Blessed One—
those self-possessed ones who are content with whatever sustains life.
Success is achieved from what is not far away; it is not so with that which is pleasing to the senses.

Indeed, the unborn Lord, having entered the mind through the Vedas, repeatedly touches that sacred ford— the majesty of one's own inner power acquired through association— which removes the passion born of the body from those who touch it.
Who indeed would not serve the prowess of Mukunda? || 5 ||
In one who possesses unconditioned devotion to the Blessed Lord,
all the gods abide through their every virtue; for one who lacks devotion to Hari, how can there be great virtues?
He runs outward with his desires even though they do not exist.
For Hari is indeed the Lord himself, the Self of all embodied beings, just as water is to fish;
if he, being great, were to become attached to a home after abandoning that [Self], then the greatness of householders would consist merely in their age.

Therefore, having abandoned the home—which is the root of passion, attachment, dejection, anger, envy, desire, fear, and wretchedness, and which is the entire cycle of worldly existence—what fear can there be for those who worship the feet of Nṛsiṃha? (8)
In this way, that lord of the Daityas also praised Nṛhari— who dwells in the lotus of the heart and is the lion that destroys the elephant of sin— with devotion day after day.
And in the region of Ketumāla, the Blessed One indeed dwells, assuming the form of Smara;
he is always to be worshipped by the lords of that region.
By means of this net of hymns, the daughter of the ocean, who is the sovereign of that region and the constant bestower of honor upon the great, is worshipped. (11)
Rāma said: Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ sma, salutations to the Blessed One Hṛṣīkeśa, whose self is distinguished by all excellent qualities.
To the sovereign lord of intentions, thoughts, minds, and distinctions;
to the one consisting of sixteen parts, composed of meters, composed of food, composed of nectar, and composed of all things; to the great glory, to vigor, to strength, and to beauty.
Salutations to you for the sake of desire; may it be fulfilled in both worlds. Women, having worshipped you, Hṛṣīkeśvara, through their vows, seek another husband in this world of their own accord.
They indeed do not protect their offspring;
for they are dependent on others, seeking wealth and life as their primary concern.
He indeed shall be a lord, free from fear from any source;
he protects from all sides the people afflicted by fear.
He alone is such, for otherwise there would be mutual fear.
Nor does he, upon attaining his own self-nature, consider anything else superior.
She who, though greedy for all desires, would not desire the worship of those lotus-feet of yours—
by her alone is that which is desired by Rādhā sought and honored.
O Blessed One, that my request has been rejected causes me such torment. || 14 ||
To attain me, the unborn Brahmā, the lords, gods, and demons perform fierce austerities with their minds fixed on the senses;
yet, O Unconquered One, they do not know me except for those who have taken refuge at your feet, for I am centered within your heart.
Therefore, O Acyuta, you have placed upon my head that lotus-hand which was laid upon the heads of the Sātvatas; for you,
O most excellent one, sustain me through your illusory power (māyā).
Who is capable of fathoming the will of the Lord? || 16 ||
Thus, for the sake of accomplishing their desires, the lords of the rain-gods, headed by Prajāpati, indeed praised Kāma, who embodies the very nature of the friend of the world.
And in the region named Ramyaka, Manu constantly praises the supreme form of the Blessed One, the Fish, who is worshipped by gods and asuras.
Manu said: Om, salutation to the Blessed One; salutation to the most preeminent, to the essence, to the vital breath, to the vigor, to the strength—to the Great Fish, salutation!
Moving with a mighty roar, your form unseen both within and without by all the world-protectors,
you are that Lord who brings this universe under his control, just as a man controls a wooden puppet woman by means of a string.
Indeed, the World-Protectors— whether acting individually or together— even though they strove, were unable to drink [the water] because of the fever of envy;
for neither bipeds nor quadrupeds were able to do so.
Whatever reptile or stationary object is seen here [is likewise subject to this]. || 20 ||
O Unborn One of great strides, by Your power, You have together with me lifted up this earth— the storehouse of herbs and creepers— from the ocean at the end of the age that is garlanded with waves.
Salutation to him, whose self is the multitude of the vital breaths of the world. || 21 ||
Thus Manu, the best among kings, praised the Lord of Gods,
the Fish Incarnation, who is the cause of the destruction of all doubts.
Through the yoga of meditation, his every impurity has been shaken off;
as the most excellent of great devotees, he remains serving the Lord with devotion.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Varṣas of Harivarṣa, Ketumāla, and Ramyaka," in the Description of the Cosmic Egg within the eighth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
In the description of the divisions of the world, follows the description of the region of Hiraṇmaya-Kimpuruṣa.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
In the region named Hiraṇmaya, the Blessed One assumes the form of a tortoise.
This very lord of yoga remains here; he is honored by Aryaman and is praised.

Aryamā said: Om, salutations to the Blessed One Akūpāra, who is distinguished by the qualities of all sentient beings, whose station is unperceived; salutations to the Body, salutations to the Earth, salutations to the Abode; salutations to You!
This form of Yours, which is Your own essential nature, presented through Your creative power (māyā), appears as a manifold variety of forms.
Homage to You, whose nature is indefinable, for whom no number exists because You are perceived beyond all categories.
The womb-born, the sweat-born, the egg-born, and the soil-born;
the moving and the unmoving; the gods, the sages, the ancestors, the elemental beings, and the senses;
heaven, space, earth, mountains, rivers, and oceans.
The single [term] "dvīpa-graha-ṛkṣa" is that which is to be designated. || 3 ||

Salutations to you, the system of Sāṃkhya, by which this enumeration— conceived by poets for that which possesses innumerable distinctions of name, form, and appearance— is removed through the vision of reality.
While Aryaman, together with the lords of the rain-gods, was thus praising the Lord of the Gods,
he sang and worshipped the Lord who is the source of all beings.
Likewise, in Uttarakuru, the Blessed One, the Person of Sacrifice (Yajñapuruṣa),
is always worshipped by the Earth in the form of the Primordial Boar (Ādivārāha).
Having worshipped the Lord according to the prescribed rites, her lotus-heart moistened by devotion to Him,
the Earth praises Hari in His form as the Sacrificial Boar, the crusher of the Daityas.
The Earth said: Om, salutations to the Blessed One, whose mark is the reality of mantra, who is the sacrificial rite,
who is the limb of the great sacrifice, salutations to the Great Boar, who is pure through action.
Salutations to you, the one who appears in the three ages. || 8 ||
The nature of whom the wise poets, desiring to behold it, plunge into with their minds as if churning wood for fire, using the intellect as a churning-stick.
The name "Gūḍha" is declared for the Self whose purpose is action.

Obeisance be to You, whose nature is beyond the reach of illusion, who are perceived by means of substances, actions, causes, time, lords, and agents— all of which are the products of Māyā— and who have dispelled the activity of Māyā through the investigation of those whose intellects perceive the Self as consisting of the limbs and their attributes.
Māyā brings about the creation, maintenance,
and dissolution of the universe, which it cannot desire to avoid by means of the qualities (guṇas) perceived by the observer;
just as iron revolves depending upon a magnet.
O pressing-stones, salutations to you, the witnesses of qualities and actions. || 11 ||
Having crushed the Daitya Prativāraṇa in battle,
that primordial Boar of the universe,
making me his fore-tooth, emerged from the ocean.
Like a sporting elephant, I bow down to that all-pervading Lord. || 12 ||
In this land of Kimpuruṣavarṣa, Śrī Hanumān praises the Blessed One, the son of Daśaratha, the Lord of all, the divine Sītārāma, the primordial Puruṣa. || 13 ||
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the one of supreme renown;
homage to him whose character and vows are noble, who has trained his self, and who is honored by the world; homage to the touchstone for the praise of the virtuous.
"Obeisance to the one who is the deity of Brahman, the Great Person, the highly fortunate one.
That which is the single essence of pure experience,
by its own splendor having destroyed the arrangement of the qualities (guṇas).
I take refuge in that which is inward-turned, profoundly peaceful, perceivable by the wise, devoid of name and form, and free from the sense of "I."
O Lord, this descent as a mortal is for the instruction of mortals and for the slaying of demons alone;
otherwise, how could there be delight for Your own Self?
The calamities suffered by the Lord on account of Sītā. || 15 ||
Indeed, that Blessed Vāsudeva, the best friend of those who possess self-mastery, is not attached to the three worlds;
he would never succumb to the dejection caused by a woman.
Nor indeed should one abandon the characteristic mark. || 16 ||
Surely neither noble birth, nor fortune, nor speech, nor intellect, nor physical form is a cause for being favored by the great;
for the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa has made friends with forest-dwellers who were rejected even by those very qualities. (17)
Whether a god, an asura, a human, or even a non-human,
whoever with their whole being worships Rāma— the supreme Knower of Good Deeds, Hari in human form— [attains the highest goal].
He who led the northern Kosalas to heaven. || 18 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
