Thus, in the land of Kiṃpuruṣa, Hanumān, the best of monkeys, [beheld] Rāma, whose promise is true, firm in his vows, and whose eyes are like lotus petals.
He praises, sings, and worships with devotion in every way;
whoever hears this wonderful narrative of Rāmacandra, having his soul purified of all sins, attains the same world as Rāma. || 20 ||

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Golden Kimpuruṣa Varṣa," in the description of the Cosmic Egg within the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The eighth chapter, concerning the description of the terrestrial sphere, is completed; herein follows the description of Bhāratavarṣa.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
In this land called Bhārata, I, the primordial Puruṣa, abide; and by you alone is my praise performed incessantly. (1)
Nārada said: Om, salutations to the Blessed One whose nature is tranquility, who has ceased from the sense of selfhood;
salutations to Him whose wealth is nothingness, the bull among sages, Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
Salutations again and again to the supreme teacher of the Paramahaṃsas, the sovereign lord who delights in the Self.
He is the agent in the acts of creation and so forth, yet he is neither bound nor slain, even though he resides within the body and is subject to bodily conditions.
The Seer is not defiled by the qualities of the seen; homage to Him, the unattached, distinct Witness. || 2 ||
For this is the skill in yoga taught by the Lord Hiraṇyagarbha, the Lord of Yogins:
that at the time of death, one's mind [should be fixed] upon you, who are devoid of qualities.
Through devotion, he cast off his wretched body. || 3 ||
For the wise man who, being greedy for desires pertaining to this world and the next, broods over children, wives, and wealth,
yet fears the destruction of this wretched body— his effort is nothing but mere exhaustion.
Therefore, O Lord Adhokṣaja, may You shatter this "I-ness" and "mine-ness" bestowed upon our wretched bodies through Your illusory power (māyā)—
a bond so difficult to break that we may quickly destroy it.
Bestow upon us the yoga that arises from your own nature.
Thus Nārada, the tiger among sages, who perceives the essence of all things through his wisdom, constantly praises the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all affliction.
Indeed, in this land of Bhārata-varṣa there are rivers and mountains;
O divine sage, I shall describe them to you—listen with a one-pointed mind. (7)
Malaya, Maṅgalaprastha, Maināka, Trikūṭaka,
Ṛṣabha, Kūṭaka, Kolla, Sahya, and likewise Devagiri.
Ṛṣyamūka, Śrīśaila, Vyaṅkaṭādri, Mahendraka, Vāridhāra, Vindhya, Muktimat, and Ṛkṣaparvata. || 9 ||
Likewise Pāriyātra, Droṇa, and Citrakūṭa mountain; Govardhana, Raivataka, Kakubha, and the Nīla mountain. || 10 ||
Gauramukha, Indrakīla, Giri, and Kāmagiri—these and other innumerable mountains are bestowers of great merit. (11)
From this [source], hundreds and thousands of rivers have arisen;
[they are beneficial] even through drinking, immersion, bathing, seeing, and chanting their praises.
And they destroy the three kinds of sins of embodied beings:
the Tāmraparṇī, the Candravaśā, the Kṛtamālā, and the Vaṭodakā. (13)
The Vaihāyasī, the Kāverī, the Veṇā, and the Payasvinī;
likewise the Tuṅgabhadrā, the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, and the Śarkarāvartakā. || 14 ||
The Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Nirvindhyā, and Payoṣṇikā; the Tāpī, Revā, Surasā, Narmadā, and Sarasvatī. (15)
The Carmaṇvatī and the Sindhu, the great rivers Andha and Śoṇa, the Ṛṣikulyā, the Trisāmā, and the great river Vedasmṛti. (16)
The Kauśikī, the Yamunā, the Mandākinī, the Dṛṣadvatī, the Gomatī, the Sarayū, the Rodhavatī, and likewise the Saptavatī. || 17 ||
The Suṣomā, the Śatadru, the Candrabhāgā, the Marudvṛdhā, the Vitastā, the Asiknī, and the Viśvā are thus proclaimed. || 18 ||
In this year, those who have taken birth through their respective actions—known as white, red, and black—attain divine, human, or hellish states. (19)
Various enjoyments accrue to all the inhabitants,
and according to the regulations of the social classes (varṇa), liberation clearly comes to pass.
And the sages who proclaim the Vedas and dwell in heaven declare that this alone is the preeminence of the year, by virtue of the accomplishment of its purpose. (21)
Aha! What auspicious deed have these people performed,
or has Hari himself become gracious toward them,
that they have obtained birth among humans in the field of Bhārata?
For our desire is indeed for that which is conducive to the service of Mukunda.

Of what use to us are difficult sacrifices, ascetic observances, vows, or acts such as giving, or even the conquest of heaven by Phalguna, if therein there is no remembrance of the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa, stolen away by the excessive festival of the senses? (23)
It is better for those with a lifespan of an eon to conquer their state through rebirth than for those with a momentary lifespan to conquer the land of Bhārata.
For by means of a mortal moment, the wise, having renounced, go to the fearless abode of Hari.
Where there is no river of the nectar of stories concerning Vaikuṇṭha, nor saintly devotees who take refuge in Him,
nor great festivals consisting of sacrifices to the Lord of Sacrifice;
Even the world of the Lord of the Gods is certainly not to be resorted to by you. || 25 ||
Those beings here who have attained human birth,
which is endowed with the aggregate of knowledge, action, and material substance,
will surely not strive for the sake of rebirth.
Furthermore, like forest-dwellers, they fall into bondage. || 26 ||

By those who, with faith upon the sacrificial grass, have offered oblations portion by portion according to the ritual, mantras, and substances—the One Lord, though invoked by various names, joyfully accepts them; He Himself is full and is the master of all blessings.

It is true that when entreated by men, He grants whatever is requested; yet He does not grant wealth simply because it is asked for, since He Himself bestows the sprout of His own feet upon those who worship Him, even if they desire nothing else, thereby concealing their worldly desires.
"If there remains for us any merit from well-performed sacrifices, charitable works, or virtuous deeds that has been stored as the fruit of heaven,
by that may we possess the memory of our births when the lotus-navelled Lord Hari bestows peace upon those who worship Him.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Thus, the gods who have gone to heaven, as well as the Siddhas and the supreme ṛṣis, proclaim the most beautiful majesty of the Bhārata. (29)
Furthermore, eight subcontinents of Jambudvīpa are recorded;
they are delineated by the oceans that purify the paths of horses. (30)
Svarṇaprastha, Candraśukra, Āvartana, Ramāṇaka, Mandara, Upākhyahariṇa, and likewise Pāñcajanya. || 31 ||
Siṃhala and Laṅkā are known as the eight sub-islands; thus has the measurement of Jambudvīpa been proclaimed in detail.
Hereafter, I shall describe the six islands beginning with Plakṣa.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of Bhārata-varṣa," within the "Description of the Cosmic Egg" (Bhuvanakośa-varṇana) in the eighth book of the Śrīmad-devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 11.
In the description of the structure of the universe, follows the description of Plakṣadvīpa and Kuśadvīpa. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Just as this Jambūdvīpa has been proclaimed, along with its dimensions;
To that extent, it is surrounded on all sides by the salt-water ocean.
Just as Mount Meru is surrounded by the ocean named Jambū,
so too is the salt-water ocean twice its size encircled by the continent named Plakṣa.
Just as a moat is indeed surrounded by an outer grove,
so too the one called Plakṣa, himself the size of a Jambū tree, assumes the form of an island.
It is certain that the golden Agni resides right there;
his son, born of Priyavata, is remembered there as Saptajihva.
Agni, whose tongue is the sacrificial fuel, was its presiding deity; and the powerful lord, having divided his own continent into seven regions, gave them to his sons.
Having himself resorted to the practice of yoga, which is honored by those who know the Self,
he approached the Blessed One by means of that very yoga of the Self.
Śiva, Yavasa, Bhadra, Śānta, Kṣema, Amṛta,
and likewise Abhaya— these are the seven regions that he, together with Satī, beheld.
Within them, seven rivers and indeed seven mountains are proclaimed: Aruṇā, Nṛmṇā, Aṅgirasī, Sāvitrī, and Suprabhātikā; (8)
The rivers are celebrated as Ṛtambharā and Satyambharā;
likewise, there are Maṇikūṭa, Vajrakūṭa, and Indrasena.
Jyotiṣmat, Suparṇa, Hiraṇyaṣṭhīva,
and Meghamāla— these are the mountains renowned in Plakṣadvīpa.
By the mere water of the rivers, through seeing, touching, and so forth,
all people were likewise cleansed of every speck of passion and freed from darkness.
The Haṃsas, the Pataṅgas, and those called the Ūrdhvāyanas—
these four castes, whose limbs are characterized by truth, [dwell] on the island of Plakṣa.
Having a lifespan of a thousand years and possessing various exemplary visions,
they worship the Sun at the gateway to heaven according to the ritual of the threefold knowledge (trayīvidyā).
We meditate upon the Sun as the Self—the form of the ancient Viṣṇu, of the Brahman whose truth is reality, and of both immortality and death. 14.
And in all the Pajja dvīpas, beginning with Plakṣa, O Nārada,
there is longevity, sensory vigor, vitality, strength, intelligence, and even fortitude.
Vikrama is the perpetual, innate accomplishment of all the worlds;
and beyond Plakṣadvīpa lies the ocean of sugarcane juice, the lord of rivers.
It stands surrounding the entire Plakṣa-dvīpa;
beyond that is the island named Śālmala, which is twice as extensive as this one.
It is surrounded by the salt ocean (Suroda) and the river Sindhu;
there indeed stands the Śālmalī tree, which is proclaimed to be as large as a Plakṣa.
That is the abode of Garuḍa, the high-souled king of birds;
for Yajñabāhu was indeed the lord of that island, born from Priyavrata.
Once born, he himself gave the earth to his seven sons;
learn now their names as they are told. (20)
Surocana, Saumanasya, Ramaṇa, Devavarṣaka, Pāribhadra, and likewise Āpyāyana, whose names are well known. (21)
In those [regions], seven mountain ranges and seven rivers each are recorded;
likewise, there are the lakes Śataśṛṅga, Vāmadeva, and Kandaka.
Kumuda, Puṣpavarṣa, and Sahasraśruti—these are the seven mountains; now the names of the rivers are being told. (23)
Anumati, Sinīvālī, Sarasvatī, and Kuhū, as well as Rajanī, Nandā, and Rākā—these are thus proclaimed. || 24 ||
All the men of that age were designated by the four social classes (cāturvarṇya):
Śrutadhara, Vīryadhara, Vasundhara, and Iṣundhara.
They worship the Blessed One, who consists of the Vedas, as Soma, the Lord;
with their own rays, they distribute [him] among the ancestors and the gods during the dark and light fortnights.
And may King Soma be gracious toward all his subjects.
Thus, it is proclaimed that [the duration] from the end of the day is twice as long as its own measure. (27)
Enveloped by the ocean of clarified butter (Ghṛtodaka), this Kuśadvīpa shines forth;
therein stands a blazing clump of Kuśa grass, which is the cause for the island's name.
Illuminating the quarters with the radiance of his own beard,
the golden-seeded Svarāṭ, the son of Priyavrata and lord of that continent, remains established there.
And he divided that island into seven parts for his seven sons:
Vasu, Vasudāna, and likewise Dṛḍharuci as the last.
Nābhigupta, Stutya, and Vrata; Vivikta, Nāma, and Devaka—these seven excellent boundary mountains are recorded as being within their respective regions. (31)
There are exactly seven rivers here; learn their names:
Cakra, Catuḥśṛṅga, Kapila, and Citrakūṭaka. || 32 ||
Devānīka, Ūrdhvaroman, Draviṇa, the seven mountains, Rasakulyā, Madhukulyā, and likewise Mitravindā. || 33 ||
Śrutavindā, Devagarbhā, Ghṛtacyut, and Mandamālikā—by their waters, all those inhabitants of Kuśadvīpa [attain purity]. 34.
The four castes are proclaimed by the names Kuśala, Kovida, Abhiyukta, and Kulaka. || 35 ||
All people who know everything, possessing the splendor of the foremost gods, worship that god in the form of Jātavedas through the skill born of ritual action. (36)
"O Jātavedas, you are the direct bearer of oblations to the Supreme Brahman;
through sacrifice, worship the Puruṣa who is the limbs of the gods.
In this manner, all the inhabitants of the continents worship the blazing Fire. (37)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of Plakṣadvīpa and Kuśadvīpa," in the description of the Cosmic Egg (Bhuvanakośa) within the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 12 ||
In the description of the cosmic egg (*bhuvanakośa*), follows the description of the islands of Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara.
Nārada said:
"O seer of all things, tell me also the measurement of the remaining islands."
By the mere knowledge of which, one becomes filled with supreme bliss. || 1 ||
Śrī Rāma-Nārāyaṇa said:
Surrounding Kuśadvīpa is the great ocean of clarified butter (ghṛtoda). Beyond that, Krauñcadvīpa is twice as large as itself in measurement.
Surrounded by the Ocean of Milk, it shines; and because the Krauñca mountain exists within it, this very [ocean] revolves as the name-giver of the continent.
He who formerly had his belly pierced by the spear of Guha was sprinkled with milk from the Ocean of Milk and protected by Varuṇa.
The illustrious son of Priyavrata, honored by all the worlds, was indeed the leader known as Ghṛtapṛṣṭha, who shone with splendor. || 5 ||
Having divided his own continent into seven parts, he gave them to his sons, establishing the rulers of the regions within those regions named after his sons.
He himself went for refuge to that Blessed One;
[namely] Āma, Madhuruha, Meghapṛṣṭha, and Sudhāmaka.
Bhrājiṣṭha, Lohitārṇa, and Vanaspati—
these seven mountains and seven rivers are renowned throughout the entire earth.
Śukla, Vardhamāna, Bhojana, Upabarhaṇa, Nanda, Nandana, and Sarvatobhadra are thus proclaimed.
Abhayā, Amṛtaughā, Āryakā, and Tīrthavatī;
likewise Vṛttirūpavatī, Śuklā, and Pavitravatikā. || 10 ||
The merit of their water is drunk by the four castes;
likewise, there are two bull-like men named Draviṇa and Devaka. (11)
Indeed, these men born of the four castes dwell there;
the men of that place [worship] the god consisting of water, the Lord of Waters.
With full cupped hands and devotion, they perform various rites, [saying]:
"O Waters, you possess the potency of Puruṣa; you are the purifiers of Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ. (13)
"May they purify us, the destroyers of disease; may they touch us with their very selves.
At the conclusion of this mantra recitation, they praise [the deities] with various hymns. (14)
Thus, situated beyond the Ocean of Milk and extending all around it,
it rests upon a circumference of thirty-two hundred thousand yojanas.
This island, Śākadvīpa, is distinguished by its own measurement and by its waters of curd-cream;
it is so called because of the Śāka tree that grows there.
O Nārada, he is indeed the cause for the designation of his own field;
its sovereign was the son of Priyavrata, known as Medhātithi. || 17 ||
Having divided the seven continents and established his own seven sons as rulers over them— each named after a continent— he himself attained the state of yoga.
Purojava, Manahpūrvaja, then Pavamānaka;
Dhūmrānīka, Citrarepha, Bahurūpa, and then Viśvadhṛk. || 19 ||
The seven boundary mountains and the seven rivers have been proclaimed;
[the mountains are] Īśāna, Ūruśṛṅga, Balabhadra, and Śatakeśara.
Sahasrasrotaka, Devapāla, and Mahāśana at the end—
these are said to be the seven mountains, and the names of the seven rivers are likewise stated.
Anaghā, Prathamā, Āyurdā, Ubhayaspṛṣṭi, Aparājitā, Pañcapadī, and Sahasraśruti. || 22 ||
Then his own steadfastness was described, as well as the seven most brilliant rivers;
and all the inhabitants of those regions were Satyavrata and Kratuvrata.
The four castes are declared to be those who observe the vows of charity and the subsequent vows;
they are united with the Lord Prāṇavāyu through the practice of prāṇāyāma.
Those who have shaken off passion and ignorance worship the supreme Hari,
who, having entered within all beings, sustains them by means of his own manifestations.
May the Inner Controller, the Lord, protect us directly— he under whose authority this world exists,
which extends far beyond the ocean of milk and is exceedingly vast.
This island named Puṣkara is twice the size of Śākadvīpa; it is surrounded by a sea of sweet water that is equal in extent to itself. || 27 ||
There stands the Puṣkara, whose bright petals resemble the crests of blazing fires,
and which possesses tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of pure golden leaves.
This seat of the illustrious Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, was prepared by the Teacher of the World out of a desire to create all the worlds. (29)
This island is indeed one alone, named Mānasottara;
it is the mountain that serves as the boundary between the inner and outer regions.
It is measured at ten thousand yojanas in both height and extent,
where indeed there are four cities in each of the four directions.
Above the world-protectors, Indra and the others, is the emergence of the sun;
for it is there that the sun revolves, circumambulating Mount Meru.
The wheel consisting of the year revolves according to the day-and-night of the gods;
the sovereign Vītihotra, son of Priyavrata, [entrusted] his two sons with it.
Having established them in succession for two years each, bearing the names of those years,
both Ramaṇa and Dhātaki became the lords of those respective years.
Created by themselves like their ancestors and devoted to the worship of the Blessed Lord,
the inhabitants of that region [worship] the Supreme Lord in the form of Brahman.
Those who have practiced well worship through the yoga of action;
that which is the *liṅga* consisting of action, the *liṅga* of Brahman, which people should revere—homage to that Blessed One, who is solitary, non-dual, and peaceful. (36)

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Cosmic Egg and Description of Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara Dvīpas," in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 13.
Description of the Sun’s Course.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Beyond that is the mountain named Lokāloka.
And that which is conceived as being in the intermediate region between the world and the non-world. || 1 ||
O divine sage, as far as there is space between Mount Sumeru and the Mānasa peak, for that same distance there exists a pure ground of gold.
It is like the surface of a mirror, devoid of all living beings;
when an object is cast into it, nothing at all is reflected back.
Therefore, O Nārada, that [mountain] is devoid of all hosts of living beings;
and as for the explanation "Lokāloka" (Light-Darkness) which is devised here, [it is as follows]: || 4 ||
And his station always exists within the Lokāloka mountain;
by the Lord, he was made the ender of the three worlds.
Indeed, by whose power the rays of the sun and other luminaries, ending with Dhruva,
extend here toward this world and spread throughout the three worlds at all times.
For as long as they do not possess the state of being turned away [from the world], O Nārada, the lord of mountains, Mahodaya, does not undergo such upward elevation.
Such is this arrangement of the worlds, characterized by their locations and dimensions,
as calculated by the poets to be fifty crores [of yojanas] in extent.
O Sage, Lokāloka mountain constitutes one-fourth of the earth's circumference;
upon it, in the four directions, by Brahmā, who is self-born, [the cities were established].
Learn the names of those world-elephants who have been stationed there:
Ṛṣabha, Puṣpacūḍa, Vāmana, and Aparājita. || 10 ||
These have been declared to be the causes of stability for the entire world;
and their own manifestations are augmented by great power.
Increasing the sovereignty of the pure being, the Blessed Lord Hari remains endowed with the eight supernatural powers (siddhis), surrounded by Viṣvaksena and others.
Surrounded on all sides by his own staff-like arms which serve as weapons,
the Supreme Lord remains for the welfare of the entire world.
The eternal Viṣṇu assumed this appearance for the duration of a kalpa,
employing his own spiritual means for the protection of this world created by his own māyā.
By this [measurement], the extent of the non-world (*aloka*) within has been explained;
for it is said that outside [the world] lies the Lokāloka mountain. (15)
Beyond that, they indeed describe the pure state of the Lord of Yoga;
it is situated within the cosmic egg, in the space between heaven and earth where the sun resides.
Between the Sun and the Egg, there are twenty-five crores [of yojanas].
Since he was born when this Egg had perished, he bears the name Mārtaṇḍa.
He is called Hiraṇyagarbha because he was born from the golden egg;
for by him the directions, the sky, the heavens, and the earth are distinguished.
Heaven and liberation, as well as hells and the abodes of the waters, belong entirely to gods, animals, humans, reptiles, and plants. (19)
The Sun is the self, the eye, and the lord of all classes of living beings;
thus far has the configuration of the terrestrial sphere been described. (20)
For by this, those who know it describe the measure of heaven, just as one describes the two halves of split pulses such as *niṣpāva* beans. || 21 ||
Between those two lies the intermediate space, joined by both;
and therein dwells the Blessed One, the Sun, the best among those who give heat.
Scorching the three worlds with its heat and illuminating them,
it reaches the northern solstice and spreads a slowness of its motion.
Having reached the point of ascent, it performs its course with slowness;
but having reached the southern solstice, it spreads its movement with great speed.
As it moves toward the place of descent, it causes the day to become shorter;
having reached the point known as the equinox (viṣuvat), it effects an equality of motion.
Then, having reached the equatorial point, he makes the days equal;
for when the sun moves through Aries and Libra, [the days and nights are equal]. (26)
When the Sun shines while situated in the five zodiac signs beginning with Taurus, the one composed of the three Vedas extends equal days and nights. (27)
Then the days increase and the nights also decrease, for when the sun, the maker of light, moves through the signs beginning with Scorpio (Vṛścika). || 28 ||
Even then, these days and nights exist in reverse order. (29)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Sun’s Motion," in the eighth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 14.
In the description of the structure of the universe, the description of the sun’s course:
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Hereafter, I shall describe the supreme movement of the Sun.
The movement of the sun is threefold, consisting of swift, slow, and other [intermediate] speeds.
O best of gods, there are only three locations for all the grahas:
Jāradgava is the southern location, Madhya is the middle, and Airāvata is the northern.
Vaiśvānara is designated as being to the south in accordance with reality;
Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, and Bharaṇī are called the Nāgavīthī (the Serpent Path). || 3 ||
Rohiṇī, Ārdrā, and Mṛgaśiras are designated as the Gaja-vīthī;
Puṣyā, Āśleṣā, and Ādityā (Punarvasu) are remembered as the Airāvatī-vīthī. || 4 ||
These three paths are called the Northern Course;
likewise, the two Phalgunīs and Maghā are considered to belong to the Bull (Arṣabhī).
Hasta, Citrā, and Svātī are called the Govīthī;
Jyeṣṭhā, Viśākhā, and Anurādhā are considered the Jāradgavī path.
These three paths are called the middle way; Mūlā, Āṣāḍhā, and Uttarāṣāḍhā are designated as the Ajavīthī.
Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Mārgī, Śatabhiṣak, Vaiśvānarī, Bhādrapadā, and Revatī are likewise proclaimed. (8)
These three paths are called the southern route;
having reached the northern solstice, they are bound within the axle of the yoke.
The drawing back of the two wind-fastened reins is known as *rohaṇa*;
from that, the chariot's movement proceeds from the inner circle.
O best of gods, dullness and the increase of the day arise, and the decrease of the night occurs; this is indeed the sequence of the northern solstice (saumyāyana).
In the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), due to the propulsion from the bond (pāśa), there is a descent;
at that time, because of the entry into the outer orbit, the speed of motion occurs.
Then the shortness of the day and the increase of the night are proclaimed;
however, at the equinox (vaiṣuva), due to the equality of the nooses (pāśa) and the sun’s state of equilibrium, they are equal.
And when those two, presided over by the Pole Star (dhruva), are drawn toward the middle of the mandala, there is equality in the length of night and day and so forth.
Then the sun revolves within the circles by means of the pair of rays released by Dhruva.
In the same way, the sun revolves externally through its orbits;
on that Mount Meru, in the eastern quarter, is the city of Indra, the abode of the gods.
To the south is the great city of Yama named Saṃyamanī;
and to the west is indeed the great city of Varuṇa named Nimlocanī.
To the north of that, the pleasant city named Vibhāvarī is said to exist;
it is by the exponents of the Veda that the rising of the sun is declared to occur in the city of Indra.
In Saṃyamanī, at midday; in Nimlocanī, sunset;
and in Vibhāvarī, it is midnight for the sun-god who is worshipped by the gods.
O Sage, I have described in their entirety those causes for the activity of living beings situated in all four directions around Meru, as well as those of the Sun.
Indeed, situated upon Meru, he always shines as if standing in its very center;
moving to the left, he makes the Golden Mountain appear on the right.
O celestial sage, [it is seen] at both sunrise and sunset, at all times directly in front,
as well as in all directions and intermediate points.
Wherever the radiant sun is seen by people, that is considered his rising;
and wherever he becomes invisible, right there occurs the setting of the sun. (23)
There is neither setting nor rising for the sun, which exists at all times;
what are called "rising" and "setting" are merely the perception and non-perception of the sun.
Abiding in the city of Śakra and the others, he touches three cities;
standing in Vikarṇa, he touches two corners and likewise two cities.
Mount Meru stands to the north of all the continents and regions;
and whichever direction the sun is seen in by those people, that alone is called "the East" (prācī).
It is determined that Mount Meru exists to its left;
and if it moves from the eastern direction for fifteen ghaṭikās, [the day proceeds].
Then, to the south, it extends for two crores and a quarter of yojanas, twelve and a half lakhs, and five thousand [yojanas]. (28)
The thousand-rayed sun, the indicator of the path of time, proceeds;
likewise, from there, the thousand-eyed one [Indra] goes toward the western, northern, and eastern directions.
The sun, the soul of Kālacakra, revolves for the sake of measuring time;
likewise do the other planets, such as the moon and others, which traverse the quarters of the sky.
They rise together with the constellations and set together with them;
in this manner, in a single muhūrta, the chariot of the Sun travels more than three hundred [yojanas].
The Lord, consisting of the three Vedas, revolves through thirty-four hundred thousand yojanas in the four directions and in the cities, by means of the wind.
The sun constantly revolves around the wheel of time known as the Pravaha,
whose single chariot-wheel has twelve spokes and three hubs.
The poets have described it as having six wheels and consisting of the year;
its axle is on the summit of Meru, at the Mānasottara mountain.
That which is described as the division between the performed and the other [the unmanifest], there the wheel-like [principle] revolves with the same speed as the oil-presser's machine. 35.
The sun revolves here around the mountain named Mānasottara;
its axis is fixed there, while the second axis is fixed at the Pole Star (Dhruva).
The upper portion of the Sun, the Lord of the worlds, is said to be like the axle of a machine, measured by a fourth part of oil. (37)
The interior of the chariot (rathanīḍa), however, is thirty-six lakhs of yojanas in length; it is proclaimed that its circumference is one-fourth of that measure.
The yoke of the sun’s chariot here consists of that much [space], and upon it are seven auspicious horses named after the Vedic meters, harnessed by the charioteer of the Sun.
They carry the divine Āditya for the sake of the happiness of the worlds;
the charioteer Aruṇa is stationed in front, while Savitṛ is yoked behind.
The elder brother of Garuḍa is engaged in the duties of the Sautya sacrifice;
likewise, there are the sages known as the Bālakhilyas, who are the size of a thumb-joint.
Numbering sixty thousand, as established by authoritative tradition, they praise the Sun before him with most beautiful hymns and prayers. (42)
Likewise, other sages, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Uragas,
Grāmaṇīs, Yātudhānas, and all the gods [worship] the Supreme Lord.
Month by month, for seven months, he [performed] the Virocana rite one by one;
the circle of the earth consists of nine crores and one hundred thousand [units].
The Lord of the gods of gods, who pervades the universe, traverses two thousand yojanas plus one gavyūti in an instant, moving without interruption.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Sun’s Motion," in the Description of the Cosmic Egg, within the eighth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 15 ||
Description of the Course of the Moon and Other Planets.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, therefore, let the wonderful course and other movements of the moon and the rest be heard.
It follows the course of men and reveals their auspicious and inauspicious deeds.
Just as when a potter’s wheel is spinning, the movement of those things resting upon it—such as insects and the like—is different from that of the wheel itself. || 2 ||
For in this way, by that wheel of time (Kālacakra), which is a multitude of aggregates, Meru and the Pole Star (Dhruva) are always carried around in a clockwise direction.
The movement of the planets, headed by the Sun, is seen to be of one kind;
likewise, because they pass through different constellations, their motion is from one constellation to another.
And these two destinies are not contradictory; this is the definitive conclusion everywhere:
he alone is the Blessed One, the primordial Person, the creator of the worlds.
Nārāyaṇa, the support of all, wandering for the welfare of the worlds and for the sake of purifying his own karma— which is indeed composed of the three Vedas— [manifested].
He who is to be sought after by both poets and the Veda became sevenfold;
he himself [manifested] in the six seasons in their proper order, beginning with spring.
Indeed, he bestows the seasonal qualities according to their pleasure;
therefore, all men always [worship] him with the threefold knowledge (trayī-vidyā).

[He was honored] by those following the path of conduct for the castes and stages of life, by the rituals prescribed in the sacred tradition, by various high and low acts performed with faith, and by the grand displays of yoga.
And those who sacrifice directly find the higher good; this is my opinion. Now, this is the Self of the worlds, situated between heaven and earth. || 10 ||
Moving through the twelve zodiac signs, Kālacakra experiences the parts of the year;
a month consists of two fortnights, and a day [of Brahmā] is a year.
And "nakta" refers to two such periods;
however, when he consumes a sixth part [of the day], it is called an "ṛtu. (12)
This portion of the year has been described by the sages as that interval during which the sun traverses half of the celestial path.
The ancient sages, honored by the wise,
describe that as the *ayana* (the path) until it returns together with the orb of the sky.
One should eat together with him in its entirety; they know that period to be a year—namely, the *saṃvatsara*, the *parivatsara*, and the *iḍāvatsara*.
The five-year cycle, consisting of Anuvatsara and Idvatsara,
has been proclaimed by those most skilled in the knowledge of time, based on the slow, swift, and even motions of the sun.
Thus has the motion of the sun been described; now learn that of the moon and the others.
In this manner, the moon is one hundred thousand yojanas above the rays of the sun. || 17 ||
Being perceived as a friend, he enjoys the food of a year;
and as the lord of medicinal herbs, he enjoys the food of a fortnight and a month.
With these two [periods] plus a quarter, he performs the daily and the fortnightly revolutions;
thus the Moon, moving with rapid speed, surely traverses the circle of the zodiac.
Bringing joy to the immortals with his waxing digits, and delighting the hearts of the ancestors with his waning digits. (20)
Spreading out days and nights through the successive series of long durations,
he is indeed the breath and the very life of the entire multitude of living beings.
And that all-pervading Lord, who is the primordial and most excellent Person consisting of sixteen parts, enjoys each single lunar mansion for thirty muhūrtas. || 22 ||
He is composed of mind and composed of food, the abode of immortality and the maker of nectar;
[he is the source] for gods, ancestors, humans, and all other beings, including reptiles and plants. (23)
Because his nature is to nourish the life-breaths (prāṇa), he is said to consist of everything;
from him, the wheel of the stars (bhacakra) revolves at a distance of three hundred thousand yojanas.
Indeed, by the circumambulation of Meru, they were joined by Īśvara and calculated as twenty-eight in number, including Abhijit.
Then, at a distance of two hundred thousand yojanas above that,
Śukra revolves together with the Sun, both in front of it and behind it.
Moving with swift, slow, or moderate speeds, this all-pervading Lord is generally said to be favorable to the worlds and brings about auspiciousness. (27)
O Sage, the descendant of Bhṛgu (Śukra) always pacifies the obstruction of rain;
from Śukra, Budha is said to be located two hundred thousand yojanas away.
With swift, slow, or moderate motions, like Venus, whenever Mercury surpasses the Sun, it is generally at that time [that the conjunction occurs]. (29)
Indicating the fear of excessive winds, the falling of clouds, rain, and so forth,
the terrestrial wind (bhauma) is situated above that at a distance of two hundred thousand yojanas.
O celestial sage, if he does not become retrograde, he traverses all twelve zodiacal signs, consuming them three signs at a time and then one by one.
For the most part, this [planet] indicates a multitude of malevolent planetary influences;
it is situated two hundred thousand yojanas from Bṛhaspati.
Then, as he moves through each individual zodiac sign, he consumes it for a year;
yet if he becomes retrograde, he is not favorable to those who discourse on Brahman.
Then, this son of the Sun, the formidable Śanaiścara, measured at two hundred thousand yojanas, revolves [around the earth] in thirty months.
The great planet moves through every single sign;
it is declared by the best among those who know Time to be inauspicious for all. (35)
To the north of that, the mandala of the Seven Sages is said to be measured at eleven lakhs of yojanas.
O Sage, those seven sages, contemplating the welfare of the worlds,
proceed toward that southern station which is the abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Movements of the Moon and Others," in the eighth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Configuration of the Dhruva-maṇḍala. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, [I shall describe] the measurement in yojanas above the circle of the sages (ṛṣi-maṇḍala).
By thirteen hundred thousand [repetitions], one attains the supreme state of Viṣṇu. || 1 ||
The illustrious and great devotee, the son of Uttānapāda, who is honored by the world, dwells there together with Indra, Agni, and Kaśyapa.
And Dhruva dwells together with Dharma, joined with him for all time;
he is always gazed upon with great respect by the onlookers standing to his right.
He, who is the means of subsistence for those living for an eon, worships the station of the Blessed One,
which belongs to all the hosts of luminaries— the planets, constellations, stars, and so forth.
By the Lord, this world was made like a supporting pillar for those wandering through time— which is unblinking and possesses manifest velocity.
Worshipped by the gods, he shines while illuminating with his own radiance,
just as oxen yoked to a central pillar for the purpose of plowing [shine] when joined to it.
These planets and all others, such as the lunar mansions and so forth, move through their respective orbits by means of the three daily libations (savana). || 7 ||
Arranged within the Kālacakra according to the division of internal and external,
they are quickly impelled by the wind while firmly supported by the Pole Star (dhruva).
Until the end of the kalpa, they move through the sky like hawks and other birds;
all of them are driven by their karma as charioteers and are subject to the power of the wind.
In this way, all the hosts of luminaries, sustained by the union of primordial nature (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa), do not fall down to the earth.
Some say that this wheel of light has the form of a sea-monster (śiśumāra),
which is useful for the Lord’s practice of yogic concentration.
O Sage, whose body is coiled with his head downward,
that Dhruva who was placed at the tip of your tail is the son of Uttānapāda.
And on his tail, it is declared, dwells the stainless Prajāpati;
Agni, Indra, and Dharma, honored by the gods, reside there as well. (13)
Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ are at the end of the tail, and then the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis) on the hips;
they assume the shape of a coil by moving in a clockwise direction.
The rays of the sun during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) are placed here on the right side,
and the rays of the sun during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) are placed here on the left side.
O son of Kaja, on both sides of his body, which is adorned with the curvature of earrings, there are an equal number of limbs.
The Ajavīthī is on the back, while the Ākāśasarit is in the belly;
Punarvasu and Puṣya are the right and left hips respectively.
Ārdrā and Āśleṣā are in the two hind feet, right and left;
Abhijit and Uttarāṣāḍhā are in the two nostrils, right and left. || 18 ||
And according to their respective order, O celestial sage, the Śruti and the Jalabha are likewise assigned by those skilled in conceptualization to the right and left eyes. (19)
Dhaniṣṭhā and Mūla are for the right and left ears respectively; and the eight lunar mansions beginning with Maghā belong here to the southern solstice.
O Sage, one should employ [the rites] in the left-side crooked constellations in their proper order,
as well as those northern constellations beginning with Mṛgaśīrṣa.
One should join [the asterisms] in reverse order upon the ribs on the right side;
likewise, Śatatārā and Jyeṣṭhā are on the right and left shoulders respectively.
Agasti is on the upper jaw, Yama on the lower jaw; Aṅgāraka is said to be in the mouths, and Mandu is said to be in the private parts.
Bṛhaspati resides in the crown of the head, Arka, the lord of the planets, in the chest;
Nārāyaṇa is in the heart, and the Moon dwells in the mind.
The Aśvins are proclaimed to be in the two breasts, Uśanas in the navel, Budha in the prāṇa and apāna breaths, Rāhu in the throat, and the Ketus [in the hair-roots]. (25)
Likewise, the hosts of stars are said to be in all his limbs and in the pores of his skin;
this is the body of the Blessed Viṣṇu, which consists of all the gods.
Every day at twilight, the sage, purified and restrained in speech, should meditate;
and the master of wisdom, while gazing [at the sun], should rise with this mantra.
"Salutation to the world of light, to Time, to the Lord of the unblinking ones;
let us address the Great Person. || 28 ||

For one who bows down to or remembers at the three times of day this [image] composed of planets, constellations, and stars— the presiding deity that removes the sins of those who have composed mantras— at the three times of day...
The sin born at that moment shall quickly perish. || 29 ||

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Configuration of Dhruva’s Mandala," in the eighth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 17.
Description of the Position of the Orb of Rāhu and Others.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Ten thousand [yojanas] below the sun, the orb of Rāhu is said to be located.
And Rāhu, though unworthy of it, moves like a star. || 1 ||
The son of Siṃhikā was the crusher of even the sun and the moon;
he obtained immortality and the status of a celestial body (kheṭa) through the grace of Viṣṇu.
That discus of the sun, which shines across ten thousand yojanas,
is known to be covered by an asura whose own extent is ten thousand times that of the sun.
The planet that eclipses the moon measures thirteen thousand [yojanas];
it is that which, at the time of the lunar nodes (parvan), becomes an eclipsing body through its persistent hostility.
From afar, he became the one who caused the obscuration of both the sun and the moon;
hearing that, Viṣṇu sent his own [discus] to both places.
The discus named Sudarśana, most terrifying with its garlands of flames,
was surrounded on all sides by its unbearable radiance.
But for a moment, his mind startled from afar,
he turned back from nearby as if thinking, "This is an eclipse."
It is said, O divine sage, let it be understood that in the midst of the world, there are worlds even more purifying than those below. || 8 ||
O best of beings, the worlds renowned for extending ten thousand yojanas, which are frequented by the meritorious, belong to the Siddhas, the Cāraṇas, and the Vidyādharas.
O celestial sage, even further below that is the supreme pleasure-ground of the Yakṣas, along with the Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Pretas, and Bhūtas.
That which is called the intermediate space (antarikṣa) is indeed as far as the wind blows and as far as the clouds rise; so it has been declared by those skilled in knowledge.
O best of the twice-born, from there downwards for a hundred yojanas,
the earth is reckoned as the domain of the Suparṇas, Śyenās, and Sārasas.
Swans and other creatures fly up; these are the earthly beings born of the earth.
Thus has the arrangement and location of the terrestrial world been accurately described.
O divine sage, it is traditionally taught that below the earth there are seven subterranean cavities,
each measuring one hundred thousand yojanas in both length and height.
Renowned for their ten-thousandfold intervals and providing happiness in all seasons,
the first is declared to be Atala, and the second is likewise Vitala.
The third is declared to be Sutala, the fourth is indeed Talātala,
Mahātala is the fifth, and the sixth is declared to be Rasātala.
O Brahmin, the seventh is Pātāla; these seven are known as the subterranean realms (vivaras).
Within these celestial caverns, there is indeed even more [splendor] than in heaven itself.
And in those worlds abundant with the pleasures of desire, enjoyments, and sovereign power, where there are eternal gardens for recreation, the savor of happiness prevails. (18)
The Daityas, the sons of Kadrū, and the powerful Dānavas were constantly delighted and devoted to their wives, children, and kinsmen. || 19 ||
Accompanied by friends, dependents, and others, these lords of households have their desires unimpeded by the Lord, yet they are full of deceit. (20)
They dwell there always joyful, endowed with the pleasures of all seasons,
in those very places which were created by Maya, the master of illusion.
In front were thousands of devotees, adorned with excellent jewels, possessing wonderful mansions, watchtowers, gateways, and other structures.
Richly adorned with the splendor of assembly halls, courtyards, shrines, and other structures— rare even among the gods—
they were filled with pairs of Nāgas and Asuras, along with pigeons and mynas.
And the great gardens, strewn with artificial grounds and adorned with the finest dwellings of the lords of the subterranean realms, shine forth in splendor.
They were pleasing to the mind with their abundance of fruits and flowers, and they shone with places fit for the amorous play of women.
With masses of water joined by flocks of various birds, with ponds filled with clear water and adorned with *pāṭhīna* fish; || 26 ||
It was likewise filled with numerous water-born creatures agitating the water, and with many varieties of lotuses:
white lilies, blue lotuses, white water-lilies, and blue and red lotuses.
They were crowded with monasteries where those who had made their dwellings resided,
and likewise with various musical sounds that provided festivals for the senses.
And they surpass even the supreme glory of the immortals;
there, indeed, there is no fear whatsoever from the limbs of Time, namely day and night.
Where the darkness is perpetually dispelled by the rays of jewels resting upon the heads of the most eminent serpents, which are ever radiant with splendor.
For those dwelling here, neither mental afflictions nor physical diseases arise, despite [the lack of] divine herbs, elixirs, juices, foods, drinks, baths, and the like. (31)
Wrinkles, gray hair, decrepitude, discoloration, perspiration, body odor, lack of enthusiasm, and the various stages of age never cause him any affliction. (32)
For those virtuous ones, there is never any fear of death from anything other than the splendor of the Blessed One and the Sudarśana discus itself. (33)
O son of Brahmā, when he enters, the masses of fetuses belonging to the wives of the Daityas generally fall away or even flow out out of fear.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Abode of the Orb of Rāhu and Others," in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 18.
A Description of the Worlds of Atala, Vitala, and Sutala.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Brahmin, in the first delightful cavity named Atala...
Māyā’s son, named Bala, exists, acting with unabated pride.
By whom ninety-six illusions were created to accomplish all purposes—those which the masters of illusion employ instantly, and some of which they themselves even wear. (2)
As that very powerful Bala yawned, throngs of women appeared, capable of enchanting the three worlds. (3)
They were well known as unchaste women, wanton women, and lustful women;
indeed, they would enter into secret hiding places where a man had gone to be alone.
Having diligently prepared it with the mercury known as hāṭaka,
[he attained success] through his own playful glances, affectionate smiles, and embraces.
And by means of conversation, amorous dalliance, and other such arts, those women also delight him;
yet when he is possessed by that [māyā], a person himself perceives it in many ways.
Thinking of himself, "I am the lord, I am perfected, I am great with the strength of ten thousand elephants," he is described as being blinded by intoxication.
Thus, O Nārada, the location of Atala has been described here;
now learn of Vitala, the second cavity.
And below the surface of the earth, in the Vitala realm, resides the Lord Bhava,
known by the name Hāṭakeśvara, surrounded by his own hosts of attendants.
For the sake of expanding even the creation fashioned by Prajāpati, he,
honored by the gods, remains united in union with Bhavānī.
The supreme river Hāṭakī, produced by the vigor of the two Bhavas,
truly drinks, as it were, the kindled fire with its own energy through the wind.
That which was spat out by him is the gold known as hāṭaka, the favorite of the Daityas;
indeed, the wives of the Daityas always wear it, for it is worthy of being their ornament.
O Sage, below the floor of that cave is the place called Sutala, the Lord of Caves (Bileśvara);
there dwells the one of meritorious fame named Bali, the son of Virocana.
Desiring to do what was most pleasing to the god Mahendra,
the Blessed Lord Trivikrama also brought Bali to Sutala.
Having snatched away the fortune of the three worlds, it is said that the king of the Daityas was established therein;
that very prosperity, which could not even be obtained by Indra and the other gods, followed after him.
He worships that very Lord of the gods with devotion;
even today, the lord of Sutala remains free from all fear.
"For this is the fruit of the gift of land when given to the Lord of All, who is a worthy recipient;
yet the high-souled ones describe it thus, O Nārada, and this is not fitting. (17)
O Brahmin, this fruit of giving is in no way appropriate for Hari, the Blessed Vāsudeva, who bestows the goals of human existence. 18.
Even by involuntarily uttering the name of that very God of gods,
one instantly shakes off the bonds of one's own karma.
Ascetics constantly perform practices such as Sāṃkhya and Yoga for the sake of severing the bonds of affliction toward the Blessed One, the Lord of all.
O Nārada, this Blessed One did not favor us,
yet he manifested the supreme sovereignty of enjoyments consisting of illusion.
The Lord Viṣṇu himself, the sovereign who knows all means, [has taught] that which is the primary cause of all afflictions and the delusion of the recollection of one's own self. (22)
His entire wealth had been stolen under the pretext of a sacrifice, leaving him with nothing but his body;
having found no other means, the Lord [bound him] with nooses born of Varuṇa.
Having bound him and then released him, as if in a mountain cave, he said:
"This Indra is a great fool, whose minister is Bṛhaspati!"
This world-wealth is exceedingly clear and unwavering;
compared to this sovereignty over the three worlds, how very trivial is [any other] power? (25)
Except for our illustrious grandfather Prahlāda, who was dear to the Blessed One, what fool would abandon the source of all blessings for the sake of worldly prosperity? (26)
He who benefits all the worlds chose servitude to that Lord,
even as an incomparable paternal sovereignty was being offered to him by Viṣṇu.
When his father, the hero, had passed away, he who was dear to the Blessed One did not desire [the kingdom],
for that man possessed incomparable majesty and was the refuge of all the world.
One like me, who has not fully digested his faults, does not understand this;
such is this Bali, the lord of the Daityas, who is most highly honored. (29)
At whose gate Hari himself serves as the doorkeeper—
once, during his world-conquering expedition, King Rāvaṇa, the "Roarer of the Worlds," [approached].
Entering Sutala, he who bestows grace upon his devotees cast it down here by ten thousand yojanas with his big toe.
Possessing such power and enjoying every happiness, this Bali remains established as the king of Sutala by the grace of the God of gods. (32)

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Worlds of Atala, Vitala, and Sutala," in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 19.
In the description of the worlds beginning with Talātala, there is an infinite description. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Below that is the cavity known as Talātala.
The great lord of the Danavas named Maya was the ruler of Tripura.
This [kingdom], which had burned three cities, was protected by Śaṅkara throughout the three worlds;
through the grace of the God of gods, it became the locus of the happiness of sovereignty.
This very one is the preceptor of illusionists, skilled in various types of magic;
he is worshipped by the terrible Rākṣasas for the successful accomplishment of all their undertakings.
Below that is clearly known as Mahātala;
there resides the great host of serpents, the offspring of Kadrū, called Krodhavaśa.
O Brahmin, I shall name for you the foremost among those with many heads:
Kuhaka, Takṣaka, Suṣeṇa, and likewise Kāliya.
Those of great wealth and great power, though they were fierce and of a fierce nature,
were all utterly distressed by the king of birds.
United with their own wives, children, friends, and family,
they sport about heedlessly, being skilled in various diversions.
And below that, in the cavity called Rasātala,
dwell the Daityas, Paṇis, and Dānavas.
Known as the Nivātakavacas, inhabitants of Hiraṇyapura, they were called the Kāleyas; they were the adversaries of the fire-eaters (the gods).
By the mere birth of Hari, who possesses great majesty, is exceedingly courageous, and is the Lord of all, their prowess was destroyed by his splendor.
For those who are constantly pierced by the words of Saramā, the messenger of Śakra, always dwell in a hole like creatures that live in the mud.
Struck by the splendor of the mantra-syllables, the asuras were indeed terrified;
even further below, in Pātāla, the lords of the world of the Nāgas [were likewise struck]. (12)
Vāsuki and the others—Śaṅkha, Kulika, Śveta, Dhanañjaya, Mahāśaṅkha, and likewise Dhṛtarāṣṭra. || 13 ||
Śaṅkhacūḍa, Kambalāśvatara, and Devopadattaka—possessing great wrath and vast coils, they dwell there, their venom most virulent. (14)
Some possessed five heads and were adorned with seven hoods;
some had ten hoods, and others likewise had a hundred heads. (15)
Certain beings with a thousand heads, wearing radiant jewels, [dispelled] the mass of darkness in the crevices of the netherworld with their own rays. (16)
And, O celestial sage, they are always filled with wrath and destroy it within the thirty-thousand-yojana interval at its base. (17)
Measured in yojanas, that portion of the Blessed One consisting of darkness, known as Ananta, dwells there, indeed worshipped by all the gods. (18)
The Sātvatas declare that he whom they call Saṅkarṣaṇa is the characteristic of the ego-conceit (ahaṃkāra), which draws together the seer and the seen.
This circle of the earth is supported upon the head of the thousand-headed Lord Śeṣa, whose form is infinite.
Indeed, the entire terrestrial globe appears like a mustard seed to that all-pervading Lord,
who desires to withdraw it at the appointed time.
From the space between his eyebrows, the mobile and immobile world emerged;
[he was] Rudra named Sāṅkarṣaṇa, adorned by the eleven-fold manifestation (vyūha).
And Trilocana himself, the great being who brings about the destruction of the great elements, rose up brandishing a three-pointed trident. (23)
Upon the two lotus-feet of whom, within the circles of his deep red, clear toenails—
which resemble shining jewel-reflectors— the great lords of serpents dwell incessantly.
Together with the foremost of the Sātvatas through the yoga of exclusive devotion,
they gazed upon his face while bowing their own heads.
Though graced by the circles of luster from the rubies of their shimmering earrings, their beautiful cheeks were radiant with the glow of the regions of their temples. (26)
The daughters of the Naga kings as well, with the luster of their beautiful limbs shining forth, likewise possessed large, bright, white, and auspicious eyes. (27)
Shining here and there with their beautiful, staff-like arms,
they were adorned with anointments of sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron paste.
Possessed by the onset of desire born from that touch, they look upon him with playful smiles and with modesty. (29)
With eyes reddened and rolling, intoxicated by the madness of passion,
yet with glances full of compassion, they likewise offered their blessings.
He is the infinite Lord, the God of infinite beings, the one of vast intent, an ocean of infinite virtues, the primordial God of great splendor. || 31 ||
Having restrained the impulse of his indignation and wrath for the welfare of the world,
he remains as a treasure-house of great beings, worshipped by all the gods.
He was constantly meditated upon by the gods, the siddhas, the asuras, and the uragas, as well as by the vidyādharas, the gandharvas, and the hosts of sages.
With eyes agitated by the incessant intoxication of joy,
he [satisfied] the gods and his own hosts of attendants with the nectar of his speech.
Growing in strength, that omnipresent Lord wore a Vaijayantī garland composed of fresh,
unfading, and translucent clusters of tulasī leaves.
Always endowed with the splendor of the humming of intoxicated swarms of bees,
the God of gods was clothed in blue garments and adorned with a single earring.

With his exceedingly thick arms placed upon the peak of the plow, the imperishable Lord of Gods, possessing noble grace, was described by the bulls among the Sāttvatas as being like Mahendra with his golden girth or a lordly elephant with its leather strap. (37)

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of Ananta," in the description of the worlds beginning with Talātala, within the eighth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Nature of Hell.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The venerable and eternal son of Brahmā described its power.
Singing in the assembly hall of Brahmā, they pay their respects. || 1 ||
The cosmic ages (kalpas), characterized by the qualities of nature such as goodness (sattva) and the rest, are the causes of this world’s origin, maintenance, and dissolution through His glance;
how indeed can one know the path of Him whose form is eternal, uncreated, and one, yet who has manifested Himself manifold within the self?
Out of great compassion for us, he assumed a form of perfectly pure being, in which this world of cause and effect shines forth;
he of noble prowess took up that faultless pastime so that the hearts of his own people might be won over, even as the lion assumes its play.

If one should recite that which has been heard—whether out of sudden impulse, or being afflicted, or fallen, or even for the sake of deception—it instantly destroys all the sins of men without exception; so, O seeker of liberation, to whom else but the Blessed Lord Śeṣa should you go for refuge?
The terrestrial globe, together with its mountains, rivers, oceans, and living beings, is like a minute atom placed upon the crown of the head of the Infinite One,
whose prowess is immeasurable due to His boundlessness.
Who, even with a thousand tongues, could enumerate his heroic deeds? || 5 ||
Such is the power of the Blessed One— boundless, with inexhaustible vigor and the majesty of vast virtues—
who dwells at the root of the nectar-stream, self-dependent.
He who, with effortless ease, sustains the earth for its stability.
For these very destinies, O best of sages, must be traversed repeatedly by men here,
just as they have been fashioned by their own past actions.
And by those who always desire sensual pleasures according to their instructions, O King of kings, there are indeed this many [pleasures] among humans, beasts, and birds. (8)
They are said to have gone to various states of fruition and likewise to be subject to the power of dharma;
they are high and low and dissimilar—understand them according to the question asked.
Nārada said:
"How was this diversity of the world created by the Blessed One, even though actions are equal? Tell us that exactly as it is. (10)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Indeed, by the power of the performer's faith alone, the destinations are of various kinds;
because they always consist of the three guṇas, their fruit here is indeed dissimilar.
Through sattvic faith, the performer always experiences happiness;
likewise, through rajasic faith, the performer experiences suffering. (12)
Suffering and delusion arise from faith characterized by tamas;
however, due to the gradations among various forms of faith, a diversity of fruits is proclaimed.
O best of the twice-born, thousands of destinies have indeed come into being, produced by the transformation of karmas fashioned by beginningless ignorance.
O best of the twice-born, I shall describe its various divisions in detail;
indeed, it is located here within the southern quarter of the three worlds.
O Nārada, beneath the earth and above the surface of the Tala-loka dwell the Agniṣvātta classes of Pitṛs and the Pitṛs themselves.
In that [city] dwell those who, through supreme meditative concentration, swiftly cause the highest blessings of their own lineages to become true for you, while indeed aspiring for them.
The Lord, the King of the Ancestors,
likewise [exercises authority] over living beings who have passed away and have been brought here to his domain by his own messengers.
Accompanied by his retinue, devoted to the commands proclaimed by the Blessed One, and upholding self-restraint,
he— possessing the vision of discernment— acts according to the deed and according to the fault.
The wise king always urges on all his own attendants—who know the truth of Dharma and execute his commands—according to the tasks assigned to them by his direction. (20)
Indeed, some describe the hells as being twenty-one in number, while others say they are twenty-eight; I shall now state them in their proper order. (21)
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, and Raurava as the third;
that named Mahāraurava and Kumbhīpāka are considered another.
Likewise, Kālasūtra, as well as Asipatravana, are cited; then Sūkaramukha, Andhakūpa, and Kṛmibhojana. (23)
The Pincers, the Heated Image, and the Thunderbolt-Prickle, as well as the Silk-Cotton Tree, O divine sage, and likewise that which is known by the name Vairatanī. (24)
Pūyoda, Prāṇarodha, and likewise Viśasana are considered [hells]; Lālābhakṣa, Sārameyādana, and after that, Mūtra. (25)
Then there is the descent into Avīci, the drinking of alkaline mud, the communal feast known as that of the hosts of Rākṣasas, and thereafter being impaled upon a trident. (26)
Daṇḍaśūka, Avaṭārodha, Paryāvartanaka, and Sūcīmukha—these are declared to be the twenty-eight hells. (27)
Thus, O Lotus-born One, these supreme realms of torment are known as the hells, which are accessible to living beings through their own actions.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of Naraka," in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 21 ||
The Description of the Sins Leading to Hell.
Nārada said:
O eternal sage, how many kinds of actions are there for me?
These grounds for undergoing torments must be heard in every way. || 1 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
He who indeed seizes the wealth, wives, or children of another is a wicked soul who falls into the domain of Yama’s attendants.
Bound by the noose of Time and seized by the most terrifying messengers of Yama,
he is cast into the hell named Tāmisra, a place of torment.
Then the messengers of Yama, equipped with nooses, inflict beating, punishment, and further threats; indeed, he falls into a state of utter exhaustion.
The son of Padmabhū, the denizen of hell, falls into a swoon, rendered helpless, he who, having deceived his husband, enjoys his wife and other possessions. || 5 ||
He is cast into the Andhatāmisra hell by the servants of Yama;
while being cast there, the living being becomes overwhelmed by agony.
One whose vision is lost and whose intellect is destroyed will surely become so without delay,
just as a tree in this world perishes when its roots are severed.
For this reason also, it has been designated by the ancients as "Andhatāmisra" (Blinding Darkness),
which consists solely of the thought "this is mine, this is I," arising through injury to living beings.
Devoted to his work, he nourishes his own family every day;
yet, having abandoned this very duty, he falls right here in this world due to his own evil deeds.
In the hell named Raurava, which brings terror to all beings, those creatures who were previously harmed by him in this world [shall suffer]. (10)
Having become those very ruru deer, they torment him in the next world;
therefore, the wise who know the Purāṇas call it Raurava.
The ancient sages have described the *ruru* as a creature even more cruel than a serpent;
likewise, there is the hell named Mahāraurava, wherein a person [suffers].
Indeed, those who have taken birth in another body and undergo torment there are called *kravyāda* ruru deer; they cause him to be slain by devouring his raw flesh.
That foolish man who is fierce and cruel, who even roasts herds of animals and flocks of birds, is himself roasted by the messengers of Yama.
O Nārada, in the Kumbhīpāka hell, they remain for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on the bodies of the animals, even while immersed in boiling oil.
That sinner who betrays his father, a Brahmin, or a priest is cast into the Kālasūtra hell;
there, the denizen of hell is tormented by fire and the sun.
Burning within and without the body from hunger and thirst, it sits, lies down, moves about, stands still, and runs. (17)
O celestial sage, even in times of non-distress, the guards seize that sinful man who departs from his own Vedic path and resorts to heresy.
And they cast him into the hell named Asipatravana;
then the hell-being who has gone there is indeed struck with whips.
Running here and there with extreme speed,
he was being sliced on both sides by the edges of sword-leaves.
With all his limbs being cut away, crying out "Alas, I am struck! and falling into a swoon, he experiences supreme agony and stumbles at every step.
The king or royal official who inflicts punishment unjustly, that person of small intellect, enjoys the fruit of heresy while following his own duty.
If he inflicts corporal punishment upon a twice-born man, that most sinful person goes to hell;
he is cast into the Sūkaramukha hell by the servants of Yama.
With his limbs shattered by those powerful ones,
he cried out with a piteous voice, fainting and overcome by dejection.
Being tormented in many ways, he indeed undergoes extreme suffering;
for even one who is detached from harming others experiences the pain of others when it is not kept at a distance. (25)
He himself inflicts suffering upon those whose livelihoods are marked by the Lord;
and he, being constrained by his betrayal of Him, falls into a blind well.
There, he is [attacked] by cruel creatures—beasts, wild animals, birds, reptiles, mosquitoes, lice, and various kinds of bedbugs. || 27 ||
There he is tormented by flies and by biting serpents in the darkness; and there, within that wretched body, he wanders about like a living creature.
But he who, though praised by the crows, eats whatever happens to be available without having performed the five sacrifices and without having shared it [with others]. (29)
That wicked man is cast by the cruel messengers of Yama into the lowest hell, Kṛmibhojana, on account of his evil deeds.
In a terrifying pit of worms extending for a hundred thousand yojanas,
having assumed the form of a worm, he himself will be devoured by them.
He who eats what has not been offered or what has not been consecrated indeed incurs sin therein;
likewise for one who, through theft or by force, takes gold or even precious gems.
O celestial sage, the followers of Yama seize that man in the hereafter who steals from a Brahmin or from anyone else when there is no state of distress.
And they tear them apart with iron balls as hot as fire—those who approach a woman who should not be approached, or a man whom she should not approach. (34)
There, even in that other world, the followers of Yama strike him with whips and embrace him with a sharp,
iron rod.
And the followers of Yama force that woman to embrace a glowing iron image,
against the man who has approached all women and accumulated a mass of evil.
In that hell, the servants of Yama plant him upon a thorny silk-cotton tree made of iron,
which is covered with spikes of diamond-hard metal.
Those kṣatriyas, royal officials, or those who follow heretical paths—who tear down the bridge of dharma—those men, having departed this life, go to the lower realms. || 38 ||
O Nārada, those who have violated the boundaries of propriety fall into the river Vaitaraṇī, which is the moat surrounding the fortress of hell.
O Nārada, though being devoured on all sides here and there by hosts of aquatic creatures, they are never separated from their own bodies nor even from their vital breaths.
And they are tormented on all sides by the ripening of their own karma, [drenched] with feces,
urine, pus, blood, hair, bones, nails, and flesh.
Those who are husbands of Śūdra women, who have lost their purity and are devoid of shame, fall into a river filled with fat and marrow. (42)
Those who have abandoned the rules of conduct and are devoted to the behavior of beasts go here to a miserable state, [drenched] with feces, urine, phlegm, and blood. (43)
Those of wicked resolve fall into that which is filled with the impurities of phlegm;
there, the hosts of Yama’s attendants devour them. (44)
Those twice-born ones who are masters of dogs, donkeys, and the like, who are constantly addicted to hunting, and who kill deer at improper places; || 45 ||
The soldiers of Yama pierce with arrows those lowest of men who have come to such misconduct, once they have become targets for their pursuit. (46)
Those lowest of men, who are hypocrites and slaughter animals in sacrifices performed with deceit— them, O soldiers of Yama, you shall then cast into the Vaiśasa hell in that world beyond.
Having cast her down, that twice-born man, deluded by passion, torments his wife of equal caste with unbearable lashes of a whip. (48)
The servants of Yama force that fool to drink his own semen in the hereafter;
they cast him into a pit of semen and compel him to drink it.
Those who are robbers, arsonists, poisoners, and plunderers of caravans—kings and royal officers who seize villages and trade routes. (50)
The messengers of Yama lead those departed ones to the Śvānakādana hell;
there are twenty-one most formidable dogs of immense size.
O Sage, it is declared in the Saptashati that they are violently devoured in the terrible hell named Śvabhojana (Dog-Eater). Hereafter, O Sage, I shall describe the hells beginning with Avīci.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Sins Leading to Hell," in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 22 ||
Description of the Remaining Hells.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Those men who always speak falsehood when giving testimony, [go to the following hells].
O divine sage, those of sinful intellect engage in the giving or bartering of wealth. || 1 ||
Having died, they indeed fall in the next world into the most terrible hell called Avīci,
from the summit of a mountain rising a hundred yojanas high.
In that place called Avīci, which is not actually space, those with their heads downward see a ground that appears like water, filled with waves.
O celestial sage, because there is no interval [of rest] in Avīci, his body is cut into pieces as small as sesame seeds; he never dies there, but is instead cast down again and again.
Or if a twice-born man—whether a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya—born of Brahman, who has drunk the Soma, should drink liquor as if it were the wife of that [Soma]. || 5 ||
But due to their negligence, O Sage, Yama’s messengers indeed cause them to fall into hell and make them drink molten iron.
O you who are born of Brahmā,
that lowest of men, though himself base, was utterly consumed by fire through his very conceit of self-importance.
That lowest of men does not hold in high regard even those superior persons who possess learning, noble birth, austerity, and the conduct prescribed for their caste and stage of life.
He is led by the servants of Yama to the hell named Kṣārakardama,
where, with his head hanging downwards, he undergoes terrible and endless torments.
O great sage, those men who, being deluded, sacrifice another man with a human sacrifice, or even women who devour a human beast, [suffer here]. (10)
Those cattle, having gathered together at the abode of Yama,
were all torn apart by him with his sharp-edged blade, like butchers.
O Sage, they drink blood, dance, and sing in many ways,
just like those insatiable man-eaters here who consume flesh.
O son of Brahmā, even those who are innocent, whether in the forest or in the village,
have been made to lose their lives by those who approached them with deceptive means while they desired to live.
Like children's toys threaded on a string or a skewer, they cause them to fall after death;
indeed, they fall into the Śūlapāta hell.
With their bodies impaled on pikes and other instruments, they are excessively tormented by hunger and thirst;
they are struck here and there by herons and cranes with sharp beaks.
For those men of violent conduct who terrify living beings remember their own many impurities when they are afflicted. (16)
For even those [who kill] snakes and such fall into hell,
specifically that place called Dandaśūka, where they rise up from all sides.
O Brahmin, those with five faces and seven mouths, possessed of cruel minds, seize those who have come to hell, just as creatures dwelling in holes do.
Those who confine [beings] in wells, granaries, caves, and the like—
those servants of the Kīnāśas [plowmen] with upraised hands shall sit upon those very things,
along with the fire named Sagara.
And they restrain those men who delight in evil deeds by means of smoke.
If a twice-born householder should look upon guests who have arrived at the proper time with an eye as if wishing to burn them, he looks upon himself with sin. (21)
For that person of evil views as well, in hell, there are the servants of Yama—
those with vajra-beaks, the kaṅkas, the kākavaṭas, and so forth.
For even the most cruel vultures forcibly tear away that man who goes about with the conceit of wealth, excessively puffed up by egoism. (23)
In this matter, that lowest of men, full of apprehension, casts sidelong glances,
constantly reflecting upon the future gain and loss of his wealth in every respect.
With his heart and mouth parched, he finds no peace at all;
like a planet, that preta guards his wealth with the servants of Yama. (25)
And by his own karma, he is cast into the Sūcīmukha hell; there, the servants of Yama treat him like weavers handling a man who has seized their wealth.
Indeed, the servants bind them all over their limbs with cords;
O Brahmin, these are the various hells for those of evil deeds.
O divine sage, there are indeed hundreds of places of torment for men, and even thousands more, whether already mentioned or yet to be told. (28)
O Sage, those who act thus enter these hells abounding in torments;
likewise, those devoted to dharma go to worlds exalted with happiness. (29)
O great sage, your own dharma has been described in many ways as consisting of the worship of the Goddess and characterized by the propitiation of the Goddess. (30)
That Goddess, when worshipped by men, is the savior from the ocean of worldly existence; merely by performing her rites, a person shall not go to hell. (31)
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Remaining Hells," in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Procedure for the Worship of the Goddess.
Nārada said:
O Father, what is the nature of that dharma characterized by the propitiation of the Goddess?
How is that Goddess propitiated so that she bestows the supreme state? || 1 ||
What is the method of propitiation? How was she propitiated, and when?
By whom does that Durgā become the bestower of protection from the difficult hells? (2)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O celestial sage, best among the learned, listen with one-pointed concentration to how the Goddess herself becomes pleased through the practice of dharma.
O Nārada, listen to me regarding the nature of one's own duty as it has been proclaimed:
in this beginningless cycle of existence, the Goddess herself created Śṛṅkhalā.
O Sage, she protects [her devotees] from terrible calamities and other such dangers;
that Goddess is worshipped by the worlds according to the prescribed rite—listen now to that procedure.
Having reached the day of the new moon, one should worship the Goddess with clarified butter;
by giving ghee to a Brāhmaṇa, one shall always be free from disease.
On the second day, one should worship the Mother of the World with sugar;
by giving sugar to a Brahmin, a man becomes long-lived.
On the third day and subsequent days, by offering milk to the Goddess during the rite of worship and giving milk to an eminent Brahmin, one shall transcend all suffering.
On the fourth day, during the worship, cakes (apūpa) should be offered to the Goddess and to the twice-born;
indeed, only cakes should be given, for one is not overcome by obstacles.
On the fifth day, one should offer a plantain fruit grown on a plantain tree to the Goddess;
that very same fruit should be given to a Brāhmaṇa, whereby one becomes a man of great intelligence.
On the sixth lunar day, honey is prescribed for the rite of worshipping the Goddess;
it should be given to a Brāhmaṇa so that beauty may arise.
O best of the twice-born, by offering molasses as a food-oblation to the Goddess on the seventh lunar day and giving molasses to a Brahmin, one becomes free from sorrow.
On the eighth day, one should offer a coconut as an oblation (naivedya) to the Goddess;
it should be given to a Brāhmaṇa, and the man shall become free from suffering.
On the ninth day, having offered parched grain to the Mother and to a brahmin, one should say:
"May he become exceedingly happy in this world and in the next. (14)
O Sage, having offered black sesame seeds to the Goddess on the tenth day and having given them to a Brāhmaṇa, one indeed has no fear of the world of Yama.
He who offers curd to the Goddess on the eleventh day and gives it to a Brāhmaṇa shall become most dear to the Goddess.
O best of sages, he who gives flattened rice (pṛthuka) to the Goddess on the twelfth day and then gives those same grains to the preceptor shall attain the state of being dear to the Goddess.
On the thirteenth day, one offers chickpeas to Durgā;
by giving those very same to a Brahmin, one shall possess a continuous lineage of progeny.
And on the fourteenth day, O divine sage, he offers groats to the Goddess;
by giving those very same to a Brahmin, one becomes beloved of Śiva. (19)
On the full-moon day, she offers milk-rice to Aparṇā and gives it to the foremost of the twice-born; thus she delivers all her ancestors from saṃsāra.
O great sage, it is taught that on those respective lunar days, an oblation should be performed for the pleasure of the Goddess;
this destroys all misfortunes through the substances prescribed for each specific day.
On Sunday, milk-rice (pāyasa) is proclaimed as the offering;
on Monday, milk is prescribed; and on Tuesday, the plantain fruit.
O twice-born one, fresh butter is prescribed for Wednesday,
and white sugar for Thursday and Friday.
On Saturday, cow's ghee is proclaimed as the appropriate food offering (naivedya).
