O Sage, now hear the food offerings for the twenty-seven lunar mansions (nakṣatras).
Ghee, sesame seeds, sugar, curd, milk, inspissated milk (kilāṭaka), *dadhikūrcī*, sweetmeat balls (*modaka*), *pheṇikā* cakes, and ghee-fried pancakes (*ghṛtamaṇḍaka*). || 25 ||
Then there was sweetmeat made from gram flour, leaves of the banyan tree, and thereafter fried cakes;
likewise, balls of wheat, *kokarasaka*, stuffed sweets, honey, and *sūraṇa* root.
Molasses, flattened rice, grapes, dates, and sugar-candy; cakes, fresh butter, mung beans, and sweetmeats as well. (27)
O Nārada, it is declared that the offering of food (naivedya) should consist of a citron;
I shall now describe the offerings for the Viṣkambha and other yogas.
When these articles have been prepared, the Mother of the World is pleased;
namely, jaggery, honey, ghee, milk, curd, buttermilk, and cakes. (29)
Fresh butter, crab, pumpkin, and sweetmeat;
jackfruit, plantain, rose-apple, mango, and sesame. (30)
Oranges, pomegranates, and jujube fruits, as well as myrobalan fruits, milk-rice, flattened rice, and chickpeas; || 31 ||
O Brahmin, coconut, rose-apple, kaseru, and likewise surana— these are the auspicious offerings for the food-oblation (naivedya) in their respective order.
O Sage, the [results] for the Viṣkambha and other yogas have been determined by the wise; now I shall describe the food offerings (naivedya) for the Karaṇas individually.
Kaṃsāra, maṇḍaka, pheṇī, modaka, vaṭapatraka, laḍḍuka, ghṛtapūra, sesame, curd, ghee, and honey. (34)
This has been proclaimed with reverence as the offering for the Goddess among all ritual acts;
now I shall further describe another supreme means that brings great delight to the Goddess. (35)
O Sage Nārada, listen with respect to that entire procedure:
on the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, a man [should approach] a Madhūka tree.
One should worship [the deity] and prepare five kinds of food as an offering;
thus, throughout the twelve months, on the third lunar day in sequence.
We shall describe the offering of food according to the prescribed rite during the bright fortnight;
O Nārada, in the month of Vaiśākha, the food offering should be accompanied by jaggery.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, honey is prescribed for the sake of pleasing the Goddess alone;
and in Āṣāḍha, fresh butter and the offering of Madhuka flowers [are prescribed]. (39)
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, curd is the prescribed offering; in the month of Bhādrapada, sugar;
in Āśvina, milk-rice (pāyasa) is declared; and in Kārttika, milk is the most excellent.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the best of froth is prescribed; in Pauṣa, curd-cakes;
and in the month of Māgha, one should offer as an oblation the finest cow's products.
And the coconut is proclaimed as the food offering for the month of Phālguna;
thus one should worship with twelve food offerings in sequence throughout the month.
Maṅgalā, Vaiṣṇavī, Māyā, the insurmountable Kālarātri, Mahāmāyā, Mataṅgī, Kālī, and Kamalavāsinī. (43)
"Śivā, Sahasracaraṇā, Sarvamaṅgalārūpiṇī—one should worship the Goddess with these names upon a Madhūka tree. (44)
Then, for the sake of fulfilling all desires and for the successful completion of the vow, one should praise the Great Goddess, the Sovereign of Gods, who resides within the Madhūka tree.
Salutations to the lotus-eyed one; salutations be to you, the mother of the universe.
Salutations to the Great Goddess, the sovereign power of Maheśvara, whose form is the source of supreme auspiciousness.
She is the supreme destroyer of sin, the bestower of the supreme path;
she is the Supreme Goddess, the source of progeny, whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman.
The giver of joy, intoxicated with bliss, accessible through honor, most exalted, wise, meditated upon by sages, and the companion of the Sun. || 48 ||
Victory to you, O Goddess of the World, O wise one, who resembles a cloud at the time of universal dissolution;
you are worshipped by gods and asuras for the sake of destroying great delusion. 49.

Salutations again and again to her who brings about the non-existence of the world of Yama, who is worshipped by Yama, who was born before Yama, and whose form is the subduer of Yama; salutations to her who is worthy of sacrifice! 50.
She is of an equal nature, the mistress of all, and entirely free from all attachment;
she is the destroyer of attachment, possessing a desirable form and a body of compassion. || 51 ||
Kaṅkālakrūrā, Kāmākṣī, Mīnākṣī, Marmabhedini, she whose form and character are sweetness, and she who is honored for her sweet voice. || 52 ||
Possessing great mantras, accessible through mantra, she brings about the favor of mantra;
she enters the minds of men and brings about the favor of the enemy of Manmatha (Śiva). || 53 ||
She resides within the Aśvattha, Vaṭa, Nimba, Āmra, Kapittha, and Badarī trees;
she takes the form of the Panasa, Arka, Karīra, and other milk-exuding trees.

Victory to you, O beloved of the Omniscient One, who are worthy of dwelling in the milk-vines, who are pitiable yet overflowing with compassion, and whose very form consists of courtesy and mercy! 55.
Thus, at the conclusion of the worship, one should praise that Goddess of gods with this hymn;
by doing so, a man always obtains the entire merit of the vow.
For that man who constantly recites this hymn which brings delight to the Goddess,
there is indeed no fear of mental anguish or physical disease, nor any fear of enemies.
One who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth; one who seeks dharma shall attain dharma;
one who seeks pleasure shall obtain pleasure; and one who seeks liberation shall attain liberation.
The Brāhmaṇa shall be perfected in the Vedas, the Kṣatriya shall be victorious, the Vaiśya shall be rich in wealth and grain, and the Śūdra shall possess abundant happiness. || 59 ||
The man who, being self-restrained, recites this hymn at the time of a śrāddha ceremony,
brings about inexhaustible satisfaction for his ancestors that lasts for an entire kalpa.
Thus has the propitiation of the Goddess, honored by the gods, been fully described;
the man who performs it with devotion shall become a partaker of the world of the Goddess. (61)
O Brahmin, through the worship of the Goddess, all desires are indeed fulfilled;
there is the destruction of all sins, and at the end, a pure intellect arises.
O Virañci, by the grace of the Mother of the World, one becomes worthy of worship and honor wherever one may be, and esteemed among those for whom honor is their wealth. 63.
By the grace of Mahāmāyā, he shall have no fear of the hells anywhere, even in his dreams; indeed, his sons, grandsons, and lineage shall increase.
One certainly becomes a devotee of the Goddess; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Thus has the characteristic of liberation from hell been fully explained to you. (65)
Indeed, the worship of the Great Goddess bestows all auspiciousness;
likewise, O Sage, is the worship with Madhūka flowers performed in the sequence of the months. (66)
O sinless one, for him who performs the entire worship known as Madhuka, no fear of affliction by disease or other such calamities shall arise.
Now I shall also describe another supreme pentad of Prakṛti, which by its name, form, and origin bestows bliss upon the world. (68)
O Sage, listen to the detailed account of the greatness of the fivefold primordial nature (prakṛti), which is indeed fascinating and bestows liberation. 69.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Worship of the Goddess," in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 24 ||
Description of the Conduct of the Original Nature.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Gaṇeśa’s mother, Durgā, Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī—
And Sāvitrī is remembered as the fivefold primordial nature (prakṛti) in the process of creation. || 1 ||
Nārada said: By whom did she manifest, and who was she, O best among the wise? What were her characteristics, O virtuous one, and how did she become fivefold?
The conduct of all [these goddesses], the procedure for their worship, their desired qualities, and the descent of each—where and whose [is it]? You should explain these to me. (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O child, who indeed would be capable of describing the characteristics of Prakṛti?
Nevertheless, I shall say something as it was heard from the mouth of Dharma.
The word *pra* denotes excellence, and the suffix *kṛti* denotes creation;
that Goddess who is the most excellent within creation is proclaimed as *Prakṛti*.
The prefix *pra-* is known to denote excellence when applied to the quality of *sattva*;
*kṛ-* is used for the intermediate *rajas*, and *ti-* is traditionally taught for *tamas*.
She whose essential nature consists of the three qualities (guṇas) and who is endowed with power (śakti),
is called Prakṛti because she is the primary cause of creation.
The first [syllable] is the letter *pra*, which signifies creation;
and that Goddess who exists at the beginning of creation is proclaimed as *Prakṛti*.
Through yoga, in the process of creation, he became twofold in form:
the male is known as the right half-body, and the female nature is the left half.
She is of the nature of Brahman, eternal, and everlasting;
as is the Self, so is Śakti, just as the power of burning resides within fire.
For this very reason, O Nārada, the lords of yogis do not perceive a distinction between female and male; for everything is composed of Brahman, O Brahmin, and Brahman is eternally the Real.
And by the will of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who consists of His own free will, that Sovereign Root-Nature suddenly manifested out of His desire to create. (12)
By His command, she is fivefold, distinguished by her creative functions; or else, she assumes forms out of compassion for her devotees to bestow grace upon them.
She who is Gaṇeśa’s mother, Durgā, whose form is Śiva and who is dear to Śiva;
she is Nārāyaṇī, the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, and her essential nature is the perfect Brahman. || 14 ||
Worshipped and praised by Brahmā and the other gods, by sages, and by Manus, she is the eternal Goddess who presides over all and whose form is the night. 15.

She who bestows the merit and fame of the truth of Dharma, she who grants auspiciousness, glory, and joy, she who bestows happiness, liberation, and delight, and she who destroys grief, affliction, and suffering. (16)
She is solely devoted to protecting those who have come for refuge and those who are miserable and distressed;
she is the supreme deity presiding over that [power], whose very nature is splendor.
The power of the Lord is eternally of the nature of all powers;
she is Siddheśvarī, the form of accomplishment, the bestower of accomplishment, accomplishment itself, and the sovereign lady.
Intellect, sleep, hunger, thirst, shadow, lassitude, compassion, memory, birth, forbearance, delusion, peace, beauty, and consciousness; || 19 ||
Contentment, nourishment, as well as fortune, fortitude, and likewise illusion—she is the embodiment of all powers belonging to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self. (20)
The merit of hearing [the scripture] has been described in the Śruti as being exceedingly small according to tradition;
however, the merit of [hearing] Anantā is infinite—now listen to that of Aparā as well. || 21 ||
Padmā, whose nature is that of pure being, belongs to the Supreme Self;
she is the embodiment of all prosperity and the presiding deity thereof.
She is beloved, exceedingly self-controlled, peaceful, virtuous, and the source of all auspiciousness;
she is devoid of greed, delusion, desire, anger, pride, and egoism.
Devoted and deeply attached to her husband, she was a chaste wife to all;
equal to the Lord’s own life-breath, she was the object of his love and spoke with sweet words.
The goddess who is the essence of all crops and the very form of the means of livelihood is Mahālakṣmī; in Vaikuṇṭha, she is the virtuous lady devoted to the service of her husband.
In heaven there is the splendor of heaven, and among kings the splendor of royalty;
likewise, in the homes of mortal householders, there is the splendor of the home.
Among all living beings and objects, she is the form of beauty and the enchanting one;
among the meritorious, she is the form of fame; and among kings, she is the form of splendor.
She appears in the form of trade for merchants, she is the sprout of strife for sinners, and she is declared to be the embodiment of compassion; as taught in the Vedas, she is honored by all.
She is worthy of all worship and worthy of all salutation; hear now of another from me:
she is the presiding deity over speech, intellect, learning, and knowledge of the Supreme Self. (29)
She who is the embodiment of all sciences is the goddess Sarasvatī;
she is the intellect, poetic inspiration, wisdom, creative intuition, and the bestower of memory upon men.
The discernment of the meanings of the various distinctions among the different systems of tenets is considered to be the very nature of the awakening of exposition, which shatters all doubt. (31)
She is the one who brings about reflection, the author of the scriptures, and whose nature is Śakti;
she is the embodiment of the cause of the harmony, melody, rhythm, and tempo of the musical scale.
She whose form consists of objects, cognition, and speech, who is the sustainer of every universe, who brings about exposition and debate, who is peaceful, and who holds a lute and a book. (33)
She is of the nature of pure being, virtuous, and beloved by the illustrious Hari;
she resembles snow, sandalwood, the kunda flower, the moon, the water-lily, and the lotus.
They worship the Supreme Self, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, with a garland of jewels;
she is the very embodiment of austerity, the bestower of the fruits of austerities, and the refuge of ascetics. (35)
She is the very nature of perfected knowledge and is always the bestower of all accomplishments;
for without her, the multitude of Brahmins is forever mute, like one who is dead.
The third Goddess has been described as the Mother of the World (Jagadambikā), declared by the Vedas;
now learn from me something more of her, according to the scriptures and to the best of my ability. (37)
The mother was an expert in the four castes, the Vedāṅgas, the meters, the mantras for the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana), and the Tantras. || 38 ||

She is the form of the twice-born caste, she is the form of silent recitation, she is the ascetic woman; she is the form of devotion to Brahman and the splendor of Brahman, and she is the embodiment of all purificatory rites.
Sāvitrī, in her pure form as Gāyatrī, is dear to Brahmā;
even the sacred fords (tīrthas) long for contact with her for the sake of their own purification. (40)
Resembling pure crystal, she is the embodiment of pure being;
she is the form of supreme bliss, the highest, and eternal.
She is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, the bestower of the state of Nirvana, the Power consisting of the splendor of Brahman, and the presiding deity thereof. 42.
O Nārada, by the dust of whose feet the entire world is purified—that Goddess has been described as the fourth; now I shall describe the fifth to you. (43)
She who is the presiding deity of the five vital breaths, whose very nature is the five vital breaths, who is dearer than life itself, and who is the supreme beauty beyond all; (44)
She is endowed with all virtues, proud of her good fortune, and possessed of dignity;
she is the very form of half of his left side, equal to him in quality and splendor.
She is the highest and the lowest, the essence, the supreme and primordial, and eternal;
she is the embodiment of supreme bliss, auspicious, venerable, and worshiped. || 46 ||
She is the presiding goddess of the rāsa-sport of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul;
she is born from the rāsa-maṇḍala and is adorned by the rāsa-maṇḍala. || 47 ||
She is the Mistress of the Rāsa, the one who delights in the Rāsa, and she who dwells in the abode of the Rāsa;
she is the Goddess residing in Goloka, assuming the guise of a cowherd maiden. || 48 ||
She is the embodiment of supreme bliss, the form of contentment and joy;
she is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), formless, untainted, and the very nature of the Self.
Devoid of effort and devoid of ego, her form is for the grace of her devotees;
she is to be known by the wise through meditation in accordance with the Vedas. 50.
She was not seen by the lords of the gods nor by the foremost of sages;
she wore garments as pure as fire and was adorned with various ornaments. (51)

She possesses a radiance like ten million moons, a form endowed with all-nourishing splendor, and she holds in her single hand devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa and servitude, which are the source of all prosperity. 52.
And in the Vārāha incarnation, she who was the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu—by the touch of whose lotus feet the earth became purified. (53)
She who was unseen by Brahmā and all others, yet seen by everyone in Bhārata,
born from the essence of the jewels of women, now rests upon the chest of Kṛṣṇa.
Just as a flash of lightning flickers in a fresh cloud in the sky, O Sage,
so too was Brahmā tormented for sixty thousand years in the past.
Those who have not seen even in a dream the sight of the toenails of his lotus feet for the sake of their own purification— what then can be said of seeing him directly?
By that very asceticism, she was beheld on earth in the forest of Vṛndāvana;
she is declared to be the fifth goddess and is celebrated as Rādhā.
In every universe, all goddesses and all women are born as portions, as parts, and as sub-divisions of parts of Prakṛti. || 58 ||
The five most perfect knowledge-deities (vidyādevīs) have been proclaimed; listen as I describe those who are the forms of their primary portions. (59)
That Gaṅgā, the purifier of the world, is the very nature of the primary constituent;
she is born from the body of Viṣṇu, eternal, and of the nature of liquid.
She is like a blazing fire for the burning away of the sins of the wicked;
she is pleasant to the touch, and through bathing and drinking her waters, she bestows the state of liberation.
She is the form of the auspicious staircase for the journey to the abode of Goloka; she is the embodiment of purity, the supreme among all sacred fords and rivers.
She is the very form of a string of pearls from the Meru-like matted locks on the head of Śambhu;
she instantly bestows the fruits of asceticism upon the ascetics in Bhārata.
Resembling the moon, a lotus, and milk, she is the very embodiment of pure beings; stainless, free from ego, virtuous, and the beloved of Nārāyaṇa.
Tulasī, the beloved of Viṣṇu, is the very nature of the primary constituent;
she is the form of Viṣṇu’s ornament and is the virtuous one who dwells at Viṣṇu’s feet.
O Sage, she accomplishes the community of asceticism, resolve, worship, and so forth;
she is the essence of flowers, ever pure and bestowing merit.
Bestowing immediate liberation through both sight and touch,
she takes the form of fire in the Kali age to burn away the fuel of worldly impurities.
By the touch of whose lotus feet the earth was instantly purified,
and by the mere touch or sight of whom even sacred fords desire purification.
Without whom all actions among all beings are fruitless;
she who grants liberation to those seeking liberation, and who fulfills all desires for those possessed by desire. (69)
She who is the very embodiment of the wish-fulfilling tree, appearing in the form of a tree in Bhārata;
she who is the supreme deity born for the delight of the people of Bhārata. (70)
She who is the very embodiment of the primary constituent (pradhāna), the daughter of Kaśyapa conceived through his mind,
the beloved disciple of Śaṅkara, and highly proficient in supreme knowledge.
She is the sister of Ananta, the Lord of the Nāgas;
she is worshipped by the Nāgas, the Mistress of the Nāgas, the Mother of the Nāgas, the Beautiful One, and she who has the Nāgas as her vehicle. || 72 ||
Accompanied by hosts of serpent-kings, adorned with serpent ornaments, saluted by the lords of serpents, she is the perfected Yoginī who reclines upon the mountains. 73.
She is the form of Viṣṇu, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and wholly intent on the worship of Viṣṇu;
she is the very embodiment of austerity, the bestower of the fruits of austerities, and an ascetic woman.
Having performed divine ascetic penance for three hundred thousand years for the sake of Hari, she is worthy of worship among ascetics in Bhārata, both among female ascetics and male ascetics. (75)
She is the presiding deity of all mantras, blazing with the splendor of Brahman;
she is the supreme embodiment of Brahman, wholly intent on the contemplation of Brahman.
The wife of the sage Jaratkāru was a devoted wife to her husband, the portion of Kṛṣṇa,
and the mother of the sage Āstīka, the most eminent among ascetics.
O Nārada, that Devasenā, whose nature consists of the primary portion [of the goddess],
is the most worthy of worship among the Mātṛkās and is proclaimed as Ṣaṣṭhī.
The virtuous Dhātrī is the giver of sons, grandsons, and so forth to the three worlds;
because she is a sixth part of Prakṛti, she is celebrated as Ṣaṣṭhī.
It is fitting that this Yoginī, who possesses the form of an aged woman, is the supreme object of worship for children;
she whose worship is performed constantly throughout all twelve months by everyone. (80)
And formerly, in the lying-in chamber, worship was performed for the infant on the sixth day,
and likewise on the twenty-first day, as a cause for prosperity.
She is bowed to by the sages; therefore, she is the supreme, eternally desirable one.
She is Mātṛkā, the embodiment of compassion, who constantly provides protection. 82.
In water, on land, in the atmosphere, and within the dwellings of children,
the Goddess Maṅgalacaṇḍikā exists in the form of the primary constituent part.
Born from the mouth of Prakṛti, she is the perpetual bestower of all auspiciousness;
in creation she is the form of auspiciousness, and in dissolution she takes the form of wrath.
Therefore, she is celebrated by the wise as Maṅgalacaṇḍī,
worshipped on every Monday and at every cosmic dissolution (viśva).
Bestowing sons, grandsons, wealth, sovereignty, fame, and auspiciousness, she is well-pleased and grants all desires to all women. (86)
When enraged, the Great Goddess, whose nature is composed of the primary constituent (pradhāna), is capable of destroying the universe in an instant;
she is Kālī, the lotus-eyed one.
Born from the forehead of Durgā in the battle against Śumbha and Niśumbha,
she was the very embodiment of half of Durgā’s own portion, equal to her in virtue and splendor.
Her body is intensely radiant, nourished by the splendor of ten million suns;
she is the foremost of all powers, powerful and supreme.
The Goddess is the bestower of all perfections, the supreme embodiment of yoga;
she is devoted to Kṛṣṇa and equal to Kṛṣṇa in splendor, valor, and virtues. (90)
Constantly darkened by devotion to Kṛṣṇa, she is eternal;
she is capable of destroying the entire universe by her mere breath.
Her battle with the Daityas was like a sport, intended as instruction for the world;
she is capable of bestowing virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation, and is thus worshipped.
Praised by Brahmā and the others, as well as by sages, Manus, and men,
she is the Earth, whose essential nature consists of the primary constituents of primordial matter (prakṛti).
She is proclaimed as the support for all and the source of all crops;
she is the mine of jewels, the womb of jewels, and the foundation of all repositories of gems. (94)
She is always honored and saluted by both subjects and lords of subjects;
she is the form upon which all depend for their livelihood and the bestower of all prosperity. || 95 ||
Without her, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings would be without support;
O Lord of Sages, learn now which of these are the various parts (kalās) of Prakṛti. 96.
I shall describe to you all of whom their respective wives are;
the goddess Svāhā is the wife of Agni and is worshipped among the Viśvedevas. (97)
Without her, the gods are not able to accept the offering of oblations;
she is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the wife of the sacrifice, and initiation (dīkṣā), honored everywhere. (98)
For without her, all ritual action among all beings is indeed fruitless; she is Svadhā, the wife of the ancestors, [worshipped] by sages, Manus, and men. (99)
For without her, the ancestral gift (pitṛ-dāna) is indeed fruitless;
Svastidevī, the wife of Vāyu, is worshipped in every universe. 100.
She, without whom both taking and giving are fruitless, the consort of Gaṇapati, is worshipped upon the surface of the earth. (101)
Without her, both men and women are utterly ruined;
yet Anantapatnī Tuṣṭi, when worshipped and saluted, shall become [gracious]. (102)
Without whom all the worlds everywhere are not contented;
she is the prosperity that is the consort of Īśāna, worshipped by gods and men alike. (103)
All the worlds are impoverished without her;
she is Dhṛti, the wife of Kapila, who is worshipped by all everywhere. (104)
All the worlds are devoid of fortitude without her;
she is the true wife, Satī, worshipped by the liberated, and beloved by the world. 105.
Without her, the world would always be devoid of kinship;
she is the virtuous wife of Delusion, Compassion, who is honored and beloved by the universe. (106)
Without her, all worlds everywhere are fruitless;
she is the meritorious wife, the foundation, who, when worshipped, always bestows merit.
O Sage, without her the entire world is like one dead while living;
she is the perfected wife of virtuous action, Fame, who is honored by the blessed. (108)
Without her, the entire world is devoid of glory, like one who is dead;
she is indeed Action, the wife of Endeavor, honored and esteemed by all. (109)
O Nārada, without her the entire world would be devoid of order;
she is the wife of Adharma, she is falsehood, yet she is worshipped by all rogues.
Without whom the entire world, created by the Ordainer, would be destroyed;
she who was invisible in the Satya age and possessed a subtle form in the Tretā age.
In the Dvāpara age, she was manifested in the form of half-a-limb;
and in the Kali age, she is exceedingly bold and forcibly pervades everywhere.
He wanders from house to house together with his brother Deceit;
and Peace and Modesty are the two honored wives of Good Conduct. (113)
Without these two, O Nārada, the entire world is as if insane;
moreover, Jñāna has three wives: Buddhi, Medhā, and Dhṛti.
Without whom the entire world is always deluded, like one intoxicated;
she is his embodied consort of Dharma, lovely in form and captivating to the mind. (115)
The Supreme Self and the flood of the universe are without support without her;
she is Lakṣmī herself, the personified form of beauty, existing everywhere as a reality. (116)
She is Śrīrūpā and Mūrtirūpā, venerable, blessed, and most highly honored;
she is Kālāgnī, the consort of Rudra, Nidrā, and Siddhayoginī. (117)
By that yoga, all the worlds were enveloped during the nights;
for Time has three wives: the twilight, the night, and the days.
Without which even the Creator is unable to calculate their number;
hunger and thirst are the two wives of greed—fortunate, honorable, and worthy of worship. (119)
By these two the entire world is pervaded, and it would remain perpetually afflicted by anxiety;
likewise, Prabhā and Dāhikā are the two wives of Tejas.
Without these two, the Lord is indeed unable to create or ordain the world;
O daughters of Time, Death and Old Age, you are the beloved and the unloved of Fever. (121)
By these two, the world was completely destroyed; yet by the Creator, they were fashioned in the ritual act:
one was the maiden Nidrā (Sleep) and the other was Tandrā (Lassitude), while the other was Prīti (Affection), who is dear to happiness.
O son of Brahmā, by these two the entire world is pervaded;
Śraddhā and Bhakti are the two honored wives of Vairāgya, according to the ordinance of Brahmā.
O Sage, from these two [powers] the entire world constantly arises— that which is considered liberation while living (jīvanmukti)—
as well as Aditi, the mother of the gods, and Surabhi, the progenitor of cows.
Diti, the mother of the Daityas, Kadrū, Vinatā, and Danu—
these who were employed in the act of creation are thus celebrated as Kalās.
There are many other Kalās; among them, learn from me some:
Rohiṇī, the wife of Candra, and Saṃjñā, the beloved of Sūrya. || 126 ||
Śatarūpā was the wife of Manu, Śacī the consort of Indra, Tārā the wife of Bṛhaspati, and Arundhatī likewise the wife of Vasiṣṭha. (127)
Ahalyā was the wife of Gautama; Anasūyā was the beloved of Atri; Devahūti was the wife of Kardama; and Prasūti was the beloved of Dakṣa. || 128 ||
Menakā, the mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs and mother of Ambikā;
likewise Lopāmudrā, Kuntī, and Kubera’s beloved wife. || 129 ||
Varuṇānī is well-known, as is Vindhyāvalī of Bali;
likewise Kāntā, Damayantī, Yaśodā, and Devakī. || 130 ||
Gāndhārī, Draupadī, Śaibyā, and that beloved Satyavatī;
the virtuous wife of Vṛṣabhānu, the mother of Rādhā, the upholder of the lineage. 131.
Mandodarī, Kausalyā, Subhadrā, and likewise Kauravī;
Revatī, Satyabhāmā, Kālindī, and Lakṣmaṇā as well. || 132 ||
Jāmbavatī, the daughter of Nagnajit, Mitravindā, and another, Lakṣmaṇā, Rukmiṇī, and Sītā—she herself is proclaimed to be Lakṣmī. || 133 ||
Kālī, Yojanagandhā—the great chaste mother of Vyāsa—as well as Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa, and her friend Citralekhā. (134)
Prabhāvatī, Bhānumatī, as well as the virtuous Māyāvatī, Reṇukā the mother of Bhṛgu, and Rohiṇī the mother of Rāma. || 135 ||
And that Ekanandā Durgā is the virtuous sister of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, in Bhārata, there are many Satīs who are indeed portions of Prakṛti herself. (136)
Whosoever may be the village goddesses, they are all portions (kalās) of Prakṛti; in every universe, women have arisen from the further subdivisions of those portions. 137.
By insulting women, one brings about the humiliation of Nature (Prakṛti);
yet by him who honors a virtuous Brāhmaṇa woman who has a husband and sons, [Nature is honored]. || 138 ||
By him, Prakṛti was honored with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste;
and an eight-year-old maiden was likewise honored with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste. (139)
By him who has worshipped the Brahmin, his own primordial nature (prakṛti) has been worshipped;
for all things—whether superior, inferior, or middling—are produced from that primordial nature.

Those who possess a portion of *sattva* should be known as the most excellent—well-behaved and devoted to their husbands; those who possess a portion of *rajas* are declared to be of middling quality and are intended for enjoyment. (141)
They are intent on the enjoyment of pleasure and always devoted to their own interests;
they are of the lowest nature, portions of darkness, and born of unknown lineages. || 142 ||

Those who have foul mouths, those who ruin their families, rogues, those who act according to their own whims, and those who delight in quarreling—those who are unchaste women on earth and the hosts of Apsarases in heaven [are all of this nature]. (143)
The portions of Prakṛti and Tamas are proclaimed to be unchaste women;
thus has the entire description of the form of Prakṛti been narrated. (144)
All of them were worshipped on earth in the meritorious field of Bhārata;
first, Durgā, the destroyer of the suffering of distress, was worshipped by Suratha.
Thereafter, by Śrī Rāmacandra, who was desirous of slaying Rāvaṇa, the Mother of the Worlds was worshipped throughout the three realms. (146)
She who was born in the beginning as the daughter of Dakṣa, having slain the Daityas and Dānavas,
then cast off her body at the sacrifice due to the censure of her husband.
He was born from the wife of Himavat and obtained Paśupati as her husband;
Gaṇeśa himself is Kṛṣṇa, and Skanda is born from a portion of Viṣṇu.
O Nārada, those two sons were born to her later;
and Lakṣmī was first worshipped by King Maṅgala.
Thereafter, among the gods, sages, and humans in the three worlds,
Sāvitrī was first worshipped by Aśvapati.
Thereafter, in the three worlds, the goddess Sarasvatī was first worshipped by Brahmā along with the preeminent gods and sages. (151)
Thereafter, Rādhā was first worshipped in the three worlds by the gods and the foremost sages in Goloka, within the circle of the Rāsa dance. (152)
On the full moon day of Kārtika, [the Lord] was with the Supreme Soul Kṛṣṇa,
along with the gopīs, the cowherds, the young girls, and the boys.
Then, following the command of Hari, with herds of cows and Surabhi, as well as by the gods headed by Brahmā and the sages, [he was honored] with supreme joy. (154)
Always worshipped and saluted with devotion by means of flowers, incense, and other offerings,
the Goddess was first honored on earth by Suyajña himself.
In the holy land of Bhārata, as instructed by Śaṅkara, and subsequently in the three worlds by the command of the Supreme Self (Paramātman), [he established it]. || 156 ||
Always worshipped with devotion by sages with flowers, incense, and other offerings, whatever arts have arisen—those too are worshipped in Bhārata. (157)
O Sage, village deities are worshipped in villages and cities;
thus has the entire auspicious history of Prakṛti been told to you. (158)
According to the scriptures, what further characteristic do you wish to hear? || 159 ||
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Character of Prakṛti," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 1 ||
The description of the origin of the five primordial natures and their presiding groups.
Nārada said: "O Lord, I have heard the entire account of the goddesses in brief."
For the sake of awakening to enlightenment, you ought to speak at length.
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me how she, who is the primordial source of creation, manifested during the process of creation, and how she became fivefold.
By which portion of their respective parts they came into being in this world consisting of the three qualities;
I now desire to hear their life stories in detail.
O wise one, describe their accounts of birth, the ritual for worship and meditation,
their hymn of praise, armor, sovereignty, valor, and auspiciousness.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The Self is eternal, as are the sky, time, and the directions;
the sphere of all universes is eternal, and Goloka itself is eternal.
Vaikuṇṭha is a single portion of that [Brahman], following its bowed aspect;
likewise, Prakṛti is eternal, and the divine play (līlā) of Brahman is everlasting.
Just as burning power in fire, beauty in the moon, and radiance in the lotus and the sun are eternally conjoined and not distinct from them, so too is primordial nature (prakṛti) in the self (ātman).
Without gold, a goldsmith is unable to fashion earrings;
indeed, without clay, a potter is not capable of making a jar. (8)
For the Self is not capable of creating the creation without that [Śakti];
she is the embodiment of all powers, by whom He is always possessed of power.
The syllable *śa* signifies sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), as well as power (*śakti*) and valor (*parākrama*).
She who bestows those two, being their very essence, is proclaimed as *Śakti*. (10)
Knowledge, prosperity, wealth, fame, strength, and fortune—
by means of these she is the Empowered Goddess (Śakti), and she is eternally of the form of the Bhaga.
Endowed with that [power], the Blessed Lord is always called the Self (Ātman);
and that God consists of His own will, being both with form and without form.
Yogis always meditate upon the form of light as being formless;
they declare it to be the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of supreme bliss.
The Vaiṣṇavas do not acknowledge Him who is invisible, the seer of all, the omniscient, the cause of all, the giver of all, and the form of all.
And they say: "To whom does this splendor belong, apart from the Splendid One?
It is the Supreme Brahmā, the Splendid One, situated in the midst of the sphere of splendor. (15)
He whose form consists of his own will, who is the embodiment of all forms, the cause of all causes, bearing an exceedingly beautiful and most enchanting appearance.

He was of youthful age, tranquil, and the most beloved of all; he was the supreme beyond the supreme, a single embodiment of splendor with the luster of a fresh rain-cloud, possessing a dark-complexioned form.
His eyes dispel the beauty of a multitude of lotuses at midday in autumn;
he is enchanting with a row of teeth that puts to shame the pure luster of pearls.
He has a crest of peacock feathers and is adorned with garlands of jasmine;
he possesses a beautiful nose, smiles gently, is lovely to behold, and acts for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees.
He is beautifully adorned with a single yellow garment as pure as a blazing fire;
he has two arms, holds a flute in his hand, and is decorated with jewel ornaments. || 20 ||
The support of all, the Lord of all, endowed with all powers, the all-pervading, the bestower of all sovereignty, the independent one, and the source of all auspiciousness. || 21 ||
The Vaiṣṇavas constantly meditate upon the eternal God of gods, the most perfectly accomplished Siddha, the Lord of Siddhas, and the bestower of spiritual success.
The supreme remover of birth, death, old age, disease, grief, and fear,
whose single blink of an eye is reckoned as the entire lifespan of Brahmā.
That Self, which is the Supreme Brahman, is designated as Kṛṣṇa; the syllable *kṛṣi* signifies devotion to Him, and the syllable *na* signifies servitude to Him. (24)
He who bestows devotion and service is proclaimed as Kṛṣṇa;
the word *kṛṣi* signifies "all," and the letter *na* signifies "seed. (25)
That Lord Kṛṣṇa, the creator of all, being alone at the beginning and desiring to create,
was impelled by his own portion, Time (kāla), as he turned toward the act of creation.
Consisting of his own will, he became twofold by his own will;
the left half was in the form of a woman, and the right half is remembered as the male.
The eternal one, possessed of great desire, beheld her, the support of all desires, who was exceedingly beautiful and resembled a lovely lotus. (28)
To the Supreme Goddess, whose pair of hips surpasses the orb of the moon,
and whose beautiful buttocks put to shame the lovely trunk of a fine plantain tree.
Her pair of breasts was as beautiful as the form of a glorious *śrīphala* fruit;
she was graced with flowers, possessed of lovely curves, slender at the waist, and captivating to the mind. (30)
Exceedingly beautiful, peaceful, and smiling, with curved eyes,
she wore garments as pure as fire and was adorned with jewel ornaments.
She was constantly and joyfully drinking in with her eyes, which were like those of the cakora bird,
the moon-like face of Kṛṣṇa, which eclipsed ten million moons.
She bore a drop of musk together with a drop of sandalwood paste below it,
and likewise a drop of vermilion in the middle of her forehead.
She bore a curved mass of hair adorned with garlands of *mālatī* flowers and a necklace of the finest gems, appearing as a woman desirous of her beloved.
She was endowed with a radiant beauty polished and nourished by the light of ten million moons;
by her gait, she destroyed the pride of royal swans and elephants. (35)
Having seen her, the Lord of the Rāsa dance, delighting in the divine rasa, performed the rāsa-krīḍā with her in the circle of the rāsa during the rāsa-exultation.
Adorned with various kinds of amorous grace, like the god of love incarnate, he enjoyed the pleasures of union for as long as the day of Brahmā lasted.
Then, exhausted, the Father of the World discharged his seed into her womb during an auspicious moment of eternal bliss.
O observer of good vows, at the conclusion of the sexual union, perspiration born of fatigue issued from every limb of that exhausted woman due to the splendor of Hari. (39)
As she was distressed by her great strides, she began to pant;
then, all that sweat born of exhaustion became the entire cosmic egg.
And that breath-wind became the support of all;
the breath-wind [is the support] of all living beings in their various states of existence. (41)
From the left side of Vāyu’s embodied form, his beloved Prāṇa emerged;
she became his wife, and their sons were the five vital breaths (prāṇas) of living beings.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—these five vital breaths (prāṇas) indeed became his sons. || 43 ||
And from the heat-water (gharmatoya) there arose the great Varuṇa as its presiding deity;
and from his left side, his wife Varuṇānī came into being.
Then that power of Kṛṣṇa’s consciousness bore Kṛṣṇa as her embryo for the duration of a hundred manvantaras, blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
She is the presiding deity of Kṛṣṇa’s life-breath, dearer to him than his own life;
she is eternally the companion of Kṛṣṇa, residing upon the surface of Kṛṣṇa’s chest.
And when a period of one hundred Manvantaras had passed, Sundarī gave birth to a supreme infant, golden-hued and the abode of the support of the universe. 47.
Upon seeing the infant, the goddess was deeply pained at heart;
and in her wrath, she cast him into the waters within the sphere of the universe.
Seeing her abandonment, Kṛṣṇa raised a cry of "Alas! Alas!
and the Lord of Gods immediately cursed the Goddess as was fitting.
"Since you have abandoned your offspring, O you who are wrathful by nature and cruel, therefore, from this day forward, you shall certainly remain childless. (50)
Whichever celestial women shall become portions of your own form,
they shall all be childless, equal to you, and eternally youthful.
In that interval, a certain girl, white in complexion and enchanting, suddenly emerged from the tip of the Goddess’s tongue. 52.
Clad in white garments, holding a lute and a book,
she is richly adorned with jewel ornaments— the presiding deity of all scriptures.
Then, after some time, she indeed became twofold in form;
from her left half emerged Kamalā, and from her right half, Rādhikā.
In the meantime, Kṛṣṇa became divided into two forms:
his right half had two arms, and his left half had four arms.
Kṛṣṇa spoke these words to her: "Become his beloved;
here indeed shall be Rādhā, the proud one, and it will be well with you. (56)
Thus, being pleased, he bestowed Lakṣmī upon Nārāyaṇa;
and the Lord of the World departed for Vaikuṇṭha together with those two.
And although you were childless, two sons were born to you, born from a portion of Rādhā;
and from the body of Nārāyaṇa, the four-armed attendants (pārṣadas) came into being.
In splendor, age, beauty, and virtues, they were equal to Hari; and from the body of Kamalā, ten million maidservants were born who were likewise equal to her.
Then, O Sage, from the pores of the hair of the Lord of Goloka,
there emerged innumerable cowherds who were equal to him in age and splendor.
By virtue of their beauty, their qualities, their strength, and their prowess,
all the attendants of the Lord became as dear to him as his own life.
From the pores of Rādhā’s body, cowherd girls were born;
they were all equal to Rādhā, her maidservants, and sweet-spoken. 62.
Richly adorned with jewel ornaments and eternally possessed of stable youth,
they were all perpetually childless due to the curse of a man.
In the meantime, O Brahmin, the goddess Kṛṣṇā suddenly appeared—
she who is Durgā, the eternal Māyā of Viṣṇu.
The Goddess Nārāyaṇī-Īśānā, whose very nature is all powers, is the presiding deity of the intellect of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self. (65)

The Goddess is the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) in the form of the seed-syllables of the goddesses; she is the Sovereign, the most perfectly full, whose nature is splendor and who consists of the three qualities (triguṇa).
She has the luster of the color of molten gold, a radiance equal to ten million suns,
a face bright with a slight smile, and is endowed with a thousand arms.
Bearing a multitude of various weapons and missiles, that three-eyed goddess wore garments purified by fire and was adorned with jewel ornaments.
And from a minute fraction of a fraction of her portion all women came into being; and all the worlds situated within the universe are deluded by her illusory power (māyā).
She is the bestower of all sovereignty upon householders who possess desires,
and she is Vaiṣṇavī, the giver of devotion to Kṛṣṇa for the Vaiṣṇavas.
She is the bestower of liberation to those seeking release and the giver of happiness to the joyful; she is the Fortune of Heaven among heavens and the Fortune of the Home within homes.
She is asceticism among ascetics, and she is the embodiment of prosperity among kings;
she is the form of burning power in fire, and the form of radiance in the sun.
She is the form of beauty in the moon and she is beautiful in the lotuses;
she who is the very embodiment of all powers resides in Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self. (73)
By whom the self is empowered and by whom the world is empowered;
without whom the entire world remains as if dead while living. (74)
And that which is the eternal seed-form of the tree of saṃsāra,
O Nārada, exists in the form of its stability, its growth, and its fruit.

She takes the form of hunger, thirst, and so forth; of sleep, lassitude, patience, and intelligence; and she possesses the nature of tranquility, modesty, contentment, nourishment, delusion, splendor, and other such qualities. (76)
Having praised the Lord of All, she sat down before Him;
the Lord of Rādhikā then granted her a jeweled throne.
In the meantime, O great sage, the four-faced one, accompanied by his consort, emerged from the navel-lotus of Padmanābha.
Holding a water-pot, glorious, an ascetic and the best among the wise,
he, blazing with the splendor of Brahman, praised him with four mouths.
Then that Sundarī was created, possessing a radiance equal to a hundred moons,
wearing garments as pure as fire, and adorned with ornaments of precious gems.
Having praised the Cause of All on a beautiful jeweled throne,
she dwelt joyfully with her Lord before Kṛṣṇa.
In the meantime, Kṛṣṇa became twofold in form:
Mahādeva was the left half of his body, and the Lord of the Gopīs was on the right.
Resembling pure crystal, possessing the radiance of a hundred million suns,
bearing a trident and a sharp-edged spear, Hara is clothed in a tiger skin.
Resplendent with the color of molten gold, bearing a mass of matted locks,
his body adorned with ashes, he was the supreme one, smiling, with the moon as his crest-jewel.
Naked, blue-throated, and adorned with ornaments of serpents,
he held a well-refined garland of jewels in his right hand.
Muttering with the five-faced [mantra] the eternal light of Brahman—Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul and Lord, whose nature is truth. (86)
He is the cause of causes, the most auspicious of all auspicious things, and the supreme remover of birth, death, old age, disease, sorrow, and fear. (87)
Having praised that Death of death, by which he is named "Conqueror of Death," he sat upon a beautiful jeweled throne in front of Hari.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Five Primordial Natures and Their Consorts," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Origin of the Deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and Others.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Now, for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā lasted, that child remained within the water.
Then, in the course of time, he suddenly became split in two.
In their midst was a single infant, radiant as a hundred million suns,
crying out piteously for a moment, his lips swollen from nursing and tormented by hunger.
Abandoned by his father and mother, without refuge in the midst of the waters,
he who is the lord of countless universes looked upward like one who is helpless.
He is also the god Mahāvirāṭ, who is both gross and most subtle by name;
yet he is like an atom, being subtler than the subtle and grosser than the gross.
This [being] is a sixteenth part of the splendor of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self;
he is Mahāviṣṇu, the primordial support of all universes. ||5||
Within each and every pore of his skin, there are all things in their entirety;
even Kṛṣṇa is not capable of speaking their number.
If there were ever a number for all the dust particles in the universe, even then no such number exists for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others. (7)
In this manner, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others exist in every universe.
That which extends from the netherworld (pātāla) up to the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) is proclaimed as a single cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). ||8||
Above that, Vaikuṇṭha is indeed outside the cosmic egg;
and above that is Goloka, extending fifty crores of yojanas.
Just as Kṛṣṇa is eternal and of the nature of truth, so too is he;
the earth, measuring seven islands and joined by seven oceans, [is his]. (10)
It contains forty-nine subcontinents, along with innumerable mountains and forests;
above it are the seven heavenly worlds, including the realm of Brahmā.
The seven netherworlds (pātālas) below, as well as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and above the earth, the world of Bhūḥ (Bhūrloka) and beyond that the world of Bhuvaḥ (Bhuvarloka). ||12||
Beyond that is Svarloka, and Janaloka is beyond that;
beyond that is Tapoloka, and Satyaloka is beyond that. (13)
Beyond that is the world of Brahmā, resembling molten gold;
thus everything, both internal and external, is artificial.
O Nārada, when that [foundation] perishes, there is the destruction of all things;
the entire collection of the universe is impermanent, like bubbles upon the water. (15)
Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha are declared to be eternal and perpetually uncreated;
it is certain that within every single pore [of the body] resides a universe. 16.
Kṛṣṇa does not know their number, so what need be said of anyone else?
Within each individual universe, there are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others. (17)
O son, there are thirty million gods everywhere;
likewise, the lords of the quarters, the guardians of the directions, the lunar mansions, the planets, and so forth. ||18||
On earth there were the four castes, and below them the moving and unmoving beings, including the Nāgas;
then, at that time, Virāṭ looked upward again and again.
And amidst the other children, there was only emptiness and nothing else;
overcome by hunger, he fell into anxiety and wept again and again. (20)
Having attained that knowledge, he then meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person;
thereafter, right there, he beheld the eternal light of Brahman. ||21||
Dark as a fresh rain-cloud, with two arms and yellow garments, smiling, holding a flute in his hand, and eager to bestow grace upon his devotees. 22.
Just as the child laughed joyfully upon seeing his father, the Lord,
the Master of Boons then granted him a boon appropriate for the occasion.
"O child, remain until the time of dissolution, equal to me, endowed with knowledge, free from hunger, thirst, and other afflictions, and residing within the countless cosmic eggs."
Free from desire and free from fear, be the bestower of boons upon all;
be devoid of old age, death, disease, sorrow, affliction, and the like.
Having spoken thus, he whispered that supreme six-syllabled great mantra— the most excellent of the Vedāṅgas— into his ear three times.
The two syllables "Kṛṣṇa," preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ), ending in the dative case,
and followed by Vahni-jāyā (Svāhā), is the supreme desired mantra that removes all obstacles.
Having bestowed the mantra, the Lord then ordained that food;
listen to it, O son of Brahmā, and understand, for I shall tell it to you. 28.
Whatever food offering a Vaiṣṇava person offers to every universe,
a sixteenth part of that belongs to the worldly Viṣṇu who has five faces.
For the Self, which is devoid of qualities and most perfectly full,
there is indeed no purpose whatsoever in the food offering (naivedya) of Kṛṣṇa.
Whatever offering any person gives to that deity,
Lakṣmīnātha, the Virāṭ, likewise eats all of that.
Having bestowed that supreme mantra, the Lord spoke to him again:
"Tell me what other boon you desire; I shall grant it to you."
Having heard Kṛṣṇa’s words, the all-pervading Virāṭ spoke to him;
meanwhile, the boy [Kṛṣṇa] addressed those words to Kṛṣṇa that were appropriate for the occasion.
The boy said:
"May unwavering devotion to your lotus feet be my boon—constant throughout my entire life, whether it be for a moment or for a very long time. (34)
In this world, one endowed with devotion to you is eternally liberated while living;
but he who is devoid of devotion to you is a fool, for though living, he is indeed dead. (35)
Of what use is the muttering of mantras, austerity, sacrifice, worship, religious observances, fasting, merit, or visiting sacred fords? (36)
The life of a fool devoid of devotion to Kṛṣṇa is in vain;
for he does not even regard as his own self that very soul by which he lives. (37)
As long as the self remains in the body, it is endowed with power;
afterwards, when that [self] has departed, all powers become independent. ||38||
And you, O illustrious one, are the soul of all, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of your own will, the first of all, the eternal light of Brahman. ||39||
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, the boy fell silent there;
Kṛṣṇa then uttered a reply that was sweet and beautiful to the ear.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Remain very firm for a very long time; as I am, so shall you be.
Even when there is the fall of countless Brahmās, no fall shall befall you. (41)
In every individual universe, you shall become a minor Virāṭ by means of a portion;
and from the lotus of your navel, Brahmā, the creator of the universe, will come into being.
And upon the forehead of Brahmā, those eleven Rudras shall indeed come into being through a portion of Śiva for the purpose of creation and dissolution. 43.
Among them, Kālāgnirudra alone shall be the cause of the dissolution of the universe;
and Viṣṇu, as the enjoyer of objects, shall become a protector through a portion of Rudra (or a small portion). 44.
By my boon, you shall always be endowed with devotion to me;
through meditation, you will certainly behold me eternally as the most desirable one. 45.
Having said to his mother, who was beautiful and seated upon his chest, "I am going to the other world; stay here, my child," he vanished.
Having gone to his own world, he spoke to Brahmā and Śaṅkara—
that very moment— to the Creator who is capable of creating and indeed of destroying.
The Blessed Lord said: "Go, my child, to create the creation; become the one born from the navel-lotus.
O Brahmā, listen now to how you shall become the Great Virāṭ within the hair-pore of the Subtle One."
"Go, my child Mahādeva; become born from the forehead of Brahmā.
And with a portion of yourself, O illustrious one, perform penance for a very long time. 49.
Having spoken thus, O son of Brahmā, the Lord of the worlds ceased;
Brahmā and Śiva, the bestower of auspiciousness, bowed to him and departed. (50)
Within a single pore of the Great Virāṭ, in the cosmic egg amidst the waters,
there arose the minor Virāṭ, who is now present as a portion of the Virāṭ.
Dark-complexioned, youthful, and clad in yellow garments, Janārdana—the pervader of the universe—lies upon a bed of water with a slightly smiling and serene countenance. 52.
In that navel-lotus, Brahmā was born as the lotus-born;
having come forth, he wandered for a hundred thousand ages within the stalk of the lotus.

The lotus-born Brahmā could not reach the end of the stalk of the lotus that served as his staff, nor did he, your father, find the limit of the lotus born from his navel; thus he fell into deep reflection.
Having returned to his own place, he meditated upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa;
then, through meditation and with divine vision, he beheld that wretched man.
And he who lies upon a bed of water, submerged within the sphere of the universe—that universe which exists within every pore of his skin—is that Supreme Lord. (56)
Having praised Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who was accompanied by the cowherds and cowherdesses in Goloka, he obtained a boon from him and then brought about creation. ||57||
The mind-born sons of Brahmā, Sanaka and the others, came into being;
thereafter, the eleven portions of Rudra are also remembered as belonging to Śiva.
And Viṣṇu became the protector on the left side of the base one;
the four-armed Lord resided in Śvetadvīpa.
And from the navel-lotus of Kṣudra, Brahmā indeed created the universe—the three worlds consisting of heaven, the mortal realm, and the netherworld, along with all things mobile and immobile. ||60||
Thus, within every single pore, the entire universe exists individually;
and within each universe, there are the minor Virāṭs, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others.
Thus, O Brahmin, has the auspicious glorification of Kṛṣṇa been described; it bestows happiness and liberation, O Brahmin. What more do you wish to hear? 62.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and Others," in the ninth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Hymn, Worship, Armor (Kavaca), and other [rites] dedicated to Sarasvatī.
Nārada said:
"Everything [concerning her], which is like nectar, has previously been heard by me through your grace."
Now, describe the individual worship of the *prakṛtis* as well.
Whose worship was performed by whom, and how was it propagated among mortals?
By whom was which goddess worshipped, and by whom was which one praised, O Lord? (2)
You should explain to me their hymn of praise, their meditation, their power, and their auspicious conduct; by whom and to whom was the boon granted? || 3 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Gaṇeśa’s mother, Durgā, Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī,
as well as Sāvitrī— these five are remembered as Prakṛti in the process of creation.
The worship of these [goddesses] is well-known, and their power is most wonderful;
their conduct is like nectar and is the cause of all auspiciousness. || 5 ||
O Brahmin, I shall tell you everything regarding the portions of Prakṛti and those Kalās, as well as their auspicious deeds; listen attentively.
Kālī, Vasundharā, Gaṅgā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Maṅgalacaṇḍikā,
Tulasī, Manasā, Nidrā, Svadhā, Svāhā, and Dakṣiṇā.
I shall relate their beautiful and concise life stories, which bestow merit and are pleasant to hear, as well as the beautiful account of the ripening of their past actions.
The extensive and great life-story of both Durgā and Rādhā, I shall likewise relate later; listen as I speak it in brief. (9)
In the beginning, the worship of Sarasvatī was established by Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
by her grace, O best of sages, even a fool becomes a scholar. (10)
Just as the goddess had appeared from the mouth of the woman of Kṛṣṇa,
she, a lustful woman capable of assuming any form at will, desired Kṛṣṇa out of passion.
And he, the omniscient one, having understood her state, spoke to that mother of all these words which were beneficial, true, and bringing happiness in the end.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O virtuous lady, worship Nārāyaṇa, who is a portion of Me, four-armed,
youthful, beautiful, endowed with all virtues, and equal to Me."
He who understands the desires of women and fulfills their every wish,
whose beauty is like that of ten million Cupids, and who is the Lord adorned with grace.
"O beloved, if you wish to remain here after making me your lover, Rādhā is more powerful than you; no good will come to you. (15)
If one who is powerful is capable of protecting another from someone else, how can he subdue others if he himself is not master of his own fate? (16)
I am the Lord of all and the Teacher of all, yet I am unable to overcome Rādhā;
for she is equal to me in splendor, as well as in beauty and virtue.
She is the goddess presiding over the vital breaths; who is capable of abandoning those very breaths?
And who indeed has a son dearer than even his own life? 18.
"O blessed lady, go to Vaikuṇṭha; it shall be well with you.
Making that Lord your husband, rejoice in happiness for a very long time. (19)
Free from greed, delusion, lust, anger, pride, and violence,
Lakṣmī is equal to you in splendor, beauty, and virtue.
In her company, your time will pass eternally in joy;
and Hari will accord equal honor to both of you. (21)
O beautiful one, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, at the commencement of learning, one should offer that great worship, full of reverence, to each and every person.
Mānavas, Manus, gods, lords of sages, and those seeking liberation;
Vasus, yogins, Siddhas, Nāgas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas. || 23 ||
By my boon, they shall perform [this] in every kalpa until the end of the dissolution (laya),
being endowed with devotion and having indeed offered the sixteen types of ritual service (upacāra).

According to the ritual prescribed in the Kaṇva recension, those who have conquered their senses and are self-restrained should perform meditation and hymns of praise toward both the water-pot and the book.
Having fashioned a golden pill anointed with fragrant sandalwood,
they will take it as armor upon their necks or on their right arms.
"And the learned shall recite [this] at the time of worship when she has been worshipped.
Having said this, he worshipped that goddess who is worshipped by all. (27)
Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others performed that worship,
as did Ananta, Dharma, and the lords of sages such as Sanaka.
All the gods, sages, kings, humans, and others—Sarasvatī was constantly honored by all the worlds. (29)
Nārada said:
[I shall describe] the procedure for worship, the armor-mantra (kavaca), and constant meditation,
as well as the food offerings suitable for worship, the flowers, the sandalwood paste, and so forth.
Speak, O best among the knowers of the Vedas; a constant curiosity dwells within my heart to hear this which is so beautiful to the ear. (31)

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe the procedure for the worship of Sarasvatī, the Mother of the World, as set forth in the Kaṇva Śākhā, complete with the rules for her ritual adoration.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, or on the day of commencing one's studies,
having made a formal agreement on the preceding day, one should remain self-controlled and pure on that day.

Having bathed and performed the daily rites, one should devoutly establish the water-pot according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic branch or, alternatively, by means of the Tantric rite.
Having first worshipped Gaṇeśa, one should then worship one's chosen deity;
having meditated with the meditation that will be described hereafter, [one should worship] firmly in the external jar.
Having meditated thus, the observer of the vow should again worship with the sixteen types of offerings.
Whatever food offering has been employed in the worship, as prescribed by the Vedas— || 36 ||
O gentle one, I shall speak a little of that according to what has been studied and according to the tradition:
fresh butter, curd, milk, parched grain, and sesame balls. (37)
Sugarcane, sugarcane juice, white-colored [substances], the five types of molasses, honey, the svastika symbol, sugar, white grain, and unbroken rice grains. (38)
The sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) as prescribed consists of flattened rice from unbroken white grains, white sweetmeats, and clarified butter mixed with rock salt. (39)
A cake made from the flour of barley and wheat mixed with ghee, as well as a *svastika* cake and a ripe jackfruit cake; (40)
Excellent rice with ghee, sweet food like nectar, coconut and its water, kaseru, and fresh ginger. || 41 ||
A ripe mango fruit, a beautiful bilva fruit, and a jujube fruit—any lovely fruit produced in the proper season and place, white and well-prepared. (42)
Fragrant white flowers, fragrant white sandalwood, a new white garment, and a beautiful conch shell, O Sage. (43)
A garland of white flowers, a white necklace, and ornaments—whatever meditation is praised in the Vedas and is beautiful to the ear [should be employed]. (44)
Understand that, O highly fortunate one, which is the cause for shattering delusion:
Sarasvatī, white in color, smiling, and most enchanting. (45)
Her form is endowed with a splendor nourished by the light of ten million moons;
she wears garments of fire-purified silk and holds a lute and a book.
Adorned with nine ornaments fashioned from the finest essence of jewels,
she was well-worshipped by hosts of gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others.
"I bow with devotion to her who is worshipped by the lords of sages through prostrations";
having meditated thus and offered everything with the root mantra, the wise one [proceeds].
Having praised her and donned the armor, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff;
O Sage, this is the daily rite for those who hold her as their chosen deity.
At the commencement of learning and at the end of the year, for everyone on the fifth day, the root-mantra useful for all purposes is the supreme eight-syllabled Vedic mantra. (50)

For those for whom there is an instruction by means of a particular [mantra], that very [mantra] is their root; and Sarasvatī [should be placed] in the dative case, ending with the wife of Agni (svāhā). 51.
This mantra, which bestows prosperity, illusion, and all else, is a wish-fulfilling tree;
in ancient times, Nārāyaṇa, the ocean of compassion, bestowed it upon Vālmīki.
He gave it on the bank of the Jāhnavī at the holy site of Bhārata;
and Bhṛgu gave it to Śukra at Puṣkara during a solar eclipse.
On the occasion of the lunar festival (Candraparvan), Mārīca joyfully gave it to Vākpati;
and Brahmā, being pleased, gave it to Bhṛgu at the Badarikāśrama.
Jaratkāru gave it to Āstika near the Ocean of Milk;
Vibhāṇḍaka gave it to the wise Ṛṣyaśṛṅga on Mount Meru.
Śiva joyfully bestowed it upon the sage Kaṇāda and upon Gautama;
and Sūrya likewise [bestowed it] upon Yājñavalkya and Kātyāyana.
The remainder he gave to Pāṇini, to the wise Bhāradvāja, and to Śākaṭāyana in the assembly of Bali in Sutala.
By reciting the mantra four hundred thousand times, it becomes perfected for men;
indeed, if one has mastered the mantra, he becomes equal to Bṛhaspati.
O best of Brahmins, listen to the armor which was given of old by Brahmā,
the creator of the universe, to Bhṛgu for the conquest of the world on Mount Gandhamādana.
Bhṛgu said: O Brahman, best among the knowers of Brahman, expert in the knowledge of Brahman;
O omniscient one, progenitor of all, Lord of all, worshipped by all! (60)
O Lord, tell me the all-conquering armor-mantra of Sarasvatī,
which is the supreme collection of mantras that has never lost its potency.
Brahmā said:
Listen, my child, I shall proclaim this armor (kavaca) which grants all desires;
it is the essence of the Vedas, pleasing to the ears, declared by the Vedas, and honored by the Vedas.
It was spoken by Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Rāsa, the all-pervading Master, in the forest of Vṛndāvana at Goloka,
during the Rāsa dance within the circle of the Rāsa.
It is exceedingly secret, supreme, and equal to the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), endowed with a collection of mantras that are unheard of and marvelous. (64)
O Brahmin, by wearing which the blessed Śukra was honored among all the Daityas,
and by wearing and reciting which Bṛhaspati became wise.
By reciting or retaining it, the sage Vālmīki became eloquent and the lord of poets;
likewise, Svāyambhuva Manu, having held it, was honored by all. (66)
Kaṇāda, Gautama, Kaṇva, Pāṇini, and Śākaṭāyana—having taken up the work they composed, Dakṣa himself [revised it] as Kātyāyana. (67)
Having divided the Vedas and all the Purāṇas, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana himself performed this by mere sport. (68)
Having retained that which Śātātapa, Saṃvarta, Vasiṣṭha, and Parāśara [taught], Yājñavalkya composed this book through its recitation. (69)
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Bharadvāja, the believer Devala, Jaigīṣavya, and Yayāti—having maintained [their vows], they were honored everywhere. (70)
O best of Brahmins, for this armor-mantra (kavaca), Prajāpati himself is the seer (ṛṣi);
the meter (chandas) is Bṛhatī, and the deity is Śāradāmbikā. 71.
Its application is proclaimed to be in the thorough knowledge of all principles, in the accomplishment of all goals, and in all forms of poetic composition. || 72 ||
Śrīṃ Hrīṃ, svāhā to Sarasvatī; may she protect my head from all sides.
Śrīṃ, svāhā to the Goddess of Speech; may she protect my forehead at all times. (73)
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Sarasvatī—may this protect the ears continuously.
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the Blessed Lady Sarasvatī—may she always protect the pair of eyes. (74)
Aiṃ Hrīṃ, Svāhā to Vāgvādinī; may she always protect my nose. Hrīṃ, Svāhā to the Goddess who presides over Knowledge; may she always protect my lips. (75)
"Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ brāhmyai svāhā"—may this always protect my row of teeth. "Aiṃ," this one-syllable mantra, may it always protect my throat. (76)
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ! May she protect my neck; may śrīṃ always protect my shoulders.
Oṃ hrīṃ! To the Goddess who presides over knowledge, svāhā! May she always protect my chest. || 77 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to her whose nature is the sovereign of knowledge; may she protect my navel.
Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, svāhā to Vāṇī; may she always protect my hands. (78)
Oṃ, svāhā to the one whose essence consists of all castes; may she always protect the pair of feet.
Oṃ, svāhā to the goddess who presides over speech; may she always protect everything. (79)
Oṃ, svāhā to her who dwells in all throats; may she always protect [me] in the eastern direction.
Oṃ, svāhā to her who dwells on the tips of all tongues; may she protect [me] in the southeastern quarter. || 80 ||
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, svāhā to Sarasvatī, the mother of the wise;
may this king of mantras always protect me on the right. 81.
The three-syllabled mantra *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ* shall protect me always in the southwest (*nairṛtya*). *Oṃ aiṃ jihvāgravāsinyai svāhā* shall protect me in the west (*vāruṇa*). || 82 ||
Oṃ, svāhā to Sarvāmbikā; may she always protect me in the northwest.
Oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ klīṃ, svāhā to Gadyavāsinī; may she protect me in the north. (83)
Oṃ Aiṃ, svāhā to the one who dwells in all scriptures; may she always protect [me] in the northeast.
Oṃ Hrīṃ, svāhā to the one worshipped by all; may she always protect [me] from above. || 84 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to her who dwells in the book; may she always protect me from below. Oṃ, svāhā to her whose nature is the seed-syllables of the scriptures; may she protect me on all sides. (85)
Thus, O Brahmin, I have told you this armor named Viśvajaya, which embodies the multitude of Brahma-mantras and is the very form of Brahman. (86)
Formerly, this was heard from the mouth of Dharma on Mount Gandhamādana;
out of affection for you, I have related it, and it must not be told to anyone.
Having worshipped the guru according to the rules with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste,
and having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, the wise man should wear the armor.
By merely reciting it five hundred thousand times, the armor-mantra (kavaca) becomes perfected; if one possesses the perfected armor, he becomes equal to Bṛhaspati.
By the grace of this armor, one shall become a great orator, a lord of poets, and a conqueror of the three worlds;
indeed, one is able to conquer everything through the power of this armor.
O Sage, this armor (kavaca) spoken in the Kaṇva recension has been told;
now hear the hymn, the ritual for worship, the meditation, and the salutation. || 91 ||

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Hymn, Worship, Armor, and Other Rites of Sarasvatī," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Sarasvatī Hymn Composed by Yājñavalkya.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen to the hymn of the Goddess of Speech, which grants all desires."
By whom the great sage Yājñavalkya praised her in the past.
Due to the curse of his preceptor, that sage became one whose knowledge was destroyed;
then, afflicted by grief, he went to the place of the Sun, which bestows great merit.
Having reached Sūrya through his ascetic penance when Lolārka came within the range of his vision, he praised the Sun and wept again and again out of grief. || 3 ||
The Lord Sūrya taught him the Veda and the Vedāṅgas;
he said, "Praise the Goddess of Speech with devotion for the sake of memory."
Having spoken thus, that Lord of the Wretched vanished;
the sage, having bathed, offered praise with his neck bowed low in devotion.
Yājñavalkya said:
"O Mother of the World, have mercy on me, whose splendor has thus been destroyed;
who am distressed, deprived of memory due to my preceptor’s curse, and bereft of knowledge."
Grant me knowledge, memory, learning, and power that awakens the disciple;
grant me the power of composing treatises and a well-established, excellent disciple. (7)
Restore once more, through the power of destiny, all that has been lost: eloquence in the assembly of the virtuous and auspicious capacity for discernment. (8)
Just as a deity brings forth a sprout from ashes,
she who is the nature of Brahman, the supreme light, and eternal.
Salutations again and again to that Vāṇī, the presiding goddess of all vidyās,
who is the very foundation within the visarga, the bindu, and the mātrās.
Salutations again and again to that eternal Goddess who presides over it;
that Goddess is the very nature of exposition, having the form of the presiding deity of exposition. (11)
Salutations again and again to that Goddess, who is the very nature of the enumeration of time, without whom it is impossible for one possessing the power of calculation to perform any reckoning. 12.
Salutations again and again to that Goddess who is the form of the established conclusion regarding delusion;
she whose nature consists of the power of memory, the power of knowledge, and the power of intellect. 13.
Salutations again and again to that power of creative intuition and imagination,
by which Sanatkumāra indeed inquired about knowledge from Brahmā.
Even Vatsa became like one mute, unable to establish a final conclusion;
then the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Controller, arrived there. 15.
He said to her, "O Prajāpati, praise Vāṇī, who is dear to you";
and by the command of the Supreme Self, Brahmā praised her.
Then, by his grace, he established that supreme Siddhānta,
when Vasundharā questioned Ananta regarding the singular knowledge.
Then, though he was like one mute and unable to formulate a refutation,
he, being terrified, praised her at the command of Kaśyapa.
Then Vyāsa established a stainless philosophical system that dispels delusion; and when he questioned Vālmīki regarding the Purāṇas and the Sūtras, [Vālmīki] composed them. 19.
Having become silent, he remembered that very Mother of the World;
then, by her boon, the lord of sages established his final conclusion.
Having attained stainless knowledge, which is a lamp for destroying the blindness of delusion,
and having heard the Purāṇasūtra, Vyāsa, who was born from a portion of Kṛṣṇa, [composed it].
He knew and meditated upon that auspicious goddess for a hundred years at Puṣkara;
then, having obtained a boon from you, he indeed became a preeminent master of poetry.
Then he performed the division of the Vedas and composed the Purāṇa,
when Mahendra questioned Sadāśiva regarding the knowledge of reality.
Having reflected upon that very matter for a moment, the Lord bestowed knowledge upon him;
and Mahendra questioned Bṛhaspati regarding the science of grammar.
And for a thousand divine years he meditated upon you at Puṣkara;
then, having obtained a boon from you for a thousand divine years—
He spoke the science of grammar and its meaning to the Lord of the Gods;
and those disciples who were taught by him, and by whom it was studied, became lords among sages.
Reflecting upon her, they proceed toward the Queen of the Gods;
for you have been praised and worshipped by the lords of sages and by human beings. (27)
He was rendered motionless by the lords of the Daityas, as well as by the gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others; he who possessed a thousand faces, five faces, and four faces.
"What human being can praise with a single mouth her whom I myself am praising?
Having said this, Yājñavalkya, his neck bowed in devotion, [fell silent]. (29)
Fasting, he prostrated and wept again and again;
even though Mahāmāyā, whose form is light, was seen by him, she spoke to him.
Having said, "May you become the lord of great poets," he departed for Vaikuṇṭha.
Whoever recites this hymn to Vāṇī composed by Yājñavalkya— || 31 ||
That lord of poets, a great orator, would become equal to Bṛhaspati;
yet he becomes a great fool and dull-witted if he should study it for only one year. || 32 ||
He will certainly become a wise and intelligent master of poets. || 33 ||

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Hymn to Sarasvatī Composed by Yājñavalkya," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Descent of Lakṣmī, Gaṅgā, and Sarasvatī onto the Earth.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "Sarasvatī herself is present in Vaikuṇṭha in the proximity of Nārāyaṇa."
Due to the curse of Gaṅgā, she became a river in Bhārata through a quarrel with Kalā.
O Sage, this abode of the meritorious bestows merit, possesses the form of merit, and is the very embodiment of holy pilgrimage sites; it is to be resorted to by those who possess merit.
She is the very form of austerity for ascetics, the embodiment of the fruit of penance,
and she has the nature of a blazing fire for burning the fuel of committed sins.
Those men on earth who die in the waters of the Sarasvatī through [the power of] knowledge,
their abode shall be in Vaikuṇṭha for a very long time in the assembly of Hari.
Even one who has committed sins in Bhārata, by bathing there effortlessly, is liberated from all sins and shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu for a long time. || 5 ||
On the full moon day of the Cāturmāsya, on the Akṣaya day, at the end of the day,
during a Vyatīpāta yoga, during an eclipse, and on any other meritorious day as well.
Even one who has bathed incidentally, or for some specific reason, or even out of faith,
will certainly attain a form similar to that of Hari in Vaikuṇṭha.
Whoever recites the Sarasvatī-mantra there for one month shall become a lord among poets, even if previously a great fool; of this there is no doubt.
That man who constantly bathes in the waters of the Sarasvatī while shaving his head shall never again dwell within a womb.
Thus has been briefly told this praise of the qualities of Bhāratī, which bestows happiness, fulfills desires, and is essential; what more do you wish to hear?
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Nārāyaṇa, Nārada, the best of sages, again quickly asked this doubt, O Śaunaka. (11)
Nārada said: How did the goddess Sarasvatī, by the curse of Gaṅgā in Bhārata,
become a merit-bestowing river through her very portion and through strife?
My curiosity increases as I hear the essence of the sacred scriptures;
I am never satiated by the nectar of your stories—for who can ever be satiated with that which leads to the highest good? (13)
How did she curse Gaṅgā, who had honored Sarasvatī—she who is the very embodiment of goodness, the giver of merit, and always the bestower of auspiciousness? || 14 ||
