covering her face with her garment, she gazes at him again and again. (42)
And you too, having gazed upon her with desire, always smiled;
while I live in Goloka, such wicked conduct has occurred. (43)
And you yourself repeatedly commit such wicked deeds;
yet out of love, I grant forgiveness, for the female nature is tender-hearted. (44)
"Taking this beloved and cherished one with you, go from Goloka, O libertine!
Otherwise, O Lord of Vraja, no good shall befall you. (45)
I saw you joined with Virajā in the sandalwood grove;
alas, I previously offered my forgiveness only at the urging of my friends. (46)
Formerly, by the mere sound of my name, you caused her disappearance;
she abandoned her body and became the river Virajā. (47)
Extending for ten million yojanas and four times that in length,
that form of your excellent fame remains even today.
And when I had gone home, she went back to his presence and wept aloud, remembering him, "O Virajā! O Virajā! (59)
Then, rising from the water through her yoga, that perfected Yoginī appeared before you in embodied form, adorned with ornaments.
Then, having seized her, you performed the act of procreation;
from that, the seven oceans were produced within her.
You were seen by Śobhā in the campaka grove accompanied by Gopī;
yet, at the mere sound of my voice, you immediately vanished from sight.
Her beauty, having abandoned her body, went to the lunar orb;
thereafter, her body indeed became smooth radiance.
Having divided it, you gave with a grieving heart something to Ratna,
something to Svarṇa, and something to Maṇivara.
A little was taken from the lotus-faces of women, a little from the king, a little from the young shoots, and also a little from the flowers. || 55 ||
A small portion from the grains that have ripened over some time, and also something from the royal and divine dwellings, as well as something from consecrated [objects]. || 56 ||
From some fresh leaves and also from some milk,
you were seen in the forest of Vṛndāvana joined with a secret splendor.
Immediately upon the mere sound of my name, you vanished;
your radiance, abandoning the body, went into the solar orb. (58)
Then her body indeed became intense radiance, for it had been previously bestowed by you with love while you were weeping. (59)
O Kṛṣṇa, out of shame and fear of me, she cast a portion from her eyes into the fire, and another portion into the Yakṣas. (60)
A little from the lions among men, a little also from the gods;
a little from the followers of Viṣṇu, and a little also from the serpents. || 61 ||
Something to the Brahmins, to the sages, and to the ascetics;
something to women endowed with good fortune, and something to those who are illustrious. || 62 ||
Having given that to all, you wept first;
and you were seen in the circle of the rāsa-dance together with Śāntigopī.
In the spring, adorned with garlands and anointed with sandalwood paste, he [should dwell] upon a bed of flowers in a palace constructed of jewels, provided with jewel-lamps. (64)
O Lord, adorned with an abundance of jewel ornaments,
he formerly enjoyed the betel nut offered by her, who was likewise decorated with jewels.
O Lord, by the mere sound of my name, you have instantly performed a disappearance;
Śānti, abandoning her body, has merged into you out of fear. 66.
Then her body indeed became preeminent in its qualities,
for it had been distributed and given by you in the past with love while weeping.
O Lord, O All-pervading One, in ancient times, a portion [of you] was given to Brahmā in the forest, a portion to me,
and a portion to Lakṣmī, whose nature is pure being (śuddhasattva).
And give something to those who worship your mantra, as well as to the Śāktas; and something to the ascetics for the sake of dharma, and to the most virtuous. || 69 ||
Previously, you were seen by me together with Gopī Kṣamā,
well-attired, wearing a garland, and anointed with fragrant sandalwood paste.
Together with her, adorned with jewels and anointed with fragrant sandalwood,
he lay happily upon a couch smeared with flowers and sandalwood paste.
Embraced by me as I slept, you immediately experienced the pleasure of a new union;
I have now awakened her, so please remember this. (72)
He wears yellow garments and a captivating flute;
he also bears a forest garland, the Kaustubha jewel, and priceless jeweled earrings. (73)
O Lord, because you were given later out of affection and at the word of your friends, you have become dark-complexioned through that sin and shame. (74)
Kṣamā, having abandoned her body out of shame, went to the earth;
thereafter, her body indeed became the most excellent of qualities. (75)
Having divided it, you gave it away out of love while weeping;
furthermore, something was given to Viṣṇu and something to the devotees of Viṣṇu.
Something for those who are righteous and for the sake of Dharma; something for the weak;
something also for ascetics, for the gods, and for the wise. (77)
All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear? O Lord, I do not know your many virtues at all. (78)
Having spoken thus, Rādhā, whose eyes were like red lotuses,
began to speak to Gaṅgā, who stood with her face bowed down, feeling ashamed.
Having understood the secret through yoga, that perfected yoginī vanished from the midst of the assembly and entered her own waters.
Having realized through the yoga of Rādhā that she was present everywhere,
the perfected Yoginī began to drink from her mouthful.
Having realized the secret of the Gaṅgā through yoga, the perfected Yoginī entered and took refuge in the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. || 82 ||
In Goloka, in Vaikuṇṭha, and likewise in Brahmaloka and other realms, Rādhā saw her everywhere; yet she did not see the Gaṅgā at all.
Everywhere it was devoid of water, with dried-up mud and globes of earth,
and it was filled with multitudes of aquatic creatures and dead bodies.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Ananta, Dharma, Indra, the Moon, and the Sun; all the Manus and Munis, as well as the gods, Siddhas, and ascetics. || 85 ||
With their throats, lips, and palates parched, they arrived at Goloka;
all of them bowed down to Govinda, the Lord of all, who is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). 86.
To the one who is the boon, the most worthy of choice, the giver of boons, the most excellent, and the supreme cause;
to the Lord who is the foremost among all the cowherd women and cowherds.
It is effortless and formless, untainted and without support;
devoid of qualities, without exertion, changeless, and stainless. || 88 ||
He is composed of His own will, possessed of form, and the bestower of grace upon His devotees;
He is the very nature of pure being (sattva), the Lord of Truth, the eternal witness.
Having bowed down to the Supreme, the Lord of Lords, the Highest, the Supreme Self, and the Sovereign, they all offered praise with their necks bent low in devotion. (90)
With voices faltering, eyes filled with tears, and their bodies covered in horripilation,
they all offered hymns of praise to the Lord of All, the Supreme Blessed One.
The Supreme Brahman, consisting of light and the cause of all causes,
was seated upon a variegated lion-throne fashioned from priceless jewels.
And he was being served by cowherds with the breeze of white chowries,
looking with a joyful smile upon the dancing and singing of the cowherd girls.
He was seated upon the breast of Rādhā, who is dearer to Him than His own life;
He had consumed the fragrant betel-leaf offered by her.
The sages, Manus, Siddhas, ascetics, and practitioners of austerity beheld the Lord of the Gods in the Rāsa dance in His most perfect form.
With delighted minds, they all experienced supreme amazement;
looking at one another, they spoke to the Four-faced One.
Having reported his desired intention to the Lord of the World,
Brahmā, upon hearing those words, placed Viṣṇu to his own right side.
To his left was Vāmadeva, who approached the presence of Kṛṣṇa;
he was filled with supreme bliss, as was she whose form is supreme bliss. (98)
The Creator beheld everything in the circle of the Rāsa dance as being composed of Kṛṣṇa;
all were dressed in identical attire and seated upon identical seats. || 99 ||
Two-armed, with a flute in his hand, adorned with a forest garland, with a crest of peacock feathers, and resplendent with the Kaustubha gem. || 100 ||
Extremely desirable and beautiful, with a tranquil form, he was endowed with virtue, ornament, beauty, splendor, youth, and radiance. (101)
Seeing that everything was most perfectly complete and endowed with all sovereign powers, he was unable to describe what was the served and what was the server. 102.
For a moment he saw its nature as light, for a moment he saw its form situated therein, and for a moment he saw it as twofold—both formless and with form. (103)
At one moment Kṛṣṇa was entirely alone, separated from Rādhā;
and at that very same moment, he was seated upon each individual throne together with her.
Is the Creator unable to conceive of Kṛṣṇa bearing the form of Rādhā and Rādhā bearing the form of Kṛṣṇa as His consort—how can a man be in the form of a woman? 105.
Having meditated upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who resides within the lotus of the heart, with the eye of meditation,
he offered praise with devotion and performed various kinds of circumambulations.
Then, opening his own eyes and by His permission once again,
he beheld Kṛṣṇa alone, seated upon the breast of Rādhā.
Seeing the Supreme Lord surrounded by his own attendants and adorned by the circle of cowherd maidens, they bowed down again and offered hymns of praise.
Having understood their intention, the Lord of Rama—
who is the soul of all, the omniscient one, the Lord of all, and the creator of all beings— spoke to them.
The Blessed Lord said: "Come, O Brahman; may it be well with you. Come, O Lord of Kamalā. Come here, O Mahādeva; may there be eternal welfare for you all."
For the illustrious lady has indeed arrived for the purpose of leading the Gaṅgā;
and the Gaṅgā herself has sought refuge at his lotus-feet out of fear. (111)
"Seeing her desiring to drink me while she is in my presence, I shall give her to you; therefore, make her free from fear. (112)
Having heard the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the lotus-born Brahmā, smiling,
praised Rādhā, who is worthy of worship and honored by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having praised him with his four faces, the four-faced creator of the four Vedas, his neck bowed in devotion, spoke.
Caturānana said: "O Lord, the Gaṅgā was born from your body within the circle of the Rāsa dance;
she emerged in liquid form from the two of you, the charming ones, at the sound of Śaṅkara. (115)
Kṛṣṇāṃśā, who is a portion of you and dear like your own daughter, having received your mantra, may she perform your worship. (116)
The four-armed Lord of Vaikuṇṭha shall become her husband;
and by a portion of her remaining on earth, the salt ocean shall be her husband. (1.7)
O Ambikā, that Gaṅgā who resides in Goloka likewise resides everywhere;
you are that Ambikā, O Queen of the Gods, and she is always your own daughter.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, she accepted them with a smile;
she emerged from the tip of the nail of Kṛṣṇa’s big toe.
Right there, honored and serene, she stood in their midst;
the presiding deity of that water rose from the water and took her seat.
Then, having placed a portion of that water in his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), Brahmā bore it upon his head,
adorned with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
The Lotus-born [Brahmā] bestowed the mantra of Rādhikā upon Gaṅgā,
as well as her hymn of praise, armor, ritual worship, procedure, and meditation.
Having likewise performed the entire sequence of preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) as prescribed in the *Sāmaveda*,
Gaṅgā worshipped that very [deity] and departed for Vaikuṇṭha.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā, and Tulasī, the purifier of the universe—
O Sage, these four are indeed the consorts of Nārāyaṇa.
Then, with a smile, Kṛṣṇa spoke to that Brahmā concerning the events of all time, which are difficult for the unwise to comprehend.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Brahmā, O Viṣṇu, O Maheśvara, receive the Gaṅgā!
Listen to the account of Time from me; O Brahmā, pay close attention. (126)
And you, as well as the other gods, sages, and Manus, and those illustrious Siddhas who have assembled here; || 127 ||
These live in Goloka, which is devoid of the wheel of time;
now, at the end of the kalpa, the entire universe has been submerged in water. 128.
O Lotus-born One, Brahmā and all others who reside in other worlds have now dissolved into me; everything except Vaikuṇṭha is submerged in water.
"Go and create once more the world of existence, beginning with the realm of Brahmā;
fashion your own cosmic egg, and afterwards Gaṅgā shall proceed. (130)
"In this manner, I shall again perform the creation of Brahmā and the others among all other universes; go quickly now along with the gods. (131)
A great deal of time has passed for you four-faced ones;
how many kinds of those creators have already gone, and how many will yet come to be? (132)
Having spoken thus, O sage, the Lord of Rādhikā went to the inner apartments;
the gods, having returned, diligently resumed the act of creation.
The Gaṅgā resides in Goloka, in Vaikuṇṭha, and in the world of Śiva;
she is situated elsewhere in the world of Brahmā, and wherever her city stands before me.
The Gaṅgā went to that very place by the command of the Supreme Self;
she emerged from the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu, and for that reason she is remembered as Viṣṇupadī.
Thus, O Brahmin, has this excellent narrative of the Gaṅgā been told—granting happiness, granting liberation, and being the very essence. What more do you wish to hear? (136)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Legend of Gaṅgā," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 13.
The Description of Gaṅgā as the Wife of Kṛṣṇa.
Nārada said:
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā, and Tulasī are the purifiers of the universe.
These four are indeed the beloved wives of Nārāyaṇa alone. || 1 ||
I have heard that Gaṅgā went to Vaikuṇṭha;
however, I have not heard how she became his wife. || 2 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
After her, Gaṅgā went to Vaikuṇṭha, and following her, the Creator of the worlds went as well;
having arrived, he bowed along with her and spoke to the Lord of the Universe.
Brahmā said:
That goddess who was produced from the bodies of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, who is liquid in form,
endowed with fresh youth, virtuous, beautiful, and excellent— (4)
She is the very nature of pure being, free from anger and ego;
born from his body, she chooses no other than him, nor does he choose anyone but her.
There, Rādhā, who is exceedingly proud, radiant, and excellent, has intentionally exerted herself to protect her, for she is afraid. (6)
He entered the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul;
having seen the entire Goloka dried up, I then departed.
In Goloka, where Kṛṣṇa resides, he—the inner self of all—having understood the intentions of everyone, [is present] for the sake of obtaining knowledge of all occurrences. || 8 ||
And Gaṅgā brought her forth from the tip of the nail of his big toe;
having bestowed upon her the mantra of Rādhikā and having filled Goloka, he released her.
Having bowed to that Lord of Rādhā and taken her here, O Lord,
accept this Queen of the Gods through the Gāndharva form of marriage.
This connoisseur of love has come to you, a connoisseur among the lords of gods;
O Lord of Gods, you are the jewel among men, and this virtuous woman is the jewel among women.
The union of the wise with the wise is virtuous;
yet that man who does not accept a maiden who has come to him of her own accord in this world [is devoid of merit]. (12)
Leaving him, Mahālakṣmī departs in anger; of this there is no doubt.
Even he who is a scholar does not despise Prakṛti. (13)
All men are products of primordial nature (prakṛti), and all women are portions of that nature;
you alone are the Blessed Lord, the Master, devoid of qualities and transcendent to primordial nature.
In ancient times, Rādhikā came into being from the left half of Kṛṣṇa’s body; Kṛṣṇa, who was two-armed, became four-armed by means of that half-body. 15.
He himself is the right side and she is the left side, as is Kamalā;
therefore, she indeed chooses you, since she was born from your own body.
"Just as Prakṛti and Puruṣa are a single part of both female and male," having spoken thus, the Creator handed her over to him and departed. (17)
Nārāyaṇa himself took her hand, which was anointed with flowers and sandalwood paste, and married her according to the Gāndharva rite. 18.
There the Lord of Ramā rejoiced with joy together with Gaṅgā;
that Gaṅgā who had gone to the earth returned once more to her own abode. (19)
Because she emerged from the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu, she is called Viṣṇupadī;
and that goddess attained a state of rapture through the play of her first union.
The passionate Vāṇī, though united with the Lord of Passionate Ones through the enjoyment of bliss, became sorrowful upon seeing her [Sarasvatī], even though she herself was not abandoned by Padmā.
The Gaṅgā, the beloved of Hari, was constantly jealous of Sarasvatī; she did not favor Sarasvatī as much as the Gaṅgā, and thus, out of anger, she cursed her in Bhārata.
O sage, that Lord of Ramā had three wives along with Gaṅgā; later, there were four including Tulasī.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Gaṅgā’s Status as Kṛṣṇa’s Wife," in the ninth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
In the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada, regarding the manifestation of Śakti,
Nārada said:
"How did that virtuous beloved of Nārāyaṇa come to be?"
Where was Tulasī born, and who was she in her previous birth? (1)
In whose family was she born, and as whose daughter did she exist in that noble lineage? By what ascetic practice did she attain that which is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti)? || 2 ||
Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Brahman, the Lord of lords, who is changeless, devoid of desire, and the very nature of the entire universe. || 3 ||
He who is to be propitiated by all, the Lord of all, the omniscient, the cause of all, the support of all, the embodiment of all, and the protector of all. || 4 ||
How did such a goddess come to attain the state of a tree?
And how did that ascetic woman become seized by an asura?
My mind is very tender and fickle, urging me on again and again;
O destroyer of all doubt, you ought to sever my uncertainty entirely.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
And Dakṣasāvarṇi Manu was indeed meritorious, a Vaiṣṇava, and pure;
he was illustrious and renowned, born from a portion of Viṣṇu.
His son was Brahmasāvarṇi, most righteous, a Vaiṣṇava, and pure;
his son was Dharmasāvarṇi, a Vaiṣṇava who had conquered his senses.
His son was Rudrasāvarṇi, who was devoted and had conquered his senses;
his son was Devasāvarṇi, who was dedicated to the vows of Viṣṇu.
His son was Indrasāvarṇi, who was devoted to Mahāviṣṇu;
and his son was Vṛṣadhvaja, who was devoted to Vṛṣadhvaja. (Variant reading:
Vṛkṣadhvaja) In whose hermitage Śambhu himself remained for three divine ages.
And Śiva’s affection for that king was even greater than for his own son.
He no longer regarded Nārāyaṇa, nor Lakṣmī, nor Sarasvatī;
he cast far away all worship of the gods.
In the month of Bhādrapada, he indeed destroyed the worship of Mahālakṣmī from me;
likewise, on the fifth day of the month of Māgha, it was forgotten by all the deities.
That wicked man performed the worship of Sarasvatī while remaining far removed from Viṣṇu; and Divākara [reproached] him who was censuring sacrifice and the worship of Viṣṇu.
The god became enraged and cursed the lord of the earth for the sake of Śiva;
Divākara cursed him, saying, "May you be deprived of your fortune. || 15 ||
Taking up his trident, Śaṅkara himself rushed toward that Sūrya;
and the Lord of Day, together with his father, went to Brahmā for refuge. (16)
Śiva, with the trident in his hand, went to the world of Brahmā in anger;
Brahmā, placing Sūrya at his head, went to Vaikuṇṭha out of fear.
Brahmā, Kaśyapa, and Mārtaṇḍa, terrified and with parched throats,
all went for refuge out of fear to Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of All.
Having approached, they prostrated themselves and praised him again and again;
they reported everything regarding the cause of their fear toward Hari.
And Nārāyaṇa, out of compassion, granted them freedom from fear, saying:
"Be steadfast, O frightened ones; what cause for fear is there while I am present? (20)
Whosoever, filled with fear in times of calamity, remembers me anywhere at all,
I go there and protect them with haste, discus in hand.
O gods, I am the protector of the worlds, and I am eternally and always their creator;
I am the creator in the form of Brahmā and the destroyer in the form of Śiva.
I am Śiva, you are I, and I am also the Sun, consisting of the three qualities;
having assumed various forms, I perform the creation and preservation [of the world]. (23)
"Go, may it be well with you; whence shall there be fear?
From this day forward, by my boon, you shall have no fear of Śaṅkara."
That Blessed Lord Śaṅkara is indeed the lord of all;
he is the protector of the virtuous, dependent upon his devotees, the very soul of his devotees, and affectionate toward his devotees.
Sudarśana and Śiva are indeed dearer to me than my own life;
O Brahman, there is no one more radiant in the cosmic eggs than these two.
The Great Lord Mahādeva is capable of effortlessly creating ten million suns and even ten million Brahmās; indeed, there is nothing that is impossible for the Lord who wields the trident.
Thinking of no external object whatsoever, day and night he meditates upon me;
with devotion, he sings my mantras and my qualities with his five mouths. (28)
I think thus day and night regarding that auspicious truth:
"In whatever way people approach me, in that very same way do I reward them. (29)
The Blessed One is of the nature of Śiva and is the presiding deity of Śiva;
because auspiciousness (śiva) arises from him, the wise know him as Śiva.
In the meantime, Śaṅkara arrived there and stood present, holding a trident in his hand, mounted upon his bull, with eyes like red lotuses. || 31 ||
Quickly descending from his bull, with his neck bowed low in devotion,
he prostrated with devotion before that peaceful one, the beloved of Lakṣmī, who is higher than the highest.
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, adorned with jewel ornaments,
wearing a crown and earrings, holding a discus, and garlanded with forest flowers.
Dark as a fresh rain-cloud, beautiful, and four-armed,
he was served by four-armed attendants with the breeze of white chowries.
O Nārada, his entire body was anointed with sandalwood paste, he was adorned and dressed in yellow garments, and he had just consumed betel-leaf offered by Lakṣmī.
He always gazes with a smile upon the dance and song of the Vidyādharīs;
he is the Lord, the Supreme Self, whose very form is the grace bestowed upon his devotees. (36)
Mahādeva bowed to him, and he too was saluted by Brahmā;
and Sūrya, trembling with devotion, bowed to the moon-crested Lord.
And Kaśyapa, with great devotion, offered praise and bowed down;
having thus praised the Lord of All, Śiva sat upon a comfortable seat.
Candraśekhara was seated comfortably on a pleasant throne, at ease,
being served by the attendants of Viṣṇu with the breeze of white chowries.
Viṣṇu spoke words as sweet as nectar, most enchanting:
"How have you come here? Tell me the cause of your anger. (40)
Mahādeva said:
"The Sun cursed my devotee Vṛṣadhvaja, who is dearer to me than my own life; this is the cause of my great anger."
Out of grief for his beloved son, he was prepared to destroy the sun;
he sought refuge with Brahmā, and that sun is now under your command.
Those who have taken refuge in you, whether by meditation or even by word alone, are free from calamity and fear; by them, old age and death have been conquered.
They have directly taken refuge; O sirs, what need is there to speak of its fruit?
The remembrance of Hari always bestows fearlessness and grants all auspiciousness.
"O Lord of the World, tell me what will become of me, your devotee, now that this fool has been slain by Śrī on account of the Sun's curse? (45)
Viṣṇu said:
Twenty-one yugas have passed by divine reckoning.
Go quickly to your abode in Vaikuṇṭha within half a ghaṭikā.
Vṛṣadhvaja died from time, which is most terrible and unavoidable;
and his son Rathadhvaja also died, struck down by misfortune.
And his two highly fortunate sons, Dharmadhvaja and Kuśadhvaja,
having been robbed of their prosperity by the curse of Sūrya, are remembered as supreme Vaiṣṇavas.
Deprived of their kingdom and deprived of their fortune, the two of them will devote themselves to the heat of the sun; and Lakṣmī shall become the wife of those two, along with Kalā.
Then those two best of kings will become endowed with prosperity;
O Śambhu, your servant is dead, so you may go and they too may go.
Having spoken thus, he who was accompanied by Lakṣmī entered the interior from the assembly hall;
the gods, greatly delighted, went to their own hermitages with supreme joy,
and Śiva, the most perfect one, departed quickly for his ascetic penance.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Śakti," in the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada within the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 15.
The description of the birth of Mahālakṣmī in the form of Vedavatī at Rājagṛha.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Sage, having propitiated Lakṣmī and those two [Brahmā and Viṣṇu] through fierce austerity...
And each obtained their own desired boon, exactly as they had wished.
By the grace of Mahālakṣmī herself, those two became lords of the earth—
Puṇyavanta and Putravanta— known as Dharmadhvaja and Kuśadhvaja.
And the virtuous Queen Mālavatī, the wife of Kuśadhvaja,
in due time gave birth to a daughter, a chaste girl who was a portion of Kamalā.
After a great length of time, she became endowed with knowledge;
having clearly uttered the sound of the Vedas, she rose from the lying-in chamber.
As soon as she was born, that girl uttered the sound of the Vedas;
therefore, the wise call her Vedavatī.
As soon as she was born, having bathed well, she went to the forest for asceticism; though restrained with great effort by everyone, she remained devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
And for the duration of one Manvantara, that ascetic woman performed most intense penance at Puṣkara with ease.
Nevertheless, she— well-nourished, unafflicted, and endowed with fresh youth—
suddenly heard a beautiful, incorporeal voice.
And in another birth, Hari himself shall become your husband;
O beautiful one, you shall obtain as your lord one who is difficult even for Brahmā and the other gods to propitiate.
Having heard this, she was delighted and once again performed austerities in an exceedingly secluded place on Mount Gandhamādana.
Having performed penance there for a very long time, she dwelt there with the entire universe;
then she beheld before her the irresistible Rāvaṇa.
Having seen him, and out of devotion to hospitality, she indeed offered him water for his feet,
as well as very delicious fruit and also very cool water.
Having eaten that, the most wicked man dwelt near her and asked this question: "Who are you, O auspicious lady, and why do you stay here? (13)
Having seen that virtuous woman of excellent hips, with full hips and breasts, her face like a festival of autumn lotuses, smiling and possessing beautiful teeth; 14.
Afflicted by the arrows of desire, the wretched man fell into a swoon;
then, drawing her toward him with his hand, he prepared to engage in amorous dalliance.
Seeing him, Satī became enraged and rendered him paralyzed;
he became motionless, unable even to speak with his hands and feet. || 16 ||
He praised the lotus-eyed goddess in his mind and approached her;
she, being pleased by his hymn of praise, performed a virtuous deed for him.
"She cursed me, saying: 'On my account, you shall perish along with your kinsmen;
for I have been touched by you out of lust, so behold now my power. (18)
Having spoken thus, she indeed abandoned her body through yoga;
and having cast her into the Gaṅgā, Rāvaṇa went to his own home.
"Aha! What wonder has been seen, or what has been done by her now?"—thinking thus again and again, he lamented repeatedly.
And in the course of time, that virtuous woman became the daughter of Janaka,
renowned as Queen Sītā, for whose sake Rāvaṇa was slain.
And she, a great ascetic through her penance from a previous birth,
obtained Rāma, the most perfect Hari, as her husband.
Having propitiated the Lord of the Universe, who is difficult to propitiate, through her ascetic penance,
that beautiful Ramā attained him and sported with Rāma for a very long time.
Remembering her former births, she did not recall the exhaustion of her past asceticism;
she easily abandoned all that suffering, as well as the pleasure found in its fruit.
Having obtained that delicate youth, the virtuous woman, herself in the full bloom of fresh adolescence, engaged in various kinds of amorous diversions for a very long time.
He obtained one who was virtuous, connoisseur of aesthetic flavor, tranquil, handsome, and unsurpassed among gods; one who was charming to women, beautiful, and exactly as desired. || 26 ||
To fulfill his father’s promise, that scion of Raghu, true to his word,
subsequently went to the forest, overcome by the power of time.
He stood near the ocean with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa;
there, Hari beheld the Fire-god in the form of a brahmin.
Seeing Rāma distressed, he too became sorrowful;
devoted to truth, he spoke these few words that were true and desired by the virtuous. (29)
The twice-born said: "O Blessed One, O Rāma, hear what time has now arrived;
this very time for the abduction of Sītā has come upon you. (30)
Fate is indeed difficult to avert, and there is nothing more powerful than fate;
having now entrusted the Mother of the World to me, protect her shadow in my presence.
"I shall give Sītā back to you at the time of the trial;
I was dispatched by the gods, and I am not a brahmin or the sacrificial fire. (32)
Having heard those words, Rāma did not reveal them to Lakṣmaṇa;
with a grieving heart, he gave his assent to the speech.
O Nārada, by means of his yogic power, Vahni created an illusory Sītā (Māyāsītā), whose every limb possessed qualities equal to those of the real Sītā, and he gave her to Rāma.
Taking Sītā with him, he departed, having forbidden her from speaking of the secret;
Lakṣmaṇa did not even know of it, so what need is there to mention anyone else? (35)
In the meantime, Rāma saw a golden deer;
Sītā urged him toward it with great effort. (36)
Having entrusted Lakṣmaṇa with the protection of Jānakī in the forest,
Rāma himself went quickly to him and pierced him with an arrow.
And uttering the word "Lakṣmaṇa," that deer, through his illusory power,
suddenly gave up his life-breaths upon seeing Hari before him, while remembering Him.
Having cast off his deer body and assumed a divine form,
he went to Vaikuṇṭha by means of a vehicle fashioned from jewels.
At the gate of Vaikuṇṭha-loka, he became a servant to the two doorkeepers;
by the command of the two doorkeepers, he went back to that gate once again.
Then, hearing that distressed cry of "Lakṣmaṇa," she urged Lakṣmaṇa toward the presence of Rāma.
And when Lakṣmaṇa had departed, the irrepressible Rāvaṇa,
having seized Sītā, proceeded toward Laṅkā with effortless ease.
Rāma was despondent upon seeing Lakṣmaṇa in the forest;
having quickly returned to his own hermitage, he did not find Sītā there at all.
He fell into a swoon for a long time, lamented intensely again and again,
and wandered about repeatedly while searching for him.
Having obtained news of him at the proper time on the bank of the Godāvarī river,
Hari took monkeys as his allies and bound the ocean.
Having gone to Laṅkā, that best of the Raghus struck him with an arrow;
in due time, having encountered and slain Rāvaṇa along with his kinsmen, he departed.
And he quickly caused that trial by fire to be performed;
at that time, the Fire-god indeed revealed the true Jānakī.
Chāyā, filled with humility, spoke to both Agni and Rāma:
"I shall do it; tell me the means by which I may do so. (48)
The illustrious Rāma and Agni said:
"O Goddess, go to Puṣkara, which bestows great merit, for the sake of penance;
by performing asceticism right there, you shall become the Fortune of Heaven. (49)
Having heard those words and having performed penance at Puṣkara for three hundred thousand divine years, she indeed became the Goddess of Fortune (Lakṣmī) of heaven.
And in time, through her ascetic penance, she was born from the sacrificial fire-pit as Draupadī,
the daughter of Drupada and the beloved wife of the Pāṇḍavas.
In the Kṛta age she was the auspicious Vedavatī, the daughter of Kuśadhvaja;
and in the Tretā age, she became Sītā, the daughter of Janaka and the wife of Rāma.
Her shadow is the goddess Draupadī, the daughter of Drupada in the Dvāpara age;
she is said to be three years old, existing throughout the three ages.
Nārada said:
"O bull among sages, how did she come to have five beloveds? Break this doubt in my mind, O destroyer of doubts. (54)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Nārada, in Laṅkā, the real Sītā, endowed with beauty and youth, attained Rāma; and the shadow [Sītā], due to her great anxiety, [remained behind]. || 55 ||
By the command of Rāma and Agni, she, afflicted by desire and anxious for her husband, worships the supreme Śaṅkara, praying to him again and again. (56)
"Give me a husband, give me a husband, give me a husband, O Three-eyed One!
Give me a husband, give me a husband!"—thus she spoke five times. (57)
Having heard her prayer, Śiva, the Lord of Rasikas, laughed and granted her a boon, saying: "O beloved, five husbands shall be yours."
Because of that, she became the beloved of the Pāṇḍavas.
Thus everything has been told to you; now hear the actual introductory account.
Then, having recovered the enchanting Sītā in Laṅkā,
Rāma gave that city of Laṅkā to Vibhīṣaṇa and returned once more to Ayodhyā.
Having ruled the kingdom in Bhārata for eleven thousand years,
he departed for Vaikuṇṭha together with all the worlds.
Vedavatī, who was a portion of Kamalā, entered into Kamalā.
This meritorious narrative has been told; it bestows merit and destroys sin.
She upon whose tip of the tongue the four Vedas themselves exist eternally in embodied form is known as Vedavatī.
Listen as I relate to you the narrative of Dharmadhvaja’s son.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Mahālakṣmī in the Form of Vedavatī at the Royal Palace," in the ninth book of the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The description of the narrative concerning the incomparable son of Dharmadhvaja.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The wife of Dharmadhvaja was renowned as Mādhavī.
And together with the king, she took delight in the Sārāma grove on Mount Gandhamādana.
Having prepared a bed that brings delight, anointed with flowers and sandalwood paste,
she whose entire body was smeared with sandalwood [was refreshed] by the breeze of flowers and sandalwood.
A jewel among women, with exceedingly beautiful limbs, adorned with jeweled ornaments,
she was created as a passionate and connoisseur-like woman, united with a connoisseur.
There was no satiety in their amorous dalliance; as they experienced that supreme pleasure, a hundred celestial years passed, and neither day nor night was perceived.
Then the king, having regained his composure, desisted from sexual union;
however, that beautiful woman, full of desire, did not reach even a slight degree of satisfaction.
That virtuous woman immediately conceived a fetus by divine power for a hundred years;
and she, pregnant with Śrī and endowed with beauty, grew more radiant day by day.
At an auspicious moment, on an auspicious day, joined with an auspicious yoga,
in an auspicious ascendant and an auspicious division, and endowed with auspicious lords and planets.
On the full moon day of Kārtika, O lotus-born one, on a Saturday,
she gave birth to that beautiful Padminī, who was a portion of Padmā.
Beholding her in the house— her face like the full moon of autumn, her eyes like autumn lotuses, her lips like ripe bimba fruit, and her smiling countenance.
With the palms of her hands and the soles of her feet reddish, with a deep navel, and beautiful;
below that, marked by the three folds [of the waist], and with rounded hips.
In the cold [season], she was pleasantly warm in all her limbs, and in the heat, pleasantly cool;
she was dark-complexioned, with beautiful hair, lovely, and well-proportioned like a banyan tree.
Having the luster of the color of a yellow campaka flower, she was the most beautiful among the beautiful;
upon seeing her, both men and women were unable to offer any comparison.
For that reason, the wise call her by the name Tulasī;
and she is most worthy of honor, just as a woman is the very embodiment of the feminine nature.
Forbidden by all, she went to the Badarī forest for asceticism;
there, for a hundred thousand years, she performed supreme penance.
She resolved in her mind that Nārāyaṇa would be her husband;
she practiced the penance of five fires in the summer, wore only water as a garment in the winter, and remained in the open air during the rainy season.
Remaining seated, she endured streams of rain day and night for twenty thousand years, subsisting only on the water of fruit juice.
For thirty thousand years that ascetic woman subsisted on leaves,
and for forty thousand years, she of the slender waist subsisted on air alone.
Then she remained without food for ten thousand years;
and seeing her standing on one foot, beyond all perception, the Lotus-born One [Brahmā] appeared.
She arrived at the supreme Badarikāśrama to grant a boon;
and having seen the four-faced one whose vehicle is a swan, she bowed down to him.
The Creator of the world, the Ordainer of all worlds, spoke to her;
Brahmā said: "O Tulasī, choose a boon that is desired in your heart. (20)
"Devotion to Hari, service to Hari, and even freedom from old age and death"—Tulasī said:
"Listen, dear father, I shall declare that which is desired in my heart. (21)
"What shame do I feel now even before the Omniscient One?
For I was formerly Tulasī, a cowherd girl, residing in Goloka. (22)
I am the beloved servant of Kṛṣṇa, a portion of her, and her dear friend;
I am she who has been enjoyed by Govinda’s love, yet remains unsatiated and swooning.
The Mistress of the Rāsa, having arrived, beheld Govinda within the circle of the Rāsa;
filled with wrath, she rebuked him and cursed me.
With these words he indeed cursed you to take birth in a human womb;
then Govinda said to me, "I am a portion of myself as the four-armed one."
"By performing penance in Bhārata, you shall obtain [your goal] through a boon from Brahmā.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods vanished.
O Guru, out of fear of the Goddess, I abandoned my body and obtained birth on earth;
I [sought] Nārāyaṇa as my beloved, who is peaceful and possesses a beautiful form.
"Now, in order to obtain him as my husband, I choose you; please grant this to me.
Brahmādeva said:
"There is a cowherd named Sudāmā, born from the body of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (28)
An exceedingly radiant portion of him was born in Bhārata;
at present, due to the curse of Rādhikā, he has been born into the lineage of Danu.
Renowned throughout the three worlds as Śaṅkhacūḍa, there was none equal to him;
having seen you formerly in Goloka, his mind was agitated by desire.
Due to the power of Rādhikā, he was unable to delay;
moreover, because he remembered his past lives, he remained forever within the ocean.
"O beautiful one, you too are a rememberer of past births and know everything;
O lovely lady, you shall now become his wife. (32)
Later, by the power of destiny and through a portion of Nārāyaṇa’s own curse, you shall indeed choose the peaceful and beloved Nārāyaṇa as your husband.
"You shall become a tree-form, purified and the purifier of the universe;
you shall be the foremost among all flowers and superior even to the life-breath of Viṣṇu. (34)
And without you, the worship of all would become fruitless;
[you shall remain] in Vṛndāvana in the form of a tree, known by the name Vṛndāvanī. (35)
With your leaves, the cowherd women and cowherds shall constantly worship Mādhava,
together with Kṛṣṇa, in the form of the presiding deity of the tree.
"You shall dwell with Gopa at your own will by virtue of my boon.
Having heard these words, she smiled, her mind filled with joy. (37)
She bowed down to Brahmā and said something to him.
Tulasī said: "Just as I have a longing for the two-armed Kṛṣṇa, the beautiful dark one... (38)
I speak the truth, O dear one, and it is not so regarding the Four-armed Lord;
for by fate, my passion was interrupted, and I remain unsatisfied with Govinda. (39)
At the very word of Govinda, I pray for the four-armed one;
by your grace, may I once again attain Govinda, who is so difficult to obtain. (40)
"I shall certainly obtain [this]; release me from the fear of Rādhā.
Brahmā said:
"Take the mantra of Rādhikā; I give it to you, the sixteen-syllabled one. (41)
And by my boon, you shall become as dear to her as her own life;
moreover, Rādhikā will not even know of the secret love between the two of you.
"O fortunate one, you shall become equal to Rādhā for Govinda.
Having spoken thus, he indeed bestowed the sixteen-syllable mantra upon the goddess. (43)

The Sustainer of the World [revealed] the mantra, the hymn of praise, the supreme armor, the entire procedure for worship, and the sequence of the rules for the preliminary rite (puraścaryā). || 44 ||
She offered him the highest auspicious blessings and performed worship;
by his grace, that goddess became perfected like Ramā herself. || 45 ||
Through the mantra, the Tulasī attained the boon as it had been described;
and she enjoyed great pleasures that are difficult to find even in all the worlds.
With a serene mind, the goddess abandoned the exhaustion of her asceticism;
for when the fruit is attained by men, both suffering and supreme happiness come to an end. 47.
Having eaten and drunk, she was satisfied and made her bed there upon a delightful couch, which was anointed with flowers and sandalwood paste.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Tulasī, Daughter of Dharmadhvaja," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada. || 17 ||
The Description of Tulasī’s Union with Śaṅkhacūḍa.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Tulasī, being thoroughly satisfied and joyful in heart, fell asleep.
She was a preeminent woman with the bull-emblem as her banner, endowed with fresh youth.
And the five-arrowed one discharged five arrows at her;
she, already scorched by the flower-weaponed god, was now smeared with flowers and sandalwood paste.
With all her limbs marked by horripilation and her eyes trembling and reddened,
she at one moment became parched and at another fell into a swoon.
For a moment he experienced agitation, for a moment the languor that brings ease;
for a moment he felt as if burning, and for a moment he attained serenity. (4)
For a moment she regained consciousness, and for a moment she fell into despondency;
rising from her bed for a moment, she would walk near for a moment.
Wandering for a moment out of agitation, staying still again for a moment,
and for yet another moment out of great distress, she fell asleep once more.
And that bed of flowers and sandalwood became exceedingly thorny;
likewise, the divine, beautiful, and pleasant fruit and water became poisonous.
A dwelling in the form of a cave, fine clothing, fire,
and even a mark of vermilion— these are like wounds and bringers of suffering.
In her state of drowsiness, the virtuous woman beheld for a moment a well-attired man—
handsome, youthful, smiling, and the lord of connoisseurs.
With all his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste and adorned with jewel ornaments, Mālyavān approached, drinking in the lotus-face of her [the goddess]. 10.
He was speaking of amorous tales, repeatedly uttering sweet words; he had enjoyed himself upon the couch and was embracing his beloved.
But as he was going away and coming back again into her presence, she said to him, "O lord of my life, where are you going? Stay! (12)
Regaining her consciousness once more, she lamented again and again;
thus, O Nārada, having attained youth, she remained right there.
The great yogi Śaṅkhacūḍa, having obtained the enchanting Kṛṣṇa-mantra from Jaigīṣavya, accomplished its perfection at Puṣkara.
And having tied around his neck the armor which is the most auspicious of all auspicious things,
he obtained from Brahmā the boon that was desired in his heart.
By the command of Brahmā, he too arrived at Badarī;
O Sage, Tulasī saw Śaṅkhacūḍa as he was approaching.
Endowed with fresh youth, possessing a splendor equal to that of the god of love, having the hue of a white campaka flower, and adorned with ornaments of jewels. || 17 ||
With a face like the full moon of autumn and eyes like autumn lotuses,
he was enchanting, seated within a celestial chariot fashioned from the finest jewels.
His cheeks were adorned with a pair of jeweled earrings, he wore a garland of *pārijāta* flowers, and he possessed a beautiful smile. (19)
Seeing him endowed with musk and saffron and anointed with fragrant sandalwood, she covered her face with a cloth out of modesty.
Smiling and gazing at him again and again with sidelong glances,
she became one whose face was deeply bowed, abashed by her first union.
She was resplendent with her own moon-like face, which surpassed the autumnal moon, and she was adorned with a necklace of priceless gems and a vermilion-colored rosary.
Adorned by the tinkling of anklets fashioned from the essence of the finest jewels, she bore a mass of hair entwined with garlands of *mālatī* flowers. (23)
She wore earrings in the shape of makaras fashioned from priceless jewels,
and she was graced by a pair of variegated earrings that illuminated her cheeks.
Her chest was radiant with a necklace of the finest essence of jewels;
she was adorned with ornaments such as jeweled bracelets, armlets, and conch-shell decorations.
Her fingers were adorned with rows of divine jewel rings;
seeing her—graceful, beautiful, virtuous, lovely, and chaste—[he was struck with wonder].
He dwelt near her and spoke sweetly to her;
Śaṅkhacūḍa said: "Who are you, whose daughter are you, and what blessed woman among women are you who are so worthy of honor? (27)
"Who are you, O proud and auspicious one, bestower of all blessings?
O beautiful lady, since your servant has become silent, please speak with me. (28)
Having heard these words, that lovely-eyed woman, filled with desire,
spoke with a smile and a downcast face to him who was likewise filled with desire.
Tulasī said:
"I am the daughter of Dharmadhvaja, and I dwell here in the penance grove engaged in asceticism. I am an ascetic woman; who are you? Go as you please. (30)
"I have heard it said that one born of noble family does not question a woman of good lineage who is alone and in private"—so I have heard from tradition. (31)
A lecher born into an ignoble family, devoid of the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras,
who has not heard the meaning of the Vedas— he, being full of desire, longs for a woman.
That woman, who is sweet at first sight yet intoxicated with death for a man,
constantly has the form of a jar of poison while her face is like nectar.
In his heart, he [perceived] her who was constantly speaking sweet words yet possessed the edge of a razor,
and who was perpetually intent upon the accomplishment of her own purpose.
She was always under the control of her master for the sake of his business, yet otherwise she was entirely dependent;
though her inner nature was dark, she possessed a serene face and eyes. (35)
In whomsoever the conduct is found to be exceedingly corrupt in the Śruti and the Purāṇas, what wise and intelligent man of noble disposition would place his trust in them? (36)
Who among them has an enemy or a friend? They constantly crave ever-new [objects of desire]; seeing a well-dressed man, they always long for him in their hearts. (37)
Externally, she diligently makes known her own purpose, her virtue, and her constant longing; she is a beautiful woman, the support of desire, and captivating to the mind. (38)
Outwardly causing distress through her playful guile, yet inwardly intent on sexual union, she laughs at her lover in secret while appearing exceedingly bashful in public. (39)
Proud when there is an absence of sexual union, she becomes angry and the source of quarrels;
she is well-pleased by abundant enjoyment, yet distressed by even a small amount of sexual intercourse. (40)
And she longed in her mind for delicious food and cool water,
and for a handsome, passionate, beloved, youthful, and ever-virtuous man.
Having heard [this], she felt supreme affection for the connoisseur of rasa;
he was her most beloved, dearer than life itself, and skilled in the arts of enjoyment. (42)
Seeing him as equal to an enemy—whether he was old or incapable of sexual union—she would constantly engage in quarrels with him, being exceedingly prone to anger. (43)
Devouring him with her speech as a serpent devours a fierce rat,
she is the very embodiment of rashness and is always the refuge of all faults.
She is difficult for even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others to overcome; she is delusion personified, the bolt barring the path of austerity, and the very door-panel of the gateway to liberation.
Separated from devotion to Hari, she is a casket of all illusions;
in the prison of worldly existence, she is eternally the form of fetters.
She is like a magical illusion, false, and dream-like in form;
she bears outward beauty while her lower parts are utterly loathsome. (47)
It is a receptacle for various kinds of feces, urine, and pus, joined with impurities;
it is possessed of foul odors and defects, consisting of blood and non-blood, and remains unrefined.
She was formerly created by the Ordainer as an illusory form for the sake of the masters of illusion;
she appeared in the form of poison to those seeking liberation, yet remained invisible even to those who longed for her.
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, Tulasī ceased;
and Śaṅkhacūḍa, smiling, began to speak.
Śaṅkhacūḍa said:
"O Goddess, that which has been spoken by you is not entirely false; some part is true and some part is false. Listen to it from me. (51)
The Creator fashioned two kinds of illusory forms that delude all beings: the female form, which is both praiseworthy and blameworthy, and the actual form. || 52 ||
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Sāvitrī, Rādhikā, and others—
the primordial creation was fashioned as the very form of the thread of emanation.
The female form is considered to be the actual partial manifestation of these [goddesses];
it is praiseworthy, the very embodiment of glory, and the bringer of all auspiciousness. (54)
Śatarūpā, Devahūtī, Svadhā, Svāhā, and Dakṣiṇā;
Chāyāvatī, Rohiṇī, Varuṇānī, and likewise Śacī. || 55 ||
And she who is the wife of Kubera, as well as Aditi and Diti, Lopāmudrā and Anasūyā, Koṭabhī and Tulasī likewise.
Ahalyā, Arundhatī, Menā, Tārā, Mandodarī, as well as Damayantī, Vedavatī, Gaṅgā, and Manasā. || 57 ||
Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Smṛti, Medhā, Kālikā, Vasundharā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Maṅgalacaṇḍī, Mūrti, and Dharmakāminī. (58)
Auspiciousness, faith, peace, beauty, supreme forbearance, as well as sleep, lassitude, hunger, thirst, twilight, night, and day. (59)
Prosperity, fortitude, fame, ritual action, splendor, radiance, and auspiciousness—
these constitute the supreme form of womanhood that has manifested in age after age.
That which consists of parts and fractions of arts, as well as celestial courtesans and the like, is indeed unpraiseworthy among all things, being merely the form of a harlot. (61)
That form which has sattva as its predominant quality and is endowed with power is the highest among all; it is the virtuous form that is praised. (62)
The wise declare that this is to be known as the real;
it is remembered as being of the nature of *rajas* and the nature of *tamas*, existing in various ways within the *kalās*.
Those who belong to the middle portion of passion (rajas) are greedy for enjoyments;
they are subject to the pleasures of happiness and are always intent upon their own interests.
Deceits are delusive and always turn one away from dharma and artha;
therefore, the state of being a virtuous wife cannot arise for that which is of the nature of rajas. (65)
The wise declare this to be the form of the middle state;
the learned know that which is of the nature of darkness, difficult to restrain, to be the lowest.
One born of noble family and wise does not inquire about another's wife, whether in a secluded place, by water, or even in private. (67)
"I come now to your side by the command of Brahmā;
O beautiful one, I shall take you as my wife through the Gāndharva rite."
I alone am Śaṅkhacūḍa, the one who causes the gods to flee;
specifically, I was Sudāmā of Danu’s lineage in the past, belonging to Hari.
I was once a cowherd among the eight cowherds and also among the attendants;
now, by the curse of Rādhikā, I am the lord of the Dānavas.
"By the power of the mantra of Kṛṣṇa, I remember my past births;
you too, O Tulasī, are a rememberer of former lives, having been enjoyed by Hari in the past. (71)
You alone were born on the land of Bhārata from the anger of Rādhikā;
I am eager to enjoy you, yet I am not able to do so due to the fear of Rādhā.
Having spoken thus, O great sage, that man fell silent;
and Tulasī, being pleased, began to speak with a smile.
Tulasī said:
"A wise man of such a nature is always praised among all people;
likewise, a beloved woman always desires such a beloved one out of love. (74)
I have now been truly defeated by you through your discernment;
for that man who is conquered by a woman is censured and impure. (75)
The ancestors, the gods, and kinsmen all censure a man who is conquered by women;
even his mother, father, and brother despise one who is mentally enslaved by women. (76)
A pure Brahmin becomes purified in ten days by birth or death, a king (Kṣatriya) in twelve days, and a Vaiśya in fifteen days. || 77 ||
A Śūdra who has been deficient in his studies for a month regarding the Vedas, who is of mixed caste,
impure, or conquered by women, shall become pure at the time of cremation on a funeral pyre.
His ancestors do not accept his offering of rice-balls and libations by their own will;
nor indeed do the gods accept his flowers, water, and other offerings. (79)
Of what use is knowledge, austerity, recitation, burnt offerings, or worship;
of what use is learning or fame for one whose mind has been stolen by women? (80)
I have tested you for the purpose of knowing the power of your knowledge;

And he gave her all of that supreme knowledge which removes every sorrow;
having obtained it, that goddess became bright-faced and bright-eyed.
Considering everything to be transitory, they played with joy;
and those two, husband and wife, while sporting, were immersed in an ocean of happiness.
O Sage, with all their limbs bristling with horripilation, they fainted in that secluded place;
joined limb-to-limb, they were deeply delighted and eager for sexual union. (79)
Just as those two were each half-bodied, so too were they like Ardhanārīśvara;
and Tulasī considered the Lord of her life to be even more supreme than her own life-breaths.
And the king regarded that virtuous lady as dearer than his own life, the mistress of his life;
they both remained there, beautiful and equal, drowsy and sleeping soundly. (81)
Well-dressed and beautiful, they remained motionless due to their enjoyment of pleasure;
for a moment, being fully conscious, they spoke, resting upon aesthetic sentiment (rasa).
They told delightful and divine stories, laughing for a moment and again for a moment engaged in play, endowed with aesthetic flavor and emotion. || 83 ||
There is no cessation in their passion; they are experts in its domain. The two are constantly victorious and are never defeated for even a moment. (84)

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gods’ Preparations for Battle with Śaṅkhacūḍa," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
The Description of the Words of Awakening Spoken by Śaṅkhacūḍa.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having meditated upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa in his mind, the Rākṣasa became solely devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
And having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* from his charming bed of flowers, || 1 ||
Having discarded his night-garment, bathed with auspicious water, put on two washed garments, and applied a brilliant tilaka; || 2 ||
He performed his daily obligatory rites and paid homage to his chosen deity;
he also beheld auspicious objects such as curd, clarified butter, honey, and parched grain.
O Nārada, he devotedly gave to the Brāhmaṇas the best of jewels, the best of gems, the finest garments, and gold, just as he did constantly.
Whatever priceless jewels there were— pearls, rubies, and diamonds— he gave them to his brahmin preceptor for the sake of the auspiciousness of the pilgrimage.
He gave everything— a jewel of an elephant, a jewel of a horse, and a captivating jewel of wealth— to the poor Brahmin Maṅgala.
With joy, he gave thousands of treasuries, two hundred thousand cities, and a hundred million villages to the Brāhmaṇa.
Having made him the king of all the Dānavas, O Indra among kings,
he entrusted his son, his wife, the kingdom, and all its prosperity to him.
He himself, equipped with armor and bow in hand, took charge of the assembly of subjects and followers, as well as the treasury, the vehicles, and so forth.
Through his servants, he gradually assembled a collection of troops consisting of three hundred thousand horses and one hundred thousand excellent elephants.
With ten thousand chariots, thirty million archers, thirty million armored warriors, and thirty million spear-bearers.
O Nārada, an immeasurable army was assembled by the lord of the Dānavas;
and in that army, there was a commander-in-chief who was highly skilled in the science of war.

He should be known as a great chariot-warrior (*mahāratha*), the foremost among charioteers in battle; having appointed him commander of an army of three hundred thousand *akṣauhiṇīs*, the lord of men [should proceed]. (13)
He indeed caused a mass of goods sufficient for thirty akṣauhiṇīs to be prepared;
then, remembering Śrī Hari in his mind, he emerged from the camp.
He ascended a celestial chariot fashioned from the finest essence of jewels;
placing his elders at the forefront, he proceeded into the presence of Śaṅkara.
On the bank of the Puṣpabhadrā river is the auspicious Akṣayavaṭa, as well as Siddhāśrama, the field of perfection for the Siddhas, O Nārada. (16)
The place of Kapila’s asceticism is a meritorious field in Bhārata,
situated to the east of the western ocean and to the west of the Malaya mountain.
On the northern part of Śrīśaila and to the south of Gandhamādana,
it is five yojanas in width and a hundred times as long.
Resembling pure crystal, bestowing great merit in Bhārata, eternal, filled with water, and auspicious, is the river Puṣpabhadrā. (19)
The beloved wife of the Salt Ocean, endowed with eternal good fortune,
emerged from the Himalayas, mingling with the river Śarāvatī.
Having kept the Gomatī to her left, she entered the western ocean;
having gone there, Śaṅkhacūḍa beheld the moon-crested Lord.

Having seen him seated at the foot of the banyan tree, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, established in the yogic posture (yogāsana), endowed with the ritual gesture (mudrā), and smiling; || 22 ||
Resembling pure crystal, blazing with the splendor of Brahman, holding a trident and a spear, clad in tiger-skin garments, he was the most excellent one. || 23 ||
He who removes death through devotion, the peaceful one, the beloved of Gaurī, the enchanting one;
the bestower of the fruits of austerities, and the giver of all prosperity. (24)
[He is] the one easily pleased, the one with a gracious countenance, who is intent on bestowing grace upon his devotees;
the Lord of the Universe, the seed of the universe, the universal form, and the source of the universe.
The sustainer of the universe, the bestower of boons upon the universe, the agent of the universe's dissolution, the cause of all causes, and the deliverer from the ocean of hell.

Having descended from his celestial chariot and beheld him— who bestows knowledge, who is the seed of knowledge, who is the eternal bliss of knowledge— the lord of the Dānavas [was struck with wonder].
Filled with devotion, he bowed his head in salutation along with everyone;
to his left was Bhadrakālī, and Skanda stood before him.
Kālī and Śaṅkara, as well as Skanda, gave him their blessings;
and seeing that he had arrived, Nandīśvara and all the others rose up.
They conversed with one another and performed their duties there at that time;
and the king, having held his discourse, remained in the presence of Śiva.
The blessed Lord Mahādeva, with a serene soul, spoke to him.
Mahādeva said: "Brahmā is the creator of the worlds, the father of Dharma, and the knower of Dharma. (31)
Marīci was his son, and he was a righteous devotee of Viṣṇu;
Kaśyapa was also his son, a most virtuous lord of creatures (prajāpati).
With affection and devotion, Dakṣa gave him thirteen daughters;
among them was the virtuous Danu, who increased his good fortune.
Danu had forty sons, the Dānavas, who were exceedingly fierce in their splendor;
among them was one named Vipracitti, possessed of great strength and prowess.
His son, the righteous Dambha, a devotee of Viṣṇu who had conquered his senses,
chanted the supreme mantra at Puṣkara for a hundred thousand years.
Having made Śukrācārya his preceptor, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul,
then obtained you as a son who was supremely devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
Formerly you were a cowherd attendant among the cowherds, most righteous even among them;
now, due to the curse of Rādhikā, you are a lord of the Dānavas in Bhārata.
The devotee of Viṣṇu indeed considered everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass as insignificant,
including even the states of residing in the same world (sālokya), sharing the same power (sārṣṭi), union (sāyujya), and proximity (sāmīpya) with Hari.
Vaiṣṇavas do not accept what is being offered without service;
moreover, a Vaiṣṇava considers even the status of Brahmā or immortality to be trivial. (39)

Whether it be the state of Indra or the state of Manu, you did not consider them even in your reckonings; for one devoted to Kṛṣṇa, what concern can there be regarding the delusions concerning the gods? (40)
"Give back the kingdom to the gods and preserve my favor, O protector of the earth! Dwell happily in your own realm, and let the gods indeed remain in their own positions. (41)
Enough with this hostility toward living beings; all are born of the lineage of Kaśyapa.
Whatever sins there may be, even including such as the killing of a Brahmin—[all these shall be removed]. (42)
O Indra among kings, if you consider it, the sins of betraying one's kinsmen do not equal even a sixteenth part of the loss of one's own prosperity. (43)
And in every state, with whom does it always attain equality?
And the concealment of Brahman occurs perpetually during the primordial dissolution.
Furthermore, his manifestation occurs through power by the will of the Lord;
likewise, the increase of knowledge and the loss of memory certainly result from ascetic penance (tapas). (45)
That Creator also brings about creation through knowledge in due order;
He is the most perfect Dharma, eternally residing in Truth within the locus of Truth.
That [portion] was reduced to three parts in the Tretā age, to two parts in the Dvāpara, and to one part in the Kali; thus, its portion diminished progressively as before.
When but a fraction of the Kali age remains, it is like the crescent of the moon on the new-moon day;
just as the splendor of the sun in midsummer is not such again in the winter.
As it is at midday during the days, so it is not at evening or dawn;
in time it rises, and it gradually reaches its state of childhood. (49)
After reaching its peak, it again sets in the subsequent time;
during the day it remains concealed, but by time it becomes manifest in the thick of a stormy day.
When seized by Rāhu, the moon trembles, yet it becomes clear once more;
on the full-moon day, it becomes the most perfectly full. || 51 ||
Such [a body] does not remain permanent;
it undergoes decay day by day, yet it attains nourishment once again, especially on the day of the new moon (kuhū).
In the bright fortnight he is endowed with prosperity, while in the dark fortnight he is withered by consumption;
on a day eclipsed by Rāhu he is faded, and on an overcast day he does not shine.
In due time, the moon will become white [waning] through the change of time and lose its splendor;
likewise, Bali will become Indra, yet he has now lost his splendor in Sutala.
In due time, the earth— rich in crops, the supporter of all, and the bearer of wealth—
became submerged in water and vanished, overwhelmed by the waters.
All things perish in time and indeed arise from time;
both the moving and the unmoving perish and come forth by means of time. (56)
The equality of the Lord, the Brahman, the Supreme Self,
is indeed such that I am the conqueror of death, because of [my mastery over] the countless dissolution of primordial nature (prakṛti).
And I shall also look into the mirror again and again, time after time;
for that which is the form of primordial nature (prakṛti) is remembered as being the very same as the person (puruṣa).
He is both the Self and the individual soul, the Supreme who assumes manifold forms;
indeed, he constantly performs the chanting of His names and qualities. (59)
In due time, he conquers death, the fear of birth and disease, and old age;
by him Vidhi was made the creator, and Viṣṇu was made the protector.
O King, having appointed Kālāgnirudra for the purpose of dissolution, we have been made the creators and destroyers of the objects of the senses. (61)
I constantly perform the chanting of his name and qualities;
by that, I am the conqueror of death and, through this knowledge, I am fearless.
"Death flees from the fear of death, just as serpents flee from Vainateya," having said this,
that Lord of All became intent upon Him with his whole being.
And Śambhu ceased speaking in the midst of the assembly, O Nārada;
and the king, having heard those words, praised them again and again.
Śaṅkhacūḍa spoke sweetly to the god with supreme humility:
"O God, that which has been spoken by you is not remembered as anything other than the truth. (65)
Nevertheless, let my report be heard as it truly is,
regarding that great sin of treachery toward kinsmen which you have just now mentioned.
Having seized all his possessions, why was Bali sent away?
O Lord, I have extracted all supreme sovereignty for myself. (67)
Even Gadādhara (Viṣṇu) was not able to rescue Hiraṇyākṣa along with his brother from that [submarine fire]; how then could he have been slain by the gods? (68)
And how were the asuras, Śumbha and the others, struck down by the gods?
Previously, during the churning of the ocean, the nectar was consumed by the deities. (69)
In that regard, we are the sharers of afflictions, while they all enjoy the fruits;
this entire universe is a plaything of Prakṛti and the Supreme Self. (70)
To whomever and wherever he gives [it], to him shall belong sovereignty at that time; the conflict between the gods and the dānavas will then be constant and perpetual. (71)
Their defeat and our victory shall occur in due course over time; therefore, in the event of conflict between us two, our coming together will be supreme and flawless.
This is a great shame for you, a kinsman and relative by marriage of the high-souled Lord, that you must now fight with us in battle. (73)
"Victory brings greater fame, while defeat results in loss"—having heard these words, the Three-eyed Lord laughed. (74)
Mahādeva spoke this appropriate reply to that lord of the Dānavas:
"In battle with you, who are born of the lineage of Brahmā... (75)
O King, what great shame or infamy is there in defeat?
For at the very beginning, Hari fought with Madhu and Kaiṭabha. (76)
O King, [he described] the battle with Hiraṇyakaśipu along with that very self,
and again the battle with Hiraṇyākṣa by that wielder of the mace.
In former times, a battle was also fought by me against the Tripuras;
it took place with Prakṛti, the sovereign of all and mother of all.
Formerly, there was a most wonderful battle with Śumbha and the others;
and you were a preeminent attendant of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul. (79)
Whichever Daityas have been slain by you, none at all are equal to you;
O King, what great shame is there for me in fighting with you? (80)
"Alas! You have been sent by Hari, the very refuge of the gods;
give back the kingdom to the deities—this is my firm resolve. (81)
"Either engage in battle with me, or what is the use of this expenditure of words?
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, Śaṅkara ceased there;
and Śaṅkhacūḍa rose up immediately along with his ministers.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Words of Awakening Spoken by Śaṅkhacūḍa," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
The Description of the Battle between Kālī and Śaṅkhacūḍa.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having bowed his head to Śiva, the powerful lord of the Dānavas [spoke].
And he quickly ascended the vehicle together with his ministers. || 1 ||
Śiva swiftly urged on his own army and the gods;
and the lord of the Dānavas, together with his army, stood ready at the commencement of the battle.
Mahendra himself fought together with Vṛṣaparvan,
and Bhāskara quickly fought with Vipracitti.
Candra engaged in a supreme battle with Dambha;
Kāla with Kālasvara, and Hutāśana with Gokarṇa. || 4 ||
Kubera was [fought] by Kālakeya, Viśvakarman by Maya,
Death by Bhayaṅkara, and likewise Yama by Saṃhāra.
Varuṇa [mounted] Vikaṅkaṇa, Samīraṇa [mounted] Cañcala, Budha [mounted] Ghṛtapṛṣṭha, and Śanaiścara [mounted] Raktākṣa.
Jayanta [was born] with Ratnasāra, the Vasus with hosts of splendors,
the two Aśvins with Dīptimant, and Nalakūbara with Dhūmra.
Dharma was borne by Dhurandhara, Maṅgala by Uṣākṣa, Bhānu by Śobhākara, and Manmatha by Piṭhara. || 8 ||
With the Godhāmukha powder, with the sword and the banner,
with the Kāñcīmukha, the Piṇḍa, and together with the smoke and Nandin.
And with Viśvapa and Palāśa, the others—the eleven Ādityas and so forth—fought; and the eleven Rudras indeed fought with the eleven Bhayaṃkaras.
Mahāmārī fought together with Ugracaṇḍā and the others,
as did all those beginning with Nandīśvara, along with the hosts of Dānavas.
And they fought in the great battle, even amidst the terrifying dissolution;
meanwhile, Śambhu stood at the foot of the banyan tree with Kālī and his son.
And all the hosts of soldiers fought continuously, O sage,
while [he] sat upon a beautiful jeweled throne together with ten million dānavas.
And Śaṅkhacūḍa, adorned with jewel ornaments, took up residence there;
as did those warriors of Śaṅkara who had been defeated by the Dānavas.
All the gods fled, terrified and with their bodies wounded;
Skanda then displayed his wrath and granted fearlessness to the gods. || 15 ||
And by his splendor, he increased the strength of his own hosts;
thus, he alone fought against the multitudes of the Dānavas.
In battle, she slew a hundred akṣauhiṇīs;
the lotus-eyed Kālī struck down the asuras.
Then, being exceedingly enraged, she drank the blood of the Dānavas—
of ten lakhs of lordly elephants, a hundred lakhs, and by the crores.
Taking them up with one hand, he playfully cast them into his mouth;
and a thousand headless trunks danced in the battle, O Sage. (19)
With a net of arrows from Skanda, the Dānavas had their bodies wounded;
terrified, they all fled, even though they possessed great prowess in battle. || 20 ||
Vṛṣaparvan, Vipracitti, Dambha, and Vikaṅkaṇa—
all of them fought with Skanda and with Vikrama.
Mahāmārī fought on and did not turn her back;
yet they became utterly agitated, oppressed by Skanda’s spear.
They did not flee out of fear; rather, a rain of flowers fell in heaven upon seeing Skanda’s battle, which was exceedingly fierce and intense.
Like a natural dissolution that brings about the destruction of the Dānavas,
the king ascended his celestial chariot and unleashed a rain of arrows.
The king's shower of arrows was like the rain from a cloud;
and there arose a most terrible darkness as well as the emergence of fire.
All the gods, as well as others such as Nandīśvara and the rest, fled;
Kārttikeya alone remained at the forefront of the battle.
And the king brought down a rain of mountains, serpents, rocks, and likewise trees—unrestrainable and terrifying. (27)
And by the king's shower of arrows, the son of Śiva was overwhelmed,
like the sun obscured by a dense mist.
The terrifying one cut apart Skanda’s bow, which was difficult to bear, and shattered his divine chariot, severing the chariot-seats as well. (29)
He rendered the peacock shattered by means of a divine weapon;
he then hurled a spear, radiant as the sun, to strike it in the chest.
For a moment he fell into a swoon, but then he regained consciousness;
taking up that divine bow which had been given by Viṣṇu in the past, he stood ready.
Mounting a chariot fashioned from the finest essence of jewels, Kārtika took up weapons and missiles and waged a fierce battle.
The son of Śiva, in his wrath, cut down the serpents, the mountains, the trees, and the rocks as well, using all [of them] with a divine weapon.
The powerful one extinguished the fire with a rain-cloud weapon (pārjanya) and effortlessly severed the chariot and bow of Śaṅkhacūḍa.
He hurled his armor, his charioteer, and his crown resplendent with a diadem, as well as a white-shining spear, into the chest of the lord of the Dānavas.
Having fallen into a swoon, the king regained consciousness;
he mounted another vehicle and quickly seized his bow.
O Nārada, that best of illusionists created a net of arrows through his power of illusion and covered Guha in battle with that web of shafts.
He seized an unwavering spear, possessing a radiance equal to a hundred suns,
having the form of the crest of the fire of universal dissolution, and enveloped by the splendor of Viṣṇu.
And in the month of Kārttika, he hurled it at her with great force and wrath;
that spear fell upon her body like a blazing mass of fire. (39)
The mighty Kārttikeya fell unconscious from the blow of the spear;
Kālī took him in her arms and brought him into the presence of Śiva.
And Śiva, by his power, restored him to life through his knowledge as a mere sport;
he granted him infinite strength, and the majestic one rose up.
Kālī, who had gone to the battlefield to protect Kārtika,
was followed by those heroes, including Nandīśvara and the others.
All the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kinnaras, as well as numerous musical instruments and hundreds of honey-carriers [were present]. (43)
Having gone to the battlefield, she then let out a lion’s roar;
and by the goddess’s lion’s roar, the Dānavas fell into a swoon.
Beholding him, he repeatedly let out a most inauspicious, loud, and boisterous laugh; he drank the honey-wine and danced at the head of the battlefield.
Ugradaṃṣṭrā, Ugradaṇḍā, and Koṭavī drank the honey-wine;
as did the hosts of Yoginīs and Ḍākinīs, the groups of gods, and others. || 46 ||
Seeing Kālī, Śaṅkhacūḍa quickly arrived at the battlefield;
the Dānavas were seized with fear, and the king granted them freedom from fear.
Kālī hurled a fire resembling the crest of the fire of universal dissolution,
but the king effortlessly extinguished it with a rain-cloud weapon (pārjanya).
She, for her part, hurled a fierce and great Vāruṇa weapon, a marvel;
and the lord of the Dānavas effortlessly cut it down with a Gāndharva weapon.
Kālī hurled the Māheśvara [missile], which resembled a crest of fire;
the king swiftly struck it down with ease using the Vaiṣṇava [missile]. || 50 ||
That goddess discharged the Nārāyaṇa weapon accompanied by mantras;
seeing it, the king descended from his chariot and prostrated himself.
That weapon, resembling the crest of the fire of universal dissolution, soared upwards;
and Śaṅkhacūḍa fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff out of devotion to him.
And she discharged the Brahmāstra with effort, preceded by the appropriate mantra;
the great king, for his part, extinguished it with the Brahmāstra.
Then that goddess discharged a divine weapon accompanied by mantras;
the king, however, extinguished it with a net of his own divine weapons.
Then the king, with great effort, hurled a spear a yojana long;
however, he shattered it into a hundred pieces with a net of divine weapons.
And the Goddess, in her wrath, seized the Pāśupata weapon purified by mantras;
and as she was about to discharge it to obstruct him, an incorporeal voice spoke. || 56 ||
For the high-souled king, there is no death by the Pāśupata weapon,
as long as the armor of Hari's mantra remains.
"As long as her virtue remains intact, and as long as the king's wives remain faithful, so long shall he be free from old age and death; such are the words of Brahmā. (58)
Having heard this, Bhadrakālī did not hurl that weapon;
instead, out of hunger, she swallowed a hundred lakhs of Dānavas with ease.
The terrifying goddess rushed with speed to devour Śaṅkhacūḍa,
but the Dānava warded her off with a very sharp divine weapon.
That goddess hurled a sword that was like the summer sun;
the lord of the Dānavas, however, shattered it into a hundred pieces with a divine weapon.
The great goddess went toward him with speed to seize him again;
the glorious lord of the Dānavas, the master of all siddhis, grew in stature.
With a swift fist, the formidable and wrathful Kālī shattered his chariot and struck down the charioteer, O virtuous one.
She hurled a trident resembling the flames of the fire of universal destruction,
but Śaṅkhacūḍa caught it effortlessly with his left hand.
With great fury and speed, the goddess struck him with her fist;
by that blow, the Daitya reeled for a moment and fell into a swoon.
Regaining consciousness in an instant, the powerful one rose up;
he did not engage in hand-to-hand combat with the goddess, but bowed down before her.
He cut down the goddess’s weapon and seized it by his own splendor;
being her devotee and a Vaiṣṇava through devotion to his mother, he did not hurl that weapon at her.
Having seized the Dānava and whirled him around again and again, the goddess,
provoked to anger, hurled him upward with great velocity.
The powerful Śaṅkhacūḍa fell down from above with great force;
having fallen, he rose up again after bowing to Bhadrakālī.
Filled with joy, he ascended a most enchanting celestial chariot fashioned from the finest essence of jewels; he had not yet rested after the great battle.
