And that goddess Bhadrakālī, driven by hunger, drank the blood of the Dānavas;
having drunk and eaten, she went into the presence of Śaṅkara.
He related the account of the battle in its proper sequence from beginning to end;
having heard it, Śambhu, the destroyer of the Dānavas, laughed.
O Lord, one hundred thousand of the lords of the Dānavas remain now in battle;
that other portion which was eaten has emerged from the mouth of her who is consuming them. (73)
And while he was about to slay the lord of the Dānavas in battle with the Pāśupata weapon, an incorporeal voice spoke: "This king is indeed unslayable by you."
The king of kings, possessed of great wisdom and great strength and prowess, did not discharge a weapon at me; rather, he cut down my arrow. (75)

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between Kālī and Śaṅkhacūḍa," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada. || 22 ||
The Description of the Slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa:
O Nārada, having heard that truth, Śiva, who is proficient in the knowledge of reality, went himself to the battlefield along with his attendants.
Having seen Śiva and descended from his celestial chariot, Śaṅkhacūḍa bowed with supreme devotion, prostrating himself on the ground like a staff with his head.
Having bowed to him, he swiftly ascended the celestial chariot;
he quickly donned his armor and took up his formidable bow.
In the past, the battle between Śiva and Dānava lasted for a full hundred years;
O Brahmin, neither victory nor defeat occurred between them.
The Blessed One had laid down his weapons, and the Dānava had laid down his weapons;
Śaṅkhacūḍa was stationed upon his chariot, while the Bull-bannered Lord was seated upon his bull.
A hundred of the Dānavas were indeed raised up;
those who had died in battle, the omnipresent Lord Śambhu restored to life.
In the meantime, an elderly brāhmaṇa,
extremely distressed, arrived at the site of the battle and spoke to the lord of the dānavas.
The old brahmin said:
"O Indra among kings, give alms now to me, a brahmin;
you are the giver of all prosperity, whatever is desired in my heart. (8)
"To you who are now inactive, aged, and thirsty, I shall speak later; for now, make your promise true. (9)
The king of kings, with a serene face and eyes, said, "Om. Then, by means of great illusion, the person said, "And I am one who seeks armor. (10)
Having heard that, Hari indeed took the divine armor and,
assuming the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa, went toward Tulasī.
Having gone there, he performed the act of impregnation through her by means of his illusory power (māyā).
Then Śambhu took up the trident of Hari against the Dānava.
It was like the midday sun of summer or the cresting flame of the fire of universal destruction;
it was irresistible, invincible, unfailing, and a slayer of enemies.
In its brilliance it was equal to a discus, the essence of all weapons and missiles,
difficult for others to bear, and terrifying even to Śiva and Keśava.
It is a thousand bows in length and a hundred cubits in breadth;
it is endowed with life, is of the nature of Brahman, eternal in form, and indefinable.
O Nārada, he who was capable of withdrawing the entire universe by his own sport, having weighed it, cast it upon Śaṅkhacūḍa.
And the king, having cast aside his bow and assumed a yogic posture with his mind, meditated with devotion upon the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having whirled his trident in a circular motion, he hurled it upon the Dānava;
then, with ease, he reduced him along with his chariot to ashes.
The King assumed a divine form as a youth dressed as a cowherd, having two arms, holding a flute in his hand, and adorned with jewel ornaments. (19)
He ascended a vehicle fashioned from the finest essence of jewels, surrounded by tens of millions of cowherds; having come from Goloka, he mounted it and proceeded toward the city.
O sage, having gone there, he bowed his head with devotion at the lotus feet of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in the forest of Vṛndāvana during the rāsa dance.
And seeing Sudāmā, their faces and eyes bright with joy,
they both embraced him very tightly out of exceeding love.
Then he went with speed to Śala and approached him with respect;
indeed, from the bones of Śaṅkhacūḍa, the Śaṅkha lineage came into being.
In various forms, it is eternally pure for the worship of the gods;
the water from a conch is highly praised and supremely pleasing to the deities. (24)
Even the very essence of the waters of sacred fords is pure only when accompanied by Śambhu;
wherever the sound of a conch resounds, there Lakṣmī is firmly established.
He who has bathed with the water from a conch shell has bathed in all sacred fords;
for the conch is the abode of Hari, and where there is a conch, there is Hari.
In that very place Lakṣmī dwells, and all inauspiciousness has been driven far away by the sounds of conchs blown by women, and especially by Śūdras. (27)
Terrified and enraged, Lakṣmī departed from that place to another land;
even Śiva, having slain the Dānava, went to the world of Śiva.
Exultant, mounted upon his bull and surrounded by his own hosts,
the gods reached their own realm, filled with supreme bliss.
Kettledrums resounded in heaven, and Gandharvas and Kinnaras sang; a continuous rain of flowers fell upon Śiva,
and the gods, as well as the foremost among the best of sages and others, offered him praise.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Greatness of Śālagrāma along with the Majesty of Tulasī.
Nārada said:
The Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa indeed performed the act of depositing his seed.
In what form does she reside within the Tulasī? You should explain that to me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: And the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, through Viṣṇu-māyā, took up the armor of Śaṅkhacūḍa during the rites of the gods.
Assuming that form once again, he went to the house of his chaste wife,
desiring to slay Śaṅkhacūḍa by destroying her devotion to her husband.
He sounded a drum near the door of the Tulasī grove and, at that doorway, announced the word "Victory! to awaken Sundarī.
Having heard that sound, the virtuous woman, filled with supreme joy,
gazed out from the window onto the royal road with great reverence.
Having given wealth to the Brāhmaṇas, he caused auspicious rites to be performed;
he gave wealth to the bards, the mendicants, and those who recited praises.
Descending from the chariot, the Lord went to the residence of the Goddess—
a beautiful and most enchanting palace fashioned from priceless jewels.
And seeing her beloved before her, she, filled with joy,
washed his feet, bowed down, and wept.
The lustful woman seated him upon a beautiful jeweled throne and gave him betel-leaf, exquisitely scented with camphor and other fragrances.
Today my birth and life have indeed become fruitful,
as I behold the lord of my life, who had gone to battle, returned once more to my home.
Smiling, casting side-long glances, filled with desire and her body bristling with horripilation,
she asked her beloved about the events of the battle in a sweet voice.
Tulasī said:
O Lord, O ocean of mercy, tell me how your victory came about in battle against the destroyer of countless universes.
Having heard Tulasī’s words, the Lord of Kamalā laughed and,
assuming the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa, spoke these nectar-like words to her.
The Blessed Lord said:
O beloved, our battle lasted for a full year;
O lovely one, there was the destruction of all the dānavas.
Brahmā himself bestowed affection upon us both, and by his command, the authority over the gods was granted to him. 15.
"I have come to my own abode; Śiva has gone to the world of Śiva.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds lay down upon his bed.
O Nārada, there the Lord of Ramā sported with Rāmā; that virtuous woman [was delighted] by the enjoyment of pleasure and the intensity of their mutual attraction.
She reflected on everything and said, "Who are you?
Tulasī said: "Tell me, O Lord of Māyā, who are you? I have been enjoyed by you through your Māyā. (18)
"Since my chastity has been violated, therefore I shall curse you!
Having heard Tulasī's words, Hari, out of fear of the curse, [acted]. (19)
O Brahmin, she effortlessly assumed a most beautiful and enchanting form;
then the Goddess beheld before her the eternal God of gods.
Dark as a fresh rain-cloud, with eyes like autumn lotuses, possessing the grace of ten million Cupids, and adorned with jewel ornaments. (21)
Seeing him with a slight smile, a serene countenance, adorned and wearing yellow garments,
that amorous woman effortlessly fell into a swoon out of desire.
Then, regaining her consciousness, she spoke to him again.
Tulasī said: "O Lord, you have no compassion for one who is like a stone."
"My master has been killed by you through deceit and the violation of dharma;
for you, O Lord, are one whose heart is like stone and who is devoid of compassion. (24)
Therefore, O Lord, may you now become stone-like;
those who speak of you as a virtuous being are indeed deluded, there is no doubt. (25)
"How was this devotee slain for the sake of another without any fault?
Thus she wept bitterly, afflicted by grief, and lamented again and again. (26)
Then, seeing her compassion, the Lord of Kamalā, who is an ocean of the essence of compassion, spoke in order to awaken her through right reasoning: || 27 ||
The Blessed Lord said: "O blessed lady, you have performed penance for my sake in Bhārata for a long time;
and for your sake, Śaṅkhacūḍa has likewise performed penance for a very long time."
Having made you his beloved, he too sported with you at that very moment;
now it is fitting that the fruit of your penance be granted to you alone.
"Having abandoned this body and assumed a divine form, sport with me in Rāma; you shall become equal to Ramā. (30)
May this body, in the form of a river renowned as the Gaṇḍakī, be pure and bestow great merit upon men in the holy land of Bhārata. || 31 ||
And your mass of hair shall become a sacred tree;
born from your hair, it shall be renowned as Tulasī.
"O fair-faced one, among all flowers and leaves in the three worlds for the worship of the gods, Tulasī shall be the most excellent. (33)
In heaven, on earth, in the netherworld, and in Goloka in my presence, become you, O Tulasī, the best of trees and the most beautiful among flowers. (34)
In Goloka, on the banks of the Virajā, in the Rāsa-dance arena, in the forest of Vṛndāvana, at the Bhāṇḍīra tree, in the lovely Campaka grove, and in the sandalwood forest; || 35 ||
May your dwelling be right here in this grove of Mādhavī, Ketakī, Kunda, Mālikā, and Mālatī flowers—a merit-bestowing place of holiness. (36)
At the roots of the Tulasī trees in sacred places, there shall be the abode of all holy fords (tīrthas), bestowing merit. || 37 ||
In that very place, O fair-faced one, is my own empowerment for all the gods,
as well as for the attainment of the falling of Tulasī leaves.
He who performs an ablution with the water from a *tulasī* leaf has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices. (39)
Whatever satisfaction Hari may derive from thousands of jars of nectar, that same satisfaction will surely arise from the offering of a Tulasī leaf. (40)
O virtuous lady, that fruit which results from the gift of ten thousand cows is obtained by the gift of a *tulasī* leaf during the month of Kārtika.
And whoever receives the water from a Tulasī leaf at the time of death is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. || 42 ||
That man who daily drinks the water from the Tulasī plant with devotion attains the merit born of a hundred thousand horse-sacrifices. (43)
A person who holds Tulasī in his hand and wears it upon his body, if he gives up his life at sacred fords (tīrthas), goes to the world of Viṣṇu. || 44 ||
The man who wears a garland fashioned from Tulasī wood certainly obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice at every step. || 45 ||
He who, having taken Tulasi in his own hand, does not maintain his commitment,
goes to the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Whatever man here makes a false oath by means of Tulasī goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Whoever receives even a single drop of Tulasī water at the time of death will certainly ascend a jewel-adorned vehicle and attain Vaikuṇṭha. (48)
On the full moon day, the new moon day, the twelfth lunar day, and during the transit of the sun,
as well as at midday, at night, and during the two twilights, one should perform an oil massage.
Those men who, during a period of impurity or at an inauspicious time, gather Tulasī while still wearing their night-clothes, they cut off the head of Hari.
O virtuous lady, a pure Tulasī leaf remains fit for three nights even if it has been kept overnight,
whether used in a Śrāddha rite, a religious vow, a gift, a consecration, or the worship of the gods.
That which has fallen on the ground or fallen into water, when offered to the virtuous Viṣṇu,
as well as a pure Tulasī leaf after it has been washed for another purpose, [is acceptable].
O goddess presiding over this tree, you shall eternally engage in perpetual play with Kṛṣṇa in the stainless realm of Goloka. (53)
The goddess who presides over the river and bestows great merit in Bhārata shall become the wife of Lavaṇoda, who is a portion of myself. (54)
And you yourself, O great virtuous lady, shall become equal to Ramā and a delight to Rāma in my presence in Vaikuṇṭha; of this there is no doubt.
"And by your curse, O Bhārata, I shall assume the form of a mountain and establish my presence on the banks of the Gaṇḍakī. (56)
There, millions of insects with sharp fangs as their primary weapons will turn my discus within the hollows of that rock.
Having a single door and four arches, adorned with a forest garland, having the appearance of a fresh rain cloud, it is named Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. (58)
Having one door and four wheels, resembling a fresh rain-cloud, it should be known as Lakṣmī-Janārdana, devoid of a forest garland. (59)
At the two gates there is a four-wheeled [sign] adorned with a cow’s footprint;
it should be known as the one named Raghunātha, devoid of a forest garland. (60)
Extremely small, having two wheels, with the luster of a fresh cloud, and devoid of a forest garland—that should be known as the one named Vāmana. 61.
The form of Śrīdhara, which is very small, has two wheels, and is adorned with a forest garland, should always be understood as bestowing prosperity upon householders.
It should be known as the one named Dāmodara, which is thick, circular in shape, devoid of a forest garland, and clearly possesses two wheels. (63)
The middle one, circular in shape, with two wheels, pierced by an arrow, and provided with a quiver for arrows, is to be known as the one named Raṇarāmā. || 64 ||
The middle [type] has seven wheels and is adorned with the ornament of a parasol;
it should be known as the Rājarājeśvara, which bestows royal prosperity upon men. || 65 ||
It has fourteen wheels, is gross, and possesses the beautiful luster of a fresh rain-cloud;
it should be known as named Ananta, bestowing the fruits of the four aims of life.
That which is wheel-shaped, possesses two wheels, is auspicious, has the luster of a water-cloud, contains a cow’s footprint, and is of medium size, should be known as Madhusūdana. (67)
Sudarśana is proclaimed as having a single wheel, Guptacakra as bearing a mace,
and Hayagrīva as having two wheels and resembling the face of a horse.
With an exceedingly wide-open mouth, two wheels, and a formidable appearance, it is easily recognized as Narasiṃha; it instantly bestows dispassion upon men. (69)
One should recognize Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha as having two wheels, a wide-open mouth, and being adorned with a forest garland; he bestows happiness upon householders. (70)
At the entrance, one should recognize Vāsudeva, who possesses two wheels, is endowed with splendor, is symmetrical, and clearly manifest; he bestows the fruits of all desires. (71)
The Pradyumna cakra is subtle, with the luster of a fresh rain cloud, abounding in hollows and apertures, and it bestows happiness upon the householder. (72)
When there are two wheels and one axle-pin, and the rear part is abundant, it should be well understood as the Saṅkarṣaṇa; it always bestows happiness upon householders. (73)
But the wise declare that the Aniruddha [mandala], which is yellowish in luster, circular, and exceedingly beautiful, bestows happiness upon householders. (74)
Wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone, there Hari is present;
right there Lakṣmī dwells, accompanied by all sacred fords.
Whatever sins there may be, including even the killing of a Brahmin, all of them perish through the worship of the Śālagrāma stone. (76)
If it is shaped like an umbrella, there will be sovereignty; if circular, great prosperity;
if shaped like a cart, suffering; and on the tip of a trident, death is certain. (77)
If the face is deformed, there will be poverty; if it is tawny, there is only loss.
If the wheel is broken, disease shall occur; if it is split asunder, death is certain.
Vows, charity, the consecration of images, ancestral rites, and the worship of deities—all these become highly meritorious through the presence of the Śālagrāma. || 79 ||
He has bathed in all sacred fords and been initiated into all sacrifices;
he has participated in all sacrifices, at all holy sites, in all vows, and in all ascetic practices.
By worshipping the Śālagrāma stone, one certainly obtains that merit which results from the study of the four Vedas and the performance of austerities. (81)
Whoever should always perform an ablution with the waters of the Śālagrāma stone obtains that merit which is found in all acts of giving, as well as that from circumambulating the earth.
The man who constantly drinks the water from a Śālagrāma stone obtains the grace desired by the gods; of this there is no doubt. (82)
All sacred fords long for even the touch of such a person;
though liberated while living and supremely purified, he goes at the end to the abode of Hari.
Right there, together with Hari, he will indeed undergo countless dissolutions into primordial nature (prakṛti),
while being appointed to the service of servitude in the performance of menial tasks.
Whatever sins there may be, even those equal to the killing of a Brahmin, flee upon seeing him, just as serpents flee from Vainateya. || 85 ||
By the dust of his feet, the goddess Earth was instantly purified;
a hundred thousand ancestors of that man would be delivered from their state from the very moment of his birth.
Whoever obtains the water from a Śālagrāma stone at the time of death, being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Viṣṇu. || 87 ||
He attains liberation through Nirvāṇa and is released from the experience of karma;
he shall become merged in the state of Viṣṇu—of this there is no doubt. (88)
Whoever, having taken up a Śālagrāma stone, speaks a false word,
goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā.
He who, having taken up a Śālagrāma stone, does not fulfill his commitment,
goes to the Asipatra hell for a period of one hundred thousand Manvantaras.
O beloved, he who breaks a Tulasi leaf upon a Śālagrāma stone will suffer separation from his wife in a future birth.
He who indeed makes a break in the *tulasī* leaves upon the conch shell shall become bereft of a wife and afflicted by disease for seven births. (92)
That great knower who keeps the śālagrāma, the tulasī, and the conch together in one place shall become beloved of Śrī Hari.
For whenever one deposits his seed in another, if that connection is severed, there will surely arise mutual suffering between them. (94)
"You shall be the beloved of Śaṅkhacūḍa for the duration of one Manvantara;
any separation from Śaṅkha will bring you nothing but sorrow. (95)
Having spoken thus to her, O Nārada, the illustrious Hari ceased;
and she, having cast off her body and assumed a divine form, [departed]. (96)
Just as Śrī dwells [upon his chest], so too did she reside upon the breast of Hari;
he, the Lord of Kamalā, went together with her to Vaikuṇṭha.
O Nārada, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā, and Tulasī—
these four became the beloveds of Hari, the Lord.
Immediately, the river Gaṇḍakī was born from that body;
and that mountain, the Lord himself, became the bestower of merit upon men on its banks.
O Sage, insects there fashion stones of many kinds;
those which fall into the water certainly become fruit-bearing. (100)
Those situated on land are to be known as Piṅgalās due to the heat of the sun.
Thus everything has been told; what more do you wish to hear? 101.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Śālagrāma Together with the Majesty of Tulasī," in the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada, within the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Ritual for Worshipping Tulasī.
Nārada said:
When Tulasī was made the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, she was to be worshipped.
Now, please tell me the procedure for her worship and her hymn of praise.
O Sage, by whom was she first worshipped, and by whom was she first praised?
And by whom did she become an object of worship there? Tell me this, O Lord! (2)
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Nārada, the bull among sages laughed and began to relate a supreme, meritorious narrative that destroys all sins.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having fully worshipped Tulasī, Hari took his pleasure with Ramā; he treated her, whose good fortune was equal to that of Ramā, with great respect.
Lakṣmī and Gaṅgā beheld her new union with him;
Sarasvatī, out of jealousy, could not endure that weight of his good fortune.
In that quarrel, the proud woman struck her in the presence of Hari;
then, out of shame and indignation, she vanished from sight.
The goddess Sarvasiddheśvarī, the yoginī who grants success to the wise, vanished from sight out of anger everywhere, O Hari! Alas! || 7 ||
Having failed to find Tulasī, Hari awakened Sarasvatī;
and having obtained her permission, he went to the Tulasī grove.
Having gone there and bathed well, Hari meditated upon the virtuous Tulasī,
worshipped her, and recited a hymn of praise with devotion.
Preceded by the seed-syllables of Lakṣmī, Māyā, Kāma, and Vāṇī, there is a ten-syllable mantra: "Vṛndāvanī" in the dative case (vṛndāvanai), ending with the wife of Fire (svāhā). || 10 ||
O Nārada, whoever worships with this king of mantras, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree, according to the prescribed rite, shall certainly attain all perfections.
With a ghee lamp, incense, vermilion and sandalwood paste, with food offerings, flowers, and ritual services, O Nārada. (12)
Pleased by the hymn of Hari, that auspicious goddess appeared from the tree;
with her lotus-feet gracious, she went for refuge.
Viṣṇu granted her a boon, saying: "May you become worthy of worship by all;
I shall carry you, so beautifully formed, upon my head and upon my chest."
"All the gods and others shall bear you upon their own heads.
Having spoken thus and taken her with him, the Lord departed for his own abode. (15)
Nārada said:
O highly fortunate one, what is the meditation, what is the hymn of praise, or what is the procedure for the worship of Tulasī? You ought to explain that to me. (16)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: When she had vanished, Hari,
afflicted by the pangs of separation, went to Tulasī in Vṛndāvana and offered her praise.
The Blessed Lord said:
Since the multitudes of forms and the trees exist together in one place, the wise know her as Vṛndā; she is my beloved, and I worship her.
In ancient times, there was a goddess who first appeared in the forest of Vṛndāvana;
because of that, she is renowned as Vṛndāvanī, and I worship her, the embodiment of auspicious fortune.
And because she is worshipped incessantly throughout all the innumerable worlds, I worship her who is known as Viśvapūjitā (Worshipped by the Universe) and who is herself the Worshipped One. || 20 ||
And you have always [established] countless and universal purifiers; I remember that Goddess, the purifier of the universe, with longing in my separation. (21)
The gods are not satisfied with this multitude of flowers without her;
therefore, out of grief, I wish to see that pure Puṣpasārā.
Since the bliss of devotion certainly arises for all beings merely by attaining her, she became renowned here as Nandinī; may she be pleased with you. (23)
Because there is no equal to this goddess among all beings in the entire universe, she is renowned as Tulasī; I go for refuge to her, my beloved. (24)
She who is the very embodiment of Kṛṣṇa’s life, the eternally beloved and virtuous one—may she, as Kṛṣṇajīvanī, protect my life. (25)
Having thus offered praise,
the Lord of Ramā stood there and beheld the virtuous Tulasī herself, bowing at his lotus feet.
Seeing his beloved weeping due to the insult she had suffered— she who was proud and honored for her self-respect— the lover quickly took her onto his chest.
Having received the command of Bhāratī, Hari went to his own abode and quickly caused her to establish affection with Bhāratī. 28.
Viṣṇu granted her this boon: "You shall be worthy of worship by all;
you shall be borne upon the heads of all, and honored and revered by me. (29)
By the boon of Viṣṇu, that goddess Sarasvatī became thoroughly pleased; having drawn her near, she caused her to dwell in her presence.
O Nārada, Lakṣmī and Gaṅgā, smiling, then drew that virtuous woman toward them and with humility caused her to enter their home.
Vṛndā, Vṛndāvanī, honored by the universe, purifier of the universe, essence of flowers, the delighter, Tulasī, and the life of Kṛṣṇa. || 32 ||
Whoever recites this hymn of eight names, which is endowed with the meaning of those names, after having worshipped her, shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. || 33 ||
On the full moon day of Kārttika, the auspicious birth of Tulasī occurs;
there, her worship was ordained by Hari in ancient times.
Whoever worships her with devotion there—she who purifies the entire universe—is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. || 35 ||
He who offers a tulasī leaf to Viṣṇu in the month of Kārtika certainly obtains the fruit of giving ten thousand cows. || 36 ||
One without a son obtains a son, one bereft of a beloved obtains a beloved, and one deprived of kinsmen obtains kinsmen, merely by hearing this hymn. (37)
The sick shall be liberated from disease; the bound shall be released from bondage;
the fearful shall be freed from fear; and the sinner shall be delivered from sin.
Thus has this hymn been told; now hear the method of meditation and worship. You yourself know that which is declared in the Veda and specifically in the Kaṇva recension. (39)
One should worship her with devotion at that tree without an invocation;
having meditated upon her with the ritual offerings, such meditation destroys all sins. (40)
Tulasī is the essence of flowers, virtuous, pure, and enchanting;
she is like a blazing crest of fire for burning the fuel of committed sins. (41)
Among flowers, there is no comparison for her; thus it is declared in the Vedas.
She is celebrated as Tulasī, the most sacred form among all. 42.
To be borne upon the heads of all, desired by everyone, the purifier of the universe, bestowing liberation while living and granting final emancipation—I worship her who grants devotion to Hari. (43)
Having meditated thus, and having worshipped and praised [her], the wise man should bow down.
The narrative of Tulasī has been told; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Worshipping Tulasī," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Regarding the narration of the ritual for the worship of Sāvitrī,
Nārada said:
"This narrative of Tulasī has been heard, which is like very sweet nectar."
Therefore, you should explain to me that narrative concerning Sāvitrī.
By whom was she first manifested? She is heard of as the mother of Śruti; by whom was she worshipped in the world at the beginning, and by whom in later times?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O sage, in the first [kalpa] the Mother of the Vedas was worshipped by Brahmā;
in the second, by the hosts of Vedas, and after that, by the hosts of the learned.
Then King Aśvapati honored him in Bhārata,
and after that, the four social orders (varṇas) likewise honored him.
Nārada said: O Brāhmaṇa, who was this Aśvapati, and by whom was that Goddess— who is worthy of worship by all— worshipped first, and by whom later?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O sage, in the land of Madra there was a great king named Aśvapati;
he was the destroyer of the strength of his enemies and the dispeller of the suffering of his friends.
He had a great queen, his principal consort, who practiced the Dharma;
she was known as Mālatī, just as Lakṣmī is to the wielder of the mace.
And that queen, though barren, O Nārada, performed the propitiation of Sāvitrī with devotion according to the instruction of Vasiṣṭha.
The queen did not receive a reply, nor did she see her;
afflicted by grief and with a burning heart, she went home.
Seeing her thus distressed, the king, having enlightened her through wise counsel,
then departed for Puṣkara out of devotion to Sāvitrī’s ascetic penance.
There he performed austerities for a hundred years with self-restraint;
yet he did not see Sāvitrī, and she became unattainable to him.
And the lord of men heard an incorporeal voice from the sky saying:
"O Nārada, perform ten lakhs of recitations of the Gāyatrī."
In the meantime, Parāśara arrived there;
the sage then bowed to him and spoke to the king.
The Sage said:
A single recitation of the Gāyatrī removes the sin born of the day;
by ten recitations alone, the sin of both day and night shall perish. (14)
Reciting it one hundred times removes the sin accumulated over a month;
reciting it one thousand times removes the defilement accumulated over a year. (15)
A hundred thousand [recitations] destroy the sin committed in this life; one million destroy that born of another life;
and ten million destroy the sin committed throughout all lifetimes. (16)
The recitation (japa) of this brings liberation to the Brahmins; it is ten times more effective than that [mere recitation].
Having formed the hand into the shape of a serpent’s hood with its opening closed, [one should perform the rite]. (17)
A twice-born man, facing east, should recite [the mantra] with his head bowed and body steady;
he should move [his fingers] from the middle of the ring finger downwards in a counter-clockwise direction.
The procedure for recitation in the hand is as follows, up to the base of the index finger;
it is performed with white lotus seeds and consecrated crystal beads. (19)

O King, having fashioned a garland, one should recite [mantras] at a sacred ford or in a temple; having placed the garland upon a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha) or a lotus, one should remain self-restrained.
Having smeared it with gorocana, the wise one should bathe it with the Gāyatrī mantra;
he should then recite the Gāyatrī a hundred times over it according to the prescribed ritual.
Alternatively, having bathed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should thoroughly consecrate the garland;
or else, having bathed with the very water of the Gaṅgā, one should make it well-consecrated.
"O royal sage, perform the recitation in this manner for ten lakhs in succession;
through the destruction of the sins of three births, you will behold Sāvitrī in person. (23)
O King, you shall perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) every single day—
at midday, at evening, and always in the morning— remaining ever pure.
One who neglects the twilight prayers (sandhyā) is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts;
whatever deed he performs during the day, he shall not partake of its fruit.
He who does not attend to the morning [prayer] and does not worship at the evening [prayer] should be excluded from all duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra. (26)
And that Brahmin who performs [this] three times at each junction of the day for as long as life lasts, is always equal to the sun in splendor and ascetic power.
The earth was instantly purified by the dust of his lotus feet;
he was a radiant one liberated while living, like a twice-born man purified by the twilight prayers.
And by the mere touch of him, even the sacred fords become purified;
consequently, sins depart from him just as serpents flee before Vainateya. (29)
The gods do not accept the worship, nor do the ancestors accept the funeral cakes and libations,
from a twice-born man who acts according to his own whims and who neglects the three daily junctures.
He who does not revere the primordial nature (Mūlaprakṛti), nor honors her mantra, and is devoid of her festivals, is like a serpent deprived of its venom. || 31 ||
A twice-born man who is devoid of the Viṣṇu-mantras, who neglects the three daily prayers,
and who omits the Ekādaśī vow, is like a serpent deprived of its venom.
A Brahmin who eats the food offered to Hari as naivedya, who serves as a washerman or a bullock-driver,
or who eats the food of a Śūdra, is like a serpent devoid of venom.
That Brahmin who burns the corpse of Śūdras is the husband of a Vṛṣalī;
and he who is the cook for Śūdras is like a serpent devoid of poison. || 34 ||
A twice-born man who accepts gifts from Śūdras, one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras,
one who lives by the sword, and one who lives by a razor are like a snake devoid of poison.

That Brahmin who sells his daughter, he who sells the name of Hari, that Brahmin who eats the food of a woman without a husband, and he who eats the food of a woman who has just bathed after her menses; || 36 ||
A Brāhmaṇa who lives by the bhaga, a usurer, or one who sells knowledge—each is like a serpent devoid of poison. || 37 ||
That twice-born man who sleeps at sunrise, who eats fish,
and who is devoid of the worship of Śiva and other rites, is like a serpent without venom.
Having spoken thus, the best of sages explained to him the entire sequence of the ritual for worship, as well as the desired meditation on Sāvitrī and other such practices. (39)
Having given everything to the lord of men, O Sage, she went to her own hermitage;
the king, having honored Sāvitrī, beheld her and obtained his boon.
Nārada said: What was the meditation of Sāvitrī, or what was the procedure for her worship?
Having given what hymn and what mantra did that Parāśara depart? (41)
By what ritual did the king worship the Mother of the Vedas, and what boon did he obtain after worshipping her according to the prescribed injunctions? (42)
I wish to hear all of that—Sāvitrī’s supreme and great secret, even the most profound secret—which is established in the Vedas, in brief. (43)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the auspicious time,
the observer of the vow should diligently and with devotion perform the rite on the fourteenth day as well.
Having observed the vow for fourteen years, accompanied by the fruits of twice seven [fortnights],
one should offer the oblation of twice seven times and perform the rites with flowers, incense, and so forth.
Having placed the garment, the sacred thread, and food according to the prescribed rules,
one should set down an auspicious jar provided with fruits and twigs.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Agni, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śivā, the twice-born man should worship his chosen deity within the pitcher once it has been invoked.
Listen to the meditation on Sāvitrī as it was taught for the midday rite,
as well as the hymn, the ritual procedure for worship, and the mantra that grants all desires.
She possessed the luster of molten gold and blazed with the splendor of Brahman,
her radiance equal to a thousand suns at the midday of summer.
With a face brightened by a gentle smile, adorned with jewel ornaments,
wearing garments as pure as fire, her very form exists for the sake of bestowing grace upon her devotees.
She bestows happiness and liberation, she is peaceful and beloved to the Creator of the worlds;
she is the embodiment of all prosperity and the giver of every kind of wealth.
I worship that Mother of the Vedas, the presiding goddess of the Vedas, whose very nature is the Vedic scriptures, and who is the essence of the seed-syllables of the Vedas. 52.
Having meditated with concentration and offered the food oblation, and placing his hand upon his own head,
the observer of the vow, having meditated again, should devoutly invoke the Goddess into the water-pot.
Having offered the sixteen services as prescribed in the Vedas accompanied by mantras,
and having worshipped and praised her, one should prostrate before the Goddess of gods according to the ritual injunctions.
A seat, water for the feet, an offering of honor, materials for bathing, unguents, incense, a lamp, food offerings, betel-leaf, and cool water. (55)
Garments, ornaments, garlands, perfumes, water for rinsing the mouth, and a charming, excellent bed—these sixteen items are to be given. (56)
Whether it be fashioned from the heartwood of trees or constructed from gold and other precious materials, I have described to you this support for the deity, which bestows merit. (57)
Holy water from sacred fords and water for the feet, which bestow merit and grant great joy—pure and forming an integral part of worship—I have offered this to you. (58)
This arghya, which is pure in form, accompanied by dūrvā grass and flower petals, bestowing merit, and sprinkled with water from a conch shell, is offered by me to you. (59)
May this fragrant scented water and the unguent that produces a sweet aroma, offered by me with devotion, be accepted as an article for bathing. (60)
O Mother, this fragrant water, produced from aromatic substances, which bestows merit, grants joy, and imparts divine fragrance, is offered by me to you with devotion. (61)
O Supreme Goddess, accept this excellent incense, which is the embodiment of all auspiciousness, the bestower of all blessings, and the giver of merit.
This lamp, endowed with fragrance, bestowing happiness, and producing light, has been offered by me to you for the sake of the worlds' vision. (63)
I have declared to you the seed-syllable that destroys darkness;
it bestows contentment, nourishment, and joy, and it annihilates hunger. (64)
May you accept this offering of food, which bestows merit and is pleasing in form;
and this excellent, delightful betel-leaf, beautifully scented with camphor and other ingredients. (65)
I have offered you this water, which bestows contentment and nourishment;
it is very cool, refreshing, and the cause for the destruction of thirst.
May life, which is the very essence of the livelihood of the worlds, be accepted;
it is the nature of bodily splendor and the enhancer of the beauty of the assembly. (67)
May garments made of cotton and those produced from silk be accepted—clothes fashioned from gold and other precious materials, which always bring prosperity and are endowed with splendor. (68)
"Accept this jewel-ornament, which bestows happiness and merit, produced from various trees and endowed with diverse forms. (69)

May that which is the very nature of the fruit, the bestower of the fruit, and the fruit itself; which is the form of all auspiciousness and the most auspicious among all auspicious things—be accepted.
"May you accept this garland, fashioned from various flowers, endowed with great beauty, bestowing joy and merit. (71)
O Goddess, please accept this merit-bestowing incense rich in fragrance, and this excellent, beautiful vermilion which greatly enhances the beauty of the forehead. (72)
And please accept this excellent ornament among all ornaments—sindūra—which is pure, bound with knots, and fashioned from a sacred thread. 73.
Let the sacred thread be taken up with a Vedic mantra;
having offered these articles with the root mantra, the wise one should recite the hymn.
Then, with devotion, the observer of the vow should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin;
[he should offer it] with the word "Sāvitrī" in the dative case, ending with the wife of Agni (svāhā). 75.
They know the eight-syllable mantra to be preceded by Lakṣmī, Māyā, and Kāma;
and the hymn spoken by Mādhyandina bestows the fruit of all desires. (76)
And learn from me as I describe the form of Viprajīvana, which Sāvitrī was given by Kṛṣṇa to Brahmā in the past at Goloka. (77)
O Nārada, she did not come with him to the world of Brahmā;
instead, by the command of Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā, out of devotion, praised the Mother of the Vedas.
Then, being highly pleased, she desired Brahmā as her husband.
Brahmā said:
"O you whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, you are the embodiment of Mūlaprakṛti. (79)
O beautiful one, be gracious in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha;
O supreme one, whose nature is splendor, you who are the embodiment of supreme bliss! 80.
O beautiful one, be pleased with the birth and form of the twice-born;
O Goddess, who are eternal, eternally beloved, and whose very nature is eternal bliss. (81)
O beautiful one, be gracious, you who are the embodiment of all auspiciousness;
O you whose nature is everything, the essence of the mantras of the Brahmins, and higher than the highest! 82.
O Goddess, bestower of happiness and liberation, be gracious, O beautiful one; you who resemble the crest of a blazing fire for the purpose of burning away the sins of the Brahmins. 83.
O Goddess who bestows great splendor, be gracious, O beautiful one!
Whatever sin a man commits through body, mind, or speech— [84]
"By the mere remembrance of that reality, it shall be reduced to ashes.
Having spoken thus, the Creator of the worlds remained right there in the assembly.
Having praised King Aśvapati with this king of hymns, Sāvitrī went to the world of Brahmā together with Brahmā. (86)

And he beheld that Sāvitrī and obtained the boon desired in his heart. Whoever, having performed the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), recites this meritorious king of hymns, obtains that very fruit which one gains from the recitation of the four Vedas. || 87 ||

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Worship of Sāvitrī," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
In the narrative of Sāvitrī, the description of the dialogue between Yama and Sāvitrī; Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having praised him with this [hymn], that Aśvapati, having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites...
There he beheld that goddess, whose splendor was equal to a thousand suns. || 1 ||
And she, being gracious and virtuous, spoke to the king with a smile,
illuminating the quarters with her luster like a mother to her own son.
Sāvitrī said:
"I know, O Great King, what is desired in your mind;
I shall certainly grant you everything that is desired by you and by your wife. (3)
Your beloved wife desires a virtuous daughter, while you pray for a son; both shall come to pass in due course.
Having spoken thus, that goddess then departed for the world of Brahmā;
the king went to his own home, and she first became his daughter.
And through her propitiation, Kamalā became supreme;
King Aśvapati gave her the name Sāvitrī.
In time, as she grew, she became more beautiful day by day; endowed with beauty and youth, she was like a digit of the moon in the bright fortnight.
She then chose as her boon Satyavat, the son of Dyumatsena,
who was truthful in character and endowed with manifold virtues.
The king gave her to him, adorned with jewel ornaments;
he too, out of curiosity, took her and went home.
And when the year had passed, Satyavān, whose valor was truth,
went out at his father’s command for the sake of gathering wood and fruit, filled with great joy.
The virtuous Sāvitrī followed after him; however, by the turn of fate, Satyavān fell from the tree and, through destiny, gave up his life. || 11 ||
O Sage, having seen that man who was bound like a thumb, Yama seized him and departed; thereafter, Satī followed after him.
Thereafter, having seen that woman of beautiful teeth, Yama, the lord of Saṃyamanī,
the great and foremost among the virtuous, spoke sweetly to that chaste lady.
The King of Dharma said:
"Aha! Where are you going, Sāvitrī, having assumed a human body?
If you shall go with your beloved, then renounce this body."
A mortal, being himself perishable, cannot go to my world while grasping this perishable body composed of the five elements; for he is always subject to destruction.
Indeed, the time for your husband's departure has arrived while the Bhārata period endures;
Satyavān goes to my abode in order to experience the fruits of his own past actions. (16)
A living being is born through karma and perishes through karma alone;
happiness, suffering, fear, and sorrow are brought about by karma alone. (17)
By his own karma a living being becomes Indra; by his own karma he becomes a son of Brahmā;
and by his own karma he may become a servant of Hari, free from birth and other such conditions. (18)
By one's own action, one shall certainly attain all perfections and immortality;
by one's own action, one may obtain the fourfold state of Sālokya and the rest from Viṣṇu.
By this deed, a man may attain the state of a god, the state of a man, and the status of a lord of kings;
likewise, he may attain the state of Śiva and even the status of Gaṇeśa.

And by one's action, the state of a lord of sages is attained; by one's own action, the state of an ascetic; by one's own action, the status of a Kṣatriya; and by one's own action, the status of a Vaiśya. (21)
One attains the state of a barbarian through action alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
Through one's own action one attains the state of a moving being, and through one's own action the state of a mountain.
Through action one attains the state of a Rākṣasa, and through one's own action the state of a Kiṃnara;
through action alone one attains sovereignty, and through one's own action the state of a tree.
By action alone one attains the state of a beast, and as a forest-dweller by his own action;
by action one becomes a low creature, and by his own action a worm. (24)
"Your status as a Daitya, a Dānava, and an Asura is due to your own karma.
Having said this to Sāvitrī, Yama indeed fell silent.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Dialogue between Yama and Sāvitrī," in the Sāvitrī-upākhyāna of the ninth book of the Śrīmad-devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 27.
In the narrative of Sāvitrī, the description of the dialogue between Yama and Sāvitrī: Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Yama, the devoted wife Sāvitrī—
Having praised him with supreme devotion, the high-minded woman spoke to him.
Sāvitrī said: What is that action? By what means is it performed, and what indeed is its cause?
Who is the embodied soul, and what is the body? Or who here is the agent of action? (2)
What is knowledge, and what is the intellect? What is the vital breath of embodied beings?
What are the senses, what is their defining characteristic, and who are their presiding deities? (3)

Who is the enjoyer, or who is the one who causes enjoyment? What is enjoyment, and what is its cessation? Who is the individual soul (jīva), and who is the supreme self (paramātman)? You should explain these to me. || 4 ||
Dharma said:
Dharma is that which is ordained by the Vedas; whatever action is auspicious is supreme. But whatever action is non-Vedic is indeed inauspicious. (5)
Service to the Divine that is causeless and free from conceptual construction,
which takes the form of uprooting karma— that alone bestows supreme devotion.
Who indeed experiences the fruit of karma, and who remains entirely untainted? That man who is a devotee of Brahman is declared in the Vedas to be liberated.
O virtuous lady, He is free from birth, death, old age, disease, sorrow, and fear;
and devotion is of two kinds, as declared in the Śrutis and approved by all. (8)
She bestows the state of Nirvana and grants the form of Hari to men;
indeed, the Vaiṣṇavas desire devotion whose very nature is the form of Hari.
Other yogins, the best among the knowers of Brahman, desire nirvāṇa;
yet [this world] is the seed-form of karma, which constantly yields its fruit.
The Blessed One, the Supreme Self, is both action and form; he is the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti).
He too exists in the form of its cause, yet the body is indeed perishable.
Earth, wind, space, water, and likewise fire—
these are the forms of the thread (sūtra) of the Existent during the process of creation.

The embodied soul is always the agent of action, the enjoyer, and the one who causes others to enjoy; it is experience, the various manifestations of power, as well as bondage and liberation itself. || 13 ||
And knowledge, which is the seed of the distinction between the existent and the non-existent, becomes manifold;
it is proclaimed as the differentiating seed of the various divisions of objects. (14)
Intellect is discernment, and it is heard in the Veda as the seed of knowledge;
the various breaths, such as prāṇa and the rest, are the forms of strength for embodied beings. 15.
And he is the most excellent among the senses, a portion of the Lord, free from pride,
the impeller of actions, and indeed difficult for embodied beings to restrain.
That which is indiscernible and invisible, yet is a differentiation of knowledge, is known as the mind (manas).
The eye, the ear, the nose, the skin, and the tongue are the sense organs (indriyas). 17.
It appears as the limbs of the possessor of limbs, as the impeller of all actions,
in the form of an enemy, in the form of a friend, and as that which bestows happiness as well as suffering.
The sun, the wind, the earth, and the deities beginning with Brahmā are traditionally taught [to be its forms];
for that which sustains the vital breath, the body, and so forth, is proclaimed as the individual soul (jīva). || 19 ||
The supreme, all-pervading Brahman, devoid of qualities and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), is called the Supreme Self (paramātman), the cause of all causes. || 20 ||
"Thus everything you asked has been told by me according to the scriptures, as well as the nature of the knowledge of the wise. Go, my child, as you please. (21)
Sāvitrī said:
"Having abandoned my beloved husband, where else could I go, for you are surely an ocean of knowledge?
Whatever question I may ask, you ought to answer it. (22)
To what various wombs does the living being go, and by what action?
By what action, O Father, does one go to heaven, and by what to hell? (23)
By what action does liberation occur, and by what does devotion toward the Guru arise?
By what action does one become a yogi, and by what action does one become diseased? (24)
By what [cause] is one long-lived, and by what action is one short-lived?
By what action is one miserable, and by what action is one happy? (25)
By what karma does one become deficient in limbs, or one-eyed, or deaf?
Or by what karma does one become blind, or even lame, or heedless? (26)
By what action does one become a despised person, excessively greedy, or a thief?
And by what does one attain the fourfold perfection, beginning with *sālokya*? (27)
By what means is one a Brāhmaṇa, and by what is one an ascetic?
By what does one obtain the enjoyments of heaven and so forth, and by what action does one attain Vaikuṇṭha? (28)
O Brahmin, by what means is Goloka the most excellent and free from all affliction?
Of how many kinds are the hells, how many are they in number, and what are their names? (29)
Who goes to which hell, and for how long does one remain there?
By what sinful deed is which disease produced?
You ought to explain to me all that I have asked regarding whatever is dear to me. (30)

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between Yama and Sāvitrī," within the Legend of Sāvitrī, in the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada, in the ninth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
In the narrative of Sāvitrī, there is a description of the ripening of karma.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Sāvitrī, Yama was struck with wonder.
Laughing, he began to speak concerning the ripening of the karma of living beings.
Dharma said: "O child, you are now twelve years of age;
yet your knowledge is supreme, like that of ancient sages, the wise, and the yogis."
By virtue of the boon granted by Sāvitrī, you were formerly obtained as a portion of Sāvitrī herself by the king through his ascetic penance; O daughter, you are equal to her.
Just as Śrī is on the lap of the Lord of Śrī, and Bhavānī is on the chest of Bhava;
just as Aditi is with Kaśyapa, and Ahalyā is with Gautama.
As Śacī is to Mahendra, as Rohiṇī is to the Moon, as Rati is to Kāmadeva, and as Svāhā is to Agni; || 5 ||
Just as Svadhā is among the ancestors, as Sandhyā is in the sun, as Varuṇānī is in Varuṇa, and as Dakṣiṇā is in the sacrifice; || 6 ||
Just as the Earth and Devasenā were [devoted] to Varāha in the month of Kārtika,
so too are you, Saubhāgyā Supriyā, dear to Satyavān.
"This boon has been granted to you, and furthermore, whatever else you desire;
listen, O illustrious goddess, I shall grant every wish."
Sāvitrī said:
"O highly fortunate one, may there be a hundred sons born of the loins of Satyavat; this is the boon I desire. (9)
"May my father have a hundred sons, and may my father-in-law regain his sight; may there be the acquisition of a kingdom—this is the boon desired by me. (10)
"After one hundred thousand years have passed, O Lord of the World, I shall go to the abode of Hari together with Satyavat; now, O Lord, take back this body of mine. (11)
I have a great curiosity to hear about the ripening of Jīvaka’s karma;
you should explain to me that which is the seed for liberation from the entire world.
The King of Dharma said:
"O great virtuous lady, everything you have desired shall come to pass.
Listen as I describe the ripening of the fruits of your past actions."
The birth of both auspicious and inauspicious karmas occurs in Bhārata, the field of merit, and nowhere else; moreover, people experience the fruits of all such actions there.
The Suras, Daityas, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, and others, as well as men who produce karma—not all of these are living beings, O Satī. (15)
Those who live by specialized means experience the results of their actions across all wombs;
whether auspicious or inauspicious, they encounter them everywhere—in heavens and in hells alike.
In particular, living beings wander through all wombs and experience the supreme fruits of their previously acquired karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious. (17)
By means of auspicious karma, one goes to the heavenly worlds and so forth;
and by means of inauspicious karma alone, they wander through the hells.
Devotion for the uprooting of karma is said to be twofold:
here, devotion in the form of liberation [is directed] toward Brahman, and [devotion] toward Prakṛti.
Through evil action one becomes diseased, and through auspicious action one becomes free from disease;
through action one becomes long-lived or short-lived, and happy or miserable. (20)
Those who are blind or otherwise deficient in their limbs, as well as those who perform despicable actions, attain success and other fruits through the most excellent of deeds. (21)
The general [method] has been told, O Goddess; now hear the specific [method], O beautiful one, which is very difficult to obtain and well-guarded even in the Purāṇas and the Smṛtis.
Human birth is difficult to attain among all births in Bhārata;
among all [humans], the Brāhmaṇa is the most excellent and is praised for all ritual acts. (23)
O Satī, among those existing in Bhārata, the twice-born who is devoted to Brahman is most venerable;
and the Brāhmaṇa is of two kinds, O Satī: one who is free from desire and one who possesses desire.
One who possesses desire is a seeker of worldly excellence, while one free from desire is truly a devotee;
the one with desire is an enjoyer of the fruits of action, whereas the one free from desire is beyond all affliction.
Having abandoned the body, he goes to that state which is free from all affliction;
for those who are free from desire, O Satī, there is no returning again.
Those devotees, assuming divine forms, worship the two-armed Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul and Lord, and they proceed toward Goloka. || 27 ||
Those possessed of desire and the Vaiṣṇavas, having gone to Vaikuṇṭha itself, return again to Bhārata; their birth occurs among the twice-born.
And when time has passed, they will gradually become free from desire;
furthermore, I shall certainly bestow upon them pure devotion.
Even those who are Brāhmaṇas and Vaiṣṇavas, if they possess desires throughout all their births and are devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu, their intellect is not pure. || 30 ||
O virtuous lady, those twice-born who reside at sacred fords and are devoted to asceticism go to the world of Brahmā, yet they return again to Bhārata.
Those who are devoted to their own duties and dwell in other holy places go to Satyaloka, and they return again to Bhārata.
In Bhārata, those Brahmins who are devoted to their own duties and devoted to the Sun go to the world of the Sun, and they return again to Bhārata. (33)
Those who are devoted to the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), free from desire, and practitioners of dharma,
go indeed to Maṇidvīpa, from which there is no return.
Devoted to their own respective duties, those devotees of Śiva, Śakti,
and Gaṇeśa go to the world of Śiva, yet they return again to Bhārata.
Those Brahmins who worship other deities, yet remain devoted to their own duty,
go to all the worlds and return again to Bhārata.
And those twice-born ones who are devotees of Hari, free from desire, and devoted to their own duty—they too go to the world of Hari by the power of devotion in due course; oh, how wonderful!
Brahmins who are devoid of their own dharma, who never worship the gods, and who have fallen from right conduct and are driven by lust, certainly go to hell. (38)
Indeed, the four castes, when devoted solely to their own duties, become the enjoyers of the fruits of auspicious action alone. (39)
And those who are devoid of their own karma certainly go to hell;
in Bhārata, they do not at all become enjoyers of the fruits of their actions.
The four castes are indeed devoted to their own duties;
the Brahmins are devoted to their own duties, and likewise [the others] are devoted to their own duties.
Those who give a maiden in marriage to a Brahmin go to the world of the Moon;
O virtuous lady, they dwell there as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
It is said that the fruit of giving a woman adorned with ornaments is twofold;
those who possess desire go to that world, but the virtuous who are free from desire do not.
Devoid of attachment to the accumulation of fruits, they go to the world of Viṣṇu;
[they offer] cow-products, silver, gold, clothing, clarified butter, fruit, and water.
Those who indeed give gifts to Brahmins go to the world of the Moon;
O virtuous lady, they dwell in that world for as long as a Manvantara.
Because those people who give gold, cows, copper, and other such things dwell there for a very, very long time, they [are so called]. (46)
They go to the world of the Sun because of their purity and their devotion to a Brahmin;
O virtuous lady, they dwell in that world for ten thousand years.
Free from disease, they dwell for a long time in a vast [abode];
he gives land to the Brahmins and abundant wealth as well. (48)
He goes to the world of Viṣṇu, the enchanting Śvetadvīpa;
there he dwells indeed as long as the moon and the sun endure.
O Sage, those people who with devotion give a house to a brahmin, the meritorious one, dwells in a vast residence for a vast duration. (50)
They go to the world of Viṣṇu, which bestows happiness for a very long time;
and in that most exalted world of Viṣṇu, [they dwell] for as long as the dust of their house remains.
When a house exists, men occupy it extensively;
and to whichever deity a man gives that house, [to him he offers his dwelling]. (52)
He goes to his world, and for as many years as there are particles of dust;
in a mansion the merit is fourfold, and in a sacred place the fruit is a hundredfold.
The Lotus-born One has said that for one who constructs a tank for the removal of all sins, the merit is double that of the aforementioned [gift] when it is of superior quality. (54)
That man goes to Janaloka and indeed to Renu-mānābda;
he always obtains ten times the fruit of [offering] at a pond.
But by the gift of a step-well, he shall obtain the fruit of a tank, provided it is clearly visible for four thousand bow-lengths. (56)
Or even less than that—such a pond is proclaimed to be contained within a *prastha*;
yet a daughter is equal to ten such ponds if she is given to a worthy recipient. (57)
If it is adorned, it yields double the fruit;
and whatever fruit is obtained from a pond, that same fruit is obtained from its excavation.
And by clearing away the mud from a pond, one obtains a fruit equal to that of constructing a pond; likewise, he who plants an Aśvattha tree and performs its consecration [obtains great merit].
O Sāvitrī, he who gives a flower garden for the welfare of all beings goes to the world of austerity (Tapoloka) for ten thousand years.
He who gives a celestial chariot to Viṣṇu while in the land of Bhārata shall certainly dwell in the world of Dhruva for ten thousand years.
He too shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu for as long as a supreme Manvantara;
and if it is joined with a painting, his fruit is fourfold.
He who, endowed with devotion, gives a palanquin to Hari, shall certainly obtain half of that very fruit which is obtained from giving a swing-temple.
O devoted wife, he who constructs a royal road provided with palatial mansions shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu for as long as a hundred manvantaras.
He too is honored in the world of Śakra for ten thousand years;
furthermore, he shall obtain a fruit equal to that of giving gifts to Brahmins and to the gods.
For that which is given is what one enjoys; what is not given does not remain [as a reward].
Having enjoyed the happiness born of heaven and other realms, the meritorious person takes birth in Bhārata.
Having enjoyed the fruits of heaven and other realms, the meritorious Brahmin in Bhārata will, in due course, be born successively among the highest and other classes of Brahmin families. (67)
Furthermore, even he may become a Brahmin, and likewise a Kṣatriya or others;
or a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya after hundreds of millions of kalpas.
"One does not attain the status of a Brahmin through austerity alone; this is heard in the Śruti.
Karma that has not been experienced does not perish even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. (69)
The fruit of every action performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, must necessarily be experienced.
One is purified through a multitude of bodies, with the assistance of deities and sacred fords.
This much has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ripening of Karma," within the Sāvitrī episode of the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada, in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 29 ||
Sāvitrī said: "O Yama, by what very same karma do people go to heaven or to another [state]?"
And how men become meritorious—you should explain that to me. || 1 ||
The King of Dharma said:
"O Bhārata, he who bestows a gift of food upon a brāhmaṇa is honored in the world of Śiva for as many years as there are grains of food."
He who gives the gift of food, even to others, performs a great gift;
and by the measure of that gift of food, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of food.
In this matter, there should be no examination of the recipient's worthiness, nor any restriction regarding the time.
O virtuous lady, if one offers a seat to the gods or to Brahmins,
one is honored in the world of Viṣṇu for ten thousand years.
He who gives a divine, milch cow to a Brahmin is honored in the world of Viṣṇu for as many years as there are hairs on that cow.
A gift given on a meritorious day yields fourfold merit, at a sacred ford (tīrtha) the fruit is a hundredfold, but in the field of Nārāyaṇa, the fruit becomes ten millionfold.
He who gives a cow to a Brahmin in Bhārata with devotion is honored in the world of the Moon for ten thousand years.
And he who makes a gift of a cow with two faces to a Brāhmaṇa is honored in the world of Viṣṇu for as many years as there are hairs on its body.
He who gives a beautiful white umbrella to a Brāhmaṇa rejoices in the abode of Varuṇa for ten thousand years.
O virtuous lady, he who gives a pair of garments to a Brahmin whose limbs are afflicted is honored in the world of Vāyu for ten thousand years.
He who gives a Śālagrāma stone along with a cloth to a Brāhmaṇa is honored in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as the moon and the sun endure.
He who gives a divine, enchanting bed to a Brāhmaṇa is honored in the world of the moon for as long as the moon and sun endure.
He who gives a lamp to the gods and to a Brahmin is honored in the world of Agni for as long as a Manvantara.
If one gives an elephant as a gift to a Brahmin in Bhārata,
that man shall dwell upon half of Indra’s throne for as long as Indra remains there.
He who gives a horse to a Brāhmaṇa in Bhārata rejoices in the world of Varuṇa for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras endure.
Indeed, he who gives an excellent palanquin to a Brāhmaṇa rejoices in the world of Varuṇa for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras endure.
O virtuous lady, he who indeed gives an excellent garden to a Brāhmaṇa is honored in the world of Vāyu for as long as a Manvantara.
He who gives a fan or a white chowrie to a Brahmin is certainly honored in the world of Vāyu for ten thousand years. || 19 ||
He who gives grain or jewels shall become long-lived and wise;
both the giver and the receiver will certainly go to Vaikuṇṭha.
The man who constantly chants the name of Śrī Hari in Bhārata is indeed long-lived; therefore, death flees from him.
The wise man who causes a swing to be set in motion in the land of Bhārata at the end of the night on the full moon day—that man shall become liberated while living. || 22 ||
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes at the end to the abode of Viṣṇu;
he shall certainly dwell there for the duration of a hundred manvantaras.
The fruit [obtained] under Uttaraphalgunī shall be even double that;
he shall live until the end of the kalpa—so said the Lotus-born One.
And whoever makes an offering of sesame seeds to a Brahmin in Bhārata rejoices in the abode of Śiva for a period of time equal to the weight of those seeds in years. (25)
Then, having attained a good birth, he shall live long and be happy;
by the gift of a copper vessel, he obtains double that fruit.

He who gives to a Brāhmaṇa in the land of Bhārata a beautiful and beloved wife, adorned with ornaments, clothed in garments, devoted to her husband, and fit for enjoyment—[attains the highest merit]. (27)
He is honored in the world of the moon for as long as the fourteen Indras endure; there he rejoices day and night together with a celestial nymph. (28)
Then, for ten thousand years in the world of the Gandharvas,
he certainly rejoices day and night with Urvaśī out of curiosity.
Then, for a thousand births, he obtains a beautiful and beloved wife— one who is virtuous, endowed with good fortune, delicate, and sweet-spoken.
And that man who gives beautiful fruit to a Brāhmaṇa is honored in the world of Śakra for as many years as there are fruits. || 31 ||
Furthermore, having attained a good womb, he obtains an excellent son;
and a thousand praised trees that bear fruit are [offered]. || 32 ||
Or, by giving the gift of the fruit alone to a Brāhmaṇa,
one dwells in heaven for a very long time and then returns to the land of Bhārata.
And he who gives a spacious house in Bhārata to a brāhmaṇa, furnished with various articles and provided with various grains; || 34 ||
He shall dwell in the world of the gods for as long as a hundred manvantaras;
thereafter, having attained a good birth, he shall become possessed of great wealth.
Whatever man, being virtuous, gives with devotion to a Brahmin land that is beautiful and endowed with crops in the meritorious field of Bhārata; || 36 ||
He is certainly glorified in Vaikuṇṭha for a hundred manvantaras;
then, having obtained a good birth once again, he becomes a great sovereign of the earth.
The earth does not abandon him for even a hundred future births;
he shall be illustrious, wealthy, possessed of sons, and a lord of subjects.
He who gives a cow-station and an excellent village to a twice-born man is honored in Vaikuṇṭha for a hundred thousand Manvantaras.
Furthermore, having attained a noble birth endowed with a hundred thousand villages,
the earth does not abandon him for even a hundred thousand lifetimes.
It was blessed with excellent offspring, preeminent, endowed with ripened crops, and filled with various lotus ponds, trees, fruits, and creepers. || 41 ||
He who gives a city to a Brahmin on the land of Bhārata is glorified on Kailāsa for ten million Indrakāla periods.
Furthermore, having attained a noble birth, he shall become a lord of kings in Bhārata;
he will obtain a hundred thousand cities—of this there is no doubt. (43)
The earth certainly does not abandon him for ten thousand births;
he shall indeed possess supreme sovereignty upon the surface of the earth.
And he who indeed gives to a twice-born man a hundred cities and a region that is very fertile, moderately fertile, and populated with subjects; || 45 ||
Endowed with ponds and lakes and graced by various kinds of trees,
he is honored in Vaikuṇṭha for the duration of ten million manvantaras.
Having attained a noble birth once again, he shall become the lord of Jambudvīpa,
endowed with supreme sovereignty upon the earth just like Śakra.
The earth does not indeed abandon him for ten million births;
he shall become a great lord of kings, living until the end of the kalpa.
He who bestows his entire office upon a twice-born man will undoubtedly obtain a fourfold reward at the end; of this there is no doubt.
Whoever gives Jambudvīpa to a Brahmin ascetic shall obtain a hundredfold fruit at the end; of this there is no doubt. || 50 ||
Of one who frequents all the sacred fords of the land of Jambudvīpa, who performs all forms of austerity, and who makes his dwelling in all [these places]; || 51 ||
For the giver of all gifts and the lord of all accomplishments, there is indeed rebirth;
however, for the devotee of the Great Lord, there is none.
They behold the passing away of countless Brahmās, the lords of the world;
they dwell on the Jewel Island in the supreme abode of the Śrī Devī.
And those who worship the mantra of the Goddess, having cast off their human bodies,
attain divine form and majesty that removes birth, death, and old age.
Having attained a form similar to that of the Goddess and performing service to her,
they behold on the Island of Jewels (Maṇidvīpa) the destruction of the world along with its divisions.
The gods and the Siddhas, along with all things in their entirety, perish;
but those devoted to the Goddess do not perish, for she removes birth, death, and old age.
He who offers Tulasī to Hari during the month of Kārtika rejoices in the abode of Hari for a duration equal to three Yugas.
Having attained a good birth once again, he will certainly obtain devotion to Hari;
he shall become the foremost among those who have conquered their senses on the earth of Bhārata.
He who bathes in the middle of the Gaṅgā at the time of sunrise rejoices in the abode of Hari for sixty thousand yugas.
Having attained a good womb once again, he will certainly obtain the mantra of Viṣṇu;
and having cast off the human body, he goes again to the abode of Hari.
There is no returning from Vaikuṇṭha to the surface of the earth;
one performs service as a servant of Hari and likewise attains the state of having the same form (sārūpya).
Bathing daily in the Gaṅgā, he becomes purified like the sun upon the earth;
at every step, he certainly obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
The earth is instantly purified by the dust of his very feet,
and he rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha as long as the moon and sun endure.
Furthermore, having attained a noble birth, he will certainly obtain devotion to Hari;
liberated while living, exceedingly radiant, he shall become the foremost among ascetics.
Devoted to his own duty, pure, learned, and with senses conquered,
he shines intensely like the sun between the signs of Pisces and Cancer.
He who gives even water that is well-scented in Bhārata rejoices on Kailāsa for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Furthermore, having attained a good birth, he shall be handsome and happy;
he shall be a devotee of Śiva, radiant, and one who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
He who gives an offering of roasted barley flour (saktu) to a twice-born man in the month of Vaiśākha rejoices in the abode of Śiva for as many years as there are particles of dust in that flour.
Whoever performs the Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī vow in Bhārata is liberated from the sins committed throughout a hundred lifetimes; there is no doubt about this. (69)
He too rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as fourteen Indras endure;
then, having attained a good birth once more, he will certainly obtain devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
Whoever observes Śivarātri right here in this land of Bhārata rejoices in the world of Śiva for the duration of seven manvantaras.
He who offers a bilva leaf to Śiva on the night of Śivarātri rejoices in the abode of Śiva for as many ages as there are leaves in that offering.
Having again attained a good birth, he will certainly obtain devotion to Śiva;
he shall become possessed of knowledge, sons, prosperity, progeny, and land. (73)
Or if, in the month of Caitra or Māgha, a practitioner of vows worships Śaṅkara and dances with devotion day and night, holding a cane in his hand; || 74 ||
Whether for a month, or half a month, or for ten, seven, or even two days,
he too is honored in the world of Śiva for an age (yuga) equal in duration to that time.
Indeed, that man in Bhārata who observes Śrī Rāmanavamī rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu for the duration of seven manvantaras.
Having attained a good birth once again, he will certainly obtain devotion to Rāma;
he shall become the foremost among those who have conquered their senses, great, and wealthy. (77)
O virtuous lady, he who performs the great autumnal festival with buffaloes, goats, rams, rhinoceroses, frogs, and other such creatures; || 78 ||
With food offerings and presents, as well as incense, lamps, and the like;
with dances, songs, musical instruments, and various auspicious festivities. (79)
He shall dwell in the world of Śiva for the duration of seven manvantaras;
then, having attained a noble birth, that man shall possess pure intellect.
He attains incomparable prosperity that increases his sons and grandsons;
endowed with great majesty, he is possessed of elephants and horses.
He too shall undoubtedly become a sovereign lord of kings;
thereafter, having reached the eighth day of the bright fortnight, he who worships Mahālakṣmī— || 82 ||
Having offered with constant devotion for one fortnight in the sacred field of Bhārata the sixteen excellent articles of worship to her, || 83 ||
He shall also dwell in Goloka for as long as the fourteen Indras endure;
then, having attained a noble birth once more, he shall become a sovereign lord of kings.
And on the full moon day of Kārttika, having fashioned the Rāsa-maṇḍala,
he likewise created a hundred cowherds and a hundred cowherdesses.
In India, one should worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa together with Rādhā with devotion upon a stone slab or in an image, offering the sixteen types of ritual services (upacāras). (86)
He shall dwell in Goloka for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā;
then, returning once more to Bhārata, he shall attain firm devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
Having gradually attained firm devotion to Hari’s mantra,
alas, he abandons his body and goes once again to Goloka.
Then, becoming a foremost attendant (pārṣada), he shall attain the same form as Kṛṣṇa;
thereafter there is no falling back, and he becomes one who removes old age and death.
Whoever observes the Ekādaśī, whether it be the bright or the dark fortnight,
rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā endures.
Returning again to Bhārata, he will certainly attain devotion to Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, he gradually makes his singular devotion to Hari very firm. (91)
Having abandoned the body, he goes once again to Goloka;
then, having attained the same form as Kṛṣṇa, he becomes an attendant.
Furthermore, there is no falling back for him; he shall become a remover of old age and death.
And that man who worships Śakra on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada [attains this]. || 93 ||
For sixty thousand years he is honored in the world of Śakra,
[having performed this on] a Sunday, at the time of the sun's passage (saṃkrānti), or on the seventh day of the bright fortnight.
He who, having worshipped the Sun, partakes of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) in Bhārata,
is honored in the world of the Sun for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
Having returned to Bhārata, he shall become healthy and endowed with prosperity;
for whoever worships Sāvitrī on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha.
He is glorified in the world of Brahmā for the duration of seven manvantaras;
then, returning to earth once more, he becomes illustrious and possessed of incomparable valor.
He who worships Sarasvatī on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha shall become long-lived, wise, and endowed with prosperity.
Having restrained himself and offered the sixteen services with devotion,
he is honored on Maṇidvīpa day and night for as long as Brahmā exists.
And having attained rebirth once more, he shall become a wise and learned poet—
indeed, he who gives land, gold, and other such gifts to a Brāhmaṇa.
For as long as one lives, if one remains endowed with devotion in Bhārata,
one dwells for a number of years equal to the hairs on the bodies of cows, and twice that many in the abode of Viṣṇu.
He rejoices together with Hari through the auspicious delights of play;
at the end of that, returning once more, he shall become a sovereign lord of kings.
In Bhārata, he who feeds sweet food to the Brāhmaṇas becomes illustrious, possessed of sons, learned, endowed with knowledge in every respect, and happy. (103)
He rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu for as many years as there are hairs on his body;
thereafter, returning here once more, he shall become happy and wealthy.
He who recites or indeed gives the names of Hari in Bhārata becomes wise, long-lived, illustrious, and possessed of incomparable valor. (105)
One who possesses the measure known as a *yuga* is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
