thereafter, returning again to this world, he shall become happy and wealthy. (106)
If the fruit at the sacred field of Nārāyaṇa were to be multiplied ten millionfold,
it would belong to him who recites the name of Hari ten million times in the field of Nārāyaṇa.
Completely liberated from all sins, he shall certainly become one who is liberated while living;
he shall not undergo rebirth again, for he is glorified in Vaikuṇṭha.
He shall attain the same form as Viṣṇu, and for him there shall be no falling away;
he shall also obtain devotion to Viṣṇu and reach the state of being identical in form with Viṣṇu.
He who constantly worships Śiva by fashioning an earthen liṅga goes to the abode of Śiva for as long as he lives.
For as many years as there are particles of dust in that clay, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
thereafter, returning here once more, he shall become a lord of kings in Bhārata.
One who constantly worships the stone and drinks the water from the stone is honored in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as a hundred Brahmās exist.
Then, having obtained rebirth and the rare devotion to Hari, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu; for him there shall be no falling back.
Having performed all austerities and every single vow,
he remains in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
Then, having obtained rebirth once more as a lord of kings in Bhārata, he shall thereafter be liberated, and no further rebirth exists for him. || 115 ||
He who, having bathed in all the sacred fords and having performed a circumambulation of the earth,
attains liberation and shall not be born again on this earth.
And he who performs an Aśvamedha sacrifice in Bhārata, the field of merit, shall occupy half of Indra’s throne for as many years as there are hairs on the horse's body. || 117 ||
A person obtains fourfold the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
for this sacrifice to the Goddess is remembered as superior even to all other sacrifices.
O lady of beautiful countenance, it was formerly performed by Viṣṇu and Brahmā,
and by Śaṅkara, the Great Lord, during the destruction of the Asura Tripura.
O beautiful one, the Śakti-sacrifice is the foremost among all sacrifices;
there exists no sacrifice equal to this in the three worlds. (120)
O Satī, in former times a great quarrel accompanied by a heated dispute took place between Dakṣa and Śaṅkara.
O Brahmins, Śeṣa cursed Nandin, and Nandin cursed the Brahmins out of anger—
for which reason the moon-crested Lord destroyed Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
In ancient times, that Prajāpati Dakṣa performed a sacrifice for the goddess, as did Dharma, Kaśyapa, Śeṣa, and Kardama. (123)
Svāyambhuva Manu, his son Priyavrata, Śiva, Sanatkumāra, Kapila, and likewise Dhruva. || 124 ||
One certainly obtains the fruit of thousands of Rājasūya sacrifices;
there is no sacrifice in the Veda that bestows greater fruit than the sacrifice of the Goddess. 125.
Living for a hundred years, he will certainly become liberated while yet alive;
through both knowledge and spiritual luster, he shall become equal to Viṣṇu in this world.
O Nārada, as Viṣṇu is among the gods and as the Vedas are among the scriptures, so is the Brāhmaṇa among the social classes. || 127 ||
Just as the Gaṅgā is among sacred fords, as Śiva is among the purifiers, as the Ekādaśī is among vows, and as Tulasī is among flowers; || 128 ||
As the moon is among the stars, as Garuḍa is among the birds, so is Rādhā among women; likewise are Vāṇī and Vasundharā. 129.
Just as the mind is among swift and flickering senses, so Brahmā is among the Prajāpatis, and the Prajāpati is among all creatures. || 130 ||
Vṛndāvana is among forests as Bhārata is among lands;
it is as Śrī is among the glorious, and as Sarasvatī is among the learned. (131)
Durgā is the foremost among devoted wives, and Rādhikā is the foremost among those possessed of good fortune;
likewise, O child, O beautiful lady, the sacrifice to the Goddess is the foremost among all sacrifices.
By a hundred horse-sacrifices alone, one certainly attains the status of Śakra;
and by a thousand, Pṛthu himself attained the station of Viṣṇu.
It is the bathing at all sacred fords, the initiation into all sacrifices, and indeed the fruit of all vows and ascetic penances. (134)
The study of the four Vedas, circumambulation of the earth, and all such fruits as these result from the service of Śakti, which bestows liberation. (135)
In the Purāṇas, the Vedas, and the Itihāsas everywhere,
the worship of the lotus feet of the Goddess is established as the very essence.
Describing him, meditating upon him, chanting his names and qualities, as well as reciting his hymns, remembering him, bowing to him, and muttering his mantra—these are [the means]. (137)
O virtuous lady, the consumption of the water from his feet and the food offerings (naivedya) is indeed always approved by all;
thus, this is desired by everyone.
Worship eternally the Supreme Brahman, who is beyond all qualities and the supreme primordial nature;
accept him as your husband, my child, and dwell happily in your home.
This auspicious ripening of karma for human beings has been told to you;
it is desired by all, approved by all, and is the supreme bestower of the knowledge of reality. (140)
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Ripening of Karma by Yama," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Eight Yamas.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the glorification of Śakti from the mouth of Yama, Sāvitrī [asked]:
With tears in her eyes and her hair standing on end, she spoke again to Yama.
Sāvitrī said:
O Dharma, the glorification of Śakti is the cause of the upliftment of all;
it removes birth, death, and old age for both the listeners and the speakers.
O Lord, the glorification and service of the Dānavas, the Siddhas, the supreme state of austerities, as well as of the Yogas and the Vedas [is established]. (3)
Liberation, immortality, and even the attainment of all supernatural powers do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit belonging to one who serves the Śrī-Śakti.
"O best among those who know the Vedas, tell me by what method I may worship; for I have heard the captivating account of the ripening of the auspicious karma of men. (5)
"And you ought to explain to me that karma which has an inauspicious ripening.
Having spoken thus, O Brahmin, Satī, with her neck bowed low in devotion, [continued].
And she praised the King of Dharma with a hymn declared in the Vedas.
Sāvitrī said:
"In former times, at Puṣkara, the Sun-god propitiated Dharma through ascetic penance. (7)
The Sun obtained Dharma as his son; I bow to that Dharmarāja, the witness of all, whose equanimity toward all beings is absolute. (8)
Therefore, I bow down to that which is called "Peace," by which the ultimate end has been made for all living beings in the universe. (9)
I bow to that Kṛtānta (the Ender), who at the proper time acts in accordance with one's desires;
he wields the staff for the sake of punishment, for the purpose of purifying the wicked. (10)
I bow to that wielder of the staff, who is the teacher of all living beings and who constantly sustains the entire universe within all things. 11.
I bow down to that Time which is exceedingly difficult to ward off;
he who is an ascetic, established in Brahman, self-controlled, and has conquered his senses.
I bow down to that Yama, who bestows the fruits of karma upon living beings;
he is one who delights in his own self, is all-knowing, and is a friend to those who perform meritorious deeds. 13.
I bow to that meritorious friend who brings affliction to sinners;
he whose birth was from a portion of Brahmā, blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
"I bow down to that Lord who meditates upon the Supreme Brahman";
having spoken thus, O Sage, Sāvitrī prostrated herself before Yama.
Yama spoke to Śaktibhaja regarding the ripening of karma:
"Whoever, having risen in the morning, should recite this *Yamāṣṭaka* daily," (16)
Because of this, he has no fear of Yama and is liberated from all evil.
If even a great sinner recites this daily, endowed with devotion,
Yama will certainly purify him through a manifestation of his own body-forms.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Eightfold Hymn to Yama," in the ninth book of the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
In the narrative of Sāvitrī, regarding the determination of the number of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas),
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Having first bestowed the great mantra of the seed-syllable of Māyā according to the prescribed rites..."
And the son of the Sun spoke to her concerning the impure ripening of karma.
The King of Dharma said:
"A human being does not go to hell as a result of the ripening of auspicious karma;
now listen as I describe the ripening of inauspicious karma. (2)
O beautiful lady, according to the various divisions of the Purāṇas and through different names,
the individual soul goes to heaven in manifold ways by means of its own actions.
Due to the ripening of auspicious karma, a person does not go to hell because of their actions;
however, through evil deeds, a person goes to various kinds of hells.
And there are various kinds of pits for the hells, according to the measurements of diverse scriptures and according to the distinctions of karma. (5)
And there are wide pits, O child, which cause affliction to the suffering,
terrifying, dreadful, and loathsome.
There are eighty-six sacrificial pits, and others as well;
learn their names as they are renowned in the sacred scriptures.
The fire-pit, the boiling-pit, the terrifying alkaline-pit, the dung-pit, the urine-pit, and the unbearable phlegm-pit. (8)
The pit of feces, the pit of excrement, and likewise the pit of fat;
the pit of semen, the pit of blood, and the loathsome pit of tears. (9)
There is a pit of bodily impurities and a pit of ear-wax;
there is a pit of marrow, a pit of flesh, and a difficult-to-cross pit of crocodiles.
The pit of hair, the pit of head-hair, and the pit of bones are difficult to cross;
the pit of copper and the pit of iron are intensely heated and grant great suffering. (11)
The pit of hides and the pit of boiling liquor are proclaimed;
as well as the pit of sharp thorns, the poison-water, and the pit of poison.
A pit of boiling oil, a pit of spears difficult to endure,
a pit of worms, a pit of pus, and a pit of serpents that brings a miserable end.
O lady of excellent vows, there is the pit of mosquitoes, the pit of gadflies, the terrifying pit of poison, and the pits of those with diamond-like fangs and of scorpions.
The pit of arrows, the pit of spears, and the terrifying pit of swords;
the pit of cows, the pit of crocodiles, and the pit of crows—a place of pure sorrow. (15)
The churning pit, the seed pit, and the unbearable diamond pit;
the pit of heated stones and the pit of sharp stones. || 16 ||
The Lālā-kuṇḍa, the Masī-kuṇḍa, and likewise the Cūrṇa-kuṇḍa;
the Cakra-kuṇḍa, the Vaktra-kuṇḍa, and the exceedingly formidable Kūrma-kuṇḍa. || 17 ||
O lady of pure smiles, there are the Jvālākuṇḍa, Bhasmakuṇḍa, and Dagdhakuṇḍa;
the Taptasūcī, Asipatra, Kṣuradhāra, and Sūcīmukha.
Gokāmukha, Nakramukha, Gajadaṃśa, and Gomukha; Kumbhīpāka, Kālasūtra, Matsyoda, and Kṛmitantuka. (19)
Pāṃsubhojya, Pāśaveṣṭa, Śūlaprota, Prakampana, Ulkāmukha, Andhakūpa, Vedhana, and likewise Tāḍana; || 20 ||
The lattice-opening, the powdering of the body, the crushing, the drying, the rubbing, the winnowing-basket, the flame-mouthed, the blinded by smoke, and the serpent-encirclement. (21)
"O Sāvitrī, these are the pits that inflict suffering upon sinners,
and they are constantly guarded by millions of hosts of Kiṅkara demons."
With staffs in their hands, nooses in their hands, intoxicated with pride, and terrifying;
with spears in their hands, maces in their hands, and swords in their hands, they were most dreadful. || 23 ||
[He was surrounded] on all sides by those possessed of darkness, devoid of compassion, and difficult to restrain;
by those full of brilliance, fearless, with eyes coppery and tawny.
By warriors endowed with yoga and supernatural powers who assume various forms,
and by sinners and all living beings whose deaths are imminent, it was beheld.
By all those devoted to their own duties—the Śāktas, the Sauras, and the Gāṇapatis—and by invisible beings, meritorious ones, Siddhas, and indeed Yogins; || 26 ||
By Vaiṣṇavas who are devoted to their own duty, or those who are widespread, independent, powerful, and fearless, as well as by those seen in dreams; || 27 ||
O virtuous lady, this description of the number of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) has been told to you;
now learn from me as I tell you which beings reside in which pit.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Number of Ponds," in the Sāvitrī episode of the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada, within the ninth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Regarding the description of the various fruits of the ripening of karma,
Dharmarāja said: "One who is devoted to the service of Hari, pure, perfected in yoga, observant of vows, and virtuous— "
An ascetic and a celibate student certainly do not go to hell. || 1 ||
That powerful man who, through harsh speech and an arrogance of strength, burns his kinsmen,
goes to the fire-pit.
Having remained there in that fire for a number of years equal to the hairs on one's own body,
one attains the womb of a beast, tormented by fierce suffering, for three births.
That fool who does not feed a Brahmin who has come to his house— thirsty, exhausted, and hungry— goes to the Taptakuṇḍa hell.
Having remained there for a period equal to the measure of his body hairs during that year of suffering,
he becomes a bird for seven lifetimes upon a heated ground and a bed of fire.
On Sundays, during the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), on the new moon day, and on the day of a Śrāddha ceremony,
a man should apply alkaline substances to his clothes alone.
He goes to the Kṣārakuṇḍa hell for as many years as there are threads [in the garment],
and he shall enter the womb of a washerwoman for seven births in Bhārata.
That lowest of men who reviles the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), as well as the Vedas, the Śāstras, and likewise the Purāṇas; || 8 ||
Likewise, there were people intent on censuring Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, as well as people intent on censuring Gaurī, Vāṇī, and the other goddesses. || 9 ||
They all go to that terrifying pit in hell;
there shall be no pit more painful than this.
Remaining there for many eons, one shall again enter the womb of a serpent;
there is no atonement for the offense of reviling a goddess. (11)
Whether it be a means of subsistence given by oneself or given by another to a god or a Brahmin,
he who destroys it shall go to Viṭkuṇḍa for sixty thousand years.
For that many years he remains there, feeding on excrement;
and for sixty thousand years he becomes a worm in dung upon the earth once again.
And he who constructs a tank upon another's tank shall,
by the fault of fate, be cast out and go to Mūtrakuṇḍa.
He remains there for as many years as there are particles of dust in that rain, subsisting on that very food;
then, when a full hundred years have passed, he shall become a bull in Bhārata once again.
Eating sweets all alone, he enters a pit of phlegm;
having consumed that food, he remains there for a full hundred years.
Then, after a full hundred years, that preta shall become pure in Bhārata;
thereafter, he eats only phlegm, urine, and pus until he becomes pure.
He who does not support his father, mother, teacher, wife, son, daughter, or the helpless, goes to Garakuṇḍa.
Having enjoyed that [food] there for a full hundred years, he remains;
thereafter he goes to Bhūtayoni, and after another hundred years, he becomes pure.
For that sinful man who, upon seeing a guest, looks askance with a crooked eye, his ancestors and the gods do not accept his water offering.
Whatever sins one may commit, such as the killing of a Brahmin and others, one experiences their consequences right here at the end, and shall go to the Dūṣikākuṇḍa hell.
Having enjoyed that [food] there for a full hundred years, he remains;
thereafter he goes to Bhūtayoni, and after another hundred years, he becomes pure.
If, after having given wealth to a Brahmin, it is then given to another,
he remains in a pit of fat for a hundred years, subsisting upon that very substance.
He shall become a chameleon for seven births in Bhārata;
thereafter, he shall be extremely fierce, impoverished, and short-lived.
Whether it be a woman who makes a man drink semen, or a man who makes a woman drink semen, he indeed goes to Śukrakuṇḍa. || 25 ||
Having eaten that [food], he remains there for a full hundred years;
then, having become pure, he shall enter the womb of a worm for a hundred years.
Having struck a venerable Brahmin and caused him to bleed,
he remains in a pit of blood for a hundred years, subsisting on that very blood.
Then he shall obtain birth as a tiger for seven births in Bhārata;
thereafter, that human being gradually attains purification. || 28 ||
That man who, upon seeing a devotee singing with a voice choked with emotion, sheds tears; yet he who indeed laughs at the congregational singing of the virtues of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (29)
He shall dwell in a pit of tears for a hundred years, subsisting on that [tears];
thereafter he becomes a Cāṇḍāla for three births, and after that, he becomes pure.
That man who constantly practices deceit toward a friend likewise goes for a hundred years to a pit of bodily impurities. (31)
Thereafter, he enters the womb of a donkey for three births;
for three births he enters the womb of a jackal, and after that, he certainly becomes pure.
He who, out of pride, laughs at or reviles a deaf person shall dwell for a hundred years in a pit of ear-wax, subsisting upon that very filth.
Thereupon, he would become deaf and impoverished for seven births;
after seven births he would be deprived of a limb, and thereafter he would certainly attain purification.
That man who, out of greed for his own sustenance, kills a living being,
shall dwell in the Marrow-pot (majjā-kuṇḍa) for a hundred thousand years, even if he eats its flesh.
Then he shall become a hare for seven births, and a fish;
for three births he shall be a boar, and a cock for seven births.
And by performing the rites beginning with the *eṇa* sacrifice, one shall certainly obtain purification from those [sins];
so too for that man who, having raised his own daughter, sells her. (37)
Out of greed for wealth, that great fool goes to the Pit of Flesh;
he remains there for as many years as there are hairs on the body of a maiden, subsisting upon that [meat].
The servants of Yama strike him with blows;
placing a burden of flesh upon his head, he licks a burden of blood out of hunger. (39)
For because of that, O Bhārata, the sinner shall become a worm in a girl's vagina for sixty thousand years, and a hunter for seven lifetimes. (40)
In three births he was a boar, in seven births a cock, and in seven births in Bhārata he was indeed a frog and a leech. (41)
For seven births he shall be a crow, after which he will certainly attain purification through the performance of vows, fasts, śrāddhas, and other rites. 42.
O beautiful one, he who performs the work of a barber is impure for all ritual acts; he remains in the pit of nails and the like. (43)
He who eats on that very day [of the lunar month] is struck by a staff;
or he who worships the earthen linga along with its hair in Bhārata.
He remains at Keśakuṇḍa for the duration of a rain of particles as small as atoms; at the end of that time, due to the wrath of Hara, he enters a Yavana womb.
After a hundred years, he attains purification; yet he certainly becomes a Rākṣasa who does not offer a funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) to his ancestors at the abode of Viṣṇu.
And he remains in a pit of bones for a year of his own hair-growth, which is exceedingly terrible;
thereafter, having attained a good womb, he is born lame in seven successive births.
That great fool who serves his own pregnant wife shall become extremely impoverished, and thereafter he shall indeed be purified from his body.
And he remains for a hundred years in a heated copper cauldron—
he who eats the food of a woman without a husband, as well as the food of a woman who has just bathed after her menses.
And he remains for a hundred years in a heated iron cauldron;
he shall go to the womb of a washerwoman and [be born as] crows for seven births.
A man who touches the property of the gods with hands smeared with leather shall thereafter become afflicted with a great ulcer and impoverished; only then does he become purified. || 51 ||
And he who, permitted by a Śūdra, eats the food of a Śūdra, remains in a leather vessel for a duration of one hundred years. (52)
That twice-born man remains in a cauldron of boiling liquor for a hundred years;
thereafter, he becomes a Brāhmaṇa who performs sacrifices for Śūdras for seven births.
And one who eats food at a Śrāddha ceremony performed by a Śūdra becomes pure only after that;
likewise, one who is corrupt in speech and harsh in his words should always strike his master. (54)
Eating that [food] there in a pit of sharp thorns, he remains there,
struck fourfold with a staff by the messenger of Yama.
Then Uccaiḥśravas said: "O pure one, that merciless man who kills a living being with poison shall suffer for seven births. (56)
And eating that [food], he remains in a pit of poison for a thousand years;
thereafter, he becomes a slayer of men and one afflicted with wounds for a hundred births.
He shall be afflicted with leprosy for seven births, and thereafter he will certainly become pure;
likewise, one who drives a bull shall strike both the cow and the bull with a staff.
Whether acting independently or through a servant, if one [fails to perform rites] in the sacred field of Bhārata,
they remain in a heated pit of oil or fire for the duration of four yugas.
After a period of years equal to the number of hairs on a cow's body, he becomes a bull;
thereafter, he who kills a living being with ease using a spear of fiery iron [is reborn as such].
O virtuous lady, he shall dwell in Kuntakuṇḍa for ten thousand years;
thereafter, having attained a good birth, he will be afflicted by diseases within the womb.
Then, by a single birth [in a lower state] due to that affliction,
a man who eats meat in vain out of greed for flesh— that lowest of the twice-born— becomes purified.
He who eats the food offered to Hari goes to the Kṛmikuṇḍa hell;
eating that [offering], he remains there for as many years as there are hairs on his body.

Then, in three births, he shall become a mleccha caste; thereafter, he becomes a twice-born man—a Brāhmaṇa who performs sacrifices for Śūdras and eats the food at the funeral rites (śrāddha) of Śūdras.
O virtuous lady, one who burns the corpse of a Śūdra shall certainly dwell in the Pit of Putrid Matter for as many years as there are hairs on the body, being punished by the rod of Yama.
Beaten by the messenger of Yama, he who consumed that food remains there;
thereafter, having returned to Bhārata, that Śūdra [remains so] for seven births.
That man who kills the serpent that devours the black lotus becomes afflicted with a great disease, impoverished, deaf, and mute. (67)
He goes to the Serpent-Pit for a period of years equal to the number of hairs on his own body;
there he is devoured by a serpent and struck by a messenger of Yama. (68)
He shall dwell as one who eats the excrement of snakes, and thereafter he will certainly become a snake;
after that, he will become a human being with a very short lifespan, afflicted by scabies.
His death will certainly come through great suffering, as if he were devoured by a serpent;
for he kills even small creatures whose lives have been granted by destiny. (70)
For a full year, he was confined in a pit with gadflies and mosquitoes;
day and night he was devoured by them, deprived of food, and filled with cries.
Bound by the hands and feet and beaten by the messenger of Yama,
he then becomes a lowly creature, and his birth shall be that of a dog.
Then he shall become a human being, but one who is deficient in limbs; thereafter he becomes pure—he who, though foolish, eats honey after having killed the honey-bees.
He alone shall dwell for a full year in a pit of poison,
devoured by poisons, scorched, and struck by the messengers of Yama.
From that [act], one becomes a member of the species of flies; from that, a man may become pure.
He inflicts punishment upon one who does not deserve it, and he also inflicts punishment upon a Brahmin. (75)
He goes quickly to the pit of the Vajradaṃṣṭra insects; there he remains day and night for as many years as there are hairs on their bodies. (76)
Devoured by those [beings] who produce sounds and struck by the messenger of Yama, O blessed lady, he utters cries of lamentation and shouts of "Alas! Alas! at every moment.
Furthermore, he is born in the womb of a pig for seven lifetimes;
then, after three lifetimes in the womb of a crow, the man becomes pure.
That fool who, out of greed for wealth, inflicts punishment upon his subjects,
will certainly dwell in a pit of scorpions for as many years as there are hairs on his body.
Then, for seven births in Bhārata, he will be born as a species of scorpion;
thereafter, he will certainly become a man who is physically deformed yet purified by disease.
A Brahmin who carries weapons, one who acts as a servant for others, a Brahmin who neglects the twilight prayers, and one who is devoid of devotion to Hari; || 81 ||
He remains for as many years as there are hairs on his body, pierced constantly by arrows and other weapons within sacrificial pits and similar sites; thereafter, that man becomes purified.
He who, being negligent through his own fault, causes the subjects to fall into a dark prison, goes to Golakuṇḍa. || 83 ||
He beheld a cow-pen-shaped pit filled with mud and heated water, shrouded in darkness and terrifying,
infested with insects possessing sharp fangs.
Pierced by insects, he shall dwell there for one year with his hair still intact;
thereafter he becomes a servant to his offspring, and from that point on, he gradually becomes purified.
The man who kills crocodiles and other creatures that have risen from the lake shall go to Nakrakuṇḍa for as many years as there are scales on the crocodile's body.
Then he will certainly become one of the species beginning with crocodiles among crocodiles and the like;
thereafter, indeed, he becomes purified immediately by means of repeated punishment alone. (87)
He who, being lustful with desire, gazes upon the chest, hips, breasts, or face of another's wife in the meritorious field of Bhārata; || 88 ||
He shall dwell in Kākakuṇḍa with his eyes pecked out by crows;
thereafter, for as many years as there are hairs on his body, he shall be burned through three births.
And that fool who steals gold from a god or a Brahmin in Bhārata shall certainly dwell in the Manthāna-kuṇḍa for as many years as there are hairs on his own body.
Beaten by the messenger of Yama, his eyes covered by churning-sticks, he shall eat that very excrement right there; thereafter, he shall be blind for three births.
For seven births he was poor, extremely cruel, and a sinner;
in Bhārata he was a goldsmith and thereafter a gold merchant.
O beautiful one, he who in Bhārata is a thief of copper or a thief of iron goes to Bījakuṇḍa for as many years as there are hairs on his body.
Eating seeds and excrement right there, with his eyes covered by seeds,
and being struck by a messenger of Yama, the man then becomes purified.
In Bhārata, a thief of gods and a stealer of divine property shall certainly dwell for as many years as he has hairs on his body in the Vajrakuṇḍa, which is difficult to cross.
Even if his body is burned by those vajras, remains without food, utters sounds, and is struck by the messengers of Yama, the man then becomes purified. || 96 ||
And whoever is a thief of silver, cows, or garments belonging to the gods or Brahmins,
shall certainly dwell for a year in a pit of heated stones, clothed in his own hair.
In three births Kaṃsa was also white in form, and in one birth he had white marks; the others were white-winged birds.
Then that man shall indeed become subject to blood disorders and colic for seven births; thereafter, he becomes purified. || 99 ||
The man who steals a vessel made of brass or bell-metal belonging to a deity or a Brahmin shall dwell for as many years as there are hairs on his body in the Tīkṣṇapāṣāṇa hell.
He shall be born as a horse for seven lifetimes in Bhārata;
thereafter, he shall be born with extra limbs, then suffer from a disease of the feet, and finally become pure.
O blessed lady, he who eats the food of an unchaste woman, or lives off one who subsists by the livelihood of an unchaste woman,
shall certainly dwell in the Pit of Saliva for as many years as there are hairs on his body.
Beaten by the messenger of Yama and eating that [food], he suffers there;
thereafter he suffers from eye-pain, and then he becomes pure in due course.
That Brahmin on the land of Bhārata who serves Mlecchas and lives by ink shall dwell for as many years as there are hairs on his body in the Pit of Ink (masīkuṇḍa), experiencing great suffering.
Beaten by the messenger of Yama, he remains there eating that [food];
thereafter, O virtuous lady, for three births he becomes a black-colored beast.
In three births he shall become a goat, and in three births a black-colored one;
thereafter he becomes a palmyra tree, and after that, he becomes a pure human being.
He who steals grain and other crops, betel leaves, a seat, or a bed from a god or a Brahmin goes to the Cūrṇakuṇḍa hell.
There he shall dwell for a hundred years, tormented by the messengers of Yama;
thereafter, he shall become a ram and a cock for three births.
Then he shall become a monkey on earth, afflicted with the disease of cough;
thereafter, he becomes lineage-less, poor, short-lived, and finally pure.
That person who seizes the property of Brahmins and thereby creates a circle of enmity shall dwell in the Cakrakuṇḍa hell for a hundred years, being beaten with clubs.
Then, in three births, he would become a human being and an oil-presser;
he would be afflicted by disease, a sick man, and thereafter, devoid of progeny, he becomes pure.
O virtuous lady, that man who practices deceit toward Brahmins who possess divine wealth goes to the Vakrakuṇḍa hell and shall remain there for a hundred yugas.
Then, for seven births, he shall have crooked limbs and deficient members;
thereafter, he shall be poor, of low lineage, and without a wife, until finally he becomes pure.
Thereafter, he would be born as a vulture for three lifetimes, and as a pig for three lifetimes;
then as a cat for three lifetimes, and as a peacock for three lifetimes.
If a Brāhmaṇa eats the forbidden meat of a tortoise,
he shall dwell in the Kūrma-kunda for a hundred years, being devoured by tortoises.
Thereafter, he would be born as a tortoise for three births, and as a boar for three births; then as a cat for three births, and as a peacock, after which he becomes pure.
That sinner who steals ghee, oil, or similar substances from gods or Brahmins goes to the Pit of Flames and the Pit of Ashes.
Having remained there for a hundred years, he shall be cooked in oil;
then, after seven births as a fish and a mouse, he becomes pure.
Whoever steals fragrant oil, myrobalan, or any other fragrant substance from a god or a brahmin in the meritorious land of Bhārata, [incurs great sin]. 119.
He shall dwell in a pit of burning coals and be scorched day and night;
for as many years as there are hairs on his body, he shall thereafter become foul-smelling.
One who possesses a foul odor [is reborn] for seven lifetimes; musk-deer [is reborn] for three lifetimes;
and for seven lifetimes one is a churning-stick (manthāna), after which he indeed becomes a human being.
In the land of Bhārata, even when it exists, a powerful man may seize the ancestral land of another through force alone, through deceit, or by means of violence. 122.
He shall dwell upon a heated needle and remain scorched day and night,
just as a living being is constantly burned in boiling oil.
The embodied soul is not reduced to ashes by the experience [of suffering], nor does it perish;
the sinner remains there, tormented, for seven manvantaras.
Struck by a messenger of Yama, the one who abstains from food utters cries;
thereafter, he becomes a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.
Then he becomes deprived of his caste and poor; thereafter he becomes pure, and having returned to his own birth, he performs auspicious deeds once again.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Fruits of the Ripening of Various Karmas," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
A description of the fruits resulting from various karmas.
Yama said:
"Devoid of compassion and extremely cruel, he cuts the living being with a sword."
In the land of Bhārata, a man who kills another out of greed for wealth destroys his own life.
He may even dwell in the Asipatra hell for as long as fourteen Indras;
he who kills Brahmins shall dwell there for a hundred Manvantaras.
With his limbs severed, he dwells there constantly upon the edge of a sword;
deprived of food and struck by the messengers of Yama, he utters loud cries.
For a hundred births he was a churning-stick, for a hundred births a boar;
for seven births a cock, and for seven births a jackal.
Struck by the messenger of Yama, he became a tiger for seven births, a wolf for three births,
and a frog for seven births.
He shall become a buffalo in the land of Bhārata, and thereafter he becomes pure;
so too for one who sets fire to villages or cities.
O virtuous lady, he might even dwell for three yugas upon the edge of a razor with his limbs severed;
thereafter, he would immediately become a *preta*, wandering the earth with fire in his mouth.
For seven births he shall be a pigeon eating impure food;
thereafter, for seven births he shall become a human being afflicted with a severe colic.
For seven births such a man suffers from leprosy; thereafter he becomes purified. He who whispers slander into another's ear while placing his own mouth there [is likewise reborn as such]. || 9 ||
One who praises great faults and reviles the gods and Brahmins shall dwell in the Sūcīmukha hell for three yugas, pierced by needles.
Thereafter, he shall become a scorpion and a serpent for seven births;
then a diamond-worm for seven births, and after that a fire-worm.
Thereafter he becomes a human being, and then he is purified;
for he who, having broken into the house of householders, commits the theft of their property, [undergoes this sequence].
He who goes to Gokāmukha with cows, goats,
and sheep shall dwell there for three yugas, being beaten by the messenger of Yama.
Thereafter, for seven births he shall be born as a cow, afflicted by disease;
for three births he shall be of the nature of a ram, and for three births, of the nature of a goat.
Then he would become a human being who is chronically ill and impoverished;
deprived of a wife and deprived of kinsmen, he would suffer and subsequently be purified.
A thief of common property goes to the mouth of a crocodile;
beaten there by a messenger of Yama, he shall dwell there for three years.
Thereafter, for seven births, he shall become an ox afflicted with disease;
thereafter he shall become a human being suffering from a great illness, and after that, he shall be pure.
He kills cows, elephants, horses, and likewise mountains;
that great sinner goes to the Gajadaṃśa hell for three yugas.
Constantly beaten with a goad by the messenger of Yama,
he shall become a species of elephant and a horse for three births.
A man born of the cow-caste or the mleccha-caste becomes pure thereafter—he who prevents a thirsty cow from drinking water. (20)
The hell is shaped like a cow's mouth and filled with heated water and worms;
there he remains tormented for the duration of a manvantara.
Then that man shall also be deprived of cattle, afflicted by great disease, and impoverished;
for seven births he shall belong to the lowest caste, after which the man becomes pure.
Indeed, he who approaches a woman who should not be approached incurs the same penalty as the killing of a cow or the killing of a Brahmin by extension;
and he who commits the murder of a woman incurs the same. (23)
In the land of Bhārata, that great sinner who commits the murder of a monk or the destruction of an embryo shall dwell in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
Beaten by the messenger of Yama and being constantly pulverized,
he falls for a moment into fire and for a moment into thorns.
For a moment he would fall into boiling oil, for a moment into [boiling] iron,
for a moment into heated metal, and for a moment into molten copper.
For a thousand births he was a vulture, for a hundred births a boar, for seven births a crow, and for seven births a serpent. (27)
For sixty thousand years he is born as a worm in excrement;
thereafter, through various births, he becomes a bull, then one afflicted with leprosy, and finally a pauper. (28)

Sāvitrī said: What constitutes the killing of a Brahmin and the killing of a cow? What is the nature of the most grievous sin? Who among men is forbidden as a guest, and who is one who has neglected the twilight prayers? (29)
Who is the man who has not been initiated, or who accepts gifts at sacred fords?
Who is the twice-born who performs sacrifices for a village, or the Brahmin who serves as a temple-priest? (30)
The cook of Śūdras and the intoxicated husband of a Vṛṣalī—
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell us all the characteristics of these.
The King of Dharma said:
"When Śrī Kṛṣṇa is present, as well as in his image, and in others in their natural state;
likewise when Śiva is present, as well as in the Śivaliṅga, and when the Sun is present, as well as in a sun-gem (sūryakānta). || 32 ||
O beautiful one, whether it be Gaṇeśa or Durgā,
he who thus conceives a sense of difference regarding them anywhere shall incur the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He who conceives a sense of duality toward his own guru, his chosen deity, his father who gave him birth, or his mother, incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He who conceives a sense of distinction between Vaiṣṇava devotees and other Brāhmaṇas shall incur the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
He who conceives a sense of duality regarding the water from a Brahmin’s feet and likewise the water from a Śālagrāma stone shall incur the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
He who conceives a sense of duality between the food offering to Śiva and the food offering to Hari shall incur the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
In Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of all lords, the cause of all causes, the primordial source of all,
the one to be served by all the gods, and the inner self of all.
He who creates a distinction between the one, indeed, qualityless Lord—who through *māyā* appears in many forms—shall incur the sin of killing a Brahmin. (39)
That mortal who harbors hatred toward a devotee of Śakti, and likewise toward the scripture of Śakti,
incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He who abandons the worship of the ancestors and the gods as ordained by the Vedas,
or he who performs what is forbidden, shall incur the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He who reviles Hṛṣīkeśa, as well as His devotee who worships His mantra—the eternal bliss of knowledge and the most sacred of all sacred things—[is lost]. 42.
Those who do not worship, and instead revile, the Lord who is the foremost of the Vaiṣṇavas and the one to be served by the gods, incur the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Those who revile the Great Goddess, who is the embodiment of the causal Brahman, who is the very nature of all powers, and who is Prakṛti, the mother of all; || 44 ||
They incur the sin of killing a Brahmin, which embodies the nature of all gods, is eternally worshipped by all, and is the form of the cause of all things.
The Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī, the Rāmanavamī which bestows great merit, as well as Śivarātri, Ekādaśī, and likewise [the day] on the Sun's day (Sunday). || 46 ||
Those men who do not observe the five auspicious festivals incur the sin of killing a Brahmin; they are more sinful than even the Cāṇḍālas. (47)
Those who dig the earth or perform water-purification rites and the like in the Ambuvācī river within the land of Bhārata incur the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He who does not support his guru, mother, father, virtuous wife, son, or daughter— provided they are blameless— incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He who has no marriage, he who does not see a son,
and he who is devoid of devotion to Hari— he shall incur the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He who eats the food offered to Hari but does not daily worship Viṣṇu,
nor the meritorious earthen liṅga— he is proclaimed to be a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
He who, seeing one striking a cow, does not restrain him, goes between the cow and the Brahmin and incurs the sin of cow-slaughter. 52.
That foolish brahmin who strikes a cow with sticks while riding upon a bull incurs the sin of killing a cow day after day; of this there is no doubt.
He who gives the leavings of food to cows, or causes a bull-driver to eat, or eats the food of a bull-driver, will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow. (54)
The man who officiates at a sacrifice for the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī), or the man who eats his food, incurs the sin of killing a hundred cows; of this there is no doubt. || 55 ||
He who places his foot in fire, or strikes cows with his foot,
or enters his home with unwashed feet, incurs the sin of cow-slaughter even after bathing.
He who eats with greasy feet, he who sleeps with greasy feet,
and he who eats at sunrise— such a person will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow.
The twice-born who eats the food of one who has no heroic sons, of one who lives by his wife,
and he who neglects the three daily prayers, incurs the sin of killing a cow.
She who harbors a sense of division toward her own husband or the deity, or strikes her beloved with harsh words, will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow. (59)
If one gives grain after clearing a path for cattle,
or at a pond or a difficult pass, he will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow.
He who commits a transgression regarding the expiation for killing a cow—whether out of a desire for a son or through ignorance—will certainly incur the sin of cow-slaughter himself. (61)
If a cowherd does not protect his cow through diligent effort against royal or divine threats, that fool who causes her suffering will certainly incur the sin of cow-slaughter. 62.
Indeed, he who steps over living beings, an image of a deity, fire, water,
an offering (naivedya), a flower, or food, will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow.
He who asserts that [the self] never exists is a speaker of falsehood, a deceiver, a hater of the gods, and a hater of the guru; he will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow. 64.
If one sees an image of a deity, or a guru, or a Brahmin,
and does not bow out of negligence, he will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow.
That twice-born man who, out of anger, does not grant a blessing to one who bows before him,
nor imparts knowledge to a seeker of learning, will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow.
The killing of a cow and the killing of a Brahmin have been described as cases of extended application;
now listen as I tell you about women who should not be approached by men. (67)
"One's own wife is to be approached by all; such is the instruction of the Vedas.
Those who know the Vedas understand that any woman other than her is not to be approached. (68)
All that has been stated is general; listen now to the particulars, O beautiful one. Understand those women who are strictly forbidden; I shall describe them to you. (69)

A Brahmin woman among Śūdras, and a Śūdra woman who desires a Brahmin, are both extremely unfit for sexual union and are censured in the world, the Vedas, and among those devoted to their husbands. (70)
A Śūdra who has approached a Brāhmaṇa woman incurs the sin of one hundred Brahman-murders;
and the Brāhmaṇa woman, being equal to him in that act, will certainly fall into the Kumbhīpāka hell.
If a Śūdra woman approaches the wife of a Brāhmaṇa,
or if a Brāhmaṇa approaches a Śūdra woman who desires him, that Brāhmaṇa indeed becomes the husband of a Vṛṣalī.
Having fallen from the status of a Brahmin, he is considered the lowest of Cāṇḍālas;
his funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) is equal to excrement, and his libation (tarpaṇa) is equal to urine.
What is given by him does not reach the ancestors or the gods;
his merit earned through ten million births and acquired through worship and austerity [is lost]. (74)
Due to lust for a *vṛṣalī*, the status of a twice-born man is surely destroyed; there is no doubt.
A Brahmin who drinks liquor, eats excrement, or is the husband of a *vṛṣalī* [is likewise lost]. (75)
A twice-born man whose body has been branded with heated seals, who is likewise marked with a heated trident, and who eats on the day of Hari, shall go to the Kumbhīpāka hell. (76)
The wife of a guru, the wife of a king, a co-wife, one's mother, a daughter, a daughter-in-law, a mother-in-law, a pregnant woman, a sister, and a chaste woman—[these must not be approached]. (77)
The wife of a uterine brother, a maternal aunt, the mother of one's father,
the mother of one's mother, her sister, a [half-]sister, and a brother’s daughter— || 78 ||
The Lotus-born One declared that a female disciple, a disciple’s wife, the beloved of a sister’s son, and even the wife of a brother’s son are women who must not be approached sexually.
That lowest of men who, out of lust, would approach these beloved women, is considered a violator of his mother in the Vedas and incurs the sin of a hundred Brahman-murders. (80)
Though unworthy of ritual action, untouchable in both the world and the Veda, and censured,
that great sinner goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell, which is most difficult to endure.
He who performs the twilight devotions improperly, or does not perform them at all,
or who avoids the three daily twilights— that twice-born man is one devoid of the twilight devotions.
He who, out of egoism, does not accept a mantra— whether Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Śākta, Saura, or Gāṇapa— is considered uninitiated.
Taking the current as the limit for a distance of four cubits,
there, within the interior of the Ganges, Lord Nārāyaṇa dwells.
One who dies there in the sacred field of Nārāyaṇa goes to the abode of Hari;
likewise at Vārāṇasī, at Badarī, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. (85)
At Puṣkara, in the sacred field of Hari-hara, at Prabhāsa, in the region of Kāmarūpa, at Haridvāra, at Kedāra, and likewise at Mātṛpura; || 86 ||
On the bank of the river Sarasvatī, in the sacred forest of Vṛndāvana, at the Godāvarī and the Kauśikī, at Triveṇī, and on the Himālaya; || 87 ||
He who accepts a gift out of desire at these sacred fords is a receiver of gifts at a holy site; he goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell.
One who serves Śūdras, performs sacrifices for Śūdras, or acts as a priest for a village is known as a Grāmayājī; likewise, one who subsists on the service of gods is proclaimed a Devala. (89)
He who lives by cooking for Śūdras is known as a *sūpakāra*;
one who is devoid of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā-pūjana*) and is negligent is considered fallen (*patita*). || 90 ||
"O blessed lady, I have described to you all the characteristics of the husband of a *vṛṣalī*.
These great sinners go to the Kumbhīpāka hell;
now listen as I tell you of the other pits (*kuṇḍas*) to which they go."

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of the Ripening of Various Karmas," within the Sāvitrī episode of the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada, in the ninth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 34 ||
Regarding the description of the various fruits of the ripening of karma,
Dharmarāja said: "O virtuous lady, without service to the gods, there can be no severing of karma."
Pure action leads to a pure seed, while hell results from evil action.
O devoted wife, that twice-born man who eats the food of an unchaste woman or has sexual intercourse with her goes, after death, to the most difficult-to-traverse Kālasūtra hell.
For a hundred years he will certainly remain fixed in the Kālasūtra hell;
having been born there as a sick man, he shall thereafter become a pure twice-born.

A woman with one husband is considered *pativratā* (devoted to her husband); with a second, she is known as *kulaṭā* (unchaste); with a third, she should be understood as *dharṣiṇī* (boldly licentious); and with a fourth, she is called a *puṃścalī* (prostitute).
In the fifth [generation] she is a courtesan, in the sixth a *puṅgī*, and in the seventh and eighth;
beyond that, she is a great courtesan (*mahāveśyā*), untouchable among all castes.
The twice-born man who approaches an unchaste woman, a wanton woman,
a harlot, a courtesan, or a great courtesan, certainly goes to Matsyoda.
One who approaches an unchaste woman incurs [the sin] for a hundred years; one who approaches a bold woman incurs four times that;
one who approaches a wanton woman incurs six times that; and one who approaches a prostitute incurs eight times that.
One who goes to a prostitute shall dwell there for ten times that duration; there is no doubt.
And one who lusts after a great courtesan shall dwell there ten times longer than that.
Right there, struck by the messenger of Yama, he suffers torment;
the partridge who goes to an unchaste woman, and the crow who goes to a bold woman.
One who approaches an unchaste woman becomes a cuckoo, one who approaches a prostitute is said to become a wolf,
and one who approaches a cow becomes a boar for seven births in the land of Bhārata.
And he who, devoid of knowledge, eats during the eclipses of the moon and the sun, is born as a *śālmalī* tree frequented by great prostitutes. (11)
He surely goes to a state of piercing pain, as well as to a year of humiliation;
thereafter, he becomes a human being afflicted by disease in the stomach.
One afflicted with a tumor, one who is one-eyed, and one who is toothless—these are pure thereafter;
as is he who gives away his own daughter, previously promised in marriage, to another man. (13)
O virtuous lady, he who steals that wealth shall dwell for a hundred years in a pit of dust,
subsisting on that very dust.
Struck by my messenger, he shall dwell upon a bed of arrows;
and that Brahmin who does not worship the earthen Śivaliṅga with devotion [shall suffer likewise]. 15.
Due to that sin, he goes to the most dreadful place impaled on a trident belonging to the Wielder of the Trident;
having remained right there for a hundred years, he becomes a beast of prey for seven births.
From that he shall become Devala for seven births, and thereafter pure;
he who, out of fear of whom the twice-born trembles, makes the Brahmin dull-witted.
One who trembles, wears a reddish garment, has hair standing on end, and whose face is contorted with rage as she looks at her husband out of anger; ||| 18 ||
He utters bitter words against him; indeed, my servant constantly hurls flaming torches into his mouth. (19)
One should strike her on the head with a staff as many times as there are hairs on her body for that year;
consequently, she shall become a human widow for seven births.
Having experienced widowhood and being afflicted by disease,
that pure Brahmin woman who was enjoyed by a Śūdra goes to the blind well.
In the darkness of the water heated by purification, she who consumes that [water] day and night shall dwell,
intensely tormented and struck by my messenger.
She remained submerged in the water for the duration of fourteen Indras;
she was a female crow for thousands of births and a sow for hundreds of births.
For a hundred births she becomes a jackal, for a hundred births a hen;
for seven births a pigeon, and for seven births a female monkey. (24)
Then she shall become a Cāṇḍālī, to be enjoyed by all in Bhārata;
thereafter she shall become a washerwoman, afflicted with consumption and a wanton woman.
Then the oil-maker shall be afflicted with leprosy and subsequently purified;
the prostitute shall dwell in a brothel, and the *puṅgī* shall be subjected to flogging with a staff.
A prostitute resides in the water-pores; an unchaste woman in the bodily powder;
a wanton woman in the crushing [of the body], and likewise a bold woman in the drying. (27)
Struck by my messenger, she shall dwell in torment,
constantly consuming feces and urine for as long as a manvantara, O virtuous lady.
Then he shall become a worm in excrement for a hundred thousand years, after which he becomes pure;
a Brāhmaṇa who approaches a Brāhmaṇa woman or even a Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya [who approaches a Brāhmaṇa woman], [shall likewise undergo this]. (29)
If a Vaiśya approaches a Vaiśya woman, or a Śūdra a Śūdra woman, or even a Śūdra [approaches a Vaiśya woman],
those people go to hell (kaṣāya) through their union with the wives of others who are of the same caste.
Having consumed the water of the Kaṣāya heated by fire, one may dwell there for a hundred years;
thereafter, a Brāhmaṇa becomes purified, and after that, indeed, the Kṣatriyas and others.
"Women also are purified," so said the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
O devoted wife, if a Kṣatriya or even a Vaiśya should approach a Brāhmaṇa woman, [the following applies]: 32.
He who approaches his mother shall dwell in the Śūrpa hell;
there he is devoured along with the Brāhmaṇa woman by worms shaped like winnowing baskets.
And he who eats heated urine, struck by my messenger,
suffers torment in that very place for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
For seven births he shall be a boar, and thereafter a goat; he who, having taken a Tulasī plant in his hand, does not fulfill his vow, shall become pure [only] after that.
He who makes a false oath shall go to Jvālāmukha;
likewise, he who takes the water of the Gaṅgā in his hand and does not fulfill his promise.
He who, having extended his right hand, does not fulfill his promise, shall go to Śilā or to a Deva-pratimā, or to Jvālāmukha. (37)
Or, having stayed in a temple of the gods, he shall go to Jvālāmukha;
by touching a Brāhmaṇa and a cow, the twice-born man shall go to Jvālāvahni.
He who does not fulfill his promise shall go to Jvālāmukha;
so too shall he who betrays a friend, the ungrateful, and he who is a violator of trust. (39)
And he who gives false testimony shall go to Jvālāmukha;
these indeed dwell there for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
Likewise, those scorched by glowing coals were struck by my messenger;
furthermore, a Cāṇḍāla who has touched Tulasī becomes pure after seven births.
O beautiful one, a Mleccha who touches the water of the Gaṅgā becomes pure after five births;
but one who touches her stone becomes a worm in excrement for seven births.
One who touches an image of a deity becomes a worm in a Brahmin's body for seven births, and thereafter becomes pure;
likewise, one who gives with the right hand alone becomes a serpent for seven births. (43)
From that, a man becomes bereft of Brahman; from that, he becomes pure [only after penance];
but one who speaks falsely in a temple of the gods becomes a *devala* for seven births.
One who touches a Brahmin or others will certainly be born as a tiger;
thereafter, he shall be mute and deaf for three births.
One devoid of a wife, one devoid of kinsmen, and one devoid of lineage is then pure;
a betrayer of friends is a mongoose, and an ungrateful person is a rhinoceros.
A betrayer of trust becomes a tiger for seven births in Bhārata;
and one who gives false testimony when it ought to be spoken becomes a frog for seven births. (47)
A twice-born man who is devoid of daily rites and possessed by dullness destroys seven ancestors, seven descendants, and himself. (48)
He who has no faith in the words of the Vedas laughs constantly and feebly;
he is devoid of vows and fasts, and is a reviler of those devoted to the words of the virtuous. (49)
He too shall dwell for a hundred years in Dhūmrāndha, subsisting on smoke;
and he shall become an aquatic creature through the succession of a hundred births.
Then one becomes various kinds of fish, and thereafter pure;
[but so too does] he who mocks the wealth of the gods or of Brahmins.
Having caused ten ancestors and ten descendants to fall,
he goes to that smoke-blind darkness filled with smoky gloom.
Afflicted by smoke and eating smoke, he shall dwell there for four times that duration;
thereafter, he will be born as a mouse for seven lifetimes in Bhārata.
From that [arose] various species of birds along with various species of insects;
from that, various kinds of trees and animals; and from that, human beings. (54)
A Brahmin who lives by astrology, one who lives as a physician or is a healer, one who trades in lac, iron, and the like, and one who sells mercury and such substances; || 55 ||
He goes to Nāgaveṣṭa, which is indeed surrounded by serpents; there he shall dwell for as many years as there are hairs on his body, bound by the nooses of the nāgas.
Then he becomes various species of birds, then a human being; thereafter, for seven births, he shall be an astrologer and a physician.
The cowherd, the blacksmith, and the dyer—these are pure;
and the well-known sacrificial pits have been described, O devoted wife. (58)
Furthermore, there are indeed other unknown and minor hells there;
in them dwell sinners who experience the fruits of their own actions, wandering through various wombs. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Various Karmic Ripenings," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Cessation of All Calamities through the Worship of the Deity.
Sāvitrī said:
"O Dharmarāja, O highly fortunate one, you who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences!"
Reveal that which is the essence found within the various Purāṇas and Itihāsas.
That which is the essence of all things, desired by all, and approved by all; which is the seed for the cessation of karma, and is praised as bestowing happiness upon men. (2)
It bestows everything upon all, and is the cause of all auspiciousness;
by means of it, indeed, all human beings perceive neither fear nor suffering. (3)
They do not see those pits, nor do they fall into them;
tell me now what that karma is by which birth and so forth would not occur.
What is the shape of those pits, or are they even man-made?
And in what form do the sinners remain there? (5)
When one's own body has been reduced to ashes, the person goes to another world;
with what body, then, does he experience the results of his auspicious and inauspicious deeds? (6)
O Brahman, how is it that the body does not perish despite the long experience of afflictions? Or what is the nature of this body? You should explain this to me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having heard the words of Sāvitrī, Dharmarāja, remembering Hari,
began to relate the narrative that cuts asunder the bonds of karma.
The King of Dharma said:
"O child, regarding the four Vedas, the Dharmashastras, the Samhitas,
the Puranas, the Itihasas, and the Pancaratra and other scriptures..."
O you of excellent vows, in all other Dharmaśāstras and Vedāṅgas,
the service of the five deities is declared to be the most desired and the very essence.
It destroys birth, death, old age, disease, grief, and torment; it is the embodiment of all auspiciousness and the cause of supreme bliss. || 11 ||
It is the cause of all perfections, the means of crossing over the ocean of hell,
the sprout that causes the tree of devotion to grow, and the cutter down of the tree of karma.
This is known as the ladder of liberation leading to the state of imperishability;
it is auspicious and bestows the rewards of dwelling in the same world, sharing the same power, possessing the same form, and being in close proximity [to the Divine]. (13)
O auspicious lady, those men who worship the five deities do not see the pits guarded by the messengers of Yama even in their dreams.
Those who are devoid of devotion to the Goddess see my abode;
likewise, those who go to Haritīrtha or observe the day sacred to Hari [attain it]. (15)
Those who constantly bow to Hari and perform worship of Hari do not go to my terrible city of Saṃyaminī.
Even Brahmins purified at the three junctions of time and endowed with pure conduct—such men will not attain liberation without service to the Goddess. (17)
Those whose conduct is devoted to their own duty, and likewise those who remain intent on their own duty—
even as they depart for the world of death, my messengers find them difficult to behold.
Terrified of the devotees of Śiva, like serpents before Garuḍa, I shall ward off my own messenger as he approaches with noose in hand. (19)
And they shall go everywhere, except to the hermitage of Haridāsa and to those who worship the mantra of Kṛṣṇa, just as serpents flee from Vainateya (Garuḍa). || 20 ||
And Citragupta, as if terrified, uses his fingernails as a stylus to cut away the names of those who worship the goddess-mantras. (21)
O virtuous lady, they repeatedly offer them the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other honors;
having transcended the world of Brahmā, they go to that higher realm.
Those by whose mere touch misfortunes are destroyed are indeed highly fortunate, for they purify a thousand lineages. (23)
And just as dry grass in a blazing fire reaches a state of total delusion upon seeing it, so too does one become terrified when beholding those [senses]. (24)
When desire exists, desire goes toward the desirer; from that, greed and anger arise.
Death is dissolved, as are disease, old age, sorrow, and likewise fear. (25)
Time, auspicious and inauspicious karma, joy, and likewise enjoyment— O virtuous lady, I have described to you those who do not undergo such suffering.
Listen; I shall describe the constitution of the body according to the traditional scriptures:
earth, air, space, fire, and water—this is clear. (27)
It is the seed of the body for embodied beings and the supreme factor in the Creator’s act of creation; it is that body which is constructed from the five elements, beginning with earth. (28)
That which is made of the thumb’s measure, fashioned as the individual soul (jīva) and the person (puruṣa), is artificial, perishable, and would here be reduced to ashes. (29)
He assumes that subtle body of such a form for the sake of experience;
yet that body would not turn to ashes in the blazing fire within my abode.
Whether by water, or by a blow struck for a very long time, or by a weapon, or by a missile, or likewise by a very sharp thorn, the embodied being is not destroyed.
In molten liquid, in heated metal, and likewise in a glowing stone; upon contact with a blazing image, and even when falling [into it] beforehand; || 32 ||
He is neither burned nor broken, yet he experiences only intense suffering.
I have described the state of the body and its causes according to the scriptures;
now, for the sake of your enlightenment, I shall tell you all the characteristics of the *kuṇḍas*.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Cessation of All Calamities through the Worship of the Goddess," in the ninth book of the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada. || 36 ||
Description of the Various Cauldrons of Hell.
Sāvitrī said:
Dharmarāja said:
O virtuous lady, the entire sacrificial pit was circular in shape like the orb of the full moon;
it was deep and had been fashioned by many through the breaking of stones.
That abode is neither perishable nor subject to dissolution, yet it is created by the will of Īśvara; it bestows affliction and is the source of all sins, manifesting in manifold forms. || 2 ||
The fire-pit is described as having the form of blazing coals, endowed with flames reaching a hundred cubits in height, and extending for a *krośa* all around.
It was filled with sinners making a great clamor,
and it was constantly guarded by my messengers who were striking them.
It was filled with boiling water, inhabited by predatory creatures,
most terrifying, and let out a harsh cry due to a powerful blow.
Measuring half a krośa, it was filled with my attendants who had been beaten by messengers and was further crowded with crows, being full of boiling alkaline water.
It was crowded with sinners, filled with wailing and terrifying, resounding with the cries of "Save me! from those struck by my messengers.
It was filled with those who were moving about without food, their throats, lips, and palates parched;
it was full of nothing but excrement, and it was wretched with its cries of distress.
It was permeated with an exceedingly foul stench and was constantly filled with sinners who had been beaten by my messengers and were consuming most dreadful food.
It was filled with the hot liquid of urine, crowded with urine-insects, and [filled] with those very insects being devoured while crying out the word "Protect! (rakṣa).

It was constantly infested by those great sinners who were like insects devouring it; it extended for a distance of two gavyūtis, was enveloped in darkness, and was filled with the incessant sounds they made.
When struck by my terrible messengers, whose throats, lips, and palates are parched, that [hell] is filled with phlegm; it is perpetually filled with insects that have subsisted upon it.
It was constantly surrounded by sinners who eat that [food],
and for half a krośa it was filled with poison-pits accompanied by those who consume poison.
It was indeed filled with sinful beings devoured by worms and insects,
and with those struck by my messengers, who were crying out and trembling.
With serpent-like, vajra-sharp fangs, parched throats, and being most terrible,
they [saw] the two eyes filled with filth and the area extending half a *krośa* teeming with insects.
It was perpetually crowded with sinful beings wandering about and devoured by insects; filled with marrow and fat, it extended for four krośas and was most difficult to endure.
One krośa in extent, Śukrakuṇḍa is filled with those sinners who ate that [food], struck by my messengers, and covered with śukra-insects. || 17 ||
It was perpetually crowded with sinful beings fleeing from it, infested by worms,
foul-smelling, filled with blood, and as deep as a large pond.
It was crowded with those who ate that [food] and with sinners; it was infested by insects, filled with tears from eyes, tormented, and inhabited by many evildoers.
And it was the size of a large pond, filled with the impurities from the bodies of men, accompanied by those sinful beings who feed upon them and wail as they are devoured by insects.
It was filled with my messengers who were beaten, agitated, and devoured by insects; it was packed with those sinners who had filled their ears with earwax and had themselves eaten that very wax.
And by those speaking of it as being the size of a fourth of a pond, [they saw] it filled with the marrow of men, consumed by worms, and possessed of a most foul stench. (22)
It was four *vāpīs* in extent, filled with great sinners and my messengers who had been struck down, their bodies covered in moist flesh.
It was crowded with evildoers, as terrifying as a vast pit,
filled with those who sell their daughters and those who eat their own kin, like insects devouring one another.
With terrifying beings who were frightened and crying out the word "Protect!",
[he struck] the four [beings] beginning with Nakha, each measuring the size of a pond and a musical instrument respectively.
It was constantly filled with sinners being beaten by my messengers,
and it contained cauldrons of molten copper along with glowing embers placed upon the copper.
It is always occupied by millions of glowing copper statues,
each embraced by a weeping sinner.
It was a vast expanse measuring a gavyūti, struck by my messengers,
filled with streams of molten iron and glowing embers.
It was filled with sinners weeping as they clung to iron images,
each one clinging to an image that was perpetually blazing with fear.
It was two gavyūtis in extent and filled with great sinners who were being beaten by messengers while crying out, "Protect us! Protect us! (30)
The iron pit (lohakuṇḍa) is proclaimed to be terrifying and filled with darkness;
likewise, there is the leather pit (carmakuṇḍa), the pit of heated liquor (taptasurākuṇḍa), and even half [of one] as well.
It is filled with those who eat and drink there and with my own struck messengers;
therefore, there is also the Śālmalikuṇḍa, adorned with the thorns of trees.
It was a hundred thousand paces in extent and measured one krośa, causing great suffering;
it was encircled by bow-lengths and extremely sharp thorns.
It was filled with those who had committed great sins, their limbs pierced one by one,
falling from the tops of trees, struck down by my messengers.
With dry palates, crying out the words "Give water!",
they were struck on the heads with staffs by those who were extremely agitated due to great fear.
It was filled with those who lived by boiling oil as they moved about,
and with the cries of Takshakas emitting poison, echoing from of old.
It was filled with sinful beings who feed upon that [flesh], and it was struck by my messengers;
it was full of boiling oil and devoid of insects and other such creatures. (37)
It was filled with great sinners who were surrounded by burning coals,
uttering piteous cries, writhing, and tormented by messengers.
Enveloped in darkness, crying out, causing affliction, and terrifying, it was surrounded by iron weapons with extremely sharp points shaped like spikes. (39)
The nature of the bed of weapons (śastratalpa) is such that it measures one *kośa* and four *turyas*;
it is surrounded by sinners pierced by spears and enveloped [by them]. (40)
And by my messengers who were beaten, their throats, lips, and palates parched, and by terrifying crawling insects as large as stakes; || 41 ||
O virtuous one, it was filled with hideous beings having sharp teeth, enveloped in darkness,
crowded with those who have committed great sins, and being struck by my messengers.
And they describe a pit of pus measuring two *gavyūtis* in size, filled with creatures that serve as its food and with my messengers who strike them down. (43)
It was covered by tens of millions of serpents as large as palm trees,
with the bodies of the sinners entwined by snakes and devoured by them.
It was crowded with my messengers who were making noise and with those being struck, and it was filled with three pits for mosquitoes and the like, teeming with mosquitoes and such creatures.
The entire treasury was half its former size and filled with great criminals, their hands, feet, and other limbs bound, amidst floods of blood and gore. (46)
While my attendants were being beaten, crying out "Alas! Alas!", the two of them filled their pit with thunderbolts and scorpions.
Or else, half [of the area] was occupied by sinners bitten by thunderbolts and scorpions;
and three sacrificial pits for the arrows and other weapons were filled with those very same things. (48)
The Golakuṇḍa pit is filled with thick darkness and boiling water, and it is joined with half of it by those pierced sinners who are blood-red.
It was filled with sinful beings who were being devoured by insects resembling spikes,
and it was crowded with terrified sinners who were themselves being eaten by those insects.
It is filled with weeping and wailing, and with my messengers who strike them;
it is pervaded by an extreme stench and is a constant source of suffering for sinners. (51)
It was filled with wicked beings of terrible and deformed appearance who were devouring [the victims],
and it was half-full— or even completely full— of millions of crocodiles dwelling in the water.
It was filled with hundreds of millions of those who consume feces, urine, and phlegm,
and it was joined by sinful beings being devoured by crows of hideous form.
The Manthāna-pit and the Bīja-pit extend for a full hundred bows each;
they are filled with sinners who have been devoured and who constantly produce sounds.
It was always crowded with sinners, filled with those who made noise and possessed adamantine fangs; it was a hundred bow-lengths long, strung with life, and utterly composed of dense darkness.
Twice the size of the pond, it was constructed of heated stones,
resembling glowing embers, and filled with moving sinners.
It was further constructed with supreme stones as sharp as razor-edges,
and it was filled with those who have committed great sins, along with pits of saliva and blood.
And for the distance of one krośa, it was filled for a hundred bow-lengths with my struck messengers, who resembled mountains of heated collyrium and were deep in depth.
It was filled with moving sinners being beaten by my messengers, full of powders and fluids, and accompanied by the wailing of the wicked. || 59 ||
By those who ate that [food], by those consumed by fire, and by my messengers who struck them,
the pit and the potter’s wheel were constantly whirling.
It was exceedingly sharp, possessed sixteen spokes, and was filled with pulverized sinners;
it was extremely crooked and depressed, measuring two gavyūtis in extent.
Its formation was like that of a mountain cave, filled with boiling water,
inhabited by great sinners, and containing devoured aquatic creatures.
It was filled with blazing, noise-making [beings] and enveloped in darkness, terrifying,
and most dreadful with tens of millions of tortoises of deformed shapes.
It was filled with those who dwell in water and joined by those sinful beings who had been devoured;
it resounded with the cries of those created from masses of flames and splendors.
It was filled with sinners who produced cries of distress, constantly causing suffering; it resounded with deep lamentations and was covered with glowing ashes. (65)
It was joined with those who constantly burned and were consumed as ashes by sinners,
and it was filled with masses of heated stones and iron.
It was filled with sinners whose limbs were scorched and whose palates were parched;
it was echoing with cries of distress, shrouded in darkness, profound, and exceedingly terrible.
It is proclaimed as Dagdhakuṇḍa because of those who have been beaten and burnt;
its water is exceedingly full of waves and is joined with scalding alkaline liquid. (68)
It was filled with aquatic creatures making various kinds of sounds,
measuring two gavyūtis in extent, deep, and enveloped in darkness.
It was filled with sinful beings who feed upon those creatures, as well as biting aquatic animals that were flaming,
making loud noises, and unable to see one another.
And the terrifying Prataptasūcīkuṇḍa is proclaimed, as well as Asidhārāpatra and the region beneath the tall Tāla tree. (71)
The pit is half a krośa in measure and filled with falling leaves;
it is certainly filled with the blood of sinners as they fall from the treetops, even while those wicked ones cry out the words, "Save me! (72).
It was deep, shrouded in darkness, and infested with red insects. || 73 ||
And that lake, known as Asīpatra, is said to be terrifying;
it measures one hundred bows in extent and is filled with weapons possessing the edge of a razor.
It was filled with the blood of sinners, terrifying with razor-sharp edges,
equipped with needle-pointed weapons, and overflowing with a flood of the blood of the wicked.
Fifty bow-lengths in extent, it causes affliction and has a needle-like opening;
it has the shape of the mouth of a certain species of creature called the *goka*.
It is deep in form like an elbow and measures twenty bows in length;
it brings about supreme and great suffering even for those who have committed the most heinous sins. (77)
And there is a pond, sixteen *dhanus* in measure, shaped like the mouth of a crocodile, where worms constantly devour those whose faces are perpetually bowed down. (78)
The form of the Gambhīra is always crowded with sinners;
it is proclaimed to be one hundred bows in measure, and is known as Gajadaṃśana. (79)
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring thirty bow-lengths and shaped like a cow’s mouth is eternally proclaimed as "Gomukha," which brings constant suffering to sinners.
Joined with the wheel of time, it revolves, terrifying, shaped like a jar, shrouded in darkness, and measuring two *gavyūtis* in extent. || 81 ||
And when a deep pit measuring a hundred thousand paces had been forgotten, there was somewhere heated oil and a vat made of copper and other metals. (82)
It was filled with the foremost of sinners and with worms that had fainted;
they were constantly perishing and making sounds against one another. (83)
Struck by the messengers of Yama with clubs and mallets,
they were reeling, falling, and fainting from moment to moment.
O beautiful one, as many sinners as there are in all the cauldrons, they weep for a moment once they have been cast down by the messengers of Yama. 85.
Thereafter, there are fourfold [times] more [sufferings] in the painful Kumbhīpāka;
being tormented for a very long time, those bodies of experience do not perish.
And Kumbhīpāka is proclaimed as the foremost of all hells;
there, sinners are bound by the thread fashioned by Time (Kāla). 87.
Raised up by messengers, they were submerged again in an instant;
held fast by their own breath for a very long time, they likewise fell once more into a swoon.
O beautiful one, it is exceedingly joined with affliction through the body and its enjoyments;
and that which is filled with boiling water is proclaimed as Kālasūtra. (89)
Avaṭa and Kūpabheda are declared to be Matsyoda;
it is filled with boiling water and measures twenty-four [yojanas]. (90)
Constantly pervaded by those who have committed great sins and by those whose limbs are scorched, it is perpetually filled with my messengers who strike them; thus is Avaṭoda proclaimed. (91)
In that pool, within a distance of a hundred bows, by the mere touch of its water, all the diseases of sinners would suddenly vanish as they fall into it.
That which is crowded with creatures being devoured by those who pierce the vital spots (aruntuda), and who utter cries of "Alas! Alas!", that indeed they know as *aruntuda*. (93)
It was strewn with glowing, burning hot sands of parched grain,
extending for a hundred bow-lengths, and was filled with sinful beings who subsisted on those sands as their food.
By merely entering, the sinner becomes encircled by the noose;
they know that the pit extends for one *krośa* and is likewise enveloped by that noose. (95)
By merely entering it, even a sinner becomes encircled by a trident;
its length is proclaimed to be twenty bows, and it is known as being impaled upon a trident.
Where there is indeed trembling for those sinners who fall,
and where it is excessively drenched with cold water for half a krośa, that is Prakampana.
For my messengers indeed deliver [the message] wherever there are meteors in the mouths of sinners;
