that place, measuring twenty bows in extent, is thoroughly crowded with those meteors.
It was a hundred bow-lengths deep and measured a hundred paces across;
it was filled with various kinds of worms and was terrifying.
It was pervaded by intense darkness, circular in shape like a well,
and filled with sinful beings who were its food, perishing as they preyed upon one another.
The Andhakūpa hell is proclaimed as being filled with scorching hot water, blazing insects, and creatures devoured by worms, where one is blinded by the darkness of the eyes.
Where sinners are pierced by floods of various kinds of weapons, that piercing is proclaimed to be twenty bow-lengths in measure. (102)
Where sinners were struck with clubs by my messengers,
that pool, measuring sixteen bows in extent, is known as Daṇḍatāḍana.
And just as sinful fish are caught by great nets, so too [are beings caught];
the opening of the net is proclaimed to be twenty bow-lengths in measure. (104)
As the sinners fall into the pit here, their bodies shall be ground to powder;
for those bound in iron shackles, the depth shall measure ten million fathoms.
A bow twenty units in length, deep and enveloped in darkness, is proclaimed as the "Body-Powder" (dehacūrṇa) for those who are unconscious and inert. 106.
Where the sinners are crushed and struck by my messengers,
that pit, measuring sixteen bow-lengths, is known as Dalana.
By that very fall, the sinner, with his throat, lips, and palate parched,
[falls] thirty bows' length into the heated sands.
Measuring a hundred paces in extent, deep and filled with darkness,
this pit is indeed a place of desiccation for sinners, bestowing suffering upon others.
The Kaṣa hell is one hundred bow-lengths wide, filled with various skins and decoctions,
and crowded with foul-smelling creatures that feed upon those [sinners].
The pit has a mouth shaped like a winnowing basket and measures twelve bow-lengths;
it is filled with heated iron sands and is occupied by sinners.
O virtuous one, that pit, filled with foul-smelling food and crowded with sinners,
has a mouth shaped like a winnowing basket and measures twelve bow-lengths in depth.
It is filled with scorching sand and inhabited by those who have committed great sins;
its mouth is perpetually pervaded by the flames of internal fire-tongues.
O beautiful one, its measure is twenty bows long,
and it is entirely filled with sinners whose limbs have been consumed by flames.
That great pit, which bestows immense suffering, is known as Jvālāmukha;
merely by falling into it, a sinful man indeed becomes unconscious. (115)
Half of it is enclosed within heated bricks and is called Jihmakuṇḍaka;
it is filled with smoke and darkness, and is inhabited by sinful beings blinded by smoke.
A distance of one hundred bow-lengths, filled with smoke through the apertures of the breath, is proclaimed as Dhūmrāndha;
by merely falling there, a sinner becomes enveloped by serpents.
A hundred bow-lengths filled with serpents—that area shall be surrounded by those serpents.
Listen now to the eighty-six sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) described by me, as well as their characteristics; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Various Pits of Hell," in the Ninth Book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada. || 37 ||
The Description of the Narrative of Sāvitrī.
Sāvitrī said:
"O Goddess, grant me devotion, which is the very essence of all essences."
It is the seed for the door of liberation for men, and the savior from the ocean of hell. || 1 ||
It is the cause of those whose essence is liberation, the destroyer of all that is inauspicious, the cutter down of the trees of karma, and the remover of the flood of committed sins. (2)

And what is the nature of liberation, and how many kinds are there? What is their defining characteristic? [Tell me] of devotion to the Goddess, the different types of devotion, and also the refutation of the *niṣeka* [rite]. (3)
The female species was created by the Ordainer as devoid of knowledge of reality;
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me some essential knowledge that possesses true substance. (4)
All charity, sacrifice, bathing at sacred fords, religious observances, and austerity do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of knowledge to the ignorant. (5)
It is certain, O Lord, that a mother is a hundred times more worthy of respect than a father;
and the teacher who imparts knowledge is a hundred times more worthy of worship than a mother.
The King of Dharma said:
"Previously, every boon desired by you in your heart was granted;
now, O child, by my favor, let there be devotion to Śakti for you."
O auspicious lady, you wish to hear the glorification of the virtues of the Goddess Śrī,
which delivers the families of those who speak, those who inquire, and those who listen.
The Residue (Śeṣa), though possessing a thousand mouths, is not able to speak it;
nor is Mṛtyuñjaya capable of speaking it even with his five faces.
Brahmā, the creator of the four Vedas and the ordainer of the worlds, is not capable [of knowing this] even with his four faces; nor is Viṣṇu, though he is all-knowing.
Kārttikeya, though six-faced, is certainly not able to describe it;
nor is Gaṇeśa capable, he who is the teacher of the lords of yogins.
And the four Vedas alone are the very essence of all scriptures;
even those who are wise do not know a mere fraction of his qualities.
Sarasvatī has become bewildered; she is not capable of describing his virtues.
Nor are Sanatkumāra, Dharma, Sanandana, and Sanātana able to do so.
Sanaka, Kapila, Sūrya, and whatever other sons of Brahmā there are who are wise—even they cannot describe it, much less others whose intellects are dull-witted. (14)

Neither the perfected ones (siddhas), nor the lords of sages (munīndras), nor likewise the yogis—what others are there besides them, or who are we—are able to describe the qualities of the illustrious Goddess. 15.
That lotus-feet of which Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others meditate are easily attained by their own devotees, but are very difficult for others to obtain.
Someone knows something; the proclamation of his virtues is auspicious. Brahmā, who is expert in the Veda, knows more than that. || 17 ||
Gaṇeśa, the teacher of the wise, knows that which exceeds even those;
but Śambhu alone, the omniscient, knows that which transcends all.
In the past, that supreme knowledge was imparted to him by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, in the utterly secluded forest of Goloka within the Rāsa-maṇḍala. (19)
In that very place, Śiva himself recounted some auspicious praise of his qualities and spoke of the Dharma in the world of Śiva.
Dharma, however, related this to the radiant one who questioned him:
"O virtuous lady, it is that very [goddess] whom even my father attained by means of his ascetic penance."
"O lady of excellent vows, I have previously refrained from taking my own domain with great effort; now, endowed with dispassion, I wish to go forth for ascetic penance."
Then my father spoke to me, praising his virtues;
I shall relate that according to tradition—listen, for it is exceedingly difficult to comprehend. (23)
She does not know its quality, so what can be said of anyone else?
O fair-faced one, it is just as space does not know its own interior.
He is the soul of all, the Lord of all, the cause of all causes;
the sovereign of all, the primordial source of all, the omniscient protector.
He is of eternal form, possessing an eternal body, eternal bliss, and yet devoid of material shape.
He is unrestrained, free from fear, devoid of qualities, and free from affliction.
He is unstained, the witness of all, the support of all, and higher than the highest;
He is distinguished by Māyā, while Prakṛti and its transformations are the products of Prakṛti.
The individual soul and primordial nature are likewise non-different from one another;
just as the power of fire is never distinct from it anywhere. (28)
This very power is Mahāmāyā, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss; though formless, she assumes form for the sake of bestowing grace upon her devotees. (29)
She first created the form of Gopālasundarī,
which was exceedingly desirable, beautiful, and most captivating.
He is a youth dark as a fresh rain-cloud, dressed in the garb of a cowherd;
he possesses the beauty of ten million Cupids and is enchanting as the abode of divine play.
His eyes surpassed the beauty of lotuses in the midday autumn sun,
and his face eclipsed the splendor of ten million full moons of the autumn season.
Adorned with various ornaments fashioned from priceless jewels,
he is ever smiling and graced by a priceless yellow garment.
He is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, blazing with the splendor of Brahman;
he is easily perceived, peaceful, the beloved of Rādhā, and infinite.
He was constantly being gazed upon by the gopīs with smiles,
standing in the midst of the circle of the rāsa dance, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne.
He has two arms, sounding his flute, adorned with a forest garland, and his chest is eternally radiant with the supreme Kaustubha jewel, the lord of gems. (36)
His body was honored with saffron, agallochum, musk, and sandalwood;
he was anointed with a beautiful garland of campaka flowers and adorned with a wreath of mālatī blossoms. (37)
Abounding in the beauty of lovely crescent moons and adorned with the splendor of the tilaka-mark upon His crest—devotees, overflowing with devotion, meditate upon Him who is thus constituted. (38)
Out of fear of whom the Creator ordains the very creation of the world, and according to [past] actions, He fashions the destiny of all deeds as they were inscribed. (39)
By whose command Viṣṇu is the bestower of the fruits of austerities and actions, and by whose fear he constantly protects everyone as their guardian. (40)
He is Kālāgnirudra, the destroyer of all universes out of fear of whom even Śiva is the conqueror of death; he is the Guru of gurus for those possessed of knowledge. || 41 ||
By the knowledge of which the Lord of Yogis becomes possessed of knowledge, a knower of wisdom, and a sovereign;
he is endowed with supreme bliss and united with devotion and dispassion. || 42 ||
Out of fear of you, O virtuous one, the wind blows, the foremost of swift-moving things, and out of fear of you the sun shines continuously. (43)
By whose command Indra pours down rain, and by whose command Death moves among living beings;
by whose command fire burns, and likewise water, though so very cool.
By his command, the guardians of the quarters protect the directions from great fear;
and out of dread of him, the planetary spheres and the celestial bodies revolve.
Out of fear the trees bear fruit, and out of fear they even flower;
honoring his command, Time itself takes away at the appointed time out of fear of him.
Likewise, by his command, those dwelling in water or on land do not perish;
he does not take away what has been pierced [by arrows] in battles or in difficult terrains at an improper time.
By His command, Vāyu supports the mass of waters, and the waters support the Tortoise;
the Tortoise supports Ananta, and he supports the earth; the earth supports the oceans, and they in turn support the mountains. (48)
And the entire earth, which possesses the form of patience and bears various jewels, is indeed where all beings abide and where [the enemy] strikes. (49)
And Indrāyu [lives] for seventy-one divine yugas;
and during the twenty-eighth fall of Śakra, it constitutes a day and night of Brahmā.
Thus, thirty days constitute a month, and two such months are known as a season (ṛtu).
Six seasons indeed make up a year, which is recorded as the lifespan of Brahmā.
Upon the dissolution of Brahmā, there is the opening of Hari’s eyes;
they know that when his eyes open, the natural (prākṛtika) dissolution occurs.
At the time of primordial dissolution, all beings, including the gods and others, both moving and non-moving,
as well as the Creator and the Ordainer, are absorbed within the lotus-navel of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
And Viṣṇu, who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk and who possesses four arms in Vaikuṇṭha,
is dissolved on the left side of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self.
In whose knowledge Śiva, the eternal Lord of Knowledge, is dissolved;
and in Durgā, who is Viṣṇu’s Māyā, all powers are dissolved. || 55 ||
She is both the intellect within Kṛṣṇa and the presiding deity of that intellect;
and Skanda, who is a portion of Nārāyaṇa, is dissolved in his chest.

And the Lord of the gods, the sovereign of the Gaṇas, who is a portion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, was born from her arm; and those who are portions of Padmā were born from Padmā, while she [Padmā] herself was born from Rādhā, O lady of virtuous vows. (57)
The Gopīs and all the celestial women were also there;
she is the presiding deity of Kṛṣṇa’s life-breaths, and she dwells within his very life-force.
Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī, the Vedas and whatever scriptures there are, as well as Speech itself, abide upon the tongue of that Supreme Self. (59)
The cowherds of Goloka have dissolved into his body hairs;
and all the vital breaths, winds, and fires of all beings have merged into his own vital breaths.
The Vaiṣṇavas, filled with supreme bliss, dissolve their water at the tips of their tongues into the digestive fire within their bellies and [place it] at the lotus-feet of Viṣṇu.
Those who drink the nectar of the essence of devotional rasa are more essential than the essential;
though they are portions of the Virāṭ, they are merged in the Great One, the Mahāvirāṭ, Kṛṣṇa.
In whose every pore all things without exception reside, and at the opening of whose eyes the dissolution of nature occurs. (63)
He whose opening of the eyes is indeed creation once again;
as much time as there is in a closing of the eyes, so much is there in an opening. (64)
Furthermore, at the end of a hundred years of Brahmā, there is again the dissolution of the threads [of creation].
O lady of virtuous vows, there is simply no end to the number of Brahmā’s creations and dissolutions.
Just as there is no way to calculate the number of particles of dust upon the earth,
so too for that Inner Self of all, whose dissolution occurs in the blink of an eye.
Upon its opening, however, creation occurs again by the will of the Lord;
for that Kṛṣṇa remains dissolved in that very Prakṛti during the dissolution.
The knowers of the Vedas understand that there was only one supreme power and the supreme Person devoid of qualities; "In the beginning, this was Being alone. (68)
The primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), though unmanifest and designated by the term "undifferentiated" (avyākṛta),
remains at the time of dissolution as that very same [nature] having attained non-difference from consciousness (cit).
Who within the cosmic eggs is capable of proclaiming his virtues?
Furthermore, the four types of liberation have been described by the four Vedas. (70)
Devotion to the Deity, centered upon that [form], is weightier even than liberation;
one bestows residence in the same world (sālokya), while the other bestows a form identical to the Divine (sārūpya). (71)
The fourfold liberation consists of proximity to Nirvāṇa and the attainment of Nirvāṇa itself;
yet devotees do not desire these without the service of the Lord. (72)
The state of Śiva, immortality, and even the state of Brahmā are held as of little consequence; likewise, wealth is no more than the fear and sorrow of birth, death, old age, and disease.
They know that the assumption of a divine form is nirvāṇa and liberation;
and liberation is devotion devoid of service, which further increases service. (74)

This is the distinction between devotion and liberation; now hear about the destruction of the seed-impregnation (niṣeka). The wise know that for those who have performed their actions, there is both impregnation and enjoyment.
The refutation of that [false doctrine] brings auspiciousness, as does the supreme service to the Lord Śrī;
this knowledge of reality, O virtuous lady, is stable in both worldly and Vedic tradition. (76)
"It has been declared that you shall go unhindered and with auspicious fortune; go, my child, as you please.
Having spoken thus, the son of the Sun restored her husband to life. (77)
Having bestowed auspicious blessings upon her, he prepared to depart;
seeing Yama departing, Sāvitrī bowed down to him. (78)
Distressed by the destruction of her virtuous husband, she wept while clutching his feet;
and hearing Sāvitrī’s lamentation, Yama, the treasury of compassion, [approached]. (79)
Being satisfied, he spoke to her and wept himself.
Dharmarāja said:
"Having enjoyed happiness for a hundred thousand years in the meritorious land of Bhārata... (80)
"You shall go before to that world where the Goddess shines resplendent;
having gone to your own home, O blessed lady, perform the vow of Sāvitrī. (81)
For women, the auspicious vow of Sāvitrī on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha is a cause for liberation throughout the span of fourteen years.
O lady of pure smiles, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should perform the vow of Mahālakṣmī; this vow of sixteen years must indeed be undertaken again and again.
The woman who worships with devotion the Goddess who bestows auspiciousness on every Tuesday goes to the abode of the Lord. (84)

Every month on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, the bestower of auspiciousness; likewise, on the day of the sun's entry into Āṣāḍha, one should worship Manasā, who grants all perfections.

Having fasted on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship Rādhā—who is dearer to Kṛṣṇa than his own life—during the Rāsa dance at the full moon of Kārtika, as well as her who bestows boons every month. (86)
[One should worship] the divine Viṣṇumāyā, Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune,
Prakṛti, and Jagadambā, as well as those women who possess husbands and sons.
Whatever woman, for the sake of wealth and progeny, should worship with devotion virtuous and pure wives, as well as mechanical images and idols; || 88 ||
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes at the end to the state of the Lord Śrī;
thus the practitioner should incessantly worship the manifestations of the Goddess. 89.
The Supreme Goddess is to be served at all times in every form;
there is nothing higher than this which bestows the state of having accomplished all that is to be done.
Having spoken thus, Dharmarāja went to his own abode;
and Sāvitrī, taking her husband with her, went to her own home.
Sāvitrī and Satyavān set out according to the traditional instructions, and Sāvitrī related her own account to the others, O Nārada.
Sāvitrī’s father obtained sons through the power of her resolve; her father-in-law regained his eyesight and his kingdom, and she herself obtained sons by means of her boon.
Having enjoyed happiness for a hundred thousand years in the meritorious land of Bhārata,
that devoted wife went to the world of the gods together with her husband.
She who is the presiding deity over Savitṛ and the presiding deity of the mantra, she is indeed the Sāvitrī of the Vedas; for that reason, she is celebrated as Sāvitrī.
Thus, O child, has this excellent narrative of Sāvitrī been told, along with the ripening of the fruits of living beings' actions; what more do you wish to hear? (96)

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Sāvitrī," in the ninth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
The Description of the Narrative of Lakṣmī.
Nārada said: Of the goddess Śrī, the primordial Prakṛti, who is Gāyatrī and yet formless—
In the dialogue between Sāvitrī and Yama, indeed stainless fame was heard.
The truthful glorification of his virtues is the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
Now, O Lord, I desire to hear the narrative concerning Lakṣmī.
By whom was she first worshipped, what was her nature, or by whom was she so in the past?
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me the glorification of her qualities.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Brahman, in the beginning of creation, long ago, the Goddess was born from the left shoulder of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, within the circle of the Rāsa dance.
Exceedingly beautiful, dark-complexioned, and well-proportioned like a banyan tree, she was like a twelve-year-old girl, yet possessed of eternal, stable youth. || 5 ||
Having the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, pleasant to behold and captivating,
her face eclipses the radiance of ten million full moons of the autumn season.
With eyes that released the splendor of lotuses at midday in autumn,
that goddess became twofold by the will of the Lord of All.
By her own form, complexion, splendor, age, brilliance, fame, dress, action, ornament, and virtue.
By means of a smile, a glance, affection,
or conciliation, Mahālakṣmī [arose] from his left shoulder and Rādhikā from his right.
First, Rādhā and others chose the Supreme Being who possesses two arms;
thereafter, Mahālakṣmī also desired that most beautiful one.
Out of respect for him, Kṛṣṇa indeed became twofold in form:
his right shoulder was two-armed, and his left shoulder was four-armed.
In ancient times, the two-armed one gave Mahālakṣmī to the four-armed one;
she by whom the entire universe is perceived and beheld incessantly with a loving glance. (12)
And having become a goddess, she is remembered as the great Mahālakṣmī;
the beloved of Rādhā has two arms, while the beloved of Lakṣmī has four arms. || 13 ||
And she, whose nature is pure being, surrounded by cowherds and cowherdesses,
while the four-armed Lord Vaikuṇṭha departed for Vaikuṇṭha together with Padmā.
Those two supreme ones, Kṛṣṇa and Nārāyaṇa, are equal in every respect;
and Mahālakṣmī, through her yogic power, assumed various forms.
And in Vaikuṇṭha, Mahālakṣmī is the most perfect Ramā,
whose nature is pure sattva and who is endowed with all auspiciousness.
She was preeminent in love among all beautiful women;
she was like the Fortune of Heaven among heavens, and the very embodiment of Śakra’s prosperity.
In the netherworld (pātāla) there is the fortune of the Nāgas; among kings, the royal fortune;
and in the houses of householders, the domestic fortune—even in a mere fraction of its parts. (18)
The very embodiment of prosperity for householders, the most auspicious of all auspicious things,
Surabhi is the progenitor of cows, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and she who desires the sacrifice.
She is the daughter of the ocean of milk, possessing the form of Śrī;
she is the very nature of splendor within the lotuses and is adorned by the orb of the sun upon the moon.
In ornaments, gems, fruits, and waters;
in kings, queens, celestial women, and palaces. (21)
In all crops, in garments, in sacred places, and in consecrated objects; in images of the gods, in auspicious items, and in water-jars. || 22 ||
She was enchanting amidst rubies and pearls, amidst garlands and among the finest gems,
diamonds, milk, and sandalwood.
In the delightful branches of trees, amidst new clouds, and among all things,
that Goddess was first worshipped by Nārāyaṇa in Vaikuṇṭha.
O Sage, she was worshipped with devotion by Brahmā in the second [kalpa], by Śaṅkara in the third, and by Viṣṇu in the Kṣīroda ocean in Bhārata.
By Svāyambhuva Manu, by the lords of men, by the foremost of sages, by the foremost of ascetics, and by virtuous householders throughout this world. (26)
She is worshipped by the Gandharvas, Nāgas, and others in the netherworlds;
and on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, worship was performed for her by Brahmā.
And with devotion, O Nārada, throughout the three worlds for the duration of a fortnight—
in the months of Caitra, Pauṣa, and Bhādrapada, on an auspicious Tuesday— 28.
And she was worshipped with devotion by Viṣṇu throughout the three worlds;
at the end of the year, on the auspicious transit of the sun into Capricorn (pauṣa-saṅkrānti) at midday, she was invoked.
Manu worshipped her, who had become the embodiment of the three worlds;
she, Maṅgalā, was worshipped by Mahendra as the very auspiciousness of auspiciousness.
By Kedāra, Nīla, Subala, and Nala; by Dhruva, Uttānapāda, Śakra, and likewise by Bali. || 31 ||
And by Kaśyapa, Dakṣa, Kardama, Vivasvat, Priyavrata, Candra, Kubera, and indeed by Vāyu. || 32 ||
She is honored by Yama, Vahni, and Varuṇa;
thus she is always honored and saluted everywhere by all.
She is the presiding goddess of all sovereignty, the very embodiment of every prosperity.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Lakṣmī," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Origin of Lakṣmī.
Nārada said:
She is the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, the supreme one who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha.
The eternal Mahālakṣmī is the presiding goddess of Vaikuṇṭha.
How did that goddess, the daughter of the ocean, come to be upon the earth?
By whom was she praised in the beginning in ancient times? You should explain that to me. || 2 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Nārada, in ancient times, due to the curse of Durvāsas, Purandara was deprived of his fortune, and the host of gods indeed became mortal in the world of mortals.
O Nārada, Lakṣmī, having abandoned heaven and other realms, departed in anger and extreme distress; she went and merged into Vaikuṇṭha as Mahālakṣmī.
Then, all of them, overcome with grief and sorrow, went to the assembly hall of Brahmā;
and placing Brahmā at their head, they proceeded to Vaikuṇṭha itself.
In Vaikuṇṭha, the gods took refuge in the supreme Nārāyaṇa;
they were filled with extreme wretchedness, their throats, lips, and palates parched.
Then, by the command of the Ancient Puruṣa,
Lakṣmī became the Daughter of the Ocean through a portion [of herself], she who is the embodiment of all prosperity.
Having thus churned the Ocean of Milk together with the hosts of Daityas,
the gods obtained Mahālakṣmī, and Viṣṇu beheld her.
Having granted boons to Surā and the others, she, with a gracious countenance and full of satisfaction, gave a forest garland to Viṣṇu, who reclines upon the ocean of milk.
O Nārada, the gods also regained their kingdom which had been seized by the asuras;
and having worshipped her together, they became free from all calamities everywhere.
Nārada said: O Brahmin, how did Durvāsas, the best of sages—most devoted to Brahman and a knower of reality—once utter a curse? By what fault was he provoked in the past? (11)
In what form did those gods and others churn the ocean?
Or by what hymn of praise did that Goddess manifest herself directly before Śakra?
"Or what conversation took place between the two? Tell me that, O Lord.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"In ancient times, the lord of the three worlds was intoxicated by the drinking of honey-wine."
The lustful one sported in secret with Rambhā;
having played with that passionate woman, his mind was captivated by her.
With his mind agitated by desire, he remained there in that great forest,
watching the best of sages as he departed from Vaikuṇṭha for the peak of Kailāsa.
Indra beheld the lord Durvāsas, blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
possessing the brilliance of a thousand suns at midday in the summer heat.
Having the appearance of molten gold, blazing with a mass of matted locks,
he wore a white sacred thread and carried a bark garment, a staff, and a water-pot.
He bore a most brilliant sectarian mark (tilaka) resembling the moon,
and was accompanied by hundreds of thousands of disciples who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Seeing him, Purandara, overcome with devotion, bowed his head;
then, filled with joy, he praised the group of disciples with great reverence.
And the Sage, together with his disciples, bestowed upon him auspicious blessings,
as well as the most enchanting Pārijāta flower given by Viṣṇu.
That flower destroys old age, disease, and death; it removes sorrow and brings about liberation. Yet Śakra, intoxicated by the prosperity of his kingdom, took that flower.
He placed that flower upon the head of the elephant at that very moment;
by the mere touch of it, the elephant was transformed in both appearance and quality.
Suddenly, by virtue of his splendor and age, he became equal to Viṣṇu;
and having abandoned Śakra, the lordly elephant went to the terrible forest. || 23 ||
O Sage, Mahendra was unable to protect him by means of his own splendor;
and seeing Śakra having abandoned that merit, the lord of sages [acted].
Greatly incensed and filled with rage, he spoke to him and cursed him.
The sage said:
"O you who are intoxicated by prosperity, how can you disregard me? (25)
A flower given by me, or whatever is offered with pride upon the head of an elephant—whether it be an offering of food, fruit, or water—to Viṣṇu; || 26 ||
It should be consumed only upon obtaining it; by rejecting it, one becomes a slayer of a Brahmin.
He shall be deprived of fortune, deprived of intellect, and fallen from his city. (27)

He who would abandon the auspicious food offering (naivedya) of Viṣṇu that has come to him by fortune, and he who eats what is offered to Viṣṇu merely because it has been obtained—he is not a devotee. (28)
Having delivered a hundred men, he himself shall become liberated while living, he who daily offers food as an oblation and bows down to Hari. (29)
Whoever worships or praises him with devotion shall become equal to Viṣṇu;
by the wind that touches him, even a multitude of sacred fords is instantly purified.
O fool, by the dust of his feet the earth is instantly purified;
[so too are] the food of a prostitute, the food of a woman whose husband is missing, and even that which follows a Śūdra’s Śrāddha.
The eating of meat in vain without first offering it to Hari, and the gift of a Śiva-liṅga given by one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras; (32)

The food of physicians and twice-born men, likewise the food of temple-priests (devalas), the food of those who sell their daughters, and the food of those who live by [providing] sexual intercourse; 33.

Food that is leftover, stale, or remains after everyone has eaten; the food of twice-born men whose wives are Śūdras or who have Śūdra husbands; and the food of those who carry corpses or who subsist on the food of such twice-born men. (34)
And the food of twice-born men who have not been initiated, of those who carry out the dead, and likewise the food of twice-born men who approach women who should not be approached; // 35 //
The food of those who betray friends, of the ungrateful, and of those who violate trust; the food of those who give false testimony, and likewise the food of Brahmins [who eat such food]; 36.
All these are purified by eating the food offered to Viṣṇu;
even a dog-eater who serves Viṣṇu shall uplift ten million generations of his lineage.
A person who is not a devotee of Hari is incapable of protecting even himself;
yet, out of ignorance, he might even take up the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) of Viṣṇu.
One is liberated from the sins accumulated over seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt—provided one partakes of Viṣṇu’s food offering (naivedya) with knowledge and devotion.
O Hari, one is certainly liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million births because a flower was placed with pride upon the head of the elephant.
Therefore, let Lakṣmī abandon you all and go to the abode of Hari;
for I am a devotee of Nārāyaṇa, and I fear neither the gods nor Brahmā.
Who else besides Time, Death, and Old Age shall I count?
And what will your father, Kaśyapa the Prajāpati, do for you? (42)
O Hari, Bṛhaspati and Guru are indeed my preceptors;
for whomsoever this flower is placed upon the head, his alone is the supreme worship.
Having heard this, Mahendra grasped the foot of the sage and,
afflicted by grief and overwhelmed with fear, wept aloud and spoke to him.
Mahendra said: "O Lord, a fitting curse that removes my power of illusion has been granted to me.
I do not ask for the recovery of my lost wealth; rather, grant me some measure of knowledge. (45)
Sovereignty is the seed of calamities, the cause for the concealment of knowledge, an axe to the path of liberation, and an obstacle to devotion. (46)
The sage said:
The seed and sprout of birth, death, old age, sorrow, and disease is supreme;
and one blinded by the darkness of worldly prosperity does not see the path to liberation.
One who is intoxicated by wealth is utterly deluded, just like one intoxicated by liquor;
even though surrounded by kinsmen, O Hari, he is truly alone because of that very state of being a kinsman.
Intoxicated by the pride of prosperity, blinded by the objects of the senses, and agitated, the passionate person of rajasic nature does not perceive the path of sattva. 49.
The blind man regarding sense-objects is said to be of two kinds: the tāmasa and the rājasa.
One who is ignorant of the scriptures is tāmasa, while one who knows the scriptures is considered rājasa. (50)
O bull among the gods, the scripture reveals two kinds of paths:
one is the seed of worldly involvement, and the other is the cause of liberation. (51)
At the beginning of worldly activity, living beings move along the path of suffering, acting according to their own will, with clarity, without opposition, and continuously. (52)
Out of greed for honey, he approaches with great effort, imagining it to be happiness,
though in its final result it is the seed of destruction and the cause of birth, death, and old age.
Having wandered joyfully through the course of many births,
he proceeded in succession through various wombs ordained by his own karma.
Then, through the supreme grace of Īśa, he attains the company of the virtuous;
for among hundreds and thousands, only one becomes the cause for crossing the ocean of worldly existence.
The virtuous one should show the path to liberation by means of the lamp of reality;
then the soul exerts effort toward the shattering of its bonds.
Through the practice of many births, by means of austerity and fasting,
one shall then attain the supreme path of liberation, which is free from obstacles and bestows happiness.
"O Purandara, that which you ask has been heard from the words of my guru;
having heard those words of the sage, he became free from passion. (58)
O Brahmin, his dispassion increased day by day;
having gone from the sage’s abode to his own home, he beheld Amarāvatī.
It was crowded with Daityas and hosts of Asuras, overwhelmed by fear,
beset by calamities, and in some places deprived of sons and kinsmen.
Seeing her utterly unstable, deprived of father, mother, and husband, and seized by enemies, she went toward the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati). 61.
On the bank of the Mandākinī, Śakra beheld his preceptor, the Lord,
standing in the waters of the Gaṅgā, meditating upon the supreme Brahman.
Facing the sun and facing the east, with faces turned in all directions,
his eyes filled with tears, his hair standing on end, and endowed with supreme bliss.
It is the most excellent and the most venerable, the most righteous and practiced by the best;
it is the dearest to one's circle of kinsmen and the most supreme among the wise.
Seeing the elder brother of the hosts of his brothers— an adversary to the gods— reciting prayers there, the Lord of the Gods stood still.
At the end of the watch, seeing his guru risen, he prostrated before him;
having bowed at his lotus feet, he wept aloud again and again.
He related the account, including the Brahmin’s curse and so forth, as well as the subsequent attainment of boons and the acquisition of knowledge, which is very difficult to obtain. (67)
And having heard the words of his disciple, Subuddhi, the best among speakers, [said]: "The Lord of the Gods shall gradually recover his own city seized by the enemy. (68)
Bṛhaspati, his eyes bloodshot with anger, spoke this.
The Guru said:
"O best of gods, everything has been heard; do not weep, listen to my words. (69)
For a wise man who understands policy is never despondent in times of adversity;
for both prosperity and adversity are transitory and take the form of toil.
The former depends on past karma, and one is oneself the agent of both;
this indeed occurs for all beings perpetually in birth after birth.
Since it follows the very sequence of a wheel’s rim, what cause for lamentation is there?
For it has been said that one's own performed karma is experienced throughout the whole of Bharata.
Whatever action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, a person experiences as the fruit of their own karma,
that karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of eons unless it has been experienced.
"Whatever action has been performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, must necessarily be experienced"—thus it has been stated in the Veda and by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self. (74)
Having addressed the Lotus-born One within the branch of the Sāmaveda, [he spoke] regarding the remainder of the experiences of birth for all those who have performed their actions (karmans). (75)
For indeed, in accordance with their own actions, they receive both the curse of a Brahmin and auspicious blessings through their deeds, whether in Bhārata or elsewhere.
Through action one may obtain great fortune, and through action one may meet with wretchedness; the karma accumulated over ten million births follows living beings.

For indeed, O Purandara, one cannot abandon the fruits of actions without experiencing them—just like a shadow—whether there be a difference in time, a difference in place, or a difference in the recipient. (78)
Indeed, there may even be a state of deficiency or excess due to one's actions;
however, through the gift of material objects, the merit for those things remains equal day after day. (79)
O God, on different days the merit is ten millionfold, or incalculable, or even greater than that; and when objects are given on level ground, the merit is equal [to the value of the land].
Depending on the difference in location, the merit is ten millionfold, incalculable, or even greater than that;
for an equal gift to an equal recipient, the merit belongs equally to both the object and the donor. (81)
When there is a distinction in the recipient, the fruit is a hundredfold, or incalculable, or even greater than that;
just as crops may yield less or more [than expected]. (82)

Just as there is a difference in yield for farmers due to differences in fields or differences in vessels, so too a gift given to a Brahmin on an ordinary day yields equal results [to that given on a sacred occasion]. || 83 ||
On the new moon day coinciding with the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), the fruit shall be a hundredfold;
and on the full moon day of the Cāturmāsya, the fruit is indeed infinite.
During a lunar eclipse, the merit is ten millionfold, and during a solar eclipse, it shall be ten times even that. || 85 ||
In the Akṣayā [tithi], that fruit is called inexhaustible and incalculable;
likewise, on other auspicious days (puṇyāha), there would be a preponderance of fruit. || 86 ||
Just as it is with giving, so it is with bathing, recitation, and other meritorious deeds;
in this way, the fruit of men's actions is to be understood in all cases. (87)
Just as a potter, the creator, fashions a jar from clay upon the ground by means of a rod, a wheel, a bowl-shaped mold, and a whirling motion; || 88 ||
In that very same way, the Creator bestows the fruit according to the thread of karma;
worship that Nārāyaṇa by whose command this universe was created. 89.
He is the ordainer of the Ordainer and the protector of the Protector in the three worlds;
he is the creator of the Creator and the destroyer of the Destroyer, the Death of Death.
"Śaṅkara has declared that for one who remembers Madhusūdana during the great calamity of saṃsāra, prosperity shall arise even in the midst of misfortune. (91)
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, the knower of reality embraced the Lord of the Gods, gave him auspicious blessings, and enlightened him regarding his desired goal.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Lakṣmī," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Narrative of Śrī Lakṣmī. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Brahmin, having meditated upon Hari, Hari went to the assembly hall of Brahmā.
Placing Bṛhaspati at their head, together with all the hosts of gods.
Having gone quickly to the world of Brahmā and beheld the Lotus-born One,
all the deities, together with Indra and their preceptor, prostrated themselves.
The preceptor of the gods related the account to Brahmā;
having heard that, the lotus-seated one laughed and spoke to Mahendra.
Brahmā said:
"O child, you are born of my lineage; you are my wise great-grandson.
You are the disciple of Bṛhaspati and yourself the sovereign of the gods."
And your maternal grandfather Dakṣa was a devotee of Viṣṇu and possessed great prowess;
how could he, whose three lineages were pure, have been filled with such ego?
How could he who has a mother devoted to her husband, a father who is pure and has conquered his senses,
and a maternal grandfather and maternal uncle [of the same character], ever become arrogant?
Due to the fault of his father, the fault of his maternal grandfather,
and the fault of his preceptor— by these three faults, a person will certainly become a sinner against Hari.
The Blessed One is the inner self of all, dwelling within all bodies;
from whose body He departs, that [body] becomes a corpse at that very moment. || 8 ||
I am the mind and the lord of the senses; for Śaṅkara is the very form of knowledge.
Viṣṇu is the vital breath, and the divine Satī is primordial nature (prakṛti) and the intellect (buddhi).
Sleep and the other powers—all these are the manifestations (kalās) of Prakṛti;
and the reflection of the Self is the individual soul (jīva), who assumes bodies for the sake of experience.
When the Lord has departed from the body, all [the senses] depart in agitation, just as attendants follow a king of men traveling on his path. || 11 ||
I, Śiva, Śeṣa, Viṣṇu, Dharma, and Mahāvirāṭ—
since you and the devotees are but portions of Him, that flower has been insulted by you.
The lotus feet of Śiva were worshipped by you with a flower;
that very flower was given there by Durvāsas, yet it was insulted by you through fate.
That merit which has fallen from the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa upon the head of someone shall be superior to the worship of all the gods.
For you have been deceived by fate, and fate is indeed most powerful;
who indeed is able to protect a foolish person devoid of fortune? (15)
That Goddess of Fortune has now departed in anger because of the rejection of Kṛṣṇa’s floral remains;
therefore, go now to Vaikuṇṭha along with me and your preceptor.
"By worshipping Śrīnātha there, he shall attain prosperity through my grace.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā, together with all the hosts of gods, [departed]. (17)
Having gone there, they beheld the Supreme Brahman, the eternal Lord, whose nature is splendor, blazing with his own radiance.
Possessing a splendor equal to hundreds of millions of suns at midday in the summer heat,
it is peaceful, without beginning, middle, or end, the beloved of the goal, and infinite.
The Lord was accompanied by his four-armed attendants and Sarasvatī;
he was surrounded with devotion by the four Vedas and by Gaṅgā.
All the gods, led by Brahmā, bowed their heads to him;
humble with devotion and with eyes full of tears, they praised the Supreme Lord.
Brahmā himself, with palms joined in reverence, related the account;
all the deities wept, for they had fallen from their respective offices.
He beheld the host of gods seized by calamity, overwhelmed with fear,
deprived of their jewel ornaments, and destitute of their mounts and other possessions.
Seeing him devoid of splendor, robbed of his glory, lusterless, and utterly terrified, he who shatters fear and dread spoke to the cowardly one.
The Blessed Lord said: "Do not fear, O Brahmin, nor you gods; for what cause for fear is there while I stand here?
I shall grant you the imperishable Lakṣmī, who increases supreme sovereignty."
Moreover, let some of my words be heard, which are appropriate for the occasion—beneficial, true, essential, and bringing happiness in the end. (26)
The countless people dwelling in the universe are perpetually under my control;
yet, just as they are so, I am dependent upon my devotees and lack independence.
Whomever my devotee, who is intent on me and free from restraint, may become angry with,
in that person's house I certainly do not dwell, even together with Padmā.
Durvāsas is a portion of Śaṅkara, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and one who has taken refuge in me;
it was due to his curse that I, together with Lakṣmī, came from your house.
Where there is no sound of the conch, no *tulasī*, no worship of Śiva, and no feeding of Brahmins, there Lakṣmī does not dwell. (30)
O Brahmin, wherever there is revilement of my devotees or of me among the gods,
Mahālakṣmī becomes greatly incensed and consequently departs, leading to their defeat.
If a fool devoid of devotion to me eats on the day of Hari or even on my birthday,
prosperity departs from his house as well.
He who sells human beings, he who sells his own daughter, and that house where a guest does not eat—from such a house my beloved departs. (33)

That brahmin who is the son of an unchaste woman, his husband who is a great sinner, and he who goes to the house of a sinner or eats the food offered at a śrāddha ceremony for a śūdra—[these are all fallen]. (34)
Then, greatly enraged, Kamalālayā departed from her abode;
that lowest of the twice-born was devoid of fortune and had cremated the corpses of Śūdras. || 35 ||
Then the goddess Kamalavāsinī, being enraged, departs from that house;
likewise for a Brāhmaṇa who is a cook for Śūdras or one who drives an ox-cart. (36)
And Kamalā departs from that man's house, fearing the drinking of his water;
for he is a twice-born man who is impure-hearted, cruel, injurious, and a reviler. (37)
The Brahmin who officiates for Śūdras and the Goddess depart from his house; likewise, the Mother of the World departs from him who eats the food of a woman without a husband. (38)
Where a Brahmin cuts grass with his fingernails, or scratches the earth with them, or remains despondent—that house, my beloved, he departs from. (39)
A twice-born man who eats at sunrise, a Brāhmaṇa who sleeps during the day,
and one who engages in sexual intercourse by day— he from whom my beloved departs.
That brahmin who is devoid of proper conduct, he who accepts gifts from a śūdra, and that fool who is uninitiated—verily, my beloved departs from him. (41)
Indeed, from the house of one who has oily feet, who sleeps naked, who is weak in knowledge,
and who is constantly talkative, that virtuous woman departs.
If one who has bathed his head with oil should touch another limb,
or play a musical instrument upon his own body, she departs from that house in anger.
That twice-born man who is devoid of vows and fasts, who neglects the twilight prayers, who is impure, and who lacks devotion to Viṣṇu—departing from him, O my beloved, I go elsewhere. (44)
He who indeed censures a Brāhmaṇa, he who constantly hates him,
he who harms living beings, and he who is devoid of compassion— after that, he goes to the womb of all species.
Wherever there is an image of Hari, and likewise wherever there is the chanting of Hari’s praises,
there that Goddess, the most auspicious of all auspicious things, resides.
O Grandfather, wherever there is praise of Kṛṣṇa or his devotee, that goddess who is dear to Kṛṣṇa dwells there perpetually. (47)
Wherever there is the sound of a conch, a conch-shell, a stone, or a *tulasī* leaf—there she resides; [where there is] service to her, salutation, and meditation. (48)
Where there is worship of the Śiva-liṅga and its auspicious glorification,
there is the worship of Durgā, her qualities, and Padmanivāsinī.
Where there is service to the Brahmins and the auspicious feeding of them, and the worship of all the gods—there, O lotus-faced one, is the virtuous woman. 50.
Having spoken thus to all the gods, the Lord of Ramā said to Ramā:
"Take birth in the Ocean of Milk by means of a portion of yourself."
Having spoken thus to her, the Lord of the World spoke again to Brahmā:
"O Lotus-born One, having churned the ocean, give Lakṣmī to the gods."
Having spoken thus, O sage, the beloved of Kamalā entered his inner apartments;
and after a long time, the gods went to the Ocean of Milk.
Having made Mount Mandara the churning-stick and the Tortoise the vessel,
and having made Śeṣa the churning-cord, the gods and the asuras churned [the ocean].
They obtained Dhanvantari, the desired nectar, the horse Uccaiḥśravas, various jewels, the jewel among elephants, Lakṣmī, and the Sudarśana discus.
O sage, that virtuous Vaiṣṇavī gave a forest garland to Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, the beautiful one who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk.
Praised and honored by the gods, as well as by Brahmā and Śaṅkara,
she bestowed her vision upon the abode of the gods through liberation from the Brahmin’s curse.
O Nārada, by the grace of Mahālakṣmī and through her granting of boons, the gods regained their own realm, which had been seized by the Daityas and was terrifying.
Thus has this entire, supreme narrative of Lakṣmī been told—granting happiness and consisting of the essential truth. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Śrī Lakṣmī," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
A Description of the Meditation and Hymn of Mahālakṣmī.
Nārada said: "O auspicious one, I have heard the glorification of Hari and that supreme knowledge concerning Him."
O Lord, please tell me the desired narrative concerning Lakṣmī, as well as the meditation and the hymn of praise.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having bathed in the sacred ford in the past and put on two clean garments, Śakra placed a pitcher in the Ocean of Milk and worshipped the six deities.
Then, having worshipped Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Agni, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śivā with devotion using flowers, perfumes, and other offerings.
And having invoked Mahālakṣmī, who is the embodiment of supreme sovereignty,
the Lord of Gods performed her worship together with Brahmā, his family priest.
O Sage, while the sages, brahmins, the preceptor Hari, the gods and others, the auspicious place, and Śiva were standing before him, there was the bliss of knowledge.
Having taken a flower from the pārijāta tree and sprinkled it with sandalwood paste,
O Nārada, he meditated upon the goddess Mahālakṣmī and worshipped her.
And understand that meditation which was formerly given by Hari to Brahmā as prescribed in the Sāmaveda; through that meditation, I shall speak it to you. (7)
I bow to the Supreme Goddess who dwells in the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus,
the Supreme One whose hands grasp the radiance of ten million full moons of the autumnal season.
Blazing with her own splendor, pleasant to behold and captivating,
she possessed the luster of molten gold— Satī herself in embodied form.
Richly adorned with jewel ornaments and beautified by yellow garments,
her face bright with a slight smile, she is eternally possessed of perpetual youth.
I worship the auspicious Mahālakṣmī, the bestower of all prosperity;
having meditated upon her, who is endowed with manifold virtues, by means of this meditation. (11)
Having worshipped according to the words of Brahmā, he offered the sixteen services with devotion and according to the prescribed rule, each preceded by its respective mantra.
They were praiseworthy, excellent, choice, and of various kinds;
they were fashioned by Viśvakarman from the essence of priceless jewels.
O Mahālakṣmī, please accept this variegated seat;
here is pure water from the Gaṅgā, which is desired and honored by all. (14)
O Abode of Lakṣmī, let the water of the Ganges, combined with flowers, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, and other offerings, be accepted as the form of the fire that consumes the fuel of sin. 15.
O dweller in the lotus, please accept this auspicious water contained within a conch shell,
as well as fragrant flower-oil and fragrant myrobalan fruit.
O beloved of Śrī Hari, let the seed of bodily beauty be accepted;
O Goddess, let clothing made of cotton and silk be accepted. (17)
O Goddess, please accept this jewel-ornament, fashioned from precious gold, which enhances the beauty of the body, brings splendor, and bestows prosperity. 18.
It is the seed of all beauty, an immediate and supreme producer of splendor, consisting of the exudation of trees and combined with fragrant substances and the like. (19)
O beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, please accept this incense and the sacred thread;
O Goddess, please accept this sandalwood paste, fragrant and bestowing happiness. (20)
O Goddess of the Suras, please accept this lamp, which is the very form of the eye of the world, pure, the dispeller of darkness, and the embodiment of bliss.
May you accept this food offering, which takes the form of various oblations, is endowed with diverse flavors, and is exceedingly delicious.
Food is the very nature of Brahman and the cause of the preservation of life;
it bestows both contentment and nourishment—O Goddess, please accept this food. (23)
O Mahālakṣmī, please accept this delicious paramānna, well-cooked from śāli rice and combined with sugar and cow's products. || 24 ||
O Supreme Goddess, accept this food offering named Svastika, cooked with sugar and cow’s milk, which is most delicious and enchanting. 25.
Various kinds of delightful cooked foods and fruits, as well as that which was exuded from the fragrant breasts—exceedingly sweet and most enchanting. (26)
"O beloved of Acyuta, please accept this mortal nectar, excellent cow's milk, which is very sweet, endowed with flavor, and produced from the sugarcane tree. (27)
Please accept this very sweet jaggery cooked by fire, produced from the flour and dust of barley and wheat grains. (28)
O Goddess, please accept this well-cooked sweet food mixed with jaggery and cow's products, as well as this cooked meal made from grain flour, served with svastika cakes and other delicacies. (29)
May you graciously accept this offering presented by me with devotion;
it provides cool breezes and is supremely comforting during the heat. (30)
O Kamalā, please accept this white chowrie-fan and this excellent, beautiful betel-leaf, exquisitely scented with camphor and other fragrances. (31)
Please accept this betel, which removes dullness of the tongue, is well-scented and very cool, and serves as the cause for destroying thirst. (32)
O Goddess, accept this life which is the very essence of the world's vitality, the seed of bodily beauty, and that which ever increases splendor. (33)
O Goddess, please accept this garment made of cotton and silk, as well as ornaments for the body and other items fashioned from red gold that enhance one's appearance. (34)

"O Goddess, please accept this ornament, which bestows beauty, brings prosperity, and is fashioned from the finest materials of various seasons, serving as a supreme repository of manifold splendor. (35)
"O Goddess, please accept this pure garland, beloved of the king of the earth;
it bestows purity, possesses a pure form, and is the most auspicious of all auspicious things. (36)
O Goddess, please accept this delightful fragrance produced from fragrant substances, as well as the pure water of sacred bathing-places, which always bestows purification. (37)
"O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, please accept this beautiful water for sipping (ācamanīyaka), fashioned from the finest jewels and other precious materials, and anointed with flowers and sandalwood paste. (38)
"O Goddess, please accept this excellent couch, richly adorned with jewel ornaments;
whatever object is unprecedented and difficult even to find upon the earth. (39)
"O Goddess, please accept this substance which is worthy of being enjoyed as an ornament for the gods;
having offered these substances with the root mantra, the preeminent among gods [should perform the rite]. (40)
He chanted the root mantra with devotion ten lakhs of times according to the prescribed rite;
by chanting ten lakhs of times, the perfection of the mantra was indeed attained.
The mantra was given by Brahmā, as was the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) on all sides;
[the names are] Lakṣmī, Māyā, Kāmavāṇī, and Kamalavāsinī, ending with the dative suffix -ṅe. 42.
This Vedic king of mantras is well-known when accompanied by the word "svāhā";
by means of this mantra, Kubera attained supreme sovereignty.
By this mantra, Dakṣa, the Sāvarṇi Manu, and Maṅgala became lords of the earth over the seven continents, as well as sovereigns of kings.
Priyavrata, Uttānapāda, Kedāra, and King Nṛpa—these Siddhas and lords of kings [attained their state] by means of this mantra, O Nārada. (45)
When the mantra was perfected, Mahālakṣmī, bestowing boons, appeared before Śakra,
seated upon a celestial chariot fashioned from the finest essence of precious gems.
Covering the earth consisting of seven islands with her splendor, she possessed the hue of a white campaka flower and was adorned with ornaments of jewels. (47)
With a face brightened by a slight smile, she is intent on bestowing grace upon her devotees;
she wears a jeweled necklace possessing a luster equal to ten million moons.
Having seen Śāntā, the mother of the world, Purandara was filled with joy;
his entire body bristling with horripilation, his eyes filled with tears, he joined his palms in reverence. (49)
And there, he was joined with the King of Hymns bestowed by Brahmā,
which is Vedic and indeed grants all desired objects.
Purandara said:
Salutations to the dweller of the lotus, salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇī;
salutations again and again to Mahālakṣmī, who is eternally the beloved of Kṛṣṇa. || 51 ||
Salutations again and again to her whose eyes are like lotus petals, and to her whose face is a lotus;
salutations again and again to her who sits upon a lotus-seat, to the lotus-like one, and to the consort of Viṣṇu. || 52 ||
Salutations again and again to her who is the embodiment of all prosperity, who is worthy of worship by all; salutations again and again to her who bestows devotion to Hari and who grants joy.
Salutations again and again to her who dwells upon the chest of Kṛṣṇa, to the Mistress of Kṛṣṇa;
salutations to her whose very form is the splendor of the moon, and who shines within the beautiful jewel-lotus.
Salutations again and again to the Great Goddess, the presiding deity of prosperity;
salutations again and again to her whose nature is growth, the bestower of growth. || 55 ||
She who is Mahālakṣmī in Vaikuṇṭha, she who is Lakṣmī in the Ocean of Milk, the Lakṣmī of heaven in the abode of Indra, and the Lakṣmī of royalty in the palace of kings; || 56 ||
She is the household fortune of householders, the domestic deity in their homes;
she was born from the ocean as Surabhi, and as Dakṣiṇā, she desires the sacrifice.
You are Aditi, the mother of the gods; you are Kamalā, whose abode is the lotus.
You are Svāhā in the offering of oblations, and you are remembered as Svadhā in the offering of ancestral rites.
For you are indeed the Earth, the support of all, whose nature is Viṣṇu;
you are the embodiment of pure goodness (sattva) and are solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Free from anger and violence, you are the bestower of boons, the auspicious Śāradā;
you are the supreme giver of the ultimate truth and the highest bestower of service to Hari.
Without her, the entire world is reduced to ashes and rendered worthless; without her, the whole universe is eternally as if dead while yet living. (61)
You are the supreme mother of all, appearing as the kinsman of all;
you are the very form of the cause for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Just as a mother is always for her suckling infants during their infancy,
so you are always the mother of all in every form.
One deprived of a mother may survive by means of her breast-milk through the power of fate;
but it is certain that no person deprived of you can ever live.
O Ambikā, you whose very nature is perfectly serene, be gracious to me;
O Eternal One, grant me that realm which has been seized by my enemies.
O beloved of Hari, as long as I am deprived of you, deprived of my kinsmen, and a mere beggar, so long shall I be destitute of all prosperity.
Grant me knowledge and the Dharma, all desired good fortune,
as well as power, majesty, and every form of authority.
"Victory, prowess in battle, and supreme sovereignty as well"—
having spoken thus, Mahendra, together with all the hosts of gods, [departed].
With eyes full of tears, he bowed down again and again with his head;
so too did Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Śeṣa, Dharma, and Keśava.
They all repeatedly made exemptions for the sake of the gods;
and having granted a boon to the deities, [he gave them] a beautiful flower garland.
In the assembly of the gods, Lakṣmī, being well-pleased, gave [herself] to Keśava;
and the gods, satisfied, went each to their own respective abode, O Nārada.
The goddess went joyfully to the abode of Hari, who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk;
and Brahmā and Īśāna also returned to their own homes, O Nārada.
Having bestowed auspicious blessings upon the gods with great affection, [the Lord said:
"That man who recites this highly meritorious hymn at the three junctions of the day," (73)
He shall become a great lord of kings, equal to Kubera;
indeed, by reciting five hundred thousand times, men shall attain perfection in this hymn. (74)
If one should recite the Siddhastotra continuously for one month, he will undoubtedly become a great happy lord of kings. (75)

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Meditation and Hymn of Mahālakṣmī," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Narrative of Svāhā.
Nārada said:
O illustrious Nārāyaṇa, O great lord Nārāyaṇa!
By his very form, by his virtues alone, by his fame, by his splendor, and by his radiance. || 1 ||
O Sage, you alone are the foremost among the wise, the perfected ones, and the yogis; you are the supreme among ascetics and sages, and the best among those who know the Vedas.
The great and wonderful narrative of Mahālakṣmī has been understood;
now, please tell us some other hidden narrative.
This must be kept strictly secret and is beneficial in every respect;
it is not to be disclosed even in the Purāṇas, as it is declared in the Vedas and is consistent with Dharma.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Brahman, how many kinds of various narratives—unrevealed from the Purāṇas, secret, and very difficult to obtain—have been heard by you? (5)
"Among those, tell me, O illustrious one, which you wish to hear—that which is the essence—or whatever else you desire; I shall speak of that further."
Nārada said: The goddess Svāhā is praised for the offering of oblations in all rites;
Svadhā is commended for offerings to the ancestors, while Dakṣiṇā is the most excellent in every respect.
I desire to hear from your mouth—their conduct, the fruit of their births, and their preeminence as well—O best among the knowers of the Vedas; please speak.
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Nārada, the best of sages smiled and began to relate the ancient tale as it is told in the Purāṇas.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In the beginning of creation, the gods formerly went for the sake of their own sustenance;
they arrived at the world of Brahmā and reached his most enchanting assembly hall.
Having gone there, they made a request to the Sage for the sake of food;
having heard this and given his promise, Brahmā attended upon the supreme Śrī Hari.
Nārada said:
Indeed, the Blessed One manifested in the form of sacrifice through his own portion;
whatever sacrificial oblation was offered to him by the Brahmins during the rite, [he received it].
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O best of sages, when Brahmins and Kṣatriyas and others offer oblations with devotion, the gods do not receive that gift at all.
All those gods became despondent and went again to that assembly;
having arrived, they reported the cause of their lack of food.
Having heard this, Brahmā took refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa through meditation;
by His command, he performed worship of Prakṛti through meditation alone. 15.
By a portion of Prakṛti herself, she is the embodiment of all powers;
she is exceedingly beautiful, dark-complexioned, delightful, and captivating to the mind.
With a face brightened by a slight smile and longing to bestow grace upon her devotees, she spoke thus before the Creator: "O Lotus-born One, choose a boon."
Having heard those words of his, Vidhi spoke to her in agitation.
Prajāpati said:
"O you who are exceedingly beautiful, become the burning power of Agni. (18)
Even the sacrificial fire is not able to burn the *prakṛtis* without you;
yet, that man who offers oblations while uttering your name at the end of the mantra [shall succeed]. (19)
The gods receive that from the gods with great joy;
she is the mistress of the household, whose nature is the prosperity of Agni and who is the very form of Śrī.
"O Mother, you are eternally worshipped by the gods, humans, and others.
Having heard these words of Brahmā, she became despondent.
Then the Goddess spoke her own intention to the Self-born One.
She said: "I shall worship Kṛṣṇa through penance for a very long time."
O Brahman, whatever else exists besides that is merely an illusion like a dream;
you are the Creator of the universe, as well as Śambhu, the all-pervading Lord who has conquered death.
Śeṣa supports the universe, and Dharma is the witness of the righteous;
he is the foremost object of worship for all gods and the lord of the Gaṇas among the hosts. || 24 ||
Nature (Prakṛti) is worthy of worship by all, for it was through her grace that the sages and seers came into being in ancient times, and they were honored by serving her.
"I constantly contemplate his lotus feet with devotion," said Padmāsya,
after addressing him as "Pādya" in accordance with the tradition of Padmanābha.
Having meditated upon the flawless Kṛṣṇa, the goddess, the lotus-born one, went forth for asceticism; she performed penance on one leg for a hundred thousand years.
Then she beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa, beyond the qualities and supreme to primordial nature; and having seen His exceedingly beautiful form, Rūpiṇī [was struck with wonder].
In due time, the lover of Kāmeśa fell into a swoon;
perceiving her intention, the omniscient one spoke to her.
Having raised her up onto his lap— she whose limbs had long been withered by asceticism—
the Blessed Lord said: "O Vārāhī, indeed, by a portion of yourself, you shall become my wife."
"O beloved, you are the daughter of Nagnajit, named Nāgnajitī;
now, O beautiful woman, become the wife of Agni and his consumer of oblations."
"By my grace, you shall become worthy of worship, embodying the very form of the limbs of the mantra;
and Vahni, having worshipped you with a spirit of devotion as the mistress of his household," (32)
"He shall sport with you, the delightful Rāmā," having spoken thus to the goddess, the divine Nārada vanished.
There, at the command of Brahmā, Vahni arrived trembling;
having meditated upon that Mother of the World according to the visualization prescribed in the Sāmaveda.
Having worshipped him, he praised him and took her hand according to the sacred mantras;
then, for a hundred divine years, he sported with Rāmā.
In an exceedingly secluded place that always provided the pleasure of enjoyment,
she conceived a child through the splendor of the Fire-god.
That goddess bore him for twelve divine years;
thereafter, she gave birth to sons who were beautiful and captivating.
The Dakṣiṇāgni, Gārhapatya, and Āhavanīya fires in succession, as well as the sages, the munis, the Brāhmaṇas, the Kṣatriyas, and the others. || 38 ||
Having uttered the mantra ending with "svāhā," they performed the offering of the oblation;
for he who takes up the praiseworthy mantra joined with "svāhā" [attains success]. (39)
All success shall belong to him merely by the grasping of the mantra;
he is like a serpent deprived of its venom, or like a twice-born man devoid of the Vedas. || 40 ||
A woman devoid of service to her husband is as contemptible as a man devoid of knowledge, or like a tree devoid of fruit and branches. || 41 ||
Likewise, a mantra devoid of "svāhā" does not grant fruit when offered;
all the twice-born were thoroughly satisfied, and the gods received their oblations. (42)
"By means of that very mantra ending in 'svāhā', everything indeed becomes fruitful. Thus has this entire, supreme narrative of Svāhā been told. (43)
"It bestows happiness, it bestows liberation, and it is the essence; what more do you wish to hear?
Nārada said:
"O Lord of Sages, [tell me] the ritual for the worship of Svāhā, as well as her meditation and hymn of praise."
"O Lord, tell me that by which he worshipped and praised Agni; [tell me] the meditation, the hymn, and the procedure for worship as declared in the Sāmaveda. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
[Listen to] the meditation, the hymn, and the procedure for worship as declared in the Sāmaveda.
Listen attentively, O Brahmin, lord of sages; I shall speak.
At the time of commencing all sacrifices, [one should worship] either in a Śālagrāma stone or in a water-pot.
Having worshipped Svāhā with diligence, one should perform the sacrifice for the attainment of the ritual parts;
she is Svāhā, endowed with the limbs of the mantra and possessing the very nature of the perfection of mantra. (47)

Having meditated thus upon her who is perfected, who bestows success upon men, and who is auspiciously the giver of the fruits of actions, a person should offer water for the feet and other offerings while reciting the root mantra. (48)
O Sage, listen: by praising with this root mantra—*oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ vahnijāyāyai devyai svāhā*—one shall obtain all accomplishments. (49)
Whoever worships her with devotion, all that is desired shall certainly come to pass.
Vahni said:
Svāhā is the beloved of Vahni, the wife of Vahni, and the one who causes him satisfaction. (50)
She is power, she is action, the giver of time, the bringer of ripeness, and the eternal.
She is the constant movement of men, the burner, and the one capable of consuming.
She is the very essence of saṃsāra and the one who carries across the terrible cycle of existence;
she is the life-force of the gods and the nourisher of the gods. || 52 ||
Whoever recites these sixteen names endowed with devotion shall attain all perfections in this world and in the next.
None of his actions shall be deficient; all his deeds will be most auspicious.
A sonless man obtains a son, and one deprived of a wife obtains a beloved spouse. 54.
And having obtained his own beloved, who resembles Rambhā, he shall attain happiness. || 55 ||

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Svāhā," in the ninth book of the *Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada. || 43 ||
The Description of the Narrative of Svadhā. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall relate the excellent narrative of Svadhā.
It brings satisfaction to the ancestors and increases the fruit obtained at the conclusion of a śrāddha ceremony.
At the beginning of creation, the Ordainer of the worlds created the groups of ancestors—
four embodied ones and three whose nature is radiant energy.
Having seen the seven classes of ancestors, who were of pleasant form and captivating,
he prepared food for them, beginning with the libations of water (tarpaṇa) and followed by the śrāddha ceremony.
Bathing up to the libations (tarpaṇa), the ancestral rite (śrāddha), the worship of the gods,
and the daily observances (āhnika) ending with the three junctions of the day— these are heard in the Veda as the duties of Brahmins.
That Brahmin who does not daily perform the Śrāddha and libations at the three junctions of the day, nor offer the bali-oblation or chant the sound of the Vedas, is like a serpent devoid of poison.
O Nārada, he who is devoid of service to the Goddess and who eats what has not been offered to Śrī Hari has his impurity ending only with his ashes; he is unfit for any sacred rite.
Having created the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and other ceremonies for the sake of the ancestors, Brahmā departed;
yet the ancestors do not receive them, even though they are offered by the Brāhmaṇas and others.
And all of them, hungry and weary, went to the assembly hall of Brahmā;
they reported everything to him, the Ordainer of the worlds.
And Brahmā created a mind-born daughter who was enchanting,
endowed with beauty and youth, and whose face resembled a hundred moons.
She was possessed of knowledge, endowed with virtues, and exceedingly beautiful; she was virtuous, possessed the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, and was adorned with jewel ornaments.
She was pure, a portion of Prakṛti, smiling, auspicious, and bestowing boons;
she was named Svadhā, possessed of beautiful teeth, and endowed with the marks of Lakṣmī. || 11 ||
And she bore the lotus-faced wife of the ancestors, born from a lotus, with lotus-eyes, whose lotus-feet were placed upon a hundred lotuses.
Brahmā gave [this] to the Pitṛs, who were satisfied, as a form of satisfaction;
and he imparted this secret instruction to the Brāhmaṇas.
Having uttered the mantra ending with "svadhā," it was also declared that [the offering] should be given to the ancestors;
in that sequence, the Brahmins of old gave the gift to the father.
Svāhā is prescribed for offerings to the gods, and Svadhā is remembered for offerings to the ancestors;
in all cases, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is prescribed, for a sacrifice without a fee is destroyed.
The ancestors, the deities, the learned brahmins, the sages, and likewise the Manus,
performed worship with the svadhā offering and praised Śāntā with supreme devotion.
The gods and others were satisfied, their desires completely fulfilled; and the Brahmins and other ancestors were gratified by the excellent offering of the Svadhā goddess.
Thus has everything been told, including the very narrative of Svadhā, which brings satisfaction to all. What more do you wish to hear?
Nārada said:
O great sage, best among the knowers of the Vedas, I desire to hear with diligence the rules for the worship of Svadhā, as well as her meditation and hymn; please speak. (19)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Brāhmaṇa, you know all the meditations and hymns of praise declared in the Vedas, which are entirely auspicious; why then do you wish to know them for the sake of your own advancement?
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śarad, under the asterism Maghā, on the day of the Śrāddha,
one should diligently worship Svadhā and then perform the Śrāddha ceremony.
If a Brahmin, possessing a sense of "I-ness," performs a śrāddha without first honoring Svadhā, he shall not partake of the fruit of that śrāddha or the libation; this is the truth.
I worship the mind-born daughter of Brahmā, who possesses eternal and stable youth,
who is worthy of worship by the ancestors and gods, and who bestows the fruits of śrāddha rites.
Having meditated thus, one should offer water for the feet and other honors to her upon a stone or in an auspicious jar with the root mantra; so it is heard in the Śruti.
"O great sage, having uttered 'oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ svadhādevyai svāhā,' the twice-born one should worship her, offer praise, and bow down to her. (25)
Listen, O best of sages, son of Brahmā, you who are learned, to this hymn which was composed by Brahmā in ancient times and which grants all desires to men. (26)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Merely by uttering the word "svadhā," a man becomes one who has bathed in a sacred ford;
he is liberated from all sins and obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. || 27 ||
If one should remember "Svadhā, Svadhā, Svadhā" in this manner three times, one obtains the fruit of the Śrāddha, as well as of the offering of bali and the libation (tarpaṇa). || 28 ||
He who, with a concentrated mind, hears the hymn of Svadhā at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony, shall obtain the very fruit arising from that Śrāddha; of this there is no doubt. (29)
The man who recites "Svadhā, Svadhā, Svadhā" thus at the three junctions of the day shall obtain a beloved, humble, virtuous wife endowed with the qualities of a mother.
You are as dear to the ancestors as their own life-breath, you are the embodiment of the livelihood of the twice-born,
the presiding deity of the Śrāddha rites, and the bestower of the fruits of the Śrāddhas and other ceremonies.
O lady of excellent vows, you are eternal and the embodiment of truth; you are the embodiment of merit.
Your manifestation and disappearance occur during creation and dissolution.
Oṃ, Svasti, Namaḥ, Svāhā, Svadhā, and Dakṣiṇā—these have been established by the four Vedas and are further praised for those engaged in ritual action. (33)
"These were created by the Lord solely for the purpose of fulfilling karma"—
having spoken thus, that Brahmā remained in his own assembly in the world of Brahmā.
And she stood there suddenly and immediately; then that Svadhā appeared, and he gave that very lotus-faced woman to the Pitṛs.
Having reached her, they and their ancestors departed filled with great joy.
Whoever listens with a concentrated mind to this meritorious hymn of praise to Svadhā shall be as one who has bathed in all sacred fords and shall obtain his desired fruit. || 36 ||

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Svadhā," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada. || 44 ||
The Description of the Narrative of Dakṣiṇā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The highly praised, sweet, and supreme narrative concerning Svāhā and Svadhā has been told.
I shall relate the narrative of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); listen with attentive mind. || 1 ||
In former times, the cowherd girl Suśīlā was the beloved of Hari in Goloka;
she was the foremost companion of Rādhā, auspicious, venerable, and enchanting. || 2 ||
She was exceedingly beautiful, a fortunate woman, virtuous, with lovely teeth;
she was learned, endowed with good qualities, and possessed of supreme beauty.
Kalāvatī was of delicate limbs, lovely, and lotus-eyed;
she possessed beautiful hips and fine breasts, was youthful, and was well-proportioned like a banyan tree.
With a face brightened by a gentle smile, adorned with jewel ornaments,
possessing the luster of a white campaka flower, she has lips like the bimba fruit and eyes like those of a deer.
Skilled in the treatises on love, the passionate woman moved with the grace of a swan; she was devoted in spirit, a knower of inner sentiments, and the beloved wife of Kṛṣṇa.
In ancient times, she who knows flavors, who is a connoisseur of aesthetic delight, and who yearned for the rasa of the Lord of Rasa,
dwelt upon the right lap of Rādhā, in front of her.
Seeing Rādhā, the most excellent among the foremost of gopīs, standing before him, Madhusūdana became humble with fear.
A passionate woman with a flushed face and eyes like red lotuses,
