her limbs trembling with anger and her lower lip quivering in rage.
Immediately after perceiving her departing with such speed,
the Blessed One, fearing conflict, vanished from sight.
Seeing that beloved being of peaceful nature and beautiful form fleeing away,
the cowherd women, headed by Suśīlā, trembled with fear.
Beholding the lecher there, ten million crores of gopīs became terrified;
with palms joined in reverence, their necks were bowed low in devotion.
Crying out "Protect us! Protect us! again and again, they went for refuge at the lotus feet of that Goddess out of fear.
O Nārada, three hundred million cowherds, including Sudāmā and others, went for refuge at his lotus feet out of fear.
Perceiving that her beloved was fleeing and that her companion Suśīlā was also fleeing, the Supreme Goddess cursed them both. || 15 ||
From this day forward, if that Gopikā comes to Goloka,
she shall be reduced to ashes by the mere act of her arrival.
Having spoken thus, the Goddess of the lords of gods, the Mistress of the Rāsa, being enraged right there in the midst of the Rāsa, summoned the Lord of the Rāsa.
Not seeing Kṛṣṇa before her, Rādhā, distressed by separation and firm in her vows,
perceived even a single moment as equal to ten million ages.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of the life-breath, come, O you who are dearer than life!
O Lord of the gods who presides over the life-breaths, my life-breaths depart without you.
A woman's pride increases day by day through her husband's good fortune; since it brings abundant happiness, she should always honor him in accordance with dharma.
He is the husband, the kinsman, the presiding deity, and the eternal refuge of noble women; he is the very embodiment of supreme prosperity, the personified bestower of enjoyments at all times. (21)
The giver of Dharma is the eternal giver of happiness, the giver of joy, and always the giver of peace;
he shines with honors, yet he bestows honor while shattering pride.
The master is the essence of essences, the increaser of kinsmen among one's kin;
indeed, no kinsman equal to a husband is seen among all kinsmen. (23)
He is called the supporter (*bhartṛ*) because of his supporting, and the lord (*pati*) because of his protecting;
he is called the master (*svāmī*) because he is the ruler of the body, and the beloved (*kānta*) because he grants desires. || 24 ||

He is remembered as a kinsman (bandhu) because he increases happiness, and as dear (priya) because of his gift of affection; he is the Lord (īśa) because he bestows sovereignty, and the Leader of Life (prāṇanāyaka) because he is the Lord of life (prāṇeśa). || 25 ||
Because he grants pleasure, the lover is dear; there is nothing dearer than the beloved.
Furthermore, a son is born from the master’s semen; therefore, he is dear. (26)
A husband is always dearer than a hundred sons to women of noble birth;
however, she who is born of an ignoble family is incapable of understanding her beloved.
It is equivalent to bathing in all sacred fords, giving the sacrificial fee at all sacrifices, circumambulating the entire earth, and performing all forms of austerity. (28)
All the vows and the like, whatever great gifts there are, the meritorious fasts, and whatever [practices] have been heard of; || 29 ||
Service to the guru, service to the brahmins, and whatever service is rendered to the gods—
all these do not equal even a sixteenth part of service to the feet of one's own master.
Among gurus, brahmins, and gods, the husband is the most venerable for all;
just as he is dear to men of noble birth, so too is the giver of knowledge.
Of the gopīs numbering hundreds of millions, and likewise of the cowherds;
and of the innumerable cosmic eggs situated therein, as well. || 32 ||

"By whose grace I have become the sovereign of all things from the beginning of the universe to the end of the cosmic egg, yet I do not know that Beloved; the nature of womanhood is difficult to overcome. (33)
Having spoken thus to Kṛṣṇa, Rādhikā meditated upon him there with her own devotion;
that Rādhā wept out of love and cried out, "O Lord! O Lord! (34).
"O Beloved, grant me your vision; I am wretched and tormented by the pain of separation.
Then, O Sage, that goddess Dakṣiṇā was cast down from Goloka.
And after performing austerities for a very long time, he entered the body of Kamalā;
then all the gods and others, having performed a most difficult sacrifice, [attained their goal]. (36)
They did not obtain the fruit of those [deeds]; despondent, they went to Vidhi.
Having heard the petition of the gods and others, Vidhi [went] to the Lord of the World.
And having meditated with devotion for a very long time, he received a response from the Lord Nārāyaṇa and from the body of Mahālakṣmī.
Having extracted the mortal splendor, he gave it as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Brahmā;
Brahmā, in turn, gave it to the sacrifice for the sake of completing the ritual acts.
Having worshipped her according to the prescribed rites, Yajña then joyfully praised her, who possessed the luster of molten gold and a radiance equal to ten million moons. (40)
She was exceedingly lovely, beautiful, and most enchanting; she had a lotus-like face, tender limbs, and large, lotus-like eyes.
She is worthy of worship by the one seated upon the lotus, born from the body of the lotus-born [Brahmā],
wearing garments as pure as fire, with lips like the *bimba* fruit, possessing beautiful teeth, and being ever virtuous.
She bore a mass of braided hair adorned with garlands of *mālatī* flowers;
her face was brightened by a gentle smile, and she was decorated with ornaments of precious gems. (43)
Well-adorned with fine garments and having bathed well, she was enchanting to the minds of sages;
she was marked with drops of musk along with fragrant sandalwood and camphor.
Even with a tiny dot of vermilion, she is radiant upon the region below her tresses;
she is endowed with highly praiseworthy hips and possesses large buttocks and breasts. (45)
Seeing her, who was the very embodiment of Kāmadeva’s power and was tormented by his arrows, the beautiful Yajña fell into a swoon.
He took her as his wife according to the rites previously prescribed by the sacred law;
and having taken her to a secluded place, he remained there for a hundred divine years.
Yajña rejoiced, filled with joy, together with Rāmeśa and Ramā;
that goddess conceived a divine embryo for twelve years. || 48 ||
Then she gave birth to a son, who was indeed the fruit of all her actions;
and when the rite was completed, that son became the bestower of its fruit.
Those who know the Vedas understand that sacrifice, together with the sacrificial fee, the son, and the fruit, is the giver of results to those who perform ritual actions.
O Nārada, having obtained the sacrificial fee and his son who bestows the fruit, the sacrifice gave the fruit of all ritual acts to everyone.
Then the gods and others, satisfied and with their desires fulfilled, all departed for their own abodes; this was heard from the mouth of Dharmavaktra.
Having performed the rite and being the performer, one should quickly give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
at that very moment one obtains the fruit—this has been declared by the Vedas, O Sage. (53)

If the performer of the rite, when the ritual is complete, does not give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins at that very moment—whether by fate or through ignorance—[he incurs a fault]. (54)
When a single moment has passed, it will certainly become twofold;
when one night has passed, it shall become a hundredfold.
In three nights it is a hundredfold; in seven days it is double that;
in a month it is said to be a hundred-thousandfold, and for Brahmins, it increases even further.
But when a year has passed, that [merit] becomes threefold;
indeed, all the ritual action of the patrons would become entirely fruitless.
And that man who seizes the property of a Brahmin is impure and unfit for ritual action;
by that sin, he becomes a sinner, impoverished and afflicted with disease.
Then Lakṣmī departs from that house after pronouncing a most terrible curse;
furthermore, the ancestors do not accept the śrāddha offerings or the libations (tarpaṇa) given by him.
In this way, the gods received that worship and the oblation of fire offered by him;
no gift was given that was not [properly] bestowed, nor did the recipient ever beg for it. (60)
Both of them go to hell like a jar whose rope has been severed,
if the sacrificer does not bestow the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) even when requested.
One who steals the property of a Brahmin will certainly go to Kumbhīpāka;
there he shall dwell for a hundred thousand years, beaten by the messengers of Yama.
Consequently, he shall become a Cāṇḍāla, afflicted by disease and impoverished;
he shall cause the downfall of seven generations of men before him and seven from his own birth.
"Thus has it been told, O Brahmin; what more do you wish to hear?
Nārada said: "O Sage, who enjoys the fruit of that ritual act which is devoid of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)?"
"Tell me first the ritual procedure for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) performed at a sacrifice.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"O Sage, how indeed can there be any fruit from a rite that is devoid of a sacrificial fee?"
O sage, only in a ritual accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) does the fruit of action proceed; and Bali, O sage, experiences the fruit of whatever ritual was performed without such fees.
O Sage, in ancient times that was given by Vāmana to Bali;
for one who is not learned in the Vedas is like a gift of śrāddha materials given without faith. (67)

Whatever offerings for worship and such were made by Brahmins who are husbands of Śūdra women, whatever sacrifice was performed by unworthy twice-born men, and whatever worship was offered to the impure; || 68 ||
Without a doubt, Bali consumes the ritual action of one who lacks devotion toward the Guru;
as does the meditation, the hymn of praise, and the sequence of the worship ritual belonging to the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 69.
I shall proclaim all of that as declared in the Kaṇva recension; listen attentively.
Long ago, having obtained her—the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) who is skilled in ritual action—Yajña [attained his purpose]. (70)
He was bewildered by her beauty and, overcome with desire, offered praise.
Yajña said:
"In former times, you were a cowherd girl in Goloka, the most excellent and noble among the cowherd girls."
Her dear friend, equal to Rādhā and beloved by Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
[is present] on the full moon day of Kārtika during the great festival of Rādhā at the Rāsa dance.
And because Lakṣmī manifested from his right shoulder, she is called Dakṣiṇā;
and formerly you were known by the name Suśīlā, O beautiful one, renowned for your virtuous character.
Having fallen from the shoulder of Lakṣmī due to the curse of Rādhā,
you have descended from Goloka and arrived here by my good fortune.
"Have mercy, O illustrious lady; make me alone your husband.
O Goddess, you alone are always the bestower of the fruits of the actions of those who perform deeds. (75)
Without you, all the actions of everyone are fruitless;
likewise, without you, the ritual action of those who perform rites does not shine. (76)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and even the guardians of the quarters and others are not capable of bestowing the fruit of action without you.
Brahmā himself is the embodiment of action, Maheśvara is the embodiment of the fruit,
Viṣṇu is the embodiment of sacrifice, and I am you— the very essence of them all.
The Supreme Brahman is the bestower of fruits; Prakṛti is supreme and devoid of qualities;
and the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa himself, together with you, is capable [of all]. (79)
O beloved, you alone are my power in birth after birth;
O fair-faced one, I am capable in every action only when together with you.
Having spoken thus, the presiding deity of the sacrifice stood before him;
that goddess, a portion of Kamalā, became pleased and attended upon him.
And whoever recites this hymn of praise for the sacrificial fee at the time of a sacrifice shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices; of this there is no doubt. || 82 ||
In the Rājasūya, Vājapeya, Gomedha, Naramedha, Aśvamedha, Lāṅgala, and the glorious Viṣṇuyajña; || 83 ||
To Dhanada, Bhūmida, Pūrta, Phalada, Gajamedhaka, Lohayajña, Svarṇayajña, Ratnayajña, and Tāmraka; (84)
In the Śiva-sacrifice, the Rudra-sacrifice, and the Śakra-sacrifice at Bandhuka;
in the rain, the Varuṇa-sacrifice, and at Kaṇḍaka during the crushing of enemies. || 85 ||
In the pure sacrifice, the dharma-sacrifice, the ritual, and the rite that liberates from sin;
in the Brahmāṇī-karma-yāga and the auspicious yoni-yāga. || 86 ||
And whoever recites this hymn at the commencement of these [rites], that entire undertaking will certainly be accomplished without obstacles. (87)
This hymn has been told; now listen to the method of meditation and worship.
A wise person should worship the Southern [Form] either in a Śālagrāma stone or in a water-pot. (88)
Born from the right shoulder of Lakṣmī, she is Dakṣiṇā, a portion of Kamalā;
she is highly skilled in all rites and the bestower of the fruits of all actions. (89)
I worship her who is the very embodiment of Viṣṇu’s power, who is honored and saluted, auspicious,
the giver of purity, whose form is purity itself, virtuous, and the bestower of well-being.
Having meditated thus, the wise one should worship the Bestower of Boons with this very root mantra,
O Nārada, after having offered water for the feet and other offerings to the Goddess according to the Vedic injunctions.
And the wise one, with devotion, should worship according to the rules Dakṣiṇā, who is honored by all, with the mantra: "Oṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Dakṣiṇā. (92)
Thus, O Brahmin, has this narrative called the Dakṣiṇā been told;
it bestows happiness, grants delight, and yields the fruit of all ritual actions. (93)
And whoever listens with a concentrated mind to this narrative of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), no action resulting in physical deficiency shall occur for them on the land of Bhārata. (94)
A sonless man shall certainly obtain a son endowed with virtues;
one deprived of a wife shall obtain an excellent, beautiful, and most virtuous wife. 95.
A wife who has beautiful hips, who has borne sons, who is humble, who speaks kindly, who is devoted to her husband, pure, and of noble birth—such is the excellent woman. 96.
One devoid of knowledge shall obtain knowledge; one devoid of wealth shall obtain wealth;
one devoid of land shall obtain land; and one devoid of progeny shall obtain progeny. || 97 ||
In times of distress, separation from kinsmen, misfortune, or likewise imprisonment, by hearing this for one month, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Dakṣiṇā," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada. || 45 ||
Description of the Narrative of the Sixty: Nārada said,
"I have heard the excellent narrative concerning many goddesses."
O Brahmin, best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me the life stories of the others.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Brahmin, the life stories of all those goddesses previously mentioned are found individually within the Vedas; which of them do you wish to hear here?
Nārada said:
"The sixth is Maṅgalacaṇḍī, who is a portion of Prakṛti produced from the mind;
I desire to hear the origin and the life-story of these [goddesses] in accordance with the truth."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: She who is the sixth part of Prakṛti is celebrated as the sixth [Goddess];
she is the presiding deity of children, the Māyā of Viṣṇu, and the bestower of children.
She who is renowned in the Mātṛkās by the name Devasenā,
that virtuous and well-vowed wife of Skanda, was dearer to him than his own life.
She bestows long life upon children, acting as their nurse and providing protection;
ever remaining by the side of infants, she is a yoginī perfected through yoga.
O Brahmin, listen to this history regarding her method of worship, which was heard from the mouth of Dharma; it is supremely bestowing happiness and granting sons. (7)
King Priyavrata was the son of Svāyambhuva Manu;
being a lord of yogis and always devoted to ascetic practices, he did not take a wife.
And by the command of Brahmā, he diligently took a wife;
yet, O sage, though he had been married for a very long time, he did not obtain a son.
Kaśyapa also caused that Putreṣṭi sacrifice to be performed;
the sage gave the sacrificial oblation (caru) to his beloved wife Mālinī.
Having consumed that sacrificial porridge of hers, she immediately became pregnant;
and that goddess bore him for twelve divine years.
Then, O Brahmin, she gave birth to a boy with the luster of gold,
endowed with all limbs, yet dead with wide-open eyes.
Seeing him, all the women and the wives of his kinsmen wept;
his mother fell into a swoon due to her intense grief for her son.
O Sage, taking the boy with him, the king went to the cremation ground;
there in the wilderness, he wept, holding his son to his chest.
The king did not abandon the boy, being intent on giving up his own life;
through the most agonizing grief for his son, he forgot the yoga of knowledge.
In the meantime, he beheld there a celestial chariot,
resembling pure crystal and fashioned from the finest of gems.
It was eternally blazing with splendor, adorned with silken garments,
enriched with various wonderful and variegated designs, and graced by garlands of flowers.
There he beheld a goddess, lovely and captivating,
with the complexion of a white campaka flower, eternally fixed in the prime of youth.
Her face was brightened by a gentle smile; she was adorned with jewel ornaments, full of compassion, perfected in yoga, and eager to bestow grace upon her devotees.
Seeing her before him, the king praised her with the utmost reverence;
he performed worship for her, leaving the child on the ground.
O Nārada, the king questioned her, who was pleased, whose radiance was like the summer sun, blazing with splendor, yet peaceful and lovely as Skanda’s own consort.
The king said:
"Who are you, O most beautiful one? O lovely lady, whose beloved are you, O woman of virtuous vows?
Whose daughter are you, O lady of excellent hips—you who are blessed and honored among women? (22)
Having heard the words of the lord of men, that Goddess Senā, the auspicious Caṇḍikā of the world and the warrior of the gods, spoke.
In ancient times, that army of the gods was seized by the Daityas;
because she granted victory to them, it was therefore called Devasenā.
The illustrious Devasenā said: "O protector of the earth, I am the mental daughter of Brahmā, the sovereign Devasenā;
having created me from his mind, the Creator gave me to Skanda. (25)
She is renowned in the Mātṛkās as the wife of Skanda and is of excellent vows;
she is celebrated among all as Ṣaṣṭhī, the supreme sixth part of Prakṛti.
She grants sons to those without sons, gives beloved things to those who desire them,
bestows wealth upon the poor, and provides their own specific duties to those engaged in work.
Happiness, suffering, fear, sorrow, joy, and even auspiciousness—prosperity as well as adversity—all come about through karma. (28)
By one's own action one has many sons, yet by one's own action one's lineage may perish;
by action one has deceased sons, and by action one lives for a long time. (29)
By his own karma one becomes endowed with virtues, and by karma one becomes deficient in limbs;
by karma one has many wives, and by karma one is deprived of a wife.
By karma the possessor of dharma becomes endowed with form; by his own karma he is constantly subject to disease.
Through karma there arises illness, and through karma alone there is health as well. (31)
"Therefore, O King, karma is supreme above all things; thus it is heard in the Śruti.
Having spoken thus, O Sage, that goddess took the boy.
By means of her great knowledge, that goddess restored him to life with ease;
the king beheld that boy, smiling and radiant as gold.
Then Devasenā, having taken leave of the king who was watching her, and taking the boy with her, the goddess prepared to ascend into the sky. (34)
Then the king, his throat, lips, and palate parched, praised her once more; by that hymn of praise, the goddess became truly gratified.
O Brahmin, she spoke to that king regarding the actions ordained by the Vedas.
The Goddess said: "In the three worlds you are the king, the son of Svāyambhuva Manu. (36)
"Having performed my worship everywhere yourself, then I shall grant you a son, a lotus of the family, who is captivating. (37)
He was renowned by the name Suvrata, virtuous and highly learned;
a master of yoga who remembered his past lives and was an embodiment of a portion of Nārāyaṇa. || 38 ||
He performed a hundred sacrifices, was the most excellent among those honored by kṣatriyas, and possessed the auspicious strength of a hundred thousand rutting elephants. (39)
He is wealthy, virtuous, and pure; he is beloved by the learned, the form of perfection for yogis and men of knowledge, and the very embodiment of asceticism for those who practice austerities. (40)
"Renowned throughout the worlds and a bestower of all prosperity"—having spoken thus, that goddess gave the child to him. (41)
King Priyavrata gave his consent for the sake of worship,
and the Goddess, having granted him an auspicious boon, went to heaven.
Accompanied by his ministers, he returned to his own home with a joyful heart;
having arrived, he related the news concerning his son. (43)
Having heard this, O Nārada, both men and women became satisfied;
they caused auspicious rites to be performed everywhere for the sake of their son.
He worshipped the Goddess and gave wealth to the Brahmins;
and every month, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, the king held a great festival.
And with great effort, he caused the rite for the Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī to be performed everywhere on the sixth day for children in the lying-in chamber, according to the prescribed ritual.
He caused that worship to be performed for twenty-one days,
as well as auspicious rites for children and the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*).
He caused it to increase everywhere and performed it himself;
listen to me regarding his meditation, the ritual of worship, and his hymn of praise. 48.
O sage of noble vows, that which was heard from the mouth of the Dharma-preacher as spoken by Kauthuma—
whether at Śālagrāma, or in a water-pot, or at the root of a banyan tree.
Or the wise man, having fashioned a statuette on a wall,
should worship it after installing that radiant image, which is pure and represents one-sixth part of Prakṛti.
She who bestows excellent sons, the giver of auspiciousness, whose form is compassion, the mother of the world;
she who possesses the luster of the color of a white campaka flower and is adorned with ornaments of jewels.
"I worship the supreme Devasenā, who is of a purifying nature.
Having meditated thus and placed a flower upon his own head, the wise one [proceeds]. (52)
Having meditated again, one should worship the virtuous Satī with the root mantra,
using water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), as well as perfumes, flowers, and lamps.
With various kinds of food offerings and beautiful fruits, one should offer according to the prescribed ritual with the mantra: "Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī. (54)
A person should recite the eight-syllabled great mantra according to his capacity;
then, having offered praise, he should bow down with devotion and a concentrated mind. (55)

And having recited one hundred thousand times the hymn from the Sāmaveda, which is excellent and bestows the fruit of a son, as well as the great eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣara), he [shall attain his goal]. || 56 ||
"He shall certainly obtain a virtuous son," so said the Lotus-born One.
"Listen, O best of sages, to this hymn which brings about all desires and auspiciousness. (57)
O Nārada, she who grants the desires of all and is hidden within the Vedas—to the Goddess, the Great Goddess, to Siddhi, to Śānti, salutations, salutations! (58)
Salutations again and again to the auspicious Goddess Devasenā, the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī;
salutations again and again to the giver of boons, the giver of sons, and the giver of wealth. || 59 ||
Salutations again and again to the Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, the giver of happiness and the giver of liberation;
salutations again and again to her who is the creation itself, whose form is the sixth part, and who is the perfected one.
Salutations again and again to Māyā, Siddhayoginī, and the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī; salutations again and again to Sārā, Śāradā, and the supreme goddess Parā. || 61 ||
Salutations again and again to the goddess who presides over children, to Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī;
to the auspicious one who bestows well-being, and who grants the fruits of actions.
Salutations again and again to the Goddess who is manifest to her own devotees, the sixth [Goddess], worthy of worship as the beloved of Skanda in all rites for all people. 63.
Salutations again and again to Goddess Shashthi, who provides protection to the gods, whose nature is pure sattva, and who is ever worshipped by men. (64)
Salutations again and again to Goddess Shashthi, who is free from violence and anger;
O Sovereign of the Gods, grant me wealth, grant me a beloved wife, and grant me a son.
Grant me honor, grant me victory, slay my enemies, O Maheśvarī!
Grant me righteousness, grant me fame; salutations again and again to Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī.
Grant land, grant progeny, grant knowledge, O highly honored one; grant auspiciousness and victory. Homage, homage to the Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī! 67.
Having thus praised the Goddess, Priyavrata, the king of kings, obtained a son of great renown through the grace of the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī. (68)
O Brahmin, he who listens to this Ṣaṣṭhī-stotra for a year shall obtain a son, a boon, who is long-lived, even if he was previously childless. (69)
And he who, having worshipped with devotion for one year, listens to this, is liberated from all sins; even a woman who has long been barren shall give birth.
By the grace of the Goddess, she gives birth to a son who is heroic, virtuous, learned, illustrious, and possessed of a very long life. (71)
A woman who is barren like a crow, or one whose children have died,
shall obtain a son after hearing [this] for a year, through the grace of the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī.
If the father or mother hears [this] for a child who is afflicted by disease, that child is liberated within a month through the grace of the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī. || 73 ||

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Ṣaṣṭhī," in the Ninth Book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada. || 46 ||
The description of the narrative concerning Maṅgalacaṇḍī and Manasā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O son of Brahmā, the narrative of Ṣaṣṭhī has been told according to tradition.
And the goddess Maṅgalacaṇḍī—listen now to her narrative.
All that she heard from the mouth of the Dharma regarding worship and other rites was indeed in accordance with the Vedas, and was thus desired even by all the learned.
She who is skillful and fierce, yet auspicious in matters of welfare;
she who is expert in auspicious rites—she is Maṅgalacaṇḍikā.
The goddess Caṇḍī who is worthy of worship, and even Maṅgala, the son of the Earth;
she who is the beloved deity of Maṅgala is indeed Maṅgalacaṇḍikā. || 4 ||
Maṅgala was a descendant of Manu and the lord of the seven islands;
his worshipful and chosen deity was Maṅgalacaṇḍikā.
Through her various forms, she is Durgā, the sovereign Mūlaprakṛti;
manifest in the form of compassion, she is the beloved deity of women.
And at the outset, she who is higher than the highest was worshipped by Śaṅkara and by Viṣṇu,
who was impelled [to act] during the terrible slaughter of Tripura.
O Brahmin, while he was in a miserable plight and in distress due to the instruction regarding the Veda,
his vehicle fell from the sky, having been struck down by a Daitya out of rage.
And Śaṅkara, instructed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, praised Durgā;
she who, through a division of forms, became Maṅgalacaṇḍī. || 9 ||
He spoke before Śambhu: "O Lord, there is no fear for you;
the Blessed One, in the form of a bull, shall become the sovereign of all for you."
"O bull-bannered one, I shall become the very embodiment of the power of battle, with Hari as my companion in the form of Māyā; of this there is no doubt."
"Go and slay the Daitya, your own enemy, who strikes down the feet of the gods.
Having spoken thus, the Goddess vanished and became the power (Śakti) of Śambhu.
With the weapon given by Viṣṇu, the Lord of Umā struck him down;
O chief of sages, when the Daitya had fallen, all the gods and great ṛṣis [rejoiced].
With their necks bowed in devotion, they praised the god Śaṅkara;
immediately, a rain of flowers fell upon the head of Śambhu.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu, being well-pleased, bestowed auspicious blessings upon him;
and likewise, Śaṅkara, having been instructed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, performed his ritual bath.
With devotion, he worshipped that goddess Maṅgalacaṇḍikā with water for the feet, respectful offerings, water for sipping, and various kinds of garments. (16)
O Sage, with various kinds of flowers, sandalwood, and food offerings made with devotion, as well as with goats, rams, buffaloes, gavayas, and birds; || 17 ||
With garments, ornaments, and garlands; with milk-rice, flour-cakes, and even honey and nectars; and with various kinds of fruits as well. || 18 ||
Accompanied by songs, dancers, musical instruments, festivals, and the chanting of his names,
one should meditate with devotion according to the meditation prescribed for the midday ritual.
O Nārada, he gave the materials with the root mantra alone:
"Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ, O Goddess worthy of all worship, O Maṅgalacaṇḍikā! (20)
"Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā" is the twenty-one-syllable mantra;
it is to be worshipped as the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru), granting all desires to its devotees. || 21 ||
By merely reciting [the mantra] one million times, the perfection of the mantra will certainly be attained.
O Brahmin, now hear the meditation as it is declared in the Vedas and approved by all. (22)
The goddess was sixteen years of age, eternally fixed in the bloom of youth, with lips like the *bimba* fruit, beautiful teeth, pure, and a face resembling an autumn lotus. || 23 ||
She has the luster of the color of a white campaka flower and eyes like beautiful blue lotuses;
she is the sustainer of the world and the bestower of all prosperity upon all beings. (24)
I always worship her whose form is light within the terrible ocean of saṃsāra;
O sage, let this meditation on the Goddess and this hymn of praise be heard. 25.
Mahādeva said: Protect, protect, O Mother of the World, O Goddess Maṅgalacaṇḍikā!
You who remove the multitude of calamities and bring about joy and auspiciousness.
O you who are skilled in joy and auspiciousness, O giver of joy and auspiciousness;
O auspicious one, skilled in auspiciousness, O auspicious Maṅgalacaṇḍikā! || 27 ||
O Auspicious One, worthy of auspiciousness, the source of all auspiciousness; O Goddess who bestows auspiciousness upon the virtuous, the abode of auspiciousness for all! || 28 ||
On the worshipful Tuesday, O auspicious tutelary deity,
you are eternally worthy of worship by King Maṅgala of the lineage of Manu.
O Goddess presiding over auspiciousness, the most auspicious among all auspicious things;
O support of the auspiciousness of worldly existence, O bestower of the auspiciousness of liberation! || 30 ||
O you who are the foundation of all auspiciousness, beyond all karmas, worthy of worship on every auspicious day, and the bestower of auspicious happiness! (31)
Having praised Maṅgalacaṇḍikā with this hymn and having performed worship on every Tuesday, Śambhu, the auspicious one, departed.
In the first [kalpa], the goddess Sarvamaṅgalā was worshipped by Śiva;
and in the second, she was worshipped by the planet Maṅgala.
On the third day, Bhadrā was worshipped by King Maṅgala;
on the fourth day, she was worshipped by beautiful women during the auspicious day of Maṅgala.
In the fifth [kalpa], Maṅgalacaṇḍikā, who is always worshipped by the Lord of the Universe (Śiva) and in every world, was worshipped by people desiring auspiciousness. || 35 ||
Thereupon, O Sage, the Supreme Goddess became worshipped everywhere by the gods, the sages, and by men and Manus.
Whoever listens with a concentrated mind to this auspicious hymn of the Goddess, may that auspiciousness be his and may no inauspiciousness come to him;
and his auspiciousness shall increase day by day through sons and grandsons. (37)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O son of Brahmā, the narrative of these two has been told according to the scriptures;
now hear with your mind the account that was heard from the mouth of Dharma.
And that maiden was the divine daughter of Kaśyapa, born of his mind;
she is the goddess who, by that very mind, sports with the mind.
And she who meditates upon the Supreme Self, the Lord, with her mind—
by that mind she is a goddess, and by that yoga she shines.
That goddess, a Vaiṣṇavī and a perfected yoginī who delights in the Self, performed penance for three yugas for Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul. (41)
And seeing that the body of Jaratkāru was withered away, the Lord, the Master, gave him the name Jaratkāru, meaning "the one whose body has decayed. || 42 ||
And the ocean of mercy, out of compassion, granted her her desire;
the Lord himself caused worship to be performed and performed it himself. (43)
In heaven, in the world of the Nagas, on earth, and up to the world of Brahma—
she who is exceedingly beautiful and captivating throughout the worlds is Gauri. Because she is thus renowned as Jagadgauri (the World-Gauri), that virtuous lady is worshipped.
And since that goddess is a disciple of Śiva, she is therefore proclaimed as Śaivī. || 45 ||
Because she was eternally and exceedingly devoted to Viṣṇu, she was celebrated as Vaiṣṇavī;
and at the sacrifice of the son of Parīkṣit, she was the protector of the lives of the Nāgas.
She is renowned as Nāgeśvarī and as the sister of the Nāgas;
because she is capable of neutralizing poison, she is remembered as Viṣaharī.
She obtained the Siddhayoga from Hara; by means of that, she became a Siddhayoginī, possessing supreme great knowledge and yoga, as well as the power to restore the dead to life.
The wise declare her to be endowed with great knowledge;
she was also the ascetic mother of Āstīka, the lord of sages.
Āstīka’s mother was well-known throughout the world and firmly established therein;
she was the beloved wife of the great-souled Jaratkāru, the lord of sages. (50)
Then Jaratkāru, the beloved of Jaratkāru, who was a yoginī perfected in mind, became the Gaurī of the world for that yogin who is worshipped by the universe.
She is Vaiṣṇavī, the sister of the Nāgas, Śaivī, and likewise Nāgeśvarī;
she is the beloved wife of Jaratkāru, the mother of Āstīka, and she who removes poison.
That goddess, endowed with great wisdom, is worshipped by the entire universe;
whoever recites these twelve names at the time of worship, [attains success]. || 53 ||
For him and for those born of his lineage, there is no fear of nāgas, even when lying on a bed infested by nāgas or in a dwelling seized by nāgas. (54)
In the great fortress adorned with serpents, whose very form is encircled by nāgas—by reciting this hymn, one is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (55)
Upon seeing one who recites this constantly, the host of nāgas flees;
indeed, by ten hundred thousand recitations of the hymn, men attain perfection in the stotra. (56)
He for whom the perfection of this hymn occurs is capable of consuming poison;
having made the serpents his ornaments, he shall have the serpents as his vehicle.
That man becomes a great adept (mahāsiddha) with a serpent-throne and a serpent-bed;
and in the end, he sports together with Viṣṇu day and night.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Narratives of Maṅgalacaṇḍī and Manasā," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada. 47.
The Description of the Narrative of Manasā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O best of sages, hear from me the procedure for worship.
And the meditation prescribed in the Sāmaveda is declared to be the ritual procedure for the Goddess. || 1 ||
She has the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, is adorned with jewel ornaments,
wears garments as pure as fire, and has a serpent as her sacred thread.
I worship her who is endowed with great wisdom, the most excellent among the foremost knowers,
the goddess presiding over the Siddhas, herself perfected and the bestower of perfection.
Having thus meditated upon that goddess, one should worship her with the root mantra alone,
using various food offerings, incenses, flowers, perfumes, and unguents.
O Sage, this twelve-syllable mantra, known as Kalpataru, is perfectly perfected; through its root-mantras declared in the Vedas, it grants the desires of devotees.
"Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ, svāhā to Manasādevī"—thus it is proclaimed.
By reciting this mantra five hundred thousand times, men shall attain mastery over the mantra.
He for whom there is accomplishment of the mantra becomes a perfected one (siddha) upon the surface of the earth;
for him, poison is like nectar, and he becomes equal to Dhanvantari.
Having bathed on the day of the sun's passage (saṅkrānti), a brāhmaṇa who diligently invokes the Goddess Īśānī in secret chambers and worships her with great devotion— || 8 ||
He who, meditating with his mind on the fifth day, offers an oblation to the Goddess,
will certainly become wealthy, possessed of sons, and renowned for his fame.
The procedure for worship has been told; now listen to its narrative.
O fortunate one, I shall relate that which was heard from the mouth of Dharma.
In ancient times, human beings on earth were overcome by fear of the nāgas;
they all went for refuge to Kaśyapa, the preeminent among sages.
Terrified and accompanied by Brahmā, Kaśyapa created mantras according to the seeds of the Vedas and through the instruction of Brahmā.
In that manner, he mentally created that goddess who presides over the mantra;
through that mental austerity, she came into being by means of his mind alone.
Having been born as a maiden, she went to the abode of Śaṅkara;
having worshipped him with devotion on Kailāsa, she praised the Moon-crested Lord.
The daughter of the sage served him for a thousand divine years,
and Maheśa, who is easily pleased, became truly gratified with her.
O sage, he bestowed great knowledge upon her and taught her the Sāman;
he gave her the eight-syllabled mantra of Kṛṣṇa, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree.
The seed-syllables of Lakṣmī, Māyā, and Kāma, followed by the word "Kṛṣṇa" in the dative case, then the name "Trailokyamaṅgala," the armor (kavaca), and the sequence of worship. || 17 ||

Having obtained the procedure for the preliminary rites (puraścaryā) as declared in the Vedas and approved by all, as well as the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, that virtuous daughter of the sage [practiced them]. (18)
By the command of Śaṅkara, the virtuous woman went to Puṣkara to perform penance;
and having performed penance for three yugas for Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, [she attained her goal]. (19)
That goddess became perfected; she beheld the Lord before her.
Seeing her, who was emaciated and young, the Treasure of Compassion was moved by pity. (20)
Hari caused worship to be performed and performed it himself;
and he granted her a boon: "May you be honored in every birth."
Having granted a boon to Kalyāṇī, Hari then vanished;
she was the first to be worshipped by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
In the second [kalpa], it was [revealed] by Śaṅkara himself, by Kaśyapa, by the god, by the sage, by Manu, by the Nāga, and by the descendants of Manu and others. || 23 ||
And she, being of virtuous vows, became honored throughout the three worlds;
in ancient times, Kaśyapa gave her to Jaratkāru, the lord of sages.
Unasked, the best of sages accepted [the bride] at the command of the Brahmin;
having performed the marriage, the great yogi rested for a long time through his ascetic power.
He slept at the foot of a banyan tree on Puṣkara upon the lap of the goddess;
that sage fell asleep, remembering the Lord, the Master of Sleep.
When evening had arrived, the sun went to its setting; then that virtuous woman, devoted to her husband, reflected in her mind.
Out of fear of violating dharma, the virtuous woman performed her reflection; she did not omit the final twilight devotion nor the daily rites prescribed for the twice-born. (28)
"My husband will incur sins such as the killing of a Brahmin—he who does not attend upon the morning [prayer] and he who does not worship at the evening [prayer]. (29)
Thinking that it was declared in the Vedas, he would always be impure in every respect and incur sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; thus she enlightened Sundarī. (30)
And that Buddha, the best of sages, became greatly enraged at her, O sage.
The sage said:
"O virtuous lady, why have you caused the interruption of my sleep while I was at ease? (31)
Futile are the vows and other observances of that woman who harms her husband; likewise futile are her asceticism, fasting, vows, and whatever gifts she may give.
For one who acts unfavorably toward her husband, everything becomes fruitless;
however, by her through whom the beloved Śrī Kṛṣṇa is honored, He himself is honored. 33.
And for the sake of the vow of devotion to her husband, Hari himself appeared in the form of a husband;
[this is equal to] all forms of giving, all sacrifices, and the visiting of all sacred pilgrimage sites.
All vows, all austerity, and whatever fasting and so forth there may be;
all dharma, truth, and the worship of all the gods—[all these are surpassed by this]. (35)
All of that does not equal even a sixteenth part of the service rendered to one's husband by her who performs the service of her husband in the meritorious land of Bhārata-varṣa. (36)
She goes to the abode of Brahmā along with her husband in Vaikuṇṭha;
she does what is displeasing to her husband and speaks what is unpleasant as if it were pleasant.
O virtuous lady, hear now the fruit of being born into an unworthy family:
she shall go to the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the moon and the sun endure. (38)
"Then she becomes a Cāṇḍālī, deprived of husband and sons.
Having spoken thus, the best of sages' lips began to quiver. (39)
At that, the virtuous woman trembled and spoke to her husband out of fear.
The virtuous woman said:
"It was only for fear of interrupting the twilight prayers that I disturbed your sleep. (40)
"O illustrious one, O observer of noble vows, bring peace to me, a wicked woman;
for he indeed brings about the destruction of my passion, food, and sleep. (41)
"He shall indeed go to the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the moon and sun exist.
Having spoken thus, the goddess mentally placed [him] at the lotus-feet of her husband.
Overcome with devotion and fear, she fell down and wept again and again upon seeing the enraged sage intent on cursing Śrīsūrya.
There the Blessed One arrived together with Sandhyā and Nārada;
having arrived there, Bhāskara himself spoke properly to the sage.

Fearing transgression of the discipline and out of respect for her, Bhāskara spoke to her as was appropriate; and seeing that it was the time of sunset, the virtuous woman, out of fear of violating dharma, [remained silent]. (45)
O Brahmin, you have awakened me; I have come to you for refuge.
Forgive me, O Blessed One, O Brahmā; it is not fitting for you, O Sage, to curse me. (46)
The hearts of Brahmins are always like fresh butter;
yet their anger lasts for only half a moment, after which the world would be reduced to ashes. (47)
Furthermore, no one other than a twice-born man is capable of creating again;
for the Brāhmaṇa, born from the lineage of Brahmā, blazes with the splendor of Brahman.
One should constantly meditate upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the eternal light of Brahman;
having heard these words of the Sun, the twice-born man became truly satisfied. (49)
Having received the blessings of the Brahmins, Sūrya went to his own abode;
meanwhile, the Brahmin Manasā abandoned [his body] in order to fulfill his vow.
Weeping, filled with grief, and with a heart burning with anguish,
she remembered her preceptor Śambhu, as well as her chosen deities Brahmā and Hari.
Afflicted by fear in her misfortune, she approached Kaśyapa, her progenitor;
there arrived the Lord of Gopīs and the Blessed Śambhu himself.
Having beheld his beloved deity, who is beyond the qualities of nature (prakṛti) and transcendent of material existence, the Brahmin mentally conceived both the ritual procedure and Kaśyapa.
He praised him with supreme devotion and bowed down again and again;
he paid homage to Śambhu, as well as to Brahmā and Kaśyapa.
He asked the question, "O gods, how did you come here?
Having heard those words, Brahmā immediately spoke what was appropriate for the occasion. (55)
Having paid homage to the lotus feet of Hṛṣīkeśa, he replied:
"If my lawful wife, who is most virtuous and devoted in mind, has been abandoned... (56)
"O Sage, produce offspring upon this wife for the sake of fulfilling your own duty;
having fathered a son upon your wife, you may then leave her."
But he who, having failed to produce offspring, abandons his beloved wife out of dispassion—his merit flows away like water from a mortar. (58)
Having heard the words of Brahmā, Jaratkāru, the lord of sages,
performed the touching of the navel through yoga preceded by mantras.
O best of sages, the best of sages spoke to her, Manasā;
Jaratkāru said:
"O Manasā, by this embryo, a son shall be born to you."
He was the foremost among those who have conquered their senses, righteous, the leader of brahmins,
radiant, ascetic, illustrious, and endowed with all virtues.
He shall be the foremost among those who know the Vedas, as well as among the wise and the yogis;
and that son, devoted to Viṣṇu and righteous, shall uplift his lineage.
All the ancestors indeed dance with joy at the mere birth [of such a child];
she who is devoted to her husband, virtuous in character, dear to him, and sweet-spoken—[she is truly blessed]. 63.
A mother of sons who is most righteous, a noble woman who protects her family, and a kinsman who bestows devotion to Hari—even these do not grant one's desired happiness. (64)
If he is a kinsman, he is also my father and the one who showed me the path of Hari;
she is the one who bore me in her womb and delivered me from dwelling within the womb. 65.
The sister is the embodiment of compassion who liberates one from the fear of Yama;
and the Guru is the giver of devotion to Viṣṇu, who bestows the mantras of Viṣṇu. (66)

And the Guru is indeed the giver of knowledge—that knowledge which consists of devotion to Kṛṣṇa—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings arises from that. 67.
Whether knowledge has become manifest or has vanished, whatever else there may be—be it born of the Vedas or born of sacrifice—the essence of all that is service to Hari. 68.
And that which is the essence of all principles—anything other than Hari is a mere mockery.
Knowledge has been imparted by me to you, for he alone is the master who bestows knowledge. (69)
One is liberated from bondage through knowledge; for he who bestows bondage is indeed an enemy, as is that teacher who does not grant knowledge endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu.
He is an enemy and a slayer of disciples, since he does not release one from bondage, nor from the mother, nor from the sufferings of the womb, nor likewise from the torments of disease.
How can he who does not liberate [others] be a guru? For he is indeed a father and a kinsman;
[he should teach] the path of Kṛṣṇa, which is of the nature of supreme bliss and imperishable.
What kind of kinsman is he who never reveals [the truth] to men? O virtuous lady, worship the Supreme Brahman, the infallible Kṛṣṇa, who is beyond all qualities.
"By serving him, the karma of men shall indeed become rootless;
I abandoned you through a deception—forgive this of mine, O beloved. (74)
In those virtuous women endowed with forbearance, anger does not exist due to their inner strength. O Goddess, I am going to Puṣkara for penance; go as you please.
The desires of those who are indifferent toward the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa [are fulfilled].
Having heard the words of Jaratkāru, she became distressed with grief in her mind. (76)
With tearful eyes, she spoke with humility to her beloved:
"O Lord, there is no fault in my mind for having interrupted your sleep; it was simply to abandon [the world]."
"Wherever I remember you constantly, there you shall come to me.
The separation from kinsmen is the greatest affliction; the separation from a son is even greater than that. (78)
The separation from the lord of one's life is more grievous than the total loss of all one's vital breaths;
indeed, for a devoted wife, her husband is dearer than even a hundred sons. (79)
Because he is dearer than everything else to women, he is called "Priya" by the wise;
as [a son] is to those with an only son, or as Hari is to the Vaiṣṇavas.
It is like eyes to the one-eyed, like water to the thirsty, like food to the hungry, and like sexual union to those filled with desire. (81)
Just as [the mind is intent] upon the property of others for thieves, upon a lover for unchaste women, upon a treatise for the learned, and upon trade for merchants; || 82 ||
"O Lord, may my mind likewise ever remain fixed on you, the beloved of virtuous women.
Having spoken thus in her mind, the goddess fell at her husband's feet. (83)
The sage, a treasure-house of compassion, took her onto his lap for a moment out of pity and bathed her with the water from his eyes and his mind.
With eyes full of tears and fearing separation, she sprinkled the sage's chest;
then, through that knowledge, both of them became free from sorrow.
Constantly remembering the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul,
the brāhmaṇa departed for ascetic penance after awakening his beloved wife.
In his mind, he went to Kailāsa, the abode of Śambhu, the Guru;
there, Pārvatī consoled Manasā, who was emaciated by grief. (87)
Śiva was exceedingly endowed with knowledge, and Śivā’s abode was likewise auspicious; on a most praiseworthy day marked by auspicious signs, the virtuous woman gave birth.
That son, an emanation of Nārāyaṇa and the teacher of yogins and wise men,
while still in the womb, heard great knowledge from the mouth of Śaṅkara.
And he became a lord of yogis, a teacher of yogis and men of knowledge;
he had his birth-chart prepared and had auspicious recitations performed. || 90 ||
And Śiva taught the Vedas to his young son;
furthermore, Śiva gave jeweled crowns studded with gems to the Brāhmaṇas.
Pārvatī [offered] a hundred thousand cows and various kinds of jewels;
and Śambhu [offered] the four Vedas as well as the other Vedāṅgas.
He taught the boy the supreme knowledge that conquers death;
likewise, his devotion was great toward his beloved, his chosen deity, and his guru. (93)
By him, she gave birth to a son named Āstīka;
and by the command of Śaṅkara, he went to Puṣkara to perform penance for Viṣṇu.
And having obtained that great mantra from the Supreme Self,
the one whose wealth is austerity performed divine penance for three hundred thousand years.
The great yogi arrived to pay homage to the Lord Śiva;
having prostrated before Śaṅkara, the boy stood right there. (96)
She went in her mind to the hermitage of her father Kaśyapa;
seeing his daughter there with her son, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) attained great joy.
O sage, he gave a hundred lakhs of jewels to the Brahmins and fed countless Brahmins for the welfare of his child.
O scorcher of enemies, both Aditi and Diti, as well as the others, attained great joy;
and she, together with her sons, remained for a very long time in her father’s abode.
I shall now relate his further narrative; listen to that.
Now, while Parīkṣit, the son of Abhimanyu, was under a Brahmin’s curse...
O Brahmin, this occurred suddenly due to the fault of destiny and past karma;
when seven days have passed, Takṣaka shall burn you.
Śṛṅgin cursed him right there with the water of the Kauśikī;
having heard the news of that, the king came to a place sheltered from the wind.
He remained there for seven days, intent on protecting his body;
and when the seven days had passed, he encountered Takṣaka on the road as he was going along.
On the road, a traveler saw King Dhanvantari, who was about to eat;
a conversation took place between them, and they felt great mutual affection. (104)
Dhanvantari obtained the jewel; Takṣaka gave it to him of his own accord.
Having taken it, he departed, satisfied and joyful in mind. (105)
Takṣaka devoured that king as he lay upon his bed;
having abandoned his body, the king departed swiftly to the other world.
O sage, Janamejaya then caused the funeral rites for his father to be performed;
the king also conducted the snake sacrifice (sarpasattra). || 107 ||
The host of serpents gave up their lives through the splendor of Brahman;
Takṣaka, indeed, being terrified, went to Mahendra for refuge.
The assembly of brahmins prepared to slay Takṣaka along with Indra;
then the gods, together with Indra, approached him in their minds.
And Mahendra, overwhelmed and agitated by fear, praised her;
then Āstīka arrived at the sacrifice by his mother’s command.
He begged the supreme lord of the earth for the lives of Mahendra and Takṣaka;
out of compassion and at the command of the Brāhmaṇa, that best of kings granted the boon. || 111 ||
Having completed the sacrifice, he joyfully gave sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins;
and the Brahmins, sages, and gods, having gone [to him] mentally, approached his presence. (112)
They worshipped Manasā and praised her individually;
Śakra, having gathered the necessary offerings, was filled with devotion and ever pure. (113)
He worshipped Manasā with great reverence and praised her;
having bowed down, he then offered the sixteen-fold service (ṣoḍaśopacāra) and a sacrificial offering dear to her.
And being well-pleased, by the command of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, he bestowed [the boon];
and having mentally worshipped the goddess Manasā, they departed for their own abodes. || 115 ||
"Thus everything has been told; what more do you wish to hear?
Nārada said:
"With which hymn did Mahendra praise the virtuous Manasā? (116)
"I wish to hear the sequence of the ritual for her worship according to its true essence.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Having bathed well, being pure and having sipped water, and having put on two clean garments... (117)
With devotion, he caused the Goddess to sit upon the jeweled lion-throne,
bathing her with the water of the celestial Gaṅgā held within a gem-encrusted pitcher.
Mahendra bathed Manasā with Vedic mantras and clothed her in two beautiful garments purified by fire.
Having applied sandalwood paste to all his limbs and being filled with devotion, he offered water for the feet (arghya) to Gaṇeśa,
the Sun, Agni, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śivā.
Having first worshipped the group of six deities, he then worshipped that virtuous Satī with the mantra:
"Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, svāhā to Manasādevī. (121)
With the ten-syllable root mantra, the leader of the gods offered everything as was appropriate;
having bestowed the sixteen services that are difficult even for gods to obtain. (122)
Impelled by Viṣṇu, he joyfully worshipped with devotion and indeed played various kinds of musical instruments there.
And by the command of Devapriyā, and there by the command of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, a rain of flowers fell from the sky upon Manasa.
With eyes filled with tears and his body marked by horripilation, he offered praise.
Purandara said:
"O Goddess, I desire to praise you, the most excellent and supreme among virtuous women. (125)
I am truly not able now to praise her who is higher than the highest and supreme;
for the characteristic of hymns in the Veda is that they are primarily devoted to describing one's own nature.
It is not possible to enumerate your virtues in this context;
you are of the nature of pure sattva, free from anger, violence, and the like.
And the sage was not able to refuse her, since he had made a request:
"O virtuous lady, you have been honored by me as my mother Aditi. (128)
O Goddess of the Suras, you are like a sister in the form of compassion and like a mother in the form of forbearance; my life, children, and wife have been protected by you.
I perform this worship of you; may my love increase forever.
O Mother of the World, although you are eternally worthy of worship everywhere, [I offer this to you]. 130.
Nevertheless, O Goddess of the Suras, I shall increase your worship;
those who shall worship you with devotion on the day of the Āṣāḍha-saṅkrānti— || 131 ||
On the fifth lunar day known as Manasī, or at the end of the month, or on every single day,
their sons, grandsons, and so forth, as well as their wealth, truly increase.
Those people who are illustrious, renowned, learned, and endowed with virtues, yet do not honor you out of ignorance, will instead revile you. (133)
They shall be devoid of fortune, and they will always face fear from the Nāgas;
for you yourself are the sovereign of all fortune, Kamalālayā, in Vaikuṇṭha.
The lordly sage Jaratkāru, an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa,
created you through his austerity, his splendor, and his mind, O Father.
For our protection alone, you were addressed by him with his mind;
O Manasādevī, you are Śakti, perfected as a yoginī through your own self.
Therefore, O Manasādevī, may you be worshipped and saluted by him;
for those who, with devotion, incessantly and fervently worship the gods of the mind.
Therefore, the wise proclaim you as the goddess of the mind;
O Goddess, you are the very embodiment of truth because of your eternal devotion to truth. 138.
For whoever would constantly meditate upon you, being intent on that, shall attain you;
and Indra, having praised you with his mind, took the boon from your sister.
Adorned with ornaments and accompanied by her retinue, that queen went to her own abode;
together with her son, she remained for a long time in her father’s house.
Constantly honored by her brothers, she was respected and saluted by all;
O Brahmin, Surabhi came there from Goloka and was most highly honored.
Having bathed her with milk, he worshipped her with reverence and imparted to her all knowledge that is secret and very difficult to attain. (142)
Honored by the gods, she returned once more to the heavenly realm;
one should worship and recite this hymn to Indra, the seed of merit for the mind. (143)
For him and for his descendants, there is no fear of serpents;
when he has accomplished the hymn, poison becomes equal to nectar.
By reciting it five hundred thousand times, a person becomes one who has mastered the hymn;
he shall certainly become a recliner upon serpents and have serpents as his vehicle. 145.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Manasā," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 48.
The Description of the Narrative of Surabhi.
Nārada said: Who indeed was that goddess Surabhi who came from Goloka?
O Brahman, I desire to hear with great effort that account of his life and deeds from his birth. || 1 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Surabhi, the presiding deity of cows, the primordial source of cows, the progenitor of cows,
and the foremost among cows, was born in Goloka.
I shall relate the life-story of the first creation; listen. In former times, his birth took place in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
Once, the playful Lord of Rādhikā,
accompanied by Rādhā and surrounded by cowherd maidens, went to the holy Vṛndāvana.
There, in that secluded place, he sported spontaneously out of curiosity;
and for him, who was composed of his own will, a desire to drink milk arose.
He effortlessly created from his left side the divine Surabhi, who was accompanied by her calf and possessed of milk; her calf was named Manoratha.
Having seen her with her calf, Śrīdāmā milked her into a new vessel;
the milk was superior to nectar and removed birth, death, and old age.
And the Lord of the Gopīs himself drank the sweet milk produced from that;
furthermore, a lake was formed by the overflow of the waters.
Extending both in length and breadth for a hundred yojanas all around,
this famous Ocean of Milk is also located in Goloka.
And by the will of the Lord, that pool for the sporting of the cowherd girls and of Rādhā became filled, being constructed from the finest jewels. (10)

Suddenly there appeared hundreds of thousands of millions of wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus), as many as there were hairs on the pores of the skin of Surabhi and all those cowherds who were there. 11.
They had many sons, indeed innumerable;
thus the creation of cows was described, and by them the world was filled.
O Sage, in ancient times the Blessed One performed worship with the Surabhi cow;
thereafter, that mode of worship became difficult to find even throughout the three worlds.
On the following day, accompanied by lamps, Surabhi became worthy of worship by the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Hari; this was heard from the mouth of Dharma.
O highly fortunate one, listen as I tell you the meditation, the hymn of praise, the root mantra, and the sequence of the ritual for the supreme rite, as declared in the Vedas. (15)
"Oṃ surabhyai namaḥ"—this six-syllabled mantra of hers is perfected by a mere hundred thousand recitations; it is a wish-fulfilling tree for devotees. (16)
Meditation is sung in the Yajurveda, and her worship is performed in every way;
she is the bestower of supernatural powers, the bestower of prosperity, the bestower of liberation, and the bestower of all desires.
The supreme consort of Rādhā, whose nature is Lakṣmī, the presiding deity of cows, the primordial cow, and the mother of cows. || 18 ||
I worship that goddess Surabhi, who is of a pure form, sanctified, the granter of all desires to her devotees, and by whom the entire universe is purified. 19.
A twice-born man should worship Surabhi in a water-pot, on the head of a cow, at a tethering post for cows, in a śālagrāma stone, or in water or fire.
He who, endowed with devotion, worships Surabhi on the following day during the forenoon while offering lamps, shall become worthy of honor upon this earth.
Once, in the three worlds during the Vārāha-kalpa, Surabhi, through the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, carried off the milk; and the gods and others were filled with anxiety.
Having gone to the world of Brahmā, they then praised Brahmā;
and by his command, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, praised Surabhi.
Purandara said:
Salutations to the Goddess, to the Great Goddess; salutations again and again to Surabhi.
O Mother of the Universe, salutations to you who are the very essence of the seed of cattle.
Salutations again and again to her who is dear to Rādhā and who is a portion of Padmā;
salutations again and again to her who is dear to Kṛṣṇa and who is the mother of cows. || 25 ||

Salutations again and again to her who is the very embodiment of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), who is eternally supreme over all, the giver of milk, the giver of wealth, and the giver of wisdom. || 26 ||
Salutations again and again to Śubhā and Subhadrā, and to Gopradā; salutations again and again to Yaśodā, Kīrtidā, and Dharmadā. || 27 ||
Merely by hearing the hymn of praise, the eternal Mother of the World, satisfied and delighted,
manifested right there in the realm of Brahmā.
Having granted a boon to Mahendra, even one that was difficult to obtain, she departed for Goloka;
and the gods and others returned to their own abodes.
O Nārada, the entire universe suddenly became filled with milk;
from that milk came clarified butter (ghṛta), from that the sacrifice, and from that the gratification of the gods.
Whoever recites this hymn of great merit with devotion shall possess cattle, wealth, fame, and likewise sons. (31)
Having bathed in all sacred fords and been initiated into all sacrifices,
he enjoys happiness in this world and goes at the end to the abode of Kṛṣṇa.
He shall dwell there for a very long time and perform service to Kṛṣṇa;
he does not return to that [mundane] existence again, but thereafter becomes a son of Brahmā.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Surabhi," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 49.
Description of the Ritual for the Worship of the Goddess’s Enclosures.
Nārada said:
"I have heard the entire narrative of the primary elements exactly as it occurred."
Having heard which, a living being is liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra. || 1 ||
Now I desire to hear the secret concealed by the Vedas—
the procedure for Rādhā and Durgā as enjoined by the Śruti.
O Lord of Sages, having heard the greatness of the other two described by you so exceedingly, whose mind would not be drawn toward them? (3)
Now tell me the procedure for those two whose portion is this entire universe, who govern all that is moving and unmoving, and through devotion to whom liberation is attained.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Nārada, I shall declare the secret enjoined by the Vedas,
which has not been told to anyone, the essence of essences, higher than the highest.
Having heard this, it must not be told to another, for it is an extreme secret concerning the arising of the world from Consciousness, whose form is that of Mūlaprakṛti.
A pair of powers, presiding over vital breath and intellect, manifested;
they are the constant controller and impeller of all living beings.
The entire universe, including the Virāṭ and all things moving and unmoving, is dependent upon them;
for as long as their grace is not obtained, liberation is indeed difficult to attain.
Therefore, for the sake of their grace, one should constantly serve those two.
First among them, O Nārada, listen with devotion to the mantra of Rādhikā.
He who is higher than the highest and is eternally served by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others;
[the mantra consists of] "Śrī Rādhe" ending in the dative case, followed by the wife of Agni (Svāhā). 10.
This six-syllabled great mantra, which illuminates the meaning of the Dharma and other truths, begins with the seed-syllable of Māyā and is remembered as the wish-fulfilling gem of desires. || 11 ||
Even with thousands of millions of mouths and hundreds of millions of tongues, it is simply not possible to describe the majesty of this mantra. (12)
Devoted to devotion, Śrī Kṛṣṇa first received the mantra from the instruction of Mūladevī in the Rāsa-maṇḍala at Goloka. (13)
Viṣṇu was instructed by him, and by him Brahmā, the Virāṭ;
by him Dharma, and by him I—such indeed is this lineage.
I recite that mantra; therefore, I am praised as a seer (ṛṣi).
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, constantly meditate upon her with joy. (15)
Since there is no authority for the worship of Kṛṣṇa without the worship of Rādhā, therefore the worship of Rādhikā must be performed by all Vaiṣṇavas. (16)
She is the presiding goddess of Kṛṣṇa’s life-breath, for the Lord is dependent upon her;
she is the Mistress of the Rāsa dance, and He never remains separated from her.
She fulfills all desires; therefore, she is celebrated as Rādhā.
Furthermore, I myself am the seer (ṛṣi) of the mantras spoken here. (18)
The goddess is Chanda and the deity here is Rādhikā;
the seed-syllable is Tāra (Om), and the power-seed is proclaimed to be Śakti. || 19 ||
The six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) should be performed with the root-mantra, as well as elsewhere. Then one should meditate upon the Great Goddess Rādhikā, the mistress of the dance.
But according to the previously mentioned method, O Sage, as sung in the Sāmaveda:
[she who] has the luster of the color of a white campaka flower and a face like the autumnal moon. (21)
Resembling ten million moons, with eyes like autumn lotuses,
with lips like the bimba fruit, broad hips, and a waist adorned with a girdle.
She was adorned with rows of teeth as beautiful as a row of jasmine flowers,
clothed in silken garments, and wearing a lower robe as pure as fire.
With a face brightened by a gentle smile, possessing breasts like the frontal globes of an elephant, eternally twelve years of age, and adorned with jewel ornaments. (24)
She is a wave in the ocean of erotic passion, ever-ready to bestow grace upon her devotees,
and is resplendent with a mass of hair adorned with garlands of jasmine and *mālatī* flowers.
With delicate, creeper-like limbs, standing in the midst of the circle of the rāsa dance, her hands bestowing boons and fearlessness, peaceful, and eternally fixed in the bloom of youth. || 26 ||
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, she is the leader of the circle of gopīs,
dearer to Kṛṣṇa than his own life-breath, the Supreme Goddess revealed by the Vedas.
Having meditated thus, one should then worship the Goddess according to the prescribed rite outside [the self], either in a śālagrāma stone, in a jar, or on an eight-petalled yantra.
Having invoked the Goddess, thereafter the seat and other offerings should be presented; having recited the root mantra, one should prepare the seat and the subsequent offerings. (29)

One should offer water for the feet (pādya) at the feet, arghya on the head as prescribed, and water for sipping (ācamanīya) in the mouth; this should be done three times with the root mantra (mūlavidyā).
Then he should offer the madhuparka and a single milch cow;
thereafter, he should lead her to the bathing hall and contemplate her right there.
Then, having prepared the ritual for bathing including anointing with oil and so forth, one should offer two garments, followed by sandalwood paste and various ornaments. (32)
Various kinds of flower garlands accompanied by tulasī buds,
as well as pārijāta blossoms, lotuses, and other such flowers.
Then, O Lord, one should perform the rite of the purifier (pavitra) and the worship of the Lord’s retinue;
the worship of the limbs (aṅga-pūjana) is performed in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and in the center.
Having done so, one should subsequently place Mālāvatī on the front petal of the eight-petaled [lotus] proceeding clockwise,
and Mādhavī in the southeast corner.
A wise man should worship Ratnamālā on the southern petal, Suśīlakā in the southwest, and Śaśikalā on the western petal. (36)
In the northwest one should worship Pārijātā, and in the north Parāvatī;
in the northeast corner, Sundarī, who acts for the beloved’s pleasure, is to be worshipped. (37)

Outside of that [the lotus], one should worship Brahmā and the others, and in the earth-fortress (bhūpura), the guardians of the directions; likewise, one should worship the weapons such as the thunderbolt and so forth—thus one should worship the Goddess.
Then, a wise man should worship the Goddess, together with her retinue, using offerings such as perfumes, along with the royal rites of service. (39)
Then one should praise the Goddess of the gods with hymns and the thousand names;
and one should diligently perform the recitation (japa) a thousand times every day.
Whoever thus worships the supreme Goddess Rādhā, the Mistress of the Rāsa dance, shall become equal to Viṣṇu and go eternally to Goloka. || 41 ||
To that wise person who celebrates the festival of Rādhā’s birth on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika, the supreme Mistress of the Rāsa dance grants her presence.
For a certain reason, Rādhā, who eternally resides in Goloka, was born in the forest of Vṛndāvana as the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu. 43.

Regarding the mantras mentioned here, according to the prescribed number of syllables, the rite of *puraścaraṇa* is declared; one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of a tenth part [of that number]. || 44 ||
One should offer oblations with sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets, with a spirit of devotion.
Nārada said:
O Sage, speak the hymn properly by which the Goddess is pleased. (45)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Obeisance to you, O Supreme Goddess, dweller in the circle of the Rāsa dance!
O Queen of the Rāsa, obeisance to you, who are dearer than life to Kṛṣṇa. (46)
Salutations to you, O Mother of the three worlds; be gracious, O ocean of compassion, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the gods beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Salutations to you in the form of Sarasvatī; salutations, O Sāvitrī, O Śaṅkarī!
O you who take the forms of Gaṅgā and Padmāvatī, O Ṣaṣṭhī, O Maṅgalacaṇḍikā!
Salutations to you in the form of Tulasī; salutations to you whose nature is Lakṣmī. Salutations to you, O Goddess Durgā; salutations to you who embodies all forms.
We worship you, who are the form of primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) and an ocean of compassion;
O Mother, lift us up from this ocean of saṃsāra and show us mercy. 50.
Whatever man recites this hymn at the three junctions of the day while remembering Rādhā, nothing whatsoever shall ever be difficult for him to attain. 51.
And at the end of the body, one shall dwell eternally in Goloka, in the circle of the Rāsa dance.
This supreme secret must not be told to anyone. 52.
Now listen, O best of Brahmins, to the ritual procedure for Goddess Durgā, by the mere remembrance of whom great calamities flee away. (53)
Indeed, there is no one anywhere who does not partake of her;
for the Śaiva power, the mother of all, is most wonderful and worthy of worship by everyone. 54.
She is the presiding goddess of all intellects, whose nature is that of the inner controller; she is celebrated on earth as Durgā because she destroys difficult obstacles.
She is to be worshipped perpetually by both Vaiṣṇavas and Śaivas;
she is the form of primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction.
I shall now declare her nine-syllable mantra, the most excellent of all mantras:
first the Vāgbhava, then Śambhuvanitā, and after that the Kāmabīja. (57)
After "cāmuṇḍāyai," the two syllables "vicce" follow;
this nine-syllable mantra is proclaimed as a wish-fulfilling tree for those who worship it.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa are proclaimed as its seers (ṛṣis);
the meters (chandas) are said to be constantly the Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, and Anuṣṭubh.
Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Sarasvatī are also deities;
likewise, there are the seed-syllables of Raktadantikā, Durgā, and Bhrāmarī.
The goddesses Nandā, Śākambharī, and Bhīmā are remembered as the Śaktis;
their application is declared to be in the pursuit of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. || 61 ||
One should place the seers (ṛṣis), meters (chandases), and deities (daivatas) on the head, the mouth, and the heart;
for the sake of accomplishing all aims, one should place the seed-syllables of the powers (śaktibījas) on the two breasts. 62.
The preceptor should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the mantra, joined with the seed-syllables, by means of three, four, two, and indeed all [of them]. (63)

One should place the syllables of the mantra on the crest-lock, the two eyes, the ears, the nose, and the mouth; then one should place them on the anus, and finally perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the entire mantra.
Holding in her hands a sword, a discus, a mace, arrows, a bow, an iron club, a trident, a *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon, a severed head, and a conch shell.
I worship Mahākālī, who has three eyes, is adorned with various ornaments, resembles blue collyrium in appearance, and possesses ten feet and ten faces.
One should meditate upon Mahākālī, who is the very embodiment of the Kāma-bīja, whom the Lotus-seated Lord (Brahmā) praised for the sake of destroying Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
And [he holds] a rosary, an axe, maces, arrows, and thunderbolts;
likewise a lotus, a bow, a water-pot, a staff, a spear, and a sword.
She holds a shield, a lotus, a bell, a vessel for wine, a trident,
a noose, and the Sudarśana discus, and she possesses a ruddy luster.
One should thus worship Mahālakṣmī, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura, who is seated upon a red lotus and whose essential nature is the seed-syllable Māyā (Hrīṃ). 70.
Holding a bell, a trident, a plow, a conch, a mace, and the Sudarśana discus,
as well as a bow and arrows in her lotus-like hands, she is radiant like a kunda flower.

One should meditate upon Mahāsarasvatī, whose form consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss, who is the destroyer of the Daityas beginning with Śumbha, and whose nature is the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāṇī). 72.
O wise one, hear now her yantra: it consists of a triangle joined with a hexagon, followed by an eight-petalled lotus and a twenty-four-petaled lotus. (73)
One should contemplate the yantra thus, as being joined with an underground chamber (bhūgṛha),
whether it be in a śālagrāma stone, in a jar, in a yantra, or in images.
Or, with one-pointed mind, one should worship the Goddess at a Bāṇaliṅga or before the Sun;
one should worship the Goddess upon a pedestal (pīṭha) joined by the powers (śaktis) such as Jayā and the rest.
In the eastern corner, one should worship the Lotus-born (Brahmā) together with Sarasvatī;
there, in the southwestern corner, one should worship Hari together with Śrī.
One should worship Śambhu together with Pārvatī in the northwest corner;
to the north of the Goddess, Siṃha is to be worshipped, and on the left, Mahāsura.
At the end, one should worship Mahiṣa; then, one should worship in sequence within the six corners Nandajā, Raktadantā, Śākambharī, and Śivā. (78)
Then, on the eight petals, [one should worship] Durgā, Bhīmā, and Bhrāmarī, as well as Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī. (79)
Then, one should worship Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Aindrī, and Cāmuṇḍā, starting from the east on the petals of the tattvas.
Viṣṇu’s Māyā, consciousness, intellect, sleep, hunger, as well as shadow, supreme power, thirst, peace, birth, and modesty; || 81 ||
Patience, faith, fame, prosperity, fortitude, conduct, sacred learning, memory, compassion, contentment, and thereafter nourishment—these are the Mothers in their respective order. (82)
Then, at the corners of the outer square (bhūpura), a wise man should worship Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapālaka, Vaṭuka, and the Yoginīs as well.

Outside of that as well, one should worship Indra and the other [guardians], together with their weapons such as the thunderbolt, according to this procedure; thereafter, one should worship the Goddess along with her retinue.
One should offer various services of royal homage for the pleasure of the Mother;
thereafter, one should recite the nine-syllable mantra preceded by the meaning of the mantra. (85)
Then one should recite the Saptaśatī hymn before the Goddess;
there exists no hymn equal to this in the three worlds. (86)
Then, by pleasing the Goddess of the Gods every day, a man becomes an abode of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. || 87 ||
Thus, O Brahmin, the ritual procedure of Śrī Durgā has been narrated to you;
this which has been told to you is that by which one attains the fulfillment of all goals. 88.
All the gods, headed by Hari and Brahmā, as well as the Manus, the sages established in knowledge, the yogis, and those in the stages of life (āśramas). || 89 ||
