Likewise, Lakṣmī and all the other goddesses meditate upon that Śivā;
indeed, there is fulfillment of one's birth at that very moment if there is remembrance of Durgā.
Even the fourteen Manus, having meditated upon his lotus feet,
attained the status of Manu, and likewise the gods attained their respective positions.
All this has been declared— the most secret of secrets— namely,
the description of the fivefold primary natures (prakṛtis) and their constituent parts.
Having heard this constantly, a person attains the four aims of human life;
there is no doubt in this matter—this truth has been spoken by me, truly, truly. (93)
A sonless man obtains a son, and one seeking knowledge shall attain it;
whatever desire he may contemplate, having heard this, he shall surely achieve it. (94)
If one recites this with a concentrated mind before the Goddess during the Navarātra, the Mother of the Universe will certainly be well-pleased. 95.
The man who recites even a single chapter every day shall have the Goddess under his control, for he acts in a manner pleasing to the Goddess.
And one should constantly examine the omens in this matter according to the prescribed rule, either by the divine hand of a maiden or from the lotus-hand of a young brahmin student. 97.
Having formed a mental resolve, one should then worship the book;
and one should prostrate again and again before the Goddess, the Sovereign of the World. (98)
Having brought a well-bathed maiden there and having worshipped her according to the prescribed rite,
one should insert a rod made of gold into the center.
Whatever occurs there, whether auspicious or inauspicious, shall come to pass; even when one is indifferent, the result will certainly be indifferent. 100.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Worship of the Goddess’s Enclosures," in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 50 ||
Nārada spoke this hymn of praise to the Goddess composed by Manu:
"O Nārāyaṇa, support of the earth, cause of the protection of all!"
The account of the Goddess’s deeds, which destroys all sins, has been narrated by you.
In all the Manvantaras, that Great Goddess manifests her appearance in whatever form she takes according to her own essential nature.
Relate all of those to us, interspersed with the majesty of the Goddess,
as well as how and by whom she has been worshipped and praised here on earth.
She who is affectionate toward her devotees fulfills the desires of those devoted to her;
therefore, [tell us] the supreme life-story of the Goddess for us who long for what is auspicious.
"Describe it, O ocean of compassion, by which one attains great happiness.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, O great sage, to this life-story that destroys all sins."
He generates devotion in his devotees and is the bestower of great prosperity;
he is the source of the universe, possessed of great splendor, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds.
O high-minded one, he who possesses four faces appeared from the navel-lotus of the Discus-wielder, the God of gods, having manifested his incarnation.
He begot from his mind the one named Svāyambhuva Manu;
that mental son of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin was Manu.
And he begot Śatarūpā as his wife, who was the very embodiment of Dharma;
that Manu [did so] on the most sacred shore of the Ocean of Milk.
The lord of the earth, having fashioned an earthen image of her, propitiated the Goddess who bestows the fruit of great fortune.
He attended upon that goddess in secret, muttering the Vāgbhava mantra,
abstaining from food, having mastered his breath, and emaciated by his observances and vows.
Standing firm upon the earth on one foot without ceasing for a hundred years, that great-souled one conquered both desire and anger.
As he remained motionless, contemplating the two feet of the Goddess within his heart,
the Goddess, who pervades the universe, appeared before him through the power of that austerity.
He spoke these divine words: "Choose a boon, O lord of the earth.
Then, having heard those joy-inducing words, the king—
He chose those boons, which were cherished in his heart and difficult even for the immortals to obtain.
Manu said:
"Victory to you, O Goddess of wide eyes! Victory to you who abide within all! (15)
O Venerable One, O Worshipful One, O Mother of the Universe, O Auspiciousness of all auspicious things!
By the glance of your side-long look, the Lotus-born creates the world.
By your command, Vaikuṇṭha protects, Hara destroys in an instant,
and the Lord of Śacī governs the three worlds.
The king of the dead instructs living beings by means of punishment, and the lord of aquatic creatures, the wielder of the noose, provides protection even for those such as me. (18)
Even Kubera, the imperishable lord of treasures, performs it;
as do Agni, Nairṛta, Vāyu, Īśāna, and Śeṣa himself. (19)
They are born from a portion of you and are empowered by your own energy;
nevertheless, O Goddess, if a boon is to be granted to me now— (20)
Then, O Śivā, may those obstacles in the work of creation perish for me;
and likewise for all those who are practitioners of the Vāgbhava mantra.
O Goddess, for those who recite and cause others to hear this dialogue, may success arise even for their most urgent tasks.
For you, O auspicious ones, worldly enjoyment and liberation shall be easily attained in this world;
may you possess the memory of past births, eloquence, and likewise excellence of speech.
May there indeed be the attainment of knowledge and the complete perfection of the path of action;
may there be the flourishing of sons and grandsons—this is my very prayer. (24)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Hymn to the Goddess Composed by Manu," in the tenth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 1 ||
The Description of the Legend of Vindhya:
The Illustrious Goddess said,
"O mighty-armed protector of the earth, all this shall come to pass."
O lord of men, I grant you that which you have requested.
"I am pleased, O Lord of Daityas, for your irresistible prowess has been firmly established through the austerity of the recitation of the Vāgbhava mantra alone. (2)
"May your kingdom be free of thorns, and may you have sons who perpetuate your lineage.
O child, may your devotion to me remain firm until liberation, when it shall lead you to the state of the True Being."
Having thus granted these boons to that great-souled one, the Great Goddess departed for the Vindhya mountain even as Manu was looking on.
That Vindhya mountain, which had been obstructed by the great sage Agastya and which, intent on blocking the path of the sun, was reaching toward the sky; || 5 ||
O best of sages, that Vindhyavāsinī, the younger sister of Viṣṇu and sovereign goddess of boons, became worthy of worship by all the worlds.
The sages said:
O Sūta, who is this Vindhya mountain, and for what reason does he touch the sky?
And for what purpose has he obstructed the path of the sun?
And how did Maitrāvaruṇi restore that great and lofty mountain to its natural state? Tell me all of this in detail.
O virtuous one, we are not satiated by drinking the nectar flowing from your mouth;
having drunk that which is called the narrative of the Goddess’s life, our thirst only increases.
Sūta said:
There was a mountain named Vindhya, honored among all the bearers of the earth,
abounding in great forest tracts and covered with massive trees.
It was covered with many well-flowered creepers and shrubs;
there were deer, boars, buffaloes, tigers, and even leopards.
Monkeys, rabbits, bears, and jackals roam everywhere, always joyful, well-nourished, and full of great energy. || 12 ||
It was filled with the waters of rivers and streams, and frequented by gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras;
it was graced by apsaras and kimpuruṣas, and by trees that yield the fruit of all desires.
Once, while wandering the earth upon such a Vindhya mountain,
the divine sage, the muni, went about according to his own will, filled with supreme delight.
Seeing him, that mountain quickly rose up in haste and,
having offered water for the feet and the guest-offering, then presented him with an excellent seat.
When the celestial sage was seated comfortably and serene, the mountain spoke:
Vindhya said:
"O celestial sage, tell me, from where has this most excellent arrival occurred?"
Because of your arrival, my humble abode has become priceless;
for your wandering, O Lord, is for the sake of granting fearlessness, just like that of the sun.
"O Nārada, tell me of that unprecedented mental state [of yours];
Nārada said:
"O enemy of Indra, my arrival from the Golden Mountain has just occurred."
There I beheld the worlds of Śakra, Agni, Yama, and Varuṇa,
as well as the abodes of all the world-protectors on every side.
"I have seen them on the Vindhya mountains, bestowing various enjoyments," having said this, he who was born of Brahmā again entered into a state of sighing.
Seeing the sage breathing again, the king of mountains asked once more:
"O divine seer, tell me, what is the cause of that breath?"
Having heard these words of Naga, the celestial sage of immeasurable luster said:
"Listen, my child, to the cause of my sighing."
Himavat, the father of Gaurī, was indeed the father-in-law of Śiva;
by virtue of that kinship with Paśupati, he was honored among the lords of the earth. (23)
In this very way, Kailāsa, the abode of the Lord Śiva,
became worthy of worship among the mountains and arose in the world as the destroyer of the flood of sins.
Niṣadha, Nīla, and Gandhamādana—indeed, all these mountains, having reached their own respective places, are worthy of worship. || 25 ||
That which the self of all, the thousand-rayed self-ruling sun,
traverses accompanied by the hosts of planets and stars— that is this very Golden Mountain.
He considers himself the best and the most excellent among the upholders of the earth, thinking:
"I alone am the foremost of all; there is no one equal to me in the worlds. (27)
"O Mountain, remembering that pride and arrogance of yours, I have released this sigh. Yet, let it be; by this much, no purpose is served for those possessed of the power of asceticism.
I have spoken to you incidentally; I shall now go to my own home."
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Legend of Vindhya," in the tenth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
In the *Devīmāhātmya*, the description of the legend of Vindhya; Sūta said:
Having thus instructed him, this supreme divine sage, the self-ruler, [departed].
The great sage, wandering at his own will, went to the world of Brahmā. || 1 ||
When the best of sages had departed, Vindhya fell into constant anxiety;
with his inner mind perpetually filled with grief, he found no peace at all. || 2 ||
"What must I do here, and how shall I conquer Meru? I find no peace at all, nor does tranquility arise in my mind. (3)

"Fie on my zeal and my pride! Fie on my fame and my lineage! Fie on my strength and my manliness! Fie on the wisdom remembered by the great-souled ones of old!"—as Vindhya was thinking thus, it became clear in his mind.
An intellect arose regarding a task to be performed that would bring about harm;
for the sun always performs the circumambulation of Mount Meru. (5)
"Accompanied by hosts of planets and constellations, this mountain is ever arrogant;
I shall block its path with my own rays."
"In that case, how could the sun, being obstructed, traverse the mountain?
Thus, the path of the sun has been blocked by me. (7)
"His pride shattered, he will surely become a divine serpent. Having thus resolved, the Vindhya mountain grew with its arms until it touched the sky.
Pervading everything with its most lofty and excellent peaks, it stands firm;
when will the sun rise, and when shall I obstruct him?
As he was reflecting thus, that night passed away;
the dawn broke clear, and the quarters of the sky became free from darkness by means of the sun's rays.
As he was departing, the sun rose upon the mountain of sunrise;
the stainless sky shone with the auspicious rays of the sun.
The lotus bed attained full bloom and the night-lily bed closed its petals;
all people, too, set about their respective duties. (12)
Increasing the offerings to the gods, the ancestors, and the spirits, as well as the oblations for the deities,
the Lord of Light [the Sun] does so according to the divisions of forenoon, afternoon, and midday.
Thus, having consoled the eastern quarter and likewise the south-eastern quarter—
both of which were separated from him like a passionate woman who has long endured separation and is now burning with grief.
Then Bhāskara, having indeed abandoned the direction of Agni,
set out swiftly from there toward the southern quarter, like a bed of lotuses.
He was unable to proceed to the front; thereupon Anūru addressed him.
Anūru said:
"O Bhānu, the Vindhya mountain, puffed up with pride, stands obstructing the sky. (16)
Desiring to obtain the circumambulation granted by you, he vies with Mount Meru.
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Anūru, the Sun indeed remained lost in thought.
"Aha! Even the path of the sky is being obstructed—how truly astonishing!
What indeed would a hero not do when standing upon a deviant path? (18)
Our path for the horse has been blocked, for destiny is indeed more powerful;
he who is distracted by the seizing grasp of Rāhu’s arm does not pause for even a moment. (19)
What can even powerful Fate do when its path has been blocked for so long? And thus, with the path obstructed, all people, including the Lord himself, [are held back].
They could find no refuge, nor did they know what ought to be done; Citragupta and all the others knew time only by means of the sun. || 21 ||
"Alas, what a reversal of fate! For when the sun was obstructed by the mountain out of rivalry, he himself has now been hemmed in by the Vindhya range. (22)
The utterances of *svāhā* and *svadhā* were lost, and the world became as if destroyed;
thus it was with the people of the West and likewise those of the South.
With eyes closed in sleep,
those from the east as well as those from the north, scorched by the intensity of the heat, sought refuge in the night itself.
The subjects died, perished, were broken, and met with destruction;
the entire world was filled with cries of "Alas! Alas!", devoid of the offerings of *svadhā* and *kavya*.
The gods, including Indra, became deeply distressed, saying, "What shall we do? (25)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Legend of Vindhya," in the Devīmāhātmya of the tenth book of the Śrīmaddevībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The prayer to Rudra:
Sūta said—
Then all the hosts of gods, headed by Mahendra, at that time...
Placing the lotus-born Brahmā at their head, they sought refuge with Rudra.
They approached the God of gods, Giriśa, whose crest is adorned by the moon, with prostrations and hymns of beautiful splendor.
The gods said:
Victory to you, O God, Lord of the hosts of deities, whose lotus feet are caressed by Umā!
To you, the bestower of the eight supernatural powers and sovereign splendors upon your devotees!
Salutations to the Supreme Self, who sports with Mahāmāyā;
to the bull-bannered Lord of the immortals, who dwells upon Kailāsa.
To Ahirbudhnya, to the venerable one, to Manu, the bestower of honor, to the unborn one of manifold forms, to Śambhu who delights in his own self; || 5 ||
Salutations to you, the Lord of the Gaṇas, the God, the Dweller on the Mountain;
salutations to you, the bestower of great prosperity, who is praised by Mahāviṣṇu.
Salutation to the one who dwells in the lotus-heart of Viṣṇu, to the one devoted to great yoga, to the one attainable through yoga, to yoga itself, and to the Lord of yogins. || 7 ||
Salutations to you, the Lord of Yogis, the bestower of the fruits of yoga, who,
though intent on giving to the wretched, possesses a form that is an ocean of compassion.
Salutations to you, who pacifies suffering, who possesses fierce valor, whose very form is virtue, who has the bull as his emblem, who is Time itself, and who is the Death of Death.
Sūta said: Thus praised by the partakers of the sacrifice, the Lord of Gods, whose banner bears the bull,
spoke with a deep voice, smiling at the foremost of the gods.
The Blessed Lord said: "O dwellers of heaven, O supreme persons, I am pleased by your hymn of praise;
O bulls among the gods, I shall fulfill the desire of you all."
The gods said:
O Lord of all gods, Giriśa, adorned with the moon upon your crest!
You are the benefactor of those in distress; O Śaṅkara of great power, bestow peace upon us.
There is a mountain named Vindhya, a very lofty rival of Meru;
indeed, it obstructs the path of the sun and causes suffering to all, O sinless one. (13)
O Īśāna, restrain its increase; become the bringer of all auspiciousness.
How can the knowledge of time arise through the obstruction of the sun’s movement? (14)
When the utterances of Svāhā and Svadhā have perished, who in this world could be our refuge?
For you alone are seen as the protector for us who are afflicted by fear. 15.
"O God, destroyer of suffering, be gracious, O Lord of Girijā!
Śrī Śiva said:
"O gods, we have no power here to cause the obstruction or destruction of that [growth]."
We shall speak thus to the Blessed Lord, the Consort of Ramā:
"He is our master and our very self; he is to be worshipped, for he assumes the form of the cause. (17)
"Govinda, the Blessed Viṣṇu, is the cause of all causes;
having gone to him, we shall speak, and our suffering will come to an end. (18)
Having heard these words spoken by the Lord of the Mountains, the gods, together with Indra and the one born from the lotus,
placed Rudra at their head and stood trembling.
They quickly departed for the realm of Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Prayer of Rudra," in the tenth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Sūta said: Having gone to the Lord of the gods, the husband of Ramā, the teacher of the world, Śrī Viṣṇu granted a boon to the deities.
They beheld Viṣṇu, whose eyes were like lotus petals, endowed with radiant splendor.
With voices faltering from devotion, they honored him with hymns of praise.
The gods said:
"Victory to you, O Viṣṇu! O Lord of Ramā! O Primordial Being, Great Person! (2)
O enemy of the Daityas, O progenitor of desire, O bestower of the fruits of all desires;
O Great Boar, O Govinda, O you whose very nature is the great sacrifice!
O Great Viṣṇu, O Lord of the Pole Star, primordial cause of the universe's creation,
you who took the form of the support for the recovery of the Vedas during your incarnation as a fish.
O Lord of the earth who upheld the vow of truth, salutations to you in the form of the fish;
victory to you, O Ocean, enemy of the Daityas, who accomplished the work of the gods!
O Lord who brings about the attainment of immortality, salutations to you in the form of the Tortoise;
you who assumed the form of the Primeval Boar for the sake of destroying the Daitya named Jaya.
Salutations to you who assumed the form of a boar and exerted yourself to uplift the earth;
salutations to him who, having assumed the body of a man-lion, tore asunder the great Daitya.
Salutations to that Nṛhari, whose limbs were proud with his claws,
who, having assumed the form of Vāmana, [overcame] him who was deluded by the sovereignty of the three worlds.
He offered the oblation to him who was in the form of a dwarf,
the destroyer of wicked kṣatriyas, and the enemy of the thousand-rayed sun.
Salutations to you, the son of Jamadagni born from the womb of Reṇukā,
who were most capable of severing the head of the wicked Rākṣasa Paulastya.
Obeisance to you, the illustrious son of Daśaratha, and to you whose strides are infinite;
[you who were oppressed] by Kaṃsa, Duryodhana, and other demons bearing the marks of earthly kings.
That great Lord, who lifted up the earth oppressed by its burden,
established the Dharma after casting sin far away.
Salutations in many ways be to that Lord Kṛṣṇa, O All-pervading One, for the purpose of destroying wicked sacrifices and for the cessation of the injury to animals. 13.
Salutations to that God who assumed the form of a Buddha while the entire world was filled with barbarians and oppressed by wicked kings.
He meditated upon the form of Kalki; salutations to you, the God of gods!
O Lord, these ten incarnations are indeed for the protection of your devotees. (15)
Therefore, for the sake of destroying the wicked Daityas, you are the remover of all suffering;
victory to you who have assumed the forms of woman, water, and the individual soul for the destruction of the afflictions of your devotees! 16.
"O Lord, by whom [is this form] seen? Who else but you is a treasure-house of compassion?
Having thus praised the Lord of the gods, the illustrious one clad in yellow garments, [he spoke]. (17)
The preeminent among the gods, filled with devotion, prostrated themselves before him with all eight limbs. Having heard their hymn of praise, the Lord Śrī Puruṣottama [responded].
Śrī Gadādhara, gladdening all the gods, spoke;
the Blessed Lord said: "I am pleased with this hymn, O gods; cast away your distress."
"I shall destroy your suffering, which is most difficult to endure;
and you, O gods, choose from me a boon that is exceedingly rare."
Being supremely pleased by the grace of this hymn, I grant [this boon] to that man who, having risen at dawn, recites this praise. (21)
O gods, having established supreme devotion toward me, sorrow shall never touch him; neither misfortune nor Kālakarṇī shall ever invade his house.
Neither calamities, nor Vetālas, nor seizing spirits, nor Brahma-rākṣasas;
neither diseases arising from wind (vātika), bile (paitta), nor those produced by phlegm (śleṣma) [shall afflict them]. || 23 ||
For him, there shall never be untimely death; his lineage shall endure for a long time, and all enjoyments, such as happiness and the like, shall be his. (24)
They shall come to exist in the house of that mortal who recites this hymn;
what more need be said? This hymn accomplishes all purposes. (25)
For those people who recite this, enjoyment and liberation are not far off.
O gods, tell me without hesitation what suffering you endure. (26)
"I shall destroy them; there is no doubt, nor even the slightest hesitation to be made in this matter.
Having heard these words of the Blessed Lord, all the inhabitants of heaven, with delighted minds, spoke again to Vṛṣākapi.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Bestowal of Boons by Śrī Viṣṇu upon the Devas," in the tenth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Agastya’s Consolation.
Sūta said: At the words of the Lord of Śrī, all the gods indeed became fully satisfied.
Having become serene in mind, they spoke to him once again.
The gods said:
O God of gods, O Mahāviṣṇu, O cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction!
O Viṣṇu, the Vindhya mountain is indeed obstructing the path of the sun.
O Great Lord, because of that obstruction by Bhānu, we have all indeed been deprived of our share of enjoyments; what can we do, and where indeed shall we go? (3)
The Blessed Lord said: She who is the creator of all worlds, the primordial one, and the increaser of the lineage—the Goddess, the Bhagavatī; the worshiper of her is possessed of supreme splendor.
That Agastya, the best of sages, resides in Vārāṇasī;
O foremost of gods, that Agastya will be the one who eclipses your splendor.
"O gods, having gone to Kāśī, propitiate that best of the twice-born, Agastya of supreme luster, and beg him for the state of ultimate liberation."
Sūta said:
Thus instructed by Viṣṇu, all those foremost of the gods,
filled with faith and bowing down, departed for the city of Vārāṇasī.
In an instant, O best of the wise, they went to the auspicious city of Kāśī;
having bathed with their clothes on at Maṇikarṇikā, they were filled with devotion.
Having gratified the gods and the ancestors and having bestowed gifts according to the prescribed rites,
he returned to the most excellent and great hermitage of the eminent sage.
It was free from the presence of predatory beasts, crowded with various kinds of trees,
and frequented by peacocks, cranes, swans, and ruddy geese.
With great boars and wild pigs, tigers and leopards as well;
with ruru deer and even more so with rhinoceroses and śarabhas. || 11 ||
Then, all of them prostrated like a staff before that best of sages, who was endowed with supreme splendor, and bowed down again and again.
The gods said:
Victory to you, O lord of the hosts of the twice-born, O venerable and worshipful one, O bull among the earth!
Salutations to you, the pitcher-born Agastya, for the destruction of Vātāpi’s strength.
O Lord of Lopāmudrā, O illustrious one born of Mitra and Varuṇa, O Agastya, treasury of all knowledge, O source of the scriptures, salutations be unto you! (14)
Salutations to you, at whose rising even the waters of the great oceans become clear and radiant. 15.
Salutations to you who cause the kāśa flower to bloom, who delight in dwelling in Laṅkā, who are adorned with a circle of matted locks, and who are accompanied by your disciples. (16)
Victory to you, O Great Sage, praised by all the immortals, heap of virtues!
Salutations be to you, the most excellent, the worshipful one, who are accompanied by your wife.
"O Lord, grant us your favor; we have come to you for refuge, O one of supreme luster, for we are afflicted by the suffering born of the mountain, which is otherwise difficult to cross. (18)
Thus praised, the most virtuous sage Agastya,
the best of the twice-born, laughed and spoke with a gracious voice.
The sage said:
"You are most excellent gods, lords of the three worlds;
you are high-souled guardians of the world, capable of both restraint and favor. (20)
He who is the lord of Amarāvatī, whose weapon is the thunderbolt,
and at whose gate stands the eightfold supernatural power— that is Śakra, the lord of the Maruts.
Vaiśvānara, the consumer of oblations to gods and ancestors, is indeed the mouth of all the immortals; for that fire, what is difficult to accomplish? 22.
The terrifying lord of the hosts of Rākṣasas is the witness of the deeds of all;
O gods, what is difficult for that deity whose hand is ever occupied with his staff? (23)
Nevertheless, O lords of the gods, if there is a task to be accomplished through my power and success, let it be told, O gods; I shall perform it without a doubt.
Having heard what was thus spoken by the best of sages, the bulls among the gods were both reassured and anxious;
with affectionate concern, they declared their own purpose.
O Great Sage, the path of the sun has been blocked by the Vindhya mountain;
because of that, the three worlds have become senseless and filled with cries of "Alas! (26).
"O Sage, arrest its growth by means of the splendor of your own asceticism.
O Agastya, by your power he will surely become humble;
for this indeed is the task that must be accomplished for us."
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Agastya’s Consolation," in the tenth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of the Obstruction by the Growth of the Vindhya Mountains.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the gods, the best of the twice-born—
"I shall perform this task for you," the sage then replied.
O best of the twice-born, when the task was then accepted by the pot-born sage, all the gods became exceedingly joyful.
Those gods took possession of their respective seats according to the words of the sage.
Then the illustrious and excellent sage spoke to the princess, his wife.
"Alas, O princess, an obstacle that causes misfortune has been encountered;
it was created by the Vindhya mountain through its obstruction of the sun's path. (4)
That reason has been understood and that ancient statement remembered,
which was sung concerning Kāśī by the sages who perceive the ultimate truth.
Those seeking liberation must never let go of Avimukta under any circumstances;
however, obstacles will surely arise for the virtuous who dwell in Kāśī.
"O beloved, while dwelling in Kāśī, this obstacle was encountered by me.
Having spoken thus to his wife, the sage, who causes great torment [to his enemies], [remained there]. (7)
Having bathed in Maṇikarṇikā, beheld the all-pervading Lord Viśveśvara,
and duly worshipped Daṇḍapāṇi, he arrived at Kālarāja.
O Kālarāja, O mighty-armed one, O remover of the fear of devotees,
why do you, as the Lord, distance yourself from the city of Kāśī?
You are the destroyer of obstacles for those dwelling in Kāśī and the protector of your devotees;
O Lord, dispeller of the suffering of your devotees, why do you distance yourself from me?
"I have spoken neither slander of others, nor calumny, nor falsehood.
By the ripening of what karma do you keep me at a distance from Kāśī? (11)
Having thus prayed to that Lord Kāla, the pot-born sage went to the witness Gaṇeśa, the warder-off of all obstacles.
Having seen him, worshipped him, and offered his prayers, the illustrious Agastya, the husband of Lopāmudrā, then departed from the city toward the southern direction.
Tormented by the separation from Kāśī, that sage— a treasure-house of great fortune—
went with his wife, remembering Kāśī at every moment.
Having mounted, as it were, the vehicle of asceticism, the sage in half a moment beheld before him that lofty Vindhya mountain, which had obstructed the sky.
Upon seeing the sage standing before him, the mountain quickly trembled,
shrinking down as if it wished to speak to the earth.
Filled with devotion, he prostrated himself on the ground with all eight limbs like a staff;
seeing that great mountain named Vindhya, whose peak was thus bowed down, [he spoke]. (17)
Then the sage Agastya, with a serene countenance, said to the Vindhya mountain:
"O child, remain thus for as long as it takes for me to return."
"O my son, I am unable to climb this boulder-like rock," having said this, the sage, eager to depart, set out toward the southern direction.
Having ascended its peaks, he descended from them in succession;
and having traveled toward the southern direction, he beheld Śrīśaila on the way.
Having reached the Malaya mountain, he became devoted to a hermitage there;
that goddess also, worshipped by Manu, arrived at the Vindhya mountains.
"And she is renowned throughout the worlds as Vindhyavāsinī, O Śaunaka," Sūta said. "This supreme life-story is the most excellent destroyer of enemies. (22)
The narrative of Agastya and Mount Vindhya destroys sins;
it grants victory to kings and increases the wisdom of the twice-born. (23)
It bestows grain and wealth upon Vaiśyas and likewise grants happiness to Śūdras;
one seeking merit attains merit, and one seeking wealth shall obtain wealth.
One who desires shall obtain their desires through devotion by hearing this even once;
thus did Svāyambhuva Manu, having propitiated the Goddess with devotion. (25)
He obtained the sovereignty of the earth for the duration of his own Manvantara.
O gentle one, this first account of the Śrī Devī, based upon the Manvantaras, has been described by me; what more shall I tell you?

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Obstruction by the Growth of the Vindhya Mountains," in the tenth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Origin of the Manus. Śaunaka said: This first and most excellent Manvantara has been described by you.
Tell me of the origin of the other Manus, who possess divine splendor.
Sūta said:
Having thus heard the origin of the first Svāyambhuva Manu,
he then inquired about the successive birth of the others.
Nārada, the supreme knower and expert in the true meaning of the Goddess's principles,
said: "O Eternal One, tell me the origin of the Manus."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O great sage, this first Manu, Svāyambhuva, has been described;
it was by worshipping the Goddess that he obtained a kingdom free from all obstacles.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, the two sons of Manu, were possessed of great luster;
they were renowned on the surface of the earth as the protectors of the kingdom.
And the second Manu is called Svārociṣa by the wise;
he was the illustrious son of Priyavrata, possessed of immeasurable prowess.
That Manu, named Svārociṣa, who brings delight to all living beings, established his residence on the bank of the Kālindī.
Subsisting on withered leaves and devoted to performing penance,
he worshipped an earthen image of the Goddess with devotion.
Thus, O dear one, as he remained in the forest practicing austerities for twelve years,
the Goddess appeared, possessing a splendor equal to a thousand suns.
Then the Goddess of gods, pleased by this king of hymns, O observer of good vows,
bestowed upon Svārociṣa the refuge of all the Manvantaras.
Consequently, through the propitiation of Tāriṇī by Svārociṣa Manu, she attained renown as the sovereign sustainer of the world.
And that powerful lord attained sovereignty, free from all enemies;
having duly established the Dharma, he ruled the kingdom together with his sons.
Having enjoyed [the world] according to the duration of his own Manvantara, he departed for the heavenly realm;
the third Manu was named Uttama, the son of Priyavrata.
Having performed austerities on the bank of the Gaṅgā while secretly muttering the Vāgbhava mantra,
he entered into the grace of the Goddess after fasting for three years.
Having praised the Goddess with excellent hymns, his mind permeated by devotion, he obtained a kingdom free from thorns and a long-lasting progeny. (15)
Having enjoyed the pleasures arising from his kingdom as well as those resulting from the age of righteousness,
he too attained the path cultivated by the best of royal sages.
The fourth Manu, named Tāmasa, the son of Priyavrata, having propitiated the Goddess who is identical with the universe on the southern bank of the Narmadā, [attained his status]. (17)
Devoted to the recitation of the Kāmarāja-koṭa mantra of Maheśvarī,
during the spring and autumn seasons, he performed worship throughout the Navarātra.
He gratified the goddess of the gods, the incomparable lotus-eyed one, having obtained her favor by bowing down with unsurpassed hymns of praise. (19)
Free from fear, he enjoyed a great kingdom without thorns;
he had ten sons, heroes who were abodes of valor and exalted by their strength.
Having procreated [offspring] upon his own wife, he ascended to the highest heaven;
he is known as the fifth Manu, Raivata, the younger brother of Tāmasa.
Resorting to the bank of the Kālindī, he recited the seed-syllable known as "Kāma," which bestows pride in the supreme speech and serves as a refuge for practitioners.
By worshipping this, one attains the unsurpassed prosperity of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*), as well as invincible power in the world that bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). (23)
Having established his auspicious lineage consisting of sons and grandsons for a long time,
having arranged the duties of dharma, and having enjoyed the objects of the senses,
that peerless hero departed for the supreme abode of Mahendra.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Manus," in the tenth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The visual description of the continuous narrative;
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, therefore, let this wonderful and supreme majesty of the Goddess be heard.
Just as the supreme kingdom was obtained by Manu, the son of Aṅga.
The son of King Aṅga was Cākṣuṣa Manu, the most excellent;
as the sixth [Manu], he went for refuge to the Brahman-sage named Supulaha.
O Brahman-sage, destroyer of the distress of those who bow before you, I have come to you for refuge;
instruct me, your servant, O Lord, so that I may attain prosperity.
"May I possess sovereignty over the earth exactly as it should be, unimpaired; may my strength of arm be unopposed, and may I be capable and skilled in the use of hand-held weapons and missiles. (4)
May my continuum endure for a long time as an unbroken and supreme age, and may there be the attainment of liberation at the end; therefore, instruct me now accordingly.
When these words reached the ears of Manu,
the illustrious sage replied concerning the supreme propitiation of the Goddess.
O King, listen to my words, which are greatly pleasing to the ear:
worship Śivā today, and by her grace this shall come to pass.
Cākṣuṣa said:
"What kind of worship of that Goddess is supremely purifying?
In what form should it be performed? Out of compassion, you ought to tell me. (8)
The Sage said:
O King, listen to the supreme and imperishable worship of the Goddess;
likewise, one should incessantly mutter the unmanifest seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbhava).
By muttering [this mantra] three times a day, a mortal shall indeed attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O delight of the royal lineage, there is no seed-mantra other than the Vāgbhava.
Through its recitation, it brings about perfection and is the supreme means for increasing vigor and strength;
by the recitation of this, even the mighty Padma became the creator of the universe.
O King, Viṣṇu, the protector of creation, is proclaimed to have arisen from the recitation of that [mantra],
and Maheśvara, the destroyer, likewise arose from its recitation.
Likewise, the world-protectors and others who are capable of both restraint and favor became arrogant with power, heroism, and pride only by relying upon him. (13)
In this same way, O King, you too, by propitiating Maheśī, the Mother of the World,
shall obtain great supernatural power before long.
Thus enlightened by Pulaha, the best of sages,
the son of Aṅga went to the Virajā river to perform austerities.
And that powerful protector of the earth performed intense austerity, devoted to the recitation of the seed-syllable consisting of speech, subsisting on withered leaves.
In the first year he subsisted on shoots; in the second, he consumed only water;
in the third year, he fed on air, remaining as motionless as a pillar.
Thus, for twelve years, as the king remained without food and constantly recited the Vāgbhava mantra, his mind became endowed with auspiciousness.
And so, as he was privately reciting the supreme mantra of the Goddess,
the Mother of the World, the illustrious Supreme Sovereign herself, appeared in person.
Resplendent, invincible, and the sovereign embodying all the gods, she,
being pleased, spoke these graceful words to that son of Aṅga.
The Goddess said:
"O protector of the earth, tell me whatever supreme boon you have contemplated;
being well-pleased by your asceticism, I shall grant it to you. (21)
Cākṣuṣa said:
O Goddess of the lords of gods, O you who are worshipped by the gods, you know everything that is desired and sought by the mind, for you exist as the inner controller (antaryāmin). 22.
Nevertheless, by my good fortune, the sight of you has occurred;
O Goddess, I say to you: grant me a kingdom lasting for a Manvantara.
The Goddess said:
"O best of kings, the sovereignty of this Manvantara has been granted to you;
and you shall have sons of great strength who will be preeminent in virtue. (24)
"The kingdom shall be free from thorns, and liberation at the end is certain";
having thus granted this supreme and excellent boon to Manu, the Goddess [departed]. (25)
She, being praised with devotion by him, immediately vanished from sight;
and that King Manu, the sixth, [attained his goal] through her grace and by taking refuge in her.
He became honored by all men, endowed with the pleasures of a sovereign ruler;
his sons were devoted to military exercises and intent upon bearing the burden of state affairs. (27)
Devotees of the Goddess who are brave and possess great strength and prowess are to be honored elsewhere as well, for they are the abodes of the happiness of great sovereignty. (28)
And thus, through the propitiation of the Goddess, the lord Manu Cākṣuṣa became the most excellent of Manus; at the end, he went to the abode of Śiva.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of Cākṣuṣa Manu," in the Devī-caritra of the tenth book of the Śrīmad-devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The description of the excellent King Suratha.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The seventh Manu has been described; the lord is Vaivasvata Manu.
Śrāddhadeva, the enjoyer of supreme bliss, is indeed honored by kings. || 1 ||
And that Vaivasvata Manu, by the grace of Paradevī and likewise through his own ascetic penance, was born as the sovereign of a Manvantara.
The eighth Manu is proclaimed as Sāvarṇi, renowned upon the earth;
having propitiated the Goddess in a previous birth, he obtained her boon. (3)
He was born as the lord of a Manvantara, honored by all kṣatriyas;
he was possessed of great prowess, steadfast, and entirely devoted to the Goddess.
Nārada said:
How was the propitiation of the Goddess born from the earth performed by that Manu in another birth? You ought to relate that to me. (5)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
In the Svārociṣa Manvantara, there was a king born of the Caitra lineage,
renowned by the name Suratha, who possessed great strength and prowess.
He was a perceiver of virtues, a wielder of the bow, honorable, excellent, a poet, and accomplished;
he was a collector of wealth and a donor within the circle of supplicants.
Proud, powerful, skilled in all weapons, and a crusher of his enemies—
he once had those kings who were destroyers of the Kolas as his adversaries.
Then the powerful enemies, accompanied by their armies, surrounded him and besieged the city of that king, whose wealth was his honor.
Then that king named Suratha, the destroyer of all enemies, surrounded by his army, marched out from his own city.
Then, in that battle, King Suratha was defeated by his enemies;
his wealth, which had been stored in the treasury, was seized by his own ministers and counselors.
Everything was taken away without exception;
then that king, possessed of supreme splendor, was tormented and expelled from the city.
Then, mounting his horse under the pretext of hunting, he went to the forest;
alone in the desolate wilderness, he wandered about with a bewildered mind.
Having come to the hermitage of a certain sage whose mind was peaceful—a place inhabited by tranquil creatures and filled with hosts of the sage’s disciples—he arrived there. (14)
For some time, that king dwelt in the most beautiful hermitage of the eminent sage Sumedhas, who possessed far-reaching vision.
Once, at the conclusion of the worship, that protector of the earth went to the sage, bowed down quickly, and, filled with humility, questioned him.
O Sage, O God upon Earth, mental suffering born of physical ailment constantly afflicts me, even though I have realized the truth and am devoid of worldly wisdom. (17)
Even for one who has been utterly defeated by enemies and stripped of his kingdom in every respect, a sense of "mine-ness" toward them clearly arises in the mind. (18)
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How may I obtain peace, O Sage?
I seek your favor; speak, O best among the knowers of the Vedas. (19)
The sage said:
Listen, O protector of the earth, to this supreme and most wonderful account of the Goddess’s majesty, which is incomparable and bestows all desires. (20)
The Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), who pervades the world and arises from Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Hara,
indeed forcibly carries away the minds of living beings.
Know this, O protector of the earth: she withdraws [the world] for the sake of delusion;
she creates the entire universe and she protects it at all times. (22)
O protector of the earth, in the form of Hara during the dissolution, she indeed withdraws all things;
she is Mahāmāyā, the granter of desires, the Kālarātri who is difficult to overcome.
Kālī, the destroyer of the universe, is Kamalā, whose abode is the lotus;
in her the entire world was born, and in her the universe is established. (24)
And she will take repose therein; therefore, she alone is higher than the highest. O King, lord of the earth, he upon whom the grace of that Goddess rests transcends delusion, and not otherwise. (25)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Conduct of King Suratha," in the tenth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 10 ||
In the *Devīmāhātmya*, the description of the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha:
The King said:
"O best among those who know the [proper] time, tell me, who is that Goddess spoken of by you?"
O twice-born one, what deludes sentient beings, and what would be the cause?
From what does the Goddess arise? What is her form and what is her nature?
O Bhūdeva, out of compassion, tell me everything in its entirety.
The sage said:
O King, listen as I describe to you the true nature of the Goddess—how the Goddess, who is identical with the universe, originated and by what means she came into being. (3)
When the divine Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Yoga, having withdrawn the universe,
spread out Śeṣa and the Blessed One lay asleep upon the ocean.
At that time, while Janārdana, the God of gods, was under the influence of deep sleep,
two Dānavas named Madhu and Kaiṭabha were born from the wax of his ears.
Then the lotus-born god, seeing those two Dānavas of terrible form intent on slaying Brahmā, [acted].
While the Lord of the gods was asleep, he fell into an insurmountable anxiety;
for the Blessed Lord was slumbering, while the two Dānavas were difficult to withstand.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go?
How indeed may I obtain peace?"—thus did that high-souled one, born from a lotus, reflect.
Then, O dear one, there arose an intellect capable of accomplishing the task,
under whose sway fell the Lord, the blessed Hari, even while he was asleep.
"I seek refuge in that Goddess, Nidrā, the mother of all.
Brahmā said: "O Goddess, O Goddess, Mother of the World, bestower of the fruits of the desires of your devotees! (10)
O Illusion of the World, O Great Illusion, O Auspicious One who reclines upon the ocean!
All beings, subject to your command, perform their respective duties.
She is the Night of Time, the Great Night, the Night of Delusion, and she who is fierce with intoxication;
she is all-pervading, she who brings others under her sway, she who is to be honored, and the unique treasure-trove of great bliss.
Worthy of honor, most adorable, illusory power, honey-sweet, and vast—
you are proclaimed as the supreme among all that is high and low.
She is modesty, nourishment, forgiveness, fame, and splendor;
she is the embodiment of compassion, the most desirable, the one worshipped by the world, and whose nature consists of the waking state and the others.
She is supreme, the sovereign mistress of the highest, and devoted to supreme bliss;
though one, she is of a singular nature, yet she possesses a companion and is dual in essence.
She is the triple Veda, the abode of the three aims of life; she is the fourth, whose nature is the state of the Fourth (turya);
she is the fifth, the mistress of the five elements; and she is the sixth, the sovereign of the sixth.
The seventh [tithi] is the mistress of the seven days of the week, the bestower of the sevenfold boons;
the eighth is the mistress of the Vasus, the sovereign composed of the nine planets.
She is the delightful essence of the nine passions, the number nine, and the sovereign of the nine;
she is the tenth, worshipped in the ten directions, the pervasive Ramā who extends through the ten quarters.
She consists of eleven aspects, is served by the eleven Rudras,
is pleased by the lunar day Ekādaśī, and is the sovereign of the eleven Gaṇas.
The goddess is the twelfth lunar day, twelve-armed, and the birthplace of the twelve Ādityas;
she consists of thirteenfold nature and is beloved by the thirteen Gaṇas.
The thirteenth is distinguished as the presiding deity of the Viśvedevas;
the fourteenth is the bestower of boons upon Indra and the progenitor of the fourteen Manus.
She is to be known as the fifteenth plus five (the twentieth), the lunar day consisting of fifteen plus five;
she is the sixteenth, possessing sixteen arms, and composed of the sixteen digits of the moon.
O Goddess of gods, you whose divine body is pervaded by the rays of the sixteen-fold moon, you are of such a form, O Nirguṇā, at the arising of Tamas. (23)
The Blessed One, the God of gods, the Lord of Ramā, has been seized by you;
these two Daityas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, are difficult to overcome and full of prowess.
"And for the sake of slaying these two, awaken the Lord of Gods.
The sage said:
"Thus praised, the Blessed One, who is of the nature of darkness (tāmasī) and beloved by the Blessed One," || 25 ||
Then, having abandoned the God of gods, he deluded the two Dānavas;
at that very moment, the Blessed Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self and Lord of the Universe, [acted].
The Lord of Gods regained consciousness and beheld the two foremost Dānavas;
then those two terrible Dānavas saw that Madhusūdana.
Having resolved to fight, the two went into the presence of Hari;
and then the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana fought with them.
For five thousand years, the omnipresent Lord, using his arms as weapons,
[fought] those two who were then intoxicated by excessive strength and deluded by the world-illusion (jagan-māyā).
"Choose a boon," they said thus to the Supreme Lord.
Having heard these words of theirs, the Blessed One, the Primordial Person, [spoke]. (30)
"Let both of us be destined for death by him today"—this was his firm resolve.
Then those two, who were exceedingly powerful, spoke again to the god Hari.
"Kill us both where the broad earth is not flooded with water.
Having said "So be it," O King, the Blessed One, who bears the mace and the conch, [acted].
Having severed their heads and hips with his discus,
O King, the Goddess was thus manifested and praised by Brahmā.
O Great King, Mahākālī is the sovereign of all masters of yoga;
likewise, O Lord of the Earth, listen to the origin of Mahālakṣmī.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha," in the Devīmāhātmya of the tenth book, within the Śrīmaddevībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 11.
The Sage said: [This is] the description of the history of Sāvarṇi Manu, together with the life of the Goddess; born from the womb of the queen, he possessed great strength and prowess.

Having defeated all the gods, Mahiṣa became the lord of the world. Having forcibly seized the offices of all the world-protectors, the great Asura enjoyed the marvelous sovereignty of the three worlds.
Then all the gods, having been defeated and cast down from heaven,
went to the highest world, placing Brahmā at their head.
Wherein the two supreme gods, Śaṅkara and Acyuta, being present,
related the account of the evil-minded Mahiṣa.
Having conquered by his own might the abodes of all the gods, that asura, arrogant with the pride of his strength and heroism, enjoys them himself.
"O lords of the immortals, destroyers of asuras, this wicked daitya named Mahiṣāsura—
let a means for his swift slaughter be devised."
Having heard these words of the gods who were oppressed by distress, the Blessed One became greatly incensed, as did Śaṅkara and the Lotus-born.
O lord of the earth, from the mouth of Hari, who was thus filled with wrath,
there emerged a divine splendor possessing a radiance equal to a thousand suns.
Then, in due order, the splendor of all the inhabitants of heaven emerged from their bodies, gladdening the lords of the gods.
The splendor that belonged to Śambhu became his face;
from the southern [quarter] and from the Vaiṣṇava [quarter], his hair and arms respectively came into being.
By the Saumya [graha] his two breasts were formed, by the Māhendra his waist;
then, O King, by the Vāruṇa his shanks and thighs came into being.
Her hips were formed from the splendor of the Earth, her feet from the splendor of Brahmā,
her toes from that of the Sun, and her fingers from those of Indra.
Likewise, O lord of the earth, his nose and teeth were produced then by the supreme splendor of Kaubera and Prājāpatya.
And by the Fire-god, a beautiful third eye was produced;
and by the twilight radiance, those two treasuries of splendor developed their frowns.
O lord of men, her two ears were born from the wind and from splendor;
and by the splendor of all [the gods], the goddess Mahiṣamardinī was born. (15)
Śiva gave him the trident, Viṣṇu the discus and the conch, the wielder of the noose (Varuṇa) the mace, Agni the spear, and Vāyu the bow and arrows. || 16 ||
Mahendra gave him a vajra and a bell from his elephant Airāvata; Yama gave him the staff of death (kāladaṇḍa), and Brahmā gave him a rosary and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
Divākara bestowed a garland of rays upon his pores, and Kāla likewise gave him a sword and a stainless shield, O lord of the earth. (18)
O King, the ocean gave him a stainless necklace, imperishable garments,
a crest-jewel, earrings, bracelets, and likewise armlets.
Filled with joy, he gave to that goddess a spotless crescent moon, anklets, a neck-ornament, and other decorations.
O Lord of the Earth, Viśvakarman gave her bangles, and Himavat gave her a lion as a vehicle and various kinds of jewels. (21)
The Lord of Wealth gave her a drinking vessel filled with wine;
and the blessed Lord Śeṣa, the all-pervading one, gave her a necklace of serpents.
Honored by all other gods without exception, she who pervades the universe—
that Great Goddess— was praised by the gods who were oppressed by Mahiṣa.
With various hymns of praise, they [worshipped] Maheśānī, the cause of the world's manifestation;
having heard their hymn, the Goddess of the Gods, who is honored by the wise, [responded].
For the purpose of slaying Mahiṣa, he let out a great roar;
by that roar, O Lord of the Earth, Mahiṣa became terrified.
Surrounded by his entire army, he approached the Mother of the World;
then that great asura named Mahiṣa fought with the Goddess.
Filling the expanse of the sky with various weapons and missiles hurled in many ways, the village chief Cikṣura, along with Senāpati, Durdhara, and Durmukha, [advanced]. (27)
Bāṣkala, Tāmraka, and another named Biḍālavadana—along with these and countless others who resembled the Destroyer at the end of an eon. || 28 ||
Surrounded by warriors, the heroic Mahiṣa, the best of the Dānavas, [advanced].
Then the Goddess, who deludes the worlds, her eyes copper-red with anger, [proceeded].
The goddess, mounted upon Mahiṣa, struck down the warriors in battle;
then, when they had been slain, that Daitya was overcome with rage.
Then the lord of the Dānavas, skilled in illusion, quickly approached the goddess; by means of his magic power, he assumed various forms.
Then she destroyed each of those various forms of his;
finally, he assumed the form of a buffalo, the tormentor of the immortals.
Having bound him very firmly with a noose and severed that head with her sword,
the Goddess struck down Mahiṣa, the destroyer of the hosts of gods.
Then the remaining army, crying out "Alas! Alas!", was broken and fled in the ten directions;
all the gods, filled with joy, praised the Goddess of the lords of gods.
Thus was Lakṣmī born as the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura;
O King, hear now how the manifestation of Sarasvatī occurred.
Once there was a Daitya named Śumbha, fierce with the intoxication of his own power, and his brother Niśumbha, who possessed great strength and prowess. (36)
O King, all the gods, oppressed by him and deprived of their splendor,
then approached the Himalayas and praised the Goddess with great devotion.
The gods said:
Victory to you, O Goddess of the gods, skilled in destroying the afflictions of your devotees! You are the one who takes the form of the destroyer of the Dānavas, ageless, immortal, and sinless.
O Goddess of gods, who are easily accessible through devotion, possessed of great strength and prowess, whose nature is that of Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, Brahmā, and others, and who possess infinite valor! 39.
O you who cause creation and maintenance, O you who cause destruction, O bestower of splendor,
O you who are well-pleased by the great *tāṇḍava* dance, O giver of joy, O Mādhavī!
Be gracious, O Goddess of the lords of gods; be gracious, O treasure-house of compassion, [from] the shoreless ocean of fear born of Niśumbha and Śumbha! 41.
"O Lord of the Earth, deliver us who have sought refuge in you, O destroyer of the distress of those who have come for protection,"— as those thirty gods were thus offering praise.
Pleased, Girijā said, "Tell me the reason for your praise.
In the meantime, she who had arisen from her treasury-form [spoke].
That Kauśikī, who is worshiped by the world, spoke this to the gods out of affection:
"O best of deities, I am pleased with your hymn of praise, which is of the most excellent form. (44)
When it was said, "Choose a boon," the gods chose a boon:
that her younger brother named Śumbha, whose elder brother is the famous Niśumbha, [be spared]. || 45 ||
O Goddess, the three worlds have been overcome by the powerful Daitya; consider his slaying, for that evil-souled one is the lord of the Dānavas. (46)
"O Goddess, he constantly oppresses [us], having surpassed us with his own power. The Goddess said: "I shall strike down Niśumbha and Śumbha, the enemies of the gods. (47)
"Remain at ease; may it be well with you; I shall destroy your thorn," said the Goddess of the lords of gods, full of compassion, to the gods including Indra. (48)
He immediately vanished from sight while the inhabitants of heaven looked on;
the gods, gathered together in joy, went to the auspicious cave of the Golden Mountain. 49.
Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa were the two servants of Śumbha and Niśumbha;
they beheld that goddess, who was enchanting to the world and beautiful in all her limbs. (50)
And those two servants, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, spoke to the king:
"O Lord, best among all the asuras, worthy of the enjoyment of jewels, O giver of honor! (51)
"O crusher of enemies, an unprecedented woman has been seen by us both;
she is indeed now fit for your enjoyment. (52)
Bring that lovely-limbed woman and enjoy her, endowed with happiness;
for there is no such woman among the asuras, nor among the gandharvas, nor among the dānavas.
"Neither a human woman nor a goddess is like that captivating lady.
Having heard these words of his servant, Śumbha, the crusher of enemy forces, [spoke].
He dispatched a messenger, a Dānava named Sugrīva;
that messenger went swiftly and with respect into the presence of the Goddess.
He related the account to the Goddess, including the words spoken by Śumbha:
"O Goddess, there is a lordly asura named Śumbha who has conquered the three worlds."
The enjoyer of all precious things, honored by the dwellers of heaven—listen to what I have said, O Goddess: "I am the imperishable enjoyer of jewels. (57)
And you too are like a jewel; therefore, O lovely-eyed one, accept me.
Among all the jewels that exist among gods, asuras, and humans— [58]
"O fortunate one, devote those very things to me alone; gratify me with the flavors born of desire.
The goddess said:
"You speak the truth, O messenger who brings joy to the king of the Daityas! (59)
How could that promise which was previously made by me be false?
O messenger, hear from me that promise which was made by me. (60)
He who shakes off my pride, he who takes away my strength,
and he who becomes my equal in power— he alone shall partake of my enjoyments.
Therefore, O Lord of Asuras, having made this promise of mine true, let him take her hand by force; for what indeed is impossible here?
Therefore, O great messenger, go and speak respectfully to my master;
that one of superior strength will also make my vow come true.
Having heard these words of the Great Goddess, that Dānava related the entire account of the Goddess to Śumbha from the beginning.
Then, having heard those unpleasant words of the messenger, the exceedingly powerful Śumbha, the lord of the Danujas, summoned a great rage.
Then the lord, the master of the Daityas, respectfully commanded the Daitya named Dhūmrākṣa: "Listen to my words, Dhūmrākṣa."
"Having struck that wicked woman by her mass of hair, bring her to my presence without delay; go quickly before me. (67)
Having received this command, the mighty lord of the Daityas, Dhūmralocana,
set out accompanied by sixty thousand asuras.
Having reached the Snowy Mountain and approached the presence of the Goddess, he quickly spoke loudly to the Goddess: "O auspicious one, quickly resort to the lord of the Daityas."
"Obtain all enjoyments from the one named Śumbha, who possesses great heroism;
otherwise, seizing you by the hair, I shall lead you to the lord of the Daityas. (70)
Having been addressed thus by the Daitya, the enemy of the gods, the goddess then said:
"O Daitya of great strength, that which you say is true."
"O King Śumbhāsura, tell me, what will you do?
Thus addressed, the lord of the Daityas, equipped with weapons, rushed forward swiftly.
The Great Goddess instantly reduced him to ashes with a roar of "huṃ";
thereafter, O Lord of the Earth, the army was routed by the Goddess's mount.
The ten directions were quickly overwhelmed by cries of "Alas! Alas! and became senseless;
having heard that news, the powerful Śumbha, the king of the Daityas, [acted].
And he became enraged with great fury, his face contorted by a frown;
then the powerful king of the Daityas, his soul overwhelmed by anger, [spoke]. (75)
The omnipresent Lord successively dispatched Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and Raktabīja;
and those three Daityas, having gone there, were valiant and possessed of great prowess.
They indeed began to exert forceful efforts to seize the Goddess;
but as they were rushing toward her, she, the Mother of the World, became intoxicated with pride.
Seizing his trident, he violently hurled it to the ground.
Hearing that the Daityas along with their army had been slain, the two lords of the Dānavas [acted].
Both Śumbha and Niśumbha arrived with great vigor;
having engaged in a most fierce battle, both Niśumbha and Śumbha [were defeated]. (79)
"The two asuras have come under the power of the Goddess and have been slain by her";
thus, having caused Śumbha, the best of the Daityas, to be killed, she who is identical with the universe—|| 80 ||
Likewise, she is praised by the wise as the supreme Vāgīśvarī herself.
Thus, O King, has this most delightful manifestation been described to you. (81)
And [the goddesses] Kālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Sarasvatī, in due order; the supreme Goddess, the Mistress of the Supreme, brings about the creation of the world. (82)
Indeed, that very Goddess maintains both preservation and dissolution;
take refuge in her, the Queen of Gods, who wards off the delusion of the world. 83.
"Worship Mahāmāyā, who is most worthy of worship; she will accomplish your purpose.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Sage, having heard these most auspicious words of the sage, the king—
He went for refuge to the Goddess, who bestows the fruits of all desires;
fasting, self-controlled, with his mind fixed on her, and composed in meditation. (85)
He worshipped the earthen image of the Goddess with devotion;
at the conclusion of the worship, he offered her a *bali* consisting of the blood from his own body.
Then the gracious Goddess, the compassionate source of the universe,
appeared before him and spoke, saying, "Choose a boon."
That king requested from the Great Goddess supreme knowledge that destroys his own delusion, as well as a kingdom free from all thorns.
The Goddess said:
"O King, a kingdom free from thorns and knowledge that destroys delusion shall be granted by me to you in this very birth. (89)
Listen to something else, O protector of the earth, concerning your activities in another birth:
having attained birth as the son of Bhānu, you shall become Sāvarṇi.
In that regard, by my boon, you shall obtain the lordship of a Manvantara, great prowess, and a vast progeny.
Having thus granted the boon, the Goddess then vanished from sight;
he too, by the grace of the Goddess, became the sovereign of a Manvantara.
Thus, O virtuous one, the birth and deeds of Sāvarṇi have been described to you. By reading or hearing this, one shall obtain the grace of the Goddess.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of Sāvarṇi Manu along with the Deeds of the Goddess," in the tenth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 12.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of Sāvarṇi Manu along with the Deeds of the Goddess," in the tenth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Bhrāmarī’s Deeds.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, therefore, listen to the wonderful origin of the remaining Anus.
By the mere remembrance of whom devotion to the Goddess arises. || 1 ||
The six sons of Vaivasvata Manu were of pure renown:
Karūṣa, Pṛṣadhra, Nābhāga, and Diṣṭa.
Śaryāti, Triśaṅku, and all those of great strength—
then those six indeed went to the excellent bank of the Kālindī.
Abstaining from food and having mastered their breath, they remained there and performed worship,
having each individually fashioned an image of the Goddess made of earth.
With great devotion, they honored her with various offerings;
and thus, all these ones, whose essence was penance, became possessed of great strength.
Eating withered leaves, subsisting on air, living on water,
inhaling smoke, and drinking [only] rays— these were their practices, involving great exertion in successive stages.
Then, as they were constantly performing worship with devotion,
a pure intellect arose within them, which destroys all delusion.
Those sons of Manu became intent solely on contemplating the feet of the Goddess;
through their pure intellect, the entire universe was [perceived] as being within the Self alone.
She quickly attained a vision [of Him], which was like a miracle;
thus, at the end of twelve years, the Goddess of the World [was reached] through austerity.
The Goddess of the gods appeared, possessing a splendor equal to a thousand suns;
seeing her, those six princes of pure soul [were filled with wonder].
With hearts bowed down by devotion and filled with intense emotion, they offered praise.
The princes said:
"Victory to you, O Maheśvarī! Victory, O Īśānī! O supreme abode of compassion! (11)
O Goddess, who are pleased by the worship of Vāgbhava, who are manifested through Vāgbhava, whose form is the syllable *klīṃ*, and who bestow delight upon the syllable *klīṃ*! || 12 ||
O giver of delight to Kāmarāja, O you who satisfy the Lord, O Great Illusion, O you who are intent on joy, O bestower of great sovereignty! || 13 ||
"O you who possess the forms of Viṣṇu, the Sun, Hara, Śakra, and the other gods; O increaser of enjoyments!"—thus was the Blessed Lady praised by the high-souled princes.
With a face bright with grace, the goddess spoke these auspicious words:
The goddess said: "O princes, you are high-souled and endowed with ascetic power. (15)
"Free from blemish and pure-minded, you have indeed become so through my worship; therefore, ask for every boon that is in your hearts without delay. (16)
"I am pleased; I shall grant you whatever resides in your hearts.
The princes said:
"O Goddess, may our kingdom be free from thorns, and may we have long-lived progeny. (17)
"Enjoyments unimpeded, as well as desire, fame, splendor, and intelligence—indeed, the state of being unthwarted by all these is the boon most beneficial. (18)
The Goddess said:
"Let it be so for all of you, according to what is in your minds;
now, listen with respect to this other word of mine. (19)
O sirs, all of these lords of the Manvantaras shall indeed have union with long-lasting progeny and manifold enjoyments.
O princes, by my grace, your strength, sovereignty, fame, splendor, and prosperity shall gradually become unimpaired. (21)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having thus granted boons to them, the Mother of the World, Bhrāmarī,
being praised by them with devotion, quickly vanished from sight.
All those princes of great prowess enjoyed, in that very birth, unsurpassed sovereignty and the pleasures available upon the earth.
Having produced an unbroken lineage upon the surface of the earth and having established their dynasties, they all became lords of the Manus.
In another birth, they shall gradually attain the status of Sāvarṇi;
the first is proclaimed as Dakṣasāvarṇi, the ninth Manu. (25)
Through the grace of the Goddess, the powerful lord became possessed of unimpeded strength;
he was the second Merusāvarṇi, who was indeed the tenth Manu.
By the grace of Mahādevī, he became the lord of a Manvantara;
he is declared to be the third Manu, named Sūryasāvarṇi.
The eleventh was Mahotsāha, who was purified by his own asceticism;
the twelfth was the powerful lord of men, Candra-sāvarṇi.
Born through the propitiation of the Goddess, he became the lord of the Manvantara;
he is known as the fifth Manu, Rudrasāvarṇi, the thirteenth Manu. || 29 ||
The powerful Mahāsattva became the Lord of the World;
he was the sixth, Viṣṇusāvarṇi, the accomplished fourteenth Manu.
By the boon of the Goddess, he became the celebrated lord of the worlds;
these fourteen Manus were endowed with great splendor and strength. (31)
By propitiating the Goddess, they shall always be worthy of worship and salutation in the worlds; through the grace of Bhrāmari, all shall possess great majesty. (32)
Nārada said:
Who is this goddess Bhrāmarī? How was she born and what is her nature?
O wise one, tell that wondrous narrative which destroys sorrow.
I do not reach satiety while drinking the nectar of the Goddess’s stories; for death does not come to those drinking nectar, whereas from hearing this [story], it does not come at all. 34.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe the wondrous deeds of the Mother of the World, whose form is inconceivable and unmanifest, which bestow liberation. (35)
Whatever conduct was displayed by the illustrious Goddess, all of it was for the sake of the world,
out of sincere compassion, just as a mother acts toward her son.
Formerly, there was a great Daitya named Aruṇa, possessed of great strength;
he was a hater of the gods and a great villain residing in Pātāla, the abode of the Daityas. (37)
Desiring to conquer the gods, he performed supreme austerity, resolving:
"He who is born from a lotus shall be our protector. (38)
Having gone to the side of the Himalayas, cooled by the waters of the Gaṅgā,
the yogi, subsisting on fallen leaves, restrained the host of vital breaths.
Devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī, yet possessed of desire and enveloped by darkness,
he then subsisted on drops of water for ten thousand years.
Then, for ten thousand years he subsisted on air alone;
thereafter, for ten thousand years he remained without food.
As he was thus performing penance, a fire arose from his body and consumed the entire world; it was like a marvel.
"What is this? What is this? cried out all the gods;
terrified, all the worlds sought refuge with Brahmā. (43)
Having heard what was requested by the best of gods, the four-faced one (Brahmā) went there joyfully, accompanied by Gāyatrī and mounted upon his swan.
With only his vital breath remaining, crowded with hundreds of veins, his belly withered and his limbs emaciated, his eyes were closed in meditation. (45)
He beheld him blazing with splendor, like a second fire.
"Choose a boon—blessings upon you, my child—whatever resides in your heart. (46)
Having heard from the mouth of Brahmā words that brought satisfaction merely by being heard— words like a stream of nectar— Aruṇa spoke.
With eyes opened wide, he beheld before him the god born from the lotus,
accompanied by Gāyatrī and attended by the four Vedas.
Seeing him with a rosary and a water-pot in his hands, muttering the eternal Brahman, [the king] rose up, bowed down, and then praised him with various hymns. (49)
He chose as his boon that death should not come to him by means of his own intellect;
hearing Aruṇa’s words, Brahmā respectfully enlightened him.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others have been swallowed by Death;
what then can be said of others, O best of Dānavas, regarding their mortality? (51)
"Therefore, tell me a suitable boon that can be granted by me;
wise people never harbor persistence in such matters. (52)
Having heard these words of Brahmā, he spoke again with reverence:
"Neither from battle, nor from weapons and missiles, nor from men, nor even from women [does danger arise]. (53)
"O Lord, O Master, grant me this boon: that my death may not come from two-footed beings, nor from four-footed beings, nor from anything possessing both forms. (54)
"And grant me abundant strength, so that there may be victory for the gods.
Having heard these words of his, he replied, "So be it. (55)
Having granted the boon, the Lotus-born One quickly departed for his own abode;
thereafter, the Daitya named Aruṇa [summoned] those residing in his own refuge from Pātāla.
Proud of the boon granted by Brahmā, he summoned the Daityas;
having arrived, all those Asuras made him their lord.
And they dispatched a messenger to Amarāvatī for the sake of war;
having heard those words of the messenger, the king of the gods trembled with fear.
Together with the gods, he went quickly toward the abode of Brahmā;
placing Brahmā and Viṣṇu at their head, they proceeded to the dwelling of Śaṅkara.
There they deliberated on the means for the slaughter of the enemies of the gods.
At that moment, he (Viṣṇu) arrived there, surrounded by the army of the Daityas.
The Daitya king named Aruṇa quickly went to heaven and seized the individual offices of the Sun, the Moon, Yama, and Agni.
O Sage, assuming various forms through his ascetic power, he performed this himself;
all those who had been displaced from their respective abodes went to the region of Kailāsa.
The gods each related their own individual suffering to Śaṅkara;
thereupon, a great deliberation arose as to what should be done hereafter. (63)
Neither by battle nor by weapons and missiles, neither from men nor from women,
neither from two-legged beings nor from four-legged beings, nor even from those of both forms.
"Death shall come to pass," for this was the word Brahmā spoke;
thus, all were overcome with anxiety and were unable to do anything at all. (65)
At that moment, an incorporeal voice arose there:
"Worship the Mistress of the World; she will accomplish your task."

"If the king of the Daityas, who is devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī, should abandon it, he would then become fit for death"—thus [the goddess spoke] in a voice that was exceedingly pleasing. (67)
Having heard that divine voice, they deliberated with great respect;
then the king of the gods, having summoned Bṛhaspati, spoke these words.
"O Guru, go toward the asuras for the sake of the gods' mission;
act in such a way that Gāyatrī may abandon him. (69)
We serve the Supreme Sovereign through the yoga of meditation;
that Blessed Lady, being pleased, will grant you her assistance.
Having thus instructed their preceptor, they all went to the Queen of Jambūdvīpa, thinking, "That beautiful lady will protect us who are terrified by the fear of the Daityas. (71)
Having gone there, they all performed austerities with great steadfastness,
intent on the recitation of the seed-mantra of Māyā and devoted to the sacrifice for the Goddess.
Then Bṛhaspati quickly went into the presence of the asuras;
and when that best of sages had arrived, the king of the Daityas questioned him.
O Sage, tell me: from where did you come, for what reason, and for what purpose?
I am not a partisan of your side; on the contrary, I am your enemy. (74)
Having heard these words of his, the leader of sages said:
"The goddess who is to be served by us is the very one you worship incessantly. (75)
"Therefore, tell me, how could you not be a partisan of our side?
Having heard these words of his, he was deluded by the divine illusion (māyā).
O best of beings, out of pride he abandoned that supreme mantra;
by abandoning the Gāyatrī, the Daitya indeed became devoid of luster.
Having accomplished his task, the Guru departed from that place once more;
he then related the entire account to the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra).
All those gods, being fully satisfied, worshipped the Supreme Goddess.
O Sage, after a long time had passed in this manner, at a certain point, [the following occurred].
The Mother of the World appeared, the bringer of auspiciousness to the world;
she shone like ten million suns and was more beautiful than ten million gods of love. 80.

The goddess was adorned with variegated unguents, clothed in a pair of colorful garments, and decorated with diverse garlands and ornaments; her fistfuls of flowers were as brilliant as multicolored bees.
She grants boons and fearlessness, peaceful, an ocean of the nectar of compassion, and is adorned with flower garlands joined by various bees. || 82 ||
She was surrounded by countless, diverse bees,
while male bees sang the mantra *hrīṃ* day after day.
Ambikā is surrounded on all sides by millions upon millions [of attendants];
she is enriched with every kind of elegant attire and is praised by all the Vedas.
She who is the soul of all, consisting of all, whose form is every auspiciousness;
she who is all-knowing, the mother of all, the All, the Sovereign of all, the Auspicious One (Śivā). 85.
Having seen her, the gods, led by Brahmā, being fickle-minded yet joyful in heart, praised the auspicious consort of Viṣṇu.
The gods said:
"Obeisance, O Goddess Mahāvidyā, you who cause creation, maintenance, and destruction!
O lotus-petal-eyed one, obeisance to you, the support of all! (87)
Salutations to her who consists of the Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, Virāṭ, and Sūtrātman;
salutations to her whose form is unmanifested, the immovable Kūṭasthā; salutations again and again.
O Durgā, who are devoid of creation and its origins, who are the bolt that restrains the wicked, and who are accessible through unimpeded love; O Bharga, O Goddess, salutations be unto you!
Homage to the venerable Kālikā, O Mother; homage to Nīlasarasvatī!
To you, O Ugratārā, O Mahogrā, there is always and ever again and again homage.
Salutations, O Goddess clad in yellow garments; salutations, O Tripurasundarī!
Salutations, O Bhairavī, Mātaṅgī, Dhūmāvatī; salutations again and again!
O Chinnamastā, salutations to you; O daughter of the Ocean of Milk!
Salutations to Śākambharī, O auspicious one; salutations to you, O Raktadantikā!
O destroyer of Niśumbha and Śumbha; O annihilator of Raktabīja;
O eradicator of Dhūmralocana; O slayer of the Asura Vṛtra! || 93 ||
O Śivā, who crushes Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa and brings an end to the Dānavas;
salutations to you, O Vijayā, Gaṅgā, Śāradā, and you of the blossoming countenance! 94.
Salutations again and again to you who are the form of the earth, the form of compassion, and the form of splendor;
salutations be to you who are the form of life-breath, the form of greatness, and the form of the elements.
O you whose form is the universe, whose form is compassion, whose form is dharma—salutations, salutations!
O you whose form is the deity, whose form is light, whose form is knowledge—homage be to you! 96.
