O Gāyatrī, O boon-granting goddess, O Sāvitrī, and O Sarasvatī! Homage, Svāhā, Svadhā, O Mother Dakṣiṇā; salutations, salutations to you! || 97 ||
We worship that Supreme Deity who is revealed by all the scriptures through the words "not this, not this," and whose nature is the witness of all. 98.
Because she is surrounded by bees, she is therefore remembered as Bhāmarī;
salutations ever to that Goddess, salutations again and again forever. || 99 ||
Salutations to you at your sides and behind; salutations to you in front, O Mother! Salutations above and salutations below; salutations, salutations everywhere.
Have mercy, O Great Goddess, dweller on the Isle of Jewels;
O Mother of the World, sovereign of infinite billions of universes! 101.
Victory, O Goddess, Mother of the World! Victory, O Goddess, Supreme beyond the supreme!
Victory, O Śrī Bhuvaneśānī! Victory, O Most Excellent of all the excellent! 102.
O Sovereign of the World, you who are the mine of the jewels of auspicious qualities; be gracious, O Supreme Goddess! Be gracious, O Gateway of the Universe! (103)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard these words of the god— words that were both bold and sweet—
the Mother of the World, who speaks with the voice of the intoxicated cuckoo, replied.
The Goddess said:
"I am always pleased, O gods; I am the crest-jewel of those who grant boons. Let all you wise ones speak whatever it is you desire to accomplish."
Having heard the words of the goddess, the gods spoke of the cause of their suffering—
the conduct of the wicked Daitya, which was the supreme cause of affliction for the world.
With great reverence, they related how there had been an insult to the gods, the Brahmins, and the Vedas, as well as their destruction and the displacement of the deities from their stations.
They related exactly how the boon had been granted by Brahmā;
then, having heard that voice from the mouth of the God, the Great Goddess [spoke].
Then Bhrāmarī urged on the bees held in her hands—
those standing at her side, those stationed in front, and likewise those assuming various forms.
He produced them in great numbers, by whom the three worlds were pervaded;
yet their entire host has now emerged like a swarm of locusts.
Then the atmosphere was pervaded by them, and darkness fell upon the earth,
as well as in the heavens, upon mountain peaks, in trees, and even in the forests.
They were transformed into bees, which was like a marvel;
rising up, they all tore open the chests of the Daityas.
Just as bees become enraged when a man steals their honey, so too there was then no means for either weapons or missiles [to prevail]. 113.
There was neither battle nor conversation; it was indeed nothing but death.
In whichever place whichever Daityas were stationed, in whatever manner [they stood], [they met their end]. 114.
And right there, all those who were full of pride met their death in that manner;
at that time, no one engaged in mutual interaction. (115)
In a mere instant, all those foremost of Daityas were destroyed;
having thus accomplished their task, the bees returned to the presence of the Goddess. || 116 ||
"This is a marvel! This is a marvel! thus the people exclaimed.
"What is so wonderful about the Mother of the World, whose power of illusion (māyā) is such as this? (117)
Then all the hosts of gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
immersed themselves in an ocean of joy and worshipped Ambikā.
With various diverse services and offerings held in their hands, they uttered cries of "Victory! and scattered flowers.
In the heavens, the kettledrums resounded and the hosts of Apsaras danced;
the best of sages recited the Vedas, while the Gandharvas and others sang.
The three worlds were pervaded by the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, murajas, vīṇās, ḍhakkās, and ḍamarus, as well as by the resonances of bells and conch shells. 121.
Then, having praised her with various hymns and likewise placing their joined palms upon their heads, they all cried out: "Victory to you, O Mother! Victory to the Sovereign! (122)
Then the Great Goddess, being pleased, granted various boons individually; and when requested by them, she bestowed upon them abundant devotion toward her.
Then, even as the gods were looking on, she vanished from sight.
Thus, I have related to you the entire great life-story of Bhrāmī.
For those who read and for those who hear it, this is the destroyer of all sins;
upon being heard, it produces wonder and is a means of crossing the ocean of saṃsāra. 125.
Thus, the life-story of all the Manus, which destroys sin and bestows auspiciousness when read or heard, is joined with the *Devīmāhātmya*. (126)
The man who constantly recites this and listens to it incessantly, being liberated from all sins, shall attain union with the Goddess. || 127 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Life of Bhrāmari," in the tenth book of the Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 13 ||
Nārada spoke this hymn of praise to the Goddess composed by Manu:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, Nārāyaṇa, Eternal One!"
The most wonderful and supreme life-story of the Goddess has been narrated. || 1 ||
The supreme manifestation of the Mother for the sake of the purpose of the enemies of the Asuras—the attainment of her office—is declared here by virtue of the full compassion of the Goddess. (2)
Now, O Lord, I desire to hear that conduct by which You always take delight and by which You fully nourish Your own devotees; please tell me that.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Nārada, knower of reality, to the sequence of rules for right conduct,
by the mere performance of which the Goddess is always pleased.
I shall now fully declare that which must be performed day by day by a twice-born man after rising in the morning, for the benefit of the twice-born.
From sunrise until sunset, the twice-born should remain engaged in virtuous deeds,
devoted to the obligatory and occasional rites, as well as other blameless optional rites.
Neither father nor mother remains for the sake of one's own companionship;
neither son, nor wife, nor kinsman remains—only dharma remains.
Therefore, always accumulate merit through its means for the sake of a companion;
for by means of that very merit as a companion, one crosses over the darkness that is so difficult to traverse.
Conduct is the primary dharma, as declared in the Śrutis and the Smṛtis;
therefore, a twice-born man should always be devoted to it for his own sake.
Through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct one obtains offspring;
through right conduct food becomes inexhaustible; and right conduct destroys sin.
Proper conduct is the supreme dharma for men; it brings about their welfare.
Having become happy in this world, one attains happiness in the next.
But for people blinded by ignorance, whose minds are deluded and bewildered,
Dharma is the great lamp that reveals the path to liberation.
"Preeminence is attained through right conduct; through right conduct, one gains mastery over action;
from action, knowledge is born"—this is the statement remembered by Manu. (13)
This conduct is the most excellent of all dharmas and the supreme austerity;
that alone is designated as knowledge, and by it everything is accomplished.
But that best of the twice-born who conducts himself here devoid of proper conduct should be excluded like a Śūdra; for he is exactly like a Śūdra. || 15 ||
Conduct is said to be of two kinds: scriptural and likewise worldly. Both should be practiced and not abandoned by one who desires welfare. (16)
O Sage, the customs of villages, the customs of castes, the customs of regions, and those arising from family lineages—all these must be observed by all men; one should never transgress them.
For a man of evil conduct is censured in the world;
he constantly partakes of suffering and is indeed pervaded by disease. (18)

One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of righteousness; and one should likewise abandon even that righteousness which results in future suffering and is despised by the world. (19)
Nārada said: "O Sage, since the scriptures here are so numerous, how can there be certainty?
Tell me, what is the authoritative measure for determining the path of dharma? (20)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"The Śruti and Smṛti are the two eyes, and the Purāṇa is remembered as the heart.
Dharma exists only in that which is declared by this triad, and nowhere else. (21)
But where there is a mutual contradiction among these three, the Śruti is the authority; in a conflict between two, the Smṛti is superior.
Where there is a conflict between two Vedic texts (śruti), both are traditionally held to be dharma;
but where there is a conflict between two Smṛti texts, the respective scope for each must be determined separately.
In some Purāṇas, they speak of a dharma exactly as it is seen in the Tantras;
one should never accept that dharma.
If a Tantra is not in conflict with the Vedas, it is authoritative; of this there is no doubt.
But that which is contradicted by direct Vedic revelation cannot be authoritative.
In every respect, the Veda alone is the authoritative means for knowing the path of dharma;
whatever is not in contradiction with it is authoritative, and nothing else.
He who, having abandoned the dharma of the Vedas, conducts himself according to other authorities—for his instruction, indeed, cauldrons dwell in the world of Yama. (27)
Therefore, with every effort, one should resort to the dharma declared in the Vedas, whether it be the Smṛti, the Purāṇa, or another Tantra or Śāstra. (28)
There would be proof for its being rooted in that [tradition], but never otherwise;
those who, through devotion to false scriptures, lead men astray in this world— (29)
With their faces downward and feet upward, those Pāśupatas who act according to their own whims and wear the sectarian marks shall go to the ocean of hell. (30)
Those who bear the mark of heated seals and follow the Vaikhānasa doctrine—all of them, having been cast outside the path of the Vedas, go to hell. (31)
Therefore, a person should always practice the true Dharma as declared in the Vedas; rising again and again, one should reflect: "What has been accomplished by me today? (32)
Whether it has been given, caused to be given, or even merely spoken with one's voice—
in all minor offenses as well as in great sins— (this applies).
Having reached the latter part of the night, one should practice meditation on Brahman,
with the feet placed upward upon the thighs, the left thigh being the uppermost.
Lying on his back with his face slightly raised and supported by his chest, with eyes closed and established in *sattva*, he should not let his teeth touch one another. (35)
With the tongue fixed against the palate, the mouth closed, and remaining perfectly motionless,
with the collection of senses fully restrained and seated on a seat that is neither too low nor too high— (36).
One should undertake breath control (prāṇāyāma) for either double or triple [the duration];
thereafter, that Lord who resides in the heart like a lamp should be meditated upon. (37)
The wise one should fix the self there and practice concentration;
it is with smoke and without smoke, with form and also without form. (38)
Prāṇāyāma is of six kinds: both perceptible (salakṣya) and imperceptible (alakṣya).
Yoga is said to be equal to prāṇāyāma; thus it is called prāṇāyāma. || 39 ||
Prāṇāyāma is said to consist of exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka); for these—exhalation, inhalation, and retention—are composed of the three phonemes.
That very syllable is declared to be the *praṇava*, and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) consists of that;
having drawn in the air through the *iḍā* [left nostril], one fills it and holds it within the abdomen. (41)
Slowly, with sixteen mātrās, one should expel that [air] by means of the other [nostril].
Thus, O Sage, the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) accompanied by smoke has been described.
In the Foundation (ādhāra), the Liṅga, the Navel, the Heart, the Root of the Palate, and the Forehead;
in the two petals, the sixteen-spoked wheel, the twenty-spoked, the ten-spoked, the twelve-spoked, and the four-spoked;
at the end of the abode, in the center of the Child (Bāla), and in the region of the throat accompanied by the letters ḍa, pha, ka, ta, sa, and ha, [are placed] the vowels.
I bow to that which is endowed with the meaning of the principles of *haṃ* and *kṣaṃ*, which resides upon all the petals, and which has the form of letters. || 43 ||
Seated upon a dawn-lotus, her complexion the color of a mass of its pollen,
marked with the signs prescribed by Hara, having the nature of a lotus fiber,
and enriched by the faces of the leaders of the Sun, Agni, and Śiva;
If he should dwell even once within the mind, he would be truly enjoyed.
Staying, going, traveling, thought, reflection, praise, and speech—I am the God who is the self of all; praise is everything, for it is your worship. (45)
"I am the Goddess, and I am none other; I am Brahman alone, not subject to sorrow.
I am of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss"—thus one should contemplate one's own Self. (46)
I take refuge in that Woman who is bliss itself, who shines forth at the first departure, who becomes like nectar upon the return journey, and who moves within the inner path. 47.
Then, one should meditate upon that Guru, who is the Lord, within one's own Brahmarandhra;
and one should worship him according to the prescribed rite with mental offerings.
The practitioner, with self-restraint, should praise with this mantra:
"The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman—salutation to that illustrious Guru. (49)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Hymn to the Goddess Composed by Manu," in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Rules for Purification.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of right conduct."
Even though he has studied the Vedas along with the six auxiliary sciences, they abandon him at the time of death, just as birds with fledged wings leave their nest. (1)
Having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, one should properly perform all of that;
furthermore, during the final watch of the night, the wise man should practice the study of the Vedas.
Then, for a short time, he should perform meditation upon his chosen deity;
the yogi, however, should practice meditation on Brahman by means of the previously mentioned path.
O Nārada, by that [means] through which the oneness of the individual soul and Brahman arises incessantly,
one becomes liberated while living at that very moment.
Fifty-five [ghaṭikās] constitute the time of dawn (uṣaḥkāla); fifty-seven is the rising of the dawn-red (aruṇodaya);
fifty-eight is morning (prātaḥ); and the remainder is recorded as the rising of the sun (sūryodaya). || 5 ||
Having risen early in the morning, that best of the twice-born should void his excrement and urine at a distance from the earth exceeding the range of an arrow-shot toward the southwest.

When voiding excrement or urine, a twice-born man in the first stage of life (the student) should place the sacred thread behind his ear; for forest-dwellers and householders, it should be worn around the neck (nivīta).
Having placed the sacred thread behind him so that it hangs from the neck, a householder may void excrement and urine; one in the first stage of life (the student) should keep it at his ear.
Having covered the ground with grass, having veiled his head with a cloth,
and having restrained his speech with effort, he should remain free from spitting and excessive breathing.
One should not perform it on ploughed land, nor in water, nor on a funeral pyre, nor on a mountain;
one should not do so in a dilapidated temple, nor on an anthill, nor on a grassy meadow.
One should not study while standing in pits inhabited by living beings, nor while walking, nor while standing on a path;
nor during the two twilights, nor while reciting prayers, nor while eating, nor while cleansing the teeth.
In rites for the ancestors and in rites for the gods, as well as when voiding urine or excrement, during exertion or sexual intercourse, and likewise in the presence of one's teacher. (12)
During a sacrifice, a gift-giving ceremony, or a Vedic study ritual (brahmayajña), a twice-born man should observe silence;
for all the deities, sages, piśācas, serpents, and rākṣasas [are present]. (13)
"May all beings depart from here; I shall prepare the ground outside.
Having thus prayed, he should thereafter perform purification according to the prescribed rule. (14)
One should never discharge feces or urine while facing the wind, fire, a learned brahmin, the sun, water, or likewise cows. 15.
One should perform [the evacuation] facing north during the day, and facing south if it is at night;
then, having covered the excrement and urine with clods of earth, leaves, grass, and so forth.
Having assumed the outward signs [of his order], he should rise and go near water;
having taken water in a vessel, he should indeed proceed elsewhere.
Taking white clay from the bank, the best of Brahmins should take it;
those of other castes should likewise take red, yellow, or black clay.
Alternatively, the earth found in that very place should be taken by the best of the twice-born,
whether from within water, from a temple, from an anthill, or from a molehill.
The five types of clay remaining after purification have not been prescribed for use;
however, it is traditionally taught that the amount of clay for purification after urination should be double, and triple after sexual intercourse.
One application of clay on the penis and three on each hand—this is declared to be the purification for urination; for [the purification after] defecation, it is declared to be double that.
For purification after voiding feces, one should apply two applications of clay to the region of the penis;
five to the anus; ten to one hand; and seven to both hands.
Placing the left foot forward and then the right,
the wise man should apply clay to each foot four times.
Thus, the purification for a householder is twofold, for a student it is threefold, for a forest-dweller it is fourfold, and for ascetics it is eightfold. (24)
For the act of purification, earth the size of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit should always be taken for each [application]; never less than that. (25)
This is declared to be the purification for a Vaiśya during the day; half of that is prescribed for it at night;
half of that again for one who is ill; and half of that for one who is traveling on a road.
For women, Śūdras, the infirm, and children, regarding the act of purification, one should perform it as many times as necessary so that the odor may be eliminated. (27)
"The purification for all castes is prescribed to continue only as long as the odor and the stain persist," so said the venerable Manu. (28)
One should perform purification with the left hand, and certainly not with the right;
the left hand is for cleaning below the navel, while the right hand is for above the navel.
This should be understood by the best of the twice-born as pertaining to the act of purification, and not otherwise;
a wise man should not take up a water vessel while voiding excrement or urine.
If one should take [the property] out of delusion, one must then perform penance;
or if, due to delusion or even through laziness, one does not perform purification for oneself. (31)
One should subsist on water for three nights; thereafter, one is purified through recitation (jāpa).
One must consider in every respect the place, time, substance, capacity, and one's own circumstances. (32)
Having understood this, one should perform purification; one should not harbor laziness in this matter. Upon voiding excrement, one should indeed take twelve mouthfuls of water for rinsing.
One should never discharge urine less than four times;
having turned his face downwards, a man should void it slowly to the left.

Having sipped water (ācamana), one should then respectfully perform the cleansing of the teeth with a twig twelve finger-breadths long, free from blemishes, and originating from a thorny or milky tree.
It should be as thick as the tip of the little finger, with a brush-like end formed at its front half.
The Karañja, Udumbara, Cūta, Kadamba, Lodhra, Campaka, and Badarī—these trees are declared suitable for cleansing the teeth. (36)
"Arrange yourselves for the sake of food; this King Soma has arrived.
Having washed my mouth with his splendor and his fortune, [he shall provide it]. (37)
O Lord of the Forest, grant us longevity, strength, fame, splendor, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence. (38)
In the absence of a tooth-stick, or on prohibited days,
one should perform the cleansing of the teeth with twelve mouthfuls of water.
That living being who performs the cleaning of his teeth on Sunday has, by that act, swallowed the Sun and destroyed his own lineage. (40)
On the first lunar day, the new moon, the sixth, the ninth, the eleventh, and on Sundays, the contact of a tooth with a wooden twig burns one's family up to the seventh generation. (41)

Having thoroughly performed the washing of the feet with pure water, one should drink it three times; then, wiping the mouth twice, one should touch the pair of nostrils with the ring finger and thumb while they hold water.

With the thumb and ring finger, one should touch the pair of eyes; with the little finger and thumb, the pair of ears; with the thumb and ring finger, the region of the navel; then the heart with the palm; and finally the head with all the fingers.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for Purification," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Greatness of Forbearance. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"The sipping of water (ācamana) is of four kinds: Śuddha, Smārta, Paurāṇa, and likewise Vaidika."
They say that what is enjoined by the Śruti is sixfold: the Tantric and the Śrauta.

The purification of feces, urine, and so forth, as well as ritual purity, has been fully described; likewise, the rites prescribed by the Smṛtis and the Purāṇas are to be performed according to the rules once one has sipped water (ācamana).
Rituals such as the Vedic and Śrauta rites, preceded by the Brahma-yajña and others,
as well as the practice of the science of weapons (astra-vidyā) and so forth, are called the Tantric procedure.
Having recollected the Oṃkāra and the Gāyatrī, one should likewise bind the topknot (śikhā).
Having sipped water again, one should touch the heart, the two arms, and the two shoulders.
Upon sneezing, spitting, being defiled by food particles from the teeth, speaking untruth, or conversing with outcasts, one should touch the right ear.
O Nārada, fire, water, the Vedas, Soma, the sun, and likewise the wind— all these abide in the right ear of the brāhmaṇa.
Then, O best of sages, having gone to a river or similar place, one should perform the purifying morning bath for the sake of cleansing the body.
The body is exceedingly impure, constantly discharging filth through its nine gates;
therefore, the morning bath is prescribed for its purification.
The sin arising from approaching those who should not be approached, the sin arising from accepting improper gifts,
and the sin committed in secret— one is liberated from all this by the act of bathing.
Since all ritual acts of one who has not bathed become fruitless,
therefore one should always perform the morning bath every single day.
One should perform one's bath and the salutation to the twilight (saṃdhyā) rites while holding darbha grass;
however, by not bathing for seven mornings, or by omitting the saṃdhyā for three days, [one incurs a fault].
A twice-born man who remains without the sacred fires for twelve days shall attain the status of a Śūdra,
because the time for the fire-oblation is short and the rite of bathing is extensive.
One should not bathe at dawn in that manner, for it is censured at the time of the fire-oblation;
indeed, there is nothing superior to the Gāyatrī, both in this world and in the next.
Because it protects one who sings it, it is called Gāyatrī;
it is joined with the Praṇava and united with the three Vyāhṛtis. (11)
A learned brahmin, endowed with Vedic knowledge and always devoted to his own duty, should conquer the wind within the wind by means of three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
He should recite Vedic mantras and never those that are worldly;
as long as there is even a mustard seed on a cow's horn, for that long his [practice] is not firm.

Neither of these two types of recitation— whether with seed-syllables (*sagarbha*) combined with chanting, or without seed-syllables (*agarbha*) consisting of mere meditation— can deliver both sides of the family, including the ancestors up to one hundred and one generations.
Having performed the libation (tarpaṇa) as an ancillary part of the bath, which gratifies the gods, sages, and ancestors,
and having put on two clean garments, he came out from the water.
The wearing of sacred ashes and the wearing of rudrākṣa beads must always be performed by practitioners of japa according to the sequential method. 16.
He who wears ten Rudrākṣas on the neck, twenty on each of the two ears, twelve on each of the two hands, sixteen on the two arms according to the digits of the moon,
one on each of the two eyes, and one hundred and eight on the crest and the chest— he himself is Nīlakaṇṭha.
O Sage, having fastened a rudrākṣa with gold or silver,
one should always wear it on the crest-lock or on the ears with a concentrated mind.
A man [should wear] the sacred thread on his hand, or around his neck, or even on his stomach, either with the glorious five-syllabled mantra or likewise with the Praṇava. || 19 ||
A wise person should joyfully wear the rudrākṣa with sincere devotion;
the wearing of rudrākṣa is the direct means for attaining the knowledge of Śiva. (20)
O Brahmin, one should contemplate that Rudrākṣa which is upon the crest-lock as the Tāra-tattva;
on both ears, one should meditate upon the God and the Goddess.
One should remember the Vedas upon the sacred thread and likewise the quarters of space in one's hand;
one should also contemplate the goddess Sarasvatī in the throat and the purifying fire as well.
The wearing of Rudrākṣas by those of all stages of life (āśramas) and castes (varṇas) is prescribed to be performed with mantras for the twice-born (dvijas), but not for those of other castes.
By wearing rudrākṣas, one becomes Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt—even while seeing forbidden things, or likewise hearing or remembering them.
Even while smelling, as well as eating, constantly prattling, always acting, walking, or even voiding, a human being [should remain absorbed]. || 25 ||
Merely by wearing rudrākṣas, one is not smeared by any sins;
whatever has been eaten by this [rudrākṣa] becomes as if eaten by the God himself. || 26 ||
That was drunk by Rudra; that was smelled by Śiva.
O great sage, those who feel shame at wearing rudrākṣas— [they are the ones who have been thus consumed]. (27)
For those who, upon seeing one wearing rudrākṣa beads, utter slander, there is no liberation from saṃsāra even through ten million births. || 28 ||
It is certain that there is indeed a confusion regarding its origin;
yet, simply by wearing Rudrākṣa beads, Rudra attains the state of Rudra-hood. (29)
The sages are of true resolve, and Brahmā attained the state of Brahmāhood;
there is nothing whatsoever superior to the wearing of Rudrākṣa beads.
He who, out of devotion, gives clothing and grain to one who wears rudrākṣa beads, being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Śiva. || 31 ||
One should joyfully feed a wearer of rudrākṣas at a śrāddha ceremony;
he attains the world of the ancestors—there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (32)
A person who washes the feet of one who wears rudrākṣa beads with water and drinks that water is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 33 ||
O best of the twice-born, by wearing with devotion a necklace, a bracelet, or even gold adorned with rudrākṣa beads, one attains the state of Rudra.

Whether it be a single rudrākṣa, O great-minded one, wherever it may be—whether accompanied by a mantra or devoid of a mantra, and lacking meditative visualization (bhāva)—it is [efficacious]. || 35 ||
Whosoever, whether a man or anyone else, should wear [this] with devotion or even out of modesty,
shall be liberated from all sins and attain perfect knowledge.
"Oh! The greatness of the rudrākṣa cannot be fully described by me;
therefore, one should wear the rudrākṣa with every effort. (37)

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Rudrākṣa," in the section on the Exposition of Right Conduct, within the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
**Description of the Greatness of Rudrākṣa.** Nārada said:
"O sinless one, such is the power of this rudrākṣa as described by you."
He is described as worthy of worship by the great; tell me, what is the reason for that?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"In this very same way, the Lord Giriśa, the powerful Rudra, was questioned in ancient times by Ṣaṇmukha; hear that which he spoke to him."
Īśvara said:
Listen, Ṣaṇmukha; I shall tell you the truth in brief.
In ancient times, there was a Daitya named Tripura who was invincible by all.
By him all the gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other deities, were conquered;
when all of them had reported this, I then set out toward Tripura.
I meditated upon the great weapon called Aghora, which is captivating,
divine, composed of all the gods, blazing, and of terrible form.
For the sake of slaying Tripura and for the deliverance of the gods,
I meditated upon the Aghora weapon, which pacifies all obstacles.
For a thousand divine years my eyes were kept open;
afterwards, drops of water fell from my agitated eyes.
There, from those drops of tears, great rudrākṣa trees were born by my command, O Mahāsena, out of a desire for the welfare of all.
And those rudrākṣas came to be of thirty-eight varieties;
twelve are remembered as being tawny (kapila), having originated from the eyes of the Sun.
Those sixteen types of white [lines] arise from the Somanetra [channel] in succession;
indeed, there are ten varieties of black [lines] arising from the Vahninetrodbhava [channel].
A white-colored rudrākṣa is said by birth to be Brāhma;
the red is Kṣatriya, the variegated is Vaiśya, and the black is Śūdra. (11)
Śiva with one face directly removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
with two faces, he is the God of gods and shall destroy manifold evil.
The three-faced Fire himself directly consumes the sin of killing a woman in an instant;
the four-faced Brahmā himself removes the sin of killing a human being.
He was Rudra himself, five-faced and known by the name Kālāgni;
[he was tormented] by the consequences arising from eating what is unfit to be eaten and from approaching women who should not be approached.
By wearing the five-faced [image], one is liberated from all sins;
that six-faced Kārttikeya, moreover, should be worn on the right hand. (15)
One is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; there is no doubt about this.
He is the highly fortunate one with seven faces, known by the name Anaṅga.
Indeed, by wearing it, one is liberated from sins such as the theft of gold;
O Mahāsena, he is the eight-faced god Vināyaka himself. || 17 ||
Likewise, one who touches Antakūṭa, Tūlakūṭa, Svarṇakūṭa, a woman of wicked lineage, or the wife of a guru; 18.
By its retention, all such evils as these are destroyed;
his obstacles perish, and at the end, he attains the supreme state. (19)
All these qualities indeed arise from wearing [the image] of Aṣṭavaktra;
however, Navavaktra Bhairava should be worn on the left arm.
It is declared to bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation; one shall become equal in power to me.
Thousands of killings of embryos and hundreds of killings of Brahmins [are thereby purified]. (21)
By the wearing of the nine-faced [liṅga], they attain immediate dissolution;
but the ten-faced one is the Lord of Gods, the manifest God Janārdana himself. (22)
Planets, piśācas, vetālas, brahmarākṣasas, and serpents are all pacified by the retention of the ten-faced [mantra]. (23)
Eleven Rudrākṣas on the face are known as the eleven Rudras;
hear now the meritorious fruit for one who indeed wears them upon the crest-lock. || 24 ||
Whatever fruit results from a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices, and a hundred thousand cows properly given as gifts; [that fruit one obtains by bathing here]. || 25 ||
One quickly obtains that fruit by wearing a single Rudrākṣa on the face, or by wearing a twelve-faced Rudrākṣa on the ear. || 26 ||
The twelve Ādityas, ever established within his mouth, are constantly gratified;
he shall obtain that fruit which is gained from the Gobheda and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
For him, there is indeed no fear of horned animals, of those bearing weapons, or of tigers and the like;
nor is there any fear of disease for him, nor is any mental affliction ever proclaimed to exist.
He has no fear whatsoever, nor does any disease arise;
he has no fear from any quarter, and he becomes happy and a lord. (29)
Having killed elephants, horses, deer, cats, snakes, mice, frogs, donkeys, dogs, jackals, and various other such creatures; || 30 ||
One is liberated from this, there is no doubt, by wearing twelve beads on the face; O child, if a thirteen-faced Rudrākṣa is obtained, [the result is even greater].
He should be known as equal to Kārttikeya, the bestower of the fulfillment of all desires and goals;
for him, both mercury and elixirs (rasāyana) shall become fully effective.
All things to be enjoyed belong to him alone; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Even he who slays his mother, his father, or his brother [is his]. (33)
O Six-faced One, one is liberated from all sins by wearing it;
O son, this is so if a fourteen-faced Rudrākṣa can be obtained.
One should constantly bear that lump of Śiva upon one's head;
O Sage, what is the use of speaking much or describing it again and again? (35)
It is constantly worshipped by the gods, and the supreme goal is attained;
therefore, even a single rudrākṣa should be worn on the head with devotion by the best of the twice-born. (36)
The garland for the head is made with twenty-six [beads], while that for the heart is made with fifty;
the armlets are made with twenty beads, and the wristbands with twelve.
O Six-faced One, having fashioned a rosary of Rudrākṣa beads with one hundred and eight, or fifty, or twenty-seven [beads]. (38)
Indeed, by wearing or even by chanting [the mantra], one enjoys infinite fruit;
if a rosary of one hundred and eight rudrākṣa beads is worn. (39)
O Six-faced One, at every moment one obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice;
having uplifted twenty-one generations of one's lineage, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Rudrākṣa," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Ritual for the Rudrākṣa Prayer Bead Rosary. The Lord said:
O Six-faced One, listen; I shall describe the characteristics of the prayer bead rosary.
Brahmā is said to be the face of the rudrākṣa, and the dot (bindu) is called Rudra. || 1 ||
Viṣṇu shall indeed be the tail, bestowing the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it consists of twenty-five syllables, has five faces, and is provided with thorns. || 2 ||
The rosary should be made from beads that are red, white, or mixed in color, strung together with holes bored through them, and shaped like the curved tail of a cow.
Having joined the mouth with the mouth, one should join the tail with the tail;
one should make Mount Meru face upwards, and above that, the serpent-noose (nāgapāśaka).
Having thus strung this garland which bestows the accomplishment of mantras,
one should wash it with scented water and then with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then, having washed [the area] with the water of Śiva, one should install the groups of mantras;
having touched it with the Śivāstra mantra, one should veil it with the Kavaca mantra.
Thereafter, one should apply the root mantra and perform the rites as before;
having sprinkled [the object] with the Sadyojāta and other mantras up to one hundred and eight times.
Having recited the root mantra and placed [the vessel] upon pure ground,
one should install Śiva, the supreme cause, together with Ambā upon it.
The garland, when properly established, shall bestow the fruits of all desires; one should worship that garland with the very mantra belonging to whichever deity it represents. || 9 ||
One should place the rosary on the head, the throat, or the ear;
likewise, with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, one should perform the recitation with a self-controlled mind.
Endowed with supreme devotion, one should constantly wear Rudrākṣas on the neck, the head, the heart, the extremities, the ears, or both arms. 11.
What is the use of speaking much more here with repeated descriptions?
Therefore, the constant wearing of rudrākṣas is praised for this reason. || 12 ||
During bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, the Vaiśvadeva rite, worship of the gods, penance, as well as at a Śrāddha ceremony, and especially at the time of initiation; || 13 ||
If a Brahmin, out of delusion, performs any Vedic rite while not wearing rudrākṣa beads, he certainly falls into hell. (14)
One should wear a Rudrākṣa on the head, on the neck, on a thread, or on the hand;
it should be pure, unadulterated with gold or gems, auspicious, and not previously worn by others. 15.
One who is impure should not wear the *akṣa*; one should always wear it with devotion alone—even blades of grass produced by the wind from the Rudrākṣa tree.
Even a man who commits sins, if he wears a rudrākṣa, shall go to the world of merit from which return is difficult to obtain. (17)
For the Jābāla Śruti declares that one crosses over all evil;
indeed, by wearing Rudrākṣa beads, even animals attain the state of Rudra.
How much more so for those men who wear a rosary of rudrākṣa beads!
Indeed, at least one rudrākṣa should always be worn on the head by those devoted to Rudra. (19)
Those who utter the names of Śambhu, the Supreme Self, proclaim the destruction of all sufferings and liberation from all sins. (20)
Those who are adorned with rudrākṣas are indeed the most excellent devotees of the Lord;
the wearing of rudrākṣas should be performed by men seeking all forms of spiritual welfare.
In the ear-lobes, the crest-lock, the neck, the hands, and likewise the belly,
reside Mahādeva, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and their various manifestations.
Likewise, other gods indeed wear rudrākṣas out of devotion;
so too do all the ancestral sages (gotrarṣis), who are the immutable and primordial forms of all beings. (23)
And all the sages born in their lineage were indeed pure, devoted to the Vedic dharma, and wearers of rudrākṣa beads. (24)
Faith does not arise directly toward that which is established by the Vedas and bestows liberation, except at the end of many births through the grace of Mahādeva. (25)
The desire to wear rudrākṣas arises spontaneously by its very nature;
indeed, the greatness of the rudrākṣa has been proclaimed with reverence by Jābāli. (26)
It is recited by all the sages and by me as well, O son:
the fruit of the rudrākṣa is indeed renowned throughout the three worlds. (27)
Upon seeing the fruit, there is merit; from touching it, the merit becomes ten millionfold;
by wearing it, a man obtains merit a hundred times ten millionfold.
Through recitation, one constantly obtains thousands of lakṣas and crores, as well as hundreds of lakṣas and crores; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (29)
Whoever wears a rudrākṣa on the hand, the chest, the throat, the two ears, and likewise on the head, is Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt. (30)
Invulnerable to all beings, he shall indeed roam the earth like Rudra;
he is to be venerated by both gods and asuras, just like Śiva.
One who constantly wears rudrākṣas is to be saluted by men, even if he is impure, engaged in improper acts, or joined with all manner of sins. (32)
One is liberated from all sins by wearing a rudrākṣa;
even if a dog dies with a rudrākṣa tied around its neck, it is released.
Even he attains liberation, how much more so a human being—
if one should wear a rudrākṣa, even if devoid of recitation and meditation.
Freed from all sins, he goes to the supreme goal;
for even by making an effort to wear a single rudrākṣa, one attains this. || 35 ||
Having extracted twenty-one [beads], one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Hereafter, I shall again proclaim the ritual procedure for the rudrākṣa.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Rudrākṣa Prayer Bead Rosary," in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
In the *Rudrākṣamāhātmya*, the description of liberation for Guṇanidhi; the Lord said:
"O Mahāsena, Kuśagranthi, Putrajīva, and others are supreme."
Not even one [other type of seed] is worth a sixteenth part of the rudrākṣa. || 1 ||
Just as Viṣṇu is among men, as the Sun is among the planets, as the Gaṅgā is among rivers, and as Kaśyapa is among sages; || 2 ||
Just as Uccaiḥśravas is among horses, just as the Lord is among the gods, and just as Gaurī is among goddesses, so too may this be the most excellent. || 3 ||
There is no hymn superior to this, nor is there any vow superior to this;
among gifts that yield inexhaustible merit, the rudrākṣa is preeminent.
One should give an excellent rudrākṣa to one who is peaceful and a devotee of Śiva;
I do not venture to describe the limit of the meritorious fruit thereof. || 5 ||
He who offers food to one who wears rudrākṣas around his neck rescues twenty-one generations of his lineage and goes to the world of Rudra.
That brahmin on whose forehead there is no sacred ash, who does not wear rudrākṣa beads on his body, and who performs no worship in the temple of Śambhu, is the lowest of outcasts.
Even one who eats meat, drinks liquor,
or associates with those of the lowest castes shall be liberated from sins if a rudrākṣa remains upon his head.
Whatever fruit is obtained through all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and the study of the Vedas,
that fruit one obtains immediately by wearing a rudrākṣa.
Whatever merit is gained through the four Vedas and by the recitation of the Purāṇas, as well as by the visiting of sacred fords and by all branches of knowledge and the like; || 10 ||
One immediately obtains that merit by wearing a rudrākṣa;
if one should die while wearing a rudrākṣa at the time of departure [from this life], [one attains liberation]. 11.
He attains the state of Rudra, and for him there is no further rebirth;
if one dies while wearing a rudrākṣa on the neck or on the arms.
Having delivered twenty-one generations of his lineage, a man shall dwell in the world of Rudra—
whether he be a Brāhmaṇa or a Cāṇḍāla, devoid of merit or possessed of merit.
Whoever wears sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads shall attain the divine state of Śiva, whether he be pure or impure, and even if he is an eater of forbidden food. (14)
Whether he be a barbarian or even a Cāṇḍāla, or one joined with all possible sins, by the mere wearing of Rudrākṣas he becomes Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt. || 15 ||
If worn on the head, it is ten million-fold; on the ears, one hundred million-fold;
bound around the neck, one billion-fold; and on the crown of the head, ten billion-fold.
Ten thousand [merits] reside in the sacred thread (upavīta), while a hundred thousand crores reside on the arm;
however, the rudrākṣa at the wrist is the supreme means for attaining liberation.
Becoming a wearer of rudrākṣa beads, whatever Vedic rite a brahmin performs with constant devotion, he obtains the great fruit thereof. (18)
Even one devoid of devotion who wears a rosary of rudrākṣas around his neck, if he is constantly engaged in sinful deeds, is liberated from all bondage. (19)
He whose mind is dedicated to Rudrākṣas, even if he does not wear Rudrākṣas himself, is a devotee of Maheśvara in this world; he is to be saluted like the Liṅga itself.
Whether ignorant or possessed of knowledge, by wearing the rudrākṣa one shall attain the world of Śiva, just as the donkey did in Kīkaṭa.
Skanda said:
O Lord, for what reason did the donkey wear rudrākṣas?
Or by whom were they given to him in Kīkaṭa? Tell me that, O Supreme Lord. (22)
The Blessed Lord said:
Listen, my son, to an ancient account. On the Vindhya mountain, there was a donkey who carried a burden of rudrākṣa beads, having been made to do so by a traveler.
Exhausted and unable to bear that burden,
the three-eyed Maheśvara, the wielder of the trident, fell to the ground, having abandoned his life-breaths.
O Mahāsena, by my grace you have come into my presence;
for the counting of the faces of the rudrākṣas is very difficult to achieve.
For as many thousands of yugas as there are [in that time], he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
this should be told to one's own disciples, but never to those who are not disciples.
One should never reveal it even to those who are undevoted or foolish;
whether he be devoted or undevoted, base or even more base. (27)
Whoever wears rudrākṣas is liberated from all sins;
with what else could the merit of wearing rudrākṣas be compared? (28)
Sages who perceive the truth declare this to be a great vow:
he who, firm in his observance, wears a thousand Rudrākṣa beads.
All the gods bow down to him; he is just like Rudra.
In the absence of a thousand arms, however, there are sixteen on each side.
One [mudrā] is on the crest-lock, twelve on each of the two hands,
thirty-two in the region of the throat, and forty on the head.

He who wears one Rudrākṣa on each ear, six on each, six on the other, six on each, six on the other, six on the ears, six on the ears, six on the chest, and one hundred and eight on the chest, is honored like Rudra himself.
He who wears Rudrākṣas combined with pearls, corals, crystals, silver, lapis lazuli, and gold shall become Śiva himself. || 33 ||
Even if one wears only rudrākṣas out of indolence,
sins do not touch him, just as darkness does not touch the sun.
A mantra recited with a rosary of rudrākṣas bestows infinite fruit;
even a single rudrākṣa on one's body grants great merit. (35)
His birth would be as futile as one who performs a head-bath while wearing a rudrākṣa on his head, yet remains devoid of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). || 36 ||
The fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā arises for him; there is no doubt about this.
Some have one face, some five faces, and others eleven mouths. (37)
Some rudrākṣas have fourteen faces and are worshipped by the world;
this rudrākṣa, whose essence is Śaṅkara, is constantly worshipped with devotion. (38)
It can even make a poor man a king on earth;
in this regard, I shall relate to you the supreme doctrine of the Purāṇas. (39)
In the land of Kosala, there was a certain twice-born man known as Girinātha;
he was immensely wealthy, righteous-souled, and a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
The son of that performer of sacrifices who was initiated for the rite was named Guṇanidhi; he was renowned for his beautiful form, youthful, and as handsome as the god of love.
Then, by means of her beauty, youth, and intoxication, she deluded Muktāvalī, the wife of the wise Guṛu.
Having united with her for some time, he then, out of fear, gave poison to his preceptor; afterwards, however, being free from fear, he [consumed it] himself.
At the very moment when his mother and father learned of some deed [of his],
he killed both his mother and father with poison.
Then, when his wealth had been exhausted through various pleasures and enjoyments,
that wicked man committed theft in the houses of Brahmins.
Then, intoxicated by the madness of drinking liquor and cast out by his kinsmen, he was expelled from the village by everyone and became a forest-dweller. || 46 ||
Accompanied by that pearl necklace, he went into the dense forest;
standing on the path out of greed for wealth, he killed many Brahmins.
When much time had passed in this manner, that lowest of men then died;
and thousands of messengers of Yama arrived to lead him away. 48.
Likewise, the attendants of Śiva arrived from the world of Śiva;
O son of Girijā, a dispute arose between the two of them.
Then the messengers of Yama said: "O servants of Śambhu, tell us if there is indeed any merit belonging to him, if you wish to lead him away. (50)
Then the messengers of Śiva said: "In the spot where he died, ten cubits below the ground, there is indeed a rudrākṣa."
"By its power, O messengers, we shall lead him into the presence of Śiva.
Then, having ascended a celestial chariot, the twice-born man assumed a divine form.
The treasury of virtues, accompanied by messengers, has gone to the abode of Śaṅkara;
thus, O observer of noble vows, has the greatness of the rudrākṣa been told to you.
Thus, the greatness of the rudrākṣa has been briefly described by me;
it destroys all sins and bestows the fruit of great merit. (54)

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of Guṇanidhi," in the Rudrākṣa-māhātmya of the eleventh book of the Śrīmad-devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 6.
Description of the Greatness of the Rudrākṣa.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Thus, O Nārada, the six-faced one was enlightened by Giriśa.
Having understood the greatness of the rudrākṣa, he became one who had achieved his life's purpose. || 1 ||
Thus have I described this Rudrākṣa, whose power is such as it is, in the context of virtuous conduct; now listen with a concentrated mind to something else.
Just as the greatness of the rudrākṣa, which bestows infinite merit, has been described,
so shall I describe its characteristics and the placement of mantras for you.
The merit from seeing it is one hundred thousandfold, and from touching it, it becomes ten millionfold;
by wearing it, a person obtains merit ten million times that amount.
A person obtains the merit of hundreds of millions and thousands of millions [of recitations] by wearing Rudrākṣa beads and by chanting them.
Indeed, from wearing the auspicious Rudrākṣas, there shall be great fruit;
that which is the size of a Dhātrī fruit is declared to be the best. (6)
The wise declare that [the size] of a jujube fruit is the medium;
the inferior is the size of a chickpea—this is the promise proclaimed by me.
By the command of Śiva, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas,
and Śūdras were born as trees upon the earth, auspicious trees belonging to those respective castes.
The Brāhmaṇas are to be known as white, the Kṣatriyas as red-colored;
the Vaiśyas are to be understood as yellow, and the Śūdras are proclaimed to be black.
A Brāhmaṇa should wear white [garments], while a king (Kṣatriya) should wear red;
a Vaiśya should wear yellow, and a Śūdra should wear black. || 10 ||
Likewise, auspicious [seeds] are those that are even, smooth, firm, and provided with thorns;
while those bitten by insects, split, broken, or lacking thorns are unfavorable.
One should avoid rudrākṣas that have six faces, those with holes, and those that are covered;
however, a rudrākṣa that has its own opening formed naturally is considered the best here.
That which is made by human effort should be considered mediocre;
one should wear [the rosary] made of smooth, firm, and round beads with a linen thread. (13)
Where a line is seen that is uniform across all limbs, perfectly even yet distinct, and which, when rubbed, has the luster of a streak of gold.
One should know that to be the supreme rosary; it is to be worn by the worshippers of Śiva.
One should wear a single rudrākṣa on the crest-lock and thirty on the head. (15)
Thirty-six [beads] should be worn on the neck, sixteen on each of the two upper arms;
twelve beads on the wrist, and there should be fifty on the shoulder. (16)
One should fashion a rosary necklace and a sacred thread with one hundred and eight beads;
one should wear it around the neck, either as a double-strand or a triple-strand.
In the earrings, the crown, the ear-ornaments, and the necklaces; likewise in the armlets, the bracelets, and the waistband. || 18 ||
A man should wear a rudrākṣa at all times, whether sleeping or drinking;
three hundred are said to be the lowest [grade], while five hundred are called the middling.
A thousand is declared to be the supreme; one should thus maintain [the count] according to the divisions:
with the Īśāna mantra on the head, and with the Tatpuruṣa mantra on the ear.
One should place [the ash] on the forehead with the Aghora mantra, and likewise on the heart;
furthermore, one should apply it to the two hands with the Aghora-bīja mantra.
One should string fifty beads with the Vāmadeva mantra on the belly;
such is the manner of wearing the rudrākṣa along with the five Brahmans and the ancillary mantras.
One should wear all the rudrākṣas strung together with the root mantra.
A one-faced rudrākṣa reveals the supreme reality.
And from the retention of the supreme reality (paratattva), its manifestation arises;
O best of sages, he becomes two-faced and Ardhanārīśvara. (24)
By wearing [this], Ardhanārīśvara is eternally pleased with him;
moreover, the three-faced Fire himself instantly consumes the sin of killing a woman.
The three-faced rudrākṣa is also the embodiment of the triple fire;
by wearing it, the Fire-god is perpetually pleased with him.
The four-faced rudrākṣa has the form of Pitāmaha (Brahmā);
by wearing it, one becomes possessed of great fortune and attains supreme, great health.
A person should wear the great wealth of knowledge for the sake of purification;
the five-faced rudrākṣa, moreover, is the very embodiment of the five Brahmans. (28)
Maheśvara is satisfied by the mere wearing of that rudrākṣa which has six faces and has Kārtikeya as its presiding deity. (29)
The wise also declare that the deity is Vināyaka;
the seven-faced rudrākṣa has the seven mātrās as its presiding deity.
It has the seven horses as its deity and the seven sages as its deity;
by its retention, there shall be great prosperity and supreme, great health. (31)
A man who possesses great wealth of knowledge and is indeed pure should wear it;
the eight-faced Rudrākṣa has the eight Mātrās as its presiding deity.
It is auspicious, pleasing to the Vasus and Aṣṭakas, and pleasing to Gaṅgā;
by wearing it, these speakers of truth shall become pleased. (33)
The nine-faced Rudrākṣa is declared to have Yama as its presiding deity; by wearing it, the fear of Yama never arises in any way whatsoever.
The ten-faced rudrākṣa is remembered as having the ten directions as its presiding deity;
there is no doubt that it generates delight for the ten directions when worn. (35)
The eleven-faced Akṣa has the eleven Rudras as its presiding deities;
they say that it has Indra as its deity and always increases happiness. (36)
The twelve-faced Rudrākṣa is the very form of Mahāviṣṇu;
it is presided over by the twelve Ādityas, and indeed, one who is devoted to it bears that [divinity].
The auspicious Akṣa, with thirteen faces, is the granter of desires and the bestower of success;
by the mere wearing of it, Kāmadeva becomes pleased. (38)
The eye with fourteen faces, born from the eye of Rudra, is the remover of all diseases and the bestower of complete health. || 39 ||
Therefore, one should avoid drinking liquor, eating meat, garlic, onions, and śigru, as well as the śleṣmātaka fruit and village pigs. 40.
During an eclipse, at the equinoxes, during the transit of the sun, as well as at the solstices, on the new moon and full moon days, and on other auspicious days,
one is immediately liberated from all sins by wearing rudrākṣa beads. (41)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Rudrākṣa," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Purification of the Elements (Bhūtaśuddhi).
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O great sage, I shall now describe the method of the purification of the elements.
Having arisen from the *mūlādhāra*, [one should contemplate] Kuṇḍalī, the supreme deity. || 1 ||
Resorting to the path of the Suṣumṇā, the practitioner should contemplate [the soul] as having reached the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
uniting the individual soul with Brahman by means of the Haṃsa mantra.
One should visualize the mandala of the earth as being from the feet up to the knees, four-cornered, marked with a vajra, known by the seed-syllable Laṃ, and golden in color. (3)

One should meditate upon the mandala of water, which extends from the knees to the navel, resembling the half-moon, marked with two lotuses, joined with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, and white in appearance.
One should meditate upon the orb of fire, red in color, extending from the navel to the heart, triangular in shape, adorned with a svastika, and joined with the seed-syllable *raṃ*.
One should meditate upon the sphere of wind, which extends from the heart to the center of the earth, circular, marked with six dots, joined with the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, and smoke-colored.

One should contemplate the sphere of space (ākāśamaṇḍala), which extends from the midpoint of the eyebrows up to the aperture of Brahmā (ābrahmarandhra), circular, transparent, and beautiful, and joined with the seed-syllable "haṃ."
Having thus reflected upon the elements, one should dissolve each one individually:
earth into water, water into fire, fire into air, and that [air] into space.
Having dissolved space into the ego, and the ego into the principle of the Great One (mahat),
one should dissolve the Great One into primordial nature (prakṛti), and that into the Self (ātman).
Having become composed of pure consciousness, one should contemplate the personification of sin (pāpapūruṣa) situated in the left side of the abdomen, black in color and the size of a thumb.
It has the head of the murder of a Brahmin, the arms of the theft of gold,
the heart of the drinking of liquor, and is joined with the hips of violating the teacher's bed.
Associated with that [sin], it consists of a pair of words, beginning with minor offenses (upapātaka);
it is black, bearing a sword and shield, facing downwards, and extremely difficult to endure.
Meditating on the seed-syllable of air, one should fill [the body] with air and dry it up;
then the mantra, joined with one's own body, should burn it away with the seed-syllable of fire.

Then, having recited [the mantra] during the retention of breath (kumbhaka), one should expel the external ash produced from the "man of sin" by means of the wind-seed syllable (vāyubīja) while exhaling.
The wise one should drench the ash produced from the body with the seed-syllable of nectar (sudhā),
and then solidify that ash like a golden rod with the seed-syllable of earth (bhū).
Meditating on the seed-syllable of the sky in the form of a pure mirror,
the wise one should fashion the limbs from the head down to the feet.
The mind should again produce the elements, beginning with space;
then, by means of the mantra, one should bring that self into the lotus of the heart.
Having taken the life-force of the kuṇḍalinī, which has become composed of nectar through contact with the Supreme,
and having established it in the heart-lotus, one should contemplate it as residing in the mūlādhāra.

May the Supreme Power of Life (Prāṇaśakti), the Goddess who is the color of the rising sun, bestow happiness upon us—she who is seated upon a vibrant red lotus on a boat in a sea of blood; who holds in her lotus-like hands a trident, a bow made of sugarcane, a jewel-string, a goad, and five arrows; who bears a skull filled with blood; who is radiant with three eyes and enriched by full, swelling breasts. 19.
Having thus meditated upon the power of breath (prāṇa-śakti) as being of the nature of the Supreme Self,
one should perform the wearing of the sacred ashes for the sake of attaining all authority and accomplishments.
I shall describe the expansion of its manifestations and the great fruit of wearing it;
the wearing of ashes is supreme, as declared by the authority of the Śruti and Smṛti. (21)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of Bhūtaśuddhi," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Description of Wearing the Tripuṇḍra along with the Śirovratam.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
By those twice-born ones who have duly performed this Śirovratam, [the following occurs].
To those very people, one should speak the supreme knowledge that sublates ignorance.
For those by whom the head-vow (śirovrata) has not been performed according to rule and with faith,
the practice of Śrauta and Smārta rites provides no benefit.
O learned one, it was solely through the practice of the head-vow that the gods, beginning with Brahmā, became deities; indeed, it was not for any other reason.
The greatness of the head-vow (śirovrata) was established by the ancients even earlier than the ancients;
so too were Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and all the deities.
Even one who is burdened with every sin is liberated from all sins by that wise person who has performed this "Head Vow" according to the prescribed rules.
This is indeed called the "Head-Vow" (śirovrata), which is stated in the Atharvaṇa Śruti upon the head;
for it is nothing other than that, and it is obtained through merit.
O tiger among sages, the names of this vow are recited differently according to the various Vedic branches; for that vow is indeed one and the same across all branches.
In all the branches [of the Vedas], there is one single reality called Śiva, who is the mass of true consciousness;
likewise, there is knowledge concerning Him, and likewise the Śirovata vow.
Even one who is devoid of the head-vow (śirovrata) and abandoned by all [other] dharmas is qualified for all branches of knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
This head-vow (śirovrata) should be performed; it burns away the wilderness of sins and is the means for attaining all vidyās. Therefore, one should practice it correctly.
One should always properly observe that vow which the subtle Atharvaṇa Śruti, illuminating the subtle reality, has spoken with affection.
With the six mantras beginning with "Agniriti," one should perform the smearing of all limbs with pure ashes; this is known as the Śirovrata.
One should perform this vow of keeping the head wet with respect during the periods of the twilights;
until the dawning of knowledge, his knowledge shall indeed be supreme.
One should perform the Śirovrata for twelve years, or one year, or half of that, or half of that again; or alternatively, one may perform it for twelve days by means of a formal resolve (saṅkalpa).
If one who has performed the head-vow (śirovrata) bath does not instruct him, his knowledge shall perish; indeed, such a teacher is merciless.
The sage who is the direct teacher of the knowledge of Brahman is indeed compassionate, just as the glorious Lord of All is gentle and truly compassionate. 16.
Only for those men who have practiced righteousness throughout thousands of previous births does faith indeed arise, and never otherwise. (17)
On the contrary, due to the abundance of ignorance, hatred alone arises;
therefore, for one possessed by intense hatred, there can be no self-knowledge. (18)
O learned one, only those who have performed the head-vow (śirovrata) are the direct qualified candidates for the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman, and no others. (19)
"The Vedic injunction is that this [teaching] should be imparted only to those twice-born who have diligently observed the Pāśupata vow. (20)
He who, by means of this vow, should abandon both the animal and that state of being an animal—having killed them, he would not become a sinner; such is the certainty of the Vedānta.
The wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) has been proclaimed with reverence by the Jābālas,
using the Tryambaka mantra, the Satarudriya, and the Śiva mantra.
One who has taken refuge in the householder stage of life should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra),
applying it three times with the syllable Om accompanied by the Praṇava (the *Haṃsa*).
"A mendicant should always wear [it]," so says the Jābāli Śruti;
with the Triyambaka mantra, the Praṇava, and the [mantra of] Śiva. (24)
The householder and the forest-dweller should also wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka),
as well as the student (brahmacārī) day after day, according to the passage beginning with "the wise one" (medhāvī).
One should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ash mixed with water;
for a Brāhmaṇa born according to the sacred law exists by means of the triple mark of ash alone.
One should always wear the horizontal smearing of ashes as a veil upon the forehead;
(due to its connection with Mahādeva, there is a corresponding affinity in that dharma). Furthermore, a Brāhmaṇa should always properly practice the dharma of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). 27.
Since the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) was worn with ashes by him who became the primordial Brāhmaṇa,
for that very reason a Brāhmaṇa should always wear the triple mark.
One should not, even out of delusion, abandon the smearing of the body with ashes established by the Vedas as the *tripuṇḍra*, nor the worship of the *rudraliṅga*. (29)
With the Tṛyambaka mantra, likewise with the one containing the Star (the Gāyatrī), with the five-syllabled mantra, and likewise with the Praṇava. || 30 ||
O great sage, one who has entered the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead, the heart, and both arms.
Alternatively, the student (brahmacārin) should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with secondary ash using the *triyāyuṣa* mantra beginning with "medhāvī" and so forth.
A Śūdra, devoted to service, should always perform the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with devotion, using only the mantra ending in "namas" dedicated to Śiva.
O Sage of excellent vows, for all others as well, the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) must be performed with devotion even without a mantra.
Smearing oneself with ashes and wearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) across the forehead are superior to all other religious duties; therefore, one should practice them constantly. || 35 ||
Having carefully taken either the ashes produced from the Agnihotra fire or those originating from the Virajā fire, and having placed them in a pure vessel; || 36 ||
Having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice with a concentrated mind,
he should slowly take up the sacred ash while reciting the five Brahma-mantras.
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one should consecrate [the water] with the mantra beginning with "Agnir...
and then consecrate it three times with those same seven mantras.
Having recited "oṃ āpo jyotiḥ" and meditated, one should utter the mantras;
first, having smeared the body with white ashes. (39)
Free from sin and free from passion, the mortal is born; of this there is no doubt.
Then, having meditated upon Mahāviṣṇu, the Lord of the World and the Master of Waters—

Having mixed water with ashes while reciting "Agnir ityādi" and other mantras, and having wiped [the body] while meditating on the Lord together with Ambā, he should then dust himself from head to toe.
With that white ash, which has become Brahmic through meditation,
[he should mark] the forehead, chest, and shoulders with the mantra appropriate for his own stage of life (āśrama).
One should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with devotion at the three times of day, using the middle, ring, and thumb fingers, both in the forward and reverse order.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Observance of the Head-Vow and the Wearing of the Tripuṇḍra," in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
In the *Bhasmamāhātmya*, the description of the *Pāśupata* vow:
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "The [vow] pertaining to fire is secondary; it destroys ignorance and accomplishes knowledge."
Know, O Brahmin, best among the knowers of Brahman, that the secondary [nature] is of many kinds.
O Sage, likewise [there is ash] born from the Agnihotra fire, that born from the Virajā fire,
that produced from the Aupāsana fire, and that originating from the Samidh fire.
[The fire] produced from a cooking fire, that arising from a forest conflagration, and for all members of the three castes, that produced from the agnihotra sacrifice. || 3 ||
O great sage, the ash produced from a smokeless fire should be worn;
for householders especially, that which has arisen from the *aupāsana* fire is prescribed.

A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) must maintain the fire produced from the sacrificial fuel (samit), while for Śūdras it is the fire arising from the cooking hearth in the house of a learned Brāhmaṇa (śrotriya). 5.
This [rite] arising from the forest fire must also be maintained by all others;
the time is the Citrā full moon, and the place is one's own domain.
A field, a grove, or a forest that is praised and possesses auspicious characteristics is suitable;
there, on the thirteenth day of the waxing moon, having bathed well and performed his daily rites, [he should proceed].
Having obtained permission from his own preceptor, having honored him and prostrated before him,
and having performed a special worship, he himself dons white garments.
Wearing a pure sacred thread, adorned with white garlands and unguents,
seated upon a seat of darbha grass and holding a handful of darbha grass.
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), facing either east or north, and having meditated upon the God and the Goddess by way of petitioning them; || 10 ||
One becomes initiated through the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), thinking, "I shall observe this vow," for as long as the body lasts, or for twelve years.
Or half of that, or half of that again, or for twelve months;
or half of that, or half of that again, or even for a single month.
It may last for twelve days, or six days,
or half of that, or even for a single day, up to the limit of the formal vow (saṅkalpa).
Having established the sacred fire according to the rules for the purpose of performing the Virajā oblation,
he offered clarified butter, sacrificial fuel, and cooked rice (caru) into it in accordance with the prescribed rites.

Having become purified, and further aiming for the purification of the principles (tattvas), one should offer oblations with the root mantra using those very same materials, such as sacrificial fuel (samidh) and so forth. || 15 ||
Recalling, "May these principles within my body be purified," one should [then contemplate] the elements and the subtle elements (tanmātras), as well as the five organs of action. (16)
Through the division of knowledge and action, there are five and five respectively;
the seven elements beginning with the skin, and the five vital airs beginning with prāṇa. (17)
Mind, intellect, ego, the qualities (guṇas), primordial nature (prakṛti) and the individual soul (puruṣa); attachment, knowledge, limited power (kalā), necessity (niyati), and time (kāla). || 18 ||
Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, Maheśvara, Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śivatattva—these they know to be the principles (tattvas) in their respective order. || 19 ||
Having offered oblations with pure mantras, that officiating priest shall become pure;
then, having taken cow dung, formed it into a ball, and consecrated it with mantras— || 20 ||
Having offered it into the fire and protected it on that day while consuming only sacrificial food (haviṣya),
one should perform everything previously described on the morning of the fourteenth day.
On that day, remaining without food, he should complete the remainder of the time;
likewise, having performed [the rites] on the morning of the festival, he should do so until the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa).
Having extinguished the fire of Rudra and carefully gathered the ashes,
he then became one with matted hair, one with a shaven head, and one with a single tuft of hair.
Having bathed after having become [so], if he should again be free from shame, he may be naked (digambara), or otherwise clothed in saffron robes, or even dressed in garments of skin or bark. (24)
Wearing a single garment, clad in bark, and possessing a staff and a girdle,
he should then wash his feet, perform the ritual sipping of water twice, and [purify] his own body.
Having gathered that ash produced from the fire free of dust (virajā),
one should apply it in due order with the six Atharvaṇa mantras beginning with "Agniriti."
Having wiped his limbs from the head down to the feet, he should touch them with those [ashes];
then, having smeared himself with ashes in that very same sequence.
One should perform the smearing of all limbs with ashes using either the Praṇava or the Śiva-mantra;
thereafter, one should fashion the sectarian mark (puṇḍra) known as the Triyāyuṣa.
Having attained the state of Śiva, one should then practice the state of Śiva;
one should likewise perform this Pāśupata vow at the three junctions of the day. || 29 ||
It bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and it brings about the cessation of the state of being a *paśu*.
Having abandoned that state of being a *paśu* and having performed the *pāśupata* vow, [one attains the goal]. (30)
Mahādeva, Sadāśiva, whose form is the Liṅga, is ever to be worshipped;
the ash-bath is supremely meritorious and the highest bestower of all happiness. (31)
Since it increases longevity, strength, health, prosperity, and nourishment, it is for the sake of protection, auspiciousness, and the full abundance of all success. (32)
For those who smear themselves with ash, there is no fear of great pestilence;
this ash is of three kinds: pacifying, nourishing, and the granter of desires. (33)

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pāśupata Vow," within the "Greatness of Ashes" section of the eleventh book of the *Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 10 ||
Description of the Greatness of the Threefold Ash.
Nārada said: How is this threefold nature of the ash proclaimed?
Tell this to me, O Lord; I have a great curiosity. || 1 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O divine sage, listen as I explain the threefold nature of the sacred ash (bhasma),
which destroys great sins and brings about supreme, great fame.
Cow dung that is still connected to its source is taken with one's own hand;
when it has been burnt with Vedic mantras, it is said here to bring about pacification.
A man, being attentive, should indeed take up that cow-dung;
having taken it into the intermediate space, he should then burn it with the six-limbed mantra.
That is declared to be nourishing (pauṣṭika), and now hear about that which grants desires (kāmada).
One should burn this with the Prāsāda mantra; it is celebrated as the ash that grants desires.
O divine sage, having risen early in the morning, pure and devoted to the vow of sacred ash,
one should go to the cow-pens and pay homage to the herd of cows.
One should take auspicious cow dung from cows that correspond to their respective castes:
the cow of a Brāhmaṇa should be white, and the cow of a Kṣatriya should be red.
The [color] of a Vaiśya is said to be yellow, while that of a Śūdra is black;
one of pure intellect [should perform this] on the full moon day, the new moon day, or the eighth day.
Having taken auspicious cow dung with the Prāsāda mantra,
one should then form it into a ball with the Hṛdaya mantra.
In a beautiful, pure place well-heated by the rays of the sun,
one should deposit [the image] with either husks, chaff, or a temple.
Or [he may take] fire produced from a forest, or that born from the house of one learned in the Vedas;
he should place it into that fire with the mantra consisting of the seed-syllable of Śiva.
Then, the wise one should take ash from the fire-pit there;
having taken a new vessel, he should deposit it with the Prāsāda mantra.
Likewise, the ketakī, the pāṭalī, uśīra, and sandalwood, as well as various fragrant substances such as saffron and others. (13)
The one of pure intellect should place [the substance] into that vessel with the *sadyo* mantra;
having first performed the water-bath, he should thereafter perform the ash-bath.
If one is unable to perform a bath in water, one should perform a bath with sacred ash;
having washed the feet, hands, and head with the Īśāna mantra. (15)
Then, after having shaken off [the impurities], one should subsequently purify the face with Tatpuruṣa,
the heart with Aghora, and thereafter the navel with Vāmadeva.
The wise one, having thoroughly dusted all his limbs with the *sadyojāta* mantra,
should discard his former garment and take up a pure garment.
Having washed both feet and hands, one should thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana);
in the absence of smearing with ashes (uddhūlana), the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is prescribed.
Before midday, it should be performed with water; after that time, it is devoid of water. One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) using the middle fingers, the ring finger, and the index finger.
The places for the ritual placement (nyāsa) are said to be the crown of the head, the forehead, the ears, the throat, as well as the heart and the two arms. || 20 ||
The preceptor should place [the marks] on the head with five fingers using the Prāsāda mantra;
he should place them on the forehead with three fingers using the Śiras mantra.
The wise one should touch the right ear with the *sadyojāta* mantra, the left with the *vāmadeva*,
and the throat with the *aghora* mantra, using the middle fingers.
The preceptor should touch the heart with the heart-mantra using three fingers;
he should then place [the mantra] on the right arm with the śikhā-mantra.
The wise one should place [the mudrā] on the left arm with the *kavaca* mantra using three fingers; he should touch the navel with the middle finger while reciting the mantra "Īśāna."
The three lines are traditionally known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
the first is Brahmā, then Viṣṇu, and above that is Maheśvara. (25)
That which is placed with a single finger—Īśvara is the deity there;
in the middle of the head is this Brahmā, while Īśvara is on the forehead.
The two Aśvin deities are in the ears, and likewise Gaṇeśa is in the throat;
the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra should likewise abandon the smearing with ashes.
For all those of the lowest castes, it should be devoid of mantra;
(for uninitiated humans as well, it should be without mantra). || 28 ||

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Three Kinds of Sacred Ash," in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 11 ||
Description of the Greatness of Wearing Ashes.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O divine sage, listen to all that regarding the fruit born from smearing oneself with ashes.
