And it contains the secret injunctions that bestow the fruits of all desires.
Having taken the clear dung of a tawny cow, it fell into the sky;
it was neither wet, nor hard, neither foul-smelling, nor dried up. || 2 ||
Having abandoned what is above and below, if [the substance] has fallen,
one should gather it together and throw it into the Śiva-fire or elsewhere, consecrated with the root mantra.
Having taken it up and covered it with a cloth, one should cast it into the fire-pit for the ashes—
[a pit] that is well-prepared, very firm, pure, washed, sprinkled, and auspicious.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) with the mantra, the practitioner of mantras should cast ashes into the vessel;
it may be made of metal, wood, clay, or even cloth.
Or one may prepare another beautiful and pure vessel for the ashes;
or, like a wealthy person, one should place the ashes in an extremely pure linen cloth.
When setting out, one should take the ashes oneself or have an attendant do so;
one should not give them to an untrustworthy person, nor should one cast them upon an impure surface.
One should not touch it with the lower parts of the body, nor should one throw it away or step over it; therefore, having taken the consecrated ashes, one should employ them.
The procedure for wearing the *vibhūti*, as proclaimed by tradition and recounted by me, has been declared;
by its very practice, one becomes equal to Śiva—of this there is no doubt. (9)
The ash prepared by Śaivas in the presence of Śiva should be accepted with supreme devotion by those who follow the Vedas; having requested it, one should worship it.
The ash accomplished according to the path taught in the Tantras by those who worship according to the Tantras—
if it is offered anywhere at all, it must not be accepted by Vaidikas.
Śūdras, Kāpālikas, or others who follow heretical paths—even they should wear that triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with devotion; one should not transgress it even in thought.
Since it is enjoined by Śruti, one who abandons it becomes fallen;
likewise, the wearing of the Tripuṇḍra with devotion and the veiling of the body [are prescribed]. (13)
A twice-born man should indeed perform [these rites] with the mantra; he who abandons them becomes fallen.
Those who do not practice the smearing of ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with devotion [are likewise fallen].
O bull among sages, for those by whom the path described as "ashes" was not maintained, there is no liberation from saṃsāra even through ten million births. (15)
O Sage, know that the birth of those men whose bodies exist without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is as fruitless as the birth of a boar. 16.
That [forehead] would be like a cremation ground and should not be beheld by people who perform meritorious deeds;
fie on the forehead devoid of ashes, and fie on the village that is an abode of inauspiciousness! 17.
Fie upon a life that does not worship the Lord! Fie upon knowledge that takes refuge in what is inauspicious!
Those who revile the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) revile Śiva himself. (18)
And those who bear [this teaching] with devotion, they alone truly bear Him;
for as a mountain does not shine when deprived of fire, so too [the bearer] does not shine without it. 19.
Even when all other means are present, those who do not perform the worship of Śiva with faith—being devoid of the smearing of ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra)—[attain no fruit]. (20)
For them, everything previously performed may even become contrary;
yet, by means of ashes, Vedic mantras, and the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), [it becomes effective]. || 21 ||
Without conduct appropriate to the Vedas, that which is performed according to the Smṛtis becomes a cause of misfortune;
by such a person, what is done remains undone, and even what has been heard becomes as if unheard.
Whether one has studied the Vedas or not, he who does not wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) has his Vedic learning in vain, his sacrifices in vain, his charity in vain, and his austerity in vain. (23)
He who does not wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) despite his vows and fasts does so in vain;
that man who desires liberation while abandoning the wearing of ashes [is deluded]. (24)
Indeed, by means of drinking poison, he makes himself eternal;
under the pretext of creation, the Creator has thus declared the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
He indeed created the forehead as oblique and upward, not circular;
for on the foreheads of all embodied beings, oblique lines are seen. (26)
Nevertheless, foolish men do not wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka);
for them there is no meditation, no liberation, no knowledge, and no austerity.
Whatever is performed by a Brahmin without the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) shall be as if it were performed by a Śūdra, who has no right to the study of the Veda. || 28 ||
Without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), a Brahmin has no authority for the worship of Śiva.
Facing east, having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) as before, [he should proceed].
Having restrained the vital breaths and made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), one should perform the ash-bath;
taking pure ashes produced from the agnihotra fire.
One should sprinkle it upon one's own head with the Īśāna mantra;
then, taking that ash, one should apply it to the mouth with the Puruṣa mantra.
One should apply ashes to the heart with that called Aghora, to the secret place with the one named Vāma,
and to both feet with the one designated Sadyojāta.
Then, one should perform the smearing of the entire body with the mantra consisting of the syllable *praṇava* alone;
this is declared by the supreme sages to be the "Agnic" (fiery) bath.
For the sake of the successful accomplishment of all rites, the wise one should first perform this;
then, having washed his hands and other limbs, he should sip water according to the prescribed rule.
The horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead, heart, and throat should be made with ashes according to the prescribed rite,
using either the five Brahma-mantras or [the appropriate mantra].
This triple mark (tripuṇḍra) made with ghee is purifying in all rites;
however, Śūdras and those of the lowest castes must never wear ashes held in their hands at any time.
One should perform ritual action smeared with ashes from the Agnihotra fire;
otherwise, all rituals will never bear fruit. || 37 ||
Truthfulness, purity, recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, visiting sacred fords, and the worship of gods and other deities—
all of this is in vain for one who does not wear the Tripuṇḍra.
The excellent Brahmin who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), who bears rudrākṣa beads, and who is pure, destroys diseases, misfortunes, ailments, famine, and thieves. || 39 ||
He attains the supreme Brahman from which he does not return again;
such a person purifies the assembly and is worthy of worship at the śrāddha rite by both brahmins and even the gods. (40)

At a funeral rite (śrāddha), a sacrifice (yajña), silent recitation (japa), an oblation (homa), the Vaiśvadeva offering, or the worship of the gods, a man who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes becomes a purified soul and conquers death. I shall describe to you once more the greatness of wearing the sacred ash (bhasma). 41.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Wearing Ashes," in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Greatness of Wearing the Tripuṇḍra. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"The multitudes of great sins (mahāpātaka) and other sins as well..."
They perish, O tiger among sages; this is the truth, the absolute truth, and not otherwise. || 1 ||
Listen to the fruit of merit for one by whom even a single measure of ash is worn:
it is said to bestow knowledge upon ascetics and to grant detachment to householders. (2)
O Sage, it likewise increases the merit of householders,
and for those established in the stage of studentship (brahmacarya), it bestows the fruit of Vedic study.
Smearing oneself with ashes and likewise wearing the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) constantly bestows merit upon Śūdras and destroys the sins of others. || 4 ||
For the protection of all beings, the Vedic revelation ordains both the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
The Vedic revelation prescribes for all of these very the status of sacrifice:
namely, the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
The Vedic revelation ordains for them, by virtue of their nature as all beings,
the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
The Vedic Śruti ordains for the sake of the Liṅga-worshippers (Māheśvaras) the smearing with ashes as well as the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra). || 8 ||
And for the sake of the realization of all things, the Vedic revelation ordains [this] through Śiva,
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and likewise the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra).
The ash, consisting of the triple-mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing (uddhūlana), was worn by Hiraṇyagarbha and by the deities such as Varuṇa who are his incarnations.
Umādevī, Lakṣmī, Vāc, and other faithful women—all of them wore sacred ash, consisting of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing of the body. || 11 ||
The ash, consisting of the triple-tilaka and the smearing of the body, is worn by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others, as well as by sages.
The ash has been worn by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and even those of mixed castes,
in the form of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and by smearing it over the body, even in Apabhraṃśa dialects.
O best of sages, only those by whom the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) have been joyfully practiced are truly cultured and wise; none others.

The Śiva-linga, the jewel, friendship, the five-syllabled mantra, sacred ash, and medicinal herbs are for men like a woman who subdues others in the rite of bringing [a person] under one's control. (15)
Wherever one who has smeared his body with ashes eats— whether he be a fool or even a scholar—
there Mahādeva, the bull-bannered god, eats together with his consort.
The man who follows one whose entire body is covered with ashes,
even if he is burdened by all manner of sins, shall soon be honored.
Whoever praises with faith one whose entire body is covered in ashes,
that person, even if burdened by all manner of sins, is honored before long.
Merely by giving alms to one who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), he has indeed studied,
he has heard the scriptures, and he has performed everything.
By whichever Brahmin the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is made upon the head with ashes—
even in the lands of the Kīkaṭas— there he is adorned with sacred ash.
A human being should always dwell [there], for that place is indeed equal to the sacred field of Kāśī;
whether he be of bad character or endowed with virtue, whether he be engaged in yoga or devoid of auspicious marks. || 21 ||

Or, he who is endowed with the teaching of prosperity (bhūti) is to be honored by me like a son; for even if one should practice the sovereign teaching of prosperity through deception, [he is still worthy]. 22.
Even with hundreds of sacrifices, one does not attain that destination which he who holds [the scripture] attains—whether by chance, through association, or even out of fear. (23)
When performed according to the prescribed rules, he indeed becomes glorious and worthy of worship just as I am;
it is the cause of satisfaction for Śiva, Viṣṇu, the gods, and Brahmā.
It is the cause of satisfaction for Pārvatī, Mahālakṣmī, and Bhāratī;
it cannot be attained through gifts, nor through sacrifice, nor through penances that are otherwise very difficult to perform. (25)
Neither by pilgrimage nor by the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is merit obtained;
[rather, it is gained through] charity, sacrifices, religious duties, and pilgrimages, O Nārada. (26)
Meditation and austerity do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
for just as a king always regards one who bears his own insignia as his own kinsman.
Likewise, whether he be of the twice-born caste or of another caste, one who applies the triple mark with pure-mindedness regards himself as Śiva, as if it were his own very self. (28)
He who wears the mark of the triple line (tripuṇḍra) has Rudra brought under his control;
even if he has abandoned the conduct of all stages of life and has ceased all ritual actions, he is such [a person]. (29)
Even he who wears the triple sectarian mark (tripuṇḍra) once across [the forehead] is liberated;
one should not examine his knowledge, nor his lineage, nor likewise his vows.
O Nārada, one whose forehead is marked with the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) is indeed worthy of worship;
there is no mantra superior to the Śiva-mantra, and nothing equal to Śiva.
Indeed, there is no merit higher than the worship of Śiva, nor any sacred site (tīrtha) equal to the ashes.
That which is the supreme sacred site of the fire of Rudra is proclaimed to be these ashes.
It is the destruction of all sufferings and the purification of all sins;
whether one is an outcaste or even a low-born person, a fool or even a scholar—33.
In whatever land he who is endowed with the teachings of prosperity may dwell,
there Sadāśiva, accompanied by the host of all beings and joined by all sacred fords (tīrthas), always makes his presence manifest.
These ashes, consecrated by the five Śiva-mantras and adorned with the limbs of the consumer of desire (Kāma),
are fashioned as triple-marks (tripuṇḍra) upon the surface of the forehead.
They erase the ill-fated lines inscribed by destiny. || 35 ||

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Wearing the Tripuṇḍra," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 13.
Description of the Greatness of Wearing the Vibhūti.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: He who joyfully gives wealth to one whose body is smeared with ashes—
All his sins are destroyed; of this there is no doubt. || 1 ||
All the Śrutis, all the Smṛtis, and even all the Purāṇas proclaim the greatness of Bhūti; therefore, a twice-born man should wear it.
Whoever applies the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with white ashes at the three junctions of the day is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 3 ||
The yogi should constantly perform the practice involving all the limbs, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, at the three junctions of the day; thus he shall quickly attain yoga.
By means of the ash-bath, a person becomes a deliverer of his lineage;
the ash-bath possesses innumerable qualities superior to the water-bath.
Whatever merit exists in all sacred fords, whatever fruit exists in all sacred fords—one obtains all that fruit from the ash-bath; of this there is no doubt.
Whether one is burdened by great sins (mahāpātaka) or even burdened by minor offenses (upapātaka),
all that is consumed by the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna), just as fire consumes fuel.
"There is no purifying bath superior to the ash-bath;
thus was it spoken by Śiva in the beginning, and then Śiva himself bathed. (8)
From that time forward, Brahmā and the other sages, seeking the welfare of Śiva,
diligently performed the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) in all their rites.
Therefore, he who performs this head-bath of the Āgneya type is indeed Rudra himself in this very body; of this there is no doubt.
Those who become fully satisfied upon seeing one who wears the sacred ash are always worthy of worship by the lords of gods, asuras, and sages; of this there is no doubt. (11)
Upon seeing that man who rises with all his limbs covered in ashes,
even the King of the Gods will prostrate himself like a staff before him.
O Sage, for those who consume what is forbidden to eat while preceded by the smearing of ashes, that very thing becomes edible for them; there is no doubt about this.
Whether he be a student, a householder, or a forest-dweller, whoever diligently bathes with ashes after having first bathed in water every day; (14)
Freed from all sins, he goes to the supreme goal;
for ascetics, bathing with sacred ash is especially distinguished. 15.
An ash-bath is better than a bath with water; the destruction of moisture is certain.
One should know that moisture is primordial nature (prakṛti), and they know primordial nature to be bondage. (16)
For the sake of abandoning primordial nature (prakṛti), bathing with ashes is prescribed;
there is nothing equal to ashes even within the three worlds, O Brahman. (17)

O Sage, in ancient times, having seen the sacred ash (bhasma), the beloved Lord formerly gave it to the Goddess for the sake of protection, for the sake of auspiciousness, and for the sake of purification.
Therefore, whoever performs this head-bath which belongs to Agni, being completely liberated from the bonds of worldly existence, is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 19 ||
Fever, rakṣasas, piśācas, pūtanās, leprosy, abdominal tumors, all types of fistulas, and the eighty diseases caused by wind (vāta). || 20 ||
There are sixty-four diseases of bile (pitta), and fifty-seven of phlegm (śleṣman);
likewise, there is fear of tigers and thieves, as well as other malevolent planetary influences.
By the ash-bath, sins perish just as elephants do before a lion;
likewise, by pure cold water and the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) made with ash. (22)
Whoever maintains the Supreme Brahman attains it, there is no doubt.
And whoever, anyone at all, maintains the supreme triple mark with sacred ash, he attains the world of Brahmā, freed from sin; there is no doubt.
By properly maintaining the power of fire upon the forehead according to the prescribed rite. || 23 ||
It certainly destroys the Yama-script written on the forehead;
by wearing it upon the neck, it destroys the sin committed there.
By wearing it on the neck, the sin committed by the neck and the enjoyment [of its beauty] is removed;
by [wearing it] on the arms, the sin committed by the arms is removed; and by [wearing it] on the chest, the sin committed by the mind is removed. (25)
O Brahmin, by holding [the breath] at the navel, one removes the sin committed with the penis; by holding it at the anus, one removes the sin committed with the anus;
and by holding it at the sides, O Brahmin, one removes [the sin of] embracing another’s wife and so forth.
The wearing of that ash is recommended everywhere as the triple mark;
it represents the wearing of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna, as well as the three sacred fires.
By that [means], indeed, the maintenance of the three worlds and their qualities was accomplished;
the learned twice-born man, covered in ashes, is freed from the consequences of great sins. (28)
One is instantly freed from defects and liberated without a doubt;
for one who is established in the ash, the defects are burned away by contact with the fire of the ash.
One whose self is purified by the bath of ashes is known as one established in the Self;
his entire body is smeared with ashes, and he bears the radiant triple mark (tripuṇḍra) made of ashes. || 30 ||
The man who sleeps on ashes is known as one established in ashes;
[by this,] ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and other such beings, as well as diseases that are exceedingly difficult to endure, [are warded off]. (31)

By the proximity of one who is devoted to the ashes, [all sins] melt away; of this there is no doubt. It is called *bhasita* because it illuminates (*bhāsana*), and it is called *bhasma* because it consumes impurities (*kalmaṣa*).
In ancient times, this ash was a source of prosperity for men and a protector that provides protection;
yet, upon seeing one who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), the spirits led by ghosts and goblins [flee].
Terrified and trembling, they perish quickly; of this there is no doubt.
Just as sin is destroyed by the mere remembrance of Rudra, [so too do these beings vanish]. || 34 ||
Even after committing thousands of improper deeds, he who bathes with ashes—
those ashes burn it all away, just as fire consumes a forest by its heat.
Even if he has committed incomparable sin, that twice-born man who, at the time of death,
becomes a bhasmasnāyin, is swiftly liberated from his sins.
For one whose soul is purified by the ash-bath, who has conquered anger and subdued the senses, having come into my presence, does not return to worldly existence again. (37)
When the moon has entered the forest (the constellation Puṣya), one whose body is smeared with ashes, upon seeing Śaṅkara worshipped there, is liberated from all sins. || 38 ||
Whether desiring long life, or seeking prosperity, or desiring liberation, a wise man—or indeed a twice-born man—should always wear the sacred ashes. (39)
The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is supremely meritorious and consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Those terrible Rākṣasas, Pretas, and other small creatures— || 40 ||
Upon seeing the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), they flee without a doubt;
having performed the rites of purification and the like, one should bathe in pure water. (41)
One should perform the smearing with ashes from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head;
this is the purely Vāruṇa bath that removes external impurities from the body.

Having performed the stainless bath of *vibhūti*, which removes both external and internal impurities, one should remain devoted to it even after leaving the ritual bath of water; of this there is no doubt. (43)
O Sage, even that which has been performed is truly as if unperformed without the bath of ashes;
the bath of ashes is declared in the Vedas and is called the "Agni-bath" (the fire-bath). (44)
One who is purified both internally and externally shall obtain the fruit of Śiva’s worship;
for that alone is the true bath which destroys even external impurity.
Even if one constantly and with devotion performs millions of ritual baths with water (vāruṇasnāna), it does not destroy that intense impurity, both internal and external, belonging to living beings.
O Sage, one does not become a purified soul without the ash-bath;
the Veda knows in truth the greatness of that ash-bath. (47)
Or rather, Mahādeva, the crest-jewel of all gods,
has declared that whoever should perform Vedic rites without having first performed the bath of ashes— || 48 ||
He who performs the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) with effort according to the prescribed rule does not truly obtain even half of a half of that ritual merit.
He alone is the one authorized for all rites, as heard in the Vedas;
and the ash-bath, the purifier of purifiers, is likewise heard in the Vedas. (50)
He who, out of delusion, does not perform this shall become a perpetrator of a great sin;
[he would lose] that merit which is obtained by twice-born men through infinite ablutions in the waters of Varuṇa.
From the ash-bath, merit many times greater than that is obtained.
The ash-bath should be performed with diligence at all three periods of the day. 52.
The ash-bath is known as Vedic; one who abandons it becomes fallen.
After the discharge of urine and other excretions, however, one must diligently perform the ash-bath.
Otherwise, human beings will not become purified;
even a twice-born man who has performed his ablutions according to the rules will not be pure without the bath of ashes. (54)
One shall not become pure in soul, nor qualified for ritual action, when the downward wind has been expelled, or during yawning, emission, or sneezing. (55)
Even when phlegm is expectorated, one should diligently perform the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*).
Only a single portion of the majesty of the glorious ash-bath has been described here. (56)
Furthermore, O bull among sages, I shall proclaim again the fruit arising from the ash-bath;
it should be heard with an attentive mind.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Wearing the Vibhūtis," in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Rules for Wearing the Tripuṇḍra and Urdhvapuṇḍra. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having purified the ashes with the mantras beginning with "Agniriti," the twice-born should respectfully apply the *tripuṇḍra* mark alone on their foreheads and other parts of the body. || 1 ||
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—all these are traditionally known as the twice-born (dvijas).
Therefore, the tripuṇḍra should be worn daily with great effort by the twice-born.
O Brahmin, he alone for whom the initiation ceremony (upanayana) has been performed is called twice-born (dvija);
therefore, the twice-born must perform the Vedic rites and the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
If one performs virtuous deeds while abandoning the wearing of the sacred ashes (vibhūti), those acts become as if unperformed; of this there is no doubt.
Even the instruction on the Gāyatrī is not [complete] without the wearing of ashes;
therefore, having applied ashes to one's limbs, one should perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī. (5)
O bull among sages, they say that the Gāyatrī itself is the very root of brahminhood;
it is not imparted by anyone in the absence of the wearing of ashes.
O Sage, there is no entitlement to the recitation of the Gāyatrī as long as the ash originating from fire has not been applied to the forehead and other parts of the body. (7)
O Brahmin, the absence of ash on the forehead is not an inferential mark for one's devotion to Brahman;
in this very way, O Brahmin, I have stated the cause that bestows great merit. (8)
He on whose forehead white ashes purified by mantra are worn—he alone is a learned Brāhmaṇa; this I tell you as the truth, the absolute truth.
O Brahmin, he who possesses an innate joy in gathering ashes as if they were jewels—he alone is a true Brāhmaṇa; this I tell you in truth, verily, truth. (10)
He who possesses no natural joy in the gathering of ashes as he does for jewels should certainly be known as a *caṇḍāla* in birth after birth. (11)
He who has no natural affection for the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), the smearing of ashes (uddhūlana), and other such rites, should be known as a Cāṇḍāla; this I speak as the truth, the absolute truth.
Those who, having abandoned the wearing of ashes, eat fruits and other such things, all of them undoubtedly fall into a terrible hell. || 13 ||

"He who worships Śiva while abandoning the wearing of the ashes is unfortunate and a hater of Śiva; that hatred brings about hell. Such a person is excluded from all rites, being devoid of the wearing of the sacred ash."
Having abandoned the wearing of sacred ashes (vibhūti), even if one performs acts equal to gold, one does not obtain the fruit thereof; indeed, such a person shall fall.

Just as the twilight rite (saṃdhyā) is not performed by twice-born men who are devoid of the sacred thread (upavīta), so too the twilight rite should not be performed by those who are devoid of sacred ash (vibhūti). 15.
In some cases, when the sacred thread has been lost, a substitute may be employed during the twilight prayers;
likewise, the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra, fasting, and other such rites may be performed [with a substitute]. || 16 ||
In the wearing of sacred ash (vibhūti), however, there is no substitute whatsoever anywhere.
If anyone performs the twilight worship (sandhyā) having abandoned the wearing of sacred ash, [he incurs a fault]. (17)
By that very act, the twice-born man indeed falls from his status and is no longer qualified;
just as a person of the lowest caste falls [from dignity] upon hearing the Vedas, so does the twice-born man. || 18 ||
One who performs the twilight rites without using ash undoubtedly falls [from grace];
therefore, the twice-born should always strive to procure the ash prescribed by the Vedas. 19.
In its absence, however, those who are composed should use either that prescribed by the Smṛtis or that which is worldly;
let it be of whatever kind it may be, for sacred ash is eternally purifying.
This dhāraṇī should be diligently maintained by the twice-born during the rites of the twilights and other ceremonies;
consequently, sins never take hold of them, just as they do not remain in ashes.
The wearing of ashes by Brāhmaṇas must indeed be performed with effort,
using precisely the three middle fingers of one's own right hand.
The measurement should be six finger-breadths in length, or even greater;
on the forehead, a radiant Tripuṇḍra should be applied according to the measure of the two eyes.
Sometimes he may perform it with ashes; he is indeed Rudra, there is no doubt about this.
The letter *A* is said to be the ring finger, and the letter *U* is the middle finger.
The letter *ma* is the forefinger;
therefore, the *tripuṇḍra*, which consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), is applied with the middle finger, the forefinger, and the ring finger in the forward direction. || 25 ||
In this regard, I shall relate to you this ancient history:
once, Durvāsas went to the world of the ancestors.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes and adorned with ornaments of rudrākṣa beads, he said:
"O Śiva, O Śaṅkara, O Soul of All, O glorious Mother, O Mother of the Universe! (27)
The crest-jewel of ascetics loudly proclaimed, "These are names," while Kavyavāḍa and the others responded with rising and salutations.
They showed great honor with offerings such as seats and other services;
then they conversed with one another on various topics.
At that time, however, a terrible cry arose from the sinners situated in the Kumbhīpāka hell, as they cried out, "Alas! We are destroyed! (30).
Some cried out, "We are dead! while others sang, "We are burned! Others wailed thus: "We are cut asunder! We are torn apart! 31.
Hearing that piteous sound, the King of Sages was distressed at heart and asked those lords of the ancestors, "To whom does this sound belong? (32)
They said, "O Sage, right here lies the supreme city of Saṃyamanī;
here resides Yamarāja, the bestower of experiences upon sinners. (33)
O sinless one, the leader is present right here in that city, accompanied by various messengers who are dark-complexioned, fearsome, and like the very form of Time (Kāla).
Therein are many pits that provide experience for sinners, surrounded by eighty-six messengers of terrible form. (35)
Among those, there exists a great and most prominent pit named Kumbhīpāka; now follows the description of the torments undergone by those who have fallen into it.
It cannot be accomplished by anyone, even in hundreds of years, by those who are enemies of Śiva as well as those who revile the Goddess. (37)
O Sage, those who are enemies of Viṣṇu fall right here;
as do those who revile the Vedas, the Sun, and Gaṇeśa.
O Sage, those who are hostile toward Brāhmaṇas fall right here;
as do those who act according to their own whims and those who are marked with heated seals.
O Sage, those who bear the trident and those who revile their mother, father, teacher, elders, and the ancient Smṛtis fall right here.
O Sage, those who are corrupters of the Dharma fall right here;
this is their most terrible sound, harsh to the ear. (41)
"We hear incessantly that which may arise from the Śruti as dispassion (vairāgya).
Having heard these words of theirs, the king of sages, desiring to see that [dispassion], [proceeded]. (42)
Having risen, he quickly set out and went near the pool;
at that very moment, O Sage, he saw [the child] below with his face cast downwards.
But for the sinners residing there, the happiness was even greater than that of heaven;
some laughed, while others sang and danced.
Intoxicated by the increase of their pleasure, they take delight in one another amidst the sounds of mṛdaṅgas,
murajas, vīṇās, ḍhakkās, and dundubhis.
Sweet breezes, adorned with the fifth musical note (*pañcama-svara*) and carrying the fragrance of spring creeper flowers, blew forth. (46)
But the sage was startled upon seeing them, and the messengers of Yama were likewise amazed;
they quickly reported this to the Knower of Dharma, Dharmarāja.
O Great King, O Lord, a great wonder has just now occurred:
that even for sinners situated in the Kumbhīpāka hell, there is a happiness greater than that of heaven. (48)
"O Lord, we do not know at all what the cause was for this;
we are all terrified and have come into your presence, O God. (49)
Having heard those words of the messenger, the King of Dharma (Yama) rose quickly;
mounted upon his great buffalo, he went to where those sinners were.
He dispatched that news to Amarāvatī by means of a messenger;
having heard it, the King of the Gods also arrived together with the hosts of deities.
From the world of Brahmā came the Lotus-born, and from Vaikuṇṭha came Viṣṭaraśravas;
and from their respective worlds, the guardians of the quarters arrived along with their hosts.
Having surrounded Kumbhīpāka on all sides,
they all beheld the living beings within it, who were immersed in a happiness even greater than that of heaven.
They were all struck with terror and did not understand the cause;
"Alas! This pit has been fashioned for the sake of experiencing sin! (54)
In that regard, when happiness has arisen, what fear can there be of sin?
How could the boundaries of the Vedas established by the Supreme Lord be destroyed? (55)
"How has the Blessed One rendered his own resolve futile?
'This is a marvel! This is a marvel!'—thus they spoke. (56)
Everyone remained indifferent, not knowing the cause therein;
in the meantime, Śauri (Viṣṇu), having consulted with the gods and others, [acted].
Accompanied by some hosts of gods, he went to the abode of Śaṅkara,
where the Lord was with Pārvatī, as beautiful as ten million Cupids.
His limbs were most delightful, a wondrous mine of beauty;
he was eternally sixteen years of age and adorned with various ornaments. (59)
He beheld the moon-crested Lord, surrounded by various hosts, caressing the supreme Śivā; he bowed down to him who is the embodiment of the four Vedas.
He related the account very clearly and with wonder, saying:
"O Lord, we do not know the cause of this in any way whatsoever."
"O Lord, tell me the cause of that, since you, O Master, are omniscient.
Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, his lotus-like face became serene.
He spoke these sweet words in a voice as deep as a thundercloud:
"Listen, O Viṣṇu, to the reason for that; there is nothing surprising in this. (63)
This is indeed the greatness of the sacred ash; for what could not be accomplished by means of ash?
Durvāsas, who was honored by the Śaivas, went to witness the Kumbhīpāka hell.
Then, with his face turned downwards, he saw from below those particles of forehead-ash falling there by the force of the wind through the turn of fate. (65)
"By him all this was produced; such is the greatness of the ashes. Beyond this, however, that sacred site belongs to those who dwell in the world of the ancestors."
There is no doubt that one will become happy by bathing there;
from now on, it shall be known by the name Pitṛtīrtha.
O best of men, the installation of the emblems of the Lord and the Goddess should be performed there;
those residing in the world of the ancestors will worship them there. (68)
Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist in the three worlds, this one shall be the most excellent among them;
by the worship of Pitrīśvarī, the three worlds become worshipped. || 69 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard these words of the god and having bowed his head to the god,
Hari took his permission and went into the presence of the gods.
He related all that reason as spoken by Śaṅkara;
the immortals said, "Excellent! Excellent! with the shaking of their heads.
O scorcher of foes, Hari, Brahmā, and the other gods, as well as the ancestors, were satisfied and praised the greatness of the sacred ash resulting from their attainment of this holy site.
On the bank of that sacred ford, the immortals installed a linga and an image of the Goddess according to the prescribed rites, and they worshipped them daily.
There, those living beings who had remained for the sake of experiencing the fruits of their evil deeds, having ascended a celestial chariot, went to the region of Kailāsa.
Those known by the name Bhadraganas indeed still dwell there even today;
furthermore, in a distant region, Kumbhīpāka was constructed.
On that very day, the gods brought about the cessation of the Śaiva path;
thus, I have related to you this entire, supreme majesty of the sacred ashes (bhasma).
O Sage, there is nothing superior or more excellent than this;
[I shall now describe] the rule for the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) according to the distinctions among those entitled to it.
O tiger among sages, I shall proclaim from the study of the Vaiṣṇava scriptures the divine measurements for the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) according to the divisions of finger-widths.
I shall now declare the letters, the mantras, the deities, and their fruits;
[this should be done] especially on a mountain peak, on a riverbank, or in a sacred field (śivakṣetra). (79)
These types of earth should be collected from the bank of a river, from an anthill, and from the base of a *tulasī* plant; one should avoid all other kinds of clay.
The dark [color] is said to bring peace; the red brings about subjugation (vaśya);
they say the yellow brings prosperity; and the white is declared to bestow dharma. (81)
The thumb is said to bestow nourishment; the middle finger brings longevity;
the ring finger constantly grants food; and the forefinger bestows liberation. (82)
One should perform these with various finger positions, but not by touching with the fingernails;
likewise, one should form the shape of a row of lamps or the shape of a bamboo leaf.
One should diligently fashion it in the shape of a lotus bud, or likewise in the form of a fish or a tortoise, and thereafter in the shape of a conch shell. 84.
A length of ten finger-breadths is said to be the most excellent;
nine finger-breadths would be middling, and eight finger-breadths is beyond that [the lowest]. (85)
The middle *puṇḍra* is recorded as being of three types, measuring seven, six, or five [finger-breadths];
the smallest *puṇḍra* should be of three types, measuring four, three, or two finger-breadths. || 86 ||
One should know Keśava on the forehead and Nārāyaṇa on the belly;
having placed Mādhava on the heart, one should place Govinda in the hollow of the throat.
In the belly on the right side, he is designated as Viṣṇu;
and between that side and the arm, he is indeed Madhusūdana. (88)
One should place Trivikrama at the region of the ear, Vāmana on the left side of the abdomen,
Śrīdhara on the left arm, and Hṛṣīkeśa at the earlobe.
One should remember Padmanābha on the back and Dāmodara on the hump;
these are the twelve names, with Vāsudeva at the head.
At the time of worship and during the fire-oblation, being composed in mind both morning and evening,
one should apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) according to the prescribed rule while uttering the names [of the deities].
Even if one is impure or lacks proper conduct and commits sin with the mind, a man marked with the *puṇḍra* on his forehead shall always remain pure. (92)
Wherever a mortal dies while wearing the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra),
even if he be a dog-cooker (outcaste), he is honored in my world, seated upon a celestial chariot.
The single-minded, highly fortunate, and stainless ones who know my true nature apply sectarian marks (puṇḍra) in the shape of Viṣṇu’s footprints, including the intervening spaces.
Even those who are supremely devoted to me, having me as their sole refuge, likewise [see] beautiful objects mixed with turmeric powder, appearing like spikes. (95)
Other Vaiṣṇavas, however, out of devotion, should apply marks that are even without gaps,
having the shapes of lamps, lotuses, or bamboo leaves.
Even those who are flawless, the exclusive Vaiṣṇavas may render flawed;
for them, there is no sin incurred in making such flaws. (97)

For those who are single-mindedly devoted, for those who have taken refuge, and even for those who are supremely single-mindedly devoted, there would be a great transgression if the unbroken sectarian mark (puṇḍra) were not applied. 98.

Furthermore, those who are Vaiṣṇavas should apply a beautiful vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) in the shape of a staff with a hollow in the middle, using the names beginning with Keśava and ending in "namaḥ. || 99 ||
That man who applies pure vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with spaces between them,
he builds a vast temple for me there.
In the center of the broad and very beautiful *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, the imperishable Viṣṇu rejoices, seated together with Lakṣmī. (101)
That lowest of the twice-born who applies the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) without leaving a gap between the lines indeed drives away both Viṣṇu and Śrī who reside therein. || 102 ||
But he who, being of deluded intellect, makes an upward *puṇḍra* that is not flawless,
goes in succession to those twenty-one hells.
One should apply straight vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) with distinct sides and intervals, resembling a staff, a lotus, a lamp, or a fish. (104)
O great sage, the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) must be worn by a twice-born man just like the topknot and the sacred thread; for if these are omitted, all ritual acts become fruitless.
Therefore, in all ritual activities, the wise Brahmin’s duty is [to apply] the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), the trident, the circular, and the square [marks]. 106.
One who is devoted to the Vedas and has taken refuge in the path of the Vedas, having received his caste status through birth, should not wear a sectarian mark such as the half-moon. || 107 ||

One should never wear a sectarian mark (puṇḍra) on the forehead even by mistake, nor for the sake of attaining fame, beauty, and other such perfections, according to the Viṣṇu Āgamas and other scriptures. (108)
A person learned in the Vedas must never wear a vertical mark (*puṇḍra*) on the forehead,
having abandoned the horizontal triple-mark (*tripuṇḍra*) prescribed by the Śrutis, even if it should happen through some delusion.
One should wear the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead with ashes;
if one wears it elsewhere than on the [prescribed] marks out of delusion, he shall become a denizen of hell.
But one who is solely devoted to the path of the Vedas, even if marked by delusion,
certainly falls— of this there is no doubt— even from another sectarian mark (puṇḍra).
One who has taken refuge in the path of the Vedas should not make a mark on the body;
for those solely devoted to the Vedic dharma, the sign is indeed that of the Vedas alone.
The insignia of those who are devoted to non-Vedic dharma is said to be non-Vedic;
however, the insignia of those deities established by the Vedas is indeed Vedic. (113)
For those who are devoted to non-Vedic systems, [their path] is indeed non-Vedic;
yet Mahādeva, established in the Veda, is the direct liberator from saṃsāra. || 114 ||
And for the benefit of his devotees, he assumes a Vedic form;
for Viṣṇu, who is established by the Vedas, possesses only a Vedic form and nothing else. (115)
Indeed, for his various manifestations as well, that very same scriptural mark—namely, the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana)—is to be understood as the sign. || 116 ||
The vertical *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* and so forth are not based on the Śruti, nor indeed is the horizontal *tripuṇḍra*;
for those who are solely devoted to the path of the Vedas, one should proceed only by the way prescribed in the Veda.
Indeed, the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) must be worn on the forehead with sacred ash.
Furthermore, he who has taken refuge in the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the supreme state,
should always wear the trident-mark on his forehead with fragrant water.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for Wearing the Tripuṇḍra and Urdhvapuṇḍra," in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 15 ||
The Description of the Sandhyā Worship.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, therefore, let the meritorious and supreme Sandhyā worship be heard.
And the greatness of wearing the sacred ash has indeed been described in detail. || 1 ||
O sinless one, I shall describe to you the ritual for the morning twilight (prātaḥsandhyā):
the morning twilight is performed while the stars are still visible, and the midday twilight when the sun is at its zenith.
They perform the three twilight devotions, including the western twilight when the sun is still visible.
O best of divine sages, listen as I shall also explain their specific divisions.
The morning twilight is considered to be of three kinds: the best is accompanied by stars; the middling has its stars obscured; and the lowest is joined with the sun. (4)

The twilight accompanied by the sun is considered the best; that occurring when the sun has set is middling; and that joined with the stars is the lowest. Thus, the evening twilight is regarded as being of three kinds.
The Brahmin is a tree; here, the twilight prayers are its roots, the Veda its branches, and righteous deeds its leaves.
Therefore, one must diligently protect the root.
When the root is severed, there is neither tree nor branch.
He by whom the twilight devotions (sandhyā) are not known, and he by whom the twilight devotions are not performed,
remains a Śūdra while living and is born as a dog upon death.
Therefore, the supreme twilight worship (sandhyopāsana) must always be performed;
for in its absence, one would certainly not be qualified for other rites and the like.
One should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) for as long as three ghaṭikās after sunrise or sunset; beyond that, it constitutes an expiation (prāyaścitta).
If a lapse of time has occurred, one should cause the fourth *arghya* offering to be presented;
or else, having first recited the mantra of the Goddess one hundred and eight times, one should perform that [offering].

At whatever time a particular rite is to be performed, one should first perform the twilight worship (sandhyopāsana) dedicated to the presiding deity of that time, and thereafter carry out the rite appropriate for that specific period.
In the home it is said to be common; in a cow-pen it would indeed be middling;
on a riverbank it would be excellent; and in the temple of the Goddess, it is most excellent.
Since this worship of the Goddess is performed, one should perform the three daily junctions (sandhyās) in the presence of the Goddess; that leads to infinity.
For these Brahmins, there exists another divine [protection]:
neither the constant worship of Viṣṇu nor likewise the worship of Śiva. (14)

Just as the worship of Gāyatrī, who is impelled by the Vedas and constitutes the essence of all the Vedas, may become [the supreme] for the Great Goddess; so too [should be the worship] of Gāyatrī. 15.
Even Brahmā and the other gods meditate upon her and recite her during the twilight hours;
the Vedas constantly recite her, and for that reason she is remembered as the one to be worshipped by the Vedas.
Therefore, all the twice-born are devotees of Śakti, neither Śaivas nor Vaiṣṇavas;
they worship Ādiśakti, Gāyatrī, the Mother of the Vedas. (17)
Having sipped water and restrained the vital breath (prāṇa), [he should worship] with the names beginning with Keśava:
Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, and Mādhava.
Govinda, Viṣṇu, and Madhusūdana;
then Trivikrama, Vāmana, and Śrīdhara. (19)
Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara; beyond these are Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
Puruṣottama, Adhokṣaja, and likewise Nārasiṃha;
Janārdana, Upendra, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa is the last.

One should cause [the disciple] to drink water preceded by the syllable *Oṃ* and followed by the name repeated twenty-four times, ending with *svāhā*; likewise, one should touch him [with the water] ending with *namaḥ*.
Having drunk [the water] three times with the [mantras] beginning with "Keśava," one should wash both hands with two [mantras];
one should wash the face with two [mantras], and likewise perform the wiping [of the face] with two [mantras].
Having sprinkled water once upon his hand, as well as his feet and his head,
he should touch the twelve limbs of the deities beginning with Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Having drunk water with the right hand, the wise man should touch it with the left;
the water is not purified until he has touched it with the left.
With his hand shaped like a cow’s ear, he should drink water in the measure of a single masha;
by drinking less or more than that, a twice-born man becomes a drinker of liquor.
With the right hand,
the fingers joined together and with the thumb and little finger released, they know that the remainder [of the hand] is for the ritual sipping (ācamana).
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) preceded by the recollection of the Praṇava,
one should recite the Gāyatrī together with its head (śiras) and joined with the fourth foot.
One should exhale the breath through the right [nostril] and fill the abdomen through the left;
the wise know that one should always hold it with retention (kumbhaka)—this is prāṇāyāma.
One should press the right channel with the thumb and likewise the left;
one should press the middle channel with the little finger and the ring finger, while leaving the index finger free.
Exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka) are declared in all the scriptures by yogis of restrained mind to be prāṇāyāma. || 31 ||
Recaka emits the breath; pūraka fills it;
that which remains in equilibrium is proclaimed as kumbhaka. || 32 ||
One should meditate upon the Great-Souled Hari during inhalation as dark as the petal of a blue lotus, established in the center of the navel, and possessing four arms. (33)
During the retention of breath (kumbhaka), however, one should meditate upon the lotus-seated Lord of the World, Prajāpati, the four-faced Grandfather, in the region of the heart.
During the exhalation (recaka), one should meditate upon Śaṅkara, the Great Lord situated on the forehead—
resembling pure crystal, stainless, and the destroyer of sins.
Through inhalation (pūraka), one attains union with Viṣṇu; through retention (kumbhaka), the state of Brahman;
and through exhalation (recaka), one shall attain the third, the supreme Lord.
O best of divine sages, the ancient rules for sipping water (ācamana) and so forth have been declared;
now listen, O sage, to the Vedic (śrauta) method of sipping water and other rites, which destroys all sins. (37)
Having first uttered the Praṇava, then the Gāyatrī verse beginning with "tat," and the three Vyāhṛtis at the beginning of each quarter, this is called the Vedic sipping of water (śrautācamana).
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its head (śiras) preceded by the Vyāhṛtis;
joined with the Praṇava at each [part], this triad constitutes the restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyama). || 39 ||
(The characteristics of breath control are now proclaimed;
it is the sole pacifier of manifold evils and the bestower of the fruit of great merit.
One should press the tip of the nose with the five fingers while reciting the *praṇava*.
This mudrā, which removes all sins, is for both forest-dwellers and householders.

For a celibate student (brahmacārī) and for one who has completed his vows (yati), the sprinkling with water from kuśa grass using the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb should be performed with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
With a concentrated mind, one should perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) either at the end of each *ṛc* verse or at the end of each quarter-verse (*pāda*),
using the hymn "āpo hi ṣṭha" accompanied by the nine *praṇavas*.
Sin accumulated over a year shall be destroyed by this cleansing.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should drink water while reciting the mantra beginning with "sūryaśca."
The sin merged within his inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is destroyed by means of the Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Gāyatrī preceded by the Praṇava. (44)
One should perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) with the hymn beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā," having drawn up water in the right hand, which is formed like the ear of a cow.
Having led it to the tip of the nose, one should visualize the sin as a black-colored person in the left side of the abdomen, and then recite the verse beginning with "ṛtam ca. (46)
Or, reciting the Drupadā verse, one should draw that evil out through the right nostril by means of the path of the breath into the water held in the hand.
Without even looking at that water, one should throw it onto a stone on the left side and contemplate:
"My body has become free from sin. (48)
Having risen from there, one should place both feet together evenly;
then, taking a handful of water, excluding the index finger and the thumb.
O tiger among sages, having looked at the sun, one should pour water consecrated with the Gāyatrī mantra three times; this is the procedure for offering the arghya.
Then one should perform circumambulation with the mantra dedicated to Āditya;
this should be done once at midday, but three times during the two twilights.
In the early morning, he should stand with his head slightly bowed; at midday, he should stand like a staff;
and when seated on his seat in the evening, the twice-born man should offer water.
One should pour water; hear now the reason for that.
There are thirty million great heroes, Rākṣasas named Mandehas. (53)
Ungrateful, cruel, and terrible, they desired to devour the sun;
thereupon all the hosts of gods and the sages whose wealth is penance [intervened].
They worship the great twilight and cast handfuls of water;
by that water, which has become like a thunderbolt, those Daityas are consumed.
For this reason, O Brahmins, they constantly perform the twilight worship;
the practice of twilight worship is said to be the source of great merit. (56)

This mantra, which constitutes a limb of the *arghya* offering, is now proclaimed; listen, O Nārada, for by its mere recitation, the full fruit of the *sandhyā* rite, including all its ancillaries, shall be attained. (57)
I am that Sun; I am the light, the Self; I am the light, the auspicious Śiva;
I am the white light of the Self; I am the essence of all lights.
Come, O boon-granting goddess Gāyatrī, whose form is Brahman;
enter my heart for the sake of accomplishing the practice of recitation. (59)
Arise, O Goddess; you must depart so that you may return again.
O Goddess, you must depart after entering my heart as the Arghya offering. 60.
Then, on a pure spot, the wise man should place his own seat;
having ascended it, he should thereafter recite the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas.
O Sage, right here, following the practice of prāṇāyāma, the khecarī mudrā is proclaimed for the performance of the morning sandhyā, O best of sages. (62)
I shall explain the meaning of that name; listen with respect, O Nārada!
Because the mind moves in the void (kha), and the tongue has gone to move in the void. (63)
The gaze directed between the eyebrows is the Khecarī mudrā;
there is no posture equal to that of the Siddhas, and no breath-control like that of the Kumbhaka.
"There is no mudrā equal to Khecarī; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Nārada.
Having diligently conquered the vital air through the sounding of the bell and the paṇava drum," 65.
O Sage Nārada, having become steady while seated firmly, free from egoism and possessiveness, listen now to the characteristics of Siddhāsana.

Having firmly placed the foot joined at the root of the thigh in the position of the womb (yoni-sthānaka), and having made the body level with the heart alone, one should stand like a pillar with restrained senses, gazing at the space between the eyebrows with a steady gaze; this is called Siddhāsana, which bestows supreme bliss upon the yogi.
May the boon-granting Goddess come, the imperishable one equal to Brahman; O Mother of the meters, Gāyatrī, may you accept this my sacred prayer. 68.
Whatever evil one commits by day, one is released from that by day;
whatever evil one commits by night, one is released from that by night. || 69 ||
O Great Goddess, you who possess all colors, O Sandhyā-vidyā, O Sarasvatī!
O undecaying, immortal Goddess, salutations be to you, O Goddess of all.
Then, with the mantra beginning "Tejo 'si," one should invoke the Goddess:
"May all that performance of yours which has been undertaken by me be complete. (71)
Then, for the sake of liberation from the curse, one should properly perform the ritual;
thus [is described] the curse of Brahmā and likewise that of Viśvāmitra. (72)
"The curse of Vasiṣṭha"—this is the threefold characteristic of a curse.
By the mere remembrance of Brahman, the curse of a Brahmin is averted. (73)
By the remembrance of Viśvāmitra, [the curse] of Viśvāmitra [is incurred];
however, by the mere remembrance of Vasiṣṭha, that curse is destroyed.
In the center of the heart-lotus, I constantly meditate upon the Person of immeasurable size, whose nature is truth, who is the very form of the entire world, and who is known as the Supreme Self.
It is the one form of consciousness, inaccessible to words.
Now I shall describe the procedure for ritual placement (nyāsa), which arises as a limb of the twilight devotion (sandhyā).
One should apply the syllable *oṃ* as before, and then recite the mantras.
Having uttered "bhūḥ," one should say "namaḥ" with the two feet;
then, preceded by "bhuvaḥ," one should say "namaḥ" with the two knees, and "svaḥ" with the hips.
Then he should assign Maharnābhya to the navel, Jana to the heart, Tapa to the throat, and Satya to the forehead. || 78 ||
One should recite "tatsavituḥ" with the two thumbs, "vareṇyakam" with the two index fingers, and "bhargo devasya dhīmahi" with the two middle fingers. (79)
With the ring fingers and the little fingers, one should say "dhiyo yo naḥ padam";
the wise practitioner should place [the hands] on the back and the palms of the hands. (80)
"Salutation to the heart of Savitṛ, whose self is Brahman;
likewise, salutation to the head, which is 'the most excellent' (vareṇyam), whose self is Viṣṇu. (81)
"Bhargo devasya" is proclaimed for the *śikhā* (topknot) to the self of Rudra;
"dhīmahi" is for the *kavaca* (armour) to the self of Śakti, following that. (82)

That which is proclaimed as the three eyes for the intellect directed toward the Self of Time (Kālātman), and that which impels all, is celebrated as the weapon for the Universal Self (Sarvātman). 83.
O Great Sage, I shall first describe the arrangement of syllables (akṣaranyāsa);
this supreme arrangement, born from the phonemes of the Gāyatrī, is the destroyer of sin. (84)
Having first uttered the Praṇava, the ritual placement of the syllables (varṇanyāsa) is proclaimed;
having first uttered the syllable "tat," one should place it on both big toes.
Likewise, one should place the syllable *sa* on the two ankles and the syllable *vi* on the two shanks;
having placed the syllable *tu* on the two knees, one should place the syllable *va* on the two thighs.
Having placed the syllable *re* in the anus and the syllable *ṇi* on the penis,
one should place the syllable *ya* here on the hips and the syllable *bha* in the region of the navel.
Having placed the syllable *go* in the heart and the syllable *de* on the two breasts,
one should place the syllable *va* in the heart and the syllable *sya* in the hollow of the throat.
One should place the syllable *dhī* in the region of the mouth, the syllable *ma* in the region of the palate,
the syllable *hi* at the tip of the nose, and the syllable *dhik* in the circle of the eyes.
One should place the syllable *yo* between the eyebrows and the syllable *yo* on the forehead;
the syllable *na* on the eastern face and the syllable *pra* on the southern face.
Having placed the syllable *co* in the western face and the syllable *da* in the northern face,
one should place the syllable *yā* on the crown and the syllable *ta* as the pervasive [syllable].
Some who are intent on recitation do not accept this procedure for ritual placement (nyāsa);
thereafter, one should meditate upon the Great Goddess Ambikā, the Mother of the World. 92.
The Supreme Goddess Kumārī has the luster of a shining hibiscus flower;
she is seated upon a red lotus throne and is anointed with red perfumes and unguents.
Wearing red garlands and garments, four-faced and four-armed,
she has two eyes and holds a *sruk* ladle, a *sruva* spoon, a rosary, and a water-pot.
[He saw] the supreme goddess, the deity of Brahman, resplendent with all ornaments, reciting the Ṛgveda, seated upon a swan-wing, and stationed in the midst of the Āhavanīya fire. 95.
One should meditate upon Maheśvarī, who has four feet, eight bellies, and seven heads; whose mouth is fire, whose crest is Rudra, and whose mind is Viṣṇu.
Brahmā is her armor, and her lineage is remembered as Sāṃkhyāyana;
one should meditate upon the Goddess Maheśvarī as residing within the solar orb. 97.
Having thus meditated upon Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, according to the prescribed rite,
one should then perform the auspicious mudrās that bring pleasure to the Goddess.
The *sumukha*, the *sapuṭa*, as well as the *vitata* and the *vistṛta*;
likewise the *dvimukha*, the *trimukha*, the *catuṣka*, and the *pañcaka*. (99)
The six-faced, the downward-facing, the pervasive-joined-palms, as well as the cart, the noose of Yama, the knotted, and the forward-facing and upward-facing. (100)
Vilamba, Muṣṭika, Matsya, Kūrma, Varāhaka, Siṃhākrānta, Mahākrānta, Mudgara, and likewise Pallava. (101)
One should display the twenty-four mudrās of Gāyatrī;
then the wise person should recite the Śatākṣara-Gāyatrī once.
Indeed, twenty-four syllables are proclaimed for the Gāyatrī;
thereafter, one should recite the Ṛc verse known by the name Jātavedas.
By revolving the verse of Tryambaka, this Gāyatrī of one hundred syllables becomes a source of great merit; it should be recited even once by the wise. (104)
Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, as well as *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*,
one should then recite the twenty-four-syllabled Gāyatrī.
Thus, a Brāhmaṇa who is the best among the twice-born should perform this recitation daily;
having obtained the complete fruit of the Sandhyā, he prospers in happiness. (106)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sandhyā Worship," in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 16 ||
Description of the Ritual Duties of the Sandhyā and Other Times.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Gāyatrī, when her feet are separated, destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
A *gāyatrī* with unseparated feet brings about the sin of killing a Brahmin. || 1 ||
Those twice-born who perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī with unbroken steps,
remaining with their faces turned downwards, shall remain so for hundreds of millions of kalpas.
O observer of noble vows, the Gāyatrī is considered to be manifold— consisting of a single *sampuṭa* and six *oṃkāras*—
in the Dharmaśāstras, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas.
The instruction is that one should recite [the mantra] conjoined with five *praṇavas*.
At the end of every eighth part of the recitation count, the fourth quarter is to be recited.
That twice-born man should be known as supreme; he shall attain the highest union (sāyujya).
However, for one who recites otherwise, that recitation becomes fruitless.
That [mantra] consisting of one *sampuṭa* and six *oṃ*s belongs to those whose vital energy is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*).
Whether a householder or a celibate student, one who seeks liberation should recite the fourth [mantra].
The fourth foot of the Gāyatrī is "parorajase sāvadom.
I shall now declare its meditation (dhyāna), which bestows the fruit of the mantra along with its limbs and recitation (japa).
In the heart, one should visualize a blossoming lotus containing the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire; it consists of the syllable *praṇava*, is inconceivable, yellow in color,
immovable, supremely subtle, and is the essence of the light of space.
May this one, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, be for my delight. || 8 ||
One should display the seven [mudrās]: the trident-yoni, the fragrant [mudrā], the rosary, the liṅga, the lotus, and the great mudrā (mahāmudrā). || 9 ||
That which is the twilight (sandhyā) is indeed Gāyatrī, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
a Brāhmaṇa should always worship her with devotion and bow down to her thereafter.
One should perform the worship of the one thus meditated upon with the five types of offerings:
"Laṃ, I offer fragrance to the self of Earth; salutations, salutations. (11)
"I offer this flower to the one whose nature is space; salutations, salutations!
And I offer this incense to the one whose nature is air"—thus he should speak thereafter.
And then one should say: "Raṃ, I offer a lamp to the one whose nature is fire (vahnyātman);
vaṃ, one should also offer the food offering (naivedya) to him, whose nature is nectar (amṛtātman)."
One should then offer a handful of flowers with the syllables *yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ haṃ*.
Having thus performed the worship, one should finally display the mudrās.
One should meditate upon the Goddess with the mind and recite the mantra slowly;
one should not shake the head or neck, nor should one show the teeth. 15.
According to the prescribed rite, one should recite it one hundred and eight times, or twenty-eight times, or ten times if unable; it should never be less than that.
Then one should dismiss the Goddess with the section beginning "uttamā".
A wise man should never recite the Gāyatrī mantra while in the midst of water under any circumstances.
For some great sages have said that she is declared to have fire as her mouth;
[she is] Surabhi, the winnowing-basket of knowledge, the tortoise, the womb, and the lotus. (18)
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should display the eight signs, including the sign of Nirvāṇa.
Whatever [mantra] has fallen from its syllables or words, or is devoid of vowels and consonants— || 19 ||
"O Goddess, beloved of Kaśyapa, may all that be forgiven;
henceforth, O great sage, the libation to Gāyatrī must be performed. (20)

The Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter (chandas), Viśvāmitra is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi), Savitṛ is proclaimed as the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the libation (tarpaṇa). || 21 ||
Having uttered "Bhūḥ," one should say, "I satiate the Person of the Ṛgveda";
and having uttered "Bhuvaḥ," one should then speak the Yajurveda.
Having uttered "Svaḥ" along with the Vyāhṛtis, one should recite the Sāmaveda;
and having uttered "Mahaḥ" at the end, one should satisfy the Atharvaveda.
A person at the end of his path should utter the Itihāsas and Purāṇas; I satisfy austerity, all the Āgamas, and the Supreme Person as well. || 24 ||
"I satisfy Truth and the Person named Satyaloka. Then one should say: "Oṃ bhūḥ! I satisfy the Person of Bhūrloka. (25)
With "bhuvaśca," I satisfy the person of the Bhuvarloka;
thereafter, with "svaḥ," I satisfy the person of the Svargaloka.
"Oṃ bhūḥ, I satiate the Gāyatrī named Ekapadā;
bhuvaḥ, I satiate the Gāyatrī named Dvipadā"—thus one should recite.
One should then say: "I satisfy Sva and the three-footed Gāyatrī," and likewise, "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" and the four-footed Gāyatrī. (28)
[He worshipped] Uṣas, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Sarasvatī, Pṛthvī—the mother of the Vedas—and likewise Ajā and Kauśikī. || 29 ||
One should recite the Gāyatrī verse of Sāṅkṛti Sārvajiti during the libation;
and at the conclusion of the libation, for the sake of pacification, one should utter the Jātavedas hymn.
A wise person should recite the mantra "mā nastoke" for the sake of peace;
furthermore, the "tryambaka" mantra is proclaimed to be for the purpose of pacification.
One should recite the mantra "tacchaṃyoḥ" specifically for the sake of pacification;
then, one should perform the touching of all limbs with the two verses beginning with "ato devāḥ."
With the mantra "Syonā pṛthivi," the best of the twice-born should perform prostration to the earth; and according to the prescribed rule, he should utter his lineage name and other particulars.
Such is the procedure for the morning twilight rite that has been proclaimed;
having completed the twilight ritual at its conclusion, one should personally perform the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Then, with a concentrated mind, one should perform the worship of the five deities;
one should likewise honor Śivā, Śiva, Gaṇapati, Sūrya, and Viṣṇu.
With a composed mind, one should perform [the rite] either with the Pauruṣa Sūkta, or with the Vyāhṛtis, or with the Mūlamantra, or with the mantra "Hrīśca te. || 36 ||
One should worship Bhavānī in the center, Mādhava in the northeast,
the Lord of Girijā (Śiva) in the southeast, and Gaṇeśa in the direction of the Rākṣasas (the southwest).
"One should worship the Sun in the north-west; such is the sequence for the stationing of the deities.
A person should offer the sixteen services with the sixteen verses. (38)
Having worshipped the Goddess, one should worship the others in sequence before her;
no merit greater than the worship of the Goddess is seen anywhere. (39)
For this very reason, the twilight worship (sandhyopāsti) has been ordained by the Vedas for the junction periods;
one should not worship Viṣṇu with unhusked grains (akṣata), nor Gaṇeśvara with Tulasī.
One should not worship Durgā with dūrvā grass, nor Maheśvara with ketakī flowers;
likewise, one should avoid the mallikā, jāti, kuṭaja, and panasa flowers.
Kiṃśuka, bakula, kunda, lodhra, karavīraka, śiṃśapā, aparājitā flowers, as well as babbūka and agastya flowers—[these are the offerings]. (42)
Madantī, sinduvāra, and likewise the flower of the palāśa;
sprouts of dūrvā grass, bilva leaves, and likewise a cluster of kuśa grass. || 43 ||
The flowers of the śallakī and mādhavī, the arka and mandāra, as well as the ketakī, karṇikāra, and kadamba blossoms. || 44 ||
Likewise, the *puṇṇāga*, the *campaka*, as well as the *yūthikā* and *tagara*—flowers such as these are dear to the Goddess. (45)
The incense should be made of guggulu, and the lamp should be made from sesame oil;
having thus performed the worship of the deity, one should then recite the root mantra.
Having thus completed the worship, the wise man should practice the study of the Vedas; thereafter,
he should provide for the maintenance of his dependents through his own lawful occupation during the third division of the day, according to the rule, being discerning in his conduct.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of Sandhyā and Other Rites," in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 17 ||
The Story of Bṛhadratha.
Nārada said:
O giver of honor, I wish to hear about the specific mode of worship of the Illustrious Goddess.
By resorting to which a person may attain the state of having fulfilled all duties. || 1 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O divine sage, listen; I shall describe the procedure for worshipping the Illustrious Ones, which directly bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and wards off all calamities.
Having sipped water (ācamana) and observed silence, one should perform the ritual resolve (saṅkalpa) and carry out the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth;
preceded by the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa), one should then perform the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
Having established the conch and prepared the general water offering (arghya),
the wise man should sprinkle the articles of worship with the Astra-mantra.
Having obtained permission from the guru, one should then commence the worship;
having first performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha-pūjā), one should thereafter meditate upon the Goddess.
Always endowed with devotion and love, he should bathe that Supreme Goddess with services such as the offering of a seat, using the essence of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and other substances.
He who bathes Maheśānī with a hundred jars filled with the juice of *pauṇḍra* sugarcane is not born again. || 7 ||
And whoever bathes the Mother of the World with mango juices in this manner, or having performed a complete recitation of the Vedas, with juice produced from sugarcane; || 8 ||
Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī shall never abandon the house of one who performs the complete recitation of the Vedas using grape juice.
The best of men, together with his family, should consecrate Maheśānī;
he is honored in the world of the Goddess for as long as the number of atoms in mercury.
While reciting the complete Vedas, one should bathe the Goddess with waters rendered turbid by the paste of camphor, agallochum, saffron, and musk.
The sins accumulated over a hundred lifetimes are reduced to ashes for one who bathes the Goddess with jars of milk while reciting the Vedas.
He shall dwell eternally in that Ocean of Milk for as long as an eon;
and he who consecrates it with curd shall become the lord of a river of curds.
By bathing [the image] with honey, clarified butter, and likewise with sugar,
one shall become the lord of rivers such as the Madhukulyā.
Bathing the Goddess with a thousand jars while being intent on devotion,
one shall become happy in this world and also happy in the other world.
By giving two garments of linen, one goes to the world of Vāyu;
by giving ornaments fashioned from jewels, one becomes a lord of treasures.
Having offered Kāśmīra sandalwood paste adorned with drops of musk, as well as vermilion for the parting of the hair and a leaf-design of red lac upon her feet; || 17 ||
Seated upon the throne of Indra, he becomes the supreme lord of the gods;
virtuous men declare that various flowers are to be used in the rite of worship. (18)
Having given those according to one's means, one personally attains Kailāsa;
he who offers unerring bilva leaves to the Supreme Śakti [attains the same].
His suffering shall never again arise, neither at any time nor in any place.
One should draw [the mantra] upon three *bilva* leaves using red sandalwood paste. (20)
One should diligently and very clearly pronounce the three seed-syllables of Māyā, which are exceedingly beautiful;
beginning with the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should utter the name ending in the dative case.
With supreme devotion, one should offer that tender leaf, ending with the word "namas," at the lotus feet of the Goddess, the Great Goddess.
He who performs this with devotion indeed attains the status of Manu;
he who [worships] with ten million petals that are thus tender and exceedingly pure— || 23 ||
One should worship Bhuvaneśānī; one shall become the sovereign of the universe by means of fresh kunda flowers, crushed with the eight fragrances.
One should worship with ten million [offerings] and will certainly obtain the fruit of the Prājāpatya penance;
likewise, by offering jasmine and mālatī flowers mixed with the eight fragrances.
By worshipping with ten million [flowers], O Sage, one is born as the Four-faced One (Brahmā); likewise, by ten billion of those very same flowers, one attains the same state.
A mortal attains the state of Viṣṇu, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain;
this vow was formerly performed by Viṣṇu himself for the sake of attaining his own station.
Even by means of hundreds of millions [of repetitions], one will certainly attain the nature of the Sūtra itself;
for this vow was formerly performed perfectly with devotion and diligence. (28)
By the power of that vow, one shall attain a golden belly;
[this applies] for the japā flower, the puṣpa flower, and the bandhūka flower. (29)
This same procedure is declared for the pomegranate flower as well;
in this manner, one should offer other flowers to the Goddess Śrī according to the prescribed rite.
Even that Lord does not know the end of the fruit of his merit,
[which was gained] by means of flowers produced in their respective seasons, numbering a thousand names.
One who is endowed with great sin, yet performs this with devotion every year without weariness, should offer it to Mahādevī. || 32 ||
Even one joined with minor offenses (upapātaka) is liberated from all sins;
at the end of the body, he attains the lotus feet of Śrī, which are difficult even for the best of gods to obtain.
O Sage, the excellent practitioner attains [this], of this there is no doubt;
[he should offer] black agallochum along with camphor and combined with sandalwood. (34)
One should offer incense to Mahādevī consisting of *śilhaka* mixed with clarified butter and combined with *guggulu*, by which the house shall be perfumed.
By that, the Goddess of the Gods is pleased and grants the three worlds;
one should offer a lamp with pieces of camphor to the Goddess continuously.
One attains the world of the Sun; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Likewise, one who is composed should offer a hundred or even a thousand lamps. (37)
One should place an offering of food (naivedya) in front of the Goddess in the form of a mountain,
consisting of things to be licked, sucked, and drunk, endowed with the six flavors and prepared with concentration.
One should constantly offer to the Goddess various divine fruits—sweet and flavorful—as well as foods placed in golden vessels. (39)
When the illustrious Mahādevī is satisfied, the three worlds become satisfied;
for everything is of her nature, just as a snake [is imagined] in a rope. (40)
Then one should offer auspicious water for drinking—great, cool water from the Gaṅgā, placed in a pitcher and mixed with camphor and vālaka. (41)
Then he offered betel leaf to the Goddess, accompanied by pieces of camphor,
combined with cardamom and cloves, which bestows fragrance upon the mouth.
One should offer [this] to the Goddess with great devotion, by which the Goddess becomes pleased,
accompanied by the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās, murajas, ḍhakkās, and dundubhis.
One should please the Mother of the worlds with most enchanting songs, as well as with the recitation of the Vedas, hymns, and the Purāṇas and other such texts. 44.
With a concentrated mind, one should offer an umbrella and two chowries to the Goddess;
one should daily present these royal honors to the auspicious Goddess.
One should perform circumambulations and prostrations to the Goddess many times;
one should repeatedly ask forgiveness from the Mother of the World, the Sustainer of the Universe. (46)
If the Goddess is pleased by mere remembrance once, what cause for wonder is there that she would be pleased by such ritual services as these? (47)
By her very nature, a mother is exceedingly compassionate toward her son;
therefore, when devotion has been rendered to her, what more need be said? (48)
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient and eternal account concerning the royal sage Bṛhadratha—a tale that is pleasing and bestows devotion. (49)
In a certain region of the Himalayas, there was a bird who was a cakravāka;
wandering through various lands, he eventually arrived at the city of Kāśī.
At the great abode of Annapūrṇā, the twice-born man, driven by the force of his past karma, went there as if helpless, out of a longing for grains of rice. 51.
Having performed a single circumambulation, he departed through the air for another land,
leaving behind that city which bestows liberation.
After some time, he died and departed toward the city of heaven;
assuming a divine form, he enjoyed all the objects of the senses as a youth.
