Having enjoyed [the fruits of his merit] for two kalpas in that manner, he returned once more to the earth;
he obtained birth in a family of Kṣatriyas, the most excellent of all the excellent.
He was renowned on the circle of the earth by the name Bṛhadratha;
he was a performer of great sacrifices, righteous, truthful, and one who had conquered his senses.
He is a knower of the three times, a sovereign emperor, self-controlled, and a conqueror of the cities of his enemies;
he possesses a recollection of his former births that is rare upon this earth.
Having heard this report, the sages arrived;
having been offered hospitality by the king of men, they sat down upon their seats.
All the sages asked: "O King, there is a great doubt:
by the power of what merit do you possess the memory of your previous birth? (58)
"By what power of merit do you possess even this knowledge of the three times?
Desiring to know that wisdom of yours, we have come into your presence. (59)
"Speak that to us exactly as it is, with a sincere disposition.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, the supremely righteous king—
He said: "O Brahman, listen, all you sages, to the entire cause of my knowledge of the three periods of time—the cause of my wisdom. (61)
The ruddy goose (cakravāka), though previously situated in a low birth, even out of ignorance, performed a circumambulation of Annapūrṇā. (62)
By the power of that merit, O observers of good vows, he dwelt in heaven for two kalpas,
and even in this birth, he possessed knowledge of the three periods of time.
Who knows how great is the fruit of remembering the feet of the Mother of the World?
Yet, having remembered her majesty, my tears fall incessantly.
Fie upon the birth of those ungrateful sinners who do not indeed worship the Goddess, the mother of all, whom they themselves should revere! 65.
Worship of Śiva is not eternal, nor is the worship of Viṣṇu likewise;
the eternal worship of the Supreme Goddess alone is ordained by the Śruti itself as being perpetual. (66)
What need is there for me to say much more? In this matter, which is beyond doubt, the lotus feet of the Blessed Lady must be served by you without interruption. (67)
There is nothing higher or more excellent than this on the surface of the earth:
the Supreme Goddess, whether she be devoid of attributes (nirguṇā) or possessed of attributes (saguṇā), is to be served. 68.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard these words of that righteous royal sage,
they all, with gladdened hearts, departed for their respective abodes.
Such is the power of that goddess; who could ask what the fruit of her worship is? It is not for anyone to say.
But for those whose birth has been fruitful, faith arises;
however, for those whose birth is a mere confusion, faith does not arise.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Bṛhadratha," within the "Glorification of the Goddess" (Devīmāhātmya) in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa consisting of eighteen thousand verses. 18.
Description of the Midday Sandhyā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, therefore, O Brahmin, listen to the auspicious midday sandhyā.
From the performance of which arises the *apūrva* (unseen merit), resulting in the most excellent fruit. || 1 ||
Sāvitrī is youthful, white in complexion, and indeed three-eyed;
she grants boons, is adorned with a rosary, and holds a trident and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands. || 2 ||
She is mounted upon a bull, the Saṃhitā of the Yajurveda, having Rudra as her deity;
she is endowed with the quality of darkness (tamas) and is established in the Bhuvarloka. || 3 ||
I bow to Māyā, the agent who causes the movement along the path of the Sun;
then, having meditated upon Ādidevī, one should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) and so forth as before.
Then, one should gather flowers for the section on the *arghya* offering;
in their absence, one should then mix *bilva* leaves with water.
Then, having thrown the arghya water upwards while facing the sun, one should present it;
everything else, including the concluding rites, is to be performed as in the morning twilight ritual.
Some desire that at midday one should recite the Sāvitrī verse beginning with "tat savituḥ"; however, performing that rite without the traditional transmission results in the loss of its efficacy.
The reason for this at the two twilights is that the Rākṣasas named Mandehas desire to devour the sun; this is the cause declared in the Śruti.
For this reason, O Brahmin, one should diligently perform the Sandhyā at both twilights daily, using the Gāyatrī and the Praṇava.

One should pour water into it with that mantra, and not otherwise, for to do so would be a violation of the sacred revelation; or one may offer flowers mixed with water while reciting the mantra "Ā kṛṣṇena."

If these are unavailable, one should diligently offer the previously mentioned *arghya* using leaves such as those of the *bilva* or *dūrvā*; thus, one shall obtain the full fruit of the *saṃdhyā* along with its ancillaries.
In this very context, I shall describe the libation; listen, O best of divine sages!
Again, for the Earth, I offer libations to Puruṣa: salutations, salutations! (12)
I satisfy the Yajurveda and I satisfy the Maṇḍala,
as well as Hiraṇyagarbha and likewise the Inner Self (Antarātman).
Then [he saw] Sāvitrī, the mother of the gods, as well as Sāṅkṛti, Sandhyā likewise, Yuvatī, Rudrāṇī, and Nirmṛjā. || 14 ||
"Accomplishing all goals and bestowing the success of the purpose of all mantras;
Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ Puruṣam tu"—thus is the midday libation.
One should perform the worship of the Sun with the hymn beginning with "ud u tyam," and one should also perform the worship of the Sun with the hymn beginning with "citraṃ devānām."
Then, intent upon the accomplishment of the mantra, one should perform the recitation (japa).
O Nārada, listen as I shall describe the various methods of recitation as well. (17)
Having placed the hands palms-upward in the morning and likewise with the hands downward in the evening,
and having placed them against the heart at midday, one should perform the recitation of the mantra.
The finger-garland (karamālā) is proclaimed to consist of two joints each, starting from the little finger in sequence up to the base of the index finger. 19.

The killer of a cow, the killer of a father, the killer of a mother, the slayer of an embryo, one who violates the teacher’s bed, the stealer of a Brahmin’s property or field, and that Brahmin who drinks liquor—[these all become purified]. (20)
By a thousand repetitions of the Gāyatrī, that person becomes purified;
[he is cleansed] of mental and verbal sin born from attachment to sense objects and the senses. (21)
A person destroys that sin across three lifetimes;
for him who does not know the Gāyatrī, his exertion is in vain. (22)
One should recite the four Vedas and chant the Gāyatrī a single time;
likewise, the chanting of the Gāyatrī is superior to the repeated recitation of the Vedas. (23)
Thus has the method for the midday twilight rite been proclaimed by me;
hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual for the Brahmayajña.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Midday Sandhyā," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 19.
The glorification of the Brahmayajña and other rites.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having first performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times, the twice-born should then perform the sprinkling (mārjana) twice.
One should touch the left hand and then sprinkle the two feet with water.
One should properly perform the sprinkling on the head, the eyes, the nose, the region of the ears, the heart, and likewise on the crown of the head.
Having recited the place and time, one should then perform the Brahma-yajña;
holding two Darbha blades in the right hand and three in the left, one should sit upon the seat once.
One should likewise perform this once each upon the sacred thread, the topknot, and the soles of the feet,
for the sake of liberation and for the destruction of all sins.
For the pleasure of the deities mentioned in the Sūtras, I perform the Brahma-yajña;
first, one should recite the Gāyatrī three times, and after that, the verse beginning with "agnim īḷe. (5)
Then, having said "yadaṅga," one should proclaim "agnir vai"; thereafter, one should likewise proclaim the Mahāvrata and this "panthā. || 6 ||
Now, therefore, [the rules] for the *saṃhitā* [text]: "vidā maghavan," "iti" (thus), likewise "mahāvratasya," and indeed "iṣe tvorje. || 7 ||
"Just as 'O Agni, come hither' (agna āyāhi) and 'the peaceful goddesses' (śanto devīḥ),
so indeed is its grammatical tradition, for it follows the rule 'vṛddhir ādaic'."
Now I shall proclaim the training known as the "Five-Year [Vow]," and one should likewise recite: "ma ya ra sa ta ja bha na" and "gau rgmā. (9)
Then, having uttered "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma," and also "Now, therefore, Brahman," as well as "May there be peace for us both" and "Salutation to Brahman," || 10 ||
Then one should perform the libation for the gods and circumambulate;
[namely] Prajāpati, Brahmā, the Vedas, the gods, and likewise the ṛṣis. (11)
And all the Vedic meters, as well as the syllable Om, the Vaṣaṭ-call, the Vyāhṛtis, and thereafter the Sāvitrī; || 12 ||
The Gāyatrī, the sacrifices, heaven and earth, the intermediate space, the days and nights, and beyond these, the Sāṃkhya. (13)
Then followed the Siddhas, the oceans, the rivers, and the mountains;
thereafter the fields, medicinal herbs, forest trees, as well as the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
One should recite the names ending with these: the Nāgas, the birds, the cows, the Sādhyas, the Brahmins, as well as the Yakṣas, the Rākṣasas, and the Bhūtas. || 15 ||
Then, having adopted the *nivīta* mode of wearing the sacred thread, he should also satisfy the seers:
the Śatarcins, the Mādhyamas, and likewise Gṛtsamada.
Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Atri, and Bharadvāja;
Vasiṣṭha, Pragātha, and thereafter the Pāvamānī hymns. || 17 ||
Kṣudrasūkta, Mahāsūkta, Sanaka, Sanandana,
as well as Sanātana and Sanatkumāra were also there.
Kapila, Asuri, Vohali, and Pañcaśīrṣaka—this libation (tarpaṇa) must be performed while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī). || 19 ||
Sumantu, Jaimini, Vaiśampāyana, and Paila, joined with the Sūtras, [composed] the Bhāṣya, the Bhārata, and so forth; thus also [is known] the Mahābhārata. (20)
And he should proclaim: "May all these teachers of Dharma be satisfied.
Bāhu, Gārgya, Gautama, and Śākala indeed know this. (21)
Bābhravya, Māṇḍavya, and Māṇḍūkeya after him;
then Gārgī Vācaknavī and Vaḍavā Prātitheyikā. || 22 ||
Then one should satisfy Sulabhāyukta and Maitreyī, and after that, Kauṣītaka and Mahākauṣītaka. || 23 ||
Bhāradvāja, Paiṅgya, Mahāpaiṅgya, Suyajñaka, Sāṃkhyāyana, Aitareya, and Mahaitareya. || 24 ||
Bāṣkala, Śākala, Sujātavaktra, Audavāhi, Saujāmi, Śaunaka, and Āśvalāyana. || 25 ||
May all other teachers likewise attain satisfaction;
and may those born in our family who died childless or without kinsmen also find fulfillment.
"May they accept this water from the wringing of my garment, which has been given by me.
Thus, O great sage, the procedure for the Brahma-yajña has been declared to you. (27)
And the practitioner who performs this supreme rite of the Brahmayajña obtains the fruit of reciting all the Vedāṅgas. || 28 ||
Thereafter, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite as well as the daily śrāddha;
and one should always practice the giving of food to guests. (29)
Then, having offered a morsel of food to a cow, he should eat together with the Brahmins;
one should perform this excellent rite during the fifth part of the day.

One should spend the sixth and seventh [parts of the day] with the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth; in the eighth, however, one should attend to worldly affairs; then, outside, one should perform the evening twilight devotion (sandhyā) once again.
Now, O great sage, I shall describe the evening twilight ritual (sāyantanī saṃdhyā),
by the mere performance of which Mahāmāyā becomes pleased.
Having sipped water and performed breath control, the practitioner, with a steady mind,
the yogi seated in the bound lotus posture, should remain firm in the evening.

In the performance of rituals prescribed by the Śruti, Smṛti, and other sources, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is "with seed" (sagarbha); however, that which consists of meditation alone is "without seed" (agarbha), and it is proclaimed to be without mantras.
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other preliminary rites— otherwise the ritual act is not proclaimed as valid—
one should meditate upon the deity for one hundred thousand times through the practices of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka).
At the evening twilight, the wise one should perform meditation upon the goddess Sarasvatī, who is aged, dark-limbed, and clad in black garments.
She holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus in her hands, has Garuḍa as her vehicle,
is adorned with various jewels shining as ornaments, and wears tinkling anklets and a girdle.
She wears a crown of priceless jewels and is adorned with strings of pearls;
her cheeks are beautified by the luster of rubies set in her earrings.
The Goddess, who wears yellow garments and whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss,
is accompanied by the Sāmaveda and joined with the path of purity.
Established in the heavenly world and following the path of the sun, I invoke the Goddess as she approaches from the solar orb. (40)
Having thus meditated upon that goddess, one should perform the twilight ritual resolve (sandhyā-saṅkalpa) with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and likewise with "agniśca".
One should perform the sipping of water (ācamana); the remainder is declared as before, having uttered the Gāyatrī mantra for the pleasure of Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
The practitioner, with a pure mind, should offer the *arghya* to the Sun;
having placed both feet evenly together and having shaken the water-offering in his hand.
Having meditated upon the deity situated within the mandala, one should then offer the arghya in sequence.
However, that foolish soul devoid of knowledge who offers the arghya into the water [alone]— || 44 ||
Having transgressed the rules of conduct and the sacred mantras, the twice-born man must perform penance;
thereafter, he should also worship the Sun with the Āditya-mantras.
Then, sitting upon a grass mat (bṛsī), one should perform the recitation (japa) of the Gāyatrī mantra one thousand times or half of that, preceded by meditation on the Goddess Śrī.
Just as one performed it in the morning, so too should one perform the ritual attendance and other rites;
and for the evening twilight and the libation, one should recite them in the proper sequence. || 47 ||
In this [verse], the sage is proclaimed to be Vasiṣṭha of Sarasvatī;
the deity is she in the form of Viṣṇu, and the meter is indeed Sarasvatī. (48)
This is the application for the libation (tarpaṇa) during the evening twilight:
having uttered "Svaḥ," [one offers to] Puruṣa and likewise to the Sāmaveda. (49)
Having likewise invoked Maṇḍala, Hiraṇyagarbha, Paramātman, and Sarasvatī, [he should worship them]. (50)
In this context, one should likewise worship Vedamātṛ, Saṅkṛti,
Sandhyā, Vṛddhā, and Uṣas, who is the very form of Viṣṇu.
And likewise Nirmṛji, who brings about all perfections,
as well as the Sovereign of all mantras, and the Puruṣa of the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
In this manner, the libation (tarpaṇa) for the twilight rite, as sanctioned by the Vedas, should be performed;
thus has been described the procedure for the evening twilight, which destroys all sins.

O best of sages, among all virtuous practices, the Sandhyā is preeminent; it removes all suffering, destroys disease, and likewise grants liberation. By performing the Sandhyā rites, the Goddess bestows the desired objects of her devotees.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Glorification of the Brahmayajña and Other Rites," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Explanation of the Procedure for the Purashcharana of Gayatri.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, therefore, O Brahmin, listen to the procedure for the Gayatri which destroys all sins.
The merit of *puraścaraṇa* bestows desired fruits according to one's wish. || 1 ||
On a mountain peak, on a riverbank, at the foot of a bilva tree, by a reservoir of water, in a cow-pen, in a temple, under an aśvattha tree, in a garden, or in a grove of tulasī; || 2 ||

A practitioner of mantra who performs the *puraścaraṇa* rite in a field of merit, in the presence of a guru, or in a place of one-pointed concentration, will certainly attain success; of this there is no doubt. (3)
Before beginning the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for any mantra whatsoever,
one should recite the Gāyatrī, conjoined with the three Vyāhṛtis, ten thousand times.
Without having first recited the Gāyatrī, all that pertains to Nṛsiṃha, Arka, and Varāha— whether Tantric or Vedic— becomes fruitless.
All these twice-born ones are said to be Śākta, neither Śaiva nor Vaiṣṇava;
they worship Ādiśakti, Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas.
Having purified the mantra with diligence,
one intent on the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) should perform the supreme purification of oneself, which is the preliminary limb preceding the purification of the mantra.
For the purification of the reality of the Self, the wise one should mutter [the mantra] three hundred thousand times,
or else one hundred thousand times, according to the path proclaimed in the Śruti.
Without purification of the self, rituals such as recitation (japa) and fire-offerings (homa) performed by the agent are to be known as fruitless; this is the reason enjoined by the Śruti.
One should scorch the body with austerity and satisfy the ancestors and the gods;
through austerity one attains heaven, and through austerity one finds the Great.
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own misfortunes through the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya, by means of wealth; and a Śūdra, O best of the twice-born, through recitation and burnt offerings.
Therefore, O lord of brahmins, one should practice austerity with great effort.
Ascetics declare that the emaciation of the body is the highest form of austerity (tapas).
One should purify [the body] according to the prescribed method through penances such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa.
Now, O Nārada, listen as I describe the means of purifying food.

The fourfold manner of subsisting on alms— known as *ayācita* (unsolicited), *uñcha* (gleaning), and *śukla* (pure)— is thus declared by both Tantrikas and Vaidikas to be the purity of food. Having brought pure alms-food and divided it into four portions:
One portion [of the food] is for the twice-born, while the second is a morsel for the cow;
the third is for guests, and thereafter, according to the specific stage of life (āśrama), one should follow the prescribed order for the ritual of eating with one's own wife.
Having first drunk cow’s urine according to one's capacity and in the proper sequence,
thereafter the number of morsels for forest-dwellers and householders shall be determined;
the measure of a morsel is prescribed as being the size of a hen’s egg.
An eight morsels for a householder, half of that for a forest-dweller; and for a student, as much as desired. Regarding cow urine, it should be taken according to the prescribed rule:
nine times, six times, or three times, after sprinkling.
Having made the hand free from gaps and mentally reciting the mantra "Tat Savitur Vareṇyam," the procedure for sprinkling is thus declared.
Whether it be a thief, a Cāṇḍāla, a Vaiśya, or likewise a Kṣatriya—
Whoever gives food [to such a person] is said to be the lowest of all rules.
Those who consume the food of a Śūdra, have contact with a Śūdra, or eat together with a Śūdra,
go to a terrible hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) should be performed for as many hundred thousand times as there are syllables in the Gāyatrī metre of the mantra;
likewise, according to the opinion of Viśvāmitra, it should measure thirty-two hundred thousand repetitions.
Just as a body devoid of life is incapable of any action,
so too is a mantra proclaimed to be when it lacks the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa). The months of Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Bhādrapada, Pauṣa, and the intercalary month (malamāsa) [are likewise unsuitable].
The day of charcoal (Tuesday), Saturday, the *vyatīpāta* and *vaidhṛti* yogas,
the eighth, ninth, sixth, fourth, and thirteenth lunar days,
as well as the fourteenth and the new moon, and likewise the evening and the night.
The asterisms of Yama, Agni, Rudra, Sarpa, Indra, Vasu, and Śravaṇa;
one should avoid Aries, Cancer, Libra, Aquarius, and Capricorn—indeed, all these should be avoided during the rite of *puraścaraṇa*. (27–28)
One should perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) especially during the bright fortnight when the moon and stars are favorable; thus, the accomplishment of the mantra arises.
One should perform the recitation of auspicious blessings (*svastivācana*) and the *nāndī-śrāddha* according to the prescribed rules.
Having diligently gratified the Brahmins with food, clothing, and other gifts,
he should thereafter begin [the rite] preceded by their permission;
facing westward in a place dedicated to Śiva, the twice-born man should recite [the mantra] in one of the other [prescribed ways].
Kāśīpurī, Kedāra, Mahākāla, Nāsika,
and Tryambaka— these five are the great sacred fields (mahākṣetra) on earth. Indeed, wherever there is a lamp, it is traditionally known as the Tortoise-throne (kūrmāsana).
From the day of commencement until the day of completion,
one should perform the recitation (japa) every single day neither deficiently nor in excess.
The lords of sages perform the *puraścaraṇa* rite without interruption.

Beginning at dawn and continuing according to the rules until midday, one should perform the recitation, along with the withdrawal of the mind, purification, meditation, and reflection on the meaning of the mantra;
as well as [knowledge of] the Gāyatrī meter and the number of syllables in the mantra. (35)
One should likewise perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for one hundred thousand times;
then one should offer oblations with ghee and milk, as well as with sesame seeds, leaves, flowers, and barley mixed with honey, using a tenth part of that number.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) by one-tenth [of the recitation]; then the mantra becomes perfected.
The Gāyatrī itself should be cultivated, for it bestows dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation. It is the supreme refuge in all three: the daily, the occasional, and the optional rites.
There is nothing superior to the Gāyatrī in this world and in the next.
Eating at midday, observing silence, devoted to bathing and worship three times a day,
the wise man, with his actions and mind focused on no other, [should recite it] three hundred thousand times in water.
Whether one performs recitation (japa) as part of a ritual act or subsequently by one's own will,
one should perform the recitation and other rites for as long as the task has not been accomplished.
The procedure for common rites performed for specific desires and so forth is now stated according to the rules.
Having bathed at sunrise, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times every day;
one will certainly obtain long life, health, sovereignty, and wealth.
After six months or three months, one shall attain perfection at the end of the year.

By offering one hundred thousand lotuses smeared with ghee into the sacrificial fire, one attains complete liberation; it is certain that success will be achieved, there is no doubt. Without the attainment of mantra-perfection, the practitioner's rites such as recitation and oblation [will not bear fruit].
Whether it be for the sake of desired objects or for liberation, everything would become fruitless.
By offering twenty-five hundred thousand oblations of curd or milk into one's own body, a living being attains success; such is the opinion of the great sages.

Whatever fruit a person obtains through the perfection of the eightfold yoga, that same fruit of perfection he attains here; no deliberation is required in this matter. Whether capable or incapable, one should practice a regulated diet.
Success shall be his within six months if he is always devoted to his guru.
For one day he should subsist on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), for one day he should subsist on air alone,
and for one day he should eat the food of a Brāhmaṇa, while performing the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra.

Having bathed in sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā, one should mutter [the mantra] a hundred times while submerged in the water; then, having drunk water a hundred times, one is liberated from all sins. One certainly obtains the fruit of penances such as the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Whether he be a king or a Brahmin, one may perform austerity in one's own home;
whether as a householder, a student, or even a forest-dweller,
by being intent upon one's specific duty, one obtains the fruit beginning with [the rewards of] sacrifice and other rites.
Rites such as those prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti are performed by those desiring liberation;
he maintains the sacred fires, follows right conduct, and is well-instructed by the learned.
Thereafter, he should diligently provide for them with fruits, roots, water, and other necessities.
One should eat pure alms-food and consume eight morsels oneself.
Having thus performed the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), one shall attain success in the mantra.
O celestial sage, by the performance of which poverty shall go to its destruction.
And having heard this, one shall attain great perfection through meritorious deeds.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Puraścaraṇa of Gāyatrī," in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The Exposition of the Ritual for the Vaiśvadeva and Other Offerings.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Now, therefore, O Brahmin, let the ritual procedure for the Vaiśvadeva be heard."
In the course of my preliminary ritual practice (puraścaryā), this has also come to my memory.
The sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to Brahman, likewise the sacrifice to beings, the sacrifice to the ancestors, and the sacrifice to humans is the fifth. || 2 ||

A householder has five slaughterhouses: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water jar; for the sake of pacifying the sin of these, [one should perform purification]. (3)

One should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite neither on the hearth, nor in an iron vessel, nor on the ground, nor in a broken pot; rather, one should perform it in a sacrificial pit or upon a consecrated mound of earth.
One should not blow upon the fire with the hand, nor with a winnowing basket, nor with pure skins and the like; one should blow upon it only from the mouth, for it was born from the mouth itself.
By [touching] a cloth, disease occurs; by a winnowing basket, the destruction of wealth;
by [touching with] the hand, one meets death; but by [touching] the mouth, there is success in one's undertakings.
One should perform [the offering] with fruits, curd, ghee, roots, vegetables, water, and so forth;
or, in their absence, with whatever is available, such as wood, roots, grass, and the like.
One should offer oblations smeared with clarified butter, avoiding oil and alkali;
or smeared with curd, or smeared with milk-rice (pāyasa); or, in the absence of these, even with water alone.
By offering dry or stale food, one becomes afflicted with leprosy; by offering the remnants of a meal, one falls under the power of enemies;
by offering coarse food, one goes to poverty; and by offering alkaline substances, one goes to a lower state.
Having removed the embers mixed with ashes from the north side of the fire,
one should indeed perform the Vaiśvadeva offering, but not with anything mixed with salt or similar substances.
But that dull-witted twice-born man who eats without having first performed the Vaiśvadeva rite,
being a fool, goes head-first to the Kālasūtra hell.
Whether it be a vegetable, or a leaf, or a root, or a fruit—
whatever food one intends to eat, with that one should also offer oblations into the fire.
If a mendicant arrives for alms while the Vaiśvadeva offering has not yet been performed,
one should set aside a portion for the Vaiśvadeva and, having given him alms, dismiss him.
A mendicant is capable of removing the fault committed by the Vaiśvadeva rite,
but the Vaiśvadeva rite does not remove the fault committed by the mendicant.
Both the ascetic and the student are the rightful owners of cooked food;
having eaten without first giving food to them, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (15)
And after the Vaiśvadeva offering, one should present a morsel of food to a cow.
I shall explain the procedure for that; listen, O you who are honored by the gods and sages! (16)
Surabhi is indeed the mother of Viṣṇu, eternally established in the station of Viṣṇu;
O Surabhi, please accept this morsel of food offered by me from a cow. (17)
Having offered worship with the words "And obeisance to the cows," one should present [the fodder] to the cow;
by this morsel for the cow, Surabhi, the mother of cows, becomes well-pleased. (18)
Then he should remain in the courtyard of his house even until the time for milking the cows;
for from whose house a guest returns with his hopes frustrated, [that man incurs great sin]. (19)
Having bestowed his misdeeds upon him and taken away his merit, he departs;
[so does] the mother, father, teacher, brother, offspring, servant, and dependent. (20)
A guest who has arrived and the sacred fire—these are declared to be those who must be supported.
Knowing this, he who out of delusion does not undertake the householder's stage of life [is at fault]. (21)
For him, by the nature of things, there is neither this world nor the next;
for he obtains that fruit which a wealthy twice-born man attains through the Soma sacrifice.
By means of the five great sacrifices performed correctly, even a poor man may attain [this merit];
now, O bull among sages, I shall describe the Prāṇāgnihotra.
By knowing which, a living being is liberated from birth, death, old age, and the like;
through full understanding, men are freed from the taints of sin.
By that means through which one enjoys [the fruits] according to the prescribed rule, he is liberated from the three debts;
such a Brahmin uplifts twenty-one generations of his lineage from hell.
One attains the fruit of all sacrifices and goes to all the worlds;
the heart-lotus is the fire-drill, and the mind is known as the churning-stick.
One should churn fire with the cord of breath; the Adhvaryu priest is the eye itself.
With the index finger, the middle finger, and the thumb, one should offer the oblation to Prāṇa.
One should offer the oblation of apāna with the middle, ring, and thumb fingers; immediately after that, the oblation of vyāna with the little, ring, and thumb fingers. (28)
One should offer an oblation to udāna with the little finger, the index finger, and the thumb;
taking food with all the fingers, one should offer an oblation to samāna.
One should recite the name-mantras preceded by the syllable Om and ending with Svāhā;
the Āhavanīya fire is in the mouth, while the Gārhapatya fire is in the heart.
The Dakṣiṇāgni fire should be at the navel; below it are the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires.
Vāc is the Hotṛ, Prāṇa is the Udgātṛ, and Cakṣus is indeed the Adhvaryu.
The mind becomes Brahmā, and the ear indeed becomes the station of the Āgnīdhra;
here, the ego (ahaṃkāra) is the sacrificial animal, and the Praṇava is said to be the milk.
And the intellect is declared to be his wife, for the householder is dependent upon her;
the chest is the altar, the body hairs are the *darbha* grass, and the hands are the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles. (33)
The seers of the Prāṇa-mantra are Rukmavarṇa and Kṣudhāgnika;
the deity here is Āditya himself, and the metre is said to be Gāyatrī. || 34 ||
Likewise, one should also utter "svāhā" at the end of the mantra for Prāṇa;
one should also say, "This is for the god Āditya, not mine. (35)
Likewise, for the Apāna-mantra, its form is as white as cow's milk;
Śraddhā is the Ṛṣi here, and Soma is indeed remembered as the deity.
One should likewise recite "To Uṣṇik meter, to Apāna, Svāhā!
and here the modification (ūha) is proclaimed as "This is for Soma, not mine. || 37 ||
The Vyāna-mantra has been declared to have a fire of lotus-colored hue;
its seer (ṛṣi) is said to be Agni, and Anuṣṭubh is proclaimed as its meter (chandas). || 38 ||
"Also for Vyāna, Svāhā! For Agni, this [is mine], not mine"—thus is the mantra for Udāna, which has the color of a *śakragopa* insect. (39)
The seer is declared to be Agni, and Vāyu is remembered as the deity;
the Bṛhatī is said to be the metre, and [the offering] is for Udāna, as before. (40)
"Vāyave idaṃ na mama"—thus the twice-born should recite;
the mantra of the Samāna-vāyu has a lightning-colored, deformed form. (41)
The seer is declared to be Agni, Parjanya is considered the deity, and Paṅkti is declared the metre; and for the Samāmnāya, it is as before. (42)
Having said, "This for Parjanya," one should offer the sixth oblation;
Vaiśvānara is proclaimed to be the great Agni, indeed the seer (ṛṣi). || 43 ||
The meter is declared to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is the Self (Ātman).
The mantra ending in "svāhā" is declared; one should recite it for the Supreme Self (Paramātman). || 44 ||
"This is not mine"—when this realization has arisen, it becomes the Prāṇāgnihotra.
Having known this and performed the rite, one is fit for becoming Brahman.
Indeed, this Prāṇāgnihotra-vidyā has been described to you in brief. (45)

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Rituals for the Vaiśvadeva and Other Offerings," in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the characteristics of the *Taptakṛcchra* and other penances.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having thus uttered the mantra "Amṛtāpidhānam," the best of practitioners...
At the end, the wise man should give food from the vessel to those entitled to receive the remnants.
"Whoever has been born in my family, including male and female slaves who have no other desires—may they all attain satisfaction on this earth through what has been given by me. (2)
May the water given by me reach those who dwell for millions of aeons in the Raurava hell, the abode of demerit, and may it become inexhaustible for those who seek it. (3)
Having untied the knot of the purifier (pavitra), one should cast it upon the ground within the mandala;
he who casts it instead into the vessel is a brahmin who defiles the row of diners.
A twice-born man who has been touched by one who is impure from eating, or by a dog, or by a Śūdra,
becomes pure after fasting for one night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If one is touched by those who have not yet finished their meal, bathing alone is prescribed;
by offering a single oblation, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
It is taught that for five [villages], the fruit is five crores, and for ten, the fruit is infinite;
this applies to one who gives food during the Prāṇāgnihotra rite. || 7 ||
Whatever merit belongs to the giver and whatever fruit belongs to the enjoyer—
both of them obtain that very same result, and both go to heaven.
That Brahmin who eats according to the prescribed rule with his hands holding the purifying grass (pavitra) obtains,
for every morsel, a fruit equal to that of consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Constant recitation, libations, fire-offerings, and feeding of Brahmins performed regularly at the three times of worship are called *puraścaraṇa*. || 10 ||
Sleeping on the ground, the righteous-souled one had conquered anger and subdued his senses;
he was modest, tranquil in mind, and ate light, pleasant, and wholesome food.
He should always bathe at the three periods of the day and always speak auspicious words;
[he must avoid] speaking with women, Śūdras, outcasts, those who have renounced their caste, atheists, or those who have consumed leftovers.
O best of sages, one should not speak the language of the Cāṇḍālas,
nor should one speak after having bowed down during the performance of recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth.
One should always, in all circumstances, avoid sexual intercourse, as well as talk about it or socializing with those who indulge in it, by means of action, mind, and speech.
The renunciation of sexual intercourse in all circumstances is declared to be celibacy;
this very celibacy is also prescribed for the king who is a householder. (15)

The union with one's own wives during their fertile periods according to the prescribed rule—having observed the season, one should diligently approach a wife of the same caste who has been consecrated by the sacraments. (16)

Traveling at night should be undertaken, for it does not destroy one's celibacy (*brahmacarya*). However, one should not depart without having cleared the three debts and without having procreated sons. (17)
Likewise, one who desires liberation after performing sacrifices goes downward;
that which is the birth of the "goat's neck" (ajāgala) is the birth ordained by the Vedas.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, one must perform the purification of the three debts;
for one is thus a debtor to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors. (19)

One should release [one's debt] to the sages through celibacy, to the ancestors with water and sesame seeds, and to the gods through sacrifice; thus one should practice the dharma of one’s own stage of life.
Subsisting on milk, or eating fruits, or eating vegetables, or consuming sacrificial ghee,
or subsisting on alms, the wise man who performs the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances should recite [the mantra].
Salt, alkaline substances, and sour things; the *gṛñjana* plant, eating from a bronze vessel, betel-leaf, eating twice a day, wearing soiled clothes, and being intoxicated. (22)
One should avoid reciting prayers at night if it contradicts the Śruti and Smṛti;
one should not waste time on gambling, women, sleep, or idle talk. (23)

One should pass the time through the worship of deities, hymns of praise, and the study of the Āgamas; likewise, one should practice sleeping on the ground, celibacy, and the observance of silence. (24)
Daily bathing at the three junctions of the day, avoidance of the duties of a Śūdra, constant worship, regular giving of gifts, and the joyful chanting of praises and glories. (25)
Worship according to the specific occasion, faith in the Guru and the Deity,
and those duties pertaining to one devoted to japa— these twelve grant excellent accomplishment.
Having performed the daily worship of the Sun, one should recite [the mantra] while facing him;
or, having worshipped an image of a deity or the like, or the fire, one should face that [object].
Devoted to bathing, worship, recitation, meditation, fire-offerings, and libations,
he is free from desire for the deity and offers all his actions as an oblation.
One who performs the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) should observe these and other such rules;
therefore, the twice-born man, with a serene mind, should be devoted to recitation (japa) and fire-offerings (homa). || 29 ||
One should be devoted to austerity and study, showing compassion toward all living beings;
through austerity one attains heaven, and through austerity one finds the Great.
For one endowed with austerity and self-restraint, rites succeed:
incantations for causing enmity, summoning, killing, and the destruction of diseases.
Whichever deity was praised by whichever sage for whatever purpose, that specific desire of each respective one was fulfilled accordingly.
I shall describe those rites and the procedures for those rites;
first, the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa), which brings about the accomplishment of the rites.
At the beginning of the practice of Vedic recitation, a twice-born man should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, he shall then become pure.
He should remain standing during the day, but at night he should remain pure and restrained in speech;
he should speak the truth, recite purificatory texts, and likewise the vyāhṛtis.
Having recited those [mantras] beginning with the syllable *jye*, as well as the Sāvitrī verse beginning with *tat*, and the purifying hymn *āpo hi ṣṭhā* which destroys sins; || 36 ||
The Pāvamānī verses, as well as those that are purifying and auspicious, should be employed everywhere at the beginning and at the end of ritual acts. (37)

One should recite [the mantra] a thousand times, or a hundred, or even ten, or perhaps ten thousand times; or one may recite the syllable *A*, the three *vyāhṛtis*, or the *Sāvitrī* ten thousand times.
Having gratified the teachers, the seers, the Vedic meters, and the deities with water, he should not speak with one who is ignoble, nor even with a Śūdra, nor with those who are censured. (39)

Nor with a woman in her courses, nor with a bride, nor with outcasts, nor with those of the lowest castes; nor with those who hate the gods and Brahmins, nor with those who revile their teachers and elders. (40)
One should not despise anyone who is hostile toward one's mother or father.
This rule for all hardships has been declared in due order. 41.
The procedure for the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra, as well as for the Sāntapana,
the Parāka Kṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa, [is now described].
One is liberated from all five mortal sins and all evil deeds;
by the Taptakṛcchra penance, one burns away all sins in an instant. (43)
Purified by three cāndrāyaṇa penances, he attains the world of Brahmā;
then, by means of eight, he shall directly behold the deities who grant boons.
Having mastered the Vedic hymns with ten [repetitions], one attains all desires;
for three days one should eat in the morning, for three days in the evening, and for three days one should eat food obtained unasked.
A twice-born man should fast for three days and then perform the Prājāpatya penance,
consuming cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with Kuśa grass.
A fast for one night is known as the Sāntapana Kṛcchra;
one should eat only a single morsel each day for three days, as previously described.
A twice-born man should fast for three days; in this manner he should perform the atikṛcchra penance.
Likewise, that which is joined with three [of these] is known as the mahāsāntapana.
A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air, each for three days, bathing once daily and remaining composed. (49)
One who drinks water while remaining self-controlled and vigilant for twelve days is said to have performed the *Prājāpatya* rite according to the traditional law. (50)
This penance called Parāka is the dispeller of all sins.
One should consume one morsel of food on the first day of the dark fortnight and increase it [by one] during the bright fortnight. (51)
One should not eat on the new moon day; such is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Having performed ablutions at the three periods of the day, this is remembered as the Cāndrāyaṇa.
A Brahmin who has performed his daily rites should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set;
this is known as the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa.
Remaining self-controlled at midday, one should eat eight morsels of sacrificial food;
this is the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
For the Rudras, the Ādityas, and the Vasus move about in this manner;
all the gods, along with the Maruts and Bhū, are indeed well.
Each one, when performed according to the rules for seven nights, purifies the skin, blood, flesh, bones, fat, marrow, and lymph. (56)
Each one is purified in seven nights; of this there is no doubt.
Having purified his soul through these vows, he should perform his duties constantly. (57)
Thus, the actions of one who is pure certainly succeed; of this there is no doubt.
One whose self is pure, who speaks the truth and has conquered the senses, should perform action. (58)
Then, one attains all desired objects without a doubt;
one should fast for three nights, abstaining from all ritual activities.
Or one may perform [the preliminary rites] for three nights; thereafter, one should commence the ritual action.
Thus has the procedure been described, which bestows the fruit of the *puraścaryā*.
O divine sage, the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) of the Gāyatrī, which bestows all desires and destroys great sins, has been described to you. (61)
First, the practitioner of mantra should perform a vow that effects the purification of the body;
thereafter, he should perform the preparatory rite (puraścaryā), and thus he shall become a partaker of all fruits.
Thus has this secret procedure for the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) been told to you;
it must not be spoken to another, since it is remembered as the very essence of the Vedas.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Taptakṛcchra and Other Penances," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Nārada spoke regarding morning reflection:
"O highly fortunate Nārāyaṇa, [I shall explain] the Gāyatrī in brief."
O treasury of compassion, please explain the ritual applications for pacification and the other [purposes].
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"O son of Brahmā, this which you have asked is an extreme secret;
it must not be told to anyone who is wicked or malicious."
Now, for the sake of pacification, the twice-born should offer oblations with fuel-sticks soaked in milk;
by means of *śamī* fuel-sticks, spirits, diseases, planetary influences, and so forth, are pacified. (3)
A twice-born man should offer oblations with moist fuel-sticks of a milk-tree,
or he may offer oblations with its chips for the pacification of elemental spirits, diseases, and other afflictions.
One should satisfy the Sun with water; by doing so with both hands, one attains peace.
Having recited [mantras] in water reaching the knees, one brings all defects to a state of calm.
Having recited [the mantra] in water reaching up to the neck, one is released from danger that threatens life;
for all rites of pacification, recitation while submerged in water is prescribed.
In a vessel made of gold, or silver, or even copper;
or one made from the wood of a milk-exuding tree, provided it is free of cracks, or even one made of clay. || 7 ||
Having offered a thousand oblations with the five products of the cow into a well-kindled fire,
one should gradually complete the remainder of the rite using wood from milk-exuding trees.
Having recited the mantra a thousand times while touching the vessel containing the offerings at each oblation,
he should sprinkle that place with those [offerings] using *kuśa* grass while recollecting the mantra.
Then, while offering the oblation (bali) therein, one should meditate upon the Supreme Deity;
thus, the malevolent spell (kṛtyā) arising from sorcery and all evil are destroyed. || 10 ||
If one thus brings gods, spirits, piśācas, and others under control,
the house, village, city, and kingdom are all liberated from them.
By digging [the earth], one is liberated from those [sins]; by writing [it], even from the middle [of the cycle].
Having drawn a trident within the mandala, or according to the previously mentioned sequence, [one is purified].
Having consecrated it with a thousand recitations, one should bury it for the sake of all-pervading peace;
[using] either a golden, silver, or even copper jar.
Having placed a new earthen vessel— divine, wound with thread, and free of cracks—
upon a sacrificial mound or a sandy bank, the knower of mantras should fill it with water while reciting the mantra.
Having brought sacred waters from the four quarters by means of the best of the twice-born,
[they offered] cardamom, sandalwood, camphor, jasmine, trumpet-flower, and mallikā.
One should likewise cast bilva leaves, krāntā, rice, barley, sesame seeds,
mustard seeds, and the tender sprouts of milk-exuding trees.
Having encompassed all [the deities], the wise Brahmin, having bathed and being composed, should recite the mantra a thousand times while holding a bundle of *kuśa* grass.
In the various directions, Brahmins learned in the three Vedas should recite mantras dedicated to the Sun;
one should sprinkle him, give him water to drink, and consecrate him with that water.
He shall be liberated from elemental spirits, diseases, and malevolent spells, and become happy;
by means of this consecration, even a man who has entered the jaws of death shall be released.
A wise king who desires to live long must certainly cause this to be performed;
O Sage, a hundred cows should be given to the officiating priests during the consecration.
Or rather, whatever sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) may bring satisfaction according to one's ability;
on a Saturday, the twice-born man, having touched an Aśvattha tree, should recite [the mantra] one hundred times.
A twice-born man shall be liberated from elemental spirits, diseases, malevolent spells, and great fear;
he should offer oblations of *guḍūcī* stalks cut at the joints and anointed with milk.
Thus, the oblation for the Conqueror of Death (Mṛtyuñjaya) destroys all diseases;
one should offer the leaves of the mango tree smeared with milk for the pacification of fever. (23)
Having offered oblations of vacā mixed with milk into the fire, one shall destroy [the affliction];
by the offering of the threefold honey, consumption (rājayakṣmā) is destroyed. 24.

Having offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*) as food to the Sun-god preceded by a fire-oblation (*homa*), one should cause a person afflicted by pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣman*) to eat it; thus he shall attain peace.
A twice-born man should cut creepers at their joints and offer them as oblations when the moon is in conjunction with the sun,
anointed with milk, for the pacification of consumption.
By offering oblations with the flowers of the Śaṅkhavṛkṣa tree, one shall destroy leprosy;
there shall be the destruction of epilepsy by means of the grains of Apāmārga.
Through the offering of oblations with fuel-sticks from milk-exuding trees, even insanity is destroyed;
through the offering of oblations with fuel-sticks from the Udumbara tree, excessive urination comes to an end.
One should pacify urinary disorders (prameha) by performing oblations with honey or sugarcane juice;
by performing oblations with the three types of honey, one brings smallpox (masūrikā) to peace.
Having offered oblations of tawny cow's ghee, one should bring peace to the disease of smallpox;
with wood from the Udumbara, Vaṭa, and Aśvattha trees, one may remove the ailments of cattle, elephants, and horses.
If an anthill containing ants and honey should arise within the house,
the twice-born man should offer oblations by the hundreds with fuel-sticks of *śamī* wood, along with food and clarified butter.
Arising from that, it attains pacification; one should offer an oblation there with the remaining [mantras].
In the case of clouds, thunder, earthquakes, and the appearance of wild cane, etc., [the following applies]: || 32 ||
If one performs the fire-oblation in this manner for seven days, the kingdom and the realm shall become happy.
In whichever direction one strikes with a clod of earth over which the mantra has been recited a hundred times, [in that direction the enemy shall be subdued]. || 33 ||
Then his fear of fire, wind, and enemies shall perish;
one who recites this with the mind alone shall be released from bondage, even if bound.

By reciting [the mantra] while touching [a person], one may liberate them from spirits, diseases, poisons, and the like; by drinking water over which the mantra has been consecrated, one shall be liberated from spirits and other such afflictions.
Having consecrated it a hundred times with mantras, one should apply the ashes for the pacification of spirits and other evils;
one should wear the ashes on the head after consecrating them with the verse beginning with "tad."
Freed from all diseases, may he live happily for a hundred years;
if he is unable, he should have the rite of pacification performed by giving a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin.
Then, by offering flowers as oblations, a twice-born man shall obtain nourishment, glory, and fortune;
one desiring prosperity should offer red lotuses and shall attain fortune.
Having offered auspicious, fresh *jātī* flowers, one obtains prosperity;
by offering an oblation of *śāli* rice grains, one obtains abundant prosperity. (39)
By offering oblations with the fuel-sticks of the *bilva* tree, one shall obtain prosperity;
likewise by offering oblations with the chips, leaves, flowers, or even the fruits of the *bilva*. (40)
One attains supreme prosperity even with the pieces of the root,
as well as with the fuel-sticks of the bilva tree, with milk-rice, and with clarified butter.
By offering oblations a hundred times each for seven days, one shall obtain prosperity;
by offering parched grain mixed with the three sweets in the fire sacrifice, one shall obtain a daughter.
By this method, a maiden obtains her desired husband;
and by offering a hundred red lotuses for seven days, she shall obtain gold.
Having offered water into the solar disc, one obtains gold situated in water;
having offered food, one obtains food; and by offering rice, one becomes a lord of rice.
By offering oblations of the powder of dried cow dung from a calf, one obtains cattle;
and through oblations of priyaṅgu, milk-porridge, and clarified butter, one shall obtain progeny.
Having offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*) as food to the Sun-god preceded by a fire-oblation (*homa*), one should feed the woman who has bathed after her menses; thus she shall obtain a supreme son. (46)
By offering oblations with fresh, sprouting twigs, one shall obtain long life;
by offering oblations with fuel-sticks from a milk-exuding tree, one shall attain longevity. || 47 ||
Having offered a hundred oblations of rice along with sprouts, fresh shoots, red flowers, and the three sweets, one shall obtain gold and long life.
Having offered a golden bud, one shall obtain a lifespan of a hundred years;
likewise by offering dūrvā grass, or even with milk, honey, or clarified butter.
By offering one hundred oblations each for seven days with *śamī* wood, food, milk, or clarified butter, one wards off untimely death.
By offering a hundred oblations each for seven days, one wards off untimely death;
having offered fuel-sticks of the *nyagrodha* tree, one should then offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) as an oblation.
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred times for seven days, one wards off untimely death;
subsisting on a diet of milk and reciting it for seven days, one shall become victorious over death.
By fasting, restraining speech, and reciting [the mantra] for three nights, one is released from Yama;
by likewise immersing oneself in water and reciting it, one is immediately liberated from death.
Resorting to a bilva tree, one should mutter [the mantra] for a month and shall obtain a kingdom;
by offering oblations of bilva—with its roots, fruits, and sprouts—one shall likewise obtain a kingdom.
Having offered a hundred lotuses for a month, one obtains a kingdom free from thorns;
having offered barley-gruel mixed with rice, one obtains a village.
Having offered oblations of *aśvattha* fuel-sticks, one shall obtain victory in battle and other such endeavors;
having offered oblations of *arka* fuel-sticks, one shall be victorious everywhere. (56)
Having offered milk-rice (pāyasa) for seven days, combined with the sap, leaves, or flowers of the reed (vetasa), one shall obtain rain. || 57 ||
Having recited [the mantra] in water reaching the navel for seven days, one shall obtain rain;
having offered a hundred oblations of ashes into the water, one shall ward off a great rain.
With fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood, one obtains spiritual splendor (*brahmavarcasa*);
by offering *palāśa* flowers, one shall obtain everything desired. (59)
Having offered milk as an oblation, one shall obtain wisdom; having offered clarified butter, one shall obtain intelligence.
Having consecrated it with mantras and drunk it, one obtains the essence of Brahman and attains wisdom.
In a flower-homa, a cloth of that same kind [is obtained] from threads;
having offered salt mixed with honey, one shall bring the desired object under control.
Having offered oblations with *lakṣmī* flowers soaked in honey, one brings [the deity] under control as desired;
standing in water, one should daily sprinkle oneself with a handful [of these offerings].

A Brahmin who performs [this rite] for another shall obtain intelligence, health, longevity, and supreme well-being; that other person for whom it is intended shall likewise attain nourishment and prosperity. (63)
Furthermore, one who desires long life should recite the Cāruvidhi mantra a thousand times every day in a pure place; thus he shall attain the highest lifespan. (64)
A twice-born man desiring long life and health should recite [the mantra] for two months; he shall obtain longevity and health. For the sake of prosperity, he should recite it for three months. (65)
Through four [repetitions], one gains longevity, prosperity, sons, wives, and so forth; through recitation, one gains fame.
Through five [repetitions], one obtains sons, wives, longevity, health, prosperity, and knowledge.
In this very manner, one should proceed toward the higher desires by means of the higher months;
standing with arms raised and without support, one should recite the mantra on one leg.
By reciting it three hundred times for a month, a Brahmin shall obtain all his desires;
likewise, by reciting it one thousand and one hundred times, he shall attain everything.
Having restrained both the prāṇa and apāna breaths, one should recite [the mantra] three hundred times for a month;
whatever one desires, that one obtains, and one may even attain the Thousandfold.
Standing on one foot with arms raised upward and having restrained the breath, one who is self-controlled shall obtain a hundred [moons] for a month, if he so desires; thus says Kauśika. (70)
Having thus recited it three hundred times, one shall obtain everything;
by reciting it a hundred times while submerged in water for a month, one shall attain one's desired goal.
Having thus recited three hundred times, one shall obtain everything;
one should recite a thousand times standing on one foot, with arms raised upward, motionless and without support.
Eating sacrificial food at night, one attains the status of a seer after one year;
likewise, by chanting this for two years, one's speech shall become unfailing.
If one recites thus for three years, there will be vision of the three times;
if one recites for four years, the Blessed Lord, the God, comes.
In this manner, within five years, one shall possess the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest;
likewise, by reciting it for six years, one attains the power of assuming any form at will (*kāmarūpitva*).
In this way, one may attain immortality in seven years;
the status of a Manu is accomplished in nine, and the status of Indra occurs in ten.
By reciting it for eleven years, one attains the state of Prajāpati;
likewise, by reciting it for twelve years, one shall surely attain the status of Brahmā.
By this very [practice], worlds were conquered through austerity by Nārada and others;
some [subsisted] on vegetables, others on roots, others on fruits, and still others on water.
Some sages subsist on clarified butter, others on Soma, and still others on sacrificial porridge; some eat only once every fortnight, while others eat only what they obtain by begging during the day.
Others, eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya), indeed perform the highest austerity;
furthermore, for the purification of secret sins, a twice-born man should recite the [Gāyatrī] three thousand times.
The best of the twice-born becomes pure from the theft of gold by [observing] a month;
one who has drunk liquor shall attain purification by reciting [the mantra] three thousand times for a month.
One who has violated the teacher’s bed shall become pure by reciting [the mantra] three thousand times for one month;
having built a hut and dwelling in the forest, one should recite it three thousand times for one month.
"A killer of a Brahmin is released from sin," so it was spoken by Kauśika;
having immersed oneself in water for twelve days, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times every day. (83)

All twice-born men who have committed great sins shall be liberated from their transgressions by reciting [the mantra] three thousand times for a month, while restraining the breath and remaining silent.
Even one joined with a great sin is liberated from great fear;
even a killer of a Brahmin is purified by a thousand breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
One should practice this six times a day with a concentrated mind, regulating the incoming and outgoing breaths;
this constitutes *prāṇāyāma*, which destroys all sins. (86)
If a king recites it a thousand times for a month, he shall attain purity;
indeed, for the killing of a cow, a twice-born man should recite it three thousand times for twelve days.
For approaching those who should not be approached, theft, killing, and eating forbidden food,
the Gāyatrī, when recited ten thousand times, shall purify a twice-born man.
Having performed a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one is liberated from all sins;
this serves for purification when there is a mixture of all kinds of evils. (89)
One who dwells in the forest and performs the daily recitation should practice it a thousand times for a month;
that three-thousand-fold recitation of this verse is equal to a fast.
Twenty-four thousand [repetitions] practiced constitute what is known as a *kṛcchra* penance;
sixty-four thousand, however, are equal to a *cāndrāyaṇa*.
Having restrained the breath at both twilights, one should constantly practice this one hundred times;
thus one attains the supreme verse beginning with "Tat," which brings about the destruction of all sins.

Having immersed oneself in the waters, one should constantly recite the verse beginning with "tat" a hundred times while meditating upon the Goddess in the form of the Sun; thus, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus have these conceptualizations of peace, purification, and so forth been correctly explained to you;
they are most secret and esoteric, and must always be kept hidden by you.
Thus has the compendium of right conduct been briefly proclaimed;
by practicing this according to the prescribed rule, Māyā-Durgā becomes pleased. (95)
A person should perform occasional rites, daily rites, and rites for specific desires according to the prescribed rules;
such a person shall partake in the attainment of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"Good conduct is the first dharma; the Lord is the master of dharma.
Thus it is stated in all the scriptures that the fruit of virtuous conduct is great. 97.
One who possesses good conduct is always pure; one who possesses good conduct is always happy;
one who possesses good conduct is always blessed—this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Nārada. (98)
Even if a mortal should hear this work, which generates the grace of the Goddess and prescribes the rules of right conduct, he shall partake in great prosperity and happiness. (99)
Through right conduct, one attains happiness both in this world and the next;
that very thing has been declared by me to you—what else do you wish to hear? (100)
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Right Conduct," in the eleventh book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
An Inquiry into the Gāyatrī:
Nārada said:
"O Lord, O Master, the rule for right conduct has been described by you."
Its majesty is likewise incomparable, destroying all sins.
I have heard from the lotus of your mouth the nectar of the Goddess’s story,
as well as those vows beginning with the Cāndrāyaṇa that were described by you.
We know those [deeds] to be difficult to accomplish, yet they are to be accomplished by the agent;
therefore, let us now perform that which is easily accomplished for embodied beings. (3)
O Lord, O Sovereign of the Gods, please graciously tell me that action which generates the grace of the Goddess and grants success in auspicious undertakings.
Regarding the procedure for the Gāyatrī that has been proclaimed in the rules for right conduct (sadācāra), what among those would be the most principal, or what would bestow the greatest merit? (5)
O Sage, regarding those syllables of the Gāyatrī that you have stated to be equal in number to the principles (tattvas), who are said to be their seers (ṛṣis) and what are their meters (chandās)?
"O Lord, which deities are said to preside over them? Tell me everything, for a great curiosity revolves within my mind. (7)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Whether he performs other rites such as formal observances or does not perform them at all,
a twice-born man who is solely devoted to the Gāyatrī becomes one who has accomplished his purpose.
O Sage, by offering the arghya libations during the twilights and performing the recitation of the Gāyatrī three thousand times, one shall become worthy of worship even by the gods.
Whether he performs the ritual placements (nyāsa) or not, let him practice the Gāyatrī alone,
meditating upon her whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss with a sincere disposition.
Through the perfect realization of that single syllable, the best of Brahmins rivals Hari,
Śaṅkara, the lotus-born Brahmā, Sūrya, Candra, and Hutāśana.
Now, therefore, O Brahmin, listen to the castes, the seers, and so forth;
likewise the meters, the deities, and indeed the principles (tattvas), in their proper order.
Vāmadeva, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Śukra, Kaṇva, Parāśara, the highly resplendent Viśvāmitra, Kapila, and the great Śaunaka. (13)
Yājñavalkya, Bharadvāja, Jamadagni—the treasure-house of austerity—Gautama, Mudgala, Vedavyāsa, and Lomaśa; || 14 ||
Agastya, Kauśika, Vatsa, Pulastya, Māṇḍūka, Durvāsas—the best among those who practice austerities—as well as Nārada and Kaśyapa. || 15 ||
Thus, O sage, these sages of the castes have been declared in order:
Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Paṅkti. (16)
The Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, and likewise the Atijagatī are considered [metres];
as are the Śakvarī, the Atiśakvarī, the Dhṛti, and the Atidhṛti. || 17 ||
Virāṭpaṅkti, Prastārapaṅkti, Kṛti, Prakṛti, Ākṛti, Vikṛti, Sakṛti, and likewise Akṣarapaṅkti. || 18 ||
"Bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ" is likewise remembered as the Jyotiṣmatī metre;
these, O great sage, are the metres that have been proclaimed. (19)
O wise one, hear now of the deities in their proper sequence:
the first is declared to be Āgneya, and the second is Prājāpatya.
The third is likewise Saumya, and Īśāna is the fourth;
Sāvitra is declared the fifth, and the sixth has Āditya as its deity.
The seventh is dedicated to Bṛhaspati, the eighth to Mitra and Varuṇa,
the ninth has Bhaga as its deity, and the tenth belongs to Aryaman.
The eleventh is remembered as belonging to Gaṇeśa; the twelfth is said to belong to Tvaṣṭṛ;
the thirteenth is declared to belong to Pūṣan; and the fourteenth belongs to Indra and Agni.
The fifteenth is dedicated to Vāyu, the sixteenth to Vāmadeva, and the seventeen-syllable [meter] is declared to have Mitrāvaruṇa as its deity. (24)
The eighteenth is indeed Vaiśvadeva, the nineteenth is Mātṛka,
the twentieth is Vaiṣṇava, and the twenty-first is declared to have the Vasus as its deity.
The twenty-first is dedicated to Rudra; the twenty-second has Rudra as its deity;
the twenty-third belongs to Kubera; and the twenty-fifth belongs to the Aśvins.

O Sage, this supreme and most excellent compendium of the twenty-four syllables and their deities has been told; it is the sole purifier of great sins, by the mere hearing of which one obtains the fruit of the recitation along with its ancillaries. 27.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Investigation of Gāyatrī," in the twelfth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 1.
The Exposition of the Powers of Gāyatrī and Others.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O great sage, listen to what the powers of the letters are.
Vāmadevī is beloved, truthful, all-auspicious, and playful. || 1 ||
Prabhāvatī, Jayā, Śāntā, Kāntā, Durgā, Sarasvatī, Vidrumā, Viśāleśā, Vyāpinī, and likewise Vimalā. (2)

She is remembered as the dispeller of darkness, the subtle one, the source of the universe, the victorious, the self-controlled, the one whose abode is the lotus, the supreme, the splendor, the auspicious, and the three-stepped. || 3 ||
The powers of the twenty-four letters have been proclaimed;
hereafter, I shall describe the colors of the letters exactly as they are.
The *campaka* and the *atasī* flower, likewise coral, that which has the appearance of crystal, and that which possesses a luster equal to the lotus flower. (5)
Resembling the rising sun, similar to a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon;
possessing the luster of coral and lotus petals, and a radiance equal to a ruby.
Pearl resembling an indranīla gem, with the luster of saffron, the hue of collyrium, red, and vaidūrya resembling honey; || 7 ||
It is turmeric-colored, resembling the luster of jasmine or milk, possessing a radiance equal to the sun;
it is like the tail-feather of a parrot, and likewise similar to a lotus petal.
Resembling the ketakī flower, possessing the luster of the mallikā blossom, and the karavīra—these are proclaimed in their respective order. (9)
The elements have been declared as the purifiers of great sins for those of all castes:
earth, water, fire, air, and space.
Smell, taste, form, sound, and likewise touch;
the generative organ, the anus, the feet, the hands, and speech, in due order. (11)
The vital breath (prāṇa), the tongue, the eye, the skin, and the ear after that;
then the out-breath (apāna), the diffused breath (vyāna), and the equalizing breath (samāna) after that. || 12 ||
These essential principles of the phonemes have been proclaimed in their proper sequence;
hereafter, I shall describe the mudrās of the phonemes in order.
Sumukha, Sampuṭa, Vitata, and likewise Vismṛta;
as well as Dvimukha, Trimukha, and likewise Catuḥpañcamukha. || 14 ||
The six-faced, the downward-facing, the pervasive, the water-dropper, as well as the cart, the noose of Yama, the entwined, and the face-to-face with the mouth turned upward. (15)
Vilamba, Muṣṭika, Matsya, Kūrma, Varāhaka, Siṃhākrānta, Mahākrānta, Mudgara, and likewise Pallava. (16)
The trident-yoni, the *surabhi*, the rosary, the *liṅga*, and the lotus are proclaimed as the great mudrās (*mahāmudrās*) which are of the nature of the fourth state (*turya*). || 17 ||
Thus, O great sage, these mudrās of the letters have been proclaimed by you;
they destroy great sins and bestow fame and splendor, O sage. (18)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Power of Gāyatrī and Others," in the twelfth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Armor of the Gāyatrī Mantra.
Nārada said:
O Lord, Master of the entire world, I have a doubt, O Prabhū.
O knower of the sixty-four arts, O foremost among those who know yoga, you who have fallen [from worldly bonds].
By what merit is one liberated, and how does one become the very form of Brahman? How, moreover, does the body specifically become the form of the deity and the form of the mantra? (2)

O Lord, I desire to hear about that action, as well as the ritual of renunciation (nyāsa) according to the prescribed rules, along with the seer, the meter, the presiding deity, and the meditation, all in accordance with the injunctions. (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: There is a certain supreme secret, namely the Gāyatrī-kavaca;
by reciting and wearing it, a mortal is liberated from all sins.
One attains all desires and is born with the form of a goddess;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the protectors of this Gāyatrī-kavaca.
O Nārada, the sages, the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, and the meters are the deities; Gāyatrī is said to be the supreme aspect of Brahman.
The seed-syllable of that is "Bharga"; this has been called Śakti by the wise.
And the "Kīlaka" is declared to be the application of the intellect for the sake of liberation. || 7 ||
The heart is said to consist of four [syllables], the head is remembered as having three letters;
the crest (śikhā) should follow with four, and the armor (kavaca) is remembered as having three.
The eye is indicated by four [units], and that weapon (astra) shall consist of four;
now I shall describe the meditation (dhyāna) which bestows the desired objects of the practitioner.

I worship Gāyatrī, who possesses three eyes with complexions like pearl, coral, gold, sapphire, and white; who wears a jeweled crown set with the moon; whose essence consists of the phonemes representing the meaning of reality; and who carries in her hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a goad, a whip, a radiant skull-bowl, a cord, a conch, a discus, and a pair of lotuses.
May Gāyatrī protect me from the east, may Sāvitrī protect me from the south; may Brahma-saṃdhyā protect me from the west, and Sarasvatī from the north.
May Pārvatī protect my southeastern direction; may she who reclines upon the waters protect the southern direction;
and may she who strikes fear into the Yātudhānas protect the southwestern direction.
May Pāvamānī, who sports as the Purifier, protect the direction;
and may Raudrī, who is Rudrāṇī and possesses the form of Rudra, protect my direction.
May Brahmāṇī protect my upper part, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī my lower part;
thus may Bhuvaneśvarī protect all my limbs and the ten directions.
May that *tat-pada* protect my feet; may the *savitṛ-pada* protect my shanks; may the *vareṇya* protect the region of my hips, and likewise may *bhargas* protect my navel. (15)
And "May we meditate upon that heart of the God" is for the two cheeks;
the word *dhiyaḥ* is for the eyes, and the word *yaḥ* is for my forehead. (16)
May *naḥ* protect my feet; may *me* impel my head;
may *tat* protect my crown; and may the syllable *sa-* protect my forehead. (17)
The syllable *tu* is in the two eyes, the syllable *tu* is on the two cheeks, the syllable *va* is in the nostrils, and likewise the syllable *re* is in the mouth. (18)
The letter *ṇa* is the upper lip, while *ya* is the lower lip;
the syllable *bha* is in the middle of the mouth, and likewise *rgo* is at the chin. (19)
The syllable *de* is at the region of the throat, while *va* is at the region of the shoulders;
*sya* is the right hand, and *dhī* is the left hand.
The syllable *ma* shall protect the heart, and likewise the syllable *hi* the belly; the syllable *dhi* is for the region of the navel, while the syllable *yo* is for the hips.
May the syllable *yo* protect our secret parts; may the syllable *pa*, the letter of the feet, protect our two thighs;
may the syllable *pra* protect our knees, and the syllable *co* protect the region of our shanks.
May the letter *da* protect the region of my ankles, the letter *ya* my pair of feet, and the consonant *ta* always protect every limb of my body. (23)
This divine armor, however, destroys hundreds of afflictions, bestows the knowledge of the sixty-four arts, and brings about liberation. (24)
One is liberated from all sins and attains the supreme Brahman;
by either reading or hearing [this], one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Description of the Gāyatrī Mantra-Kavaca," in the twelfth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Nārada spoke the Gāyatrī-hṛdaya:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Sovereign of the past, future, and present worlds!"
And the divine armor has been heard, which is the very embodiment of the Gāyatrī mantra.
Now I wish to hear the supreme Gāyatrī-hṛdaya, by the retention of which all the merit arising from the recitation of the Gāyatrī is obtained. (2)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Nārada, the Heart of the Goddess has been clearly proclaimed in the Atharvaṇa;
that very same [Heart], which is the most secret of secrets, I shall now proclaim.
Having meditated upon Gāyatrī, the Mother of the Vedas, who is the Great Goddess in the form of Virāj,
one should then meditate upon these deities within her limbs.
Because of the identity between the individual body and the cosmic egg,
the practitioner should likewise contemplate his own body as having the form of the Goddess, in order to become one with her.
"An non-god should not worship a god"—thus those who know the Vedas understand;
therefore, for the sake of non-duality, one should contemplate these deities within one's own body.
Now I shall proclaim that [teaching], through which one may become absorbed in that;
for this Gāyatrī-hṛdaya, I alone am traditionally remembered as the seer (ṛṣi).
The Gāyatrī metre is prescribed, and the deity is the Supreme Goddess (Parameśvarī).
One should perform the six limbs in sequence according to the method previously described.
Seated on a seat in a secluded place, one should meditate with a one-pointed mind. (8)
The ritual assignment (*nyāsa*) is as follows:

the deity of the sky is on the head; the two Aśvins are on the rows of teeth; both twilights are on the lips; Agni is on the mouth; Sarasvatī is on the tongue; Bṛhaspati is on the neck; the eight Vasus are on the breasts; the Maruts are on the arms; Parjanya is on the heart; space (*ākāśa*) is on the belly; the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*) is on the navel; Indra and Agni are on the hips; Prajāpati, the mass of consciousness, is on the buttocks; Kailāsa and Malaya are on the thighs; the Viśvedevas are on the knees; Kauśika is on the shanks; and the path of the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*) is on the private parts.

The ancestors are the thighs; the earth is the feet; the trees are in the fingers; the seers are the body hairs; the moments (*muhūrta*) are the nails; the planets are in the bones; blood and flesh are the seasons; the years are the twinkling of an eye; day and night are the sun and the moon. I take refuge in the preeminent, divine Gāyatrī, the thousand-eyed one, for protection. *Oṃ*, obeisance to that desirable Savitṛ. *Oṃ*, obeisance to that primordial victory. Obeisance to that Āditya of the morning.

Therefore, "Salutation to the Sun as the Foundation at Dawn. Studying this in the morning destroys the sin committed during the night; studying it in the evening destroys the sin committed during the day; studying it both in the evening and in the morning, one becomes sinless. One becomes as if bathed in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*); one becomes known by all the gods. One becomes purified from speaking what should not be spoken; one becomes purified from eating what should not be eaten; one becomes purified from consuming what should not be consumed; one becomes purified from sucking what should not be sucked.
