One becomes purified by the accomplishment of what is otherwise unattainable; one becomes purified from hundreds of thousands of ill-gotten gifts; one becomes purified from all forms of receiving gifts; one becomes purified from defiling the assembly at a meal; one becomes purified from speaking falsehoods. Furthermore, even one who is not a celibate student becomes a celibate student. By studying this *Hṛdaya*, it is as if a thousand sacrifices have been performed. The fruits of reciting six million *gāyatrīs* are obtained. One should correctly instruct eight Brahmins [in this]; for him, success (*siddhi*) comes to pass.
"The Brahmin who studies this daily, being pure in the morning, is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Brahmā. Thus spoke the Blessed Lord Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Heart of Gāyatrī," in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Glorious Gāyatrī Hymn.
Nārada said: O compassionate one toward devotees, O omniscient one, [you have described] the heart that destroys sin.
Since the Gāyatrī has been described [to you], therefore recite the hymn of the Gāyatrī.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Primordial Power, Mother of the World, bestower of grace upon devotees, all-pervading and infinite Śrī Sandhyā; salutations be unto you!
You alone are the twilight, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī;
you are Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Raudrī, as well as red, white, and black.
In the morning she is a young girl, and at midday she becomes established in youth;
in the evening she is an old woman—the Goddess is thus always meditated upon by the sages.
Seated upon a swan, mounted on Garuḍa, and likewise borne by a bull—
she who is seen on earth by ascetics as she studies the Ṛgveda.
Reciting the Yajurveda, she shines resplendent in the intermediate space;
likewise, as a singer of Sāmans, she wanders everywhere upon the earth.
For you have indeed gone to the world of Rudra and dwell in the world of Viṣṇu;
you alone, O immortal one, bestow grace in the world of Brahmā.
She is the delighter of the Seven Sages, the source of illusion who bestows many boons;
she indeed arose from the tears and sweat produced by the hands and eyes of Śiva and Śivā.
Durgā, the progenitor of bliss, is celebrated in ten forms:
Vareṇyā, Varadā, Variṣṭhā, and Varavarṇinī; || 9 ||
The seventh is Gariṣṭhā, Varārhā, and Varārohā;
likewise Nīlagaṅgā and Sandhyā, who always bestow both enjoyment and liberation.
The goddess Bhāgīrathī flows in the world of mortals, and Bhogavatī in Pātāla; she is the river that carries the three worlds and dwells in these three abodes.
In the world of Bhūr you alone are the earth, the sustainer of the worlds;
in the world of Bhuvas you are the power of the wind, and in the world of Svar you are the treasury of splendors.
In Maharloka she is Mahāsiddhi; in Janaloka she is also known as Janā;
in Tapoloka she is Tapasvinī; and in Satyaloka she is Satyavāk.
Kamalā resides in the world of Viṣṇu, Gāyatrī bestows the world of Brahmā, and Gaurī, dwelling in half of Hara’s body, resides in the world of Rudra. 14.
For you are indeed proclaimed as the primordial nature (prakṛti) of both the individual soul and the Great Soul;
you are indeed the essence of the state of equilibrium, possessing the form of the variegated Brahman.
Therefore, you are indeed sung of as the supreme, transcendent Power;
you are the power of will, the power of action, and the power of knowledge—the bestower of the three powers.
The Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, the Vipāśā and the Sarasvatī, the Sarayū, the Devikā, the Sindhu, the Narmadā, and likewise the Airāvatī. || 17 ||
The Godāvarī, the Śatadrū, the Kāverī that flows to the world of the gods, the Kauśikī, the Candrabhāgā, the Vitastā, and the Sarasvatī; || 18 ||
The Gaṇḍakī, Tāpinī, Toyā, Gomatī, and Vetravatī;
and likewise Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā as the third.
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and likewise Apūṣā;
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, Śaṅkhinī, and Prāṇavāhinī. || 20 ||
And you are sung of by the ancient wise ones as the *nāḍī* (channel) situated within the body;
you are the vital power (*prāṇa-śakti*) residing in the heart-lotus, and the mistress of dreams residing in the throat. (21)
You are always situated in the palate as the Support; you are in the Bindu as the Garland of Bindus. You are the power Kuṇḍalī at the root, and as Vyāpinī, you reside at the roots of the hair.
For you are seated in the middle of the crest-lock, while Manonmanī resides at the tip of the crest-lock;
what more need be said in abundance regarding whatever exists within the three worlds? (23)
"O Great Goddess, all that [is for] prosperity; O Sandhyā, obeisance be to you!
Thus has this hymn been proclaimed, which bestows great merit when recited at the twilight. (24)
It pacifies great sins and bestows great siddhis;
whoever recites this hymn with a concentrated mind at the time of the twilights [shall attain these]. (25)
One without a son shall obtain a son; one seeking wealth shall obtain wealth;
and he shall attain the fruit of visiting all sacred fords, performing austerities, giving gifts, offering sacrifices, and practicing yoga.
Having enjoyed pleasures for a long time, he shall attain liberation in the end;
whoever recites this hymn composed by ascetics at the time of bathing [shall obtain the same]. (27)
Wherever one may be immersed in water, one obtains the fruit born of bathing at the twilight;
of this there is no doubt, O Nārada, it is the truth, it is the truth. (28)
Whoever listens to this with devotion is liberated from sin;
these words, spoken at the junction of day and night (saṃdhyā) by Nārada, are like nectar. (29)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Śrī Gāyatrī Stotra," in the twelfth book of the Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Thousand-Name Hymn of Gāyatrī.
Nārada said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, expert in all scriptures!
The secret of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas has been heard from your own mouth.
O God, by what means does the knowledge that removes all sins proceed? What is the realization of Brahman, and what indeed is the means to liberation? || 2 ||
O lotus-eyed one, by what means is the goal of the Brahmins attained, or by what is death destroyed? And by what is the fruit of this world and the next obtained? (3)
"You ought to explain everything in its entirety, without omission, from the very beginning.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly wise one! You have asked rightly, O sinless one. (4)
Listen, I shall carefully recite eight thousand auspicious and divine names of Gāyatrī, which destroy all sins. (5)
I shall tell you that which was previously spoken by the Blessed One at the beginning of creation:
Brahmā is proclaimed as the seer (ṛṣi) of the one thousand and eight [verses].
The meter is known to be Anuṣṭubh, and the goddess is Gāyatrī;
the consonants are its seeds (bījas), and the vowels are said to be its powers (śaktis). || 7 ||
The placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the placement of the hands (karanyāsa) are now described by means of the letters of the Mātṛkā.
Next, I shall indeed proclaim the meditation (dhyāna) for the benefit of practitioners.

I worship this maiden Gāyatrī, who is seated upon a lotus, resplendent with three eyes, red in complexion, adorned with a fresh red garland and clusters of jewels; she is joined by [the colors] red, white, golden, blue, and pale-white, and holds a water-pot and a lotus in her palms.
I worship her who holds a lotus-stalk and an excellent garland, and who is mounted upon a swan. || 9 ||
She whose nature is inconceivable and unmanifest, yet who is the Great Sovereign of the objects of cognition;
though situated in the midst of the ocean of nectar, she is unconquered and invincible.
She is the support of the qualities such as *aṇimā* and others, yet she resides within the solar orb; she is free from old age, birth, and other defects, and she holds a rosary in her hand.
She who begins with the letter 'A' and ends with the letter 'Kṣa', who pierces the six internal enemies;
she who resembles the mountain of collyrium (Añjanādri) and dwells upon that mountain of collyrium. 12.
She is Aditi, the unborn knowledge, with eyes like lotuses;
she dwells both within and without, destroying ignorance, and is the innermost self.
She is unborn, her abode is the mouth of the Unborn (Aja), and her face resembles a lotus;
she bestows the knowledge of the meaning of the half-measure (ardhamātrā) and crushes the circle of enemies.
She is the slayer of Asuras, the New Moon night, the destroyer of misfortune when worshipped by the lowest castes;
she is primordial fortune, the primal power, the embodiment of form, and the one with the vast countenance.
She moves along the path of the sun and is frequented by the sun;
she follows the conduct of the preceptor and dwells in the primordial form.
She is of the nature of fire, she possesses a chowrie, she is the primordial one, she is to be worshipped, and she is seated upon her throne;
she is the support residing in the foundation, and she dwells within the limits of space.
She is conjoined with the first letter, has the form of the intermediate space,
resides within the solar orb, and destroys the inner darkness.
Indirā, Ceṣṭadā, Ceṣṭā, Indīvaranibhekṣaṇā, Irāvatī, Indrapadā, Indrāṇī, and Indurūpiṇī. || 19 ||
Equipped with a sugarcane bow and drawing a shaft,
she has a form like sapphire and the appearance of tawny hair.
She is Indrākṣī, the sovereign goddess, free from the three [guṇas] here;
she is Umā, Uṣā, resembling the stars, and her face is like the fruit of the urvāruka gourd.
Uḍuprabhā, Coḍumatī, Uḍupā, and Uḍumadhyagā;
Ūrdhvā, Ūrdhvakeśī, and Ūrdhvādhogatibhedinī. || 22 ||
She who holds her beloved with uplifted arms, who bestows the knots of speech adorned with garlands of waves;
she who is Truth, the Seer, the one possessed of Truth, and she who is saluted by seers and gods. (23)
She is the Rigveda, the remover of debt, and she who moves within the circle of the Ṛṣis;
she is the bestower of prosperity, established on the straight path, the embodiment of upright dharma, and the giver of the cosmic order (Ṛta). || 24 ||

She whose abode is the Ṛgveda, who is straightforward, who sets in motion the lost dharma, who is born from the foremost of spiders, and who removes the poison of spiders and other [venomous creatures]. || 25 ||
Consisting of a single syllable and a single mora, she is established as one and alone;
indeed, she is Aindrī, mounted upon Airāvata, and the bestower of both worldly and otherworldly fruits.
She is indeed the syllable Oṃ, the medicinal herb, and she who dwells as the warp and woof;
she is the submarine fire Aurva, endowed with medicinal herbs, and the bestower of the fruits of domestic ritual duties.
The Goddess situated in the center of the Egg, whose form corresponds to the syllable *cāḥ*, is Kātyāyanī, Kālarātri, Kāmākṣī, and Kāmasundarī. (28)
Kamalā, Kāminī, Kāntā, Kāmadā, Kālakaṇṭhinī;
she whose breasts bear the weight of an elephant's frontal globes, and who dwells in Karavīra.
She is auspicious, adorned with earrings, a dweller of Kurukṣetra;
she has the form of a kuruvinda petal, wears earrings, and resides in the white water-lily.

Kālajihvā (Black-tongued), Karālāsyā (Terrifying-faced), Kālikā (The Black One), Kālarūpiṇī (She whose form is Time), Kamanīyaguṇā (Possessing lovely qualities), Kānti (Splendor), Kalādhārā (Bearer of arts), and Kumudvatī (The Moon-lotus-like one). || 31 ||
Kauśikī is lotus-shaped and the destroyer of the movement of desire; Kaumārī has compassionate side-glances, reaches to the ends of the quarters, and is dear to elephants. || 32 ||
She who has tawny hair, she who is praised by Keśava, she who is fond of Kadamba flowers;
she who is the Yamunā, she who is dark-hued, she who is the girdle, and she who is extolled by the one born from a water-jar (Agastya).
Kāmamātā, Kratumatī, Kāmarūpā, Kṛpāvatī;
Kumārī, Kuṇḍanilayā, Kirātī, and Kīravāhanā. 34.
She is Kaikeyī, whose speech is like the warbling of the cuckoo; she is fond of the ketakī flower; she bears a water-pot; she is Kālī; and she is the one who effects the uprooting of karma. || 35 ||
With the gait of a swan, her armpits adorned with festive auspicious marks, bearing a tilaka of musk, lovely, with the movement of a lordly elephant, she was like the voice of the cuckoo. (36)
She who is smeared with camphor, she who is black, she who is tawny, she who dwells in caves;
she who is immovable, she who bears the mountains, she who is beautiful, and she who resides within the belly of all the worlds.
Holding a sword and a shield, she is short in stature; she is Khecarī, whose vehicle is a bird.
She is renowned as the bearer of a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), seated upon the king of birds.

The destroyer of the threshing floor, the one who has shattered old age, the giver of the narrative called Khaṇḍa, she whose tilaka-mark is a crescent moon, Gaṅgā, who is worshipped by Gaṇeśa and Guha. (39)
She is Gāyatrī, Gomatī, Gītā, Gāndhārī, and she who is fond of singing;
she is Gautamī, Gāminī, and Gāthā, served by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
She is stepped upon by the feet of Govinda; she is manifested through the three qualities (guṇas);
she is the Gandharvī, the Gahvarī, the Gotrā, the Girīśā, the Gahanā, and the Gamī. || 41 ||
Dwelling in the cave, possessed of virtues, and the destroyer of great sins;
she is weighty, virtuous, secret, to be protected, and the bestower of qualities.
Girijā, Guhyamātaṅgī, the beloved of him whose banner bears Garuḍa;
she who removes pride, Godā, she who dwells in Gokula, and Gadādhara. 43.
Residing in Gokarṇa, she dwells within the secret maṇḍala;
she is the giver of heat, the giver of clouds, the bell, and the crusher of the terrible dānavas.

She whose voice consists of the mantra of compassion, who bestows a heavy downpour [of grace], who is fond of the sound of bells, who is the sense of smell, and who brings satisfaction through the sun. || 45 ||
She is the dense circle of enemies, she who whirls, she who is dripping with clarity, and she who possesses dense velocity;
she is the meditation consisting of the element of gnosis, she who is well-anointed, and she who smiles beautifully.
She is agile, fierce, and variegated, adorned with wonderful garlands;
she has four arms and beautiful teeth, and she bestows the fruit of clever conduct.
Cūlikā, Citravastrāntā, Candramas-karṇakuṇḍalā, Candrahāsā, Cārudātrī, Cakorī, and Candrahāsinī. || 48 ||
Candrikā, Candradhātrī, Caurī, Caurā, Caṇḍikā, Cañcadvāgvādinī, Candracūḍā, and Coravināśinī. || 49 ||
Her limbs were smeared with beautiful sandalwood paste, she was fanned by waving yak-tail whisks, she possessed a lovely waist and a graceful gait; Candilā was as radiant as the moon.
She who loves beautiful oblations, whose conduct is lovely, who possesses arms like a wheel;
she who dwells in the center of the lunar orb and for whom the lunar orb is a mirror. || 51 ||
She whose breasts are like ruddy geese, whose movements are variegated, who is beautiful and playful;
she whose nature is consciousness, who is Candravatī, who is like the moon, and who is fond of sandalwood.
She is the impeller, possessed of ancient wisdom, the cātaka bird, and the source of beautiful causes;
she is the one who moves under the parasol, the bearer of the parasol, the shadow, and whose retinue is her own will.
Chāyādevī has nails with gaps, she pervades through the concealed senses;
her meter is Anuṣṭubh ending in Pratiṣṭhā, and she is the destroyer of calamities arising from defects. || 54 ||
Chedā, Chatreśvarī, Chinnā, Churikā, and Chedanapriyā; the Mother, who is free from birth, Jātavedā, and the one whose essence is the universe. || 55 ||
Jāhnavī, Jaṭilā, Jetrī, free from old age and death;
she who dwells in Jambūdvīpa, the flame, the victorious one, and she who abounds in water. || 56 ||
She who has conquered her senses, conquered anger, and conquered her enemies; she who is beloved by the world; whose tongue is like gold; the daughter of Janaka; the earth; and old age. 57.
The mother, the daughter of Jahnu, who desires the welfare of the three worlds;
Jvālāmukhī, the practitioner of mantra-recitation, the destroyer of fever, who has conquered the universe. 58.
She who consists of the conquest of all, the flame, the ever-awake goddess of fever,
the blazing one, the giver of water, the eldest, she whose quarters of the horizon resound with the twang of her bowstring.
Jambhinī, Jṛmbhaṇā, Jṛmbhā, she whose earrings are blazing rubies;
Jhiṃjhikā, she whose resonance is the sound *jhaṇ*, she who possesses the speed of a violent storm.
Skilled in playing the jhallarī drum, she is known as Ñarūpā and Ñabhujā;
equipped with a ṭaṅka and an arrow, she is Ṭaṅkinī and Ṭaṅkabhedinī.
She who utters the sound of the ṭaṅka weapon, whose great chest is worthy of being struck with a ṭaṅka,
the Goddess who produces the sound of clanging, and who resounds with the syllables "ṭha-ṭha."
She is Ḍāmarī, the Ḍākinī, the child-like one (Ḍimbhā), who alone has conquered the demon Ḍuṇḍubha;
she stands upon the path of the Ḍāmarī Tantra and resounds with the sound of the ḍama-ḍamaru drum.
She who dwells upon the foam, who is devoted to the playful games of children,
the mother of the elephant-headed Lord of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa), who holds a drum in her hand, and who is the multitude of the syllable Ḍhi.
The river Narmadā is eternal knowledge, incomparable, and devoid of qualities;
she is the triple-stranded lute with three strings, and the young Tulasī tree.
Trampled by the foot of Trivikrama, she who goes upon the fourth step;
resembling the rising sun, she is both dark as night and cool as frost.
She is endowed with knowledge of the three times, the triple-streamed confluence, and the three-eyed one;
she is the triple-power, Tripurā, the lofty one, and likewise the horse-faced one.
She is the devourer of the *timiṅgilas*, the fierce one, the three-streamed, the bringer of darkness,
the knower of the distinctions of *tantras* and *mantras*, the slender-waisted, and the one who dwells in the triple heaven.
She who is the three junctions of the day, who has three breasts, who is established in contentment, who blazes like a palmyra tree;
she who wears earrings, who has the luster of frost, and who dwells on the snowy mountain.
She is endowed with a web of threads, fond of strings of pearls,
devoted to oblations of sesame seeds, a sacred ford, and possesses the form of the Tamāla flower.
She has three stars, she is slender, she is surrounded by Triśaṅku;
she has a flat belly, she is adorned with sesame seeds, and she wears earrings that are dear to her.
Trijatā, Tittirī, and Tṛṣṇā—these three were of youthful form;
they resembled molten gold and were adorned with ornaments of molten gold.
She belongs to Tryambaka, she consists of the three goals of life, and she bestows knowledge of the three periods of time;
she is the one who offers libations, the giver of satisfaction, the satisfied one, the one characterized by Tamas, and she who is praised by Tumburu.

Seated upon Tārkṣya, she whose form consists of the three guṇas, her slender creeper-like body bent in three places; she who utters the sound "thāt," who is praised as "thāra," and who ends with "thā"; she who bestows boons and is compassionate toward the distressed. 74.
Durgā, the destroyer of the Dānavas; the slayer of the demon Durga; the course of the gods; day and night; Draupadī; she whose voice is like the sound of a drum. 75.
Devayānī, difficult to dwell with, the divider of poverty by day, beloved of Dāmodara, radiant, naked, and the deluder of the directions. || 76 ||

Dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, she is the wielder of the staff (Daṇḍinī), worshipped by the gods, saluted by the deities, an enemy of the dwellers of heaven, and possessing the form of a Dānava. || 77 ||
She is praised by the poor and the helpless; she is initiation (dīkṣā) and the very embodiment of the deities and others;
she is the nurse, the wielder of the bow, the cow, the sustainer, and the follower of righteousness.
She is the sustainer of the earth, the support of the world, the giver of wealth, and the milker of grain;
she is virtuous in character, the presiding deity of riches, and highly skilled in the science of archery.
Fortitude, the blessed one, she who has established her feet, the beloved of the King of Dharma, the eternal;
she who possesses smoke, she whose hair is smoke, the illuminator of the treatises on Dharma. (80)
Nandā, Nandapriyā, Nidrā, Nṛnutā, Nandanātmikā, Narmadā, Nalinī, Nīlā, and she who has her abode in the Blue-throated One (Nīlakaṇṭha). || 81 ||
She is the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, eternal, stainless, devoid of qualities, a treasure-trove;
she is without support, incomparable, eternally pure, and untainted.
She who transcends sound, the drop, and the digit; whose nature consists of sound, the drop, and the digit;
the lioness among men; the upholder of the mountain; adorned with kings and serpents. 83.
She quiets the afflictions of hell, she is born from the feet of Nārāyaṇa;
she is irreproachable, formless, and acts for the pleasure of Nārada.
She is known as the manifold light, the bestower of treasures, and pure in essence;
she upholds the nine threads, is the guiding principle, and brings about the absence of affliction.
Born of joy, enriched with the nine gems, dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest,
fond of fresh butter, a woman whose voice is like the sound of dark clouds.
She who blinks, she whose form is a river, she with the blue throat, the sovereign of night,
the series of names, the slayer of Niśumbha, and the dweller in the world of the Nagas.
Resembling fresh Jāmbūnada gold, she is the presiding deity of the world of the Nāgas;
with her feet adorned by anklets, she brings delight to the hearts of men. 88.
Her eyes were submerged and reddened; her voice was like the roar of a thunderclap;
she dwelt in the Nandana grove and moved about upon the palace turrets.
Pārvatī is supremely generous, identical with the Supreme Brahman, and transcendent;
she is liberated from the five sheaths and is the destroyer of the five great sins.
She knows the dispositions of others' minds, she is fivefold, and possesses five forms;
she is the full moon, supreme joy, and the illuminator of the splendor of the beyond. (91)
Ancient, belonging to Puruṣa, auspicious, with eyes like lotuses,
submerged in the depths of Pātāla, she is pleased and the increaser of joy.
She is the purifier, endowed with feet, graceful, and subsisting on air; she is the Lord of Creatures, weary from creation, and her breasts are the rounded peaks of mountains. 93.
She who is fond of lotuses, who dwells upon a lotus, whose eyes are like lotuses, who is born from a lotus;
she who has lotus petals, whose feet are like lotuses, who is the mistress of the lotus-pond, and who speaks with affection.
She is liberated from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa), the lady of the city, the dweller within the city;
she is abundant, the supreme person, the knower of the joints of existence, and she is fond of the flowers of the Pārijāta tree.
Devoted to her husband, pure of limb, intent on smiles like flowers, the daughter of Prajñāvatī, the granddaughter of Pautra, honored by her sons, and full of milk. || 96 ||
The row [of trees] bearing silken cords bestows the world of the ancestors;
it is ancient, virtuous by nature, and the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before it. || 97 ||
She is the mother of Pradyumna, she is nourishing, she is the consort of the Grandfather (Brahmā),
she dwells in the city of Puṇḍarīka, and her face is like a white lotus.
She has broad shanks, broad arms, broad feet, and a broad belly;
she possesses the beauty of coral sprouts, has tawny eyes, wears yellow garments, and is exceedingly fickle.
She is the progenitor, the giver of nourishment, the meritorious, the foundation, and the goal of the syllable Om;
she possesses five colors, the fivefold speech, is the quintessence (pañcikā), and resides within the cage.
She is the supreme, the highest light, the supreme joy, and the supreme goal;
she is the ultimate limit, the sovereign of the beyond, the purifier, and she whose luster is like fire. || 101 ||
Puṇyabhadrā, Paricchedyā, Puṣpahāsā, Pṛthūdarī, Pītāṅgī, Pītavasanā, Pītaśayyā, and Piśācinī. || 102 ||

She whose activity is yellow destroys the piśācas; she who has eyes like the pāṭala flower performs clever deeds; her conduct is fond of the five kinds of food; she is the slayer of the life-force of pūtanās. || 103 ||

Situated in the midst of a forest of *punnāga* trees, frequented by sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*), she is the supreme power (*parāśakti*) possessing five limbs, who brings about the highest bliss. (104)
She who abides in the flower-arrowed god, who nourishes all the worlds, who is fond of drinking, who has five tufts of hair, and who reclines upon a serpent. 105.
The earth consists of five elements; she is the traveler and the yielder of abundant milk.
She is the Purāṇas, Nyāya, and Mīmāṃsā, and she is fragrant with the scent of Pāṭalī flowers.
She is the bestower of merit and progeny, whose sole domain is the supreme path;
she possesses the beauty of coral, her hopes are fulfilled, she is the syllable Om (praṇava), and her belly is like a tender sprout. 107.
She who bears fruit, who bestows fruit, who is fragile, who hisses, whose form is like a shield;
she who reclines upon the coils of the lord of serpents, and who is adorned by the circle of hooded snakes. || 108 ||
She who is honored by children, whose garments resemble the heat of the sun, the beloved of Balabhadra, the venerable one, the mare, and she who is praised by the intellect. 109.
Bandīdevī, Bilavatī, Baḍiśaghnī, Balipriyā, Bāndhavī, Bodhitā, Buddhi, and Bandhūkakusumapriyā. || 110 ||
She who creates the radiance of the rising sun, the divine Brāhmī, the deity of the Brahmins;
she who is praised by Bṛhaspati, Vṛndā, who sports in Vṛndāvana. || 111 ||
She has youthful breasts, feeds on mice, dwells in holes, and drinks much water;
she has many eyes, many feet, and many earrings.
She is endowed with many arms, the embodiment of the seed-syllable, and possesses manifold forms;
she transcends the bindu, nāda, and kalā, yet has the nature of bindu and nāda.
She wears leather arm-guards and finger-protectors; she dwells in the hermitage of Badarī;
she is the object of worship for the gods; she has broad shoulders; she is vast; and she is the one who strikes with arrows.
The leader of the Vṛnda, praised by many, a woman of great prowess,
sat with her legs crossed in the lotus posture upon a surface of bilva leaves.
She whose natural abode is the Bodhi tree, who is established in the Bindu-mirror, the youthful maiden who possesses the bow of Bāṇa, and who has the speed of the submarine fire (vaḍavānala). 116.
She who dwells both outside and within the cosmic egg, she who threads the bracelet of Brahmā,
Bhavānī, the formidable one, the future, and the remover of fear.
Bhadrakālī, Bhujaṅgākṣī, Bhāratī, she whose intent is toward the Bharatas; Bhairavī, of terrifying form, the bestower of prosperity, garlanded with prosperity. || 118 ||
The passionate woman, devoted to enjoyment, the bestower of prosperity, she of vast prowess;
she whose dwelling is the elements, the creeper-like Bhṛgu, the daughter of Bhṛgu, and she who is worshipped by the gods on earth.
Bhāgīrathī, Bhogavatī, Bhavanasthā, Bhiṣagvarā, Bhāminī, Bhoginī, Bhāṣā, Bhavānī, and Bhūridakṣiṇā. || 120 ||
She whose essence is splendor, she who is formidable, she who liberates from the bonds of worldly existence;
she who is to be worshipped, the sustainer of all beings, she who is delighted, the Sovereign Lady of the World. 121.
She who has serpent-bracelets, the formidable one, Bheruṇḍā, the fortunate one;
the Mother, Māyā, Madhumatī, Madhujihvā, and Madhupriyā. 122.
The great queen, highly fortunate, wearing a garland, with eyes like those of a fish;
she who has transcended illusion, full of sweetness, possessing honey and meat, and flowing with honey.
Born from the honey, she is the daughter of Manu and the resident of the city of Mithilā;
she is the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the Earth, and she who wears a garland of clouds.
Mandodarī, Mahāmāyā, Maithilī, Masṛṇapriyā, Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, Mahākanyā, and Maheśvarī. || 125 ||
She belongs to Mahendra, she is the daughter of Meru, she is worshipped with Mandāra flowers;
her feet possess charming anklets, she is the bestower of liberation, and she is sweet-voiced.
Madhuradrāviṇī, Mudrā, Malayā, and she who is accompanied by Malaya; Medhā, who is dark-green like an emerald, Māgadhī, and Menakātmajā. || 127 ||
Mahāmārī, Mahāvīrā, Mahāśyāmā, praised by Manu;
Mātṛkā, resplendent as the sun, and she whose stride reaches the feet of Mukunda. || 128 ||
The charming one residing in the *mūlādhāra*, dwelling in the *maṇipūraka*, the deer-eyed one mounted upon a buffalo, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura. 129.
She is the posture of yoga, accessible through yoga, and the yoga that rests upon youth;
she is the youthful maiden, standing in the midst of battle, the Yamunā river, and the upholder of the ages.
She was a Yakṣiṇī engaged in yoga, born of a Yakṣa king;
she was skilled in the rites of processions and vehicles, and she was born of the Yadu lineage.
Beginning with the letter *ya* and ending with the letter *ha*, she belongs to the Yajurveda and is the embodiment of sacrifice;
she is the night, devoted to yoga, and the terrifier of demons.
Rukmiṇī, the delightful Rāmā, Revatī, Reṇukā, and Rati;
Raudrī, whose form is dear to Rudra, the mother of Rāma, and she who is fond of Rati. || 133 ||
She is Rohiṇī, the bestower of sovereignty, the Revā, Ramā, and the lotus-eyed one;
she is the full-moon goddess, endowed with beauty, and seated upon a jeweled lion-throne.
Wearing red garlands and garments, anointed with red perfumes and unguents,
Rambhā is mounted upon a royal swan and is fond of red offerings.
She is the support of the delightful age, she who illumines the entire surface of the earth;
she is clothed in the skin of a deer, a chariot-warrior adorned with garlands of jewels. (136)
The mistress of disease, the pacifier of disease, the awakener, the one who causes the hair to stand on end;
she who is stepped upon by the feet of Rāmacandra and the one who effects the destruction of Rāvaṇa. || 137 ||
Clad in garments of jewels, seated upon a chariot, adorned with golden ornaments, she is the restless presiding deity of modesty; she is graceful and wears the *liṅga*. 138.
Lakṣmī, the fickle one, she who has destroyed poison, the observer, world-renowned;
Lajjā, the goddess Lambodarī, the woman, the sustainer of the worlds. || 139 ||
The bestower of boons, the one who is saluted, the knowledge, the one belonging to Viṣṇu, she of pure form;
Vārāhī, the stainless one, the showerer, the excellent Lakṣmī, the playful one. 140.
Vinatā, who stands in the midst of the sky; she who is seated upon the lotus-throne;
Vāruṇī, born from the bamboo; Vītihotrā, the multiformed one. || 141 ||
Abiding in the midst of the circle of wind, she is the form of Viṣṇu, beloved of Brahmā;
she is the consort of Viṣṇu, Viṣṇumatī, the large-eyed one, and Vasundharā.
She is beloved by Vāmadeva, the shore, the wielder of the thunderbolt, and the milker of wealth;
her limbs are encompassed by the syllables of the Vedas, and she bestows the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. || 143 ||
She is the mother of Vāma, the consort of Vāsava, the supreme dweller in Vaikuṇṭha;
she is the beloved of Vyāsa, the bearer of armor, and she who is served by Vālmīki. || 144 ||
Śākambharī, Śivā, Śāntā, Śāradā, the refuge for those who seek shelter; she of the slender waist, of auspicious conduct, and the crusher of the demon Śumbha. || 145 ||
She is the radiant one, whose form is auspicious, who forms half the body of Śaṅkara;
she is crimson, pure in intention, brilliant white, and the one who effects the union with the head.
Śarāvatī, Śarānandā, Śarajyotsnā, Śubhānanā, Śarabhā, Śūlinī, Śuddhā, Śabarī, and Śukavāhanā. || 147 ||
The illustrious Śrīdharānandā, who bestows the bliss of hearing;
Śarvāṇī, who is to be worshipped by the night; she who possesses the six languages and is fond of the six seasons. || 148 ||
The Goddess resides in the six supports; she acts for the pleasure of the Six-faced One.
She is of the nature of the six limbs, possesses excellent intelligence, and is saluted by gods and asuras. (149)
Sarasvatī is the eternal support, the bringer of all auspiciousness;
she is fond of the chanting of the Sāman, subtle, the mother Sāvitrī, and born from the Sāman. 150.
She dwells in all abodes, is eternally blissful, possesses beautiful breasts, and has the ocean as her garment;
she is fond of all sovereignty, is perfection itself, and possesses the prowess of a virtuous kinsman.
She resides within the circle of the Seven Sages and dwells in the lunar orb;
she is omniscient, possesses intense compassion, and is devoid of equals or superiors. (152)
She is most exalted, free from attachment, possessed of excellent qualities, and the bestower of all desired things;
she is the honey-bee, the daughter of the Sun, the one with beautiful hair, and the embodiment of the Moon. 153.
Golden-hued, tawny, the utterer of the syllable *hrīṃ*, borne by swans, her limbs draped in silken garments, the daughter of the Ocean of Milk, she is Forgiveness itself. 154.
Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Pārvatī, and Sarasvatī; Vedagarbhā, Varārohā, Śrīgāyatrī, and Parāmbikā. || 155 ||
Thus, O Nārada, this collection of a thousand names of Gāyatrī bestows merit, destroys all sins, and grants great prosperity. (156)
Indeed, these names of Gāyatrī produce satisfaction;
they should especially be recited on the eighth lunar day together with the twice-born.

Having performed the recitation (japa), and especially having performed the fire-oblation (homa), worship (pūjā), and meditation (dhyāna), [this] must not be given to just anyone, and this is especially true for the Gāyatrī. || 158 ||
This should indeed be told to one who is devoted, a good disciple, and a worshiper of the gods;
it should not be shown to fallen practitioners or to mere kinsmen. 159.
In whose house a scripture is written, no fear from anyone arises;
even though she is fickle, Kamalā remains there, having become steadfast. (160)
This is a great secret, more hidden than the most hidden;
it bestows merit upon men and provides a treasure for the poor. (161)
It bestows liberation upon those seeking release and grants all desires to those possessed by longing;
indeed, the sick are freed from disease, and the bound are released from bondage.
Men who have committed the murder of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, the theft of gold, or even sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife, are released from that sin by doing this once. (163)
One is liberated simply by reciting [this] from the sin of accepting improper gifts, especially from eating what should not be eaten, and from [associating with] heretics, liars, and the like. 164.
O Lotus-born one, this stainless secret has been spoken by me;
it bestows union with Brahman upon men—this is the truth, the absolute truth, there is no doubt. || 165 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Thousand-Name Hymn of Gāyatrī," in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Ritual for Mantra Initiation.
Nārada said: I have heard the [section] called the Thousand Names of the Illustrious Gāyatrī, which bestows its fruit.
This hymn brings about great exaltation, confers supreme fortune, and is most excellent. || 1 ||
Now I wish to hear the supreme definition of initiation (dīkṣā),
without which there can be no eligibility for the mantra of the Goddess.
O Lord, describe in detail everything according to the general rule for Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and likewise for women.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, I shall explain the initiation for disciples of purified soul,
by which they obtain the qualification for the worship of the gods, the fire, the guru, and so forth.
That which bestows divine knowledge and brings about the destruction of sins is indeed declared as *dīkṣā* by those proficient in the Vedas and Tantras.
That [initiation] must certainly be performed, since it is considered to yield abundant fruit;
moreover, both the teacher and the disciple must be exceedingly pure in this regard.
The Guru, having duly performed all his morning duties, and having performed the bath, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and everything else according to the prescribed rules; || 7 ||
Carrying his water-pot and observing silence, he should go from the riverbank to his home;
having reached the sacrificial pavilion, he should enter there and take his place upon an excellent seat.
Having sipped water and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should properly prepare water mixed with fragrance and flowers,
over which the Astra-mantra has been recited seven times.
With that water, while reciting the Astra-mantra, the wise one should sprinkle the entire doorway; thereafter, he should perform the worship.
At the top of the Udumbara tree, one should worship the Lord Gaṇanātha, as well as Śrī and Sarasvatī, with perfumes and flowers while reciting their respective name-mantras.
One should worship Gaṅgā and Vighneśa on the right jamb of the door,
and Kṣetrapāla and Sūryajā on the left jamb of the door.
One should worship the deity of the weapon at the threshold with the weapon-mantra, while contemplating everywhere that all that is visible is composed of the Goddess. 13.
One should dispel divine obstacles by the recitation of weapon-mantras (*astramantra*);
terrestrial obstacles with kicks of the feet; and obstacles situated in the intermediate space [by gazing].
Then, touching the left branch [of the door], one should enter with the right foot.
Having entered and established the water-pot, and having prepared the general arghya offering; || 15 ||
And with that water for the guest-offering (arghya),
one should worship the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha), who is born from a lotus, in the south-western direction with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth.
Then the Guru should prepare the *pañcagavya* and, with that along with the *arghya* water,
sprinkle the pavilion as far as the arches and pillars.
One should indeed contemplate with the mind that all this is composed of the Goddess;
while reciting the root mantra with devotion, the sprinkling should be performed with the arrow-mantra.
Having recited the Śara-mantra, one should strike the edge of the pavilion;
then, having recited the Huṃ-mantra, one should perform the sprinkling.
One should fumigate the interior with incenses and then scatter the *vikirāḥ* (scattered offerings);
thereafter, one should sweep them away again with a broom made of *kuśa* grass.
O Sage, having formed that heap in the northeastern direction, one should establish it;
then, having performed the Puṇyāhavācana rite, one should satisfy the poor and the helpless.
Afterwards, having prostrated before one's own guru, one should sit upon a soft seat facing east and, according to the prescribed rule, meditate upon the deity of the mantra to be imparted.

O Sage, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other rites according to the very path previously described, one should indeed perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seer (ṛṣi) and other factors for the mantra to be imparted.
One should place the Sage upon the head, the Vedic meter upon the mouth,
the Deity within the lotus of the heart, and the Seed-syllable on the feet.
Having placed the *śakti* [mudrā] thereafter, and then from the sound of three claps (*tāla*),
the person should subsequently perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) with three snaps of the fingers (*choṭikā*).
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) while recollecting the root mantra, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā upon the body; that procedure is now described.
Having uttered "Oṃ Aṃ Namaḥ," the knower of mantras should place it on the head;
O Sage, in this very same manner, he should indeed place them in all the locations.
The best of beings should perform the placement of the root mantra and the six limbs upon the limbs,
sequentially on the fingers beginning with the thumb, and on the heart and other parts.

The sixfold ritual of the limbs (ṣaḍaṅgaka) is performed with exactly six mantras, beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ), and joined with the words *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, as well as *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*.

Thereafter, one should apply the placement of the syllables (*varṇanyāsa*) and so forth of the root mantra in the respective locations as prescribed in the specific ritual manual (*kalpa*); this is remembered as the procedure for placement (*nyāsavidhi*).
Then, one should contemplate a beautiful seat within this own body;
one should place Dharma on the right shoulder and Jñāna on the left shoulder.
O Sage, one should place detachment on the left thigh and sovereignty on the right thigh; one should then meditate upon unrighteousness in the region of the face.
On the left side at the region of the navel, and likewise on the right side,
one should again place the [qualities] beginning with non-existence (nañ) and those beginning with knowledge (jñāna), exactly as previously described.
O best of sages, dharma and the other [qualities] are said to be the feet of the seat;
whereas adharma and the others are remembered as its limbs by the preeminent sages. (34)
One should place Ananta in the center at the location of the heart on a spot with a soft seat;
upon that, one should place the pure lotus of the phenomenal world (prapañca), and within it, the sun, moon, and fire.
The practitioner of mantra should place [the deities] together with their constituent parts (kalās); I shall describe them briefly:
the twelve kalās of the Sun are known, and those of the Moon are sixteen.
The ten digits (kalās) of Fire have been declared; one should remember them as being endowed with those [digits], and then one should place Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas upon them.

The wise one should install the Self (ātman), the inner self (antarātman), the supreme self (paramātman), and the self that is knowledge (jñānātman); such is the conceptualization of the seat (pīṭha).
Having worshipped the seat with the mantra "Obeisance to [Name]’s seat," the practitioner should then meditate upon the Supreme Mother within it.
The mantra-practitioner should worship the deity of the mantra to be given, according to the procedure prescribed in the Kalpa,
with mental offerings and in accordance with the rules.
The wise one should display the mudrās prescribed in the ritual manual (kalpa) which cause delight;
for by performing them, joy arises for the Goddess.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, on the front of his own left side, he should properly draw a circular mandala upon a hexagon, joined with a square in its center.
Having drawn a triangle in the center, one should display the conch mudrā;
then one should worship the six limbs within the six corners with flowers and other offerings.
O best of sages, one should perform the worship of the six limbs in the corners starting from the southeast;
then, O best of sages, taking up the supporting vessel for the conch—
Having sprinkled [it] with the Astra-mantra, one should establish it there in the mandala;
having uttered "Maṃ" for the fire-mandala, and then for that which consists of ten kalās.
"Obeisance to the vessel for the arghya of such-and-such a goddess"—this mantra is also declared by the wise for the placement of the base of the conch. (46)
On the support (ādhāra), beginning from the east and proceeding in a clockwise direction, one should worship the ten fire-potencies (vahnikalā) situated within the fire-mandala. || 47 ||
Then, having sprinkled that excellent conch with the root mantra, one should place it upon its base while recollecting the root mantra. (48)
Having uttered "Aṃ" for the solar disc, which consists of twelve parts at the dvādaśānta, one should then recite: "Obeisance to the arghya-vessel of such-and-such a goddess. (49)
Having uttered the word "śaṃ" for the conch, one should pronounce "namaḥ";
with that [mantra], one should sprinkle the conch and worship it twelve times therein. || 50 ||
Having recited the twelve digits (kalās) of the Sun, beginning with Tapantī in their proper order,
one should then recite the Mātṛkā in reverse and the root mantra in reverse.
One should fill the conch with water and place there a digit of the moon,
having uttered "Oṃ, to the lunar orb," followed by "to the self of sixteen digits."
The mantra ending with the heart-mantra is remembered as: "O Amṛtā, [accept] this such-and-such arghya. One should worship the water with that mantra using the *sṛṇi* mudrā.
Having invoked the sacred fords (tīrthas) right there, one should mutter the mantra eight times;
having assigned the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅgas) to the water, one should worship the waters with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
One should recite the root mantra eight times and cover [the vessel] with the *matsyamudrā*.
Then, one should place the *prokṣaṇī* (sprinkling vessel) upon the conch in the southern direction.
Having poured a little water from the conch, one should sprinkle it everywhere;
thereafter, one should contemplate the objects of worship and one's own self as being completely purified.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, having drawn a Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala upon the altar in front of himself,
he should fill the center of the pericarp with rice grains.
Having spread darbha grass right there, one should place a ritual seat (kūrca) possessing the proper characteristics;
then, beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with the Pīṭhamaṇu, one should perform worship.
Having taken a flawless jar whose interior has been washed with water consecrated by mantras,
one should wrap it with a triple-stranded thread that is reddish-brown in color.

The preceptor should place [the vessel], which has nine gems within its belly, is provided with a tuft of grass, and is worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, upon that pedestal while reciting the Tāra mantra.
O Sage, one should contemplate the unity of the pitcher and the pedestal, and then fill it while reciting the Mātṛkā in reverse order with water from sacred fords.
Having recited the root mantra, one should fill [the vessel] with the thought that it is the deity itself,
using tender, fresh sprouts of the Aśvattha, Panasa, and Āmra trees.
The wise one should cover the mouth of the jar with a cup containing fruit and unbroken rice;
he should establish it and wrap it with a pair of cloths.
One should perform the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇasthāpana) with the mantra for installing the vital breaths;
one should gladden the supreme deity with the mudrās of invocation and the others. 64.
One should meditate upon that Supreme Sovereign Lady according to the method prescribed in the Kalpa;
one should then utter words of welcome and inquiries after her well-being in the presence of the Goddess.
Then one should offer water for the feet (pādya), and after that, the respectful offering (arghya) and water for sipping (ācamanīyaka);
then one should present the honey-mixture (madhuparka) along with an oil massage, and finally offer the bath to the Goddess.
Then he should give two garments made of pure, red silk;
thereafter, he should provide ornaments studded with various collections of gems.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the limbs of the Goddess according to the rules of the Mātṛkā using the phonemes encapsulated by Manu, one should worship her with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
O Sage, the fragrance consists of black agallochum combined with camphor,
as well as saffron and sandalwood together with musk.
One should offer flowers such as the *kundapuṣpa* and others to the Supreme Goddess.
For incense, one should use a great collection of *aguru*, *turuṣka*, *uśīra*, sandalwood, and sugar. (70)
It is traditionally taught that offerings mixed with honey are always dear to the Goddess in the form of incense.
Then, having offered many lamps, the wise man should present the food offering (naivedya).
One should offer water for each individual substance from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, and not otherwise;
thereafter, one should perform the worship of the limbs (*aṅgapūjā*) and the enclosures (*āvaraṇas*) as prescribed in the ritual manual.
Then, having worshipped the Goddess along with her attendants, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the south and having placed the fire there.
Having invoked the deity residing in the image there and worshipped it in due order,
one should then perform oblations with the Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, and indeed with the root mantra.
O Sage, one should then offer oblations twenty-five times with milk-rice mixed with ghee, and subsequently, one should again perform the sacrifice with the *vyāhṛti* mantras.
Having worshipped the Goddess with perfumes and other offerings, one should unite her with the pedestal;
then, having dismissed the fire, one should scatter an oblation of sacrificial food all around.
Then, having offered the fivefold service (pañcopacāra) consisting of perfumes, flowers, and so forth, along with betel, an umbrella, and chowries, to the attendants of the deity.
Then one should give [the offering] to the Goddess and recite the mantra a thousand times;
having offered the recitation, one should scatter [the offerings] in the northeast direction.
One should place a *karkarī* (water-pot) upon it, invoke Durgā therein, and worship her while reciting "Protect! Protect! and sprinkling water from its spout.
Chanting the weapon-mantra (astramantra), he should sprinkle the site while circumambulating it;
he should place the water-pot (karkarī) in its proper place and worship the deity of the weapon.
Thereafter, the guru, restrained in speech, should eat together with the disciple;
on that night, he should diligently sleep upon that very altar.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O sage, I shall now describe in brief, according to the prescribed rules and ritual injunctions, the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the altar (sthaṇḍila).
Having recited the root mantra, one should gaze at [the object] with the weapon mantra;
one should sprinkle it and perform the striking with that very armor mantra.
Sprinkling is thus prescribed; thereafter, one should draw lines all around, three by three, with their tips pointing eastward and northward.
Having sprinkled the pedestal with the *praṇava*, one should worship the pedestal of the Goddess,
beginning with the *ādhāraśakti* and ending with the *pīṭhamantra*.
Having invoked Śiva and Śivā, the supreme causes, upon that seat,
one should worship them with concentration using offerings such as fragrances and the like.
One should meditate on the Goddess, having bathed after her menses, closely united with Śaṅkara;
one should contemplate their amorous play for some time as they are overcome by passion. (87)
Then, having taken up the fire with a vessel, one should place it in front,
having set aside the portion for the flesh-eaters (kravyāda) by means of the previously mentioned rites of inspection and so forth.
Having consecrated the fire and uttered the seed-syllable *raṃ* immediately thereafter,
one should unite consciousness within it and consecrate it with the *praṇava*.
Then the Guru should display the *dhenumudrā* seven times;
having protected [the object] with the arrow-mantra, he should veil it with the armor-mantra.

Having circumambulated it three times in a clockwise direction, the best of beings, muttering the *tāra* mantra over the sacrificial pit while touching the ground with his knees, [performed the rite]. || 91 ||
With the thought that it is the seed of Śiva, one should cast the fire into the womb of the Goddess;
then, one should offer water for sipping to the God and to the Goddess, the Mother of the World.
"CIT PIṄGALA HANA DAHA PACA YUGMAṂ, followed by SARVAJÑA ĀJÑĀPAYA SVĀHĀ"—this is the mantra for the kindling of the fire. (93)
I worship Agni, the blazing one, the knower of all beings, the consumer of oblations—pure, golden-hued, kindled, and facing in every direction. 94.
With this mantra, he should praise that fire with supreme devotion;
then the best of preceptors should perform the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) of the fire-mantra.
Sahasrārcis, Svastipūrṇa, Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa, Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, and Dhanurdhara are remembered in this order. (96)
One should place the six limbs, joined with their respective seed-syllables, in the previously mentioned locations;
one should meditate upon the Fire-god as being golden-colored, three-eyed, and seated upon a lotus.
Then, the knower of mantras should sprinkle the supreme auspicious vessel— which holds the *iṣṭa*, the *śakti*, the *svastika*, and the *abhī*— over the *mekhalā* of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
One should strew darbha grass around [the altar] from the west, and then place the enclosing sticks (paridhis).
[The mandala] consists of a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, an eight-petaled lotus, and an outer enclosure (bhūpura).
One should either visualize the yantra of fire or draw it beforehand;
then, O Sage, one should worship Agni in its center with this mantra.
O Vaiśvānara, O Jātavedas, bring [the deity] from the west here;
having uttered the word "Lohitākṣapada," accomplish all rites. || 101 ||
The mantra ends with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā); with that, one should worship Vahni in the center and in all six corners—namely Hiraṇyā and likewise Gaganā.
One should worship those seven tongues— Red, Black, Radiant, Multiform, and Deep-Red— as well as the worship of the limbs upon the filaments.
On the petals, one should worship the forms [of the deities]: Śaktidhāriṇī, Svastikadhāriṇī, Jātavedas, Saptajihva, and Havyavāhana. (104)
Another is known as Aśvodaraja, while another is called Vaiśvānara;
Kaumāratejas is one, and Viśvamukha is remembered as Devamukha. (105)
The forms of the fires (Vahni-mūrtis) should begin with the word "tārāgnaye" and end with "namaḥ.
One should [place] the world-protectors (Lokapālas) in the four directions, equipped with their weapons, such as the thunderbolt (vajra), and so forth. 106.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Then, having performed the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles as well as the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*), one should perform the oblation (*homa*); having taken the ghee with the *sruva* ladle, one should indeed proceed.

From the southern portion of the clarified butter, one should offer it into the right eye of the fire with the mantra "Svāhā to Agni"; likewise, from the other [northern] side, one should offer it into the left [eye].
O best of men, having taken ghee from the middle [portion] with the mantra "Svāhā to Soma," he should then offer it into the middle channel with the mantra "Svāhā to Agni and Soma. (109)
Then, taking ghee from the southern portion and placing it in the mouth, one should subsequently offer it with the mantra: "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā! (agnaye sviṣṭakṛtsvāhā).
Then the practitioner should offer oblations with the seven vyāhṛtis;
thereafter, he should offer them three times with the fire-mantra (agnimantra). || 111 ||
Then, O Sage, for the sake of performing the purificatory rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna), one should offer eight oblations of clarified butter at a time, using the syllable Om alone.

The rite of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), followed by the birth-rite (jātakarma), the naming ceremony (nāmakarma), and likewise the first outing (upaniṣkramaṇa). || 113 ||
The feeding of rice, as well as the tonsure ceremony, the tying of the sacred thread, and likewise the Mahānāmnī vow, followed by the Upaniṣad vow. (114)
The sacraments of the Godāna and the marriage have been declared as enjoined by the Vedas;
thereafter, having worshipped Śiva and Pārvatī, one should bid them farewell.
The practitioner should offer five fuel-sticks (samidh) directed toward the fire;
thereafter, he should also offer one oblation for each of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇas). || 116 ||
O Sage, having taken ghee into the *sruk* ladle four times with the *sruva* spoon, and having covered it with that very same spoon while remaining seated on one's own seat; 117.
Then, one should offer oblations into the fire with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
and subsequently offer ten oblations with the Mahāgaṇeśa mantra.
Having worshipped the seat in the fire and meditated upon the deity of the mantra to be offered within the fire,
one should [offer it] twenty-five times into its mouth.
One should offer oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of unifying the faces, while contemplating the identity of the fire and the deity together with oneself. (120)
Then the best of practitioners should meditate upon [the deity] as unified;
he should offer oblations separately for the six limbs of the deities.
O best of sages, one should offer exactly eleven oblations;
by this, O sage, the union of the channel occurs between the fire and the deity.
O Sage, one should likewise offer oblations with clarified butter, following the sequence of each individual repetition.
Then, one should perform oblations with the substances prescribed in the ritual manual, or else with sesame seeds,
a thousand times for each syllable of the root mantra of the deity, using the Gajendramokṣaṇa mantra.
O Sage, having performed the oblation in this manner, one should then meditate upon the Goddess as being satisfied,
as well as the presiding goddesses of the enclosures and the deities of fire and the other directions.
Then, [he should initiate] the disciple who has bathed well, performed the rites beginning with the *saṃnyāsa*,
is provided with two garments, and is endowed with golden ornaments.
Holding a pure water-pot in his hand, he should approach the vicinity of the sacrificial pit;
then the disciple, having paid homage to the gurus and the members of the assembly, [should proceed]. (127)
Having paid homage to the family deity, he should then enter there and sit upon a seat;
thereafter, the Guru should look upon that disciple with a compassionate gaze.
One should contemplate that consciousness as being united within one's own body; thereafter follows the purification of the paths (adhvan) residing within the body of the disciple. 129.
The wise one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) by means of divine vision, so that the self may become purified and fit for the grace of the gods and other beings. 130.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: One should meditate upon the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) within the body of the disciple in their proper sequence:
the path of the Kalās (kalādhvāna) in the feet, and then the path of the Tattvas (tattvādhvaka) in the navel.

One should place the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) at the navel, the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan) at the heart, the path of the words (padādhvan) at the forehead, and the path of the mantras (mantrādhvan) at the head.
Touching the disciple with the *kūrca* grass while [offering] sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter, he should recite the mantra:
"I purify this path, svāhā! (133).
One should indeed offer oblations eight times for each path, beginning with the path of Tārā;
thereafter, one should contemplate those six paths as dissolved into Brahman.

Therefore, the Guru should indeed generate it again by means of the path of emanation (sṛṣṭimārga), and then join that consciousness, which resides within himself, once more with the disciple. || 135 ||
Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should lead the deity into the water-pot;
then, having again offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* as well as the limb-oblations (*aṅgāhuti*) to the fire.
Having offered each one individually, the Guru should dissolve the fire into himself;
thereafter, the Guru should bind the eyes of the disciple with a cloth.
With the Netra-mantra, he should lead that disciple from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to the mandala;
he should cause the disciple, by means of his hand, to offer a handful of flowers to the principal goddess.
Having removed the blindfold, he should cause [the disciple] to sit upon a seat of kuśa grass;
then he should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) within the body of the disciple according to the prescribed method.
Then, having performed the ritual placements (nyāsa) as prescribed by the mantra upon the body of the disciple,
one should cause the disciple to enter the mandala, while [the other deities] remain within the water-pot.
One should place the *pallava* upon the head of the disciple and recite the *mātṛkā*;
then one should bathe the disciple with the waters contained in the jar, which are identical in essence to the deity.
And one should immediately perform the sprinkling of water from the *vardhanī* for the sake of protection;
then the disciple, having risen and put on two garments, [should proceed]. (142)
Having smeared himself with ashes, he should lie down in the presence of the Guru.
Then, the Guru [should visualize] Śivā, who has emerged from his own heart.
The treasury of compassion should meditate upon her having entered the heart of the disciple;
he should worship her with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, while indeed contemplating the identity of the two.
Then, placing his own hand upon the head of the disciple, the Guru should impart the great mantra of the Great Goddess into the disciple's right ear; this is the thirty-first [rite]. 145.
O Sage, the disciple should also recite the mantra one hundred and eight times,
and prostrate himself on the ground like a staff before that Guru, who is the very embodiment of the deity.
One should offer one's entire possession to him for as long as one lives, with a mind focused on no other;
having given sacrificial fees to the officiating priests, one should also feed the Brahmins. || 147 ||
One should [feed] married women, maidens, and young brahmins in every way, as well as the wretched, the helpless, and the poor, while remaining free from stinginess regarding wealth. 148.
Realizing that one's own purpose has been accomplished, one should constantly propitiate the Manu.
Thus has the unsurpassed ritual of initiation been correctly explained to you. (149)
Having reflected upon this in its entirety, take refuge in the lotus feet of the Goddess;
for there exists no other supreme dharma for a Brahmin here on earth. (150)

A follower of the Vedas should teach the Manu according to the sequence prescribed in his own Gṛhya-sūtra; however, a follower of Tantra should do so according to the Tantric method—this is the eternal rule.
Those various [beings] shall perform those respective applications as they have been taught, and not otherwise.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"O Nārada, everything that was asked by you has thus been explained by me."
Henceforth, worship eternally the lotus feet of Parāmbā;
by worshipping her constantly, I have attained supreme bliss.
Vyāsa said:
O King, having thus spoken all this unsurpassed teaching to Nārada,
he closed his eyes in meditative absorption and contemplated the lotus feet of the Goddess.
Then the blessed Nārāyaṇa, the crest-jewel of the best of sages,
and Nārada as well, having bowed to their supreme teacher Nārāyaṇa,
immediately departed for penance, longing for a vision of the Goddess. || 155 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Initiation into Mantras," in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the Manifestation of the Supreme Power.
Janamejaya said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, best among those who have mastered all the scriptures!
For all the twice-born, however, the worship of Śakti is declared in the Vedas.
O Lord, why would the twice-born, having abandoned her who is to be performed daily at the three junctions of time or at other times, accept other deities? || 2 ||
Some Vaiṣṇavas are indeed seen, and others are Gāṇapatyas;
there are Kāpālikas, those devoted to the path of the Cīnas, and those wearing bark garments.
Digambaras, Buddhists, Cārvākas,
and others like them are seen in great numbers in the world, devoid of faith in the Vedas.
O Brahman, you ought to tell me what the cause is here;
for these men are intelligent, learned, and experts in various systems of logic.
Indeed, they do exist even within the Vedas, though they are devoid of faith;
for no one here desires to abandon their own welfare through their own intelligence.
What is the reason for this? Therefore, speak, O best among the knowers of the Vedas;
the greatness of Maṇidvīpa was previously described by you.
O sinless one, tell that to me, your devoted and faithful follower: what is that supreme and most exalted abode of the Goddess like? || 8 ||
"When the gurus are pleased, they indeed speak even that which is secret.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the king, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa [spoke]. (9)
Then, O lords of sages, he narrated everything in due order, hearing which the faith of the twice-born in the Vedas increases. (10)
Vyāsa said:
You have asked well, O King, at the proper time and what is appropriate for that time. You are wise regarding the Vedas, and you are clearly seen to be full of faith.
Formerly, O great king, the Daityas, arrogant with pride, waged war against the gods for a hundred years, which was a source of great wonder.
O King, their battle was truly one that brought about the destruction of the world, featuring various weapons and missiles and variegated with diverse illusions.
Through the entry of the grace of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), the gods conquered the Daityas in battle;
abandoning the earth and heaven, they went to the abode of Pātāla.
Then the gods, filled with great joy and full of pride, began to describe their own prowess to one another everywhere out of delusion.
Why should victory not be ours, since our greatness is such? O Daityas, where is he who is superior to all, and where are you, base and devoid of prowess? (16)
We are all illustrious ones who bring about creation, preservation, and destruction;
what talk can there be of base men or even of Daityas before us? (17)
Not knowing the power of the Supreme Śakti, they fell into delusion;
at that very moment, the Mother of the World (Jagadambikā) acted to bestow her grace upon them.
O King, he appeared in the form of a Yakṣa, filled with compassion, resembling ten million suns in brilliance yet as cool as ten million moons. (19)
Having seen that supremely beautiful splendor, which was never seen before, possessing a luster equal to ten million flashes of lightning and devoid of hands, feet, and other limbs; || 20 ||
Then, filled with wonder, they said: "What is this? What is this? "Is this the deed of the Daityas, or is it some great illusion? (21)
Or was she created by someone as a source of wonder for the gods?
Then they all gathered together and held an excellent deliberation.
Having gone near the yakṣa, one should also ask, "Who are you?
Then, having ascertained his strength or weakness, the counter-measure should be undertaken. (23)
Then Indra, the lord of the gods, having summoned Agni, spoke:
"Go, O Agni, for you are our most excellent mouth. (24)
Then, having gone there, find out what this yakṣa is;
thus spoke the Thousand-eyed One, his words filled with his own prowess. (25)
Emerging with speed, that fire went into the presence of the Yakṣa;
then the Yakṣa spoke to the consumer of oblations: "Who are you? (26)
"And what is this vigor in you? Tell me all of that before me.
He replied, "I am Agni; likewise, I am Jātavedas. (27)
"The power to burn everything resides within me;
therefore, this supreme Yakṣa, who is a blazing fire, has placed a blade of grass before me. (28)
If you indeed possess the power to burn this universe,
then the Fire-god exerted every effort with all his might.
He was unable to burn even a blade of grass; ashamed, he went before the gods.
When questioned by the gods regarding the matter, the consumer of oblations (Agni) related everything that had occurred.
"O gods, our pride regarding the lordship over all things and other such matters is indeed in vain.
Then the slayer of Vṛtra summoned Vāyu and spoke these words.
The entire universe is woven upon you, and it moves by means of your activities;
you are the form of the vital breath for all, the sustainer of every power.
Go yourself and find out what this yakṣa is;
there is no one else capable of knowing that supreme splendor which is the yakṣa.
Having heard the words of the Thousand-eyed One, which were woven with the weight of his virtues,
he went quickly with pride to where the Yakṣa was shining.
Having seen the Yakṣa, he then spoke to Vāyu in gentle words: "Who are you? What power do you possess? Tell me everything before me. (35)
Then, having heard the words of the yakṣa, Marut spoke out of pride:
"I am Mātariśvan," and he said, "I am Vāyu. (36)
Indeed, my vigor lies in the moving and grasping of everything; through my activity, the entire world becomes possessed of all its functions. (37)
Having heard these words of Vāyu, the Supreme Light spoke:
"This [world] is but a blade of grass before you; move it as you wish. (38)
"Otherwise, abandon this pride and go ashamed to Vāsava.
Having heard the words of the Yakṣa, Vāyu, endowed with all powers, [departed]. (39)
He made an effort, yet he did not move from his own place;
then that Wind-god, casting aside his pride, went bashfully to the side of the God.
He related the entire account, the cause for the quenching of their pride:
"We, who were conceited with false pride, were not capable of knowing this. (41)
A supernatural, extremely terrible, and yakṣa-like radiance appeared;
thereupon, all the hosts of gods addressed the Thousand-eyed One.
"Since you are the king of the gods, you must know this yakṣa in its true nature.
Thereupon, Indra, out of great pride, rushed toward that yakṣa.
Then that supreme splendor in the form of a yakṣa, higher than the highest, fled;
thereafter, that yakṣa vanished from the presence of Vāsava.
Even Vāsava, the king of the gods, became exceedingly ashamed;
due to the absence of conversation with the Yakṣa, he felt a sense of insignificance in his mind. (45)
Henceforth, I must not go to the assembly of the gods;
for what could I say there to the deities that would not appear as my own insignificance? (46)
Therefore, the abandonment of the body is better; for pride is indeed the wealth of the great.
When pride is lost, life is undoubtedly equal to death. || 47 ||
Having thus resolved and abandoned his pride right there, the Lord of the Gods sought refuge in him whose life-story is such as this. (48)
At that very moment, a celestial voice arose in the sky:
"O Thousand-eyed One, chant the seed-syllable of Māyā; by that, become happy. (49)
Then, subsisting on no food for a hundred thousand years with eyes closed in meditation, he recited the supreme seed-syllable of Māyā, which is higher than the highest.
Suddenly, on the ninth day of the month of Caitra, while the sun was at the meridian,
that very same light manifested once again in that very same place.
In the center of a circle of light is a young maiden in the bloom of youth,
with a luster like a shining hibiscus flower and a radiance like ten million rising suns.
She wears the cool-rayed moon as her crown, with her breasts revealed by the hem of her garment;
she holds in her four excellent hands the boon-granting gesture, the noose, the goad, and the gesture of fearlessness.
I bow to the Mother, who possesses beautiful limbs and delicate creeper-like arms, who is auspicious, who is a wish-fulfilling tree for her devotees, and who is adorned with various ornaments. (54)
She has three eyes and is adorned with a mass of hair in the form of a jasmine garland;
she is praised from the four directions by the four Vedas personified.
With her rows of teeth she has made the ground all around as red as rubies;
with a face of peaceful smiles, she is more beautiful than ten million gods of love.
[He saw] the goddess named Umā, the auspicious daughter of Himavat, standing before him, clothed in red garments and anointed with red sandalwood paste. (57)
There, Vāsava beheld the embodiment of unfeigned compassion, the cause of all causes, his inner heart faltering with love.
Then, with eyes filled with tears of love and his body covered in horripilation, he prostrated himself like a staff at the feet of the Lord of the World. (59)
With his neck bowed in devotion, he praised him with various hymns;
being exceedingly pleased, he asked: "What is this? Is it a Yakṣa? (60)
"And why did it manifest? Tell me all of that, O beautiful one.
Having heard his words, she, an ocean of compassion, spoke: 61.
This form of mine is Brahman, the cause of all causes;
it is the substratum of Māyā, the witness of all, and free from all affliction.
That state which all the Vedas declare, which all austerities proclaim,
and desiring which they lead a life of celibacy— [that state I shall tell you briefly].
I shall declare that state to you in brief. || 63 ||
"Oṃ," the single-syllable Brahman, they say is identical to "hrīṃ";
these two seed-syllables are my primary mantras, O best of gods. (64)
Since I create the entire universe possessing two parts,
one of those parts is proclaimed to be named Saccidānanda.
The second portion is said to be that which is designated as Māyā-prakṛti;
and that Māyā is the Supreme Śakti, while I, the Sovereign Goddess, am the Possessor of Power (Śaktimat).
O best of gods, this Māyā of mine has attained non-difference from me, just as moonlight is inseparable from the moon; she consists of the state of equilibrium.
At the time of dissolution, she remains non-different from me alone;
indeed, by the power of the ripening of the karma of living beings, [she manifests] once again.
Thus, that form which is unmanifest attains manifestation;
however, that state which is inward-turned is designated as Māyā. (69)
But that illusion which is directed outward is designated by the word "tamas";
from that tamas, which is of an outward-turned nature, the arising of sattva is born. (70)
O best of gods, it is at the beginning of creation that the quality of rajas arises;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are said to consist of the three qualities.
Brahmā has a predominance of the quality of rajas; Viṣṇu would have a predominance of sattva;
and Rudra, who assumes the form of the cause of all, has a predominance of tamas.
The gross body is Brahmā; the subtle body is remembered as Hari; Rudra is the causal body, but the fourth state is indeed I myself.
But that state of equilibrium which has been described as having the form of the inner ruler of all—
beyond that is the Supreme Brahman, my own form, devoid of all material form.
My form is said to be twofold: devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and possessed of qualities (saguṇa).
That which is devoid of qualities is free from māyā; that which is possessed of qualities is joined with māyā. (75)
Having created the entire world and having entered into its midst,
I incessantly impel the individual soul according to its karma and according to its acquired knowledge.
Indeed, I alone impel Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— the very essence of the cause— toward creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Out of fear of me the wind blows, and out of fear the sun moves;
Indra, Agni, and Death likewise act so; thus I am remembered as the supreme among all. (78)
"By my grace, victory has been obtained by you in every way;
I cause you to dance like wooden puppets. (79)
Sometimes there is victory for the gods, and sometimes victory for the Daityas;
independent and by my own will, I perform everything in accordance with the law of karma.
Having forgotten me, who am the soul of all, out of your own pride, you—
your selves shrouded by egoism— have fallen into an endless delusion.
Then, in order to bestow grace, my unsurpassed splendor suddenly emerged from your body as a Yakṣa. || 82 ||
Henceforth, having abandoned pride born of the body along with all worldly attachments, take refuge in me alone, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss. 83.
Vyāsa said: Having spoken thus, the Great Goddess, the Sovereign Primordial Nature (Mūlaprakṛti),
immediately vanished while being praised with devotion by the gods.
Then, having abandoned all pride, they all properly propitiated the supreme lotus feet of the Goddess, who is higher than the highest.
At all times, during the three junctions of the day, they were all constantly intent on the recitation of the Gāyatrī;
they always worshipped the Goddess with their shares of the sacrificial offerings and other rites.
Thus, in the Satya Yuga, all were intent upon the recitation of the Gāyatrī,
their minds fully absorbed in the recitation of both the Tāra and the Hṛllekhā.
Nowhere in the Veda is the worship of Viṣṇu declared to be obligatory;
likewise, there is no mandatory initiation (dīkṣā) for Viṣṇu, nor is there any for Śiva.
The meditation on the Gāyatrī is eternal and proclaimed by all the Vedas;
without it, there is certainly a downfall for the Brāhmaṇa in every respect. (89)
To that extent alone is the twice-born one’s duty fulfilled; indeed, he has no further dependence on anything else.
A twice-born man who is proficient in the Gāyatrī alone shall attain liberation.
"Whether one performs other rites or does not perform them," Manu himself has declared;
yet, having abandoned that Gāyatrī, one should be solely devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu. (91)

A Brahmin devoted to the worship of Śiva goes to hell in every way. Therefore, O King, in the first age, all the best of the twice-born were intent on the chanting of the Gāyatrī and were devoted to the lotus feet of the Goddess.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Supreme Power," in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
An exposition on the causes for the faith of the Brahmins and others in the worship of deities other than Gāyatrī.
Vyāsa said: "O Lord, once upon a time, after fifteen years had passed..."
Due to the power of the karma of living beings, Śatakratu did not send rain.
Due to a lack of rain, there occurred an extreme famine that caused total destruction;
indeed, it was impossible to count the number of corpses in every single house.
Some, afflicted by hunger, devour horses or wild boars;
and other people eat the corpses of men.
Afflicted by hunger, all those men set out to devour the child, the mother of the child, the woman, and even the man. || 4 ||
Many Brahmins there engaged in excellent deliberation: "Gautama, whose wealth is asceticism, exists; he will remove our distress. (5)
Now everyone must go together to the hermitage of Gautama,
to the hermitage of Gautama who is currently intent upon the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra.
"It is heard that there is plenty of food there, and many living beings have gone thither.
Having reflected thus, the Brahmins, who were householders maintaining the sacred fire-rituals, [set out].
Accompanied by their cattle and their horses, they went to the hermitage of Gautama;
