some came from the eastern region, and others from the southern region.
Those from the west and those from the north arrived from various directions;
seeing the assembly of brahmins, Gautama prostrated himself before them.
He honored the Brahmins with offerings such as seats and the like,
and then inquired after their welfare and the purpose of their arrival.
Smiling, they all related their respective accounts;
seeing those Brahmins distressed, the sage granted them freedom from fear.
"This is your dwelling; I am your servant in every respect.
O Brahmins, what concern is there for you when I, your servant, am present? (12)
I am blessed at this moment, O you all whose wealth is asceticism; by the mere sight of you, my evil deeds turn into meritorious acts.
They all purify my home with the dust of their feet;
who else but I could be so fortunate through your grace? (14)
"All must remain here in comfort, devoted to the twilight prayers and the recitation of mantras.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus consoled them all, the sage Gautama, the king of sages, then—
With his neck bowed in devotion, he prayed to Gāyatrī:
"Obeisance to you, O Goddess Mahāvidyā, Mother of the Vedas, who are higher than the highest! (16)
O Mother, who consists of the great mantras beginning with the *vyāhṛtis*, who takes the form of the *praṇava*,
whose nature is the state of equilibrium, salutations to you who take the form of the syllable *hrīṃ*.
I bow to you, O Goddess, whose very nature is *svāhā* and *svadhā*, the bestower of all goals, the wish-fulfilling creeper for devotees, and the witness of the three states of existence. (18)

She whose nature transcends the fourth state (turyātīta), who consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss, who is to be known through all the Vedāntas, and who dwells within the solar orb. || 19 ||
In the morning I bow eternally to her as a girl of red complexion; at midday, to her as a supreme young woman; and in the evening, to her as an old woman of black complexion.
"O Goddess, who brings all beings under your control, O Supreme Sovereign, forgive me!
Thus praised, the Mother of the World granted her direct vision.
She gave him a full vessel by which all nourishment would be provided;
that Mother said to the sage, "Whatever desire you wish for," (22)
"A vessel that fulfills his merit shall be given by me.
Having spoken thus, the goddess Gāyatrī, the supreme power, vanished.
From that [place], O King, heaps of food resembling mountains emerged,
as well as various foods of six flavors and diverse kinds of grasses.
And divine ornaments, silken garments, the commencement of sacrifices, and various ritual vessels; || 25 ||
O King, whatever was desired by that high-souled sage,
all of that emerged from that full vessel of Gāyatrī.
Then, having summoned all the sages, Gautama, the king of sages,
joyfully gave them wealth, grain, ornaments, and garments.
Cows, buffaloes, and other animals emerged from the full vessel;
he gave away the sacrificial implements that had come forth, such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
All of them, having gathered together at the word of the sage, performed sacrifices;
that very place became preeminent, resembling heaven itself.
Whatever beautiful object is seen within the three worlds,
all that is produced there from the vessel bestowed by Gāyatrī.
The wives shine like celestial damsels with their ornaments and other finery;
the sages resemble gods with their garments, sandalwood paste, and decorations. (31)
A perpetual festival commenced within the circle of the sage’s hermitage;
there was no fear whatsoever of disease or the like, nor was there any fear of demons anywhere.
That hermitage of the sage extended for a hundred yojanas on all sides;
and whatever other living beings there were, they too gathered there. (33)
Then that self-possessed one, having granted them all freedom from fear,
nourished them through various kinds of great sacrifices duly performed for the sake of the gods.
They attained supreme satisfaction and sang the praises of the sage;
then the highly illustrious slayer of Vṛtra again recited a verse in the assembly.
"Aha! This wish-fulfilling tree of ours, once firmly established, surely fulfills our desires;
otherwise, where would there be such an offering of oblations or sacrificial fat at such an untimely moment?"
But where the hope for life is extremely difficult to maintain. || 36 ||
In this manner, for twelve years, that king of sages, entirely devoid of even a scent of pride, nurtured the preeminent ascetics like his own sons. (37)
The best of sages established the supreme abode of Gāyatrī, where the Mother of the Universe is worshipped by all the foremost of sages. (38)
Even today, that Goddess is seen there in the morning as a young girl, due to the performance of purificatory rites with supreme devotion three times a day.
At midday she appeared as a young woman, but at evening she was seen as an old woman;
once, at that place, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived.
Jingling his ornaments and singing of the supreme qualities of Gāyatrī,
he sat down in the midst of the assembly of sages whose souls were purified.
Honored most highly by Gautama and others, he, whose mind was tranquil,
recounted various stories concerning the glory of Gautama.
O Brahman-sage, in the assembly of the gods, the king of the gods sang of your manifold, pure, and supreme fame arising from your nurturing of the sages.
Having heard the words of the Lord of Śacī, I have come to see you;
you are blessed, O best of sages, by the grace of the Mother of the World. 44.
Having spoken thus to that best of sages, he went to the abode of Gāyatrī;
with eyes blossoming with love, he beheld that Mother of the World.
Having praised the Goddess according to the prescribed rites, he returned once more to heaven.
Then, those Brāhmaṇas who were staying there, supported by the sage, [remained]. (46)
Having heard of the sage’s excellence, they became distressed with envy and thought:
"We must certainly act in every way so that his fame shall not increase. (47)
"It shall happen later when the time has arrived"—this was certain for all of them.
Then, after some time, rain fell upon the surface of the earth.
O best of kings, there was abundance in all lands;
hearing news of this prosperity, all the Brāhmaṇas gathered together.
"Alas, alas, O King! They have made an effort to curse Gautama;
blessed indeed are their parents, from whom such an offspring was born! (50)
O King, who indeed is able to describe the greatness of Time?
O monarch, a single cow was created by Māyā as an old woman on the verge of death.
And at that time, during the hour for the fire-sacrifice, she entered the hermitage of the sage;
being driven away by his shouts of "Hum hum," she gave up her life at that very moment.
"The cow has been killed by this wicked one! thus cried out those twice-born ones.
Having completed the fire-oblation, the sage was struck with the utmost amazement. (53)
With eyes closed in meditative concentration, he reflected upon the cause;
having realized that all this had been done by the twice-born, he understood it at that very moment.
He harbored a supreme wrath like that of Rudra at the time of universal dissolution,
and with eyes bloodshot from anger, he cursed all the sages.
If you are not oriented toward the Mother of the Vedas, Gāyatrī, nor toward meditation upon her or the recitation of her mantra, you are in every way the lowest of Brahmins. (56)
"You are always averse to the Vedas, to the sacrifices prescribed in the Vedas, and likewise to the occupations related to them; you are the lowest of Brahmins. (57)
O lowest of Brahmins, you have always been averse to Śiva, to His mantra, and likewise to the scripture of Śiva. (58)
"O lowest of Brahmins, you are always averse to meditation upon and the stories of Śrī Devī, the primordial nature. (59)
Likewise, regarding the mantra of the Goddess, her sacred site, and the performance of ritual acts, you have always been averse to these, O lowest of Brahmins. (60)
In your desire to witness the festival of the goddesses and in the chanting of the names of the goddesses, you have always been averse;
you are the lowest of Brahmins. (61)
O lowest of Brahmins, you have always been averse to the presence of a devotee of the Goddess as well as to the worship of a devotee of the Goddess. (62)
O lowest of Brahmins, you have always been averse to the desire to witness the festival of Śiva and to the worship of a devotee of Śiva. (63)
"Rudrākṣa beads, bilva leaves, and likewise pure ashes—you base Brahmins are always turned away from these. (64)
"You are always averse to the Vedic and Smārta traditions, to right conduct, and likewise to the path of knowledge; therefore, you are the lowest of Brāhmaṇas. (65)
"You are always the lowest of Brahmins, for you are never inclined toward the practice of peace, self-control, and other such means, nor toward steadfastness in the knowledge of non-duality. (66)
"Even regarding the performance of daily rites and the means for the Agnihotra and other sacrifices, you are always averse; you are the lowest of Brahmins. (67)
You are always averse to the private recitation of the Vedas, to formal study, and likewise to the teaching of them; you are the lowest of Brahmins. (68)
Indeed, in matters such as the gift of cows and other charities, as well as in the ancestral śrāddha rites, you have always been averse to them; you are the lowest of Brāhmaṇas. (69)
"O lowest of Brahmins, you are always averse to performing penances such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa."
Those who possess faith and devotion toward deities other than the Śrīdevī, and who are marked with the conch, discus, and so forth, are the lowest of Brāhmaṇas. (71)
O lowest of Brahmins, may you be ever devoted to the doctrines of the Kāpālikas, take delight in the Buddhist scriptures, and be intent upon the conduct of heretics. 72.
Likewise, those who sell their father, mother, son, brother, or daughter, as well as those who sell their wife—behold, they are the lowest of Brahmins. (73)
Likewise, those who sell the Vedas, those who sell sacred pilgrimage sites, and those who sell dharma—such are the lowest of Brahmins. (74)
O lowest of Brahmins, may you become possessed of faith in the Pañcarātra, in the science of erotics (kāmaśāstra), in the Kāpālika doctrine, and in Buddhism! 75.
Those who approach their mother’s daughters and likewise those who approach their sisters, and all those who are lustful for the wives of others—be they the lowest of Brahmins! (76)
Those born of your lineage— both women and men alike—
shall be consumed by the curse I have given you and shall become just like you.
What is the use of my speaking at length? The Supreme Gāyatrī, the primordial nature and sovereign lady, has indeed become enraged with you. (78)
"May your dwelling always be in pits such as blind wells.
Vyāsa said:
Having uttered such a verbal punishment, he then touched water for purification.
Filled with supreme devotion, he went for the purpose of beholding Gāyatrī;
he prostrated before the Great Goddess, and she too, the goddess higher than the highest, [honored him].
Having seen the work of the Brahmins, he indeed felt wonder in his heart;
even today, her face is seen to be filled with that same wonder. (81)
With her lotus-face smiling, she said to that best of sages:
"Milk offered to a serpent only results in poison. (82)
"O illustrious one, bring peace; such is the course of karma.
Having thus prostrated before the goddess, he then departed for his own hermitage.
Then, by the Brahmins consumed by the curse, the masses of the Vedas were forgotten;
Gāyatrī was forgotten by everyone, and that was like a marvel. (84)
Then, having all assembled together and filled with remorse,
they prostrated themselves before that best of sages, falling upon the ground like a staff.
They did not utter a single word, but stood with their faces cast down in shame, saying again and again, "Be gracious! Be gracious! Be gracious! (86)
Having surrounded the lord of sages on all sides, they made their request;
then the sage, his heart filled with compassion, spoke to them.
"Your stay shall be in Kumbhīpāka until the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa;
know this in every way that my word shall not be false. (88)
Thereafter, in the Kali age, you two shall indeed take birth on earth;
all this that I have spoken shall certainly come to pass, and not otherwise.
If you have any desire for the liberation of the fisherman, then the lotus-feet of Gāyatrī should always be served by all. (90)
Vyāsa said:
Having thus dismissed them all, Gautama, the best of sages,
attained peace in his heart, thinking that what was destined to happen had come to pass.
For this reason, O King, when the wise Kṛṣṇa had departed and the Kali age had set in, they emerged from the Kumbhīpāka hell.
Those Brāhmaṇas born on earth who were formerly consumed by curses, those who are devoid of the three daily junctions (sandhyās), and those who lack devotion to the Gāyatrī; || 93 ||
Devoid of devotion to the Vedas and following heretical doctrines, they are bereft of the performance of virtuous rites such as the Agnihotra, as well as the utterances of Svadhā and Svāhā.
Some never understand the unmanifest primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti),
while others, marked with heated seals, are devoted to sensual conduct.
The Kāpālikas, the Kaulikas, the Buddhists, the Jains, and others— even though they are all learned scholars— they are all promoters of wicked conduct.
Those who are lecherous toward the wives of others and devoted to wicked conduct shall all,
by their own deeds, go again to the Kumbhīpāka hell.
Therefore, O King, the Supreme Goddess should be served with one's whole being;
neither the worship of Viṣṇu nor the worship of Śiva is as constant.
And the constant worship of Śakti is that without which one falls downward;
everything you asked, O sinless one, has been told by me in brief. 99.
Henceforth, listen to the beautiful description of Maṇidvīpa, which is the supreme abode of the Primordial Bhuvaneśī, the forest-fire to the world of existence. 100.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Causes for the Faith of Brāhmaṇas and Others in the Worship of Deities Other than Gāyatrī," in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of Maṇidvīpa. Vyāsa said:
Above the world of Brahmā lies that world which has been heard of as existing.
That very place is Maṇidvīpa, where the Goddess shines resplendent.
Because he is superior to everything, he is therefore remembered as the "All-world" (Sarvaloka);
in ancient times, this was fashioned by the Supreme Mother herself through the desire of her mind.
In the very beginning, for the purpose of his own dwelling, by means of his primordial nature (prakṛti),
he created a world superior to Kailāsa and even more excellent than Vaikuṇṭha.
The entire world is remembered as superior even to all of Goloka;
indeed, nothing as beautiful as that exists anywhere within the three worlds.
O best of beings, that very [Lord] is the parasol for the three worlds, destroying the heat of worldly existence,
and is the shade for all cosmic eggs.
The ocean of nectar, extending for many yojanas and being equally deep, surrounds the Island of Jewels on all sides.
It was crowded with hundreds of waves tossed up by the friction of the Maruts;
it possessed sands as bright as jewels and was filled with large fish and conchs.
It was cooled by droplets from the waves produced by the friction of the ripples,
and it was filled with the coming and going of various ships equipped with diverse banners.
Then, a great mountain, radiant on all sides with jewel-trees upon its slopes,
fashioned from the northern region of Ayodhātu, appeared in the sky.
A great rampart seven yojanas wide extends there;
[the guards] are skilled in various weapons and missiles, and are experts in various modes of warfare.
Guardians dwell here, rejoicing on all sides;
it is provided with four gates and attended by hundreds of gatekeepers.
O King, surrounded by various hosts of goddesses full of devotion, those gods who come for the sake of beholding the Lord of the Universe [arrive]. (12)
Their hosts dwell here, as do their mounts;
for that place is filled with the sound of bells clashing together from hundreds of celestial chariots.
The quarters of the sky were deafened by the harsh neighing of horses,
while [the enemies] were struck by the hosts with cries of "kilakila" and with canes held in their hands.
The attendants of the hosts of gods shone there, O lord of the earth;
in that clamor, O King, no sound could be heard by anyone anywhere. (15)
To some, it is heard as being exceedingly tumultuous with various sounds; yet at every step, there are lakes completely filled with sweet water.
O King, there were various gardens adorned with jewel-trees;
beyond that was a mandala fashioned from the essence of great precious substances.
There is another great *sāla* tree whose summit touches the sky; this latter tree is a hundred times more brilliant in splendor than the former *sāla*. (18)
It was provided with gate-towers and gates and endowed with many trees;
whatever species of trees exist, all of them were present there.
They were constantly covered with flowers, always endowed with fruit, possessed of fresh sprouts, and filled with mutual fragrances. || 20 ||
Panasa, bakula, lodhra, karṇikāra, and śiṃśapā trees;
devadāru, kāñcanāra, mango trees, and sumeru trees [were there]. || 21 ||
Likucas, hiṅgulas, elās, lavaṅgas, and kaṭphalas; likewise pāṭalas, mucukundas, phalinīs, and jaghanephalas. (22)
Tālas, astamālas, sālās, kaṅkolās, nāgabhadrakas, punnāgas, pīlavas, sālvakas, and indeed camphor-bearing trees; || 23 ||
Aśvakarṇas, Hastikarṇas, Tālaparṇas, and pomegranates; Gaṇikās, Bandhujīvas, Jambīras, and Kuraṇḍakas. || 24 ||
There were *cāmpeya* trees, *bandhujīva* flowers, as well as golden trees, black aloe-wood trees, and likewise sandalwood trees. (25)
Date palms, jasmine, tālaparṇī, and likewise sugarcane;
milky trees, khadira, ciñcā, and bhallātaka as well. || 26 ||
There were rucaka and kuṭaja trees, as well as bilva trees;
likewise, there were groves of tulasī and of mallikā jasmine.
O Lord of the Earth, there are forests and groves of various species of trees such as these, provided with hundreds of diverse ponds. (28)
Resounding with the cries of cuckoos and adorned by humming bees, all those excellent trees exude resinous sap and possess lush, cool shade. (29)
The trees, produced by various seasons and crowded with diverse birds,
were exceedingly beautified by rivers flowing with various juices.
With the breezes from the wings of flocks of pigeons, parrots,
and mynas, and with the gusts of wind arising from the wings of swans, the trees were set in motion.
That excellent forest was filled with breezes carrying fragrant scents and was joined by herds of does running hither and thither.
That divine forest, dripping with honey on all sides, resounded with the pleasure-inducing cries of flocks of dancing peacocks. || 33 ||
To the north of the bell-metal wall (kāṃsyasāla) is proclaimed the copper wall (tāmrasāla);
it is square in shape and seven yojanas in height.
Between those two palaces, O lord of the earth, the Kalpavāṭikā grove is said to be situated; the flowers of the trees therein possess the luster of gold.
The leaves have the luster of gold, and their seeds and fruits are made of jewels;
indeed, their fragrance spreads in all directions for ten yojanas. || 36 ||
O King, that forest was guarded day and night by the season of spring,
which sat upon a throne of flowers and shone with a parasol of blossoms.
Adorned with floral ornaments and reeling from the intoxication of flower-liquor,
he had two esteemed wives, Madhuśrī and Mādhavaśrī.
As they played with smiling faces using jasmine clusters as balls, the forest became exceedingly beautiful, dripping with honey on all sides. (39)
For an extent of ten yojanas, it was filled with a breeze fragrant with flowers and with divine gandharvas together with their wives, who were eager for song.
That divine forest was resplendent, resounding with the songs of intoxicated cuckoos; endowed with the beauty of spring, it increased the desires of those who long for love.
To the north of the Tāmrasāla mountain, the Sīsasāla mountain is proclaimed;
its height is also recorded as being seven yojanas in measure.
O King, within the garden-enclosure of those two palaces,
the fragrance of the flowers extends ten yojanas in every direction.
The flowers were golden-hued and in full bloom without interval,
and the fruits were sweet, imbued with the essence of nectar.
O best of kings, the leader of that garden during the summer season was Śukraśrī; he had two esteemed wives, Śukraśrī and Śuciśrī.
But the world, terrified by the heat, took refuge at the roots of trees;
[the Lord], surrounded by various Siddhas and accompanied by various gods, [remained there]. || 46 ||
By throngs of playful women, smeared with the paste of liquid sandalwood, adorned with flower garlands, and holding palm-leaf fans in their lotus-like hands. || 47 ||
O King, the wall was beautiful, lined with those who frequent cool waters;
and further to the north of the lead and sāla trees, it was auspiciously made of brass.
O King, there stands a rampart measuring one *muni-yojana* in length;
between those two, a grove of *haricandana* trees is recorded.
The lord of those two months is the rainy season (Varṣartu), who has clouds as his vehicle;
he is remembered as having eyes tawny with lightning and armor made of clouds.
Resounding with the roar of thunderbolts and possessing rainbows on all sides,
he remains surrounded by his hosts, discharging thousands of streams of water.
Nabhaḥśrī, Nabhasyaśrī, Svarasyā, Rasamālinī,
Ambā, Dulā, Niratni, Abhramantī, and Meghayantikā.
Varṣayantī, Cipuṇikā, and Vāridhārā are considered the twelve powers (śaktis) of the rainy season; they are said to be intoxicated with passion.
There were trees with fresh sprouts accompanied by young creepers,
and the entire earth was covered with green grass.
The currents of rivers and streams flow with great force, and lakes of turbid water are like the minds of those possessed by passion. (55)
The gods and the Siddhas who perform service for the Goddess dwell there, as do the ponds, wells, and tanks dedicated for the sake of the Goddess. (56)
Those hosts dwell here, full of grace and accompanied by their women;
in front of it is a mountain made of brass, seven yojanas in length.
The Sāla tree in the center consists of the five metals; within it is a grove of Mandāra trees, strewn with various flowering creepers and adorned with various sprouts. || 58 ||
The season of autumn is declared here to be its presiding deity, free from ailment;
it has two esteemed wives, Iṣulakṣmī and Ūrjalakṣmī.
Various perfected beings dwell here together with their women and their retinues.
In front of it is [a mountain] made of five metals, seven yojanas in length.
Blazing with great peaks, it stands with silver salākās;
in the midst of the Pārijāta forest, it is adorned with clusters of blossoms.
Flowers with a fragrance that extends for ten yojanas on all sides gladden all the hosts who perform the work of the goddesses.
O King, the season of Hemanta is proclaimed there as its presiding lord; it is exceedingly radiant, accompanied by its attendants and weapons, delighting all those possessed of passion.
Sahaśrī and Sahasyaśrī were his two esteemed wives;
the Siddhas who perform the vow of the goddess also dwell there.
In front of the silver wall, there is a golden wall said to be seven yojanas in length,
fashioned from molten gold.
In the center, however, was a grove of Kadamba trees, adorned with flowers and sprouts;
from it, streams of Kadamba wine flowed forth by the thousands.
The season of Śiśira, which brings great prosperity, is proclaimed there as its presiding lord, by whose sipped and swallowed [waters] one's own bliss is experienced. (67)
Tapaḥśrī and Tapasyaśrī were his two esteemed wives;
he, appearing like the cool season (Śiśira), lived joyfully together with them.
Endowed with various amusements and surrounded by various groups, the great Siddhas who bestow gifts upon the Goddess dwell there. (69)
Endowed with great bliss arising from various enjoyments,
they were accompanied by their women and surrounded by their retinues in great numbers.
In front of the golden *sāla* tree stands a *sāla* tree made of ruby, one *yojana* in length,
its form as reddish as saffron.
The ground, the forests, and the groves are made of topaz;
even the jeweled trees and their basins are recorded as being composed of topaz.
The walls were made of whatever jewel they were, and likewise the trees, the forest grounds, the birds, and the waters were all of the color of those same jewels. (73)
The pavilions, the pillars of the pavilions, the lakes, and the lotuses—whatever else may be there within the enclosure wall, all of that shall be identical to that [original]. (74)
O Lord, this description has been set forth regarding the Ratnasālā and the other halls;
O King, each subsequent hall is a hundred thousand times more radiant than the preceding one.

The guardians of the quarters (dikpālas) of all those existing within every universe dwell here, appearing as the collective embodiment of all such guardians, with their excellent weapons flashing forth. (76)
In the eastern direction stands Amarāvatī with its lofty peaks;
there, Mahendra shines, surrounded by various groves.
And whatever splendor there may be in heaven,
even more than that is the collective splendor of the Hundred-eyed One (Indra), remembered as being a thousandfold greater.
Mounted upon Airāvata, thunderbolt in hand,
the majestic Śatakratu shines here, surrounded by the divine army.
There Śacī, accompanied by hosts of celestial nymphs, shines resplendently;
O King, in the south-eastern corner is the city of Agni, resembling the abode of Fire.
There the Fire-god shines resplendent, joined with Svāhā and Svadhā,
enriched by his own vehicle and ornaments, and surrounded by his own hosts of deities.
In the southern direction lies the city of Yama; there dwells the great wielder of the staff, O King, surrounded by his own soldiers led by Citragupta.
The son of the Sun, the great Yama, endowed with his own power, resides in the south-western direction, the quarter of the Rākṣasīs, surrounded by Rākṣasas. (83)
Nirṛti stands quivering, wielding a sword and joined by his own Śakti;
in the western quarter is King Varuṇa, powerful and holding a noose. 84.
Mounted upon a great fish, overwhelmed by the intoxication of wine,
he was accompanied by his own Śakti and joined by his own hosts of aquatic creatures.
In the western quarter is the world of Varuṇa, crowded with Varuṇānīs and waters;
in the northwestern corner is the world of Vāyu, where Vāyu presides.
Surrounded by yogis who have attained perfection through the practice of breath-control (vāyusādhana),
he stands with a banner in his hand, possessing large eyes, and is seated upon a deer as his vehicle.
Surrounded by the hosts of Maruts and endowed with his own power,
O protector of the earth, there exists in the northern direction the great realm of the Yakṣas.
There dwells the sovereign lord of the Yakṣas, the leader of wealth, pot-bellied and endowed with the nine treasures, as well as powers such as growth and prosperity. (89)
Maṇibhadra, Pūrṇabhadra, Maṇimān, Maṇikaṃdhara;
adorned with jewels, wearing jeweled garlands, and bearing a jeweled bow. || 90 ||
Thus, accompanied by the Yakṣa generals and endowed with his own powers, the exceedingly great world of Rudra is proclaimed to be in the northeast corner. (91)
Therein resides Rudra as the presiding deity, inlaid with priceless jewels; he is full of wrath, with blazing eyes, and has his great quiver fastened to his back.
With his left hand brandishing a bow, he was supported by countless Rudras who were equal to himself, holding strung bows and bearing excellent tridents as their weapons. (93)
With distorted faces, with gaping mouths, vomiting fire from their mouths;
with ten hands, a hundred hands, or endowed with a thousand arms. (94)
With ten feet, ten necks, and three eyes, they possessed fierce forms;
those who were known to move through the atmosphere and those who moved upon the earth.
The Rudras are remembered in the Rudrādhyāya; he was surrounded by all of them, together with ten million Rudrāṇīs and the Mothers, Bhadrakālī and the others.
O King, Rudra shines forth, surrounded by the hosts of Ḍāmarīs and others endowed with various powers, accompanied by Vīrabhadra and his followers. 97.
Wearing a garland of skulls, with bracelets of serpents and a serpent as his necklace, he is clothed in a tiger skin with an elephant hide as an upper garment. || 98 ||
His limbs were smeared with the ashes of funeral pyres, he was surrounded by hosts of Pramathas and other attendants,
and the quarters of the sky were deafened by the sounds of his rattling ḍamaru drums.
Filling the vault of the sky with the sounds of loud laughter and the slapping of arms,
Maheshvara— the abode of spirits— is possessed by hosts of bhūtas;
he is the lord of the northeastern quarter and is known by the name Ishana.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of Maṇidvīpa," in the twelfth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
Description of the excellent rampart constructed from rubies and other gems.
Vyāsa said:
In front [of it], its body was reddish like saffron, made of topaz.
The wall in the center was made of ruby, and the ground likewise was of the same material. || 1 ||
It was ten yojanas in length and provided with gate-towers;
O King, there were hundreds of pavilions there, adorned with jeweled pillars.
Seated in the middle upon the ground were sixty-four Kalās,
heroic warriors bearing various weapons and adorned with jewel ornaments.
Each world belongs to them, for they are the leaders of their respective worlds;
they always remain surrounding the Padmarāga gem on all sides.
They are frequented by the inhabitants of their respective worlds and are characterized by their own vehicles and weapons;
I shall state their names—listen, O Janamejaya.
Piṅgalākṣī, Viśālākṣī, Samṛddhi, Vṛddhi,
Śraddhā, Svāhā, she known as Svadhā, Māyā, Saṃjñā, and Vasundharā.
She is the sustainer of the three worlds, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, and the sovereign of the thirty gods; she is the one of beautiful form and many forms, the mother of Skanda, and the beloved of Acyuta.
Likewise, she is Vimalā, Amalā, Aruṇī, and Āruṇī;
she is primordial nature (prakṛti), transformation (vikṛti), as well as creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
She is Sandhyā, the Mother, the Swan-like One, Mardikā, Vajrikā, and the Supreme;
she is the Mother of the Gods, the Blessed One, Devakī, and the Lotus-seated One.
Another has three faces, another seven faces, and she is the crusher of gods and demons;
she has hanging lips, upward-pointing hair, many heads, and the belly of a wolf.
After her was the one named Ratharekhā, then another, Śaśirekhā;
followed by Gaganavegā, Pavanavegā, and then Vegā.
First there would be Bhuvanapālā, followed by Madanāturā;
likewise Anaṅgā, Anaṅgamathanā, and Anaṅgamekhalā. (12)
Then there is Anaṅgakusumā, followed by Viśvarūpā and Surādikā; thereafter the Śakti Kṣayaṅkarī and Akṣobhyā. (13)
Then Satyavādinī, Bahurūpā, Śucitavratā, and the one named Udārā, as well as Vāgīśī— these are remembered as numbering sixty-four.
With all our tongues blazing, vomiting forth fierce fire, we shall drink up all the water and annihilate the god of fire. 15.
"Today we shall paralyze the wind and devour the entire world!"—
thus they cried out, their eyes bloodshot with rage.
All of them, bearing bows and arrows, were constantly eager for battle alone,
deafening the quarters of the sky with the "kaṭakaṭa" clashing sounds of their fangs.
Those with tawny hair standing erect are said to always hold bows and arrows in their hands;
for each one of them, an army of a hundred akṣauhiṇīs is proclaimed.
O best of kings, the power of each single weapon is sufficient to destroy a hundred thousand universes;
such is the army consisting of a hundred akṣauhiṇīs.
"What could he not accomplish in this world? It is impossible even to describe;
O Sage, the entire equipment for battle was present within that śāla tree. (20)
There is no counting of the chariots, nor likewise of the horses and elephants; similarly, there is no counting of the weapons, and likewise no counting of the hosts.
In front of the one made of ruby,
there stands a great rampart constructed from gomedaka gems, ten yojanas in length.
The middle region of that [world] has the luster of a shining hibiscus flower,
and the dwellings of its inhabitants are likewise fashioned from gomedaka gems.
The birds, the excellent pillars, the trees, the ponds,
and the lakes were all fashioned from *gomedaka* stone, their forms reddened like saffron.
Situated in their midst are the thirty-two great goddesses known as Śaktis;
they wield various weapons and missiles and are adorned with go-meda gems.
O King, each of those who dwell in the world, having surrounded [the city] on all sides,
were equipped with go-meda armor and possessed faces like piśācas.
Constantly worshipped by the inhabitants of the heavenly realm, those who wield the discus, with eyes red with wrath, cried out: "Pierce! Cook! Cut! Burn! (27)
With hearts burning with the desire for battle, they constantly utter these words:
"Ten akṣauhiṇīs are considered the strength of each single great power. (28)
Even there, a single army possesses the power to destroy a hundred thousand universes;
O King, how can such a great army be described?
There was no counting of chariots, nor likewise of mounts;
there, the entire undertaking of battle shone forth for the Goddess.
I shall state their names, which destroy all sins:
Vidyā, Hrī, Puṣṭi, Prajñā, Sinīvālī, and likewise Kuhū. (31)
Rudrā, Vīryā, Prabhā, Nandā, Poṣiṇī, Ṛddhidā, Śubhā, Kālarātri, Mahārātri, Bhadrakālī, and Kapardinī. || 32 ||
Vikṛti, Daṇḍinī, Muṇḍinī, Śikhaṇḍinī who bears a crescent moon, the destroyer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, and the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura. || 33 ||
Indrāṇī, Rudrāṇī, who forms half the body of Śaṅkara;
Nārī, Nārāyaṇī, and also Triśūlinī, the protectress. || 34 ||
Ambikā and Hlādinī—these are remembered as the powers (śaktis).
If these goddesses become enraged, then there will be the destruction of the universe.
For there is never, at any time or place, defeat for these [goddesses].
In front [of them] is a gem made of *gomedaka*, fashioned with excellent diamonds.
It was ten yojanas high, provided with gate-towers and doors, secured with door-panels and chains, and resplendent with nine kinds of trees.
The *sāla* tree, the ground in its center, and everything else is said to be composed of diamonds;
likewise the houses, the lanes, the streets, the great highways, and the courtyards. (38)
The trees were like tree-basins; even the deer were of that same nature.
There were rows of oblong ponds, square ponds, lakes, and wells. (39)
There, the attendants of the illustrious Bhuvaneśvarī reside;
each one is served by a hundred thousand maidservants and is proud with intoxication. (40)
Some held palm-leaf fans, others had lotus-like hands adorned with goblets;
some, exceedingly proud, carried vessels of betel-leaf.
Some were holding sunshades, others were waving chowries;
some wore various garments, while others held lotuses in their hands.
Some were applying various ointments, some were smearing saffron paste, others were wearing collyrium, and still others held cups of vermilion.
Some were makers of decorative paintings, intent on massaging the feet; others were makers of ornaments, wearing various kinds of jewelry. || 44 ||
There were many such other excellent women, skilled in fashioning flower ornaments, adept at arranging floral decorations, and proficient in various graceful amorous gestures. (45)
All the young women were dressed in their formal lower garments;
by virtue of even a slight portion of the Goddess's grace, they held the three worlds in contempt.
These goddesses are known as the messengers (dūtīs), proud with the intoxication of passion;
I shall declare their names, O best of kings—listen to me. (47)
The first is Anaṅgarūpā, the second is Anaṅgamadanā;
then the third is proclaimed as Sundarī Madanāturā. (48)
Then there would be Bhuvanavegā, as well as Bhuvanapālikā;
there would be Sarvaśiśirā, Anaṅgavadanā, and Anaṅgamekhalā. (49)
With limbs like streaks of lightning, adorned with jingling girdles,
and feet with tinkling anklets, they moved here and there both outside and inside.
Running about, they all shone like streaks of lightning;
skilled in all tasks, they stood on every side with canes in their hands.
Likewise, in the eight directions and even outside the rampart,
their palaces shine resplendent with various vehicles and weapons.
At the foremost part of the Vajra-hall, there was a palatial hall constructed of lapis lazuli;
it was ten yojanas high and adorned with gate-towers and portals. || 53 ||
The entire ground is of beryl, as are the various houses;
the alleys, streets, and great highways are all fashioned from beryl.
The ponds, wells, and tanks, as well as the banks of the rivers and all the sand,
were fashioned from lapis lazuli gems.
There, O best of kings, the mandala of Brāhmī and the other goddesses shines forth in all eight directions, surrounded by their respective retinues.
These are declared to be the collective forms (samaṣṭi) of the Mothers of every universe:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī. (57)
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā, along with the seven Mothers; Mahālakṣmī is the eighth—these are the Mothers as they are named. (58)
They are remembered as being equal in form to the gods, such as Brahmā and Rudra;
they bring about the welfare of the world and are surrounded by their respective armies.
O King, at the four gates of that palace, the mounts of the Great Lord are always kept ready and adorned with ornaments. (60)
There were tens of millions of elephants as mounts, and likewise tens of millions of palanquins;
there were swans, lions, Garuḍas, peacocks, and bulls.
O prince, there were likewise tens of millions of chariots equipped with those [warriors], joined by rear-guard forces, their banners kissing the sky. (62)
There were tens of millions of celestial palaces, adorned with various emblems,
equipped with diverse musical instruments, and furnished with great banners.
Beyond the Vaidūrya-maṇi palace, another palace is recorded;
it is ten yojanas high and constructed of sapphire stone.
The central area, as well as the pathways, the great roads, the houses,
and all the ponds, wells, and tanks, were constructed from that very jewel.
There, a lotus is said to exist, extending for many yojanas,
with sixteen petals, radiant like another Sudarśana discus.
There, the various abodes of the sixteen Śaktis indeed dwell, complete with all requisites and in full prosperity. (67)
I shall state their names; listen to me, O best of kings:
Karālī, Vikarālī, Umā, and Sarasvatī. (68)
Śrī Durgā, Lakṣmī, Śruti, Smṛti, Dhṛti,
Śraddhā, Medhā, Mati, Kānti, and Āryā— these are the sixteen Śaktis.
Resembling dark blue clouds, with lotus-like hands grasping swords, they were equally equipped with shields and possessed minds intent upon the commencement of battle.
All these generals are remembered as the leaders of the powers (śaktis) residing in every Brahmāṇḍa, belonging to the illustrious Goddess, the Sovereign of the World. (71)
They cause the agitation of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), are augmented by the powers of the Goddess, are mounted upon various chariots, and are accompanied by various energies (śaktis). || 72 ||
Even one with a thousand mouths would not be able to describe this prowess, which extends far before the great sapphire tree. (73)
A wall of pearls rises, ten yojanas in length;
the central ground is described as being as before, and in its center is an eight-petaled lotus.
It was extensive, strewn with clusters of pearls and gems, and possessed filaments;
there, they always bore the same form as the Goddess and carried her weapons. (75)
These eight ministers have been proclaimed as the awakeners of the world's affairs;
they enjoy pleasures equal to the Goddess herself, and being learned, they understand even the slightest gestures.
They were skilled in all tasks, devoted to the service of their master, capable of understanding the queen's intentions, clever, and exceedingly beautiful. (77)
Endowed with various powers, they perceive the conduct of living beings residing within each individual universe through their power of knowledge.
I shall tell you their names; listen to me, O best of kings:
she who is called Anaṅgakusumā is also known as Anaṅgakusumāturā. (79)
Anaṅgamadanā, likewise Anaṅgamadanāturā, Bhuvanapālā, and Gaganavegā after that. (80)
Then follow Śaśirekhā and Gaganarekhā;
they bear the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, and their bodies are of a reddish hue. 81.
On the upper part of the pearl pavilion, another great emerald constantly provides news concerning the entire world.
The excellent Sāla tree is described as being ten yojanas in length,
endowed with various forms of beauty and possessed of manifold enjoyments.
The middle ground is said to be of that same nature, and the dwellings are likewise;
here, the hexagon is extensive—now hear of the deities stationed at its corners.
In the eastern corner is Brahmā, four-faced and accompanied by Gāyatrī;
he is the supreme one, bearing a water-pot, a rosary, the gesture of granting boons, and a staff as his weapons.
Then the goddess Gāyatrī, the supreme deity, bearing her weapons, appeared;
all the Vedas were present in embodied form, as were the various Śāstras. || 86 ||
Indeed, the Smṛtis and the Purāṇas dwell here in embodied form—those who possess the body of Brahman and those who possess the body of Gāyatrī. (87)
Indeed, the personified forms of the Vyāhṛtis are always present there;
in the southwest corner is the one whose lotus-like hands hold the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
The Sāvitrī-mantra prevails there, and Mahāviṣṇu is likewise present;
so too are all those who possess the forms of Viṣṇu, such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and the rest.
Indeed, all those who are embodiments of Sāvitrī are present there;
in the northwestern corner [is one] endowed with an axe, a rosary, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
Mahārudra resides here, and Sarasvatī is likewise present there; O King, so too are all the various forms of Rudra, such as Dakṣiṇāmukha and the others.
Indeed, all the various forms of Gaurī reside there,
as do the sixty-four Āgamas and whatever other Āgamas are traditionally known.
Indeed, they all dwell right there in embodied form;
likewise, in the south-eastern corner, there is a jewel-pitcher as well as a casket of gems.
Kubera, the bestower of wealth, holding [his treasures] with his own two hands, is accompanied by various market-streets and attended by Mahālakṣmī. || 94 ||
The Lord of Treasures (Kubera) dwells with the Goddess, surrounded by his own qualities;
and in the great corner of Varuṇa is Madana, united with Rati.
He always shines resplendent, bearing a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows;
the personified forms of the erotic sentiment are ever present there. (96)
In the northeast corner, the heroic Vighneśa, eternally endowed with nourishment,
shines resplendent as the remover of obstacles, bearing a noose and a goad.
O best of kings, whatever manifestations of Gaṇeśa exist,
they all dwell here, endowed with great sovereignty.
These are declared to be the collective manifestations of Brahmā and the others who reside in every individual universe;
these very beings, Brahmā and the rest, serve the Sovereign Goddess of the World. 99.
In front of the Mahāmārataka tree, there is another coral *sāla* tree, a hundred *yojanas* in length, its body as red as saffron.
The central ground is said to be of that same nature, and the dwellings are as before;
in their midst there are five mistresses of the five elements.
Hṛllekhā, Gaganā, and the fourth, Karālikā, who is red,
and Mahocchuṣmā as the fifth— these possess a radiance equal to the five elements.
Holding nooses, goads, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, they are adorned with countless ornaments;
richly attired in garments similar to those of the Goddess, they are proud of their fresh youth. (103)
O King, at the tip of the coral branch there is a great tree made of the nine precious gems, extending for many yojanas.
And there, too, were many dwellings for the goddesses of the sacred tradition,
as well as ponds and lakes made entirely of the nine precious gems.
Indeed, those who are the incarnations of the Śrī Devī reside there;
O King, the great Vidyās and the great Bhedas are also present in that very place.
Together with their own attendant goddesses, ornaments, and vehicles,
all the goddesses shine resplendent, possessing a brilliance equal to ten million suns.
Indeed, there dwell seventy million deities of great mantras;
and before it stands a vast palace of wish-fulfilling jewels made of the nine gems.
But the mere substance there was fashioned from wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi),
as well as from stones that glow at sunrise and stones that glow at moonrise.
Thousands of pillars were fashioned from gems with the brilliance of lightning, such that by their radiance, no object situated within them could be seen. (110)

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Wall Constructed of Padmarāga and Other Gems," in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 11 ||
The Description of Maṇidvīpa. Vyāsa said:
That very abode of the Goddess shines resplendent in the central region.
In those [four directions], there were four pavilions, each provided with a thousand pillars. || 1 ||
There is one Śṛṅgāramaṇḍapa and also a Muktimaṇḍapa;
the third is proclaimed by the name Jñānamaṇḍapa. || 2 ||
The fourth is proclaimed to be the solitary pavilion;
it is provided with various canopies and perfumed with various incenses.
The auspicious pavilions shine with a splendor equal to ten million suns;
it is said that around those pavilions lies a grove of saffron trees.
O King, there stands the grove of Mallikā and Kunda flowers where the Puṣkalakas reside; it is filled with countless musks and flows with their secretions.
Likewise, the Mahāpadma forest was constructed with jeweled staircases;
it was filled with the essence of nectar and resounded with the humming of intoxicated bees.
Crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, its horizons filled with fragrance;
the Island of Jewels was exquisitely perfumed by the sweet scents of the forest groves.
In the Śṛṅgāra-maṇḍapa, the goddesses sing with various melodies; the excellent gods are the members of the assembly, and in their midst is the illustrious Mother of the Universe.
In the middle of the Liberation Pavilion, Śivā constantly grants liberation;
O King, she imparts the instruction of knowledge in the third pavilion.
And in the fourth pavilion, the Mother of the World constantly contemplates the protection of the universe together with her female attendants.
O King, in the palace of the wish-fulfilling gem, the couch, composed of the supreme Śakti-tattva,
shines forth, joined by ten steps.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—these are said to be the bed-legs, while Sadāśiva is the plank. || 12 ||
Above him shines Mahādeva, the Lord of the World;
and that Goddess, for the sake of her own divine play, became manifest in two forms.
At the beginning of creation, however, he was indeed this very Maheśvara, whose half-body was hers,
and who was as beautiful as ten million Kandarpas intent on destroying the pride of Kanda.
He has five faces and three eyes, is adorned with jewel ornaments,
and holds in his own arms a deer, the gesture of fearlessness, an axe, and a boon-granting mudrā.
That great Lord of all, appearing as a sixteen-year-old youth,
was resplendent like ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons.
Resembling pure crystal, three-eyed, and possessing cool radiance,
the goddess Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī is seated upon his left side.
She was resplendent with a girdle-string studded with clusters of nine gems,
and adorned with bangles of vaidūrya set in refined gold.
Her lotus-face was adorned with earrings shaped like golden śrī-cakras, and the splendor of her forehead’s beauty surpassed the moon, the source of nectar. || 19 ||
She was adorned with lips that eclipsed the luster of the bimba fruit,
and her face was made radiant by a tilaka mark of shimmering saffron and musk.
With the expansive, shimmering moon and sun [reflected] in her divine crest-jewel,
she was radiant with a nose-ornament as pure as a rising lotus.
She was adorned with clusters of pure pearls suspended from her thought-ornaments,
and her breasts were embellished with sandalwood paste, camphor, and saffron.
Adorned with various and manifold ornaments, her neck was like a conch shell,
and she was resplendent with rows of teeth resembling the seeds of the pomegranate fruit.
Her head was adorned with a crown fashioned from priceless jewels;
her lotus-face was enriched by locks of hair shimmering with swarms of intoxicated bees.
Her face resembles the autumn moon, free from blemish and waning;
she is adorned with a navel as beautiful as a whirlpool in the waters of the Ganges.
Her fingers were adorned with rings set with fragments of rubies,
and she was beautiful with three eyes shaped like the petals of a white lotus.
Her radiant luster is like that of a great ruby of pure passion fashioned [of light];
she is adorned with jeweled bracelets and equipped with jeweled tinkling bells. || 27 ||
Her feet shine with a continuous series of anklets made of strings of gems and pearls;
her hands gleam with a web of light spread from her jewel-adorned fingers.
The radiance of her body was enhanced by the infinite luster of various jewels set in her bodice;
her hair, fragrant with jasmine, was adorned with jasmine flowers and a swarm of bees.
Śivā is languid from the weight of her well-rounded, firm, and lofty breasts;
she possesses four arms, which shine with the gestures of granting boons, the noose, the goad, and the protection-bestowing mudrā.
Richly adorned with every elegant ornament, her creeper-like limbs are delicate;
she is the very essence of the stream of beauty and is composed of unfeigned compassion. (31)
She who surpasses Sarasvatī with the sweetness of her own conversation,
and who possesses a supreme splendor that outshines millions upon millions of suns and moons.
She was surrounded on all sides by various female friends, maidservants, celestial nymphs, and all the deities.
Endowed with the power of will (icchā-śakti), the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), and the power of action (kriyā-śakti),
she is accompanied by modesty, contentment, nourishment, fame, splendor, forgiveness, and compassion.
Buddhi, Medhā, Smṛti, and Lakṣmī are remembered as women in embodied form; likewise are Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā. (35)
Nityā, Vilāsinī, Dogdhrī, Aghorā, Maṅgalā—
these nine are the powers of the seat (pīṭhaśakti) who serve the Supreme Mother.
On its two sides are those two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padmaka;
likewise, there are rivers carrying the nine jewels as well as those flowing with gold.
O best of kings, the seven rivers carrying the [seven] elements have issued forth from the two treasures; they all flow toward the ocean of nectar.
That Goddess Bhuvaneśānī shines upon His left lap;
for the Great Lord’s status as the Lord of All arises solely from her association, and not otherwise. (39)
O protector of the earth, hear the dimensions of this house of the wish-fulfilling gem;
they declare it to be one thousand yojanas in extent and truly vast.
To the north of that, the Mahāśālas are recorded as being twice the size of the former;
this [region] shines forth, situated in the intermediate space and devoid of support.
Its contraction and expansion occur incessantly, like a cloth, due to the necessity of its effects during dissolution and creation. (42)
Among all the halls, the abode of the Cintāmaṇi jewel is declared to be the ultimate limit of all splendor, wherein resides the Goddess Mahāmāyā.
Whosoever the lay devotees (upāsakas) may be who exist throughout every universe—among the gods, in the worlds of the nāgas, among humans, and others. || 44 ||
O King, all those who, devoted to the worship of the Goddess, give up their lives here in the field of the Goddess, go to that very place of the Śrīdevī.
They all go to that very place where the goddess’s great festival is held;
there are streams of ghee, streams of milk, streams of curd, and flows of honey.
All the rivers flow there, as do other supreme streams carrying nectar;
some carry grape juice, while others carry the juice of the jambu fruit. (47)
There were thousands of rivers flowing with mango juice and sugarcane juice,
as well as trees that yielded the fruits of one's desires, along with ponds and wells.
It yields fruits and drinks according to one's desire; indeed, there is no deficiency whatsoever.
Neither disease nor graying hair, nor even old age, ever occurs there. (49)
There was neither anxiety nor envy, nor likewise desire, anger, and so forth;
all were young men accompanied by their wives, possessing a radiance like that of a thousand suns.
There they constantly worship the goddess Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī;
some have attained residence in the same world (salokatā), while others have reached proximity (sāmīpyatā). || 51 ||
Some have attained similarity of form (sarūpatā), while others have attained equality of power (sārṣṭitā);
such are the various deities residing there within each respective cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Established as a collective whole, they serve the Sovereign of the Universe;
the seventy million great mantras worship her in embodied form.
And all the great vidyās [worship] that Śivā, whose nature is the state of equilibrium, who is the form of the causal Brahman, and whose body is variegated by māyā. (54)
Thus, O King, has the most magnificent Maṇidvīpa been described by me;
there neither the sun nor the moon exists, nor lightning, nor even ten million fires.
They are not equal even to a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth part of its radiance;
in some places it resembles coral, and in others it has the luster of emerald.
In some places its luster was equal to the flash of lightning, and in others it was like the midday sun;
in some places it was spread across with a beautiful expanse of great torrents resembling ten million flashes of lightning.
In some places it possesses a luster resembling vermilion, sapphire, and great rubies; in others, the horizons are set ablaze by the intense radiance of the great interior of diamond-essence. 58.
In its radiance it was like a forest fire, resembling molten gold;
in some places it emitted moonstones, and in others it emitted sunstones.
It was equipped with jeweled peaks, possessed jeweled walls and gate-towers,
and was completely adorned with jeweled leaves, jeweled fruits, and jeweled breasts.
It was radiant with the cries of flocks of dancing peacocks and the cooing of pigeons,
and it was graced by the sweet warbling of cuckoos and the speech of parrots.
It was surrounded by lakes extending for hundreds of thousands of yojanas, with waters exceedingly delightful and beautiful,
and in their centers shone blossoming lotuses made of jewels.
It was perfumed on all sides for a hundred yojanas by fragrant scents,
and filled with trees swaying, stirred by a gentle breeze.
The sky was overspread with the radiance of clusters of wish-fulfilling gems,
while the horizons on all sides blazed with a brilliant glow from the luster of jewels.
It was filled with the great fragrance of tree-borne winds and wind-blown scents;
it was perfumed with incense, O King, and radiant with the light of jewel-lamps.
With the shimmering inner luster of its latticework of gems and its slightly perforated openings,
this [palace], joined with the surface of a mirror, causes confusion regarding the directions.
Of complete sovereignty, of all aesthetic charm, of omniscience, and indeed of all splendor; (67)
O King, here is the culmination of all valor, of every supreme quality, and of all compassion. (68)
Starting from the bliss of the King up to the realms ending with the world of Brahmā, all the blisses that exist are indeed included within this very one. (69)
Thus, O King, has this most magnificent Maṇidvīpa been described to you—the supreme abode of the Great Goddess, the highest of all that is excellent in all the worlds. (70)
By remembering this, all sin is instantly destroyed;
moreover, by remembering it at the moment of the departure of the vital breaths, one goes to that very place.
If one should recite these five chapters daily with a concentrated mind,
there shall indeed be no affliction from spirits, ghosts, demons, and the like.
In the construction of a new house as well as in the Vāstu sacrifice, this should be recited with effort; by that, auspiciousness arises.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of Maṇidvīpa," in the twelfth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 12.
Janamejaya’s description of the liberation of his ancestors through the performance of the Ambā sacrifice and the hearing of the Devībhāgavata.
Vyāsa said:
"O sinless King, I have thus narrated to you everything that was asked by you."
That which was spoken by Nārāyaṇa to the high-souled Nārada.
Having heard this most wonderful Purāṇa of the Great Goddess, a mortal becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose; indeed, he is the most beloved of the Goddess.
O King, perform the Ambā sacrifice for the sake of truly rescuing your father,
O Indra among kings, since you have become distressed upon learning of your father’s miserable state.
Accept this mantra of the Great Goddess, the most excellent of all excellences,
which, when applied according to the prescribed ritual, bestows the fulfillment of one's birth.
Sūta said: Having heard that, the tiger among kings requested the lord of sages for that very great mantra known as the Devī-Pranava.
The best of kings received the initiation according to the prescribed rite;
then, at the commencement of the nine-night festival, he summoned Dhaumya and the others.
Free from stinginess regarding his wealth, he quickly performed the Ambā-yajña;
meanwhile, he had the Brahmins recite this most excellent Purāṇa.
In the presence of the illustrious Goddess, for the pleasure of Ambikā, he fed countless Brāhmaṇas and married women with the supreme Devībhāgavata.
Having satisfied the maidens, the vaṭukas, and likewise the poor and the helpless with gifts of wealth, the lord of the earth [performed the rite]. || 9 ||
Indeed, while he remained established in the conclusion after completing the sacrifice,
Nārada descended from the sky at that very moment.
Sounding his great lute, resembling a blazing crest of fire,
he rose up in haste upon seeing that sage Nārada.
The lord of the earth honored him with offerings such as a seat and,
having inquired after his welfare, asked the reason for his arrival.
The king said:
"O virtuous one, from where have you come? Tell me, what may I do for you? By the mere reason of your arrival, I am provided with a protector and my purpose is fulfilled."
Having heard these words of the king, the best of sages replied:
"O best of kings, today I witnessed a marvel in the world of the gods."
Having reached your presence in great astonishment to report that matter, I find your father has fallen into a miserable state due to the reversal of his own karma. (15)
Indeed, having now assumed this very same divine form and body,
he is being properly praised on all sides by the gods of gods and by the apsarases.
Having ascended an excellent celestial chariot, he went to Maṇidvīpa by virtue of the fruit arising from hearing this Devībhāgavata.
Even by the fruit of a single oblation to Ambā, your father has gone to a happy state;
you are blessed, you have accomplished your purpose, and your life is fruitful.
O ornament of the lineage, your father has been rescued from hell by you;
today your vast fame has spread throughout the world of the gods. (19)
Sūta said:
Having heard what was spoken by Nārada, his heart faltering with love,
he fell at the lotus feet of Vyāsa, whose deeds are marvelous.
O God, O Great Sage, by your grace I have achieved my purpose;
what else could I do for you in return, other than offer salutations? (21)
"O Sage, I must always be favored by you in this very manner.
Having heard these words of the king and having greeted him with blessings, [the sage replied]. || 22 ||
The venerable Bādarāyaṇa spoke these gentle words:
"O King, renouncing everything, take refuge in the lotus feet of the Goddess. (23)
Recite the Devībhāgavata daily with a concentrated mind;
always perform the Ambāmakhya sacrifice with devotion, remaining ever-vigilant.
By that [means], you shall be liberated from the bonds of existence without effort.
There are other ancient [Purāṇas] as well, such as those headed by the Hari and Rudra Purāṇas. (25)
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of this Devībhāgavata;
it is the essence of all the Purāṇas and the Vedas in every respect. (26)
O best of kings, how could that which teaches this very primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) be anything other than a Purāṇa? It would be equal to one. How else could it be, O supreme ruler? (27)
O Janamejaya, that which possesses merit equal to the Veda upon recitation—indeed, that alone should be studied with effort by the best of the wise. (28)
Having spoken thus to that best of kings, the sovereign of sages departed;
and the stainless sages, headed by Dhaumya, likewise returned to their respective abodes.
They offered the highest praise indeed to the Devībhāgavata.
Then, with a satisfied mind, the king ruled the earth,
while the Devībhāgavata was being read and heard in his presence.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of His Father by Janamejaya through the Performance of the Mother-Sacrifice and the Hearing of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam," in the twelfth book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. 13.
Description of the Fruit of Hearing the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said:
That which consists of even half a verse, having emerged from the lotus-like mouth of the Goddess—
The work known as Śrīmad Bhāgavata is that which reveals the established conclusions of the Vedas. || 1 ||
That which was taught to Viṣṇu, who dwells upon the banyan leaf—
extending for a hundred crores [of verses]— was formerly composed by Brahmā.
Having gathered its essence together for the sake of Śuka, Vyāsa composed it in eighteen thousand verses, consisting of twelve books.
The Purāṇa named Devībhāgavata was composed in ancient times;
even today, it remains indeed very extensive in the world of the gods.
There is no merit equal to this, which is purifying and destructive of sin;
at every step, a human being obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. || 5 ||
Having honored a reciter of the Purāṇas with garments, ornaments, and other gifts,
and having heard this from his mouth with the thought that he is Vyāsa himself, one should remain fasting.
O Sage, having had it written down with his own hand or by a scribe on the full moon day of the month of Bhādrapada, accompanied by a golden lion; || 7 ||
Then he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the reciter of the Purāṇa: a tawny cow that yields milk, adorned with ornaments, accompanied by her calf, and wearing a golden garland.
At the conclusion, he should feed Brāhmaṇas equal in number to the chapters [of the text],
as well as an equal number of married women, virgins, and young boys.
One should worship them with the thought that they are goddesses, using garments, ornaments, and so forth,
as well as excellent milk-rice, perfumes, garlands, flowers, and the like.
By this gift of a Purāṇa, one obtains the fruit of a gift of land;
having become happy in this world, he shall go to the city of the Goddess at the end.
For one who constantly listens with devotion to the supreme Devībhāgavata,
there is indeed nothing whatsoever that is difficult to attain, anywhere, at any time.
One without a son shall obtain sons; one seeking wealth shall attain wealth;
and one seeking knowledge shall acquire knowledge, his fame adorning the surface of the earth. (13)
Whether a woman is barren, or one whose children are like crows (stillborn), or one whose children have died, she shall undoubtedly be freed from those defects by hearing this. 14.
In whichever house this book remains worshipped, Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī shall never abandon that home. (15)
There, the vetālas, dākinīs, rākṣasas, and other such beings do not look [upon him].
Having touched a man afflicted by fever, one should recite this with a concentrated mind. (16)
One suffers the destruction of one's circle [of followers] and fever accompanied by burning sensations;
however, by reciting this a hundred times, the disease of consumption (kṣayaro ga) is destroyed.
That man who, having performed his twilight devotions, recites even a single chapter at each junction of the day with a concentrated mind, shall become possessed of knowledge.
One should indeed observe the omens regarding what should and should not be done;
O Sage, the manner of doing so has already been explained by me previously.
If one recites this daily with great devotion during the autumnal Navarātra,
Ambikā, being well-pleased, bestows upon him a fruit exceeding his desires.
Rama and Uma are always pleased by the Vaiṣṇavas and the Śaivas,
as well as by the Sauras, the Gāṇapatyas, and those who worship their own chosen deity (iṣṭa-śakti), for the sake of their satisfaction.
O Sage, it should be recited with effort during the four nine-night periods, and daily by those following the Vedic tradition for the sake of pleasing their own Gāyatrī.
This should be recited with effort; there is no contradiction here for anyone.
Indeed, the worship of all [deities] is always endowed with power. (23)
This should always be recited by the twice-born for the sake of pleasing that very power;
however, a woman or a Śūdra, being deluded, should never recite this.
One should listen from the mouth of a twice-born man; this is the constant rule.
What is the use of saying more? I shall state the essence according to the truth.
O best of the twice-born, this meritorious Purāṇa is the essence of the Vedas;
its recitation is equal to the recitation of the Vedas, and likewise its hearing.
I bow to that Goddess, whose nature is Truth-Consciousness-Bliss, who is expressed by the Gāyatrī, who consists of the syllable Hrīṃ, and who impels our intellects. (27)
Having heard these words of Sūta, the ascetics of Naimiṣa honored Sūta, the best of Paurāṇikas, with exceedingly great praise.
With hearts full of clarity, all those who worship the lotus feet of the Goddess attained supreme bliss through the power of the Purāṇa. (29)
They bowed again to the Sūta, seeking his forgiveness repeatedly, saying:
"O dear one, you alone are indeed our raft across the ocean of worldly existence."
Having thus caused this Purāṇa of Durgā— the secret of all the Vedas— to be heard before the best of sages,
and having honored the assembly of sages with blessings after they had bowed down, Sūta, the bee at the lotus-feet of his mother, then departed.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Fruit of Hearing the Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa," in the twelfth book of the Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses.
The forty-fourth chapter is completed.
The twelfth book is completed.
The glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa is complete.
